body: In mathematics, the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem limits the number of sets in a family of sets for which every two sets have at least one element in common. Paul Erdős, Chao Ko, and Richard Rado proved the theorem in 1938, but did not publish it until 1961. It is part of the field of combinatorics, and one of the central results of extremal set theory.
title: Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; F0124_C19 version 1; status: independently checked proof. For two-sided nearest-neighbor iid increments with 0<p<1, q=1-p, independent iid fair sign scenery and n>=1, define r(k)=+1 for k=0,1 mod4 and -1 otherwise. For a=0 or 1 let E_a be the EXTRA event that every scenery site z in [-n,n] equals either r(z+a) for all z or r(z+a+2) for all z. These two complete assignments have equal prior probability. Given E_a and ANY exterior word eta on 0<|t|<=n, if eta_-1=eta_1 then P(C0=+1|E_a,eta)=1/2. If eta_-1 differs from eta_1, P(C0=eta_1|E_0,eta)=p^2/(p^2+q^2), whereas the E_1 value is q^2/(p^2+q^2). Each site has one neighbor of each color, so its next observed color uniquely determines an increment. Within a phase pair the forward paths coincide in phase after their first step, as do the backward paths; every later likelihood factor cancels. The first paired weights are pq versus qp for equal neighbors, p^2 versus q^2 otherwise. Extra scenery conditioning is not an admissible remote color-tail modification. Even hypothetical perfect phase-pair forcing would give no gap for equal immediate neighbors or p=1/2. A separate mechanism is needed; no badness or novelty is asserted.

[Thm 66 (The key estimate with general initial data in all dimensions) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Consider any (microscopic) sequence of measures $\nu_N$ on $I$ for which the associated (macroscopic) sequence of initial conditions $\mathfrak H^N(0,\bullet)$ as defined in \eqref{hn} is a good sequence in the sense of Definition \ref{goodseq}, converging weakly as measures on $\mathbb R^n$ to a measure $\mathfrak H_0$. Let $Q_N(t,\bullet; \nu_N^{\otimes 2})$ be as in \eqref{qfield}. Then, we have the limits:
     \begin{itemize}
        \item If $d=1$ and $N^{1/4p}   \varsigma_N\to   0$ then we have 
            $$\lim_{N \to \infty}\;  \Ex\big[ Q_N^f(t,\phi; \nu_N^{\otimes 2})\big] =\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}(f)\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb R} \big((G_s * \mathfrak H_0)(a)\big)^2 \phi(a)\dr a\dr s.$$
     
         \item If $d=2$ and $(\log N)^{1/2p}   \varsigma_N\to   {\boldsymbol v}$ with $|\boldsymbol v|$ sufficiently small, then we have 
            $$\lim_{N \to \infty}\;  \Ex\big[ Q_N^f(t,\phi; \nu_N^{\otimes 2})\big] =\frac{\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}(f)}{1- \frac12 \gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}(  {\boldsymbol v})^2}\cdot 2\pi \cdot \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb R^2} \big((G_s * \mathfrak H_0)(a)\big)^2 \phi(a)\dr a\dr s.$$
         \item if $d\ge 3$ and if $  \varsigma_N\to   {\boldsymbol v}$ with $|\boldsymbol v|$ sufficiently small, then 
         $$\lim_{N \to \infty}\;  \Ex\big[ Q_N^f(t,\phi; \nu_N^{\otimes 2})\big]= \Theta_{\mathrm{eff}}^2(f;   {\boldsymbol v}) \cdot c_d\cdot \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb R^d} \big((G_s^{(  {\boldsymbol v})} * \mathfrak H_0)(a)\big)^2 \phi(a)\dr a\dr s,$$ where $\Theta_{\mathrm{eff}}^2( f,  {\boldsymbol v})$ is as in Proposition \ref{4.1c}.
     \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: The key estimate with general initial data in all dimensions

[Proposition 117 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Fix $\eps>0$. There exists $\delta>0$ such that for each of the four types \emph{void-band-void}, \emph{void-band-saturated}, \emph{saturated-band-void}, \emph{saturated-band-saturated}, each $\hat{n} \in \big(\eps,\frac{1}{\eps}\big)$ and $\theta \in \big(\eps,\frac{1}{\eps}\big)$, each $\hat A_1'$, $\hat B_1'$
 satisfying
 \[
 \max\big(\hat B'_1- \hat A'_1- \theta \hat n,| \hat B'_1-\hat A'_1 -2\theta \hat n|\big) > \eps \qquad \textnormal{and} \qquad \max\big(|\hat A'_1|,|\hat B'_1|\big) < \frac{1}{\eps}
 \]
 and each interval $(\alpha,\beta)$ such that
 \[
 0 < \alpha - \hat A'_1 < \delta \qquad \textnormal{and} \qquad 0 < \hat B'_1 - \beta < \delta,
 \]
 we can find $\hat A'_2$ and $\hat B'_2$ such that the equilibrium measure $\widetilde \mu$ of Theorem~\ref{Proposition_ZW_equilibrium_measure} has the prescribed type and the band $(\alpha,\beta)$. Moreover, $\hat A'_2$ and $\hat B'_2$ can be chosen to depend smoothly on $\alpha,\beta, \hat A'_1, \hat B'_1, \hat n, \theta$.

 For the types \emph{void-band-void} and \emph{saturated-band-saturated}, if we additionally set $\alpha - \hat A'_1 = \hat B'_1 - \beta$, it is sufficient to require $|\hat B'_1-\hat A'_1 - 2\theta \hat n|\neq 0$ instead of $>\eps$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Diaconis asks which perfect matching to add to a connected d-regular graph with an even number n of vertices to obtain fastest mixing of nearest-neighbor random walk on the (d+1)-regular augmentation. The problem includes accurate convergence rates for a cycle with an added matching. A separate variation adds a weighted edge to a finite reversible chain and Metropolizes the result to preserve its stationary law, asking which edge best improves mixing or spectral gap. These variants must distinguish total-variation mixing time, ordinary gap, absolute gap, and any laziness convention. A single unadjusted edge changes degrees and generally changes stationary law. Bounded-degree random-matching cutoff is known (Hermon-Sly-Sousi); the present bounded literature check does not certify current openness of general deterministic optimization. This is an open-question record, not a theorem.
connected d-regular base graph
even finite vertex count
perfect matching augmentation; metric must be specified

body: Unproved model-specific input for square-lattice bond percolation at p=1/2 with precisely fixed Dobrushin exploration and boundary crossing events: on each positive-separation localization of marked Loewner coordinates 0<X_delta<Y_delta,1<Y_delta,2, the correctly oriented bounded conditional crossing martingales P_delta,i should satisfy E sup_{t<=T wedge tau_delta}|P_delta,i(t)-C(X_delta,t/Y_delta,i,t)| -> 0 as delta -> 0. Here C(u)=B(1/3,1/3)^(-1) integral_0^u [v(1-v)]^(-2/3)dv. Compatible joint driver/mark convergence and limiting filtration are also required. This draft provides no proof of this estimate; rotational symmetry, self-duality and a local parafermion equation do not by themselves establish it. No C0017 solution or novelty is claimed.
title: UNPROVED: stopped square bond Cardy approximation

If R is a Noetherian ring (every ideal finitely generated, equivalently the ascending chain condition on ideals), then the polynomial ring R[x] is Noetherian. By induction R[x_1, ..., x_n] is Noetherian; in particular every ideal in a polynomial ring over a field is finitely generated.

[Lemma lem:burning of arXiv:2605.19419, 'Tail exponents of the three-dimensional uniform spanning tree and Abelian sandpile'] Let $K\Subset\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ contain $0$ and all nearest neighbours of $0$. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an event of subsets of $K$ such that every $A\in\mathcal{A}$ contains at least one nearest neighbour of $0$. Then
\begin{equation}
\nu_{K}\bigl(W_{1,K}\in\mathcal{A}\bigr)
= g_{K}\,\nu_{K}^{(0)}\bigl(\mathfrak{T}_{K}\in\mathcal{A}\bigr),
\qquad
 g_{K}:=\frac{|R_{K^{\circ}}|}{|R_{K}|}=G_{K}(0,0),
\end{equation}
where $G_{K}$ is the inverse of the finite-volume toppling matrix.

Let T = (R/LZ)^d carry Lebesgue measure dx, of total mass L^d, and for F in L^1(T) and xi in L^(-1) Z^d let F^(xi) = integral over T of F(x) e^(-2 pi i xi.x) dx. For F in L^2(T), F = L^(-d) sum over xi of F^(xi) e^(2 pi i xi.x) in L^2, and integral over T of |F|^2 dx = L^(-d) sum over xi of |F^(xi)|^2. For F, G in L^1(T) the convolution (F * G)(x) = integral over T of F(y) G(x - y) dy has (F * G)^(xi) = F^(xi) G^(xi). For F, G in L^2(T), (F G)^(xi) = L^(-d) sum over eta of F^(eta) G^(xi - eta). At L = 1 these are the usual formulas with no factors.

[Proposition prop:6 of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] Almost surely, for any fixed $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z}\in \mathbb{C}$ and simultaneously for all $0<t<s$, the following hold.
      \begin{enumerate}
      \item There is a finite set of points $\mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})\subseteq \partial \mathcal{B}_t^\bullet(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ such that every leftmost $D_h$-geodesic from $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z}$ to a point on $\partial \mathcal{B}_s^\bullet(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ passes via some $x\in \mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$.
      \item  There is a unique $D_h$-geodesic from $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z}$ to $x$ for each $x\in \mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$.
      \item For $x\in \mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$, let $I_x$ denote the set of $y\in \partial \mathcal{B}_s^\bullet(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ for which the leftmost $D_h$-geodesic from $0$ to $y$ passes via $x$. Each $I_x$ for $x\in \mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ is a connected arc of the Jordan curve $\partial \mathcal{B}_s^\bullet(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ and $\partial \mathcal{B}_s^\bullet(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$ is a union of the arcs $I_x$ for $x\in \mathcal{X}_{t,s}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$, with any two such arcs being disjoint.
      \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let A be a closed operator on a Banach space with resolvent set rho(A) and resolvent R(z) = (z I - A)^{-1}. Then: (i) the FIRST RESOLVENT IDENTITY R(z) - R(w) = (w - z) R(z) R(w) holds for z, w in rho(A), so resolvents at different points commute; (ii) rho(A) is OPEN and R is analytic on it, with the Neumann expansion R(z) = sum over k >= 0 of (w - z)^k R(w)^{k+1} valid whenever |z - w| is strictly less than 1 / ||R(w)||; (iii) consequently the distance from w to the spectrum is at least 1 / ||R(w)||, so the resolvent norm blows up at least like the reciprocal of the distance to the spectrum as z approaches it. For a BOUNDED A the series R(z) = sum over k >= 0 of A^k / z^{k+1} converges for |z| > the spectral radius.
A closed (so that the resolvent is bounded by the closed graph theorem) and the resolvent set nonempty.
The lower bound on the distance to the spectrum is an equality only for normal operators on Hilbert space;
for a non-normal operator the resolvent norm can be enormous far from the spectrum, which is the pseudospectrum phenomenon and the reason spectral information alone does not control transient behaviour.

body: In mathematics, the four color theorem, or the four-color map theorem, states that no more than four colors are required to color the regions of any map so that no two adjacent regions have the same color. Adjacent means that two regions share a common boundary of non-zero length. It was the first major theorem to be proved by use of a computer. Initially, this proof was not accepted by all mathematicians because the computer-assisted proof was infeasible for a human to check by hand. The proof has gained wide acceptance since then, although some reservations remain.
title: Four color theorem

Owner-own-work research draft; status proof (unaudited), independent review and priority assessment pending. Fix k>=2, D>=k+1, L>=0, M>=kappa>0, H>=0 and 0<lambda<=1. Let h extend C2 to a neighborhood of [0,1]^k with |grad h|<=L and kappa I<=D2h<=M I on the cube. Put F(x)=(x,h(x)), with any isometric embedding into R^D. Let p be a probability density with p>=lambda and Lip(p)<=H, and let mu=F#(p dx). For continuous scalar-input piecewise-affine generators with at most N pieces, including plateaux, the infimum W1 error from uniform noise is between c_lower N^(-beta) and c_upper N^(-beta) for every N>=1. Here beta=2/(2k-1), b=sqrt(1+L^2), omega_(k-1) is unit-ball volume in R^(k-1), A=5^k+8 omega_(k-1) sqrt((2L+3)/kappa), c_lower=(lambda/2)(2A)^(-beta), C0=b(sqrt(k-1)+sqrt(k))/2+bH/4+M/8, and c_upper=8C0+b sqrt(k). The new lower proof bounds every affine-line tube preimage by A r^(k-1/2) for 0<r<=1: near-vertical lines have diameter <=5r; other lines are sliced into two-sided height bands of kappa-strongly convex one-dimensional functions, whose total length is <=8 sqrt(epsilon/kappa). The upper half depends on the unaudited general C2 construction T1-003 v1. For exactly uniform surface probability on any such graph, the area density J=sqrt(1+|grad h|^2), V=integral J, p=J/V satisfies p>=1/b and Lip(p)<=M; take lambda=1/b and H=M. Thus the matching exponent covers a whole nonquadratic strongly convex graph class and its uniform-surface laws. This is not a theorem for every C2 image, a closed-manifold class, merely bounded varying densities without a common regularity bound, or deep generators.
All graph, curvature, density and generator assumptions in the statement. Matching upper depends on unaudited T1-003 v1. No independent audit or priority claim.

[Corollary 2 (Modified Lyons--Sidorova conjecture) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, let $\gamma:[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous tree-reduced bounded-variation path, and let $v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0$. Then
\[
R\bigl(\log S(\gamma)\bigr)=\infty
\]
if and only if there is a based prefix $\beta$ of $\overline\gamma=\gamma-\gamma_0$ such that
\begin{equation}
\overline\gamma
 \sim_{\mathrm{rep}}
\beta*\lambda_v*\overleftarrow{\beta}.
\end{equation}
When $v=0$, the tree-reduced path is constant. When $v\neq0$, $S(\beta)$ is the gate from the identity to the unique minimum-displacement axis of left multiplication by $S(\gamma)$ in the signature tree. This prefix is unique up to waiting intervals and weak increasing reparametrisation. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Modified Lyons--Sidorova conjecture

body: [Theorem 5 of arXiv:2512.19063, 'Sharp Decoupling Inequalities for the Variances and Second Moments of Sums of Dependent Ra'] For any nonnegative dependent square-integrable variables $d_{1},...d_{n}$, and the mutually independent variables $z_{1},...,z_{n}$ such that $z_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathcal{L}}}{{=}}d_{i}$ for all $i=1,...,n$, we have the following sharp inequality $\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_{i}\right)^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{i}\right)^{2}.$

[Proposition prop:collision-exact-sequence of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] The map
\[
 \partial_q:\mathcal C_q(A)\longrightarrow\mathbb R^m,
 \qquad
 \partial_q\!\left(\sum_u\gamma_ue_u\right)=\sum_u\gamma_u u,
\]
has image $L_q(A)$, contained in the coordinate-sum-zero subspace.  With
\[
 \mathcal N_q(A)=\ker\partial_q,
 \qquad \operatorname{cnul}_q(A)=\dim\mathcal N_q(A),
\]
there is an exact sequence
\begin{equation}
 0\longrightarrow\mathcal N_q(A)
 \longrightarrow\mathcal C_q(A)
 \xrightarrow{\partial_q}L_q(A)
 \longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Consequently, if $\Delta_q(A)=M_{q,m}-|qA|$, then
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\Delta_q(A)=r_q(A)+\operatorname{cnul}_q(A).}
\end{equation}
For $C=\Sigma_{\ell,c}A$,
\begin{equation}
 \Delta_q(C)
 =\sum_{j=0}^{\min(q,\ell-1)}\Delta_{q-j}(A)
  +\sum_{j=\ell}^{q}M_{q-j,m},
\end{equation}
where the second sum is empty for $q<\ell$.

[Lem FVlip of arXiv:2608.06500, 'Free energy of Ising models under a spectral condition'] For any $\alpha$-good potential $V$ and $C>0$, there
    exists a constant $L>0$ depending only on $V$ and $C$ such that
    for any positive semidefinite $N\times N$ matrices $\text{\boldmath $B$}_1$ and
    $\text{\boldmath $B$}_2$ with spectrum contained in $[0,C]$ and vectors
    $\text{\boldmath $h$}\in\mathbb{R}^N$ with $\|\text{\boldmath $h$}\|_\infty\le C$, we have that

    \begin{align*}
|F_V(\text{\boldmath $B$}_1,\text{\boldmath $h$})-F_V(\text{\boldmath $B$}_2,\text{\boldmath $h$})|\le L\|\text{\boldmath $B$}_1-\text{\boldmath $B$}_2\|.
\end{align*}

   In other words, $F_V(\text{\boldmath $B$},\text{\boldmath $h$})$ is a
    Lipschitz function of $\text{\boldmath $B$}\in\{\text{\boldmath $M$}:{\boldsymbol 0}\preceq\text{\boldmath $M$}\preceq C\text{\boldmath $I$}\}$
    under the  operator norm.
title: Lem FVlip of arXiv:2608.06500

body: In mathematical analysis and in probability theory, a σ-algebra is part of the formalism for defining sets that can be measured. In calculus and analysis, for example, σ-algebras are used to define the concept of sets with area or volume. In probability theory, they are used to define events for which a probability can be defined. In this way, σ-algebras help to formalize the notion of size.

[Theorem thm:local-monotonicity of arXiv:2607.08551, 'Weighted-threshold Coupon Collection'] Fix $\theta\in(0,1)$ and let $\alpha_{s,\theta}$ be defined by
\[
F_s(\alpha_{s,\theta})=\theta.
\]
Then, as $s\downarrow 0$,
\[
\alpha_{s,\theta}
=
\alpha_{0,\theta}
+
\frac12\,\alpha_{0,\theta}\bigl(\alpha_{0,\theta}-2\bigr)s^2
+o(s^2),
\qquad
\alpha_{0,\theta}=-\log(1-\theta).
\]
In particular, with
\[
\theta_c:=1-e^{-2},
\]
one has:
\begin{itemize}
\item if $\theta>\theta_c$, then $\alpha_{s,\theta}>\alpha_{0,\theta}$ for all sufficiently small $s>0$;
\item if $\theta<\theta_c$, then $\alpha_{s,\theta}<\alpha_{0,\theta}$ for all sufficiently small $s>0$.
\end{itemize}

Let $g \in L^2(\mathbb{R}, \gamma)$ have Hermite rank $d \ge 1$, and let $\sum_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} |\rho(k)|^d < \infty$. For $t \in [0, 1]$, define the continuous-time empirical path $F_n(t) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n t \rfloor} g(Y_k) + \frac{nt - \lfloor nt \rfloor}{\sqrt{n}} g(Y_{\lfloor nt \rfloor + 1})$. body: In 1933 Karol Borsuk conjectured that every bounded subset of n-dimensional Euclidean space can be partitioned into at most n+1 pieces, each of strictly smaller diameter than the original set. This is TRUE for n=1, 2, 3, and for all smooth convex bodies in every dimension. The conjecture is FALSE in general: Kahn and Kalai showed in 1993, adapting a counterexample of Frankl and Wilson, that partitioning into only n+1 smaller-diameter pieces fails for all sufficiently large n; the smallest dimension with an explicit known counterexample was later narrowed to 64 by Jenrich and Brouwer in 2014. The truth for intermediate dimensions, roughly 4 through 63, remains open.
title: Borsuk's conjecture

body: Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and f: Omega -> R (or C) a measurable function. The essential supremum of |f| is ess sup |f| = inf{M >= 0 : mu(|f| > M) = 0}, with the infimum of the empty set taken to be infinity. The space L-infinity(mu) consists of equivalence classes, under equality mu-almost everywhere, of measurable functions f with ess sup |f| < infinity, normed by ||f||_infinity = ess sup |f|; with this norm L-infinity(mu) is a Banach space. body:
Let S be a compact C^k hypersurface in R^n with k >= 2. Then there is delta > 0 such that on the tubular neighbourhood { x : dist(x, S) < delta } the nearest point of S to x is UNIQUE, the projection map is C^{k-1}, and the signed distance function d is C^k with gradient of unit length equal to the outward normal at the projected point. The largest such delta is governed by the REACH of S, which is bounded below by the reciprocal of the supremum of the principal curvatures and shrinks where the surface nearly self-touches. For a merely C^1 hypersurface the reach can be zero and the projection can fail to be unique arbitrarily close to the surface, so no tubular neighbourhood of uniform width need exist - the standard trap when a proof written for C^2 surfaces is applied to a C^1 one.
C^2 (or better) regularity and compactness;
the width of the neighbourhood depends on curvature bounds and is not uniform over all surfaces.
For a convex set the projection is globally unique and 1-Lipschitz with no curvature hypothesis, which is a different theorem, resting on convexity rather than smoothness.

body: [Proposition 3.1 of arXiv:2608.08073, 'eIRWR: Enhanced Iterative Random Walk with Restart for Scalable Root Cause Analysis in Mic'] shows that basic IRWR is not a new graph model at all. The ablation in Section 4.3 confirms this equality numerically and shows that walking on the true transpose W ⊤(a genuinely “backward” matrix) is in fact catastrophic. The consequence for evaluation is that basic IRWR must be benchmarked against a restart-tuned PPR, not the default; once that is done, its advantage disappears.

[Lem 29 of arXiv:2607.21759, 'Marchenko--Pastur law for tensor powers of exchangeable unconditional vectors'] For $0<k<\infty$, let $(X_1,\dotsc,X_n) \sim \Inv_k(R)$. Then \[
        \E(X_1^4\dotsm X_r^4 X_{r+1}^2\dotsm X_{2d - r}^2) = \frac{\Gamma(5/k)^r \,\Gamma(3/k)^{2d - 2r}}{\Gamma(1/k)^{2d - r}} \cdot \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{n}{k}\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{n+4d}{k}\bigr)}\cdot \E(R^{4d}).
    \]
    Let $r = 0$ and replace $2d$ by $d$, we get \[
        \E(X_1^2\dotsm X_d^2) = \frac{\Gamma(3/k)^d}{\Gamma(1/k)^d} \cdot \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{n}{k}\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{n+2d}{k}\bigr)}\cdot \E(R^{2d}),
    \] and taking $d = 1$ gives \[
        \E(X_1^2) = \frac{\Gamma(3/k)}{\Gamma(1/k)} \cdot \frac{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{n}{k}\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{n+2}{k}\bigr)}\cdot \E(R^{2}).
    \]

[Proposition 30 (Averaged lower bound under sparsity and edge-density control) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(u\in[0,1]\), \(\theta>0\), and let
\[
c_{\theta,u}:=1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}.
\]
Also define
\[
C_\theta:=
\begin{cases}
1, & \theta=1,\\[1ex]
\dfrac{\theta |\log \theta|}{|\theta-1|}, & \theta\neq 1.
\end{cases}
\]

Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with \(|V|=n\), and assume that for some \(\eta,\varepsilon>0\),
\[
e_G(S)\le (1+\varepsilon)|S|
\qquad\text{for every }S\subset V\text{ with }|S|\le \eta n.
\]
Assume moreover that
\[
\frac{|E|}{n}\in [m_-,m_+]
\]
for some \(m_-,m_+>0\).

Then for every \(a\ge 0\) and every \(s>0\),
\[
\frac1s\int_a^{a+s}\Pbb^G_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\,\dd t
\ge
\frac{
m_- - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)-C_\theta/s
}{
(1+\theta)m_+ - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)
},
\]
provided the denominator is positive.

Let N=N(n) with N/n->c in (0,infinity). For all n,i,j let X_ij^(n) be real independent identically distributed random variables with mean zero, variance one, and E|X_ij^(n)|^(4+epsilon)<infinity for some epsilon>0. Let sigma_ij(n) be deterministic real numbers uniformly bounded in absolute value. Let A_n be deterministic real N-by-n matrices whose row Euclidean norms and column Euclidean norms are uniformly bounded over all n and all rows and columns. Put (Y_n)_ij=sigma_ij(n) X_ij^(n)/sqrt(n) and Sigma_n=Y_n+A_n. For the relevant N,n, write A=A_n and sigma_ij=sigma_ij(n), D_j=diag(sigma_1j^2,...,sigma_Nj^2), and Dtilde_i=diag(sigma_i1^2,...,sigma_in^2). Let S_plus consist of the functions z->integral_[0,infinity) (lambda-z)^(-1) nu(dlambda) for probability measures nu on [0,infinity), analytically continued to C minus [0,infinity). Define the unique S_plus-valued solution psi_i,psitilde_j by psi_i(z)=-1/[z(1+tr(Dtilde_i Ttilde(z))/n)] and psitilde_j(z)=-1/[z(1+tr(D_j T(z))/n)], where Psi=diag(psi_i), Psitilde=diag(psitilde_j), T(z)=[Psi(z)^(-1)-z A Psitilde(z) A^T]^(-1), and Ttilde(z)=[Psitilde(z)^(-1)-z A^T Psi(z) A]^(-1). Both trace terms in these canonical equations use division by n. For fixed s>0, use natural logarithms and define C_n(s)=E[log det(I_N+Sigma_n Sigma_n^T/s)]/N and Cbar_n(s)=integral_s^infinity [1/omega-tr(T_n(-omega))/N] domega. Then C_n(s)-Cbar_n(s)->0 as n->infinity. Furthermore, evaluating all canonical matrices at -s, Cbar_n(s) equals (1/N)log det[Psi(-s)^(-1)/s+A_n Psitilde(-s) A_n^T]+(1/N)log det[Psitilde(-s)^(-1)/s]-(s/(n N)) sum_{i=1}^N sum_{j=1}^n sigma_ij(n)^2 (T_n(-s))_ii (Ttilde_n(-s))_jj. Both logarithmic determinants are divided by N, including the determinant of the n-by-n matrix. The first quantity C_n is an expectation, as defined in equation (4.1). Equivalently Cbar_n(s)=integral log(1+lambda/s) pi_n(dlambda), with pi_n specified by tr(T_n)/N.

    \begin{equation}
        C_1 2^{-n(1+\xi_{\alpha}(1,1))} \le \Pb(D \in K_{j,n}) \le C_2 2^{-n(1+\xi_{\alpha}(1,1))},
    \end{equation}
    and, for any pair of cubes $D,E$ of side length $2^{-n}$ with
    distance in $[2^{-m-1},2^{-m}]$,
    we have
    \begin{equation}
        \Pb(D,E \in K_{j,n})\le C_3 2^{(-2n+m)(\xi_{\alpha}(1,1)+1)}.
    \end{equation}
    Furthermore, 
    \begin{equation}
        \Pb(D\in F_{j,n}) \le C_4 2^{-n(2+\xi_{\alpha}(1,1))}.
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, split B, full calibration, paired). The two-vertex blend of the transductive covariance penalty keeps the simplex's gain on EMIT and closes three quarters of its deficit to the pool's hand-tuned heuristic on OCO-2 (-0.27 there); the heuristic is itself label-free, so it was added as a third vertex with barycentric weights chosen by the same criterion. P26 (a) REFUTED: on OCO-2 the three-vertex blend reads -0.09 vs the pool best and +0.18 vs the two-vertex blend; (b) HELD: on EMIT it reads +4.78 vs the pool best and +0.05 vs the two-vertex blend; (c) HELD: mean weights (simplex, least squares, pool) are (0.09, 0.44, 0.47) on OCO-2 and (0.59, 0.24, 0.17) on EMIT; falsifier (three-vertex worse than two-vertex by more than 0.5 on either corpus) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P27, split C, pre-registered before the split-B result was read): P27 (a) HELD: on split C OCO-2 the three-vertex blend reads -0.12 vs the pool best and +0.20 vs the two-vertex blend; (b) HELD: on EMIT +4.83 vs the pool best and +0.18 vs the two-vertex blend; (c) HELD: mean weights (simplex, least squares, pool) (0.11, 0.42, 0.48) on OCO-2 and (0.57, 0.26, 0.17) on EMIT; falsifier (three-vertex worse than two-vertex by more than 0.5 on either corpus) not triggered.
the three bases are fitted on the calibration rows only (simplex = long-only relative-metric stack; least squares = per-output ridge 1e-6; pool heuristic = per-output ridge with a GCV lambda shrunk toward the pooled convex weights by a 5-fold-CV amount); barycentric weights on the 0.1 grid (66 points); the criterion is the 5-fold cross-validated squared relative error on the calibration rows plus the excess pairs-bootstrap variance (B = 8) of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows; the two-vertex blend is the face with zero pool weight, so its comparison is exact

body:
[Thm 96 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Given any $\acute{b},\acute{\sigma},\acute{w},p,\acute{\zeta},
\acute{\zeta}^\Ising$, let  
\begin{align*}
    d Z(t) &= p'(t)^{1/2} \ab_t\,dt + s(t) \asig_t\,dB(t)\,,
    \\
    dZ^{\Ising}(t)
    &= \aw_t\,dW(t)\,,
    \end{align*}
on the time interval $q_0 \le t \le 1$, with $Z(q_0)\sim\acute{\zeta}$ and $Z^\Ising(q_0)\sim\acute{\zeta}^\Ising$. Assume the following:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item 
The coefficients
$\ab,\asig,\aw$ are 
progressively measurable processes on the time interval $[q_0,1]$;

\item 
$\bE[(\aw_t)^2]=1$ for all $t\in[q_0, 1]$;

\item  $p\in\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ with
$p(q_0)\ge 1/L$
and $\|p\|_{C^2([q_0,1])}\le L$;

\item 
The coefficients $\ab,\asig,\aw$ obey the budget constraints \eqref{eq:is-budget-constraint}, that is,
	\[
	\bE \bigg[(\ab_t)^2 + \frac{(tp)'(t)}{p(t)}(\asig_t-1)^2\bigg]
        \le \frac{(\bE \aw_t)^2 }{ \alpha}\,,\]
for all $t\in [q_0,1]$;

\item 
$|Z^{\Ising}(1)|=1$ almost surely;

\item 
$Z(q_0)=0$ almost surely, and $\bE[Z^{\Ising}(q_0)^2]=q_0$;

\item 
$\zeta^\Ising\in\cP([-1,1])$,
the space of Borel probability measures on $[-1,1]$.\footnote{We note that since $Z^\Ising$ is a martingale with $|Z^{\Ising}(1)|=1$ almost surely, the initial distribution cannot have support outside of $[-1,1]$.}
\end{enumerate}
Given any
$q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$
(same $p$ as above),
let $X,X^\Ising$ be given by \eqref{e:sde.x} and \eqref{e:sde.x.ising} on the time interval $[q_*,1]$, with $X(q_*)\sim\zeta$ and $X^\Ising(q_*)\sim\zeta^\Ising$.
Then for any $\epsilon>0$ there exist parameters $q_*,b,\sigma,w,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising$ such that the following hold: 
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 
$b_t= b(t,X_t)$, $\sigma_t=\sigma(t,X_t)$, and $w_t= w(t,X_t)$,
for $C$-Lipschitz functions
$b:[q_*,1]\times\R\to[-C,C]$
and $\sigma,w:[q_*,1]\times\R\to[0,C]$, for a constant $C=C(L,\epsilon)$.
 
\item 
 $|\bE[(w_t)^2] -1| \le\epsilon$
 for all $t\in[q_*,1]$. 
 
\item 
 $X$ and $X^{\Ising}$ approximately obey the budget constraints at each time $t$, that is,
	\[\bE \bigg[(b_t)^2 + \frac{(tp)'(t)}{p(t)}(\sigma_t-1)^2\bigg]
        \le \frac{(\bE w_t)^2 }{ \alpha}
        +\epsilon\]
for all $t\in[q_*,1]$.

\item  The initial distributions of $(X,X^\Ising)$ and $(Z,Z^\Ising)$ are close:
\[\begin{aligned}
\bbW_2(\zeta,\acute{\zeta}) &= 
\bbW_2(\Law(X(q_*)),\Law(Z(q_0)))
\leq \epsilon\,,\\
\bbW_2(\zeta^\Ising,\acute{\zeta}^\Ising)
&= \bbW_2(\Law(X^{\Ising}(q_*)),
        	\Law(Z^{\Ising}(q_0)))
\leq \epsilon\,.
\end{aligned}\]

\item  
The initial time $q_*$ lies in $[q_0,q_0+\epsilon]$.
\end{enumerate}
Lastly, we have
	\beq
    \begin{aligned}
	\bbW_2(\Law(X(1)),\Law(Z(1)))
	&\leq \epsilon\,,\\
	\bbW_2(\Law(X^{\Ising}(1)),
        	\Law(Z^{\Ising}(1)))
	&\leq \epsilon
    \end{aligned}
	\eeq
Thus the more general diffusions $(Z,Z^\Ising)$ are well approximated by the Markovian SDE solutions
$(X,X^\Ising)$. Finally, if $\Law(Z^{\Ising}(t))$ is even for each $t$, then we can take $w_t$ to be even for each $t$, that is, $w(t,x)=w(t,-x)$ for all $(t,x)\in [0,1]\times \bbR$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 18 of arXiv:2606.16164, 'A Low-Regularity Semigroup Sewing Lemma via Quotient Structures'] Let $\tau\in[0,T]$ and $\beta\in\mathbb R$. If $\gamma\in(0,1)$, then
\[
\Lambda_\tau^{\mathrm d}: ZC^{\gamma}(\Delta^3_\tau;B_\beta)\to C^{\gamma}(\Delta^2_\tau;B_\beta)
\]
is linear, satisfies $\delta\Lambda_\tau^{\mathrm d}h = h$ and obeys the estimate $\|\Lambda_\tau^{\mathrm d}h\|_{\gamma,\beta;\tau}\le C_\gamma\|h\|_{\gamma,\beta;\tau}$. 
If $\gamma=1$, then
\[
\Lambda_\tau^{\mathrm d}: ZC^{1}(\Delta^3_\tau;B_\beta)\to C^{1}_{\mathrm{log}}(\Delta^2_\tau;B_\beta)
\]
is linear, satisfies $\delta\Lambda_\tau^{\mathrm d}h = h$ and obeys the estimates $\|\Lambda_\tau^{\mathrm d}h\|_{1,\log;\tau,\beta} \le C_{1,T}\|h\|_{1,\beta;\tau}$, as well as, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$,  $\|\Lambda_\tau^{\mathrm d}h\|_{1-\varepsilon,\beta;\tau}\le C_{\varepsilon,T}\|h\|_{1,\beta;\tau}$.

[Proposition prop locality of arXiv:2609.04138, 'The conformally invariant metric on $\CLE_4$ I:\\ subsequential limits of the non-simple C'] Let $\Gamma, D$ be the random variables appearing in the subsequential limits~(equation eq cv ball of the paper) and~(equation eq cv subsequence boundary of the paper). Let $V \subseteq \BD$ be a deterministic simply connected subdomain and $I \in \SCS$ a deterministic segment. Let $V^\star$ be the open set obtained by removing from $V$ the closure of the union of the domains encircled by the loops of $\Gamma$ which are not included in $V$. Let $V_j$ for $j\ge 1$ be the connected components of $V^\star$ in decreasing order of Lebesgue measure. For all $j\ge 1$, let $Z_j$ be an independent random point in $V_j$ sampled uniformly with respect to Lebesgue measure. Let $\phi_j$ be the unique conformal mapping from $\BD$ to $V_j$ sending $0$ to $Z_j$ and such that $\phi_j'(0)>0$.

	Then, there exist random distances $D_j$ on $\phi_j^{-1}(\Gamma\vert_{V_j})$, coupled with $(\Gamma, D)$, such that
	\begin{itemize}
		\item Conditionally on $\{ \SCL \in \Gamma: \SCL \not \subseteq V\}$, 
		$\{\SCB_t(\SCL): \SCL \in \Gamma, \  \SCL \not\subseteq V, t \in [0, D(\SCL, \partial V^{\star}))\}$ and $\{\SCB_t(I): t \in [0, D(I, \partial V^\star))\}$, the $(\phi_j^{-1}(\Gamma\vert_{V_j}), D_j)$'s are i.i.d.\ and their conditional law is that of $(\Gamma, D)$.
		\item For all $j$, for all $\SCL_1, \SCL_2 \in \Gamma\vert_{V_j}$, we have
		\[
		D(\SCL_1, \SCL_2) \le D_j(\phi_j^{-1}(\SCL_1), \phi_j^{-1}(\SCL_2)).
		\]
		\item For all $j$, for all $\SCL \in \Gamma\vert_{V_j}$, for all $t \in [0, D(\SCL, \partial V_j))$, the image under $\phi_j$ of the metric ball of radius $t$ for $D_j$ centered at $\phi_j^{-1}(\SCL)$ is $\SCB_t(\SCL)$.
	\end{itemize}

[Definition 16 of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] We use $B$ to denote a standard Brownian motion on $\mbb R^2$. For any $x,y\in\mbb R^2$ and $t>0$,
we let $B^x=(B|B(0)=x)$ denote the Brownian motion started at $x$, and let $B^{x,y}_t=(B|B(0)=x,~B(t)=y)$
denote the Brownian bridge from $x$ to $y$ on the time interval $[0,t]$. Finally, when we require multiple
independent copies of Brownian motion, we use the notation ${_1}B,{_2}B,{_3}B,\ldots$
(in particular, we use ${_i}B^{x_i}$ and ${_i}B^{x_i,y_i}_t$, $i\geq1$, to denote independent Brownian motions
started at $x_i$ and independent Brownian bridges from $x_i$ to $y_i$ on the time interval $[0,t]$).

[Proposition 28 of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $n,m \in \N$. Then, for any $Q \in \conbodo[m]$, and any compact set $K\subset \R^n$ with positive volume such that $o\in \operatorname{int}\operatorname{conv}(K)$,
\[\Vol(K^{\star,Q}) \vol(K^\circ)^{-m} \leq \Vol((\B)^{\star,Q}) \vol(\B)^{-m}.\]

 For a fixed $Q$, there is equality when $K=E$ for some centered ellipsoid $E\subset\R^n$ up to removal of null sets. For a fixed $K$, there is equality when $Q=[0,1]^m$.

Fix t>0, let X have density p(x)=(sqrt(2)/2) exp(-sqrt(2)|x|), and let G~N(0,1) be independent. Put Y=X+sqrt(t)G and a(y)=Var(X|Y=y). Then 0<=a(y)<=t and a(y) tends to t as y tends to positive infinity. For any nonzero smooth phi supported in (0,1), let f_L(x)=integral_{-infinity}^x phi(u-L)du and h_L(Y)=E[phi(X-L)^2|Y]. As L tends to positive infinity, E[a(Y)h_L(Y)]/(t E h_L(Y)) tends to 1. Consequently no fixed q<1 controls this ratio for every test function even for this one fixed isotropic log-concave measure.
X is the specified variance-one centered Laplace law
G independent standard Gaussian
t>0 fixed
phi nonzero smooth and supported in (0,1)

Take the centered Laplace density p(x)=(lambda/2) exp(-lambda|x|), lambda=sqrt(2), so Var X=2/lambda^2=1. Its posterior has variance a(y)<=t. [Definition defi_strong_sol of arXiv:2603.26307, '\LARGE The incompressible Navier--Stokes--Fourier system with thermal noise'] Let Assumption (Ass:noise of the paper) hold, $(\Omega,\mathfrak{A},\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space equipped with a filtration $\mathscr{F}$ satisfying the usual conditions and $3$-dimensional standard $\mathscr{F}$-Brownian motions $(W_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$ and $3\times 3$-matrix valued $\mathscr{F}$-Brownian motions $(B_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$ with covariance structure (equation Eq_noise_matrix_covariation of the paper) be independent. Then a local strong solution to (equation Eq_new_var of the paper), defined up to a stopping time $\tau >0  $, is a tuple of continuous, adapted  processes $U \colon [0,\tau ) \to C^1(\mathbb{T}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ and $\Psi \colon [0,\tau ) \to C^1(\mathbb{T}^3)$, such that for a strictly increasing localizing sequence $0\le \tau_j\nearrow \tau $ the following holds for any $j\in \mathbb N$:
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item  We have $\mathrm{inf_{(t,x) \in [0,\tau_j] \times \mathbb{T}^3}} \Psi(t,x)>0$, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely.
		\item  For every divergence-free $\varphi\in C^{{\infty}}(\mathbb{T}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ it holds
		\begin{align}\begin{split}
				& \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}  U_t\cdot \varphi\,\mathrm{d} x \,-\, 
				\int_{\mathbb{T}^3} U_0 \cdot \varphi\,\mathrm{d} x
				\\&\quad=\,  \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3} -  \Bigl(\frac{1}{2}+ \frac{F_1}{4}\Bigr) \nabla U: \nabla  \varphi \,+\, U\otimes U:\nabla \varphi \,\mathrm{d} x\,\mathrm{d} s \,+\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}^3}\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}\Psi f_n \nabla \varphi\,\mathrm{d} x :\mathrm{d} B_{n,s},
			\end{split}
		\end{align}
		and $\nabla \cdot U_t = 0$  for all $t\in [0,\tau_j]$, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely.
		\item 
		For every $\eta\in C^{{\infty}}( \mathbb{T}^3)$ it holds
		\begin{align}\begin{split}
				&\int_{\mathbb{T}^3} \Psi_t  \eta  \, \mathrm{d} x  \,-\, \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}
				\Psi_0 \eta
				\,\mathrm{d} x \,=\,  \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}  \frac{\eta}{\Psi} \bigl(
				|\nabla \Psi|^2+|\nabla_\mathrm{sym} U|^2
				\bigr) \,\mathrm{d} x \, \mathrm{d} s
				\\&\qquad+\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3} - \bigl(1+ {F_1}/2 +G_1/2\bigr) \nabla \Psi\cdot \nabla  \eta \,+\,\Psi U\cdot \nabla \eta   \,-\, (F_2/2+G_2/8) \Psi \eta \,\mathrm{d} x\,\mathrm{d} s 
				\\&\qquad + \sum_{i=1}^3
				\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}^3}\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3} \Psi g_n \partial_i \eta  + \frac{1}{2} \Psi \eta \partial_ig_n   \,\mathrm{d} x \, \mathrm{d} W_{n,s}^i
				\,-\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}^3}\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb{T}^3}\eta f_n \nabla U\,\mathrm{d} x :\mathrm{d} B_{n,s},
			\end{split}
		\end{align} for all $t\in [0,\tau_j ]$, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely.
	\end{enumerate}

[Defn def:flowblowdown of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\Phi$ be a smooth flow on a closed $3$-manifold $M$. A \textbf{blowup} of $(M, \Phi)$ along a closed orbit $\gamma$ of $\Phi$ is a pair $(M^\circ,\Phi^\circ)$, where $M^\circ$ is a compact $3$-manifold with torus boundary and $\Phi^\circ$ is a flow on $M^\circ$ tangent to the boundary, together with a map $\pi:M^\circ \to M$ such that 
        \begin{enumerate}
        \item There exist smooth local coordinates $(r, \theta, \phi)$ around $\partial M^\circ$ (where $r$ parametrizes the normal direction, $\phi$ parametrizes the longitudinal direction, $\theta$ parametrizes the meridional direction) and cylindrical coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$ in a neighborhood of $\gamma$ (where $\gamma$ lies along $\{r=0\}$), such that $\pi$ has the form 
        $$\pi(r,\theta,\phi) = (f(r),\theta,\phi)$$
        for some smooth function $f:[0,1]\to [0,1]$. In particular, $\pi$ sends $\partial M^\circ$ to $\gamma$, collapsing leaves of a linear foliation on $\partial M$ to points.
        \item $\pi$ restricts to a smooth orbit equivalence between $(\interior M^\circ, \Phi^\circ\vert_{\interior M^\circ})$ and $(M, \Phi\vert_{M\setminus \gamma})$.
        \end{enumerate}
    We say that $(M, \Phi)$ is a \textbf{blowdown} of $(M^\circ, \Phi^\circ)$ along the slope $\phi=const$.

[Proposition 7 (Fixed-threshold almost-flat/torus-bundle alternative) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(M\) be \(\TT^3\), a compact \(\Nil\) torus bundle with nontrivial
unipotent monodromy, or a compact \(\Sol\) torus bundle with hyperbolic
monodromy, and let \(g(t)\) be an immortal Ricci flow on \(M\).  Let \(K\) be
a Type-III constant supplied by Proposition~\ref{input:bamler-typeIII}.
Fix any \(c_0\in(0,1)\) such that
\begin{equation}
        Kc_0^2<\eps_{\mathrm{af}}.
\end{equation}
The parameter \(c_0\) is used only as the diameter threshold separating the two
geometric alternatives below; it is not an analytic smallness parameter and will not
be decreased later to meet compactness or stability tolerances.

There exist a finite time \(T_B(c_0)<\infty\) and a nonincreasing function
\[
        \eps_B^{c_0}:[T_B(c_0),\infty)\longrightarrow(0,\tfrac12],
        \qquad \eps_B^{c_0}(t)\longrightarrow0,
\]
with
\begin{equation}
        \eps_B^{c_0}(t)<c_0,
        \qquad t\geq T_B(c_0),
\end{equation}
such that every \(t\geq T_B(c_0)\) belongs to exactly one of the following
diameter-defined alternatives.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
If
\begin{equation}
        \diam(M,g(t))<c_0\sqrt t,
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
 \bigl(\sup_M|\sec_{g(t)}|\bigr)\diam(M,g(t))^2
 <Kc_0^2<\eps_{\mathrm{af}}.
\end{equation}
Thus the slice is quantitatively almost flat.

\item
If
\begin{equation}
        \diam(M,g(t))\geq c_0\sqrt t,
\end{equation}
then there exist a torus fibration \(\pi_t^B:M\to S_t^1\) and an invariant metric \(g_t^B\), in the sense described in
Subsection~\ref{subsec:torus-bundle-conventions}, such that
\begin{equation}
        (1+\eps_B^{c_0}(t))^{-1}g_t^B\leq g(t)
        \leq(1+\eps_B^{c_0}(t))g_t^B.
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every integer \(m\) with
\(0\leq m<\bigl(\eps_B^{c_0}(t)\bigr)^{-1}\), the metric
\(t^{-1}g_t^B\) is \(\eps_B^{c_0}(t)\)-close to \(t^{-1}g(t)\) in
\(C^m\), relative to \(t^{-1}g(t)\), and every fiber has
\(g(t)\)-diameter at most \(\eps_B^{c_0}(t)\sqrt t\).
\end{enumerate}
Labels~(\ref{item:bamler-small-slice}) and~(\ref{item:bamler-large-slice})
refer only to the diameter inequalities.  A torus comparison
may also exist in the first alternative, but it is not used there.  In the
second alternative the fibration, quotient circle, and comparison metric may
depend on \(t\), with no asserted compatibility or uniqueness. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Fixed-threshold almost-flat/torus-bundle alternative

[Defn d:sharp-dperc of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] For a graph $\Psi = {\Psi(\cdot)}$ defined on the input process \( \mathcal{P} \), the {\em critical probability $q_c$ for  percolation} is defined as  
\begin{equation}
q_c := \sup\Bigl\{q \in [0,1] :  \forall p \in \mathbb{N} , \, 
\text{the function $\tilde{\mathfrak{a}}_{p,q}(r)$ is fast decreasing as $r\to\infty$}\Bigr\},
\end{equation}
where for $r > 0$
\begin{equation} \tilde{\mathfrak{a}}_{p,q}(r):=\sup_{n \geq 1} \sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p\in W_n}
\mathbb{P}_{\bk x1p,q}\bigl( x_1 \stackrel{(\mathcal{P}_n\cap B_{r}(x))_{*q}}{\longleftrightarrow} \mathcal{P}_n \cap B_r(x_1)^c \bigr), \,
\end{equation}
where the underlying graph is $\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n)$ and recall that
\(
\{x \stackrel{{{\cal X }'}_{*q}}{\longleftrightarrow} \mathcal{Y}\} = \{x \stackrel{\perc{\Psi({\cal X })}{{\cal X }'}{q}}{\longleftrightarrow} \mathcal{Y} \}
\)
means that there exists an open path in~\(\Psi({\cal X })\) from~\(x\in{\cal X }'\subset{\cal X }\) to
\(\mathcal{Y}\subset {\cal X }\)  through vertices in ${\cal X }'_{*q}$, the thinned subset of ${\cal X }'$ where vertices in~\({\cal X }'\) are
independently open/retained with probability~\(q\), while all other vertices in ${\cal X }$ are
always open, and where \(\mathbb{P}_{\bk x1p,q}\) incorporates this additional percolation randomness on top of Palm distribution.

[Corollary Main Corollary of arXiv:2608.27248, 'Optimal Transport and the ABP Method in Higher Codimension'] Let $n\geq2$ and $1\leq m\leq4$.  Let
$X:\Sigma\to\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ be a smooth immersion of a compact $n$-dimensional
manifold with smooth boundary, where the boundary may be empty, and let
$\mathcal E$ be a centered ellipsoid.  Then every positive
$f\in C^\infty(\Sigma)$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \int_\Sigma h_{\mathcal E}(\nabla^\Sigma f+fH)\,\mathrm d\mu
 +\int_{\partial\Sigma}f h_{\mathcal E}(\eta)\,\mathrm d\sigma
 \geq nV_*(\mathcal E)^{\frac1n}
 \left(\int_\Sigma f^{\frac n{n-1}}\,\mathrm d\mu\right)^{\frac{n-1}{n}}.
\end{equation}
Equality holds if and only if $\Sigma$ is connected, $f$ is constant, and,
for some $n$-plane $P$ realizing $V_*(\mathcal E)$, $X$ is an embedding onto
$x_0+r\,\overline{\operatorname{proj}_P\mathcal E}$ for some
$x_0\in\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ and $r>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem Inverse transport theorem of arXiv:2608.27248, 'Optimal Transport and the ABP Method in Higher Codimension'] Let $m\geq1$, let $X:\Sigma^n\to\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ be a smooth immersion of a
compact manifold, possibly with smooth boundary, and let
$\mathcal K\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+m}$ be a bounded open convex set.  Let
$u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\Sigma)$, understood up to the boundary, for some
$\alpha\in(0,1)$.  If $\partial\Sigma\ne\varnothing$, assume
$\langle\nabla^\Sigma u,\eta\rangle=h_{\mathcal K}(\eta)$ on
$\partial\Sigma$.  With $v$, $Q$, $\Phi$, $\mathcal{C}$, and $\vartheta$ defined
above, the following conclusions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item One has $Q_x(y)\geq0$ on $\mathcal{C}$ and, for every Borel function
$\varphi:\mathcal K\to[0,\infty]$,
\begin{equation}
 \int_{\mathcal{C}}\varphi(\Phi(x,y))\frac{\det Q_x(y)}{\vartheta(x)}
 \,\mathrm d\mu(x)\,\mathrm dy
 =\int_{\mathcal K}\varphi(\xi)\,\mathrm d\xi.
\end{equation}
Both sides are understood as extended nonnegative integrals.

\item Let $\rho$ be a nonnegative Borel function satisfying
$\int_{\mathcal K}\rho\,\mathrm d\xi=1$, and set
\[
 I_\rho(x)=\int_{\mathcal{C}_x}\rho(\Phi(x,y))\det Q_x(y)\,\mathrm dy,
 \qquad
 \mathrm d\lambda_{u,\rho}(x)=\frac{I_\rho(x)}{\vartheta(x)}\,\mathrm d\mu(x).
\]
By part \textup{(i)}, $I_\rho(x)<\infty$ for $\mu$-almost every $x$.
For $0<I_\rho(x)<\infty$, define
\begin{equation}
 \mathrm d\nu_{x,\rho}(y)
 =\frac{\rho(\Phi(x,y))\det Q_x(y)}{I_\rho(x)}
 \mathbf1_{\mathcal{C}_x}(y)\,\mathrm dy.
\end{equation}
On $\{I_\rho=0\}\cup\{I_\rho=\infty\}$ set
$\nu_{x,\rho}=\delta_0$.  Then $x\mapsto\nu_{x,\rho}$ is a Borel
probability kernel, $\lambda_{u,\rho}$ is a probability measure, and the plan
$\pi_{u,\rho}$ defined by
\begin{equation}
 \int \zeta\,\mathrm d\pi_{u,\rho}
 =\int_\Sigma\int_{N_x\Sigma}
 \zeta(x,v(x)+y)\,\mathrm d\nu_{x,\rho}(y)\,\mathrm d\lambda_{u,\rho}(x)
\end{equation}
for bounded Borel $\zeta$ has marginals $\lambda_{u,\rho}$ and
$\rho\,\mathrm d\xi$, and is optimal for
$c(x,\xi)=\frac12|X(x)-\xi|^2$.

\item Let
\begin{equation}
 \Psi(\xi)=\max_{z\in\Sigma}
 \{\langle X(z),\xi\rangle-u(z)\}.
\end{equation}
As a supremum of affine functions, $\Psi$ is convex and hence differentiable
almost everywhere.  Then $T=\nabla\Psi$ is the Brenier map from
$\rho\,\mathrm d\xi$ to $X_\#\lambda_{u,\rho}$ and
\begin{equation}
 T_\#(\rho\,\mathrm d\xi)=X_\#\lambda_{u,\rho}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Graph matrix, see e.g. [RT23] Definition 4.4]
Given a shape $\tau$, the associated graph matrix ${\bf M}$ : $\Omega \rightarrow {\mathbb R}^{d_1 \times d_2}$ is a matrix-valued function such that
$$
{\bf M} [I,J] = \sum_{\substack{\varphi \in {\mathcal T}^k_n: \\ \varphi(U_\tau) = I, \varphi(V_\tau) = J }} \prod _{(u,v) \in E(\tau)} G_{\varphi(u),\varphi(v)}.
$$
In other words, ${\bf M}$ maps an input graph $G \in \Omega$ to a $\frac{n!}{(n-|I|)!} \times \frac{n!}{(n-|J|)!}$ matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by $I$ and $J$ respectively.

The PDF (v2, 4 May 2021), printed p.8, states for H={sum_(i=1)^d alpha_i x_i^2}, Gaussian input, and orthogonally equivariant learners:
  N_star(A,P,epsilon) >= [d(d+3)/2](1-epsilon)-1.
The formula was visually checked in papers/theorem54_page.png; this is not inferred only from PDF text extraction. The definition directly above it normalizes mean square prediction error by E[y^2].

Counterexample to the literal lower bound: take d=2. Any symmetric quadratic x^T A x has only D=d(d+1)/2=3 coefficients. Given n=3 Gaussian observations, solve least squares over Sym(2) and select the minimum Frobenius-norm solution on rank-deficient samples. This algorithm is orthogonally equivariant on every dataset: conjugation A->R A R^T maps the least-squares solution sets into each other and preserves Frobenius norm, while the minimum-norm solution is unique. Hence predictions transform as required by source Definition 3.2.

For three generic Gaussian inputs, the 3 by 3 quadratic evaluation design is invertible almost surely. Its determinant is a polynomial that is not identically zero: inputs (1,0), (0,1), (1,1), with coefficient coordinates (A_11,A_12,A_22), give rows (1,0,0), (0,0,1), (1,2,1), with determinant -2. A nonzero polynomial vanishes on a Lebesgue-null set; independent Gaussian inputs are absolutely continuous. Thus the algorithm reconstructs EVERY symmetric A exactly almost surely, in particular every diagonal target in H, and has zero population squared error. For each fixed target, N_star<=3 at every epsilon>0, including the normalized definition. The zero target also has zero error and poses no division issue because the definition is an inequality against epsilon E[y^2].

At epsilon=1/10, the printed bound is 5*(9/10)-1=7/2>3, a contradiction. More generally, D Gaussian samples exactly reconstruct every symmetric d by d quadratic, so the printed expression cannot hold when it exceeds D.

This does not assert that the other source moment calculations are correct, nor propose their full repair. The interpolation counterexample alone refutes the literal theorem constant, independently of those calculations.

Let G be an m x n matrix (m >= n) with independent standard Gaussian entries, and let s_max(G) >= s_min(G) denote its largest and smallest singular values (the extreme values of |G x| over unit vectors x in R^n). Then sqrt(m) - sqrt(n) <= E s_min(G) <= E s_max(G) <= sqrt(m) + sqrt(n). Both maps G |-> s_max(G) and G |-> s_min(G) are 1-Lipschitz in the Frobenius (Euclidean) norm, so Gaussian concentration gives, for every t >= 0, P( s_max(G) >= sqrt(m) + sqrt(n) + t ) <= exp(-t^2/2) and P( s_min(G) <= sqrt(m) - sqrt(n) - t ) <= exp(-t^2/2). In words: an m x n Gaussian matrix with m substantially larger than n is a well-conditioned near-isometry, with condition number about (sqrt(m) + sqrt(n)) / (sqrt(m) - sqrt(n)); for square matrices (m = n) the lower bound degenerates to 0 and the smallest singular value is of order n^{-1/2} (a separate theorem). The constants are sharp in the sense that both bounds match the Marchenko-Pastur edges (1 +- sqrt(n/m)) sqrt(m) to first order.
G has independent N(0,1) entries, m >= n

body: In statistics, the Neyman–Pearson lemma describes the existence and uniqueness of the likelihood ratio as a uniformly most powerful test in certain contexts. It was introduced by Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson in a paper in 1933. The Neyman–Pearson lemma is part of the Neyman–Pearson theory of statistical testing, which introduced concepts such as errors of the second kind, power function, and inductive behavior. The previous Fisherian theory of significance testing postulated only one hypothesis. By introducing a competing hypothesis, the Neyman–Pearsonian flavor of statistical testing allows investigating the two types of errors. The trivial cases where one always rejects or fails to reject the null hypothesis are of little interest but it does prove that one must not relinquish control over one type of error while calibrating the other. Neyman and Pearson accordingly proceeded to restrict their attention to the class of all $\alpha$ level tests while subsequently minimizing type II error, traditionally denoted by $\beta$. Their seminal 1933 paper, which includes the Neyman–Pearson lemma showed not only the existence of tests with the most power that retain a prespecified level of type I error ( $\alpha$), but also provided a way to construct such tests. The Karlin-Rubin theorem extended the Neyman–Pearson lemma to settings involving composite hypotheses with monotone likelihood ratios.

body: Cayley's formula: For every positive integer n, the number of labeled trees on the vertex set {1, 2, ..., n} (that is, trees whose vertices are distinguishable) is n^{n-2}. For example the count is 1 for n = 1 and n = 2, 3 for n = 3, and 16 for n = 4. Equivalently, the number of spanning trees of the complete graph K_n is n^{n-2}.
title: Cayley's formula

[Thm 1 of arXiv:2603.27433, 'The $k$-cycle shuffling with repeated cards'] Let $(n_N)_{N\ge 1},(k_N)_{N\ge 1}$, and $(t_N)_{N\ge 1}$ be sequences of positive integers, such that $\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}n_N=\infty$. For all $N\ge 1$, let $t'_N:=t_N-\frac{n_N\log n_N}{k_N}$. Also, let $P_{n_N,k_N}^{*t_N}$ be defined as in \Cref{defi: Pnk and its convolution}, and $\nu_{n_N,k_N}^{t_N}$ be defined as in \Cref{defi: construction of nu}. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item Suppose that 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $k_N\ge 2$ for all $N\ge 1$, and $\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{k_N\log n_N}{n_N}=0$.
\item $t_N'=cn_N/k_N$, where $c\in\R$ is an absolute constant.
\end{enumerate}
Then, we have
$$\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}d_{TV}(P_{n_N,k_N}^{*t_N},\nu_{n_N,k_N}^{t_N})=0.$$ 

\item Suppose that 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $k_N\ge 2$ for all $N\ge 1$, and $\limsup_{N\rightarrow\infty}\log_{n_N}k_N\le c_0$, where $c_0\in[0,1)$ is an absolute constant.
\item $\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\log\log n_N-|2k_Nt_N'/n_N|=+\infty$.
\end{enumerate}
Then, we have
$$\limsup_{N\rightarrow\infty}\log_{n_N}d_{TV}(P_{n_N,k_N}^{*t_N},\nu_{n_N,k_N}^{t_N})\le c_0-1.$$

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For the lower bound, magnetization from all plus has mean N*(1-1/N)^t and variance at most N, whereas stationary magnetization has variance N. Thus at t=(N/2)*(log N-C) the means are separated by order exp(C/2)*sqrt(N). Check: For distinct spins, E[sigma_i*sigma_j]=(1-2/N)^t <=(1-1/N)^(2t), so their covariance is nonpositive and the variance bound follows. Chebyshev separates the two magnetization laws as C grows. This independently recovers the factor log N between random updates and one sweep. Obstruction: The product case shows why the logarithmic allowance is necessary. body: A Markov chain on a countable state space S with transition matrix P is reversible with respect to a probability distribution pi on S if the detailed-balance equations hold: pi(x) P(x,y) = pi(y) P(y,x) for every pair of states x, y in S. Detailed balance is sufficient but not necessary for pi to be a stationary distribution of P: summing the detailed-balance equation over x gives sum_x pi(x) P(x,y) = pi(y) sum_x P(y,x) = pi(y). [standard, e.g. Levin and Peres, Markov Chains and Mixing Times]
title: Reversible Markov Chain (Detailed-Balance Condition)

[Theorema 3 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(k\) be a perfect field of characteristic \(p>0\).
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Let \(X\) be a smooth quasi-\(F\)-split \(k\)-variety, and let \(D\)
be a simple normal crossings divisor on \(X\).  Then \((X,D)\) is
log HT-split (\Cref{qFs-to-HT}).

\item
Let \(X\) be a smooth \(k\)-variety, and let \(D\)
be a simple normal crossings divisor on \(X\).
Let \((X,D)\) be a log HT-split pair, and let
\[
\pi\colon Y \defeq \operatorname{Bl}_Z(X) \to  X
\]
be the blow-up along a stratum \(Z\) of \(D\) and $D_Y \defeq (\pi^{-1}D)_{\red}$. 
Then \((Y,D_Y)\) is log HT-split.  In particular, \(Y\) is HT-split (\Cref{HT-ascent-stratum-blowup}).

\item
Let \(T\) be a toric variety with Cox ring \(S_T\).  
Suppose that a smooth
closed subvariety \(Z\subseteq T\) is defined by a homogeneous regular sequence.
Then \(Z\) is HT-split (\Cref{complete-intersection}).

\item Let $\pi \colon X \to Y$ be a morphism of smooth $k$-varieties.
If $\cO_Y \to R\pi_*\cO_X$ splits and $X$ is HT-split, then $Y$ is HT-split (\Cref{finite-cover}).
In particular, if $\pi$ is a linearly reductive good quotient and $X$ is HT-split, then $Y$ is HT-split.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorema 3 of arXiv:2609.00567

    t_m(X,G) :=\sum_{\substack{f:[n]\rightarrow[N]\\f(1)=m}} \left( \prod_{i\in[n]}
\prod_{\ell=1}^k h_{\ell,f(i)}^{d_{\ell,i}} \right) \left( \prod_{i\le
j\in[n]} a_{f(i)f(j)}^{w_{ij}} \right).
\end{align*}

    A \emph{local vector} 
     is a vector-valued function on weighted
    graphs $G$ that can be expressed as a finite linear combination of

Fix p in (0,1] and a probability law mu on R that is symmetric about zero, has mean zero and variance one, has finite moments of every order, and has no atoms anywhere. Write mu_4 for its fourth moment. For positive layer widths n_0,...,n_d, let W^(i) be n_i by n_(i-1) matrices with iid mu entries, let D^(i) be diagonal n_i by n_i matrices with iid Bernoulli(p) diagonal entries, and assume all these random objects are mutually independent. Put X^(i)=(p n_(i-1))^(-1/2) D^(i) W^(i), M=X^(d)...X^(1). For a deterministic unit vector u in R^n_0 define Z=(n_0/n_d)||Mu||_2^2, S_2=sum_(i=1)^d n_i^(-2), and beta=(3/p-1)sum_(i=1)^d n_i^(-1)+(mu_4-3)||u||_4^4/(p n_1). For beta in a fixed compact interval [b,B] contained in (0,infinity), the Kolmogorov distance between log Z and a normal law of mean -beta/2 and variance beta is O(S_2^(1/5)); for a possible Z=0 interpret log Z=-infinity and compare distribution functions at finite real arguments. The implicit constant may depend on mu,p,b,B, and is uniform over the widths, depth and unit vector. Moreover, for every fixed integer k>=0 with k(k-1)/2 < min_(1<=i<=d)n_i, E[Z^k]=exp(k(k-1)beta/2+O(S_2)), with an error constant depending on k,p and the moments of mu. In particular, if beta tends to beta_* in (0,infinity) and S_2 tends to zero, log Z converges in distribution to N(-beta_*/2,beta_*), and Z converges to the corresponding lognormal law. The distributional assertion is a separate quantitative CLT; it is not deduced from convergence of lognormal moments.
All W entries iid from a symmetric atomless mean-zero unit-variance law with all moments finite
All matrices and Bernoulli gates mutually independent; p fixed in (0,1]
u deterministic with Euclidean norm one; X^(i) normalized by (p n_(i-1))^(-1/2)
CLT bound: beta in a fixed compact subset of (0,infinity)
Moment statement: k fixed nonnegative integer and k(k-1)/2<min_i n_i

body: In mathematics, Itô's lemma or Itô's formula is an identity used in Itô calculus to find the differential of a time-dependent function of a stochastic process. It serves as the stochastic calculus counterpart of the chain rule. It can be heuristically derived by forming the Taylor series expansion of the function up to its second derivatives and retaining terms up to first order in the time increment and second order in the Wiener process increment. The lemma is widely employed in mathematical finance, and its best known application is in the derivation of the Black–Scholes equation for option values.
title: Itô's lemma

body: In mathematics, especially group theory, two elements $a$ and $b$ of a group are conjugate if there is an element $g$ in the group such that $b=gag^{-1}.$ This is an equivalence relation whose equivalence classes are called conjugacy classes. In other words, each conjugacy class is closed under the maps $a\mapsto gag^{-1},$ with $g$ an element of the group.

Let X be a Banach space with dual X*. The duality set of x ∈ X is J(x) = {x* ∈ X* : ⟨x, x*⟩ = ‖x‖² = ‖x*‖²}, which is nonempty by the Hahn-Banach theorem. A linear operator A: D(A) ⊂ X → X is dissipative if for every x ∈ D(A) there exists some j ∈ J(x) with Re⟨Ax, j⟩ ≤ 0. Equivalently (Lumer-Phillips lemma), ‖(λ − A)x‖ ≥ λ‖x‖ for all λ > 0 and all x ∈ D(A). In a Hilbert space (J(x) = {x}) this reads Re⟨Ax, x⟩ ≤ 0 for all x ∈ D(A). A is m-dissipative (maximal dissipative) if it is dissipative and Ran(λ − A) = X for some λ > 0 (then for every λ > 0). A is accretive (m-accretive) if −A is dissipative (m-dissipative). For a dissipative A, λ − A is injective for λ > 0 and its inverse on Ran(λ − A) has norm at most 1/λ.
X is a real or complex Banach space
A is linear on a subspace D(A)

body:
[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Let $(\vertexset,w)$ be a weighted graph, let $x_0,y_0 \in \vertexset$ two distinct vertices, and let
 \[
  w'(x,y) =
  \begin{cases}
   w(x,y) ,& (x,y) \neq (x_0,y_0) ,\\
   \infty ,& (x,y) = (x_0,y_0) .
  \end{cases}
 \]
 (In other words, we consider the weighted graph $(\vertexset',w')$ obtained from $(\vertexset,w)$ by contracting $(x_0,y_0)$ to a single vertex.)
 Let $R$ (resp.\ $R'$) the effective resistance associated with $w$ (resp.\ $w'$).
 Then
 \[ R(x,y) \le R'(x,y)+\frac{1}{w(x_0,y_0)} \quad\text{for each } x,y \in \vertexset . \]
title: Lemma 19 of arXiv:2512.04807

[Lemma 18 (Explicit flat zero-diagonal endpoint) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let
\(
 S_N^0=N^{-1}(\one\one^{\mathsf T}-I)
\)
and \(\sigma_N=1-N^{-1}\).  Let \(m_N^0(z)\) be the scalar Dyson solution
\begin{equation}
 -\frac{1}{m_N^0(z)}=z+\sigma_Nm_N^0(z),
 \qquad m_N^0(z)\sim-z^{-1}.
\end{equation}
Uniformly for \(z,w\in\Gamma\),
\begin{align}
 N\bigl(m_N^0(z)-m(z)\bigr)
 &\longrightarrow-\frac{m(z)^3}{1-m(z)^2},
 \\
 \Tr\!\left[(S_N^0)^2(I-m(z)^2S_N^0)^{-1}\right]
 &\longrightarrow\frac{1}{1-m(z)^2},
 \\
 \Tr\!\left[S_N^0(I-m(z)m(w)S_N^0)^{-2}\right]
 &\longrightarrow
 \frac{1}{(1-m(z)m(w))^2}-1.
 
\end{align}
Consequently, if the summed fourth cumulants converge to \(\kappa\), the
Li--Xu bias together with the finite-flat Dyson correction converges to
\(m_{\varphi,\Gamma}^{\rm base}(\kappa)\) in
\eqref{eq:base-mean-definition}, and the covariance kernel converges to
\(\mathcal K_{\rm Wig}^{(\kappa,0)}\) in
\eqref{eq:Wigner-kernel}.
title: Explicit flat zero-diagonal endpoint

[Problem The rank-constrained Gaussian maximum of arXiv:2607.14087, 'Stochastic Domination of Gaussian Maxima: A Resolution of the Weak Simplex Conjecture'] \label[problem]{prob:rank-constrained}
Fix integers $m\geq3$ and $1\leq d<m-1$, and fix $\lambda>0$.  Determine
\[
  \max\left\{
    \mathbb E\exp\!\left(\lambda\max_{1\leq i\leq m}\xi_i\right):
    \xi\sim\mathcal N(0,G),\ G\text{ a correlation matrix},\ \rank G\leq d
  \right\},
\]
and characterize all maximizing covariance matrices.  In particular, determine
whether the maximizing configuration depends on $\lambda$. (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

  T} | \mathbb{E} [F (\mathcal{Z}_t)] | \lesssim_T \| F \|_{L^2 (\mu)}$ for
  all $T > 0$ and $F \in \mathcal{C}$. We say that $\mathcal{Z}$ is a solution to the
  {\textit{martingale problem associated to $(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{D}_{\max} (\mathcal{L}))$ }} if, for all
  $F \in \mathcal{D}_{\max} (\mathcal{L})$, the process 
  \[ F (\mathcal{Z}_t) - F (\mathcal{Z}_0) - \int_0^t \mathcal{L} F
     (\mathcal{Z}_s) \; \dd s, \qquad t \geqslant 0, \]
  is a martingale w.r.t. the filtration generated by $\mathcal{Z}$.

Let K>=1 be an integer, let a,b,c>0, and let d_2,...,d_(K+1) be real numbers such that for every k=1,...,K, d_(k+1)<=a/k+b(1+log k)+c sum_(ell=2)^k d_ell/(k-ell+2), with the empty sum zero. Then for every such k, d_(k+1)<=[a/k+b(1+log k)] sum_(i=0)^(k-1)[2c(1+log k)]^i. In particular, if 2c(1+log K)<=1/2, the right-hand geometric factor is at most two for every k<=K. Source: Liu--Zhou Lemma E.2. The finite comparison also extends to zero coefficients by a positive perturbation and a limit.
K is a positive integer
a,b,c are positive constants
The displayed scalar recurrence holds for every k=1,...,K; no sign condition on d is needed

Let X_0 have any probability law on R^d with finite second moment. Let X_u=e^{-u}X_0+sqrt(1-e^{-2u})G, where G is an independent N(0,I_d), and denote its density for u>0 by q_u. Fix T>0 and let the exact reverse diffusion satisfy Y_0~q_T and dY_t=(Y_t+2 grad log q_{T-t}(Y_t))dt+sqrt(2)dB_t for 0<=t<T, so Y_t~q_{T-t}. Set S_t=grad log q_{T-t}(Y_t) and H_t=Hess log q_{T-t}(Y_t). Then dS_t=-S_t dt+sqrt(2)H_t dB_t. In particular M_t=e^t S_t is a square-integrable martingale on every closed interval [0,T-delta] with delta>0, and E||M_t-M_s||_2^2=2 integral_s^t e^{2r} E||H_r||_F^2 dr for 0<=s<=t<T. The Gaussian smoothing and the finite-second-moment estimates in Lemma 6 ensure that this integral is finite on each such interval.

For n>=2 and any nonnegative q_v summing to one on each of the n antidiagonals of the n-vertex up/right path triangle, define B_n(t)=sum_v q_v^(1+tanh(t/2)) and J_n=int_0^infinity e^(-t)B_n(t)dt. Then J_n>=(n-1)/log n, and B_n(n^(-alpha))/n tends to one for each fixed alpha>0. Consequently this direct unweighted one-site hypercontractive upper certificate cannot establish an O(n^(1-epsilon)) variance bound for fixed epsilon>0. The result is no lower bound on actual path overlap or variance.

[Lemma 25 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(\sigma,\tau\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\). Assume that
\(\check\sigma,\check\tau\in L^1(\mathbb R)\) and
\[
\int_0^\infty x\left(
|\check\sigma(x)|^2+|\check\sigma(-x)|^2
+|\check\tau(x)|^2+|\check\tau(-x)|^2
\right)\,\mathrm dx<\infty .
\]
Then, for every \(L>0\), \(W_L(\sigma\tau)-W_L(\sigma)W_L(\tau)\) is trace
class on \(L^2(0,L)\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|W_L(\sigma\tau)-W_L(\sigma)W_L(\tau)\|_1
&\le
\left(\int_0^\infty x|\check\sigma(x)|^2\,\mathrm dx\right)^{1/2}
\left(\int_0^\infty x|\check\tau(-x)|^2\,\mathrm dx\right)^{1/2} \\
&\quad+
\left(\int_0^\infty x|\check\sigma(-x)|^2\,\mathrm dx\right)^{1/2}
\left(\int_0^\infty x|\check\tau(x)|^2\,\mathrm dx\right)^{1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2608.30138, 'High-frequency wave propagation for the viscoelastic wave equation with singular memory'] There exists $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that, for every $0\le \varepsilon\le \varepsilon_0$,
the eikonal equation \r{eik2} 
admits a solution $\psi\in C^\infty(B(0,R_T))$, which also depends smoothly on $\varepsilon \in [0,\varepsilon_0]$ and on $\omega$. Consequently, $\psi$ admits a Taylor expansion in $\varepsilon$,
\[
\psi(x,\eps)
\sim \sum_{j\ge0}\varepsilon^j\psi_j(x)
\qquad \text{in } C^\infty(B(0,R_T)),
\]
with
\[
\psi_0(x)=x\cdot\omega,
\qquad
\psi_j(x)=\frac1{j!}\,\partial_\varepsilon^j\psi(x,\eps)\big|_{\varepsilon=0},
\]
and the coefficients satisfy
\begin{equation}
2\,\omega\cdot\nabla \psi_j
=
(-1)^j\sigma_{\mathfrak{m}}^j
-
\sum_{\ell=1}^{j-1}\nabla\psi_\ell\cdot\nabla\psi_{j-\ell},
\qquad j\ge1,
\end{equation}
together with
\[
\psi_j(x)=0
\qquad \text{for } x\in B(0,R_T),\quad x\cdot\omega<-R.
\]

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2609.03946, 'The groups $\SL_2(\F_{13})$ and $\SL_2(\F_{19})$ are Galois over $\Q$'] Let $\ell\in\{13,19\}$. For $\ell=13$, let $f_\ell\in\Z[x]$ be the degree $14$ polynomial displayed in Example~\textup{\ref{ex:f13}}, and for $\ell=19$, let $f_\ell\in\Z[x]$ be the degree $20$ polynomial in
Appendix~\textup{\ref{app:f19}}.  Then $f_\ell$ is irreducible,
all $\ell+1$ of its roots are real, and its splitting field $L_\ell$
satisfies
\[
 \Gal(L_\ell/\Q)\cong\PSL_2(\F_\ell).
\]
This isomorphism carries the action on the roots of $f_\ell$ to the action of
$\PSL_2(\F_\ell)$ on $\PP^1(\F_\ell)$.  Moreover, for every odd rational prime $q$
whose ramification index $e(q)$ in $L_\ell$ is even, the residue degree
$f(q)$ satisfies
\[
 f(q)\ \text{is odd}
 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
 q\equiv1\pmod4 .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Defn ribbon of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Given a foliation $\mathcal{F}$ on $M$, a \textbf{ribbon} is a smoothly embedded strip $R =  [-T, T] \times [0,\varepsilon] \subset M$ transverse to $\mathcal{F}$ such that the arcs $\{\pm T\} \times [0,\varepsilon]$ lie on $\partial M$, $(-T,T)\times [0,\varepsilon]$ lies in $\interior M$, and the induced foliation $\mathcal{F}|_R$ is topologically isotopic rel.~boundary to the standard foliation by lines $[0,T]\times \{y\}$, $y\in [0,\varepsilon]$. We use parameters $T$ and $\varepsilon$ for the width and height to emphasize that ribbons are usually short and long.
title: Defn ribbon of arXiv:2608.30031

body: [Theorem 9 of arXiv:2506.16259, 'Two-dimensional Rademacher walk'] Suppose that $B\subseteq \Z_+\setminus\{0\}$ is good. Then there exists a sequence $a_1,a_2,\dots$   which contains all elements of the set $B$, and each element only finitely many times, such that the $a$-walk $S_n$ is recurrent. [Corollary Point-incoherent frames of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[corollary]{cor:point-incoherent}
Let \(\overline\sigma_{N-1}\) denote normalized surface measure on
\(\mathbb S^{N-1}(1)\), and define
\[
 D_{N,L}=\left\{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1):
 \left\lVertx\right\rVert_\infty\le L\sqrt{\frac{\log N}{N}}\right\},
 \qquad
 \widehat\mathcal O_{N,L}
 =\{(v_1,\ldots,v_n,x)\in\mathbb O(N):x\in D_{N,L}\}.
\]
Let \(\widehat\mathcal Z_{N,L}^J\) be defined by replacing \(\mathcal O_{N,L}\) with
\(\widehat\mathcal O_{N,L}\) in (equation eq:Z-def of the paper).  Every conclusion of
(thm:bulk-universality of the paper) remains valid for
\(\widehat\mathcal Z_{N,L}^J\), with the same quantitative bound.  For Gaussian
disorder, (equation eq:Gaussian-Z-exact of the paper) remains valid with
\(\nu_N(\mathcal O_{N,L})\) replaced by
\(\overline\sigma_{N-1}(D_{N,L})\).  In particular, for \(L>L_0\) the
set \(D_{N,L}\) has spherical measure tending to one, while for every
fixed \(L>0\) the Gaussian variational pressure limit is unchanged.

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, paired). The per-output long-only stack on the relative-metric error covariance was shrunk toward the pooled simplex weights, $w_d \mapsto w_g + (1 - s)(w_d - w_g)$. The ceiling of the family - the amount chosen by five-fold cross-validation on the calibration rows - adds $+0.59$ percent on EMIT and $+0.20$ on OCO-2 at full calibration (28 of 40 and 26 of 30 cells). A positive-part James-Stein amount $s = \min(1, \sum_d \operatorname{tr} V_d / \sum_d \|w_d - w_g\|^2)$ with $V_d$ the naive $n$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap covariance of the long-only weights over 20 resamples recovers $+0.10$ / $+0.15$ (worst cells $-2.6$ / $-0.0$) with amounts $0.18$ against the cross-validated $0.14$ on EMIT: it overshoots, because the long-only weights have coordinates at the boundary and the naive bootstrap is inconsistent there (Andrews 2000; resampled fits flip members between zero and positive weight). The $m$-out-of-$n$ subsampling repair ($m = n/2$, variance scaled by $m/n$; Politis-Romano) gives amounts $0.11$ / $0.12$ against $0.14$ / $0.57$ and gains $+0.43$ / $+0.09$ (worst $-1.3$ / $-0.0$). Reading: the residual pooling amount is not recoverable from resampling to the accuracy the ceiling requires and remains the one cross-validated quantity in the neighbourhood of the long-only estimator, which alone sits within that ceiling

B = 20 bootstrap resamples per fit; the CV amount from 5 folds of the calibration rows in the relative metric

Proof (unaudited), elementary route obstruction; no novelty claimed. Let K>=2 be even, N=Kn, and let a ReLU tree committee have independent standard Gaussian input blocks, spherical hidden weights of norm sqrt(n), fixed balanced readout signs and zero threshold. Labels are fixed independently of inputs. Restrict to classifiers in which every unit is inactive on every opposite-label pattern, but allow assignments to depend arbitrarily on all inputs and allow same-sign overlaps. Conditional on positive and negative label counts M_+,M_-, strict storage probability is at most q(M_-,n)^(K/2) q(M_+,n)^(K/2), where q(0,n)=1 and q(m,n)=2^(1-m) sum_{r=0}^{min(n-1,m-1)} binom(m-1,r) for m>=1. Uniformly in labels this is at most q(ceil(P/2),n)^(K/2), so for fixed K storage probability tends to zero when n tends to infinity and P/N tends to a>4/K. With balanced labels and P=4n the conditional bound is 2^-K. Thus positive sequential wide-limit load requires allowing wrong-sign active votes in this model; this is not an upper bound on unrestricted ReLU capacity.
Even fixed K>=2, N=Kn, n>=1, P>=1; independent Gaussian blocks and patterns
Hidden weights have norm sqrt(n), both readout signs occur K/2 times, threshold zero, ReLU hidden activation
Labels fixed or random independently of inputs; no balance or inter-label independence required for asymptotic exclusion
Every unit is inactive whenever its readout sign differs from the pattern label; arbitrary input-dependent assignments and same-sign overlaps are allowed

body: In mathematics, Parseval's theorem usually refers to the result that the Fourier transform is unitary; loosely, that the sum of the square of a function is equal to the sum of the square of its transform. It originates from a 1799 theorem about series by Marc-Antoine Parseval, which was later applied to the Fourier series. It is also known as Rayleigh's energy theorem, or Rayleigh's identity, after John William Strutt, Lord Rayleigh.
title: Parseval's theorem

body: Publication record. Problem 19.30 of S. Janson's survey (Probab. Surveys 9, 2012; 18.30 in arXiv v1) asks whether two consequences of his Theorem 19.7 remain true when the offspring variance is infinite: (ii) if n P(xi >= h(n)) -> 0 then Y_(1) < h(n) with high probability; (iii) if n P(xi >= h(n)) -> infinity then Y_(j) >= h(n) with high probability for every fixed j. Y. Shmalo, The second largest outdegree of conditioned Galton-Watson trees with infinite variance (October 2026) shows that (iii) can fail at lambda = nu with sigma^2 = infinity: along a sequence n_r one vertex has outdegree (r + 1/2) L_r and every other vertex has outdegree at most L_r/(64 (log n_r)^2), although n_r P(xi >= L_r) >= r. Part (ii) was answered negatively by Kortchemski and Richier (Ann. Appl. Probab. 29, 2019, Theorem 3); (iii) for j = 1 remains open. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/second-largest-degree-infinite-variance (commit ba626a83fe32). Not refereed; an outside audit is owed.
title: Janson Problem 19.30 (arXiv 18.30) answered in part: the second largest outdegree of conditioned Galton-Watson trees with infinite variance (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/second-largest-degree-infinite-variance)

[Lemma Strict finite-support profile of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[lemma]{lem:strict-profile}
Let \(K\) be a compact neighborhood in \(\mathbb S^{N-1}(1)\), let \(x_0\) lie in its relative interior, and suppose a continuous function \(P\) satisfies
\[
 P(x_0)=\max_KP,
 \qquad
 \Delta:=P(x_0)-\max_{\partial K}P>0.
\]
If \(\left\lVertr\right\rVert_\infty\le M\) and \(b\Delta>2M\), then \(bP+r\) has a local maximum in the interior of \(K\), with value in
\[
 [bP(x_0)-M,bP(x_0)+M].
\]
If \(P,r\) are \(C^1\), this point is a spherical critical point.

[Proposition 13 (Control of the adaptive log-survival term) of arXiv:2605.04048, 'Catastrophe--dispersion models in random and varying environments across generations'] In Example~\ref{ex:RE-adaptive}, assume that $\psi_0$ has a continuous distribution on $(0,1)$ and
that $\mathbb E[|\log \psi_0|]<+\infty$. Let $\pi_p$ denote the invariant
distribution of the Markov chain $(p_n)$ defined by
\[
p_{n+1}=\min\{1,\;a p_n+(1-a)\psi_{n+1}\},\qquad a\in(0,1).
\]
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textnormal{(i)}]
$\log p_0\in L^1(\pi_p)$ and
\[
-\infty < \mathbb E_{\pi_p}[\log p_0] < 0.
\]
\item[\textnormal{(ii)}]
The map $a\mapsto \mathbb E_{\pi_p}[\log p_0]$ is continuous and nondecreasing on
$(0,1)$.
\item[\textnormal{(iii)}]
The following bounds hold:
\[
\mathbb E[\log \psi_0]
\;\le\;
\mathbb E_{\pi_p}[\log p_0]
\;\le\;
\log\!\bigl(a+(1-a)\mathbb E[\psi_0]\bigr).
\]
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition 31 (Total mass) of arXiv:2607.24561, 'Range convergence and sharp one-arm asymptotics\\for the critical percolation cluster in h'] The law of $\mu(\R^d)$ under $\bN$ is atomless, has infinite mean on
$\{\mu(\R^d)>\eps\}$ for every $\eps>0$, and $\bN$ is an infinite but
$\sigma$-finite measure. The explicit Laplace transform

($\theta>0$) holds, giving the tail
$\bN\bigl(\mu(\R^d)>\eps\bigr)=\sqrt{2/(\pi\gamma)}\,\eps^{-1/2}$; this
explicit form is used for the cluster-tail consistency check
(Remark~\ref{rem:tailknown}) and for the finiteness of the restricted masses
$\bN(\mu(\R^d)>\eps)$; the rest of the paper requires only atomlessness.

Fix integers d>=2 and L>=1. Let (U_z)_{z in Z^d} be independent uniform(0,1) labels. Almost surely every finite set has a unique minimum. Put W_x=x+[-L,L]^d (integer vertices), and a(x)=argmin_{z in W_x} U_z. Declare x good if a(y)=a(x) for every nearest neighbor y of x. Let X_x be its indicator.

The field X is stationary, ergodic, and r-dependent with r=2L+2 in the sup norm: X_x is determined by labels in the union of W_y over y=x and its neighbors, which lies in x+[-L-1,L+1]^d. For two sets at sup-norm distance greater than 2L+2, their determining label sets are disjoint; independence applies to the corresponding sigma-fields, not merely individual pairs. Ergodicity follows because X is a measurable translation-equivariant factor of the ergodic iid label field.

Every nearest-neighbor component of good vertices is finite. If x and y are adjacent good vertices, their anchors coincide. Hence all vertices of any connected good component share an anchor a. Each such vertex x satisfies a in W_x, so the component lies in a+[-L,L]^d and has at most (2L+1)^d vertices.

Its exact good density is

    q(d,L) = (2L-1)^d / [(2L+1)^(d-1) (2L+1+2d)].

Proof of the formula: write I=intersection_{y=x or y~x} W_y and J=union_{y=x or y~x} W_y. All anchors agree iff the unique minimum on J belongs to I. Necessity holds because a shared minimum belongs to every W_y and minimizes the union; sufficiency is immediate. Now |I|=(2L-1)^d. The union is W_x and 2d disjoint outer faces of size (2L+1)^(d-1), giving the denominator. The minimum is uniformly located on J by exchangeability of continuous iid labels.

Consequently q(d,L)->1 as L->infinity while every good component is finite. This refutes the inference that marginal good probabilities tending to one plus finite dependence at each scale suffice for percolation when the dependence range is allowed to grow. [Proposition prop:lattice_potts of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $\Lambda_k$ be a collection of $k$-cells, $\Omega = \{0,1\}^{\Lambda_k}$, $\Sigma =\ker(\partial_k)$,  $x_{\mathbf{c}}\in (0,1)$ for all $\mathbf{c}\in \Lambda_k$,  $f:\Omega\to 2^{\Sigma}$ be defined by $f(\omega)= \Sigma^{\downarrow}(\omega):=\{\eta \in \Sigma\mid \operatorname{supp}(\eta) \subset \omega\}$  and
	\[\rho[\omega] \propto \prod_{\mathbf{c}\in \Lambda_k (\omega)} \frac{x_{\mathbf{c}}}{1-x_{\mathbf{c}}}, ~\forall \omega\in \Omega, ~\gamma[\eta]\propto 1, ~\forall \eta\in \Sigma. \]
    	Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
    \item[(a)] The marginal  $\mathscr{P}_\Sigma = \ell^q_{\Lambda_k,x}$.
          For $\omega\in\Omega,$ the  conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega]$  is uniform on $\Sigma^{\downarrow}(\omega)$, i.e. a uniform divergence free $q$-coloring of $\omega$.
		\item[(b)] The marginal $\mathscr{P}_\Omega= \phi^q_{\Lambda_k,p}$, with $x_{\mathbf{c}}=\frac{p_{\mathbf{c}}}{p_{\mathbf{c}}+q(1-p_{\mathbf{c}})}$.
        For each $\eta\in\Sigma$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \eta] = \mathbb{P}_x \cup \delta_{\operatorname{supp}(\eta)}$,  Bernoulli percolation on $\Lambda_k$ with parameter $(x_{\mathbf{c}})_{\mathbf{c}\in \Lambda_k}$ conditioned on all $k$-cells in $\operatorname{supp}(\eta)$ being open. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
