[Theorem thm:kac-moment of arXiv:2608.08375, 'Algebraic formulas for first-passage times of Markov processes in the linear framework: ge'] Let $G$ be a strongly connected graph and choose $u \in \mathcal{V}(G)$. The $r$-th moment of the recurrence time to $u$ is given by,
\[
    \tau^{(r)}_u(G) = \frac{r!}{\left( \lambda_u(G) \, x_u^*(G) \right)^r} \sum_{(i_1, \dotsc, i_r) \in \mathcal{V}(G)^r}{\left( \prod_{j=0}^{r-1}{\psi_{i_{j+1}|i_j,u} \, x_{i_{j+1}}^*(G)} \right)} \,,
\]
where the exchange factor takes the form,
\begin{align*}
    & \psi_{i_{j+1}|i_j,u} = 1 \,\, + \\
    & \sum_{\substack{m \in \mathcal{V}(G) \setminus \{i_{j+1}\} \\ m \to_G u}}\left( \frac{w(\Phi_{\{u,i_{j+1}\} \to \{m,i_{j+1}\}}(G)) - w(\Phi_{\{i_j,i_{j+1}\} \to \{m,i_{j+1}\}}(G))}{w(\Phi_{\{i_{j+1}\}}(G))} \right) \ell(m \to_G u) \,.
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Generalised Kac lemma

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; tested by direct Monte Carlo simulation of the Poisson-weighted infinite tree (4000 replicates, k=2,5,10,12), agreeing with the recursion within about 1.5 standard errors] This is the campaign's branching-walk identification behind Conjecture 1 of H. Stepanyants, P. L. Krapivsky, H. Hartle and D. Krioukov, The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees, arXiv:2608.04303. Let the Poisson-weighted infinite tree have root position zero, with children of each vertex at the points of an independent rate-one Poisson process on (0,infinity), translated by their parent's position. Let M_k be the minimum position of generation k, and set M_0=0. Define s_0(y)=1 for y>=0 and s_k(y)=1-exp(-integral_0^y s_{k-1}(z)dz) for k>=1. Put bar_ell_k=integral_0^infinity s_k(y)exp(-y)dy and ell_k=bar_ell_k-bar_ell_{k+1}. In the source, ell_k is the limiting fraction of vertices in layer k of a random recursive tree, formed by joining each new vertex j uniformly to one of vertices 1,...,j-1. Layer zero consists of the initial leaves, and subsequent layers are obtained by successive leaf removals. For every k>=0 and y>=0, s_k(y)=P(M_k<=y). Consequently bar_ell_k=E[exp(-M_k)] and ell_k=E[exp(-M_k)-exp(-M_{k+1})]. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
Independent rate-one Poisson offspring displacement processes.
The layer-tail recursion is the one stated in the source paper.

Direct stationary hitting calculations give J/tau2=b*(a+b)/(a^2+b^2)=(1+r)/(1+r^2), r=a/b. This ratio ranges up to(1+sqrt2)/2, attained at r=sqrt2-1. Thus the converse cannot hold with constant1 even for two states, although a universal larger constant is consistent with this control. Check: E_pi T0=a/[b(a+b)] and E_pi T1=b/[a(a+b)]. Substituting the two maxima into the harmonic mean gives the formula; differentiating(1+r)/(1+r^2) gives its exact maximum. Meeting occurs at the first jump of either distinct coordinate, total rate a+b. Obstruction: The two-state calculation does not bound J/max E M on arbitrary chains. Rare spatial bottlenecks can affect stationary hitting times and two-particle meeting differently.

For real a,b and C=[[a,-b],[b,a]], the real block J=I_r tensor C+delta N_r tensor I_2 obeys the same bound ||exp(tJ)||_2<=exp((a+delta)t). For delta>0, a diagonal change of basis with successive power weights changes a Jordan superdiagonal of 1 to delta; use repeated power weights for the real form of a conjugate pair. Consequently, let A be a real finite matrix with algebraically simple real eigenvalue lambda_1>max{Re(lambda_j):j>=2}. For any rho with max_{j>=2}Re(lambda_j)<rho<lambda_1, a real basis S can be chosen with S^-1 A S=diag(lambda_1,B) so that ||exp(t S^-1 A S)-exp(lambda_1 t)e_1 e_1^T||_2<=exp(rho t) for every t>=0. These constant-one bounds concern the chosen coordinates: in the original Euclidean norm the corresponding estimate carries ||S||_2||S^-1||_2.
Finite-dimensional real matrices and Euclidean operator norm
t>=0 and delta>=0 for block bounds; delta>0 for the similarity
For the final assertion the leading eigenvalue is real and algebraically simple and strictly dominates all other real parts

\[
R\bigl(\log S(X)\bigr)=\infty
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
R\bigl(\log S(Y*X*\overleftarrow{Y})\bigr)=\infty.
\]
More precisely, if $l=\log S(X)$ and $a=S(Y)$, then

\log S(Y*X*\overleftarrow{Y})=a l a^{-1}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:intro-two of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $\boldsymbol\kappa=(\kappa_1,\kappa_2)$ satisfy
$\kappa_1>0>\kappa_2$, and let
$(\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})\in\Lambda_2(D)$
be a strict local minimum point of the corresponding Kirchhoff--Routh function
$W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}$ defined in (equation eq:intro-KR of the paper).  Fix
$M_i,R_i>0$ for $i=1,2$.  For each $\varepsilon>0$, let
$\mathbf a_{1,\varepsilon},\mathbf a_{2,\varepsilon}\in D$, and let
$\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}\in L^\infty(D)$ be nonnegative and satisfy
\[
  \int_D\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}\,\mathrm d\mathbf x=|\kappa_i|,
  \qquad
  \|\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}\|_\infty\leq M_i\varepsilon^{-2},
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}
  \subset B_{R_i\varepsilon}(\mathbf a_{i,\varepsilon}),
  \qquad i=1,2.
 \]
Suppose that
\[
  (\mathbf a_{1,\varepsilon},\mathbf a_{2,\varepsilon})
  \longrightarrow
  (\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2}),
  \qquad
  \mathcal A(\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0})\longrightarrow0
  \quad(i=1,2)
\]
as $\varepsilon\to0$.  Set
$\omega_{\varepsilon,0}
:=\zeta_{1,\varepsilon,0}-\zeta_{2,\varepsilon,0}$.
Let $\omega_{\varepsilon,t}$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the corresponding
Yudovich solution of (equation eq:euler-intro of the paper), and, for $i=1,2$, let
$\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,t}$ denote the transport of
$\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}$ by the associated Euler flow map
(so that
$\omega_{\varepsilon,t}
=\zeta_{1,\varepsilon,t}-\zeta_{2,\varepsilon,t}$
for every $t\in\mathbb R$; see (rk:decomvor of the paper)).
Then, as $\varepsilon\to0$,
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\mathcal A(\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,t})
  \longrightarrow0
  \qquad(i=1,2),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\ \sup_{(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)\in
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{1,\varepsilon,t})\times
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{2,\varepsilon,t})}
  |(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)
  -(\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})|
  \longrightarrow0.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Global persistence: two opposite-sign vortices

[Defn 1 of arXiv:2607.21759, 'Marchenko--Pastur law for tensor powers of exchangeable unconditional vectors'] Let $\binom{[n]}{d}$ be the collection of subsets of $[n]$ with size $d$, and let $[n]^{d}=\{1,\dotsc,n\}^d$. These index sets have sizes $\binom{n}{d}$ and $n^d$, respectively. Further, let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $\R^n$ and let $\mathbf X = (X_1,\dotsc, X_n) \sim \nu$. We define the following random tensor models.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*.]
    \item Set $p = \binom{n}{d}$ and index the coordinates of  $\R^p$ by $\binom{[n]}{d}$. We define a random vector $\mathbf x \in \R^p$ by
    \[
         \mathbf x = \biggl(\prod_{\alpha \in i} X_\alpha\biggr)_{i \in \binom{[n]}{d}}.
    \] In this case, we say $\mathbf x$ is a \df{principal tensor generated from the base distribution $\nu$}, and denote its law by $\PrincipalT(n,d,\nu)$.
   \item Set $q = n^d$, and index the coordinates of $\R^q$ by $[n]^d$. We define another random vector $\mathbf x \in \R^q$ by \[
       \mathbf x = \biggl(\prod_{j=1}^d X_{i_j}\biggr)_{i \in [n]^d},
    \]
    where $i=(i_1,\dots,i_d)\in[n]^d.$ In this case, we say $\mathbf x$ is a (full) \df{tensor power generated from the base distribution $\nu$}, and denote its law by  $\PowerT(n,d,\nu)$.
        \end{enumerate}
    With a slight abuse of notation, we will usually write $\mathbf X$ in place of $\nu$, or omit them completely when the context is clear. When we are discussing both models simultaneously, we will just call them the tensor power models.
title: Definition 1 of arXiv:2607.21759

[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2605.21155, 'Asymptotic Probabilities of Attaining the Maximum in Heterogeneous Gaussian Samples'] For $\sigma>1$,  the sequence
  $\mathbb P (M^{(1)}_{n_1}>M^{(2)}_{n_2} )$
converges to a limit in $(0,1)$ if and only if \eqref{eq:N1N2} holds for some $C\in(0,\infty)$.  Moreover, in this case,
\begin{equation}
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P\!\left(M^{(1)}_{n_1}>M^{(2)}_{n_2}\right)
=
\mathbb P\!\left(\Lambda_1>\sigma^2(\Lambda_2-\kappa(C,\sigma))\right)
=
\int_0^\infty \exp\left(-y - e^{-\kappa(C,\sigma)} y^{1/\sigma^2}\right) \mathrm dy,
\end{equation}
where $\Lambda_1$ and $\Lambda_2$ are independent Gumbel random variables, and
\begin{align}
 
 \kappa(C,\sigma)
=
\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\log\frac{C}{\sigma}
+\frac12\left(1-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\right)\log(4\pi).
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3 of arXiv:2605.21155

[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2608.27433, 'Scalar curvature on K\"ahler blow-ups and systolic inequalities'] Let \(X^{m+r}\) be a compact K\"ahler manifold admitting an almost holomorphic fibration \(f:X^{m+r}\dashrightarrow Z^m\) onto a normal compact K\"ahler space \(Z\) which is not uniruled. Assume
that a general fibre of \(f\) is biholomorphic to \(\PP^r\). If \(\omega\) is a K\"ahler metric on \(X\) with positive scalar curvature, then, for every \(1\le q\le r\),
\begin{equation}
        \min_X S(\omega)\cdot\sys_{2q}(\omega)^{1/q}
        \le 2\pi r(r+1).
\end{equation}
Moreover, for a fixed \(q\), equality holds if and only if the universal cover
\[
        (\widetilde X,\widetilde\omega)
        \cong
        (\PP^r,a\omega_{FS})\times(Y,\omega_{\mathrm{FS}}),
\]
where \(a=[\omega]\cdot[L]\) for a line \(L\) in a general fibre,
\(\omega_{\mathrm{RF}}\) is Ricci-flat, and \(\sys_{2q}(\omega)\) is realized by a
fibrewise linear \(\PP^q\subset\PP^r\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3 of arXiv:2608.27433

Let X be a real random variable and let M(t) = E[e^{tX}] be its moment generating function. For every real a and every t > 0 with M(t) < infinity, P(X >= a) <= e^{-ta} M(t); hence P(X >= a) <= inf_{t > 0} e^{-ta} M(t). Likewise for every t < 0 with M(t) < infinity, P(X <= a) <= e^{-ta} M(t). For a sum X = X_1 + ... + X_n of independent variables, M(t) = prod E[e^{tX_i}], which gives the usual exponential tail bounds; for instance, if the X_i are independent Bernoulli with mu = E[X], then P(X >= (1+delta) mu) <= (e^{delta} / (1+delta)^{1+delta})^{mu} for every delta > 0.
M(t) finite at the value of t used
independence is needed only for the product form of M

Let U ⊂ R^n be open, let F = F(p,z,x) be C^1 on R^n × R × U, and let u ∈ C^2(U) satisfy F(Du(x), u(x), x) = 0 for all x ∈ U. Let x(·): I → U solve the ODE x'(s) = D_pF( p(s), z(s), x(s) ), where p(s) := Du(x(s)) and z(s) := u(x(s)). Then on I: z'(s) = D_pF(p(s),z(s),x(s))·p(s) and p'(s) = -D_xF(p(s),z(s),x(s)) - D_zF(p(s),z(s),x(s)) p(s). Thus (x(·),z(·),p(·)) solves the characteristic system x' = D_pF, z' = p·D_pF, p' = -D_xF - p D_zF, and F(p(s),z(s),x(s)) ≡ 0 along it. The curve x(·) is called a projected characteristic.
F of class C^1 in all its arguments
u of class C^2 (second derivatives exist and are symmetric); C^1 is not enough for this computation
x(·) solves the projected characteristic ODE and stays in U on the interval considered

[Lem 77 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\gamma:[q_0,1]\to[q_0,1]$ be a monotone and absolutely continuous function, and define its generalized inverse
	\[
	\lambda:[q_0,\gamma(1)]\to[q_0,1]\,,\quad
	\lambda(s)
	\equiv\inf\Big\{
	t : \gamma(t)>s
	\Big\}\,.
	\]
Then the set $\{s : \gamma'(\lambda(s))=0 \}$ has zero Lebesgue measure.

\begin{proof}
It is straightforward to verify that $\lambda$ is a right-continuous function with $\gamma(\lambda(s))=s$ for all $s$. For any measurable set $A\subseteq\R$, consider the preimage $\lambda^{-1}(A)$: we have $s\in \lambda^{-1}(A)$ if and only if $\lambda(s)\in A$, which implies $s=\gamma(\lambda(s)) \in \gamma(A)$. This proves that 
	\[\lambda^{-1}(A)
	\subseteq \gamma(A)\]
(the converse need not hold). Let $A=\{t\in[q_0,1] : \gamma'(t)=0\}$: by absolute continuity of $\gamma$, we have
	\[|\gamma(A)|
	= \int_{q_0}^1 \gamma'(t)
	\ind\{t\in A\}
	\,dt = 0\,.\]
Since $\lambda^{-1}(A)\subseteq \gamma(A)$, it follows that
	\[
	|\lambda^{-1}(A)|
	=\bigg| \Big\{s : \gamma'(\lambda(s))=0
	\Big\}\bigg|=0\,,
	\]
as claimed.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 77 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Thm mr2 of arXiv:2411.06571, 'Moment-based approach for two erratic KPZ scaling limits'] Fix some $p\in\Bbb N$. Consider the SPDE 
    \begin{equation}\tag{dSHE}\partial_t z^\epsilon(t,y) = \tfrac12 \partial_y^2 z^\epsilon(t,y) + \epsilon^{p-\frac14} z^\epsilon(t,y) \partial_y^p\eta^\epsilon(t,y),\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; t\ge 0, y\in \Bbb R,
    \end{equation}where $\eta^\epsilon:= \varphi_\epsilon *\eta$ for a standard Gaussian space-time white noise $\eta$ on $\Bbb R_+\times\Bbb R$ and where the convolution is in space only, and where $  \varphi_\epsilon (y):= \epsilon^{-1} \varphi(\epsilon^{-1}y)$ for some fixed smooth even mollifier $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\Bbb R)$.

    Let $Z^\epsilon_{s,t}(x,y)$ denote the associated family of propagators given by the It\^o-Walsh solution $z^\epsilon$ to the equation (equation dshe of the paper). Then $Z^\epsilon$ converges in law as $\epsilon\to 0$ to the family of propagators given by the It\^o-Walsh solution of the SPDE $$\partial_t \mathcal U(t,y) = \tfrac12 \partial_y^2 \mathcal U(t,y) +  \sigma_p \mathcal U(t,y) \xi(t,y), \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\sigma_p^2 := \int_{\Bbb R} (\varphi * \varphi^{(2p-1)}(x))^2 dx$$ where $\varphi^{(k)}$ is the $k^{th}$ derivative and $\xi$ is another space-time white noise. Convergence is in the sense of finite-dimensional laws $(Z^\epsilon_{s_1,t_1},...,Z^\epsilon_{s_m,t_m}),$ where each coordinate has the topology of $\mathcal M(\Bbb R^2)$, for any finite collection of indices $s_j\le t_j$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Scaling limit of the SHE with derivative noise

[Thm -2 of arXiv:2411.13403, 'Path weighting method for spot sensitivities and its variance reduction'] Let $S_{t}$ and $\tilde{S}_{t}$ be the processes
defined by 
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}S_{t_{i+1}} & =H_{i+1}(S_{t_{i}},\sqrt{\Delta t_{i+1}}Z_{i+1}),\;i\ge1,\\
S_{t_{1}} & =H_{1}(s,\sqrt{\Delta t_{1}}Z_{1}),\\
S_{t_{0}} & =s,
\end{aligned}

\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}\tilde{S}_{t_{i+1}} & =H_{i+1}(\tilde{S}_{t_{i}},\sqrt{\Delta t_{i+1}}Z_{i+1}),\;i\ge1,\\
\tilde{S}_{t_{1}} & =H_{1}(s,\sqrt{\Delta t_{1}}(Z_{1}+\epsilon Y)),\\
\tilde{S}_{t_{0}} & =s,
\end{aligned}

\end{equation}
where $Y$ is an $\mathbb{R}^{n}$-valued random variable such that
$Y$ is independent of $Z_{2},\dots,Z_{N}$, and
\[
\mathbb{E}(Y)=0,
\]
and
\[
\mathbb{E}(e^{\lambda|Y|})<\infty
\]
for any $\lambda>0$. Let $F(S)=F(S_{t_{2}},\dots,S_{t_{N}})$ be
a payoff function which does not contain $t_{1}$ as an event date.

\]

 2. \quad  for all

Writing delta=|E[Y]-M| and x_+=max(x,0), for every t>=0 one has P(|Y-E[Y]|>=t)<=min(1,2 c exp(-a (t-delta)_+^2)). For t>delta the deviation event implies |Y-M|>=t-delta; for t<=delta use probability at most 1. The assumption at t=0 implies c>=1/2.

[Lemma of arXiv:2510.18792, 'The frog model with death revisited'] \thlabel{lem:biased-walk-bounds}
Let $(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a nearest-neighbor random walk on $\mathbb Z$ with $X_0=n> 0$ that moves left with probability $0<p<1/2$ and right with probability $1-p$ at each step. Let $\rho = p/(1-p)$. We let $\Geo(r)$ denote the geometric distribution supported on the nonnnegative integers. 
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item
For $\tau_{n-1}=\inf\{t\ge1: X_t=n-1\}$, it holds that
$$\frac{\tau_n-1}{2} \preceq \Geo\left(r\right) \quad 
\text{ with } \quad r = \exp\left(-\frac{3(1 - 2p)^2}{2(1 + 4p)} \right).$$

\item Let $T_n = \max \{t \colon X_t =n\}$ be the time of the last visit to $n$. It holds that 
    $$\frac{T_n}{2}\ \preceq \Geo(s) \quad \text{ with } \quad s=(1-2p)r.$$
\item
Suppose the walk is conditioned to never go left of $n$ i.e.\ conditioned on the event $A=\{X_t \geq n \text{ for all $t \geq 0$}\}$. 
Let $T_n'$ denote the time of its last return to $n$. Then $T_n' \preceq T_n$. 

\end{enumerate}
It follows that the length of each excursion between steps taken by the recursive frog model on $\mathbb T_d$ is stochastically dominated by the $2\Geo((1-p)(1-\rho)r) +1$ distribution. Moreover, these excursion lengths are independent between non-backtracking steps by the strong Markov property of random walk.

Let P=product_{j=1}^k P_j on Euclidean coordinate blocks, and supply the fixed separable OU score field g_t(x)=(g_{j,t}(x_j))_j. All blocks have the same specified OU output endpoint u. If block algorithm j exists using at most L_j adaptive rounds and q_j queries per round, and has output TV error <=delta_j at endpoint u, then independent copies compose into a product-oracle sampler using at most max_j L_j rounds and sum_j q_j queries per round, with TV error <=sum_j delta_j. Query times may differ within a batch. If the block fields have uniform squared L2 score errors <=e_j^2, the product error is <=sum_j e_j^2; block algorithms must exist at these tighter tolerances. This does not give an upper bound from a known block lower bound, does not cover arbitrary nonseparable approximate product-target oracles, and does not exclude precision-driven amplification. It prevents adding independent blocks' round lower bounds without a separate sequential-dependence argument.

Common OU endpoint and arbitrary query times permitted within a batch
Independent private sampling randomness across block algorithms

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:a5101e5de8f756b93c904e96db4d1847bfea252d737b0388db99c8f27afcad06","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/a5/a5101e5de8f756b93c904e96db4d1847bfea252d737b0388db99c8f27afcad06.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:bff1003339ad9f1f8b4babfc21550fec444a8764df17bfd1ea9ec544151ebed9","bundle_entry_key":"product-score-round-composition","bundle_id":"population.t306-product-ou-round-composition-obstruction-008","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"diffusion sampling, oracle complexity and adaptive parallel rounds","draft":"w720/bundle_008.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.diffusion:product-ou-score-oracles-parallel-round-composition-w720-c14","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C14: independent products do not force additive adaptive rounds

Kind: route-failure. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited).
Elementary conditional simulation; no novelty or frontier exponent claimed.

## Exact statement

For j=1,...,k let P_j be laws on R^{m_j}, and let g_{j,t}(x_j)
be fixed jointly measurable block score fields. Supply the product field
g_t(x)=(g_{1,t}(x_1),...,g_{k,t}(x_k)) for P=product_j P_j.
All blocks share the OU time parameter and the prescribed endpoint u.

Suppose algorithm A_j uses at most L_j adaptive rounds and q_j queries
per round at any requested points and times, and its output law is within
TV delta_j of OU_u(P_j). With independent private randomness across
blocks, one product-oracle algorithm uses at most max_j L_j rounds and
sum_j q_j queries per round, and its output law is within TV sum_j delta_j
of product_j OU_u(P_j)=OU_u(P).

If each block field has uniform OU squared L2 error <=e_j^2,
then the product field has uniform squared error <=sum_j e_j^2.
These assertions require the supplied separable product field, not just
the fact that the target law is a product. A general approximate oracle
for a product target need not be separable and is not covered.

## Proof

Gaussian OU smoothing acts independently on the coordinate blocks.
At positive times the density is a product of positive smooth densities,
so the gradient of its log is the concatenation of their scores.
Integrating the squared Euclidean norm of the blockwise error gives
exactly the sum of the block integrals. The same holds at zero if the
scores exist and the stated error promises there are assumed.

Run every A_j with its own randomness. In round r, every unfinished
algorithm proposes its batch using only that block's earlier responses.
For each proposed query (x_j,t), query the full field at the point whose
j-th block is x_j and whose other blocks are zero, at time t, and extract
only response block j. By separability this is exactly g_{j,t}(x_j),
independently of the other coordinates. All the proposed queries form
one batch, even if their times differ. Their count is <=sum_j q_j.
After receiving this batch, each A_j advances one round. Finished blocks
are padded by doing nothing, so max_j L_j rounds suffice. Adaptivity is
preserved: no algorithm used another block's response, and all within-
round queries were chosen before that round's answers.

For fixed hidden block instances, the outputs are independent because
the oracles are fixed and the block algorithms use independent random
seeds and disjoint extracted responses. Thus the output law is the
product of the block output laws. Replacing one marginal at a time
and using TV contraction under adjoining a common independent marginal
gives TV(product outputs, product targets)<=sum_j delta_j.
No multiplication of conditional success probabilities is used.

If block guarantees instead hold only on events in a distribution of
hidden instances, use the union bound for their failure events. Neither
independence of those events nor universal instance success follows
from individual high-probability guarantees.

## Consequence for the attempted Target 2 route

For k equal m-dimensional blocks, D=km. At prescribed total OU score
tolerance e and TV delta, it suffices to invoke the block algorithms at
score tolerance e/sqrt(k) and TV tolerance delta/k. The conditional upper
bound is max block round cost at THESE stricter parameters, not k times
that cost. Per-round query cost sums; this remains polynomial in D if
k and the block query budgets are polynomial. With covariance spectra
in a common interval [c,C], the product condition number stays <=C/c;
the second moments sum. Thus conditioning alone does not impose serial
dependence between blocks.

This does NOT establish an upper bound for the Xun-Price hard family:
its known square-root lower bound is not an algorithmic upper bound.
It does NOT exclude amplification through precision dependence, coupled
nonseparable oracles, hidden inter-block dependence, or restricted batch
size. It refutes the attempted inference that independent blocks must
be completed sequentially in the polynomial-batch round model. Merely
summing their individual round lower bounds is unjustified.

NEXT: A useful composition must introduce genuine sequential information
dependence while retaining covariance conditioning, uniform absolute OU
accuracy and the same smoothed endpoint; independent repetition supplies
none of that dependence by itself.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:e6366dc993ba4de7287e5b175666c415d73e5a111555f618da2faad053b34ab2","revision_digest":"sha256:06d33e5dd8ba88f6ce2b2e5511a9d03843a1c347be9360ae99765ee58e4236bf","source_id":"owner-own-work:w720-T306-C14","source_revision":"C14 v1; proof (unaudited); no novelty claim","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Corollary c:conddist of arXiv:2605.05904, 'Schr\"odinger's problem with constraints'] Assume the setting of Theorem (thm:first of the paper). Then, for $i,j\in\{1,2\}, i\neq j$: 
\[
P^*(X^i_t \in dx_i|\cF^{X^j}_t)= \frac{h^{(i)}(t,x_i, X^j_t)R(X^i_t\in dx_i)}{\pi^i(t,X^j_t)}, \quad t\in[0,1],\; x_i\in E_{\ell},
\]
where  $\bbF^{X^j}=(\cF_t^{X^j})_{t\in[0,1]}$ is the minimal filtration generated by $X^j$ satisfying the usual hypothesis,
$h^{(i)}(t,u,v)$ equals $h(t,(u,v))$ (resp. $h(t,(v,u))$) if $i=1$ (resp. $i=2$), and 
\[
\pi^i(t,x_j)=\int_{E_{\ell}}h(t,x)R(X^i_t\in dx_i),
\]
with $x=(x_1,x_2)$.

body:
[Definition def:qRacah_ensemble of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] The $q$-Racah ensemble
	$\mathfrak{R}^{qR(N)}_{M,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}$
	depending on the parameters satisfying (equation eq:qRacah_parameters_nonnegative of the paper),
	is a probability measure on $N$-tuples of particles $(x_1<\ldots<x_N )$ in $\{0,1,\ldots,M \}$,
	with probability weights given by
	\begin{equation}
		
		\mathfrak{R}^{qR(N)}_{M,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}(x_1,\ldots,x_N )=
		\frac{1}{Z(N,M,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)}
		\prod_{1\le i<j\le N}\left( \mu(x_i)-\mu(x_j) \right)^2
		\prod_{i=1}^{N}w^{qR}(x_i).
	\end{equation}
	Here $Z(N,M,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta)$ is the normalization constant ensuring that the total probability is~$1$. The condition $M \ge N-1$ in (equation eq:qRacah_parameters_nonnegative of the paper) is required so that $N$ particles can fit into $\{0,1,\ldots, M \}$.
title: Definition def:qRacah_ensemble of arXiv:2507.22011

[Definition 4 (Bessel Kernel) of arXiv:2608.07365, 'A pathwise Ito formula \\for weakly differentiable functions'] The Bessel kernel $g_{\alpha}\colon \Rr^d\to \Rr,\, \alpha>0$ is defined by its Fourier transform
\[
\hat g_{\alpha}(\xi):= \frac 1 { (1+4\pi ^{2}\vert \xi \vert ^{2})^{\alpha/2}}.
\]
where the Fourier transform is defined as
\[
\hat {f}(\xi )={\mathcal {F}}(f)(\xi)=\int _{\mathbb {R} ^{d}}f(x )e^{-2\pi i\, x\cdot \xi }\,\d x.
\]
Equivalently, one has
\[
 (I-\Delta )^{-\alpha/2}f=g_{\alpha}\ast f,
\]
where $\Delta:= \sum_{i=1}^{n}{\frac {\partial ^{2}}{\partial x_{i}^{2}}}$ is the Laplace operator.

body:
[Definition NEW-d:lip_assum of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] The jointly measurable functions $(b,\sigma) :[0,\infty) \times \mathbb {M}  \times \hat\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb {M} }\to \mathbb{R}^{d'}\times (\mathbb{R}^{d'} \times \mathbb{R}^{d'})$ are said to be \emph{Lipschitz diffusion coefficients} if they satisfy the non-anticipative property, meaning that for all $t \in [0,t_0]$, $x \in {\cal X }$, any finite subset ${\cal X }' \subset {\cal X }$, and for $m_1[x]$, $m_2[x] \in \mathbb {M} $, with $m_1[{\cal X }']:=\sum_{x'\in{\cal X }'}\delta_{m_1[x']}\in\hat \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb {M} }$, and similarly for $m_2[{\cal X }']\in\hat\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb {M} }$, we have: 
\begin{align*}b(t,m_1[x], m_1[{\cal X }']) &= b(t,m_2[x],m_2[{\cal X }']),\\
\sigma(t,m_1[x], m_1[{\cal X }']) &= \sigma(t,m_2[x], m_2[{\cal X }'])\\ \noalign{whenever}
m_1[x,t] &= m_2[x,t],\\
m_1[{\cal X }',t] &= m_2[{\cal X }',t].
\end{align*}
Furthermore, there exists a {\em Lipschitz diffusion constant} $K_t < \infty$ such that:
\begin{align*}
& \sup_{s\in[0,t]}|b(s,m_1[x], m_1[{\cal X }']) - b(s,m_2[x], m_2[{\cal X }])|
+ |\sigma(s,m_1[x],m_1[{\cal X }']) - \sigma(s,m_2[x], m_2[{\cal X }'])| \\
& \qquad \leq K_t \Big( \|m_1[x,t] - m_2[x,t]\| + \frac{1}{|{\cal X }'|}\sum_{x' \in {\cal X }'} \|m_1[x',t] - m_2[x',t]\| \Big),
\end{align*}
with the convention that $\frac{1}{|{\cal X }'|}\sum_{x'\in{\cal X }'}(\dots)=0$ if ${\cal X }'=\emptyset$. We assume, moreover, that  $\sup_{t\in[0,t_0]}K_t<\infty$ and that $K_t$ are increasing in $t$.
Finally, using the zero-function notation $0[x]\in\mathbb {M} $ and $0[{\cal X }']):=\sum_{x'\in{\cal X }'}\delta_{0[x']}$, the coefficients $(b,\sigma)$ satisfy (uniformly in $x$ and ${\cal X }'$)
$$\int_0^{t_0}(|b(s,0[x],0[{\cal X }'])|^2 + |\sigma(s,0[x],0[{\cal X }'])|^2) \mathrm{d} s < K_{t_0}.$$
title: Lipschitz diffusion coefficients

A function f : [a,b] -> R is absolutely continuous if and only if it satisfies all three of the following: f is continuous on [a,b], f is of bounded variation on [a,b], and f has Lusin's property (N), that is, f maps every Lebesgue null subset of [a,b] to a null set. Dropping any one of the three destroys the equivalence: the Cantor function is continuous and of bounded variation but fails (N) and is not absolutely continuous.
All three hypotheses are needed.
Property (N) alone does not imply bounded variation, and bounded variation alone does not imply (N).

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:1f9415e1a1e7c43df37374fe372230934c52bbf29faa25aba348cf0662e14732","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/1f/1f9415e1a1e7c43df37374fe372230934c52bbf29faa25aba348cf0662e14732.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:3a820a0b5fe01445903a950ccb85776dae8e17f9caf4fbfb91ab2caf1fbc14f7","bundle_entry_key":"t410-w739-c007-v1","bundle_id":"population.t410-w739-background-obstructions-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"oracle computational complexity; weighted sampling; hidden witnesses; average-case inversion","draft":"w739/bundle_009.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:complexity.cryptography:t410-w739-c007-v1","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Zero-background protected-block ensembles almost surely fail C003 A

C007 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: route-failure. Target: 2.
This rules out an almost-sure construction strategy, not every exceptional
oracle, not every protected-block construction, and not Target 2. No novelty
priority is claimed. The check for this route returned go ahead.

## Setup

Use the random protected blocks of C006 v2: h_n=2^floor(n/2) fixed protected
inputs of length n, independent fair bits b_y and independent uniform witnesses
of length n^2. Put ZERO witness answers on all unprotected inputs. The auxiliary
oracle, conditional on all other blocks, ranges over at most 2^a(n) fixed
reference oracles independent of the remaining block, with a(n) polynomial.
The selected reference may depend arbitrarily on the remaining block. This
is the exact total-leakage hypothesis from C006, not a bound on answer length.

Then with probability one over the protected variables, C003 A fails for
one explicit uniformly efficiently weighted family, defined below. In fact,
for every fixed uniform polynomial-time sampler S, S is within TV 1/(100L)
of this family at only finitely many distinguished lengths, almost surely.
Countably many possible S are allowed, including a sampler chosen after O.

## Weighted law and what repeated sampling would reveal

At length L(n)=1+n+n^2 give 0^L weight 1 and give each word 1 y w weight 4
exactly when the witness oracle accepts (y,w). All other words have weight
zero. At nondistinguished lengths put all mass at 0^L. The quadratic length
map is injective and recognizable in polynomial time; evaluating a weight
uses one oracle query. Recognizing the protected set is NOT necessary.
The only accepted words correspond to protected yes inputs, by zero background.

Fix a block, write h=h_n, M=2^(n^2), and s for its number of yes bits. Each
of its s valid witness words has target mass p=4/(1+4s). Suppose S's output
law B is within tau=1/(100L) of the target. If s=0 the all-zero bit guess is
already correct. Otherwise call a valid word bad if B(word)<p/2. Since the
sum of positive target-minus-B differences equals TV, the number k of bad
words satisfies

    k < 2 tau/p = tau(1+4s)/2 <= tau(1+4h)/2 < h/8.

Every other valid word has B-probability at least p/2>=1/(3h). Run S afresh
t=6h(n+2) times, with independent random tapes, verify every returned witness,
and guess b_y=1 exactly for observed valid words. There are no false positives.
The probability of missing any good valid word is at most

    h (1-1/(3h))^t <= h exp(-2(n+2))
       <= h 2^(-2(n+2)) <= 1/16.

Thus, if S has the claimed TV accuracy for this oracle, this procedure guesses
the full protected bit vector with at most floor(h/8) errors with probability
at least 15/16 over the independent tapes. The samples are independent only
conditional on the fixed oracle; that is precisely where the coupon bound is
used. There is no multiplication of conditional guarantees across different
oracle choices or different prefixes.

## Hamming-ball extension of C006 and contradiction in probability

For a fixed transcript, C006 bounds the largest posterior mass of a single
bit vector by F. The posterior mass of any Hamming ball of radius r is at
most V(h,r)*F, where V(h,r)=sum_{j=0}^r binom(h,j). This is a finite union
bound, independent of where the guessed center is chosen. The same expected
potential proof, and the union over reference oracles, give

    Pr[at most r errors] <= V(h,r) 2^(a-h) (1+1/M)^Q.        (1)

Randomized procedures also satisfy (1), by first fixing their random tapes
independently of the hidden variables and then averaging. A polynomial-time
sampler uses at most q(n) direct witness queries per call for some polynomial
q; verification adds one query. Hence the repeated procedure has
Q<=6h(n+2)(q(n)+1).

For r=floor(h/8), the binomial generating function at x=1/4 gives

    V(h,r) <= (5/4)^h 4^(h/8) <= 2^(3h/4).

The last inequality follows by taking fourth powers of the bases:
2*(5/4)^4=1250/256<8. Therefore (1) is at most

    2^(a(n)-h_n/4) exp(6h_n(n+2)(q(n)+1)/2^(n^2)).         (2)

Let E_n be the event, over the protected tables and the selected auxiliary
oracle, that S has TV accuracy tau at L(n). Conditional on each oracle in
E_n, the learner succeeds with probability at least 15/16. Outside E_n its
success probability is nonnegative. Thus Pr(E_n) is at most 16/15 times (2).
Since a and q are polynomial and h_n is exponential, these upper bounds are
summable. The tail union bound implies E_n occurs infinitely often with
probability zero. This argument remains valid after conditioning on other
blocks because the reference-oracle bound is uniform; integrate afterwards.

Apply the result to each of the countably many uniform polynomial-time oracle
samplers. The countable union of null events is null. Therefore almost surely
no such sampler approximates this one weight family at all sufficiently large
distinguished lengths, contrary to A.

## What this does and does not rule out

The zero-background ensemble satisfies C006's circuit-hardness conclusion but
almost surely fails A under its polynomial total-leakage hypothesis. Thus the
independent-oracle or small-total-leakage shortcut cannot by itself deliver
the proposed almost-sure common-oracle construction. Measure-zero exceptional
oracles are NOT ruled out, nor are auxiliary interfaces with greater total
dependence, nor protected blocks mixed with substantial background witnesses.
No claim about B is needed: this obstruction already concerns A.

The next unpaid step is a background-witness construction that prevents every
uniformly efficient weight family from concentrating on the protected bits,
while valid sampling/inversion interfaces preserve a circuit lower bound.
Neither the present proof nor C006 constructs that invariant. Let f be a locally integrable function on R^n (Lebesgue measure). Then for Lebesgue-almost every x, lim_{r -> 0} (1/|B(x, r)|) integral_{B(x, r)} |f(y) - f(x)| dy = 0; in particular lim_{r -> 0} (1/|B(x, r)|) integral_{B(x, r)} f(y) dy = f(x) for almost every x. Such x are called Lebesgue points of f. The balls may be replaced by cubes centred at x, or by any family of sets E_r shrinking nicely to x (E_r contained in B(x, r) with |E_r| >= c |B(x, r)| for a fixed c > 0).
f locally integrable
the averaging sets shrink nicely; for general families of sets the conclusion can fail

[Prop 63 (Limit formula for the QVF in $d\ge 3$) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Let $d \geq 3$. Assume that we are in the setting of Assumption \ref{ass:QVBounds}. Then there exists $\epsilon_{\mathrm{thr}}>0$ (possibly depending on $F$ and $d$) and a function $\Theta_{\mathrm{eff}}^2(f,\bullet):B_{\mathbb R^d}(0,\epsilon_{\mathrm{thr}})\to \mathbb R$ equal to $\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}(f)$ at $  {\boldsymbol v}= 0$, such that for all $t>0$ and $  {\boldsymbol v}\in \mathbb R^d$ with $|  {\boldsymbol v}|<\epsilon_{\mathrm{thr}}$, if $  \varsigma_N\to   {\boldsymbol v}$ then 
		\begin{align}
			
			\lim_{N \to \infty}\;  \Ex\big[ Q_N^{f_N}(t,\phi;    a^N_1,   a^N_2)\big] = \Theta_{\mathrm{eff}}^2(f;  {\boldsymbol v}) \cdot c_d \cdot \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb R^d} G^{(\boldsymbol{v})}(2s,   a_1-   a_2) G^{(\boldsymbol{v})}(2s,   y) \phi(\tfrac12(   y+   a_1+   a_2)) \dr    y\dr s,
		\end{align}
        where $G^{(\boldsymbol{v})}(t,x)$ is the heat kernel with respect to the operator $\mathrm{div}(H_{  {\boldsymbol v}}\nabla)$, 
where $H_{  {\boldsymbol v}}$ is the Hessian matrix of $\log M$ at $  {\boldsymbol v}$, and where $M$ is the moment generating function of $\mu$ as in \eqref{dn}.
        The explicit expression for $\Theta_{\mathrm{eff}}^2(f;  {\boldsymbol v})$ is given by $$\int_I  \left[f(y) +  \left(e^{\boldsymbol u_{  \boldsymbol v}(   y)} -1\right) \mathbf E_y^{(\boldsymbol v,\mathrm{diff})} \left[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{1 \leq s_1\le ...\le s_{n} < \infty} g_{\mathrm{count}}( \vec s) \boldsymbol u_{  \boldsymbol v}(X_{s_1}) \cdots \boldsymbol u_{  \boldsymbol v}(X_{s_{n}}) \left(\sum_{s = s_{n} +1}^{\infty} f(X_{s})\right) \right] \right]\pi_{\boldsymbol v}^{\mathrm{inv}} (\dr y). $$ 
        Here $\pi_v^{\mathrm{inv}}$ is the invariant measure for the difference process (see Proposition \ref{diffproc}) of the tilted two-point chain $\boldsymbol q^{(2)}_{ v}$ from \eqref{qk}, and 
        \begin{equation} g_{\mathrm{count}}( \vec r):= \prod_{n \in \mathbb Z} \frac{1}{\left(\#\{i: r_i = n\}\right)!}.\end{equation}
        In the particular special case of $f=\boldsymbol{\vartheta}_{   v}:= e^{\boldsymbol u_{   v}}-1,$ 
        we have the simpler form which matches with Theorem \ref{main4}: \begin{equation} \Theta_{\mathrm{eff}}^2(\boldsymbol{\vartheta}_{   v};    v) = \int_I \big( e^{\boldsymbol u_{   v }(y) }-1 \big) \mathbf E_y^{(v,\mathrm{diff})} \bigg[ e^{\sum_{s=1}^\infty \boldsymbol u_{   v} (X_s)} \bigg] \pi_{   v}^{\mathrm{inv}} (\dr y).\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Limit formula for the QVF in $d\ge 3$

body:
Two hypotheses of the Riesz-Thorin theorem are load-bearing and are routinely dropped in write-ups. (1) COMPLEX SCALARS. The proof interpolates through an analytic family f_z, so the conclusion ||T||_{p_theta -> q_theta} <= M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta} is a theorem about complex L^p spaces. Counterexample for real scalars: on R^2 with the l^p norms let T(x_1, x_2) = (x_1 - x_2, x_1 + x_2). Over the REALS, ||T||_{l^infinity -> l^1} = 2 (the maximum of |x_1-x_2| + |x_1+x_2| = 2 max(|x_1|,|x_2|) over the unit cube) and ||T||_{l^2 -> l^2} = sqrt(2) (T is sqrt(2) times a rotation). Interpolating the endpoints (p_0,q_0) = (infinity,1) and (p_1,q_1) = (2,2) at theta = 1/2 gives (p,q) = (4, 4/3) and the putative bound 2^{1/2} (sqrt 2)^{1/2} = 2^{3/4} = 1.6818...; but the real operator norm from l^4 to l^{4/3} is about 1.7320 (already the vector (1, 1/2) gives the ratio 1.7268 > 1.6818). No contradiction with the complex theorem: over C the norm ||T||_{l^infinity -> l^1} is 2 sqrt 2 (take (1, i)), and the complex bound becomes (2 sqrt 2)^{1/2} (sqrt 2)^{1/2} = 2, which is consistent. Remedy: for a real-linear T, complexification costs at most a factor 2, so the real conclusion holds with constant 2 M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta}. (2) LINEARITY. Riesz-Thorin is false as stated for merely sublinear operators, and it also requires STRONG endpoint bounds; an operator with only weak endpoint bounds, or one that is sublinear (such as a maximal operator), must be interpolated with the Marcinkiewicz theorem instead, whose constant is not M_0^{1-theta} M_1^{theta} and blows up at the endpoints.
the counterexample is a 2-dimensional real l^p computation (the ratio at (1, 1/2) is 1.7268 and the maximum over x = (1,t) is attained near t = 0.62 at about 1.7320)
complexification bound: ||T_C f||_q <= ||T u||_q + ||T v||_q for f = u + i v
title: Pitfall: Riesz-Thorin needs complex scalars and a linear operator

PROOF (UNAUDITED), w741-T422-C04 v1. Not independently checked. For noiseless fresh Gaussian online least squares on l2 with H=diag(j^-alpha), alpha>1, deterministic nonzero e0 in l2, any fixed eta>0 and integer B>=1, the single-example instantaneous covariance ratios R_ell(e_t), ell=1,2, have no finite almost-sure upper bound at any finite deterministic t>=1, including any finite first expected-risk hit. This rules out a deterministic finite almost-sure upper calibration by a finite critical-batch quantity. It does not rule out high-probability bounds, expectation-of-ratio bounds, or ratios of expectations.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:390d6a263f5a9d2ed6f8a0e4220389544e4b8b4458f1d8f6354189821867aea6","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/39/390d6a263f5a9d2ed6f8a0e4220389544e4b8b4458f1d8f6354189821867aea6.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:600216d8983c2f7421e60ae16539f04683a4be1f9cd03189c761a3b9ef7e33a7","bundle_entry_key":"t422-instantaneous-support-obstruction","bundle_id":"population.t422-instantaneous-support-obstruction-002","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"stochastic optimization","draft":"w741/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.stochastic:gaussian-sgd-instantaneous-noise-scale-has-unbounded-support","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T422 Target 2: no finite almost-sure bound for the instantaneous endpoint scale

Status: proof (unaudited). This is a scope obstruction, not a solution of the
averaged or high-probability comparison. It does not change C02 or C03.

## Precise statement

Let H on real l2 have eigenvalues h_j=j^(-alpha), alpha>1. Let e_0 be a
deterministic nonzero l2 initial error. In particular, the exact power-law
initialization h_j e_0,j^2=j^(-gamma) is allowed when gamma>alpha+1.
Use noiseless online least squares, independent fresh x_(s,b)~N(0,H), a
positive integer batch B, and any fixed eta>0:

    e_(s+1)=e_s-(eta/B) sum_(b=1)^B x_(s,b) <x_(s,b),e_s>.

For an instantaneous error e, let G(e)=H e and let Sigma(e) be the covariance
of the single-example gradient x<x,e>, conditional on e. For ell=1,2 put

    R_ell(e)=tr(H^(ell-1) Sigma(e)) / <e,H^(ell+1)e>.

The ratio is considered on e!=0. For every finite deterministic t>=1 and
every finite L, there is an event of strictly positive probability on which
e_t!=0 and R_ell(e_t)>L. Thus R_ell(e_t) has no finite deterministic almost-sure
upper bound, for either the unweighted or Hessian-weighted convention.

This applies, in particular, when t is the first index at which EXPECTED
risk reaches a prescribed target, provided such a finite index exists.
That index is deterministic. No assertion is made for a sample-path stopping
time defined by the realized risk.

## Gaussian full support, proved directly

Since sum h_j<infinity, E||x||^2=tr H<infinity, so x is l2 almost surely.
Every l2 ball centered at a prescribed u has positive Gaussian probability.
Indeed, for radius r>0 choose N so that ||u_(j>N)||<r/4 and
sum_(j>N)h_j<r^2/32. Markov's inequality gives

    P(||x_(j>N)||<r/4)>1/2.

The first N independent coordinates have an everywhere positive density,
so ||x_(j<=N)-u_(j<=N)||<r/2 has positive probability. It is independent
of the tail event. On their intersection ||x-u||<r, by the triangle
inequality. This proves the claim. A finite product of these Gaussian laws
therefore gives positive probability to every product of l2 balls.

## A finite training history can approach any chosen high mode

Put c=||e_0||/2>0, and for each n let y=c u_n, where u_n is the nth standard
basis vector. Set z=e_0-y. Cauchy--Schwarz gives

    <z,e_0>=||e_0||^2-c e_0,n >= ||e_0||^2/2 >0.

Choose the deterministic input

    x_star=z/sqrt(eta <z,e_0>).

Then eta x_star <x_star,e_0>=z. A training history having all inputs zero
for its first t-1 steps, and all B inputs equal to x_star on its last step,
maps e_0 exactly to y. These prescribed points are used only to identify
the support; no event of exactly zero inputs is assigned positive probability.

The map from the finite Bt inputs in l2^(Bt) to e_t in l2 is continuous:
each update is a finite sum of continuous inner products and scalar-vector
products. Consequently every neighborhood of y contains e_t for all inputs
in a sufficiently small product of balls about this prescribed history.
The full-support argument gives this event strictly positive probability.

## The ratio is arbitrarily large near these reachable modes

The Gaussian fourth-moment identity gives

    Sigma(e)=<e,He> H + (He)(He)',
    R_ell(e)=1+tr(H^ell)<e,He>/<e,H^(ell+1)e>.

All operators here are bounded and H^ell is trace class. The denominator
is strictly positive for every nonzero e, because every h_j>0. The ratio
is therefore continuous near each y!=0. At the chosen y=c u_n,

    R_ell(y)=1+zeta(ell alpha) h_n^(-ell)
            =1+zeta(ell alpha) n^(ell alpha).

Given L, choose n making this expression larger than L. By continuity,
some open ball about y excludes zero and has R_ell>L throughout. The
reachable-support argument assigns that ball positive probability. This
proves the statement for any B, eta and finite t>=1, without a stability
or monotonicity assumption.

The finite-dimensional Gaussian fourth-moment identity extends here by l2
truncation: x has finite fourth l2 moment, e is fixed in l2 when conditioning,
and x<x,e> is dominated in norm by ||e|| ||x||^2. Thus the conditional
covariance and its weighted traces are finite and the displayed formulas
follow by dominated convergence. The finite iterate construction remains in
l2; finite-time moments exist by the finite Gaussian polynomial update.

## Consequence and limitations

Even at a deterministic first EXPECTED-risk hit, an instantaneous scale can
exceed any specified finite multiple of a finite deterministic critical-batch
quantity with positive probability. Hence a deterministic finite pathwise
two-sided calibration cannot be the intended universal theorem in this model.
The theorem does not rule out quantile bounds, expectation-of-ratio bounds,
or the ratios of expectations treated by C03. It gives no quantitative lower
bound on the exceptional probability, which can be extremely small.

The hardest remaining piece for an instantaneous interpretation is a
quantitative small-denominator/tail estimate with a specified confidence
level, evaluated at the intended hitting rule. This file does not provide it.

Provenance: the model and conditional Gaussian covariance are the same as in
the settled T422 diagnostics and C03. McCandlish et al., arXiv:1812.06162,

body: Let f be holomorphic on an open set U in C except for isolated singularities, and let gamma be a closed, rectifiable curve in U, avoiding all singularities, that is null-homotopic in U (for instance a positively oriented simple closed contour whose interior lies in U). Then the contour integral of f along gamma equals 2 pi i times the sum, over singularities a inside U, of the winding number of gamma around a times the residue Res(f, a). For a simple closed positively oriented contour this reduces to 2 pi i times the sum of residues at the singularities enclosed by gamma.
title: Residue theorem

body: The Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem concerns the mathematical properties of solutions to the Navier–Stokes equations, a system of partial differential equations that describe the motion of a fluid in space. Solutions to the Navier–Stokes equations are used in many practical applications. However, theoretical understanding of the solutions to these equations is incomplete. In particular, solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations often include turbulence, which remains one of the greatest unsolved problems in physics, despite its immense importance in science and engineering.
title: Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Split by growth type and identify the remaining cases precisely. Result: By Trofimov's theorem a quasi-transitive graph of polynomial growth is quasi-isometric to a Cayley graph of a virtually nilpotent group, and the critical behaviour of percolation is not a quasi-isometry invariant in general, so this does not reduce directly to Z^d; however the known proof for Z^2 (Harris-Kesten) and the high-dimensional proof (lace expansion, d >= 11) do not transfer either. Exponential growth is Hutchcroft's theorem. The remaining cases are (a) polynomial growth of degree 3 to 10 (and all virtually nilpotent non-abelian cases, e.g. the Heisenberg group of growth degree 4), where the problem is at least as hard as C0023, and (b) intermediate growth (Grigorchuk-type groups), where Hutchcroft's argument fails because it uses that the number of vertices at distance n grows exponentially to compare the cluster with a branching structure. For case (b) I checked the two known routes: the nonamenable route (Burton-Keane fails, so uniqueness monotonicity gives theta(p_c)=0 through the Benjamini-Lyons-Peres-Schramm argument) does not apply since intermediate-growth groups are amenable; the exponential-growth route uses a subadditivity argument on the expected number of vertices at distance n reached by the cluster, which requires growth rate > 1 in the exponential sense. Intermediate growth groups have growth exp(n^alpha), alpha < 1, which is superpolynomial, and Hutchcroft's argument actually needs only that the growth is faster than any polynomial? His proof uses the growth to show that the susceptibility is finite at p_c in a spherically-averaged sense via a comparison with a branching random walk with killing at rate given by the growth; I believe the argument requires exponential growth for the comparison to be uniform, so intermediate growth is a genuine gap. Recorded: the open cases are polynomial growth (degree 3 to 10 and non-abelian nilpotent) and intermediate growth. Obstruction: Polynomial growth is the Z^d problem; intermediate growth defeats the exponential-growth comparison.

body:
[Lem 245 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Assume that $L\ge1$ and that condition \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} holds. Let $\vX\equiv \vX^N$ be the process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp} and \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising}. Then the process $X^\RomI$ satisfies the estimate
	\[ \max_{a\in[M]}
	\E\bigg[ \max_{0\le d\le\dmax}
	 \Big(X^\RomI(q_d,a)
	 -\E X^\RomI(q_d,a)\Big)
	 ^8\bigg] \le L^{O(1)}\,,\]
with the estimate holding uniformly in $N$.
\begin{proof} Similarly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising}, let us abbreviate
	\[
	\frac{\Delta X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	\equiv \mathfrak{y}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\equiv \frac{(\bmeta^a(q_{d+1}),\by(q_{d+1}))}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
Define truncated $\tilde{\bmeta}$ and $\tilde{\by}$ similarly as
in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising}, and define
	\[
	\frac{\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	\equiv \tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\equiv \frac{(\tilde{\bmeta}^a(q_{d+1}),
		\tilde{\by}(q_{d+1}))}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
By the same argument as for \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4.step2} or for \eqref{e:RomII.tilde.discrepancy.second.mmt.bound}, we have
	\beq
	\bigg|\E\bigg[
	\Big(
	\mathfrak{y}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	- \tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\Big)^8
	\bigg]\bigg|
	\le e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
Let $\tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$ be the process started from zero with increments
$\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$. (As before, we regard this as a process indexed by time $q_d$, for fixed $a\in[M]$.) Applying \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4.step2.RomI} gives
	\beq
	\E\bigg[ \max_{0\le d \le \dmax}\Big(
	X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)- \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)\Big)^8\bigg]
	\le o_N(1)\,.
	\eeq
Then consider the centered increments
	\begin{align*}
	\frac{\Delta \bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	&\equiv
	\frac{\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
	-\E\bigg[
	\frac{\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)}{\delta_d p'(q_d)^{1/2}}
		\,\bigg|\, \cG(q_d)
		\bigg]\\
	&= \tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	- \E\Big[\tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
		\,\Big|\,\cG(q_d)\Big]\,.
	\end{align*}
Each increment above is a Lipschitz function of the gaussian noise, with Lipschitz constant $L^{O(1)}\delta_d$, and has mean zero conditional on $\cG(q_d)$.
Let $\bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$ be the process started from zero with increments
$\Delta \bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$. (Again, we regard this as a process indexed by time $q_d$, for fixed $a\in[M]$.)
Then $\bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)$ is a \emph{martingale}, whose increments are subgaussian with variance proxy $L^{O(1)} (\delta_d)^2$. Similar arguments as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising} give (cf.\ \eqref{e:bar.X.II.martingale.exponential.concentration})
	\[
	\E \Big[\exp\{ \theta \bar{X}^{\RomI}(1,a)\}\Big]
	\le \exp( \theta^2 L^{O(1)} \delta)\,,\]
and combining with Doob's $L^p$ martingale inequality gives (cf.\ \eqref{e:martingale.bar.X.II.application.of.Doob})
	\beq
	\E\Big[ \max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\bar{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)^8\Big] 
	\le L^{O(1)} \delta^4\,.
	\eeq
It remains to address the discrepancy between $X^{\RomI}$ and $\bar{X}^{\RomI}$. Since $\tilde{X}^{\RomI}$ has subgaussian increments, we have
	\[
	\E\bigg[
	\Big( \Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a) - \E \Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\Big)^8\bigg] \le  L^{O(1)}\delta^8\,,
	\]
and summing over increments gives
	\beq
	\E\bigg[ \max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\Big(
	 \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a) - \E \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)\Big)^8\bigg]
	 \le L^{O(1)}\,.
	\eeq
It also follows from  
\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4.step2.RomI}
or \eqref{e:martingale.X.I.to.tilde.X.I.error}
that
 \beq
 \max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
 \bigg|\E \Big[ \tilde{X}^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
 - X^{\RomI}(q_d,a) \Big] \bigg| \le o_N(1)
 \eeq
 where we recall $\E X^{\RomI}(q_d,a)
 = \E X(q_d,a)$.  Combining \eqref{e:martingale.X.I.to.tilde.X.I.error}, \eqref{e:martingale.tilde.X.I.close.to.mean}, and \eqref{e:martingale.tilde.X.I.close.to.X.I} gives the conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 245 of arXiv:2608.29416

A two-layer ReLU network f(c,x)=sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j dot x+v_j dot c+b_j), with all displayed parameters trainable and no shared output bias, uses one-hot task controls, Rademacher x in dimension d and task probabilities p_t. Partition neurons into owning blocks B_t. Let each isolated block half-squared-loss gradient flow exist through local time p_t*T and satisfy the chain-rule energy identity, with initial loss ell_t0. If every neuron in B_t initially has preactivation at most -gamma_t on every foreign task input, and gamma_t>sqrt((d+1)*p_t*T*ell_t0), then concatenating the isolated block flows at local times p_t*s and keeping foreign-control coordinates fixed constructs a joint gradient-flow solution through T with zero interference and exactly the isolated task losses. Large initial foreign margins are an explicit additional hypothesis; ordinary small iid initialization and single-task emergence are not established.

Let N_m be orthogonal projections on a finite-dimensional real Euclidean space, sampled iid from a fixed law, Q=E N_m and Phi(Y)=E[(I-N_m)Y(I-N_m)]. Suppose Phi preserves the span of nonzero pairwise orthogonal projections E_1,...,E_L summing to I. The covariance map preserves a commutative unital algebra. Then Phi^k(Q)<=2Q for all k>=0, and for e_(k+1)=(I-N_(i_(k+1)))e_k, E[e_k^T Q e_k]<=2||e_0||^2/(k+1). This covers coordinate sign-symmetric unit-normal rank-one task laws in every dimension, allowing arbitrary mixtures of coordinate magnitudes; individual task projections need not commute. It does not cover arbitrary noncommutative covariance orbits.

[Corollary 15 (Entropic rates of convergence on compact groups) of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent random variables in a connected, 
compact and metrizable abelian group $G$. Let $S_n = \sum_{i=1}^nX_i$
and write $j^*$ for the index that achieves
$$h(X_{j^*})=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}h(X_i),$$
with any ties broken arbitrarily. Then
$$
D(S_n\|U_G)
\leq
\Big[
\prod_{1\leq i\leq n, i\neq j^*}r(h(X_i))\Big]
D(X_{j^*}\|U_G)
\leq
r\Bigl(\min_{1\leq i\leq n} h(X_i)\Bigr)^{n-1}
\min_{1\leq i\leq n}D(X_i\|U_G),
$$
where
$$
r(x)
=
1-\min\left\{
\frac14,
\frac{\bigl(1-\operatorname{sinc}(e^{6x-2})^2\bigr)^2}
{8+16\frac{\operatorname{sinc}(e^{6x-2})^2}{e^{6x-2}}}
\right\},
\qquad x\in(-\infty,0],
$$
and as usual $\mathrm{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x}, x \in \mathbb{R}.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Entropic rates of convergence on compact groups

[Theorem thm:conservation of arXiv:2607.04620, 'The Exact Ville Identity\\ \large From the Absorbing Case to the General Law\\ with an App'] Let $\{X_n\}$ be a mean-zero martingale and $T$ an extended-valued stopping time for its filtration, with $\mathbb{E}|X_T|\mathbf{1}(T<\infty)<\infty$. Then there is a finite real number $L$ with
\[
  \mathbb{E}[X_T\mathbf{1}(T<\infty)]=L
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[X_n\mathbf{1}(T>n)]=-L.
\]
Neither $L$ nor $\mathbb{P}(T=\infty)$ need be zero. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 61 (General Laurent differential expansion) of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] For every zero-framed knot $K$, there is a unique sequence
\[
 G_k(K;A,q)\in\Z[A^{\pm1},q^{\pm1}],\qquad k\ge1,
\]
such that
\begin{equation}
 \HH_r(K;A,q)
 =1+\sum_{k=1}^{r}Z_{r,k}(A,q)G_k(K;A,q)
 \qquad(r\ge0).
\end{equation}
It satisfies
\begin{equation}
 G_k(K;-A,q)=(-1)^{k+1}G_k(K;A,q).
\end{equation}

DRAFT audit material, independent review pending. In dimension one let right-jump probabilities be iid, equal to 3/4 with probability 3/4 and to 1/4 otherwise. With rho_i=(1-p_i)/p_i and q=P_{0,omega}(T_{-1}=infinity), harmonic scale gives q^-1=1+sum_{k>=0} product_{j=0}^k rho_j. For lambda>=0, E q^-lambda is finite exactly when lambda<1: for 0<lambda<1, it is at most 1/[1-(3/4)3^-lambda-(1/4)3^lambda]; at lambda=1 Tonelli and E rho=1 make it infinite. In particular E q^-1/2<=4+2sqrt(3), although the first crossing mean is infinite and the walk's speed is zero. This same q appears in the layer-iid d>=2 lift omega(x,+e1)=p_x1/2, omega(x,-e1)=(1-p_x1)/2, omega(x,+/-ej)=1/[4(d-1)] for j>=2; the lift is not site iid. A small positive inverse moment alone therefore cannot replace an integrable duration estimate. This is not a C0041 counterexample and does not refute the public claimed proof's stronger crossing estimate.
Critical one-dimensional iid law, outside C0041

body: In linear algebra and functional analysis, a spectral theorem is a result about when a linear operator or matrix can be diagonalized. This is extremely useful because computations involving a diagonalizable matrix can often be reduced to much simpler computations involving the corresponding diagonal matrix of eigenvalues. The concept of diagonalization is relatively straightforward for operators on finite-dimensional vector spaces but requires some modification for operators on infinite-dimensional spaces. In general, the spectral theorem identifies a class of linear operators that can be modeled by multiplication operators, which are as simple as one can hope to find. In more abstract language, the spectral theorem is a statement about commutative C*-algebras. See also spectral theory for a historical perspective.
title: Spectral theorem

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Look for a discrete holomorphic observable on the square lattice analogous to Smirnov's on the triangular lattice. Result: Smirnov's argument needs the three-arm colour-switching symmetry, which on the triangular lattice comes from site self-duality; on Z^2 bond percolation the dual is the shifted square lattice and the exploration interface lives on the medial lattice, where the parafermionic observable F(z) = E[e^{i sigma W(z)} 1_{z on interface}] with spin sigma = ... satisfies only half of the discrete Cauchy-Riemann relations (the contour-integral relations, as for FK models with q not 2). A concrete check: for the q=1 FK model the parafermionic observable has spin sigma = 2/3 and the relation sum over edges around a face vanishes, which gives crossing exponent bounds but not holomorphicity; the missing half is what conformal invariance needs. No new observable found. Obstruction: Only the weak (contour) half of discrete holomorphicity holds for the q=1 parafermion on the square lattice.

[Theorem Davies-Mandouvalous of arXiv:2411.09614, 'Moment estimates for the stochastic heat equation on Cartan-Hadamard manifolds'] Suppose $t>0,x,y\in \mathbb{H}^{n}_1$, the $n-$dimensional hyperbolic space. The heat kernel $P^1_t(x,y)$ satisfies
    for some $c,C>0$ depending on $n$ $$ch(t,d(x,y))\leq P^1_t(x,y)\leq Ch(t,d(x,y)),$$
    where the Davies-Mandouvalous function $h:\mathbb{R}_+\times \mathbb{R}_+\to \mathbb{R}+$ is defined by $$h(t,z):=t^{-\frac{n}{2}}(1+t+z)^{\frac{n-3}{2}}(1+z)\exp\left(-\frac{z^2}{4t}-\frac{(n-1)^2t}{4}-\frac{(n-1)z}{2}\right).$$

Kind: bound, conditional reduction. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited).
This does not inherit the C06 v1 PASS and does not construct a hard seed.

Let d>=1, 0<tau<=1, 0<epsilon<=1. Write P_tau=P*N(0,tau^2 I).
Assume a fixed jointly measurable seed OU score field b_t has squared
L2 error at most epsilon^2/16 under OU_t(P_tau), for EVERY t>=0.
Set

K=4(d+1)/(epsilon tau^2),
eta=min{1/(2d),epsilon^2/[4(K+d/tau)^2]},
Q=(1-eta)P+eta H, R=Q*N(0,tau^2 I).

Then G_t=projection onto the Euclidean ball of radius K of b_t is a
fixed OU oracle for R with squared error at most epsilon^2/2 for every
t>=0. H may be any probability law for this accuracy assertion.
One query to b_t simulates one query to G_t at the SAME point and time.
In particular the seed OU tolerance is epsilon/4, with no extra tau factor.

## Proof

Fix t and put a=exp(-t), v=1-a^2+a^2 tau^2. Then tau^2<=v<=1.
OU_t(P_tau) is the law of aY+sqrt(v)Z with Y~P and Z standard normal,
independent. The corresponding H law has the same Gaussian noise v,
and OU_t(R) is their mixture with weights 1-eta and eta.

For a mixing law L define D_L(g)=E||g(aY+sqrt(v)Z)+Z/sqrt(v)||^2.
Conditional expectation gives its minimizer s_L, the score of this
smoothed law, and D_L(g)-D_L(s_L)=E||g-s_L||^2.
The same identity and conditional Jensen give
E||s_P||^4<=E||Z||^4/v^2=d(d+2)/v^2.

Projection is nonexpansive; comparing the projected field and projected
true score, then using (u+w)^2<=2u^2+2w^2 and truncation, yields

E_P||G_t-s_P||^2
 <=epsilon^2/8+2E||s_P||^4/K^2
 <=epsilon^2/8+2d(d+2)/(K^2 tau^4)
 <=epsilon^2/4.                                             (A)

The last term is at most epsilon^2/8 because d(d+2)<=(d+1)^2.
The mixture denoising risk is D_Q=(1-eta)D_P+eta D_H.
Subtracting the optimal Q risk and using D_P(s_Q)>=D_P(s_P)
and D_H(s_Q)>=0 bounds its excess risk by

E_Q||G_t-s_Q||^2
 <=(1-eta)E_P||G_t-s_P||^2+eta D_H(G_t).

Minkowski and ||G_t||<=K give D_H(G_t)<=(K+sqrt(d/v))^2
<=(K+d/tau)^2. Its eta-weighted contribution is <=epsilon^2/4.
Together with (A) this proves epsilon^2/2. Bounded G_t has finite
denoising risk even without moments for H. Cross-risks of s_Q are finite
because positive mixture weights dominate their component integrals.
Every estimate is uniform in t. No per-query independence is asserted.

As a coordinate check, additional VE noise sigma^2=exp(2t)-1 has
T^2=tau^2+sigma^2 and T^2/(1+sigma^2)=v>=tau^2.
In those coordinates the same construction clips at K/sqrt(1+sigma^2),
and the seed VE squared error is epsilon^2/[16(1+sigma^2)].
Thus it directly matches the OU profile, instead of requiring the
stronger epsilon^2 tau^2/(16T^2) sufficient profile of C06 v2.

since ||mu||^2<=1 and eta<=1/(2d). Also E_Q||Y||^2<=2.
Hence Cov(R) has condition number <=3 and E_R||Y||^2<=2+d tau^2,
which is <=3 if tau<=1/sqrt(d).

For any fixed desired output OU endpoint u>=0,
TV(OU_u(R),OU_u(P_tau))<=eta by Markov contraction.
A seed lower bound L rounds, TV failure r, instance probability rho,
therefore transfers with the same L and rho and failure r-eta, provided
it holds for THIS seed oracle accuracy and THIS smoothed endpoint.
The simulation is deterministic and uses one oracle query per query,
so adaptive batches and public data are unchanged. Assume r>eta for
a meaningful positive failure bound. Hardness at a different endpoint
cannot be substituted. Normalization may change all these parameters.

This removes an unnecessary extra tau factor from the sufficient seed

body:
[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2606.11068, '2606.11068'] Let \(D^*\) be the maximal two-sided displacement of a single active particle
 and let \(D^\to\) and \(D^\leftarrow\) be the corresponding one-sided maximal
 displacements to the right and to the left.
 \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item If \(\E(\eta)<\infty\) and
 \[
   \limsup_{n\to\infty} n\Pbb(D^*\ge n)
   <
   \frac{1}{2\E(\eta)},
 \]
 then the frog model dies out almost surely.
 \item If \(\Pbb(\eta=0)<1\) and, for one of the two directions,
 \[
   \liminf_{n\to\infty} n\Pbb(D^\to\ge n)
   >
   \frac{1}{\E(\eta)}
\] or \[
   \liminf_{n\to\infty} n\Pbb(D^\leftarrow\ge n)
   >
   \frac{1}{\E(\eta)},
 \]
 where \(1/\E(\eta):=0\) when \(\E(\eta)=\infty\), then the frog model survives
 with positive probability.
 \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 2 of arXiv:2606.11068

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] For  $\eps > 0$ small enough, for any $\delta \in (0,1)$, there exist $c_\eps, C_\eps > 0$ and $k \geq 0$ such that 
\begin{itemize}
\item The dynamics has the $(\eps, k)$-matching of the digits property.
\item For any $n\geq 0$, 
\[
\P[ \mathsf{NC}(n,n) ] \leq \exp(-c_\eps n) + C_\eps\P[\lfloor \mathsf{NC}((1-\delta)n,(1-\delta)n) \rfloor_k].
\] 
\end{itemize}

[Proposition 53 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(q\in Y^{\rm prod}\).
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item At every fixed limiting point based at \(q\), the underlying
K\"ahler metric flow of every tangent space is the smooth shrinking
cylinder
\[
 \bigl(\C^m\times\PP^1,
       g_{\rm E}+(-s)g_{S^2}\bigr)_{s<0},
 \qquad \Rc(g_{S^2})=\tfrac12g_{S^2}.
\]
\item The fixed fibre satisfies
\[
 \sup_{0\le t<1}\sup_{x\in F_q}
 (1-t)|\Rm(g(t))|_{g(t)}(x)<\infty.
\]
\item Fix \(x_0\in F_q\) and one anchored limiting point
\(\xi=(\mu_t)_{t<1}\) obtained from poles \((x_0,s_j)\),
\(s_j\nearrow1\).  For every \(\tau_i\searrow0\), choose
\(H_{2m+2}\)-centres \(p_i\) of
\(\mu_{i,-1}:=\mu_{1-\tau_i}\) with respect to
\(g_i(-1)=\tau_i^{-1}g(1-\tau_i)\) at backward scale one.  After a
realizing subsequence there is \(D<\infty\) such that
\[
 F_q\subset B_{\tau_i^{-1}g(1-\tau_i)}(p_i,D),
\]
and, for every finite \(A\ge0\), the curvature is uniformly bounded
on the radius-\(D+A\) ball.
\end{enumerate}

body: Definition 10. A transversal design of order n and block size k, denoted TD(k, n), is a triple (V, G, B), where V is a set of kn elements (or points); G is a partition of V into k classes, called groups, each of size n; B is a collection of k-subsets of V, called blocks; and every unordered pair of elements from V is contained in one group, or one block, but not both. If the blocks can be resolved into n rounds of n blocks, the design is said to be a resolvable transversal design, RTD(k, n). An RTD(k, n) can be obtained by removing one of the groups from a TD(k + 1, n).

[Proposition prop:doublecurrent-Xor of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected graph. Let $\Omega:=\{0,1\}^E$ be the space of bond configurations and $\Sigma:=\{-1,+1\}^V$ be the space of spin configurations. Let $f:\Omega\to 2^{\Sigma}$ be given by $f(\omega)=\{\sigma\in \Sigma\mid \omega\subset S(\sigma)\}$ (so $|f(\omega)|=2^{\kappa(\omega)}$). For any $A, B\subset V$ with $|A|, |B|$ even, let
	\[\rho[\omega] \propto \mathbf{P}^{A\triangle B}_{2J}[\omega \mid \mathcal{F}_A],~\forall \omega\in\Omega,~\gamma[\sigma]\propto 1, ~\forall \sigma\in \Sigma.\]
	Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(a)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$ is $\mu^{A,B}$ defined by
		\[\mu^{A,B}[\sigma] \propto \langle \tau_{A \triangle B} \rangle_{S(\sigma),2J} \mathbf{P}^{A\triangle B}_{S(\sigma),2J}[\mathcal{F}_A]  \mu^{\XOR}[\sigma],\]
		where $ \langle \tau_{A \triangle B} \rangle_{S(\sigma),2J}$ is the expectation of the product of Ising spins  $\tau_{A \triangle B} = \prod_{x\in A \triangle B}\tau_x$, $\tau_x \in \{-1,1\}$  under the Ising measure defined on $S(\sigma)$ with couplings $(2J_e)_{e\in E}$. For each $\omega\in\Omega$ with  $\omega\in\mathcal{F}_A \cap \mathcal{F}_B$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega]$ on $\Sigma$ is realized by tossing independent fair coins to get $\pm$ for each open cluster of $\omega$.
		\item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$ is $\mathbf{P}^{A,B}$.  For each $\sigma\in\Sigma$ with $\mu^{A,B}[\sigma] \neq 0$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \sigma] = \mathbf{P}^{A\triangle B}_{S(\sigma),2J}[\;\cdot \mid \mathcal{F}_A]$, the single random current measure on $S(\sigma)$ with sources $A\triangle B$ and couplings $2J=(2J_e)_{e\in E}$ conditioned on $\mathcal{F}_A$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:doublecurrent-Xor of arXiv:2506.10765

[Lem 18 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] (Existence of
solutions to the penalized equation)
Let Assumption \ref{assu:assu for existence} and Assumption \ref{assu:assum for F} hold for some $p\in [2,\infty)$.

For fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, as $\alpha\to0$ and $n\to\infty$,
there exists a subsequence of $\{u_{\alpha,n,\varepsilon}\}_{(\alpha,n)\in(0,1)\times\mathbb{N}}$ that converges almost surely on the original probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ in $L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times[0,T])$ to some limit $u_{\varepsilon}$.
This limit $u_{\varepsilon}$ is a stochastic kinetic equation
of \eqref{eq:penalized eq} in the sense of Definition \ref{def:def of stochastic kinetic solution without obstacle}, meaning that the kinetic function $\chi_{\varepsilon}(x,\xi,t):=\mathbf{1}_{\{0<\xi<u_{\varepsilon}(x,t)\}}$ satisfies almost surely, for every $\phi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T))$,
\begin{align}
& -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\chi_{\varepsilon}(x,\xi,s)\partial_s\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}s\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})\nabla_x u_{\varepsilon}\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})]^{2}\nabla_x u_\varepsilon+\sigma(u_{\varepsilon})\sigma^{\prime}(u_{\varepsilon})F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla_x\phi)(x,u_{\varepsilon},s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}m_\varepsilon(x,\xi,s)-\int_0^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u_\varepsilon,s)\nabla_x \cdot g(u_\varepsilon)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\

Both theories provide interpretations of classical mechanics and describe the same physical phenomena.

[Definition 10 of arXiv:2609.02699, '\vspace{-0.5 cm}Gauge theory and symplectic structures'] Let $(M,g,J)$ be a closed K\"ahler $3$-fold. For $S_+=\oplus_p\Omega^{0,2p}(\mathcal{L}), A\in\mathcal{A},$ one can write $A=A^{\mathrm{Ch}}+2B$ with abuse of notation. Here $A^{\mathrm{Ch}}$ is the Chern connection on the $K^{-1}$ and $B$ is a unitary connection on $\mathcal{L}$. Given such an $A=A^{\mathrm{Ch}}+2B,\beta\in$ Re$(\Omega^{0,3}),\phi\in\Gamma(S_+)$, we define the energy of $(A,\beta,\phi)$ to be 
\begin{align*}
    &\mathcal E(A,\beta,\phi)\\
    &:=\int\Big(|\nabla_{A,\beta}\phi|^2+\frac{s}{4}|\phi|^2+2|F_B|^2+4|d^{*}\beta|^2+\frac{3r^2}{16}+\frac{1}{48}(3|\phi^0|^2-|\phi^{0,2}|^2)^2+\frac{1}{2}|\phi^0|^2|\phi^{0,2}|^2\\
    &\hspace{5 ex}-\frac{2}{3}|\Lambda(F_B)|^2-2|\beta|^2|\phi|^2-\frac{r}{8}(3|\phi^0|^2-|\phi^{0,2}|^2)+\big\langle 4(F_B)^{1,1}_p+2F_{A^\mathrm{Ch}},q(\phi)\big\rangle\Big)dv\\
    &\hspace{5 ex}-2\pi r\mathrm{deg}(\mathcal L)
\end{align*}

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked against a direct linear-algebra solve on twelve graphs, with the complete graph and the cycle as independent controls at the two extremes.] This is the proved identity behind the campaign reduction of Open Problem 7.31 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html). Let G be a finite connected simple distance-regular graph with n>=2 vertices, valency k, and diameter d: for vertices at distance i, the numbers of neighbors one step closer to or farther from the target are constants c_i and b_i depending only on i. Use c_1=1, b_0=k, b_d=0. Let k_i be the number of vertices at distance i from a fixed vertex, so k_0=1, k_1=k, k_{i+1} c_{i+1}=k_i b_i, and n=sum_{i=0}^d k_i. For the simple random walk, let T_y be the first hitting time of y, measured in steps, and define tau_0=max_{x,y} E_x[T_y]; here tau_0 is the maximum mean hitting time, not the spectral Kemeny sum. Then tau_0=k sum_{i=1}^d (k_i+k_{i+1}+...+k_d)/(k_i c_i). In particular tau_0>=n-1, with equality exactly for complete graphs. The distance to a fixed target is a birth-and-death chain with downward probability c_i/k, upward probability b_i/k, and stationary mass k_i/n, so the formula requires only the intersection array. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
G is finite, connected, simple, distance-regular, and n>=2.

[Theorem 1 (Variational characterization) of arXiv:2609.02590, 'Directional Optimal Sub-Gamma Scales for Infinitely Divisible Laws'] For the signed canonical remainder of \Cref{thm:factorization},
\begin{align}
 \cplus(X)&=\max\left\{0,\sup_{t>0}\Psi_+(t)\right\},
 &\Psi_+(t)&=\frac{1-M_{R_X}(t)^{-1}}{t},
 \\
 \cminus(X)&=\max\left\{0,\sup_{t>0}\Psi_-(t)\right\},
 &\Psi_-(t)&=\frac{1-M_{R_X}(-t)^{-1}}{t}.
 
\end{align}
Here $1/\infty=0$. If the value on the right is finite, it is itself a feasible
scale. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \cplus(X)<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\tplus(X)>0,
 \qquad
 \cminus(X)<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\tminus(X)>0.
 
\end{equation}

Author-proved draft; w376 scoped KEEP, designated referee pending. On Z^d, d>=2, let undirected nearest-neighbor edge weights be iid, nondegenerate, and satisfy 0<r<=t_e<=R<infinity. Let T be the unrestricted minimum passage time and mu=E t_e. Choose two separated support sets of positive masses, with weights at most a on the lower set and at least b on the higher set, and an integer k with k*b>(k+2)*a. Let S_k be the sum on a k-edge axial path, and H_k the sum on its edge-disjoint height-one (k+2)-edge detour. Then delta=E[(S_k-H_k)_+]>0, E T(0,n*e1)<=n*mu-floor(n/(k+1))*delta, and almost surely limsup T(0,n*e1)/n<=mu-delta/(k+1). The directed axial path has passage-time ratio tending to mu, giving a strictly positive raw linear gap. For any per-n coupling of the two marginal laws and any 0<c<delta/(k+1), P((T_directed-T)/n>=c) tends to one. Different centering may still permit a comparison. This result supplies no fluctuation or wandering exponent and does not solve P0110.

body: [Theorem 4 of arXiv:2609.02197, '2609.02197'] Let $\left(f_r\right)_{r \in \mathbb{R}_+}$ be a stochastic process of state space $\left(\mathscr{S}',\mathcal{B}\left(\mathscr{S}'\right)\right)$ and $\left(\alpha,\beta,\theta\right) \in \mathbb{R}^2\times \mathbb{R}_+^*$ such that $\beta<\alpha$ and $\theta>\max\left(\frac{2d}{\alpha-\beta},1\right).$ If for all $U \in \mathbb{R}_+,$ there exists $\left(\mu,\gamma\right) \in \left(\mathbb{R}_+^*\right)^2$ such that for every $\left(r_1,r_2,j,x\right) \in \left[0,U\right]^2\times \mathbb{N}\times \mathbb{T}^d,r_1\neq r_2,$ $$\left(\mathds{E}\left[\left|\left(\delta_{j-1}f_0\right)\left(x\right)\right|^\theta\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{\theta}}+\left|r_2-r_1\right|^{-\gamma-\frac{1}{\theta}}\left(\mathds{E}\left[\left|\left(\delta_{j-1}f_{r_2}\right)\left(x\right)-\left(\delta_{j-1}f_{r_1}\right)\left(x\right)\right|^\theta\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{\theta}}\leq \mu2^{-\alpha\left(j-1\right)},$$ then there exists a stochastic process $\left(g_r\right)_{r \in \mathbb{R}_+}$ of state space $\left(\mathscr{C}^\beta,\mathcal{B}\left(\mathscr{C}^\beta\right)\right)$ such that the sample paths of $\left(g_q\right)_{q \in \mathbb{R}_+}$ are continuous and for all $r \in \mathbb{R}_+$ and for $\mathds{P}$-almost every $\omega \in \Omega,g_r\left(\omega\right)=f_r\left(\omega\right).$

DRAFT proof-audit material, independent referee check pending. For iid nearest-neighbour bond percolation on Z^d with p_c>0, let a_n(p) be the probability of an open path from 0 to the vertex boundary of B_n=[-n,n]^d intersect Z^d, using edges internal to B_n. Let I_n(p) be the sum of the pivotal probabilities of those edges for that event. Then theta(p)=lim_n a_n(p). The assertion theta(p_c)=0 is equivalent to lim_(delta down to 0) sup_n integral_(p_c-delta)^(p_c) I_n(p)dp=0, where 0<delta<p_c. Finite-product differentiation identifies the integral with a_n(p_c)-a_n(p_c-delta). This is an equivalence identifying the open input, not a proof of the required uniform estimate in dimensions 3 through 10; continuity of each finite-event polynomial is insufficient.

[Defn Coarse slope of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{G}$ be an oriented foliation on $\mathbb{T}^2$ and $\ell$ is a leaf of $\mathcal{G}$ not lying in the interior of a Reeb annulus, we define its $\textbf{(coarse) slope}$, $\slope(\ell)$ which is an element of $(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus \{0\})/\mathbb{R}_{>0} \cong S^1$, where $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ acts on $\mathbb{R}^2\setminus \{0\}$ by scaling. It is defined as 
$$\slope(\ell) \coloneqq \left[ \lim_{t\to +\infty} \frac{\varphi_t(x)-x}{t} \right],$$ 
where $\varphi_t$ denotes a flow directing the universal cover $\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $x\in \ell$; up to positive scalars, the limit does not depend on these choices. We are usually concerned with slopes having non-negative $x$-coordinate; we call these the \textbf{admissible} slopes. The admissible slopes can be identified with $\mathbb{R} \cup \{\pm \infty\}$ via $(1,x) \mapsto x$.

If $\mathcal{G}$ has no Reeb annuli, all of its leaves have the same (coarse) slope which we denote by $\slope(\mathcal{G})$. If $\mathcal{G}$ has Reeb annuli, $\slope(\mathcal{G})$ is not well-defined.
title: Coarse slope
