{"artifact_digest":"sha256:82d204866c9de546a5e644cda77c2c41837d0caad12cd981f4e6f519f060ff48","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/82/82d204866c9de546a5e644cda77c2c41837d0caad12cd981f4e6f519f060ff48.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:8b760dc91eda60d4cd7c62b6f0f23ca76907e671f84fa206bdc6aeacc114379f","bundle_entry_key":"conditional-endpoint-two","bundle_id":"population.t232-conditional-endpoint-and-variational-transport-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"deep linear networks; saddle-to-saddle gradient flow","draft":"w704/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.deep_linear_networks:t232-conditional-dimension-two-endpoint","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T232 target 1: conditional complete second step when min(m,n)=2

Status: proof draft, independent review pending; a corollary of existing local escape theory. No novelty or unconditional Gaussian result is claimed.

## Statement
Let X in R^(n x N) have full row rank, Y in R^(m x N), and min(m,n)=2. Let C(P)=||PX-Y||_F^2/(2N), with its unique unconstrained minimizer M=YX^T(XX^T)^(-1) of rank two. Let w>=2 and the asymmetric factors obey B'=-G A^T, A'=-B^T G, G=grad C(BA). Let P1 be a globally best rank-at-most-one product, with a corresponding critical rank-one factor theta1=(b1,a1^T); put u1=(b1;a1), Z1=u1u1^T. Assume that this is the rank-one endpoint being approached by the given initialization family. Use the block lift, residual singular vector v, and the strong arrival-alignment hypothesis of C001. In particular there are nonnegative arrival times T_alpha with Z_alpha(T_alpha)->Z1 and
  liminf a_alpha/||Z_alpha(T_alpha)-Z1||_F>0,
where a_alpha=v^T Z_alpha(T_alpha)v. Then the known canonical local escape orbit selected at the time shift log(1/a_alpha)/(2s) has a width-two factor realization whose product tends to M as t->infinity. Its factor path tends to a finite critical width-two parameter theta2 representing M, hence a global (in particular width-two local) minimum. The original family converges to that width-two factor path after a hidden orthogonal rotation depending on alpha but fixed in time, on each fixed compact interval of shifted time.

No hypothesis that XX^T is isotropic or commutes with the target is used. No Gaussian arrival-alignment assertion is made. The theorem conditions on the rank-one arrival and exact strong Gram alignment, just as the existing local theorem does.

## The single hardest piece still open beyond this conditional statement
For the actual small Gaussian initialization, prove the required quantitative arrival alignment (or replace it by a weaker hypothesis proved to suffice). In dimensions at least three on both sides, identifying the forward rank-two local-minimum endpoint also needs more than the energy argument below.

## 1. Existing local result and nontriviality
C001 specializes Section 3 and Theorem G.2 of Li-Luo-Lyu, arXiv:2012.09839. Its local complete-extension argument handles the source's all-real-time convention. The selected Gram path Z*(t) has rank at most two and tends to Z1 as t->minus infinity. The canonical simple-top escape is nonconstant: the local estimates in Appendix E, Lemmas E.3-E.6, compare the shifted orbit at sufficiently negative t with a nonzero top eigenmode of size exp(2s t), with quadratic error. Thus that mode cannot disappear identically in the limit. This is the outgoing orbit, rather than the constant stationary solution.

For this data class s is automatically simple and positive when P1 is critical and nonglobal. Indeed G1 a1=0 and G1^T b1=0, with both b1 and a1 nonzero (M rank two excludes the zero product as a best rank-one solution). Consequently rank G1<=min(m-1,n-1)=1. Since XX^T is positive definite, G1=0 would imply P1=M, which contradicts their ranks. Thus rank G1=1 and its positive top singular value is simple. Every cancellation here uses nonzero b1,a1 and positive-definite XX^T.

## 2. A factor realization, strict descent and rank two
At any fixed time, factor the PSD matrix Z*(0)=U*(0)U*(0)^T using at most two columns. Solve U'=-H(Z)U, equivalently the asymmetric two-factor flow. Uniqueness of the induced Gram ODE identifies UU^T with Z*. Backwards on every finite interval the prescribed continuous H(Z*(t)) defines a linear factor ODE, so this realization covers the complete Gram orbit. The known rank-at-most-two Gram constraint is preserved. To check the backward PARAMETER endpoint as well, the canonical local estimates give ||Z*(t)-Z1||_F=O(exp(2s t)) as t->minus infinity. Let H1=H(Z1). The factor norm is bounded there since ||U||_F^2=tr Z*. Since H1 Z1=0,
  ||H1 U||_F^2=tr(H1^2 Z*)=tr(H1^2(Z*-Z1))=O(exp(2s t)).
Also H(Z*)-H1=O(exp(2s t)) because H is smooth. Therefore ||Uprime||_F=O(exp(s t)), integrable at minus infinity. Hence U*(t) converges to a finite factor Uminus with Uminus Uminus^T=Z1. This is precisely the width-one saddle inclusion up to a single hidden orthogonal rotation.

Along factor flow,
  d C(BA)/dt = -||GA^T||_F^2-||B^TG||_F^2.
A nonconstant gradient trajectory cannot have a stationary time, by uniqueness. Its loss is therefore strictly decreasing; as t->minus infinity it tends to C(P1). Hence C(B(t)A(t))<C(P1) for every finite t. Since P1 is globally best among all rank-at-most-one products, rank(B(t)A(t))>=2. Combining this with the width-two realization gives rank two at every finite time.

## 3. Forward boundedness, with the constants and dimensions shown
For any forward factor trajectory set P=B^TB, Q=AA^T, K=P-Q (these are w-by-w matrices). Differentiate to see K'=0. Exact trace expansion gives
  ||P||_F^2+||Q||_F^2=2||BA||_F^2+||K||_F^2.
By nonincreasing loss and the triangle inequality, ||BA X||_F is uniformly bounded forward. If lambda>0 is the smallest eigenvalue of XX^T, then
  lambda ||BA||_F^2 <= ||BA X||_F^2.
So BA is bounded. Cauchy-Schwarz on the 2w nonnegative eigenvalues of P,Q then yields
  ||B||_F^2+||A||_F^2 = tr(P)+tr(Q)
  <= sqrt(2w) sqrt(2||BA||_F^2+||K||_F^2).
This bounds both factors uniformly. The polynomial vector field cannot blow up in a finite positive time while its state is bounded, so the forward solution is global. This proof does not assume initial balance K=0.

## 4. Why boundedness gives a stationary limit here
The factor loss L(B,A)=C(BA) is polynomial, hence real analytic. We spell out the standard analytic-gradient argument rather than infer convergence from boundedness alone (compare the analytic argument in Li-Luo-Lyu, proof of Theorem 5.8, PDF p.32).

Since L decreases and is bounded below, L(t)->ell. Boundedness gives a cluster point z0, with L(z0)=ell. Moreover integral_0^infinity ||grad L||^2 dt=L(0)-ell is finite. On the compact forward orbit the Hessian and gradient are bounded, so ||grad L||^2 is uniformly continuous in time. A nonnegative uniformly continuous integrable function tends to zero (otherwise disjoint fixed-width intervals around its positive peaks force a divergent integral). Thus grad L(z0)=0.

The analytic gradient inequality supplies c>0, theta in [1/2,1) and a neighbourhood of z0 on which ||grad L(z)||>=c |L(z)-ell|^theta. Write e=L-ell>=0 along this trajectory. If e ever reaches zero, energy monotonicity makes the remaining trajectory stationary. Otherwise, while inside that neighbourhood,
  -d(e^(1-theta))/dt
  =(1-theta)e^(-theta)||grad L||^2
  >=c(1-theta)||grad L||.
Choose a sufficiently late cluster time with z(t_k) arbitrarily close to z0 and e(t_k) small enough that e(t_k)^(1-theta)/(c(1-theta)) is less than the distance to the boundary of a fixed smaller ball. The displayed length bound forbids exit from that ball, and bounds the remaining arc length. The trajectory is Cauchy and converges to z0. All uses of theta require theta<1, and no division by e is made in the e=0 case. Hence B(t)->B2, A(t)->A2, a finite stationary factor pair.

## 5. The endpoint is the global regression minimizer
Fix any finite t0. Monotonicity gives C(B2A2)<=C(B(t0)A(t0))<C(P1). Thus the ENDPOINT product also has rank two; the strict inequality is inherited from the fixed finite t0, not from taking a limit of merely pointwise strict inequalities without a uniform margin.

If m=2, rank(B2A2)=2 forces B2 to have full row rank two. Its transpose is injective, so stationarity B2^T G2=0 forces every column of G2 to be zero. If n=2, A2 has full column rank two, so stationarity G2 A2^T=0 forces G2=0 instead. Either case gives
  G2=(B2A2 XX^T-YX^T)/N=0,
and XX^T invertible yields B2A2=M. This is a global minimum of C and of the width-two factor loss.

## 6. Recovering parameters modulo one hidden rotation per alpha
Gram convergence alone must not be mistaken for convergence of the original factors. Here it suffices as follows. At shifted time zero, choose two linearly independent row vectors of the limiting rank-two Gram factor; their 2-by-2 Gram determinant is strictly positive. The corresponding rows of U_alpha remain independent for all sufficiently small alpha. Apply Gram-Schmidt to these two rows to obtain the first two columns of a hidden orthogonal basis Q_alpha, completing it arbitrarily. The coefficients of every other row on those first two basis vectors converge, because they are obtained from converging Gram inner products and strictly nonzero limiting pivot norms. The squared norm in the orthogonal complement is the Schur-complement residual and tends to zero, since the limiting Gram matrix has rank two. Therefore U_alpha(shift)Q_alpha converges to a width-two realization with zero extra columns.

Keep this SAME Q_alpha at all times. Right orthogonal equivariance of factor gradient flow and continuous dependence on its initial state give convergence to the corresponding width-two solution on every fixed compact time interval. Backward dependence is used only on finite intervals where the limiting path exists, and the positive shift tends to infinity so the original flow is defined there. Factors of the same Gram matrix differ by a right orthogonal transformation, so this limiting realization has the endpoint from Sections 3-5.

## Literature scope and novelty
Li-Luo-Lyu explicitly supply the asymmetric lift and conditional local theorem. Their Appendix H treats later endpoints as generic; the dimension-two endpoint conclusion here is an elementary corollary of their local result plus standard bounded analytic gradient convergence. Zhang-Saxe-Latham, arXiv:2512.20607, Sections 4-5, explicitly call the subsequent trajectory arguments heuristic; their Theorem 4 is about the LINEARIZED dynamics (10), not a full nonlinear second-phase limit. This check does not establish priority for the corollary; no claim of specialist novelty is made.

## Adversarial checks and scope boundary
scripts/check_endpoint_algebra.py checks exact stationarity implications in rectangular two-dimensional examples and a noncommuting covariance example. It also supplies a genuine boundary to THIS PROOF: in dimension three, a nonoptimal rank-two stationary product can have loss strictly below the best rank-one value. Take S=[[1,1,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]], D=diag(5,4,3), C(P)=||PS-D||_F^2/2 and P=diag(5,0,3)S^(-1). This P is stationary for rank-two factors, with loss 8<25/2 (best rank one), but the best rank-two loss is 9/2. It is not a counterexample to saddle-to-saddle dynamics; it shows why the dimension hypothesis cannot simply be omitted from the endpoint argument.

On a FINITE measure space, uniform integrability plus convergence in measure gives L^1 convergence. On a general (for instance sigma-finite but infinite) measure space this is FALSE and a third hypothesis is needed. The correct statement: let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and f_n in L^1(mu) with f_n -> f in measure (or mu-a.e.). Then f_n -> f in L^1(mu) if and only if (i) {f_n} is uniformly integrable, meaning sup_n integral_{|f_n| > K} |f_n| dmu -> 0 as K -> infinity, AND (ii) {f_n} is uniformly tight, meaning for every eps > 0 there is a set A with mu(A) < infinity and sup_n integral_{Omega \ A} |f_n| dmu < eps. Counterexample showing (ii) is not implied by (i): on R with Lebesgue measure take f_n = 1_{[n, n+1]}. Then |f_n| <= 1 so the family is uniformly integrable and dominated, f_n -> 0 pointwise everywhere, yet ||f_n||_1 = 1 for every n. Mass escapes to infinity; on a finite measure space it has nowhere to go, which is exactly why the finite-measure statement can omit (ii). [standard; e.g. Bogachev, Measure Theory, Vol. I, Section 4.5]

body:
Let $E = \frac{1}{n} X^T X$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $C$ (rows $C^{1/2} z_i$ with $z_i$ having i.i.d. entries of mean zero, variance one and finite twelfth moment), in the regime $p, n \to \infty$ with $q = p/n \to q_0 \in (0, \infty)$, and assume the spectral distribution of $C$ converges to a limit with bounded support. Let $\lambda_k, u_k$ be the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors and let $g_E(z) = \frac{1}{p}\operatorname{tr}(z I - E)^{-1}$ be the Stieltjes transform of the sample spectrum, with $g(\lambda - i0) := \lim_{\eta \downarrow 0} g_E(\lambda - i\eta)$ inside the bulk. THEOREM (Ledoit and Peche, 2011, Theorem 4; in the form of Bun, Bouchaud and Potters 2017). The oracle eigenvalues $\xi_k^{\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$ converge, uniformly in $k$ inside the bulk, to $$\xi(\lambda_k) = \frac{\lambda_k}{\big|\, 1 - q + q\, \lambda_k\, g_E(\lambda_k - i0) \,\big|^2}.$$ This limit depends on the population covariance $C$ only through the observable sample spectrum, so it is a consistent, computable estimator (the rotationally invariant estimator, RIE, or nonlinear shrinkage): replace each sample eigenvalue by $\xi(\lambda_k)$, keep the sample eigenvectors. In practice $g_E$ is evaluated at $\lambda_k - i\eta$ with a small $\eta$ of order $n^{-1/2}$ times the eigenvalue scale, and the result is floored at a small positive fraction of the bulk level. When $C = \sigma^2 I$ the formula returns $\sigma^2$ for every eigenvalue (the Marchenko-Pastur spread is entirely removed); for a spike above the bulk it returns approximately the debiased population spike. Applying the formula to a matrix whose largest eigenvalue is a signal one is trying to keep, and flooring relative to that top eigenvalue, destroys the small eigenvalues that the inverse depends on.

body:
Let K be a compact convex subset of a locally convex Hausdorff topological vector space, and suppose K is metrizable. Then the set ext K of extreme points of K is a G_delta set, and for every x in K there is a Borel probability measure mu on K, concentrated on ext K, whose barycenter is x: phi(x) = integral phi dmu for every continuous linear functional phi. Without metrizability, the Bishop-de Leeuw theorem gives a probability measure that vanishes on every Baire set disjoint from ext K. The Krein-Milman theorem, that K is the closed convex hull of ext K, is the qualitative counterpart. Uniqueness of the representing measure for every x characterises the Choquet simplices.
K compact and convex in a locally convex Hausdorff space
K metrizable for the measure to live on ext K itself

body: The transitive closure of a set x, denoted \mathrm{TC}(x), is the unique smallest transitive set containing x as a subset. It is given by \mathrm{TC}(x) = \bigcup_{n < \omega} x_n, where x_0 = x and x_{n+1} = \bigcup x_n.

[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2609.02444, 'The Hasse norm principle for $A_4$-quartic extensions of global function fields'] Let $K/k$ be an $A_4$-quartic, 
i.e.\ a quartic extension whose normal closure $L/k$ has Galois group $A_4$. Then the Hasse norm principle holds for $K/k$ if and only if there exists a place $v$ of $k$ whose decomposition group $D_v\subset A_4$ contains a copy of $V_4$.

OWNER RESULT DRAFT, proof (unaudited), C007 v1; no novelty claim.
Let a fixed zero-mean finite-rank Gaussian process have a supplied feature map phi with ||phi(x)||<=R, independent Gaussian observation noise of variance s>0, and at most n context observations. All context/query input locations and context length are jointly independent of the GP and all noises. Context labels may be correlated and are not bounded or conditioned. Put V=s+R^2. Given the full original context W, let P_W=N(m,v) be the exact noisy posterior predictive. Clip each context label to [-B,B], B>0, and recompute the mean m_B with the same design; v is unchanged. Suppose a Gaussian predictor h_B=N(mhat,vhat), depending only on clipped context and supplied features, has vhat>=s and KL(N(m_B,v)||h_B)<=eps_c for every possible context and design. Then on the ORIGINAL unconditioned task law,
E_W KL(P_W||h_B) <= 2 eps_c + (2 sqrt(2) n^2 R^4 V/s^3) exp(-B^2/(4V)).
In particular, for eps>0, eps_c=eps/4 and B=sqrt(4V log(max(e,4 sqrt(2) n^2 R^4 V/(s^3 eps)))) make the expected KL at most eps. If nR=0 the bias is zero. This does not assert that N(m_B,v) is the conditional law given clipped labels. The supplied-feature comparator exists by the separately audited C002 construction; this clipping lemma itself awaits independent review.
Zero-mean fixed finite-rank GP, supplied feature norms <=R, independent Gaussian noise variance s>0
At most n context labels; all input locations and context length jointly independent of latent GP and noises; iid tasks
Full original posterior is the target; only the predictor clips context labels at the explicit deterministic B

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:a250ad9398f1c4933949faa963228203bbd7e06273ae41e4c3b12a15bddf5155","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/a2/a250ad9398f1c4933949faa963228203bbd7e06273ae41e4c3b12a15bddf5155.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:6e69c763cd0e656f01ac2e4370a7dfcabc4e0f0adc984422a40d12b0be364059","bundle_entry_key":"t336-w727-c007-clipping","bundle_id":"population.w727-t336-gp-context-clipping-004","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian process predictive approximation; context truncation","draft":"w727/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.transformers:draft-t336-w727-c007-gp-context-clipping-kl","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C007: ERM on the original, unconditioned GP task law

Claim T336-w727-C007 v1. Kind: bound. Target: none (the reviewer-authorized
generalization continuation). Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty is claimed.
The hardest step is retaining the original conditional target after clipping
the observed context. The comparison below keeps that target unchanged.

## 1. Task law and clipping comparator

Fix a zero-mean finite-rank GP with supplied feature map phi into R^p,
k(x,x')=<phi(x),phi(x')>, ||phi(x)||<=R, and independent observation
noise of variance s>0. Each task has at most n context observations and one
query observation. The joint law of all input locations and the context
length is independent of the latent GP and all observation noises. Locations
within a task need not be independent. Tasks are iid, with fresh GP/noise
draws. Write W for the FULL context labels, locations and query location.
Thus P_W, the query law given W, is the exact Gaussian posterior predictive.
No label-based selection, rejection, or conditioning of tasks is made.

Put V=s+R^2. Conditional on the input design alone, every observed label
is centered Gaussian of variance at most V. The context labels can be
correlated. Given W, the posterior variance v is in [s,V].

For B>0, replace each context label y_i by c_B(y_i)=max(-B,min(B,y_i)).
Let m and m_B be the posterior means computed from the original and clipped
labels. Their computed predictive variances are the same v, since that
variance depends only on the input design. The Gaussian N(m_B,v) is an
auxiliary predictive; it is NOT asserted to be the conditional law given
clipped labels.

Set A=s I_p+sum_i phi_i phi_i^T. The coefficient of y_i in the predictive
mean is phi_*^T A^{-1} phi_i, whose absolute value is at most R^2/s.
For r_i=y_i-c_B(y_i), Cauchy-Schwarz therefore gives, for any context
length l<=n,

    |m-m_B|^2 <= (R^4/s^2) l sum_i r_i^2.                 (1)

For a centered Gaussian G of variance tau<=V,

    E[G^2 exp(G^2/(4V))]
       = tau (1-tau/(2V))^(-3/2) <= 2 sqrt(2) V.

This follows by differentiating the elementary Gaussian square-mgf;
it also holds for tau=0. Since r_i^2<=y_i^2 1{|y_i|>B}, conditioning
on the design and then averaging yields

    E|m-m_B|^2 <= 2 sqrt(2) n^2 R^4 V/s^2
                         * exp(-B^2/(4V)).              (2)

Only a sum of marginal expectations was used, not independence of labels.

Apply the independently checked C002 v1 construction to clipped context
labels with its pointwise accuracy eps_c>0. Let its output be
h_B=N(mhat,vhat), with vhat>=s. Pointwise in every full W, C002 gives

    KL(N(m_B,v) || h_B) <= eps_c.

The variance part d_v=(log(vhat/v)+v/vhat-1)/2 is nonnegative. Splitting
m-mhat=(m-m_B)+(m_B-mhat) and using (a+b)^2<=2a^2+2b^2 gives

    KL(P_W || h_B) <= 2 KL(N(m_B,v) || h_B)+(m-m_B)^2/s.

Consequently, on the ORIGINAL task law,

    E_W KL(P_W || h_B) <= 2 eps_c+Ctail exp(-B^2/(4V)),
    Ctail=2 sqrt(2) n^2 R^4 V/s^3.                       (3)

For any eps>0 choose

    eps_c=eps/4,
    B=sqrt(4V log(max(e,2 Ctail/eps))).                  (4)

Then (3) is at most eps. This formula also makes sense when Ctail=0:
the bias vanishes. If R=0 or n=0, the exact constant predictive N(0,v)
can alternatively be used. body:
Let n>=2, K>=2 and d>=1. Let each f_i:R^d->R be convex C1 with globally L_i-Lipschitz gradient, L_i>0. Let psi:R^d->R union {+infinity} be proper closed convex. Set f=(1/n)sum_i f_i, F=f+psi, and suppose x* minimizes F with F(x*) finite. Start at x_1 in dom psi. Write D=||x_1-x*||, Lbar=(1/n)sum_i L_i, Lmax=max_i L_i, s=1+log K, sigma_any^2=(1/n)sum_i ||grad f_i(x*)||^2 and sigma_rand^2=sigma_any^2+n||grad f(x*)||^2. Use a fixed positive step eta<=1/[4n sqrt(2 Lbar Lmax s)]. In epoch k, set z_0=x_k, take z_i=z_(i-1)-eta grad f_(sigma_i)(z_(i-1)) for i=1,...,n along a permutation sigma, and set x_(k+1)=prox_(n eta psi)(z_n), where prox_(n eta psi)(z) minimizes psi(x)+||x-z||^2/(2n eta). There is an absolute constant C such that, for every sequence of permutations, F(x_(K+1))-F(x*)<=C[D^2/(n eta K)+(n eta)^2 Lbar sigma_any^2 s]. If fresh independent uniform permutations are used in each epoch, E[F(x_(K+1))-F(x*)]<=C[D^2/(n eta K)+n eta^2 Lbar sigma_rand^2 s]. These are bounds for the last epoch iterate, with no strong-convexity assumption. For D>0, balancing eta under the stated cap gives respectively O(D^2 sqrt(Lbar Lmax s)/K+D^(4/3)(Lbar sigma_any^2 s)^(1/3)/K^(2/3)) and O(D^2 sqrt(Lbar Lmax s)/K+D^(4/3)(Lbar sigma_rand^2 s)^(1/3)/(n^(1/3) K^(2/3))). The fixed-step bounds also cover D=0. All norms are Euclidean. Source: Zijian Liu and Zhengyuan Zhou, On the Last-Iterate Convergence of Shuffling Gradient Methods, Theorem 4.4 and its full version Theorem C.1.
Finite-dimensional Euclidean space; n>=2 components and K>=2 epochs
Convex C1 f_i with globally L_i-Lipschitz gradients, L_i>0
Proper closed convex psi and an attained finite minimum of F=f+psi
x_1 is in dom psi; eta is constant, positive, and satisfies the displayed K-dependent cap
For the expected random-reshuffling bound, use fresh independent uniform permutations
For the optimized-rate corollaries assume D>0; the fixed-step inequalities do not require D>0

body: [Definition 3.2 (δ-hyperbolic (Gromov, 1987) of arXiv:2606.10238, 'Hyperbolic Neural Population Geometry Benefits Computation'] A geodesic metric space (X , d) is δ-hyperbolic if every geodesic triangle in X is δ-thin. Equivalently for all x, y, z, w ∈X , d(x, z) + d(y, w) ≤ (3.1) max {d(x, y) + d(z, w), d(y, z) + d(x, w)} + 2δ, which is called the 4-point condition. In general, low δ means the geodesic metric space is more tree-like, as tree triangles (Chiswell, 2001) are 0-hyperbolic.
title: Definition 3.2 (δ-hyperbolic (Gromov, 1987) of arXiv:2606.10238: Hyperbolic Neural Population Geometry Benefits Computation

body: Exact rank three for the bounded-density conjecture: what is proved and what is open. (1) The step 'a rank-three coarea bound ||p_S||_inf <= K ||rho||_inf^{2/3} for S = sum_{j<=3} lambda_j Y_j^2' is false for general bounded densities rho on R^3: a density rho <= B that puts mass 2hB A(s) on the shell {|S - s| < h} gives p_S about B A(s) near s, where A(s) = d/ds vol{S <= s} = 2 pi s^{1/2}/sqrt(lambda_1 lambda_2 lambda_3) for a definite form, unbounded as s grows; a bound needs regularity of rho beyond its supremum. (2) Orthonormal 3D projections of product densities have that regularity on spheres: their spherical means satisfy M_{y0}(r) <= 6/(pi r) uniformly in the centre, and definite rank-three forms have density <= 82 for every linear term. (3) The marginal bound is sharp and law-free: the projection onto a k-dimensional subspace of a vector with independent coordinates of densities <= 1 has density <= min{(n/(n-k))^{(n-k)/2}, 2^{k/2}} (Livshyts, Paouris and Pivovarov 2016); Ball's cube slicing is the uniform case and Rudelson-Vershynin give (CK)^d with an unspecified absolute C. (4) Indefinite exact rank three is bounded with any c-pivot, when every leverage is at most 1/2 (<= 12), for a leak-free hub with the linear term in the range (<= 278), and for a leaking hub with a spread light frame up to a factor log(1/eps); the no-pivot indefinite case with a hub (a hub plus a small cross term) is open and is the single-hub core of the general conjecture.

Random variables X_n converge in distribution to X if and only if their characteristic functions converge pointwise, phi_{X_n}(t) -> phi_X(t) for every t. More usefully: if phi_{X_n}(t) -> psi(t) pointwise and psi is continuous at t = 0, then psi is the characteristic function of some random variable X and X_n -> X in distribution. This is the engine that turns the characteristic-function computation in the Central Limit Theorem into convergence in distribution.

Let f: [t_0-a,t_0+a] x B(y_0,b) -> R^n be continuous, where B(y_0,b) subset R^n is the closed ball of radius b around y_0, and suppose f is Lipschitz in its second argument uniformly in the first: there is L >= 0 with |f(t,y_1)-f(t,y_2)| <= L|y_1-y_2| for all t in the interval and y_1,y_2 in B(y_0,b). Let M = max|f(t,y)| over this compact domain and h = min(a, b/M). Then the initial value problem y'(t) = f(t,y(t)), y(t_0)=y_0, has a unique solution y on [t_0-h, t_0+h]. (When M = 0, read b/M as infinity, so h = a.) Continuity alone does not give uniqueness: y' = 2 sqrt(|y|), y(0) = 0 has infinitely many solutions. If f is continuous and locally Lipschitz in y on an open domain D, the local solutions through (t_0, y_0) patch together into a unique maximal solution, which leaves every compact subset of D as t approaches either end of its interval.

body:
[Lemma Lem:pathcounting of arXiv:2411.13030, 'Classification of the limit shape for 1+1-dimensional FPP'] Given integers  $M \ge k \ge 1$, let $S(M,k)$  be the number of distinct $k$-tuples $(a_1,...,a_k)$ of integers whose absolute values sum up to $M$. We then have that
\[
S(M,k)= \sum_{\rho=0}^{M-1} \binom{k}{\rho}\binom{M-1}{\rho}2^{\rho}+\binom{k}{M}2^{M}
\]

body: Corollary 5. Let t >= 2 be an integer and G = {G_i | i in [1, t]} be a multiset of simple graphs of order at least 2. Then we have the following. (i) If G_j is discrete for some j in [1, t], then r(G) = min{|V(G_i)| | G_i is discrete and i in [1, t]}. (ii) If G_1, ..., G_t are non-discrete graphs and r(G_{I_00}) = r(G) - 1, then r(G) = max{|V(G_j)| | delta(G_j) = 0 and j in [1, t]} > max{|V(G_j)| | delta(G_j) >= 1 and j in [1, t]}. Here r(G) = r(G_1, ..., G_t) is the multicolour Ramsey number; a graph is discrete if chi(G) = 1, that is, if it has no edges; delta is the minimum degree; I_0 := {i in [1, t] | delta(G_i) = 0} and I_00 := {i in I_0 | |V(G_i)| = r(G)}; and for J in [1, t] the paper's multiset G'_J replaces G_i, for i in J, by G_i with one isolated vertex removed (by G_i itself when delta(G_i) >= 1).

body: For a sign fibre A subset {+-1}^r the entropy defect is ell(A) = r - log_2|A|. d_cb(A) is the minimum signed-selector residual rank after optimizing over ALL coordinate bases drawn from the full dual of A: pick a coordinate basis, pick for each full-dual form a signed basis selector, require all assignment residuals to lie in one common space R, and minimize dim R over basis and selector choices. Notes: S6 uses ell and d_cb throughout without re-deriving them; the quantifier 'optimizing over all coordinate bases in the full dual' is the load-bearing part (it is what makes d_cb weaker than a fixed-basis d(H)).

body:
[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2609.02017, 'Optimal girth-dependent bounds for the Bethe approximation of the permanent'] Let $G=(L\sqcup R,E)$ be a bipartite graph of girth at least $g$, with
$|L|=|R|=n$. Let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on the perfect
matchings of $G$, and let $
  p_e:=\P_{M\sim\mu}(e\in M)$, $\bs{p}:=(p_e)_{e\in E}$.
Then
\[
  H(\mu)\leq\Phi_G(\bs{p}).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  H(\mu)-H_{\mr B}(\bs{p})
  \leq\frac2g\sum_{v\in V}F(\bs{p}_v).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 11 of arXiv:2609.02017

Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). Given that the long-only gain is the estimation variance the constraint removes at the rows the stack is scored on, the amount of constraint was chosen with the evaluation inputs: a blend w(t) between the simplex and least-squares stacks with t minimising the cross-validated calibration error plus the excess bootstrap variance of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows, and a per-row version t_i = 1/(1 + kappa v_i/median v) that leans to the simplex where least squares is uncertain. P24 (a) HELD: on EMIT the per-cell blend reads +0.08 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 39 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 t* is at or above 0.5 on 30 of 30 cells and the blend reads +0.66 vs least squares; (c) REFUTED: the per-row blend vs the per-cell blend is +0.70 on Y2 and -0.14 on EMIT overall; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P25, split C, SPLIT_SEED 11, the criterion uses no evaluation targets): P25 (a) HELD: on split C the EMIT blend reads +0.63 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 35 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend reads +0.84 vs the simplex (wins 30 of 30) and +0.65 vs least squares; (c) HELD: t* averages 0.34 on EMIT and 0.67 on OCO-2; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Bootstrap-size stability (P28, B = 16 against B = 8 on split B): P28 (a) HELD: t*(16) equals t*(8) on 86 pct of the 70 cells and is within 0.2 on 100 pct; (b) HELD: the blend's mean gain against the simplex moves from +0.08 to +0.06 on EMIT and from +0.83 to +0.83 on OCO-2, and the both-endpoints win count on OCO-2 is 30 of 30 at B = 16; falsifier (agreement below 50 pct or a gain moving by more than 0.5) not triggered. Break test: a fixed midpoint t = 0.5 matches the criterion on OCO-2 (+0.96 / +1.01 against +0.83 / +0.84 on the two splits) but loses 1.6 and 4.4 pct on EMIT where the criterion stays at +0.08 and +0.63 - the criterion's value is knowing, without labels, when not to leave the simplex; the EMIT shortfall against the hindsight-best t is the bias-shift term of the risk identity. Scarce calibration (P30, 240 of the calibration rows per cell, split B): P30 (a) HELD: at n = 240 the simplex beats least squares by +14.10 on EMIT (full calibration +8.83); (b) REFUTED: t* averages 0.22 on EMIT and the blend reads -2.61 vs the simplex; (c) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells and the simplex reads +2.27 vs least squares (full calibration -0.18); falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT) TRIGGERED. The observable part of the bias shift (P31): adding t^2 (D_ev - D_cal), the shift in the two bases' mean squared disagreement between the evaluation and calibration rows, to the criterion - P31 (a) REFUTED: the R'-blend reads -0.71 vs the simplex on EMIT split B (R-blend +0.08) and +0.71 on split C (R-blend +0.63); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the R'-blend is -0.11 vs the R-blend on split B and -0.12 on split C; (c) REFUTED: mean t** 0.39 against t* 0.33 on EMIT, share of the hindsight optimum 0.07 -> -0.62; falsifier (R'-blend worse than the R-blend by more than 0.3 on any corpus or split) TRIGGERED. Per-output mixing weights (P34, the criterion decoupled across outputs): P34 (a) REFUTED: the per-output blend reads -0.41 vs the per-cell blend on EMIT split B and -0.53 on split C; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 -0.02 and -0.08 on split C; (c) REFUTED: on Y2 the share of outputs at t_d = 0 is 0.20 and at t_d >= 0.5 is 0.34; falsifier (per-output worse than per-cell by more than 0.3 anywhere) TRIGGERED. A nearest-neighbour proxy for the bias shift (P35, the simplex's out-of-fold residuals at the nearest calibration rows standing in for its bias at the scored rows): P35 (a) REFUTED: the full-shift blend reads -0.69 vs the R-blend on EMIT split B and -0.12 on split C; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 -0.08 and -0.14 on split C; (c) REFUTED: cross-only vs full on EMIT -0.05 vs -0.62 (split B); falsifier (either variant worse than the R-blend by more than 0.3 anywhere) TRIGGERED. Scarce calibration, the ratio-metric criterion (P41, 240 calibration rows, split B, three-vertex form, registered and R_1 choices side by side): P41 (a) HELD: at n_cal = 240 the R_1 blend reads +1.17 vs the simplex on EMIT (within 1.0; the registered three-vertex blend reads -1.83); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the R_1 blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells (at least 25); (c) HELD: R_1 vs the registered blend on EMIT +1.38 (at least +1.0); falsifier (R_1 worse than the simplex by more than 2.0 on EMIT) not triggered. So the P30 caveat is confined to the squared-loss criterion; the criterion in the score's own metric keeps the simplex where it should at scarce calibration. P44: the shipped tool against the driver (P44): P44 (a) REFUTED: the tool's mixing weight is within 0.2 of the driver's on 14 (squared) and 11 (ratio) of 14 cells; (b) HELD: the tool's blend scores within 1 pct of the driver's on 12 / 12 of 14; (c) HELD by the clause's wording (worse than both endpoints by more than 1 pct while the driver beats one: none); under the stricter test the analyzer was first written with (worse than the better endpoint by more than 1 pct): one cell, emit s102 Y3 (ratio); falsifier not triggered by the clause's wording, TRIGGERED under the stricter test. P55: the seed-102 diagnostic (P55): P55 (a) REFUTED: with the target norms at the scored rows the tool's ratio choice is within 0.2 of the driver's on 0 of 3 cells; (b) REFUTED: with the shipped convention at B = 32 on 2 of 3 (at most one); (c) REFUTED: on Y3 arm A stays at the least-squares endpoint; falsifier TRIGGERED (the draw decides - raise B before the ratio metric is the default). P49: scarce calibration on the held-out split (P49): P49 (a) HELD: on split D at 240 rows the R_1 blend reads +0.56 vs the simplex on EMIT (within 1.0; the registered blend -0.52); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 it beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells; (c) HELD: R_1 vs the registered blend on EMIT +1.00 (at least +1.0); falsifier (R_1 worse than the simplex by more than 2.0 on EMIT) not triggered.

body: In commutative algebra and algebraic geometry, localization is a formal way to introduce the "denominators" to a given ring or module. That is, it introduces a new ring/module out of an existing ring/module R, so that it consists of fractions ${\frac {m}{s}},$ such that the denominator s belongs to a given subset S of R. If S is the set of the non-zero elements of an integral domain, then the localization is the field of fractions: this case generalizes the construction of the field $\mathbb {Q}$ of rational numbers from the ring $\mathbb {Z}$ of integers.

body:
[Theo 22 (Explicit threshold, compact-support branch and onset amplitude) of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Let $0<\alpha<1$ and $n\ge2$. Consider the problem
\[
\begin{cases}
	-u''=\lambda u+m_n(x)u^\alpha,& -1<x<1,\\
	u(-1)=u(1)=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Define
\[
\lambda_{c,n}:=
\frac{\pi^2}
{\left((1-\alpha)+\dfrac{1+\alpha}{n}\right)^2}.
\]
Then
\[
\frac{\pi^2}{4}
<
\lambda_{c,n}
<
\lambda_n^*.
\]
At $\lambda=\lambda_{c,n}$ there exists an even positive flat solution
$u_{c,n}$ satisfying $u_{c,n}(\pm1)=u_{c,n}'(\pm1)=0$. For every
$\lambda\in(\lambda_{c,n},\lambda_n^*)$ there exists a unique even
non-negative solution in the above class whose connected support is
\[
\operatorname{supp}u_{\lambda,n}
=
[-b_{\lambda,n},b_{\lambda,n}]
\Subset(-1,1),
\]
where
\[
b_{\lambda,n}
=
\frac{1}{1-\alpha}
\left(
\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{\lambda}}
-\frac{1+\alpha}{n}
\right).
\]
For $x\ge0$ the solution is
\[
u_{\lambda,n}(x)
=
\begin{cases}
	A_{\lambda,n}\cos(\sqrt{\lambda}\,x),
	& 0\le x\le\dfrac1n,\\[2mm]
	\displaystyle
	\left(
	\frac{2}{(1+\alpha)\lambda}
	\right)^{\frac1{1-\alpha}}
	\sin^{\frac{2}{1-\alpha}}
	\left[
	\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\sqrt{\lambda}\,
	(b_{\lambda,n}-x)
	\right],
	& \dfrac1n\le x\le b_{\lambda,n},\\[3mm]
	0,
	& b_{\lambda,n}\le x\le1,
\end{cases}
\]
and it is extended evenly to $(-1,0)$. Moreover,
\[
A_{\lambda,n}
=
\|u_{\lambda,n}\|_{L^\infty(-1,1)}
=
\left(
\frac{2}{(1+\alpha)\lambda}
\right)^{\frac1{1-\alpha}}
\cos^{\frac{1+\alpha}{1-\alpha}}
\left(\frac{\sqrt{\lambda}}{n}\right).
\]
For each fixed $n$, the mapping $\lambda\longmapsto A_{\lambda,n}$
is strictly decreasing on $(\lambda_{c,n},\lambda_n^*)$, and
$A_{\lambda,n}\longrightarrow0\hbox{ as }\lambda\uparrow\lambda_n^*$. If
\[
A_n:=\|u_{c,n}\|_{L^\infty(-1,1)},
\]
then
\[
A_n=
\left[
\frac{2}{(1+\alpha)\pi^2}
\left(
(1-\alpha)+\frac{1+\alpha}{n}
\right)^2
\right]^{\frac1{1-\alpha}}
\cos^{\frac{1+\alpha}{1-\alpha}}
\left(
\frac{\pi}{n(1-\alpha)+(1+\alpha)}
\right),
\]
and
\[
\lambda_{c,n}\uparrow
\lambda_{c,\infty}:=
\frac{\pi^2}{(1-\alpha)^2},
\]
while
\[
A_n\longrightarrow
A_\infty:=
\left[
\frac{2(1-\alpha)^2}
{(1+\alpha)\pi^2}
\right]^{\frac1{1-\alpha}}
>0.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\frac{\lambda_{c,n}}{\lambda_n^*}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Moreover, $H_\lambda(u_{\lambda,n})=M_n(u_{\lambda,n})<0$, and therefore
$E_\lambda(u_{\lambda,n})>0,\ E_\lambda''(u_{\lambda,n})<0$. Thus, these
explicit solutions have the variational character of the
branch $u_{\lambda,n}^-$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Explicit threshold, compact-support branch and onset amplitude

[Theorem Voiculescu of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $A_1 = U_1 \text{} \ensuremath{\operatorname{diag}} (a^{(1)}_1, \ldots,
  a^{(1)}_N) U_1^{\ast}$ and $A_2 = U_2 \ensuremath{\operatorname{diag}} (a^{(2)}_1, \ldots,
  a^{(2)}_N) U_2^{\ast}$ be Hermitian random matrices of size $N$, where $U_1,
  U_2$ are chosen independently at random with respect to the Haar measure
  on the unitary group $U (N)$ and $\{ a_i^{(j)} \}_{i, j}$ are fixed and such
  that for $j = 1, 2$ the empirical distribution of $A_j$ converges weakly to
  a probability measure $\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_j$. Then the random empirical
  distribution of $A_1 + A_2$ converges weakly, in probability to a
  deterministic probability measure $\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_1 \boxplus
  \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_2$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Voiculescu

body:
[Theorem thm:scaled-murmuration of arXiv:2609.00777, 'Universal murmuration and Hecke augmentation'] Let $k\geq 2$ be fixed.  Let $P\neq 2$ be a prime, and suppose that $P$, $X$, and $Y$ tend to infinity.
Assume that
\[
Y=(1+o(1))X^{1-\delta_1},
\qquad
P^k\ll X^{1+\delta_2},
\]
where
\[
0<2\delta_2<\delta_1<\frac18,
\qquad
(k-1)\delta_2<1.
\]
Put
\[
\eta=\frac{\delta_1}{2}-\delta_2,
\qquad
y=\frac{P^k}{X}.
\]
Let
\[
A=\prod_p\left(1+\frac{p}{(p+1)^2(p-1)}\right),
\]
\[
B=\prod_p\left(1-\frac{p}{(p^2-1)^2}\right),
\]
and
\[
C(r)=\prod_{p\mid r}
\left(1+\frac{p^2}{p^4-2p^2-p+1}\right).
\]
Then, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
\begin{multline*}
\frac{
\displaystyle
\sideset{}{'}\sum_{N\in[X,X+Y]}
\ \sum_{f\in H_{\mathrm{new}}(N)}
P^{k/2}\lambda_{\operatorname{sym}^k f}(P)\,\varepsilon(f)
}{
\displaystyle
\sideset{}{'}\sum_{N\in[X,X+Y]}
\ \sum_{f\in H_{\mathrm{new}}(N)}1
}
\\
=
\frac{12}{\pi D_0}
\left(
A\sqrt y
+
B\sum_{1\leq r\leq 2\sqrt y}
C(r)\sqrt{4y-r^2}
-\pi y
\right)
+
O_{k,\varepsilon}\left(
X^{-\eta+\varepsilon}
+X^\varepsilon\frac{\sqrt y}{P}
+\frac{1+y}{P}
\right).
\end{multline*}
Here the prime indicates that the sum is restricted to squarefree integers $N$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:scaled-murmuration of arXiv:2609.00777
Green‘s function comparison theorem at the edge

body:
Let (M_n) be a martingale with respect to a filtration (F_n) and let tau be a stopping time for the same filtration. Then E[M_tau] = E[M_0] under any one of the sufficient conditions: (a) tau is bounded; (b) tau is almost surely finite and (M_n) is uniformly bounded; (c) E[tau] < infinity and the increments |M_n - M_{n-1}| are uniformly bounded. For a submartingale the equality becomes E[M_tau] >= E[M_0] (and <= for a supermartingale). Some integrability condition is essential - without one the martingale of a simple symmetric random walk stopped at first hitting of +1 has E[M_tau]=1 != 0.
(M_n) a martingale for (F_n)
tau a stopping time
one of the sufficient integrability conditions (a)/(b)/(c)

Let $u(t, x)$ be the mild solution to a stochastic partial differential equation (such as the stochastic heat equation $\partial_t u = \frac{1}{2} \Delta u + \sigma(u) \dot{W}$ or stochastic wave equation) driven by space-time white noise $\dot{W}$ on $\mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}^d$. For a non-linear test function $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ and an expanding domain $B_R = [-R, R]^d$, the spatial statistic is $S_R(t) := \frac{1}{R^{d/2}} \int_{B_R} (g(u(t, x)) - \mathbb{E}[g(u(t, x))]) \mathrm{d}x$. Viewed as a function of time $t \in [0, T]$, $S_R$ is a random element of $K = L^2([0, T])$.
u is a mild solution of an SPDE driven by space-time white noise
B_R = [-R, R]^d is the spatial domain
K = L^2([0, T])
title: Spatial Statistics Functional for Stochastic PDEs

eigenvalues.  The family $(\Lambda_{n_i}^\mu)_{i=1}^M$ is called
\emph{response-transverse} if its response functionals in
(equation eq:abstract-response-functionals-Q of the paper) are linearly independent on
$\mathcal Q$.  Equivalently, for real $a_1,\ldots,a_M$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{i=1}^Ma_i\ell_{n_i}^\mu(q)=0
 \quad\text{for every }q\in\mathcal Q
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_1=\cdots=a_M=0.
 
\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:abstract-coherent-fiber of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] Let
\[
 H_N:=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_N\}\subsetH_{\mathrm{reg}},
\]
where $e_1,\ldots,e_N$ are linearly independent.  Put
$v_t:=\sum_{k=1}^Nt_ke_k$, and let
$t(x)$, $x^\perp$, and $\mathbb P_{H_N}^\perp$ be the corresponding slice
objects from (equation eq:abstract-slice-coordinates of the paper) and
Lemma~(lem:abstract-gaussian-disintegration of the paper).  Let
$\Omega_0\in\mathcal B(X)$ satisfy
$\Omega_0\subset\Omega_{\rm can}$ and $\mathbb P(\Omega_0)=1$; in the
applications below, $\Omega_0=\Omega_{\rm str}$.
For $\mathbb P_{H_N}^\perp$-almost every $x^\perp$, the set
\begin{equation}
 T_0(x^\perp)
 :=\{t\in\mathbb R^N:x^\perp+v_t\in\Omega_0\}
 
\end{equation}
satisfies
\[
 T_0(x^\perp)\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^N),
 \qquad
 \mathcal L^N(\mathbb R^N\setminus T_0(x^\perp))=0.
\]
For such $x^\perp$ and any
$s\in T_0(x^\perp)$, define
\begin{equation}
 \mu_t^{\rm coh}
 :=e^{\kappa(v_t-v_s)}\mu_{x^\perp+v_s},
 \qquad t\in\mathbb R^N.
 
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{align}
 d\mu_t^{\rm coh}
 &=e^{\kappa(v_t-v_r)}\,d\mu_r^{\rm coh},
 &&r,t\in\mathbb R^N,
 \\
 \mu_t^{\rm coh}
 &=\mu_{x^\perp+v_t},
 &&t\in T_0(x^\perp).
 
\end{align}
If $\Omega_0\subset\Omega_{\rm str}$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mu_t^{\rm coh}\in\mathcal M_{\rm adm},
 \qquad t\in\mathbb R^N.
 
\end{equation}

Let (X,d) be a compact metric space and T : X -> X continuous. Define the Bowen metric d_n(x,y) = max over 0 <= k < n of d(T^k x, T^k y). A set E is (n, eps)-SEPARATED if distinct points of E are at d_n-distance greater than eps; a set F is (n, eps)-SPANNING if every point of X is within d_n-distance eps of some point of F. Let s(n,eps) be the largest cardinality of an (n,eps)-separated set and r(n,eps) the smallest cardinality of an (n,eps)-spanning set. Then the topological entropy is h_top(T) = lim as eps -> 0 of limsup_n (1/n) log s(n,eps) = lim as eps -> 0 of limsup_n (1/n) log r(n,eps), and this agrees with the open-cover definition of Adler, Konheim and McAndrew. The quantity does not depend on the metric, only on the topology, and is invariant under topological conjugacy.
X compact, T continuous.
The two limits in eps are monotone so they exist in [0, infinity];
separated and spanning counts interleave by r(n,eps) <= s(n,eps) <= r(n, eps/2), which is why the two definitions agree.
title: Bowen-Dinaburg definition of topological entropy by spanning and separated sets

Let d>k>=2, y be a k-parity, and independent online x have law (1-rho) uniform signs plus rho product signs of mean mu. For f=m^(-1)sum a_r ReLU(w_r dot x+b_r), use exact simultaneous hinge-SGD with common step eta, h=eta/m, no neuron-specific randomness. Both initial groups a=+/-1/4 must be nonempty, with w=0,b=1/4. Each group stays internally identical. Group masses p,1-p enter f and its hinge indicator, but the per-neuron step remains h, not eta p. In the all-active regime hT(d+1)<=1/8, set A=(a_plus+a_minus)/2,D=(a_plus-a_minus)/2,U=(u_plus+u_minus)/2,V=(u_plus-u_minus)/2,u=(w,b),z=(x,1). Exact sample increments are Delta A=h y U dot z, Delta U=h y A z, Delta D=h y V dot z, Delta V=h y D z. With v=E[yz], conditional drifts replace yz by v without factorizing any state products. D has zero sample increment initially, so common output noise cancels from it at that step. Pathwise 3/14<=D<=2/7 gives support-ordering failure probability at most k(d-k)exp(-9Tg^2/128) for V, g=rho mu^(k-1)(1-mu^2). The predictor remains affine only in this regime: beta=p a_plus u_plus+(1-p)a_minus u_minus, H=p(u_plus u_plus^T+a_plus^2 I)+(1-p)(u_minus u_minus^T+a_minus^2 I), M=E[zz^T]. Its exact conditional drift is h H v+h^2 M beta; the second-order term comes from simultaneous multiplication of parameter increments. Full gated equations and exact polynomial formulas for the unconditional means of A,D,U,V are in proofs/two_group_drift.md. Means of beta cannot be obtained by multiplying those state means. Numerical evidence is limited to finite exact checks; final parity fitting after gate changes is open. Lean returned runtime UNVERIFIED, so no formal certificate exists.

[Proposition 14 of arXiv:2608.15874, '2608.15874'] Let $X$ have distribution
\[
  \P{X=2}=\P{X=-2}=\frac1{36},\qquad \P{X=0}=\frac{17}{18}.
\]
Then $X$ is centred with $v:=\E X^2=2/9$, and satisfies the two-sided sub-Poisson condition with variance proxy $v$:
\[
  \log\E e^{sX}=\log\E e^{-sX}\leq v\psi_h(s),\qquad s\geq0.
\]
It therefore also satisfies the two-sided sub-gamma condition with the same variance proxy:
\[
  \log\E e^{sX}=\log\E e^{-sX}\leq v\psi_b(s),\qquad 0\leq s<3.
\]
Moreover, for each $f\in\curlyb{h,b}$,
\[
  \E U_\rho^f(X,v)=1+\frac{1}{54\rho^2}+O(\rho^{-3}),\qquad \rho\to\infty,
\]
so $\E U_\rho^f(X,v)>1$ for all sufficiently large $\rho$.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, A Levy random drift destroys compactness for every confining power (2026). Let V be a two-sided semi-selfsimilar Levy process of index alpha in (0,2) and L^{w+V} = (1/2)(Delta - grad(w+V).grad) on L^2(R; e^{-(w+V)} dx), with w_1 = |x|^delta and w_2 = -|x|^delta; the unperturbed semigroups are compact exactly when delta > 1. Shiozawa and Wang (arXiv:2607.07410, Proposition 5.2) proved the perturbed semigroups noncompact for delta <= 1/alpha and left delta > 1/alpha open (their Remark 5.3(ii)). For delta > 1/alpha: if the Levy measure of V on one of the two half-lines charges (-infinity,0), the bottom of the essential spectrum of -L^{w_1+V} is 0 almost surely, and if one charges (0,infinity) the same holds for -L^{w_2+V}; in either case the semigroup is noncompact. If V changes sign and either alpha < 1 or the jumps go both ways (for instance V symmetric), both semigroups are noncompact for every delta > 0. The case alpha in [1,2) with both Levy measures on the same half-line is left open for one of the two operators. The proof uses test functions with disjoint supports around large jumps of V. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/levy-drift-noncompact (commit f3a3d2c42394). Not refereed.
title: A Levy random drift destroys compactness of the diffusion semigroup for every confining power delta > 1/alpha, on a question of Shiozawa and Wang (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/levy-drift-noncompact)

body: Lemma (campaign status: proved): Assume affine spanning and coordinate-full homogenization; put $R=\dim\widehat W=m-2$, $M=m+1$. Then after a linear choice of intrinsic coordinates, $\widehat A_t$ becomes an antipodal spanning subset $A\subset\{\pm1\}^R$ (tag 6) which is full closed and whose projective full dual satisfies $|D(A)|=M=R+3$ (tag 7). Notes: Proof: choose $R$ independent full-dual members as a basis and let $\Phi(w)=(g_1(w),\dots,g_R(w))$ (tag 8), a linear isomorphism mapping $\widehat A_t$ into the intrinsic cube. The $M$ displayed homogenized coordinate forms are projectively distinct (if $\widehat f_i=\pm h$ on $\widehat W$, restriction to $U=\ker h=\ker C\times\{0\}$ would give $f_i=0$ on $\ker C$, contradicting old projective simplicity). Closure: if $y\in\operatorname{cl}(A)$ and $w=\Phi^{-1}(y)$, every displayed coordinate of $w$ is a sign, so $w\in\widehat W\cap\{\pm1\}^M=\widehat A_t$.

For nonempty compact sets A, B in R^n and their Minkowski sum A + B = {a + b}, the n-th roots of volumes satisfy vol(A + B)^{1/n} >= vol(A)^{1/n} + vol(B)^{1/n}, with equality for homothetic convex bodies. ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine the small parameter of the lace expansion and whether a different expansion parameter exists for d in {7,...,10}. Result: The lace expansion converges when the triangle diagram at p_c is small, which for nearest-neighbour percolation is controlled by the random-walk quantities: the triangle at p_c is bounded by a constant times (2d)^{-1} times sum over n of the return probabilities, i.e. by beta_d = O(1/d); the NoBLE refinement replaces 1/d by a numerically computed constant and the bootstrap closes for d >= 11 because the computed bound on the triangle at d = 10 exceeds the threshold. Below d = 11 there is no small parameter: the triangle diagram is of order 1 but finite for d > 6, and finiteness alone does not make the expansion converge; convergence needs smallness. An alternative is to bootstrap from d = 11 downward using a continuous interpolation in the dimension (long-range or spread-out interpolation), but the interpolated models at d = 10 are spread-out models, whose infrared bound is already known, and the interpolation does not return to the nearest-neighbour model at d = 10 without passing through a non-small regime. So the obstruction is structural: the method requires a small parameter and there is none for nearest-neighbour d in {7,...,10}. A rigorous partial statement: the infrared bound holds for the nearest-neighbour model in d in {7,...,10} on any lattice whose triangle diagram at p_c is below the NoBLE threshold, which fails for Z^d but holds for some non-Z^d lattices of higher coordination number (e.g. the body-centred or the D_d-type lattices in d = 7, 8 where the coordination number is larger); I did not verify the threshold numerically for those lattices. Obstruction: No small parameter for nearest-neighbour Z^d with 7 <= d <= 10.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Exact identities, finite controls and structural obstruction Result: Writing J_i=E[eta_i*(1-eta_(i+1))], stationarity of eta_i gives J_(i-1)-J_i=kappa*1_(i=0)*E eta_0. There is also an exact obstruction to any independent Bernoulli invariant law whose site densities r_i all lie strictly between0 and1. For adjacent sites, subtract the derivative of r_i*r_(i+1) from the generator derivative of E[eta_i*eta_(i+1)]. At a product law the covariance derivative equals J_i*(r_(i+1)-r_i), with killing terms cancelling. Stationarity therefore forces all adjacent densities equal. The one-site balance at0 then forces kappa*r_0=0, a contradiction. Check: The internal jump i to i+1 leaves eta_i*eta_(i+1) equal to0 both before and after, whereas it changes the two marginal means by -J_i and +J_i. Incoming and outgoing exterior jumps factor under the product law, giving the displayed covariance derivative. Independent killing at0 contributes the same product term in both expressions and cancels. Obstruction: Thus even a piecewise Bernoulli product with strictly interior densities cannot be the desired invariant law. The source matrix-product approach needs nontrivial correlations and a telescoping identity at the killing defect. Neither this obstruction nor the current-balance equation supplies that identity or classifies the correlated stationary measures.

[Proposition 20 (Girsanov is not tight) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Let $\Prob_{\mathrm{true}}$ and $\Prob_{\mathrm{dir}}$ be the laws of the full and the directed (single-parent-conditioned) systems on a time interval $[0,\tau]$. The Radon--Nikodym density is
\[
\log\frac{d\Prob_{\mathrm{true}}}{d\Prob_{\mathrm{dir}}}=\int_0^\tau\langle b^{-1}\Delta_t,dW_t\rangle-\frac12\int_0^\tau\|b^{-1}\Delta_t\|^2\,dt,
\]
where $\Delta_t=\gamma\,\sigma\big(s^{(v)}_t-\theta_{vu}\big)$ is the back-reaction drift. On the cascade timescale $\|\Delta_t\|=\Theta(1)$ whenever the child is active, so the quadratic-variation term is $\Theta(\tau)$ and the density is not tight toward $1$ as $G_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{BS}}T$. Hence Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red} cannot be obtained by a change of measure showing $d\Prob_{\mathrm{true}}/d\Prob_{\mathrm{dir}}\to1$.

[Definition Def:limit_shape of arXiv:2411.13030, 'Classification of the limit shape for 1+1-dimensional FPP'] For $G\neq \delta_0$ and $0\le \theta \le \frac \pi 2$, we define the curve
\[
\mathcal B(\theta)=\frac 1 {\Lambda(\tan(\theta))\cos(\theta)}.
\]
The \emph{limit shape} $\mathcal B_G$ is the closed area embodied by the four symmetrical copies of the curve $\mathcal B(\theta)e^{i\theta}$, 
$\mathcal B(\theta)e^{-i\theta}, -\mathcal B(\theta)e^{i\theta}, -\mathcal B(\theta)e^{-i\theta}$. The union of the four curves then form the boundary of the limit shape $\partial \mathcal B_G$.

body:
[Prop countlayered of arXiv:2609.03081, 'Non-attacking rook placements on crossword grids'] Suppose $m_1, m_2 > 0$ and let $m = \min(m_1, m_2)$. For the layered permutation $w \in S_n$ of shape $(m_1, 1,1,\dots,1, m_2)$, the number of rook placements on $\operatorname{Grid}(w)$ is given by 
    \[
    \sum_{i = 0}^{m-1} S(m_1, m - i)S(m_2, m - i)\left((m-i)^{n - m_1 - m_2} \cdot (m-i)!\right)^2.
    \]
    In particular, if $m > 1$ then for the layered permutation in $S_n$ of shape $(m,1,1,\dots,1,m)$, the number of rook placements on $\operatorname{Grid}(w)$ is given by 
    \[
    \sum_{k = 1}^m \left[S(m, k) \cdot k^{n-2m} \cdot k!\right]^2.
    \]
title: Prop countlayered of arXiv:2609.03081

[Lemma lem:coupr of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Let $I=\llbracket a,b\rrbracket$ for some $-\infty \le a < b \le \infty$. 
Take real parameters $\gamma_0<\gamma_1$ and $\{\beta_i\}_{i\in I}$, such that $\gamma_0+\beta_i>0$ for each $i\in I$.

Let $\{A_i,B_i\}_{i\in I}$ be independent random variables with
$A_i\sim \operatorname{Gamma}^{-1}(\gamma_0+\beta_i)$, $B_i\sim \operatorname{Gamma}^{-1}(\gamma_1+\beta_i)$.
Similarly, let $\{C_i,D_i\}_{i\in I}$ be independent random variables with
$C_i\sim \operatorname{Gamma}^{-1}(\gamma_1+\beta_i)$, $D_i\sim \operatorname{Gamma}^{-1}(\gamma_0+\beta_i)$.

Then these two families of random variables can be coupled so that almost surely, for any $x\le y\in I$,
\begin{equation}
\sum_{j=x}^y \prod_{i=x}^j A_i \prod_{i=j}^y B_i
=
\sum_{j=x}^y \prod_{i=x}^j C_i \prod_{i=j}^y D_i .
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:coupr of arXiv:2604.10020

Known result, source-bound formulation of Blum-Dick-Manoj-Zhang (2020), Theorem 1.2 and Corollary B.3. Let d>=2, 2<=p<=infinity (1/infinity=0), B>0 and 0<delta<1. Let R_p(B,delta) be the supremum of radii r>=0 for which some fixed Borel probability law D on R^d satisfies E_D||Z||_2^2<=B and TV(D,D+v)<=delta for every v with ||v||_p<=r, with TV(P,Q)=sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|. Then (2*delta/9)*sqrt(B)*d^(1/p-1) <= R_p(B,delta) <= sqrt(800)*delta/sqrt(1-delta)*sqrt(B)*d^(1/p-1). In particular B=d*sigma^2 gives matching dimension exponent d^(1/p-1/2) at fixed delta and sigma. Arbitrary dependence and nonzero means are allowed for the upper bound; the lower construction is isotropic Gaussian. Fixed classifier accuracy alone does not imply the uniform-TV hypothesis. This does not settle input-dependent smoothing certificates.
d>=2 and 2<=p<=infinity
0<delta<1 and B>0
One fixed Borel noise law; uniform TV over every shift in the l_p ball
Uncentered second moment E||Z||_2^2<=B

body: [Prop hahnbanach of arXiv:2605.10908, 'On Talagrand's Convexity Conjecture'] Suppose $A$ is a bounded, symmetric, open subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, and $b, c \in (0, 1)$ satisfy $2b +c < 1$, and are such that $b^{-1}(A+A+A)$ does not contain a symmetric convex body of Gaussian measure at least $c$. [Proposition 5 (Triangular detector response) of arXiv:2609.02788, '\textbf{Quantized Einstein Metrics on \(S^7\) with \(SU(3)\)-Symmetry}'] At the $p_2$ sine cone, the differential of the reflection detector respects
the Weyl splitting.  The odd response contributes at first order only to
$F_1$, and its complex transfer coefficient is nonzero; equivalently, its
real $F_1$-response is a nontrivial sinusoid of the odd phase.  The regular
even mode contributes at first order only to $F_2$, and its transfer
coefficient is positive.  Thus, in parity-adapted coordinates, the response
has nonzero odd transfer and a positive even diagonal entry.

[Lem 4 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any constant $\delta > 0$, there exists $c = c(\alpha, L, \delta) > 0$ such that with probability $1-e^{-cN}$,
    \begin{align}
        
        \bigg|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1\bigg| &\le \delta\,,\\
    
        \bigg|\frac{\E[ \|\hat{\by}\|^2 | \bG]}{N} - 1\bigg| &\le
        \frac{\delta}{2}\,.
    \end{align} 
Moreover, conditional on any realization of $\bG$ satisfying \eqref{e:fp-y-cond-conc} the following holds. Let $\hat{\bx} = N^{1/2} \bar{\bx}  / \|\bar{\bx}\|$ (we set this arbitrarily to $\bone \in \R^N$ if $\bar{\bx} = \bzero$). Let $\bXi'$ be an independent copy of $\bXi$ and $\hat{\by}' = \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi')$. Then
    \beq
        
        \lt|\frac{\|\hat{\by}\|^2}{N} - 1\rt|\,,
        \frac{|(\hat{\bx},\hat{\by})|}{N},
        \frac{|(\hat{\by},\hat{\by}')|}{N} \le \delta
    \eeq
   with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$.

\begin{proof}
    Since $\bG \mapsto \|\bar{\bx}\|$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $\|\bar{\bx}\|$ is $O(1)$-subgaussian by gaussian concentration of measure.
    Combined with $\E \|\bar{\bx}\|^2 = N$ this implies \eqref{e:fp-x-conc}.
    We next argue that the function
    \[
        f(\bG) = \E[ \|\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|^2 | \bG]^{1/2}
    \]
    is also $L$-Lipschitz. Indeed,
    \[
        \nabla f(\bG)
        = \frac{\E[ (\nabla_\bG \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi))(\bG,\bXi) \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi) | \bG]}{\E[ \|\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|^2 | \bG]^{1/2}}\,,
    \]
    and thus
    \[
        \|\nabla f(\bG)\|^2
        = \frac{\|\E[ (\nabla_\bG \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)) \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi) | \bG]\|^2}{\E[ \|\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|^2 | \bG]}
        \le \frac{\E[ \|\nabla_\bG \hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|_\op^2 \|\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|^2 | \bG]}{\E[ \|\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)\|^2 | \bG]}
        \le L^2\,.
    \]
    Thus $\E[ \|\hat{\by}\|^2 | \bG]^{1/2}$ is also $O(1)$-subgaussian.
    Combined with $\E \|\hat{\by}\|^2 = N$ this proves \eqref{e:fp-y-cond-conc}. 
    The first inequality of \eqref{e:fp-y-conc} follows similarly to \eqref{e:fp-x-conc}, applying gaussian concentration on $\bXi$ conditional on $\bG$.
    The second inequality of \eqref{e:fp-y-conc} holds by gaussian concentration because $\bXi \mapsto (\hat{\bx},\hat{\by}) / N$ is $L/N^{1/2}$-Lipschitz and $\E[\hat{\by} | \bG] = \bzero$. 
    The third inequality of \eqref{e:fp-y-conc} follows similarly, conditioning further on a realization of $\hat{\by}$ such that $\|\hat{\by}\| \le 2N^{1/2}$ (which holds with probability $1-e^{-cN}$).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 3 (Radial order-statistic representation) of arXiv:2608.24964, 'Common-Center Geometry and Certified Radial Reconstruction for Energy-Form Full Conformal '] Assume $I_1,\ldots,I_m$ are each star-shaped about the same point $c$.  For
\[
u\in\mathbb S^{d-1},
\]
define
\[
R_j(u)=\sup\{r\ge0:c+ru\in I_j\}\in[0,\infty].
\]
Let
\[
R_{(1)}(u)\le\cdots\le R_{(m)}(u)
\]
be the ascending order statistics.  For $0\le\varepsilon<1$ and
\[
1\le k=\lfloor(m+1)\varepsilon\rfloor\le m,
\]
the radial function of $\Gamma^\varepsilon$ about $c$ is
\[
R_\varepsilon(u)
=
\sup\{r\ge0:c+ru\in\Gamma^\varepsilon\},
\]
and satisfies
\[
R_\varepsilon(u)=R_{(m-k+1)}(u).
\]
If $k=0$, then
\[
\Gamma^\varepsilon=\mathbb R^d,
\qquad
R_\varepsilon(u)=+\infty.
\]
At $\varepsilon=1$, the prediction set is empty.  For the power-distance specialization with $m=1$, one has
\[
I_1=\mathbb R^d,
\qquad
R_1\equiv+\infty.
\]
Thus finite power-distance radial reconstruction begins at $m\ge2$.

Let P be a PRODUCT probability measure on {0,1}^E with E finite (the infinite case follows by approximation). Call f : {0,1}^E -> R increasing if f(omega) <= f(omega') whenever omega_e <= omega'_e for every e. Then for increasing f and g in L^2(P), E[f g] >= E[f] E[g]. In particular, for INCREASING events A and B, P(A and B) >= P(A) P(B), and for two DECREASING events the same inequality holds. For one increasing and one decreasing event the inequality REVERSES: P(A and B) <= P(A) P(B). The hypothesis that both functions are monotone IN THE SAME DIRECTION is the whole content; nothing is claimed for events of mixed or no monotonicity. The result extends beyond product measures to any measure satisfying the FKG LATTICE CONDITION mu(x or y) mu(x and y) >= mu(x) mu(y), which covers the random-cluster and ferromagnetic Ising measures; that extension is the FKG inequality proper, Harris's version being the product case. [Harris (1960); Fortuin, Kasteleyn and Ginibre (1971); see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.4]

[Definition 1 (Extended mapping) of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^n$, let $d\in\mathbb N$,
and let
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\colon \mathbb R^n\to \mathbb R^k$ be a measurable mapping
such that
\[
0<\sigma_{f_j}^2:=\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f_j)<\infty
\quad \forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.
\]
Let
\[
\hat f_j
=
\sigma_{f_j}^{-1}
\biggl(f_j-\int_{\mathbb R^n} f_j\,d\mu\biggr)
\quad \forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\},
\]
and set
$\hat f:=(\hat f_1,\ldots,\hat f_k)$.
Assume also that
\[
\hat f^{\mathbf m}:=\hat f_1^{m_1}\ldots \hat f_k^{m_k}\in L^2(\mu)
\quad \forall \mathbf m=(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\in\mathbb Z_+^k
\quad\text{with}\quad
1\le |\mathbf m|\le d^{k-1}.
\]
We define the \emph{extended mapping} of order $d$ by
\[
F_\mu^d(f)
=
\bigl(\hat f^{\mathbf m}\bigr)_{1\le |\mathbf m|\le d^{k-1}},
\]
and set
\[
\Sigma_\mu^d(f):=\operatorname{Cov}_\mu \bigl(F_\mu^d(f)\bigr).
\]
In other words, $\Sigma_\mu^d(f)$ is the matrix, in the monomial basis, of the quadratic form
\[
Q\mapsto \operatorname{Var}_\mu\bigl(Q(\hat f)\bigr),\quad Q\in\mathcal P_{d^{k-1}}(\mathbb R^k),\quad
Q(0)=0.
\]
title: Extended mapping

body:
Let f be in L^1(mu). For every eps > 0 there exists delta > 0 such that integral_A |f| dmu < eps whenever A is measurable with mu(A) < delta. Equivalently, the finite measure nu(A) = integral_A |f| dmu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu in the strong epsilon-delta sense, not merely in the sense that mu(A) = 0 implies nu(A) = 0. The two senses coincide for FINITE nu but not in general: with mu Lebesgue measure on (0,1) and nu(A) = integral_A dx/x, nu vanishes on mu-null sets yet nu(0, delta) = infinity for every delta. A single integrable function is therefore automatically a uniformly integrable family of one element. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.5]
f in L^1(mu); the conclusion fails for f merely locally integrable with a non-integrable singularity

[Theorem teoBismutLip1 of arXiv:2605.07832, 'A Bismut -Elworthy formula for BSDEs with degenerate noise'] Assume that Hypotheses (hyp:base of the paper), (ip-psiphi-li of the paper) and (hyp:operatorG1 of the paper) and condition (equation link_gat_der_mall_der of the paper) hold true.
Then for every $0\leq s< t\leq T$ and $x,h\in H$ 
we get the following Bismut formula
\begin{align}
\widetilde{\mathbb E}\left[ \langle \nabla_x\,Y^{s,x}_t,h\rangle \right]
= & 
\widetilde{\mathbb E}\int_t^T\psi\left(r,X_r^{s,x},Y_r^{s,x},Z_r^{s,x}\right)
\int_s^r\langle \widetilde u_{h,s,x,r}(\sigma),d\widetilde W_\sigma\rangle_{U}\,dr \notag \\
&+\widetilde{\mathbb E}\displaystyle\int_t^T Z_r\widetilde G(r)^{-1}P\bar B(r,X_r^{s,x})\int_s^r\langle\widetilde u_{h,s,x,r}(\sigma),d\widetilde W_\sigma\rangle_U dr \notag \\
& 
+\widetilde{\mathbb E}\left[  \phi(X_T^{s,x})\int_s^T\langle \widetilde u_{h,s,x,T}(\sigma),d\widetilde W_\sigma\rangle_{U}\right].
\end{align}
Moreover, if $h=Ja$, $a\in U$, then equality (equation Bismut-lip of the paper) holds true also for $t=s$ and there exists a positive constant $C$, which depends on $A,\bar B,\widetilde G,J_1,S,K_\phi,K_\psi,L_\psi$ and $T$, such that
\begin{align}

|\langle \nabla_xY_s^{s,x},Ja\rangle_U|
\leq \frac{C(1+|x|^m)|a|_U}{(T-s)^{\frac12+\beta}}, \qquad s\in[0,T), \ a\in U.
\end{align}

[Definition Tree number of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] The tree number $\tau(C)$
of a component $C$ is defined recursively. 
If $C$ is a TC then $\tau(C)=0$. Otherwise, 
if $C$ is formed by merging some $C_1,\ldots,C_h$
with $H_j^*$, we let $\tau(C)=\sum_{i=1}^h\tau(C_i)+\tau_j$, where 
 $\tau_j$ is the number of tree parts
in the various $C_i$  
that are added to the bad part $B$ of $C$ after the merge.
When such a tree part $T$ is
added to $B$, we say that 
it has become {\it compromised}.

Method: Strong convergence of high-dimensional representations of a fixed compact group structural calculation Result: The one-generator SU(2) case has an elementary complete answer. A Haar element has eigenvalues exp(plus/minus i*theta), with theta/pi irrational almost surely. Its N-th symmetric power has eigenvalues exp(i*(N-2k)*theta),0<=k<=N. These become dense on the unit circle, so every Laurent-polynomial norm converges to the supremum on the circle, the regular Z norm. Uniform continuity then proves norm convergence for each Laurent polynomial. Geometric sums give convergence of every nonzero normalized trace moment to0. NOVELTY: UNCHECKED (an extension of the good-site argument; priority is not assessed).
Status: proof (unaudited).

## Statement

Under the critical analytic assumptions and nonempty time window in notes/boundary_comb.tex, for almost every iid tooth environment with P(H_0>t)~C t^(-1/3), two independent walks started together at the backbone origin collide infinitely often at height h, for every fixed integer h>=1, almost surely. These are separate countably many fixed-height assertions, not a uniform statement at heights growing with the spatial scale.

## What the source says

KNOWN (De Ambroggio–Ng–Nitzschner–Scali, arXiv:2609.05343v1, Theorem 4.1): its pair-collision classification concerns collisions anywhere in the comb, infinite for gamma>1/3 and finite for gamma<1/3 under its power-tail assumptions. It does not classify positive-height collisions separately at the boundary.

KNOWN AS A SOURCE REMARK (Section 4 introduction, p.16): collisions far above the backbone are described as strongly correlated and unsuitable for the paper's second-moment count. Its mechanism is crossings of the backbone between long excursions, rather than both walks sharing one long trapping tooth. This remark is not a theorem saying there are only finitely many collisions in the teeth.

KNOWN (same source, Corollary 5.2): its stated triple-collision result covers every gamma in (0,1), including 1/3, conditional on the paper's analytic estimates. It concerns simultaneous collisions of three walks and does not settle pair collisions at positive heights. No new triple-collision claim is made here.

## Positive-density good roots with a sufficiently long tooth

Fix an integer h>=1. The tail assumption implies s_h=P(floor(H_0)>=h)>0. Retain the deterministic kernel envelope constant A from Lemma A of the note. Its events E_K increase to probability one. Choose a deterministic K_h>=3 so that P(E_(K_h)^c)<s_h/2. Define

    G_h = {z: theta_z omega in E_(K_h), floor(H_z)>=h}.

Its stationary density is p_h=P(E_(K_h) intersect {floor(H_0)>=h})>=s_h/2>0. Under the iid two-step shift it has that same positive density in each backbone parity class. Every z in G_h has sum_{j=1}^T r_j(z)<=K_h+A(1+log T).

## One-scale backbone opportunities at G_h

For same-color starts v,w in the scale-N rectangle plus boundary, count killed backbone collisions whose root belongs to G_h intersect [-N,N] during the same time horizon T_N=ceil(c_u N^3) as Lemma B. The first-moment computation gives

    E Z_(N,h) >= a_h := p_h c_9^2(c_u-c_l)/(4 c_u^(4/3))>0

for all sufficiently large N. The Markov second-moment sum at a counted root uses K_h rather than K and gives

    E Z_(N,h)^2 <= E Z_(N,h)[1+2K_h+2A(1+log T_N)].

Therefore there is deterministic d_h>0 with

    P(Z_(N,h)>0) >= d_h/(1+log N),

uniformly over those starts. These steps are the full first/second moment calculation of Lemma B with the indicated constants; selection of the tooth event does not change the quenched Markov property.

## Raise both walkers to height h

Let rho be the first such counted backbone collision, on the event that it occurs before the box exit and horizon. This is a stopping time defined by the current pair position and the fixed environment. At rho both walks are at (z,0) for some z in G_h, hence every upward edge up to height h exists.

Conditional on the pair history at rho, the probability that both walkers follow exactly h consecutive upward steps is at least 3^(-2h). Every individual edge choice has probability at least 1/3, and the two future walks remain independent under their quenched product transition kernel. The probability bound follows by multiplying these conditional transition probabilities along this specified finite path; no independence between unrelated events is presumed.

On this event the two walkers collide at (z,h) at time rho+h. The whole specified path remains in the outer box: |z|<=N<bN and h<(bN)^(3/2) for all sufficiently large N. Thus the corresponding exit block does not end during these h steps. The resulting height-h collision occurs before the outer box exit. The strong Markov property at rho therefore gives the uniform one-scale lower bound

    P(a height-h collision before outer box exit)
        >= 3^(-2h) d_h/(1+log N).

## Infinitely many blocks

Use the geometric exit blocks sigma_m of C1. At sigma_m both starts are same-color and in the appropriate inner closure. For the event B_(m,h) of a height-h collision in [sigma_m,sigma_(m+1)), the preceding bound and strong Markov property give

    P(B_(m,h) | F_(sigma_m))
        >= 3^(-2h) d_h/(1+m log b)

for all sufficiently large m. These events are F_(sigma_(m+1))-measurable. The conditional product argument of C1 applies directly, since the lower bounds have a divergent harmonic sum. It proves infinitely many successful disjoint blocks at height h almost surely.

All environment and quenched probability-one events used above can be intersected over the countable set h=1,2,... . Hence the conclusion holds simultaneously for every fixed height h.

## Limits

This argument provides no uniform frequency as h grows, no control of collisions at heights proportional to N^(3/2), and no distribution of the highest collision. Its constants d_h and finite environment thresholds may deteriorate with h.   $$\mathbb{Q}_t(\Gamma) = \frac{W^{(2)} (\mathbf{1}_{\Gamma} F_t)}{ W^{(2)} (F_t)}$$

Moreover, the following penalisation result holds: for all $s \geq 0$, $\Gamma_s \in \mathcal{F}_s$,

NOVELTY: UNCHECKED (a direct consequence of the specified heat-kernel inputs; no priority claim).
Status: proof (unaudited).

## Statement

Assume the critical versions of source Lemma 4.9, Lemma 4.10 and Proposition 4.11, with deterministic constants and a nonempty lower window 0<c_l<c_u, as stated in notes/boundary_comb.tex. Assume iid finite tooth heights with P(H_0>t)~C t^(-1/3), C>0. Let G,A,K be the good-root set and constants of I0012-L1 v1. For two independent walks started at a good backbone root (z,0), put

    C_T = sum_{n=1}^T 1{X_n^1=X_n^2 on the backbone}.

For almost every environment and every z in G, E_{(z,0),(z,0)} C_T is of exact order log T: there are deterministic 0<d_0<=d_1<infinity and an environment/root-dependent finite threshold T_z such that

    d_0 log T <= E C_T <= d_1 log T,   T>=T_z.

Including the collision at time zero changes the count by one and not its order. This is conditional on the analytic inputs; it does not resolve their upstream proof qualifications in UPSTREAM_CHECK.md.

## Upper bound

Independence gives E C_T=sum_{n=1}^T r_n(z), with r_n as in L1. For z in G, L1 gives

    E C_T <= K+A(1+log T).

For T>=e this is at most d_1 log T with d_1=K+2A, independent of the particular good root.

## Lower bound

Apply source Lemma 4.9 in the environment translated by z. Since Z is countable and the environment is iid and shift-invariant, the source's almost-sure event holds simultaneously at every fixed translated root after taking a countable intersection. The constants c_l,c_u,c_9 remain deterministic and unchanged; only the finite starting threshold depends on z and the environment.

For sufficiently large N, start both walks at (z,0) and choose backbone targets (y,0) with |y-z|<=N of the parity prescribed by time n. There are at least N/2 such targets. For each n in [c_l N^3,c_u N^3], the parity/nonnegativity condition is met and the killed lower bound gives

    P_z(X_n=(y,0)) >= c_9 n^(-2/3),

because dropping killing and converting from p to q only increases the bound (deg(y)>=1). Therefore

    sum_{n in [c_l N^3,c_u N^3]} r_n(z)
        >= ( (c_u-c_l)N^3/2 ) * (N/2) * c_9^2 c_u^(-4/3) N^(-4)
        = a_0,

where a_0=c_9^2(c_u-c_l)/(4 c_u^(4/3))>0. Integer rounding is handled by increasing the starting threshold, as in C1.

Choose an integer R>=2 so that R^3>c_u/c_l, and use N_j=R^j. The time windows [c_l R^(3j),c_u R^(3j)] are disjoint. After a finite index j_z, every such window supplies at least a_0 to E C_T if its upper endpoint is at most T. The number of these windows is at least

    (log T)/(3 log R)-D_z

for a finite environment/root-dependent D_z. Consequently

    E C_T >= a_0( (log T)/(3 log R)-D_z ).

Increasing T_z makes the right-hand side at least d_0 log T, with d_0=a_0/(6 log R)>0. This proves the lower bound. It actually holds at any fixed backbone root; the good-root restriction is needed for the uniform logarithmic upper bound.

## What this does not give

An expectation of order log T does not establish almost-sure growth of order log T, nor concentration, nor a limiting constant. The diagonal Green bound alone allows large fluctuations. The almost-sure infinite-collision implication uses the separate adapted-scale argument in C1, not this expectation calculation. ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Analyse the covariance of the dyadic prime-block increments and the failure of independence. Result: The increments Y_h(l) = sum over primes with log p in (2^{l-1}, 2^l] of Re(p^{-i(tau+h)}) p^{-1/2} have, for tau uniform on [0,T], exact joint moments given by counting solutions of multiplicative equations among primes (Montgomery-Vaughan), so their joint law is asymptotically that of independent uniform phases as long as the number of primes involved is o(log T / log log T) in the moment order; this gives asymptotic independence of any FIXED number of increments at fixed moment order, but the branching-random-walk machinery needs exponential moments of sums of all n = log log T increments simultaneously, i.e. moments of order growing with n, where the multiplicative counting develops correlations from products of primes exceeding T. The dichotomy (50) for the covariance holds exactly for the random model and up to O(1/log T) errors for zeta by the prime number theorem in short intervals. So the decomposition EXISTS with the right covariance structure; what fails is independence at high moment order, precisely for the finest 1/log log T fraction of scales. Reduction: the structural question is equivalent to controlling exponential moments of the full prime sum truncated at T^{1-eps} (which is the ABR approach for the upper bound) and separately handling the last block, and the honest status is that the decomposition is available for all but the last O(1) scales, which is why the O(1) term (C0103) is where the difficulty concentrates. Key identity: Fixed-order joint moments of dyadic prime blocks match independent phases; the failure is at moment order growing with the number of scales. Obstruction: High-moment dependence of the last blocks.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded and open, $T>0$, $a^{ij},b^i,c\in L^\infty(U_T)$ with $a^{ij}=a^{ji}$ and $a^{ij}\xi_i\xi_j\ge\theta|\xi|^2$ for some $\theta>0$, $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(U))$, $g\in L^2(U)$. Put $B[u,v;t]=\int_U\big(a^{ij}u_{x_j}v_{x_i}+b^iu_{x_i}v+cuv\big)dx$. A function $u\in L^2(0,T;H^1_0(U))$ with weak time derivative $u'\in L^2(0,T;H^{-1}(U))$ is a weak solution of $u_t-\partial_i(a^{ij}u_{x_j})+b^iu_{x_i}+cu=f$ in $U_T$, $u=0$ on $\partial U\times[0,T]$, $u=g$ on $U\times\{0\}$, if $\langle u'(t),v\rangle+B[u,v;t]=(f(t),v)_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H^1_0(U)$ and a.e. $t\in[0,T]$, and $u(0)=g$. The initial condition is meaningful because (Lions-Magenes lemma) every such $u$ agrees a.e. with a function in $C([0,T];L^2(U))$, and $t\mapsto\|u(t)\|_{L^2}^2$ is absolutely continuous with $\frac{d}{dt}\|u(t)\|_{L^2}^2=2\langle u'(t),u(t)\rangle$ for a.e. $t$; this identity is what justifies testing the equation with $u$ itself.
