# E0018-C6 v1: a simpler two-Hurwitz witness (three degree-16 certificates)
Status: proof (unaudited), 2026-10-14.

Let A0=[[-3,-100],[100,-3]]/100 and A1=[[35,55],[-55,-75]]/100.
Under symmetric constant-rate r switching, for every fixed nonzero deterministic
initial vector and either initial state, the almost-sure norm exponent L(r) exists,
is continuous, and obeys
L(1)>.00588, L(20)<-.00504, L(100)>.02118.
Both individual matrices are Hurwitz. The open instability set {r:L(r)>0} therefore
has at least two disjoint interval components. The arithmetic mean is unstable.
This is a simpler explicit witness to Malrieu Open question 3 (PDF p.10); it leaves
the stronger all-convex-combinations-Hurwitz variant unresolved. No novelty claim.

## Matrices and scalar shift

Put J=[[0,-1],[1,0]], B0=J, B1=(11/20)[[1,1],[-1,-1]].
Then B1^2=0 and A0=B0-(3/100)I, A1=B1-(1/5)I.
A0 eigenvalues are -3/100+-i, and A1 has repeated eigenvalue -1/5.
Thus both matrices are Hurwitz, although A1 is not diagonalizable.
The switched fundamental matrix for Ai is exp[-integral a_{I_s}ds] times that for
Bi, since scalar matrices commute. Symmetric occupation times converge to 1/2,
so L(r)=G(r)-(3/100+1/5)/2=G(r)-23/200.
The mean (A0+A1)/2 has eigenvalues -23/200+-sqrt(1/10)/2; the larger is positive
because (sqrt(1/10)/2)^2=1/40>(23/200)^2.

## Angular generator and the certificate principle

For phi=2 arg X modulo 2pi and Y=log||X||, direct differentiation for Bi gives
f0=2, g0=0, f1=-(11/10)(1+sin phi), g1=(11/20)cos phi.
For bounded C1 periodic hi define residuals
R0=2h0'+r(h1-h0),
R1=(11/20)cos phi-(11/10)(1+sin phi)h1'+r(h0-h1).
The compensated angular corrector is a martingale with bounded jumps and variance
rate O(r). Chebyshev at times n^2 and Doob maximal bounds between n^2 and (n+1)^2
are summable after dividing by n^2; hence M_t/t->0 almost surely.
The identity
Y_t-Y_0=integral_0^t R_{I_s}(phi_s)ds-h(phi_t,I_t)+h(phi_0,I_0)+M_t
therefore places liminf/limsup growth between global minimum/maximum of R.
This is the complete argument of E0018-C2 v1 (both independent audits PASS), applied
to phi rather than theta; no invariant-density numerical approximation is needed.

## Exact finite certificate

All three hi polynomial pairs have degree 16 and denominator D=10^12, in files
nilpotent_corrector_r1_m16_rational.json,
nilpotent_corrector_r20_m16_rational.json,
nilpotent_corrector_r100_m16_rational.json.
Run python -X utf8 certify_nilpotent_correctors.py.
The proof inputs are those exact integers; float least-squares discovery is not proof.

The verifier recomputes residual Fourier numerators with denominator 100D:
state-0 derivative terms are +200k b0k (cos), -200k a0k (sin);
state-1 constant drift terms are -110k b1k (cos), +110k a1k (sin);
state-1 sine drift terms are +55k a1k at cos(k-1), -55k a1k at cos(k+1),
-55k b1k at sin(k+1), +55k b1k at sin(k-1), omitting sine degree zero.
Switching is 100r times h_other-h_i. The radial term is 55D at state-1 cos(phi).
Differentiation and product-to-sum prove these coefficients; equality with the
stored residuals is asserted by the verifier.

The integer interval algorithm uses scale S=10^30. Every product computes all
endpoint products and floors its lower/S and ceilings its upper/S; positive-integer
division also rounds outward. Sine/cosine of exactly 1/1024 are enclosed by Taylor
sums through degrees 41/40; exact rational omitted-term comparisons show a one-unit
pad encloses the true values, since the alternating terms decrease.
Interval rotation recurrence encloses sin/cos at j/1024 for j=0..7168 on [0,7],
and another recurrence encloses every frequency. Each point is within 1/2048 of
a grid point. Adding the global derivative bound
sum_{k>=1}k(|cos numerator_k|+|sin numerator_k|)/(100D) times 1/2048,
with outward rounding, proves residual bounds over [0,7], a full period since 2pi<7.
No floating-point math or library trigonometric function enters this check.

The exact common output denominator is 10^44. The relevant extrema numerators are
r=1 lower: 12088236150482936277350659928241797476156055;
r=20 upper:10995857615608850524167701952489394405567105;
r=100 lower:13618306137000586568465166260842916361390230.
Compare with threshold (23/200)*10^44=
11500000000000000000000000000000000000000000.
Thus G(1)>.12088, G(20)<.10996, G(100)>.13618; subtracting .115 proves all three
strict stated signs. These are conservative rigorous bounds, not fitted exponent values.

## Exponent existence, continuity, and several intervals

Observe projective theta modulo pi after each B0 rotation, before the next B1
sojourn. A cycle is an independent T~Exp(r) B1 sojourn and S~Exp(r) rotation.
The angular cycle transition is theta_next=F_T(theta)+S modulo pi, with F_T the
projective flow of exp(B1 T)=I+T B1 (invertible since det=1).
The rotation density modulo pi is q_r(z)=r exp(-rz)/(1-exp(-r pi)).
It is bounded below by a positive constant; the cycle kernel therefore has Doeblin
constant epsilon_r=pi*r exp(-r*pi)/(1-exp(-r*pi))>0 and a unique invariant law pi_r.
The same holds uniformly on a compact neighborhood of any positive r.

The cycle log norm reward W satisfies |W|<=||B1||T= (11/10)T; rotation adds zero.
Its conditional second moment is uniformly finite. Subtracting its bounded expected
reward m_r(theta) makes martingale differences; the sum of their variances/n^2 is
finite, so martingale convergence and Kronecker's lemma prove their averages vanish.
For f=m_r-pi_r(m_r), geometric Doeblin contraction makes v=sum K_r^j f converge
uniformly. The Poisson identity v-K_rv=f telescopes along the angle chain; the
bounded martingale differences in this telescoping also average to zero.
Thus the cycle reward average is pi_r(m_r) from every direction. Cycle lengths
average 2/r, and exponential-tail Borel-Cantelli makes unfinished cycles negligible.
It follows that G(r)=(r/2)pi_r(m_r) exists and is independent of the fixed start.

As r changes locally, the joint density of (T,S) changes continuously in L1.
Pushing forward gives uniform-in-theta total-variation continuity of the transition
kernel. Stationarity and the local Doeblin contraction give total-variation
continuity of pi_r. The bound |W|<=(11/10)T also gives uniform continuity of m_r by
weighted L1 continuity of the exponential T density. Hence G and L are continuous.
The set U={r>0:L(r)>0} is open, contains 1 and 100, and excludes 20. The two
components containing 1 and 100 are distinct open intervals. This completes the proof.

The hard stronger open piece is several intervals with a Hurwitz average or all
convex combinations Hurwitz. [campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the criterion reproduces the source's worked example, and every algebraic step was confirmed symbolically] This is the upper bound in the campaign answer to Problem 3.3 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution. For t>0 let S(0,t) be the centered semicircle law of variance t, with density sqrt(4t-x^2)/(2pi t) on |x|<=2sqrt(t). Let mu be compactly supported with positive diameter D=sup{|x-y|: x,y in supp(mu)}. Then mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for every t>=D^2. Proof route: by the source's Lemma 3.1 (Biane's description), non-unimodality at time t gives some R>0 and a separating local minimum u_0 of xi_R with xi_R(u_0)<=1/t. The stationary-kernel lower bound, rescaled to diameter D, gives xi_R(u_0)>=1/D^2, so t<=D^2. At t=D^2, equality would hold in that lower bound. This forces mu to be the symmetric two-point law with atoms at u_0±D/2 and R^2=3D^2/4, which is unimodal at t=D^2 by the source's Example 2.1. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
mu has compact support of positive diameter D.
t>D^2.

body:
For complex matrices B (k by n) and A (m by k) and 1 <= p, q, r <= infinity, ||AB||_{p->r} <= ||A||_{q->r} ||B||_{p->q}. When A and B are nonzero, equality holds exactly when some x with ||x||_p = 1 satisfies ||Bx||_q = ||B||_{p->q} and ||A(Bx)||_r = ||A||_{q->r} ||Bx||_q: a norming vector of B that B maps to a norming vector of A. Here ||x||_p = (sum_i |x_i|^p)^(1/p) for 1 <= p < infinity and ||x||_infinity = max_i |x_i| on C^n, and for a complex m by n matrix A, ||A||_{p->r} = max over x != 0 of ||Ax||_r / ||x||_p, with ||A||_p = ||A||_{p->p}.

[Lemma 14 (Bounded divisorial barrier) of arXiv:2608.29736, '2608.29736'] There exists \(a>0\) sufficiently small such that
\[
\psi:=e^{a\rho}\quad\text{on }M\setminus Z,
\qquad
\psi|_Z:=0,
\]
satisfies
\[
\psi\in C^0(M)\cap C^\infty(M\setminus Z),
\quad 0\leq\psi\leq 1,\quad\widetilde\chi
:=
\chi+\sqrt{-1}\partial\bar\partial\psi>0,
\]
\begin{equation}
F_{n-1}(\widetilde\chi)>0
\quad\text{on }M\setminus Z,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\frac{F_n(\widetilde\chi)}{\omega^n}
\longrightarrow+\infty
\qquad\text{as }x\longrightarrow Z.
\end{equation}
Finally, for every \(u\in C^\infty(M)\), the function \(u-\psi\)
cannot attain a local minimum at a point of \(Z\).

	The correlation kernel of the $N$-particle $q$-Racah OPE
	on $\{0,1,\ldots,M\}$
	is given by
	\begin{equation}
		
		K^{qR}(x,y)=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f_n(x)f_n(y).
	\end{equation}
	This is a kernel of the orthogonal projection operator onto
	$\operatorname{\mathrm{span}}\left( f_0,f_1,\ldots,f_{N-1}  \right)$
	in the Hilbert space
	$\ell^2\left( \left\{ 0,1,\ldots,M  \right\} \right)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\left\langle

G^a
:=\widetilde W\,dy^a(\mathcal Q).$$

body: The Nash embedding theorems, named after John Forbes Nash Jr., state that every Riemannian manifold can be isometrically embedded into some Euclidean space. Isometric means preserving the length of every path. For instance, bending but neither stretching nor tearing a page of paper gives an isometric embedding of the page into three-dimensional Euclidean space because curves drawn on the page retain the same arc length however the page is bent.
title: Nash embedding theorems

[Prop p:FLT of arXiv:2605.08983, 'A functional limit theorem for self-normalized linear processes with random coefficients a'] Let $(Z_{i})_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}$ be a strictly stationary and strongly mixing sequence of regularly varying random variables satisfying $((e:regvar of the paper))$ and $((eq:pq of the paper))$ with $\alpha \in (0,2)$, such that the local dependence condition $D'$ and conditions $((e:oceknula of the paper))$ and $((e:sim of the paper))$ hold. If $\alpha \in [1,2)$, also suppose that condition $((e:vsvcond of the paper))$ holds. Let
 $(C_{i})_{i \geq 0 }$ be a sequence of random variables independent of $(Z_{i})$ such that the series defying the linear process
 $$ X_{i} = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}C_{j}Z_{i-j}, \qquad i \in \mathbb{Z},$$
  is a.s.~convergent.

Then, as $n \to \infty$,
\begin{equation*}

\widetilde{L}_{n}(\,\cdot\,) := \bigg( \sum_{i = 1}^{\lfloor n \, \cdot \, \rfloor} \frac{CZ_{i}}{a_{n}}, \sum_{i = 1}^{\lfloor n \, \cdot \, \rfloor} \frac{C^{S} Z_{i}^{2}}{a_{n}^{2}}  \bigg) \xrightarrow{d}  (C^{(1)}V(\,\cdot\,), C^{(2)}W(\,\cdot\,))
\end{equation*}
 in $D^{2}$ with the weak $M_{1}$ topology,
where $V$ is an $\alpha$--stable L\'{e}vy process with characteristic triple $(0, \mu, b)$, with $\mu$ as in $((eq:mu of the paper))$,
$$ b = \left\{ \begin{array}{cc}
                                   0, & \quad \alpha = 1,\\[0.4em]
                                   (p-r)\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}, & \quad \alpha \in (0,1) \cup (1,2),
                                 \end{array}\right.$$
with $p$ and $r$ defined in $((eq:pq of the paper))$, $W$ is an $\alpha/2$--stable L\'{e}vy process with characteristic triple $(0, \widetilde{\mu}, \alpha/(2-\alpha))$ with $\widetilde{\mu}(\mathrm{d} x) = (\alpha /2) x^{-\alpha/2-1} 1_{(0,\infty)}(x)\,\mathrm{d} x$,
and $(C^{(1)}, C^{(2)})$ is a random vector, independent of $(V, W)$, such that
$(C^{(1)}, C^{(2)}) \stackrel{d}{=} (C, C^{S})$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Explicit model calculation, comparison identities and remaining hypothesis obstruction Result: An exactly solvable continuous-state control model shows how covariance enters the correction. Let dX_i=(-a*X_i+b*M_N)dt+sigma*dB_i with a>b>=0 and independent Brownian motions. The empirical mean is an OU process of rate a-b and variance sigma^2/[2(a-b)N]. Orthogonal deviations have marginal variance sigma^2*(1-1/N)/(2a). Therefore E X_i^2=sigma^2/(2a)+(sigma^2/(2N))*(1/(a-b)-1/a), an exact first-order correction with no further error. Check: The orthogonal projection onto the constant vector and its complement diagonalizes the linear drift. Their independent Brownian projections give the two variances, and summing them reproduces the one-coordinate stationary variance directly from the Lyapunov equation. Obstruction: This classical Gaussian calculation is a baseline, not a solution for the least-workload PDMP. Its interaction involves routing minima and a reflecting or sticky empty boundary; the appropriate infinite-dimensional covariance and response equations must be derived and solved with certified truncation and tail error. The source empirical approximation lambda^2/[2(1-lambda)] is not asserted exact.

[Theorem thm:Lyapunov of arXiv:2605.30707, 'Sharp behavior of the free energy for the two-dimensional directed polymer model'] There are universal constants \(c,c'>0\) such that, as \(\beta \downarrow 0\), we have:
       \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
              \item 
              If \(p\in (0,1)\),
                     \[
                     - c\, p\wedge (1-p)\, \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\pi}{\sigma^2(\beta)}}  \leq \mathtt{F}_p(\beta) \leq - c'\, p\wedge (1-p)\, \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\pi}{\sigma^2(\beta)}} \,.
                     \]
              \item 
              If \(p >1\),
                     \[
                     c'\, (p-1)\, \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{\pi}{\sigma^2(\beta)}}  \leq \mathtt{F}_p(\beta) \leq  (p-1)\, \mathtt{F}_{\lceil p \rceil}(\beta) \,.
                     \]
       \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 22 (Failure of marginal Torelli reconstruction) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $G_1,G_2$ be independent standard Gaussian variables and set
\begin{equation}
 X=G_1(G_1^2+G_2^2),
 \qquad
 Y=G_1^3-3G_1G_2^2.
 
\end{equation}
Then $X$ and $Y$ have the same law, but their defining polynomials are not
related by an orthogonal change of variables.  More precisely, with the
probabilists' Hermite polynomials,
\begin{equation}
 X=H_3(G_1)+G_1H_2(G_2)+4G_1,
 \qquad
 Y=H_3(G_1)-3G_1H_2(G_2),
 
\end{equation}
so, writing $(P_t)_{t\ge0}$ for the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck semigroup, their
correlation profiles are respectively
\begin{equation}
 \ip{X}{P_tX}_{L^2}=16e^{-t}+8e^{-3t},
 \qquad
 \ip{Y}{P_tY}_{L^2}=24e^{-3t}.
 
\end{equation}
Thus a marginal law does not determine the terminal chaos grading or its
minimal graded support.

Let a(n,j) be the probability that the strictly descending chain with transitions q(n,j)=1/((n-j)H_(n-1)), 1<=j<n, visits j, where H_k=sum_(r=1)^k 1/r. Put a(j)=6H_(j-1)/(pi^2(j-1)) and g(j)=j when j=2^r for some r>=1, zero otherwise. For every fixed integer L>=0, along n=2^K+L+1 the ratio [sum_(j=2)^(n-L-1) a(n,j)g(j)]/[sum_(j=2)^n a(j)g(j)] tends to infinity. The same holds with the denominator stopped at n-L-1. Thus deleting any fixed-width near-root band does not repair the divergent-series occupation ansatz for polynomially bounded weights.
L is fixed as K tends to infinity
The chain uses the displayed harmonic-descent transition probabilities

[Theorem 1 (local existence and uniqueness below the classical threshold) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Fix $\breg\in(\frac12,1)$. Let $n\ge2$, let $\frac{n+1}2<s\le\frac n2+1$, let
$\Bzero\equiv\Binf\in\Rn\setminus\{0\}$, and let $v_0\in H^{s}(\Rn)$ be divergence-free. There are
constants $C\ge1$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$, depending only on
$n,s,\breg$ and $v_{\rm A}$, and there exist a time $T_*>0$, a distributional
solution $(v,B, p)$ of \eqref{eq:mhd} on $[0,T_*]\times\Rn$ with data
$(v_0,\Binf)$, with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item writing $b:=B-\Binf$, the fields $v$, $b$ and $p$ lie in
$C([0,T_*],H^{s}(\Rn))$. The pressure is normalised by
\[
 p=\Riesz_i\Riesz_j
 \big(v^iv^j-\Binf^ib^j-b^i\Binf^j-b^ib^j\big),
\]
where $\Riesz_i$ are the Euclidean Riesz transforms;
\item writing $X=\mathrm{id}+w$, the solution is carried by a Lagrangian flow
$X:[0,T_*]\times\Rn\to\Rn$ with $X(0,\cdot)=\mathrm{id}$, uniformly bi-Lipschitz
and volume-preserving, $\det dX\equiv1$, such that $v=(\partial_tX)\circ X^{-1}$ and
$B=(\mathcal BX)\circ X^{-1}$;
moreover there is a spatially exact spacetime field
$\Ufield\in H^{s-1,1}_{\breg}(\Rst)$ such that
$\Ufield=dw$ on $[0,T_*]\times\Rn$ and, for constants fixed by
the standing parameters (one may take $C=2C_{\rm lin}$, with $C_{\rm lin}$
the constant of the linear estimate \eqref{eq:linear}),
\begin{equation}
 \|\Ufield\|_{H^{s-1,1}_{\breg}}
 \le C\|v_0\|_{H^s},
 \qquad
 \sup_{t\in[0,T_*]}\|dw(t)\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}\le\delta;
\end{equation}
here $\delta$ is chosen so that the second bound implies
$\|dw\|_{L^\infty_{t,y}}\le\frac12$;
\item the renormalised energy $E$ and cross helicity $H_{\rm c}$ of \eqref{eq:energy} are
conserved on $[0,T_*]$;
\item the solution is unique among all distributional solutions with the same
initial data for which $v$ and $B-\Binf$ belong to
$C([0,T_*],H^s)$. 
\end{enumerate}
The existence time is governed by the longitudinal regularity of the datum. We
distinguish the following two regimes.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textbf{\emph{(R1)}}]  $T_*$ depends on $n,s,\breg,
v_{\rm A}$, on $\|v_0\|_{H^{s}}$ and on the function
$T\mapsto\omega_{v_0}(T)$ defined in \eqref{eq:datum-modulus}.
\item[\textbf{\emph{(R2)}}] If $\|\nabla v_0\|_{Y^{s-1,\rpar}}<\infty$
for some $\rpar\in(0,1]$, then $T_*$ depends on $n,s,\breg,\rpar,v_{\rm A}$
and on $\|v_0\|_{H^{s}}+\|\nabla v_0\|_{Y^{s-1,\rpar}}$ alone. Moreover,
the spacetime field in~(2) satisfies
\[
 \|\Ufield\|_{H^{s-1,1+\rpar}_{\breg}}
 \le C\|\nabla v_0\|_{Y^{s-1,\rpar}}.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: local existence and uniqueness below the classical threshold

body: [Definition def:commute of arXiv:2606.14895, 'Effective Resistances and Commute Times in Sparse Random Geometric Graphs'] Define the commute time between nodes $u$ and $v$ as $C_{uv} = H_{uv}+H_{vu}$, i.e., the expected number of steps for a random walk started at $u$ to first reach $v$ and then return to $u$. Unlike hitting times, commute times are symmetric by construction: $C_{uv} = C_{vu}$.
title: Commute Time

body: Cover's theorem is a statement in computational learning theory and is one of the primary theoretical motivations for the use of non-linear kernel methods in machine learning applications. It is so termed after the information theorist Thomas M. Cover who stated it in 1965, referring to it as counting function theorem.

body: [Defn 13 of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Let $m,k\in \mathbb N$ and consider the multi-index $\mathbf j = (\vec j_1,...,\vec j_m) \in \big( \{1,...,k\}\times \{1,...,d\}\big)^m$. [Lemma eq:variance-completion of arXiv:2607.14087, 'Stochastic Domination of Gaussian Maxima: A Resolution of the Weak Simplex Conjecture'] \label[lemma]{lem:variance-completion}
Let $S$ be an $m\times m$ positive-semidefinite matrix with $S_{ii}\leq1$,
and let $Y\sim\mathcal N(0,S)$.  Define
\[
  D=\diag(1-S_{11},\ldots,1-S_{mm}),
\]
and let $W\sim\mathcal N(0,D)$ be independent of $Y$.  Then $G=S+D$ is a
correlation matrix and
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb E\max_iY_i\leq\mathbb E\max_i(Y_i+W_i).
\end{equation}

PROOF (UNAUDITED); elementary matrix example, no novelty claimed. For every integer m>=1, let rho=1-m^(-2), Y=[[1,rho],[rho,1]], b(t)=(1/(2m)+t)(1,-1)^T, and G(t)=[[Y,b(t)],[b(t)^T,1]], for 0<=t<=1/(8m). Every G(t) is positive definite of rank 3 with unit diagonal. Its Schur complement s(G(t))=1/2-2mt-2m^2t^2 lies in [7/32,1/2]. The endpoint Frobenius distance is 1/(4m), while the Schur-complement difference is 9/32 and its square-root difference is (4-sqrt(7))/(4sqrt(2)). Hence square-root sensitivity is >m/2. This shows that unit marginal variances, fixed rank and positive conditional innovations alone do not bound the raw Gram-map Lipschitz constant. It is a source-proof obstruction for quantitative Gaussian conditioning, not a realized Tensor Program convergence-rate lower bound or a general necessity statement.
m a positive integer
The exact real symmetric 3-by-3 matrix family displayed above
Frobenius metric for the full Gram matrix; scalar Schur complement in its last coordinate
No identification of m with a realizable network depth

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:9e82299d74c221fab2fc02c11eb6de175ae2e995b7f05ee8cbf4d5991d2191e6","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/9e/9e82299d74c221fab2fc02c11eb6de175ae2e995b7f05ee8cbf4d5991d2191e6.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:c8855a3bdc71b37d214f900012ae8a546b8d7c0730d5c0ca1858c84e133f24c2","bundle_entry_key":"t250_w712_c024","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c024-schur-conditioning-obstruction","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability and Gaussian conditioning","draft":"w712/bundle_018.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:schur-complement-unit-diagonal-gram-conditioning-obstruction","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C024 v1: explicit Gram-map obstruction in the length-constant route

Kind: route-failure. Target: 4 (and the stability assumptions needed for Target 1).
Status: proof (unaudited). Elementary matrix calculation; no novelty claimed.

## What this establishes
In Section 4.2 of arXiv:2607.06290, covariance stability applies a differentiability estimate to the square root of a Schur complement of the previous-parent Gram matrix, in order to obtain equation (4.9). Unit marginal variances, fixed rank, and even a uniform positive lower bound on the new conditional innovation variance do not bound the Lipschitz constant of that raw Gram-data map. A conditioning Gram spectral parameter, or an argument exploiting additional structure instead of this raw Lipschitz estimate, is needed for a uniform extraction from this step.

This is NOT a Tensor Program convergence-rate counterexample. It does not realize the Gram family below by a fixed-activation critical chain or by a length-L program with fixed structural constants. It neither disproves Target 1 nor asserts a necessary condition for every possible coupling proof. It identifies a specific obstruction to reading the desired length bound off this source proof. Standard linear algebra is not claimed as new research.

## The exact family
Let m>=1 be an integer, let delta=1/m^2, rho=1-delta, e=(1,-1)^T, and define

Y_m = [[1,rho],[rho,1]],
b_m(t)=(1/(2m)+t)e,
G_m(t)=[[Y_m,b_m(t)],[b_m(t)^T,1]],
0<=t<=1/(8m).

Every diagonal entry of G_m(t) equals 1. The two eigenvalues of Y_m are 2-delta and delta, both positive. Thus Y_m is invertible, Y_m^(-1)e=m^2 e, and its smallest eigenvalue is m^(-2).

Let s(G)=G_33-G_3,[1,2] Y_m^(-1) G_[1,2],3 be the Schur complement. Direct multiplication gives

s(G_m(t))=1-2m^2(1/(2m)+t)^2
         =1/2-2mt-2m^2t^2.

This function decreases on the specified interval. At the endpoints it equals 1/2 and 7/32. Consequently 7/32<=s(G_m(t))<=1/2 throughout the interval.

For completeness positive definiteness of G follows without invoking an unstated eigenvalue estimate. For u in R^2 and v in R,

(u,v)^T G (u,v)
=(u+Y^(-1)b v)^T Y (u+Y^(-1)b v)+s(G)v^2.

Both coefficients are positive, so this is positive for every nonzero (u,v). Thus every G_m(t) is positive definite of rank 3, with unit diagonal and conditional innovation variance bounded below by 7/32.

## Exact amplification
Put G0=G_m(0), G1=G_m(1/(8m)). The four changed off-diagonal entries have absolute value 1/(8m), so

||G1-G0||_F=1/(4m).

The Schur complement changes by 9/32. Therefore

|s(G1)-s(G0)|/||G1-G0||_F=9m/8.

For the square-root map used in source equation (4.9), the ratio is exactly

|sqrt(s(G1))-sqrt(s(G0))|/||G1-G0||_F
= m (4-sqrt(7))/sqrt(2) > m/2.

The strict inequality follows from sqrt(7)<3 and sqrt(2)<2. Therefore no finite Lipschitz constant, independent of m, holds even on this unit-diagonal, positive-definite family with uniformly nonvanishing conditional innovations. This is not caused by crossing a rank boundary or a zero of the scalar square root: the entire segment remains in the same positive-definite stratum and s stays at least 7/32.

The raw regression coefficient also illustrates the separate mean estimate: beta(G)=Y_m^(-1)b_m(t). Its change has Euclidean norm sqrt(2)m/8, so

||beta(G1)-beta(G0)||_2/||G1-G0||_F=m^2/sqrt(2).

This is an estimate on raw coefficients only. Combining the coefficients with correlated Gaussian parent variables may produce cancellations; we do not replace that joint analysis by the coefficient bound or assert an actual network error from it.

## Connection to the primary proof and what remains unpaid
The source's Section 4.2 states (4.6) as an induction on the number of program lines. The NonLin step explicitly multiplies parent errors by Lip(phi). Equations (4.8) and (4.9) bound conditional mean and conditional square-root covariance errors with a generic constant c. The covariance proof identifies f(X) as a Schur complement and invokes differentiability of sqrt(f) at the infinite-width Gram point; it does not display a bound uniform over the Gram family above. Section 3 notes that the generic constant may change from line to line. Hence these displayed estimates, as written, are not an explicit O(sqrt(L)) corollary.

If m=2^j, the raw square-root stability constant exceeds 2^(j-1) despite all marginal variances being one. The integer j here is a matrix-family parameter, NOT a proven network depth or line count. An exponential-in-depth lower bound would require a program realization with controlled structural constants and a lower bound on its actual law distance; neither is supplied here.

The unpaid source step is to replace this local raw Gram Lipschitz estimate by a quantitative bound in an appropriate conditioning-weighted norm, or assume and propagate suitable conditioning-Gram spectral control, and then avoid multiplicative accumulation over program lines. For a chain with fresh weights there are no previous uses of the current weight; this particular reused-weight conditioning obstruction may disappear. The remaining chain obstruction is therefore still a separate problem.

Primary locator: Agazzi, Mosig Garcia, Trevisan, arXiv:2607.06290, Section 4.2, (4.6), (4.8), (4.9), covariance-stability paragraph immediately preceding (4.9); Section 3, definition (3.1). Existing local primary bytes: papers/2607.06290.pdf and .html; the saved text includes formulas in both rendered text and LaTeX. No assertion is made about a stronger bound elsewhere in the literature.

## Checks and status
The universal argument above is exact and self-contained. scripts/c024_schur_checks.py independently expands rational determinants, inverses and endpoint Schur complements for several m, including m=2^20; these finite checks are supporting author checks, not a proof of the universal statement and not independent reviewer PASS. No floating-point inequality is used. Brysiewicz and Sinn (Local dimension testing via quadratic obstructions, arXiv:2609.02818, 2026) show that the realization space of the 24-cell has the expected local dimension at its symmetric regular realization, completing the local-dimension program for regular 4-polytopes begun by Rastanawi, Sinn and Ziegler. The expected dimension from the vertex-facet incidence count d(f_0 + f_3) - f_{03} is 4(24 + 24) - 144 = 48, which exceeds dim PGL(5,R) = 24, so the symmetric 24-cell has projectively inequivalent deformations and is not locally projectively rigid. The certificate is a second-order (quadratic obstruction) isolation test applied on linear slices, whose cost is governed by the nullity of the Jacobian.

Assumes: realization space of the 24-cell's face lattice, at the regular realization

A pair $(x,\mu)$ is a solution

\[
x(0) = x_0 \quad \text{ a.s.}, \qquad \mu(0)=\mathsf{Law}\left(x_0\mid \mathscr{F}^{\mathsf{W}}_0\right) = \mu_0,

as well as

\]

[campaign status: unreviewed - author-checked against the source's exact wording; verification unreviewed] For a transversal Volterra quadratic stochastic operator the ITINERARY of a trajectory is the sequence of fixed-point neighbourhoods it visits; Rozikov (2009, p. 4) asks whether some trajectory has a periodic itinerary. CLAIM, in two halves. (i) YES at m = 3, by an example already in the literature: for the cyclic Volterra operator with a = b = c = 1, matrix A = [[0,1,-1],[-1,0,1],[1,-1,0]], whose leading 2x2 minor is 1 so the operator is transversal and whose fixed-point set - the three vertices and the centre - is finite, the itinerary of every non-fixed interior point is periodic, 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> ..., with sojourns 12, 51, 1073, ... growing geometrically by the heteroclinic-cycle mechanism of Ganikhodzhaev and Zanin (2004). (ii) OPEN at m = 4: in the proof of Theorem 5 of Ganikhodjaev and Zanin (arXiv:1205.3841) the trajectory passes between the epsilon-neighbourhoods of the vertices along the routes 1-4-3-2-1, 1-4-2-1 or 1-4-3-1, and a simulated cyclic-type m = 4 map produced the mixed finite prefix 1,4,3,2,1,4,2,1. [Defn 1 (Log-concavity, PF$_2$, and TP$_2$) of arXiv:2605.18751, '\mytitle'] A positive function \(a:J\to(0,\infty)\) on an interval \(J\subseteq E\) is \emph{log-concave} if \(\log a\) is concave on \(J\). In the discrete case this is equivalent to \(\Delta^2\log a(k)\le0\) for every admissible \(k\in J\) and in the continuous case it is equivalent to \((\log a)''(x)\le0\) wherever the second derivative exists.

For a sequence \(b=(b_k)_{k\in\Z}\), we say that \(b\) is a \emph{P\'olya frequency sequence of order 2} (PF$_2$) if \(b_k\ge0\) for all \(k\), the support \(\{k:b_k>0\}\) is an interval in \(\Z\), and \(b\) is log-concave on its support.  A probability distribution \(F\) on \(\N_0\) is PF$_2$ if its mass sequence, extended by zero outside its support, is PF$_2$.

A nonnegative kernel \(M:I\times J\to[0,\infty)\) on two totally ordered sets is \emph{totally positive of order 2} (TP$_2$) if
\[
M(i,j)M(i',j')\ge M(i,j')M(i',j)
\]
whenever \(i\le i'\) and \(j\le j'\). See~\cite{Karlin1968} for the general total positivity theory.
title: Log-concavity, PF$_2$, and TP$_2$

body: Publication record. Problem 19.9 of S. Janson's survey (Probab. Surveys 9, 2012; 18.9 in arXiv v1) asks whether the conclusion of his Theorem 19.7 at lambda = 0 also holds when m/n -> 0. Y. Shmalo, Poisson limits for large boxes in sparse random allocations (October 2026) answers it: it holds for every m -> infinity if and only if the support of the weights lies in aZ, a = min{k >= 1 : w_k > 0}; bounded m fails; for b coprime to a the sequences along which it holds are characterized by c_n = n P(xi = b) and m mod a, and for c_n -> c in (0, infinity) the number of boxes with at least b balls is asymptotically Poisson(c) conditioned on a residue class. nontrivial weakly mixing probability-preserving Borel
$\Gamma$-space. Then the induced $\mathbb R^d$-space
$\operatorname{Ind}_\Gamma^{\mathbb R^d}(Z)$ admits a generating
stealthy Delone cross-section $Y$ for which
\[
    \sigma_Y
    =
    \sigma_Y^{\mathrm{tor}}
    +
    \sigma_Y^Z,
    \qquad
    \operatorname{supp}\sigma_Y^{\mathrm{tor}}
    \subset
    \Gamma^*\setminus\{0\},
\]
and
\[
    0\neq\sigma_Y^Z
    \ll
    \widetilde{\mathfrak m}_{Z,\nu}^0.
\]
In particular, $\sigma_Y$ has a nonzero continuous component. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A homeomorphism between topological spaces X and Y is a bijection f from X to Y such that both f and its inverse map f^(-1) are continuous. If such a map exists, X and Y are called homeomorphic. Homeomorphic spaces are indistinguishable by topological properties: any property expressed purely in terms of open sets (compactness, connectedness, Hausdorffness, and so on) holds for X if and only if it holds for Y. A continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism in general; it is one, for example, whenever X is compact and Y is Hausdorff.
title: Homeomorphism

Let X and Y be centered Gaussian vectors in R^p with covariance matrices Sigma^X and Sigma^Y respectively. The Kolmogorov distance between their coordinate-wise maxima satisfies sup_{z >= 0} |P(max_{1 <= i <= p} |X_i| <= z) - P(max_{1 <= i <= p} |Y_i| <= z)| <= C * Delta^(1/3) * (ln(p))^(2/3), where Delta = max_{1 <= i, j <= p} |Sigma_{i,j}^X - Sigma_{i,j}^Y| and C is a universal constant.
X, Y are centered Gaussian vectors in R^p
Delta is the maximum coordinate-wise covariance discrepancy

body:
[Lemma 223 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Functions $\mathfrak{c}$ have the following properties (see also Table~\ref{table:sumf}):

\begin{itemize}
\item For each $g \in [H]$, the $H$-tuple of functions $\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{c}}^{\textnormal{1st}}_{\bullet;g}(z)$ satisfies the master Riemann--Hilbert problem with zero source. Besides, we have $\mathfrak{c}^{\textnormal{1st}}_{h;g}(z) = \frac{\delta_{h,g}}{z} + O(\frac{1}{z^2})$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$ for any $g,h \in [H]$; equivalently: $\oint_{\gamma_h} \frac{\dd z}{2\ii\pi} \mathfrak{c}^{\textnormal{1st}}_{h;g}(z) = \delta_{h,g}$. And, it is tame with exponent $1$.
\item For each $\boldsymbol{f}$, the $H$-tuple of functions $\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{F}}^{\textnormal{I}}[\boldsymbol{f}](z)$ satisfies the master Riemann--Hilbert problem with source
\[
\forall h \in [H]\qquad D_h^{\textnormal{I}}[\boldsymbol{f}](z) = - \oint_{\gamma_h} \frac{\dd\zeta}{2\ii\pi}\, \frac{f_h(\zeta)}{(z - \zeta)^2}.
\]
where $z$ is \emph{inside} the contour of integration. Besides, it behaves as $O(\frac{1}{z^2})$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$. And, it is tame with exponent $1$.
\item For each $\boldsymbol{f}$, the $H$-tuple of functions $\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{F}}^{\textnormal{II}}[\boldsymbol{f}](z)$ satisfies the master Riemann--Hilbert problem with zero source. Besides, it is $O(\frac{1}{z^2})$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$, and it becomes tame with exponent $1$ after subtraction of $(\frac{1}{2} \partial_z(\sigma_h(z)f_h(z)))_{h = 1}^H$.
\item For each $\boldsymbol{f}$, the $H$-tuple of functions $\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{F}}^{\textnormal{III}}[\boldsymbol{f}](z)$ satisfies the master Riemann--Hilbert problem with source
\[
\forall h \in [H] \qquad D_h^{\textnormal{III}}[\boldsymbol{f}](z) = \oint_{\gamma(\alpha_h)} \frac{\dd\zeta}{2\ii\pi}\,\frac{f_h(\zeta)}{(z - \zeta)^2}+\oint_{\gamma(\beta_h)} \frac{\dd\zeta}{2\ii\pi}\,\frac{f_h(\zeta)}{(z - \zeta)^2}.
\]
Besides, it is $O(\frac{1}{z^2})$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$, and it becomes tame with exponent $1$ after subtraction of $(\frac{1}{2\theta_{h,h}} \partial_z f_h(z))_{h = 1}^H$.
\item For each $g \in [H]$ and $\zeta \in \amsmathbb{C} \setminus \amsmathbb{B}$, the $H$-tuple of functions $\boldsymbol{\mathfrak{c}}^{\textnormal{3rd}}_{\bullet;g}(z;\zeta)$ satisfies the master Riemann--Hilbert problem with respect to $z$ and with source
\[
\forall h \in [H] \qquad D_{h;g}(z;\zeta) = -\frac{\delta_{h,g}}{z - \zeta}.
\]
Besides, it is $O(\frac{1}{z^2})$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$. If $\zeta$ is away from the endpoints $\alpha_g,\beta_g$ it is tame with exponent $1$. If $\zeta$ is located at $\alpha_g$ or $\beta_g$, it becomes tame (with respect to the variable $z$) with exponent $1$ after we subtract $\frac{1}{2\theta_{g,g}}\boldsymbol{D}_{\bullet;g}(z;\zeta)$.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Also, let $\{\sigma_d : {\mathbb R}^d \rightarrow [1, \infty)\}$ be a sequence of smooth maps. For $d \in {\mathbb N}\setminus \{0\}$,
        define the joint target distribution 
        on ${\mathbb R}^d \times {\mathbb R}^d$ by
        $\mu_\sigma^{(d)} ({\mathrm d} x, {\mathrm d} v) \coloneqq  {(2\pi \sigma_d^2(x))^{-d/2}} \exp(-|v|^2/(2\sigma_d^2(x))) \,{\mathrm d} v\, {\mathrm d}\mu^{(d)}( x )$.\\
        
        (i) Assume that $\log \chi^2(\mu_0^{(d)} \| \mu_\sigma^{(d)}) =  O(d)$. \\
        (ii) Assume that $(\mu^{(d)}, \sigma_d)$ satisfies~(ass:wpi of the paper),~(ass:sigmabounds of the paper) and~(ass:curvature of the paper) with $m = \widetilde \Omega(d^{-l})$ (for some $l \in {\mathbb R}_+$), $M_D = O(1)$, $M_H = O(d^{1/2})$, $M_{U, \sigma} = O(d)$ and $K = O(d)$.\\
        Then we have that $t_\mathrm{mix}(1, \mu_0^{(d)}) =  O(d^{l+ 5})$.
        
        In particular, for $\mu^{(d)}({\mathrm d} x) \propto \langle x \rangle^{-d - r_d} {\mathrm d} x$ for $r_d > d$ or $\mu^{(d)}({\mathrm d} x) \propto \exp( -\langle x \rangle^{p}) \,{\mathrm d} x$ for $p \in (0, 1)$ with the tempering $\sigma_d = \langle x\rangle$ or $\langle x \rangle^{1 - p}$ respectively, assumption (ii) is satisfied for $l = 1$. Then, for initial distributions $\{\mu_0^{(d)}\}_{d \in {\mathbb N}\setminus \{0\}}$ satisfying assumption (i), we have that $t_\mathrm{mix}(1, \mu_0^{(d)}) =  O(d^{6})$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Exact integral manipulation, Palm calculus, mass transport, limiting obstruction or conditional construction Result: The vertex graph has constant degree d+1. Under its stationary Palm law, rerooting at a uniformly selected neighbor preserves the marked-vertex marginal by mass transport: send f of the receiving marked vertex along every directed edge with weight 1/(d+1). Outgoing expectation is the neighbor average and incoming mass is f at the root. Thus the separation mark of a uniformly chosen neighbor also has the source Gamma(d+1) marginal. Any proposed joint neighbor formula must reproduce this law, not the Exp(1) law for a volume-typical point. Check: Constant degree makes the incoming weights sum to one. Without constant degree the stationary neighbor-rooted law would instead be degree-biased. The mass transport applies to the full marked configuration. Obstruction: Marginal preservation does not determine dependence between neighboring separation marks, lengths or angles. A joint Palm/Mecke calculation remains missing.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0409-joint-law-of-neighboring-ideal-voronoi-vertices

body: For n >= 1 let zeta_n = exp(2 pi i / n) be a primitive n-th root of unity. The n-th cyclotomic field is Q(zeta_n). Facts: (1) the minimal polynomial of zeta_n over Q is the n-th cyclotomic polynomial Phi_n(x) = prod over 1 <= k <= n with gcd(k, n) = 1 of (x - zeta_n^k), which has integer coefficients and is irreducible over Q (Gauss for n prime, Kronecker/Dedekind in general), so [Q(zeta_n) : Q] = phi(n), Euler's totient; (2) Q(zeta_n)/Q is a Galois extension with Galois group canonically isomorphic to (Z/nZ)^*, the automorphism sigma_a sending zeta_n to zeta_n^a; in particular it is abelian, and by the Kronecker-Weber theorem every finite abelian extension of Q lies in some cyclotomic field; (3) the ring of integers of Q(zeta_n) is Z[zeta_n]; (4) a prime p not dividing n is unramified and splits into phi(n)/f primes of residue degree f, where f is the order of p in (Z/nZ)^*; a prime p dividing n ramifies, totally so in Q(zeta_{p^k}) where p is the phi(p^k)-th power of a prime, and p O_K = (1 - zeta_{p^k})^{phi(p^k)}; the discriminant of Q(zeta_{p^k}) is +- p^{p^{k-1}(pk - k - 1)}, and in general the primes ramified in Q(zeta_n) are exactly the primes dividing n (for odd n; 2 ramifies only when 4 divides n); (5) Q(zeta_n) contains the quadratic field Q(sqrt(p^*)) with p^* = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} p for each odd prime p dividing n (Gauss sums), which is one route to quadratic reciprocity; (6) the maximal real subfield is Q(zeta_n + zeta_n^{-1}) of degree phi(n)/2 for n > 2; (7) the class number h_n of Q(zeta_p) is 1 exactly for the primes p <= 19; Kummer proved Fermat's last theorem for regular primes (p not dividing h_p) using the arithmetic of Z[zeta_p]. Cyclotomic fields are the class field theory of Q made explicit and the model case of Iwasawa theory.

For each 0<tau<T, continuous mapping at the positive continuous limit gives

    (n theta_floor(nt))_[tau,T] => (1/U_t)_[tau,T],
    (log theta_floor(nt)+log n)_[tau,T] => (-log U_t)_[tau,T].

These are weak path-law statements, with exceptional degenerate paths assigned
any fixed finite extension. Indeed C002 makes their probability vanish, and
the minimum of U on [tau,T] is strictly positive almost surely. Under a
Skorokhod representation the first assertion is a uniform relative angle
approximation on this interval; it is not a same-space coupling claim about
the original network and a newly drawn SDE.

In particular, for L/n -> t>0,

    L theta_L => t/U_t =_law 3pi/A_t,
    L^2(1-cos theta_L) => t^2/(2 U_t^2),
    A_t = (1/t) integral_0^t exp(s+sqrt(2) W_s) ds.

The equality in law follows by time-reversing Brownian increments in C017's
explicit solution. If q_t=t^2/(2U_t^2), then

    Var(log U_t) = Var(log q_t)/4
                = Var(log integral_0^t exp(s+sqrt(2) W_s) ds).       (V)

This is the predicted centered log-angle variance. It is finite: the absolute
value of log(U_t/(a t)) in this equality-in-law representation is bounded by
t+sqrt(2) sup_(s<=t)|W_s|, whose moments of every finite order are finite.

There is a rigorous truncated network statement, but not an unqualified raw
variance limit. Define the continuous bounded function on [0,infinity)

    g_R(u)=clip(-log u,-R,R) for u>0, and g_R(0)=R.

C006 and convergence of both bounded moments imply, for fixed R and t>0,

    Var(g_R(U_n(L/n))) -> Var(g_R(U_t)),  L/n -> t.

Any extension on degenerate paths gives the same bounded-moment limit. Then
dominated convergence using the just-proved finite log moments gives

    lim_(R->infinity) lim_(n->infinity) Var(g_R(U_n(L/n)))
        = Var(log U_t).                                            (TV)

The order in (TV) is essential. At every finite width there is positive
probability of an exact zero angle or extinction (C001/C002), so an
unconditional real-valued log-angle variance is not defined. Even conditioning
on nondegeneracy does not follow from C006 alone: convergence of that full
conditional variance requires a separate uniform-integrability argument for
the squared centered logarithms. We do not claim it here. Conditional sample
variances in ANGLE_VARIANCE_COMPARISON.md are numerical diagnostics of (V),

[Proposition prop:zero-cell-continuity of arXiv:2608.13452, 'Wasserstein stability of the zero cell of a Poisson hyperplane tessellation under directio'] Let \(\phi_n,\phi\in\mathcal{P}(S^{d-1})\) be even probability measures, and let \(\gamma_n,\gamma > 0\).
For each \(n\), let \(Z_0^n\) be the zero cell of the stationary Poisson hyperplane process \(\Psi_n\) with intensity measure
\(\Theta_n=(\phi_n \otimes \gamma_n \lambda)\circ \mathfrak{q}^{-1}\) and let \(Z_0\) be the zero cell of the stationary Poisson hyperplane process \(\Psi\) with intensity measure \(\Theta=(\phi \otimes \gamma \lambda)\circ \mathfrak{q}^{-1}\).
Then, \(\phi_n \Rightarrow \phi\) (weakly) and \(\gamma_n \to \gamma\) if and only if \(Z_0^n\) converges to \(Z_0\) in distribution as random convex bodies as $n \to \infty$.

Let d>=2, N>=2, and let C be a set of N distinct points on the unit sphere S^(d-1). Let t_1<...<t_m<1 be exactly the distinct inner products between distinct points of C, m>=1, and assume C is a spherical (2m-1)-design: every polynomial on R^d of degree<=2m-1 has the same average over C as under normalized uniform surface measure. Put F(t)=product_(i=1)^m(t-t_i). Let P_l be the degree-l polynomial orthogonal for weight (1-t^2)^((d-3)/2) on [-1,1], normalized by P_l(1)=1. Every coefficient of F in the basis P_0,...,P_m is strictly positive. This is strict positive definiteness in the coefficient sense used by Cohn-Kumar; it is not an assertion that every Gram matrix of F(<x,y>) is nonsingular. The case m=1 is included.

m>=1 counts all distinct off-diagonal inner products; F is monic
C is a spherical (2m-1)-design
fixed-dimension normalized zonal basis P_l(1)=1

PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. For a deterministic K=1 NK-form landscape on 2m bits with F(x)=sum_i J_i 1{x_(2i-1)=x_(2i)}, J_i>0, there are 2^m strict single-bit local maxima, all global. Two distinct peaks differing on pair set D connect by a single-bit path inside {F>=max F-delta} exactly when delta>=max_{i in D} J_i. Every level-set component contains a peak and the component count is 2^(number of J_i>delta). For J_i=1, all peaks are isolated below deficit one and the whole level set is connected at deficit one. This is a deterministic block model, not the typical iid Gaussian NK model with overlapping neighborhoods.

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The ordinary generating function of $H$ is
  \[
    \phi_H(z) = (1-p)^m \binom{m/z - 1}{m}^{-1}.
  \]
  \begin{proof}
    We use the Laplace--Borel transform with $m$ applications of integration
    by parts:
    \begin{align*}
      \frac{\phi_H(x)}{(1-p)^m} &= \int_0^\infty
        \left( e^{xt/m} - 1 \right)^m
        e^{-t} \, dt\\
      &= \underbrace{\left. \left( e^{xt/m} - 1 \right)^m \left(-e^{-t}\right)
          \right|^{t=\infty}_{t=0}}_0\\
      &\quad + \int_0^\infty m\left( e^{xt/m} - 1 \right)^{m-1} \left(\frac{x}{m} \, e^{xt/m}\right)
      e^{-t} \, dt\\
      &= \frac{m\left(x/m\right)}{1} \int_0^\infty \left(e^{xt/m}-1\right)^{m-1}
            e^{-(1-x/m)t} \, dt\\
      &= \frac{m \left(m-1\right) (x/m)^2}{1-x/m} \int_0^\infty \left( e^{xt/m}-1\right)^{m-2}
            e^{-(1-2x/m)t} \, dt\\
      &\ \,\vdots\\
      &= \frac{m!\left(x/m\right)}{\left(m/x - 1\right)^{\underline{m-1}}} 
            \int_0^\infty e^{-(1-x)t} \, dt\\
      &= \frac{m!}{\left(m/x-1\right)^{\underline{m}}} = \binom{m/x - 1}{m}^{-1},
      \quad 0 < x < 1.
    \end{align*}
    The right-hand side is a rational function of $x$, say
    $f(x) / g(x)$ where $f(z)$ and $g(z)$ are real polynomials in $z$.
    Then $f(z) \, g(z)^{-1}$ is a well-defined object in the ring 
    of formal power series $\mathbb{R}[[z]]$ and we can
    restate our result for $\phi_H(z)$;
    see Section~\ref{language}.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 10 of arXiv:2605.14206

[Lemma 22 of arXiv:2604.01978, 'Homogenized Transformers'] Let $X\in(\S^{d-1})^{n}$ and let $R\in\R^{n\times n}$ be its Gram matrix.
Set
\(
R(\gamma)\coloneqq (1-\gamma)I_n+\gamma\,\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^{\sT}.
\)
Then there exists $L>0$ such that for all $\gamma\in(-1/(n-1),1)$,
\begin{equation*}
\max_{1\leq i\neq j\leq n}|\cD_{ij}(R)-b(\gamma)|
\leq L\max_{(i,j)\in[n]}|R_{ij}-R(\gamma)_{ij}|.
\end{equation*}
(Note that $\mathscr{D}_{ij}(R(\gamma))= b(\gamma)$.)
Moreover one can take $L=O(1+d\sigma_{\bA}^{4}\upbeta^{2}n)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 7 (Varying environment: interval bounds) of arXiv:2605.04048, 'Catastrophe--dispersion models in random and varying environments across generations'] Consider the Poissonian growth with binomial survival of Example~\ref{ex:poisson-binomial}. Let $(\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a deterministic environment sequence whose components satisfy, for all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
\theta_n\in[\theta_-,\theta_+],\quad
\lambda_n\in[\lambda_-,\lambda_+],\quad
p_n\in[p_-,p_+],\quad
d_n\in[d_-,d_+],
\]
with $0<\lambda_-\le\lambda_+<\theta_-\le\theta_+<+\infty$, $0<p_-\le p_+\le1$, and integers $1\le d_-\le d_+$. Then, for every dispersion mechanism $\Delta^{(j)}$, $j=1,2,3,4$:
\begin{itemize}
  \item if
  $\displaystyle p_+<\frac{\theta_-}{\theta_-+\lambda_+}$,
  the process becomes extinct almost surely;
  \item if
  \[
    \frac{d_-}{d_--1}\,\frac{1-p_-}{p_-}\,
    {}_2F_1\!\Bigl(1,1;d_-;-\frac{\lambda_-p_-}{\theta_+}\Bigr) + {}_2F_1\!\Bigl(1,1;d_-+1;-\frac{\lambda_-p_-}{\theta_+}\Bigr)< \frac{1}{p_-},
  \]
  where ${}_2F_1$ is the hypergeometric function, then the process survives with positive probability.
\end{itemize}

\Delta_{\bar{j}}f :=  {\mathcal{F}}^{-1} (\theta_{\bar{j}} {\mathcal{F}}f )\;.
$$
The sequence $(\Delta_{\bar{j}}f)_{\bar{j}\in \mathbb{N}^2}$ is called a hyperbolic Littlewood-Paley analysis of $f$.
\end{itemize}

body: A twin-prime pair consists of two positive prime integers p and p+2. Examples include (3,5), (5,7), (11,13), (17,19), and (41,43). Either member can be called a twin prime. The pair (2,3) is not a twin-prime pair because its gap is one. The twin-prime conjecture asserts that infinitely many such pairs exist; this definition supplies no proof of the conjecture.
title: Twin primes: definition and complete examples

body: Let X_1, X_2, ... be iid random variables in a Polish space X with common law mu, and let L_n = (1/n) sum_{i=1}^n delta_{X_i} be the empirical measure, an element of the space of probability measures on X with the weak topology. Sanov's theorem states that L_n satisfies a large deviation principle, as n -> infinity, with rate function I(nu) equal to the relative entropy D_KL(nu || mu) when nu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu, and I(nu) = +infinity otherwise: for Borel sets Gamma of measures, the log-probability (1/n) log P(L_n in Gamma) has upper limit at most -inf_{closure of Gamma} I and lower limit at least -inf_{interior of Gamma} I. Due to Ivan Sanov.
title: Sanov's theorem

body:
[Proposition prop:Bartlett-torus-base-decomposition of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $(Z,\nu)$ be weakly mixing, and let $Y\subset X$ be a Delone
cross-section. Its Bartlett spectrum has a unique decomposition
\[
    \sigma_Y
    =
    \sigma_Y^{\mathrm{tor}}
    +
    \sigma_Y^Z,
\]
where
\[
    \sigma_Y^{\mathrm{tor}}
    :=
    \sigma_Y|_{\Gamma^*\setminus\{0\}},
    \qquad
    \sigma_Y^Z
    :=
    \sigma_Y-\sigma_Y^{\mathrm{tor}},
\]
and
\[
    \sigma_Y^Z
    \ll
    \widetilde{\mathfrak m}_{Z,\nu}^0.
\]
In particular, $\sigma_Y^Z$ is atomless.

body:
[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] For $m\ge0$, let
\[
 \mathscr P_m
 =\{\lambda:\ell(\lambda)\le n,\ |\lambda|\le m\},
 \qquad
 E_m=\bigl(G_\lambda(p_\mu)\bigr)_
       {\mu,\lambda\in\mathscr P_m},
\]
where
\[
 p_\mu=(Q^{\mu_1+n-1},Q^{\mu_2+n-2},\ldots,Q^{\mu_n}),
\]
and the rows and columns are ordered by any linear extension of
inclusion.  Then $E_m$ is lower triangular and
\[
 G_\lambda(p_\lambda)
 =u_\lambda\prod_{\square\in\lambda}
       (1-Q^{h(\square)}),
 \qquad u_\lambda\in R_{\mathrm{ev}}^\times.
\]
In particular,
\[
 D_m:=\det E_m\in R_{\mathrm{ev}}\setminus\{0\}
\]
is a Laurent unit times a product of cyclotomic polynomials, and
\[
 D_mE_m^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(E_m)
 \in\operatorname{Mat}_{\mathscr P_m}(R_{\mathrm{ev}}).
\]

If $F=\sum_\lambda b_\lambda G_\lambda\in
\Lambda_n^{\mathrm{pol}}$ and
\[
 \mathbf v_m(F)=\bigl(F(p_\mu)\bigr)_{\mu\in\mathscr P_m},
 \qquad
 \mathbf b_m(F)=\bigl(b_\lambda\bigr)_{\lambda\in\mathscr P_m},
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf v_m(F)=E_m\mathbf b_m(F).
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every ideal $J\subseteq R_{\mathrm{ev}}$,
\[
 F(p_\mu)\in J\quad(\mu\in\mathscr P_m)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 b_\lambda\in D_m^{-1}J
 \quad(\lambda\in\mathscr P_m).
\]

body:
Two realizations P_1, P_2 of a d-polytope in R^d are projectively equivalent if there exists a projective transformation T in PGL(d+1, R) preserving the upper halfspace that maps the vertices of P_1 to the vertices of P_2.
P_1, P_2 are realizations of the same combinatorial polytope
title: Projective Equivalence of Polytope Realizations

body: Index of open problems answered in papers by Y. Shmalo posted in 2026, as public repositories under github.com/yspennstate (several also on arXiv and ResearchGate); none is refereed as of 14 October 2026. Answered in the negative: Aldous-Fill Open Problems 7.27 (arc-transitive-graphs-that-mimic-the-cycle), 4.49(ii) (flow-parameter-diameter), 4.30 (relaxation-time-normal-approximation) and 4.48(a) (variation-threshold-stationary-times); Ding-Lee-Peres Question 5.2 (cover-time-fluctuations); Ganikhodzhaev-Rozikov Problem 11 (strictly-nonvolterra-qso-fixed-points); Thévenin's 2020 conjecture on degree counts (non-gaussian-degree-counts); Janson Problems 19.41 (uniform-condensation-windows), 19.42 and 19.43 (condensation-two-giant-boxes) and 19.30(iii) (second-largest-degree-infinite-variance); Leskelä's form of Ross's second queueing conjecture (Ross-s-second-queueing-conjecture, arXiv:2609.25084); Hasebe-Ueda-Wang Problems 4.3, 4.7 and 4.11 (free-multiplicative-log-unimodality); Agresti-Veraar Problems 4 and 5 (critical-allen-cahn-noise); Pete's Question 13.2 for 0 < q < 1 (random-cluster-not-monotone); Aldous-Janson Open Problem 14, linear growth instead of n log^4 n (beta-splitting-drawn-length); Vu's Conjecture 9.5 (gaussian-integer-spectra); Lyons-Peres Question 17.18 (nonergodic-galton-watson-flow-rule); Holroyd-Levine-Meszaros-Peres-Propp-Wilson Question 6.2 for H >= -1 (sandpile-holes-corner-angles). Answered in the affirmative or proved: Hasebe-Ueda Problem 3.3 with the sharp constant (free-brownian-unimodality-sharp-constant) and Problem 3.11 (free-strong-unimodality); Lyons-Peres Question 6.20 for finite-faced regular tessellations (outer-vertex-isoperimetry); Bradley's Question 5 (phi-mixing-interlaced-rho-mixing-markov); Janson Problem 19.10 with its joint extension (joint-allocation-extremes), Conjecture 19.4 (sparse-allocation-largest-box), Problem 19.9 (sparse-allocation-poisson-limits) and Conjecture 21.1 (level-width-moments); Aldous-Fill 6.13, Kemeny half (maximal-kemeny-constant), and 4.48(b); Garban-Pete-Schramm Section 11 Question 1 and Kalai's Conjecture 8 for crossings (percolation-crossing-entropy, arXiv:2609.15388); the FEI inequality for every linear threshold function (fourier-entropy-threshold-functions, arXiv:2610.16069); Aldous's coagulation-fragmentation mixing item (linear-polymer-relaxation); Kosygina-Zerner Problem 5.3 (positive-cookie-ballisticity); the Krauth-Mézard capacity at zero margin (ising-perceptron-capacity, arXiv:2607.11010). Other results: exact Toeplitz and Hankel moments to order 14 (toeplitz-hankel-exact-moments); the Bubeck-Li-Nagaraj law of robustness up to one logarithm (arXiv:2607.07778); the Gaussian Balan-Wang phase-retrieval base 1/4 (arXiv:2607.06249); Matrix Spencer for Toeplitz and Hankel matrices (ResearchGate 407239961); a new proof of Atanassov's conjecture (arXiv:1708.07175, 2017). Of the 200 famous open problems on the owner's list of 14 October 2026 none is solved; its item T069, the Krauth-Mézard capacity, is the preprint arXiv:2607.11010. CAUTION ON THE NAME: this is the other result commonly called 'Rosenblum's argument' - the contour-integral solution of the Sylvester equation; the scattering-theory Hilbert-Schmidt estimate is a different theorem of the same author, so a citation naming Rosenblum must be matched to its context. STATEMENT: let H and K be complex Banach spaces, A a bounded operator on H, B a bounded operator on K, and suppose their spectra are disjoint: sigma(A) intersect sigma(B) is empty. Then for every bounded operator C from K to H the equation A X - X B = C has a UNIQUE bounded solution X from K to H, and it is given by X = (1 / (2 pi i)) times the contour integral over Gamma of (A - z)^(-1) C (B - z)^(-1) dz, where Gamma is a finite union of positively oriented rectifiable Jordan curves lying in the resolvent set of B, encircling sigma(A) once and sigma(B) not at all. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) disjointness of the spectra is what gives both existence and uniqueness. With A = B and C = 0 the equation A X - X A = 0 is solved by every operator commuting with A, so uniqueness fails badly; and with A = B = 0 on a one-dimensional space the equation is unsolvable for nonzero C. (ii) It is the SPECTRA, not the norms, that matter: no smallness of C is assumed, the solution depends linearly on C, and the bound on X is controlled by the length of Gamma and by the size of the two resolvents on Gamma - a bound that blows up as the spectra approach each other, which is the quantitative content usually needed in perturbation arguments. (iii) The theorem as stated is for BOUNDED A and B; for unbounded operators the analogous statement requires separate hypotheses (sectoriality, semigroup generation), and the contour formula must be justified anew. (iv) Finite-dimensional corollary: for matrices, A X - X B = C is uniquely solvable precisely when A and B have no common eigenvalue.
H and K are complex Banach spaces
A and B are BOUNDED linear operators on H and K respectively
sigma(A) and sigma(B) are disjoint compact subsets of C
C is a bounded operator from K to H
Gamma is a cycle in the resolvent set of B winding once around sigma(A) and not at all around sigma(B)

body: The conditional block bridge is not a proof of critical nonpercolation. Its unproved premise is a fixed, finite, deterministically compatible block construction from theta(p_c)>0 with error delta small enough for its actual sigma-field dependence range r. One self-contained sufficient condition is delta<64^(-(r+1)^2). Qualitative uniqueness and a sequence of high marginal densities with uncontrolled growing range do not supply this certificate: the local-anchor counterexample has densities tending to one and only finite good components. Peer w430 has supplied a coarsening criterion delta<64^(-4)/(r+1)^2, pending designated referee w431; it reduces the promising numerical hurdle but does not construct critical blocks.
title: C0023 compatible finite-block construction: the remaining gap

[Thm P exact Haus of arXiv:2608.25471, 'Exact Hausdorff measures and fine geometry of collisions of independent Markov processes'] [Exact Hausdorff measure for collision points] 
  Assume that $\hat{d}_{\mathrm{s}} > 2$.
  Then there exist a deterministic function
  $c_1\colon (0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ and a deterministic constant
  $c_2\in(0,\infty)$ such that,
  $\hat{P}_{\bm{\rho}}$-a.s., for all $t \in (0,\infty)$ and for every Borel subset $A$ of $M$,
  \begin{equation}
    c_1(t)\Pi_t(A)
    \leq
    \mathcal{H}_{\Psi_{\mathrm{cp}}}(A\cap\mathcal{P}_t)
    \leq
    c_2\Pi_t(A).
  \end{equation}
  In particular, 
  $0<\mathcal{H}_{\Psi_{\mathrm{cp}}}(\mathcal{P}_t)<\infty$ for all $t \in (0,\infty)$, 
  $\hat{P}_{\bm{\rho}}$-a.s. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For every n>=1 and d>=1, the operator f -> T_df=(1/d!)D^dF_f(0), from L2(mu) to the ordered-index Hilbert--Schmidt tensor space, has norm exactly sqrt(binom(2d-2,d-1)). Thus ||T_df||<=2^(d-1)||f||_2 and R=2 is the smallest base valid in ||T_df||<=R^d||f||_2 for all degrees in this family. The proof separates orthogonal coordinate supports before bounding each positive frame-operator trace. The law is isotropic and log-concave but nonsmooth, so this direct calculation does not invoke the regularity-dependent BKL criterion. It does not supply the input for arbitrary log-concave laws.

STATUS: proof (unaudited); owner-own-work draft; no novelty assertion. Every period-dividing-two orbit of simultaneous joint-head factored-attention GD with nonzero key-query imbalance is a fixed point, at every eta>0. Every nonstationary nonbalanced finite periodic orbit of any period requires delta squared >=2 at some iterate, where delta=eta vG. These exact algebraic obstructions do not prove full-space convergence or exclude balanced cycles. For every eta>0 a distinct-example coupled factored logistic attention family has the exact balanced period-two orbit (2/eta,1,-1) <-> (2/eta,-1,1), with constant loss log 2 and transverse two-step multiplier 9. Thus excluding imbalance-zero points is essential in 014, and an every-initialization GD classification containing only fixed points and endpoint escapes is false; no positive-measure or almost-everywhere failure is claimed.

# Target 1: two-cycle exclusion and necessary overshoot for periodic GD

Version 1, proof unaudited. This excludes possible third fates; it does not
classify all factored-GD trajectories or prove convergence.

Consider the factored model of claim 010 with any eta>0. More generally the
argument applies to any real update
 v_+=v+eta F(v,kq),
 k_+=k+delta q, q_+=q+delta k,
 delta=eta v G(v,kq),
where G is strictly positive at every finite point and F(0,s) has a unique
zero p_bar. The softmax logistic model satisfies these conditions.

1. Every orbit of period dividing two with k^2-q^2!=0 is a fixed point.
   It lies on v=0,kq=p_bar. This holds at every fixed step size.
2. Every nonstationary finite periodic orbit with k^2-q^2!=0 at one (hence
   every) iterate must contain an iterate with delta^2>=2. Equivalently,
   any periodic orbit on which |eta vG|<sqrt(2) throughout is stationary.

Neither statement excludes balanced-plane cycles, long cycles with large
overshoot, unbounded nonconvergent orbits, or nonperiodic bounded invariant
sets. This is a special obstruction result, not a scored global classification.

## Proof of two-cycle exclusion

Let U=k+q and D=k-q. Their exact simultaneous updates are
 U_+=(1+delta)U, D_+=(1-delta)D.
The nonzero imbalance is C=UD, so U,D are both nonzero initially.
For a returning two-step orbit, with a=delta_0,b=delta_1,
 (1+a)(1+b)=1, (1-a)(1-b)=1.
Expansion and addition yield 2ab=0; subtraction yields 2(a+b)=0.
Over the reals this forces a=b=0. Since eta>0 and G>0, v_0=v_1=0.
The factors therefore do not move. The head update then forces
F(0,kq)=0, hence kq=p_bar. This is a fixed point, as claimed.

## Proof of the overshoot requirement

The exact imbalance update is C_+=(1-delta^2)C. If an r-step orbit returns
with C_0!=0, no intermediate C can vanish, and
 product_{t=0}^{r-1}(1-delta_t^2)=1.
If every delta_t^2<2, every absolute factor is <=1, strictly less than 1
whenever delta_t!=0. The product can have absolute value 1 only if every
delta_t=0. Then every v_t=0, the factors stay fixed, and F(0,kq)=0.
Thus any nonstationary periodic orbit requires at least one delta_t^2>=2.

## Relation to the remaining gap

The flow's invariant imbalance is unavailable in GD, but its multiplicative
replacement still excludes every nonbalanced two-cycle, including at steps
beyond the normal-stability threshold of claim 013. A loss of an attracting
normal multiplier therefore does not by itself provide a two-cycle witness.
The unresolved step is controlling general, possibly large factor updates
well enough to show eventual entry into one of claim 010's escaping regions,
or finding a third fate that persists off the balanced planes.


# Target 1: exact balanced two-cycle and its transverse multiplier

Version 1, proof unaudited. Boundary check for claim 014, not a positive-volume
counterexample to an almost-everywhere theorem.

Fix any n>=2 and any distinct positive kappa_i. Put
 b_i=2 cosh(kappa_i)^2/kappa_i,
 a_i=b_i tanh(kappa_i).
These satisfy 0<a_i<b_i. In the usual coupled factored model
h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s), all links have
 h_i(-1)=0, h_i'(-1)=2.

For EVERY fixed eta>0, simultaneous Euclidean GD on the average logistic
loss has an exact two-cycle
 (v,k,q)=(2/eta,1,-1) <-> (2/eta,-1,1).
At both points the loss is log 2, the product is -1, and k^2-q^2=0.
The two-step Jacobian has a transverse multiplier 9 normal to k=-q.

delta=eta vG=2. The factor update sends

different nonlinear scales, rather than requiring repeated identical examples.

linearization gives dU_+=(1+delta)dU=3dU; the term U d(delta) vanishes.

of every finite initialization by stationary points and escaping selections
alone would be false at any positive constant step. The exceptional balanced
plane must be allowed, as it is in claim 012's flow statement (which is a
different dynamical system).

   every) iterate must contain an iterate with delta^2>=2. Equivalently,
   any periodic orbit on which |eta vG|<sqrt(2) throughout is stationary.

overshoot, unbounded nonconvergent orbits, or nonperiodic bounded invariant

Let U=k+q and D=k-q. Their exact simultaneous updates are
 U_+=(1+delta)U, D_+=(1-delta)D.
The nonzero imbalance is C=UD, so U,D are both nonzero initially.
For a returning two-step orbit, with a=delta_0,b=delta_1,

The exact imbalance update is C_+=(1-delta^2)C. If an r-step orbit returns

body: When $M$ predictors of the same target are trained on the same data, their error vectors are nearly collinear: the error covariance has a few large eigenvalues and a long tail of tiny ones. Its participation ratio $M_{\mathrm{eff}} = (\sum_k \lambda_k)^2 / \sum_k \lambda_k^2$ counts the independent error directions. Measured on the EMIT lookup-table pool (23 members, 932 calibration rows, seed 101): $M_{\mathrm{eff}} = 2.2$ to $3.4$, with spectra spanning sixteen decades (top / median / smallest eigenvalue $5.9 \times 10^{-4}$ / $6 \times 10^{-6}$ / $5 \times 10^{-20}$ on one component; condition numbers $10^5$ to $10^{16}$). Two consequences. First, the Marchenko-Pastur regime is not the relevant one: with $q_{\mathrm{eff}} = M_{\mathrm{eff}}/n$ between $0.002$ and $0.06$ the Pafka-Kondor inflation of the plug-in minimum-variance stack predicts gains of $0.1$ to $3$ percent from cleaning, while the measured gains of nonlinear shrinkage over least squares were $+4$, $+10$, $+14$, $+22$ percent at $n = 932, 240, 120, 60$ on the hardest component - an order of magnitude more. Second, the mechanism is different: the minimum-variance inverse $\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf{1}$ is dominated by the smallest eigenvalues, which are numerical noise around zero, so the plug-in stack wanders in the members' near-null space (the raw inverse is far worse than least squares at small $n$: $0.31$ against $0.058$ at 60 rows on one component), and any cleaning of that bottom of the spectrum is a large regularisation. Which cleaning matters depends on the component: where the gain is small (two of four components) a floor at the noise level, a cross-validated ridge and the Ledoit-Peche shrinkage agree within one percent; where the gain is large (the other two) the nonlinear shrinkage without any floor equals the shrinkage with the floor and beats every fixed floor by $4$ to $20$ percent and the cross-validated ridge by about $4$ percent, with no tuning. The number to compute before applying a random-matrix result to an ensemble is $M_{\mathrm{eff}}$, not $M$.

The normalized tilt coefficient T_d f=F_f^(d)(0)/d! is E[f(X)q_d(Y)], where q_d(y)=y^d/d!-y^(d-1)/(d-1)! for d>=1. [Lemma 11 (Uniform inner--outer matching) of arXiv:2609.02788, '\textbf{Quantized Einstein Metrics on \(S^7\) with \(SU(3)\)-Symmetry}'] There is a function $\varepsilon(b)\to0$ such that, uniformly for
$|\mu|\le\mu_0$,
\begin{align}
 F_2(b,\mu)&=\mathcal E(\mu)+O(\varepsilon(b)),\\
 b^{-5/2}F_1(b,\mu)
 &=\Re\!\left(C_o(\mu)Qe^{i\omega\log(1/b)}\right)
   +O(\varepsilon(b)).
\end{align}
With $\delta_b=b^{1/2}$ one may take
\begin{equation}
 \varepsilon(b)
 =C\left[
   \kappa_b+\delta_b^\sigma+\delta_b^2
   +\left(\frac b{\delta_b}\right)^5
 \right](1+|\log\delta_b|).
\end{equation}
In particular \(\varepsilon(b)\to0\) as \(b\downarrow0\).  Indeed,
\(\beta_+=(-5+3\sqrt5)/2\in(0,2)\),
\(\rho(b)=O(b^{\beta_+/m})\), and with
\(\delta_b=b^{1/2}\), \(\tau_b=b^{-1/2}\), every power occurring in
\(\kappa_b\) and \((b/\delta_b)^5\) is strictly positive; multiplication by
\(1+|\log\delta_b|\) therefore still tends to zero.
title: Uniform inner--outer matching

[Proposition prop:Eproduct of arXiv:2507.10531, 'Quantitative central limit theorems for exponential random graphs'] For any fixed $k$, let $e_1, \dotsc, e_k \in \binom{[n]}{2}$ be distinct potential edges and suppose that
either of the following two conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
	\item The density $p$ is the unique global maximizer of $L_\beta$, i.e.\ $M_\beta = U_\beta = \{p\}$.
	\item The edges $e_1, \dotsc, e_k$ form a forest in $K_n$, the complete graph on $[n]$.

body:
For a least-squares predictor yhat(x) = x' beta_hat fitted on n rows, the textbook variance at a new point x is sigma^2 x'(X'SX)^(-1) x (sigma^2 times the leverage), and the hat matrix H = X(X'SX)^(-1)X'S has trace equal to the number of parameters. Both statements require X'SX to be invertible. On a design that is rank-deficient - here, an ensemble whose members include exact duplicates, so the member-prediction Gram of every output is singular by the number of duplicates - the leverage is undefined: the trace of the hat matrix drops to the rank (21 instead of 24 on the s104 Y1 cell of the EMIT pool), and inverting through a tiny ridge assigns any new point that leaves the duplicates' span an arbitrarily large leverage (a load 11.8 times the whole prediction error on that cell), which is a property of the ridge, not of the predictor actually used. The pairs bootstrap sidesteps this: resample the n rows with replacement B times, refit the predictor exactly as it is fitted in production (with its own ridge or pseudo-inverse and its own constraints), and take the empirical variance of the B predictions at x. Under Freedman's (1981) conditions for the pairs (correlation-model) bootstrap - independent rows, finite fourth moments of the regressors and errors, and a design whose empirical second-moment matrix converges - the bootstrap variance of a linear predictor is consistent for its sampling variance, and it remains well defined on a singular design because every resample is fitted by the same regularised map as the original. It is the right variance estimator when the estimator's regularisation, rather than an invertible Gram, determines its behaviour; it also applies unchanged to a constrained estimator (a long-only stack) for which no closed form exists. Cost: B refits per cell; B = 8 was enough to rank rows and cells in the RMT ensemble program (the ranking, not the level, was used).
rows independent and identically distributed (the pairs bootstrap resamples rows, not residuals, so heteroscedasticity is allowed)
finite fourth moments and a converging empirical second-moment matrix (Freedman 1981); the predictor is a fixed measurable map of the sample, applied identically to every resample

body: Let pi(x) denote the number of primes less than or equal to x. The prime number theorem states pi(x) is asymptotic to x / log(x) as x tends to infinity, meaning the ratio pi(x) / (x / log x) tends to 1; equivalently pi(x) is asymptotic to the logarithmic integral Li(x), a sharper approximation. Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, the error term satisfies pi(x) = Li(x) + O(sqrt(x) log x). First proved independently in 1896 by Jacques Hadamard and Charles Jean de la Vallee Poussin, using nonvanishing of the Riemann zeta function on the line Re(s) = 1.
title: Prime number theorem

body: For a household size h and contacts vector X = (X_G, X_L), let B(p) be the branching process approximating the early epidemic when each local contact is replaced by a global one independently with probability p. The extinction probability rho_p of B(p) is decreasing in p (Lemma 5.2). Proof: for 0 <= p < q <= 1, B(p) and B(q) are built on one probability space so that the i-th individual makes the same X_{G,i} + X_{L,i} attempted births and Y^(p)_{T,i} <= Y^(q)_{T,i} of its local contacts are converted to global ones; a lower-bound process B^(p, q), with the Y^(q) - Y^(p) extra contacts made 'ghost contacts', gives rho_q <= rho_p. Consequently the probability of a major outbreak increases in p for any distribution of X_L, while the limiting final size z increases in p when the pgf of X_L is log-convex and can fail to otherwise.

[Definition defi_solution_ep of arXiv:2603.26307, '\LARGE The incompressible Navier--Stokes--Fourier system with thermal noise'] A  \emph{weak martingale solution 
		to (equation ep_approx of the paper)--(equation eqn354865865 of the paper)} 
	consists of a probability space $(\Omega,\mathfrak{A},\mathbb{P})$, a filtration $\mathscr{F}$ satisfying the usual conditions, independent $3$-dimensional standard $\mathscr{F}$-Brownian motions $(W_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$ and $3\times 3$-matrix valued $\mathscr{F}$-Brownian motions $(B_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$ with covariance structure (equation Eq_noise_matrix_covariation of the paper), a weakly continuous and adapted  $L^2(\mathbb{T}^3 ;\mathbb{R}^3)$-valued process
	$u_{\epsilon}$, as well as   progressively measurable   $\psi_{\epsilon} \in L^\infty(0,T;L^2( \mathbb{T}^3))$ and  $q_{\epsilon}\in \mathcal{M}_+([0,T]\times \mathbb{T}^3)$, such that the following holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item  We have the additional regularity {$u_{\epsilon}\in L^{2}(0,T;H^2(\mathbb{T}^3 ;\mathbb{R}^{3}))$ and $\psi_{\epsilon} \in  L^{2}(0,T;H^2(\mathbb{T}^3))$}, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely.
		\item   It holds $\psi_{\epsilon}>0$, $\mathbb{P}\otimes \mathrm{d} t \otimes \mathrm{d} x$-a.e., and  $q_{\epsilon} \ge \frac{1}{\psi_{\epsilon}}(|\nabla \psi_{\epsilon}|^2 + |\nabla_\mathrm{sym} u_{\epsilon}|^2+\epsilon)$,  as measures  on $[0,T]\times \mathbb{T}^3$, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely. 
		\item   For every divergence-free $\varphi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ it holds
		\begin{align}\begin{split}
				& \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}  u_{\epsilon,t}\cdot \varphi\,\mathrm{d} x \,-\, 
				\int_{\mathbb{T}^3} u_0 \cdot \varphi\,\mathrm{d} x\,+\,\epsilon\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb{T}^3} u_{\epsilon}\Delta^2\varphi\,\mathrm{d} x\,\mathrm{d} s
				\\&\quad=\,  \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3} -  \Bigl(\frac{1}{2}+ \frac{F_1}{4}\Bigr) \nabla u_{\epsilon}: \nabla  \varphi \,+\, u_{\epsilon}\otimes u_{\epsilon}:\nabla \varphi \,\mathrm{d} x\, \mathrm{d} s \,+\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}^3}\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}\psi_{\epsilon} f_n \nabla \varphi\,\mathrm{d} x :\mathrm{d} B_{n,s},
			\end{split}
		\end{align}
		and $\nabla \cdot u_{\epsilon,t} = 0$ for all $t\in [0,T]$, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely.
		\item  
		For every $\zeta\in C_c^{\infty}([0,T) \times \mathbb{T}^3)$ it holds
		\begin{align}\begin{split}
				&-\,
				\int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{T}^3} \psi_{\epsilon}  \partial_t \zeta  \, \mathrm{d} x\, \mathrm{d} t \,-\, \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}
				\psi_0 \zeta
				\,\mathrm{d} x\,+\,\epsilon\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb{T}^3} \psi_{\epsilon}\Delta^2\zeta\,\mathrm{d} x\,\mathrm{d} s 
				\\&\quad=\,  \int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{T}^3} - \bigl(1+ {F_1}/2 +G_1/2\bigr) \nabla \psi_{\epsilon}\cdot \nabla  \zeta \,+\,\psi_{\epsilon} u_{\epsilon}\cdot \nabla \zeta   \,-\, (F_2/2+G_2/8) \psi_{\epsilon} \zeta \,\mathrm{d} x\,\mathrm{d} t \,+\, \int_{[0,T]\times\mathbb{T}^3} \zeta \,\mathrm{d} q
				\\&\qquad + \sum_{i=1}^3
				\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}^3}\int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{T}^3} \psi_{\epsilon} g_n \partial_i \zeta  + \frac{1}{2} \psi_{\epsilon}  \zeta \partial_ig_n \,\mathrm{d} x \, \mathrm{d} W_{n,t}^i
				\, +\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sum_{i,j =1}^3\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}^3}\int_0^T \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}u_{\epsilon,j}\partial_i (\zeta f_n) \,\mathrm{d} x \,\mathrm{d} B_{n,t}^{ji},
			\end{split}
		\end{align}  $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely.
	\end{enumerate}
title: Weak martingale solution to \eqref{ep_approx}--\eqref{eqn354865865}

[Corollary Recovery from sampled trajectories of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] There
exist constants \(C,C_{low},C_{up},\varepsilon_{0},c > 0\) such
that if \(0 < \varepsilon < \varepsilon_{0}\),
\[T \geq C\left( s_{0} + \kappa_{d}(\varepsilon)^{- 1}\left( \log N_{\varepsilon}(M) + \log\frac{1}{\delta} \right) \right)\],
and \(\omega_{X}(\Delta) \leq c\varepsilon\), then with
probability at least \(1 - \delta\),

\begin{multline*}
H_{q}\left( \left( \Gamma_{T}^{\Delta} \right)^{r} \right) \cong H_{q}(M)\\
\text{for every }q = 0,\ldots,d\text{ and every }C_{low}\,\varepsilon \leq r \leq C_{up}\, \operatorname{reach}(M).
\end{multline*}

Blachère–den Hollander–Steif (2011), Theorem 1.3, restricted to zero holding probability: let iid increments X_n in {-1,+1}, n>=1, have P(X_n=+1)=p in [1/2,1], let S_0=0 and S_n=sum_{j=1}^n X_j, and let C_z be independent iid fair black/white scenery. Set Y_n=C_{S_n}. Badness and goodness refer to the conditional law of Y_0 given the ONE-SIDED future record (Y_n)_{n>=1}, using finite-cylinder tail-tampering discontinuity. (i) There exists p0<1 such that every future record is good when p0<p<=1. (ii) Every future record is bad when 1/2<p<4/5. (iii) At p=1/2 both good and bad future records exist. These conclusions do not classify two-sided exterior records. The paper's more general walk has holding probability epsilon; all three conclusions stated here assume epsilon=0. Locator: arXiv:1103.1780v3, Theorem 1.3, PDF page 5; one-sided restriction Section 1.1, PDF page 2.
