OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; C18 v1 status SKETCH, independent audit pending, no novelty claim; not a certified theorem. Proposed diagnostic: for a finite public Gaussian family N(mu_theta,v0 I_d), d>=1 and v0>0, every finite set of OU time-point pairs (t_j,x_j), t_j>=0, and epsilon>0 admit instance-specific jointly smooth estimated fields b_theta equal to zero on those pairs with E_{OU_t(P_theta)} ||b_theta-s_theta,t||^2 <= epsilon^2 for every t>=0. Each field has some finite global spatial Lipschitz constant uniform over t; no prescribed, polynomial, or efficient-computability bound is supplied. The fields need not be gradients or scores of an OU-consistent family. Construction: choose smooth time bumps h_j and small spatial bumps g_j, set chi=1-product_j(1-h_j g_j), and b_theta=(1-chi)s_theta. The Gaussian envelope and chi^2<=chi<=sum_j h_j g_j make the uniform error arbitrarily small. For a sampler with a uniform finite query cap Q and a selected finite set S of query-randomness seeds, form at most Q|S| query pairs from all-zero-reply adaptive paths. The resulting fields are fixed before drawing the realized seed and produce identical replies on every seed in S. If S has probability at least 1-eta, two output laws have TV at most eta, so for target separation delta one target has sampling TV error at least (delta-eta)/2. Independent continuous randomness after the query phase is allowed. Finite sets of individual continuously distributed query seeds can instead have zero probability. Smoothness without a quantitative modulus does not justify query discretization. Thus this does not prove a lower bound for continuously randomized diffusion samplers, a prescribed Lipschitz oracle class, or Target 2. The real missing step is continuous adaptive transcript indistinguishability, not finite path interpolation. Only finite mask algebra was checked; the construction and coupling await review.
Finite public Gaussian family with common positive spherical variance; d>=1
Finite prescribed set of nonnegative OU time-point pairs; epsilon>0
No prescribed Lipschitz constant, gradient constraint, or OU-consistency assumption for estimated fields
Adaptive application assumes identical public input, uniform finite query cap, and a finite selected set of query-randomness seeds
Finite-seed masking does not establish continuously randomized query hardness

[Corollary cor:robustness of arXiv:2503.21737, 'High-intensity Voronoi percolation on manifolds'] Let \(r, \delta > 0\).

Method: Mixing of the random-pair binary crossover chain structural calculation Result: The naive Hamming coupling in the source has exact one-column drift E(W_next|W=w)=w-w^2/[2(K-1)]. At the last possible disagreement w=2, the chance of removing it is1/(K-1), so this coupling itself requires order K further steps from that state. It therefore cannot prove logarithmic K mixing simply by improving its large-w drift estimate. Check: When w=2 there is one opposite mismatch of each sign. They coalesce only if paired, probability1/(K-1), and then the prescribed opposite-swap coupling agrees forever. Waiting is geometric. This is a limitation of the coupling, not a mixing-time lower bound. Obstruction: One needs a different coupling, entropy estimate or representation argument which does not insist on coordinatewise agreement at every generation. Marginal one-column mixing also does not automatically control joint mixing because pairings are shared across all columns.

body: Let A be a real symmetric (or complex Hermitian) n by n matrix, and define its inertia as the triple (n_+, n_-, n_0) of the numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues of A, counted with multiplicity (n_+ + n_- + n_0 = n). If B = P* A P for some invertible n by n matrix P (a congruence transformation), then B has the same inertia as A. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis]
title: Sylvester's Law of Inertia

body: Let G = (V, E) be a finite graph. A proper k-coloring of G is a function c: V -> {1, ..., k} such that c(u) is not equal to c(v) whenever {u,v} is in E. The chromatic number chi(G) is the smallest integer k for which a proper k-coloring of G exists. [standard, e.g. Diestel, Graph Theory]
title: Chromatic Number of a Graph

body: If a countable first-order theory, over a countable language, has an infinite model, then it has models of every infinite cardinality. The downward Lowenheim-Skolem theorem gives, for any infinite model, an elementary substructure of any smaller infinite cardinality down to that of the language; the upward part gives elementary extensions of every larger cardinality. Consequently no countable first-order theory with an infinite model can determine a unique infinite structure up to isomorphism, as illustrated by the Skolem paradox for axiomatic set theory. Proved by Leopold Lowenheim (1915) and Thoralf Skolem (1920, 1922).
title: Lowenheim-Skolem theorem

[Theorem 18 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $(X_t)$ be an ergodic Markov chain with state space $\Omega$ and transition matrix $P$. Let $\Phi$ be an eigenfunction of $P$ with real eigenvalue $\alpha$ satisfying $1/2 < \alpha< 1$. Let $R>0$ such that:
   \[\mathbb{E}_x\left(|\Phi(X_1)-\Phi(x)|^2\right)\leq R,\quad \forall x\in \Omega\]
   Then for any $x\in \Omega$ and $\epsilon\in (0,1)$,
   \[t_\text{mix}(\epsilon) \geq \frac{1}{2\log(1/\alpha)}\left[\log \left(\frac{(1-\alpha)\Phi(x)^2}{2R}\right) + \log\left(\frac{1-\epsilon}{\epsilon}\right)\right]\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Method: Bootstrap thresholds on the line and the three-regular tree Result: On Z the one-neighbor bootstrap threshold is zero, whereas the two-neighbor threshold is one because any initially vacant adjacent pair stays vacant. On the three-regular tree with threshold two, the final vacant set is the two-core of the initial vacant percolation. If its density q<=1/2, all vacant clusters are finite almost surely and leaf pruning empties them. If q>1/2, with positive probability a vertex has two surviving vacant branches, giving a bi-infinite vacant path that remains vacant. Hence the complete-occupation threshold is p=1/2. Check: An infinite bi-infinite path supplies a stable set since each vertex has two vacant neighbors. Finite trees have an exposed leaf and are exhausted by the pruning process. Critical Binomial(2,1/2) clusters die out. Obstruction: This illustrates both the amenable endpoint behavior and a nonamenable interior threshold. [Definition Random environment system of arXiv:2606.13264, 'Interference Queueing Networks: A Replica Mean-Field Approach in the Symmetric Setting'] Fix \(p\in[0,1]\). For each \(i\in\{1,\dots,N\}\), let
\(D_i^p\) be a Poisson random measure on
\[
\mathbb R_+\times\mathbb R_+\times\{0,1\}^{N-1}
\]
with intensity
\[
\mathrm du\,\mathrm dz\,\nu_p(\mathrm d\theta),
\]
where \(\nu_p\) is the product measure of \(N-1\) independent Bernoulli
random variables with parameter \(p\).

For \(\theta=(\theta_m)_{m\neq i}\in\{0,1\}^{N-1}\), define
\[
\mu_i^p(\theta)
=
B\log_2\left(
1+
\frac{1}{1+\sum_{m\neq i}\theta_m l(d(i,m))}
\right).
\]
The random-environment system is defined, for each
\(i\in\{1,\dots,N\}\), by
\[
q_i^p(t)
=
q_i^p(0)
+
A_i[0,t]
-
\int_{\{0,1\}^{N-1}}\int_{\mathbb R_+}\int_0^t
\mathbf 1_{\{u\leq \mu_i^p(\theta)\}}
\mathbf 1_{\{q_i^p(z^-)>0\}}
\,D_i^p(\mathrm du,\mathrm dz,\mathrm d\theta).
\]
title: Random environment system

body: For a complex m by n matrix A, s_1(A) >= s_2(A) >= ... >= 0 are its singular values (padded with zeros to min(m, n) entries). For 1 <= p < infinity the Schatten p-norm is ||A||_{S_p} = (sum_i s_i(A)^p)^(1/p), and ||A||_{S_infinity} = s_1(A), the spectral norm. Zero singular values do not change the value. These norms are unitarily invariant, ||U A V||_{S_p} = ||A||_{S_p} for unitary U and V, and S_1 is the nuclear (trace) norm, S_2 the Frobenius norm and S_infinity the spectral norm.

body: In the localized FPP problem on a finite region of Z^2 (weights restricted to a finite edge set), define G as the set of edges lying in EVERY geodesic between two fixed points. Then membership is Borel outright: e belongs to G if and only if the passage time computed with e forbidden strictly exceeds the unrestricted passage time, and both are continuous functions of finitely many weights. No measurable selection of a geodesic is needed for any argument consuming G, and geodesic non-uniqueness only SHRINKS G (more geodesics means more constraints), so uniqueness assumptions are unnecessary for upper bounds on |G|. Confirmed in independent review (2026-08-10) of an entropy-method derivation that had carried a measurable-selection caveat it turned out not to need.

body:
[Thm 1 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Suppose that $\sqrt{N} W_{ij}$ $(1 \leq i<j \leq N)$ are i.i.d., symmetric, and strictly sub-Gaussian random variables with variance $1$. Suppose that $\sqrt{N} x_k$ $(1 \leq k \leq N)$ are i.i.d., symmetric, and strictly sub-Gaussian random variables with variance $1$, independent of $\sqrt{N} W_{ij}$. Let
\beq 
	Z_N \equiv Z_N(\beta) = \E_{\caX} \left[ \exp \left( \beta N \sum_{i<j} W_{ij} \frac{x_i x_j}{\| \bsx \|^2} \right) \right], \qquad F_N \equiv F_N(\beta) = \frac{1}{N} \log Z_N.
\eeq
(When $\| \bsx \| = 0$, we define $x_i x_j / \| \bsx \|^2 = 0$ for all $i, j$.) Then, for any $\beta \in (0, 1)$,
\[
	F_N(\beta) \to F(\beta) := \beta^2 /4
\]
and
\[
	N(F_N(\beta) - F(\beta) ) \Rightarrow \caN(m_F, V_F),
\]
as $N \to \infty$, i.e., $N(F_N(\beta) - F(\beta) )$ converges in distribution to the Gaussian with mean $m_F$ and the variance $V_F$ as $N \to \infty$. Here,
\[
	m_F = \frac{1}{4} \log (1- \beta^2) + \frac{\beta^2 (1-m_4)}{4} + \frac{\beta^4 (w_4-3)(m_4^2 -3)}{48}
\]
and
\[
	V_F = -\frac{1}{2} \left( \log (1- \beta^2) + \beta^2 - \frac{\beta^4 (w_4-3)}{4} \right),
\]
where we let $w_4 = N^2 \E[W_{ij}^4]$ and $m_4 = N^2 \E [x_1^4]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:Lambda_J_approach1 of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let Assumptions~(ass:dynamics of the paper) hold, such that the symmetric part
$\mathcal{L}_S$ satisfies the Poincar\'e inequality~(equation eq:poincare of the paper) with
spectral gap $\lambda_\mathrm{gap}>0$. Then for all 
$0 \leq k < \lambda_\mathrm{gap}/\|W-\E^\mu[W]\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}$,
\begin{align}
\Lambda^J(k)
&\leq
k\E^\mu[W]
+ \frac{k^2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(W)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap} - k\|W - \E^\mu[W]\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}}
+ k^2\|Q\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}
\\
&\leq
k\E^\mu[W]
+ \frac{k^2 \bigl(\mathrm{Var}_\mu(W) + \lambda_\mathrm{gap}\|Q\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}\bigr)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap} - k \|W - \E^\mu[W]\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}}.

\end{align}

[Corollary 22 of arXiv:2608.18557, 'Randomly Permuted Orthogonal Products and Fast Dimension Reduction'] There exist universal constants \(c,C>0\) such that the following
	holds. Let \(X\subseteq \mathbb S^{d-1}\) with \(|X|=N\geq d\),
	\(0<\eps<1\), \(0<\eta<1/2\), and
	\(I\subseteq [d]\) with \(|I|=m\). Let \(Q_T\) be a Kac walk with
	\(T\geq Cd\log(d/\eta)\), let \(D_\xi\) be an independent
	Rademacher diagonal, and let \(\pi\) be an independent uniform
	permutation on \(S_d\). Define
	\[
	\Phi=\sqrt{\frac dm}\,P_IQ_TD_\xi P_\pi.
	\]
	Assume the admissibility condition
	\[
	m\log\left(\frac d\eta\right)
	\log\left(\frac{Nd}{\eta}\right)
	\log\left(\frac{Nm}{\eta}\right)
	\leq c d.
	\]
	If $m\geq C\eps^{-2}\log(N/\eta)$,
	then, with probability at least \(1-\eta\),
	\[
	\sup_{x\in X}
	\left|
	\norm{\Phi x}_2-\norm{x}_2
	\right|
	\le
	\eps\norm{x}_2.
	\]

[Proposition 25 of arXiv:2608.25785, 'Proper Actions on Homogeneous Spaces of the Upper Triangular Matrix Group via Coarse Geome'] Let $G_1,G_2$ be locally compact Hausdorff groups and $f$ a map from $G_1$ to $G_2$.
    Consider that $G_1$ and $G_2$ are equipped with LR-coarse structure.
    Then the following six assertions hold:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Assume that  $f$ is a continuous group-homomorphism. Then $f$ is controlled.
        \item Assume that  $f$ is a continuous anti-group-homomorphism. Then $f$ is controlled.
        \item Assume that  $f$ is a topological closed embedding group-homomorphism. Then $f$ is coarse. 
        \item Assume that  $f$ is a topological closed embedding anti-group-homomorphism. Then $f$ is coarse. 
        \item Assume that  $f$ is an isomorphism of topological groups. Then $f$ is a coarse equivalence. 
        \item Assume that  $f$ is an anti-isomorphism of topological groups. Then $f$ is a coarse equivalence. 
    \end{enumerate}
    In particular, for a group and its closed subgroup, the inclusion map is coarse. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Owner-own-work research draft; proof (unaudited), independent review and priority assessment pending. Fix k>=2, D>=1, 0<alpha<1, b>0, M,K>=0 and 0<lambda<=1<=Lambda. Let F:[0,1]^k->R^D extend C1 to a neighborhood with ||DF||<=b and Lip(DF)<=M, and let p be a probability density with lambda<=p<=Lambda and Lip(p)<=K. There are C,W0 depending only on these constants such that, for W>=W0, a common scalar-input ReLU feedforward DAG with at most W charged edge weights and biases and depth O(W) satisfies sup_(F,p) inf_theta W1((G_theta)#Unif[0,1], F#(p dx))<=C W^(-2(1+alpha)/k). Skip connections, unrestricted real precision and discontinuous target-to-weight assignments are allowed. All fixed coefficients, affine biases, output translations and scalar-source conversion edges are charged. The proof reflects p evenly to a 2-periodic positive density, invokes Caffarelli-Li periodic Monge-Ampere C2,alpha regularity and uniqueness, and derives uniform potential bounds by compactness and the mean-zero periodic Schauder implicit-function theorem. Reflection symmetry forces S=x+grad u to preserve every cube face; det DS=p implies its inverse R samples p exactly. F composed with R lies in a common C1,alpha ball; the Yarotsky-Zhevnerchuk function approximation theorem and a logarithmic-size tent-map scalar-source conversion give the rate. For (a,b)-bi-Lipschitz maps with Lip(DF)<=M, exactly uniform surface laws are included by lambda=(a/b)^k, Lambda=(b/a)^k, K=k b^(k-1) M/a^k. Thus every exponent 4/k-eta with fixed 0<eta<2/k is available, but no endpoint 4/k, bounded-bit upper or arbitrary closed-manifold-class upper is claimed. The least-trusted analytic step is uniformity of the mean-zero periodic Schauder/implicit-function argument, not certified by finite algebraic controls.
Unrestricted real weights and discontinuous weight selection; skip connections allowed and all fixed coefficients, biases and source conversion charged. Cube images may have boundary; no arbitrary closed-manifold class or bounded-bit upper. Standard periodic linear Schauder theory and Banach implicit-function theorem are explicit analytic inputs.
Proof (unaudited); the step-2 uniform periodic transport argument and its primary-source inputs require independent review.

[Theorem thm:fullII of arXiv:2607.01463, 'Two Multi--Draw Coupon Collector models with different retention rules'] The full asymptotic expansion of the expectation of the random variable $T_{N,1}$ (of Theorem (result2 of the paper)) regarding the $d$ coupon collector problem, where we draw $d$ coupons each time, but keep the \textbf{least} collected coupon so far, is (as $N \rightarrow \infty$)
\[
\mathbb{E}[T_{N,1}]
\sim
\frac{N}{d}\log N
+\left(\frac{\gamma}{d}+
C_d\right)N
+
\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}
\bigl(\alpha_{j+1}(d)\log N+u_j(d)\bigr)N^{-j},
\]
where,
\begin{equation*}
C_d:
=
\int_0^1
\left(
\frac{1}{1-(1-x)^d}-\frac{1}{dx}
\right)\,dx,
\end{equation*}
\[
u_j(d)
=
\gamma\,a_{j+1}(d)
+
\int_0^1 h_{j+1}(x;d)\,dx
+
\frac{a_j(d)+h_j(1;d)-h_j(0;d)}{2}
\]
\[
\qquad
-
\sum_{r=1}^{\lfloor (j+1)/2\rfloor}
\frac{B_{2r}}{2r}\,a_{j+1-2r}(d)
+
\sum_{r=1}^{\lfloor (j+1)/2\rfloor}
\frac{B_{2r}}{(2r)!}
\bigl(
h_{j+1-2r}^{(2r-1)}(1;d)-h_{j+1-2r}^{(2r-1)}(0;d)
\bigr),
\]
and, as usual, $\lfloor x\rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. The quantities $\alpha_j$ and $h_j$ are defined in the Appendix in relations ((a3 of the paper)) and ((a4 of the paper)). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In statistical mechanics, the Griffiths inequality, sometimes also called Griffiths–Kelly–Sherman inequality or GKS inequality, named after Robert B. Griffiths, is a correlation inequality for ferromagnetic spin systems. Informally, it says that in ferromagnetic spin systems, if the 'a-priori distribution' of the spin is invariant under spin flipping, the correlation of any monomial of the spins is non-negative; and the two point correlation of two monomial of the spins is non-negative.
title: Griffiths inequality

body: In Riemannian geometry, the sectional curvature is one of the ways to describe the curvature of Riemannian manifolds. The sectional curvature $K(\sigma _{p})$ depends on a two-dimensional linear subspace $\sigma _{p}$ of the tangent space at a point $p$ of the manifold. It can be defined geometrically as the Gaussian curvature of the surface which has the plane $\sigma _{p}$ as a tangent plane at $p$, obtained from geodesics which start at $p$ in the directions of $\sigma _{p}$ (in other words, the image of $\sigma _{p}$ under the exponential map at $p$). The sectional curvature is a real-valued function on the 2-Grassmannian bundle over the manifold.

Let Delta_(t+1)=(I-M_t)Delta_t in finite-dimensional real space, where the random self-adjoint matrices M_t are independent, satisfy 0<=M_t<=I, and have a common mean Q. Unit rows give uniform sampling. The rate is for the true last iterate and is independent of condition number; it does not establish inverse-time convergence.

Let q be a prime power and 1 <= k <= q. Choose C_0, ..., C_{k-1} independent and uniform in F_q and let P(t) = C_0 + C_1 t + ... + C_{k-1} t^(k-1). Then the family (P(a))_{a in F_q} is k-wise independent and each P(a) is uniform on F_q. If k < q, no k + 1 of the evaluations are independent: for distinct a_1, ..., a_{k+1}, P(a_{k+1}) is a function of P(a_1), ..., P(a_k), and the (k+1)-tuple takes only q^k of the q^(k+1) possible values.

  probability measure of the 3-$d$ Bessel bridge, namely, the law of
  $\left\{\left|B_t\right|\right\}_{t \in [0,1]}$ conditioned to $B_1 = 0$.  The
  set $K_{0}$ is introduced in (equation E:def-Kalpha of the paper) with $\alpha=0$. We consider a
  measure $\nu^{G}$ on $K_0$ defined as follows: for all $\xi \in K_0$,
  \begin{align}
    \nu^G (\ensuremath{\mathrm{d}} \xi) \coloneqq e^{2 G(\xi)} \nu(\ensuremath{\mathrm{d}} \xi),
  \end{align}
  where $G$ is given by~(equation E:def-Gxi of the paper). Then, $\nu^G$ is an invariant measure
  for~(equation E:reflect of the paper) reflected at $0$.

body: [Prop poincare of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Every Reebless $C^0$-foliation $\mathcal{G}$ on $\mathbb{T}^2$ of slope $s$ is monotone equivalent to a linear foliation $\mathcal{G}_s$ of slope $s$. When $s$ is irrational, the monotone equivalence can be taken to be a blowup along countably many leaves. When $s$ is rational, the monotone equivalence can be taken to be a blowup along countably many leaves, each inserting a $\sharp$ or $\flat$ annulus, followed by a blowdown of countably many $\natural$ annuli. The invariant measure on $\mathcal{G}_s$ pulls back to an invariant transverse measure on $\mathcal{G}$ whose support is the union of all minimal sets of $\mathcal{G}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop poincare of arXiv:2608.30031

body: In mathematics, Hall's marriage theorem, proved by Philip Hall, is a theorem with two equivalent formulations. In each case, the theorem gives a necessary and sufficient condition for an object to exist:The combinatorial formulation answers whether a finite collection of sets has a transversal—that is, whether an element can be chosen from each set without repetition. Hall's condition is that for any subset of sets from the collection, the total unique elements they contain is at least as large as the number of sets in the subset. The graph theoretic formulation answers whether a finite bipartite graph has a perfect matching—that is, a way to match each vertex from one group uniquely to an adjacent vertex from the other group. Hall's condition is that any subset of vertices from one group has a neighbourhood of equal or greater size.
title: Hall's marriage theorem

body:
[Proposition 26 of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $V$ be a strictly convex, $p$-homogeneous, $C^2$ function on $\R^n$, $p>1$, satisfying $V(o)=0$. Then, the geometric inequality
    \begin{equation}
    
        \vol(K)\vol\left(\nabla \mathcal{L}V(K^\circ)\right)^{p-1} \leq \vol\left(\left\{V\leq \frac{1}{p}\right\}\right)^p, \qquad \forall \,K \in \mathcal{C}^n,
    \end{equation}
    holds if and only if for every $f \in \mathcal{F}_n$ and all measurable functions $g:\R^n\to\R_+$ and $\Omega:\R_+\to\R_+$, where $\Omega$ is non-increasing, that satisfy the pointwise bound
    \[
        f(x)^{\frac{1}{p}}g(y)^{\frac{p-1}{p}} \leq \Omega\left(\frac{\langle x,y \rangle}{p}\right), \qquad \forall \,\,x, y \in \R^n \text{ with } \langle x,y \rangle>0,
    \]
    one has the functional inequality:
    \begin{equation}
    
        \left(\int_{\R^n}f(x)dx\right)\left(\int_{\R^n}g(\nabla V(z))dz\right)^{p-1} \leq \left(\int_{\R^n}\Omega(V(z))dz\right)^p.
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 26 of arXiv:2609.01460

body: [Lemma lem:likeliness of arXiv:2609.04138, 'The conformally invariant metric on $\CLE_4$ I:\\ subsequential limits of the non-simple C'] Fix distinct $x,y \in \partial \BD$ and let $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ be such that $\varepsilon < \min\{1/2, |x-y| / 3\}$. For each $n \in \BN$, let $\eta_n$ be a chordal $\SLE_{\kappa_n}(-1;-1)$ in $\BD$ starting from $x$ and targeting $y$, where the force points are located at $x^-$ and $x^+$ respectively. [Definition defWellPoseHadmard of arXiv:2411.05534, 'Inverse problems for stochastic partial differential equations'] Consider the equation

\begin{equation}
F(u) = v, \qquad u\in U,\; v \in V.
\end{equation}

The equation (equation defWellPoseHadmard-eq1 of the paper) is called well-posed in the sense of Hadamard if the following three conditions are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item For any $ v \in V $, there exists a solution $ u \in U$ such that $ F(u) = v $.
    \item This solution is unique.
    \item The solution $ v = F^{-1}(u) $ depends continuously on $ u $ in $U$.
\end{enumerate}
If at least one of these conditions is failed, the problem is called ill-posed.
title: Definition defWellPoseHadmard of arXiv:2411.05534

[Thm prop.convipvt of arXiv:2412.00822, '\textsc{Ideal Poisson--Voronoi tessellations \\ beyond hyperbolic spaces}'] Let $\mathbf{X}^{(\lambda)}=(X_i^{(\lambda)} \, \,;\; \, i\geq 1 )$ be a PPP of intensity measure $\lambda \cdot \mathrm{Vol}_{ \mathcal{M}}$, where the points of $\mathbf{X}^{(\lambda)}$ are ranked by increasing values of $d(X_i^{(\lambda)},\mathbf{o})$. Then the following convergence in law holds
$$
\mathrm{Vor}(\mathbf{X}^{(\lambda)}) \underset{\lambda \downarrow 0}{\overset{\rm law}{\Longrightarrow}}\mathrm{Vor}( \boldsymbol{\Theta}, \boldsymbol{\Phi}, \mathbf{D}) \; ,
$$
where $\boldsymbol{\Theta}=(\Theta_{1},\ldots)$ and $\boldsymbol{\Phi}=(\Phi_{1},\ldots)$ are i.i.d.~uniform on $\partial\mathbb{H}_2 \times \partial\mathbb{H}_2$ and $\mathbf{D}=(D_{1},\ldots)$ is s.t.~$\left(\pi^{2}e^{D_{i}}\right)_{i\geq 1}$ is a rate-1 homogeneous PPP on $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$. The processes $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$,  $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$, $\mathbf{D}$ are all pairwise independent. We call $\mathrm{Vor}( \boldsymbol{\Theta}, \boldsymbol{\Phi}, \mathbf{D})$ the \textbf{\textit{ideal Poisson–Voronoi tessellation}} of $\mathcal{M}$ and denote it by $\text{\rm IPVT}(\mathcal{M})$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textsc{Convergence towards IPVT($\mathcal{M}$), extended version}

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT; mathematical review pending; C0052 is not solved or refuted. Fix 0<gamma<3. Let G_x, x in Z^3, be a stationary centered unit-variance Gaussian field with covariance R_gamma(x-y)=(1+|x-y|^2)^(-gamma/2), and sigma_x=sign(G_x). These are stationary spin-flip symmetric positively associated +/-1 spins with E[sigma_0 sigma_x]=(2/pi)arcsin R_gamma(x), asymptotic to (2/pi)|x|^(-gamma), and on-site fourth cumulant -2. For every finite list of compactly supported smooth real tests f, N^(-3+gamma/2)sum_x f(x/N)sigma_x converges jointly to a Gaussian vector with covariance (2/pi)integral integral f(u)h(v)|u-v|^(-gamma)du dv. The nonlinear remainder after subtracting sqrt(2/pi) times the similarly scaled G-field has squared L2 norm O(N^(-2gamma)) for gamma<1, O(N^(-2)log N) at gamma=1, and O(N^(-(3-gamma))) for gamma>1; constants depend on fixed gamma and test. No nearest-neighbor Ising Gibbs, reflection-positivity, random-current, distribution-space tightness, or fourth-moment-convergence assertion is made.

[Lemma sumconvergestoexpectationas of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] Let $(\widetilde\Omega,\widetilde\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space. Let $(A_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be 
a sequence of independent events in $\widetilde\Omega$, and let $(a_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be a 
bounded sequence of positive numbers. Suppose that $(N_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ is a strictly
increasing sequence of natural numbers such that 
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty E_n^{-1}<\infty,
\]
where $E_n:=\sum_{k=N_{n-1}+1}^{N_n}\widetilde\mathbb{P} (A_k)a_k> 0$. For all 
$\tilde\omega\in\widetilde\Omega$, define 
\[
S_n(\tilde\omega):=\sum_{k=N_{n-1}+1}^{N_n} \chi_{A_k}(\tilde\omega) a_k.
\]
Then $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{S_n}{E_n}=1$ almost surely.

[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2608.16752, 'Absorption Probabilities for Random Convex Hulls: Distribution-Freeness via the Wall-Cross'] Let $N,d\geq1$ and  $q_1, \dots, q_N \in \R^d$.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item[(i)] $0 \notin \Conv(q_1, \dots, q_N)$ if and only if
        there is $v \in \R^d$ with $\langle q_m, v \rangle > 0$ for all
        $m$.
        \item[(ii)] $0 \in \Int \Conv(q_1, \dots, q_N)$ if and only if
        there is \emph{no} $v \neq 0$ with $\langle q_m, v \rangle \ge
        0$ for all $m$.
        \item[(iii)] If $q_1, \dots, q_N$ are in general linear position, then
        either $0 \notin \Conv(q_1, \dots, q_N)$ or $0 \in \Int
        \Conv(q_1, \dots, q_N)$.
        \item[(iv)] Let $N \ge d+1$ and $0 \in \partial \Conv(q_1, \dots, q_N)$.
        If there is exactly one $d$-element set $I\subseteq [N]$ such that
        the vectors $(q_i)_{i \in I}$ are linearly dependent, then the points $q_i$, $i \in I$,
        are affinely independent,
        $0 \in \relint \Conv(q_i : i \in I)$, and there is a unique unit
        vector $\nu$ such that $$\langle q_i, \nu \rangle = 0 \text{ for } i \in I
        \quad
        \text{and}
        \quad
        \langle q_m, \nu \rangle > 0 \text{ for }\, m \notin I.$$

    \end{itemize}

body:
[Definition AvoidBB of arXiv:2410.23899, 'Tightness for interlacing geometric random walk bridges'] Fix $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $\vec{x}, \vec{y} \in W_k^{\circ}$, $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and $f: [a,b] \rightarrow (-\infty, \infty]$ and $g: [-\infty, \infty)$ be two continuous functions. The latter means that either $f: [a,b] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is continuous or $f = \infty$ everywhere and similarly for $g$. We also assume that $f(t) > g(t)$ for all $t \in [a,b]$, $f(a) > x_1$, $f(b) > y_1$, $g(a) < x_k$ and $g(b) < y_k$. 

With the above data we define the $(f,g)$-avoiding Brownian line ensemble on the interval $[a,b]$ with entrance data $\vec{x}$ and exit data $\vec{y}$ to be the $\llbracket 1 , k \rrbracket$-indexed line ensemble $\mathcal{Q}$ on $\Lambda = [a,b]$ whose law is the same as that of $\{B_i\}_{i = 1}^k$ (with law $\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{free}}^{a,b, \vec{x}, \vec{y}}$), conditioned on the event
$$E = \{f(r) > B_1(r) > B_2(r) > \cdots > B_k(r) > g(r) \mbox{ for all $r \in [a,b]$} \}.$$
We denote the law of $\mathcal{Q}$ by $\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{avoid}}^{a,b,\vec{x},\vec{y},f,g}$, and expectations with respect to this measure by $\mathbb{E}_{\operatorname{avoid}}^{a,b,\vec{x},\vec{y},f,g}$.
title: Definition AvoidBB of arXiv:2410.23899

body:
[Lemma S34L of arXiv:2410.23899, 'Tightness for interlacing geometric random walk bridges'] Fix $p, M_1, M_2, A \in (0,\infty)$, $\delta_1 \in (0,1/2)$, and $\sigma = \sqrt{p(1+p)}$. There exist $N_4 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\epsilon > 0$, depending on $p,M_1,M_2, A, \delta_1$ such that the following holds for all $n \geq N_4$. Suppose that $x,y \in \mathbb{Z}$ are such that $x\leq y$, $|x| \leq M_1 n^{1/2}$, $|y - np| \leq M_1 n^{1/2}$ and $B \in [-M_2, M_2]$. Let $f^t, f^b \in C([0,1])$ be defined through
$$f^t(t) = f(t|A, B, \sigma^{-1} n^{-1/2} x, \sigma^{-1} n^{-1/2}(y- pn), \delta_1) $$
$$f^b(t) = f(t|-A, B, \sigma^{-1} n^{-1/2} x, \sigma^{-1} n^{-1/2}(y- pn), \delta_1), $$
where we recall that $f(t|A,B,x,y,\delta)$ is as in ((S34E1 of the paper)). If $\mathcal{Q}_1\in C([0,1])$ is defined by $\mathcal{Q}_1(t) = \sigma^{-1}n^{-1/2}(Q_1(tn) - ptn)$, we have
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{Geom}}^{0,n, x, y} \left( f^t(t) \geq \mathcal{Q}_1(t) \geq f^b(t) \mbox{ for all } t\in [0,1] \right) > \epsilon.
\end{equation}
title: Lemma S34L of arXiv:2410.23899

body: The wedge product is the associative bilinear product on differential forms, wedge : Omega^k x Omega^l -> Omega^{k+l}, that is graded-anticommutative: alpha wedge beta = (-1)^{kl} beta wedge alpha for a k-form alpha and l-form beta. In particular dx^i wedge dx^j = - dx^j wedge dx^i, so a repeated differential vanishes. It makes the direct sum of form spaces into the exterior algebra of the manifold.

body:
Fix an integer k>=1. Let n,p tend to infinity with C^(-1)<=p/n<=C for a fixed C. Let X have iid rows x_i in R^p. For each j<=k let C_{j,p} be a nonempty compact set of Euclidean radius at most a fixed R. Write C_p^k=product_j C_{j,p}, interpreted as the allowed columns of Theta in R^{p by k}. Let the nonnegative regularizer r_p be locally Lipschitz in Frobenius norm, with its Lipschitz constant on each fixed bounded ball uniform in p. Let g_p~N(mu_p,Sigma_p). For each j assume the following bounds, with constants uniform in n,p: sup_{theta in C_{j,p}, ||theta||_2<=1}||x_i^T theta||_{psi_2}<=K; sup over the same set of ||Sigma_p^(1/2)theta||_2<=K; and ||mu_p||_2<=K. Let independent eps_i be independent of X and of the Gaussian comparison matrix G, whose rows are iid copies of g_p, and assume max_i||eps_i||_{psi_2}<=K. Let the nonnegative loss ell:R^k x R->R be globally Lipschitz jointly in its two arguments, with a uniform constant. Assume all C_{j,p} are contained in one symmetric convex domain S_p of Gaussianity for x_i versus g_p: for every bounded Lipschitz phi, sup_{theta in S_p}|E phi(theta^T x_i)-E phi(theta^T g_p)|->0. Define R_n^*(X)=min_{Theta in C_p^k}{n^(-1)sum_i ell(Theta^T x_i,eps_i)+r_p(Theta)}, and define R_n^*(G) by replacing x_i by g_i and keeping the same noise law. Then for every bounded Lipschitz psi:R->R, |E psi(R_n^*(X))-E psi(R_n^*(G))|->0. For every real rho, R_n^*(X) converges in probability to rho if and only if R_n^*(G) does. This is the globally Lipschitz-loss branch of Theorem1; convexity of the loss, regularizer or constraint sets is not required. It compares optimized objective values; it does not by itself identify minimizers, their fitted projections, or test risk.
Fixed projection dimension k; proportional p/n regime; iid feature rows.
Uniformly bounded compact column constraints and locally Lipschitz nonnegative penalty.
Restricted subgaussianity and Gaussian comparison bounds exactly as in source Assumption4.
Independent uniformly subgaussian noise and a nonnegative globally Lipschitz loss (Assumption5 branch1).
All allowed columns lie in one symmetric convex domain of Gaussianity.

body: Empirical Bayes methods are procedures for statistical inference in which the prior probability distribution is estimated from the data. This approach stands in contrast to standard Bayesian methods, for which the prior distribution is fixed before any data are observed. Despite this difference in perspective, empirical Bayes may be viewed as an approximation to a fully Bayesian treatment of a hierarchical model wherein the parameters at the highest level of the hierarchy are set to their most likely values, instead of being integrated out.

[Lemma Lem one but not other of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Let $(B_t)_{t\geq 0}$ denote a standard Brownian motion on
$\mathbb{C}$,
and denote by
$\mathbb{P}_z$ the probability associated to the initial condition
$B_0=z$.
Denote by $T_{2\partial\mathbb{D}}$ the first time this Brownian motion hits the circle $2\partial\mathbb{D}$.
There is a universal constant 
$C''_{\rm univ}>0$,
such that for every
$\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2$ as above,
and the associated $\Gamma = f_{\Gamma_1}(\Gamma_2)$,
$\widetilde{\Gamma}$ and $\widetilde{\Gamma}_2$,
and for every $\theta\in [0,2\pi)$,
we have
\begin{equation}

\mathbb{P}_{e^{i\theta}}
(B([0,T_{2\partial\mathbb{D}}])
\text{ intersects } \widetilde{\Gamma}
\text{ but not } \widetilde{\Gamma}_2
)
\leq 
C''_{\rm univ} R^{+}(\Gamma)^{1/2},
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}

\mathbb{P}_{e^{i\theta}}
(B([0,T_{2\partial\mathbb{D}}])
\text{ intersects } \widetilde{\Gamma}_2
\text{ but not } \widetilde{\Gamma}
)
\leq 
C''_{\rm univ} R^{+}(\Gamma)^{1/2}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Let R=UV^T, X=R/sqrt(N), and Y=sqrt(s)X+G with independent standard real Gaussian noise. For finite-second-moment products define L_R=E||R-E[R|Y]||_F^2/(NP) and m_X=E||X-E[X|Y]||_F^2/(NP). Exactly L_R=N*m_X, and for i_N(s)=I(R;Y)/(NP), I-MMSE gives i_N derivative=m_X/2=L_R/(2N). If U,V have independent standard Gaussian entries of sizes N by M and P by M, beta_N=M/N, then m_X(s)>=beta_N/[1+s(1+beta_N+1/N)] and L_R(s)<=M for all s>=0. Revealing U gives a lower bound E tr[C(I+sC)^(-1)]/N, C=UU^T/N; Cauchy-Schwarz and E tr(C)/N=beta_N, E tr(C^2)/N=beta_N(1+beta_N+1/N) give the explicit inequality. Thus when M/N tends to a positive finite constant and s is fixed, raw NP-normalized loss grows linearly in N. A finite scaled loss instead divides raw error by N^2 P. This is a standard normalization and conditioning calculation, not a novelty claim; independent audit pending.
Independent standard Gaussian factors for the lower bound; arbitrary finite-second-moment products for the scaling identity and I-MMSE.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:011181908c05c624a799bd14e194fe9ed76fccaead15d5e8e53089ab65c975d2","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/01/011181908c05c624a799bd14e194fe9ed76fccaead15d5e8e53089ab65c975d2.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:235e82196ece14cc4302c0cd85fe5c21acc54bb11c4aacd75c90153e26068f72","bundle_entry_key":"product-mmse-normalization-genie-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-gaussian-product-logconcavity-mmse-and-normalization-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:product-mmse-normalization-genie-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Product-loss normalization and a Gaussian lower bound

Proof draft, unaudited. This is a normalization correction and a standard
Gaussian-conditioning calculation; no novelty is claimed.

Let R=UV^T, X=R/sqrt(N), and observe

    Y=X+sqrt(Delta)G, Delta>0,

where G has independent standard Gaussian entries. Write s=1/Delta;
rescaling the observation gives sqrt(s)X+G and leaves its information and
conditional expectations unchanged. Define the two per-entry losses

    L_R=E||R-E[R|Y]||_F^2/(NP),
    m_X=E||X-E[X|Y]||_F^2/(NP).

Linearity of conditional expectation gives exactly

    L_R=N*m_X.                                       (1)

Thus m_X equals the raw product loss divided by N^2 P. Normalizing the raw
product error only by NP gives a different large-size scale.

## The literal raw loss diverges for Gaussian factors

Let U,V have independent standard Gaussian entries, of sizes N by M and
P by M, respectively. Put beta_N=M/N and C=UU^T/N. Revealing U in addition
to the observation can only reduce Bayes squared error. Conditional on U,
each column of X is centered Gaussian with covariance C. Completing the
Gaussian square for its latent V row gives posterior covariance

    C(I+sC)^(-1).

This identity remains valid when C is singular: write A=U/sqrt(N), complete
the square with covariance (I_M+s A^T A)^(-1) for that V row, and use
A(I_M+s A^T A)^(-1)A^T=C(I_N+sC)^(-1). All inverted matrices are positive
definite. The P independent observation columns have the same conditional
covariance. Therefore

    m_X(s)>= E tr[C(I+sC)^(-1)]/N.                    (2)

Let lambda denote a uniformly selected eigenvalue of C, including any zero
eigenvalues, with the expectation also over U. Cauchy-Schwarz applied to
sqrt(lambda/(1+s lambda)) and sqrt(lambda(1+s lambda)) gives

    E[lambda/(1+s lambda)] >= (E lambda)^2 /
                                    (E lambda+s E lambda^2).

The two required Gaussian moments are exact:

    E lambda=beta_N,
    E lambda^2=beta_N(1+beta_N+1/N).

For completeness, expanding tr[(UU^T)^2] has four index cases. Their
expectations and counts are: i=k,a=b gives 3 NM; i=k,a!=b gives
NM(M-1); i!=k,a=b gives N(N-1)M; and i!=k,a!=b gives zero by independence
and centering. Their sum is NM(N+M+1); division by N^3 gives the second
displayed moment. No asymptotic spectral law is used.

Combining these identities proves

    m_X(s) >= beta_N/[1+s(1+beta_N+1/N)],
    L_R(s) >= M/[1+s(1+M/N+1/N)].                    (3)

The zero estimator gives L_R<=M. Hence, if M/N tends to beta in (0,infinity)
and Delta is fixed positive, L_R is of order N and diverges. This applies
for every P>=1, including the proportional-aspect regime. The scaled loss
m_X is the bounded quantity relevant to a finite per-entry limiting curve.

## I-MMSE convention

For any finite-second-moment product R, let

    i_N(s)=I(R;sqrt(s/N)R+G)/(NP).

body:
Let (F_n) be a sequence of distribution functions on R, that is nondecreasing right-continuous functions with values in [0,1]. Then there exist a subsequence (F_{n_k}) and a nondecreasing right-continuous F : R -> [0,1] such that F_{n_k}(x) -> F(x) at every continuity point x of F. The limit F need NOT be a distribution function: mass can escape to plus or minus infinity, and with F_n the distribution function of the point mass at n one gets F identically 0. This is exactly the gap that tightness closes: the family is tight, meaning sup_n (1 - F_n(M) + F_n(-M)) -> 0 as M -> infinity, if and only if every such subsequential limit is a proper distribution function, which is Prokhorov's theorem on R. Nothing is assumed about the F_n beyond monotonicity, right-continuity and the range [0,1] - no continuity, no tightness, no common support. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.2.6]

body: A topological space X is compact if every open cover of X has a finite subcover: whenever X is the union of a family of open sets {U_i : i in I}, there are finitely many indices i_1, ..., i_n such that X is the union of U_(i_1), ..., U_(i_n). A subset K of a space is compact if it is compact in the subspace topology; equivalently, every cover of K by sets open in the ambient space admits a finite subfamily covering K. For metric spaces, compactness is equivalent to sequential compactness (every sequence has a convergent subsequence) and to being complete and totally bounded; for subsets of R^n it is equivalent to being closed and bounded (Heine-Borel theorem).

  \big(\hat{X}^{\ell,\eta}
  -\hat{X}^{\ell,0}\big)^2
  \Big]
  =0.\eeq
Similarly for $\hat{M}^{\ell},\hat{V}^{\ell},\hat{Y}^{\ell},\hat{U}^{\ell}$.

OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited), no novelty established. Let d>=2, E^T E=I_2, Lambda=diag(1,9), and let the teacher be (1/3)sum_j N(a E diag(1,3)u_j,I_d) with unit equilateral vertices. For the canonical equal-weight identity-covariance mixture score, optimize all means by physical Euclidean unit-step population DDPM GD at this fixed noise level. Write M=a b 1^T+a sqrt(3/2) Z V^T and Z=(E sqrt(2C)+Y)O_theta, E^T Y=0. Let H(theta)=[(61/4)(cos(3theta)-1)^2+(189/4)sin(3theta)^2]/2, beta=acos(-61/128), l=beta/3, r=(2pi-beta)/3, and cbar_a(theta)=c_a(theta)+a^2(0,Hprime(theta)/40,0), where c_a is the centered planar covariance critical section. Fix 0<delta<(r-l)/4 and a sufficiently large fixed K. There exist dimension-independent rho,a_0>0 such that, if 0<a<a_0, ||b_0||<=K a^4, ||(c_0-cbar_a(theta_0),Y_0)||<=rho and theta_0 is in [l+2delta,r-2delta], the unrestricted trajectory converges to the strict non-global minimum in that sector. Throughout, ||b_k||<=K a^4 and normal error is at most rho exp(-lambda a^2 k)+C a^4; after O(a^(-2)log(1/a)) steps theta remains in [l+delta,r-delta]. The same holds in permutation-equivalent sectors and the other determinant branch. This conditional local basin lemma is not a random-initialization probability, empirical/finite-precision guarantee, annealed-GD obstruction or general K=3 result.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:b5b1184cda3946a62346cde3d51e43f3cb99b3dc94bd0e7382953e44d0543236","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/b5/b5b1184cda3946a62346cde3d51e43f3cb99b3dc94bd0e7382953e44d0543236.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:189395fa8a762194df2b369495233f8cb82db069c750663d89ee0bde2e2e2d4b","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c18","bundle_id":"population.t309-unrestricted-anisotropic-trapping-draft","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian mixture learning and diffusion objectives","draft":"w721/bundle_011.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:gaussian-mixture-ddpm-unrestricted-anisotropic-post-entry-trapping","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; T309-w721-C18 v1; proof (unaudited); Target 2 route 12 auxiliary lemma.

# Post-entry angular trapping with a free centroid and perpendicular directions

This extends C15's local basin statement to unrestricted population mean GD after C17's covariance entry. It is conditional on local entry, not yet a random-initialization failure-probability theorem. All analytic dependencies remain unaudited. No novelty claim, annealed-GD obstruction or general T309 resolution is made.

## Statement and coordinates

Use C17's equal-weight teacher, D=E Lambda E^T, Lambda=diag(1,9), and its physical unit-step population DDPM GD. Write M=a b 1^T+a sqrt(3/2) Z V^T. On either orientation branch near the covariance orbit, write

    Z=(E L+Y) O_theta,  L=sqrt(2C), E^T Y=0,
    c=(C11,C12,C22), c_*= (1/2,0,9/2).

Here Y has d-by-2 entries with columns perpendicular to E. The coordinates come from the polar decomposition of E^T Z; all norms below are Euclidean/Frobenius product norms. On the determinant-negative branch use O_theta=R_theta J, where J is a fixed reflection that permutes the equilateral vertices u_j. Then R_theta J U=R_theta U Pi for a permutation matrix Pi, so label symmetry gives precisely the same sectors and reduced angular function there.

Use H, beta, l, r and the lag section cbar_a from C15. Fix 0<delta<(r-l)/4 and a fixed K sufficiently large to dominate C17's centroid bound and the bound below. There are rho>0 and a_0>0, independent of ambient dimension, such that

    ||b_0||<=K a^4,
    ||(c_0-cbar_a(theta_0),Y_0)||<=rho,
    theta_0 in [l+2delta,r-2delta], 0<a<a_0

imply convergence of unrestricted physical GD to the strict bad minimum in this sector. Along the motion

    ||b_k||<=K a^4,
    ||(c_k-cbar_a(theta_k),Y_k)||
             <=rho exp(-lambda a^2 k)+C a^4.       (1)

The angular interval [l+delta,r-delta] traps the trajectory after O(a^(-2)log(1/a)) steps. Constants can depend on fixed K and delta, but not d. The claim uses exact population gradients at a fixed noise level.

## 1. Keep the centroid small instead of assuming it vanishes

On a fixed enlarged neighborhood of this covariance orbit, C17's exact update gives

    ||b_+||<=||b||/2+C_b a^4.                     (2)

Choose K>=2 C_b. Then ||b||<=K a^4 is forward invariant as long as the shape remains in this neighborhood. C17 supplies the initial bound for a suitable fixed K.

Let F_a^0(Z)=F_a(0,Z). C17's differentiated expansion, now with two bounded derivatives, gives

    F_a(b,Z)=a^2||b||^2
      +a^4[||ZZ^T-D||_F^2/4-b^T ZZ^T b]+a^6 H_a(b,Z).

Subtract the shape updates at b and at zero, holding Z fixed. The explicit b-quadratic term contributes O(a^2||b||^2); the remainder contributes O(a^4||b||). Thus

    ||Z_+(b,Z)-Z_+(0,Z)||<=C_K a^8.              (3)

The polar coordinate inverse has bounded first derivatives on the enlarged neighborhood, so (3) also bounds the differences of c_+, theta_+ and Y_+. This is a one-step comparison at the current state. No comparison over the entire slow interval by Gronwall is assumed.

These dimension-free derivative bounds use the same finite-span dominated Gaussian argument as C06/C17, with at most a fixed number of differentiation directions. The chart itself consists of a two-by-two polar map and right multiplication of Y by a two-by-two orthogonal matrix; its operator derivative bounds are uniform in d for Frobenius norms.

## 2. The new perpendicular linearization

For zero centroid the leading shape field is gamma f_D, gamma=2a^2/3. Put Z=(E L+Y)O and E^T Y=0. Direct multiplication gives

    E^T f_D(Z) O^T=(Lambda-L^2)L-L Y^T Y,
    P_perp f_D(Z) O^T=-Y(L^2+Y^T Y).             (4)

At C=c_*, Y=0, the perpendicular derivative is -Y Lambda. Consequently its physical-GD normal block is

    Y_+=Y-(2a^2/3)Y Lambda+higher-order terms.    (5)

Its two column contraction coefficients are 2/3 and 6, both strictly positive. The planar covariance block is C15's B=diag(4/3,20/3,12). There is no leading linear coupling between these blocks: every Y contribution in the planar equation in (4) is quadratic, and the perpendicular equation vanishes at Y=0.

For b=0, exact reflection symmetry across the teacher plane makes Y=0 invariant, including the higher-order DDPM terms. Therefore there is no independent perpendicular forcing at Y=0. Passage to the rotating chart contributes Y times the angular increment; it is bounded by C(a^2||e||^2+a^4||e||), where e=(c-cbar_a(theta),Y).

At Y=0, C15 supplies the lag cancellation and the angular drift. Combining (3)--(5), the differentiated expansion, and the inverse-chart Taylor remainder yields

    e_+=(I-a^2 B_full)e+R_e,
    ||R_e||<=C[a^2||e||^2+a^4||e||+a^6],        (6)
    theta_+=theta-a^4 H'(theta)/15+R_theta,
    |R_theta|<=C[a^2||e||+a^6],                 (7)

where B_full is block diagonal: B on c, and right multiplication by (2/3)Lambda on Y. Its eigenvalues lie in [2/3,12]. The extra centroid error O(a^8) is absorbed by the displayed a^6 term.

For completeness, the zero-centroid normalized shape step is O(a^2||e||+a^4). Its inverse-chart Taylor remainder is O((a^2||e||+a^4)^2), exactly as in C15. Terms linear in Y from the higher-order field are O(a^4||Y||); leading planar terms quadratic in Y are O(a^2||Y||^2). Subtracting cbar(theta_+) adds O(a^6+a^4||e||+a^4||e||^2). These bounds account for every term in (6). At fixed e and b, the angular map has derivative 1+O(a^2||e||+a^4); (3) remains valid after one angular derivative by one additional bounded derivative of H_a. None of these assertions require the covariance critical section to be invariant.

## 3. Normal confinement and angular trapping

For sufficiently small a, ||I-a^2 B_full||=1-(2/3)a^2. Choose a fixed small normal neighborhood so its quadratic term in (6) consumes at most one sixth of a^2||e||, and then choose a so its linear remainder consumes at most another sixth. For lambda=1/3,

    ||e_+||<=(1-lambda a^2)||e||+C a^6.          (8)

Choose rho smaller than half that neighborhood and then a so C a^4/lambda<rho. Equations (2),(8) close a simultaneous stopped induction: neither b nor the shape leaves the enlarged neighborhood. Solving (8) proves (1).

Choose a fixed small w>0. After N=O(a^(-2)log(1/a)) steps, ||e_N||<=w a^2. Through that interval (7),(8) give

    sum_{k<N}|theta_{k+1}-theta_k|
          <=C rho+C a^2(1+log(1/a))<delta/2,    (9)

by choosing rho and then a. This follows by summing the geometric normal transient; it does not sum a persistent order-rho error over the slow interval.

At the two endpoints of I=[l+delta,r-delta], the leading angular drift in (7) points strictly inward. Choose w so Cw is less than one fourth of the smaller endpoint drift coefficient, and then a so C a^2 is smaller than another fourth. Thus for ||e||<=w a^2 both endpoint images point inward. The fixed-(e,b) angular map is increasing on I by the derivative bound after (7), so it maps all of I into I. Equation (8) preserves ||e||<=w a^2 once C a^4/lambda<=w a^2. Equation (2) simultaneously preserves the centroid bound. By (9), the trajectory is inside I at time N, and hence stays there forever.

## 4. Unrestricted convergence

On this bounded normalized-mean neighborhood the physical mean Hessian has centroid block (2/3)I+O(a^2), shape block O(a^2), and mixed block O(a^2). The leading centroid eigenvalue is below one. For small a its full operator norm is below a fixed number less than two, including on the short GD segments in a slightly enlarged neighborhood. The descent lemma therefore gives F(M_+)<=F(M)-c||grad_M F(M)||^2 with c>0. Nonnegativity implies grad_M F(M_k)->0.

All iterates lie in a compact set for each fixed d, so every accumulation point is critical. Criticality first uniquely eliminates b=O(a^4) by its uniformly positive centroid Hessian; the parameter-dependent implicit function theorem applies to a^(-2) partial_b F, whose derivative is 2I+O(a^2). Substitution changes the centered risk by O(a^10), with bounded derivatives: partial_b F(0,Z)=O(a^6), b_critical=O(a^4), and the centroid quadratic cost is O(a^10).

After this elimination, the leading covariance-normal Hessian divided by a^4 is diag(2,4,2), and the perpendicular Hessian is right multiplication by Lambda, positive with smallest eigenvalue one. On a fixed sufficiently small normal neighborhood the full normal Hessian is uniformly positive. It therefore gives a unique normal critical section for each angle, by the same uniform implicit-function/strong-convexity argument. Reflection symmetry forces its perpendicular coordinate to be zero. Its reduced risk has derivative a^6[H'(theta)+O_C^1(a^2)]. As in C15, this has exactly one zero in I, the strict bad minimum inherited from C06. Thus there is exactly one accumulation point, and the unrestricted trajectory converges to it.

## Scope and remaining step

This is a local unrestricted trapping lemma with an O(a^4) centroid entry hypothesis. It pays the transfer left by C17; it does not itself quantify how much of C17's random entry lies in the required angular sectors or handle the two determinant branches probabilistically. That coupling and the resulting precise failure-probability statement remain to be written. Even such a statement would concern a fixed high-noise objective for this teacher, not all schedules or general K=3 learnability. body: Watson's lemma gives the asymptotic expansion, as a positive parameter x tends to infinity, of Laplace-type integrals of the form the integral from 0 to b (b positive or infinite) of e^{-x t} f(t) dt, where f has, near t=0, an asymptotic expansion f(t) ~ sum over n >= 0 of a_n t^{n+lambda-1} for some lambda > 0, and f satisfies mild growth and integrability conditions away from 0. Then the integral is asymptotic to the sum over n >= 0 of a_n Gamma(n+lambda) / x^{n+lambda}, obtained by formally integrating the local expansion of f term by term against e^{-x t}, since the large-x behavior is dominated by t near 0. Named after G. N. Watson.
title: Watson's lemma

body: [Proposition 5 (Lloyd--Max optimality \citep{lloyd1982lsq,max1960quantizing}) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Assume $\E[X^2]<\infty$ and that the support of $X$ contains at least $L$ points, so that no optimal cell has zero probability. Then every optimal fixed-rate scalar quantizer satisfies, up to sets of probability zero, (i) the \emph{nearest-neighbor} condition $b_i=\tfrac12(c_i+c_{i+1})$ for the interior boundaries $i=1,\dots,L-1$ and (ii) the \emph{centroid} condition $c_i=\E[X\mid X\in(b_{i-1},b_i]]$. Alternating (i) and (ii) (Lloyd's algorithm) never increases $D$, though its stationary points need not be local minima. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lloyd--Max optimality \citep{lloyd1982lsq,max1960quantizing}

body:
Fix input dimension d>=1 and a finite normalized training horizon T>=1. Data (x,y) are sampled independently at successive steps from a distribution P with bounded support in R^d times R. Let sigma be C^2, bounded and Lipschitz, with bounded first and second derivatives. Set sigma_*(x;(a,w))=a sigma(w.x), v(w)=-E[y sigma(w.x)] and u(w,w_prime)=E[sigma(w.x)sigma(w_prime.x)]; assume v and u are differentiable with bounded Lipschitz continuous gradients (Assumption 1). The initial neuron parameters (a_i,w_i) are iid with common bounded-support law rho_0 on R^(d+1), independently of the training samples. The two-layer mean-field network is f_N(x;theta)=N^(-1) sum_i a_i sigma(w_i.x). Use noiseless, unregularized SGD with source scaling xi=1/2, namely theta_i^(k+1)=theta_i^k+epsilon [y_k-f_N(x_k;theta^k)] grad_theta sigma_*(x_k;theta_i^k). The horizon here is the nonlinear-dynamics time k epsilon, as in Appendix B.2; this differs by a fixed factor from the sum of the source step sizes s_k=epsilon/2. These smooth-activation restrictions are an explicitly narrower case of the source; in particular ReLU is excluded. Let rho_t be the deterministic mean-field law, and let bar_theta_i(t) solve d bar_theta_i/dt=-grad V(bar_theta_i)-integral grad_1 U(bar_theta_i,theta) rho_t(dtheta), with the same initial parameter as neuron i. Here V(a,w)=a v(w) and U((a,w),(a_prime,w_prime))=a a_prime u(w,w_prime). The comparator trajectories are independent across i and each has law rho_t. body: In mathematics, the uniform boundedness principle or Banach–Steinhaus theorem is one of the fundamental results in functional analysis. Together with the Hahn–Banach theorem and the open mapping theorem, it is considered one of the cornerstones of the field. In its basic form, it asserts that for a family of continuous linear operators whose domain is a Banach space, pointwise boundedness is equivalent to uniform boundedness in operator norm.
title: Uniform boundedness principle

[Definition $(r-2)_*$-BP of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] Let $T$ be a $K_r$-tree
and $S\subset V(T)$ a set of {\it seeds}, 
which we consider to be initially {\it infected}. 
Then, in each step of the process, either 
\begin{itemize}
\item {\it (usual step)} some vertex $v$ with at least $r-2$ 
infected neighbors becomes infected; or else
\item {\it (special step)} if no such $v$ exists, but 
for some internal edge $e$, there are two cliques $H_i\neq H_j$ 
containing $e$ such that $H_i$ has $r-4$ infected vertices 
and $H_j$ has $1$ infected vertex,  
and all $r-3$ of these vertices are not in $e$, 
then  we infect an arbitrarily chosen vertex $u\in e$; and 
otherwise, 
\item {\it (terminal step)} if neither type of step is possible, 
then the process terminates. 
\end{itemize}
We call this process {\it $(r-2)_*$-BP} 
on $T$, 
and let $\langle S;T\rangle_*$ denote the set of 
eventually infected vertices in $T$ started with 
the seed set $S$.
title: $(r-2)_*$-BP

[Definition def:circuit-output of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix a circuit state $\tau$.  A component atom is a physical two-front
atom, with all ancillary legs and circuit fragments left in their declared
slots, presented as $XY^*$ at its two correlated Hilbert--Schmidt fronts.
Every other fixed letter is either a safe gate or fixed raw circuit wiring.
The cost of an atom is
\[
 \|X\|_2\|Y\|_2
 \prod_G\|G\|_{\rm op},
\tag{2.3.16}
\]
where the product contains only safe gates and prescribed bounded maps,
not the raw cups, caps, or bases belonging to the circuit wiring.  Let
$\mathscr P_\tau$ be the algebraic $\ell^1$-projective sum of tensors of
such atoms and let $\|\cdot\|_{\mathscr P_\tau}$ be the corresponding
projective cost.  All named boundary variables remain multilinear slots.

If $\mathcal R_\tau^{\rm in},\mathcal R_\tau^{\rm out}$ are retained root
words, define $\|T\|_{\tau,\varepsilon}$ by inserting operator-norm-one
matrix tests in every nonroot slot and taking the trace norm on the joint
ordered root word.  With no retained root, take absolute value after the
terminal scalar closure.

[Definition 9 of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Let \(\mathscr E\subseteq\Sym^2T^*\Mcal\) be a relaxation bundle and let \(\mathscr F\subset\mathscr E\) be an open fiber domain containing its zero section. A \textbf{Navier--Stokes potential} is a smooth scalar function
\be
\chi=\chi(\beta,\zeta),
\qquad
\beta\ \text{future timelike},
\qquad
\zeta\in\mathscr F,
\ee
satisfying the following conditions.
\bei

\item \emph{Euler equilibrium.} For every future timelike~\(\beta\), one has
\be
\chi(\beta,0)=\chi_{\rm E}(\beta).
\ee

\item \emph{Dominant energy condition.} The potential-generated stress-energy tensor satisfies
\be 
T_\chi^{\alpha\beta}(\beta, \zeta) X_\alpha Y_\beta
=
\frac{\del^2\chi}{\del\beta_\alpha\del\beta_\beta}(\beta, \zeta)
X_\alpha Y_\beta
\geq0
\ee
for all future-directed causal vectors~\(X,Y\), all future timelike~$\beta$ and all $\zeta\in\mathscr F$. 

\item \emph{Causal hyperbolicity.}  With \(\Xi=(\beta,\zeta)\), define the symmetric principal matrices
\bel{eq:pot-principal}
K^{\alpha AB}(\Xi)
\coloneqq
\frac{\del^3\chi}
{\del\beta_\alpha\del\Xi_A\del\Xi_B}(\Xi).
\ee
For every future-directed timelike vector~\(n\), the quadratic form
\be
-n_\alpha K^{\alpha AB}(\Xi)Z_AZ_B
\ee
is positive for every non-zero variation~\(Z\) of\/~\(\Xi\) and every state \((\beta,\zeta)\) in the constitutive domain.
\eei

body: Let X_1, ..., X_n be convex subsets of R^d with n >= d+1. If every d+1 of the sets X_1, ..., X_n have a point in common, then all n sets have a point in common. The same conclusion holds for an arbitrary, possibly infinite, family of compact convex subsets of R^d, provided every d+1 of them have a common point. [Helly (1923); see Matousek, Lectures on Discrete Geometry]

Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and 1 <= p < infinity with conjugate exponent q = p/(p-1) (q = infinity when p = 1). For 1 < p < infinity the map g -> (f -> integral f g dmu) is an isometric isomorphism from L^q(mu) onto the dual space L^p(mu)^*, for ANY measure space. For p = 1 the same map from L^infinity(mu) onto L^1(mu)^* is an isometric isomorphism provided mu is sigma-finite (or, more generally, localizable); without such a hypothesis it can fail to be surjective. The dual of L^infinity is strictly larger than L^1 whenever L^infinity is infinite-dimensional: on ([0,1], Lebesgue) a Banach limit or a Hahn-Banach extension of the functional f -> lim_{x -> 0} f(x) from C[0,1] gives an element of (L^infinity)^* not represented by any L^1 function. So the duality chain (L^1)^* = L^infinity does NOT continue to (L^infinity)^* = L^1, and L^1 is not reflexive; L^p is reflexive exactly for 1 < p < infinity. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 6.15]
1 <= p < infinity
for p = 1: mu sigma-finite (or localizable)
no hypothesis on mu for 1 < p < infinity

Fix constants0<p<1/2,0<=q<1/2,and a logarithm base b>1. Let lambda<=n(lambda)<=poly(lambda),ell(lambda)<=poly(lambda),and tau(lambda)<=log_b n(lambda). Assume an efficiently evaluable tau-local family F_s:{0,1}^n->{0,1},indexed by a uniform ell-bit seed,is a noisy weak PRF at noise q:polynomial-time adversaries receiving fresh uniform inputs and noisy labels under one shared seed cannot distinguish that sample oracle from samples of one shared uniform random function,except negligibly in lambda. All parameter functions and Bernoulli(q) sampling used below are polynomial-time implementable. Write a=log_b(1/(1-2*p))>0. For an absolute sufficiently large C0,choose integer m=ceil(C0*(1-2*q)^(-4)*n^(4*a)) and N=3*m*(n+1)^2,with the usual efficiently implementable rounding within a fixed constant factor permitted. Algorithm1,with a shared uniform seed,pad and permutation,encodes the sole empty message by concatenating m fresh uniform n-bit inputs with their q-noisy F_s labels,filling uniformly to length N,XORing the pad,and permuting coordinates. Decode by undoing pad and permutation and accepting the empty message exactly when the number W of agreeing recovered input/label pairs exceeds m/2+ln(m)*sqrt(m),otherwise reject. Inputs of length different from N are rejected. This is a binary secret-key zero-bit pseudorandom code:sound on every fixed key-independent word,undetectable against polynomially many repeated encoding-oracle queries under one key,and robust to every word-only channel that makes at most p*N substitutions almost surely on every input. More generally,the robustness conclusion holds if that budget fails only negligibly on an independent uniform N-bit input. The positive-p restriction and implementable integer lengths are explicit;this card does not claim the unmodified Eq4 choice at p=0 has negligible soundness error.

body: FIRES WHEN you read a numerically computed spectrum of a strongly non-normal matrix, and in particular whenever a computed max|eig| appears to GROW with dimension. THE MEASUREMENT: for the clock-shift sum A_q = U_q + V_q, whose characteristic polynomial is exactly z^q so that the whole spectrum is the origin, a standard double-precision eigenvalue routine returns a maximum modulus of 0.755 at q = 64 and 1.385 at q = 256. Nothing is converging to a real spectrum; these matrices are extremely non-normal and the eigenvalues of a nilpotent matrix are the textbook ill-conditioned case - the computed eigenvalues track the pseudospectrum, whose radius does grow. CONDITION OF FAILURE: high non-normality, which a condition number of the eigenvector matrix will show immediately. WHAT TO DO INSTEAD, and it is what settled it here: compute the characteristic polynomial EXACTLY in the right algebraic setting - over Z[m] reduced modulo the minimal polynomial of m = e^{i pi / q} - and verify A^q = 0 as a matrix identity. That was done at q = 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 13 and the determinant is z^q on the nose.

body: The spiked covariance model (Johnstone, 2001) is the family of $p \times p$ population covariance matrices $\Sigma = \sigma^2 (I_p + \sum_{k=1}^{r} \theta_k u_k u_k^T)$ with orthonormal vectors $u_1, \dots, u_r$, spike sizes $\theta_1 \ge \dots \ge \theta_r > 0$, and a fixed rank $r$ that does not grow with $p$. The data are $n$ independent rows $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^p$ with covariance $\Sigma$ (Gaussian in the sharpest results; finite fourth moments suffice for the eigenvalue statements), and the object studied is the sample covariance $S = \frac{1}{n} \sum_i x_i x_i^T$ in the proportional regime $p, n \to \infty$ with $p/n \to \gamma \in (0, \infty)$. All but $r$ population eigenvalues equal the noise level $\sigma^2$ (the bulk); the model asks which spikes are visible in $S$ and how far the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors are from the population ones. With $\theta_k = 0$ for all $k$ the sample spectrum follows the Marchenko-Pastur law with ratio $\gamma$ and variance $\sigma^2$, whose support is $[\sigma^2 (1 - \sqrt{\gamma})^2, \sigma^2 (1 + \sqrt{\gamma})^2]$.

[Lemma 33 (Monotonicity of the edges) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Fix a finite graph $G$ and some $\beta\in[0,\infty)$.
    Let $E'\subset E$ and $uv\in E\setminus E'$.
    Define $G':=(V,E')$.
    For any $\tau'=(\alpha',\omega',\eta')\in\Pi_{G'}$, write
    $\mu^{\omega_{uv}}_{\tau'}$ and $\mu^{\eta_{uv}}_{\tau'}$ for the laws of $\omega_{uv}$ and $\eta_{uv}$ in the conditional measure
    \(
        \mu_{G,\beta}[\blank|\{\tau|_{G'}=\tau'\}]
    \).
    Then
    \[
        \tau'\preceq\tau''
        \qquad
        \implies
        \qquad
        (
        \mu_{\tau''}^{\omega_{uv}}\leqstoch\mu_{\tau'}^{\omega_{uv}}
        \quad\text{and}\quad
        \mu_{\tau'}^{\eta_{uv}}\leqstoch\mu_{\tau''}^{\eta_{uv}}
        )
    \]
Notice also that $\omega$ and $\eta$ are independent in this conditional measure.
Moreover, $\mu^{\omega_{uv}}_{\tau'}$ only depends on the values of $\alpha_u$, $\alpha_v$,
and the partition of $\{x\in V:xy\in E\setminus E'\}$ into $\omega'$-connected components.
The same holds true for $\mu^{\eta_{uv}}_{\tau'}$ (mutatis mutandis).

[Theorem main-thm-2 of arXiv:2608.23202, 'Locally finite Fixed points of Branching Brownian Motion'] Let $\Pi$ be a fixed point of BBM with drift $\lambda \geq \sqrt{2}$ and $\theta$ be a point process. Then,   
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For $\lambda > \sqrt{2}$, $\theta \in Dom_{\lambda}(\Pi)$ if and only if $\theta$ satisfies (H1), (H2), (H3). In that case, $\Pi \overset{d}{=}\widetilde{\mathcal E}_\infty^\lambda(\cdot - S)$ with $S = \log(Z)/\mu$, where $\widetilde{\mathcal E}_\infty^\lambda$ and $Z$ are sampled independently of each other \footnote{Note that the random variable $Z$ appearing here can be $0$ with positive probability. As such, comparing with Remark (infinite-S of the paper), $S$ is a $[-\infty, \infty)$-valued random variable and $\Pi = \widetilde{\mathcal E}_\infty^\lambda(\cdot - S)$ is an empty point process on the event $S= -\infty$.}. \\

\item For $\lambda = \sqrt{2}$, $\theta \in Dom_{\lambda}(\Pi)$ if and only if $\theta$ satisfies (A1), (A2), (A3). In that case, $\Pi \overset{d}{=}\widetilde{\mathcal E}_\infty(\cdot - S)$ with $S = \log(Z)/\sqrt{2}$, where $\widetilde{\mathcal E}_\infty$ and $Z$ are sampled independently of each other\footnote{The critical case $\lambda = \sqrt{2}$ in this result was also addressed in [Shekhar_Domain] although with an additional assumption of $\theta$ having a finite top particle and with a slightly stronger notion of convergence as compared to Definition (Def_DOA of the paper).}. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let U and V be open subsets of R^n and let phi : U -> V be a C^1 DIFFEOMORPHISM: phi is a bijection of U onto V, phi is continuously differentiable, and its inverse is continuously differentiable. (By the inverse function theorem it is equivalent to assume phi is injective, C^1, onto V, with det Dphi(x) nonzero for every x in U.) Let Dphi(x) denote the Jacobian matrix. Then for every Lebesgue measurable f : V -> [0, +infinity], the integral of f(y) dy over V equals the integral of f(phi(x)) |det Dphi(x)| dx over U, both sides being simultaneously finite or infinite; the same identity holds for complex-valued f, with f integrable over V if and only if (f composed with phi) times |det Dphi| is integrable over U. Taking f an indicator gives the measure statement: the Lebesgue measure of phi(E) equals the integral of |det Dphi| over E, for every measurable E contained in U. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) the ABSOLUTE VALUE of the determinant is required. The density is |det Dphi|; the sign records orientation and belongs to the theory of differential forms, not to Lebesgue integration. (ii) Injectivity cannot be dropped without paying for multiplicity: for a general C^1 map the correct statement is the area formula, the integral of f(phi(x)) |det Dphi(x)| dx over U equals the integral over V of f(y) N(y) dy, where N(y) is the number of preimages of y in U; N identically 1 is exactly injectivity. (iii) Smoothness cannot be relaxed to 'differentiable almost everywhere'. One needs the Luzin (N) property, that null sets map to null sets, which C^1 and Lipschitz maps have: in dimension one the Cantor function is continuous and nondecreasing with derivative 0 almost everywhere, yet it maps a null set onto a set of measure 1, and the naive substitution formula is false for it. (iv) The hypothesis is a diffeomorphism between OPEN sets; for maps defined on closed or lower-dimensional sets the statement must be routed through the area or coarea formula.
U and V are open subsets of R^n of the same dimension n
phi : U -> V is a bijection, continuously differentiable, with continuously differentiable inverse (equivalently injective C^1 with nonvanishing Jacobian determinant and image V)
Lebesgue measure and Lebesgue measurable functions are used on both sides
f is measurable and either nonnegative or integrable

[Definition Order of TWGs of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] The {\it order} $\vartheta(T)$ of a TWG 
$T$ for $e$ is defined inductively. 
If $T$ consists of a single edge then $\vartheta(T)=0$, otherwise
\[
\vartheta(T)
=1+\sum_{f\in E(H^{(e)}\setminus e)}\vartheta(T_f),
\]
where $H^{(e)}$ is the root of $T$.
If $\vartheta(T)=k$, then we call $T$ a {\it $k$-TWG}.
title: Order of TWGs

Let m_n be deterministic, a_n>0, and Y_n=(X_n-m_n)/a_n converge in distribution to a nondegenerate real Z. Then Z has finite fourth moment, its variance is positive, and

    Var(X_n)/a_n^2 -> Var(Z) in (0,infinity).

Its mass is at least 1-p, so its contribution to variance yields

    |mu_n-m_n| <= M a_n + sigma_n/sqrt(1-p).

This bound also holds if the mean is inside the interval. Both sigma_n/a_n and (mu_n-m_n)/a_n are uniformly bounded eventually. [Theorem 6 (Gaussian tail and conditional excess limit) of arXiv:2607.20714, 'High Minima of Gaussian Processes: Overshoots and Minimizer Locations'] Let $\boldsymbol X$ be a centred Gaussian vector in $\mathbb R^n$ with
positive definite covariance matrix $\Sigma$, and let $\boldsymbol p$ be
the minimizer of the following problem:
\[
 \sigma_*^2=\min_{\boldsymbol v\geq0,
             \,\boldsymbol1^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol v=1}
             \boldsymbol v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma\boldsymbol v.
\]
Put
\[
 I=\{i:p_i>0\},\qquad J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus I,
 \qquad  
 \qquad \boldsymbol\theta=\Sigma_{II}^{-1}\boldsymbol1_I.
\]
Then
\[
 \boldsymbol\theta=\frac{\boldsymbol p_I}{\sigma_*^2}>0,
 \qquad
 \boldsymbol r_J=\Sigma_{JI}\Sigma_{II}^{-1}\boldsymbol1_I\geq\boldsymbol1_J,
 \qquad
 \boldsymbol1_I^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\theta=\frac1{\sigma_*^2}.
\]
Write $r_j$ for the $j$th component of $\boldsymbol r_J$.
Let
\[
 P=\{j\in J:r_j=1\},\qquad N=\{j\in J:r_j>1\},
\]
and let $G_P$ be centred Gaussian with covariance matrix
\[
 \Gamma_P=\Sigma_{PP}-\Sigma_{PI}\Sigma_{II}^{-1}\Sigma_{IP}.
\]
Set $c_P=\Pp\{G_P>0\}$, with $c_P=1$ when $P$ is empty.  If
$M=\min_{1\leq i\leq n}X_i$, then, as $u\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \Pp\{M>u\}\sim
 \frac{c_P}{(2\pi)^{|I|/2}\det(\Sigma_{II})^{1/2}
                  \prod_{i\in I}\theta_i}
 u^{-|I|}\exp\left\{-\frac{u^2}{2\sigma_*^2}\right\}.
 
\end{equation}
Let $(\xi_i)_{i\geq1}$ be independent unit exponential random variables.
If $P$ is nonempty, let $G_P^+$ have law
$\mathcal L(G_P\mid G_P>0)$ and be independent of $(\xi_i)_{i\geq1}$.
Furthermore, as $u\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal L\left(
 \left(
   (u(X_i-u))_{i\in I},
   (X_j-u)_{j\in P},
   \frac{\boldsymbol X_N}{u}
 \right)
   \ \middle|\ M>u\right)
 \Longrightarrow
 \mathcal L\left(
   (\xi_i/\theta_i)_{i\in I},
   G_P^+,
   \boldsymbol r_N
 \right).
 
\end{equation}
The $G_P^+$ and $\boldsymbol r_N$ blocks are omitted
when $P$ and $N$, respectively, are empty. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Gaussian tail and conditional excess limit

Conjecture (not a theorem): Let G be an infinite connected locally finite graph whose automorphism group has finitely many vertex orbits. In independent Bernoulli site percolation, if the critical parameter p_c(G) is below 1, then at p_c(G) there is almost surely no infinite open vertex cluster. This is the site-percolation form of Benjamini and Schramm's 1996 Conjecture 4; the p_c<1 assumption is essential.
G infinite, connected, locally finite
finitely many vertex orbits under Aut(G)
independent Bernoulli site percolation
p_c(G)<1
title: Benjamini–Schramm criticality conjecture, original site form

body:
Every continuous map f from the sphere S^n to R^n sends some pair of antipodal points to the same value: there is x with f(x) = f(-x). Equivalently, no continuous antipode-preserving map S^n -> S^{n-1} exists. Consequences include the ham-sandwich theorem (bisect n masses in R^n by one hyperplane) and, famously, that at any moment two antipodal points on Earth share temperature and pressure.
f continuous on S^n into R^n

Condition sparse synchronous parking on holes at 0,e1, particles at 2e1,3e1, and zero excess elsewhere in B3(0) union B3(e1). With q=1/(2d), the time-three conditional hole covariance equals [1-q-(4d-3)q^3](1-q^2)q^4>0. In d4 it is 27405/134217728. The conditioning event has positive probability for every fixed 0<p<1/2, so conditional hole pairwise negative correlation is not universal. Assumptions: d>=1; uniform nearest-neighbor synchronous model; Sparse iid law signs each p, otherwise zero, 0<p<1/2; Specified finite initial pattern; horizon three; source finite propagation. Limitation: Finite-time conditional obstruction only; does not exclude averaged influence-energy estimates or determine the d4 long-time limit. Novelty: KNOWN finite-walk method; UNCHECKED exact conditional counterexample. Status: independently checked proof. The model is discrete-time uniform nearest-neighbor synchronous parking on Z^d with stationary capacity-one holes; A_t(x) is the active-particle count and H_t(x) the unfilled-hole indicator. In the sparse law eta(x) is initially +1 and -1 each with probability p, and zero otherwise, independently across sites. B3(x) is the graph-distance ball of radius three, e1 is the first coordinate unit vector, and covariance is conditional on the specified initial pattern.
d>=1; uniform nearest-neighbor synchronous model
