{"artifact_digest":"sha256:45c177ec0e48d6d43de93b941ad98567843757a71608ce24384965e7a7703f16","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/45/45c177ec0e48d6d43de93b941ad98567843757a71608ce24384965e7a7703f16.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:d573087f35a7b32ffd59589ea853e28d563fa1f54ff9ce13dc859d0863f48a69","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c20","bundle_id":"population.i0005-final-exploration-energy-and-charge-007","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"parking and interacting particle systems","draft":"w661/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:sparse-parking-positive-conditional-hole-covariance-time-three-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C20 v1: conditional hole covariance can be positive in dimension four

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN finite-walk enumeration method;
UNCHECKED this exact conditional parking counterexample. This is an actual
source-model example, not a Gaussian proxy or a different parking rule.

In Z^d, d>=1, let e=e_1, q=1/(2d), and condition the sparse iid initial
law on this pattern in C=B_3(0) union B_3(e): holes at 0,e, one active
excess particle each at 2e,3e, and zero excess at every other site of C.
For every 0<p<1/2 this event has probability

    p^4(1-2p)^(|C|-4)>0.

By source finite propagation, signs outside C do not affect H_3(0),H_3(e).
Conditional on this pattern,

    f:=P(H_3(e)=1)=[1-q-(4d-3)q^3](1-q^2),
    P(H_3(0)=1)=1-q^4,
    P(H_3(e)=H_3(0)=1)=f,
    Cov(H_3(e),H_3(0))=f q^4>0.

For d=4 this covariance is exactly 27405/134217728. Therefore hole
indicators are not always negatively correlated after conditioning on
the initial configuration. In particular instruction randomness cannot
simply be declared to contribute only negative hole correlations.
No unconditional long-time correlation bound is claimed.

## 1. Horizon and geometry

Call the particles starting at 2e and 3e P and Q. A path from P to 0
through time three can arrive only at time two, by two consecutive -e
steps; it first hits hole e at time one and settles there. Parity excludes
an arrival to 0 at time three. Thus P cannot fill the deeper hole.

Q can reach 0 through time three only by taking three consecutive -e
steps. It reaches e at time two and can pass it only if P already filled
e at time one, which requires P's first step to be -e. These four
specified steps have independent probability q^4. Hence the deeper hole
fills with probability exactly q^4. Every filling of 0 requires a prior
filling of e, so H_3(e)<=H_3(0) pathwise.

The two initial particle parities differ, and after each synchronous round
they still differ. They cannot arrive at the same hole in the same round.
Thus this example is independent of tie-breaking choices.

## 2. Survival of the nearer hole

The nearer hole survives exactly when both independent free particle paths
avoid e through time three. Any path relevant to a first hit of e stays
inside C. The only other initial hole is 0, and neither particle can
settle there before visiting e within this horizon, by the preceding
geometry. Therefore free-path avoidance is equivalent to actual survival.

For P, the displacement to the target is e. Its first hit can occur at
time one or three. The probability at time one is q. For three steps,
the number of walks with displacement e is 3+6(d-1)=6d-3: either two
+e steps and one -e step, or one +e step and a cancelling pair on another
axis. Thus p_3(e)=(6d-3)q^3. Of these visits at time three, paths that
already hit at time one contribute q p_2(0)=q^2=(2d)q^3. The probability
of first hitting at time three is consequently (4d-3)q^3. P avoids the
nearer hole with probability 1-q-(4d-3)q^3.

Q has displacement 2e to the nearer hole. By parity it can hit through
time three only at time two, requiring two -e steps, with probability
q^2. Its avoidance probability is 1-q^2. Independence proves the formula
for f. Both factors are positive (for d=1 they are 3/8 and 3/4;
for larger d they are positive as well).

## 3. Conditional covariance

The pathwise implication in Step 1 makes the joint survival probability
equal to f. Subtracting the product f(1-q^4) gives f q^4>0. In d=4,
q=1/8, f=(435/512)(63/64)=27405/32768; multiplication by q^4=1/4096
gives 27405/134217728.

## Conditioning and the scope of the obstruction

All relevant initial signs were fixed in a finite cone, an event of
positive probability under the actual sparse iid law. Conditional on the
entire initial configuration, outside signs still cannot affect the two
time-three events, so the same positive covariance holds on this
positive-probability family of initial configurations. The example
refutes a blanket conditional pairwise-negative-correlation premise.
It does not rule out a proved averaged energy estimate for conditional
influences, or a bound for some other times, initial patterns or observables.

Primary model and finite propagation: Bou-Rabee--Panagiotis,
arXiv:2609.02820v1, Section 2 and Theorem 1.6's sparse law. The finite
path probabilities and event implication are derived above explicitly.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:910b07332d3c65bdc4ce5cdeda4b2465d185fe70eef164a8962607b3724a5daf","revision_digest":"sha256:1062cf5401bc1af803d047469816863e364ff981e667e89e3b0194da8d160109","source_id":"owner-own-work:w661:I0005-C20:v1","source_revision":"v1; packaged 2026-10-14T07:46:54.3984460+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

For sparse critical parking, q=p/(1-p), conditional on active-exploration history through t that excludes unrevealed initial hole/empty labels, surviving holes are independent Bernoulli(q) on V_t sites with no initial active particle and no arrival. Thus h_t=q P(V_t(0)=1), and with N_t counting V_t sites strictly inside the nearest-active graph radius, P(F_t)=E[1-(1-q)^N_t]. It lies between q P(N_t>=1) and P(N_t>=1), so fixed-p zero-limit questions are equivalent. The other-hole Palm field is dominated by iid Bernoulli(q) via an explicit posterior coupling. Assumptions: d>=1; fixed 0<p<1/2; sparse iid signs each p; Synchronous independent walks, capacity-one holes; Exploration filtration includes initial active indicators and used paths/arrivals but excludes unvisited initial trap coins; Graph metric; extended-ball conventions if nearest active distance is infinite. Limitation: Unexplored-site geometry relative to active sites is unresolved in d4; no fixed-law limit obtained. Novelty: KNOWN deferred-decision method; UNCHECKED exact parking posterior and nearest-event reduction. Status: independently checked proof. The model is discrete-time uniform nearest-neighbor synchronous parking on Z^d with stationary capacity-one holes; A_t(x) is the active-particle count and H_t(x) the unfilled-hole indicator. In the sparse law eta(x) is initially +1 and -1 each with probability p, and zero otherwise, independently across sites. F_t is the event that the origin is strictly closer in graph distance to an unfilled hole than to an active particle; active distance is infinite if no active site exists, and the corresponding strict ball is all finite-distance sites.

Synchronous independent walks, capacity-one holes
Exploration filtration includes initial active indicators and used paths/arrivals but excludes unvisited initial trap coins

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:f1a62227238ada58ac7f3867f52e37e36bf907ad6e27418a82a4593061dca15e","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/f1/f1a62227238ada58ac7f3867f52e37e36bf907ad6e27418a82a4593061dca15e.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:d573087f35a7b32ffd59589ea853e28d563fa1f54ff9ce13dc859d0863f48a69","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c23","bundle_id":"population.i0005-final-exploration-energy-and-charge-007","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"parking and interacting particle systems","draft":"w661/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:parking-unrevealed-hole-posterior-nearest-unexplored-reduction-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C23 v1: deferred holes and an exact unexplored-site reduction

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN deferred-decision method;
UNCHECKED this exact parking posterior/reduction formulation. All statements
use the explicit exploration filtration below, which does not reveal
unvisited initial hole/empty labels.

For the sparse critical synchronous particle-hole process on Z^d, d>=1,
P(eta=1)=P(eta=-1)=p, P(eta=0)=1-2p, 0<p<1/2, put q=p/(1-p).
Let E_t be the information generated by the initial active-particle
indicators, active trajectories and actual arrivals/settlements through
round t. It includes A_t, but reveals an initial hole/empty label only
when an arrival tests that site. Define the E_t-measurable eligible field

    V_t(x)=1{A_0(x)=0 and no particle has arrived at x in rounds 1,...,t}.

Conditional on E_t, the surviving-hole indicators H_t(x) are independent
Bernoulli(q) coins on the set V_t=1, and are zero elsewhere. Consequently,

    h_t=q P(V_t(0)=1),
    P(H_t(0)=H_t(z)=1)=q^2 P(V_t(0)=V_t(z)=1), z!=0.

Let D_A be the graph distance from the origin to the nearest active site
at time t, and let

    N_t=number of V_t sites in B_(D_A-1)(0),

with an empty ball when D_A=0 and a limiting union when D_A=infinity.
Then the exact closer-hole probability is

    P(F_t)=E[1-(1-q)^N_t].

In particular

    q P(N_t>=1)<=P(F_t)<=P(N_t>=1).

For one fixed p, the closer-hole probability tends to zero if and only
if the probability of an eligible never-arrived site strictly nearer than
an active site tends to zero. This is an exact reduction; the unexplored
geometry remains unproved in d4.

## 1. Independent latent coins for the source initial law

Generate iid initial-particle indicators I_x with probability p. Independently
generate iid Bernoulli(q) coins B_x and all walks/tie randomness. Set eta(x)=1
when I_x=1. When I_x=0 set eta(x)=-1 if B_x=1 and eta(x)=0 otherwise.
This gives probabilities p,(1-p)q=p,(1-p)(1-q)=1-2p, exactly the source law.
Coins at initial particle sites are irrelevant.

Simulate by revealing B_x at the first arrival to a site with I_x=0.
If B_x=1, one arriving particle settles; otherwise none does. After that
first visit there is no unfilled hole there in either case. Before the
first arrival the coin has no effect on any trajectory or tie choice.
This is a law-equivalent deferred-decision construction.

## 2. Exact conditional distribution, including adaptive exploration

For a finite set S, the event that all its sites are eligible is determined
without reading any of their coins. To see this without assuming that
the explored set is independent of the coins, fix all initial indicators,
external coins and walk/tie randomness. Vary the coins at S. If no site
in S receives an arrival, the history through t is identical for every
choice. If some first arrival to S occurs, its occurrence is determined
before reading the first such coin, and the event that all S are eligible
is already false. Thus for any nonnegative E_t-measurable F,
F product_{x in S}V_t(x) is invariant under changing B_S.

Pointwise H_t(x)=B_x V_t(x). Integrating over the independent coins at S
therefore gives

    E[F product_{x in S}H_t(x)]
       =q^|S| E[F product_{x in S}V_t(x)].

This holds for all nonnegative F in the exploration sigma-field, and so
determines all conditional joint moments. Binary inclusion-exclusion
then identifies the conditional finite-dimensional law as independent
Bernoulli(q) on eligible sites, zero elsewhere. This proves the posterior
claim and its one- and two-site consequences. It does not condition on
the full initial eta configuration; doing so would reveal these coins.

## 3. Exact nearest-event formula

D_A and V_t are exploration-measurable. For each finite value D_A=k,
strictly nearer holes are exactly holes in the deterministic ball B_(k-1).
Conditional independence gives the probability that none of its N_t
eligible sites carries a hole as (1-q)^N_t. Partition by k to obtain
the formula. The k=0 case has N_t=0. For infinite D_A, take increasing
finite balls and use continuity of conditional probabilities; adopt
(1-q)^infinity=0. Thus no finite-nearest-distance assumption is necessary.

For each integer n>=1, q<=1-(1-q)^n<=1, and for n=0 the expression
vanishes. The bounds follow on averaging; fixed q>0 proves the stated
equivalence of zero limits. This does not hold uniformly if p is reselected
and q tends to zero.

## 4. Palm domination is now justified by a coupling

Given exploration, generate fresh independent Bernoulli(q) coins at all
eligible sites to realize the conditional hole field. It is coordinatewise
bounded by an iid Bernoulli(q) field on all sites. Mixing over exploration
preserves this domination even after conditioning on the final active
field. After conditioning additionally on H_t(0)=1, the origin is eligible
and its coin is fixed to one; all other remaining coins still have their
independent Bernoulli(q) law. Hence the other-hole Palm field is dominated
by iid Bernoulli(q), via this explicit coupling. This conclusion is not
inferred merely from C5's factorial-moment inequalities.

The moment consequences in C5/C8 become immediate from the displayed
identity. They do not constrain the geometry of V_t: for example the
two-hole upper bound q h_t reduces to the trivial bound
P(V_t(0)=V_t(z)=1)<=P(V_t(0)=1). A finite Palm count at mean spacing
still requires information about the actual unexplored set.

## Sources and remaining piece

Primary model: Bou-Rabee--Panagiotis arXiv:2609.02820v1, Sections 2 and
8.2, capacity-one sparse law. The latent-variable construction, adaptive
invariance argument and nearest-event reduction are explicitly proved
above. The unresolved task is the geometry of never-arrived eligible
sites relative to current active particles for one fixed d4 law.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:910b07332d3c65bdc4ce5cdeda4b2465d185fe70eef164a8962607b3724a5daf","revision_digest":"sha256:10667b77db602237787d0f4f48383239ddf147d74a90e24f5fd523c092a83032","source_id":"owner-own-work:w661:I0005-C23:v1","source_revision":"v1; packaged 2026-10-14T07:46:54.3984460+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Corollary cor:charac-Y-reflexive of arXiv:2609.00794, 'On operators whose adjoints or second adjoints attain their norms'] Let $Y$ be a Banach space. Then the following are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \itemsep0.25em
        \item $Y$ is reflexive.
        \item $\operatorname{QNA}(X,Y) = \operatorname{NA}_1(X,Y)$ for every Banach space $X$.
        \item $\operatorname{QNA}(\ell_1,Y) = \operatorname{NA}_1 (\ell_1,Y)$.
    \end{enumerate}
    If, moreover, $Y$ contains no isomorphic copy of $\ell_1$, then these conditions are also equivalent to 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*), start=4] 
\itemsep0.25em
        \item $\operatorname{NA}_1(X,Y) = \operatorname{NA}_2(X,Y)$ for every Banach space $X$.
        \item $\operatorname{NA}_1(\ell_1,Y) = \operatorname{NA}_2 (\ell_1,Y)$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lem 133 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $t\notin \oJ$ (recall Lemma~\ref{l:bad.J}) and parameters as in \eqref{eq:order-of-limits}: 
    \[\bE\Big[|tp'(t) - \trrr_t|\Big]
    \leq  
    o_{\trK}(1)
    \]
for $ \trrr_t\equiv \trrr(t,X^\plus(t))$. 

\begin{proof}
Let $\bar{P}(t)$ be the temporal smoothing of $tp'(t)$. Then for $t\notin\bar{J}$ we have
	\[
    \bE\Big[|tp'(t) - \trrr_t|\Big]
    =
    \bE\Big[|tp'(t) - \bar P(t)|\Big]
    +\bE\Big[|\bar P(t) - \trrr_t|\Big]
    = O(\lambda)
    +\bE\Big[|\bar P(t) - \trrr_t|
    \Big]\,.
    \]
Let $\bar{P}^N$ be the temporal smoothing of $t(p^N)'(t)$. It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:limit.coefs} that $\bar{P}^N$ converges pointwise to $\bar{P}$, and $\trrr^N$ converges pointwise to $\trrr$. It follows by the bounded convergence theorem that we also have convergence in expectation, so
	\[
	\bE\Big[|\bar P(t) - \trrr_t|\Big]
	=\bE\Big[|\bar P^N(t) - (\trrr^N)_t|\Big] + o_N(1)\,.
	\] 
We then note that $\bar{P}^N-\trrr^N$ is the smoothing (via Definitions~\ref{d:sp.smooth} and \ref{d:t.smooth}) of 
	\begin{align} \nonumber
	A^N(t,\vy)
	&\equiv t(p^N)'(t)-\rrr^{\plus,N}(t,\vy)
	= t(p^N)'(t)-\sum_{B^\frozen \subseteq B^{\frozen,\coarse}}
    \frac{|B|}{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|}
    \rrr^{\trunc,N}(t,B) 
    \\
	&\qquad= \bigg(
	1-\frac{|B^{\frozen,\coarse} \cap [M]|}{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|} 
	\bigg)
	t(p^N)'(t)
	+ \sum_{B^\frozen \subseteq B^{\frozen,\coarse}} \frac{|B|}{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|}
	\bigg(
	t(p^N)'(t) -
	\rrr^{\trunc,N}(t,B)\bigg)\,,
	
	 \end{align}
where the correspondence between $\vy$ and $B^{\frozen,\coarse}$ is as described around \eqref{e:review.P}. For the first term in
\eqref{e:P.N.r.frozen.twoterms}, at any fixed time $t$, we have
\[\bE\bigg[ 1-\frac{|B^{\frozen,\coarse} \cap [M]|}{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|} \bigg]
    = 1 - \sum_{B^{\frozen,\coarse}}
    \frac{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|}{M^\frozen}
    \frac{|B^{\frozen,\coarse} \cap [M]|}{|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|}
    = 1 - \frac{M}{M^\frozen}
    = o_{\trK}(1)\,,
\]
by recalling the choice of $M^\frozen$ from Definition~\ref{d:froze}. For the second term in \eqref{e:P.N.r.frozen.twoterms},  we argued in the proof of Proposition~\ref{p:budget-constraints-without-frozen}\ref{it:Ising-budget-constraint} that the total fraction of particles ever frozen is with high probability at most $o_{\trK}(1)$, so this term is also small on average at any fixed time for the process $Y$. Altogether this shows
	\beq
	\bE\Big[ |A^N(t,\vY^{\frozen,N,\RomI:\RomIII}(t)) |\Big]
	= \int_{\R^3} |A^N(t,\vy)| \varrho_{N,t}(d\vy)
	\le o_{\trK}(1)\,.
	\eeq
Let $\tilde{A}^N$ be the spatial smoothing of $A^N$, via Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth}. Let $\tvY^{\frozen,N}(t)\equiv \vY^{\frozen,N}(t)+\xxx$, and denote the projection onto the sum of the first three coordinates as
 $\tilde{Y}^{\frozen,N} = \tilde{Y}^{\frozen,N,\RomI}+\tilde{Y}^{\frozen,N,\RomII}+\tilde{Y}^{\frozen,N,\RomIII}$. Then
	\begin{align*} &\bE\Big[ |\tilde{A}^N(t, \tilde{Y}^{\frozen,N}(t)) |\Big]
	= \int_{\R} |\tilde{A}^N(t,y)| \overline{\varrho_{N,t}*\sphi}(y)\,dy \\
	&\qquad = \int_{\R} \bigg|
	\int_{H(y)} \int_{\R^3} \sphi(\vy-\vx) A^N(t,\vx)
		\,\rho_{N,t}(d\vx)\,d\vy \bigg| \,dy \\
	&\qquad\le  \int_{\R^3}
	|A^N(t,\vx)| \bigg( \int_{\R^3}
		 \sphi(\vy-\vx) \,d\vy\bigg)
		\,\rho_{N,t}(d\vx) =  \int_{\R^3}
	|A^N(t,\vx)|\rho_{N,t}(d\vx) \le o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\end{align*}
using the previous estimate \eqref{e:AN.small.finiteN}. This shows that the bound \eqref{e:AN.small.finiteN} can be passed to the spatially smoothed quantity $A^N$. Similarly, let $\bar{A}^N$ be the temporal smoothing of $\tilde{A}^N$, via Definition~\ref{d:t.smooth}. Then
	\begin{align*}
	&\bE\Big[ |\bar{A}^N(t,\tilde{Y}^{\frozen,N}(t))| \Big]
	=\int_{\R} |\bar{A}^N(t,y)| \overline{\varrho_{N,t}*\sphi}(y)\,dy\\
	&\qquad\le \int_{\R}  
	\bigg( \int_{\R}\tphi(t-s) |  \tilde{A}^N(s) |\,ds  \bigg) \,
	 \overline{\varrho_{N,t}*\sphi}(y)\,dy \\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)

Fix an integer d>=2 and normalized uniform surface measure sigma on S^(d-1). Let H_l be the real degree-l spherical harmonics, h_l=dim H_l, and Y_(l,1),...,Y_(l,h_l) any orthonormal basis in L2(sigma). Let P_l be the degree-l polynomial orthogonal to lower-degree polynomials for weight (1-t^2)^((d-3)/2) on [-1,1], normalized by P_l(1)=1. Then sum_(j=1)^(h_l) Y_(l,j)(x)Y_(l,j)(y)=h_l P_l(<x,y>). In particular P_l(<x,y>) is a positive semidefinite kernel: for any finite x_i on the sphere and real c_i, sum_(i,j)c_i c_j P_l(<x_i,x_j>)>=0. For a real polynomial u=sum_l a_l P_l, its zonal kernel u(<x,y>) is positive semidefinite if and only if every a_l>=0. The product of two such polynomials again has nonnegative P_l coefficients. If every coefficient through the respective degrees is strictly positive, the product also has every coefficient through its degree strictly positive. Here d=2 uses the normalized Chebyshev polynomials, and d>=3 the Gegenbauer polynomials rescaled to value 1 at 1. Positive semidefinite kernels allow zero quadratic forms; strictly positive coefficients do not mean strict positivity of every finite Gram matrix.

P_l(1)=1; fixed dimension throughout
polynomials have finitely many coefficients

[Definition D:asy-Feller of arXiv:2412.03521, 'On ergodic properties of stochastic PDEs'] A Markov transition semigroup $P_t$ on a Polish space $\mathcal{X}$ is called
  asymptotically strong Feller at $x$ if there exists a totally separating
  system of pseudo-metrics $\left\{d_n; n\ge1\right\}$ for $\mathcal{X}$ and a
  sequence $\left\{t_n; n\ge 1\right\}$ with $t_n>0$ such that
  \begin{align*}
    \liminf_{U\in \mathcal{U}_x}\: \limsup_{n\to\infty}\: \sup_{y\in U}\Norm{P_{t_n}(x,\cdot)-P_{t_n}(y,\cdot)}_{d_n}=0,
  \end{align*}
  where $\mathcal{U}_x$ is the collection of all open sets containing $x$. It is
  called asymptotically strong Feller if this property holds at every $x \in
  \mathcal{X}$.
title: Definition D:asy-Feller of arXiv:2412.03521

[Definition def:subdivided-graph of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] For $r\in{\mathbb N}_0$, the \emph{$2^r$-subdivision}
$G_r=(\Lambda_r,E_r)$ of $G$ is obtained by replacing every edge by a series
of $2^r$ edges as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\Lambda_r$ is obtained from $\Lambda$ by adding $2^r-1$ new vertices $v_{e,2^{-r}j}$,
  $j=1,\ldots,2^r-1$ for
  any edge $e\in E$. We say that these new vertices are located on the edge $e$. 
  In particular, $\Lambda\subseteq \Lambda_r$. 
\item Every edge $e\in E$ is replaced by a series of $2^r$ edges $e_{1,r},\ldots,e_{2^r,r}$ as follows.
  For bookkeeping purposes only, we endow $e$ with a direction, and 
  call $v_{e,0}$ and $v_{e,1}$ the two vertices it consists of. Then, $e$ is
  replaced by the new edges $e_{j,r}=\{v_{e,2^{-r}(j-1)},v_{e,2^{-r}j}\}$, $1\le j\le 2^r$,
  which we view as being located on the edge $e$. Thus, 
  $E_r=\{e_{j,r}:e\in E, 1\le j\le 2^r\}$.
\end{itemize}
Note that $\Lambda_0=\Lambda$ and $\Lambda_r\subseteq\Lambda_{r+1}$. 
For technical convenience, we introduce also the set of
direct self-loops $\Delta_r:=\{\{i,i\}:i\in\Lambda_r\}$.

[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2506.15159, 'Conditional central limit theorems for exponential random graphs'] Denote the edge set of $H_l$, $1\leq l \leq m$, by $k_{l_1},\dots, k_{l_{e_l}}$.
    Denote by $s(H_l\backslash k_{l_j})$ and $t(H_l\backslash k_{l_j})$ the numbers of two stars and triangles in graph $H_l\backslash k_{l_j}$, respectively. We have $|\widetilde{p}-p-c^* n^{-1}|\leq C n^{-3/2}$ with
\begin{align*}
       c^*=\frac{p(1-p)}{1-\varphi^{\prime}(p)}&\bigg[\sum_{l=1}^m\beta_l\sum_{j=1}^{e_l}\left(4s(H_l\backslash k_{l_j})p^{e_l-3}\frac{q^2\sum_{r=2}^m\beta_rs_rp^{e_r}}{1-2\sum_{r=2}^m\beta_rs_rp^{e_r-1}q}\right.\\
       &\left.\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad+12t(H_l\backslash k_{l_j})p^{e_l-4}q^3\sum_{r=2}^m\beta_rs_rp^{e_r}\right)\\
        &+(1-2p)\left( \frac{8(\sum_{l=2}^m \beta_ls_l p^{e_l-2})^2pq}{(1-2\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_ls_lp^{e_l-1}q)}+36\big(\sum_{l=2}^m \beta_lt_l p^{e_l-2}\big)^2q^2\right)\\
        &-\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_le_lp^{e_l-1}\left(v_l-2\right)\left(v_l-3\right)\bigg].
    \end{align*}

body:
[Lem 107 (spatial smoothing of domain constraint) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\sV^N$ and $\sU^N$ be the spatially smoothed quantities from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth}. Then, analogously to \eqref{e:domain.plus.coarse}, with high probability we have
	\[
	\svvv^N(t,y)
	=\frac{\sV^N(t,y)}{p^N(t)}
	\ge
	\frac{\sU^N(t,y)^2}{p^N(t)
		\cdot  \srrr^N(t,y)}
	-\frac{\eta^2}{2}
	\ge 
	\frac{\sU^N(t,y)^2}{p^N(t)
		\cdot  t (p^N)'(t)}
	-\frac{\eta^2}{2}
	=\suuu^N(t,y)^2
	-\frac{\eta^2}{2}
	\]
for all $(t,y) \in[q_0,1]\times\R$.

\begin{proof}
We use the abbreviations introduced above. In particular, recall from Definition~\ref{d:disc.rescaled.coeffs} that we can regard $V$ as a function of $(t,\vy)$ for $\vy\in\R^3$. 
Using 
\eqref{e:discrete.ratio.occ.V}, we can rewrite
	\[
	\rho_{V,t}*\sphi(\vy)
	= \int_{\R^3} \sphi(\vy-\vx) V(t,\vx)\,\varrho_t(d\vx)\,.
	\]
It follows that we can express 
$\sV(t,y)\equiv 
\sE_{t,y} V(t,\xxx)$ where $\sE_{t,y}$ 
refers to expectation with respect to the law of $(\vy,\xxx)\sim\tilde{\bP}_{t,y}$ defined by
	\beq
	\tilde{\bP}_{t,y}(d\vy\,d\vx)
	= \frac{ 
		\varrho_t*\sphi(\vy)}
		{\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}
		(y)}
		\cdot 
		\frac{\sphi(\vy-\vx)\,
		\varrho_t(d\vx)}
		{\varrho_t*\sphi(\vy)} \, d\vy
	\eeq
for $\vx\in\R^3$ and $\vy\in H(y)$ where
	\beq
	H(y)
	\equiv \bigg\{\vy\in\R^3 : (\vI,\vy)=y\bigg\}\,.\eeq
Here $H(y)$ is equipped with the Hausdorff measure inherited from Lebesgue measure on $\R^3$, and in \eqref{e:tilde.bP} $d\vy$ denotes integration with respect to this measure. Similarly, $\sU(t,y) = \sE_{t,y} U(t,\xxx)$ and $\srrr(t,y)=\sE_{t,y} \rrr(t,\xxx)$. One can check that the function
	\[
	(u,r) \mapsto \begin{cases}
	 \frac{u^2}{r} & r>0\,,\\
	0 & u=r=0
	 \end{cases}
	\]
is convex on the domain $\{u\in\R,r>0\}  \cup\{u=r=0\}$, so Jensen's inequality gives
	\[
	\frac{\sV(t,y)}{p(t)}
	= \frac{\sE_{t,y} V(t,\xxx)}{p(t)}
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:domain.plus.rewrittten}}{\ge}
	\sE_{t,y} \bigg[
		\frac{U(t,\xxx)^2}{p(t) 
		\cdot \rrr(t,\xxx)}
		- \frac{\eta^2}{2}\bigg]
	\ge 
	\frac{\sU(t,y)^2}{p(t) 
	\cdot  \srrr(t,y)}
		- \frac{\eta^2}{2}\,,
	\]
as claimed.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: spatial smoothing of domain constraint

Let Omega in R^n be bounded and open with C^2 boundary, and let Lu = -sum D_i(a^{ij} D_j u) + sum b^i D_i u + c u with a^{ij} = a^{ji} in C^1(closure of Omega), b^i, c in L^infinity(Omega), and uniform ellipticity sum a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j >= lambda |xi|^2 with lambda > 0. Let f in L^2(Omega) and let u in H^1_0(Omega) be a weak solution of Lu = f. Then u is in H^2(Omega), Lu = f holds almost everywhere (u is a strong solution), and ||u||_{H^2(Omega)} <= C ( ||f||_{L^2(Omega)} + ||u||_{L^2(Omega)} ) with C depending only on Omega and the coefficients; if the Dirichlet problem is uniquely solvable (for instance b = 0 and c >= 0), the term ||u||_{L^2} may be dropped. Interior H^2 regularity (u in H^2_loc with the corresponding estimate on compactly contained subsets) needs only a^{ij} in C^1(Omega) and no boundary hypothesis. The C^2 boundary hypothesis can be relaxed to C^{1,1}, and for L = -Laplacian to convexity of Omega, but it cannot be dropped: on a domain with a reentrant corner the conclusion is false.
Omega bounded open in R^n with C^2 (or C^{1,1}) boundary for the global statement
a^{ij} = a^{ji} in C^1(closure of Omega) (Lipschitz is enough); b, c in L^infinity
uniform ellipticity with lambda > 0
f in L^2(Omega) and u in H^1_0(Omega) a weak solution

[Thm Thm_strict_monotonicity of arXiv:2606.22183, 'Expected loss of quasi-arithmetic means of exchangeable random variables'] Let $I\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a nonempty open interval, $f:I\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous and strictly increasing function,
 and $(\xi_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of exchangeable random variables with values in $I$ such that
 $\mathbb{D}^2(f(\xi_1))\in(0,\infty)$.
Let $\mu\in\mathbb{R}_+$ and $L:I\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function such that the function $L\circ f^{-1}: f(I)\to\mathbb{R}$ is strongly convex with modulus $\mu$
 and $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}(\vert L(\xi_1)\vert)<\infty$.
Then, for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, we have that $\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\big(L\big( \mathscr{A}_n^{f}(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n) \big)\big)\in[-\infty,\infty)$ and the sequence
\[
  \bigg(\operatorname{\mathbb{E}}\big(L\big( \mathscr{A}_n^{f}(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n) \big)\big)-\frac{\mu(1-\varrho)}{n}\mathbb{D}^2(f(\xi_1))\bigg)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}
\]
is decreasing, where
 \[
   \varrho:=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(f(\xi_1),f(\xi_2))}{\sqrt{ \mathbb{D}^2(f(\xi_1)) \mathbb{D}^2(f(\xi_2)) } }
           = \operatorname{Corr}(f(\xi_1),f(\xi_2)).
 \]

[Lemma Survival from a killed eigenfunction of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] Let
\(B \subseteq M\) be closed of positive capacity, let
\(\lambda_{B}\) denote the principal eigenvalue of the process
killed on \(B\), and let \(\varphi_{B} \geq 0\) be a
corresponding principal eigenfunction normalised by
\(\parallel \varphi_{B} \parallel_{L^{\infty}(M)} = 1\). Then for
every \(x \in M\) and every \(t \geq 0\),

\[\mathbb{P}_{x}\left( \tau_{B} > t \right) \geq \varphi_{B}(x)\, e^{- \lambda_{B}t}.\]

[Proposition 27 (Maximum principle for particle-production Navier--Stokes flows) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Fix a Navier--Stokes triple $(\mathscr F,\chi,\mathscr B)$ that is admissible (\autoref{def-pot-admissible-triple}) and torus-adapted (\autoref{def-NS-torus-adapted}).
Let $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$ be a sufficiently regular particle-production Einstein--Navier--Stokes areal flow $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$ on $[t_0,t_1]\times\Tbb^3$.
If the density $\mu>0$ is positive throughout, in terms of the characteristic flow~\eqref{eq:section-8-characteristics} of $\velo$, one has
\bel{eq:pot-characteristic-contraction}
\aligned
\Gammaunpar_\chi\bigl(t,X(t;t_0,x)\bigr)&=\exp\left(-\int_{t_0}^t\frac{\mathfrak d_{\mathscr B}^{\rm ar}}{\rho_\chi}\bigl(r,X(r;t_0,x)\bigr)\,dr\right)\Gammaunpar_\chi(t_0,x),\\
\Gammazero\bigl(t,X(t;t_0,x)\bigr)&=\Gammazero(t_0,x),
\endaligned
\ee
hence the ranges of $\Gammaunpar_\chi(t,\cdot)$ and $\Gammazero(t,\cdot)$ obey
\bel{eq:pot-radial-hull}
\operatorname{Ran}\Gammaunpar_\chi(t,\cdot)\subset\left\{\lambda z\middle|\ 0\leq\lambda\leq1,\ z\in\operatorname{Ran}\Gammaunpar_\chi(t_0,\cdot)\right\},\qquad \operatorname{Ran}\Gammazero(t,\cdot)=\operatorname{Ran}\Gammazero(t_0,\cdot).
\ee
For flows including the vacuum $\mu=0$, a weaker statement holds: the convex hull of $\{0\}$ and the range of~$\Gammaunpar$ is contained in the same convex hull at initial time.

	of non-negative numbers, such that $F_{n,k}=0$ when $k>n$ and such that the following recursion is satisfied:
	\begin{align}
	F_{n,k}	=\sum_{i\geq 0}A_{i,k} F_{n-1,i-1},	
	\qquad n\geq 1,\quad k\geq 0,
	\end{align}
	where we make the convention $F_{n,-1}=0$ for all $n\geq 0$.
	If the array $A$ is TP2, then so is the array $F$.

Suppose (mu_n)_{n in N} in M_1(X) is sequentially tight along compact sets (K_epsilon^delta)_{delta > 0}. Then there exists a collection of finite sets (F_epsilon^delta)_{delta, epsilon > 0} that is increasing with decreasing delta and epsilon along which (mu_n)_{n in N} is sequentially tight. Furthermore, F_epsilon := overline{bigcup_{delta > 0} F_epsilon^delta} is a separable and complete subspace of X for every epsilon > 0.

body:
Consider a finite simple graph with an FK(p,q) law, 0<p<1 and q>=1, with no imposed identification of vertices outside a chosen subgraph H. Suppose H has at least two distinct boundary vertices and boundary vertex v has k incident edges outside H. If xi is the partition of the boundary induced by open paths using only exterior edges, then P(xi is not the one-block wired partition)>=(1-p)^k. In a family of maximum degree D this is at least (1-p)^D>0. Therefore uniqueness of a giant component alone cannot justify an assertion that every fixed boundary vertex is wired together with probability tending to one.

body:
[Theorem 6 (Wendel's formula: Probabilistic version) of arXiv:2608.16752, 'Absorption Probabilities for Random Convex Hulls: Distribution-Freeness via the Wall-Cross'] Let $\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n$ be random vectors in $\R^d$ whose joint distribution is invariant under sign flips, that is,
$$
(\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n) \stackrel{d}{=} (\eps_1 \xi_1, \dots, \eps_n \xi_n)
\qquad \text{for every } \eps \in \{\pm 1\}^n.
$$
Suppose additionally that the configuration $X := (\xi_1 \,|\, \dots \,|\, \xi_n)$ is regular almost surely, i.e.\ $\pr(X \in \mathcal D) = 0$. Then
\begin{align*}
    \pr\big( 0 \notin \Conv(\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n) \big)
    = \frac{1}{2^{\,n-1}} \sum_{j=0}^{d-1} \binom{n-1}{j}.
\end{align*}
Note that neither independence nor exchangeability of $\xi_1, \dots, \xi_n$ is assumed.

[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2511.16973, '2511.16973'] Suppose Condition \ref{cond noise} is satisfied.
Then there exist constants $C_0,C_1>0$ such that for any $t>s\ge0$ and $x,y>0$,
$$
W_V(P_{s,t}(x,\cdot),P_{s,t}(y,\cdot))\le C_0 d_V(x,y)\mathrm{exp}\left(-C_1\int_s^tb_0(r)\,\dd r\right),
$$
where $d_V$ and $W_V$ denote the metric defined in \eqref{metric of dv} and the Wasserstein distance introduced in \eqref{wasserstein dist}, respectively. In particular, if
$$
\limsup\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\left( t^{-1}\int_\cdot^tb_0(r)\,\dd r\right)>0,
$$
the process is exponentially contractive in the $W_V$-distance. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

PRIVATE CONDITIONAL RESOLUTION, author-recorded, sources not re-fetched. Procaccia, Rosenthal and Sapozhnikov (PTRF 2016) prove a quenched invariance principle for random walk on the infinite cluster of correlated percolation models satisfying a polynomial decoupling condition, local uniqueness and a density condition; for the vacant set these were known for u < u** at the time. Duminil-Copin, Goswami, Rodriguez, Severo and Teixeira (2023) prove u* = u** = bar u, so the inputs hold for every u < u*, and the conclusion of PRS should extend to the whole supercritical phase, answering Open Problem 16.7 of Heydenreich-van der Hofstad for the vacant set (the interlacement set itself was already covered for all u > 0). Verification owed: that the decoupling inequalities of the sharpness paper have exactly the PRS form and that constants may depend on u.

[Definition 35 of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] A point $(t,x) \in L  \cdot (\Z_{\leq 0}\times\Z^d)$ is said to be $(L  ,\delta)$-good is the following three conditions are satisfied:
\begin{itemize}
\item  For all $r \in [-L  (t+1), -L  t]$, the two configurations $R^{\Lambda_{2n_L  }(v), -(t+1)n_L  , -r}(\tau^\pm )$ coincide on the space box $\Lambda_{n_L  }(v)$.
\item For all $-r \in [-L  (t+1), -L  t] $, there exists no $\om$-open cluster of $R^{\Lambda_{2n_L  }(v), -(t+1)n_L  , -r}(\tau^+ )$ crossing the space box $\Lambda_{L  }(v)$.

[Corollary 23 (The Weighted Functional Santal\'o inequality) of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $q \in (0, n)$, let $a\in L^\frac{n}{q}(\s)$ be non-negative and define $$C_{n,q}(a) = \frac{n-q}{n\|a\|_{L^1(\s,\sigma_{n-1})}} \left(\frac{n}{n-q}\|a\|_{L^\frac{n}{q}(\s,\sigma_{n-1})}\right)^{\frac{n}{2n-q}}.$$ Then, for every function $f \in \mathcal{F}_n$ and any non-negative measurable function $g$ on $\R^n$ that satisfy the pointwise bound
    \[
        f(x)^{\frac{n-q}{2n-q}} g(y)^{\frac{n}{2n-q}} \leq \Omega(\langle x, y \rangle) \quad\forall \,x, y \in \R^n \text{ with } \langle x,y\rangle>0,
    \]
    where $\Omega: \R_+ \to \R_+$ is a measurable, non-increasing function, one has:
    \begin{equation}
        
        \left(\int_{\R^n} \!\!\!f(x) dx \right)^{\frac{n-q}{2n-q}} \left(\int_{\R^n} \!\!\!\!g(y) |y|^{-q}a\left(\frac{y}{|y|}\right) dy \right)^{\frac{n}{2n-q}} \leq C_{n,q}(a) \int_{\R^n}\!\!\! \Omega(|z|^\frac{2n-q}{n}) |z|^{-q}a\left(\frac{z}{|z|}\right) dz.
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: The Weighted Functional Santal\'o inequality

body:
Let (X_n) be a submartingale with sup_n E[X_n^+] < infinity. Then X_n converges almost surely to a limit X_infinity with E|X_infinity| < infinity. For a MARTINGALE the hypothesis is equivalent to sup_n E|X_n| < infinity, since E[X_n] is constant and E|X_n| = 2E[X_n^+] - E[X_n]. Convergence is ONLY almost sure: it need not hold in L^1, and E[X_infinity] need not equal E[X_0]. Standard failure: let (X_n) be the product of independent nonnegative mean-one factors, for instance X_n = prod_{k <= n} (1 + eps_k) with eps_k = +1 or -1 with probability 1/2 each - equivalently X_n = 2^n on the event that all signs were +1 and 0 otherwise. Then X_n is a nonnegative martingale with E X_n = 1 for every n, so it is L^1-bounded and converges a.s., but the limit is 0 almost surely and E X_infinity = 0 != 1 = E X_0. Nonnegative supermartingales always converge a.s. because X_n^+ = X_n has bounded expectation; upgrading to L^1 convergence is exactly what uniform integrability supplies. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.2.11]
(X_n) a submartingale for a filtration (F_n)
sup_n E[X_n^+] < infinity (for a martingale: sup_n E|X_n| < infinity)
no uniform integrability is assumed, and without it convergence is only almost sure

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2606.29512, '2606.29512'] A $\mathcal V$-valued optional process
$u=(u_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$
is a solution to \eqref{SNS2}--\eqref{bin2} on $[0,T]$ if
$u\in L_2([0,T],\mathcal V)\cap L_\infty([0,T],\mathcal H)\, \text{(a.s.)}, $
and for each
$\varphi\in\mathcal V$
the identity
\begin{equation} 
                                             
\begin{aligned}
(u_t,\varphi)&=(u_0,\varphi)-
\int_0^t\Big[(a_s^{ij}D_j u_s+\mathfrak{f}_s^i(u_s),D_i \varphi)
+(u_{s(u_s)},\varphi)\Big]\,ds                              \\
&\quad
+\int_0^t\big(\gamma_s^{ki}D_i q_s^k+f_s(u_s,Du_s),\varphi\big)\,ds\\
&\quad
+\int_0^t\big(\sigma_s^{ik}D_i u_s+h_s^k(u_s),\varphi\big)\,dm_s^k
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
holds for $\mathbb P\otimes dt$-almost every
$(\omega,t)\in\Omega\times[0,T]$, 
and 
\begin{equation}
                                 
\nabla q_t^k=R\big(\sigma_t^{ik}D_i u_t+h_t^k(u_t)\big)
\quad
(\bP\otimes dt\otimes dx\text{-a.e.})\quad \text{for $k\in\bZ$}. 
\end{equation}
We call
$(u_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$
an $\mathcal H$-solution if it is an $\mathcal H$-valued 
$\mathcal F_t$-adapted c\`adl\`ag process such that
$u\in L_2([0,T],\mathcal V)\ \text{(a.s.)}$, 
and almost surely \eqref{hl_sol} holds for all
$t\in[0,T],\,\varphi\in\mathcal V$, 
and \eqref{pressure_assumption} is satisfied.

[Lemma 11 (All surplus component bound) of arXiv:2608.04799, '2608.04799'] There is an absolute constant \(A<\infty\) such that, for every \(k\ge1\)
and \(r\ge1\),
\begin{equation}
  c(k,k+r-1)
  \le \left(\frac{A}{r}\right)^{r/2}k^{k+3r/2-2}.
\end{equation}
For every \(0<b<\infty\), there are constants \(C_b,D_b<\infty\) and an
integer \(n_b\), depending also on \(\lambda\), such that, whenever
\(n\ge n_b\) and \(1\le k\le bn^{2/3}\),
\begin{align}
  t_n(k)&\le C_b n k^{-5/2},                                      \\
  \E N_n(k,r)&\le t_n(k)\left(\frac{D_b}{r}\right)^{r/2},
       \qquad r\ge1.                                               
\end{align}

AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Core double-cover graph bound via st-ordering, including local bridges. Let B be a finite connected loopless multigraph with q vertices and e edges, each edge bearing exactly two distinct labels among v>=2 labels. The label multigraph G is connected and stays connected after deleting any vertex. Each label subgraph B_t is nonempty, connected and has minimum degree at least2. Then q-e+v<=2. If some B_t has cycle rank>=2, then q-e+v<=1. A self-contained st-order and contraction/leaf proof pays this without a bridgeless or Eulerian hypothesis. In loopless entropy diagrams the global equality-class graph is such a B; every higher raw block forces the strict bound, including odd blocks and bridge-containing local graphs. No dimension-uniform Taylor remainder follows. Novelty unestablished.
Finite connected loopless multigraph B; parallel edges remain distinct
Every edge has exactly two distinct labels, v>=2
Label graph connected, and remains connected after any one vertex is deleted
All label subgraphs are nonempty, connected, minimum degree>=2
Strict case: at least one label subgraph has cycle rank>=2

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:3eb4c72118a0c98b85af5b199155f8951f52c2c3b4f0e70884c258772e8b604b","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/3e/3eb4c72118a0c98b85af5b199155f8951f52c2c3b4f0e70884c258772e8b604b.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:13469eb43ce2832dcdec7940e941823fddca997fdd31a9e3d4f7045f3065ea4d","bundle_entry_key":"core-double-graph-cover-st-numbering-index-bound-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-general-core-cover-asymmetric-coefficients-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Graph cycle ranks and extensive-rank Gaussian-channel information","draft":"w718/bundle_011.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:core-double-graph-cover-st-numbering-index-bound-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Core double covers and st-ordering: the bridge-free restriction is unnecessary

Target1 supporting graph lemma. Proof draft, UNAUDITED; novelty is
unestablished. This extends claim030 to local graphs with bridges. It
does not supply the analytic, size-uniform remainder required by Target1.

## 1. Abstract theorem

Let B be a finite connected loopless undirected multigraph, with q
vertices and e edges. Assign every edge two distinct labels from a set
of v>=2 labels, and let G be the label multigraph: its vertices are the
labels and its edges are the edges of B with those label endpoints.
For each label t let B_t be its edge-induced subgraph, without isolated
vertices. Suppose:

* G is connected and G-t is connected for every vertex t; the graph
  with one vertex is regarded as connected.
* Every B_t is nonempty, connected, and has minimum degree at least two.

Then q-e+v<=2. If at least one B_t has cycle rank at least two, then
q-e+v<=1. Degree counts include the multiplicities of parallel edges.

The statement does NOT assume that the B_t are bridgeless or Eulerian.
The proof below is self-contained; its st-ordering device is a standard
graph method, not a novelty assertion.

## 2. Adding a core subgraph increases cycle rank

Let A and H be finite connected subgraphs of a loopless multigraph.
Assume A meets H, H has minimum degree at least two, and H has an edge
not in A. Then

    b(A union H) >= b(A)+1,     b(J)=|E(J)|-|V(J)|+1.

Proof. Contract the entire connected A in A union H to a single root,
and discard the edges of A. Retain all edges outside A, including any
loops created by contraction. The resulting graph K is connected and

    b(K)=|E(H) minus E(A)|-|V(H) minus V(A)|
        =b(A union H)-b(A).

If b(K)=0, K is a tree. It has at least one edge. A nontrivial finite
tree has a leaf different from the root. This leaf corresponds to an
original vertex outside V(A), so all its incident edges in A union H
are edges of H, and none was altered or removed by the contraction.
Its degree in H is therefore one, contradicting the assumption. A
connected graph has nonnegative cycle rank, so b(K)>=1. QED.

This step uses a graph contraction and a leaf contradiction, not an
independence assertion about different local cycle spaces.

## 3. An st-order with any prescribed first vertex

Choose any vertex s of G and any neighbor z of s. There is a linear
ordering of the vertices starting at s and ending at z in which every
other vertex has both an earlier and a later neighbor. Here is a
construction, included to avoid assuming an unstated graph theorem.

Begin with the ordered set [s,z]. Suppose a proper vertex set S is
already ordered with that property. A component C of G-S has at least
two distinct neighbors in S. It has a neighbor since G is connected;
if its only neighbor were w, deleting w would disconnect C from the
nonempty S minus {w}, contradicting connectedness of G-w.

Choose distinct neighbors x,y in S and a simple path from x to y whose
internal vertices lie in C: join their adjacent vertices through the
connected component C, and simplify the resulting walk. Orient the
path so x precedes y in the current ordering. Insert its internal
vertices, in path order, immediately after x. Every new vertex has an
earlier and a later path neighbor, and the earlier/later neighbors of
old vertices keep their relative positions. The first and last vertices
stay s and z. At least one vertex is added. Iteration ends with the
required ordering. The construction also covers v=2 without iteration.

## 4. Proof of the theorem, including strictness

If there is a label s with b(B_s)>=2, choose it as the first vertex of
the preceding order. Otherwise choose any s. The last label z may be
any neighbor of s. Write the ordered labels t_1=s,...,t_v=z, and set

    A_j = union of B_(t_i) for i<=j.

All A_j are connected: each new label has an earlier neighbor, and the
edge of G to that neighbor is an edge common to the new B_t and the
previous union. For 2<=j<=v-1, label t_j also has a later neighbor.
The edge to that later neighbor is absent from A_(j-1), because its
only labels are t_j and that later label. Thus the lemma of Section2
gives b(A_j)>=b(A_(j-1))+1.

Every edge of B already lies in A_(v-1): its two labels are distinct,
so at least one is different from the last label. Therefore

    b(B) >= b(B_s)+(v-2).

A nonempty finite connected graph of minimum degree two has cycle
rank at least one. This proves b(B)>=v-1, equivalently q-e+v<=2.
If b(B_s)>=2, it proves b(B)>=v and hence q-e+v<=1. QED.

## 5. Exact application to raw cumulant diagrams

The entropy contraction graph G has v tensor vertices and e Wick edges;
by claim010's exact entropy cancellation it is loopless, connected and
has no articulation. The surviving terms have v>=2. At each tensor
vertex t, the raw cumulant expansion is indexed by row and column
partitions with connected join and no singleton blocks. Its local
bipartite graph H_t has the raw row and column blocks as vertices and
the incident tensor positions as edges. It is connected and has minimum
degree two; odd blocks and bridges are allowed.

Let B have one vertex per global row equality class and one per global
column equality class. Each Wick pair is a distinct edge joining its
row and column classes. Its labels are the two tensor vertices joined
by the Wick pair. Those labels are distinct because G is loopless.
For a fixed t, no two local tensor positions are identified as the
same Wick edge; otherwise that pair would be a self-loop at t. Thus
H_t maps edge-bijectively onto B_t, identifying only vertices of the
same row/column type. In particular B_t is connected and has minimum
degree two. Connectedness of G implies connectedness of the union B.

If a raw block has size>=3, H_t has a vertex of degree>=3 while all
degrees are>=2. For h vertices and d edges this implies 2d>=2h+1,
so integer d>=h+1 and b(H_t)=d-h+1>=2. Vertex identifications cannot
decrease cycle rank of a connected graph. Hence b(B_t)>=2 and the
strict form of the theorem applies.

As B has q=c_i+c_j vertices, this proves

    c_i+c_j-e+v<=1

whenever at least one higher raw block occurs. The weak bound<=2
holds for every term. This pays the previously open odd-block graph
step, including the two-cycle-plus-bridge local graph.

## 6. Audit boundaries

The abstract graph theorem is independent of probability. Its translation
uses the loopless/no-articulation entropy-graph reduction from claim010;
that statistical reduction remains independently unaudited. The next
coefficient theorem also needs the existing finite-dimensional Taylor
coefficient representation and moment hypotheses. None of this bounds
posterior connected cumulants uniformly in dimension at positive SNR.

Least trusted new application step: the edge-bijection from H_t to B_t
depends on excluding contraction self-loops BEFORE applying this lemma.
The proof does not apply to a graph with self-loop tensor contractions.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:5dc5e55fd52de17190c46ce82824b733f184b71e297dcfbd13ccb4dc60f2d10c","revision_digest":"sha256:1130e3377af7cbbff31fa89abc6abbdc189cea3af1b6c09a0ca864ad0a0d417b","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:core-double-graph-cover-st-numbering-index-bound-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

For a language model on a finite alphabet Sigma, a supported prefix t[1:i-1], and i<j, empirical substring entropy is H_e^[i:j)(t)=-ln P_Model(T[i:j-1]=t[i:j-1] | T[1:i-1]=t[1:i-1]); it equals the sum of the realized token surprisals along that substring. A watermark has PPT algorithms Setup,Wat,Detect and a polynomial output-length cap Lmax. Soundness bounds the key-averaged acceptance probability for every fixed key-independent word of length at most Lmax by a negligible function. Undetectability compares polynomially many oracle samples from one fixed watermark key with independent model samples. For a threshold beta, the high-entropy event for a length ell=j-i substring is H_e^[i:j)(t)>=beta(ell)*ln|Sigma|. CAUTION: the displayed Definition2.6 and LemmaC.6 Eq37 sample tprime from E(t), where t is the full watermarked text, and require negligible probability of detection failure together with existence of such a high-entropy interval. The following Definition2.6 prose and C.6 Step1 instead give the channel the selected substring, setting tprime=E(t[i:j-1]). These are distinct experiments when the edit budget is measured relative to the channel input length. This card records the distinction and does not silently replace the displayed definition or certify Theorems5.1-5.2.
All conditional token probabilities use the same language model and realized prefix; logarithms are natural.
Strings may be END-padded to Lmax for selecting intervals; the input actually given to the channel must be specified.
This is a source-definition record, not a watermark construction guarantee.

\(
\operatorname{tr}(T_{a,L})=L\lambda_a,
\)
and has kernel \eqref{eq:reduced-kernel}. Moreover, for every \(\theta\in\mathbb{C}\),
\begin{equation}

\mathbb{E}\exp(\theta N_a(L))
=
\det\left(\operatorname{Id}+(e^{\theta}-1)T_{a,L}\right).
\end{equation}

Kac-Rice: slab first moment equals the proxy rate 0.0082 d; proxy two-point complexity below twice the one-point rate for 0<q<=0.95 and near the diagonal (3af); band maxima are marginal (3ag), so the count is kappa-gapped: kappa=0.02 gives Theta 0.0025-0.0046 with a matching second moment (3ah); separation is local (3ai, 3aj). The E part of the two-point integrand loses only e^(O(ln^2 n)) up to the diagonal (3ao), in-plane rows a power of ln d (3ap). High probability: the q=0 pair log-dets keep Corr 0.2-0.4, so Paley-Zygmund alone fails, but given the x-free S1, S2 the correlation is noise, also under the critical-point tilt (3aq, 3ar); the shared mode is dF/dS1 = -m(x0) sqrt(d/3), checked to 2 pct at d=80 (3as); given S1, S2 the residual pair has an order-one kernel K(q), zero at q=0, so the pair integrand gains a bounded factor equal to 1 at q=0 and the Laplace step reduces to the proxy constant (3at); K is the universal Chebyshev-mode kernel -2 log(1-m^2 rho(q)) given the x-free modes plus a finite-p/n term of order d^(-1/2), with no in-plane part (3au, 3av). PRIVATE REDUCTION, author-recorded. Barsky-Grimmett-Newman: at p_c(Z^d) the half-space N x Z^{d-1} has no infinite cluster. To conclude theta(p_c) = 0 in Z^d (open for 3 <= d <= 10) one would show that a unique infinite cluster (Burton-Keane) cannot be made of infinitely many finite half-space clusters connected through the boundary hyperplane. In d = 2 this works because the half-plane susceptibility at p_c is infinite. The reduction: theta(p_c) = 0 in Z^d follows from (i) infinite half-space susceptibility at p_c(Z^d), and (ii) a gluing lemma showing that finite half-space clusters linked across the hyperplane force an infinite half-space cluster on one side at a slightly larger parameter. Both (i) and (ii) are open for 3 <= d <= 10; (i) is a natural intermediate target because it is a statement about a single half-space cluster rather than about the full-space cluster.

body: In number theory, the sum of two squares theorem relates the prime decomposition of any integer n > 1 to whether it can be written as a sum of two squares, such that n = a^{2} + b^{2} for some integers a, b. An integer greater than one can be written as a sum of two squares if and only if its prime decomposition contains no factor p^{k}, where prime $p\equiv 3{\pmod {4}}$ and k is odd.

body: [Theorem 2.4 (Erdős–Rényi, SBMs and logistic RDPGs) in the first version of arXiv:2512.18592, 'Wavelet Latent Position Exponential Random Graphs'] Fix $c\in\mathbb{R}$ and a real symmetric Hilbert–Schmidt matrix $S=(s_{rs})_{r,s\geq 0}$, and let $G_{n}\sim\mathrm{WL\mbox{-}ERG}(c,S)$ be generated as in Definitions 2.1 – 2.3. 1. (Erdős–Rényi.) If $s_{rs}=0$ for all $(r,s)\neq(0,0)$, then $G_{n}$ is Erdős–Rényi $G(n,p)$ with $p=\sigma(c+s_{00})$. 2. (Haar/SBM special case.) Assume the underlying wavelet system is the Haar system and fix an integer $J\geq 0$. Let $\{I_{\ell,J}\}_{\ell=0}^{2^{J}-1}$ be the dyadic partition of $(0,1)$, define $\phi_{\ell,J}(x):=2^{J/2}\mathbf{1}_{I_{\ell,J}}(x)$, and let $V_{J}:=\mathrm{span}\{\phi_{\ell,J}:0\leq\ell\leq 2^{J}-1\}\subset L^{2}(0,1)$. If the logit satisfies $f_{S}\in V_{J}\otimes V_{J}$, equivalently if there exist real coefficients $\alpha_{\ell k}$ such that $f_{S}(x,y)=\sum_{\ell,k=0}^{2^{J}-1}\alpha_{\ell k}\,\phi_{\ell,J}(x)\phi_{k,J}(y)\quad\text{in }L^{2}\big((0,1)^{2}\big),$ then $G_{n}$ is a stochastic block model with $2^{J}$ blocks. In particular, there are constants $\beta_{\ell k}:=2^{J}\alpha_{\ell k}$ such that $f_{S}(x,y)=\beta_{\ell k}$ for a.e. $(x,y)\in I_{\ell,J}\times I_{k,J}$, and hence the block connectivity probabilities are $p_{\ell k}=\sigma(c+\beta_{\ell k})=\sigma(c+2^{J}\alpha_{\ell k}).$ Under $U_{i}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$, the block proportions are $\pi_{\ell}=2^{-J}$. 3. (Finite-rank PSD $\Rightarrow$ logistic RDPG.) Assume $S$ is positive semidefinite as an operator on $\ell^{2}$ and has finite rank $d$. Then there exist functions $g_{1},\dots,g_{d}\in L^{2}(0,1)$ such that $f_{S}(x,y)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}g_{k}(x)g_{k}(y)\quad\text{in }L^{2}\big((0,1)^{2}\big).$ Consequently, for a measurable representative $\Phi(x):=(g_{1}(x),\dots,g_{d}(x))\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ (defined a.e.), $W_{c,S}(x,y)=\sigma\!\bigl(c+\Phi(x)^{\top}\Phi(y)\bigr)\quad\text{for a.e. }(x,y).$ Therefore $G_{n}$ is a logistic random dot product graph: with latent positions $X_{i}=\Phi(U_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, the edges are independent conditional on $X$ and satisfy $\mathbb{P}(A_{ij}=1\mid X)=\sigma(c+X_{i}^{\top}X_{j})$ for all $i<j$.

For n >= 5 the general polynomial equation of degree n, x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} + ... + a_n = 0 with independent indeterminate coefficients over Q (the field Q(a_1, ..., a_n)), is not solvable by radicals: there is no formula for its roots built from the coefficients by field operations and extraction of k-th roots. Moreover specific polynomials over Q are not solvable by radicals, for instance x^5 - x - 1 and x^5 - 4x + 2, whose Galois groups over Q are S_5. For n <= 4 the general equation IS solvable by radicals (the quadratic formula; Cardano's formula for cubics, 1545; Ferrari's method for quartics). GALOIS'S CRITERION, which subsumes the theorem: a polynomial over a field of characteristic 0 is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is a solvable group.
characteristic 0 (over Q or a field containing Q); the criterion needs the field to contain, or to be extended by, roots of unity
'general' means indeterminate coefficients; a particular polynomial of degree >= 5 may well be solvable (x^5 - 2 is)

(1) Galois's criterion: a finite extension obtained by adjoining radicals lies in a Galois extension whose group has a chain of normal subgroups with cyclic quotients (adjoining a primitive root of unity gives an abelian extension; adjoining a k-th root of an element, in the presence of the k-th roots of unity, gives a cyclic Kummer extension); a group with such a chain is solvable, and subgroups and quotients of solvable groups are solvable, so the Galois group of a polynomial solvable by radicals is solvable. Conversely a solvable Galois group yields a radical tower, again by Kummer theory. (2) The Galois group of the general polynomial of degree n over Q(a_1, ..., a_n) is the full symmetric group S_n: the roots are algebraically independent and the coefficients are the elementary symmetric functions of them, so every permutation of the roots extends to an automorphism fixing the coefficient field. (3) S_n is not solvable for n >= 5: its only nontrivial proper normal subgroup is A_n, and A_n is simple and non-abelian for n >= 5 (every element of A_n is a product of 3-cycles, all 3-cycles are conjugate in A_n for n >= 5, and any nontrivial normal subgroup of A_n contains a 3-cycle). Hence the general quintic is not solvable by radicals. (4) For the explicit examples: x^5 - 4x + 2 is irreducible over Q by Eisenstein at p = 2; it has exactly three real roots (its derivative 5x^4 - 4 vanishes at two points and the values there have opposite signs), so complex conjugation acts as a transposition; irreducibility makes the group transitive of order divisible by 5, so it contains a 5-cycle; a 5-cycle and a transposition generate S_5. The same argument, with the reduction of x^5 - x - 1 modulo 2 and 5 to produce the needed cycle types, gives S_5 for x^5 - x - 1 (irreducible modulo 5 since it has no root and no quadratic factor there). For n <= 4, S_4 is solvable (S_4 > A_4 > V_4 > 1 with abelian quotients), which is why the cubic and quartic formulas exist.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:e6f2a04e4ac8507250bf39ca99bd4be01dc87b100ccb98a635efbbbcfd665292","revision_digest":"sha256:115d87a98ec962f9b30fe189acf038bc99ce62e12c2461843b01819a67bf4895","source_id":"rederived:claude-98979b96","source_revision":"standard-theorem-2026-09-03; stated and proved in outline by the author from Galois's criterion and the simplicity of A_n; references: Dummit and Foote, Abstract Algebra, section 14.7 (Theorem 39 and Corollary 40); Stewart, Galois Theory, chapters 8 and 15; Artin, Galois Theory","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Let Sigma and Gamma be finite alphabets with N=|Sigma|>=2 and k=|Gamma|>=1. Let P be any fixed probability distribution on Sigma, H=-sum_a P(a)*ln P(a) its Shannon entropy in nats, with0*ln0=0, and let phi:Sigma->Gamma be a uniformly random function, so the labels phi(a) are independent uniform samples. Write r(b)=sum_{a:phi(a)=b}P(a). Then P_phi(sum_{b in Gamma}min(1/k,r(b))>=H/(4*ln N))>=1-2^(k-H*exp(H/2)/(4*ln N)). This is the stated Golowich-Moitra C.1 bound with an explicitly corrected proof: the source light-set mass estimate is not valid unconditionally, but follows in the only regime where this probability lower bound is positive. This card is unaudited and does not claim a new concentration theorem.
N>=2 and k>=1; natural logarithms; fixed P independent of the uniform random map.
Uniform random function means fully independent output labels, not merely an arbitrary pairwise-independent hash family.
Source-proof repair is explicitly labeled and awaits independent review.

PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. Let G be a countable connected graph of maximum degree Delta>=2 with iid finite nonnegative edge weights W. If for some theta>0, (Delta-1) E exp(-theta W)<1, then almost surely every vertex pair has a finite path attaining its passage-time infimum. Counting simple paths, exponential Markov bounds and Borel-Cantelli make all bounded-cost competitors have bounded lengths. In particular (Delta-1)P(W=0)<1 suffices, even without a positive lower bound or a finite mean. On Z^d this gives the known sufficient subrange P(W=0)<1/(2d-1), leaving the arbitrary-law question unresolved.

There are only finitely many such simple paths, a nonempty set, so one attains the infimum over all finite walks.

Let A = (a_ij) be a complex n x n matrix and for each i let R_i = sum_{j != i} |a_ij| be the i-th deleted absolute row sum and D_i = { z in C : |z - a_ii| <= R_i } the i-th Gershgorin disc. Then every eigenvalue of A lies in the union of the discs D_1, ..., D_n. Applying the theorem to the transpose, every eigenvalue also lies in the union of the column discs (radii the deleted column sums), so the spectrum lies in the intersection of the two unions. Refinement: if a union of k of the discs is disjoint from the union of the other n - k, then exactly k eigenvalues (counted with algebraic multiplicity) lie in the union of those k discs. Consequences: a strictly diagonally dominant matrix (|a_ii| > R_i for all i) is invertible, since 0 lies in no disc; a Hermitian strictly diagonally dominant matrix with positive diagonal is positive definite; and the discs can be shrunk by a diagonal similarity D^{-1} A D, which changes the radii to sum_{j != i} |a_ij| d_j / d_i.

Let $W$ be $n \times n$ with i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1/n)$ entries. Then $\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}} \to 2$ almost surely as $n \to \infty$; equivalently, for entries $\mathcal{N}(0,\alpha/n)$, $\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}} \to 2\sqrt{\alpha}$. Consequently $\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}} \le 1$ eventually almost surely when $\alpha<1/4$, and fails eventually almost surely when $\alpha>1/4$. At the critical value $\alpha=1/4$ neither holds: the edge fluctuation is of Tracy-Widom type, so $\mathbb{P}(\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le 1)$ converges to a limit strictly between $0$ and $1$, and the threshold is approached but not attained.

The non-attainment at the critical value follows from the Tracy-Widom limit for the fluctuation of the largest eigenvalue at the soft edge, which places the limiting probability strictly inside $(0,1)$.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:fd2305ab353cdabdde0a2f8ca382a959e6ebfd3c9bb824899315aaa85f392721","revision_digest":"sha256:119e9ad3b696badba8ad174eb176fbc82653b181884986712ea6e15569c92321","source_id":"wikipedia:Marchenko-Pastur distribution","source_revision":"as-read-2026-08-20","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Corollary 16 of arXiv:2609.03946, 'The groups $\SL_2(\F_{13})$ and $\SL_2(\F_{19})$ are Galois over $\Q$'] For each $\ell\in\{13,19\}$ there is a continuous surjection
\[
 \rho_\ell\colon\GQ\twoheadrightarrow\SL_2(\Z_\ell)
\]
unramified outside a finite set of primes, whose reduction modulo $\ell$ cuts
out $M_\ell$, for which every complex conjugation lies in $\ker\rho_\ell$.
Consequently, the fixed field $M_{\ell,n}$ of
$\ker(\rho_\ell\bmod\ell^n)$ is totally real with
$\Gal(M_{\ell,n}/\Q)\cong\SL_2(\Z/\ell^n\Z)$, the fields satisfy
$M_{\ell,n}\subset M_{\ell,n+1}$, and all are unramified outside one fixed
finite set.

body:
Fix input dimension d>=1 and a finite normalized training horizon T>=1. Data (x,y) are sampled independently at successive steps from a distribution P with bounded support in R^d times R. Let sigma be C^2, bounded and Lipschitz, with bounded first and second derivatives. Set sigma_*(x;(a,w))=a sigma(w.x), v(w)=-E[y sigma(w.x)] and u(w,w_prime)=E[sigma(w.x)sigma(w_prime.x)]; assume v and u are differentiable with bounded Lipschitz continuous gradients (Assumption 1). The initial neuron parameters (a_i,w_i) are iid with common bounded-support law rho_0 on R^(d+1), independently of the training samples. The two-layer mean-field network is f_N(x;theta)=N^(-1) sum_i a_i sigma(w_i.x). Use noiseless, unregularized SGD with source scaling xi=1/2, namely theta_i^(k+1)=theta_i^k+epsilon [y_k-f_N(x_k;theta^k)] grad_theta sigma_*(x_k;theta_i^k). The horizon here is the nonlinear-dynamics time k epsilon, as in Appendix B.2; this differs by a fixed factor from the sum of the source step sizes s_k=epsilon/2. These smooth-activation restrictions are an explicitly narrower case of the source; in particular ReLU is excluded. Train networks A and B independently using this same initialization law, training distribution and scheme, and stop them at k=floor(T/epsilon). For every delta in (0,1) and err>0 there is N_min such that for all N>=N_min there is epsilon_max(N)>0 such that for all 0<epsilon<=epsilon_max(N), with probability at least 1-delta there exists one permutation pi of all N neuron pairs (a_i,w_i) in B such that for P_x-almost every x, simultaneously for all t in [0,1], |t f_N(x;theta_A)+(1-t)f_N(x;theta_B) -f_N(x;t theta_A+(1-t)pi theta_B)|<=err. The permutation acts on both incoming weights and the corresponding output coefficients. No dimension-free width bound or trained deep-network conclusion is asserted.
fixed finite dimension and horizon; bounded training-data and initialization support
bounded smooth Lipschitz activation and bounded Lipschitz interaction gradients
mean-field normalization; iid initial neurons; fresh iid data at successive SGD steps
no gradient noise and no weight decay; constant source step size epsilon/2

\)

[Lemma lem:exp-decay of arXiv:2411.10419, 'Lower bounds on the top Lyapunov exponent for linear PDEs driven by the 2D stochastic Navi'] In the same setting as in Theorem~(thm:main of the paper), for every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a random constant $D_\varepsilon(\omega,u_0)$ satisfying $D_\varepsilon \in (0,1]$, $\mathbb{P}\times \mu$ almost surely, and a closed random subspace $F(\omega,u_0)\subset L^2_{*}$ with $\mathrm{codim}\,F(\omega,u_0) = m \in (0,\infty)$, such that for all $ \varrho_{0} \in L^{2}_{*}$ we have for all $t\geqslant 0$
\begin{equ}
   \|\varrho_t\| \geqslant  D_\varepsilon(\omega,u_0)\|\varrho_0\| \sin\angle(\varrho_0,F(\omega,u_0))e^{(\lambda^{\kappa}_1-\varepsilon) t}\;,
\end{equ}
where
\[
\sin\angle(\varrho_0,F) = \inf_{\varphi\in
F(\omega,u_0)}\frac{\|\varrho_0-\varphi\|}{\|\varrho_0\|}\;.
\]

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2608.29075, 'The 2-Monoidal Structure of Symmetric Sequences'] Let $\C$ be a (locally small) monoidal category and $X,Y \in \text{Ob}(\text{Fun}(\C,\textbf{Set}))$. We define the \textit{Day convolution} of $X$ and $Y$ as the left Kan extension of their external product $$X\Tilde{\times}Y: (c,d) \mapsto X(c) \times Y(d)$$ along the bifunctor given by the internal monoidal law $\otimes$ of $\C$. 
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{\C \times \C} && \Set \\
	& {\C}
	\arrow[""{name=0, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{{X \Tilde{\times} Y}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["\otimes"', from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{{\text{Lan}_\otimes (X\Tilde{\times} Y) =: X \otimes_{\mathrm{Day}}Y }}"', dashed, from=2-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[shorten <=3pt, Rightarrow, from=0, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]

The Day convolution, denoted by $\otimes_{\mathrm{Day}}$, assembles into a bifunctor and gives $\text{Fun}(\C,\Set)$ the structure of a closed monoidal category, as shown in Proposition 3.1 of \cite{nlab:day_convolution}.
title: Definition 5 of arXiv:2608.29075

For a continuous-time birth-death queue with birth rate lambda, death rate mu>lambda, killed on hitting zero, the expected busy duration from k>=0 is k/(mu-lambda) and the expected integral of queue length before extinction is k^2/[2(mu-lambda)]+(lambda+mu)k/[2(mu-lambda)^2]. The quadratic function has generator equal to minus k; negative drift gives exponential jump-count tails, which justify stopping and passage to the limit. These identities also average over a Poisson initial queue.

Assume Poisson arrivals of rate lambda>0, independent exponential service of rate mu>lambda, FCFS, and a single server. After becoming empty, it remains on for a deterministic grace period g in [0,infinity], then switches off. An arrival to an off server starts a deterministic setup of duration tau>=0. Setup is not cancelled; arrivals during setup wait and are served when setup ends. Define p=exp(-lambda g) (p=0 for g=infinity), x=lambda tau, v=mu-lambda, and rho=lambda/mu.

The stationary mean queueing wait, excluding service, is

W(g)=lambda/[mu(mu-lambda)] + tau(1+lambda tau/2) p/(1+lambda tau p).

The long-run fractions of time busy, on-idle, off, and in setup are respectively

rho, (1-rho)(1-p)/(1+xp), (1-rho)p/(1+xp), (1-rho)xp/(1+xp).

If their powers are B,I,O,U, average power is

P(g)=rho B+(1-rho) I+(1-rho)[O+xU-(1+x)I] p/(1+xp).

Thus W and P lie on an affine line as g varies (power may be constant when the bracket vanishes); all later arrivals and the busy period are included.

Setup occurs with probability p and contributes tau p expected time. After setup the initial busy-period queue is K=1+Poisson(x), whereas after a hot arrival it is K=1.

For the birth-death queue killed at zero, its expected busy duration from k is k/v. Its expected area under the queue length is

F(k)=k^2/(2v)+(lambda+mu)k/(2v^2).

The generator satisfies LF(k)=-k and F(0)=0. A justification avoiding an unbounded optional-stopping assumption is as follows: embed at jump epochs, whose increments are iid with probabilities lambda/(lambda+mu) and mu/(lambda+mu). Negative drift and bounded increments give an exponential tail for the hitting time of zero from each fixed k, by a Chernoff bound on the unconstrained walk when survival forces its position to stay positive. Queue height is at most k plus the number of jumps. This tail makes the stopped quadratic boundary term vanish and the queue area integrable; apply the stopped generator identity and let the cutoff tend to infinity. The Poisson initial queue also has all moments and exponential moments sufficiently near zero, so the same formulas can be averaged over K.

E[K]=1+x, E[K^2]=1+3x+x^2 after setup, and the expected setup queue area is tau+lambda tau^2/2. Thus the expected cycle duration is

C=mu/[lambda v] (1+xp),

and its expected queue area is

A=mu/v^2 [1+mu tau p+lambda v tau^2 p/2].

Renewal reward gives E[N]=A/C. Little's law gives response time E[N]/lambda, and subtracting 1/mu yields the displayed W. body: A smooth manifold of dimension n is a topological space M that is Hausdorff and second-countable, together with a smooth atlas: a collection of charts {(U_alpha, phi_alpha)} where the U_alpha are open sets covering M and each phi_alpha: U_alpha -> R^n is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of R^n, such that whenever U_alpha and U_beta overlap, the transition map phi_beta o phi_alpha^{-1} between open subsets of R^n is smooth (infinitely differentiable). Two atlases are considered to define the same smooth structure if their union is again a smooth atlas.

Let $\varphi\in C_b^7\left(\R^d\right)$ and let
$\sigma_t^2\left(\varphi\right)$ be the limiting fluctuation variance from
Definition~\ref{def:uniform-time-limiting-variance-abs-assump}. Assume that
there exists a constant $\underline \sigma > 0$ such that
\begin{equation}

\inf_{t \ge 0}\sigma_t^2\left(\varphi\right)\ge \underline \sigma^2.
\end{equation}
Then, there exists a constant $C>0$ such that for every $N\ge 1$,
\begin{equation}

\sup_{t \ge 0}
W_1\left(
G_t^N\left(\varphi\right),
\mathcal N\left(0,\sigma_t^2\left(\varphi\right)\right)
\right)
\le
\frac{C}{\sqrt{N}}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Uniform-in-time quantitative CLT for the fluctuations

body: Let X be a normed vector space, X** its bidual (the dual of the dual X*), and J: X -> X** the canonical isometric embedding defined by J(x)(f) = f(x) for f in X*. Let B_X and B_{X**} denote the closed unit balls of X and X**. Then J(B_X) is dense in B_{X**} with respect to the weak-star topology sigma(X**, X*) on X**. When X is reflexive, J(X) = X** and the statement is immediate; the theorem's content is that weak-star density of J(B_X) in B_{X**} holds even when X is not reflexive. [Goldstine (1938); see Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis]
title: Goldstine's Theorem

\widehat G$ and $\kappa \in (0, \frac 12)$ being arbitrarily fixed,
there exists a constant ${\cal C}$ and a subdomain $\widetilde G \subset
\subset G$ with $\widehat G\subset \subset \widetilde G$, such that
for any solution $\tilde y$ to the equation (equation system-sp1 of the paper), it
holds that

\begin{align}\notag
    &   {\mathbb{E}} \int_{\frac T 2 - \kappa T}^{\frac T 2 + \kappa T}\int_{\widehat G}
    \big(|\nabla \tilde y|^2 + \tilde y^2\big)dx dt\\
    &   \leq {\cal C}\Big[ \exp\Big (\frac {\cal C}
    \varepsilon\Big ) {\mathbb{E}}\! \int_0^T\int_{G_0}\big( \tilde y^2 \!+ |\nabla \tilde y|^2\big)dx dt +
    \varepsilon{\mathbb{E}}\! \int_0^T  \int_{\widetilde G}(\tilde y^2 \!+\! |\nabla
    \tilde y|^2)dxdt\Big],
\end{align}
for all $ \varepsilon > 0 $. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

The Malliavin derivative on the Wiener-Poisson space is defined as the closed unbounded operator D = (D^{(1)}, D^{(2)}): D^{1, 2} subset L^2(Omega) -> L^2([0, T] x Omega) x L^2([0, T] x R_0 x Omega). For F in D^{(1)}, D_t^{(1)} F represents the stochastic gradient in the Brownian direction defined via directional perturbations along Cameron-Martin paths. For F in D^{(2)} with chaotic expansion F = sum_{n=0}^infinity I_n(h_n) with respect to Poisson integrals, D_{t, z}^{(2)} F = sum_{n=1}^infinity n * I_{n-1}(h_n(t, ., z)) denotes the difference operator F(omega + delta_{(t, z)}) - F(omega). The Hilbert space domain D^{1, 2} is equipped with the graph norm ||F||_{D^{1, 2}}^2 = ||F||_{L^2}^2 + ||D^{(1)} F||_{L^2([0, T] x Omega)}^2 + ||D^{(2)} F||_{L^2([0, T] x R_0 x Omega)}^2.
F in D^{1, 2} = D^{(1)} cap D^{(2)}
title: Directional Malliavin Derivatives on Wiener-Poisson Space

[Definition 4 (Colored height function) of arXiv:2604.06532, 'Random permutations from $q$-Demazure products'] For a color threshold $c \in \{0, 1, \dots, n\}$, a row $S$, and a column $Y$, define
\[
  H(c;\, S,\, Y)
  \;:=\;
  \#\bigl\{\, Y' \ge Y : \text{the vertical arrow at column } Y',\, \text{row } S
  \text{ has color } \le c \,\bigr\}.
\]
At the top row $S = n$, this is related to the permutation height function by
$H(c;\, n,\, Y) = c - Y + 1 + n \cdot H_\sigma\!\bigl(\tfrac{Y-1}{n},\, \tfrac{c}{n}\bigr),$
since $H(c;\, n,\, Y)$ counts colors $\le c$ at positions $Y' \ge Y$, while $H_\sigma$ counts positions $i \le \lfloor nx \rfloor$ with $\sigma(i) > \lfloor ny \rfloor$.
title: Colored height function

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the annulus fields phi_k as exactly independent rather than approximately so, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the coupling error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the independence used in the concentric decomposition is an approximation that must be explicitly controlled, and skipping this step is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.
Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions
Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics
Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk
title: Technique: Concentric Decomposition of the 2D Gaussian Free Field

[Proposition prop:conditioned_Bernoulli2 of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite graph, $p_e\in(0,1), x_e>0$ for each $e\in E$. Let $\Omega = \{0,1\}^E$, $\Sigma \subset \Omega$ and $f(\omega)= \Sigma^{\uparrow}(\omega):=\{\eta \in \Sigma \mid \eta \supset \omega\}$, and 
	$$\rho[\omega] = \mathbb{P}_{p}[\omega], ~\forall \omega\in \Omega, ~\gamma[\eta] = \mathbb{P}_{\frac{x(1-p)}{1+x(1-p)}}[\eta \mid \Sigma]\propto \prod_{e\in \eta} x_e(1-p_e) , ~\forall \eta\in \Sigma.$$
    	Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)]  The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$ is $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta]\propto \prod_{e\in \eta} x_e$. For each $\omega\in\Omega$ with $\mathscr{P}_\Omega[\omega] \neq 0$, the  conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega]=\mathbb{P}_{\frac{x(1-p)}{1+x(1-p)}}[\; \cdot  \mid \Sigma^{\uparrow}(\omega)]$.
        \item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$ is $\mathscr{P}_{\Omega} = \mathscr{P}_{\Sigma} \cap \mathbb{P}_{p}$.  
        For each $\eta\in\Sigma$ with $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta] \neq 0$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \eta] = \mathbb{P}_p \cap \delta_{\eta} = \mathbb{P}_{\eta,p}. $ 
    \end{enumerate}
title: Proposition prop:conditioned_Bernoulli2 of arXiv:2506.10765

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Asymptotic influence bounds for polynomial thresholds exact calculation or structural obstruction Result: The desired C*d*sqrt(n) bound holds when the polynomial is a product of d affine linear forms with no cube zeros. Indeed its sign is a product of d threshold functions. If that product changes on a coordinate flip, at least one factor changes, so its influence is at most the sum of the factor influences. For a threshold g, unateness gives Inf_i(g)=|ghat(i)| and hence I(g)<=sqrt(n)*sqrt(sum_i ghat(i)^2)<=sqrt(n). Check: For a monotone coordinate of a Boolean function, its discrete derivative is either0 or1 after the conventional half-difference, so its expectation equals its flip probability. Cauchy-Schwarz and Parseval then give the threshold bound. A union bound gives the product estimate. Obstruction: A general multivariate polynomial need not factor into real affine forms. The argument supplies a genuine subclass result, not a reduction for arbitrary polynomial thresholds.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0173-asymptotic-influence-bounds-for-polynomial-thresholds
