[Theorem 1 (The \JKL{} formulation of Einstein areal flows) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Consider four-dimensional spacetimes $(\Mcal,\guntrois)$ with spatial topology $\Tbb^3$ and two commuting spacelike Killing fields with closed orbits, admitting a foliation by the area~$|t|$ of the symmetry orbits. Consider a constitutive law $p=p(\mu)$ (pressure vs.\ mass-energy density) satisfying hyperbolicity and asymptotic conditions (stated in~\eqref{hyperbolic-eos-zero}, below). Then the following properties hold.
\bei

\item \textbf{Perfect-fluid matter model.} In the class of regular flows, the Einstein--Euler system 
\bel{equa-49F}
G^{\alpha\beta} = T^{\alpha\beta},
\qquad
\nabla_\alpha T^{\alpha\beta}=0
\ee
is equivalent to an \emph{evolution--constraint, first-order differential system} in terms of the variables \eqref{equa-phipsi}, as  given in \eqref{eq:T2-1234-def}--\eqref{equa-9385}, below, and referred to as the \JKL{} system. Its evolution subsystem has essentially \emph{quadratic nonlinearities} with a partial \emph{null structure} and, away from vacuum, is strongly hyperbolic.   All differential operators in the formulation 
remain defined on the full (closed) state space, including cavitation and near-light speed fluid propagation, although the hyperbolicity degenerates at non-zero null states.  

\item \textbf{Particle-production dissipative model.} Analogous properties hold for the following class of Einstein--Navier--Stokes systems
\bel{eq:pot-production-system0}
G^{\alpha\beta}=T_\chi^{\alpha\beta},
\qquad
\nabla_\alpha T_\chi^{\alpha\beta}=0,
\qquad
\nabla_\alpha A_\chi^{\alpha\beta\gamma}
=-\mathscr B^{\beta\gamma}, 
\ee
namely an extension of the Einstein--Euler system by adjoining to the fluid variables a symmetric two-tensor relaxation field~$\zeta$. The tensors $T_\chi$ and $A_\chi$ are defined from second-order derivatives
of a \emph{Navier--Stokes potential} denoted by~$\chi$, which is assumed to satisfy suitable equilibrium, dominant-energy, and causal-hyperbolicity conditions in \autoref{def-pot-hyperbolic}. The relaxation rate tensor~$\mathscr B$ is prescribed and satisfies suitable stable-equilibrium and positivity conditions in \autoref{def-pot-source}. In particular, the coupled evolution equations are symmetric hyperbolic in the interior of the state space, and both Einstein equations and Bianchi equations are satisfied.  The associated particle-number current~$\vNumb_\chi$ satisfies $\nabla_\alpha \vNumb_\chi^\alpha = \zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}\geq 0$.

\item \textbf{Dissipated-energy dissipative model.} 
Analogous properties also hold for the following class of Einstein--Navier--Stokes systems
\bel{eq:pot-dissipated-system0}
\begin{aligned}
G^{\alpha\beta}
&=T_\chi^{\alpha\beta}+T_{\rm aux}^{\alpha\beta}, \quad
&
\nabla_\alpha T_\chi^{\alpha\beta}
&=-\sigma n^\beta, \quad
&
\nabla_\alpha A_\chi^{\alpha\beta\gamma}
&=-\mathscr B^{\beta\gamma},
\end{aligned}
\ee 
with 
\be
\begin{aligned}
T_{\rm aux}^{\alpha\beta}
&=\sigma \underline\pi^{\alpha\beta},
&
\sigma & \coloneqq \frac{\zeta_{\alpha\beta} \mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}}{-n_\alpha\beta^\alpha} \geq 0. 
\end{aligned}
\ee 
Here $\underline\pi^{\alpha\beta}$ is the (rescaled) projection onto the symmetry orbits, $n_\alpha$ is the future-directed normal to the areal foliation, and $\beta$ is the rescaled fluid momentum.
The model includes an auxiliary stress tensor~$T_{\rm aux}$ (\autoref{def-diss-en}), which compensates the mass-energy dissipated by~$T_\chi$. In particular, the coupled evolution equations are symmetric hyperbolic in the interior of the state space, and both Einstein equations and Bianchi equations are satisfied.
The associated particle-number current~$\vNumb_\chi$ is divergence-free.
\eei
\noindent For all three systems, the Einstein constraints propagate from one areal hypersurface, and the metric variables are reconstructed from the transport, constraint, and periodicity equations. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: The \JKL{} formulation of Einstein areal flows

body: Let X be a normed vector space over R or C, and let X* be its continuous dual space equipped with the weak-* topology (pointwise convergence on X). Then the closed unit ball B* = {f in X* : ||f|| <= 1} is compact in the weak-* topology. More generally, the polar of any neighborhood of 0 in X is weak-* compact. Completeness or separability of X is not required; the proof rests on Tychonoff's theorem, and if X is separable then B* with the weak-* topology is also metrizable.
title: Banach-Alaoglu theorem

body: Publication record. Question 17.18 of R. Lyons and Y. Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks (Question 3 of Section 10 of Lyons, Pemantle and Peres, Ergodic theory on Galton-Watson trees, 1995) asks whether a flow rule with a stationary measure equivalent to the Galton-Watson measure GW must give an ergodic chain. Y. Shmalo, A nonergodic flow rule with Galton-Watson stationary measure (October 2026) answers no: for the offspring law p_2 = 3/5, p_3 = 2/5 an AND/OR colouring is a function of the tree, the flow rule that spreads the flow evenly over the children of the root that share its colour has GW stationary, and the event that the root has colour 1, of probability 1/2, is invariant, so the chain is not ergodic; GW(.|C = 1) and GW(.|C = 0) are its ergodic components. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/nonergodic-galton-watson-flow-rule (commit 837dd0c8da7d). Not refereed; an outside audit is owed.

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical, priority and scope audit pending. Let d>=1,N>=2d+1,K>=2,1<=r<K,F=K-r,gcd(r,F)=1. There are d unknown A/S context pairs with r arbitrary truths in A and all K truths in S, others known S. The source selects contexts uniformly then truths uniformly. Observe n iid untagged facts and independent uniform ell-subsets of truths in BOTH variable contexts, including S. Assume ceil(K/2)<=ell<=r and 0<=n<=r-ell. Each realized generator must have source Mis_infinity<=c in every compatible world at exact generator-score bins, 0<=c<1/(2NrK). Let h_i be the smaller observed-plus-certified truth union size in pair i,H=max_i h_i,b_h=[1/K+(r-h)/(r(K-h))]/(2N),tau_h=F/(2(K-h)). Every feasible generator has false mass at least sum_i F*b_hi-c*tau_H in EACH compatible world. Selecting h_i known truths from each sibling, pooling paired residuals, then moving c mass from a largest-h residual group to fixed S attains equality in all worlds. Thus the exact global expected robust minimax frontier is Gamma(c)=E[sum_i F*b_hi]-c*E[tau_H], with exact polynomial-time occupancy coefficient evaluation in the proof. For the same-data supplied-partition oracle, let a_i be the known union size in actual A context i. Its pointwise value is sum_i F*(r-a_i)/(Nr(K-a_i))-c*max({F/(K-a_i):a_i<r} union {0}). Its expectation is the exact global oracle O(c), and Gamma(c)-O(c) is the matching experiment-specific learning penalty. Zero-residual groups a_i=r must not supply a slope-one coefficient. The proof is pointwise weighted Cauchy-Schwarz on invariant-bin residual objects, not averaging conditional maxima. The class has VC dimension d. This is a fractional-verifier infinite family with n allowed to grow with K, but not a classical labeled ERM/PAC theorem or unrestricted longer-sample result.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:2c717d067c6da4462e3891f795f17fbed5873c863178801bd02b0ed6b1b8b79f","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/2c/2c717d067c6da4462e3891f795f17fbed5873c863178801bd02b0ed6b1b8b79f.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:95600de25cf48b65e1daccbc99890b8c66135dd36230ee6224a754dc6396e301","bundle_entry_key":"high-fraction-partial-verifier-global-frontier","bundle_id":"population.t379-high-fraction-partial-verifier-global-vc-frontier-20261020","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"calibrated generation; partial truth verification; global VC minimax","draft":"w709/bundle_015.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.calibration:kalai-vempala-high-fraction-partial-verifier-arbitrary-vc-global-frontier","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# High-fraction partial verification: arbitrary-VC global frontier

T379-C023 v2, proof (unaudited); exact checks PASS. Target1; secondary target2.

## Model and conditional theorem candidate

There are d>=1 independent A/S pairs and N-2d>=1 known S contexts, K
candidates per context, r arbitrary truths in A and K truths in S.
Put F=K-r and assume gcd(r,F)=1. Source p chooses contexts uniformly,
then truths uniformly. Observe actual untagged iid facts and independently
uniform ell-subsets of truths from BOTH variable contexts, including S.
For observed-plus-certified union sizes j_x, suppose ALL pairs remain
unresolved (every j_x<=r) and h_i=min(j_iL,j_iR)>=K/2.
Let H=max_i h_i and 0<=c<1/(2NrK). Every realized generator is required
to satisfy source Mis_infinity<=c in all compatible worlds.

Define
 b_h=[1/K+(r-h)/(r(K-h))]/(2N), tau_h=F/[2(K-h)].

Pointwise matching candidate theorem (unaudited):

 EVERY feasible g has H_theta(g)>=sum_i F*b_hi-c*tau_H
 in EACH compatible actual world theta. A causal pooling rule attains
 equality simultaneously in every world.                       (1)

This strengthens the C019 conditional worst-world assertion in the
high-known-count regime. It does not average a conditional maximum.

## Hardest step: a weighted cell inequality

C019's bin-mass lattice and coprime support expansion apply: every
score-bin source mass is world-invariant, and forgetting surplus known
truths down to the smaller count h_i preserves the same generator's
source bin masses and actual false-count vectors for every orientation.
Fix any actual world in the expanded balanced-minimum game. Write

 C=(K+r)/(2NrK), E=1/(Nr), q_i=2(K-h_i)/F.

Use its fair orientation mean only to COMPUTE common source bin masses;
do not substitute fair orientations for actual sampling likelihoods.
The invariant-bin classification gives the following components:

* A common residual bin of pair i peels k_i<=h_i known truths from each
  sibling. Its object has m=2(K-k_i) atoms, f=F actual false atoms, and
  source mass m*b_ki=C*m-E*f. Thus m>=f*q_i.
* If the two outside bins differ, each contains a whole context. The
  actual A context is an object m=K,f=F, source mass1/N. Since h_i>=K/2,
  m>=f*q_i. Its source mass is >=C*m-E*f, with excess F/(2Nr).
  The actual S context is safe with density lambda=1/(NK).
* Both saturated h_i=r,r may split outside atoms into balanced sub-bins.
  A balanced outside component has m=2v,f=v, source mass lambda*m/2
  =C*m-E*f, and q_i=2. Known truths in these bins are safe.
  A coprime unbalanced bin contains a whole context and uses the previous
  case. No assertion forces ALL saturated outside atoms into one bin.
* Remaining certified/fixed atoms are safe and have mean source density
  >=lambda; safe whole-S components have density lambda.

All risk-bearing objects have mean source density <=lambda. For a bin
containing them, analytically remove its safe components of density
>=lambda. This weakly lowers its mean source density and therefore its
actual false mass. This is a scalar inequality, not a new generator or
a data-dependent deletion. Let its remaining objects have sizes m_a,
false counts f_a>0 and targets q_a=q_i of the originating pair.
Put M=sum m_a, f=sum f_a. Its original false mass is at least

 f*(sum object_source)/M >= C*f-E*f^2/M
 >= C*f-E*sum_a(f_a/q_a)
 =sum_a f_a*b_hi.                                      (2)

Here M>=sum f_a*q_a and weighted Cauchy--Schwarz gives
f^2/(sum f_a*q_a)<=sum f_a/q_a.
Every pair has total actual false count F among its objects, so summing
bins proves H_theta(p0)>=sum_i F*b_hi for the common coarsened source p0.

The SAME component bounds give actual false fractions <=1/q_i=tau_hi:
common residual objects have k_i<=h_i, whole-A objects satisfy K>=2(K-h_i),
and saturated split objects have fraction1/2=tau_r. Safe atoms only lower
the fraction. Hence every actual score-bin risk is <=tau_H. Calibration
TV c reduces actual false mass by at most c*tau_H, proving (1).

Attain (1) by selecting h_i known truths in each sibling and pooling
their paired 2(K-h_i) residuals at their common source density. Remove
c mass from any count-H residual group and transfer it to fixed S.
Every group source mass is invariant and its actual false fraction is
tau_hi. The strict budget is smaller than every positive group mass.
Ties/selections may be randomized as policies; never average output laws.

## Actual iid global regime and exact frontier

Assume ceil(K/2)<=ell<=r<K and 0<=n<=r-ell. Then every possible data
outcome has j_x<=ell+n<=r and h_i>=ell>=K/2. Thus (1) applies to ALL
outcomes, and the exact global expected robust minimax is

 Gamma(c)=E[sum_i F*b_hi]-c*E[tau_H].                    (3)

Both bounds are pointwise in each world before expectation. The class has
VC dimension d. The estimator has polynomial arithmetic complexity in
n,NK. This is an experiment-specific expected robust frontier, not a
classical labeled-sample ERM/PAC theorem.

The expectation in (3) has a polynomial-time exact coefficient formula.
For m in {r,K} define the truth-union occupancy probability

 P_m(j|u)=binom(m-ell,j-ell)/m^u
           *sum_{a=0}^{j-ell}(-1)^a binom(j-ell,a)(j-a)^u,

using 0^0=1. All polynomials below are truncated after degree n.
For one actual A/S pair let

 B_h(z)=sum_{u+v<=n} z^(u+v)/(u!v!)
           *sum_{a=ell}^r sum_{b=ell}^K
                1_{min(a,b)=h} P_r(a|u) P_K(b|v).
 E_t(z)=sum_{h=ell}^t B_h(z).

Then E_r(z)=exp(2z) modulo z^(n+1). Set

 G_t=n!/N^n *[z^n] exp((N-2d)z)*E_t(z)^d.

This is the exact CDF P(H<=t); the coefficient handles multinomial
context counts without assuming independent learned counts. Therefore

 Gamma(c)=d*n!/N^n *[z^n] exp((N-2)z)*sum_h F*b_h*B_h(z)
   -c*(tau_ell+sum_{h=ell+1}^r(tau_h-tau_(h-1))*(1-G_(h-1))). (4)

This expression holds for every fixed world because support/certificate
permutations carry the full experiment to each other.

## Same-data supplied-partition oracle

Let a_i be the known union size in actual A context i. Its residual
source density is A_a=(r-a)/(Nr(K-a)), false fraction alpha_a=F/(K-a).
The pointwise oracle value in the same small-budget regime is

 O(D,c)=sum_i F*A_ai
          -c*max({alpha_ai:a_i<r} union {0}).             (5)

Groups with a_i=r have zero residual source mass, and must not contribute
a slope-one coefficient. Ordered residual-density/risk tails, or the
already saved C009 known-partition argument, prove (5); native residual
groups and transfer to fixed S attain it in every support.

For an explicit expectation define, for ell-1<=t<=r-1,

 A_t(z)=sum_{u=0}^n z^u/u! *
            sum_{j in ({ell,...,t} union {r})}P_r(j|u),
 F_t=n!/N^n *[z^n] exp((N-d)z)*A_t(z)^d.

Thus F_t is the probability that every A union is either saturated r or
<=t; F_(ell-1) is the probability all A unions are saturated.
Let

 T(z)=sum_{u=0}^n z^u/u!*sum_{j=ell}^r P_r(j|u)*F*A_j.

The exact global oracle is

 O(c)=d*n!/N^n*[z^n]exp((N-1)z)*T(z)
  -c*(alpha_ell*(1-F_(ell-1))
       +sum_{j=ell+1}^{r-1}(alpha_j-alpha_(j-1))*(1-F_(j-1))). (6)

Empty sums have value zero. The exact matching learning penalty is
Gamma(c)-O(c), with (4) and (6). It is not claimed equal to ordinary
binary classification error.

## Limits, source and pending verification

For ell<r this is a genuine fractional-verifier family, with arbitrary d
and n up to r-ell, not just an isolated sample size. E.g. r=K-1 is always
coprime, ell=ceil(K/2) permits n growing linearly with K. Lower verifier
fractions, longer samples with resolved pairs, noncoprime saturation and
larger calibration budgets remain open here. Full verifier ell=r with
arbitrary n was separately handled by C022.

[Theorem 27 (Widom {\cite[Theorem~3) of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] {Widom1982}}]

Let \(\sigma\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})\), and let \(W_L(\sigma)\) be the truncated Wiener--Hopf operator on \(L^2(0,L)\). Suppose that there exists a bounded determination \(\psi\) of \(\log\sigma\) whose inverse Fourier transform \(\check{\psi}\) satisfies
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}}|x|\,|\check{\psi}(x)|^2\,\mathrm{d}x<\infty.
\]
Then \(W_L(\sigma)\exp(-W_L(\psi))\) is of determinant class, and
\[
\det\bigl(W_L(\sigma)\exp(-W_L(\psi))\bigr)
\to
\exp\left(
\int_0^{\infty}x\check{\psi}(x)\check{\psi}(-x)\,\mathrm{d}x
\right)
\]
as \(L\to\infty\). If, in addition, \(\psi\in L^1(\mathbb{R})\), then
\[
\det W_L(\sigma)
\exp\left(
-\frac{L}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\psi(\xi)\,\mathrm{d}\xi
\right)
\to
\exp\left(
\int_0^{\infty}x\check{\psi}(x)\check{\psi}(-x)\,\mathrm{d}x
\right),
\]
where \(\det W_L(\sigma)\) denotes the Fredholm determinant of \(W_L(\sigma)=\operatorname{Id}+W_L(\sigma-1)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Combining this result with012v2 and024v2 gives the following sharper
critical-line classification for the SAME standard initialization,
under the explicit hypothesis x_l,0 != 0:

 x_l,0 != 0: [A_t->38 and liminf S_t>38] IFF [x_h,t->0]. (1)

is automatic once both coordinates converge to zero and the critical
coordinate's initial position is nonzero. This covers every high cap
theta_h>38, including cycle-neutral and stable-cycle cap parameters;
it is not an origin-basin avoidance or generic-tracking theorem.

PRIOR WORK AND HARDEST STEP
The recurrence theorem used below is CLASSICAL, not a new method:
Borcea--Friedland--Shapiro, arXiv0909.1216v1, actual version title
"On Asymptotic Ratio of a Sequence of Functions Obeying a Finite
Recurrence Relation", Theorem3 (headed Poincare--Perron), printed p4. The ratio-convergence
part used here is Poincare's theorem (1885).
The paragraph before it states the discrete version. Coefficient limits
and characteristic roots of distinct absolute values give the ratio
limit for each nontrivial, not-eventually-zero solution. Here every
last recurrence coefficient is nonzero and the position pair never
vanishes. There is no need for summable coefficient convergence or an
assumed generic coefficient of the dominant root. Perron's additional
root-attainment conclusion for nonvanishing last coefficients is not
used: we do not claim that either root occurs for a standard Adam start.

The new Adam step is to combine this pointwise scalar conclusion with
the supercritical origin rate q<b in025v1. The earlier inverse-Lyapunov
pair bound gave only a dominating SUBSEQUENCE of scalar positions.

1. CHECK THE ACTUAL SCALAR RECURRENCE
For either coordinate put
P_t=sqrt(v_(t+1)/(1-d^(t+1)))+epsilon,
a_t=eta/[(1-b^(t+1))*P_t]>0.
Eliminate raw momentum from x_(t+1)=x_t-a_t*m_(t+1) and
m_(t+1)=b*m_t+(1-b)*lambda*x_t. For t>=1,

 x_(t+1)=[1+b*a_t/a_(t-1)-(1-b)*lambda*a_t]*x_t
                         -b*a_t/a_(t-1)*x_(t-1).       (2)

Along any fixed actual trajectory these are a particular scalar linear
recurrence's coefficient sequences. Their dependence on the trajectory
does not obstruct applying a deterministic recurrence theorem after
the trajectory is fixed.

If x_t->0, the stable raw variance recursion gives v_t->0, so P_t->epsilon,
a_t->eta/epsilon and a_t/a_(t-1)->1. At cap theta_l=38 the limiting
characteristic polynomial is

 r^2-[1+b-(1-b)*38]*r+b = (r+1)*(r+b).                  (3)

At every finite t the last coefficient in(2) is nonzero. Since

eventually zero. Poincare's ratio theorem applies to(2): its limiting roots

roots. This is a statement about EVERY such nontrivial solution, not
only the dominant-root solutions.

For the high coordinate tending to its origin,025v1 Section2 supplies

Choose nu with q<nu<b. The ratio conclusion for the low coordinate

|x_l,t|>=c*nu^t for every sufficiently large t. Thus

 |g_h,t/g_l,t| <= (lambda_h*C)/(lambda_l*c)*(q/nu)^t ->0. (4)

[Theorem 20 (Convergence theorem \cite{Yakymiv}) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Let $X$ and $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be random variables with moment-generating
  functions $M_X$ and $M_{X_1}, M_{X_2}, \dots$ respectively.
  Assume these \textsc{mgf}s are finite
  on some interval $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ that is bounded, open and non-empty.
  Then $M_{X_m}$ converges pointwise to $M_X$ on $I$
  if and only if
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $X_m$ converges weakly to $X$; and
    \item $\sup_m M_{X_m}(t) < \infty$ for all $t \in I$.
  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let a Poisson(lambda) Galton-Watson process have lambda>1 and extinction probability q in (0,1), satisfying q=exp(-lambda(1-q)). Conditional on extinction its offspring law is Poisson(lambda q). If I(a)=a-1-log a, then I(lambda q)=I(lambda) exactly. For lambda=1+epsilon with epsilon decreasing to zero, lambda q=1-epsilon+(2/3)epsilon^2+O(epsilon^3). This is a branching-process mechanism for discrete duality; it does not prove that hypercube clusters after deleting the giant have this law.

body: [Theorem 11 of arXiv:2512.19063, 'Sharp Decoupling Inequalities for the Variances and Second Moments of Sums of Dependent Ra'] With the same setting as Theorem 6, we have a Chebyshev-type inequality for any $t>0$, $\mathbb{P}\left(|S_{n}-\mathbb{E} S_{n}|>t\right)\leq\frac{2\operatorname{Var}(S^{\prime}_{n})}{t^{2}}.$ (15) If in addition $S_{n}\geq 0$ a.s., we have a Paley-Zygmund-type inequality for any $0<\theta<1$, $\mathbb{P}(S_{n}>\theta\,\mathbb{E} S_{n})\geq(1-\theta)^{2}\,\frac{(\mathbb{E} S_{n})^{2}}{2\mathbb{E}{S^{\prime}}_{n}^{2}-(\mathbb{E} S_{n})^{2}}=(1-\theta)^{2}\,\frac{1}{\frac{2\mathbb{E}{S^{\prime}}_{n}^{2}}{(\mathbb{E} S_{n})^{2}}-1}.$

Let D = {z in C : |z| < 1} and let f : D → D be holomorphic with f(0) = 0. Then |f(z)| ≤ |z| for every z in D, and |f'(0)| ≤ 1. Moreover, if |f(z0)| = |z0| for some z0 in D with z0 ≠ 0, or if |f'(0)| = 1, then f is a rotation: f(z) = λz for a constant λ with |λ| = 1. (The hypothesis f(D) ⊂ D may be weakened to |f| ≤ 1 on D, since a nonconstant such f maps D into D by the open mapping theorem and the constant must be 0.) Without f(0) = 0 the correct statement is the Schwarz–Pick theorem.

body:
[Lem 38 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] There exists a constant $C_8=C_8(\alpha,\iota)$ such that the following holds with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$ over $\dot{\bg}_+, \hat{\bg}_+$, where $c$ is an absolute constant. 
    For any $\|\by\|^2=N$, the function
    \[
        \btheta_+ \mapsto
        \frac{2(\hbg_+,\btheta_+)}{M}
        + \frac{2\|\btheta_+\|(\dbg_+,\by)}{M\sqrt{N}}
        - \frac{((\hbD_+)^{-1} \btheta_+, \btheta_+)}{M}
    \]
    attains its supremum over $\R^{B_+}$ at some $\btheta_+$ satisfying
    $\|\btheta_+\| \le C_8N^{1/2}$.
    (We take the assertion to be vacuously true if $B_+ = \emptyset$.)

\begin{proof}
    Since the function tends to $-\infty$ as $\|\btheta_+\| \to +\infty$, the supremum is attained at a local maximizer $\btheta_+$.
    The function is differentiable everywhere except possibly at $\btheta_+=\bzero$, so the only possible local maximizer are $\btheta_+=\bzero$ and stationary points $\btheta_+$. 
    The stationarity condition gives
    \[
      \btheta_+
     =\hbD_+\bigg(   \hbg_+
        + \frac{(\dbg_+,\by) \btheta_+}{N^{1/2} \|\btheta_+\|}
        \bigg) \,.
    \]
With probability $1-e^{-cN}$, we have $\|\hbg_+\| \le 2 M^{1/2}$, $\|\dbg_+\| \le 2 N^{1/2}$, and consequently $|(\dbg_+,\by)| \le 2N$. Since the operator norm of $\hbD_+$ is at most $\hv_1$, it follows that any stationary point $\btheta_+$ must satisfy
    \[
        \|\btheta_+\|
        \le\hv_1 \bigg(
            \|\hbg_+\|
            + \bigg|
            \frac{(\dbg_+,\by) }{N^{1/2} }
            \bigg|
        \bigg)
        \le
        2\hv_1\Big( M^{1/2} + N^{1/2}
         \Big)
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:reduced-normalization}}{\le}
        \frac{4(\alpha^{1/2}+1)}{\iota} N^{1/2}\,.
    \]
This proves the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 38 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Theorem thm:intro-one of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $\mathbf a_*\in D$ be a strict local minimum point of $H$.  Fix
$\kappa,M,R>0$.  For each $\varepsilon>0$, let
$\mathbf a_\varepsilon\in D$ and let
$\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\in L^\infty(D)$ be nonnegative and satisfy
\begin{equation}
  \int_D\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\,\mathrm d\mathbf x=\kappa,
  \qquad
  \|\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\|_\infty\leq M\varepsilon^{-2},
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\omega_{\varepsilon,0}
  \subset B_{R\varepsilon}(\mathbf a_\varepsilon).
\end{equation}
Suppose that
\begin{equation*}
  \mathbf a_\varepsilon\longrightarrow\mathbf a_*,
  \qquad
  \mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,0})\longrightarrow0
  \qquad\text{as }\varepsilon\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation*}
Let $\omega_{\varepsilon,t}$, $t\in\mathbb R$, denote the corresponding
Yudovich solution of (equation eq:euler-intro of the paper).
Then, as $\varepsilon\to0$,
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})\longrightarrow0,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\ \sup_{\mathbf b\in
  \mathsf C(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})}
  |\mathbf b-\mathbf a_*|\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Global persistence: one concentrated vortex

[Prop 26 of arXiv:2606.11271, '\LARGE The $K$-th nearest neighbor random walk on a Poisson point process gets trapped'] Let $(Y^L_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be the Markov chain on $\{0,1,\ldots,3L\}$ with $Y^L_0=0$ and transition probabilities:
\[
\P(Y^L_{n+1}=j \mid Y^L_n=i) = \begin{cases} 
(1-p)\mathbf{1}_{j=1}+p\mathbf{1}_{j=2} & \text{if } i=0 \\
(1-p)\mathbf{1}_{j=i+1}+p\mathbf{1}_{j=i-1} & \text{if } i\equiv 0 \pmod 3 \text{ and } 0<i<3L \\
(1-p)\mathbf{1}_{j=i-1}+p\mathbf{1}_{j=i+1}  & \text{if } i\not\equiv 0 \pmod 3 \text{ and } 0<i<3L \\
(1-p)\mathbf{1}_{j=3L-1}+p\mathbf{1}_{j=3L-2}  & \text{if } i=3L.
\end{cases}
\]
If $\mu = \mu_0$, then on the event $\cH_L$, the walk $(X_n)_{n\ge 0}$ has the law of $(x_{Y^L_n})_{n\ge 0}$.

[Defn $\sharp$ and $\flat$ modifications of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a cooriented $C^0$-foliation on the $2$-torus $\mathbb{T}^2$, and $p \in \mathbb{T}^2$. We choose a smooth closed arc $c$ transverse to $\mathcal{G}$ and containing $p$ in its interior. After some arbitrarily small $C^0$ isotopy, we may assume that $\mathcal{G}$ is smooth in a neighborhood of $c$, and we choose coordinates $N(c) \cong (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)_x \times (-2,2)_y$ near $c$, in which $c$ is identified with $\{0\} \times [-1,1]$, $p=(0,0)$, and $\mathcal{G}$ is tangent to $\partial_x$. 

    Let $h : [-1,1] \rightarrow [-1,1]$ be a smooth diffeomorphism satisfying 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $h \geq \mathrm{id}$ (resp.~$h \leq \mathrm{id}$),
        \item $h = \mathrm{id}$ near $\partial [-1,1]$,
        \item $h > \mathrm{id}$ (resp.~$h < \mathrm{id}$) on $[-1/2, 1/2]$.
    \end{itemize}

    We modify $\mathcal{G}$ in $(-\varepsilon/2, \varepsilon/2) \times (-2,2) \subset N(c)$ so that the parallel transport along the leaves of $\mathcal{G}$ from left to right is $h$, and moreover the new $C^0$-foliation $\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}$ is everywhere either tangent or positively (resp.~negatively) transverse to $\partial_x$ in $N(c)$. Choosing $h$ sufficiently $C^0$-close to $\mathrm{id}$, we can further arrange that $T\widetilde{\mathcal{G}}$ is $C^0$-close to $T\mathcal{G}$. 
    
    We call the resulting $C^0$-foliation a $\sharp$ (resp.~$\flat$) modification of $\mathcal{G}$ near the point $p$. This modification can be made arbitrarily $C^0$-small and close to $p$.
title: $\sharp$ and $\flat$ modifications

[Theorem thm:wobbling of arXiv:2607.04620, 'The Exact Ville Identity\\ \large From the Absorbing Case to the General Law\\ with an App'] Let $\{M_n,\mathcal{F}_n\}$ be a mean-zero martingale and fix a level $r\ge0$. Let $T_r$ be the first $n\ge1$ with $M_n>r$, and $\infty$ if no such $n$ exists. Suppose
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item (sufficient wobbling)
\[
  \lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\limsup_{k\to\infty}
  \mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{n\ge k}|M_n-M_k|>\varepsilon\right)=1,
\]
\item (bounded expected overshoot) there is $B<\infty$ with $\mathbb{E}[M_n\mid T_r=n]\le r+B$ a.s. for every $n\ge1$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\mathbb{P}(T_r<\infty)=1$ and $\mathbb{E}[M_{T_r}]\le r+B$; moreover $\limsup_{n\to\infty}M_n=+\infty$ almost surely. Condition (i) ensures the martingale wobbles arbitrarily far out; condition (ii) bounds the overshoot of $M_{T_r}$ beyond $r$. [Theorem Thm:BesovLog of arXiv:2412.03366, 'Regularity of Weighted Tensorized Fractional Brownian Fields and associated function space'] Let $s, \beta \in \mathbb{R}$ and $0 < p,q\leq \infty$ and $p'$ the conjugate exponent of $p$. We have the following embeddings
\begin{itemize}
\item if $q<+\infty$
\begin{equation}
\widetilde{B}^s_{p,q,\vert \log \vert^{\beta - r_1/q}}(\mathbb{R}^2) \hookrightarrow B^s_{p,q,\vert \log \vert^{\beta}}(\mathbb{R}^2) \hookrightarrow \widetilde{B}^s_{p,q,\vert \log \vert^{\beta +r_2/q}}(\mathbb{R}^2)
\end{equation}
where $$r_1 = \begin{cases}q(\frac{1}{p}-1)+ \max(q-1,0) & \text{ if } p \le 1 \\ 
\max( \frac{q}{\min(p,p')}-1,0) & \text{ if }p>1 \end{cases}$$
and
$$
r_2 = \begin{cases}1  & \text{ if } p < 1 \\ 
\max(1- \frac{q}{\max(p,p')}-1,0) & \text{ if }p\ge 1 .\end{cases}$$

\item if $q=+\infty$
\begin{equation}
\widetilde{B}^s_{p,\infty,\vert \log \vert^{\beta - \max(1/p-1,0) -1}}(\mathbb{R}^2) \hookrightarrow B^s_{p,\infty,\vert \log \vert^{\beta}}(\mathbb{R}^2) \hookrightarrow \widetilde{B}^s_{p,\infty,\vert \log \vert^{\beta }}(\mathbb{R}^2)
\end{equation}

\item if $q=2$, the Sobolev spaces $H^{s}_{2,\vert \log \vert^{\beta}}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ coincide with the classical Besov spaces $B^{s}_{2,2,\vert \log \vert^{\beta}}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ and with the hyperbolic Besov spaces $\widetilde{B}^{s}_{2,2,\vert \log \vert^{\beta}}(\mathbb{R}^2) $.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem Thm:BesovLog of arXiv:2412.03366

Method: Explicit stationary law of the leftmost Hammersley drift-jump particles structural calculation Result: The established rank representation can be expanded into a convergent combinatorial density series. Let B=(1=b1<...<bk) be the limiting first-row labels of the insertion tableau, and let q_B be its probability. The first b=bk labels form a uniform permutation, so q_B=(1/b!)*sum over partitions lambda of b with first row length k of f^lambda times the number of standard tableaux of shape lambda with first row B. Independent unit-rate Poisson spacings then give density exp(-xk)*sum_B q_B*product_(i=2..k)[(x_i-x_(i-1))^(b_i-b_(i-1)-1)/(b_i-b_(i-1)-1)!]. Check: Restriction of an insertion tableau to labels at most b is the tableau of the corresponding restricted subword. The last specified first-row entry b pins the first k labels, irrespective of later larger labels. Conditional on B, the Poisson arrival times have independent gamma increments, so every term is a normalized conditional density and nonnegative summation is valid. For k1 this gives Exp(1); known Poissonized LIS formulas give P(X2>x)=exp(-x)*I0(2sqrt(x)) and E X2=e. Obstruction: This repackages a known representation into explicit but rapidly growing finite-tableau coefficients and an infinite sum. It does not establish a new tractable closed joint law or its novelty, and should not be promoted as a full solution to the source request.

[Thm 6 (Main result in spatial dimension $d=1$) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Let $\{K_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ denote an environment satisfying Assumption \ref{a1}, and let $\mathfrak H^N$ be as in \eqref{hn}. Assume as in Definition \ref{goodseq} that one has a good sequence of deterministic initial data $\mathfrak H^N(0,\bullet)$ converging weakly as measures to some limit $\mathfrak H_0$. There is an explicit Banach space $X$ of distributions on $\mathbb R$, which is continuously embedded in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R)$, such that the rescaled and recentered collection $\{ \mathfrak F^N\}_{N \ge 1}$ is tight with respect to the topology of $C([0,T], X)$. Furthermore any limit point as $N\to \infty$ is as follows. 
\begin{itemize} 
\item (Bulk fluctuations in $d=1$) If $N^{1/2}\varsigma_N \to \boldsymbol{\varsigma} \text{ as } N\to\infty$, then the limit point is unique and coincides with the law of $(t,x)\mapsto e^{\varsigma\bullet x +\frac12 |\varsigma|^2 t} \mathcal U(t,x+\varsigma t)$ where $\mathcal U$ is the solution of the additive-noise SPDE \begin{equation}\partial_t \mathcal U(t, x) = \frac12\partial_x^2 \mathcal U(t, x) + \gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot \partial_x^p \big((\mathfrak H_0 *G_t)(x)\;\xi(t, x)\big),
\end{equation}started with initial data $\mathcal U(0, x)=0$. 

\item (Extremal fluctuations up to location scale $N^{1-\frac1{4p}}$ in $d=1$) If $N^{-1/2}\ll  |\varsigma_N|\ll  N^{-1/4p} \text{ as } N\to \infty,$ then the limit point is unique and coincides with the law of the solution of the additive-noise SPDE \begin{equation}\partial_t \mathcal U(t, x) = \frac12\partial_x^2  \mathcal U(t, x) + \gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot   (\mathfrak H_0 *G_t)(x)\; \xi(t, x),
\end{equation}started with initial data $\mathcal U(0, x)=0$. 
\end{itemize} Here $G_t(x) = G(t,x)= (2\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2t}$ is the standard heat kernel, $*$ denotes spatial convolution, and $ \xi$ is a standard space-time white noise defined on $\mathbb R_+\times \mathbb R.$ Furthermore in either case we have the noise coefficient $$\gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}^2:=  \frac1{(2p)!}\int_{I} \bigg[ \int_{I^2}( x- y)^{2p}\mu(\mathrm d x)\mu(\mathrm d y)-\int_I ( a- z)^{2p} \pdif( z,\mathrm d a)\bigg]
\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}(\mathrm d z).
$$Here $\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}$ is the invariant measure of the Markov kernel $\pdif$, under its unit normalization (see Definition \ref{def:unit}). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Main result in spatial dimension $d=1$

Work as d->infinity with integers N=N(d)->infinity and M=M(d)>=1. Let (X_d,nu_d) and (Omega_d,tau_d) be probability spaces and sigma_d in L2(nu_d times tau_d). Use its singular expansion sigma_d(x,theta)=sum_j sqrt(mu_j) psi_j(x) phi_j(theta), with ordered nonnegative mu_j, sum_j mu_j<infinity, positive mu_(M+1) and positive denominators in the displayed tail conditions, and orthonormal families psi_j in L2(nu_d), phi_j in L2(tau_d). Let D_d be the closed span of the psi_j and P_<=M its orthogonal projection onto the first M modes. Define the feature kernel U_d(theta,thetaprime)=E_x~nu_d sigma_d(x,theta)sigma_d(x,thetaprime), its spectral tail U_>r=sum_(j>r) mu_j phi_j phi_j^T, and kappa_r=sum_(j>r)mu_j>0 for each cutoff used. Draw theta_1,...,theta_N independently from tau_d and let K_ij=U_d(theta_i,theta_j). All stochastic rates below are as d->infinity. (H) There is one sequence u(d)>=M(d) such that, for every fixed real q>=1, all g in span{phi_1,...,phi_u} satisfy ||g||_(L2q(tau_d))<=C_q||g||_(L2(tau_d)), with C_q independent of d and g. (E) For the same u there is a fixed delta_E>0 such that N^(2+delta_E)<=kappa_u^2/sum_(j>u)mu_j^2 eventually. (Sa) There is a fixed delta_a>0 with N^(1+delta_a)<=kappa_M/mu_(M+1) eventually. Let Phi_ij=phi_j(theta_i) for j<=M, A=diag(sqrt(mu_1),...,sqrt(mu_M)), and Lambda=diag(U_>M(theta_i,theta_i)/kappa_M). Theorem6 gives a symmetric Delta such that K=Phi A^2 Phi^T+kappa_M(Lambda+Delta), and there exists a fixed delta_prime>0 with E||Delta||_op=O(N^(-delta_prime)). In particular the remainder is controlled in expectation, not only numerically. If additionally M<=N^(1-delta_h) for some fixed delta_h>0, then ||Phi^T Phi/N-I_M||_op=o_P(1). These conclusions do not require Dupper, Dlower, or the eigenvalue ratio part of Sb.

body: For an elliptic curve E over the rational numbers, the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture asserts that the rank of the finitely generated abelian group E(Q) of rational points equals the order of vanishing of the curve's L-function L(E,s) at s=1. A refined form further predicts the leading Taylor coefficient of L(E,s) at s=1 in terms of arithmetic invariants of E: the order of the Tate-Shafarevich group, the regulator, the real period, and the Tamagawa numbers. The conjecture is OPEN in general, one of the seven Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, though proved when the analytic rank is 0 or 1 by Gross, Zagier, and Kolyvagin.
title: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture

Let (X_t)_{t in T} be a stochastic process on a metric space (T, d) with SUB-GAUSSIAN INCREMENTS, meaning P( |X_s - X_t| > u ) <= 2 exp( - u^2 / (2 d(s,t)^2) ) for all s, t and u > 0. Then there is an absolute constant C with E sup_{t in T} X_t <= C integral_0^{diam(T)} sqrt( log N(T, d, u) ) du, where N(T, d, u) is the covering number, the smallest number of d-balls of radius u needed to cover T. If the process is not centred one should read the statement for X_t - X_{t_0} with a fixed base point. Two standard cautions: the bound can be LOOSE - for a centred Gaussian process the sharp answer is Talagrand's generic chaining and the majorizing measure theorem, and Dudley's integral can overshoot by an unbounded factor; and the integral must converge, so a class with covering numbers growing faster than exp(u^{-2}) is not handled. Sudakov's minoration provides the matching lower bound E sup_t X_t >= c sup_{u > 0} u sqrt( log N(T, d, u) ) for centred GAUSSIAN processes, so the two differ exactly by the integral versus the supremum. [Dudley (1967); see Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, Theorem 8.1.6]

For positive differentiable unconditional and conditional densities p_t(x) and p_t(x|c), let s_u=grad_x log p_t(x), s_c=grad_x log p_t(x|c). At guidance strength gamma in R, the classifier-free guidance score is s_gamma=(1-gamma)*s_u+gamma*s_c. It is the gradient of log[p_t(x)^(1-gamma)*p_t(x|c)^gamma]. If the product has finite positive integral Z_(t,gamma), it is also the score of the normalized instantaneous density q_(t,gamma)=p_t^(1-gamma)*p_t(.|c)^gamma/Z_(t,gamma). This identity is pointwise in noise time t; it does not assert that the forward diffusion of q_(0,gamma) has marginals q_(t,gamma), or that a guided reverse process samples q_(0,gamma).

body:
[Proposition 1 (Dichotomy recurrence/transience for $\Tree_{\infty}$-walk) of arXiv:2608.30668, 'Recurrence and capacity of stable branching random walks'] Assume that \(\theta\) is not supported by a strict subgroup of \(\Z^d\). Consider the \emph{total escape} event
\(\esc= \bigl(W_{\Tree_{\infty}}(u) \neq 0\ \forall u \in \Tree_{\infty}\!\setminus\! \{ c_0 \} \bigr)\).

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item
  If \(\P(\esc)=0\) then almost surely, for every \(x \in \Z^d\),
  \(\sum_{u \in \Tree_{\infty}} \1_{W_{\Tree_{\infty}}(u)=x} = +\infty\)
  \emph{i.e.} \(x\) is visited infinitely often by
  \(W_{\Tree_{\infty}}\).
\item
  If \(\P(\esc)>0\) then almost surely, for every \(x \in \Z^d\),
  \(\sum_{u \in \Tree_{\infty}} \1_{W_{\Tree_{\infty}}(u)=x} < +\infty\).
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, \[\P(\esc)=0 \text{ if and only if } \P(\esc_{+})=0,\] where
\(\esc_{+}= \bigl(W_{\Tree_{\infty}}(u) \neq 0\ \forall u \in \Tree_{+} \bigr)\)
as in \eqref{eq:LinkFiniteInfinite}, and in the recurrent case we actually have that almost surely, for every \(x \in \Z^d\),
  \(\sum_{u \in \Tree_{+}} \1_{W_{\Tree_{\infty}}(u)=x} = +\infty\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Dichotomy recurrence/transience for $\Tree_{\infty}$-walk

[Corollary 6 (\textsf{Law of small numbers}) of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Let $(B_{n,k})_{1\leq k\leq N_n}$ be independent 
$\{0,1\}$-valued Bernoulli variables
with success probabilities $p_{n,k}$, and put

\noi
\begin{align}
 X_n:=\sum_{k=1}^{N_n}B_{n,k}
 \AND
 \theta_n:= \E[X_n] =\sum_{k=1}^{N_n}p_{n,k}.
\notag
\end{align}
If

\noi
\begin{align}
 \theta_n\to\lambda>0
\AND
 \max_{1\leq k\leq N_n}p_{n,k}\to0,
\notag
\end{align}
then $X_n$ converges to $\Pois(\lambda)$ in total variation and its
first four moments converge to those of the limit. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textsf{Law of small numbers}

body:
[Theorem intro-th:sec-order-main of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] (Theorem (th:sec-order-main of the paper))

  Let $A$ be a random Hermitian matrix of size $N$ and assume that for every
  finite $r$ one has
  \begin{equation} 
  \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^2 \left( \frac{1}{N} \log \mathbb{E}[H
     \text{} C (x_1, \ldots, x_r, 0^{N - r} ; \lambda_1 (A), \ldots, \lambda_N
     (A))] - \sum_{i = 1}^r \Psi (x_i) - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i = 1}^r \Phi (x_i)
     \right) = \sum_{i = 1}^r \mathrm{T} (x_i), 
     \end{equation} 
  where $\Psi, \Phi, \mathrm{T}$ are smooth functions in a complex neighborhood of $0$ and
  the above convergence is uniform in a complex neighborhood of $0^r$. Then the $1 /
  N^2$ correction of the average empirical distribution of $N^{- 1} A$
  is given by
  \[ \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^2 \left( \frac{1}{N^{k + 1}}
     \mathbb{E}[\ensuremath{\operatorname{Tr}} (A^k)] -\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k - \frac{1}{N}
     \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'_k \right) =\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}''_k
     +\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\nu}}''_k, \]
  where $(\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}, (\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'_k)_{k \in
  \mathbb{N}}$ are given by ((intro-topg of the paper)),((intro-G of the paper)) respectively. The sequences
  $(\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}''_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}, (\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\nu}}''_k)_{k \in
  \mathbb{N}}$ are given by
  \[ \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}''_k = \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 1} \frac{k!}{m! (m + 1) ! (k -
     m - 1) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi' (x))^{k - m - 1}
     \mathrm{T}' (x)) \right|_{x = 0} \]
  \begin{equation}
    \text{{\hspace{10em}}} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 2} \frac{k!}{m! (m
    + 1) ! (k - m - 2) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
    (x))^{k - m - 2} (\Phi' (x))^2) \right|_{x = 0} 
  \end{equation}
  and
  \[ \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\nu}}''_k = \frac{1}{24} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 3} \frac{k!}{m! (m
     + 1) ! (k - m - 3) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
     (x))^{k - m - 3} \Psi''' (x)) \right|_{x = 0} \]
  \[ \text{{\hspace{4em}}} + \frac{1}{12} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 3} \frac{k!}{m! (m
     + 2) ! (k - m - 3) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
     (x))^{k - m - 3} \Psi''' (x)) \right|_{x = 0} \]
  \begin{equation}
    \text{{\hspace{10em}}} + \frac{1}{12} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 4} \frac{k!}{m! (m
    + 2) ! (k - m - 4) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
    (x))^{k - m - 4} (\Psi'' (x))^2) \right|_{x = 0} . 
  \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

(a) Let Z be standard Gaussian on R and f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| < infinity. Then E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ]. (b) Multivariate: if X is centred Gaussian on R^n with covariance Sigma and f is differentiable with the appropriate integrability, then E[ X_i f(X) ] = sum_j Sigma_{ij} E[ d f / d x_j (X) ]. (c) STEIN'S CHARACTERISATION: a real random variable Z is standard Gaussian IF AND ONLY IF E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ] for every bounded, continuously differentiable f with bounded derivative. This is the identity that makes Stein's method work: to show a law is close to Gaussian, one bounds E[ Z f(Z) - f'(Z) ] over a class of test functions f solving Stein's equation. (d) ISSERLIS-WICK FORMULA: for a centred Gaussian vector, E[ X_1 X_2 ... X_{2m} ] = sum over all PERFECT MATCHINGS of {1, ..., 2m} of the product of the covariances of the matched pairs, and any odd moment vanishes. For 2m = 4 this reads E[X_1X_2X_3X_4] = Sigma_{12}Sigma_{34} + Sigma_{13}Sigma_{24} + Sigma_{14}Sigma_{23}, and in particular E[Z^4] = 3 for a standard Gaussian, which is the '3' that the fourth moment theorem tests against. Centring is essential in (d); for a non-centred Gaussian one must first subtract the means. [standard; Isserlis (1918), Stein (1972); see Nourdin and Peccati, Normal Approximations with Malliavin Calculus, Chapter 3]
(a) f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| finite
(c) the characterisation quantifies over a rich enough class of test functions
(d) the Gaussian vector must be CENTRED

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:b06d9caf4499e373ff65611423270da513ac5c9944263938539642c041560074","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/b0/b06d9caf4499e373ff65611423270da513ac5c9944263938539642c041560074.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:0f5a7de4ce67fffcf1173bf993c31713fb08f0f899b640c0c3d1c53764d47571","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c5","bundle_id":"population.i0005-four-dimensional-parking-partials-002","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"interacting particle systems and random-walk potential theory","draft":"w661/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:i0005-c5-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C5 v1: multi-hole deletion bound and a Palm exponential-moment bound

Novelty: UNCHECKED. The source proves a two-hole deletion bound in Lemma 8.4. This is a strengthened two-hole constant and a multi-hole extension of that KNOWN argument. Literature search was limited to the source, companion paper, later author/title lists and relevant brain recalls; no assertion of priority.

For the iid sparse particle–hole initial law P(η=1)=P(η=−1)=p and P(η=0)=1−2p, assume 0<p<1/2. Use synchronous nearest-neighbor simple random walks on Z^d, stationary holes of capacity one, and any d≥1. Let h_t=P(H_t(0)=1)>0 and q=p/(1−p)∈(0,1).

For distinct sites x_0,...,x_k and every finite integer t≥0,

P(H_t(x_i)=1 for every 0≤i≤k)≤h_t q^k.

In particular the source's two-hole constant p/(1−2p) can be replaced by p/(1−p). For any finite S⊂Z^d\{0}, N_t(S)=sum_{x∈S}H_t(x), and λ≥0,

E[exp(λN_t(S)) | H_t(0)=1]≤(1+q(e^λ−1))^{|S|}.

This is an exponential-moment inequality, not a claim of stochastic domination by a Bernoulli product process.

## Proof of the multi-hole inequality

Let E be the event that all k+1 specified holes are unfilled at time t. Then η(x_i)=−1 for every i, and no particle has arrived at any x_i by time t: with capacity one an arrival would fill that hole permanently.

Fix a subset J⊂{1,...,k}. Replace η(x_j)=−1 by 0 at the sites indexed by J, and leave every other initial variable and every walk/stack instruction unchanged. No particle ever visits one of these sites by round t in the original evolution. The changed evolution is identical away from these sites until its first putative arrival at any changed site. Before that arrival all particle moves are identical, so it would also be an arrival in the original evolution, a contradiction. Thus there is no such arrival, and all particles elsewhere evolve identically up to t. In particular the original hole at x_0 remains unfilled.

Call the image of E under this replacement E_J. The replacement map is injective on E after the fixed original −1 values are restored. These events E_J are pairwise disjoint: at x_j, their initial values are exactly 0 if j∈J and −1 otherwise. Each is a subset of {H_t(x_0)=1}. Conditional on all other initial variables and instructions, the probabilities of the specified coordinate assignments have ratio ((1−2p)/p)^{|J|}. Hence

P(E_J)=((1−2p)/p)^{|J|}P(E).

Only finitely many initial sites and instructions can affect the finitely many targets by time t (finite propagation and bounded initial particle count), so this change-of-variables identity can be understood entirely in a finite product space. Alternatively it follows by conditioning on all variables except the k changed initial coordinates.

Summing over the 2^k disjoint images gives

h_t≥sum_J P(E_J)
=P(E)(1+(1−2p)/p)^k
=P(E)((1−p)/p)^k.

Translation invariance gives P(H_t(x_0)=1)=h_t, proving the assertion. For k=0 the identity reduces to h_t=h_t.

## Proof of the exponential-moment inequality

For s=e^λ−1≥0 and binary H,

(1+s)^{N_t(S)}=product_{x∈S}(1+s H_t(x))
=sum_{J⊂S}s^{|J|}product_{x∈J}H_t(x).

Multiplying by H_t(0), taking expectations, and applying the multi-hole estimate term by term yields

E[H_t(0)(1+s)^{N_t(S)}]≤h_t sum_{J⊂S}(sq)^{|J|}
=h_t(1+sq)^{|S|}.

Divide by h_t. No independence of the surviving holes is used. Positivity of h_t follows, for finite t, by requiring all initial sites in a sufficiently large finite neighborhood of the target to contain holes and no particles.

## Limit of this result

The Palm expected number of other surviving holes in S is at most q|S|. This controls balls of radius O(p^−1/d), uniformly in time, but it does not control balls of radius O(h_t^−1/d), whose volume grows like h_t^−1. The missing time-dependent thinning/decorrelation input in C2 remains missing.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:a717cab0408ba62fa14a8ae11b44e2c6621727ffa391b3ed98fd0857f08973f1","revision_digest":"sha256:1568d6f055efd1ea5822dd15d9b32a500c860bb2e3f333eef82afbe389f07225","source_id":"owner-own-work:w661:I0005-C5:v1","source_revision":"v1; 2026-10-14T05:23:59.4615090+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Almost surely these span C^2. The real-linear measurement map from the four-dimensional Hermitian 2-by-2 space to R^3 has a nonzero kernel element H. H cannot be positive or negative semidefinite: a_i^* H a_i=0 for a spanning set would force H=0. Thus H has one positive and one negative eigenvalue and can be written xx^*-yy^* with noncollinear x,y. Their three intensity measurements agree. Hence p_2=0. Check: Dimension gives a nonzero H without assuming generic rank three; the spanning condition rules out semidefinite kernel elements. Spectral decomposition independently verifies equal squared magnitudes. Obstruction: For M>2 a nonzero kernel matrix need not have rank at most two with one eigenvalue of each sign. [Cor 14 of arXiv:2604.25725, 'What is The Probability That A Random Graph With A Given Degree Sequence is Connected?'] Fix $0<\eps<10^{-6}$. Let $\cD$ be such that $m$ is large enough and $n_1,n_2  \le 10^{-6}m$. Let $v\in[n]$. Then for any $1 \le i \le m$, if $i$ is such that $d_i(v_i)>\sqrt{m}(\log m)^{-2}$ and 
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item $X_{i-1} \neq 0$,
    \item $2|E(H_{i-1})|+|X_{i-1}| \le \epsilon m$, and
    \item  $D^*\leq\eps m$,
\end{enumerate}
then $\Cprob{X_i-X_{i-1}< 0.9d_i(v_i)}{H_{i-1}}<m^{-m^{1/3}}$.

body:
For a nondegenerate centered real stationary Gaussian sequence X and any n>=1, rho(n)=r(n) and rho*(n)=r*(n). Here r(n) is the supremum of absolute normalized covariance of finite linear combinations supported in the past and future across gap n, and r*(n) is the same supremum for arbitrary finite separated index sets; complex coefficients are permitted and the norm of a linear form is (E|sum a_k X_k|²)^(1/2). Zero-norm forms are excluded. The rho coefficients instead allow arbitrary centered square-integrable functions of the respective coordinate sigma fields, including infinite sets. This Gaussian equality does not hold for general non-Gaussian sequences. Primary author formulation: Bradley (2005), equation (7.1), PDF p.27, with (6.7) and attribution to Kolmogorov-Rozanov (1960), Theorem1 on PDF p.28.
Centered real stationary jointly Gaussian sequence
Finite positive variance
All correlations exclude zero-norm variables

For every finite real martingale (M_k,F_k), k=0,...,N, with M_0=0 and M_N in L^4, let D_k=M_k-M_{k-1} and Q_N=sum_{k=1}^N D_k^2. Then E M_N^4<=81 E Q_N^2 and E Q_N^2<=81 E M_N^4. Also sum E[M_{k-1}^2D_k^2]<=16 E Q_N^2, sum |E[M_{k-1}D_k^3]|<=4 E Q_N^2, and sum E D_k^4<=E Q_N^2. No independence or conditional symmetry of the differences is assumed.

    sum E[M_{k-1}^2 D_k^2] <= 16 E Q_N^2,
    sum |E[M_{k-1} D_k^3]| <= 4 E Q_N^2,
    sum E D_k^4 <= E Q_N^2.

    E S^4 <= (4/3) E[|M_N| S^3]
             <= (4/3) ||M_N||_4 ||S||_4^3,
    ||S||_4 <= (4/3) ||M_N||_4.

body: The Banach–Tarski paradox is a theorem in set-theoretic geometry that states the following: Given a solid ball in three-dimensional space, there exists a decomposition of the ball into a finite number of disjoint subsets that can be put back together in a different way to yield two identical copies of the original ball. Indeed, the reassembly process involves only moving the pieces around and rotating them, without changing their original shape. The pieces themselves are not "solids" in the traditional sense, but infinite scatterings of points. The reconstruction can work with as few as five pieces.
title: Banach–Tarski paradox

On Z^4 let G be the full-space nearest-neighbor discrete-time SRW Green kernel, k_N(z)=G(z)1{|z|_2<=N}, sigma_N^2=sum_z k_N(z)^2, and xi_z independent standard Gaussians. Define Y_N(x)=sum_z k_N(x-z)xi_z/sigma_N and H_N(x)=1{Y_N(x)>=2sqrt(log N)}. Its density is (1+o(1))N^(-2)/(2sqrt(2pi log N)). For each fixed 0<beta<1/sqrt(2), the graph ball of radius floor(N^beta) contains no H_N hole with probability tending to one. For 1/2<beta<1/sqrt(2), its expected hole count nevertheless diverges. This is a Gaussian comparison field, not parking, and uses a spatial cutoff distinct from C11. Novelty: KNOWN Gaussian coarse/fine method; UNCHECKED exact cutoff statement. Status: independently checked proof.
Full-space discrete-time nearest-neighbor SRW Green kernel
Independent standard Gaussian input; spatial Euclidean kernel cutoff N

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:5a02b3868a47db55b6c952754e0268e213007ba978b87214b867a12bad064e55","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/5a/5a02b3868a47db55b6c952754e0268e213007ba978b87214b867a12bad064e55.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:55088415a049af5e8a9143cfc14291cb5e0f4cfd2f31ee7339c148e76a5f0314","bundle_entry_key":"i0005-c16","bundle_id":"population.i0005-correlation-energy-and-active-moments-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"parking and comparison fields","draft":"w661/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.particle-hole:spatial-green-gaussian-hole-typical-void-scale-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# I0005-C16 v1: typical Gaussian vacancy scale exceeds mean spacing

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN coarse/fine Gaussian method and
Green asymptotic; UNCHECKED prior appearance of this exact cutoff statement.
This is a comparison field, not the parking process. Its spatial cutoff
differs from C11's time cutoff; no equality of the fields is asserted.

For full-space discrete-time nearest-neighbor SRW on Z^4, let G be its
Green function, k_N(z)=G(z)1{|z|_2<=N}, and xi_z iid standard Gaussians.
Put sigma_N^2=sum_z k_N(z)^2 and

    Y_N(x)=sum_z k_N(x-z)xi_z/sigma_N,
    H_N(x)=1{Y_N(x)>=2 sqrt(log N)}, h_N=E H_N(0).

For every fixed 0<beta<1/sqrt(2),

    P(there is an H_N hole in B_floor(N^beta)) --> 0,

where B is a graph ball. Yet for 1/2<beta<1/sqrt(2), the expected number
of holes in the same ball tends to infinity. In particular mean intensity
does not determine typical nearest-hole distance, even at a polynomial
separation of scales. No active-particle field is defined here.

## Variance and marginal density

Lawler--Limic Theorem 4.3.1 gives
G(z)=(2/pi^2)|z|_2^(-2)+O(|z|_2^(-4)). Squaring and summing over lattice
annuli gives

    sigma_N^2=A log N+O(1),  A=8/pi^2.

Indeed sum_{1<=|z|_2<=N}|z|_2^(-4)=2pi^2 log N+O(1), by comparison
with unit cubes and the integrable derivative error; the sphere area in
four dimensions is 2pi^2. Terms from the Green error are summable. Normal
Mills bounds then give

    h_N=(1+o(1)) N^(-2)/(2 sqrt(2pi log N)).

The mean spacing h_N^(-1/4) is N^(1/2+o(1)). The unnormalized threshold
in the numerator field is

    s_N=2 sqrt(log N) sigma_N=2 sqrt(A) log N+O(1).

## Coarse noise is nearly constant on a smaller ball

Set r=floor(N^beta). Split the numerator field W_N(x) into F_x+C_x,
using respectively the noise sites |z|_2<=2r and |z|_2>2r. These are
independent centered Gaussian components. For all |x|_1<=r and sufficiently
large N, 3r<N, so

    Var(F_x)<=sum_{|w|_2<=3r}G(w)^2<=A beta log N+O(1).

We next show Var(C_x-C_0)<=C uniformly over |x|_1<=r. On the region
where both shifted kernels are inside their cutoff and |z|_2>2r,
the same Green asymptotic and the derivative of |z|^(-2) give

    |G(z-x)-G(z)|<=C r |z|_2^(-3)+C|z|_2^(-4).

Its squared lattice sum is bounded by
C r^2 sum_{|z|>2r}|z|^(-6)+C sum_{|z|>2r}|z|^(-8)<=C.
If exactly one shifted kernel is inside its cutoff, then
N-r<=|z|_2<=N+r. This shell has O(N^3 r) sites and each squared kernel
is O(N^(-4)), giving O(r/N)<=C. Else both kernels vanish. This proves
the asserted uniform increment variance without assuming differentiability
of a random field.

For any fixed epsilon>0, the Gaussian tail bound and a union bound yield

    P(max_{x in B_r}|C_x-C_0|>epsilon log N)
       <=C r^4 exp(-c epsilon^2 (log N)^2) -->0.

Also Var(C_0)<=A log N+O(1), so
P(|C_0|>epsilon log N)<=2N^(-epsilon^2/(2A)+o(1)) tends to zero.
Thus max_{x in B_r} C_x<=2epsilon log N with probability tending to one.

## Fine-noise maximum upper bound

Let u_N=(2sqrt(A)-3epsilon)log N, with epsilon small enough that u_N>0.
The fine variance bound and the cardinality |B_r|=O(N^(4beta)) give

    P(max_{x in B_r}F_x>u_N)
       <=N^[4beta-(2sqrt(A)-3epsilon)^2/(2A beta)+o(1)].

At epsilon=0 the exponent is 4beta-2/beta, which is strictly negative
exactly when beta<1/sqrt(2). Choose a sufficiently small fixed positive
epsilon so it remains negative. Then the fine maximum is at most u_N
with probability tending to one. Combining the two maximum bounds makes
max_{x in B_r}W_N(x)<s_N eventually with probability tending to one.
This proves the claimed vacancy probability.

## Diverging expectation despite the void probability

For beta>1/2, stationarity and the graph-ball count yield

    E sum_{x in B_r}H_N(x)=h_N |B_r|
      =N^(4beta-2+o(1)) -->infinity.

For beta additionally below 1/sqrt(2), the preceding result says the ball
is nevertheless empty with probability tending to one. The rare occupied
configurations account for this divergent expectation. This is an explicit
warning against treating an annealed expected hole count as a typical
spatial count in a logarithmically correlated comparison field.

## Limits of the comparison

The proof gives an upper bound on the probability of finding a hole in
these balls; it gives no matching upper bound on nearest-hole distance.
It does not identify the source parking field with this Gaussian field.
C9's finite-Palm criterion is sufficient, not proved necessary, and neither
a favorable interlacement proxy nor this unfavorable Gaussian proxy decides

[Lem 240 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,L,\epsilon,\delta>0$, and $\fq\in [1,2)$, there exists $c = c(\alpha,L,\delta) > 0$ such that the following holds for sufficiently large $N$. For any $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$, we have
	\[
		\P\bigg(
			\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)
			\Big) \le \delta
		\bigg) \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,,
	\]
for $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)$ as defined by \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L}. The analogous estimate holds likewise for $\bbW_\fq(\mu_{\bG,\sym}(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))$ and $\cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon))$, where the latter is defined by \eqref{e:cM.Lip.union.L.SYM}. 

\begin{proof}
	Throughout this proof, $c$ denotes a constant that depends on $\alpha,L,\delta$, which can change line by line.
	By \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, for $C = C(\alpha)$ as defined therein, we have
	\beq
		\P\bigg(
			\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)) \in \cP_2(\R,C)
		\bigg) \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
We now define
	\[
		S_\delta \equiv
		\Big\{ \mu \in \cP_2(\R,C) : \bbW_\fq(\mu, \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta \Big\}
	\]
(note this differs slightly from the set $S_\delta$ defined in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.lip.trunc.to.ideal}). 
	By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_2(\R,C)$ endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric is compact.
	The set $S_\delta$ is closed with respect to the $\bbW_\fq$ metric, and therefore also compact. We may thus cover $S_\delta$ with finitely many $\bbW_\fq$-balls,
	\[S_\delta = \bigcup_{\mu \in T_\delta} \cB_{\fq,\delta/5}(\mu)
		\,,\]
	where $T_\delta \subseteq S_\delta$ is a finite set depending on only $\fq, \delta$, and
		\[\cB_{q,\delta/5}(\mu) 
		\equiv\bigg\{
			\mu' \in S_\delta : \bbW_\fq(\mu,\mu') \le 
			\frac{\delta}{5}
		\bigg\}\,.\]
	Note that for each $\mu \in S_\delta$, we have
	\begin{align*}
		\bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu) 
		&\ge \bbW_\fq(\mu,\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon))
		- \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \\
		&\ge \delta - \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon))\,,
	\end{align*}
where the last term on the right-hand side above does not depend on $
\mu$, and is $o_N(1)$ by
	Proposition~\ref{p:confinement}. It follows that for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[
		\inf_{\mu \in S_\delta} \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu) \ge 
		\frac{4\delta}{5}\,.
	\]
	For each $\mu \in T_\delta$,  Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound} implies
	\[
		\E \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu\Big)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound}}{\ge} \bigg(\Big[\bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^2 - o_N(1)\Big]_+\bigg)^{1/2}
		\ge \frac{3\delta}{5}
	\]
	for sufficiently large $N$.
	Note that the $o_N(1)$ term above may depend on $\mu$; however, as $T_\delta$ is a finite set independent of $N$, the above estimate can be taken to hold simultaneously for all $\mu \in T_\delta$. By Lemma~\ref{l:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc} combined with a union bound over
$\mu \in T_\delta$, we obtain
	\[
		\P\bigg(
			\min_{\mu \in T_\delta} \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux),\mu\Big)
			\ge \frac{2\delta}{5}
		\bigg)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.tail}}{=} 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
	\]
	(This $c$ depends on $\alpha,L,\delta$ only, as $\epsilon,\fq$ affect only the $N$-independent number of terms $|T_\delta|$ in the union bound.)
	On this event, we further have
	\[\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)), S_\delta\Big)
		\ge \min_{\mu \in T_\delta} \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu\Big) - \frac{\delta}{5}
		\ge 
		\frac{\delta}{5}\,,\]
	and therefore $\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)) \not\in S_\delta$.

PRIVATE AUTHOR-CHECKED DRAFT, no independent review. Let Gamma be a finite group and Q a Gamma-equivariant positive contraction on l^2(Gamma) with 0 < Q < I, and let P_Q be the determinantal probability measure on subsets of Gamma with kernel Q. Let HM(Q) be the harmonic mean of the eigenvalues of Q. Then P_Q stochastically dominates the product Bernoulli measure of density HM(Q), and symmetrically P_Q is dominated by the product measure of density 1 - HM(I - Q). This is strictly weaker than Lyons's Conjecture 5.7 (ICM 2014), which asserts the same with the geometric mean (Fuglede-Kadison determinant) in place of the harmonic mean; the conjecture is the harmonic-to-geometric upgrade, and numerical monotone-coupling linear programs on Z/nZ, n <= 6 (102 random symmetric circulant contractions), satisfy the geometric-mean bound exactly, with density FK(Q) + 0.01 already failing on a tested instance.

body: In vector calculus, Green's theorem relates a line integral around a simple closed curve C to a double integral over the plane region D bounded by C. It is the two-dimensional special case of Stokes' theorem. In one dimension, it is equivalent to the fundamental theorem of calculus. In two dimensions, it is equivalent to the divergence theorem.
title: Green's theorem

A weak joint shape/length limit does not determine conditional shape at a prescribed lattice length. For even n, let L_n be uniform on {1/n,2/n,...,1} and let X_n=0 except at L_n=1/2. Their conditional features at L_n=1/2 are respectively +1 and -1; that atom has mass 1/n. Thus the required transfer must control relative conditional errors, not just a weak mixture limit. Let 0<epsilon<1/2 and 0<p<1, and let F=(1-p)Uniform[0,epsilon]+p Uniform[1-epsilon,1]. Its mean is mu=p+(1/2-p)epsilon. Put r=n epsilon/[2(1-epsilon)]. If F is n-CM, then:

- If np is noninteger, r>=max({np},1-{np}), where {np} denotes its fractional part.
- If np is an integer and n>=2, F is in fact n-CM.

Proof of necessity. In any complete mix define K to be the number of coordinates in the high interval. Since the intervals are disjoint and every marginal has high mass p, E[K]=np. Pathwise,

    (1-epsilon)K <= sum_i X_i <= (1-epsilon)K+n epsilon.

The sum equals n mu=np(1-epsilon)+n epsilon/2, hence |K-np|<=r. Therefore np belongs to the convex hull of the allowed integers in [np-r,np+r] intersect [0,n]. If np is noninteger, this convex hull contains np only if both floor(np) and ceil(np) are allowed. The distances from np to these integers are {np} and 1-{np}; this gives the stated inequality. There is no independence assumption.

Proof of sufficiency when np is an integer k and n>=2. A centered uniform law is n-CM for every n>=2 by the explicit uniform triple plus symmetric pairs in D0007-C001 (even n consists of pairs, odd n one triple plus pairs). Thus choose U_1,...,U_n all uniform on [0,epsilon], with sum n epsilon/2. Add 1-epsilon to exactly k of their coordinates. The resulting sum is n epsilon/2+k(1-epsilon)=n mu. Apply an independent uniform coordinate permutation. Each marginal is the desired mixture F, because every coordinate receives a high label with probability k/n=p.

In the sparse critical law of I0005-C3, now allow any fixed p in (0,1/4]. Let h_t=P(H_t(0)=1). For any fixed b>0 set r_t=floor(bh_t^−1/4), x_t=(r_t,0,0,0), and K_t(x)=sum_{n=0}^t(n+1)p_n(x). Then

The O(1) constant can depend on b and the initial law. Thus simply replacing equation (46)'s infinite-time kernel by a time-t cutoff, even if such a replacement were justified, does not restore bounded decorrelation at the mean hole spacing.

Corollary 1.3, equation (8), gives c/(t+1)≤h_t≤C log(t+2)/(t+1), since EA_t(0)=h_t for the sparse law. In particular h_t→0. Consequently r_t→∞, r_t²=b²h_t^−1/2(1+o(1)), and r_t²/t→0 by the lower density bound. The log-positive branch in I0005-C1 is therefore eventually the ordinary logarithm, giving

K_t(x_t)=(4/π²)log(t/(1+r_t²))+O(1)
=(4/π²)(log t+(1/2)log h_t−2log b)+O(1).

The density bounds imply log h_t=−log t+O(log log(t+2)); inserting them proves the second formula. More precisely, the correction (1/2)log(th_t) is bounded below and at most (1/2)log log(t+2)+O(1).

## Scope of the obstruction

The source's pair bound in d≥5 has an exponential involving log(1/h_t) times a spatially decaying infinite-time kernel. At d=4 the displayed cutoff kernel is already of order log t at the mean spacing, so substituting it into that form yields an uncontrolled order-(log t)^2 exponent. This is a failure of that estimate, not a proof that true hole correlations are that large. Cancellation, conditioned killing, or another argument might still give the missing Palm pair-sum bound.

Multiplying the spacing by (log t)^α for a fixed real α only changes log(t/r_t²) by −2α log log t+O(1); it does not remove the leading logarithm. Moreover, positive density g_t≥c h_t of disjoint isolated-hole balls of radius R_t requires g_t|B_{R_t}|≤1 by translation invariance, hence R_t=O(h_t^−1/4). A divergent positive log factor in R_t conflicts with that geometry. This excludes a radius-only logarithmic repair of the particular isolation argument, not other counterexample constructions.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:a717cab0408ba62fa14a8ae11b44e2c6621727ffa391b3ed98fd0857f08973f1","revision_digest":"sha256:15a2ad445a69ab55806d22082f59eebc9323c12d5deda12a19b4bd4916f684cf","source_id":"owner-own-work:w661:I0005-C4:v1","source_revision":"v1; 2026-10-14T05:23:59.4615090+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: If a linear operator T is bounded from L^{p0} to L^{q0} with norm M0 and from L^{p1} to L^{q1} with norm M1, then for every theta in (0, 1) it is bounded from L^{p_theta} to L^{q_theta} with norm at most M0^{1-theta} M1^{theta}, where the intermediate exponents interpolate harmonically: 1/p_theta = (1-theta)/p0 + theta/p1 and likewise for q. The proof runs through the Hadamard three-lines theorem applied to an analytic family built from the duality pairing. Interpolation converts two endpoint estimates into the whole scale - the engine behind Hausdorff-Young and Young's convolution inequality.
title: Riesz-Thorin Interpolation Theorem

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT, independently checked proof: claude-738954b6 PASS on T421-W706-006 v2, 2026-10-20 11:09. There exist kappa>0,a0>0 such that for every eta>0, epsilon=eta outside sqrt, and fixed H=diag(lambda_1,lambda_2) with 38<lambda_i<38+kappa, ordinary bias-corrected full-batch Adam at beta1=9/10,beta2=999/1000 started with m0=v0=0 and 0<|x_i,0|<eta*a0 in both coordinates approaches a nonzero product two-cycle by parity. Both eta active curvature and eta top preconditioned sharpness tend to 38. Equivalently, any absolutely continuous initialization supported in this small eta-scaled box obeys the conclusion almost surely. The constants are existential; no explicit kappa or a0 bound, arbitrary initialization, or p>1 result is asserted.

p=1:epsilon=eta>0 added outside sqrt
