{"artifact_digest":"sha256:800692cd47180d36b48bc5a16ddadef3ecc1ccc5604665005d3a36ac4b9c1d22","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/80/800692cd47180d36b48bc5a16ddadef3ecc1ccc5604665005d3a36ac4b9c1d22.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:8fb7bff6ab0721702779e931d401d4bb65fef1493a35724caa6d8b9c7bdb3a65","bundle_entry_key":"standard-adam-entry","bundle_id":"population.t421-standard-adam-p1-entry-and-center-graph-002","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"deterministic adaptive optimization","draft":"w706/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.adam:adam-bias-corrected-standard-moment-near-threshold-p1-entry-w706","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"T421-W706-006 v2; target 1; kind narrowed; rung proof (unaudited).

THE STATEMENT
There exist kappa>0 and a0>0 such that for every eta>0, epsilon=eta,
H=diag(lambda_1,lambda_2) with 38<lambda_i<38+kappa, and standard m0=v0=0
with 0<|x_i,0|<eta*a0, ordinary bias-corrected full-batch Adam at
beta1=9/10,beta2=999/1000 approaches a nonzero product two-cycle by parity.
Both eta times the active curvature and eta times top preconditioned
sharpness tend to 38 as t->infinity. The eigenvalues are fixed during a run.
This does not assert arbitrary initialization or any p>1 behavior. kappa
and a0 are existential, not numerical bounds.

PRIMARY THEOREM USED
van den Berg, Hetebrij and Rink, More on the parameterization method for
center manifolds, arXiv:2003.00701, Theorem 1.1 pp.4-5 and Remark 1.4 p.6;
equivalently their arXiv:1905.00264 Theorem 2.1 pp.5-6.
The finite-dimensional special case used here: a C3 map fixing zero with
derivative diag(I_c,A_s), spectral radius(A_s)<1, has a locally invariant
C3 center graph tangent to the center subspace, parameterized by its center
coordinates (choose k_c=0). To match the theorem, choose an adapted norm
with ||A_s||<1; A_c=I satisfies all spectral-gap inequalities for n<=3;
the unstable space is zero. Subtract the linearization and multiply the
remaining O(||z||^2) nonlinearity by a smooth compact cutoff. Its derivative
supremum tends to zero as support shrinks, exactly as Remark 1.4 requires.
The cutoff changes nothing in the eventual local domain. This applies to
the parameter-augmented map (delta'=delta), so no separate parameter theorem
or stable-foliation theorem is needed.

SCALAR PROOF
Write b=9/10,d=999/1000,c=1/19,D=1/38. For scalar curvature lambda set
 X=x/eta, M=m/(eta lambda), V=v/(eta lambda)^2,
 rho=epsilon/(eta lambda)=1/lambda, delta=D-rho.
For X!=0 set y=|X|, q=M/X, r=V/X^2, and add clocks
alpha=b^(t+1), sigma=d^(t+1). Define u=dr+1-d, h=bq+1-b and
 A=1-h/[(1-alpha)*(rho+y*sqrt(u/(1-sigma)))].
On the open region A<0 this is the EXACT corrected recursion:
 (y,q,r,alpha,sigma)'=(-Ay,h/A,u/A^2,b alpha,d sigma).             (1)
All square roots and denominators are regular on a full open neighborhood
of z*=(0,-c,1,0,0,delta=0): u=1, rho=D>0, A=-1 there.
Thus (1), augmented by delta'=delta, extends C-infinity across y=0 locally.

The fixed-delta Jacobian at z* is
 [[1,0,0,0,0],[-4,.9,0,2/19,0],
  [152,-342/5,.999,-4,0],[0,0,0,.9,0],[0,0,0,0,.999]],
where the decimal entries denote the EXACT fractions 9/10 and 999/1000.
The center directions in (y,q,r,alpha,sigma;delta) are
 v_y=(1,-40,2888000,0,0;0),
 v_delta=(0,40,-2888000,0,0;1).
Their eigenvalue is 1; the other four eigenvalues are b,b,d,d. These
identities and invertibility are checked exactly in scripts/verify_center.py.

The subspace alpha=sigma=0 is invariant. Apply the primary center-graph
theorem to the restriction to this subspace with delta appended. Choose
center coordinates exactly (y,delta), since stable directions have zero
y and delta components. This gives q=Q(y,delta), r=R(y,delta), clocks=0,
with derivatives Q_y=-40,Q_delta=40,R_y=2888000,R_delta=-2888000 at zero.
View the same graph as an invariant center graph of the full clock map.
Denote its scalar center update by f_delta(y).

In coordinates e=(q-Q(y,delta),r-R(y,delta),alpha,sigma), the map has form
 y'=y B(y,e,delta),  e'=T(y,e,delta),  delta'=delta,
with T(y,0,delta)=0. At zero D_e T has eigenvalues b,b,d,d. Choose an
adapted e-norm and then shrink the neighborhood so
 ||T(y,e,delta)||<=theta||e||, theta<1.                           (2)
This follows from the mean-value formula and continuity of D_e T; no
phase projection or foliation theorem is being invoked.

We next identify the exact center normal form. The y=0 graph has y'=0,
so f_delta(0)=0. The extended full map has the EXACT fixed branch
 (y,q,r,alpha,sigma)=(delta,-c,1,0,0)                            (3)
for every sufficiently small real delta, including negative delta in the
smooth extension. Every such fixed point lies on our graph: its transverse
coordinate would otherwise satisfy e=T(y,e,delta) with ||e||<=theta||e||,
contradicting theta<1. Thus f_delta(delta)=delta.
Exact differentiation on the graph gives
 f_delta(y)=y+1444 delta*y-1444 y^2+O((|y|+|delta|)^3).
For example the y^2 coefficient is -76+(171/5)*(-40)=-1444,
and the delta*y coefficient is 76+(171/5)*40=1444.
These are exact symbolic checks, not floating-point estimates.
Two applications of Hadamard's lemma therefore give the EXACT factorization
 f_delta(y)=y+y(delta-y) K(y,delta), K(0,0)=1444,                 (4)
where K is C1. Choose a small interval |y|,|delta|<r_* on which K is
positive and f_delta is strictly increasing in y. For 0<delta<r_*/4,
f_delta maps (0,delta) into itself above the diagonal and (delta,r_*)
into itself below the diagonal. Every positive center orbit in that
interval consequently converges to delta.

NOW PROVE NEARBY ATTRACTION DIRECTLY, RATHER THAN ASSUMING A FOLIATION.
Smoothness of B implies, on a sufficiently small product neighborhood,
 |B(y,e,delta)-B(y,0,delta)|<=L||e||.
Along any orbit that remains there, (2) yields ||e_n||<=theta^n||e_0||,
so its amplitude satisfies
 y_(n+1)=f_delta(y_n)+y_n E_n,
 |E_n|<=L theta^n||e_0||.                                     (5)
The original map has A<0 throughout the neighborhood, hence y_n>0.

The neighborhood is forward invariant after shrinking the allowed initial
box. Indeed monotonicity and f_delta(delta)=delta imply
 f_delta(y)<=max(y,delta) for y>0 in the local interval. Equation (5) gives
 y_n<=max(y_0,delta)*exp[L||e_0||/(1-theta)].                    (6)
Choose y_0,delta<r_*/4 and ||e_0|| small enough that the exponential is <2
and the transverse coordinates remain strictly inside the local domain.
Induction using (2),(5),(6) gives y_n<r_*/2 and the required transverse
bound for all n. Apply the estimates on a slightly larger product box
to avoid circularity at the boundary; all its images are defined by the
cutoff center graph, which agrees with the original map on the smaller box.

For completeness, summable errors in (5) give y_n->delta, not just boundedness.
Fix 0<h<delta with delta+h<r_*/2. On y<=delta-h, for all sufficiently
large n the multiplier in (5),(4) is >=1+h*min(K)/2. On y>=delta+h
it is <=1-h*min(K)/2. These inequalities force finite exit from either
outer region. Moreover f_delta maps [delta-h,delta+h] strictly inside
itself at the endpoints: its endpoint margins are positive by (4).
For n large, the perturbation |y_n E_n| is smaller than these margins
and smaller than h/2. Strict monotonicity of f_delta prevents a step
from jumping across the entire middle interval. Hence the orbit enters
and remains in [delta-h,delta+h]. Since h is arbitrary, y_n->delta.
Then e_n->0 and continuity of Q,R imply q_n->-c,r_n->1,clocks->0.
This proves a uniform local positive-amplitude tube of attraction for
all sufficiently small delta>0. The tube may contain arbitrarily small
positive y; no lower bound depending on delta was assumed.

STANDARD ZERO MOMENTS ENTER THIS TUBE.
At m0=v0=0 the ratio values are q0=r0=0; clocks alpha0=b,sigma0=d.
Analyze first the extended boundary orbit y=delta=0. For q in [-c,0],
h=bq+1-b lies in [c,1-b] and
 A_t=1-h/[(1-b^(t+1))*D]<=-1.
Its q update maps [-c,0] into itself. Direct differentiation gives
 d(h/A_t)/dq=b/A_t^2<=b.
At q=-c the discrepancy from -c is 2c*b^(t+1)/(1+b^(t+1)). Thus
 |q_t+c|<=b^t*c+2c*t*b^t ->0.                                  (7)
Also 0<=r_t<=1 because r'=(d r+1-d)/A_t^2, and
 |r_(t+1)-1|<=d|r_t-1|+|1-A_t^(-2)| ->0.                       (8)
The convergence in (8) follows by splitting the geometric convolution
of its vanishing forcing into a finite initial part and a uniformly
small tail. The clocks vanish, so this boundary orbit approaches z*.

Choose a FINITE N placing it strictly inside the local tube's transverse
and amplitude upper bounds. Every preceding denominator is strictly
positive, u>=1-d>0, sigma_t<1, and A_t<=-1. By continuity of this
FINITE composition, some delta0>0 and a0>0 ensure that all physical
0<delta<delta0,0<y_initial<a0 have A<0 through time N and land inside
the same tube with y_N>0. Equations (2)-(8) then prove convergence to
(3). This establishes entry from actual time-0 ordinary bias correction,
without a warm-start or a stable-foliation hypothesis.

TWO COORDINATES AND CURVATURE.
Shrink delta0 further if needed and choose kappa>0 with
0<D-1/lambda<delta0 whenever 38<lambda<38+kappa.
The scalar maps are decoupled, with identical clocks. Each coordinate
converges by parity to |x_i|=eta*(D-1/lambda_i)>0,
m_i=opposite-sign lambda_i*|x_i|/19 and v_i=lambda_i^2*x_i^2.
Since the bias corrections tend to one,
sqrt(vhat_i)+epsilon ->eta*lambda_i*(D-1/lambda_i)+eta
                       =eta*lambda_i*D.
Each preconditioned eigenvalue therefore tends to 1/(eta D)=38/eta.
The active curvature is their Rayleigh average, and the limiting gradients
in both coordinates are nonzero. It and their maximum have the same limit.

WHAT WAS CHECKED / LIMITS
scripts/verify_center.py checks the complete augmented Jacobian, its spectrum,
both center tangent equations, the quadratic coefficients, the exact fixed
branch and boundary derivative. scripts/check_entry_cases.py checks 96 exact
physical/ratio identities and 1050 exact boundary invariance cases. Those
finite checks corroborate the identities; the formulas above prove them
on their full domains. Initial zero coordinates violate the nonzero-cycle
and top-curvature conclusion (they stay dormant with eta curvature=lambda).
lambda=38 collapses the cycle; below 38 the purported positive amplitude
is negative. Exact beta2=.999 is stronger than this local argument needs:
the center argument only needs 0<d<1; it is retained to match the target.
Numerical examples in logs/entry_numerics.json are diagnostics, not bounds.
Lean checks previously timed out; this is not a Lean-checked proof.

Hardest still-open part of target 1: p>1 from standard initialization,
and the remaining p=1 eigenvalue/initial-amplitude range. This theorem
does not prove or disprove o(1)-tracking there.

OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited), claim w730-T355-C009 v1; novelty unestablished.

Let d,q be finite positive integers. Let H be constant SPD with eigenvalues
in [m,M], m>0, and let sigma,D,kappa>=0. Let 0<rho<2 and

    0<eta<=rho/M, gamma=min(m,M(2-rho)/rho),
    eta kappa^2 <= gamma/2, B=I-eta H.

An adapted recursion starts from deterministic u0,v0 and satisfies

    u_{k+1}=u_k-eta xi_k^u,  v_{k+1}=B v_k-eta xi_k^v,
    E[xi_k^u | F_k]=0, E[xi_k^v | F_k]=0,
    E[|xi_k^v|^2 | F_k] <= sigma^2 tr H + kappa^2 |v_k|^2,
    E[|xi_k^u|^2 | F_k] <= sigma^2 D^2 |v_k|^2.           (1)

The filtration contains the state before the kth increment. No iid,
symmetry or moments beyond these conditional second moments are required
for the oracle estimate. If the target's on-manifold covariance identity
is desired, additionally impose Cov(xi^v | state (u,0))=sigma^2 H.
The tangent condition then forces tangent and cross covariance to vanish
there, giving sigma^2 diag(0,H), proportional to the population Hessian.

Define V=|v0|, alpha=sigma^2 tr H, and

    c_V=2(alpha+kappa^2 V^2)/gamma,
    R_T=sigma^2 D^2 (V^2/gamma+T c_V).

For F in C_b^2(R^{d+q}), let F_uu,F_uv,F_vv be the global operator-norm
bounds of its second derivative blocks. For every T>=0,

    sup_{integer 0<=K<=floor(T/eta^2)}
      |E F(u_K,v_K)-F(u0,B^K v0)| <= eta C(T,V),
    C(T,V)=F_uu R_T/2+F_uv sqrt(c_V R_T)+F_vv c_V/2.    (2)

Thus a=1, with explicit constants, in a larger normal-noise class than
C007's uniformly bounded conditional covariance class. This is not a
claim that the new constants improve those of C007 when kappa=0.

When v0=0, (2) compares against the constant slow limit (u0,0) at every
index. For general fixed v0 and F_v=sup ||D_v F||, comparison against
(u0,0) has bound eta(C(T,V)+F_v) at every integer

    ceil(log(max(1,V/eta))/(eta gamma))<=K<=floor(T/eta^2).

An empty interval covers no indices. The initial-layer cutoff is the
same deterministic contraction argument as C008; it is not a logarithm
in the weak-error constant. No comparison against (u0,0) is asserted at
K=0 from nonzero v0 for arbitrary ambient observables.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:244728a849d0a0273035f52e0137197699edcca82854a8bce162cb3d0dec94bb","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/24/244728a849d0a0273035f52e0137197699edcca82854a8bce162cb3d0dec94bb.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:6518fe05d8bbe55bac96f1ab89d543b62784c45796ef59251e53ff0c15072f06","bundle_entry_key":"w730-t355-c009-normal-variance-growth","bundle_id":"population.w730-t355-normal-variance-growth-v1","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"probability","draft":"w730/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.stochastic_approximation:w730_t355_c009_normal_variance_growth","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Normal variance growth: explicit flat-manifold slow-clock weak estimate

Claim w730-T355-C009 v1. Kind: narrowed. Target: 1.
Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty and literature priority unestablished.

## Statement

Let d,q be finite positive integers. Let H be constant SPD with eigenvalues
in [m,M], m>0, and let sigma,D,kappa>=0. Let 0<rho<2 and

    0<eta<=rho/M, gamma=min(m,M(2-rho)/rho),
    eta kappa^2 <= gamma/2, B=I-eta H.

An adapted recursion starts from deterministic u0,v0 and satisfies

    u_{k+1}=u_k-eta xi_k^u,  v_{k+1}=B v_k-eta xi_k^v,
    E[xi_k^u | F_k]=0, E[xi_k^v | F_k]=0,
    E[|xi_k^v|^2 | F_k] <= sigma^2 tr H + kappa^2 |v_k|^2,
    E[|xi_k^u|^2 | F_k] <= sigma^2 D^2 |v_k|^2.           (1)

The filtration contains the state before the kth increment. No iid,
symmetry or moments beyond these conditional second moments are required
for the oracle estimate. If the target's on-manifold covariance identity
is desired, additionally impose Cov(xi^v | state (u,0))=sigma^2 H.
The tangent condition then forces tangent and cross covariance to vanish
there, giving sigma^2 diag(0,H), proportional to the population Hessian.

Define V=|v0|, alpha=sigma^2 tr H, and

    c_V=2(alpha+kappa^2 V^2)/gamma,
    R_T=sigma^2 D^2 (V^2/gamma+T c_V).

For F in C_b^2(R^{d+q}), let F_uu,F_uv,F_vv be the global operator-norm
bounds of its second derivative blocks. For every T>=0,

    sup_{integer 0<=K<=floor(T/eta^2)}
      |E F(u_K,v_K)-F(u0,B^K v0)| <= eta C(T,V),
    C(T,V)=F_uu R_T/2+F_uv sqrt(c_V R_T)+F_vv c_V/2.    (2)

Thus a=1, with explicit constants, in a larger normal-noise class than
C007's uniformly bounded conditional covariance class. This is not a
claim that the new constants improve those of C007 when kappa=0.

When v0=0, (2) compares against the constant slow limit (u0,0) at every
index. For general fixed v0 and F_v=sup ||D_v F||, comparison against
(u0,0) has bound eta(C(T,V)+F_v) at every integer

    ceil(log(max(1,V/eta))/(eta gamma))<=K<=floor(T/eta^2).

An empty interval covers no indices. The initial-layer cutoff is the
same deterministic contraction argument as C008; it is not a logarithm
in the weak-error constant. No comparison against (u0,0) is asserted at
K=0 from nonzero v0 for arbitrary ambient observables.

## New normal-moment estimate

Put r=||B||<1. For each eigenvalue lambda in [m,M],
1-|1-eta lambda|=min(eta lambda,2-eta lambda)>=eta gamma.
Hence 1-r^2>=1-r>=eta gamma>0, in particular eta gamma<=1.
Let b_k=B^k v0 and w_k=v_k-b_k. Conditional centering gives E w_k=0.
The finite second moments used here follow inductively from (1).
Consequently E|v_k|^2=|b_k|^2+E|w_k|^2. Writing s_k=E|w_k|^2,

    s_{k+1} <= r^2 s_k + eta^2(alpha+kappa^2 E|v_k|^2)
             <= a s_k + eta^2(alpha+kappa^2 V^2),
    a=r^2+eta^2 kappa^2, s_0=0.

This is the extra term absent from the uniform-covariance proof. The
stated step condition gives 0<=a<=1-eta gamma/2<1. Summing the finite
geometric series yields, for every k>=0,

    s_k <= eta^2(alpha+kappa^2 V^2)/(1-a) <= eta c_V,
    E|v_k|^2 <= r^{2k} V^2+eta c_V.                     (3)

No commutation of random covariance matrices with H is assumed. Only
the scalar trace bound in (1) is used. The k=0 empty sum is zero.

## Passing the new estimate to the weak bound

The centered increments of u form a square-integrable martingale.
Distinct increments are orthogonal in expectation: condition the later
increment on its past, which contains the earlier increment. Thus for
K eta^2<=T, (1) and (3) give

    E|u_K-u0|^2
      <=eta^2 sigma^2 D^2 sum_{j=0}^{K-1} E|v_j|^2
      <=eta^2 sigma^2 D^2 V^2/(1-r^2)
         +K eta^3 sigma^2 D^2 c_V
      <=eta R_T.                                      (4)

Also E(u_K-u0)=0. Fix K and its deterministic b=b_K. Taylor expansion
in u at fixed b gives

    |E F(u_K,b)-F(u0,b)| <= F_uu eta R_T/2.

Taylor expansion in w_K gives a remainder bounded in expectation by
F_vv eta c_V/2. For its linear term, E w_K=0 lets us subtract the
constant D_v F(u0,b), leaving

    |E[(D_v F(u_K,b)-D_v F(u0,b)) dot w_K]|
      <=F_uv sqrt(E|u_K-u0|^2 E|w_K|^2)
      <=eta F_uv sqrt(R_T c_V).

This is Cauchy-Schwarz for correlated variables; no independence of
u_K and w_K is used. Adding the three bounds proves (2). All constants
are finite and independent of eta in the stated range. sigma=0,
kappa=0, D=0, V=0 and T=0 introduce no division by these quantities.
The post-layer comparison follows from ||B^K v0||<=exp(-eta gamma K)V
and the global derivative bound F_v, with the cases V=0 and V<=eta
handled by contraction alone.

## An actual nonnegative sample-loss family beyond C007

Let A:R^d -> R^{q x q} be C1 with A^T A=H and
sup_u sum_i ||A_i(u)||_op^2<=D^2. Let z have mean zero and covariance I_q;
let zeta be independent of z with probabilities 1/2 at -1 and +1.
Fresh iid pairs are independent of the past. Fix 0<tau<1 and define

    ell_{z,zeta}(u,v)
       = (1+tau zeta)/2 * |A(u)v + sigma z/(1+tau zeta)|^2.

Every sample loss is nonnegative and differentiable. Its expectation is
v^T H v/2 + sigma^2 q/[2(1-tau^2)], so its minimizing manifold and
Hessian are exactly the desired flat manifold and diag(0,H).
Differentiating A^T A=H shows v^T A_i^T A v=0. The centered gradient
components therefore are

    xi^u_i = sigma z^T A_i(u)v,
    xi^v = tau zeta H v + sigma A(u)^T z.

Independence and centering cancel the cross term, giving

    E[|xi^v|^2 | (u,v)] = sigma^2 tr H + tau^2 |Hv|^2
                          <=sigma^2 tr H + tau^2 M^2 |v|^2,
    E[|xi^u|^2 | (u,v)] <=sigma^2 D^2 |v|^2.

Thus the theorem applies with kappa=tau M. At v=0 the full gradient
covariance is sigma^2 diag(0,H). For nonzero v the normal covariance is
sigma^2 H+tau^2 Hv v^T H. Its trace is unbounded as |v| grows, so no
single uniform normal covariance bound of the C007 form covers this
whole state space. This demonstrates added scope with actual sample
losses, not merely an abstract oracle. The slow limit remains constant.

## Stability warning and scope

Even the usual deterministic window eta M<2 need not stabilize the
multiplicative normal second moment. For scalar H=1, tau=1/2, eta=9/5,
its second-moment coefficient is
(1-eta)^2+eta^2 tau^2=29/20>1, despite eta<2.
This is a warning about moments at that step size, not a counterexample
to a small-eta asymptotic statement for bounded observables. The extra
condition here is sufficient and is not claimed optimal.

General curved manifolds, nonquadratic population losses and invariant
laws remain outside the result. Literature priority and all claims of
novelty are unresolved. The independent reviewer should check the
normal recurrence coefficient a, its stability margin, and the actual
sample-loss gradient calculation first. Let w: {0,1,...} -> {0,1,...} be a deterministic nondecreasing function with

    limsup_(n -> infinity) w(n)/sqrt(log n) < 1/sqrt(C).

For any fixed integer y_0, almost surely no geodesic ray has a tail entirely in

    T_w(y_0) = {(x,y) in Z^2: |y-y_0| <= w(|x|)}.

Proof. For R=2^k set W=w(2R), m=m(W), and J=floor(R/(m+1)). Use J slabs with left columns A_j=R+j(m+1), 0 <= j < J. Their endpoints lie between R and 2R, and all tube vertices there have height within W of y_0. By Lemma 2 the required edge sets are disjoint. Therefore

    P(no trap among these J slabs) = (1-q_W)^J <= exp(-J q_W).

Put L=limsup w(n)/sqrt(log n). Choose a number theta strictly between C L^2 and 1. For all sufficiently large R, C(W+1)^2 <= theta log R. Thus q_W >= R^(-theta). Also W+1 <= D sqrt(log R) for some finite D and all large R, so

    J >= R/[2(K+1)(W+1)]

for all sufficiently large R. Hence J q_W >= c R^(1-theta)/sqrt(log R) for some c>0. The no-trap probabilities are summable over dyadic k. By the first Borel-Cantelli lemma, almost surely every sufficiently distant positive dyadic annulus contains a trap. Reflection gives the same conclusion on the negative x side. Independence BETWEEN annuli is not needed.

Suppose a geodesic ray has a tail in T_w(y_0). For each M, the part of this tube with |x| <= M is a finite vertex set. An injective ray eventually leaves it permanently. Nearest-neighbor steps prevent infinitely many switches between the two sides after that departure. Consequently the x coordinate tends to +infinity or -infinity.

Consider the +infinity case and any sufficiently distant trapped slab with columns A and A+m, beyond the beginning of the confined tail. Choose an index at column A and a later first index at column A+m, then choose the last column-A index before that arrival. Between the chosen indices the x coordinate is in [A,A+m], by the nearest-neighbor property. The entire subpath is therefore in the height-W strip. It is a finite geodesic crossing forbidden by Lemma 1. The negative-side argument follows by reflection. QED.

The assertion excludes all rays on the probability-one trap event; it is not merely an assertion about one preselected random ray.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:175bff8bc57c3f6c71ef4d5776f74f54a6d8366f39b726ee67970a79a7faf19c","revision_digest":"sha256:15afe5a66a7e023a64918d9e2cb5906d8b4b2e5d3c38b6f1f88c578a9ec9c660","source_id":"owner-probability-campaign:w390:P0117:2026-10-10","source_revision":"author-proof-v1-pending-independent-review-w392","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma 15 of arXiv:2607.06428, 'Impact of spinning on the early-warning signs in non-Markovian stochastic systems'] Let $H\in(0,1)$ and $(x_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be a solution to \eqref{eq:fast system simplified} in the setting \nameref{S1}. Then, for any $\delta>0$, there is a local regime $|A(\lambda)|>\delta$ in which $S_x(\delta)$ has power-law behavior with exponent $-2$ meaning  
    $$\frac{\txtd \log(S_x(\delta))}{\txtd \log(|A(\lambda)|)} = -2.$$
    Furthermore, for $\lambda\to\lambda^*$ we have
    $$S_x(\delta)\xrightarrow{\lambda\to\lambda^*}\sigma^2\Gamma(2H+1)\sin(\pi H)|\delta|^{-1-2H}.$$

Let(U,V) be centered jointly Gaussian with unit variances and correlation0<=sigma<1; put tau=sqrt(1-sigma^2). Fix real p>=0 and q with p+q>=0. For lambda>0 let A_lambda={|U|<=lambda|V|}, M(lambda)=E[|U|^p|V|^q 1_A_lambda], and S(lambda)=E[sgn(UV)|U|^p|V|^q 1_A_lambda]. The integrand on V=0 is defined as0 (a null set); |U|^0=1. These expectations are finite and continuously differentiable on(0,infinity). Define mu_+^2=(1+lambda^2+2 sigma lambda)/tau^2, mu_-^2=(1+lambda^2-2 sigma lambda)/tau^2, D=p+q+2, and J_D=integral_0^infinity t^(D-1)exp(-t^2/2)dt. Then Mprime(lambda)=lambda^p J_D/(pi tau)[mu_-^(-D)+mu_+^(-D)] and Sprime(lambda)=lambda^p J_D/(pi tau)[mu_-^(-D)-mu_+^(-D)]. In particular S(lambda)>=0; if p+q=2, J_D=2. This is Corollaries3.3-3.4 pp9-10 of2101.03540, with the explicit additional restriction p>=0; negative q such as p3,q-1 are allowed.

[Corollary eq:expected-max of arXiv:2607.14087, 'Stochastic Domination of Gaussian Maxima: A Resolution of the Weak Simplex Conjecture'] \label[corollary]{cor:mean-width}
Let $S$ be an $m\times m$ positive-semidefinite matrix with $S_{ii}\leq1$,
and let $Y\sim\mathcal N(0,S)$.  Then
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb E\max_iY_i
  \leq \mathbb E\max_i\xi_i^\triangle
  =\sqrt{\frac{m}{m-1}}\,\mathbb E\max_i Z_i,
\end{equation}
where $\xi^\triangle\sim\mathcal N(0,G_\triangle)$.  Equality holds if and only if
$S=G_\triangle$.

Consequently, among convex hulls of $m$ points contained in the Euclidean unit
ball of $\mathbb R^d$, for every $d\geq m-1$, the regular $(m-1)$-simplex uniquely
maximizes mean width, up to rotation and relabeling. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Gaussian maxima and the Simplex Mean Width Conjecture

[Cor 195 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, let $p^\sigma\equiv p^\sigma(\bXi)$ denote the empirical averages
	\[
	\frac1M\sum_{a\le M}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\ind \Big\{
	X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a)
	\notin  [-\trK,\trK)\Big\}\,.
	\]
Similarly, let $p^\Ising\equiv p^\Ising(\bXi)$ denote the empirical average
	\[
	\frac1N\sum_{i\le N}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\ind \Big\{
	X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i)
	\notin  [-\trK,\trK)\Big\}\,.
	\]
Then $p^\sigma(\bXi) \le o_{\trK}(1)$
for all $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$, with probability
at least $1- \exp(-N^{1/2})$.

\begin{proof}
Let $\bar{p}^\sigma$ be defined as $p^\sigma$, but with $[-\trK+1,\trK-1)$ in place of $[-\trK,\trK)$.
Let $f:\R\to\R$ be the Lipschitz function defined by
	\[f(x)=\begin{cases}
	0 & \textup{if $|x|\le \trK-1$,}\\
	1 & \textup{if $|x|\ge \trK$,}\\
		|x|-(\trK-1)
		&\textup{if $\trK-1
			\le |x| \le \trK$}\,.
	\end{cases}\]
Since $\ind\{x\notin[-\trK,\trK)\} \le f(x)
\le \ind\{x\notin[-\trK+1,\trK-1)\} 
$, for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$ we have
	\[p^\sigma(\bXi)
	\le
	F^\sigma(\bXi)
	\equiv
	\frac1M
	\sum_{a\le M}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	f(X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a))
	\le \bar{p}^\sigma(\bXi)
	\,.
	\]
We first argue that the \emph{annealed} expectation of $\bar{p}^\sigma$ is small for each $\sigma$. Note that since $\vX^{\trunc,\RomI:\RomIII}$ is frozen upon leaving $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ (Definition~\ref{d:trunc}), the probability that $\vX^{\trunc,\RomI:\RomIII}(q_d,a)$ lies outside $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ is maximized at time $d=\dmax$. From the spatial rerandomization (Definition~\ref{d:rerand}), this is the same as the probability that $\vY^{\RomI:\RomIII}(q_d)$ lies outside $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ at time $d=\dmax$. This (annealed) probability can be bounded using the proof of  Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}: recall from \eqref{e:A.H} that the event $A(H)$ has probability tending to zero as $H\to\infty$. On the complement of $A(H)$, the paths
$\bar{D}^\RomI$,
$Y^\RomII$, $Y^\RomIII$, $Y^\Ising$
are all $\gamma$-H\"older with H\"older norm $O(H)$, and in particular the maximum deviation of each path must be $O(H)$.
Moreover, since $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges uniformly to zero, the discrepancy between $\bar{D}^\RomI$ and $Y^\RomI$ converges uniformly to zero, so we can conclude that the maximum deviation of $Y^\RomI$ is also $O(H)$.
If we take $H$ to be a small constant multiple of $\trK$, then we conclude that $\E[\bar{p}^\sigma(\bXi)] \le o_{\trK}(1)$ for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$. A similar argument gives 
$\E[\bar{p}^\Ising(\bXi)] \le o_{\trK}(1)$. 

The above implies that the annealed expectation of each $F^\sigma$ is also small. It remains to show that $F^\sigma$ is highly concentrated about this expectation. For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$,
it follows by Corollary~\ref{c:conc.empir.avg} 
that $F^\sigma$ is $(L^{O(1)}/(\delta N^{1/2}))$-Lipschitz on the set $U_\MAX$. It follows by 
Assumption~\ref{a:params} that this Lipschitz constant is very small, for instance,
	\[
	\frac{L^{O(1)}}{\delta N^{1/2}}
	\ll \frac{1}{N^{1/3}}\,.
	\]
By the Kirszbraun extension theorem, there exists a function $\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)$ which agrees with $F^\sigma$ for $\bXi\in U_\MAX$, but such that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is $(1/N^{1/3})$-Lipschitz on the entire space. 
It follows by standard concentration bounds (see e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}) that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is highly concentrated about its mean $\E[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)]$. We finally bound
	\[
	\E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	\le \E\Big[F^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	+ \E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi);(U_\MAX)^c\Big]
	\le 
	\E\Big[F^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	+\bigg\{ \E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)^2\Big]
	\P\Big((U_\MAX)^c \Big)
	\bigg\}^{1/2}
	\le o_{\trK}(1)\,.
	\]
In the last step, we used that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is Lipschitz so its second moment must be bounded, while  \eqref{e.MAX.bound} implies that $\P((U_\MAX)^c)$ is very small. This proves the claim for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, and a similar argum (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:partial_coupling of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite graph, $p_e\in(0,1), x_e>0$ for each $e\in E$. Let $\Omega = \{0,1\}^E$, $\Sigma \subset \Omega$ and $f:\Omega\to 2^{\Sigma}$ be defined by $f(\omega)= \Sigma^{\downarrow}(\omega):=\{\eta \in \Sigma\mid \eta \subset \omega\}$ and
	\[\rho[\omega] = \mathbb{P}_{p}[\omega], ~\forall \omega\in \Omega, ~\gamma[\eta]= \mathbb{P}_{\frac{x}{p+x}}[\eta \mid \Sigma]\propto 
   \displaystyle \prod_{e \in \eta} \frac{x_e}{p_e} , ~\forall \eta\in \Sigma. \]
   	Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$ is $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta] \propto \prod_{e\in \eta} x_e$. 
        For each $\omega\in\Omega$ with $\mathscr{P}_\Omega[\omega] \neq 0$, the  conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega]
        = \mathbb{P}_{\frac{x}{p+x}}[\;\cdot \mid \Sigma^{\downarrow}(\omega)]$. 
        \item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$ is $\mathscr{P}_\Omega= \mathscr{P}_{\Sigma} \cup \mathbb{P}_p$.
        For each $\eta\in\Sigma$ with $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta]\neq 0$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \eta] = \mathbb{P}_p \cup \delta_{\eta}$, Bernoulli percolation on $E$ with parameter $(p_e)_{e\in E}$ conditioned on all edges in $\eta$ being open.
    \end{enumerate}
title: Proposition prop:partial_coupling of arXiv:2506.10765

Method: Forced network urn convergence and diffusion scaling structural argument Result: A complete fixed-step classification follows. On any event Z_n->z, the update forces X_n to converge to a binary vector x and hence eventually equal it. The bounded martingale-difference strong law gives x=Qz. The update limit gives z=(r x+f p)/(r+f). A binary coordinate of Qz can equal0 or1 only when all its positive-weight predecessors have the same x-value and matching p-value. Irreducibility then forces x and p to be the all-zero or all-one vector. Conversely if p=0, the positive stationary vector pi gives E[pi.Z_n]=(1-f)^n E[pi.Z_0], and Markov plus Borel-Cantelli yields Z_n->0; p=1 follows by complementing. Check: The proof needs no conditional independence. The strong law follows from summable variances of martingale increments divided by n, then Kronecker. The maximum principle can also be checked by propagating the set of zero coordinates backwards through irreducibility. Obstruction: This resolves the fixed-step convergence subquestion under the stated assumptions, but not the whole diffusion question. body: In mathematics, the Riemann series theorem, also called the Riemann rearrangement theorem, named after 19th-century German mathematician Bernhard Riemann, says that if an infinite series of real numbers is conditionally convergent, then its terms can be arranged in a permutation so that the new series converges to an arbitrary real number, and rearranged such that the new series diverges. This implies that a series of real numbers is absolutely convergent if and only if it is unconditionally convergent.
title: Riemann series theorem

body:
Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and f_n measurable. (a) If f_n >= 0 for every n then integral sum_n f_n dmu = sum_n integral f_n dmu in [0, infinity], with no integrability hypothesis. (b) If sum_n integral |f_n| dmu < infinity then sum_n f_n converges absolutely mu-almost everywhere, the sum is in L^1(mu), and integral sum_n f_n dmu = sum_n integral f_n dmu. The hypothesis in (b) is on the sum of the integrals of the ABSOLUTE VALUES; convergence of sum_n integral f_n alone is not enough. Failure: on R with Lebesgue measure let f_n = 1_{[n, n+1]} - 1_{[n+1, n+2]} for n >= 0. Each integral f_n = 0 so sum_n integral f_n = 0, but the partial sums telescope to 1_{[0,1]} - 1_{[N+1, N+2]}, so sum_n f_n = 1_{[0,1]} pointwise off the integer endpoints, with integral 1. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.15 and its corollary]
(a) f_n >= 0 measurable
(b) sum_n integral |f_n| dmu < infinity

[Theo 6 of arXiv:2609.02261, 'Quantization and process'] Let $F\in D_h (\R^{2n})$.   
     
       i) The expression,

       
  \be  {\rm Op}_h^{\rm Wick}(F) =
  (2 \pi h)^{-2n} \int _{\R^{4n} }  \Pi _{X h} 
   F^{\rm ext}(Y, X)  \Pi _{Y h} dX  dY\ee 
   defines a bounded operator in     $L^2 (\R^{n})$.
   
   
   ii) We have,  
   
    $$\sigma_h^{\rm Wick}( {\rm Op}_h^{\rm Wick}(F)) = F.$$
    
   iii)  The operator  ${\rm Op}_h^{\rm Wick}(F) $ is belonging to $C_h$ 
 and we have,
   
   $$ \Vert {\rm Op}_h^{\rm Wick}(F) \Vert_{C_h} 
      \leq C 
     \Vert F \Vert_{D_h ( \R^{2 n })} .$$ 
      
      iv) We have, 
 
 $$ W_h(T)^{\star}  {\rm Op}_h^{\rm Wick}(F)  W_h(T) = 
  {\rm Op}_h^{\rm Wick}(F_T),$$
  where,  for each $T\in\R^{2n}$,
  $ W_h(T) $ stands for the Weyl translation operator in $L^2 (\R^{n})$ defined in (\ref{trans-Weyl}) and
 $ F_T(X) = F(X+T)$, for all $X\in\R^{2n}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theo 6 of arXiv:2609.02261

body:
[Lemma Delta-bound of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Fix $q\in[0,1)$ and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $[-1,1]$ with
		$\int m^2\,\mu(\mathrm{d} m)=q$.
		For $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$, let $(X_t^{\mu,\zeta})_{t\in[q,1]}$ be the
		Auffinger--Chen process (equation eq:AC mu of the paper), set
		\[
		u_\zeta(t,x):=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,x),
		\]
		and define
		\begin{equation}
			\Delta_\zeta^\mu
			:=
			\int_{[q,1]}
			\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\bigl[u_\zeta(t,X_t^{\mu,\zeta})^2\bigr]-t\Bigr)\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\end{equation}
		Then:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item
			For every $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$,
			\[
			|\Delta_\zeta^\mu|\le 1.
			\]
			
			\item
			Let $\zeta_\mu$ be the unique minimizer of $\mathrm{TAP}(\mu,\cdot)$ on $\mathcal P([q,1])$.
			Assume that $\mu$ is supported in $[-1+\delta,1-\delta]$ for some
			$\delta\in(0,1)$, and let $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$ satisfy
			\[
			\zeta(\{q\})\ge u_0>0.
			\]
			Then there exists $C=C(\xi,u_0)$ such that
			\[
			|\Delta_\zeta^\mu|
			\le \frac{C}{\delta}\,\mathrm{dist}(\zeta,\zeta_\mu).
			\]
		\end{enumerate}

\begin{equation}
 g_i(s)=\tau_i^{-1}g(T+\tau_i s),\qquad

is included in the definition.  The limiting point is fixed before the
scales are selected.  If
\(d\mu_t=v_t\,dV_{g(t)}\), then the density of \(\mu_{i,s}\) relative

Let n>=1, 0=t_0<t_1<...<t_n=1, and w_i>0 for 0<=i<n, with sum_i w_i(t_{i+1}-t_i)=1. Let p be the probability density equal to w_i on [t_i,t_{i+1}], with endpoint choices irrelevant to the law. Set b_0=0 and b_i=sum_{j=0}^{i-1} w_j(t_{j+1}-t_j) for 1<=i<=n. Set a_0=1/w_0 and a_i=1/w_i-1/w_{i-1} for 1<=i<n. With rho(z)=max(z,0), the function f(u)=sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i rho(u-b_i) pushes Uniform[0,1] exactly to the law with density p. In particular it is an n-term one-hidden-layer ReLU representation of a continuous, strictly increasing quantile map on [0,1]. Its coefficients are unrestricted real numbers; the theorem supplies no uniform bound on their bit complexity. Source: arXiv:2006.16664v2, Theorem 3.3, PDF pp4--5.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Random-cluster measures with 0 < q < 1 are not monotone in p (2026) shows that for every q in (0,1) there are a finite graph G, an edge e and p1 < p2 with phi_{G,p1,q}(e open) > phi_{G,p2,q}(e open), so the measures phi_{G,p,q}, 0 <= p <= 1, admit no monotone coupling. This answers Question 13.2 of G. Pete, Probability and Geometry on Groups, in the negative for 0 < q < 1. The graphs are theta graphs, an edge e = uv with m internally disjoint u-v paths: when all paths have length l, the probability that e is open fails to be increasing in p for all large m exactly when q < 1 - e^(1-1/l)/l. For the arboreal gas (q -> 0 with p/(1-p) = beta q) the smallest theta graph satisfying the corresponding criterion has ten edges, and on it the probability that e is open increases up to beta* ≈ 13.574 and decreases after. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/random-cluster-not-monotone (commit 964e68294429). Not refereed.
title: Pete's Question 13.2 (Probability and Geometry on Groups) answered negatively for 0 < q < 1: random-cluster measures are not monotone in p (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/random-cluster-not-monotone)

where $T=V|T|$ is the polar decomposition.

Moreover, the intermediate projections $\delta(t)$, $t\in(0,1)$ are the  graphs of bounded operators: $\delta(t)=P_{Gr(B(t))}$, where $B(t)\in\b(\h)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \to M_d(\mathbb{R})$ a measurable cocycle with $\log^+ \|A\| \in L^1(\mu)$; write $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x)\cdots A(x)$.

ONE-SIDED (FILTRATION) VERSION - no invertibility of $T$ or of $A$ needed. For $\mu$-a.e. $x$: (a) the limit $\Lambda(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \big(A^n(x)^{\mathsf T} A^n(x)\big)^{1/2n}$ exists (a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix); (b) there are an integer $1 \le k(x) \le d$, exponents $\infty > \lambda_1(x) > \lambda_2(x) > \dots > \lambda_{k(x)}(x) \ge -\infty$ (only the smallest may be $-\infty$; this happens whenever $A$ is singular with positive probability, and can also happen for a.e.-invertible $A$ when $\log^+\|A^{-1}\|$ is not integrable), and a filtration of linear subspaces $\mathbb{R}^d = V_1(x) \supsetneq V_2(x) \supsetneq \dots \supsetneq V_{k(x)}(x) \supsetneq V_{k(x)+1}(x) = \{0\}$, measurable in $x$, such that $A(x) V_i(x) \subset V_i(Tx)$ and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x) \quad\text{for every } v \in V_i(x) \setminus V_{i+1}(x);$$
(c) $k$, the $\lambda_i$ and the multiplicities $m_i = \dim V_i - \dim V_{i+1}$ are $T$-invariant functions of $x$ (constants when $T$ is ergodic); (d) $\lim \frac1n \log |\det A^n(x)| = \sum_i m_i \lambda_i(x)$, and more generally $\lim \frac1n \log \|\Lambda^p A^n(x)\|$ (norm on the $p$-th exterior power) equals the sum of the $p$ largest exponents counted with multiplicity; (e) the $\lambda_i$ with multiplicities are exactly the limits $\lim \frac1n \log \sigma_j(A^n(x))$ of the singular values, i.e. the logarithms of the eigenvalues of $\Lambda(x)$.

TWO-SIDED (SPLITTING) VERSION. If moreover $T$ is invertible, $A(x) \in GL_d(\mathbb{R})$ a.e. and $\log^+ \|A^{-1}\| \in L^1(\mu)$, then for a.e. $x$ all exponents are finite and there is a measurable $A$-equivariant splitting $\mathbb{R}^d = E_1(x) \oplus \dots \oplus E_{k(x)}(x)$, $A(x)E_i(x) = E_i(Tx)$, $\dim E_i = m_i$, with $\lim_{n \to \pm\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x)$ for all $v \in E_i(x) \setminus \{0\}$ (the SAME exponent forwards and backwards), $V_i(x) = \bigoplus_{j \ge i} E_j(x)$, and the angles between the Oseledets subspaces decay subexponentially along orbits: $\lim_{n\to\pm\infty} \frac1n \log \sin\angle\big(E_i(T^n x), \bigoplus_{j\ne i} E_j(T^n x)\big) = 0$.

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without $\log^+\|A\| \in L^1$ the limits need not exist: for $d = 1$ the theorem IS Birkhoff's theorem for $\log|a|$, which fails when $\log^+|a| \notin L^1$. (2) Without $\log^+\|A^{-1}\| \in L^1$ (or with $T$ non-invertible) there is in general NO equivariant splitting, only the forward filtration: the subspaces of vectors with exponent exactly $\lambda_i$, $i \ge 2$, are not canonically defined and the 'slow' directions are not invariant under $A$. (3) The exponents depend on the measure $\mu$: different ergodic measures for the same $T$ and $A$ generally have different exponents, and a point outside the full-measure set need not have exponents at all. (4) Convergence is not uniform in $x$, and the Oseledets subspaces are only measurable, in general not continuous, in $x$. (5) The theorem is about $\|A^n(x)v\|$ along ONE orbit; it says nothing about eigenvalues of $A^n(x)$ or about $\|A^n\|$ averaged over $x$.
T is measure-preserving on a probability space; for the one-sided version T need not be invertible
A is measurable with log^+ ||A|| integrable
the splitting version additionally needs T invertible, A(x) invertible a.e., and log^+ ||A^{-1}|| integrable
all statements hold for mu-a.e. x; exponents depend on mu

body: [Theorem 1.5 of arXiv:2512.17823, 'van den Berg-Kesten--type correlation inequalities for disjoint polymers in the KPZ univer'] Fix any real numbers $x_{1}<x_{2}$ and $y_{1}\in\mathbb R$. Let $\mathsf{A}\subseteq\mathcal{C}([0,K],\mathbb R)$ for some $K>0$ be an increasing Borel measurable set. Then for any $s<t$, $R>0$, and a.e. $f\in\mathcal{C}([y_{1}-R,y_{1}],\mathbb R)$, $\displaystyle\mathbb P\Bigl(\log\mathcal{K}_{2}((x_{1},x_{2}),s;(y_{1},\bm{\cdot}),t)|_{[y_{1},y_{1}+K]}-\log\mathcal{Z}(x_{1},s;y_{1},t)\in\mathsf{A}\ \Big|\ \log\mathcal{Z}(x_{1},s;\bm{\cdot},t)|_{[y_{1}-R,y_{1}]}=f\Bigr)$ $\displaystyle\leq\mathbb P\Bigl(\log\mathcal{Z}(x_{2},s;\bm{\cdot},t)|_{[y_{1},y_{1}+K]}\in\mathsf{A}\Bigr).$ The same also holds when the conditioning is replaced by $\log\mathcal{Z}(x_{1},s;\bm{\cdot},t)|_{[y_{1}-R,y_{1}]}\geq f$. The same also holds under both conditionings when $x_{1}<x_{2}$, $+K$ and $-R$ are simultaneously replaced by $x_{1}>x_{2}$, $-K$ and $+R$ in the above.

[Corollary 8 of arXiv:2609.01681, 'Large induced subgraphs with $k$ vertices of maximum degree'] Let \(k\ge 2\) be fixed, and let \(c_3 = c_3(k)\) be the constant from Lemma~\ref{lem:exact-independent}. 
Suppose \(G\) is a graph with \(s_k(G) > |D| + 2k(k-1)\), where \(S\) and \(D\) arise from the minimum-edge construction for some choice of \(t\) with \(0<t<|V(G)|\).
Then for every integer \(x\), 
\(\bigl|\{v\in D : d_S(v) = x\}\bigr| < R(k, c_3)\).

body: [Theorem thm:flt of arXiv:2411.02362, 'Limit theorems for random Dirichlet series: boundary case'] Assume that $\mathbb{E}[\eta]=0$ and $\sigma^2=\mathbb{E} [\eta^2]\in (0,\infty)$. Then $$\Big(\frac{1}{(\log 1/s)^{1/2}}\sum_{k\geq 2}\frac{(\log k)^{-1/2}}{k^{1/2+s^t}}\eta_k\Big)_{t\geq 0}~\Longrightarrow~ (\sigma B(t))_{t\geq 0},\quad s\to 0+$$ on $C[0,\infty)$, where $(B(t))_{t\geq 0}$ is a standard Brownian motion. [Lemma 18 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The \textsc{mgf} of $T_{m,p}$ has the following form for $t \leqslant 0$,
\[
  M_{T_{m,p}}(t)
  = \binom{m\,e^{-t}}{m}^{-1} \times
    (1-p)^m
    \left[
      1
      -
      \int_0^1 p \, m
      \left(1-x\right)^{m\exp(-t)-m}
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx
    \right]^{-1}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] For every finite nonempty \(T\subset\mathbb D\), the full family
\(\{\nu_F^T:F\in\mathcal I_T\}\) is tight, and the directed net
\((\nu_F^T)_{F\in\mathcal I_T}\) converges to a unique law \(\nu^T\) as
\(F\uparrow\mathbb D\).  The family \((\nu^T)\) is projectively consistent.
Consequently, if
\begin{equation}
  h_n\downarrow0,
  \qquad L_n^-\to\infty,
  \qquad L_n^+\to\infty
  
\end{equation}
with dyadic, grid-aligned parameters, then
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal L_{Q_{h_n,L_n^-,L_n^+}}(B_T)
  \Longrightarrow\mu^T:=(-\operatorname{id})_*\nu^T.
  
\end{equation}
The limit is independent of the relative rates in
\eqref{eq:wall-parameter-limit}.

PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. For integer d>=2 let a_d=1-1/d and F_d(z)=[(1-z)^(-1)+exp(-d)(1-z/a_d)^(-1)]/[1+exp(-d)]. Its Taylor coefficients are nonnegative, F_d(0)=1, and its first pole is a_d. On every fixed [0,1-epsilon], |F_d(z)-(1-z)^(-1)|<=3 exp(-d)/epsilon for all large d, giving the same asymptotic expansion to every order in 1/d, yet its first pole is shifted by 1/d. Thus compact subcritical expansions alone cannot locate a critical point; the lace-free susceptibility route requires additional control near criticality or exclusion of small-residue poles. This is an analytic countermodel to an inference, not a percolation counterexample.

body:
[Theorem thm:cyclic-suspension of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Put $C=\Sigma_{\ell,c}A$ and $D=\max A$.  For
$q\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$, let $L_q(A)$ be the real span of the homogeneous
relation vectors of relation degree at most $q$, and put
$r_q(A)=\dim L_q(A)$.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For every $q\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$,
\begin{equation}
 |qC|=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(q,\ell-1)}|(q-j)A|.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, for $X\in\{A,C\}$ put
\[
 \mathcal H_X(z)=\sum_{q\geq0}|qX|z^q.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal H_C(z)=\mathcal H_A(z)[\ell]_z,\qquad
 [\ell]_z=1+z+\cdots+z^{\ell-1}.
\end{equation}

\item Let
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 S_A&=K[x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}],&
 \psi_A&:S_A\longrightarrow K[u,v],\\
 \psi_A(x_i)&=u^{D-a_i}v^{a_i},&
 I_A&=\ker\psi_A,\qquad R_A=S_A/I_A.
 \end{aligned}
\]
be the standard-graded projective semigroup ring of $A$.  Put
$S_C=S_A[y]$, and let $I_C$ be the kernel of the homogeneous toric map
\[
 x_i\longmapsto u^{\ell(D-a_i)}v^{\ell a_i},\qquad
 y\longmapsto u^{\ell D-c}v^c,
\]
so that $R_C=S_C/I_C$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 R_C\cong
 R_A[y]\big/\bigl(y^\ell-x_0^{\lambda_0}\cdots
 x_{m-1}^{\lambda_{m-1}}\bigr).
\end{equation}
The displayed polynomial is homogeneous and regular.  In particular, if
$R_A$ is Cohen--Macaulay, then so is $R_C$.

\item Define the ambient $K$-polynomials by
\[
 \mathcal K_A(z)=(1-z)^m\mathcal H_A(z),\qquad
 \mathcal K_C(z)=(1-z)^{m+1}\mathcal H_C(z).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal K_C(z)=\mathcal K_A(z)(1-z^\ell).
\end{equation}
If $\beta^A_{i,j}$ and $\beta^C_{i,j}$ are the standard-graded Betti
numbers over $S_A$ and $S_C$, respectively, extended by zero outside their
natural homological and internal degree ranges, then
\begin{equation}
 \beta^C_{i,j}
 =\beta^A_{i,j}+\beta^A_{i-1,j-\ell}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, with $\xi$ an indeterminate recording homological degree, put
\[
 \mathcal B_A(\xi,z)=\sum_{i,j}\beta^A_{i,j}\xi^iz^j,
 \qquad
 \mathcal B_C(\xi,z)=\sum_{i,j}\beta^C_{i,j}\xi^iz^j.
\]
Then
\[
 \mathcal B_C(\xi,z)=\mathcal B_A(\xi,z)(1+\xi z^\ell).
\]

\item Label the coordinates of $C$ by the tuple
$(\ell a_0,\ldots,\ell a_{m-1},c)$.  They need not be in increasing order;
this changes $L_q(C)$ only by a coordinate permutation.  Put
\[
 w_{\ell,c}=(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_{m-1},-\ell).
\]
Under the old-coordinate embedding,
\begin{equation}
 L_q(C)=
 \begin{cases}
  L_q(A),&q<\ell,\\[2mm]
  L_q(A)\oplus\mathbb Rw_{\ell,c},&q\geq\ell.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Hence
\begin{equation}
 r_q(C)=r_q(A)+
 \begin{cases}
  0,&q<\ell,\\
  1,&q\geq\ell,
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
and the multiset of active-relation birth degrees is the old multiset with
$\ell$ adjoined.

\item Define the order-$q$ Freiman dimension by
\[
 \operatorname{fdim}_q(A)=m-1-r_q(A).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{fdim}_q(C)=
 \begin{cases}
  \operatorname{fdim}_q(A)+1,&q<\ell,\\
  \operatorname{fdim}_q(A),&q\geq\ell.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}

\item One has
\begin{equation}
 \max C=\ell D,\qquad
 \operatorname{ndiam}(C)=\ell\operatorname{ndiam}(A).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

body: Let K be a nonempty, compact, convex subset of a Banach space X, and let f: K -> K be continuous. Then f has at least one fixed point in K, that is, there exists x in K with f(x) = x. This extends Brouwer's fixed-point theorem from finite-dimensional balls to compact convex sets in arbitrary Banach spaces. [standard, e.g. Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis]
title: Schauder Fixed-Point Theorem

For the actual zero-initial-bias one-step ReLU gradient G with proportional n,m,d, iid N(0,I_d) input rows, iid unit-sphere or N(0,I_d/d) initial neurons, independent Rademacher initial readout, and labels y=f_*(X)+xi with independent iid centered noise of variance s^2>0 and uniformly bounded fourth moment, every fixed epsilon in (0,1) satisfies P(||G||op^2 >= (1-epsilon)s^2 d/(4n), ||G||F^2 >= (1-epsilon)s^2 d/(2n))->1. No signal-size bound is needed for these gradient lower bounds. Therefore both gradient-norm reciprocals are O_P(1). With signal RMS O_P(1), C08 gives ridge-readout delocalization for the exact unfloored rule eta=c N/||G||, for either norm, N=1 or ||W0||op, at fixed raw ridge lambda>0, without a further gradient-nondegeneracy hypothesis. Explicitly, for F_(i,k)=ReLU(x_i^T(w_k+eta g_k)) and objective ||Fu-y||^2/n+lambda||u||^2, the corollary gives ||u||infinity=O_P(sqrt(log(m)/m)) and ||u||2<=||y||/sqrt(n lambda). Proof method (shifted quadratic lower tail with fourth moments): for deterministic PSD A with tr(A)>0, any deterministic mu, independent iid centered xi_i with variance s^2>0 and E xi_i^4<=K4, and epsilon in (0,1), P((mu+xi)^T A(mu+xi)<(1-epsilon)s^2 tr(A)) <= (||A||op/tr(A))*(2*(K4+2*s^4)/(epsilon^2*s^4)+2/epsilon), uniformly over mu. The same estimate holds conditionally when A and mu are jointly independent of xi. No zero-third-moment assumption is required. Scope: Independent review pending. The label-noise result does not cover arbitrary C08 designs, arbitrary initial biases, zero-variance noise, noise-dependent signal, multiple steps, or C05 scalar-gain limits. No exhaustive literature-priority claim. Lean scalar target remains RUNTIME_UNVERIFIED; this is not a Lean-checked theorem.

STATUS: proof (unaudited), owner-work draft. For Gaussian ReLU with critical variance 2/n, let V be the log first-input diagonal scale and U=1/(n theta). On any fixed 0<d<=u<=K, the same good-event self-loop kernel as C004 has joint generator A f=-(5/2)f_v+(2u+1/(3pi))f_u+(5/2)f_vv+2u*f_vu+u^2*f_uu, with O(n^-1/2) error for bounded C^3 tests with bounded derivatives. In particular n E[Delta V Delta U]=2u+O(n^-1/2); radial and fine-angle noises are not independent. Bounded-test exact-kernel agreement has exponentially small one-step error. Scope: Only a compact joint generator; no independent audit, entrance-boundary joint convergence, or literature novelty claim.
Zero biases; independent Gaussian weight matrices; width n; positive first-input Gram scale; u in a fixed compact subset of (0,infinity); explicit G regularization as C004; constants depend on compact and test.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:320d8db0aa92c5810cec5de0a341c0317d0887ff205bf04f679217dbfa2a77d8","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/32/320d8db0aa92c5810cec5de0a341c0317d0887ff205bf04f679217dbfa2a77d8.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e7963929c5b7ca586eadbacffa69648feee97a3091faf5d967ac624ee540936f","bundle_entry_key":"relu-joint-lognorm-angle","bundle_id":"population.t244-relu-joint-generator-draft-003","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_003.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:gaussian-relu-joint-lognorm-reciprocal-angle-generator","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Joint log-norm and reciprocal-angle compact generator

Status: proof draft (unaudited), Target 1. This builds on the reviewer-checked compact angular generator C004. It does not assert a complete joint functional limit from the entrance boundary or literature novelty. The hardest unresolved piece remains the independently unchecked entrance/removal-of-stopping argument C005-C006.

Consider a width-n zero-bias Gaussian ReLU network at variance 2/n. Let K_1 be its first input's positive diagonal Gram scale, V=log(K_1/q_1), and U=1/(n theta). Conditional on a state (v,u) with 0<d<=u<=K<infinity, use the Gaussian rows a,g and the good-event self-loop regularization G of compact_generator.md. On G,

    V'=v+m, m=log(2S/n),
    U'=u exp(-z), z=log(theta'/theta).

Off G self-loop both coordinates, so m=z=0. Uniformly on the fixed u compact, for bounded C^3 functions on R^2 with bounded derivatives through order three,

    n E[f(V',U')-f(v,u)]
      = -(5/2) f_v +(2u+1/(3pi)) f_u
        +(5/2) f_vv +2u f_vu +u^2 f_uu +O_(d,K,f)(n^-1/2).

In particular, the radial and angular noises cannot be treated as independent: n E[(V'-v)(U'-u)]=2u+O(n^-1/2). Good-event failure is exponentially small, so the same bounded-test generator holds for the exact chain killed at degeneracy. The killing convention only affects a bounded test at this step.

## Single-input moments under the same truncation

Let k=#{a_i>0} and I={n/3<=k<=2n/3}. On I, conditional on k, S~chi-square_k and R~chi-square_(k-1) are independent. Put

    m0=log(2S/n), z0=(log R-log S)/2.

These expressions are used only on I, so no logarithm of a zero norm is taken. Cauchy-Schwarz with higher central-k logarithm moments and P(G^c)<=Cexp(-cn) permits replacing I by G at exponentially small cost. Uniformly for central k,

    E[m0|k] = log(2k/n)-1/k+O(k^-2),
    Var(m0|k) = psi_1(k/2)=2/k+O(k^-2),
    E[z0|k] = -1/(2k)+O(k^-2).

Here psi_1 is the trigamma function, equivalently the variance of log chi-square. Its displayed asymptotic follows by differentiating the gamma moment formula E S^h=2^h Gamma(k/2+h)/Gamma(k/2). The same formula, or the central moments plus exponentially small chi-square tails, gives uniformly bounded rescaled third absolute logarithm moments.

Write h=k-n/2. On I, Taylor expansion with binomial central moments gives

    E[log(2k/n);I] = -1/(2n)+O(n^-3/2),
    Var(log(2k/n)1_I) = 1/n+O(n^-3/2),
    E[1/k;I]=2/n+O(n^-2).

For instance log(1+2h/n)=2h/n-2h^2/n^2+O(|h|^3/n^3), E h=0, E h^2=n/4, and E|h|^3=O(n^(3/2)). Central-set truncation changes the first two equalities only exponentially. Combining conditional and between-k variances gives

    E m = -5/(2n)+O(n^-3/2),
    E m^2 = 5/n+O(n^-3/2),
    E|m|^3=O(n^-3/2).

These are moments of m=log(2S/n)1_G, not of an untruncated multiplier with a zero atom.

## Mixed moment without false independence

Conditional on k, only S and R, not the flip correction, are independent. Thus exactly

    Cov(m0,z0|k)=-(1/2) Var(log S|k)=-(1/2) psi_1(k/2).

Its average on I is -E[1/k;I]+O(n^-2)=-2/n+O(n^-2). The product of conditional means contributes O(n^-3/2): the central-k L2 norm of E[m0|k] is O(n^-1/2), while that of E[z0|k] is O(n^-1). Hence

    E[m z0;G] = -2/n+O(n^-3/2).

C004's decomposition gives ||(z-z0)1_G||_2=O(n^-1) on the fixed u compact. Indeed theta=O(n^-1), the flip-ratio L2 norm is O(n^-1), the log Q norm is O(n^-3/2)+O(n^-2), and the arctangent term is O(n^-2). Cauchy-Schwarz therefore yields

    E[mz]=-2/n+O(n^-3/2).

No independence between m and the flip correction has been imposed. Since |z| is bounded on G,

    Delta U = -u z+O_(d,K)(z^2),
    |E[m Delta U]+u E[mz]| <= C E[|m|z^2] <= C ||m||_3 ||z||_3^2
                                               = O(n^-3/2).

Consequently E[m Delta U]=2u/n+O(n^-3/2), with the positive sign shown in the generator. The mixed sign arises because a larger S both increases the norm and decreases the angle multiplier sqrt(R/S), hence increases its reciprocal.

## Taylor expansion and the compatible coupled SDE

C004 supplies E Delta U=(2u+1/(3pi))/n+O(n^-3/2), E(Delta U)^2=2u^2/n+O(n^-3/2), and E|Delta U|^3=O(n^-3/2). Combined with the moments above, E(|m|+|Delta U|)^3=O(n^-3/2). The multivariate Taylor remainder for bounded third derivatives is therefore O(n^-3/2) per step. Its mixed quadratic term is f_vu E[m Delta U], with no extra factor of 1/2. This proves the stated generator.

The diffusion matrix is

    [[5, 2u], [2u, 2u^2]], determinant 6u^2.

One compatible representation, using independent standard Brownian motions W1,W2, is

    dV = -(5/2) dt +sqrt(5) dW1,
    dU = (2U+1/(3pi)) dt +(2/sqrt(5))U dW1 +sqrt(6/5)U dW2.

The covariance between V and U is 2U dt. The scalar U marginal agrees with C004 up to Brownian sign convention. A joint entrance theorem would start (V,U) at (0,0), and its output pair would use exp(V_t/2) times a shared independent final Gaussian coordinate, with unequal deterministic input norms restored. This last sentence describes the remaining joint limit route, not a theorem established by a compact generator alone.

[Theorem 8 (The $m$th-order Santal\'o inequality on $M_{n,m}(\R)$) of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Fix $Q\in\conbodo[m].$ Consider a compact set $L\subset M_{n,m}(\R)$ with positive volume and non-empty interior. If either $L_{\circ,Q}$ or $(L_{\circ,Q})^\circ$ has center of mass at the origin, then
  $$\Vol(L)\vol(L_{\circ,Q})^m \leq \vol(\B)^m \Vol((B_2^n)^{\star,Q}),
$$
with equality if and only if $L=E^{\star,Q}$ for some centered ellipsoid $E\subset\R^n$ up to removal of null sets. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Use the balanced paired model with one variable pair, even N>=16, K>=2 and 1<=r<K, uniform context marginal, all K candidates true in systematic contexts, and a random r-subset true in arbitrary contexts. Replace annotated training by n>=1 iid factual context/candidate samples from the truthful target. Average the sample law over the random subsets. The two pair-orientation data laws D0,D1 satisfy TV(D0,D1)<=T=min(1,n(n-1)/(r*N^2)). Every pair-orientation estimator has worst-orientation expected classification error >=(1-T)/N. Taking K=2r and r>=2n(n-1)/N^2 keeps this >=1/(2N), so there is no uniform O(VCdim/n) rate over this unannotated family, although the partition class has VC dimension one. Let X be a random variable with finite mean mu = E X and finite variance sigma^2 = Var X. Then for every t > 0, P(|X - mu| >= t) <= sigma^2 / t^2; equivalently P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2 for every k > 0. The inequality is sharp: for t >= sigma the variable taking the values mu - t and mu + t with probability sigma^2 / (2 t^2) each and the value mu otherwise has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(|X - mu| >= t) = sigma^2 / t^2 exactly. It gives no information for t <= sigma, and it is the classical route to the weak law of large numbers: for i.i.d. X_i with finite variance, P(|(X_1 + ... + X_n)/n - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2 / (n eps^2) -> 0.
E X^2 < infinity (finite variance); with only a finite mean use Markov on |X - mu|

\begin{itemize}
\item[a)]
If
\(\int_\Omega m(x)\varphi_{1,\Omega}^{\alpha+1}\,dx<0\), then, as
$\lambda\downarrow\lambda_{1,\Omega}$,
\[
E_\lambda(u_\lambda^-)\rightarrow+\infty,
\qquad
\|u_\lambda^-\|\rightarrow+\infty,
\]
and, after normalizing $\|\varphi_{1,\Omega}\|=1$,
\[
\frac{u_\lambda^-}{\|u_\lambda^-\|}
\longrightarrow\varphi_{1,\Omega}
\qquad\text{strongly in }H_0^1(\Omega).
\]	
\item[b)]
If $|\Omega^+|>0$, then, as $\lambda\to-\infty$,
\[
E_\lambda(u_\lambda^+)\rightarrow0,
\qquad
\|u_\lambda^+\|\rightarrow0.
\]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 12 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] A weak solution of \eqreftag{eq:MV-a} consists of a filtered probability space
\((\Omega,\Fc,\F,\P)\) supporting a \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motion \(B\), a
random variable \((X,Y_0)\) with law \(\pi_0\), and an \(\F\)-adapted continuous
process \(Y=(Y_t)_{t\ge0}\), such that \(B\) is independent of \((X,Y_0)\) and the
following conditions hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item 
    There exists \(p>1\) such that, for every \(T>0\),
    \[
    \int_0^T
    \E\left[
    \left|
    \hat A_t
    -
    a\bigl(t,X,Y_t,\Lc(Y_t\mid X)\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(Y_t)
    \right|^p
    \right]\,dt
    <\infty,
    \]
    where $
        \hat A_t
        :=
        \E [
            a (t,X,Y_t,\Lc(Y_t\mid X) )
            \mid Y_t
        ].
    $

    \item 
    The process \(Y\) satisfies, in the weak sense,
    \[
    dY_t
    =
    \left(
    \hat A_t
    -
    a\bigl(t,X,Y_t,\Lc(Y_t\mid X)\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(Y_t)
    \right)dt
    +
    \sqrt{2}\,dB_t .
    \]
\end{enumerate}

body: [Lem straightening of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{G}_1,\dots,\mathcal{G}_k$ be Reebless $C^0$-foliations of $\mathbb{T}^2$, possibly with infinite slopes. Then there are $C^0$-isotopies $h_1^t,\dots,h_k^t$, $0\leq t \leq T$, of $\mathcal{G}_1,\dots,\mathcal{G}_k$ respectively such that the isotoped foliations $h_i^T (\mathcal{G}_i)$ are tangentially $C^0$-close to linear foliations. In particular, if $\mathcal{G}_i$ and $\mathcal{G}_j$ have different slopes, then $h_i^T(\mathcal{G}_i)$ is transverse to $h_j^T(\mathcal{G}_j)$. Moreover, if any pair of the foliations start out transverse, they remain transverse during the isotopy, and if any foliation is smooth, then the corresponding isotopy is smooth as well.

body: [Theorem 1 of arXiv:2511.18562, 'Ensuring Calibration Robustness in Split Conformal Prediction Under Adversarial Attacks'] Assume $f$ the predictive probability distribution of class true label $y$ given observed input $x$ is smooth for a trained neural network. In the case of a neural network, this corresponds to the probability assigned to each class after applying the softmax transformation to the model’s output scores. Denote function $g(f_{y}(x))$ as the density of $f_{y}(x)$. Suppose $g$ is second-order differentiable w.r.t. $f_{y}(x)$. Let $C_{\epsilon_{cal}}(x_{test}+\epsilon_{test}A_{test})$ be the prediction set produced by the Split CP algorithm using calibration set with attack strength $\epsilon_{cal}$ given the adversarially attacked test input $x_{test}+\epsilon_{test}A_{test}$. Then for any fixed $\epsilon_{cal}=o(1)$, the coverage of $C_{\epsilon_{cal}}(x_{test}+\epsilon_{test}A_{test}))$ satisfies: $\displaystyle|\mathbb{P}(y_{test}\in C_{\epsilon_{cal}}(x_{test}+\epsilon_{test}A_{test}))-(1-\alpha)|\leq$ $\displaystyle e_{train}+d_{cal}+e_{cal}$ $\displaystyle+\left((2\epsilon_{test}-\epsilon_{cal})||\nabla f_{x_{test}}||-\epsilon_{cal}\cdot c\right)$ $\displaystyle g(Q_{1-\alpha}(f_{y_{cal}}(x_{cal})))+o\left(\epsilon_{cal}^{2}+\epsilon_{test}^{2}\right).$ where we rewrite the attack as $\epsilon_{test}A_{test}$ and $\displaystyle A_{test}$ $\displaystyle\propto$ $\displaystyle\frac{\partial L(f(x_{test}),y_{test})}{\partial x_{test}}$ $\displaystyle=$ $\displaystyle\frac{\partial L(f(x_{test}),y_{test})}{\partial f_{y_{test}}(x_{test})}\frac{\partial f_{y_{test}}(x_{test})}{\partial x_{test}}$ with $||A_{test}||=1$.

Thus E[U_k^(-p);alive]<=C_T*n^p/(k+1)^p, U_k=1/(n theta_k). The result holds for C032 regularization and the exact chain, and permits additional killing on U>K. Model: n independent Gaussian/ReLU row pairs x=max(g,0), y=max(cos(theta)g+sin(theta)h,0), g,h independent standard Gaussians, independent across layers; output angle between the resulting n-vectors. Kill at zero norm, zero angle, or exit from the stated interval. The regularized version self-loops outside a fixed small concentration box for sample averages of (x^2+y^2,(x-y)^2/theta^2,(x^2-y^2)/theta) about their population mean. Limit: Unaudited proof. Upper occupation bounds only; no sharp asymptotic occupation coefficient and no network weak-rate theorem.

Version 1, 20 October 2026. Target 1, kind moved, proofs (unaudited).
These use the normalized-Gram construction of C032 and C036; neither
claim is a complete network weak-rate theorem.

## C037: inverse occupation is a positive angle-moment problem

For every finite T, there are epsilon>0 and constants C_T,n0 such that the
following holds. Start the Gaussian/ReLU angle chain at any deterministic
theta0 in (0,epsilon], with width n>=n0. Kill it when it leaves that angle
interval or becomes degenerate, and set its killed angle to zero. One may
also kill it when u=1/(n theta) exceeds any fixed K. For p=1,2 and 0<=k<=Tn,

    E[theta_k^p; alive at k] <= C_T/(k+1)^p.                 (1)

This holds both for the normalized-Gram self-loop regularization and for
the exact chain. In particular, with U_k=1/(n theta_k) only on alive states,

    E[U_k^(-p); alive at k] <= C_T n^p/(k+1)^p.             (2)

Here inverse powers at the cemetery are excluded by the alive indicator.
The statement is a small-angle stopped-chain estimate; it does not assign
the initial time of entrance from an arbitrary fixed theta0.

Proof. Write the normalized output multiplier as theta'/theta=1/T_theta
on the C032 good box. For p=1,2 the coordinate test Phi_p=T_theta^(-p)
has uniformly bounded first and second derivatives on that box for all
small theta. Its deterministic value is (F(theta)/theta)^p, where F is
the deterministic ReLU angle map. A second-order sample-average Taylor
bound, uniform normalized row second moments, and exponential deletion
outside the box imply

    E[(theta'/theta)^p]
       <= (F(theta)/theta)^p+C_p/n
       =1-p a theta+O_p(theta^2)+C_p/n,  a=1/(3pi).

To justify the first inequality explicitly, the linear centered-average
term has mean zero before good-box truncation and an exponentially small
deleted mean; the quadratic Taylor remainder is bounded by the coordinate
Hessian bound times E|Zbar-mu_theta|^2=O(1/n). Off the good box the
regularized multiplier is one. No reciprocal-angle moment is used.

Choose epsilon small so the O(theta^2) term is at most p a theta/2. Killing
only decreases positive angle moments. Thus, for p=1,2 and constants c_p>0,

    E[theta_(k+1)^p | theta_k=theta]
       <= theta^p(1+C_p/n)-c_p theta^(p+1).

Let m_k=E theta_k^p, with theta_k=0 after killing. Jensen gives

    m_(k+1) <= rho m_k-c_p m_k^(1+1/p), rho=1+C_p/n.

Put v_k=rho^(-k)m_k. Since rho>=1,

    v_(k+1) <= v_k-(c_p/rho)v_k^(1+1/p).

Decrease the constant if necessary so z=(c_p/rho)v_k^(1/p)<=1/2; this is
possible because v_k<=m_k<=epsilon^p. If v_(k+1)>0, the elementary inequality
(1-z)^(-1/p)>=1+z/p implies

    v_(k+1)^(-1/p) >= v_k^(-1/p)+c_p/(p rho).

If a term becomes zero, the killed nonnegative chain has zero subsequent
moments and the desired bound is immediate. Otherwise summing yields
v_k<=C/(k+1)^p. As rho^k<=exp(C_p T), (1) follows for the regularized chain.

For the exact chain, use the same independent Gaussian rows until a
good-box failure. Its conditional probability is at most C exp(-cn),
uniformly in every alive small angle. A union bound through k<=Tn gives
disagreement probability at most C k exp(-cn). Both killed angles lie in
[0,epsilon], so their pth moments differ by at most
C epsilon^p k exp(-cn). For k<=Tn this is bounded by C_T/(k+1)^p,
uniformly in n>=n0. This proves (1) for the exact chain, and (2) is the
identity U_k^(-p)=n^p theta_k^p on alive states.

## C038: summing the C036 local remainder after a layer cutoff

Use the regularized stopped chain of C037, with the additional upper
cutoff U<=K. Let N<=Tn, 0<=m<N, and let f_(n,k) be deterministic bounded
C^5 tests whose supremum and derivative bounds through order five are
uniform in n,k. Define the *unstopped-kernel* local remainder, evaluated
only at alive prestop states, by

    R_(n,k)(u)=n(P_n f_(n,k)-f_(n,k))(u)
                               -A f_(n,k)(u)-B f_(n,k)(u)/n.

Choose the angle cutoff epsilon at most C036's theta_star. Then

    (1/n) sum_(k=m)^(N-1) E[|R_(n,k)(U_k)|; alive at k]
      <= C_(K,T)[n^(-3/2)+log(n+1)/n^2
                             +1/(n(m+1))+n exp(-cn)].         (3)

The same estimate holds using the exact kernel and its stopped chain.
This is an accumulated estimate for the indicated local remainders. It
does not discard boundary terms or prove a stopped-semigroup comparison.

Proof. C036 applies to every alive state, since 0<U_k<=K and
theta_k=1/(nU_k)<=epsilon. Its (u+sqrt(u))/n^(3/2) term sums after the
outer factor1/n to at most C_(K,T)n^(-3/2). The constant/n^2 term sums to
C_T/n^2. By (2), the other two algebraic terms contribute at most

    C/n^3 sum_(k=m)^(N-1) n/(k+1) <= C_T log(n+1)/n^2,
    C/n^3 sum_(k=m)^(N-1) n^2/(k+1)^2 <= C_T/[n(m+1)].

The exponential term sums to C_T n exp(-cn). This proves (3), separately
for each chain using the C037 moment bounds and C036's exact-kernel bound.

For any m=m_n tending to infinity, the right side is o(1/n). This pays
for the pointwise Taylor-remainder accumulation after a growing cutoff.
The main singular correction B-A^2/2 still needs an asymptotic occupation
calculation matched to the early network chain. An upper bound for its
occupation is not that asymptotic calculation. Neither (1) nor (3) proves
that the network coefficient is D_t/(2pi).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:ef5cf8d24593c8c15d39382f642a60f6bd9f0b66fde78d07f243e32a0c98ecb5","revision_digest":"sha256:170bec1daa3230b4a97204e8d39975a706b1d3faf00a05db0919072f841476e0","source_id":"owner-own-work:T244-w691-C037:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Definition 20 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Blockage in the finite range case.}

For $\landsc$ a landscape, and $(x, y)\in \Half$ a point, the blocking building of $(x, y)$ in $\landsc$ is, when it is well defined, 
\[\tau (x, y, \landsc) = (x_b, y_b) := \underset{\substack{(a, b) \in \landsc \\a\in ]x, x+R]}}{\text{argmax}} \frac{b-y}{a-x}.\]
And $\tau(x, y, \landsc) = (-\infty, -\infty)$ when there is no building in $]x, x+R]$.

We define the blockage angle $\theta$ and its tangent $\mathrm{t}$ similarly to the infinite range case (with the convention that $\mathrm{t} = -\infty$).
title: Definition 20 of arXiv:2605.03851

[Lemma lem:rooted-component-allocation of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix a fully colored circuit-anchored spatial state and a selected set of
$q$ resource-bearing component roots.  Let $B_{\rm tok}$ be the number
of surplus nonsingleton packet tokens and explicit linear Jacobi
resources, including such resources fused into a selected root
supernode.  Let $T_{\rm nf}$ be the number of singleton supernodes not
fused into a selected root.  Then, for $r\le L\log n$,
\[
 \boxed{
 q^{B_{\rm tok}+T_{\rm nf}}N^{-B_{\rm tok}}
 n^{-\delta T_{\rm nf}}\le A_L^r,
 \qquad \delta=\frac1{16}.}
\tag{3.4.1x$_7$}
\]
Consequently the retained debits sum all assignments of these tokens and
nonfused singleton supernodes to the selected roots with exponential
cost.  The assertion does not include port-open singleton occurrences
whose weak-time node is a selected root supernode.

body: [Proposition 3.2 of arXiv:2512.19517, 'Spiking and Resetting'] Let $0<a\leq b<1$ and $A=[a,b]$. For any $n\geq 0$ and any real numbers $0=s_{0}<s_{1}<s_{2}<s_{n}<t=s_{n+1}$, conditionally to the event $\{e_{1}^{\varepsilon}\geq t\}$, the random vector $\begin{split}\big(N^{\varepsilon}_{(s_{i},s_{i+1}]}(A)\big)_{0\leq i\leq n}\end{split}$ converges in law, as $\varepsilon$ goes to $0$, to the random vector $\begin{split}\big({\bar{N}}_{i}\big)_{0\leq i\leq n}\end{split}$ composed of independent random variables such that for any $i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, $N_{i}$ is a Poisson random variable with parameter $(s_{i+1}-s_{i})\lambda_{*}(A)$.

body: In the mathematical field of dynamical systems, an attractor is a set of states toward which a system tends to evolve, for a wide variety of starting conditions of the system. System values that get close enough to the attractor values remain close even if slightly disturbed.

[campaign result 2026-09-14, Author-checked only, no independent read.] This is a complementary characterization reported in the campaign note on the Chapter 4 question of David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html), recorded as intake row I0024. That question asks whether the relaxation time can be characterized exactly as an infimum over flows. The note attributes the characterization to its companion note on Open Problem 4.49. Let P be a finite irreducible reversible transition matrix on V with stationary probabilities pi_i, and let tau_2=1/(1-lambda_2), where lambda_2 is the second-largest eigenvalue. For an unordered edge e={i,j} with i!=j and p_ij>0, put c_e=pi_i p_ij=pi_j p_ji. Call a symmetric array d(a,b) of negative type here if d(a,a)=0 and d is a squared Euclidean distance array, d(a,b)=||v_a-v_b||^2 for some finite-dimensional real vectors v_a. Triangle inequalities for d are not imposed. The record reports 2 tau_2 = max {sum_{a,b in V} pi_a pi_b d(a,b) : d is such a squared-distance array, sum_e c_e d(i,j)=1}, where the first sum is over ordered pairs and the second over unordered edges. It contrasts this with the dual of the flow-congestion program of Open Problem 4.49, which is the same objective and normalization taken over the cone of metrics. The squared-distance cone is not polyhedral and the program is semidefinite, so the rational-linear-program obstruction does not extend to this formulation. Its variables are vectors, not flows. The record refers to the companion note for the variational derivation rather than supplying a complete proof. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The chain has at least two states and is irreducible and reversible.
The squared-distance cone is used, without an additional triangle-inequality constraint.

body:
[Proposition 18 (Bethe verification) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] On $T_d$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red} is exact.) By vertex-transitivity all transmission probabilities equal a single $p=p^{\ex}$, the harmonic measure is uniform on the end space $\Sigma^{\mathbb N}$, $\Sigma=\{1,\dots,d-1\}$, there is no failure-strength heterogeneity across siblings (all forcings identical), and the failed cluster is exactly a Galton--Watson process with offspring law $\mathrm{Bin}(d-1,p)$. The mean matrix is the scalar $M=(d-1)p$, so $\rho(M)=(d-1)p$.
\item (Theorem~\ref{thm:gap} is an equality.) The boundary is homogeneous, $p_ew_e\equiv p$, so $\ell=\log(d-1)+\log p$ and $e^{\ell}=(d-1)p=\rho(M)=p_{\min}^{-\dimH}$ with $p_{\min}=1/d$; the Jensen gap is zero. At criticality $(d-1)p=1$ the weighted dimension is $0$.
\item (Theorem~\ref{thm:32}.) At criticality the offspring law is $\mathrm{Bin}(d-1,1/(d-1))$, mean $1$, variance $1-1/(d-1)<\infty$ for $d\ge3$, giving $C_d=(2\pi(1-1/(d-1)))^{-1/2}>0$ and the $n^{-3/2}$ tail. The binary tree $d=2$ is the degenerate variance-zero case and is excluded.
\item (Theorem~\ref{thm:stab}.) $\rho=(d-1)p(\theta,\gamma)$ with $p$ decreasing in $\theta$ and increasing in $\gamma$; $\mathcal M_+=\{p>1/(d-1)\}$ is convex, $\mathcal M_-$ its complement is contractible by the $\gamma$-retraction, the critical curve is smooth, and $(1-(d-1)p)^{-1}$ is the explicit expected cluster size.
\item (Theorems \ref{thm:pressure}, \ref{thm:dimS} and \ref{thm:crt}.) The pressure is affine, $\varphi(\beta)=\log(d-1)+\beta\log p$, so the convexity gap vanishes, consistent with item 2. In the supercritical regime $(d-1)p>1$ the failed boundary has $\dimH(\partial S)=\log((d-1)p)<\log(d-1)=\dimH(\partial T)$: the cascade survives along an exponentially thin bundle of rays, of relative codimension $\log(1/p)$. At criticality, the cluster is single-type with bounded offspring, so the exponential-moment hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:crt} is automatic and the conditioned cluster rescaled by $\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{off}}}{2\sqrt n}$, $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{off}}=1-\frac{1}{d-1}$, converges to the CRT by Aldous' theorem \cite{Ald93}.
\end{enumerate}

Let V be an affine algebraic set and p a point on V. The point p is called an isolated point of V if {p} is an irreducible component of V. Equivalently, in the Euclidean topology (over C or R), there exists an open neighborhood U of p such that V intersect U = {p}, which corresponds algebraically to local dimension dim_p(V) = 0.

[Defn of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $M$ be a compact oriented $3$-manifold with $n$ framed toroidal boundary components, and $\Phi$ be a nonwandering flow on $M$ tangent to $\partial M$. We define
    $$\mathcal{Z}(\Phi) \coloneqq \big\{\bm{s} \mid \text{$\exists$ foliation $\mathcal{F}$ transverse to $\Phi$ with boundary multislope $\bm{s}$}\big\} \subset \mathbb{R}^n.$$
    We refer to $\mathcal{Z}(\Phi)$ as the \textbf{(foliation) ziggurat} of $\Phi$, borrowing the evocative terminology coined by Calegari--Walker for related sets arising in circle dynamics (see \zcref{sec:circledynamics}).
title: Unnumbered defn of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'

[Proposition 4 (Finite first moments and exact moment identities) of arXiv:2608.12839, 'Spiking Neural Networks with Elephant Reinforcement'] Assume
\[
\mathbb E[V_i(0)+K_i(0)+|S_i(0)|]<\infty,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.
\]
Then for every \(T>0\),
\[
\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}
\mathbb E[V_i(t)+K_i(t)+|S_i(t)|]<\infty.
\]
Moreover, for almost every \(t\geq0\),
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E[V_i(t)]
=
\beta_{i-1}(t)+\beta_{i+1}(t)
-
\gamma\mathbb E[V_i(t)]

-
\mathbb E\bigl[V_i(t)\lambda_i(t)\bigr],
\end{align}
\begin{equation}

\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E[K_i(t)]
=
\beta_i(t),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}

\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E[S_i(t)]
=
(2p-1)
\mathbb E\left[
\frac{S_i(t)}{K_i(t)}\lambda_i(t)
\right].
\end{equation}
Here
\[
\lambda_i(t)
=
\lambda(V_i(t),S_i(t),K_i(t)).
\]

(\Omega, \mathcal{A}, \pi) is the latent space
\bm{\xi}_i are latent variables
\bm{B}_i are independent Brownian motions
