body: Theorem 3 (Estimating the number of communities). Assume that the average degree satisfies d >= 2 and Assumption 1 holds. For any epsilon > 0 small enough, the following holds with high probability for sufficiently large n: N_eps(sqrt d) = N(sqrt d + eps) = r_+ and N_eps(-sqrt d) = N(-sqrt d - eps) = r_-. The above is also valid when taking eps = eps_n = log(n)^{-c} for any c > 0. Here, for a stochastic block model with r communities, proportions pi and connectivity P: d := sum_j P_ij pi_j > 1 for all i is the average degree; Assumption 1 says pi_i, P_ij (and hence d, r and r_0) do not depend on n; r_+ and r_- count the positive and negative informative eigenvalues of the signal matrix Q = P diag(pi) (those mu with mu^2 > d); H(t) := t^2 - tA + (D - I) is the Bethe-Hessian of the graph (A its adjacency matrix, D its degree matrix); N_eps(t) is the number of eigenvalues of H(t) below -eps and N(t) the number of negative eigenvalues of H(t).

body: Skolem's Paradox is the apparent contradiction arising from Downward Löwenheim-Skolem: if ZFC has a model, it has a countable model M, yet M proves the existence of uncountable sets (such as \mathbb{R}). The resolution is that 'uncountable' is not absolute: the bijection between \mathbb{R}^M and \omega exists outside M but is not an element of M.
title: Skolem's Paradox

body:
Let mu be a probability measure on {0,1}^{E(Z^d)} that is (i) invariant under the lattice translations, (ii) ERGODIC with respect to them, and (iii) has the FINITE ENERGY property: for every edge e, the conditional probability that e is open given the states of all other edges lies almost surely strictly between 0 and 1. Then the number of infinite open clusters is almost surely a constant taking the value 0 or 1. Each of the three hypotheses does work. Ergodicity is what makes the number a constant rather than a random variable; without it a mixture of two percolation measures is a counterexample. Finite energy is what rules out infinitely many infinite clusters, by allowing local modifications; a measure that deterministically forbids certain local patterns can have infinitely many. And the argument uses AMENABILITY of Z^d - on a regular tree or another nonamenable transitive graph there is genuinely a regime with infinitely many infinite clusters, so the theorem is false there. Bernoulli percolation satisfies all three hypotheses for every p, so its infinite cluster is unique whenever it exists. [Burton and Keane (1989), Comm. Math. Phys. 121; see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 8.1]

Step 1: rule out 2 <= N = k < infinity. If exactly k infinite clusters exist with k >= 2, choose a box large enough that with positive probability it meets at least two of them. Finite energy allows one to open all edges inside that box with positive conditional probability, which merges those two clusters into one and leaves at most k - 1 infinite clusters on an event of positive probability - contradicting that N is almost surely the constant k. Step 2: rule out N = infinity. Call a vertex x a TRIFURCATION if x lies in an infinite cluster, x has exactly three open incident edges, and deleting x splits its infinite cluster into exactly three infinite pieces. If N = infinity then by the same finite-energy local modification - take a box meeting three distinct infinite clusters and rewire its interior to join them through a single vertex of degree three - the probability that the origin is a trifurcation is strictly positive, say delta > 0. By translation invariance the expected number of trifurcations in a box of side 2n + 1 is delta (2n+1)^d. But a purely combinatorial fact about trees bounds the number of trifurcations inside a box by the size of its BOUNDARY: contracting each cluster gives a forest in which the trifurcations are branch vertices of degree at least three and the distinct infinite branches must exit through distinct boundary vertices, so the number of trifurcations in the box is at most the number of boundary vertices, of order n^{d-1}. For large n, delta (2n+1)^d exceeds C n^{d-1}, a contradiction. This step is exactly where amenability - the fact that boundary is of smaller order than volume - is used.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:0a10dca57c02792c802de68a722e918c5119beec63f791aa1a02a4d2b2b22ace","revision_digest":"sha256:19571635c9811ef2c4fa9bf7413abff7ada34807a8dc3b1fc48636004a01b663","source_id":"rederived:claude-8e06e1f7-M9","source_revision":"re-derived-2026-08-22; statement, the role of each hypothesis and the two-step trifurcation proof were written and checked by the author; textbook cross-reference in the statement, source not fetched this session","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Given a Markov chain with kernel P and a nonnegative P-harmonic function h, the Doob h-transform defines a new Markov chain with kernel P^h(x,y) = P(x,y) h(y)/h(x), representing the law of the original chain conditioned, in an appropriate limiting sense such as conditioning to survive forever or on an asymptotic event, to respect the weighting given by h. Applied to a critical or subcritical Galton-Watson branching process conditioned to survive forever, or, for critical trees, conditioned to have total size n with n -> infinity, the Kesten tree construction realizes the limiting law as an explicit infinite random tree: a single infinite spine, with each spine vertex additionally carrying an independent number of extra children distributed according to the size-biased-minus-one offspring law, each extra child then supporting an ordinary, unconditioned Galton-Watson subtree. This gives the exact local weak limit of large conditioned critical or subcritical branching trees and underlies scaling-limit results, such as convergence to the continuum random tree, that first pass through this explicit infinite-tree description. It does not directly give scaling limits of the whole tree's metric structure, which requires an additional contour or height-function argument, and the exact form of the spine's offspring law is specific to the conditioning event used, since conditioning on survival forever and conditioning on total size n give related but generally distinct limiting infinite trees. Typical failure: Confusing the different conditioning regimes for the conditioned Galton-Watson tree, such as conditioning on survival to infinity versus conditioning on total progeny exactly n as n -> infinity versus conditioning on height n, as if they all give the identical Kesten tree limit; they give related but generally distinct limiting infinite trees, differing in the spine's offspring bias and finer distributional details, and using one variant's known properties for a computation set up under a different conditioning is a frequent, easy-to-miss error. Canonical reference: Doob, 1957, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Lyons, Pemantle and Peres, 1995, Annals of Probability.
a Markov chain, here a Galton-Watson branching process, with an identified P-harmonic function h appropriate to the conditioning event
for Kesten's tree specifically: finite-mean offspring distribution with criticality or subcriticality correctly identified, and a precisely specified conditioning event
existence of the relevant weak-convergence limit of the conditioned law to the h-transformed law, which must be checked rather than assumed
correct identification of the size-biased offspring law along the spine, which differs from the original offspring law
title: Technique: Doob h-Transform and Kesten's Tree (Conditioned Galton-Watson Tree)

[Lemma 16 of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be a connected compact abelian group, let $\mu$ be its Haar 
probability measure, and let $\chi \in \widehat G$ be a nontrivial 
continuous character. For a measurable set $S \subset G$ with 
$\mu(S)\in(0,1],$ write $g_S:=\frac{ \mathbb{I}_S}{\mu(S)}.
$
Then:
$$ 
\bigl|\widehat{g_S}(\chi)\bigr|
=
\left|
\frac{1}{\mu(S)}\int_G   \mathbb{I}_S(x)\,\overline{\chi(x)}\,d\mu(x)
\right|
\leq
\frac{\sin(\pi\mu(S))}{\pi\mu(S)}.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A Poisson process of rate lambda > 0 is a counting process {N(t) : t >= 0} with N(0) = 0, independent increments, and N(t+s) - N(s) distributed Poisson(lambda t) for all s, t >= 0 (stationary increments). Equivalently: the inter-arrival times are i.i.d. Exponential(lambda). Equivalently: increments are independent, N(t) has a.s. jumps of size 1, and P(N(h) = 1) = lambda h + o(h), P(N(h) >= 2) = o(h).
title: Poisson Process

body: The quadratic variation [X]_t of a process X is the limit in probability of sum (X_{t_{i+1}} - X_{t_i})^2 over partitions of [0, t] with mesh tending to zero. For Brownian motion [W]_t = t; for continuous martingales the quadratic variation is the increasing process making X^2 - [X] a martingale, and it is the object that makes second-order terms survive in stochastic calculus.

[Definition def:hill of arXiv:2608.08375, 'Algebraic formulas for first-passage times of Markov processes in the linear framework: ge'] The vertices of $\mathcal{H}_u[G]$ are the non-terminal vertices of $G$, $\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{H}_u[G]) = \overline{Z}$. The edges and labels of $\mathcal{H}_u[G]$ are acquired from those of $G$ through the following rules.
\begin{enumerate}[topsep=1em]
    \item If $j, k \in \overline{Z}$ are non-terminal vertices with $k \neq u$ ($j = u$ is allowed) and there is an edge $j \to_G k$, then there is an edge $j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} k$ with, 
    \[
        \ell(j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} k) = \ell(j \to_G k) \,.
    \]
    \item If $j \in \overline{Z}$ is a non-terminal vertex and there is an edge $j \rightarrow_G u$, then there is an edge $j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u$ with, 
    \[
        \ell(j \to_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u) = \ell(j \to_G u) + \sum_{j \rightarrow_G z ,\, z \in Z} \ell(j \rightarrow_G z) \,.
    \]
    \item If $j \in \overline{Z}$ is a non-terminal vertex other than $u$ ($j \neq u$) without an edge to $u$ ($j \not\to_G u$) but with at least one edge, $j \to_G z$, to some $z \in Z$, then there is an edge $j \rightarrow_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u$ with, 
    \[
        \ell(j \rightarrow_{\mathcal{H}_u[G]} u) = \sum_{j \rightarrow_G z ,\, z \in Z} \ell(j \rightarrow_G z) \,.
    \]
\end{enumerate}
There are no other edges in $\mathcal{H}_u[G]$.
title: Definition def:hill of arXiv:2608.08375

For geometric offspring with pgf f(s)=1/(2-s), iteration gives f_l(s)=(l-(l-1)*s)/(l+1-l*s). Thus survival has probability 1/(l+1), and the conditional positive population is geometric with success 1/(l+1). The conditional tail at floor(l*x) is (l/(l+1))^floor(l*x), tending to exp(-x). Obstruction: No EWT Yaglom or Q-process theorem is proved. body:
Read the ladder result (every consistent cleaner ties inside the long-only stack; floors and linear shrinkage lose) through the entrywise bound. Unconstrained minimum variance depends on $\hat\Sigma^{-1}$, so its error is governed by the SPECTRUM of $\hat\Sigma$: the ratio $q = M/n$, the bulk edge, the near-null directions - the territory of random-matrix cleaning, where the Ledoit-Peche oracle, its analytical estimate and NERCOME differ from the sample covariance by design. The long-only plug-in's excess risk is bounded by twice the ENTRYWISE error $\varepsilon = \max_{ij}|\hat\Sigma_{ij} - \Sigma_{ij}|$, which is $O(\sqrt{\log M/n})$ for the sample covariance and of the same order for every consistent estimator (a consistent nonlinear shrinkage moves the eigenvalues by $O(n^{-1/2})$ relative, hence the entries by the same order) - so all of them obey the same bound and, on the well-conditioned active submatrix, produce the same weights. A fixed floor $f\sigma^2$ on the small eigenvalues, or a linear shrinkage $\rho(\mu I - \hat\Sigma)$, is a BIAS of size $f\sigma^2$ (or $\rho|\mu - \Sigma_{ii}|$) in the entries spanned by those directions that does not vanish with $n$; it cannot tighten the bound and it displaces the plug-in wherever an active member has weight in a floored direction. With case weights $s_i$ (the per-sample relative metric $s_i = 1/\|y_i\|^2$) the bound holds with $n$ replaced by the effective sample size $n_{\mathrm{eff}} = (\sum_i s_i)^2/\sum_i s_i^2$, which a few tiny-norm cases can make much smaller than $n$: that is why the relative-metric fit overfits without the constraint and why the long-only form still pays a little at very small $n$. Measured on the EMIT pool (2026-09-05, seed 101, diag_entrywise.py): the bound holds on every output of Y1/Y2/Y4 at $n = 932$ and of Y2/Y4 at $n = 60$, and is loose by one to three orders of magnitude (median $2\varepsilon$ over the oracle risk 10 to 1000 against a realised excess of 0.02 to 0.5 at full calibration) - it delivers finiteness and the right dependence, not a tight number; the unconstrained plug-in on the same matrices carries weights of median absolute size 68,000 on Y1 and 1,800 on Y2; the effective sample size of the $1/\|y\|^2$ weighting is 150 of 932 rows on Y2 (615 on Y1, 634 on Y4) and 8.7 of 60 in the $n = 60$ arm.

[Dfn 186 (discrete quadratic variation processes) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\vY$ and $\vY^\frozen$ be the spatial rerandomization processes from Definitions~\ref{d:rerand} and \ref{d:rerand.Ising}. Let $\vD$ and $\vD^\frozen$ be the associated drift processes from Definition~\ref{d:D}.
We now let 
	\begin{align*}
	\vZ &\equiv \vY-\vD\,,\\
	\vZ^\frozen 
		&\equiv \vY^\frozen-\vD^\frozen\,,
	\end{align*}
so these are martingales with respect to the filtration $\cG(q_d)$ from \eqref{e:gaus.filt}. In this subsection we consider the ``quadratic variations'' (and ``covariations'') for the $Z$ processes. To this end, for $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$, define 
$Q^{\sigma,\tau}$ to be the piecewise linear process with increments
	\beq
	\Delta Q^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d) 
	=  \bE \bigg[
		\Big( \Delta Z^\sigma(q_d)\Big)
		\Big(\Delta Z^\tau(q_d)\Big)
		\,\bigg|\, \cG(q_d)
		\bigg]\,,\eeq
started from $Q^{\sigma,\tau}(q_0)=0$. Clearly $Q^{\sigma,\tau}=Q^{\tau,\sigma}$; and we will also abbreviate $Q^{\sigma}\equiv Q^{\sigma,\sigma}$. We define likewise $Q^{\frozen,\sigma,\tau}$.
title: discrete quadratic variation processes

For a normal n by n matrix A, sigma_min(zI - A) = dist(z, spec A) for every z, so Lambda_epsilon(A) is the union of the closed disks of radius epsilon about the eigenvalues. Every eigenvalue of A + E lies within ||E|| of spec A, and if A and A + E are both normal, the Hausdorff distance between their spectra is at most ||E||. If moreover rho = min |lambda| over the eigenvalues of A is positive, every eigenvalue mu of A + E has an eigenvalue lambda of A with |mu - lambda| / |lambda| <= ||E|| / rho.

body: Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent, f non-negative and (a, b)-self-bounding with a >= 1/3, and Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) with finite mean; put c = (3a - 1)/6. Then for t > 0, P(Z - E[Z] >= t) <= exp(-t^2 / (2(a E[Z] + b + c t))) (Theorem 1 of arXiv:2509.22375, after Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart). For the lower tail, P(Z - E[Z] <= -t) <= exp(-t^2 / (2(a E[Z] + b + t/3))) for t > 0 (Theorem 2 there); and when the X_i take values in {0,1}, P(Z <= E[Z] - t) <= exp(-t^2 / (2(a E[Z] + b))) for 0 < t <= E[Z] (Theorem 3.3 of arXiv:1005.2791). With b = 0 and a = 1 the upper tail is exp(-t^2 / (2 E[Z] + 2t/3)).

body:
[Proposition prop:HB of arXiv:2608.25279, 'Provable Non-Acceleration of Standard Strang\\ Splittings of Kinetic Langevin Dynamics'] Let $(X_k,V_k)_{k\ge0}$ be the OBABO chain (equation eq:obabo1 of the paper)-(equation eq:obabo5 of the paper). Let $\xi_0^{(2)}$ be a $\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{Id}_d)$ variable independent of the pairs $(\xi_k^{(1)},\xi_k^{(2)})_{k\ge1}$ driving the chain. Alternatively, let $\xi_0^{(2)}$ be the zero vector. Define the auxiliary variable $X_{-1}$ by
\begin{equation}
 V_0=r\left(\frac{X_0-X_{-1}}h-\frac h2\nabla U(X_0)\right)
      +\sigma\xi_0^{(2)}.
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 X_{k+1}=X_k+\beta(X_k-X_{k-1})
 -s\nabla U(X_k)+\zeta_{k+1},
 \qquad
 s=\frac{h^2}{2}(1+\beta),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
 \zeta_{k+1}=h\sigma\bigl(r\xi_k^{(2)}+\xi_{k+1}^{(1)}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Distinct $\zeta_k$ depend on disjoint noises and are therefore
independent centered Gaussians. If
$\xi_0^{(2)}\sim\mathcal N(0,\mathrm{Id}_d)$, they are identically distributed
with covariance
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb E[\zeta_k\zeta_k^\top]
 =h^2(1-\beta^2)\mathrm{Id}_d.
\end{equation}
If $\xi_0^{(2)}=0$, then
\[
 \zeta_1=h\sigma\xi_1^{(1)},\qquad
 \mathbb E[\zeta_1\zeta_1^\top]=h^2(1-\beta)\mathrm{Id}_d,
\]
while (equation eq:zetacov of the paper) holds for every $k\ge2$.

    Let $(x, y)$ be a point of $\Half$ and $\landsc$ be a landscape of buildings. Then the angle formed by $(x, y)$ and its blocking building $\tau(x, y)$ is greater than that formed by $\tau(x, y)$ and its own blocking building $\tau (\tau (x, y))$. In other words, the sequence of shades $\left(S^{\tau^{(n)}(x, y)}_{\tau^{(n+1)}(x, y)}\right)_{n\in \N}$ is non increasing with respect to inclusion. [Corollary 16 of arXiv:2608.08242, 'Bang--bang representation of $3\times 3$ embeddable stochastic matrices'] Let $A\in \mathcal M_+$.  Suppose that $A\in R_n\setminus\bigl(R_{n-1}\cup\V\bigr)$
 and $n\geq 6$.
	Then $A$ has a minimal representation
	\[
	A=(X_n\cdots X_6)(X_5\cdots X_1),
	\]
	where each $X_\ell$ is a homogeneous elementary matrix and
	\[
	A'=X_5\cdots X_1\in\V
	\]
	satisfies exactly one vestibule equality. Moreover, in any such
	representation, if the unique vestibule equality is
	$V_{ij}(A')=0$ and $k$ is the remaining state, then, read in the order in which the moves are applied, the move types of
	$X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are, successively,
	\[
	(i,k),\ (k,j),\ (j,i),\ (i,k),\ (k,j),\ (j,i),\ldots .
	\]

\[
    \left|\psi^{(j)}(x+iy)\right|
    \leq
    C_{j,N}
    e^{2\pi\sigma|y|}
    (1+|x|)^{-N}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
    \operatorname{supp}\widehat\psi
    \subset[-\tau,\tau].
\]

Let $b:Z\to[-1,1]$ be a Borel injection and define
\[
    H_z(w)
    :=
    \sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}
    b(T^nz)\psi(w-n).
\]
The series and all its derivatives converge locally uniformly on
$\mathbb C$. The map
\[
    z\longmapsto H_z
\]
is Borel for the topology of locally uniform convergence, and
\[
    H_z(n)=b(T^nz),
    \qquad
    H_{Tz}(w)=H_z(w+1).
\]
For every $j\geq0$,
\[
    \left|H_z^{(j)}(x+iy)\right|
    \leq
    C_j e^{2\pi\sigma|y|}
\]
uniformly in $z\in Z$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R$. Finally,
\[
    \operatorname{supp}\widehat H_z
    \subset[-\tau,\tau]
    \qquad
    (z\in Z).
\]

[Lem 168 (errors from spatial rerandomization) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\vY$ be the spatial rerandomization of $\vX^\trunc$, defined by \eqref{e:def.Y}
with indices $(a(q_0), \ldots, a(\dmax))$ sampled according to Definition~\ref{d:rerand}. Then we have
	\begin{align*} 
	\max\bigg\{
	\Big|\Delta Y^{\sigma}(q_d)
		-\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d, a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
		: \sigma\in\{
		\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII
		\}
		\bigg\}
		&\le 2\eta\,,\\
	\bigg|
	\Delta Y^{\Ising}(q_d)
	-\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg|
	&\le2\eta\,.
	\end{align*}
for all $0\le d\le \dmax-1$. The same holds with $(\vY^\frozen,\vX^\frozen)$ in place of $(\vY,\vX^\trunc)$.

\begin{proof}
We prove the estimate for
$Y^{\RomI}$ versus $X^{\trunc,\RomI}$; the other bounds follow by the same argument. It follows from the definition~\eqref{e:def.Y} that
	\[
	\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)
	= \sum_{a\in B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))}
	\frac{X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a)}{|B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))|}
	-\sum_{a\in B(q_d,a(q_d))}
	\frac{X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)}{|B(q_d,a(q_d))|}\,.
	\]
Marginally, $a(q_d)$ is a uniformly random index from $[M]$. Conditional on $\cG(q_d)$, the index $a(q_{d+1})$ is sampled uniformly at random from  $B=B(q_d,a(q_d))$, the bucket at time $q_d$ that contains $a(q_d)$. 
It follows from the definitions of the buckets (see~\eqref{e:bucket}) that
	\begin{align*}
	\max\bigg\{ \Big|X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a)
	-X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	: a\in B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg\} &\le \eta\,,\\
	\max\bigg\{ \Big|X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)
	-X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	: a\in B(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))
	\bigg\} &\le \eta\,,
	\end{align*}
where the second bound uses that
$a(q_{d+1})$ and $a(q_d)$ are in the same bucket $B$ at time $q_d$.
Since $\vY(q_d)$ is obtained by averaging $\vX^\trunc(q_d,a)$ over $a\in B$, we immediately obtain
	\[
	\max\bigg\{
	\Big|Y^{\RomI}(q_d)
	- X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_d))\Big|,
	\Big|Y^{\RomI}(q_d)
	- X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	\bigg\} \le\eta\,.
	\]
Likewise, since $\vY(q_{d+1})$ is obtained by averaging 
$\vX^\trunc(q_{d+1},a')$ over $a'\in B'=B(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))$, we have
	\beq
	\Big|Y^{\RomI}(q_{d+1})
	- X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_{d+1},a(q_{d+1}))\Big| \le\eta\,.
	\eeq
Combining these gives the claimed bound.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition 92 of arXiv:2609.03875, 'Measure theory without infinities'] Let $\mf A$ be an HTM and $\mu$ be an $\mf A$-valued map. Given a set $A$, we say that $\mu$ is $A$-exhaustive and write $\ex{\mf A}{A}\mu$ if $\mu(\mb A(n))\to 0$ in $\mf A$ as $n\to\infty$ whenever $\mb A\colon\N\to D_\mu$ is a disjoint family such that $\mb A(n)\subset A$ for every $n\in\N$. We call $\mu$ weakly exhaustive if $\ex{\mf A}{A}\mu$ for every $A\in D_\mu$.

Let f : {-1,1}^n -> R with the uniform product measure and let Delta_i f (x) = ( f(x) - f(x^{(i)}) ) / 2, where x^{(i)} flips coordinate i. Then there is a UNIVERSAL constant C with Var(f) <= C sum_{i=1}^n || Delta_i f ||_2^2 / ( 1 + log( || Delta_i f ||_2 / || Delta_i f ||_1 ) ), with the convention that a term is 0 when Delta_i f = 0. The unimproved bound Var(f) <= sum_i ||Delta_i f||_2^2 is the Efron-Stein inequality on the cube; Talagrand's refinement gains a LOGARITHMIC factor for every coordinate whose influence is spread out, that is whose L2 and L1 norms are far apart, and gains nothing for a coordinate whose discrete derivative is essentially an indicator. This is precisely the inequality Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm apply to first-passage percolation with two-valued weights to obtain Var <= C n / log n, and the reason their theorem carries a two-point weight hypothesis is that the L1-L2 comparison must be run on that specific cube structure. The p-biased and Gaussian analogues exist with modified constants; the Gaussian version replaces the log ratio by an entropy term (Falik-Samorodnitsky). [Talagrand (1994), 'On Russo's approximate zero-one law', Ann. Probab. 22; used in Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm (2003)]
uniform product measure on the discrete cube {-1,1}^n
f real-valued and square integrable on the cube
C is a universal constant, in particular independent of n and of f

Set r=T/kappa_T, A=x0^2/2, D=n/(n-1) for even n and (n+1)/n for odd n, B=A*exp(-4r), H=2*s2*D*T/kappa_T^2, and let u>0 uniquely solve u^2*exp(u)=H/B. Put V=B*(exp(u)*(1+u)-1). Then (min_eta>=0 E[final function error]-B)/V->1, and every global minimizing constant-step sequence obeys 2*r*(2-kappa_T*eta_T)/u->1. Thus the total optimal error is asymptotic to B*exp(u)*(1+u). Status: proof draft (unaudited). No priority or full-T362 claim.

## Statement

Use C001's normalized common-Hessian model, fixed n>=2, fixed deterministic x0!=0,y0 and fixed zero-sum linear terms with mean squares s1>=0,s2>0. Epoch permutations are fresh, independent and uniform, shared across coordinates. Let T=nK and suppose only kappa*log(T)/T->4. Set

    r=T/kappa,  A=x0^2/2,
    D=n/(n-1) for even n, (n+1)/n for odd n,
    B=A*exp(-4r),  H=2*s2*D*T/kappa^2,
    lambda=H/B.

Let u>0 be the unique solution u^2*exp(u)=lambda, and put

    V=B*(exp(u)*(1+u)-1).

For the exact expected final-epoch objective P_T,

    (min_{eta>=0} P_T(eta)-B)/V ->1.                     (1)

Consequently min P_T ~ B*exp(u)*(1+u). Every sequence of global minimizers satisfies

    [2r*(2-kappa*eta_T)]/u ->1.                          (2)

These statements permit oscillating subleading corrections in kappa, including lambda tending to zero, a positive constant, infinity, or having no limit. In particular (1) is an excess-error equivalent, stronger than a relative equivalent for the total error when V=o(B).

## Scalar optimizer lemma

For lambda>0, f_lambda(z)=exp(z)-1+lambda/z on z>0 is strictly convex, diverges at both endpoints and has unique minimum at u satisfying u^2 exp(u)=lambda. Indeed f'=exp(z)-lambda/z^2 and f''=exp(z)+2lambda/z^3>0. Its minimum is exp(u)*(1+u)-1.

We also need this uniform stability statement: for arbitrary sequences lambda>0 and z>0,

    f_lambda(z)/f_lambda(u)->1 implies z/u->1.            (3)

Proof of (3). Pass to a subsequence with u tending in the extended interval [0,infinity]. If u->0, f_lambda(u)~2u and lambda=u^2 exp(u). The lower bounds f_lambda(z)>=z and f_lambda(z)>=lambda/z force z/u to stay bounded above and bounded away from zero. Along any convergent subsequence z/u->a>0, the ratio tends to (a+1/a)/2; equality to 1 forces a=1. If u tends to a finite positive value, continuity, endpoint coercivity and strict uniqueness give z->u. If u->infinity, any z/u<=1-epsilon has ratio at least

    [u*exp(u)/(exp(u)*(1+u)-1)]/(1-epsilon)
        ->1/(1-epsilon)>1.

Any z/u>=1+epsilon has ratio at least [exp((1+epsilon)u)-1]/[exp(u)*(1+u)-1], which diverges. Thus (3) holds in all subsequences, without assuming lambda itself converges.

## Scales and candidate step

1. Write ell=log T. The ratio assumption implies r~ell/4, kappa~4T/ell, and

    B=T^(-1+o(1)), H=T^(-1+o(1)), log(lambda)=o(ell).

It follows that u=o(ell), u=T^(o(1)) and 1/u=T^(o(1)). For u<=1 use 2log u+u=log lambda; for u>=1 use u<=log lambda. Also exp(u)=T^(o(1)). Since

    V=B*(exp(u)-1)+H/u,

both an upper bound and the positive lower bound H/u show V=T^(-1+o(1)). These are logarithmic-scale statements, not relative equivalents with fixed prefactors.

2. Use delta_c=u/(2r), q_c=2-delta_c, eta_c=q_c/kappa. Then delta_c->0 and delta_c*T=u*kappa/2=T^(1+o(1))->infinity, so eventually 0<q_c<2. C006's fixed-n endpoint residue is

    J_n(2-delta)~D/delta,

where the stiff finite-horizon variance is (s2/kappa)*J_n(q)*(1-(1-q)^(2T)). The residue comes from W_n(2)=4 floor(n/2)ceil(n/2); its denominators are positive for 0<q<2. Thus the stiff variance at this candidate is (1+o(1))*H/u.

3. The flat deterministic contribution is

    A*(1-eta_c)^(2T) = B*exp(u)*(1+O(T/kappa^2)).

This follows from the uniform logarithm expansion at eta_c=O(1/kappa); T/kappa^2=T^(-1+o(1))->0. Its absolute error is T^(-2+o(1))=o(V). The flat variance is O(kappa^-3)=o(V). The stiff deterministic term is at most kappa*y0^2*exp(-u*kappa)/2=o(V), because u*kappa=T^(1+o(1)) dominates log T. The finite-horizon variance multiplier tends to one by the same bound. Hence

    min P_T <= B+(1+o(1))*V = T^(-1+o(1))->0.            (4)

## Unrestricted optimizer localization

4. Global minimizers exist by the coercive exact polynomial in C001. Put q_T=kappa*eta_T for ANY sequence of them. The exact stiff variance is

    R_T=[s2*q_T^2*W_n(q_T)/(2(n-1)*kappa)]
           *sum_{j=0}^{K-1}(1-q_T)^(2nj),
    W_n(q)>=q^2.

If q_T>=2, every summand is >=1 and R_T>=8s2*K/((n-1)kappa), which diverges like log T, contradicting (4). Therefore q_T<2 eventually. If q_T<=2-epsilon along a subsequence, the flat transient is at least T^(-1+epsilon/2+o(1)), also contradicting (4). Thus q_T->2 from below. Write delta_T=2-q_T->0.

5. Necessarily delta_T*T->infinity. Otherwise, along a subsequence delta_T*T<=M, every summand of the variance sum is at least exp(-4M) eventually, using log(1-delta)>=-2delta for delta<=1/2. It follows that R_T>=const*K/kappa->infinity. Therefore the stationary residue and the vanishing finite-horizon correction apply along every minimizer sequence.

## The excess-error comparison

6. Put z_T=2r*delta_T>0. Since delta_T->0 and r~ell/4, z_T=o(ell). The flat deterministic contribution has the expansion

    B*exp(z_T)+O((T/kappa^2)*B*exp(z_T)).

Here B exp(z_T)=T^(-1+o(1)), so the absolute remainder is T^(-2+o(1))=o(V), even when V=o(B). The stiff variance is (1+o(1))*H/z_T, by step 5. All other contributions are nonnegative. Define

    F(z)=B*(exp(z)-1)+H/z = B*f_lambda(z).

Subtracting the exact retained baseline B and controlling the flat remainder therefore gives

    P_T(eta_T)-B >= (1-o(1))*F(z_T)-o(V).                (5)

This is valid because both summands of F(z) are nonnegative on z>0: a relative error in H/z can be bounded by the same relative error in F(z). No uncontrolled subtraction of asymptotic equivalents is used. Since F(z)>=F(u)=V, (4)-(5) prove (1), and also F(z_T)/V->1. Applying scalar stability (3) proves z_T/u->1, exactly (2).

## Scope, side conditions and audit focus

All logarithms occur only for sufficiently large T. n-1>0, kappa>0, B>0, H>0, lambda>0 and u>0; the stationary denominator is used only after 0<q<2 is established. Fixed n is needed for the pole residue; nonzero s2 supplies variance localization, and x0!=0 makes B positive. The fresh-epoch recursion is inherited from the row. Coordinate-noise independence is not assumed.

This fills the general ratio-only c=4 window of named target 1 in draft form. It includes the exact path C006 without replacing its proof or rechecking the settled recursion. It does not settle general Hessians, growing n, x0=0, s2=0, or the full T362 conjecture. Independent audit should focus on (3), the T^(-2+o(1)) absolute remainder versus V=T^(-1+o(1)), and the excess-error comparison (5). No priority claim is made from the bounded prior-art search recorded with C004. body: Let v_1, ..., v_n be vectors in an inner product space H (real or complex). The Gram matrix G, with entries G_{ij} = <v_i, v_j>, is Hermitian positive semidefinite. Moreover G is positive definite if and only if v_1, ..., v_n are linearly independent. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis]

body: A function f between metric spaces is Lipschitz with constant L if d(f(x), f(y)) <= L d(x, y) for all x, y in its domain. The Lipschitz constant Lip(f) is the smallest such L. For real-valued f on a normed space this reads |f(x) - f(y)| <= L ||x - y||.

body: Liouville's theorem: every bounded entire function is constant. Precisely, if f is holomorphic on all of C and there is a constant M with |f(z)| <= M for every z in C, then f is constant. Equivalently, a nonconstant entire function has unbounded image. It follows from the Cauchy estimates: |f'(a)| <= M/R for every disk of radius R about a, and letting R go to infinity gives f' = 0. Standard consequences: the fundamental theorem of algebra (a nonconstant complex polynomial attains a root, else 1/p would be a bounded entire function), and an entire function growing at most like a polynomial of degree n is a polynomial of degree at most n.
title: Liouville's theorem (complex analysis)

body: Let X be a normed vector space and Y a proper closed linear subspace of X. Then for every theta in (0,1) there exists x in X with ||x|| = 1 and dist(x, Y) = inf_{y in Y} ||x - y|| >= theta. Consequently, the closed unit ball of an infinite-dimensional normed space is never compact: one can inductively construct a sequence of unit vectors with pairwise distances at least 1/2. [standard, e.g. Conway, A Course in Functional Analysis]
title: Riesz's Lemma (Almost-Orthogonal Elements in a Normed Space)

body:
Let f : {-1,1}^n -> R with the uniform measure, with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_{S subset [n]} fhat(S) chi_S where chi_S(x) = prod_{i in S} x_i. For 0 <= rho <= 1 define the noise operator T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} fhat(S) chi_S. Then for all 1 <= p <= q < infinity, || T_rho f ||_q <= || f ||_p whenever rho <= sqrt( (p-1)/(q-1) ). Two standard specialisations: taking p = 2 gives || T_rho f ||_q <= || f ||_2 for rho = 1/sqrt(q-1); and for f of DEGREE at most d, meaning fhat(S) = 0 whenever |S| > d, one gets || f ||_q <= (q-1)^{d/2} || f ||_2 for every q >= 2, and by duality || f ||_2 <= (q-1)^{d/2} ||f||_{q'} for the conjugate exponent. The degree-d moment comparison is the workhorse: it says low-degree functions on the cube have all L^q norms comparable to their L^2 norm with a constant depending only on the degree and q, not on n, which is exactly the dimension-free input that KKL and Talagrand's variance inequality consume. The measure must be the UNIFORM (or a fixed p-biased, with a different constant) product measure - the theorem is about product measures on the cube. [Bonami (1970), Beckner (1975); see O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Chapter 9]
the uniform product measure on {-1,1}^n
1 <= p <= q < infinity and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1))
the constant is independent of n
metadata_json: {"artifact_digest":"sha256:c4ed3530c52be6e7fc9375618cdb99ac4420db31d2e95f4547441daccfae5281","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/c4/c4ed3530c52be6e7fc9375618cdb99ac4420db31d2e95f4547441daccfae5281.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:5d0af25fb2bb6ea6e0afced86be983845a6c3262052b9ee136bb54da2d02c09b","bundle_entry_key":"thm-bonami-beckner","bundle_id":"population.martingales-and-concentration-001","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"claude-8e06e1f7-M9/bundle_ap02.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.concentration:bonami-beckner-hypercontractivity-on-the-discrete-cube","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"The proof has exactly two steps, and the second is where the dimension-free constant comes from. STEP 1, the two-point inequality: for n = 1 the claim is that for real a, b, ( E |a + rho b x|^q )^{1/q} <= ( E |a + b x|^p )^{1/p} with x uniform on {-1,1} and rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1)). Normalising a = 1 and expanding both sides as power series in b, one compares coefficients termwise; the inequality reduces to the elementary fact that the binomial-type coefficients of (1 + rho b)^q + (1 - rho b)^q are dominated by those coming from the p-side under the stated constraint on rho, which is checked directly for the first two orders and follows for the rest from the same constraint. STEP 2, tensorization: the hypercontractive constant of a product is the minimum of the constants of the factors. Precisely, if T_rho is a contraction from L^p to L^q on each factor space then it is a contraction from L^p to L^q on the product. This is proved by applying the one-dimensional bound in one coordinate at a time and using Minkowski's integral inequality, valid because q >= p, to exchange the order of the L^q norm in the remaining coordinates with the L^p norm in the coordinate being processed.  \nu(\dd x)=\frac{V}{2c^3}e^{-x/c}\one_{(0,\infty)}(x)\,\dd x.

Fix delta > 1 and x_0 > 0. Let V be a real, locally bounded, cadlag function on (0,infinity), and set B_l(x) = (integral_{x_0}^x exp(y^delta+V(y)) dy)(integral_x^infinity exp(-y^delta-V(y)) dy), allowing an infinite product. Suppose V has a downward jump of size m > 0 at a sufficiently large time tau, so V(tau-) - V(tau) = m. Put h = min(tau^(1-delta),1), assume tau-h > x_0, and define O_1 = sup_{tau-h<=y<tau}|V(y)-V(tau-)| and O_2 = sup_{tau<=y<=tau+h}|V(y)-V(tau)|. Then B_l(tau) >= exp(-4 delta) tau^(2-2 delta) exp(m-O_1-O_2). So the logarithmic cost of a quiet well at tau is (2 delta-2) log tau, while its jump depth contributes m. The bound uses only the integrals over [tau-h,tau] and [tau,tau+h], so it holds with x_0 replaced by any R < tau-h. This is an unrefereed campaign result.

[Def Def_quasi_arithmetic of arXiv:2606.22183, 'Expected loss of quasi-arithmetic means of exchangeable random variables'] Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $I\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a nonempty open interval, and let $f:I\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous and strictly increasing function.
The $n$-variable quasi-arithmetic mean $\mathscr{A}_n^{f}:I^n\to I$ is defined by
 \[
  \mathscr{A}_n^{f}(x_1,\ldots,x_n):= f^{-1} \bigg( \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)\bigg), \qquad x_1,\ldots, x_n\in I,
 \]
where $f^{-1}$ denotes the inverse of $f$. The function $f$ is called the generator of $\mathscr{A}_n^{f}$.

[Cor 163 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $0<q_1<q_2<\dots<q_m<1$. For small enough $\delta,\epsilon>0$ there exists $c>0$ such that for $N$ sufficiently large and $K=e^{cN}$, with probability $1-e^{-cN}$ the following holds for any $(L,\epsilon)$-good $(p,\sigma,b,w)$: 
 there exist points $(\by_w :w\in [K]^m)$, taking values in $\Sigma_N(\iota)$ (or $S_N(\iota)$) such that
  \beq
  \bbW_2\Big(
  \mu^{\sym}_{\bG}(\by_w),
  \mu^{\sym}(p,\sigma,b,w)
  \Big) \le\epsilon\eeq
for all $w\in [K]^m$, and
  \beq
  \lt|\frac{( \by_w,\by_{w'})}{N}-q_{w\wedge w'}\rt|
  \leq \epsilon\eeq
for all $w,w'\in [K]^m$. In fact, we can take $\by_w=\cA_{\chaos}(\bz_w)$ where $(\bz_w:w\in [K]^m)$ is an ensemble of gaussians that are suitably correlated with $\bz\equiv(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 

\begin{proof}
Choose $\epsilon\ll q_1$ small. We will take $c$ small in order to union bound over $e^{O(cN)}$ exponentially unlikely events in the proof. Let $\cA_{\chaos}$ be as defined in 
Proposition~\ref{ppn:chaotic-amp-still-works}, taking inputs $\bz=(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. Let $\chi$ be the correlation function associated to $\cA_{\chaos}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:chaotic-iamp-is-chaotic}, we have
  \[p_i\equiv \chi^{-1}(q_i)
  \ge 1-\epsilon\]
for all $1\leq i\leq m$. Let $T$ denote the $K$-ary tree of depth $m$, and identify the leaves with $[K]^m$. Generate a jointly gaussian ensemble
$(\bz_w: w\in [K]^m)$ such that $\bz_{1^m}=\bz=(\bG,\bg^\aux)$, and such that the correlation between $\bz_u$ and $\bz_v$ is $p_{|u\wedge v|+1}$ for any $u,v\in [K]^m$. Let $\by_w\equiv \cA_{\chaos}(\bz_w)$ for $w\in[K]^m$. 
By taking $\eta$ small enough in the 
definition of $\cA_{\chaos}$, and 
applying
Proposition~\ref{ppn:chaotic-amp-still-works} together with a union bound over $w\in[K]^m$, we obtain
that with probability at least $1- e^{-10cN}$, we have 
  \begin{equation}
  
  \bbW_2\Big(
  \mu^{\sym}_{\bG_w}(\by_w),
  \mu^{\sym}(p,\sigma,b,w)
  \Big)\leq \epsilon
  \end{equation}
for all $w\in[K]^m$. Another union bound gives that with probability at least 
 $1-e^{-10cN}$, we have
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  \max\bigg\{
  \frac{\|\by_w\|}{N^{1/2}}
  : w\in[K]^m\bigg\}
  &\le 2\,,\\
  \max\bigg\{
  \frac{\|\bG_w-\bG_{w'}\|_{\op}}{M^{1/2} + N^{1/2}}
  : w,w'\in[K]^m
  \bigg\}
  &\leq 10\epsilon^{1/2}\,.
  \end{aligned}
  \]
On the event that the above conditions hold, we have deterministically
  \[
  \bbW_2\Big(\mu^{\sym}_{\bG_w}(\by_w),\mu^{\sym}_{\bG}(\by_w)\Big)
  \leq 
  \bbW_2\Big(\mu_{\bG_w}(\by_w),\mu^{\sym}_{\bG}(\by_w)\Big)
  \leq 
  \frac{\|(\bG_w-\bG)\by_w\|}{
    (MN)^{1/2}}
  \leq 
  O(\epsilon^{1/2}).
  \]
Combining with \eqref{eq:outputs-good-for-perturbed-disorder} and adjusting $\epsilon$ gives \eqref{eq:all-outputs-good}. Next we note that
  \[
  \bbE\bigg[\frac{( \by_w,\by_{w'})}{N}\bigg]
  =
  \chi(p_{w\wedge w'})=q_{w\wedge w'}\,,
  \]
so \eqref{eq:overlaps-ultrametric} follows from concentration of measure (again taking a union bound with $c$ small enough).  
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
DRAFT, proof (unaudited), T318-C2 version 2; no priority claim. Take n/p->gamma>0, p/d->psi>0, independent f_j uniform on the sphere of radius sqrt(d), g_i~N(0,I_d), and features x_ij=rho(f_j^T g_i/sqrt(d))/sqrt(p), with rho a fixed nonzero odd globally Lipschitz activation. Use the shared-feature teacher y_i=x_i^T w_*+epsilon_i with independent w_*~N(0,s_*^2 I_p), epsilon_i~N(0,sigma^2), and inference prior N(0,s_p^2 I_p), where sigma^2,s_p^2>0, s_*^2>=0; prediction always integrates the original likelihood with noise sigma^2. Put lambda=sigma^2/s_p^2, r=s_*^2/s_p^2, v=E rho(G)^2, b=(E G rho(G))^2, tau=v-b, G~N(0,1). The conditional feature covariance has limiting law H=law(tau+b W), W~MP_psi. The weighted resolvent m(a) is the positive fixed point m=integral t/[a+gamma*t/(1+m)] dH(t), and m_2=-m', m_3=m''/2. Whole-posterior tempering keeps the mean fixed and uniquely minimizes limiting predictive log loss at T_W=1+(r-1)lambda*m_2(lambda)/m(lambda), with 0<lambda*m_2/m<1. Hence r<1 gives a nonvanishing cold margin for fixed model parameters. Likelihood tempering uses a=lambda*T, q=a*m, R=r*a^2*m_2+lambda*(m-a*m_2); its excess log risk over known-teacher noise entropy is 0.5*[log((lambda+q)/lambda)+(lambda+R)/(lambda+q)-1]. Interior optimal a satisfy 2*(r*a-lambda)*(m_2-a*m_3)*(lambda+a*m)+(m-a*m_2)*(a*m-r*a^2*m_2-lambda*(m-a*m_2))=0. There are finitely many positive critical points; compare them with the a->0 limit and set T=a/lambda. Infinite temperature cannot minimize; no uniqueness of the likelihood optimum is claimed. The fixed point is algebraic via the shifted-MP quadratic, giving an algebraic root prescription, not a radical formula. For rho(t)=sqrt(3)*erf(t/sqrt(2)), v=1,b=3/pi,tau=1-3/pi. Noise normalization lambda is essential; the unnormalized target cannot depend only on gamma,psi,s_p/s_*. Convergence is in probability for expected test log loss conditional on typical realized training data and features. Non-odd activations and trained hidden layers are outside this result.
Exact assumptions are in the self-contained statement; DRAFT proof (unaudited).

Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with n >= 2, and let A be measurable, bounded and uniformly elliptic on Omega (alpha|xi|^2 <= A(x)xi.xi, |A(x)| <= Lambda, alpha > 0). Let f be in L^1(Omega) and let f_m be any sequence in L^infinity(Omega) with ||f_m||_{L^1} <= ||f||_{L^1} and f_m -> f in L^1 (for instance f_m = T_m(f), the truncation of f at level m). Let u_m in H^1_0(Omega) solve -div(A grad u_m) = f_m weakly. Then: (i) for every q with 1 <= q < n/(n-1) the sequence (u_m) is bounded in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) by a constant depending only on n, q, alpha, |Omega| and ||f||_{L^1}; (ii) up to a subsequence u_m converges strongly in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) and almost everywhere, together with its gradients, to a function u in W^{1,q}_0(Omega) which is a distributional solution: integral_Omega A grad u . grad phi = integral_Omega f phi for every phi in C_c^infinity(Omega); (iii) the limit satisfies the Marcinkiewicz (weak-Lebesgue) bounds u in M^(n/(n-2)) for n >= 3 and |grad u| in M^(n/(n-1)), with norms controlled by ||f||_{L^1}. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) the endpoint q = n/(n-1) is genuinely excluded - the fundamental solution of the Laplacian (the limit case f = Dirac mass) has |grad u| comparable to |x|^(1-n), which lies in weak-L^(n/(n-1)) but not in L^(n/(n-1)); (b) for n >= 3 one has n/(n-1) < 2, so the limit u need not belong to H^1_0 and the energy formulation is unavailable - u is only a distributional solution; (c) distributional solutions with L^1 data are NOT unique: Serrin's example gives a bounded measurable uniformly elliptic A and a nonzero u in W^{1,q}_0(Omega), q < 2, that solves the homogeneous equation distributionally. Uniqueness is restored only in the entropy-solution or renormalized-solution formulation of Benilan-Boccardo-Gallouet-Gariepy-Pierre-Vazquez. (d) The estimate is a bound on approximations plus a compactness statement; it does not by itself say that every distributional solution obeys it.
Omega is a bounded open subset of R^n, n >= 2
A is measurable, bounded and uniformly elliptic (no continuity assumed)
f is in L^1(Omega); the data may also be a bounded Radon measure with the same conclusions
the approximating data f_m are bounded, converge to f in L^1, and have L^1 norms bounded by ||f||_{L^1}
q is strictly less than n/(n-1)
conclusions are for the approximating sequence and its limit, not for an arbitrary distributional solution

body: Let A be an n by n Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues lambda_1 >= ... >= lambda_n, and let V be an n by k matrix, k <= n, with orthonormal columns (V* V = I_k). Let B = V* A V, a k by k Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues mu_1 >= ... >= mu_k. Then lambda_i >= mu_i >= lambda_{i+n-k} for every i = 1, ..., k. Taking V to be the matrix obtained by deleting one standard basis column recovers the Cauchy interlacing theorem as the case k = n-1. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis]

[Lemma lem:finite-block-weighted-growth-paper of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Let 
\(
(A_0,A_1)
\)
be a pair of almost surely finite nonnegative random variables, and define the possibly extended-valued function 
\(
\kappa:[0,1]\to[0,\infty]
\)
by
\[
\kappa(\theta)
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf 1_{\{A_0>0\}}+\mathbf 1_{\{A_1>0\}}\right],
& \theta=0,\\[8pt]
\displaystyle
\mathbb{E}\left[A_0^\theta+A_1^\theta\right],
& 0<\theta\le1.
\end{cases}
\]
Assume that 
\[
\inf_{0\le\theta\le1}\kappa(\theta)>1.
\]

Let 
\(
\mathcal T=\bigcup_{n\ge0}\{0,1\}^n
\)
be the full binary tree, with root \(\varnothing\). Let
\[
\bigl\{(A_0(v),A_1(v)):v\in\mathcal T\bigr\}
\]
be an i.i.d. family of copies of 
\(
(A_0,A_1)
\).
For 
\(
u=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)\in\{0,1\}^n
\),
write 
\(
u|_{j-1}=(u_1,\ldots,u_{j-1})
\),
with 
\(
u|_0=\varnothing
\),
and define
\[
A_u
=
\prod_{j=1}^{n}A_{u_j}(u|_{j-1}),
\qquad
A_\varnothing=1.
\]
Then there exist 
\(
N\ge1
\), 
\(
\tau>0
\),
and 
\(
\beta>1
\)
such that 
\[
\beta\tau>1 \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbb{E}\#\{u\in\{0,1\}^N:A_u\ge\tau\}>\beta.
\]

body: Euler's formula: for every real number x, e^{ix} = cos x + i sin x, where e is the base of the natural logarithm, i the imaginary unit, and cos, sin the trigonometric functions; the right-hand side is sometimes written cis x. With the exponential defined by its power series the identity holds for every complex x, and the special case x = pi gives e^{i pi} + 1 = 0.

Let U ⊂ C be open and connected, let f_n be holomorphic on U, and let f_n → f uniformly on compact subsets of U, where f is not identically zero. If the closed disk |z - a| ≤ r lies in U and f has no zero on the circle |z - a| = r, then for all sufficiently large n the functions f_n and f have the same number of zeros, counted with multiplicity, in the open disk |z - a| < r. Consequences: (a) if every f_n has no zeros in U, then the limit f either has no zeros in U or is identically zero; (b) if every f_n is injective on U, then f is either injective on U or constant.
U ⊂ C is open and connected
each f_n is holomorphic on U
f_n → f uniformly on compact subsets of U
f is not identically zero (for the counting statement and (a)); f is not constant (for (b))
the counting circle lies in U and avoids the zeros of f

[Lemma 2 (Expectation under uniform dispersal $D4$) of arXiv:2605.04048, 'Catastrophe--dispersion models in random and varying environments across generations'] Let $d\ge1$ and let $Y:=N_{\eta(T)}$ be an $\mathbb N_0$-valued random variable with probability generating function
\[
G_Y(z)=\mathbb E[z^Y], \qquad 0\le z\le1.
\]
Under dispersal mechanism $D4$, the expected number of founded colonies satisfies
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[\Delta^{(4)}(Y)\right]
=
\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{dY}{Y+d-1}\mathbf 1_{\{Y\ge1\}}\right].
\]
In particular, if $d\ge2$, then
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[\Delta^{(4)}(Y)\right]
=
d
-
d(d-1)\int_0^1 z^{d-2}G_Y(z)\,dz.

[Prop 13 of arXiv:2608.30357, 'Mean convergence for Banach space-valued random elements indexed in measure spaces'] Let $p \in [1, \infty)$ and assume that $\{X^n_s : s \in S_n, n \ge 1\}$ is $(\nu_n)$-$\CUI(p)$ in the sense of  \cref{def:CUI-uniform}. Assume that for each $n \ge 1$ there exists $D_n \in \cS_n \otimes \cS_n$ such that:
\begin{enumerate}[\rm (a')]
		\item  $\lim_{n \to \infty} (\nu_n \otimes \nu_n) (D_n) = 0$,
		
		\item  $X^n_s$ and $X^n_t$ are diagonally negatively dependent for $(\nu_n \otimes \nu_n)$-a.e.\ $(s, t) \in (S_n \times S_n) \backslash D_n$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Then, \cref{eq:thm:bounded-masses} holds.

body: [Theorem 2.5 (Conditional exponential family (finite symmetric truncation)) in the first version of arXiv:2512.18592, 'Wavelet Latent Position Exponential Random Gr'] Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and latent positions $U=(U_{1},\dots,U_{n})\in(0,1)^{n}$. Let $\{\psi_{r}:r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\}$ be the wavelet basis from Definition 2.1, and let $I\subset\mathbb{N}_{0}\times\mathbb{N}_{0}$ be a finite index set. Let $\theta=\bigl(c,(s_{rs})_{(r,s)\in I}\bigr)$ and define the truncated coefficient matrix $S_{\theta}=(\tilde{s}_{rs})_{r,s\geq 0}$ by $\tilde{s}_{rs}:=\begin{cases}s_{rs},&(r,s)\in I,\\ 0,&(r,s)\notin I.\end{cases}$ Assume $S_{\theta}$ is symmetric, i.e. $\tilde{s}_{rs}=\tilde{s}_{sr}$ for all $r,s\geq 0$ (equivalently: whenever both $(r,s)$ and $(s,r)$ lie in $I$ we impose $s_{rs}=s_{sr}$, and any unpaired index in $I$ must have coefficient $0$). Define $\eta_{\theta}(x,y):=c+\sum_{(r,s)\in I}s_{rs}\,\psi_{r}(x)\psi_{s}(y),\qquad W_{\theta}(x,y):=\sigma\!\bigl(\eta_{\theta}(x,y)\bigr).$ Under $\mathrm{WL\mbox{-}ERG}(c,S_{\theta})$, the conditional distribution of $A$ given $U$ has pmf $\mathbb{P}_{\theta}(A\mid U)=\exp\Bigl\{c\,S_{00}(A)+\sum_{(r,s)\in I}s_{rs}\,S_{rs}(A,U)-\Psi_{n}(\theta;U)\Bigr\},$ with log–partition function $\Psi_{n}(\theta;U):=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\log\!\Bigl(1+\exp(\eta_{\theta}(U_{i},U_{j}))\Bigr).$ Because $\psi_{0}\equiv 1$, if $(0,0)\in I$ then $s_{00}$ is confounded with $c$ (the family is not minimal); one may remove $(0,0)$ from $I$ or absorb $s_{00}$ into $c$.

body:
For a finite collection of self-avoiding paths with weights x to the power of path length, x>0, conditioning on length n makes the law uniform among the n-step paths in that same collection, because all surviving weights equal x^n. A prescribed terminal vertex and bounded domain remain part of that collection. Weak convergence of the unconditioned variable-length laws alone does not identify a conditional law at a length whose probability tends to zero; a relative local-limit estimate or another explicit transfer theorem is required before a chordal critical-fugacity result can address Grimmett's uniform n-step free-endpoint question.

Positive fugacity

Let R be a commutative ring with identity and let A be an n x n matrix over R. Let p_A(t) = det(t I_n - A) in R[t] be its characteristic polynomial, a monic polynomial of degree n. Then p_A(A) = 0, the n x n zero matrix, where p_A(A) is formed by substituting A for t and the identity matrix for the constant term. Consequently the minimal polynomial of A over a field divides p_A, and A^n lies in the R-span of I, A, ..., A^{n-1}.

[Theorem thm:orthant of arXiv:2607.14087, 'Stochastic Domination of Gaussian Maxima: A Resolution of the Weak Simplex Conjecture'] Let $R$ be an $m\times m$ correlation matrix satisfying
\[
  R-\frac1mJ\succeq0,
\]
and let $X\sim\mathcal N(0,R)$.  Then
\begin{equation}
  \mathsf M_X\leq_{\mathrm{st}}\mathsf M_Z.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb P\{X\leq c\mathbf 1\}\geq\Phi(c)^m
  \qquad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb R.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
  \mathsf M_X\stackrel{d}{=}\mathsf M_Z
  \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
  R=I_m.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Metropolis relaxation for geometric-time Cayley targets explicit structural calculation Result: Monotone decrease is false already on the two-element Cayley group, with relaxation defined by1/(1-lambda_2). For the nonlazy base walk that flips states, mu_p=(1/(2-p),(1-p)/(2-p)), and its Metropolis matrix is[[p,1-p],[1,0]]. Its second eigenvalue is p-1, hence tau(p)=1/(2-p), which is strictly increasing. The same conclusion survives a lazy base walk: the base matrix has all entries1/2, mu_p=((1+p)/2,(1-p)/2), the Metropolis off-diagonal rates are(1-p)/(2*(1+p)) and1/2, and tau(p)=1+p. Check: For the flip walk, sum the geometric probabilities over even versus odd times. For the lazy base, X_0 is the identity and X_k is uniform for every k>=1. The nontrivial eigenvalue of a two-state stochastic matrix is1 minus the sum of its off-diagonal probabilities, giving both formulas directly. If laziness is imposed after forming the nonlazy Metropolis kernel, tau becomes2/(2-p), still increasing. Obstruction: The literal monotonicity direction is refuted under the standard spectral-gap relaxation convention, but this does not answer the other universal-bound questions or resolve the source undefined tau(infinity). If relaxation meant inverse absolute gap for a nonlazy chain, that convention differs; the lazy example has nonnegative spectrum and removes that ambiguity. Prior-art status remains unverified.

OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; source-scope observation, proof (unaudited), no novelty claim. In Hidden Progress in Deep Learning: SGD Learns Parities Near the Computational Limit, arXiv:2207.08799v3, Proposition 9 converts an initialization derivative Fourier gap gamma into support recovery: if every relevant gradient-coordinate magnitude exceeds every irrelevant one by at least gamma, a coordinatewise gradient estimate with error strictly below gamma/2 identifies the parity support by taking its k largest absolute coordinates. The n^(k-1) scale arising from the initialization gap is a gradient-estimation sample scale, not a sharp conditional-loss onset-time theorem. The full MLP Theorem 4 in Appendix B.1 concerns even parity degree, structured symmetric initialization, hinge loss and prescribed minibatch and rate schedules; first-layer weights and biases have zero learning rate after the first step. The conclusion bounds expected minimum population hinge loss over the iterates. These results do not by themselves establish a sharp MSE loss onset or a persistent learned plateau for continuing feature-learning GD with small Gaussian initialization. This is a statement about this citation, not an assertion that no other source supplies such an onset theorem.
Scope limited to arXiv:2207.08799v3, main Theorem 4, Appendix B.1, Appendix B.2 Proposition 9 and Section C.1

[Lemma lem:completion of arXiv:2608.28007, 'Exact Risk Ratios for Weighted Data Selection in Linear Regression'] Let a whitened system in $\mathbb{R}^d$ contain a positive circuit $C$ of gradients
with $|C|=r+1$, $P=\operatorname{span}\{g_i:i\in C\}$, $\dim P=r$, and weights
$\alpha_i>0$, $\sum_{i\in C}\alpha_ig_i=0$. Define
\[
E(P)=\frac1N\sum_{i:\,\Pi_{P^{\perp}}\xi_i\ne0}\eta_i^2 .
\]
Then there is a strictly convex, strictly positively weighted selection of at
most $d+1$ points with $\lVert \hat q\rVert^2\le(d-r)\,E(P)$.

[Conjecture 25 (Front-Markov property, full saturated regime) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] In the full saturated regime --- without the dissipative condition $\kappa<1$ of \eqref{eq:kappa}, and uniformly through the critical window --- there is a constant $C$ such that, for the cluster law in $G_n$,
\[
\dTV\Big(\mathcal L(\text{failed cluster}),\ \mathcal L\big(\text{multitype GW with }M\big)\Big)\le C\big(\varepsilon(\delta)+\eta_n\big),
\]
with $\eta_n\to0$ as $G_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{BS}}T$ and $\varepsilon(\delta)\to0$ as the saturation margin $\delta\to\infty$. Equivalently, the cascade front is asymptotically Markov: conditional on the set of failed vertices at generation $k$ and their types, the failures into generation $k+1$ are asymptotically independent of generations $<k$. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Front-Markov property, full saturated regime

For the exact equal-variance critical-tanh infinitesimal-angle kernel, E log M_q=psi(n/2)+log2-logn-2n*q/(n+2)+O(q^2 log(2n)^2), while E log H_q=[psi((n-1)/2)-psi(n/2)]/2+O(q^2 log(2n)^2), uniformly for n>=2,q>0. The linear-q angular term cancels exactly. Thus at q=x/n, x<=C, nE(log M_q,log H_q)->(-1-2x,-1/2); the scaled absolute third moments vanish. Assumptions: Exactly C050/C051: Gaussian critical weight variance 1/n, no bias or shaping, equal preactivation variances q>0, angular derivative at zero taken first, n>=2. Constants absolute in remainder, scaled limits uniform over fixed bounded x. Scope: One-step infinitesimal-angle coefficients only. {"artifact_digest":"sha256:0ac8425e5c9f1644b8533a31409b21ecd08762f9733ed2b1288506d86d82eec2","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/0a/0ac8425e5c9f1644b8533a31409b21ecd08762f9733ed2b1288506d86d82eec2.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:fa509c687b9afa97b92a88db5623a80bd94fc45dccfd39e89fd71d69cd194507","bundle_entry_key":"tanh-tangent-angular-drift-cancellation","bundle_id":"population.t244-tanh-tangent-angular-drift-cancellation-018","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_018.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-tanh-tangent-angular-drift-cancellation","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C052: critical tanh tangent log drift and cancellation

Target 3; proof draft, unaudited. All variables and the conditional
Gaussian quadratic-form coupling are those of C050/C051. For n>=2,
q>0 let A_q=log M_q and B_q=log H_q. There is an absolute constant c
such that

    E A_q = psi(n/2)+log(2)-log(n)
                -[2n/(n+2)]q + O(q^2 log(2n)^2),
    E B_q = [psi((n-1)/2)-psi(n/2)]/2
                              + O(q^2 log(2n)^2).

The constants in O are independent of n,q. In particular, uniformly
over x in (0,C] and q=x/n,

    n E A_q = -1-2x+o(1),
    n E B_q = -1/2+o(1).

Together with C051, these identify the leading first two moments of
the one-step radial/angular tangent log kernel. Also
n E(|A_q|^3+|B_q|^3)->0 uniformly in that range. These are not claims
about a full multilayer tanh tangent or correlation process.

## Conditional Taylor coefficients

Write S=||g||^2, T4=sum g_i^4, Z=max_i|g_i|, v0=g/sqrt(S), and
v(q)=tanh(sqrt(q)g)/||tanh(sqrt(q)g)||, defined continuously at q=0.
The normalized radial ratio is

    r(q)=||tanh(sqrt(q)g)||^2/(qS),
    r(0)=1,  r'(0)=-(2/3)T4/S.

Let O(q) be the orthogonal rotation carrying v0 to v(q), using the
plane they span and the identity on its orthogonal complement. One
explicit formula is O=I+J+J^2/(1+c), with
J=v(q)v0^T-v0 v(q)^T and c=v0 dot v(q)>0. Thus no antipodal issue
arises. On v0-perp define the positive definite matrix

    C(q)=P_g O(q)^T D(q)^2 O(q) P_g.

Its eigenvalues are the nonzero eigenvalues in C050, because O(q)
maps v0-perp to x-perp. At q=0, C(0)=I on this (n-1)-dimensional
space. Differentiating O^T O=I cancels its first-order terms, so

    C'(0)=-2 P_g diag(g_i^2) P_g.

With nu uniform on the unit sphere of v0-perp, the exact conditional
mean angular correction relative to q=0 is

    F_g(q) = (1/2) E_nu log(nu^T C(q) nu) - (1/2)log r(q).

This follows from the Gaussian polar decomposition in dimension n-1;
the independent radial factor is chi-square_(n-1). It is also valid
at n=2, when the sphere is the two-point sphere in dimension one.
Its derivative is

    F'_g(0) = -(S-T4/S)/(n-1) + (1/3)T4/S.

## Remainders, without inverse singularities

For q Z^2<=delta, with fixed sufficiently small absolute delta>0,
the scalar functions tanh(sqrt(q)g_i)/sqrt(q), extended at q=0, and
sech^2(sqrt(q)g_i) have first and second derivatives bounded by
C Z^2 and C Z^4 times their natural zeroth-order norm. This follows
by differentiating their convergent even Taylor series on the fixed
interval |sqrt(q)g_i|<=sqrt(delta). Normalizing the first vector gives
||v'||<=C Z^2 and ||v''||<=C Z^4. The explicit rotation formula above
then gives ||C'||<=C Z^2 and ||C''||<=C Z^4, with eigenvalues bounded
away from zero by an absolute constant. Consequently both
log(nu^T C(q)nu) and log r(q) have second derivatives bounded by
C Z^4, uniformly in nu. Taylor's theorem bounds their remainders by
C q^2 Z^4, independently of dimension.

For q Z^2>delta use the global logarithmic bounds from C051 instead:
|F_g(q)|<=q Z^2 and |log r(q)|<=2q Z^2. The explicit first derivatives
at zero are also bounded by C Z^2 (for n>=2). The resulting deviation
from the linear term is <=C q Z^2<=C q^2 Z^4/delta. Thus the same
quadratic remainder bound holds for ALL g and q>0. Integration uses
E Z^4<=C log(2n)^2. No small-eigenvalue event has been discarded.

## Exact cancellation after Gaussian averaging

Gaussian polar decomposition g=sqrt(S)v0 makes S independent of v0.
E S=n and E sum_i v0_i^4=3/(n+2), so

    E(T4/S)=3n/(n+2).

The radial coefficient is therefore -(2/3)E(T4/S)=-2n/(n+2), while

    E F'_g(0)
      = -[n-3n/(n+2)]/(n-1)+n/(n+2) = 0.

This cancellation is exact for every n>=2. Add the baseline means
E log(S/n)=psi(n/2)+log2-log n and
E log sqrt(R/S)=[psi((n-1)/2)-psi(n/2)]/2 to obtain the theorem.
The standard Gamma log-moment asymptotics
psi(n/2)-log(n/2)=-1/n+O(n^-2) and

Finally, centered chi-square logarithms have fourth moment
3 psi_1(z)^2+psi_3(z)=O(n^-2), where z=n/2 or (n-1)/2.
Their means are O(n^-1) in the combinations used here. Thus their
uncentered absolute third moments are O(n^-3/2). C051's pointwise
log-error bounds and E Z^6=O(log(2n)^3) add at most
C q^3 log(2n)^3. Multiplication by n proves the stated vanishing
third-moment condition when q<=C/n.

Status: complete author-checked candidate counterexamples to two explicitly numbered questions in a 2025 primary survey. No independent proof review or originality certification is claimed. Current-literature searches are incomplete. This packet is research, not a promoted solution.

## Source and exact target

Agresti and Veraar, *Nonlinear SPDEs and Maximal Regularity: An Extended Survey*, NoDEA (2025), Problems 4 and 5, journal page 130 of 150, PDF page 131 (the repository adds a cover page). Primary published PDF: https://repository.tudelft.nl/file/File_783e6459-5d3b-4957-bcd3-64da5b8d9025 . Archived SHA256: a66ffa2c1d88f2b46d563a3e4d3963bbc0f8623492e7e1837b4ae089008ad091. The arXiv version https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18561 has the questions on PDF page 92. The published page was rendered and visually read in this campaign.

Problem 4 asks for an expected squared maximal-energy bound in the setting of Theorem 6.4. Its explicit model is the Ito equation on the one-dimensional torus

$$du=(\Delta u+u-u^3)\,dt+\gamma u^2\,dW,$$

with one scalar Brownian driver, and it singles out $\gamma^2=2$ as unresolved. Problem 5 asks whether convergence of initial conditions in $L^2(\Omega;H)$ implies convergence of solutions in $L^2(\Omega;L^2(0,T;V)\cap C([0,T];H))$ under the same general assumptions. These are distinct bounds and continuity questions, not parameter copies. Both fail for the same critical equation.

## Scalar reduction and global construction

Normalize the torus volume to one and take the deterministic constant initial condition $u_0(x)=a>0$. A spatially constant solution is $u(t,x)=U_t$, where

$$dU_t=(U_t-U_t^3)\,dt+\sqrt2 U_t^2\,dW_t,\qquad U_0=a.$$

Set $s(t)=(e^{2t}-1)/2$. Let $R_s$ be a four-dimensional Bessel process, starting at $r=1/(\sqrt2 a)$ and satisfying

$$dR_s=dB_s+\frac{3}{2R_s}\,ds.$$

It is the radial part of four-dimensional Brownian motion started at a point of length $r$ and never hits zero. Define

$$U_t=\frac{e^t}{\sqrt2 R_{s(t)}}.$$

Ito's formula for $z(R)=1/(\sqrt2 R)$ gives drift $-z^3$ and diffusion $-\sqrt2 z^2$. Deterministic time change followed by multiplication by $e^t$ yields drift $U-U^3$ and diffusion $-\sqrt2 U^2$; replace the scalar Brownian driver by its negative. This proves the displayed SDE. Positivity and nonexplosion follow from the Bessel construction: a continuous positive Bessel path has a positive minimum on each compact time interval. Local Lipschitz coefficients give pathwise uniqueness; therefore this construction gives the law of the unique global strong solution for any prescribed scalar Brownian driver.

## A finite-time Bessel minimum lemma

For $0<b<r$, define $\tau_b=\inf\{s\ge0:R_s=b\}$. Fix $S>0$. The function $h(x)=|x|^{-2}$ is harmonic away from zero in dimension four. Its stopped process at $\tau_b$ is bounded by $b^{-2}$. Optional stopping at $\tau_b\wedge S$ gives the exact identity

$$\frac{\mathbb P_r(\tau_b\le S)}{b^2}=\frac1{r^2}-\mathbb E_r[R_S^{-2};\tau_b>S].$$

Since the process never hits zero, $\mathbf1_{\{\tau_b>S\}}\to1$ almost surely as $b\downarrow0$. The required integrability and strict loss of harmonic expectation can be computed directly. If $x\in\mathbb R^4$ has length $r$ and $B_S^{(4)}\sim N(0,SI_4)$, then Tonelli's theorem and a Gaussian integral give

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_r[R_S^{-2}]&=\int_0^\infty(1+2S\lambda)^{-2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lambda r^2}{1+2S\lambda}\right)d\lambda\\
&=\frac1{2S}\int_0^1\exp\!\left(-\frac{r^2(1-v)}{2S}\right)dv\\
&=\frac{1-e^{-r^2/(2S)}}{r^2}.
\end{aligned}$$

Dominated convergence in the stopped identity therefore proves

$$\lim_{b\downarrow0}\frac{\mathbb P_r(\tau_b\le S)}{b^2}=\frac{e^{-r^2/(2S)}}{r^2}>0.$$

No infinite-horizon hitting probability has been substituted for a finite-horizon one. The strict positive constant is explicitly derived for every $S>0$.

## Failure of Problem 4

Let $M_S=\sup_{0\le s\le S}(2R_s^2)^{-1}$. Substituting $b=(2x)^{-1/2}$ in the preceding lemma shows

$$\lim_{x\to\infty}x\,\mathbb P_r(M_S\ge x)=\frac{e^{-r^2/(2S)}}{2r^2}>0.$$

Thus $\mathbb E M_S=\infty$ by integration of the tail. For $S=s(T)$, the scalar construction gives

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}U_t^2\ \ge\ M_{s(T)},\qquad \mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}U_t^2=\infty\quad(T>0).$$

Consequently, $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}\|u(t)\|_{L^2(\mathbb T)}^2=\infty$, although $u_0$ is a smooth bounded deterministic function. The proposed bound fails for each positive finite time, not merely asymptotically.

At each fixed positive time, by contrast,

$$\mathbb E U_t^2=e^{2t}a^2\left(1-\exp\!\left[-\frac1{4a^2s(t)}\right]\right)<\infty.$$

This is consistent with the existing theorem's pointwise second-moment bound. The rare finite-time maxima have a $1/x$ tail for squared amplitude; replacing a localized stochastic integral by a mean-zero integrable martingale would miss exactly this issue.

## Verification of the abstract assumptions

There is already a finite-dimensional counterexample: choose the Gelfand triple $V=H=V^*=\mathbb R$, $A=I$, $B=0$, $F(v)=2v-v^3$, and $G(v)=\sqrt2 v^2$. Then the evolution equation $du+Au\,dt=F(u)\,dt+G(u)\,dW$ is the scalar SDE above. The linear coercivity condition holds with $\theta=1,M=0$. The nonlinear condition is

$$v(Av-F(v))-\tfrac12|G(v)|^2=-v^2\ge |v|^2-2|v|^2-2,$$

so Theorem 6.4's coercivity holds with $\theta'=1,M'=2$. Polynomial local Lipschitz bounds satisfy Assumption 6.1 with $\rho=2$, $\beta=2/3$, since $(2\beta-1)(\rho+1)=1$. All interpolation norms on this one-dimensional triple are equivalent. No compactness or infinite-dimensionality is required in the source assumptions.

For the stated torus model, take $V=H^1(\mathbb T)$, $H=L^2(\mathbb T)$, $A=I-\Delta$, $B=0$, $F(v)=2v-v^3$, and the same one-dimensional noise. Then

$$\langle v,Av-F(v)\rangle-\tfrac12\|G(v)\|_{L^2}^2=\|\nabla v\|_2^2-\|v\|_2^2=\|v\|_{H^1}^2-2\|v\|_2^2.$$

The polynomial Lipschitz condition follows from $(H^{-1},H^1)_{2/3,1}\hookrightarrow H^{1/3}\hookrightarrow L^6$ in one dimension, using Holder for the cubic drift and the resulting $L^4$ embedding for the quadratic diffusion. Thus the same critical indices $\rho=2$, $\beta=2/3$ suffice. The unique solution from Theorem 6.4 agrees with the spatially constant strong solution above.

## Failure of Problem 5

Use a common scalar Brownian driver and initial conditions $u_0^{(n)}(x)=1/n$, with limiting initial condition $u_0=0$. The solutions exist strongly and can be constructed simultaneously for this countable family. Their initial conditions converge deterministically in $L^2$. The limiting solution is identically zero, since both drift and diffusion vanish at zero. For every $n$ and every $T>0$, the preceding calculation applied with $a=1/n$ gives

$$\mathbb E\|u^{(n)}-0\|_{C([0,T];H)}^2=\infty.$$

Therefore convergence in the claimed $L^2(\Omega;L^2(0,T;V)\cap C([0,T];H))$ space cannot hold under the general hypotheses. This does not contradict convergence in probability or the stated $L^p$ convergence for $p<2$. In particular, tiny tail coefficients for small initial conditions do not make an infinite second maximal moment finite.

## Adversarial checks and remaining review

The argument's load-bearing checks are the Ito rather than Stratonovich convention; the scalar spatially constant driver allowed by the published model; the factor $\sqrt2$ and Bessel dimension four; the finite-horizon stopping identity; and the distinction between a fixed-time moment and the expected supremum. All are explicit above. The zero initial condition alone is not a counterexample, and $\gamma^2<2$ is outside this construction's critical claim.

A first later-literature search found the 2026 paper *Fractal dimension of singular times for SPDEs: Energy bounds, criticality, and weak-strong uniqueness*, arXiv:2602.21981. Its abstract concerns singular-time dimensions and does not resolve these two endpoint questions. Its full archived text has not yet been completely reviewed. Searches and an author's publication page are not a novelty certificate. The Bessel and Gaussian facts themselves are classical; the claimed candidate contribution is their application to the two precisely sourced questions. Scoped independent review is recorded below; human review and novelty remain pending.


## Moment-order and continuity-scope clarification

Only the fixed-time second moment is asserted finite. The fixed-time fourth moment is infinite: a nondegenerate four-dimensional Gaussian has a strictly positive continuous density at the origin, so the expectation of its inverse fourth radial power diverges logarithmically. The continuity counterexample addresses the numbered general Problem 5. It does not assert a resolution of the narrower surrounding prose with additional mapping or growth hypotheses. AUTHOR PROOF DRAFT, unaudited; novelty is unestablished. Unconditional Gaussian-reference replica second moments cannot give the desired size-uniform entropy remainder. Let X=UV^T/sqrt(N), d=NP, s>0, and q_v=N(0,v I_d), v>1/2 finite. The exact second moment is (v^2/(2v-1))^(d/2) E exp{s[2v<X,Xprime>-(v-1)(||X||^2+||Xprime||^2)]/[2(2v-1)]}, with an independent replica. For iid Rademacher factors, coherent rare states give (1/d)log(1+chi^2)>=log(v^2/(2v-1))/2+s M^2/[N(2v-1)] -2M(N+P)log2/(NP). At fixed positive finite aspect ratios this diverges for fixed s>0 and either v=1 or v=1+sM/N. For iid Gaussian factors, chi^2 is infinite for every positive finite N,P,M,s and every finite v>1/2. KL and MI remain finite. The obstruction concerns the unconditional annealed bound, not the actual information. Elementary proof draft, novelty unestablished.
Independent factor replicas and independent standard Gaussian channel noise
Positive integer N,P,M; s>0; finite v>1/2
Rademacher claim uses iid symmetric signs in both factors
Gaussian claim uses iid standard Gaussian entries in both factors
Divergence in size assumes P/N,M/N converge to positive finite limits

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:6a9effd3a34726d61fa1442ac7312545998e512fe754277a5621b71abee16732","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/6a/6a9effd3a34726d61fa1442ac7312545998e512fe754277a5621b71abee16732.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f022f02353ea0aa3676743ca3a75db70243ec4ed5a65fd3a833c8610a1dca57d","bundle_entry_key":"coherent-factor-states-gaussian-reference-second-moment-obstruction-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-uniform-cubic-one-gaussian-factor-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Extensive-rank matrix inference, Gaussian channels and high-noise expansions","draft":"w718/bundle_012.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:coherent-factor-states-gaussian-reference-second-moment-obstruction-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Uniform-remainder route: an unconditional Gaussian-reference second moment fails

Target1 route finding, not a solution or a novelty claim. Proof draft,
UNAUDITED. This isolates the positive-SNR annealed overlap obstruction
left after the fixed-order coefficient proof032.

## 1. Exact Gaussian integral, including its domain

Let X in R^d be any random vector, Z an independent N(0,I_d), and
p_s the density of sqrt(s)X+Z. Put q_v=N(0,v I_d), where s>0 and
v>1/2 are finite. Let X' be an independent copy of X. Tonelli's
theorem and completion of the square give, as an equality in [0,infinity],

 1+chi^2(p_s||q_v)
 = [v^2/(2v-1)]^(d/2)
   E exp{ s/[2(2v-1)]
      [2v<X,X'>-(v-1)(||X||^2+||X'||^2)] }.             (1)

No moment-generating-function assumption is needed for (1); either
side can be infinite. The determinant/variance factors are positive
under v>1/2. In particular for v=1 the expectation is E exp(s<X,X'>).

If X is centered with covariance b I_d and v=1+sb, then

   I(X;sqrt(s)X+Z)=d log(v)/2-D(p_s||q_v).

The proposed entropy control D<=log(1+chi^2) is Jensen under p_s,
with an infinite right side allowed. The following examples show that
this unconditional bound cannot furnish a size-uniform remainder.

## 2. Bounded iid Rademacher factors: coherent rare states

Set d=NP, X=UV^T/sqrt(N), with independent Rademacher factors of
sizes N by M and P by M. All three dimensions are positive integers.
The event that both independent factor pairs have every entry +1
has probability 2^[-2M(N+P)]. On it X=X', every entry is M/sqrt(N),
and ||X||^2=NP M^2/N. Its contribution to (1) proves the exact bound

 (1/(NP))log(1+chi^2(p_s||q_v))
 >= (1/2)log[v^2/(2v-1)]
    +s M^2/[N(2v-1)]
    -[2M(N+P)/(NP)]log2.                               (2)

For fixed s>0, P/N->alpha>0 and M/N->beta>0, choose either v=1
or the covariance-matched v_N=1+sM/N. The positive term in (2) grows
linearly in N and the entropy cost stays bounded. The normalized
log-second-moment therefore diverges to +infinity. Nevertheless the
normalized KL for covariance matching is bounded above by log(v_N)/2,
because information is nonnegative. This is a failure of the annealed
upper bound, not a divergence of the actual normalized information.

The input entries are bounded and have moments of every order. Entry
boundedness alone therefore cannot justify this positive-SNR replica
second-moment interchange. Coherent configurations with exponentially
small probabilities can dominate it.

## 3. Gaussian factors: the second moment is infinite at every finite size

Now take all factor entries independent standard real Gaussian. For
any positive N,P,M and every s>0, v>1/2, the expectation in (1) is
infinite. Here is a direct lower-tail proof.

Hold all entries other than U_11,V_11,U'_11,V'_11 in [-1,1]. This
event has positive probability, independent of the four displayed
coordinates. For large T restrict these four coordinates to
[T,(1+epsilon)T], with epsilon>0 sufficiently small depending only on v.
Then X_11 and X'_11 equal T^2/sqrt(N) times factors arbitrarily close
to one, up to bounded terms. All other entries of X and X' are O(T).

At equal positive leading coordinates, the quartic term in the exponent
in (1) is s T^4/[N(2v-1)]>0. By continuity, for a sufficiently small
fixed epsilon it is uniformly at least c T^4 on the indicated boxes,
minus a fixed O(T^3+T^2+1) error from the other coordinates. Their
Gaussian probabilities are at least c_1 exp(-c_2 T^2) for large T.
Take disjoint boxes at T=2^k. Each contributes at least

   c_3 exp(c_4 T^4-c_5 T^3-c_6 T^2-c_7),

which tends to infinity. Thus the expectation is infinite. Finite
noise variance or covariance matching does not cure these product
tails. The KL and MI remain finite by finite second moments.

## 4. A limited repair: condition on an operator-norm event first

This calculation explains a possible next route, not a proof of the
required higher-order remainder. Let U be any random N by M matrix,
independent of an iid standard Gaussian P by M matrix V, and assume
||U||op<=L sqrt(N) almost surely. Put C=UU^T/N and let C' arise from
an independent U'. Conditional on U,U', the columns of X and X'
are independent Gaussian vectors with covariances C,C'. For

     0<=s<L^(-2),

the standard-reference second moment is

 E[exp(s<X,X'>)|U,U']
   =det(I-s^2 C^(1/2)C'C^(1/2))^(-P/2)
   <=exp{NP s^2 L^4/[2(1-s^2 L^4)]}.                  (3)

For L=0, X=0 and the statement is read directly. For L>0, (3)
follows by Gaussian integration, 0<=C,C'<=L^2 I, and the scalar
inequality -log(1-u)<=u/(1-r) for 0<=u<=r<1.
Consequently, writing a=E||X||^2/(NP),

 0 <= s a/2-I(X;sqrt(s)X+Z)/(NP)
   <= s^2 L^4/[2(1-s^2 L^4)].                         (4)

This only provides a first-order uniform bound in a conditional-Gaussian
model. It is not a higher-order expansion, does not handle both general
non-Gaussian factors, and does not identify a prior-dependent limiting
term. Applying such truncation to the original laws still requires an
explicit entropy/risk coupling error and appropriate covariance
self-averaging. Those steps have not been supplied here.

NEXT: a viable second-moment route must first remove the coherent and
heavy-tail events, pay that removal in information, and then control the
covariance-matched tilted overlap to the required order. Finite polynomial
overlap moments alone do not pay those exponential tails.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:aa41163a9dc9aba1cc4d5da34f092bda06f0aa84d13cfef271e192be25fcc597","revision_digest":"sha256:1a90d582611c9e24c65c0b366e61069cd817b45dd998415afc9b348958a068fb","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:coherent-factor-states-gaussian-reference-second-moment-obstruction-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma 18 (Clusterwise integral interpolation) of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] Let $\cO$ be a complete DVR with fraction field $L$, and let
$x_0,\ldots,x_k\in\cO$ be pairwise distinct in $L$.  Partition the indices
into residue clusters $C$ according to equality of $\bar x_i$.  Suppose
that, for each cluster $C$, there are $c_C\in\cO$ and
$F_C(U)\in\cO[[U]]$ such that
\begin{equation}
 x_i-c_C\in\pi\cO,
 \qquad
 y_i=F_C(x_i-c_C)
 \quad(i\in C).
\end{equation}
Then the unique polynomial $P(T)\in L[T]$ of degree at most $k$ satisfying

[Lemma lem:lpineq of arXiv:2411.16366, 'Connections between sequential Bayesian inference and evolutionary dynamics'] Consider a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ on which a scalar valued Wiener process is defined.  Suppose $f(s,\omega)$ for $\omega \in \Omega$ is an $\mathcal{F}_t$-adapted process.  Then the following inequality holds for $q > 1$

\begin{align}
\mathbb{E} \left[ \left| \int_0^t f(s,\omega)dW_s \right|^{2q} \right] \leq t^{q-1}(q(2q-1))^q \mathbb{E} \left[ \int_0^t  | f(s,\omega) |^{2q} ds  \right]
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For probability mass functions p and q on the same finite or countable set, the Kullback-Leibler divergence D(p||q) = sum_x p(x) log(p(x)/q(x)) (a term with p(x) = 0 is 0, a term with p(x) > 0 = q(x) is +infinity) satisfies D(p||q) >= 0, with equality if and only if p = q. When the entropy -sum_x p(x) log p(x) is finite this is the same as -sum_x p(x) log p(x) <= -sum_x p(x) log q(x): the entropy of p never exceeds its cross-entropy against q.
