OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; T419-C023 v2, proof (unaudited), no novelty claimed. Let integers r>=1, p>=r, m>=r be arbitrary. Let Delta be a real m-by-p matrix of rank exactly r, normalized so sigma_1(Delta)=1, and write mu=sigma_r(Delta)>0. Let 0<rho<1, and define

 d=rho/2, a=d/(10r^(3/2)), b=sqrt(rp/d),
 K0=sqrt(r)(b^2+1+4sqrt(r)), gamma=1/(6K0+1), delta=gamma a^2/4,
 S=max{1,sqrt(2r)/a}.

Assume mu>1-delta, equivalently the condition number kappa=1/mu satisfies

 1<=kappa<1/(1-delta).

This includes the equal-spectrum case and a nonempty interval of unequal spectra for every rank and pair of dimensions. Set beta=mu-1+delta>0. For every s>=S initialize B0=0 and A0=sG, where G is r-by-p with independent standard normal entries. Use simultaneous ordinary GD on q(B,A)=||BA-Delta||F^2/2 with the one fixed step eta=gamma/s^2. With probability at least1-rho, for every integer t>=1,

 ||B_t A_t-Delta||F <=sqrt(r) exp[-gamma beta^2(t-1)/(2s^4 K0)].

For every 0<eps<sqrt(r), a sufficient fitting time is

 1+ceil[(2s^4 K0/(gamma beta^2)) log(sqrt(r)/eps)].

The event and eta are independent of eps. In the equal-spectrum case mu=1, beta=delta, giving exponent gamma^3 a^4/(32s^4 K0). If mu>=1-delta/2, the exponent is at least gamma^3 a^4/(128s^4 K0). The scale threshold S is explicit and polynomial in r and rho^{-1}; for r>=1, S=10sqrt(2)r^2/d. The very conservative rate has no claim of optimality. Every proper bottleneck m,p>r is included. This is a large-scale, nearly flat-spectrum interval, not all initialization scales or all condition numbers. No finite-sample risk conclusion is made.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:cf9cc5498f7a21219b2e926de80b5a2b440051356a9993957ddefbd783bdbe02","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/cf/cf9cc5498f7a21219b2e926de80b5a2b440051356a9993957ddefbd783bdbe02.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:466b6527f59870a8d400e57b299f3b255028af70ecbea77feb3262d2710d8047","bundle_entry_key":"operator-margin-large","bundle_id":"population.t419-all-aspect-ratios-large-scale-operator-margin-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"LoRA population convergence, discrete operator-norm drift, unbalanced Gaussian initialization","draft":"w705/bundle_012.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.lowrank:lora-all-aspect-ratios-large-gaussian-scale-operator-margin-gd","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T419-C023 v2: operator-margin GD at large Gaussian scales, all aspect ratios

Kind: moved. Target:1. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.

The hardest step is a replacement for the Frobenius deficiency-margin argument: the residual operator norm may increase under simultaneous GD, but its total upward drift is bounded by eta times the remaining loss. This allows a first-step operator margin to persist. The argument below proves that statement before using any full-rank or convergence conclusion.

Known ingredients are credited to Du-Hu-Lee, arXiv:1806.00900, Theorem2.2 and AppendixB ClaimB.1 (imbalance method), Min-Tarmoun-Vidal-Mallada, arXiv:2105.06351, Corollary5 printedp10 (sufficient-margin idea for flow), and Zhang-Liu-Chen, arXiv:2502.01235, Theorem3.1/C.10 (invariant output span). Related unbalanced-flow results in Kunin et al., arXiv:2406.06158, Theorem4.2 require scalar imbalance and structural widths; their AppendixA.2.4 is rank one. The primary abstract of arXiv:2511.09925 concerns four-layer factorization with balancing regularization, rather than this ordinary two-factor recursion. None of these scope checks establishes novelty or an absence of other applicable literature. Reviewer assessment remains necessary.

## Statement

Let integers r>=1, p>=r, m>=r be arbitrary. Let Delta be a real m-by-p matrix of rank exactly r, normalized so sigma_1(Delta)=1, and write mu=sigma_r(Delta)>0. Let 0<rho<1, and define

 d=rho/2, a=d/(10r^(3/2)), b=sqrt(rp/d),
 K0=sqrt(r)(b^2+1+4sqrt(r)), gamma=1/(6K0+1), delta=gamma a^2/4,
 S=max{1,sqrt(2r)/a}.

Assume mu>1-delta, equivalently the condition number kappa=1/mu satisfies

 1<=kappa<1/(1-delta).

This includes the equal-spectrum case and a nonempty interval of unequal spectra for every rank and pair of dimensions. Set beta=mu-1+delta>0. For every s>=S initialize B0=0 and A0=sG, where G is r-by-p with independent standard normal entries. Use simultaneous ordinary GD on q(B,A)=||BA-Delta||F^2/2 with the one fixed step eta=gamma/s^2. With probability at least1-rho, for every integer t>=1,

 ||B_t A_t-Delta||F <=sqrt(r) exp[-gamma beta^2(t-1)/(2s^4 K0)].

For every 0<eps<sqrt(r), a sufficient fitting time is

 1+ceil[(2s^4 K0/(gamma beta^2)) log(sqrt(r)/eps)].

The event and eta are independent of eps. In the equal-spectrum case mu=1, beta=delta, giving exponent gamma^3 a^4/(32s^4 K0). If mu>=1-delta/2, the exponent is at least gamma^3 a^4/(128s^4 K0). The scale threshold S is explicit and polynomial in r and rho^{-1}; for r>=1, S=10sqrt(2)r^2/d. The very conservative rate has no claim of optimality. Every proper bottleneck m,p>r is included. This is a large-scale, nearly flat-spectrum interval, not all initialization scales or all condition numbers. No finite-sample risk conclusion is made.

## 1. Gaussian event, independent of the dynamics and requested accuracy

Take a thin SVD Delta=U Lambda V^T, with U m-by-r, V p-by-r having orthonormal columns, and Lambda diagonal with entries between mu and1. Right rotation invariance of the independent standard Gaussian rows implies H=GV is an r-by-r iid standard Gaussian matrix. No independence between H and ||G||F is asserted or required.

We use the joint event

 sigma_min(H)>=a, ||G||F<=b.

Its probability is at least1-2d=1-rho. To prove the first bound without a random-matrix citation, H is nonsingular almost surely. Let l_j be the distance of its j-th column from the span of the other r-1 columns. Conditional on those columns, l_j has the law |N(0,1)|. The norm of row j of H^{-1} is l_j^{-1}. If sigma_min(H)<a, then ||H^{-1}||F>1/a, so some l_j<a sqrt(r). The normal density bound and a union bound give

 Pr[sigma_min(H)<a] <=r sqrt(2/pi)a sqrt(r)<d.

Markov gives Pr[||G||F>b]<=rp/b^2=d. A final union bound gives the claimed joint event. All following statements are deterministic for a G on this event.

## 2. Global factor bounds and summable gradients, before any margin argument

The deterministic lemma C014 is saved in proofs/C014_empirical_boundedness.md and appended in full to this result's queued card. Apply it with C=I, D=W=Delta. Its constants satisfy

 q0=||Delta||F^2/2<=r/2,
 J=||A0 A0^T||F+1<=s^2 b^2+1,
 R=||Delta||F+sqrt(2q0)<=2sqrt(r),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R)<=s^2 K0.

Because K0>=4r, gamma<=1/(1+r). Also eta(6K+1)<=gamma(6K0+1/s^2)<=1. Thus eta<=1/(1+2q0) and eta<=1/(6K+1), the two hypotheses of C014. It follows that, for all t>=0,

 q_(t+1)<=q_t-(eta/2)||grad q_t||F^2,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=s^2 K0,
 sum_(j=T)^(infinity) ||grad q_j||F^2<=2q_T/eta, for any integer T>=0.

The last inequality follows by telescoping the first from T to any finite endpoint, and then taking the increasing limit of nonnegative partial sums. In particular eta||B_t||op^2 and eta||A_t||op^2 are at most gamma K0<1. No positive margin, full-rank iterate, or global optimization conclusion has been used in these bounds.

## 3. Operator norm of the residual: bounded total upward drift

Put E=BA-Delta, gB=E A^T, gA=B^T E. The simultaneous update has the exact residual identity

 E_next=E-eta(BB^T E+E A^T A)+eta^2 gB gA.

The sign and multiplication order of the last term matter. The first-order expression equals

 (1/2)[(I_m-2eta BB^T)E + E(I_p-2eta A^T A)].

For a positive semidefinite matrix M with eta||M||op<=1, every eigenvalue of I-2eta M is in [-1,1], hence its operator norm is at most1. Section2 therefore makes each of the two summands an operator-norm contraction of E. Triangle inequality and arithmetic-geometric mean yield

 ||E_next||op<=||E||op+eta^2||gB||F||gA||F
             <=||E||op+(eta^2/2)||grad q||F^2.

For every integer t>=T, summing these one-step inequalities and using section2 gives

 ||E_t||op <=||E_T||op+eta q_T.

This is a drift bound, not a claim that ||E_t||op decreases at every step. It does not need the gradient terms to be independent, and it does not assume that the residual is already small. This is the key replacement for a Frobenius-margin proof when the input dimension is large.

## 4. The first step creates enough margin

At B0=0, gA0=0, so A1=A0 and B1=eta Delta A0^T. Write L=A0^T A0, a positive semidefinite p-by-p matrix. Then E1=Delta(eta L-I). Since eta||L||op<=gamma b^2<1, the Loewner inequality eta^2 L^2<=eta L holds. In the target output coordinates,

 U^T E1 E1^T U
 =Lambda V^T(I-2eta L+eta^2 L^2)V Lambda
 <=Lambda[I-eta V^T L V]Lambda.

Here V^T L V=(A0 V)^T(A0 V)>=s^2 a^2 I. Multiplying this Loewner inequality by Lambda on both sides needs no commutation between Lambda and V^T L V. Hence

 U^T E1 E1^T U <=(1-eta s^2 a^2)Lambda^2
                         <=(1-gamma a^2)I.

The scalar 1-gamma a^2 is positive because a<1, gamma<1. Also col(E1) is contained in col(U), so the same upper bound controls all nonzero singular values of E1. Consequently

 ||E1||op<=sqrt(1-gamma a^2)<=1-gamma a^2/2.

Section3 with T=1, together with q1<=q0<=r/2 and s^2>=2r/a^2, now proves for every t>=1

 ||E_t||op <=1-gamma a^2/2+eta r/2
            <=1-gamma a^2/2+gamma a^2/4
            =1-delta.

The total possible future upward drift was bounded before asserting persistence. Thus this step is not a circular use of the conclusion it is intended to establish.

## 5. Gradient domination and Frobenius fitting

The zero output initializer and the B update give B_t=U R_t, where R_t is square r-by-r, at every time. This known invariant follows directly by induction since Delta and every B_t lie in col(U). Thus

 E_t=U(R_t A_t-Lambda V^T).

For t>=1, section4 and Weyl's singular-value inequality imply

 sigma_min(R_t A_t)>=mu-||E_t||op>=mu-1+delta=beta>0.

For a square R and any r-by-p A,

 sigma_min(RA)<=||A||op sigma_min(R).

To see this, take a unit x minimizing ||R^T x|| and bound ||A^T R^T x||. With the section2 factor bound, this yields

 sigma_min(R_t)>=beta/(s sqrt(K0)).

The A gradient equals R_t^T(R_t A_t-Lambda V^T). Therefore

 ||grad q_t||F^2>=||gA_t||F^2
                  >=beta^2 ||E_t||F^2/(s^2 K0).

Substitute into the descent inequality to get

 ||E_(t+1)||F^2 <=[1-eta beta^2/(s^2 K0)]||E_t||F^2.

The bracket belongs to (0,1), since 0<beta<=delta<1, s>=1 and gamma<1. Iterating, using ||E1||F<=sqrt(r) from descent, and sqrt(1-x)<=exp(-x/2), proves the theorem. This is one fixed step for all times and all requested accuracies, not an algorithm with a step change after reaching the margin.

## Scaling and exact scope

For a target with largest singular value alpha>0, divide Delta by alpha and both factors by sqrt(alpha). The normalized initializer scale is s/sqrt(alpha). If s>=sqrt(alpha) S and mu=sigma_r(Delta)/alpha>1-delta, the same original step eta=gamma/s^2 gives

 ||B_t A_t-Delta||F<=alpha sqrt(r) exp[-gamma beta^2 alpha^2(t-1)/(2s^4 K0)].

This follows because the normalized GD step is alpha eta. Dimension, confidence and condition-number restrictions remain as above. Arbitrary condition numbers and moderate/small normalized scales are not covered by this argument. For those, an operator margin may never be reached by the presently proved estimate. With positive label noise the exact output-span reduction fails, so this proof alone gives no statistical-risk comparison. Exact rational matrix identities check the update algebra but do not independently certify this theorem. Prior results may already imply special cases; specialist novelty assessment and independent review are pending.


Full deterministic boundedness component C014:
# T419-C014 v1: empirical GD boundedness with an initialization-dependent step

Kind: bound. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.
This is an explicit anisotropic version of the published Gram-imbalance/descent method, not a solution of Target 2. It proves a trajectory component without assuming the iterates are bounded. The prior source is Du-Hu-Lee, arXiv:1806.00900, Theorem 2.2 and Appendix B, Claim B.1; its full convergence theorems have different initialization/step hypotheses. C009 already identifies the exact covariance metric and C010 the positive-noise empirical landscape.

## Statement

Let C be any real positive definite p-by-p matrix, D any real m-by-p matrix, and r>=1. Put lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op, ell=||D||op, W=D C^(-1), and

 q(B,A)=(1/2)||(BA-W) C^(1/2)||F^2,

with B m-by-r and A r-by-p. This is the empirical regression objective up to a constant when C=XX^T/n and D=ZX^T/n. Initialize at any finite deterministic factors B0,A0, and define

 q0=q(B0,A0), J=||A0 A0^T-B0^T B0||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R), L=6Kc+ell.

For any fixed

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/L},

simultaneous ordinary factor GD satisfies, for every integer t>=0,

 q_t<=q0,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=K,
 ||(A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t)-(A0 A0^T-B0^T B0)||F<=2eta q0<1,
 sum_(t>=0) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/eta.

In particular the gradient tends to zero, every accumulation point is critical, and for every integer T>=1,

 min_(0<=t<T) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/(eta T).

All constants are finite and computable from C,D and the initialization. There is no Gaussian assumption and no low-rank assumption on W. No iterate-convergence, saddle-avoidance or statistical-risk assertion is included.

## Exact identities and product/factor bounds

Let G=BA C-D. The two factor gradients are G_B=G A^T and G_A=B^T G. With E_t=A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t the first-order cross terms cancel exactly, giving

 E_(t+1)-E_t=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B),
 ||E_(t+1)-E_t||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2).

This cancellation only uses dependence on BA and does not require isotropic C. Also

 (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2
 <=r [||AA^T-B^TB||F^2+4||BA||F^2].

To verify it, write P=B^TB,Q=AA^T. Scalar trace Cauchy-Schwarz gives (tr(P+Q))^2<=r tr((P+Q)^2), and cyclicity of trace gives tr((P+Q)^2)=||P-Q||F^2+4 tr(PQ), tr(PQ)=||BA||F^2. No commutation is assumed.

When q<=q0, positivity of C gives ||BA-W||F<=sqrt(2q0/lambda), hence ||BA||F<=R. If additionally ||E-E0||F<=1, then ||E||F<=J, so the preceding trace bound implies

 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2<=sqrt(r) sqrt(J^2+4R^2)<=K.

The initialization meets these conditions and therefore has pair norm at most sqrt(K).

## Descent established before closing the boundedness induction

Suppose at the current iterate the pair norm is at most sqrt(K), and preceding steps have valid descent inequalities. Then

 ||grad q||F<=||BA C-D||op sqrt(||B||F^2+||A||F^2)
             <=(Kc/2+ell)sqrt(K).

Because eta<=1/(6Kc+ell), the proposed next point has pair norm at most 2sqrt(K). The connecting segment also lies in that ball. On that ball the Hessian quadratic form in a perturbation (dB,dA) is

 ||(dB A+B dA) C^(1/2)||F^2+2<BA C-D,dB dA>.

Its absolute value is at most

 [c(||A||op^2+||B||op^2)+||BA C-D||op]
 times (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2)
 <=[4Kc+(2Kc+ell)] (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2).

Here the first summand uses Cauchy-Schwarz on dB A+B dA; the cross term uses |<G,dB dA>|<=||G||op||dB||F||dA||F. Thus the Hessian operator norm on the segment is at most L. Taylor's theorem along that segment proves

 q_next<=q-eta||grad q||F^2+(L eta^2/2)||grad q||F^2
        <=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2.

In particular q_next<=q0. Telescoping the descent inequalities, including the proposed step, and using q>=0 yields

 sum_(j=0)^t eta^2||grad q_j||F^2<=2eta q0
 <=2q0/(1+2q0)<1.

Summing the imbalance increments now proves ||E_next-E0||F<=2eta q0<1. The product/factor bound therefore puts the endpoint back in the smaller ball of pair radius sqrt(K). This closes the induction without assuming a bound before proving descent on the required larger segment. The q0=0 case is included: both gradients vanish, the sequence is constant, and all inequalities still hold.

## Consequences and exact remaining gap

Telescoping for every finite horizon gives the infinite summability bound. A nonnegative summable sequence tends to zero, so the gradients vanish. Bounded finite-dimensional factor pairs have convergent subsequences; gradient continuity makes every subsequential limit critical. The running-minimum bound follows by averaging the finite sum. These statements do not require that the entire sequence converges to one point.

For B0=0 and a Gaussian A0, this provides an allowed positive step after observing the initialization, conditional on every full-row-rank design. It does not supply a single positive step independent of the unbounded Gaussian initializer. C013 shows that unconditional expected-limit risk with such an initialization-independent fixed step can diverge even at rank one.

Combining this bound with the already verified empirical strict-saddle landscape C010 is insufficient to conclude global optimization. One must additionally show that the specified zero/Gaussian initialization does not approach a nonglobal critical point, with all hypotheses of a saddle-avoidance theorem checked for its lower-dimensional initial support and step rule. Vanishing gradients do not establish that. Even convergence almost surely would not by itself justify passing to expected population risk; a failure-tail/integrability or finite-stopping argument is separately required. The usual full-ambient absolutely-continuous random-initialization theorem cannot simply be cited for the plane B0=0.

Independent reviewer audit and any novelty assessment remain pending. [Lem of arXiv:2505.11700, 'Distribution of the cokernels of determinantal row-sparse matrices'] (A generalization of [Mes23])
The following statements hold. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item
We have $f\left(\frac{\mathbb{1}}{|G|} \right) = 0$.
\item 
The gradient of $f$ at $\frac{\mathbb{1}}{|G|}$ is $0$. 
\item 
The Hessian matrix of $f$ at $\frac{\mathbb{1}}{|G|}$ is $Q$. 
\item 
$Q$ is positive definite and $\det(Q) = |G|^{|G|}$.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma trace inequality of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] Let ${\bf A}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ for $i=1,2,\dots, m$ and $r\geq 1$. Then
    $$
    \tr \Bigg \vert \sum_{i=1}^m {\bf A}_i \Bigg \vert ^r ~ \leq ~ m^{r-1} \tr \left(\sum_{i=1}^m |{\bf A}_i|^r\right),
    $$
    where $|{\bf A}_i| = ({{\bf A}_i}^{\mathsf{T}}{\bf A}_i)^{1/2}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem spinmain of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a simple  point process on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with summable exponential mixing correlations as in Definition (def.A2 of the paper) and bounded reduced  Palm intensity function of the ground process $\mathcal{P}$, i.e., for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$
\begin{equation} 
\sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_p \in \mathbb{R}^d} \sup_{y \in \mathbb{R}^d} \rho^{(1)}_{\bk x1p}(y) \leq \hat{\kappa}_p<\infty.
\end{equation}
Let $\Psi = \Psi(\cdot)$ be a stabilizing interaction graph on finite windows with respect to $\mathcal{P}$ as in Definition~(d:stabilizing-graph of the paper). 
Assume the Gibbs specification~(equation eqn:gibbs of the paper) satisfies  averaged weak spatial mixing on~$\Psi(\mathcal{P})$,  as in  Definition~(d:ssm-pp of the paper).
Denote by $\{V_x\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}_n}= \{V_x(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n))\}_{x \in \mathcal{P}_n}$  the spin configuration on $\mathcal{P}_n$
assuming for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ that  $Z(\mathcal{P}_n) > 0$.
Assume moreover  for all $p>1$ the following moment condition 
\begin{equation}
\sup_{1 \leq n< \infty} \sup_{q\le p } \sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_q \in W_n} \mathbb {E} _{\bk x1{q}}[ \max(1,|V_{x_1}(\Psi(\mathcal{P}_n))|^{p})]
< \infty\,.
\end{equation}

Put
 $$
 \mu_n^{\Psi} :=  \sum_{x \in \mathcal{P}_n} V_x \delta_{n^{-1/d}x}.
 $$
 
If  $f \in \mathbb{B} (W_1)$ satisfies

${\rm Var}{\mu_n^{\Psi}(f)} = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$, then as $n \to \infty$

$$ ({\rm Var}{\mu_n^{\Psi}(f)})^{-1/2}(\mu_n^{\Psi}(f) - \mathbb {E} [\mu_n^{\Psi}(f)]) \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Coro 2 of arXiv:2606.22960, '2606.22960'] For the uniform random recursive tree ($\alpha=\beta=0$)
    one has
	\[
	R_{\mathrm{maj}}(q)\le 
    \frac{\Gamma^2(2-2q)}{\Gamma(3-4q)}
    \left(1+\frac{1}{1-4q}\right)-1 \quad\text{for all } q\in[0,1/4).
	\]
    Moreover,
    $$
    R_{\mathrm{maj}}(q)
    \le 8\left(\frac{9\Gamma^2(3/4)}{4\sqrt{\pi}}-1\right)q
    \le 7.25 q \quad\text{for all } q\in[0,1/8)
    $$
    and
    $$
    R_{\mathrm{maj}}(q)\le 8 q \quad\text{for all } q\in[0,1].
    $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.06038, 'Efron type identities\\ for stopping sets and Poisson hulls'] Let $\eta$ be a Poisson process with locally finite intensity
  measure $\lambda$ on a localized Borel space $(\BX,\cX)$.  Assume
  that $Z$ is a stopping set.  Then on the event
  $\{\eta(Z(\eta))<\infty\}$ the conditional distribution of $\eta$
  restricted to $Z(\eta)^c$ given $\eta_{Z(\eta)}$ is (almost surely)
  the distribution of a Poisson process with intensity measure
  $\lambda$ restricted to $Z(\eta)^c$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.06038

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT. Status: proof (unaudited), claim w730-T355-C002 version 2; not independently checked. The scalar tangential coordinate is u in R; v is in R^q. Let A:R -> R^{q x q}
be C^4, q>=1 an integer, H=A^T A, and assume, globally,

    0 < m I <= H(u) <= M I,
    ||A'(u)|| <= D,  ||H^(j)(u)|| <= B_j, j=1,2,3,4.

Matrix norms are operator norms. Constants m,M,D,B_j are finite and independent
of eta. Let sigma>=0. The iid label noises z_k have a centrally symmetric law,
E z_k z_k^T=I, and mu_6=E|z_k|^6<infinity; put mu_4=E|z_k|^4. No almost-sure noise bound is assumed. In particular E z_k=0. Set
eta_0=min(1,1/M), 0<eta<=eta_0. Start from deterministic (u_0,0).
Consider full-vector label-noise SGD for residual A(u)v and loss
L(u,v)=|A(u)v|^2/2:

    d_k=u_{k+1}-u_k
       =-eta v_k^T H'(u_k)v_k/2 -eta sigma z_k^T A'(u_k)v_k,
    v_{k+1}=(I-eta H(u_k))v_k-eta sigma A(u_k)^T z_k.

On v=0 its noise covariance is sigma^2 Hess L. The limiting ODE is

    U'=b(U),  b(u)=-sigma^2 tr H'(u)/4,  U(0)=u_0.

This is the known limiting flow of Li-Wang-Arora, Corollary 5.2, arXiv
2110.06914v4, printed pp.8-9 and 33. Their Theorem 4.6 supplies convergence,
not the explicit error estimate below. The hardest quantitative step here
is averaging with a coefficient that depends on u and shares the same noise
as the normal update. Section 4 computes that correlation rather than
discarding it as a martingale.

## 1. Constants and conclusion

Let F:R^{1+q}->R be bounded C^3, with bounded derivatives. Write
f(u)=F(u,0), F_j=sup |f^(j)|, j=1,2,3, and
F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||. The displayed bound uses only these seminorms.
Define

    c2=sigma^2 q M/m,
    c4=[sigma^2 M(2q+4)c2 + sigma^4 M^2 mu_4]/m,
    c6=[sigma^2 M(3q+12)c4 + 15 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 c2
        + sigma^6 M^3 mu_6]/m,
    J2=B_1^2 c4/4+sigma^2 D^2 c2,
    Jcv=B_1^2 c6/4+B_1^2 sigma^2 M q c4/4
         +sigma^2 D^2 q c4+sigma^4 D^2 M mu_4 c2.

For j=0,1,2,3 put beta_j=sigma^2 q B_{j+1}/4. For T>=0 set

    G1=F_1 exp(beta_1 T),
    G2=exp(2 beta_1 T)(F_2+beta_2 T F_1),
    G3=exp(3 beta_1 T)[F_3+3 beta_2 T F_2
                     +(beta_3 T+3 beta_2^2 T^2/2)F_1],
    Gtu=beta_1 G1+beta_0 G2,
    Gtt=beta_0 beta_1 G1+beta_0^2 G2.

Define

    S0=B_1/(2m),
    S1=(B_2+2B_1 S0)/(2m),
    S2=(B_3+2B_2 S0+4B_1 S1)/(2m),
    C0=G1 S0/2,
    C1=(G2 S0+G1 S1)/2,
    C2=(G3 S0+2G2 S1+G1 S2)/2,
    Ct=Gtu S0/2.

Finally let

    Qg=G2 J2/2 + Gtu sqrt(J2) + Gtt/2,
    Qc=C0 M^2 c2
       +C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 q M c2)/2
       +2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(M) D c2
       +2 C2 Jcv + Ct c2,
    C(T)=(C0+F_vv/2)c2 + T(Qg+Qc).

Then, simultaneously for all integers 0<=k<=T/eta^2,

    |E F(u_k,v_k)-F(U(k eta^2),0)| <= C(T) eta.       (1)

The exponent is a=1. The finite constant is explicit in the hypotheses and
the stated observable seminorms. H and H' need not commute. This includes
every finite normal dimension q, and arbitrary smooth rotating output
frames A satisfying the bounds. The tangential dimension remains one.
It permits unbounded symmetric noise, including Gaussian labels. Fixed
off-manifold initialization is not addressed.
A in C4(R,R^{q x q})
0<mI<=H<=MI globally
sup norm A prime<=D; sup norm H^(j)<=B_j, j=1..4
iid z independent of past, z equal in law to -z, EzzT=I, E|z|6 finite
sigma>=0; eta in (0,min(1,1/M)]
u0 deterministic; v0=0
F bounded C3 with bounded derivatives

       +C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 q M c2)/2
       +2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(M) D c2
       +2 C2 Jcv + Ct c2,
    C(T)=(C0+F_vv/2)c2 + T(Qg+Qc).

Then, simultaneously for all integers 0<=k<=T/eta^2,

    |E F(u_k,v_k)-F(U(k eta^2),0)| <= C(T) eta.       (1)

The exponent is a=1. The finite constant is explicit in the hypotheses and
the stated observable seminorms. H and H' need not commute. This includes
every finite normal dimension q, and arbitrary smooth rotating output
frames A satisfying the bounds. The tangential dimension remains one.
It permits unbounded symmetric noise, including Gaussian labels. Fixed
off-manifold initialization is not addressed.

## 2. Uniform normal bounds

Write r=|v|, w=(I-eta H)v, e=-eta sigma A^T z. Since eta M<=1,
|w|<=(1-eta m)r. The updates map finite states to finite states for every
finite iteration, almost surely; all coefficients are global. The moment
recurrences below also show all expectations used are finite.

Conditioning on the entire past F_k,

    E[|v'|^2|F_k]=|w|^2+eta^2 sigma^2 tr H
       <=(1-eta m)r^2+eta^2 sigma^2 qM.

Induction from v_0=0 gives E|v_k|^2<=c2 eta. Central symmetry kills odd
moments of e, so

    E[|w+e|^4|F_k]
      =|w|^4+2|w|^2 E|e|^2+4 E(w.e)^2+E|e|^4
      <=(1-eta m)r^4+eta^2 sigma^2 M(2q+4)r^2
        +eta^4 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4.

Using eta<=1 and the second-moment bound gives E|v_k|^4<=c4 eta^2.
The exact sixth-moment expansion, conditional with w frozen, is

    E|w+e|^6=|w|^6+3|w|^4 E|e|^2+12|w|^2 E(w.e)^2
             +3|w|^2 E|e|^4+12 E[(w.e)^2 |e|^2]+E|e|^6.

Since E(w.e)^2<=eta^2 sigma^2 M|w|^2 and
E[(w.e)^2|e|^2]<=|w|^2 E|e|^4,

    E[|v'|^6|F_k]
      <=(1-eta m)r^6+eta^2 sigma^2 M(3q+12)r^4
        +15 eta^4 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 r^2+eta^6 sigma^6 M^3 mu_6.

Induction gives E|v_k|^6<=c6 eta^3: its forcing is <=m c6 eta^4.
All three recurrences use (1-eta m)^j<=1-eta m for j>=1 and
eta m in [0,1]. Only z_k, not u_k and v_k, is independent of the past.

## 3. Backward observable and Lyapunov corrector

Fix any terminal integer K with tau=K eta^2<=T. Let S_t be the flow of b,
and g(t,u)=f(S_{tau-t}(u)), 0<=t<=tau. The bounded Lipschitz vector field b
has a global flow. Its first three spatial variational equations give

    |J_s|<=exp(beta_1 s),
    |K_s|<=beta_2 s exp(2 beta_1 s),
    |L_s|<=(beta_3 s+3 beta_2^2 s^2/2)exp(3 beta_1 s).

Indeed J'=b'J; K'=b'K+b''J^2; L'=b'L+3b''JK+b'''J^3.
Variation of constants and exp(beta_1 t)<=exp(beta_1 s) for t<=s give
these bounds even when beta_1=0; no division by beta_1 is made.
Consequently |g_u|<=G1, |g_uu|<=G2, |g_uuu|<=G3.
The transport equation g_t=-b g_u implies
|g_tu|<=Gtu, |g_tt|<=Gtt.

There is a unique symmetric matrix S(u) satisfying

    H S+S H=H'.

For any symmetric Q the solution of H X+X H=Q is
int_0^infty exp(-sH)Q exp(-sH)ds, with norm <=||Q||/(2m).
Exponential decay justifies this integral and integration by parts.
Differentiating the finite-dimensional invertible linear system twice gives

    H S'+S'H=H''-H'S-SH',
    H S''+S''H=H'''-H''S-SH''-2H'S'-2S'H'.

This proves ||S||<=S0, ||S'||<=S1, ||S''||<=S2. Smoothness follows from
smooth inversion of this uniformly invertible finite-dimensional operator.
Set

    C(t,u)=-g_u(t,u)S(u)/2,
    G(t,u,v)=g(t,u)+v^T C(t,u)v.

Then ||C||<=C0, ||C_u||<=C1, ||C_uu||<=C2, ||C_t||<=Ct, and

    HC+CH=-g_u H'/2,
    sigma^2 tr(CH)=-sigma^2 g_u tr(H')/4=b g_u.       (2)

The trace identity uses tr(HC+CH)=2 tr(CH), not commutation.

## 4. One-step defect, including shared-noise correlation

Put delta=eta^2 and t=k delta. All coefficients in the following conditional
computations are evaluated at (t,u_k); w,e,d use u_k,v_k,z_k.
Taylor expansion in u followed by t (both on the whole real line in u) gives

    E[g(t+delta,u+d)-g(t,u)]
       =delta E g_t - eta E[g_u v^T H'v]/2 + Rg,
    |Rg|<=Qg eta^3.

For completeness, the three remainders are bounded by
G2 E d^2/2, delta Gtu E|d|, delta^2 Gtt/2. Conditional centering gives

    E d^2<=eta^2[B_1^2 E r^4/4+sigma^2 D^2 E r^2]<=J2 eta^3.

Therefore E|d|<=sqrt(J2)eta^(3/2)<=sqrt(J2)eta, and eta^4<=eta^3.
The term linear in z has conditional mean zero.

For the quadratic part, first freeze C at (t,u): exactly,

    E[v'^T C v'-v^T C v|F_k]
       =-eta v^T(HC+CH)v
         +eta^2 v^T HCH v+eta^2 sigma^2 tr(CH).       (3)

The middle term in (3) has unconditional absolute expectation at most
C0 M^2 c2 eta^3.

Next expand C(t,u+d)=C(t,u)+C_u(t,u)d+R_C,
||R_C||<=C2 d^2/2. To bound this without a deterministic radius use

    d^2<=2 eta^2[B_1^2 r^4/4+sigma^2 D^2 |z|^2 r^2],
    |v'|^2<=2r^2+2 eta^2 sigma^2 M|z|^2.

Multiplication, independence of z_k from F_k, and E|z|^2=q give

    E[d^2 |v'|^2]<=4 eta^2[B_1^2 c6 eta^3/4
       +eta^2 B_1^2 sigma^2 M q c4 eta^2/4
       +sigma^2 D^2 q c4 eta^2
       +eta^2 sigma^4 D^2 M mu_4 c2 eta]<=4 Jcv eta^3.

Every actual exponent is at least four; eta<=1 justifies the relaxation.
The coefficient remainder costs at most 2 C2 Jcv eta^3.
Replacing time t by t+delta costs at most
delta Ct E|v'|^2<=Ct c2 eta^3.

The remaining linear coefficient term is E[d v'^T C_u v']. Its drift part
has absolute value at most

    eta C1 B_1 E[r^2 E(|v'|^2|F_k)]/2
      <= C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 q M c2) eta^3/2.

Here E(|v'|^2|F_k)<=r^2+eta^2 sigma^2 qM, so the second product is
of order eta^4 and is relaxed to eta^3 using eta<=1.

For the noise part write a=A'v and B=C_u. Conditional on F_k,

    E[(z^T a)(w-eta sigma A^Tz)^T B(w-eta sigma A^Tz)]
        =-2 eta sigma w^T B A^T a.

The constant term vanishes by E z=0, the cross term uses E zz^T=I,
and the cubic term vanishes by central symmetry. Multiplying by -eta sigma
shows that this part is bounded in absolute expectation by
2 eta^2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(M)D E r^2
<=2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(M)D c2 eta^3. This is the correlation that a false
conditional-martingale argument would miss.

Combining these bounds with (2), (3), and g_t+b g_u=0 yields

    |E[G(t+delta,u_{k+1},v_{k+1})-G(t,u_k,v_k)]|
         <=(Qg+Qc)eta^3.                            (4)

All remainder estimates are unconditional after conditioning on the past.
They are uniform in k and use normal moments rather than pathwise smallness.

## 5. Telescope and restore ambient observables

At time zero, v_0=0 and G(0,u_0,0)=f(U(tau)). At the terminal time,
G(tau,u_K,v_K)=f(u_K)+v_K^T C(tau,u_K)v_K. Summing (4) gives

    |E f(u_K)-f(U(tau))|
       <=[C0 c2+T(Qg+Qc)]eta.

To restore F, the joint law of (u_k,v_k) is invariant under (u,v)->(u,-v).
At step k this follows by applying (v,z)->(-v,-z): the u update is unchanged
and the v update changes sign. The iid centrally symmetric noise and v_0=0
start the induction. Therefore
E[D_v F(u_k,0)v_k]=0. Taylor's theorem with bounded normal Hessian gives

    |E[F(u_k,v_k)-f(u_k)]|<=F_vv E|v_k|^2/2<=F_vv c2 eta/2.

This proves (1). K was arbitrary and every constant uses the common upper
horizon T, proving the supremum in (1), including K=0.

## Scope and unpaid steps

The constant-Hessian target in the initial brief has zero tangential drift;
that is settled ground in the dossier and is not reproved here. The result
above concerns its explicitly repaired, varying-curvature model. It gives
a candidate rigorous rate for noncommuting matrix curvature, beyond the
scalar proof claim and the two-output numerical diagnostics already present.
Novelty against later quantitative literature remains unestablished.
The next unpaid extensions are multiple tangential coordinates and fixed
off-manifold initialization. The latter requires an explicit initial-layer
correction for a supremum including time zero. Central symmetry is used in
the cubic shared-noise term and ambient linear-term cancellation. The
nonsymmetric-noise case is not claimed here.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:e7ceb436532dd0b75711e8251e575790b1b747c36755c6b2874314daef39328f","revision_digest":"sha256:1acc06ed77c5a3544de7b5d174203e8bbf687cbf55975a914b5375320d1a09ac","source_id":"owner-own-work:w730:T355:C002:v2","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v2-unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Let $\hat\theta_n$ be an estimator from $n$ i.i.d. observations of a parameter $\theta$ such that $\tau_n(\hat\theta_n - \theta)$ converges in law to some limit distribution $J$ with $\tau_n \to \infty$ (for instance $\tau_n = \sqrt n$). For a block size $b = b_n$ with $b \to \infty$ and $b/n \to 0$, let $\hat\theta_{n,b,i}$ be the estimator computed on the $i$-th of the $N = \binom{n}{b}$ subsets of size $b$, and define the subsampling distribution $L_{n,b}(x) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{1}\{\tau_b(\hat\theta_{n,b,i} - \hat\theta_n) \le x\}$ (in practice an average over a random subset of the $N$ subsets, which changes nothing below). Then $L_{n,b}(x) \to J(x)$ in probability at every continuity point $x$ of $J$. No assumption on the FORM of $J$ is made - it need not be normal, and the result holds when $\theta$ lies on the boundary of the parameter space, where the $n$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap is inconsistent (Andrews 2000). If in addition $\{\tau_b^2(\hat\theta_{n,b,i} - \hat\theta_n)^2\}$ is uniformly integrable, the subsampling variance $\tau_b^2 \cdot \frac{1}{N}\sum_i(\hat\theta_{n,b,i} - \bar\theta_{n,b})^2$ converges to the variance of $J$, so $\frac{b}{n}\operatorname{Var}_{\text{sub}}(\hat\theta_{n,b}) $ estimates $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_n)$ when $\tau_n = \sqrt n$ - the $m$-out-of-$n$ variance estimate.
i.i.d. observations; tau_n(theta_hat_n - theta) converges in law to some J with tau_n -> infinity
b -> infinity and b/n -> 0 (so tau_b / tau_n -> 0)
for the variance statement: uniform integrability of the squared scaled subsample deviations

Every matrix A in C^{m x n} with m >= n has a factorisation A = Q R with Q in C^{m x m} unitary and R in C^{m x n} upper triangular (full QR); equivalently A = Q_1 R_1 with Q_1 in C^{m x n} having orthonormal columns and R_1 in C^{n x n} upper triangular (reduced QR). If A has full column rank n, the reduced factorisation with R_1 having positive real diagonal entries exists and is unique, and the columns of Q_1 span the column space of A, with the first k columns of Q_1 spanning the span of the first k columns of A for every k. Real A gives real Q and R. Three constructions: Gram-Schmidt (R holds the coefficients; numerically unstable in its classical form, better modified), Householder reflections (n reflections H_k = I - 2 v v^* / (v^* v) zeroing one column at a time, backward stable, 2 m n^2 - 2 n^3 / 3 flops), and Givens rotations (for sparse or structured matrices). Uses: least squares min ||A x - b|| solved by R_1 x = Q_1^* b without forming A^* A (condition number kappa(A) instead of kappa(A)^2), the QR algorithm for eigenvalues, and orthonormal bases of subspaces.
m >= n for the statement as given (for m < n the same argument gives A = Q R with R upper trapezoidal)
full column rank for uniqueness of the reduced factorisation with positive diagonal

body: Let $x_1, \dots, x_p$ be independent uniform points on the sphere $S^{d-1}$ with $p = d(d+1)/2$ the dimension of $\mathrm{Sym}_d$, let $z_i = x_i x_i^\top$ (the Veronese embedding, centred and normalised so that $E[z z^\top] = I_p$ in the Frobenius inner product), and let $A \in \mathrm{Sym}_d$ be the unit normal to the span of $z_1, \dots, z_{p-1}$ (the leave-one-out normal, computable from a single linear solve $v = (-Z_1^{-1} z, 1)$). Conjecture, supported by measurement: the normalised moments $d^{k-1}\,\mathrm{Tr}(A^{2k})$ converge to the Catalan numbers $C_k = 2, 5, 14, 42$ for $k = 2, 3, 4, 5$, i.e. the spectral measure of $\sqrt d\, A$ is Wigner's semicircle law, exactly as for a uniformly random unit direction in $\mathrm{Sym}_d$. Measured over 2,300 designs: $d\,\mathrm{Tr}(A^4) = 1.976 + 7.93/d$; the $1/d$ correction is about twelve times the one a Haar-random direction gives, so the Veronese structure shows only at the next order. What is proved: the law of $A$ is invariant under conjugation $A \mapsto O A O^\top$ for orthogonal $O$ (the design is rotation invariant) and $E[zz^\top] = I_p$ exactly, which fixes the second moment; the higher moments are the conjecture. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov falsifier against the semicircle on the eigenvalues tracks its Haar control. The lemma (L-b) of the Veronese hard-edge reduction in the ProofNet24 kernel program (Target 4) is the $k=2$ case, and the reduction $\mathrm{Tr}(A^4) \le \|A\|_{op}^2$ loses exactly the factor $2$.

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] The Rook's Walk with dimension $d\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}$ and board length $n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 3}$ is transitive.
  \begin{proof}
  Fix $x,y\in \Omega$ and let $d = (y-x \bmod n+1)$. Define, $\xi_{(x,y)}: \Omega \to \Omega$ as,
  \[v \overset{\xi_{(x,y)}}{\longmapsto} v + d,\quad  \quad \forall v\in \Omega\]
  Now, notice that,
  \begin{align*}
   \xi_{(x,y)}(x) &= x + d\\
   &= (x\bmod n+1) + (y-x \bmod n+1)\\
   &= (y\bmod n+1)\\
   &= y
  \end{align*}
  Therefore, $\xi_{(x,y)}$ satisfies our first condition. Now, fix $z,w \in \Omega$. Notice that the transition probability $P(z,w)$ is dependent only on the Hamming distance between $z$ and $w$ (Recall that $||z-w||_0$ is the Hamming distance). Further we have,
  \[||\xi_{(x,y)}(z) - \xi_{(x,y)}(w)||_0 = ||(z+d)-(w+d)||_0= ||z-w||_0\]
  That is, Hamming distance is invariant under $\xi_{(x,y)}$ and, by extension, \[P(z,w) = P(\xi_{(x,y)}(z), \xi_{(x,y)}(w))\]
  Therefore, the Rook's Walk is transitive.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 8 (Terminal-time Schauder estimate) of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Let $\LinearOp_s$ be as in \eqref{eq:LinearOp} with 
\[
    a_2,a_1\in \ParaHoelderzero{\alpha}([0,1]\times\R),
    \qquad
    \inf_{[0,1]\times\R} a_2\ge\kappa>0.
\]
Then, for every
\[
    b\in \ParaHoelderzero{\alpha}([0,1]\times\R),
    \qquad
    \varphi\in C_b^{2+\alpha}(\R),
\]
the terminal-value problem
\[
\begin{cases}
-\partial_su(s,x)=\LinearOp_su(s,x)+b(s,x),
& (s,x)\in[0,1)\times\R,\\[0.5ex]
u(1,x)=\varphi(x),
& x\in\R,
\end{cases}
\]
has a unique solution
\[
    u\in \ParaHoelder{\alpha}([0,1]\times\R).
\]
Moreover,
there exists a constant \(C\) depending only on \(\alpha,\kappa\), and the
\(C_b^{\alpha/2,\alpha}\)-bounds of \(a_2,a_1\)
such that
\[
    \norm{u}_{1+\alpha/2,2+\alpha}
    \le
    C
    \left(
        \norm{b}_{\alpha/2,\alpha}
        +
        \norm{\varphi}_{C_b^{2+\alpha}(\R)}
    \right),
\]

body: Janson Problem 18.40 is not settled: the claimed theorem that for every weight sequence with w_0 > 0 and rho = 0 (m/n -> lambda) one box takes all m balls with probability tending to 1 along a subsequence is false. Counterexample: w_k = k! on the full support {0,1,2,...}, where P(Y_(1) = m) -> e^{-1/lambda} (exact 0.3567 at m = n = 40 against e^{-1} = 0.3679). The proof's inequality (3) omits a Theta(m) mixing-entropy term. The weaker statement that Y_(1)/n does not tend to 0 holds in the k! example (Y_(1) = m - Poisson(1/lambda)) but is not proved in general; the reduction for Problem 18.39 inherits the gap.

body: [Theorem 2.1 (ii) of arXiv:2503.23159, 'Hall's marriage theorem'] gives a necessary and sufficient condition for the permanent to be non-zero. This was proved indepently by Egorychev [11] and Falikman [12] in 1980.

[Lemma det asymp of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Let $\zeta$ be a probability measure on $[0,1]$ with prefix $\{0,q\}$ with $q\in (0,1)$. Let $f\in \mathbb{R}$. There exists $C_\varepsilon>0$, depending only on $\varepsilon$, $f$, and $\xi$, with $C_\varepsilon\to 0$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$, such that the following holds uniformly over $\mathbf{m}\in \mathrm{SUSY}_1(\zeta,\varepsilon)$: Letting $\mathcal{B}:=\{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0,\, F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf\}$,
		\begin{equation*}

			- \log\prod_{i=1}^N\partial_{mm}h_\zeta(q,m_i)

			\right|
			\leq C_\varepsilon N.
		\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma det app of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Fix $q\in(0,1)$, $\delta\in(0,1)$, and let $\zeta\in\mathcal P([0,1])$.
		For every $s\in[0,1]$, set
		\[
		\pi_s\zeta:=\zeta|_{(s,1]}+\zeta([0,s])\delta_s,
		\qquad
		T_{\zeta,s}(m):=\partial_{mm}h_{\pi_s\zeta}(s,m)
		+\xi''(s)\int_s^1 \pi_s\zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t,
		\qquad m\in[-1,1].
		\]
		Assume that there exist $\varepsilon_0>0$ and $u_0>0$ such that
		\[
		[q-\varepsilon_0,q+\varepsilon_0]\subset (0,1)
		\qquad\text{and}\qquad
		\zeta([0,s])\ge u_0
		\quad\text{for every } s\in[q-\varepsilon_0,q+\varepsilon_0].
		\]
		Let $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, let $\mathbf{m}\in[-1+\delta,1-\delta]^N$ satisfy
		\[
		q_\mathbf{m}\in(q-\varepsilon,q+\varepsilon),
		\qquad
		\mathrm{dist}\!\bigl(\zeta_\mathbf{m},\pi_q\zeta\bigr)\le \varepsilon,
		\]
		and let $f\in\mathbb{R}$. Writing $T_\zeta:=T_{\zeta,q}$, one has
		\begin{multline}
			\log \mathbb{E}\Bigl[
			\bigl|\det(\nabla^2F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}))\bigr|
			\;\Bigm|\;
			\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0,\,
			F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf
			\Bigr]
			\\=
			N\int \log|x|\,\mathrm{d}\Bigl((T_\zeta\#\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})})\boxplus \sigma_{\xi''(q)}\Bigr)(x)
			+O\!\left(\left(\varepsilon+\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right)N\right)+o(N).
		\end{multline}
		The implicit constant in the $O(\cdot)$ term depends only on $\xi$, $f$, $u_0$, and $\varepsilon_0$; the $o(N)$ term is the error from the deformed GOE asymptotics and is uniform over $\mathbf{m}$ satisfying the stated constraints.

body:
[Thm 24 of arXiv:2603.27433, 'The $k$-cycle shuffling with repeated cards'] Let $l\ge 2$ be a fixed integer, $(n_N)_{N\ge 1},(m_N)_{N\ge 1},(k_N)_{N\ge 1}$, and $(t_N)_{N\ge 1}$ be sequences of positive integers that satisfy the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $n_N=m_N\cdot l$ for all $N\ge 1$.
\item $\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}m_N=\infty$.
\item $k_N\ge 2$ for all $N\ge 1$, and $\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}\frac{k_N\log n_N}{n_N}=0$.
\item $t_N=\frac{n_N}{k_N}(\log n_N+c)$ for all $N\ge 1$, where $c\in\R$ is an absolute constant.
\end{enumerate}
Then, we have
$$\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}d_{TV}(\sim_{l}\backslash P_{n_N,k_N}^{*t_N},\sim_{l}\backslash U_{\S_{n_N}})=d_{TV}(\Pois(l+\exp(-c)),\Pois(l)).$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 24 of arXiv:2603.27433

[Proposition classiquedecomposition of arXiv:2607.14792, 'On the degree distribution of large tentacular Bienaymé--Galton--Watson trees'] Let $(X_i)_{i \geq 1}$ and $(Y_i)_{i \geq 1}$ be the i.i.d. increments of $W$ and $W'$, respectively. We define $(\widehat{X}_i)_{i \geq 1}$ as the sequence obtained from $(X_i)_{i \geq 1}$ by removing all steps equal to $-1$. 
     Let $f : \mathbb{R}^{n-k_n} \to \mathbb{R}_+ $ be a measurable and stable by cyclic permutation function.
     Then, we have the following equality:
     \begin{align*}
   & \mathbb{E}\left[ f\left( (\widehat{X}_i)_{1\leq i \leq n-k_n}\right) \1_{ W_n=-1, \ W_i \geq 0 \, \forall i \in [\![1,n-1]\!], \ |\{i \in [\![1,n]\!] : X_{i}=-1\}|=k_n  }\right] \\ & \qquad = \frac{1}{n}\binom{n}{k_n}\mu(0)^{k_n}\left(1-\mu(0) \right)^{n-k_n}  \mathbb{E}\left[ f\left( (Y_i)_{1\leq i \leq n-k_n}\right) \1_{W'_{n-k_n}=k_n-1} \right].
   \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition classiquedecomposition of arXiv:2607.14792

[Lemma lem:AsympSimplexD1 of arXiv:2609.01825, 'On everywhere locally soluble varieties \\ in families over toric bases'] Let $f \colon \mathbb R^s \to \mathbb R$ be given by $f(\vec t) = \prod_{i=1}^s (t_i + 1)^{\ell_i}$ for any $\vec \ell \in \mathbb R^s$. Let $C \in \mathbb R_{\geq 0}$, $\vec c \in \mathbb R_{>0}^m$, $\vec x \in \mathbb R^s$ and $W \in \mathbb R^{s \times m}$ be a matrix such that $W \vec t + \vec x \in \mathbb R_{\geq 0}^s$ for all $\vec t \in C \Delta^m$. Then uniformly in all $C \geq 0$, we have
	\begin{multline*}
		\int_{C \Delta^m} \exp\Bigl(-\sum_{i=1}^m c_i t_i \Bigr) f(W \vec t + \vec x) \,\mathrm d\vec t = \frac{ f(\vec x)}{c_1 \cdots c_m}\\
		+ O_{W, \vec c}\Bigl( \mathrm e^{-\min_i c_i C} (C+1)^{m-1} \max_{\vec t \in C \Delta^m} |f(W \vec t + \vec x)| \Bigr)\\
		+ O_{W, \vec c}\biggl( \int_{C \Delta^m} \exp\Bigl(-\sum_{i=1}^m c_i t_i \Bigr) \tilde f(W \vec t + \vec x) \,\mathrm d\vec t \biggr),
	\end{multline*}
	where $\tilde f(\vec t) = f(\vec t) (\min_i t_i + 1)^{-1}$.
title: Lemma lem:AsympSimplexD1 of arXiv:2609.01825

For disjoint vertex sets A, B of a graph let d(A, B) = e(A, B) / (|A| |B|) be the edge density; the pair is epsilon-regular if |d(A', B') - d(A, B)| <= epsilon for all A' subset A, B' subset B with |A'| >= epsilon |A| and |B'| >= epsilon |B|. The lemma: for every epsilon > 0 and every integer m >= 1 there is M = M(epsilon, m) such that every graph on at least m vertices admits a partition of its vertex set into k parts V_1, ..., V_k with m <= k <= M, all part sizes differing by at most one, and all but at most epsilon k^2 of the pairs (V_i, V_j) epsilon-regular. The bound M cannot be better than a tower of twos of height proportional to a power of 1 / epsilon (Gowers, 1997).
finite simple graph
an equitable partition is asked for; the number of parts depends on epsilon and m only, not on the graph

body: [Definition 4 of arXiv:2507.23376, 'Combinatorial solutions to the Social Golfer Problem and Social Golfer Problem with Adjace'] Let K be a subset of positive integers and let λ be a positive integer. A pairwise balanced design (PBD) of order v with block sizes from K is a pair (V, B), where V is a finite set (the point set) of cardinality v and B is a family of subsets (blocks) of V that satisfy (1) if b ∈B then |b| ∈K and (2) every pair of distinct elements of V occurs in exactly λ blocks of B.

[Prop 9 of arXiv:2607.16707, 'Vertex reinforced branching random walks and generalized time-dependent P\'olya urns'] Consider a GPU process with weight function $w$ and drawing sequence $(\sigma_n)_{n\ge 1}$. Assume that there are initially $B_0\ge 0$ blue balls. Then 
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]
$$\sum_{n\ge 1} \frac {\sigma_n}{w(\tau_{n-1}-B_0)} <\infty   \quad  \Longleftrightarrow \quad \mathbb P(B_\infty= B_0 ) >0,$$ 
\item[(ii)] 
$$ \sum_{n\ge 1} \frac {\sigma_n}{w(\tau_{n-1})} =\infty   \quad  \Longrightarrow \quad \mathbb P(R_\infty = B_\infty = \infty) =1,$$ 
\item[(iii)] 
$$\mathbb P(R_\infty = B_\infty = \infty) =0 \quad  \Longrightarrow \quad \sum_{n\ge b+1} \frac {\sigma_n}{w(\tau_{n-1}-b)} <\infty, \ \text{for all }b>0.$$ 
\end{itemize}

body: [Theorem thm:cycle_size_count_dist of arXiv:2605.06511, 'Logarithmic Mixing of Random Walks on Dynamical Random Cluster Models'] Let $G$ be a random $d$-regular graph on $n$ vertices with cycle counts $\left(\mathcal{C}_k \colon k \geq 3\right)$. Let $\left(\mathcal{Z}_k \colon k \geq 3\right)$ be independent Poisson random variables with $\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{Z}_k\right] = \frac{(d-1)^k}{2k}$. For any $n \geq 1$ and $r, d \geq 3$, $\TVD{\left(\mathcal{C}_3, \dots, \mathcal{C}_r\right)}{\left(\mathcal{Z}_3, \dots, \mathcal{Z}_r\right)} = O\left(\frac{\sqrt{r} (d-1)^{3r/2 - 1}}{n}\right)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Assume strong rho-dependence in l-infinity distance: sigma-fields generated by any two index sets separated by distance greater than the integer rho>=0 are independent. Suppose P(X_z=0)<=q for every z and set K=(rho+1)^2. If q<=101^(-K), then the probability that 0 belongs to an infinite nearest-neighbour component of good sites is at least 378252/81240057>0. Residue coloring and enclosing bad star-contours give the bound 1-q-9t(1+t)/(1-t)^3 with t=8q^(1/K). At q<=101^(-K), q<=1/101 and t<=8/101 give the stated positive value. This uses independence of separated sets, not mere pairwise independence. It weakens the base-800 sufficient error requirement when only positivity is needed. It supplies no estimate achieving that error for critical lattice blocks.
Strong rho-dependence of separated index SETS
rho is an integer>=0
q<=101^(-(rho+1)^2)
Good paths use nearest-neighbour adjacency and bad contours use star adjacency
title: A Peierls sufficient condition for positive block percolation

[Lemma 13 (Local graph property) of arXiv:2609.03958, '2609.03958'] The map $T$ is a local $C^2$ diffeomorphism and
\begin{equation}
 J(x)=\det DT(x)>0,
 \qquad x\in B_{10}.
\end{equation}
Let $U\subset B_{10}$ be any open set such that
$T|_U:U\to V:=T(U)$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism.
Then the restriction $Y|_U$ parametrizes the graph of a function
$\widetilde u\in C^2(V)$; that is,
\[
 Y(U)=\{(y,\widetilde u(y)):y\in V\}.
\]
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
  D_y\widetilde u(y)=Du(x),
 \qquad y=T(x), \qquad x\in U.
\end{equation}
In particular, the graph factors of the original and parallel graphs
agree at corresponding points:
\[
 \sqrt{1+|D_y\widetilde u(T(x))|^2}
 =\sqrt{1+|Du(x)|^2}=W(x),
 \qquad x\in U.
\]

Pourkamali-Macris Proposition2, with the standing spectral regularity made explicit. Let N<=M_N and N/M_N->alpha in (0,1]. Let mu be a probability density on [0,K] for a finite deterministic K. Its symmetrization mu_bar on R is assumed to have finite logarithmic energy integral integral log|x-y| dmu_bar(x)dmu_bar(y)>-infinity and integral log|x| dmu_bar(x)>-infinity, as in source Assumption2. Draw an infinite iid sequence of nonnegative singular values with law mu and, for each N, put its first N values (ordered if desired) on the diagonal of the rectangular N by M_N matrix Sigma_N. Condition on this singular-value sequence. The signal is S_N=U_N*Sigma_N*V_N^T, with independent normalized Haar orthogonal matrices U_N in O(N), V_N in O(M_N). Independently let Z_N have iid centered real Gaussian entries of variance1/N, and observe Y_N=sqrt(lambda)*S_N+Z_N for fixed lambda>0. In the partition function the candidate X has this same fixed-spectrum Haar prior P_N, and Zcal_N(Y)=integral exp(N*sqrt(lambda)*Tr(X^T*Y)-N*lambda*||X||_F^2/2) P_N(dX). Define F_N(lambda)=-(1/(N*M_N))*E[log Zcal_N(Y_N) | Sigma_N], where expectation includes the planted Haar orientations and Gaussian noise. Define I_N,M(A,B)=integral_{O(N)xO(M)} exp(N*Tr(A^T*U*B*V^T)) dU dV and J_N,M(A,B)=log I_N,M(A,B)/(N*M). Let mu_lambda be the pushforward of mu under x->sqrt(lambda)*x, and let nu_alpha be the limiting empirical SINGULAR-VALUE law of Z_N under this normalization. Write mu_lambda rectangular-free-plus_alpha nu_alpha for the singular-value law of sqrt(lambda)*Sigma_N+Z_N. Let J_alpha[mu_lambda,mu_lambda rectangular-free-plus_alpha nu_alpha] denote the corresponding deterministic limit of J_N,M_N(sqrt(lambda)*Sigma_N,sqrt(lambda)*Sigma_N+Z_N), in precisely this N*M normalization. Then for almost every singular-value sequence, F_N(lambda)->(lambda*alpha/2)*integral x^2 dmu(x)-J_alpha[mu_lambda,mu_lambda rectangular-free-plus_alpha nu_alpha]. This is the auxiliary quenched fixed-spectrum free energy in Section5.6.1, not an assertion that the original prior has iid singular values. Bounded support gives the bounded empirical second moments of source Assumption3. The source calls nu_alpha the Marchenko-Pastur law; here it is explicitly the nonnegative singular-value law, rather than confusing it with the law of squared singular values. No atomic, divergent-log-energy or unbounded-support extension is asserted.
N<=M_N, N/M_N->alpha in (0,1], fixed lambda>0; normalized real orthogonal Haar measures.
Nonnegative iid auxiliary singular values from a compactly supported density; finite symmetrized logarithmic energy and logarithmic moment.
Signal orientations, posterior candidate orientations, and centered Gaussian noise follow the matched fixed-spectrum model explicitly defined above; noise variance1/N.

[Lemma lem:strictly-perturbed-compactness of arXiv:2609.00556, 'Higgs--Demailly System and Positivity of Higgs Bundles'] Fix \(0<\gamma<1\).  Let
\[
 c_j\in C^{0,\gamma}(M,\mathbb R),
 \qquad
 F_j\in C^{0,\gamma}(M,\operatorname{End} E),
\]
and suppose that, for some constants \(c_-,c_+,C_0>0\),
\[
 0<c_-\leq c_j\leq c_+,
 \qquad
 \|c_j\|_{C^{0,\gamma}}
 +\|F_j\|_{C^{0,\gamma}}
 \leq C_0.
\]
Let \(g_j>0\) be \(h_{\rm ref}\)-Hermitian endomorphisms satisfying
\(\det g_j=1\) and
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 &\sqrt{-1}\Lambda_\omega
 \left(
  \bar\partial(g_j^{-1}\partial^{h_{\rm ref}}g_j)
  +[\theta,
    g_j^{-1}\theta_{h_{\rm ref}}^*g_j
    -\theta_{h_{\rm ref}}^*]
 \right)\\
 &\hspace{45mm}
 +c_j\log g_j=F_j.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
If
\[
 \|\log g_j\|_{C^0}\leq L,
\]
then
\[
 \|g_j\|_{C^{2,\gamma}}\leq C,
\]
where \(C\) depends only on the fixed background data,
\(c_-,c_+,C_0,L\), and \(\gamma\).  More generally, uniform
\(C^{k,\gamma}\)-bounds for \(c_j\) and \(F_j\) imply uniform
\(C^{k+2,\gamma}\)-bounds for \(g_j\).

body: Let K be a number field of degree n over the rationals, with r1 real embeddings and r2 pairs of complex conjugate embeddings, so n = r1 + 2 r2, and let O_K be its ring of integers. Dirichlet's unit theorem states the unit group of O_K, the elements with a multiplicative inverse in O_K, is isomorphic to the direct product of a finite cyclic group of roots of unity in K and a free abelian group of rank r1 + r2 - 1. Real quadratic fields thus have unit rank 1, generated modulo torsion by a fundamental unit, while imaginary quadratic fields have unit rank 0. Proved by Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet in 1846.
title: Dirichlet's unit theorem

body: Every strictly stationary phi-mixing Markov chain on a standard Borel space is interlaced rho-mixing, with rho*(n) <= min{1, 2 sqrt(2 phi(n))} and, for phi(n) <= 1/4, rho*(n) <= 2 sqrt(2 phi(n) (1 - 2 phi(n))). Route: a phi(n) bound puts every n-step transition row within phi of the marginal (row diameter 2 phi); the chi-square SDPI-versus-Dobrushin bound gives a robust channel coefficient kappa <= sqrt(2 phi) uniformly in the input law; merging same-colour observation times into alternating blocks makes the prefix-conditioned correlation matrix of Peyre's tensorization kappa times a path's bipartite adjacency (adjacent blocks keep their kernel, non-adjacent blocks decorrelate through a Markov separator); Peyre's N-against-M theorem gives ||E|| ^ 1 <= 2 kappa and the Z-against-Z theorem the arcsine bound; a finite-coordinate martingale approximation extends to infinite index sets. The reset chain P(i,0) = 1-q, P(i,i+1) = q is exponentially phi-mixing with psi'(n) = 0 for every n, so Bradley's 1997 lower-psi criterion does not cover it.

body:
Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and 1 ≤ p < ∞.

(A) Poincaré–Friedrichs inequality (zero boundary values). Suppose Ω is bounded in one direction: Ω ⊂ {x : a < x_1 < a + d} for some a and some finite d (in particular any bounded Ω, with d = diam Ω). Then for every u ∈ W^{1,p}_0(Ω)
   ||u||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ d ||∂_1 u||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ d ||∇u||_{L^p(Ω)}.
For p = 2 the sharp constant for a slab of width d is d/π: ||u||_{L^2} ≤ (d/π)||∇u||_{L^2} for u ∈ H^1_0(Ω). NO regularity of ∂Ω is required and Ω need not be connected. Consequently ||∇u||_{L^p} is a norm on W^{1,p}_0(Ω) equivalent to the full W^{1,p} norm, the Dirichlet form ∫|∇u|^2 is coercive on H^1_0(Ω), and for bounded Ω the best constant C_P in ||u||_2 ≤ C_P||∇u||_2 satisfies 1/C_P^2 = λ_1(Ω), the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of −Δ.

(B) Poincaré–Wirtinger inequality (mean-zero functions). Suppose Ω is bounded, connected, and has Lipschitz boundary (or is bounded, connected and convex; more generally a bounded connected W^{1,p}-extension domain). Then there is C = C(Ω, p) with
   ||u − u_Ω||_{L^p(Ω)} ≤ C ||∇u||_{L^p(Ω)}  for all u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω),  u_Ω = (1/|Ω|) ∫_Ω u dx.
For convex Ω and p = 2 the sharp constant is diam(Ω)/π (Payne–Weinberger). Consequently u ↦ ||∇u||_{L^p} + |∫_Ω u| is a norm on W^{1,p}(Ω) equivalent to the W^{1,p} norm, and the Neumann problem is coercive on the mean-zero subspace.

Where it fails. (A) fails without zero boundary values: constants lie in W^{1,p}(Ω) with zero gradient. (A) fails on any domain containing balls of arbitrarily large radius (R^n, half-spaces, exterior domains): dilating one test function shows no constant works. (B) fails for disconnected Ω (a function equal to different constants on two components). (B) fails on some bounded connected domains with bad boundary (rooms-and-passages domains, sufficiently sharp outward cusps), where functions that are ≈0 in one part and ≈1 in another can have arbitrarily small gradient energy; Lipschitz boundary rules this out. In (B) the constant depends on Ω and blows up as the domain degenerates (e.g. a thin neck).
1 ≤ p < ∞
(A): u ∈ W^{1,p}_0(Ω), Ω contained in a slab of finite width d (no boundary regularity needed)
(B): Ω bounded, connected, Lipschitz boundary (or convex), u ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω)

body:
Let H be a complex Hilbert space (inner product linear in the first slot) and T: D(T) ⊂ H → H linear and densely defined. The adjoint T* has domain D(T*) = {y ∈ H : x ↦ ⟨Tx, y⟩ is bounded on D(T)}, and for y ∈ D(T*), T*y is the unique z ∈ H with ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, z⟩ for all x ∈ D(T) (uniqueness uses density of D(T); without density T* is not a well-defined operator). T is symmetric (Hermitian) if it is densely defined and ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, Ty⟩ for all x, y ∈ D(T), i.e. T ⊂ T*. T is self-adjoint if T = T*, which includes the equality of domains D(T) = D(T*). T is essentially self-adjoint if it is symmetric and its closure T̄ is self-adjoint (equivalently, T is symmetric and has exactly one self-adjoint extension). For a closed symmetric T the deficiency subspaces are K_+ = ker(T* − i) = Ran(T + i)^⊥ and K_- = ker(T* + i) = Ran(T − i)^⊥, and the deficiency indices are n_± = dim K_± ∈ {0, 1, 2, ..., ∞}. A symmetric T is bounded below (semibounded) with bound c ∈ ℝ if ⟨Tx, x⟩ ≥ c‖x‖² for all x ∈ D(T); positive if c = 0 works. For symmetric T one always has T ⊂ T̄ ⊂ T* and T̄ = T**.
H is a complex Hilbert space
T is densely defined (needed for T* to be an operator)
title: Adjoint, Symmetric, Self-Adjoint and Essentially Self-Adjoint Operators

body: In mathematical logic, Goodstein's theorem is a statement about the natural numbers, proved by Reuben Goodstein in 1944, which states that every Goodstein sequence eventually terminates at 0. Laurence Kirby and Jeff Paris showed in 1982 that Goodstein's theorem is unprovable in Peano arithmetic. This was the third example of a true statement about natural numbers that is unprovable in Peano arithmetic, after the examples provided by Gödel's incompleteness theorem and Gerhard Gentzen's 1943 direct proof of the unprovability of ε0-induction in Peano arithmetic. The Paris–Harrington theorem gave another example.
title: Goodstein's theorem

body:
[Thm RT of arXiv:2603.15323, '\Large \bf Small-time heat decay for stable processes on fractal drums'] Suppose that a map $f:{\mathbb R}\to {\mathbb R}$ satisfies the renewal equation (equation eqn:RE of the paper) with
\[
\lim_{z\to-\infty}f(z)=0,
\]
and 
\[
|\phi(z)|\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}|z|}, \quad z\in {\mathbb R},
\]
for some constants $c_1,c_2>0$. Then, the solution of the renewal equation (equation eqn:RE of the paper) is given by
\[
f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}L^{n}\phi(z)=\phi(z)+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{i_1,\cdots, i_n} 
c_{i_1}\cdots c_{i_n}L_{\gamma_{i_1}}\cdots L_{\gamma_{i_{n}}}\phi(z),
\]
where $i_1,\cdots, i_n$ take values from 1 to $N$ and are not necessarily different.
Furthermore, if $\{\gamma_{j}\}$ is non-arithmetic, then 
$$
f(z)=\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}c_{j}\gamma_{j}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(x)dx +o(1) \text{ as } z\to\infty.
$$ 
If $\{\gamma_{j}\}$ is arithmetic with span $\gamma$, then
$$
f(z)=\frac{\gamma}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}c_{j}\gamma_{j}}\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(z-k\gamma) +o(1) \text{ as } z\to\infty.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Renewal Theorem \cite{LV1996}

body:
[Lemma lem:nonexplosive_from_moments of arXiv:2605.15401, 'Noise Tradeoffs, Stationary Information Flow, and Structural Balance in Unit-Birth Network'] Consider the unit-birth CTMC on $S=\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}^N$ with transition rates
$q(x,y)$ and total exit rate
\[
\Lambda(x):=\sum_{y\neq x}q(x,y).
\]
Suppose Assumption~(ass:standing of the paper) holds. Then
\begin{equation}
\sum_{x\in S}\pi(x)\,\Lambda(x)=\mathbb{E}_\pi[\Lambda(X)]<\infty.
\end{equation}
In particular, by [anderson2018non], the CTMC is nonexplosive.

[Definition 48 (Raw factor feedback) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] For a common graded module $M$, write $A=P_Mx$, $r=P_{M^\perp}x$.  For each input
weight $q$, let $\widehat Y_q$ be the branch-labeled direct sum of unsymmetrized
contraction output spaces and set
\begin{equation}
 \widehat\Lambda_q h
 =
 \left(
 r_{a,p}\otimes_s P_{M_q^\perp}h
 \right)_{\substack{a,p,s\\1\le s\le p\wedge q\$p,q,s)\ne(q,q,q)}}
 \oplus
 \left(
 A_{a,p}\otimes_s P_{M_q^\perp}h
 \right)_{\substack{a,p,s\\1\le s\le p\wedge q}} .
 
\end{equation}
All indices and contraction orders are separate orthogonal branch labels.  Put
\begin{equation}
 \widehat N_q=\widehat\Lambda_q^*\widehat\Lambda_q,
 \qquad
 \widehat{\mathfrak H}_Q(A,r)
 =
 \sum_{b,q}
 \ip{r_{b,q}}{\widehat N_qr_{b,q}}.
 
\end{equation}
The omitted residual branch is precisely total covariance; total mixed contractions vanish
by the grade-wise orthogonality of the active and residual modules.

[Lemma 25 of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] Let $t>0$ and $x\in\mbb R^2$ be fixed. For every $\eps>0$ and $A\subset[0,t]^2$,
\[\be^{\eps}_A(B^{x,x}_t)\deq t\,\be^{\eps/t}_{A/t}(B^{0,0}_1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\be^{\eps}_{A}(B^x)\deq t\,\be^{\eps/t}_{A/t}(B^0).\]
In particular, if $A=[a,b]^2_{\leq}$ for $0\leq a<b\leq t$, then by Theorem \ref{Theorem: Existence of SILT}-(2),
\[\ga_A(B^{x,x}_t)\deq t\,\ga_{A/t}(B^{0,0}_1)
\qquad
\text{and}
\qquad
\ga_{A}(B^x)\deq t\,\ga_{A/t}(B^0).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be $1$-periodic and of bounded variation on $[0,1]$ (hence bounded and integrable, with one-sided limits everywhere). Then for every $x$, $S_Nf(x)\to\frac12\big(f(x^+)+f(x^-)\big)$; in particular $S_Nf(x)\to f(x)$ at every point of continuity. The convergence is uniform on every closed interval on which $f$ is continuous at each point. By Riemann localization the conclusion at a single point $x$ only needs $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ together with bounded variation on some neighbourhood of $x$. Note that near a genuine jump the convergence cannot be uniform: the Gibbs phenomenon produces an overshoot of about $8.95\%$ of the jump on each side.
f is 1-periodic and of bounded variation on a period (or, for the pointwise statement at x, f in L^1(T) and of bounded variation near x)
conclusion is for the symmetric partial sums S_N
at jumps the limit is the midpoint of the one-sided limits, not f(x) itself

body: [Lemma ERWgSRRW of arXiv:2604.07227, 'Transition probabilities of step-reinforced random walks'] The ERW on the Cayley graph $G_{\Gamma}$ of a finitely generated group $G$ with respect to a symmetric generating set $\Gamma$ is a generalized SRRW.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:45306651fcca61bdd2c0de7c2fa93b35392ccb87a5bc037879ecb4764834a169","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/45/45306651fcca61bdd2c0de7c2fa93b35392ccb87a5bc037879ecb4764834a169.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:d31a6a3366ca0f3daf94f4773a35ed91ee9b53b12dd33c7cfd8d35bd507ea5fd","bundle_entry_key":"2604-07227-lemma-8-erwgsrrw","bundle_id":"population.tex-extract-s0_103","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"tex-extract-v2-20260907/bundle_s0_103.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:harvest.arxiv.mathematics:arxiv-2604-07227-lemma-8-erwgsrrw","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Paper's own proof, opening: We may assume that $\Gamma=\{g_1,g_2,\dots,g_d\}$ where $d\geq 2$. When the memory parameter $p\geq 1/d$, the ERW is a usual SRRW on $G$ with parameter $\alpha=(dp-1)/(d-1)$ and step distribution $\mu$ uniformly on $\Gamma$, see [mukherjee2025elephant]. When $p < 1/d$, we let $\sigma$ denote the rotation $(123\dots d)$. Then define $(T_n)_{n\geq 2}$ by 
$$
T_n(g_i):= g_{\sigma^{Y_n}(i)}, \quad \text{for } i\in \{1,2,\dots, d\},

[Theorem thm:existence of arXiv:2606.02003, 'Higher-Order Multifractional Stable Motion:\\ Definition and Fundamental Properties'] Under Assumption~(ass:params of the paper), the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \textbf{Well-definedness.}
  For each $t \in \mathbb{R}$,
  $f_n(t,\cdot;H,\alpha) \in L^\alpha(\mathbb{R})$,
  so $X^{(n)}_H(t)$ is a well-defined S$\alpha$S random variable.

\item \textbf{Finite-dimensional distributions.}
  For any $m \in \mathbb{N}^*$, $t_1,\ldots,t_m \in \mathbb{R}$,
  and $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m \in \mathbb{R}$:
  \begin{equation}
  
  \mathbb{E}\!\left[
  \exp\!\Bigl(i\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j X^{(n)}_H(t_j)\Bigr)
  \right]
  = \exp\!\left(
  -\int_\mathbb{R}\Bigl|\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j f_n(t_j,u)\Bigr|^\alpha\,du
  \right).
  \end{equation}

\item \textbf{S$\alpha$S property.}
  For any $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m \in \mathbb{R}$,
  the linear combination $\sum_{j=1}^m\theta_j X^{(n)}_H(t_j)$
  is S$\alpha$S. In particular, $(X^{(n)}_H(t_1),\ldots,X^{(n)}_H(t_m))$
  is a jointly S$\alpha$S random vector.

\item \textbf{Scale.}
  $\bigl\|X^{(n)}_H(t)\bigr\|_\alpha^\alpha
  = \int_\mathbb{R}|f_n(t,u)|^\alpha\,du < \infty$.

\item \textbf{Higher-order increment stationarity.}
  For $H$ constant ($H(t) \equiv H \in (n-1,n)$), the
  $n$-th order increment process
  \begin{equation}
  
  \Delta^n_h X^{(n)}_H(t)
  := \sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^{n-k}\binom{n}{k}X^{(n)}_H(t+kh),
  \quad h \in \mathbb{R},
  \end{equation}
  is stationary in $t$. For functional $H(\cdot)$, the distribution
  of $\Delta^n_h X^{(n)}_H(t)$ depends on $t$ only through the
  values $H(t), H(t+h), \ldots, H(t+nh)$.
\end{enumerate}

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Aizenman-Barsky (1987), for Bernoulli percolation on Z^d (and general transitive graphs), work with the magnetisation M(p,h) = P(0 is connected to a ghost vertex attached to every site with probability 1 - e^{-h}) and prove two differential inequalities: M <= h dM/dh + M^2 + p M dM/dp and dM/dp <= |J| M dM/dh (|J| the coordination constant), the first of Simon-Lieb type via the pivotal decomposition, the second from Russo's formula. Integrating them gives: (i) sharpness of the phase transition, i.e. the susceptibility chi(p) is finite for every p < p_c, hence exponential decay of connectivities below p_c; (ii) the mean-field bounds M(p_c,h) >= c h^{1/2} (delta >= 2) and theta(p) >= c (p - p_c) for p > p_c (beta <= 1). What they do NOT prove: continuity of theta at p_c (theta(p_c) = 0 is open for 3 <= d <= 10), or the matching upper bounds beta >= 1, delta <= 2 (those need the triangle condition, i.e. the lace expansion in high dimensions). The same inequalities transfer to the Ising model via the random-current representation (Aizenman-Barsky-Fernandez). Typical failure: Conflating the auxiliary percolation ghost field h with an actual physical parameter of the underlying model, or applying the conclusion theta(p_c)=0 to a percolation variant where FKG fails for the ghost-augmented measure, such as certain dependent percolation models; the entire argument rests on FKG holding for the specific augmented construction, and this needs to be re-verified for each new model rather than assumed to transfer automatically from ordinary Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Aizenman and Barsky, 1987, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Aizenman, Kesten and Newman, 1987, Communications in Mathematical Physics.

Russo's formula and the pivotal decomposition (Simon-Lieb type inequality)
Conclusions are one-sided mean-field bounds and sharpness, never continuity at p_c

body: In functional analysis and related branches of mathematics, the Banach–Alaoglu theorem states that the closed unit ball of the dual space of a normed vector space is compact in the weak* topology. A common proof identifies the unit ball with the weak-* topology as a closed subset of a product of compact sets with the product topology. As a consequence of Tychonoff's theorem, this product, and hence the unit ball within, is compact.
title: Banach–Alaoglu theorem

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.19396, '\bf Penalisation of Two-Dimensional Brownian Motion'] Let $q$ be a nonnegative function from $
\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{R}$, compactly supported and such that its integral on $
\mathbb{C}$ is positive and finite. 
Then, there exists a unique continuous, strictly positive function $\varphi_q$ from $\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{R}$ satisfying the Sturm-Liouville equation $\Delta \varphi_q = q 
\varphi_q$ in the sense of Schwartz distribution, and such that the radial derivative of $\varphi_q$ at $z$ is well-defined for $|z|$ large enough 
and equivalent to $1/(\pi |z|)$ when $|z| \rightarrow \infty$. 
Under the Wiener measure $W^{(2)}$, and for 
$$A_s^{(q)} := \int_0^s q(X_u) du$$
the process 
$$\left( M_s^{(2,q)} = \frac{\varphi_q(X_s)}{
\varphi_q(0)} \exp \left(- \frac{1}{2} A_s^{(q)} \right) 
\right)_{s \geq 0}$$
is a martingale with respect to the filtration $(\mathcal{F}_s)_{s 
\geq 0}$, and there exists a probability measure $W_{\infty}^{(2,q)}$ on 
$\Omega$, such that for all $s \geq 0$, its restriction to the $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F}_s$ has density 
$ M_s^{(2,q)}$ with respect to $W^{(2)}$. 
Moreover, under $ W_{\infty}^{(2,q)}$, $A_{\infty}^{(q)}$ is almost surely finite, and the $\sigma$-finite measure $
\mathbf{W}^{(2)}$ given by 
$$\mathbf{W}^{(2)} = \varphi_q(0) \exp 
\left( \frac{1}{2} A_{\infty}^{(q)} 
\right) 
\cdot W_{\infty}^{(2,q)} $$ 
does not depend on $q$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let M be a symmetric alpha-stable-like jump process on R^d with d > alpha in (0,2). For potential w(x) asymp (1+|x|)^p, the operator L - w satisfies the Liouville property if and only if p >= -alpha.

body:
Let sum a_n be a series of complex numbers. ROOT TEST (Cauchy): put L = limsup |a_n|^{1/n}. If L < 1 the series converges absolutely; if L > 1 it diverges (the terms do not tend to 0); if L = 1 the test is inconclusive. RATIO TEST (d'Alembert): suppose a_n != 0 for large n. If limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n| < 1 the series converges absolutely; if liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n| > 1 (in particular if |a_{n+1}/a_n| >= 1 for all large n) it diverges; otherwise the test is inconclusive. Comparison: for every sequence, liminf |a_{n+1}/a_n| <= liminf |a_n|^{1/n} <= limsup |a_n|^{1/n} <= limsup |a_{n+1}/a_n|, so whenever the ratio test decides, the root test decides the same way, and the root test is strictly stronger: for a_n = (1/2)^n for n even and (1/3)^n for n odd, the ratios oscillate between (2/3)^n -> 0 and (3/2)^{n} -> infinity so the ratio test says nothing, while |a_n|^{1/n} takes the values 1/2 and 1/3, limsup 1/2 < 1, and the series converges. Both tests are inconclusive for sum 1/n (divergent) and sum 1/n^2 (convergent), which have L = 1; the radius of convergence of a power series sum c_n z^n is 1 / limsup |c_n|^{1/n} (Cauchy-Hadamard), the root test in its most used form.
complex (or real) terms; the ratio test needs a_n != 0 eventually
limsup and liminf are taken in [0, infinity]; when the limits exist the tests read with the plain limit

[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2608.27569, 'Laplace and Dolbeault operators on Sasakian manifolds'] On the $\left( 2n+1\right) $-dimensional
Sasakian manifold with Lefschetz operator $L$ and adjoint $\Lambda $ and operator $H$, we have for all positive integers $b$, 
\begin{align*}
[L^{b},H] &= 2bL^{b}, \\
[L^{b},\Lambda] &= (-bH-b(b-1))L^{b-1}.
\end{align*}
As a consequence, the map $L^b:\Omega^m\to \Omega^{m+2}$ is injective for $m\leq n-b$ and $\Lambda^b:\Omega^m\to \Omega^{m-2}$, for $m\geq n+2b$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 18 of arXiv:2608.27569

Let x_1,...,x_N be deterministic vectors in R^n, with integers N,n>=2, and let eps_1,...,eps_N be independent signs with probabilities1/2 for each of +/-1. Put r=min(N,n), M=max_i||x_i||_2 and H=sum_i x_i x_i^T. There is an absolute constant C such that E_eps||sum_i eps_i x_i x_i^T||_op<=C sqrt(log r) M ||H||_op^(1/2). The logarithm is natural. The N,n>=2 restriction makes the displayed logarithmic factor positive. This is the spectral-norm Rudelson inequality in Vershynin1011.3027v7, Corollary5.28 p19.

[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2604.09248, '\bfseries Limit laws for longest edges in empty region graphs'] Let $\xi$ be the point process defined by \eqref{eq:DefXi}, and assume that $\mathbf{L}(\mathbb{Y})<\infty$, {\eqref{eqn:assumption_xS},} \eqref{eqn:assumption_g}, and \eqref{eqn:assumption_f} are satisfied. Let $\zeta$ be a Poisson process on $\mathbb{Y}$ with a finite intensity measure $\mathbf{M}$, and define
\begin{align*}
E_2 & := \frac{2}{(k!)^2} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \mathbbm{1}\{S_{\mathbf{x}}\cap S_{\mathbf{z}}\neq\varnothing\} \mathbb{E}[ g(\mathbf{x},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}})] \mathbb{E}[g(\mathbf{z},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) ] \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{z}) \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{x}) \\
E_3 & := \frac{2}{(k!)^2} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \mathbbm{1}\{S_{\mathbf{x}}\cap S_{\mathbf{z}}\neq\varnothing\} \mathbb{E}[ g(\mathbf{x},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) g(\mathbf{z},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) ] \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{z}) \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{x}) \\
E_4 & := \frac{2}{k!} \sum_{\varnothing \subsetneq I \subsetneq \{1,\hdots,k\}} \frac{1}{(k-|I|)!} \int_{\mathbb{X}^k} \int_{\mathbb{X}^{k-|I|}} \mathbb{E}[ g(\mathbf{x},\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) g((\mathbf{x}_I,\mathbf{z}),\eta+\delta_{\mathbf{x}}+\delta_{\mathbf{z}}) ] \, \mathbf{K}^{k-|I|}(\dint \mathbf{z}) \, \mathbf{K}^k(\dint \mathbf{x})
\end{align*}
with $(\mathbf{x}_I,\mathbf{z}):=(x_{i_1},\hdots,x_{i_m},z_1,\hdots,z_{k-m})$ for $I=\{i_1,\hdots,i_m\}$.
Then,
$$
\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{KR}}(\xi,\zeta) \leq \mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathbf{L},\mathbf{M}) + E_2 + E_3 + E_4.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:induced-spectral-decomposition of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $\smash{\mathfrak m_{Z,\nu}^0}$ be a representative of the maximal
spectral type of the $\Gamma$-action on $L^2_0(Z,\nu)$. The
maximal spectral type of the induced $\mathbb R^d$-representation
on $\smash{\mathcal K_{\mathrm{tor}}^0}$ is the counting-measure class on
the set $\smash{\Gamma^*\setminus\{0\}}$. Its maximal spectral type on $\smash{\mathcal K_Z}$ is the periodic lift
$\smash{\widetilde{\mathfrak m}_{Z,\nu}^0}$.

translation representation on $L^2(\mathbb R^d/\Gamma)$.

Its Fourier basis consists of the characters indexed by
$\Gamma^*$. The character indexed by $0$ is constant, so the
maximal spectral type on $\mathcal K_{\mathrm{tor}}^0$ is the
counting-measure class on the set
$\Gamma^*\setminus\{0\}$.

The representation on $\mathcal K_Z$ is naturally equivalent to
the representation induced from the $\Gamma$-representation on
$L^2_0(Z,\nu)$. By the spectral theorem for unitary
representations of abelian groups, it is enough to describe what

Let M be a q-by-p real matrix, q<=p, of full row rank, whose q positive singular values are pairwise distinct. For any hidden width r>=1, let U be q-by-r, V be p-by-r, and g(U,V)=(1/2)||UV^T-M||F^2. Every local minimum of g is a global minimum over its factor domain. Every nonglobal critical point has a strictly negative Hessian eigenvalue. Consequently every second-order stationary point is globally optimal for rank-at-most-r approximation. This is the one-hidden-layer specialization of Kawaguchi, Deep Learning without Poor Local Minima, arXiv:1605.07110, section 2.3, Theorem 2.3 and Corollary 2.4 (printed p.3), with artificial data X=I_p,Y=M. It is a landscape theorem and does not itself assert convergence of a specified gradient-descent initialization.

Let T preserve a probability measure mu on X and let A have mu(A) > 0. By the Poincare recurrence theorem the first-return time n_A(x) = min { n >= 1 : T^n(x) in A } is finite for mu-almost every x in A. The INDUCED transformation T_A(x) = T^{n_A(x)}(x) preserves the normalised restriction of mu to A; Kac's formula says the integral of n_A over A with respect to mu equals mu of the union of the forward orbit of A, hence equals 1 when T is ergodic, so the mean return time is 1/mu(A). Conversely, the KAKUTANI TOWER (skyscraper) over T_A with height function n_A reconstructs T on the union of the orbit of A: the tower is the set of pairs (x,k) with x in A and 0 <= k < n_A(x), the map sends (x,k) to (x,k+1) below the top and (x, n_A(x)-1) to (T_A x, 0). Induced maps and towers are ergodic exactly when the original system restricted to the orbit of A is.
mu(A) > 0 and mu a finite invariant measure (Poincare recurrence).
Kac's formula in the form 'mean return time is 1/mu(A)' needs ERGODICITY;
without it the integral computes the measure of the orbit of A instead.
title: Induced (first-return) transformation and the Kakutani tower

body: [Definition 12 of arXiv:2609.02755, 'The Sharp Rate of Probabilistically Strong Convergence to the KPZ Equation'] A rooted tree is a finite connected acyclic graph $\tau$ with a distinguished root vertex, where each edge is typed with an element of a set $\tilde{\mathfrak{L}} = \tilde{\mathfrak{L}}_+ \sqcup \tilde{\mathfrak{L}}_-$ of edge types, and equipped with node decorations $\mathfrak{n} : N(\tau) \to \mathbb{N}^d$ and edge decorations $\mathfrak{e} : E(\tau) \to \mathbb{N}^d$. We write $E(\tau)$ for the set of edges of $\tau$ and $N(\tau)$ for the set of nodes of $\tau$. We write $L(\tau)$ for the set of leaves of $\tau$ and $E_\pm(\tau)$ for the set of edges of $\tau$ with kernel and noise types respectively. In particular, we emphasise that noises are represented by edges of noise type that are incident to a leaf.

body: Let f be a Schwartz function on the real line, smooth with all derivatives decaying faster than any polynomial, and let f_hat be its Fourier transform, f_hat(xi) equal to the integral over all real t of f(t) e^{-2 pi i xi t} dt. The Poisson summation formula states the sum over all integers n of f(n) equals the sum over all integers k of f_hat(k). It holds more generally for f in suitable Sobolev-type spaces, and generalizes to a lattice L in R^d, equating a sum over L with a sum over the dual lattice divided by the covolume of L. It underlies the functional equation of the Riemann zeta function and identities for theta functions.
title: Poisson summation formula
