[Proposition 33 (Monotonicity for Einstein--matter areal flows) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] 1. In the future-contracting regime $[t_0,t_1]\subset(-\infty,0)$, the conformal length~$\mathcal L$, the orbit area~$|t|$, the volume~$\mathcal V$ and its rescaling $|t|^{-3/4}\mathcal V$, and the energy $|t|\mathcal E_\chi$ are monotonically non-increasing in time.

2. In the future-expanding regime $[t_0,t_1]\subset(0,+\infty)$, the conformal length~$\mathcal L$, orbit area~$t$, volume~$\mathcal V$ and rescaled volume~$t^{-3/4}\mathcal V$ are monotonically non-decreasing, while the energy $t^{-2}\mathcal E_\chi$ is monotonically non-increasing.  In the Euler case, the exponent of~$t$ in the energy bound can be improved, namely $t^{-1}\mathcal E_{\rm E}$ is monotonically non-increasing.

As a result, the upper bound~\eqref{estimate-SE} on the energy~$\mathcal E_\chi(t)$ holds, and the upper/lower bounds~\eqref{estimate-LV} on $\mathcal L(t),\mathcal V(t)$ hold in the future-contracting/expanding regimes, respectively. Let X be a complex Banach space and T in K(X) compact. Then: (a) every nonzero point of the spectrum sigma(T) is an eigenvalue of T, of finite geometric multiplicity; (b) for each nonzero lambda in sigma(T) the operator T - lambda has finite ascent and descent p = p(lambda) >= 1, and X = N ⊕ R with N = ker (T - lambda)^p finite-dimensional and R = ran (T - lambda)^p closed, both T-invariant; T - lambda is nilpotent on N and invertible on R, and dim N is the algebraic multiplicity of lambda; (c) each nonzero lambda in sigma(T) is an isolated point of sigma(T), and the Riesz projection P_lambda = (1/(2 pi i)) times the contour integral of (z - T)^{-1} around a small circle about lambda is a projection of finite rank dim N onto N; (d) sigma(T) is at most countable and its only possible accumulation point is 0; equivalently, for every eps > 0 there are only finitely many eigenvalues with |lambda| > eps; (e) if dim X = infinity then 0 is in sigma(T); (f) sigma(T) = sigma(T'), and for lambda nonzero dim ker(T - lambda) = dim ker(T' - lambda) < infinity. (For real Banach spaces the statements about real nonzero lambda remain valid; the spectrum itself should be taken in the complexification.)
X is a complex Banach space
T: X -> X is compact
lambda is a nonzero scalar in the statements (a)-(c), (f)

[Question of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{B}(\Omega),\mathscr{P}_{\Omega})$ and $(\Sigma,\mathcal{B}(\Sigma),\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma})$ be Polish measure spaces and let $f:\Omega\to \mathcal{B}(\Sigma)$ be measurable\footnote{There is a natural $\sigma$-algebra on $\mathcal{B}(\Sigma)$ generated by the Borel measures.}.
    What assumptions on $\mathscr{P}_{\Omega}$, $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}$ and $f$ are needed for there to exist a probability measure $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega\times \Sigma$ with $\mathscr{P}_{\Omega}$ and $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}$ as marginals and such that the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega]$ is supported on $f(\omega)$ almost surely? Do the graphical representations of the quantum Ising model satisfy any such assumptions? (Stated as a question by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Unnumbered question of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'

body: Let (S, d) and (T, rho) be metric spaces and F a family of functions from S to T. F is equicontinuous at a point x_0 in S if for every epsilon > 0 there exists delta > 0 such that, for every f in F and every x in S with d(x, x_0) < delta, rho(f(x), f(x_0)) < epsilon; F is equicontinuous (on S) if it is equicontinuous at every point, and uniformly equicontinuous if a single delta works for every x_0 in S for each epsilon. The key feature is that the same delta serves every function in the family, not merely every point for a fixed function. [standard, e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis]
title: Equicontinuous Family of Functions

[Proposition prop:AGG of arXiv:2607.22291, 'Rare subtree patterns in size-conditioned Bienaymé trees: Poisson approximation and declum'] Let $(I^{n}_i)_{i \in [n]}$ be indicator random variables with
$q^{n}_i = \mathbb{E}[I^{n}_i]$, $\lambda^{n} = \sum_{i=1}^n q^n_i$,
$W^n = \sum_{i=1}^n I^n_i$.
For each $i \in [n]$, let $B^n_i \subseteq [n]$ be such that $i \in B^n_i$. Then there exists a function $f_n$ with $||f_n||_{\infty} \leq 1$  such that
\[
  d_{\mathrm{TV}}\bigl(W^n,\, \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda^{n})\bigr)
  \leq  2 (b^n_1 + b^n_2 + b^n_3)
\]
with $$ 
b^n_1= \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \in B^n_i} q^n_i\, q^n_j,  \quad  b^n_2 = \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j \in B^n_i \setminus \{i\}} \mathbb{E}[I^n_i I^n_j], \quad 
  b^n_3 = \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n \left| \mathbb{E}\bigl[(I^n_i - q^n_i)\, f_n\big( 1 +\sum_{j\in [n]\setminus B^n_i} I^n_j\big)\bigr] \right|.
  $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Arratia, Goldstein \& Gordon

[Theorem thm:codiff-asymp of arXiv:2606.02003, 'Higher-Order Multifractional Stable Motion:\\ Definition and Fundamental Properties'] Under Assumptions~(ass:params of the paper) and~(ass:limits of the paper), for fixed
$s \in \mathbb{R}$ and as $t \to +\infty$:
\begin{equation}

\tau\!\bigl(X^{(n)}_H(s),\, X^{(n)}_H(t)\bigr)
\sim C(s)\, t^{(\alpha-1)H_+ + H(s) - n},
\end{equation}
where the constant $C(s) > 0$ is given by
\begin{equation}

C(s)
= \frac{\alpha\,|\kappa_\infty|^{\alpha-1}\,|C_n(s)|}
{n - (\alpha-1)H_+ - H(s)},
\end{equation}
with
\[
\kappa_\infty := \frac{\binom{H_+-1/\alpha}{n}}{\Gamma(H_++1-1/\alpha)},
\]
and $C_n(s)$ is the leading tail coefficient of $f_n(s,\cdot)$ from
Lemma~(lem:kernel-asymp of the paper)(iii). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Asymptotic codifference of $n$-MFSM

body: [Proposition 22 of arXiv:2606.23099, 'Path-dependent Affine Processes'] Let $\mu \in \ccM([0,T], \R)$ satisfy $\mu([t,T]) \leq 0$ for all $t \in [0,T]$ and let $\psi \in L^2([0,T], \R)$ denote the unique global solution of \eqref{eq:riccati-pd-vol}. Then $\exp(Y)$ with $Y$ defined by \eqref{eq:Y-pd-vol} is a true martingale. In particular, the exponential-affine transform formula \eqref{exp-affine-formula} holds.

[Theorem 58 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] Under the law \(\mu_H\) of
\eqref{eq:unique-entrance-mixture}, define
\begin{equation}
  J_\infty
  :=\int_0^Ue^{-L(s)}\,\mathrm ds
    +\int_0^\infty e^{-R(s)}\,\mathrm ds.
  
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
  0<J_\infty<\infty
  \quad\text{almost surely},
  
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
  J_a\Longrightarrow J_\infty,
  \qquad
  \widehat{\EE}_a[J_a^{-1}]
  \longrightarrow
  D_H:=\EE_{\mu_H}[J_\infty^{-1}]
  \in(0,\infty).
  
\end{equation}
title: Theorem 58 of arXiv:2607.21374

The adaptive particle-weight system consists of $N$ agents with states $\bm{X}_i(t) \in \mathbb{D}$ (where $\mathbb{D} = \mathbb{R}^d$ or $\mathbb{T}^d$) and interaction weights $\bm{W}_{i, j}(t) \in \mathbb{R}$ co-evolving according to the coupled system of SDEs: $\mathrm{d}\bm{X}_i = \mu(\bm{X}_i) \mathrm{d}t + \nu \mathrm{d}\bm{B}_i + \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j \in [N] \setminus \{i\}} \bm{W}_{i, j} \sigma(\bm{X}_i, \bm{X}_j) \mathrm{d}t$ and $\mathrm{d}\bm{W}_{i, j} = \alpha(\bm{X}_i, \bm{X}_j) \bm{W}_{i, j} \mathrm{d}t + \beta(\bm{X}_i, \bm{X}_j) \mathrm{d}t$ for all $i, j \in [N], i \neq j$, where $(\bm{B}_i)_{i \in [N]}$ are independent standard Brownian motions, $\nu \ge 0$, and $\mu, \sigma, \alpha, \beta$ are globally Lipschitz continuous functions.
\mathbb{D} is \mathbb{R}^d or \mathbb{T}^d
\bm{B}_i are independent Brownian motions
\mu, \sigma, \alpha, \beta are globally Lipschitz
title: Coupled Particle-Weight SDE System with Adaptive Plasticity

[Theorem 19 of arXiv:2506.10856, 'The space of multifurcating ranked tree shapes: enumeration, lattice structure, and Markov'] The tree $\ddot{T}_N$ with the maximum backwards degree in $\mathcal{MT}_N$ is the multifurcating tree with the following properties 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item It has $K=\lfloor \frac{N-2}{2} \rfloor+1$ internal nodes.
    \item Each of the $\lfloor \frac{N-2}{2} \rfloor$ non-root internal nodes subtend distinct cherries descending from the root.
    \item The rest of the $L=2 + (N \text{ mod } 2)$ tips are leaves descending from the root.
\end{enumerate}
The backwards degree of $\ddot{T}_N$ is \[ \text{deg}^-(\ddot{T}_N) = \big (3+ (N \text{ mod } 2) \big) 2^{\left \lfloor \frac{N}{2} \right \rfloor} - \left \lfloor \frac{N}{2} \right \rfloor - 3 .\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 19 of arXiv:2506.10856

body: A power series sum a_n (x - c)^n has a radius of convergence R in [0, infinity] given by the Cauchy-Hadamard formula 1/R = limsup |a_n|^{1/n}: it converges absolutely for |x - c| < R and diverges for |x - c| > R (behavior on |x - c| = R varies). Within the open disk of convergence the series is infinitely differentiable and integrable term by term, and equals the Taylor series of its sum. This is the bridge from analytic functions to their coefficient sequences.
title: Power Series and Radius of Convergence

Let $\mathcal{S}(K)$ be the class of smooth cylindrical $K$-valued random variables of the form $F = \sum_{i=1}^m f_i(W(h_1), \dots, W(h_n)) k_i$ with $f_i \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$. The Malliavin derivative $D F$ is the random element in $L^2(\Omega; \mathcal{H} \otimes K)$ defined by $D F = \sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n \partial_j f_i(W(h_1), \dots, W(h_n)) (h_j \otimes k_i)$. The operator $D$ is closable from $L^p(\Omega; K)$ into $L^p(\Omega; \mathcal{H} \otimes K)$, and its domain is denoted by $\mathbb{D}^{1, p}(K)$.
F is a smooth cylindrical K-valued random variable

body: On four equally likely points {0, 1, 2, 3}, the systems A_1 = {0, 1}, A_2 = {0, 2}, A_3 = {1, 2} and B_1 = {0, 1}, B_2 = {0, 2}, B_3 = {0, 3} both have every event of probability 1/2 and every pairwise intersection of probability 1/4, so they share every bound computed from first and second order data, including the Gallot-Kounias value 3/4. But the first union has probability 3/4 and the second has probability 1. The first system attains the bound; the second falls short by 1/4.

[Def weighted projective stack and curve of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Consider the $(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$-weighted action of $\mathbb{G}_m$ on $n$-dimension affine space $\mathbb{A}^n$, i.e., \[t \cdot (x_1, \ldots, x_n) = (t^{a_1}x_1, \ldots, t^{a_n}x_n)\] where each $a_i > 0.$ 
Then, the {\em weighted projective stack} $\mathcal{P}(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ is given by the stack quotient
\[
\mathcal{P}(a_1, \ldots, a_n) := [(\mathbb{A}^n \setminus 0)/\mathbb{G}_m].
\]
When $n = 2$, we refer to the weighted projective stack $\mathcal{P}(a,b)$ as a {\em weighted projective curve}.
title: weighted projective stack and curve

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:46cbd9f702496a40b4aa2fe562f442ed7be2339f9cc0c13fc02e8c87e0c7880d","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/46/46cbd9f702496a40b4aa2fe562f442ed7be2339f9cc0c13fc02e8c87e0c7880d.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:691d9e53bfe0740916bcf5228b229f125186c483b263d7a128676e5ad034b679","bundle_entry_key":"t336-w727-c016","bundle_id":"population.w727-t336-raw-rbf-prior-averaged-erm-011","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"Transformer approximation and generalization; amortized Bayesian Gaussian-process prediction","draft":"w727/bundle_011.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.transformers:draft-raw-rbf-original-task-prior-averaged-erm","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C016 v1: prior-averaged raw-input RBF prediction by approximate ERM
Kind: bound. Target: none (reviewer-authorized generalization continuation).
Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty, efficient-training or independent-audit claim.

## 1. Task law and theorem
Fix d>=1, n>=0, ell,s,epsilon>0. On X=[0,1]^d let f be a zero-mean GP with kernel k(x,z)=exp(-||x-z||^2/(2 ell^2)). Observations are f(x) plus independent N(0,s) noises. Each task consists of at most n context observations and one fresh noisy query. The joint law of context length and all input locations is independent of f and the noises. Within-task locations and labels need not be independent. Tasks are iid with fresh GP/noise draws. There is no label-based rejection or input selection. Let W denote the FULL, unclipped context, its locations and the query location; P_W denotes the exact noisy query posterior given W.

For m>=1 training tasks, confidence alpha in (0,1), output cover tolerance gamma>0 and empirical optimization error xi>=0, define the explicit architecture and constants below. Let theta_hat be any measurable xi-approximate empirical minimizer over that bounded parameter cube for the displayed Gaussian loss. With probability at least 1-alpha over the training tasks,

    E_fresh W KL(P_W || h_theta_hat(c_B(W))) <= epsilon + 2 E_m + xi.    (1)

The expectation is over a fresh ORIGINAL task, conditional on training. Only the predictor's encoding uses clipped context labels. Its input is raw coordinates, clipped labels and fixed flags/constants, with no supplied kernel-feature oracle. The deterministic approximation and cover lemmas invoked below, and this composition, remain unaudited. In particular (1) is not an additional independently checked MOVE.

## 2. Completely specified architecture and class
Put V=s+1 and

    C_tail=2 sqrt(2) n^2 V/s^3,
    eps_c=epsilon/4,
    B=sqrt(4 V log(max(e,2 C_tail/epsilon))).

Use C013 v1 with tolerance eps_c and this B. For convenience its explicit size recipe is restated, without re-proving that saved construction:

    b_mu=sqrt(s eps_c), b_v=min(s/2,s sqrt(eps_c)),
    C_mu=nB/s+n^2 B/s^2, C_v=1+2n/s+n^2/s^2,
    tau=min(1/2,b_mu/[3(1+C_mu)],b_v/[3C_v]),
    a=d/ell^2, t=ceil(max(1,2e a,log(1/tau)/log(2))),
    p=binomial(d+t-1,d),
    E_mu=nB(3/s+6n/s^2), E_v=3+12n/s,
    rho=min(1,b_mu/[3(1+E_mu)],b_v/[3E_v]),
    g=max(1,ceil(d sqrt(p)/(ell rho))), J=(g+1)^d,
    eps0=min(eps_c/9,1/36), kappa=1+4max(1,n)/s, M=4nB/s,
    delta0=min(1/2,s/8,sqrt(s eps0)/(1+M),s sqrt(eps0)/4),
    T_c=ceil(sqrt(kappa) log(2/delta0)/2),
    N=n+1, D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ,
    H=2Jd+pJ+4p+1, L=T_c+5+ceil(log(J)/log(2)).

The class has L attention-then-residual-MLP layers, five normalized ReLU attention heads per layer (zero padding unused heads), token width D, MLP hidden width H, and a two-output linear readout on the query token. All layer and readout matrix entries range over [-W_max,W_max], where C015 v1 supplies

    W_max=N max(4,s,2/s,1/ell), K0=max(1,B,s),
    P=L(15D^2+2DH)+2D.

The fixed, parameter-independent input placement has bound K0; encoder coefficients are counted as trainable parameters. The exact clipping map c_B clips each observed context label to [-B,B]. Fixed output clips impose

    mu_theta in [-U,U], U=nB/s+sqrt(s eps_c)+1,
    v_theta in [v0,v1], v0=s, v1=1+2s.

C015 proves those clips leave the C013 comparator unchanged. No general monotonicity of Gaussian KL under variance clipping is required. Fixed label/output clips and affine input placement are excluded from the trainable count, as in C004/C013.

## 3. Explicit cover and statistical constants
Use the saved C014 recurrence, starting K_0=K0,F_0=0:

    Kbar_j=K_j+5D^4 W_max^3 K_j^3,
    Fbar_j=(1+15D^4 W_max^3 K_j^2)F_j+15D^4 W_max^2 K_j^3,
    K_(j+1)=(1+HD W_max^2)Kbar_j,
    F_(j+1)=(1+HD W_max^2)Fbar_j+2HD W_max Kbar_j,
    Lambda=D W_max F_L+D K_L.

Here F is the sensitivity recurrence, renamed to avoid confusion with E_m. Set

    q=max(1,ceil(2W_max Lambda/gamma)), J_cover=(q+1)^P,
    C=0.5 log(v1/v0)+U^2/v0, A=V/v0, K_loss=4(C+A),
    u=log(4 J_cover/alpha), t_query=log(4m/alpha),
    T_query=sqrt(2V t_query),
    Q=1/(2v0)+(U+sqrt(V))/v0+(U^2+V)/v0^2,
    L_query=1/(2v0)+(T_query+U)/v0+(T_query+U)^2/(2v0^2),
    beta=4sqrt(2) K_loss sqrt(u/m)+2K_loss u/m,
    E_m=beta+gamma(Q+L_query).                              (2)

These are finite explicit real constants, not an efficient numerical prescription. One may evaluate u using P log(q+1), without materializing an enormous cover. For fixed approximation parameters and alpha, taking gamma=1/m gives E_m=O(sqrt(log(m)/m)+log(m)/m) as m tends to infinity (m>=2). Constants depend on d,n,ell,s,epsilon and alpha through the displayed formulas. This rate describes estimation above the fixed approximation error epsilon; it does not assert efficient dependence on dimension or on epsilon.

Use normalized Gaussian log loss

    loss_theta(W,Y)=0.5 log(v_theta/v0)+(Y-mu_theta)^2/(2v_theta).

An xi-approximate empirical minimizer has empirical risk at most infimum empirical risk plus xi. No algorithm for finding it is asserted.

## 4. New bridge: clipping bias for the full Gaussian kernel
We extend the saved C007 finite-feature clipping argument to the non-finite-rank kernel, rather than asserting that an infinite-dimensional feature input was supplied.

Fix a deterministic context of length l<=n and its query. Their (l+1)-point real positive-semidefinite Gram matrix admits a finite Gram realization by vectors z_1,...,z_l,z_* in R^(l+1). Each vector has norm one because the kernel diagonal is one. Let F have rows z_i^T, let K_ctx=F F^T, and set A_ctx=sI+F^T F. Both ridge matrices are positive definite. The identity

    A_ctx F^T = F^T(sI+K_ctx)

implies F^T(sI+K_ctx)^(-1)=A_ctx^(-1)F^T. Therefore the coefficient a_i of y_i in the exact posterior mean satisfies

    a_i=z_*^T A_ctx^(-1) z_i,   |a_i|<=1/s.              (3)

The last inequality uses ||A_ctx^(-1)||_op<=1/s and unit vector norms. This is a pointwise finite-matrix argument for each design; a globally selected Gram factor is not needed as a measurable input to the predictor.

Let mu and mu_B be the exact-kernel posterior formulas evaluated at full and clipped labels respectively. The computed variance v is identical for the two formulas. N(mu_B,v) is an auxiliary Gaussian, NOT the conditional law given clipped labels. For r_i=y_i-c_B(y_i), Cauchy-Schwarz and (3) give

    |mu-mu_B|^2 <= (l/s^2) sum_i r_i^2.

Conditional on the input design, each y_i is centered Gaussian with variance at most V (in fact V for this kernel). For G of variance tau<=V the elementary square-mgf identity gives

    E[G^2 exp(G^2/(4V))]=tau(1-tau/(2V))^(-3/2)<=2sqrt(2)V.

Since r_i^2<=y_i^2 1{|y_i|>B}, multiplication by the indicator and the positive exponential yields

    E|mu-mu_B|^2 <= 2sqrt(2) n^2 V/s^2 exp(-B^2/(4V)).  (4)

This uses a sum of marginal expectations, not independence of correlated context labels. The Gaussian square-mgf needs tau<=V and the argument 1/(4V)<1/(2tau); it is available from the exogenous Gaussian task law, not from a mere second-moment bound.

C013 at eps_c gives a raw-input comparator h_B=N(muhat,vhat) with vhat>=s and KL(N(mu_B,v)||h_B)<=eps_c for every clipped context. C015 places it in the bounded class and preserves it through the fixed output clips.

Writing d_v=0.5(log(vhat/v)+v/vhat-1)>=0, the scalar inequality (a+b)^2<=2a^2+2b^2 gives

    KL(P_W||h_B)
      <= 2 KL(N(mu_B,v)||h_B)+(mu-mu_B)^2/s.

The direction uses vhat>=s and nonnegativity of d_v. By (4),

    E_W KL(P_W||h_B) <= 2eps_c+C_tail exp(-B^2/(4V)) <= epsilon. (5)

If C_tail=0 the tail term vanishes; otherwise the definition of B gives exp(-B^2/(4V))<=epsilon/(2C_tail). Empty contexts are included. All expectations in (4)-(5) retain the original task law.

## 5. Apply the saved concentration result with the new cover
C007 Section 3 is a uniform concentration statement whose predictor dependence enters only through bounded output intervals and a fixed gamma-cover. Its attention-only cover is replaced here by C014, not used for an architecture containing uncounted MLPs. C015 supplies the comparator radius and intervals. The query marginal conditional on exogenous design is centered Gaussian with variance <=V even though its conditional mean given W need not be bounded.

For clarity the hypotheses and directions of the invoked tail argument are explicit. The pointwise loss envelope is 0<=loss<=C+Y^2/v0. Its finite exponential moment satisfies E exp(loss/K_loss)<2; no independence of Y and the predictor is used. C007's moment expansion gives, for |z|<1/(2K_loss),

    log E exp(z(loss-E loss)) <= 8K_loss^2 z^2/(1-2K_loss|z|).

IID tasks allow multiplication of their mgfs. The Chernoff exponential-Markov argument then gives two-sided tail at most 2exp(-u) at threshold beta in (2). This is an exponential-moment argument, not Chebyshev's second-moment inequality. Union over the fixed J_cover predictors costs alpha/2. The Gaussian marginal query bound 2exp(-T_query^2/(2V)), unioned over m tasks, costs alpha/2. No within-task independence is used.

The loss derivatives on the output rectangle give the output-distance bound gamma L(Y), where

    L(Y)=1/(2v0)+(|Y|+U)/v0+(|Y|+U)^2/(2v0^2).

C007 proves E L(Y)<=Q from E|Y|<=sqrt(V), EY^2<=V and (|Y|+U)^2<=2Y^2+2U^2. On the query-tail event L(Y_i)<=L_query. The fixed cover therefore yields, with probability >=1-alpha,

    sup_theta |R(theta)-Rhat(theta)| <= E_m.

This is precisely the saved statistical lemma applied to the correct architecture and original task law; it is not a fresh independent audit of C007. An empirical xi-minimizer then obeys R(theta_hat)<=inf_theta R(theta)+2E_m+xi.

Finally, conditional Gaussian entropy is integrable because s<=v(W)<=V. For every fixed predictor,

    R(theta)=E_W KL(P_W||h_theta(c_B(W)))
                  +0.5 E_W log(v(W)/s)+0.5.

Subtract the same finite constant from the risk comparison and insert (5). This proves (1), including data-dependent theta_hat on the uniform event.

## 6. Sources, status and limitation
Dependencies: C007 Sections 1 and 3-4 (saved original-task loss concentration and clipping template); C013 (raw-coordinate Gaussian-kernel approximation); C014 (trainable attention-plus-MLP cover); C015 (explicit coefficient and output bounds). Accepted C002/C004 are not re-audited. C013 uses the Taylor feature facts in Cotter, Keshet and Srebro, arXiv:1109.4603v1, Section 3 equations (6)-(11), PDF pages 4-5; those facts are known, not new here. Bai et al., arXiv:2306.04637v2, Section 5.1 Theorem 20, PDF pages 14-15, is the related square-loss ERM framework, not a cited Gaussian-log-loss theorem. The main new composition step here is (3)-(5) for the full raw-input kernel and the fully specified bounded hypothesis class.

No novelty is claimed. Independent review is required for C007 and C013-C016. This is noisy predictive forward KL averaged over the prior and original exogenous task law. If a set S of natural numbers contains 0 (or 1) and contains n+1 whenever it contains n, then S is all of N. Equivalently (strong induction) if S contains n whenever it contains all m < n, then S = N. Both are equivalent to the well-ordering principle (every nonempty subset of N has a least element).

[Proposition 7 (A law-weighted Brownian error with sublinear spatial growth) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\wt\eta\in(1/\alpha,1)$, $0<\lambda<1$, $\kappa\ne0$, and let $0<\theta<\alpha/2$. Put
\[
  \phi_\theta(x):=(1+x^2)^{\theta/2},\qquad x\in\R,
\]
and let $r\in L^2(0,T)$ be deterministic. Consider
\[
  b(t,x)=\wt b(t,x)\equiv0,
  \qquad
  a(t,x)\equiv\kappa,
  \qquad
  \wt a(t,x)=\kappa+r(t)\phi_\theta(x),
\]
and
\[
  \sigma(t,x)=\wt\sigma(t,x)=1+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr).
\]
Then the stable coefficient is bounded, bounded away from zero, and H\"older while failing to be Lipschitz at the origin. The perturbed Brownian coefficient is spatially Lipschitz. For any coupled solution pair satisfying Assumption~\ref{ass:solutions},
\[
  B=0,
  \qquad
  A^2=\int_0^T |r(t)|^2\,\E \phi_\theta(X_t)^2\dd t,
  \qquad
  S=0.
\]
Moreover, $A<\infty$ and
\[
  A^2\le C_{\theta,T}\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^2,
\]
where $C_{\theta,T}$ depends on the baseline moment $\sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t|^{2\theta}$, which is finite by Proposition~\ref{prop:baseline-moments}. Consequently, for every $R>0$ there exists $C_R>0$ such that, whenever $\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}\le R$, $x_0=\wt x_0$, and $A<1$ (for instance, for sufficiently small $\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}$),
\[
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}
  \le C_R\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}}.
\]

body: In mathematics, and in particular linear algebra, the Moore–Penrose inverse ⁠⁠ of a matrix ⁠⁠, often called the pseudoinverse, is the most widely known generalization of the inverse matrix. It was independently described by E. H. Moore in 1920, Arne Bjerhammar in 1951, and Roger Penrose in 1955. Earlier, Erik Ivar Fredholm had introduced the concept of a pseudoinverse of integral operators in 1903. The terms pseudoinverse and generalized inverse are sometimes used as synonyms for the Moore–Penrose inverse of a matrix, but sometimes applied to other elements of algebraic structures which share some but not all properties expected for an inverse element.

body: [Lemma lem:det_lemma of arXiv:2510.06891, 'Multivariate CLT for L\'evy processes: convergence rates without moment assumptions'] Let $\bm{M}(t)$ be a $d \times d$ positive definite matrix (i.e. with strictly positive eigenvalues), such that $\bm{M}(t) \to \bm{I}_d$ as $t\to\infty$. Let $\bm{M}(s,t)\coloneqq s\bm{I}_d +(1-s)\bm{M}(t)$ and $D_t(s)\coloneqq\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}[\det(\bm{M}(s,t))^{-1}]$ for $s \in [0,1]$ (with the derivatives at $s\in\{0,1\}$ being one-sided) and $t \geqslant 1$. Then, for every $t\geqslant 1$, the function $s\mapsto D_t(s)$ is well-defined, continuous and finite on $[0,1]$. Moreover, $\det(\bm{M}(s,t))\sim 1$ and $D_t(s) \sim -\mathrm{tr}(\bm{I}_d-\bm{M}(t))$ uniformly in $s\in [0,1]$ as $t \to \infty$.

[Definition 22 (Admissible stage start) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Fix a torus structure and constants \(\Lambda,\eta,\theta>0\).  We call the
pair \((q_0,r_0)\), where \(r_0=\overline{q_0}\), an \emph{admissible stage
start with constants \(\Lambda,\eta,\theta\)} if \(r_0\) is Riemannian and
\begin{equation}
 \BG_N(r_0;\Lambda),\qquad
 \|q_0-r_0\|_{C^{N,\sigma}(M,r_0)}<\eta,\qquad
 d_{\TT^2}(r_0)<\theta.
\end{equation}
The Riemannian condition and the first two displayed conditions are the
\emph{analytic start conditions}; the last displayed condition is the
\emph{geometric start condition}.  Stage preparation and positive-time
smoothing reproduce bounded geometry and control the endpoint error;
finite-time decay and averaging contract that error, while fibration comparison
reproduces the geometric condition.  No quotient-length condition is part of
an admissible stage start; the required lower bound is reconstructed from the
large-diameter hypothesis inside each block.
title: Admissible stage start

Let a<b and let f:[a,b]->R be continuous on [a,b] and differentiable on (a,b). Then there is c in (a,b) with f'(c)=(f(b)-f(a))/(b-a). In particular if f(a)=f(b), some c has f'(c)=0 (Rolle's theorem). For a continuous f:[a,b]->V into a real or complex normed vector space, differentiable on (a,b) in norm, a single-point vector equality need not hold; however ||f(b)-f(a)|| <= (b-a) sup_{x in (a,b)}||f'(x)|| whenever the supremum is finite (and the estimate is vacuous if it is infinite). Complex-valued functions use the usual complex modulus as norm.

body:
[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2606.17381, 'Large deviation principle for friendship-biases\\ in Galton--Watson trees'] {\bf [LDP for type fractions along a random path]}

Under the joint law of the Galton--Watson tree $\mathcal{T}_\infty$ and the random exploration path, the family of random variables $\{\Upsilon_j\}_{j\in\N_4}$ satisfies the LDP in the Polish space $(0,\infty) \times \mathcal{S}_2$ with rate $j$ and with good rate function $J$ given by
\[
J(x,s) = \inf_{\nu \in \Phi(x,s)} I(\nu), \qquad x \in (0,\infty),\, s \in \mathcal{S}_2.
\]
Here,
\begin{itemize}
\item 
$I\colon\,\mathcal{P}(E) \to [0,\infty]$ is the good rate function given by
\[
I(\nu) =
\begin{cases}
H\left(\nu\,\middle\|\, \pi_{1,2}\nu \otimes \zeta^{\otimes 2}\right), & \text{if } \pi_{1,2}\nu=\pi_{2,3}\nu,\\[1ex]
\infty, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{cases}
\]
where $H(\cdot\, \|\, \cdot)$ denotes relative entropy and $\pi_{1,2}$, $\pi_{2,3}$ denote the projection onto the first two, respectively, the last two of the three coordinates.
\item
The constraint on $\nu$ is to the subset of $\mathcal{P}(E)$ given by
\[
\Phi(x,s) = \big\{\nu \in \mathcal{P}(E)\colon\,\|G(\nu)\|_1 = x,\,G(\nu)/\|G(\nu)\|_1 = s\big\},
\qquad x \in (0,\infty),\,s \in \mathcal{S}_2,
\]
where $G = (G^\chi)_{\chi \in S}$ with $G^\chi\colon\,\mathcal{P}(E) \to [0,\infty]$ is given by
\[
G^\chi(\nu) = \int_{E} h^\chi\,\mathrm{d}\nu
\]
with $h^\chi\colon\,E \to \N_0$ given by
\[
\begin{aligned}
h^{-}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\, c>0\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\,c=0,\, c^\prime>0\}}, \\[6pt]
h^{0}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= c-\mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}}-\mathbbm{1}_{\{c>1\}}
+ \mathbbm{1}_{\{b=0,\,c=0,\,c^\prime=0\}}, \\[6pt]
h^{+}\big((a,a^\prime),(b,b^\prime),(c,c^\prime)\big)
&= \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>0\}} + \mathbbm{1}_{\{c>1\}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 3 of arXiv:2606.17381

Let (X_n)_{n=1}^\infty be independent real random variables, and fix c > 0. Define the truncated variables Y_n = X_n \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_n| \le c\}}. Then the series \sum_{n=1}^\infty X_n converges almost surely if and only if all three of the following series converge: (1) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb{P}(|X_n| > c) < \infty; (2) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb{E}[Y_n] \text{ converges in } \mathbb{R}; (3) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \text{Var}(Y_n) < \infty.

PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. Let S_k=max_{j<=k} X_j and a_n=sqrt(n) log(n). If for every finite T, max_{k<=floor(nT)} |S_k-X_k|/a_n tends to zero in probability, and S_floor(nt)/a_n converges in the Skorokhod J1 topology to a continuous process Y, then X_floor(nt)/a_n also converges to Y. The identity time change bounds their J1 distance by the displayed uniform norm. A uniform O_P(sqrt(n)) backtracking estimate suffices; a fixed-time estimate alone does not establish this hypothesis. [Theorem thm:root-comparison of arXiv:2607.08551, 'Weighted-threshold Coupon Collection'] Fix $\theta\in(0,1)$ and $0<\delta<t_{N,\theta}$. Define
\[
\Delta_{N,\theta}(\delta):=
\min\Bigl\{
\theta-m_N(t_{N,\theta}-\delta),
\,
m_N(t_{N,\theta}+\delta)-\theta
\Bigr\}.
\]
Then $\Delta_{N,\theta}(\delta)>0$ and
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(|\tau_{N,\theta}-t_{N,\theta}| > \delta\bigr)
\le
4\exp\!\left(
-\frac{\Delta_{N,\theta}(\delta)^2}
{2w_N^\ast+\frac23 w_N^\ast \Delta_{N,\theta}(\delta)}
\right).
\]

Consider the autonomous system y'=f(y) on an open set U subset R^n containing an equilibrium y* (f(y*)=0), with f locally Lipschitz. Suppose there is a continuously differentiable V: W -> R on a neighborhood W of y* with V(y*)=0, V(y)>0 for y in W\{y*} (V positive definite), and V_dot(y) = grad V(y).f(y) <= 0 for all y in W (V is a Lyapunov function). Then y* is stable: for every epsilon>0 there is delta>0 such that |y(0)-y*|<delta implies |y(t)-y*|<epsilon for all t>=0. If in addition V_dot(y)<0 for y in W\{y*}, then y* is asymptotically stable: stable, and y(t) -> y* as t -> infinity for all initial conditions sufficiently close to y*.
f is locally Lipschitz near the equilibrium y*
V is C^1, positive definite at y*, with V_dot <= 0 (resp. < 0) near y*

body: The functional form of Brunn-Minkowski: if h((1-t)x + ty) >= f(x)^{1-t} g(y)^t for all x, y, then the integral of h is at least (integral of f)^{1-t} (integral of g)^t. Applied to indicator functions it recovers Brunn-Minkowski in multiplicative form; applied to log-concave densities it proves that log-concavity is preserved by marginals and convolutions, and it yields Gaussian concentration arguments without isoperimetry.
title: Prekopa-Leindler Inequality

body:
Let L/K be a finite Galois extension and G=Gal(L/K). The assignments H->L^H={x in L:sigma(x)=x for every sigma in H} and E->Gal(L/E) are inverse inclusion-reversing bijections between subgroups H of G and intermediate fields K subseteq E subseteq L. They satisfy [L:L^H]=|H| and [L^H:K]=[G:H]; moreover, H is normal in G exactly when L^H/K is Galois, in which case Gal(L^H/K) is isomorphic to G/H.
L/K is a finite Galois extension
G=Gal(L/K)

body: A twin prime is a prime number that is either 2 less or 2 more than another prime number—for example, either member of the twin prime pair or (41, 43). In other words, a twin prime is a prime that has a prime gap of two. Sometimes the term twin prime is used for a pair of twin primes; an alternative name for this is prime twin or prime pair.
title: Twin prime

The connected Lorentz group $O^{+\uparrow}(1,2)$ consists of orientation- and orthochronous-preserving linear isometries of $\mathbb{R}^{1,2}_1$. Every non-identity element in $O^{+\uparrow}(1,2)$ is conjugate to exactly one of three rotational types: (1) elliptic (rotation fixing a timelike axis), (2) hyperbolic (boost fixing a spacelike plane pointwise), or (3) parabolic (null rotation fixing a lightlike line).
O^{+\uparrow}(1,2) is the identity component of the Lorentz group in 3 dimensions

[Lemma 22 (\textsf{Zero-set bound}) of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Let
$
 P\in\bigoplus_{j=0}^s\cC_j^{\mathsf{R}}
$
be nonzero with $s\in\N_0$, and let $r:=\deg(P)\leq s$.
Then, for every
$(i_1,\ldots,i_r)\in\Delta_r$ such that
$
 D_{i_r}\cdots D_{i_1}P\not\equiv 0,
$
one has

\noi
\begin{align}
 \PP(P\ne0)
 \geq
 \prod_{\ell=1}^r
 \min\{p_{i_\ell},q_{i_\ell}\}.
 
\end{align}
Consequently, if, for some
$\eps\in(0,\frac12]$,
\[
 \eps\leq p_k\leq1-\eps
\]
for every coordinate on which $P$ depends, then
\noi
\begin{align}
 \PP(P\ne0)
 \geq\eps^r
 \geq\eps^s.
 
\end{align}

[Lemma lem:m1-sup of arXiv:2605.10617, 'Logarithmic scaling of selective sweep curves:\\ from tents to houses'] For $I= [\alpha, \beta]$, $t\in I$ and $f\in \mathcal D_I$ let 
    $$
      \overline f(t)
        := \max_{\alpha \le t'\le t} f(t'), \qquad
      \widetilde f(t)
        := \max_{\beta +\alpha  -t \le r\le \beta} f(r)
    $$
    be the running maximum of $f$ and of its time-reversal, respectively.
    Then
    $${\rm a)} \quad d_{M_1}(f,\overline f)\le \sup_{t\in I} | \overline f(t)-f(t) |, \qquad  \quad {\rm b)}\quad  d_{M_1}(f,\widetilde f)\le \sup_{t\in I} | \widetilde f(t)-f(t) |. $$

Let (X_{n, k})_{1 \le k \le r_n} be a triangular array of row-wise independent random variables with \mathbb{E}[X_{n, k}] = 0, \sum_{k=1}^{r_n} \text{Var}(X_{n, k}) = 1, and the uniform asymptotic negligibility (UAN) condition \lim_{n \to \infty} \max_{1 \le k \le r_n} \text{Var}(X_{n, k}) = 0. If \sum_{k=1}^{r_n} X_{n, k} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, 1), then the array necessarily satisfies the Lindeberg condition: for every \epsilon > 0, \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^{r_n} \mathbb{E}[X_{n, k}^2 \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_{n, k}| > \epsilon\}}] = 0.

[Theorem 33 of arXiv:2609.03070, 'Variants of order semicontinuity in Banach lattices'] Assume that $F$ is $r$-demicontinuous. Then:
\item[(i)] $F^{L}$ is an $r$-monotonically complete Banach lattice.
\item[(ii)] The norm of $F$ has an $r^{2}$-demicontinuous extension to $F^{L}$, equivalent to $\|\cdot\|_{L}$.
\item[(iii)] The norm completion of $F$ is $r^{2}$-demicontinuous.
\item[(iv)] If $T:F\to E$ is a contractive order continuous homomorphism into a demicontinuous normed lattice, then there is a unique order continuous extension $T^{L}:F^{L}\to E^{L}$ of $T$. Moreover, $T^{L}$ is a contractive homomorphism.
\item[(v)] If $G$ is a normed lattice which isomorphically contains $F$ as an order dense sublattice, then there is a unique injective order continuous homomorphism $J:G\to F^{L}$ which leaves $F$ in place.
\item[(vi)] If $F$ is $r$-semicontinuous, then so is $F^{L}$. In particular, the Lorentz completion preserves topological semicontinuity.

[Theorem Thm:lower_deviation_dir of arXiv:2411.13030, 'Classification of the limit shape for 1+1-dimensional FPP'] For each $\varepsilon>0$ and $v_0\ge 0$, there exist constants $A,B$ such that for all $n\ge 1$ and $v\in [0,v_0]$:
\[
\Prob{T((0,0),(n,{\lceil v n \rceil}))\le n (\Lambda(v)-\varepsilon)}\le A \exp(-Bn). 
\]
The same holds for the SJ model when $G$ corresponds to a Bernoulli distribution. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 12 of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] Let $S=(S_1,\dots,S_n)$ and $S'=(S'_1,\dots,S'_n)$ be two 
    Bernoulli path ensembles with  endpoints $(p_1=(x_p,y_{p_1}),\dots,p_n=(x_p,y_{p_n})),(q_1=(x_q,y_{q_1}),\dots,q_n=(x_q,y_{q_n}))$ for $S$,  and $(p'_1=(x_p,y'_{p'_1}),\dots,p'_n=(x_p,y'_{p'_n})),(q'_1=(x_q,y'_{q'_1}),\dots,q'_n=(x_q,y'_{q'_n}))$ for $S'$. Assume that $y_{p_i}\ge y'_{p'_i}$ and $y_{q_i}\ge y'_{q'_i}$
    for every $i=1,\dots,n$. Then, we can couple $S,S'$ in such a way that, almost surely, the $S_i$ is weakly above $S'_i$ for every $i=1,\dots,n$.

	More generally, fix functions $V^\pm_i,W^\pm_i:(x_p,x_q)\mapsto \mathbb R$  such that $V_i^\pm \ge W_i^\pm$. Condition  $S$ to the event that $S_i$ is above $V^-_i$ and below $V^+_i$ for every $i=1,\dots, n$, and condition $S'$ to the event that $S'_i$ is above $W^{-}_i$ and below $W^+_i$ for every $i=1,\dots,n$ (we assume that $(V_i^\pm , W_i^\pm)_{i=1,\dots,n}$ are such that these events are nonempty). Then, we can couple $S,S'$ in such a way that, almost surely, the $S_i$ is weakly above $S'_i$ for every $i=1,\dots,n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 12 of arXiv:2605.26664

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Partition quadratic stochastic operators converge to the empty body (2026). An F-quadratic stochastic operator acts on the simplex over types {0, 1, ..., m}, where 0 is the empty body: parents of the same sex, or a pair containing 0, produce 0; Rozikov and Zhamilov proved that every such operator has the unique fixed point e_0 and that every trajectory converges to it exponentially fast. Problem 10 of Ganikhodzhaev, Mukhamedov and Rozikov, Quadratic stochastic operators and processes: results and open problems (arXiv:0902.4207), asks whether the same holds when the two sexes are replaced by the blocks E_1, ..., E_q of an arbitrary partition of {1, ..., m}, with same-block pairs producing the empty body. The answer is yes: with y = 1 - x_0, every such operator V satisfies y(V(x)) <= (1 - 1/q) y(x)^2, so e_0 is the unique fixed point and y(V^n(x)) <= c^{-1} (c y(x))^{2^n} with c = 1 - 1/q, and the inequality is an equality at every step along some trajectories for each q. Without the rule that pairs containing 0 produce 0 the statement fails: (x_0, x_1) -> (x_0^2 + x_1^2, 2 x_0 x_1) has a second, attracting fixed point (1/2, 1/2). Exact rational checks and a Lean 4 file accompany the paper. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/partition-qso-empty-body (commit f3a2991ab8c5). Not refereed.
title: Partition quadratic stochastic operators converge doubly exponentially to the empty body, answering Problem 10 of Ganikhodzhaev, Mukhamedov and Rozikov (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/partition-qso-empty-body)

[Theorem thm:conva of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Let $\Phi_D$ be a zero boundary GFF on a bounded simply-connected domain $D$ and $\tilde \phi_m$ be a sequence of zero boundary metric graph GFFs on $\widetilde D_m$ that are coupled with the GFF $\Phi_D$ such that a.s., 
$\tilde \phi_m \to \Phi$ in $H^{-\varepsilon}(\mathbb{C})$, for some $\varepsilon>0$.
Further, take 
$(\widetilde C_k^m,  \tilde\nu_k^m,\tilde s_k^m)
_{k \geq 1}$ 
the excursion decomposition of $\tilde \phi_m$, where 
$\widetilde C_k^m$ are the connected components of 
$\{\tilde \phi_m \neq 0\}$, 
$\tilde \nu_k^m$ are given by $|\tilde \phi_m|$ restricted to $\widetilde C_k^m$, and $\tilde s_k^m$ are the sign of 
$\phi_m$ on $\widetilde C_k^m$. 
Moreover, the clusters are ordered by decreasing size of diameter.

For every $k>0$,  we have the joint convergence in probability of $ \widetilde C_k^{(m)}\to C_k$, 
$\tilde\nu_k^{(m)}\to \nu_k$ and $\tilde s_k^{(m)}\to s_k$ as $m\to \infty$, in the Hausdorff topology\footnote{This is the topology on closed sets given by the Hausdorff distance.} for the first component, and in the weak topology of measures for the second component. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 18 (Fixed-time moment formula) of arXiv:2607.24561, 'Range convergence and sharp one-arm asymptotics\\for the critical percolation cluster in h'] For $k\ge1$, $t_1,\dots,t_k>0$ and $\phi_1,\dots,\phi_k\in\Cc$,
\begin{equation}
\bN\Bigl[\prod_{i=1}^k X_{t_i}(\phi_i)\Bigr]
=\gamma^{\,k-1}\sum_{T\in\T_k}
\int
\prod_{\{a,b\}\in E(T)} p_{\,s_b-s_a}\bigl(y_b-y_a\bigr)
\prod_{v\in V_{\mathrm{int}}(T)} ds_v\,dy_v\,
\prod_{i=1}^k\phi_i(z_i)\,dz_i ,
\end{equation}
where each vertex $a$ of $T$ carries a space-time point $(s_a,y_a)$; the
root is pinned at $(0,0)$, the leaf $i$ at $(t_i,z_i)$; the edges
$\{a,b\}$ are written with $a$ the endpoint closer to the root; internal
vertices are integrated over $(0,\infty)\times\R^d$; and $p_s\equiv0$ for
$s\le0$ (which enforces the genealogical time-ordering). Here $\gamma$ is the branching parameter of \eqref{eq:laplace} (Section~\ref{sec:SBM}) and $p_s(x)=(2\pi s)^{-d/2}e^{-|x|^2/2s}$ is the heat kernel of Section~\ref{sec:notation}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2506.16259, 'Two-dimensional Rademacher walk'] Let $C>0$ and $z\in\Z^2$ with $\norm{z}\le C$, and $b'$ and $b''$ are positive integers which are coprime. Then there exist three positive integers $c',c'', N_0$  such that $N_0$ depends on $c',c''$ and~$C$ only and
$$
\P(T_m=z\text{ for some }m\le N_0)\ge 1/2
$$
where
$$
T_m=\sum_{i=1}^m \tilde Z_i    \text{     with }
\tilde Z_i=b'(\xi_{i,1}'+\dots+\xi_{i,c'}')+b''(\xi_{i,1}''+\dots+\xi_{i,c''}'')
$$
and $\xi'_{i,k},\xi''_{i,k},$  are i.i.d.\ two-dimensional Rademacher random variables.

Let X and Y be Banach spaces, I ⊆ R an interval, and K : I × I → B(X,Y) a kernel that is continuous in the operator norm. Let 1 ≤ p < q ≤ ∞ and suppose the (untruncated) operator T f(t) = ∫_I K(t,s) f(s) ds satisfies ‖T f‖_{L^q(I;Y)} ≤ A ‖f‖_{L^p(I;X)} for all f ∈ L^p(I;X). Then the retarded (causal) truncation T̃ f(t) = ∫_{s ∈ I, s < t} K(t,s) f(s) ds satisfies ‖T̃ f‖_{L^q(I;Y)} ≤ C(p,q) A ‖f‖_{L^p(I;X)}, with C(p,q) depending only on p and q (it blows up as q ↓ p). The strict inequality p < q is necessary: the conclusion is false for p = q.

1 ≤ p < q ≤ ∞, strictly
the untruncated operator is bounded L^p(I;X) → L^q(I;Y)

[Theorem multilinear:intro of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Restatement of (homo multilinear recursion of the paper)]

Let ${\bf x} = \{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequence of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. Let $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n}$ be a multi-indexed sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define a permutation symmetric, homogeneous multilinear polynomial random matrix of degree $d$ as
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right).
$$
Let $a,b,c\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $d = a+b+c$. Then for $2 \leq t \leq \infty,$
$$
{\mathbb E} \ensuremath{\left\lVert {\bf F}({\bf x}) \right\rVert}_{4t}^{4t} ~\leq~ \sum_{\substack{a,b,c: \\ a+b+c=d}} (48dt)^{4dt} \cdot L^{4ct} \norm{{\bf F}_{a,b,c}}_{4t}^{4t}.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem multilinear:intro of arXiv:2412.07936

[Definition 8 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Let $D \subsetneq \C$ be a simply connected domain.  Fix $N \in \N_0$ and let $\ul{x} = (x_1,\ldots,x_{2N})$ be a collection of distinct prime ends which are ordered counterclockwise.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item We call $(D;\ul{x})$ a \emph{marked domain}. Let $\markeddomain{2N}$ be the collection of marked domains with $2N$ marked points.
\item Suppose that $(D;\ul{x}) \in \markeddomain{2N}$, and we have a non-crossing collection of paths $\ul{\gamma} = (\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_N)$ outside of $D$ where each $\gamma_i$ connects a distinct pair of marked points. The paths $\ul{\gamma}$ induce a planar link pattern $\beta$ on the exterior of $D$, formally described by a partition of the marked points into pairs $\beta = \{\{a_1,b_1\},\ldots,\{a_N,b_N\}\}$ where $\{a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_N,b_N\} = \{1,\ldots,2N\}$, $a_r<b_r$, and such that the configuration $a_r<a_s<b_r<b_s$ does not occur. We let $\eldomain{2N}$ be the collection of exterior link pattern decorated marked domains.
\item Suppose that $(D;\ul{x}) \in \markeddomain{2N}$, and we have a non-crossing collection of paths $\ul{\eta} = (\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_N)$ in $D$ where each $\eta_i$ connects a distinct pair of marked points. We will also consider the planar link pattern $\alpha$ on the interior of $D$ induced by the paths $\ul{\eta}$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition 8 of arXiv:2512.04807

[Lem 57 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\star$ as in \eqref{e:star.options} and $\mu \in \sM^\star(\alpha,q_0)$, we have
        \[\|\mu\|_{L^2}^2 \le
    \frac{10}{\alpha}
    +6 + O(\epsilon)\,.\]
\begin{proof}
Let $X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main}. Let us write
$X(1)= X(q_*)+\textup{(a)}+\textup{(b)}$ where (a) denotes the drift term and (b) denotes the martingale term.
We have $\bbE[X(q_*)^2] \le \epsilon$ under either of the initialization conditions \ref{it:6.1} or \ref{it:6.2}. Next, using the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    &= \E\bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1
    p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt\bigg)^2
    \bigg]
    \le \E\bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1 p'(t)\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg(\int_{q_*}^1 (b_t)^2 \,dt
        \bigg)\bigg]
    \le
    \int_{q_*}^1 \E[(b_t)^2] \,dt\\
    &\le \int_{q_*}^1 \Cost(t)\,dt
    \le \int_{q_*}^1 \budget(t;\alpha)\,dt + \epsilon
    \le \frac{1+\epsilon}{\alpha} + \epsilon\,,
    \end{align*}
where the last two inequalities hold under any of the budget conditions
\ref{it:4.1}, \ref{it:4.2}, or \ref{it:4.3}
combined with either condition
\ref{it:2.1} or \ref{it:2.2}. Lastly, we have from \eqref{e:loc.mg.L2.bounded} that 
    \[
    \E[\textup{(b)}^2]
    \le \int_{q_*}^1 s(t)^2
    \E[(\sigma_t)^2] \,dt
    \le 2\bigg\{ \frac{1+\epsilon}{\alpha}
        + \epsilon + 1\bigg\}\,.\]
Combining the above bounds gives altogether
    \[
    \E[X(1)^2]
    \le 3\bigg\{
    \E[X(q_*)^2]
    +\E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    +\E[\textup{(b)}^2]\bigg\}
    \le 3\bigg\{
    \frac{3(1+\epsilon)}{\alpha}
    +2 + 4\epsilon\bigg\}\,,
    \]
proving the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 57 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Proposition prop:remainder of arXiv:2608.27828, 'Scaling limit of the 3D abelian Yang--Mills Langevin dynamics'] Fix $T>0$ and $M,r\ge1$.
Suppose that, almost surely,
\begin{equ}
  \|\theta^\varepsilon(0)\|_{\mathcal C^\eta_\varepsilon}
  \le M,
 \qquad
  -\frac23+\frac53\kappa < \eta.
\end{equ}
There exist constants $C_{M,T}<\infty$ and
$\varepsilon_0=\varepsilon_0(M,T, r)>0$ such that for every
$\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, on the event $\Omega_{r,\varepsilon}(T)$ from (equation eq:GoodEvent of the paper) we have
\begin{equ}[e:no-exit]
  \widehat\tau_\varepsilon>T
\end{equ}
and
\begin{equ}[eq:v-apriori-final]
  \|\widehat v^\varepsilon\|_
  {\mathcal C^{4\kappa,T}_{0,\varepsilon}}
  \le
  C_{M,T}\varepsilon^{\kappa/2}r^5.
\end{equ}
Consequently,
$\widehat \theta^\varepsilon$ agrees with the original
Langevin process $\theta^\varepsilon$ on $[0,T]$ and $\tau_\varepsilon>T$ on $\Omega_{r,\varepsilon}(T)$.

body: Let (X_n)_{n=0}^N be a submartingale with respect to a filtration (F_n), and for real numbers a < b let U_N[a,b] denote the number of upcrossings of the interval [a,b] by X_0, ..., X_N, that is, the number of disjoint time intervals during which the process passes from at or below a to at or above b. Then E[U_N[a,b]] <= E[(X_N - a)^+] / (b - a), where x^+ = max(x, 0). This bound is the key step in the proof of the martingale convergence theorem. [Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples]

Method: Explicit calculation or obstruction with source-specific scope Result: The no-switch-over comparison has an exact simplification: if all jobs require deterministic time2 and arrivals are the superposition of independent Poisson streams, total workload is the workload of a work-conserving M/D/1 queue, independently of the polling order. Introducing deterministic switch-over times destroys work conservation even when the sum of a service time and a switch time remains2. Empty visits then consume capacity, and their boundary frequencies enter the two-dimensional reflected limit. Check: Total unfinished service decreases at unit rate whenever any work is present in the first system. In the second it is constant during each switch, including switches caused by an empty queue. Thus equal nominal time per saturated visit does not imply equal sample-path workload. Obstruction: The missing boundary occupation and reflection structure prevent identifying the limiting joint law from a scalar workload formula. The source suggests a two-dimensional transform boundary-value problem. No solution of that problem or valid interchange of its heavy-traffic limit is supplied.

[Prop contractionprinciple of arXiv:2604.23751, 'Large deviation principles for pattern-avoiding permutations, and limit shapes for constra'] Assume that $(X_n)$ satisfies an LDP at speed $a_n$ with good\footnote{A rate function is said to be \textit{good} if its level sets $\{x \in E: \, I(x) \le M\}$ are compact.} rate function $I$ on some space $E$.   
 Let $F:E \rightarrow G$ be a bounded continuous function. 
 Then, the sequence of random variables $Y_n=F(X_n)$ satisfies an LDP at speed $a_n$ with good rate function $J$ given, for any $y\in G,$ by
 \[ J(y) =  \inf\{ I(x) : F(x)=y\}.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Lemma lem:lift of arXiv:2609.02953, 'Alon's Question on Connectivity Graph-Codes: $f(d)=2^d$ for Every $d\geq 4$'] Let $B$ be a finite graph with an edge labelling in $\mathbb{F}_{2}^{d}$ such that every selected graph $B_{a}$, $a\ne 0$, is connected, spanning and contains a cycle. Then there are infinitely many finite covers $\widetilde{B}$ of $B$ in which every lifted selected graph $\widetilde{B}_{a}$ is connected and spanning. If $B$ is finite, simple, bipartite and $d$-regular, the covers may be chosen with all of these properties.

body: Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent real random variables with densities bounded by K, A a real symmetric n x n matrix, b in R^n, c in R, and Q = X^T A X + b^T X + c. If A has five eigenvalues of modulus at least s > 0 (s_5(A) >= s), Q has a density bounded by 270 K^2/s, whatever n, the other eigenvalues, the signature of A, b and c; with three such eigenvalues, sup_a E|Q - a|^{-1/2} <= 77 K/sqrt(s), and one is not enough (X_1 uniform on [0,1] and Q = X_1^2 give E X_1^{-1} = infinity). The nine-eigenvalue bound 400 K^2/s and the 17- and 33-eigenvalue versions are special cases. The proof turns 2m - 1 large eigenvalues into m large singular values of one off-diagonal block by random sign decoupling on the eigenvectors and applies a Fourier decay bound for that block. The conjecture itself, with three eigenvalues of modulus at least 1 and a universal constant, and the case of four are open; the sign-decoupling route cannot go below five.

[Theorem teo:2 of arXiv:2601.00291, 'The probability of connection between two vertices cannot be monotone with the distance fo'] For every $d \geqslant 2$, there exists a critical value $\lambda_c(\mathbb{Z}^d) \in (0,\infty)$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[a)] If $\lambda > \lambda_c$, then $\mathbb{P}_{\lambda}\left(o\longleftrightarrow \vec{e}\, \right) > \mathbb{P}_{\lambda}\left(o\longleftrightarrow t\vec{e}\, \right)$ for all $t\in (0,1)$.

\end{enumerate}
Where $\vec e = (1,0,\ldots,0)\in\mathbb{Z}^d$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let p(x) = x^n + c_{n-1} x^{n-1} + ... + c_1 x + c_0 be a monic polynomial with complex coefficients. The companion matrix of p is the n by n matrix C(p) with 1 in every position (i+1, i) for i = 1, ..., n-1 (the subdiagonal), with -c_{i-1} in position (i, n) for i = 1, ..., n (the last column), and 0 elsewhere. The characteristic polynomial of C(p) equals p(x), so the eigenvalues of C(p), with multiplicity, are exactly the roots of p. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis]
title: Companion Matrix of a Monic Polynomial

[Theorem gaussian recursion of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] Let ${\bf x} \sim \gauss{0}{\mathbb{I}_n}$ and $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in [n]^d}$ be multi-indexed sequences of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define a degree-$d$ homogeneous Gaussian polynomial random matrix as
$$
{\bf P}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in [n]^d} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right).
$$
Let $a,b \in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$. Then for $2 \leq t \leq \infty,$
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf P}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf P}({\bf x})}_{2t}^{2t} ~\leq~ (2^d \sqrt{2}t)^{2t} \left( \sum_{1 \leq a+b \leq d}\norm{{\mathbb E} {\bf P}_{a,b}}_{2t}^{2t} \right).
$$

Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty: KNOWN elementary rare-density/product
expansion method; UNCHECKED separate prior appearance of the exact range
coefficient below. This is an actual particle-hole process statement at
fixed finite time, not a fixed-density long-time theorem.

For the source's sparse critical synchronous particle-hole process on Z^d,
d>=1, with signs +1 and -1 each having probability p, write h_t(p) for
one-hole survival probability and j_t(p,z) for joint survival at 0,z!=0.
Let R_t={X_0,...,X_t} be the range of one free nearest-neighbor SRW and
M_t=E_0|R_t|. For any integer t>=0 and z!=0 with p M_t<=1/4, uniformly in t,z,

    h_t(p)=p[1-p(M_t-1)+O(p^2 M_t^2)],
    j_t(p,z)/h_t(p)^2
      =1+p I_t(z)+O(p^2 M_t^2),
    I_t(z)=sum_y P_y(the path through t visits both 0 and z)
          =E_0 |R_t intersect (R_t-z)|.

In addition, for d>=3 only, with full-space escape-probability capacity
and g=G(0),

    I_t(z)/(t+1) --> 2/g-cap({0,z})
                  =2G(z)/[g(g+G(z))].

This limit concerns the first-order coefficient; the uniform remainder
is useful only in the dilute regime p M_t<=1/4.

The errors have absolute constants: at most (5/2)p^2 M_t^2 for the
singleton bracket and at most 100p^2 M_t^2 for the displayed pair ratio. In particular for |z|_1=2 and t=2,

    I_2(z)=2p_2(z)>0.

Thus these same-parity holes are positively correlated at time two for
all sufficiently small p. C14 proves they are negatively correlated at
time one for every p>0. Neither a blanket association statement nor a
time-propagated same-parity negative-correlation claim follows from the
one-round signs. This includes d=4.

## 1. Conditional survival and a finite product derivative

For a fixed finite target set K let phi_K(p) be the probability that no
particle enters K by time t, conditional on all its sites initially being
holes. The exact survival probability is p^|K| phi_K(p). Only initial
values and instructions in a finite backward time-t cone can affect this
event, by source finite propagation. After averaging the finitely many
relevant instructions, phi_K is a polynomial in p: each initial sign has
probabilities p,1-2p,p. In particular it has a Taylor remainder O(p^2)
at zero with a finite constant depending on K,t.

At p=0 all sites off K are empty and there are no particles, so phi_K(0)=1.
Differentiate the finite product law one coordinate y outside K at a
time. The derivative replaces that coordinate's empty state with +1 and
-1, each with coefficient one, and subtracts twice its empty state.
If its replacement is a hole, the configuration still has no particles
and the event has probability one. If it is a particle, it follows a free
SRW until its first visit to K, where it settles. There are no other
holes or particles. The no-arrival probability is therefore
1-P_y(T_K<=t). The coordinate contributes -P_y(T_K<=t). Summing gives

    phi_K(p)=1-p S_K(t)+O_{K,t}(p^2),
    S_K(t)=sum_{y outside K}P_y(T_K<=t).

The sum is finite because a walk takes at most t steps. The presence of
arbitrarily many random instructions creates no analytic issue: the event
averaged over them is a bounded function of a finite set of initial signs.

## 2. Singleton and pair coefficients

Translation of one free path and Tonelli give

    sum_y P_y(T_0<=t)=E_0|R_t|=M_t.

The y=0 term is one, hence S_{0}=M_t-1. For K={0,z}, inclusion-exclusion
for a single free path gives

    sum_y P_y(T_K<=t)=2M_t-I_t(z).

The y=0 and y=z terms of this union event are both one; therefore

    S_{0,z}=2M_t-I_t(z)-2=2S_0-I_t(z).

Substitution into p phi_{0} and p^2 phi_{0,z}, followed by expansion of
the strictly positive denominator phi_0(p)^2 near p=0, proves the displayed
ratio. For the range identity, fix one free path from 0 and translate it
by its starting point y. It visits both 0 and z exactly when -y is in
R_t and z-y is in R_t. The number of such y equals
|R_t intersect (R_t-z)|. Averaging proves the identity.

## 3. Time two and the correlation flip

If |z|_1=2, a two-step path visiting both targets must start at one target
at time zero and reach the other at time two. There is no time to visit
both from a different starting point, since their distance is two.
Therefore I_2(z)=P_0(X_2=z)+P_z(X_2=0)=2p_2(z).
For z=2e_i this equals 1/(2d^2); for z=e_i+e_j, i!=j, it equals 1/d^2.
The same constants hold after sign changes of coordinates. The coefficient
is positive, so the ratio exceeds one for all sufficiently small positive p.
At time one C14's exact ratio is [(1-2q)/(1-q)^2]^m<1, q=p/(2d).

## 4. Exact last-visit identity and capacity rate

For any finite K define M_K(t)=sum_y P_y(T_K<=t). On a path that visits
K through time t there is a unique last visit, at a site s in K and time
n between zero and t. The Markov property gives

    P_y(T_K<=t)=sum_{n=0}^t sum_{s in K}
                  P_y(X_n=s) P_s(T_K^+>t-n).

Sum over y. Each transition-kernel column sums to one by translation
invariance. Hence, after changing m=t-n,

    M_K(t)=sum_{m=0}^t sum_{s in K}P_s(T_K^+>m).

The summands decrease to sum_s P_s(T_K^+=infinity)=cap(K), so Cesaro
averaging gives M_K(t)/(t+1)->cap(K). This identity is valid in all
dimensions; in recurrent dimensions the limiting capacity is zero.

For d>=3, M_{0}(t)=M_t and cap({0})=1/g. Inclusion-exclusion from
Step 2 gives I_t(z)=2M_0(t)-M_{0,z}(t). The claimed rate now follows.
The two-point capacity identity 2/(g+G(z)) is Sznitman's Proposition 1.5,
equations (1.58)-(1.59), with the same full-space normalization.

## 5. Uniform dilute-regime remainder from free paths

Condition on initial holes at a finite K of size k. Give every possible
initial particle an independent full free walk, retaining its unused
suffix after actual settlement. A particle follows this prefix until
settlement; tie-breaking only chooses which arriving particle settles.
The no-arrival event for all free walks implies no actual arrival to K.
For y outside K put a_y=P_y(T_K<=t), S=sum_y a_y=S_K(t). Independence
of initial particle indicators and their free walks gives the free void
probability Q=product_y(1-p a_y). Bonferroni gives

    1-pS <= Q <= 1-pS+(pS)^2/2.

If there is a free arrival to K but no actual arrival, some free K-hitting
particle must have settled earlier at an initial hole outside K. A union
bound over those initial holes and particles, using p^2 for the opposite
signs at distinct outside sites, bounds this discrepancy probability by

    p^2 sum_{y outside K} E_y[1{T_K<=t}|R_t|]
       <=p^2 k E_0|R_t|^2.

The last inequality follows by fixing one translated free path: the
number of its translations hitting K is at most k times its range size.
Initial signs at the particle's own site or fixed target sites cannot
produce an outside hole and may harmlessly be included in the upper bound.

For completeness, E|R_t|^2<=2M_t^2. Sum over ordered pairs x,z of sites
visited. Every joint visit has either T_x<=T_z or T_z<=T_x. Strong Markov
at the first entrance to the earlier site bounds the respective sums by
sum_x P_0(T_x<=t) sum_z P_x(T_z<=t)=M_t^2. Including equal visit times
twice only enlarges the bound. Hence

    0<=phi_K(p)-(1-pS_K(t))
              <=(k^2/2+2k)p^2 M_t^2.

This establishes the singleton bracket error 5p^2 M_t^2/2 and pair
bracket error 6p^2 M_t^2, uniformly in time and separation.

Write a=M_t-1, I=I_t(z), b=2a-I, phi_0=1-pa+e_1,
phi_{0,z}=1-pb+e_2. Here 0<=e_1<=2.5p^2 M_t^2,
0<=e_2<=6p^2 M_t^2, 0<=a<=M_t, and 0<=I<=2M_t.
If pM_t<=1/4 then phi_0>=3/4. Expanding its square gives

    phi_0^2=1-2pa+r,   |r|<=6.4p^2 M_t^2.

Indeed the remainder is p^2a^2+2(1-pa)e_1+e_1^2, bounded by
(1+5+6.25/16)p^2M_t^2<6.4p^2M_t^2. Consequently

    |phi_{0,z}-phi_0^2(1+pI)|
        =|e_2-r+2p^2aI-pIr|<=20p^2 M_t^2.

Division by phi_0^2>=9/16 gives a ratio error below
36p^2M_t^2; the stated constant 100 is conservative.

## Quantifier limitation and sources

The uniform estimate requires p M_t<=1/4 and its error is quadratic in
p M_t. For fixed p>0, M_t tends to infinity, so the dilute regime ends.
The range-intersection coefficient therefore cannot be inserted into a
fixed-p long-time survival formula using this argument. This differs from C6's triangular-law
nonuniformity result and does not settle I0005.

Primary model and finite propagation: Bou-Rabee--Panagiotis,
arXiv:2609.02820v1, Sections 2 and 8.2. The finite-set conditional
survival identity is also proved in I0005-C13. All expansion and
inclusion-exclusion steps are given above explicitly.
The capacity normalization is additionally verified in Sznitman,
arXiv:0704.2560v3, (1.5)-(1.7) and Proposition 1.5. The last-visit
identity and Cesaro argument are proved here directly.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:a1e8e0a4e9d3ea844deb3d838cd3e61ce199607ccdf1c6da584de03b25d96ae0","revision_digest":"sha256:1e11da4481898b83bd6939f334cb4fbf73268f079529b5d5ea351a666f4a7eee","source_id":"owner-own-work:w661:I0005-C15:v3","source_revision":"v3; 2026-10-14T06:38:57.0934370+03:00","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma lem:1-a_SV of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\ell\in\mbox{SV}_\infty$ be $C^1$ with derivative $t\mapsto\wt\ell(t)/t$, where $|\wt\ell|\in\mbox{SV}_\infty$. Then, for each $x>0$, we have $(\ell(t)-\ell(xt))/\wt\ell(t)\to-\log x$ as $t\to\infty$. Defining $L_x(t) \coloneqq 1-\ell(x t)/\ell(t)$ for $t,x>0$, the function $|L_x|$  is  asymptotically equivalent to the quotient $|\wt\ell(t)\log x|/\ell(t)\sim |L_x(t)|$ as $t\to\infty$ and, if $x\neq 1$, slowly varying at infinity. Moreover,  for $x>0$, the function $\Sigma(x)\coloneqq \sup_{t>0, y\in [x\wedge 1,x\vee1]}\wt\ell(yt)/\wt\ell(t)$  satisfies
\[
\big|L_x(t)\big|
=\bigg|\frac{\ell(xt)}{\ell(t)}-1\bigg|
\leqslant \frac{|\wt\ell(t)|}{\ell(t)}
    \cdot\Sigma(x)|\log x|
\qquad \text{ for all }t,x>0.
\]
title: Lemma lem:1-a_SV of arXiv:2411.03609

body:
Let Ω ⊂ R^n be open and F: Ω × R × R^n → R continuous. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 in Ω if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local maximum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity supersolution if for every φ ∈ C^1(Ω) and every x0 ∈ Ω at which u - φ has a local minimum, F(x0, u(x0), Dφ(x0)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. For the evolution equation u_t + H(x,Du) = 0 in R^n × (0,T) apply the definition in the variables (x,t), with test functions φ(x,t) of class C^1 and F((x,t), r, (p,s)) = s + H(x,p); so at a local maximum of u - φ one requires φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≤ 0, and at a local minimum φ_t + H(x0, Dφ) ≥ 0. Equivalent variants giving the same class: C^1 test functions may be replaced by C^2 or C^∞ ones, local extrema by strict local extrema, and one may normalize φ(x0) = u(x0). The definition is NOT invariant under F ↦ -F: in general the viscosity solutions of F = 0 and of -F = 0 differ. The correct symmetry is: u is a viscosity subsolution of F(x,u,Du) = 0 iff -u is a viscosity supersolution of G(x,r,p) = 0, where G(x,r,p) := -F(x,-r,-p).
Ω ⊂ R^n open
F continuous on Ω × R × R^n
u continuous on Ω

On the uniform cube {-1, 1}^n let f be real, f^(S) = E[f chi_S] its Walsh coefficients and W_k = sum over |S| = k of f^(S)^2. For rho in [-1, 1], T_rho is the noise operator: T_rho f(x) = E[f(Y)] where the Y_i are independent with P(Y_i = x_i) = (1 + rho)/2, so T_rho chi_S = rho^|S| chi_S. Let E_k be the span of the chi_S with |S| = k. For 0 < |rho| < 1, a linear operator A on functions on {-1, 1}^n commutes with T_rho iff A(E_k) is inside E_k for every k. For a permutation pi and signs eps, the map (U f)(x) = f(g x) with (g x)_i = eps_i x_{pi(i)} commutes with T_rho for every rho in [-1, 1]; for a finite group G of such maps, P_G = |G|^(-1) sum over g of U_g is the orthogonal projection onto the G-invariant functions and commutes with T_rho. The condition 0 < |rho| < 1 is needed: at rho = 0 the map sending chi_{1} to chi_{12} and killing the other characters commutes with T_0; at rho = 1, T_1 = I commutes with everything; at rho = -1 the map sending chi_empty to chi_{12} commutes with T_{-1}.

Two equal-length strands may leave different complementary regions and therefore different loop partition functions. Check: Summing the joint weight x^(|gamma|+total loop length)*n^(number of loops) over compatible loop families factors out x^|gamma| and leaves exactly the stated complementary partition function. Obstruction: The environmental partition-function factor is the missing ingredient in a reduction to self-avoiding walk. Its conformal asymptotics have not been derived here.

Let $S$ be symmetric positive semidefinite and $w^*$ a solution of $\min_w w^T S w$ subject to $\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$, $w \ge 0$. Let $A = \{i : w^*_i > 0\}$ be its active set and $S_{AA}$ the principal submatrix on $A$. Then $w^*_A$ solves the equality-constrained problem on $A$ alone: if $S_{AA}$ is nonsingular, $w^*_A = S_{AA}^{-1}\mathbf{1}_A / (\mathbf{1}_A^T S_{AA}^{-1}\mathbf{1}_A)$, and $w^*_i = 0$ for $i \notin A$. The inactive rows and columns of $S$ enter only through the inequalities $(S w^*)_i \ge \lambda^*$ for $i \notin A$ that certify optimality, where $\lambda^* = w^{*T} S w^*$ is the optimal value. Consequently two covariance estimates that agree on $S_{AA}$ and both satisfy the inactive inequalities produce the same long-only weights, whatever they do to the eigen-directions supported on the inactive members.
S symmetric positive semidefinite
S_AA nonsingular for the closed form (otherwise w*_A is any solution of S_AA w = c 1_A on the simplex)

PRIVATE AUTHOR-CHECKED DRAFT (revision 2), no independent review. Let Gamma be a finite group and Q a Gamma-equivariant positive contraction on l^2(Gamma) with 0 < Q < I, and P_Q the determinantal measure with kernel Q. Let HM(Q) be the harmonic mean of the eigenvalues of Q. Then P_Q stochastically dominates the product Bernoulli measure of density HM(Q), and P_Q is dominated by the product measure of density 1 - HM(I - Q). Precise chain: the minimal conditional ODDS of presence is s_min = 1/(J^{-1})_ee = HM/(1 - HM) with J = Q(I-Q)^{-1}, and the minimal conditional PROBABILITY is s_min/(1 + s_min) = 1/(Q^{-1})_ee = HM(Q) (revision 2 states the odds and the probability separately, after a reviewer noted the two had been conflated in a side note). This is weaker than Lyons's Conjecture 5.7 (geometric mean / Fuglede-Kadison determinant), which numerical monotone-coupling linear programs on Z/nZ, n <= 6, satisfy exactly, with FK + 0.01 failing on a tested instance; those LP results are floating-point evidence, not certificates.

    =delta_{ij}/n.

Hence each row consists of independent N(0,1/n) variables. With its natural filtration and trivial initial sigma-field it is a martingale-difference row. Its predictable total variance is exactly one. For a standard normal G, its conditional Lindeberg sum is

    E[G^2 1{|G|>epsilon sqrt(n)}] -> 0.

Yet the row sum is exactly Z for every n. It already has the required N(0,1) marginal distribution, while it cannot converge to a normal independent of the whole underlying sigma-field in the stable sense. For the bounded underlying variable H=1{Z>0} and bounded continuous f(x)=tanh(x),

    E[H f(sum_k D_{n,k})] = E[1{Z>0} tanh(Z)] >0,

whereas independence of a new standard normal G would give E[H]E[tanh(G)]=0. Thus convergence of distributions does not establish asymptotic independence from all existing randomness. The sequence does converge stably to Z itself; it is the independent-limit strengthening that fails. A statement of stable or mixing convergence must name its reference sigma-field and sufficient cross-row/filtration assumptions.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:3d98775b15e063ab5412171ff78b20512070def0754220a3225c1c8341903839","revision_digest":"sha256:1e57aebcac7ed74d5fa6d8f0f5e3e1d81931f2e3117b1a374eee9ce41b4a7aa2","source_id":"owner-original:martingale-proof-repair-weak-not-mixing-20260909","source_revision":"3e58922009ba6e8ebf59675d733230e5df71f2a1d414abf3276d7d9b587523cb","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the scale walk S_k as an exact random walk with identically distributed increments, as if the field were an exact branching random walk, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the comparison of S_k with a random walk (scale-dependent variances, the bounded error terms (iii)) must be explicitly controlled, while the Gibbs-Markov pieces themselves are exactly independent; skipping this control is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.
Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions
Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics
Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk

A family $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ in $L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ (or a sequence $K_N$ with $N\to\infty$; the same definition works on $\mathbb T$) is an approximate identity if (i) $\int K_\varepsilon=1$ for every $\varepsilon$; (ii) $\sup_\varepsilon\|K_\varepsilon\|_1<\infty$; (iii) for every $\delta>0$, $\int_{|x|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\,dx\to0$ as $\varepsilon\to0$. If $K\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ with $\int K=1$, the dilates $K_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\varepsilon)$ form an approximate identity. Standard examples: the Gauss-Weierstrass (heat) kernel $\varepsilon^{-d}e^{-\pi|x|^2/\varepsilon^2}$, the Poisson kernel of the half-space, the Fejer kernel $F_N$ and the Poisson kernel $P_r(x)=\sum_n r^{|n|}e^{2\pi i n x}$ ($r\uparrow1$) on $\mathbb T$. Non-example: the Dirichlet kernel $D_N$ satisfies (i) but not (ii), since $\|D_N\|_1\to\infty$; this is the root of the divergence phenomena for Fourier series. Some texts add the stronger condition $\sup_{|x|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(x)|\to0$, which is the convenient hypothesis for convergence at a point of continuity of a merely integrable $f$ (the tail is then controlled by $\|f\|_1$). Almost-everywhere convergence at Lebesgue points needs more than either condition: the usual hypothesis is the dilation structure $K_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-d}K(x/\varepsilon)$ together with an integrable radially nonincreasing majorant of $|K|$.
each K_eps is Lebesgue integrable
