{"artifact_digest":"sha256:80d97294b8e92df1cf0787bcb370b1de67dd6b177e2773265a99c045c266fd6b","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/80/80d97294b8e92df1cf0787bcb370b1de67dd6b177e2773265a99c045c266fd6b.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:2f3275b96176775d8eb5dc40419f498be81655f87995faf6f4fc0f29ccdd72c9","bundle_entry_key":"haar-orbit-mi-mmse-comparison-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-finite-moment-and-orbit-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:haar-orbit-mi-mmse-comparison-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Orbit mixing and a dimension-uniform Gaussian comparison

Target 2. Proof draft of an abstract comparison lemma, unaudited.
The application to iid products requires a primary-source check of
their common limiting singular-value law and of the Gaussian reference
mutual-information limit. These are separate inputs, not assumed proved
by the finite-size Taylor expansion.

Let A_n and B_n be random N_n by P_n real matrices with finite second
moments, d_n=N_n P_n. Suppose B_n is invariant in law under independent
left and right orthogonal transformations. Let their singular-value
vectors, in the same decreasing order and padded to min(N_n,P_n), be
coupled so that

 e_n^2 = E sum_j (sigma_j(A_n)-sigma_j(B_n))^2/d_n -> 0.    (1)

Assume i_{B,n}(s)=I(B_n;sqrt(s)B_n+G_n)/d_n converges to a finite
function i_B(s) for all s>0. Gaussian noise has independent standard
entries and is independent of each signal. Write m_{A,n}(s) for the
normalized product-signal MMSE, and likewise for B.

Then the claimed conclusions are

 limsup_n i_{A,n}(s) <= i_B(s),                          (2)
 limsup_n m_{A,n}(s) <= 2 i'_{B,-}(s),   s>0.            (3)

At every differentiability point of i_B,

 m_{B,n}(s) -> 2 i'_B(s),
 limsup_n m_{A,n}(s) <= lim_n m_{B,n}(s).                (4)

The finite concave function i_B has at most countably many
nondifferentiability points on (0,infinity). Thus the MMSE comparison
holds outside at most a countable exceptional set. If i_B is
differentiable throughout (0,infinity), it holds everywhere there.

## 1. Gaussian-smoothed entropy is Lipschitz in input Wasserstein distance

For any coupled R^d-valued U,V with finite second moments and an
independent standard Gaussian G,

 |I(U;sqrt(s)U+G)-I(V;sqrt(s)V+G)|
    <= sqrt(sd) (E||U-V||^2)^(1/2).                     (5)

For bounded U,V, interpolate U_t=(1-t)U+tV and let p_t be the density
of sqrt(s)U_t+G. Differentiating the Gaussian kernel gives

 partial_t p_t(y)=-sqrt(s) div E[(V-U)phi(y-sqrt(s)U_t)].

The continuity equation and integration by parts yield

 |partial_t h(p_t)|
 <= sqrt(s) [E||U-V||^2]^(1/2) J(p_t)^(1/2).

Indeed the conditional velocity E[V-U|sqrt(s)U_t+G=y] has square
integral at most E||V-U||^2, by conditional Jensen. The score identity

 grad log p_t(sqrt(s)U_t+G)=-E[G|sqrt(s)U_t+G]

gives J(p_t)<=E||G||^2=d. Integrating in t proves (5); the Gaussian
conditional entropy h(G) is the same for both channels.

For finite-second-moment inputs truncate the coupled pair in L^2.
Their convolved densities converge pointwise, have a common Gaussian
lower bound on every tail derived from a fixed input ball, and are
bounded above by (2pi)^(-d/2). Convergence in L^2 of the inputs gives
uniform integrability of the squared output norms, hence convergence
of output entropies by the compact-plus-tail argument used in
finite_moment_expansion.md, Section C. Thus (5) passes to the limit.
All constants in (5) are explicit and the dimension dependence is
exactly sqrt(d).

## 2. Haar mixing increases both quantities exactly at finite dimension

Let tilde A=Q A R^T with independent Haar orthogonal Q,R, independent
of A. The input law of tilde A is a mixture of orthogonal images of
the input law of A. Output entropy is concave in the input law;
Gaussian noise and Frobenius loss are invariant under these images.
Therefore

    I(A;sqrt(s)A+G) <= I(tilde A;sqrt(s)tilde A+G).        (6)

The Bayes MMSE is the infimum, over estimators f, of a risk linear in
the input law. Hence it too is concave in the input law and

    mmse(A;sqrt(s)A+G) <= mmse(tilde A;sqrt(s)tilde A+G).  (7)

This uses no assertion that singular vectors of A are already Haar.

Under the singular-value coupling (1), draw the same independent Haar
left and right matrices for the rectangular diagonal singular-value
representatives of A_n and B_n. The first resulting matrix has the
law of tilde A_n; the second has the law of B_n by its assumed
bi-orthogonal invariance. Their squared Frobenius distance is exactly
the sum in (1). Equation (5), divided by d_n, gives

    |i_{tilde A,n}(s)-i_{B,n}(s)| <= sqrt(s) e_n.         (8)

Equations (6) and (8) prove (2). They also show that i_{tilde A,n}
converges pointwise to i_B, rather than merely lying below it.

## 3. Concavity transfers the MMSE comparison

For a Gaussian channel, I-MMSE gives i'_{tilde A,n}(s)=m_{tilde A,n}(s)/2;
this derivative is nonincreasing, so each i_{tilde A,n} is concave.
Its finite pointwise limit i_B is concave as well. For 0<h<s,

    m_{A,n}(s)/2 <= i'_{tilde A,n}(s)
       <= [i_{tilde A,n}(s)-i_{tilde A,n}(s-h)]/h.

Take limsup in n and then let h decrease to zero. The left difference
quotient tends to i'_{B,-}(s), proving (3). For the reference B_n,
the usual two secant bounds for a concave function give convergence of
its derivatives wherever i_B is differentiable. This proves (4).
No differentiation of a one-sided MI inequality is used.

## 4. Precise iid-product application still to be discharged

For centered iid unit-variance factors A_n=UV^T/sqrt(N), the normalized
matrix A_n/sqrt(N)=UV^T/N has a deterministic limiting empirical
singular-value law depending only on the two aspect ratios, under
the usual iid product-matrix spectral hypotheses. The Gaussian-factor
product B_n has the same law in the limit and is bi-orthogonally
invariant. To invoke the lemma it remains to attach a primary theorem
with exactly these iid rectangular dimensions and moment assumptions.

If the normalized empirical laws converge in W2 in probability and
their squared W2 distances are uniformly integrable, independent
singular-value samples can be coupled through their ordered quantiles
and the deterministic common limit. Writing r=min(N,P),

 E||tilde A_n-B_n||_F^2/(NP)
    = (r/P) E W2(mu_{A_n/sqrt(N)},mu_{B_n/sqrt(N)})^2 ->0.

This is condition (1). Finite factor fourth moments give a convenient
uniform-integrability estimate, since

 E[(||A_n||_F^2/(NP))^2] <= E[A_{11}^4]
   =3(M/N)^2+(M/N^2)(E U^4 E V^4-3),

which is bounded under fixed aspect ratios. Convergence of the
empirical second singular moment also needs to be justified, rather
than inferred from weak spectral convergence alone. Its variance is
computed from shared-row/shared-column covariances and is O(N^-2)
under fixed aspect ratios and finite factor fourth moments.

The other external input is the finite Gaussian-factor limiting MI,
treated in rotationally invariant rectangular denoising papers. The
all-SNR MMSE assertion further requires differentiability of that
limit; without it (2)-(4) are the exact conclusions.

Hardest unpaid step for a full application: verify the singular-law
theorem's hypotheses and the Gaussian reference regularity directly
from primary sources. The abstract lemma itself does not establish
these inputs. Finite-size reversal at SNR tending to zero with n is
compatible with all of (2)-(4).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:8f63ff0321a76b62e9dac113608ece73cd7dca48d071ce1c705e60d4b4dbfd27","revision_digest":"sha256:1e9902bf6f9a60114b953a59d6a753588520e4041acbe46cff07d15df14fb81b","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:haar-orbit-mi-mmse-comparison-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Theorem 18 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(n\ge2\).  For each \(j\), let
\[
 (M_j^{2n},g_j(s),J_j,\nu^j_s,x_j),\qquad -A_j\le s\le0,
\]
be a pointed compact K\"ahler--Ricci flow with its point conjugate heat
kernel based at \((x_j,0)\), in the standard real convention
  \(\partial_sg_j=-2\Rc(g_j)\), where $A_j\ge1$.  Assume:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item \(A_j\to\infty\), the pairs are uniformly \(H_{2n}\)-concentrated,
  and
  \[
            \inf_j\mathcal N^{g_j}_{x_j,0}(1)>-\infty;
  \]
\item the pointed metric-flow pairs converge in \(\mathbb F\) on every
  compact negative time interval to
  \((\mathcal Z,g_{\mathcal Z}(s),\nu^Z_s,z)\);
\item the limit is a connected noncollapsed metric soliton and convergence is smooth
  on its full regular spacetime;
\item on the regular convergence charts, \(J_j\) converges smoothly to a
  parallel K\"ahler complex structure \(J_Z\), while the distinguished
  point-kernel densities converge smoothly to the distinguished soliton
  density.
\end{enumerate}
Put \(Z:=(\mathcal Z_{-1},d_Z)\), let
\(\mathcal R:=\mathcal R_{-1}\), and denote the limiting regular
K\"ahler structure by \((g_Z,J_Z,\omega_Z)\).  Then the following two
conclusions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item The space \(Z\) carries a compatible normal complex-analytic
structure with klt singularities.  Its analytic and metric topologies
agree, and its analytic regular locus is precisely \(\mathcal R\).
\item The form \(\omega_Z\) extends locally across \(\Sing Z\) as a
positive current with bounded potential.  Every \(p\in Z\) has a
neighbourhood \(U\), a closed holomorphic embedding
\(\iota_U:U\hookrightarrow\Omega_U\subset\C^L\), and \(c_U>0\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \omega_Z\ge c_U\,\iota_U^*\omega_{\C^L}
 \qquad\text{on }U\cap\mathcal R.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

In a simple theory, let $a \mathop{\mathpalette\setbox0=\hbox{$x$}\kern\wd0\hbox to 0pt{\mathchardef \nn=12854\hss$\nn$\kern1.4\wd0\hss}\hbox to 0pt{\hss$\mid$\hss}\lower.9\ht0 \hbox to 0pt{\hss$\smile$\hss}\kern\wd0{}}_{C} b$. The obstacle to identifying it with ordinary unimodular rerooting is the reproductive f0 bias: unimodularity is a mass-transport identity for the root law, while the spine favors descendants through the right eigenfunction. body: In mathematics, theta functions are special functions of several complex variables. Fundamentally, they are a family of continuous functions which encode the behavior of discrete multi-dimensional periodic systems, such as crystal lattices or points on a torus. Because they are smooth, they allow the study and manipulation of discrete combinatorial systems using the tools of analysis.

body:
[Lemma lem:nointersect of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Let $F_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}$ denote the event that at least two different odd CLE$_4$ gaskets of nested CLE$_4$ intersect both 
$\mathbb{D}(z_1, \varepsilon_1)$ and $\mathbb{D}(z_2, \varepsilon_2)$. Then
\begin{itemize}
    \item Let $E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{\rm{odd},k}(z_1,z_2)$ denote the event that the $k$-th odd nested CLE$_4$ gasket intersects 
    $\mathbb{D}(z_1,\varepsilon_1)$ and $\mathbb{D}(z_2,\varepsilon_2)$. Then there is a constant $C > 0$
    such that for all $k \geq 1$,
    $$\mathbb{P}(F_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2} \cap E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{\rm{odd},k}(z_1,z_2)) 
    \leq C(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{1/4}\left(\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{\rm{odd},k}) + 
    \1_{k \geq 2}\mathbb{P}(E_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}^{\rm{odd},k-1})\right).$$
    \item Further, for some $\widetilde C > 0$, 
    for all $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2 > 0$ sufficiently small, 
$$\sum_{k \geq 1}\mathbb{P}(E^{\rm{odd},k}_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)) < 
\widetilde C\mathbb{P}(E^{\rm odd}_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)).$$
    \item In particular, $\mathbb{P}(F_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2})$ is bounded by 
    $C(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{1/4}\mathbb{P}(E^{\rm odd}_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1, z_2))$ for some $C > 0$ as 
    $\max(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2) \to 0$. 
\end{itemize}
Further, the same holds when we replace odd by even everywhere. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma supportinequality of arXiv:2507.16188, 'The noisy voter model with general initial conditions'] {LubetzkySly14}}] 
For any $t \geq \hat t \geq 0$ and any set $W$ of vertices at time~$t$ in the space-time slab, if $\hat W$ denotes the (random) history of $W$ at time $\hat t$, we have
\[
\left\|\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_0}(X_{t}(W)\in \cdot)-\mu_G\mathord{\upharpoonright}_{W}\right\|_{\textsc{tv}} \leq \mathbb{E}\left[\big\|\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_0}(X_{\hat t}(\hat W)\in \cdot)-\mu_G\mathord{\upharpoonright}_{\hat W}\big\|_{\textsc{tv}}\right]\,,
\]
where the expectation is with respect to the update sequences along $[\hat t,t]$. Furthermore, if $\{X_t^{(i)}\}$ are i.i.d.\ copies of the dynamics, and $\tau_i\in[0,t]$ are stopping times for their backward dynamics, then
\[
\left\|\prod \mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_0}\big( X_{t}^{(i)}(W_i)\in \cdot\big)-\prod \mu^{(i)}_G\mathord{\upharpoonright}_{W_i}\right\|_{\textsc{tv}} \leq \mathbb{E}\left[\big\|\prod \mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_0}(X_{t-\tau_i}(\hat W_i)\in \cdot)-\prod \mu_G\mathord{\upharpoonright}_{\hat W_i}\big\|_{\textsc{tv}}\right]\,.
\]

body:
[Thm 221 (\textbf{informal statement of main result}) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] A measure $\mu$ can be approximated by $\mu_{\bG}(\bx)$, with $\bx$ the output of a Lipschitz algorithm \eqref{eq:algorithms-as-maps},
if and only if:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item  (for the spherical setting, where $\bx$ must lie near $S_N$)  $\mu$ lies in 
$\bar{\cM}^{\sph}(\alpha)$;
\item  (for the Ising setting, where $\bx$ must lie near $\Sigma_N$) $\mu$ lies in 
$\bar{\cM}^{\Ising}(\alpha)$.
\end{enumerate}
The sets
$\bar{\cM}^{\sph}(\alpha)$ and 
$\bar{\cM}^{\Ising}(\alpha)$
are specified by Definition~\ref{d:achievable-msrs}. Moreover they coincide with the sets
$\ocM^{\sph, \concave}(\alpha)$ and
$\ocM^{\Ising, \concave}(\alpha)$ respectively. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \textbf{informal statement of main result}

body:
[Proposition 25 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Length of the typical relaying zone.}

Let us consider $H$ a random variable distributed following $\mathcal{L}$. Let us further consider the landscape $\tilde{\landsc} := \landsc\cup \{(0, H)\}$. Then expectation of the length of the zone of the typical eventual relaying $\zone (0, H)$ is 
\[\e[\ell(\zone(0, H))] = \frac{1}{\lambda}\e[T],\]
where $T$ is the hitting time of the cemetery state $(-\infty, -\infty, -\infty)$ for the Markov chain $(\tilde{x}_n, \mathrm{t}_n, H_n)$ started at 
$(0, 0, +\infty)$:
\[\e[T] = \sum_{n\geq 1} \displaystyle\int_{\Half^{n+1}} g_n \delta_{(0, 0)}\displaystyle\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n} (\Leb \otimes \mathcal{L}).\]
title: Proposition 25 of arXiv:2605.03851
Lem l:1104.1 of arXiv:2602.21277

[Theorem thm:intro-abstract-response of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] In the abstract setup above, suppose
Assumptions~(ass:admissible-forms of the paper)--(ass:spectral-borel of the paper) hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item The positive spectrum is almost surely simple:
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P\!\left\{x\in\Omega_{\rm str}:
  \dim\ker(A_{\mu_x}-\Lambda_n^{\mu_x})=1
  \text{ for every }n\ge1
 \right\}=1.
 
\end{equation}
\item Fix $M\ge1$ and $1\le n_1<\cdots<n_M$.  If, for
$\mathbb P$-almost every $x\in\Omega_{\rm str}$, the selected positive
eigenvalues form a response-transverse family in the sense of
Definition~(def:abstract-response-transversality of the paper), then
\begin{equation}
 (\Lambda_{n_1}^{\mu_x},\ldots,\Lambda_{n_M}^{\mu_x})_\#\mathbb P
 \ll\mathcal L^M.
 
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:intro-abstract-response of arXiv:2608.02459

body:
[Lemma sublemma of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] For $\omega \in \Omega$ and $n\in \mathbb{N}$, define a measure $\mu_n^{\omega}$ by
\[
\mu_n^{\omega}\coloneqq \sum_{D\in \mathcal{D}_n}\nu(D)a_{n,D}\sum_{k=M_n}^{N_n} 
  \chi_{D\cap (C-V_k)}(\omega_k )\delta_{\omega_k}.
\]
Then $\mu_n^{\omega}\to \nu$ almost surely in the weak-$\ast$ topology.
title: Lemma sublemma of arXiv:2506.10448

body:
Let S_t be the square-integrable Cox-CIR jump-diffusion asset price and X_t = ln S_t with running maximum M_T = sup_{0 <= t <= T} X_t. Then M_T admits the explicit Clark-Ocone martingale representation M_T = E[M_T] - int_0^T E[ 1_{[0, tau]}(t) * int_t^tau mu_bar_s D_t^{(1)} lambda_s ds | F_t ] dW_t + int_0^T int_{R_0} psi(t, z, M_t - J_{t, z}) d N_tilde^c(dt, dz), where mu_bar_s = int_{R_0} (e^{J_{s, z}} - 1) nu(dz), tau = inf{t : X_t = M_T}, and the jump kernel is given by psi(t, z, y) = 1_{J_{t, z} >= 0} int_y^{M_t} int_0^infinity F_bar_{t, x, r} dr dx - 1_{J_{t, z} < 0} int_{M_t}^y int_0^infinity F_bar_{t, x, r} dr dx, with joint tail probability F_bar_{t, x, r} = P(sup_{t <= s <= T} X_s > x, sup_{t <= s <= T} lambda_s > r | F_t).
S_t is square-integrable
Feller condition holds for CIR intensity lambda_t

body:
[Theorem thm_longest_paths of arXiv:2606.09488, 'The temporal stochastic block model'] Suppose assumptions (ass1 of the paper) and (ass2 of the paper) hold. Fix $u,v \in V$. Then, 
\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
    \item $|\gamma_{\mathrm{max}}| \in (e\theta\log n,\alpha(\theta)\log n)$ whp, where $$\alpha(\theta)\coloneqq \inf\left\{x>0: \log\left(\frac{x}{e\theta}\right)=1 \right\}  ;$$
	\item $|\gamma_{\mathrm{max}}(v)| \sim_p e\theta\log n$;
	\item if $\theta>1$, then $|\gamma_{\mathrm{max}}(u,v)| \sim_p \beta(\theta)\log n$ and $|\gamma_{\mathrm{min}}(u,v)| \sim_p \gamma(\theta)\log n,$, where
    $$\beta(\theta) \coloneqq \sup\left\{x>0:x\log\left(\frac{x}{e\theta}\right)=-1\right\},$$
    $$\gamma(\theta) \coloneqq \inf\left\{x>0:x\log\left(\frac{x}{e\theta}\right)=-1\right\}. $$
    However, if $\theta<1$, then whp there is no increasing path between $u$ and $v$. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm_longest_paths of arXiv:2606.09488

body: [Definition 2 of arXiv:2512.19517, 'Spiking and Resetting'] Given $0< t \le T$, we say that the process $X^\varepsilon$ does not jump from $0$ to $1$ during the time interval $(0,t)$ if and only if for any $r \in (0,t)$, we have $0 \le X_r^\varepsilon \le y_*^\varepsilon$, i.e. $e_1^\varepsilon \ge t$. This is equivalent to saying that for all $i\ge 1$ such that $\tau_i^\varepsilon \in (0,t)$, the condition $0<\tau^{\varepsilon}_{i+1} -\tau_i^\varepsilon<T_*^\varepsilon$ holds.
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2512.19517

[Proposition 48 (Bounded rough transform criterion) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Assume \(f\in L^\infty\), \(\E_\nu f=0\), \(\E_\nu f^2=1\), and assume the density \(p\) satisfies the translation expansions
\[
        \|p(\cdot-s)-p+s p'\|_{L^1}=o(|s|),
\]
\[
        \left\|p(\cdot-s)-p+s p'-\frac{s^2}{2}p''\right\|_{L^1}=o(s^2).
\]
Then Condition~\ref{cond:profile-admissibility} holds with
\[
        a_1=-\int f(y)p'(y)\,dy,
        \qquad
        b_1=-\int f(y)^2p'(y)\,dy,
\]
\[
        b_2=\frac12\int f(y)^2p''(y)\,dy.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:9a287e11c4fc6d547505bfe46b3666427527117c3d97ad9f0ec895023140b991","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/9a/9a287e11c4fc6d547505bfe46b3666427527117c3d97ad9f0ec895023140b991.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:06a88ee1522ab6b1a7013f7130d967e9b06b608ef15dff3a349e0a4e221db2dd","bundle_entry_key":"w338-c0021-02","bundle_id":"population.open-problems-w338-exact-majority-and-scoped-lemmas-001","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"w338/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.boolean:iterated-three-majority-depth-two-optimal-revealment-and-composition","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C0021: exact depth-two decision tree and composition

Status: exact computational certificate plus a proved composition lemma; pending w346 KEEP. No novelty or full solution is claimed. Local status source is Garban and Steif, *Noise Sensitivity of Boolean Functions and Percolation* (2012), Exercise VIII.5 note, p. 97. The 7 September intake still labels the exponent unverified and unresolved.

Let f_k be iterated majority of three on 3^k independent fair bits. Algorithms query bits and must always return the exact output. Revealment is the largest probability that an individual bit is queried, under the uniform input and internal randomization.

For k=2, the minimum expected number of queries is 393/64 = 6.140625. Its minimum revealment is 131/192 = 0.6822916667. The usual recursive algorithm has expected cost 25/4 and revealment 25/36. Thus the verified finite-block cost decreases by 1.75%.

The certificate in check_majority.py examines all 19,683 partial assignments. At a partial assignment with m free bits, let A(s) be the sum of the remaining query counts over its 2^m compatible complete inputs. A(s)=0 if the function is forced; otherwise A(s)=2^m+min_i[A(s with bit i=0)+A(s with bit i=1)]. Every zero-error decision tree must choose an unqueried bit at a nonterminal state, so induction on m proves this recurrence gives the optimum. Randomization cannot beat the minimum of its deterministic trees. All computations use integers; the only division is by 2^9 at the root.

The independent checks use the 512-entry truth table to verify the terminal condition in every partial assignment, verify every Bellman residual and chosen action, and execute the complete policy on every input. All three error counts are zero; all outputs are correct and the sum of the 512 query counts is 3144. The policy is in majority_policy.json.

Randomize the policy by a uniform automorphism of the full ternary tree. This finite group preserves f_2 and acts transitively on its nine leaves. Each leaf then has revealment (393/64)/9 = 131/192. Conversely, any algorithm's maximum revealment is at least its expected query count divided by nine. This proves the finite-block optimum, subject to audit of the certificate.

For any k, evaluate each logical bit requested by this depth-two policy using a recursively composed policy on an independent descendant subtree. A logical subtree is selected before any of its own inputs are examined, so its selection event is independent of its bits and fresh internal randomness. At each block, the nine outputs are independent fair bits. A fixed leaf's query probability is consequently the product of the block probabilities. Hence

    delta_k <= (131/192)^floor(k/2) * (5/6)^(k mod 2).

For even k=2m this is n^(-0.17399134015245032), improving the exponent 0.16595623285353023 of the usual recursive construction. It is an achievable bound, not the exact asymptotic exponent. The former influence lower bound delta_k >= (2/3)^k still applies.

For NONNEGATIVE real numbers a_1, ..., a_n, (a_1 + ... + a_n)/n >= (a_1 a_2 ... a_n)^(1/n), with equality if and only if a_1 = ... = a_n. WEIGHTED FORM: if w_1, ..., w_n >= 0 with w_1 + ... + w_n = 1 and a_1, ..., a_n >= 0, then w_1 a_1 + ... + w_n a_n >= a_1^(w_1) ... a_n^(w_n), with the convention 0^0 = 1, and with equality if and only if all a_i with w_i > 0 are equal. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) nonnegativity is essential. With n = 2 and a_1 = a_2 = -1 the arithmetic mean is -1 while the product is 1 and its positive square root is +1, so the inequality as usually read reverses; the theorem is about nonnegative entries, never about arbitrary reals. (ii) With at least one zero entry and n >= 2 the geometric mean is 0 and the inequality is strict unless every entry is 0. (iii) The weights must be nonnegative AND sum to 1; dropping the normalisation makes the statement false, and the correct inhomogeneous relative is Young's inequality ab <= a^p/p + b^q/q with 1/p + 1/q = 1. (iv) The inequality is homogeneous of degree one, so it can be rescaled but never used to compare means of different orders; that is the power mean inequality, of which AM-GM is the limiting case as the exponent tends to 0.

in the weighted form the weights are nonnegative and sum to exactly 1
the geometric mean is the nonnegative real root of the product

Method: Local finiteness of scale-invariant network traffic measures structural attempt Result: For a bounded area A, translation invariance and Tonelli give expected full-network traffic through A equal to area(A)*integral_R2 |z|^-beta*E len R(0,z) dz. body: The real numbers are complete: every nonempty set of reals that is bounded above has a least upper bound (supremum) in R. This distinguishes R from Q (the rationals lack sup for e.g. {x : x^2 < 2}). Equivalent formulations: every bounded monotone sequence converges; every Cauchy sequence converges; nested closed bounded intervals have nonempty intersection; R has no gaps (Dedekind completeness). Completeness is the single axiom from which Bolzano-Weierstrass, the intermediate and extreme value theorems, and the whole convergence theory follow.
title: Completeness of the Reals (Least Upper Bound Property)

[Dfn 56 (measure classes) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the definition of the endpoint measure $\mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)$ from \eqref{e:control.problems.endpoint.measures}.
    For $\star$ as in \eqref{e:star.options}, we define
    \[
        \cM^\star(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon,L_0,\epsilon_0) 
        \equiv \bigg\{
            \mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta) : (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^\star(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon,L_0,\epsilon_0)
        \bigg\}\,.
    \]
When $\Adm^\star(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon,L_0,\epsilon_0)$ does not depend on some of these parameters we will sometimes omit them from the notation, writing e.g. $\cM^\BOGP(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon) = \cM^\BOGP(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon,L_0,\epsilon_0)$ for all $L_0,\epsilon_0$. Define
    \[
        \sM^\star(\alpha,q_0) 
        = \adjustlimits 
        \bigcap_{\epsilon_0 > 0} 
        \bigcup_{L_0>0}
        \bigcap_{\epsilon>0}
        \bigcup_{L>0}
        \cB_{\epsilon_0}(\cM^\star(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon,L_0,\epsilon_0))\,.
    \]
Note that this order of quantifiers corresponds to the limit \eqref{e:control.problems.limiting.regime}.

Let A be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H and let B be symmetric with D(A) ⊂ D(B) and ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ for all x ∈ D(A), where 0 ≤ a < 1 and b ≥ 0. Then A + B, defined on D(A + B) = D(A), is self-adjoint, and it is essentially self-adjoint on every core of A. If in addition A is bounded below by M, then A + B is bounded below by M − max{b/(1 − a), a|M| + b}. (Wüst's theorem covers the borderline a = 1: if B is symmetric with D(A) ⊂ D(B) and ‖Bx‖ ≤ ‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖, then A + B is essentially self-adjoint on D(A), though possibly not self-adjoint there.) Standard application (Kato): for n ≤ 3 and V ∈ L²(ℝⁿ) + L^∞(ℝⁿ) real valued, multiplication by V has −Δ-bound 0, so −Δ + V is self-adjoint on H²(ℝⁿ) and essentially self-adjoint on C_c^∞(ℝⁿ); this covers V(x) = −γ/|x| in ℝ³, the hydrogen Hamiltonian.

TECHNIQUE CARD. Normal approximation for a sum of locally dependent variables: when each summand is independent of all but a few others, Stein's method bounds the distance of the standardized sum from the normal law by the neighbourhood size and the third and fourth moments. Ross, Definition 3.1: a collection of random variables (X_1, ..., X_n) has dependency neighborhoods N_i ⊆ {1, ..., n}, i = 1, ..., n, if X_i is independent of {X_j}_{j∉N_i}. Theorem 3.5: let X_1, ..., X_n be random variables with E[X_i⁴] < ∞, E[X_i] = 0, σ² = Var(Σ_i X_i), and W = Σ_i X_i/σ; let (X_1, ..., X_n) have dependency neighborhoods N_i with D = max_i |N_i|. Then for Z a standard normal random variable, d_W(W, Z) ≤ (D²/σ³) Σ_i E|X_i|³ + (√26 D^{3/2}/(√π σ²)) √(Σ_i E[X_i⁴]) (3.8). Ross applies it to the number of triangles in the Erdős-Rényi graph G(n,p) (Section 3.2.1).

[Lemma lem:initial-robin of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $\kappa,R>0$, $\mathbf a_*\in D$, and $\rho>0$ satisfy
$B_\rho(\mathbf a_*)\Subset D$.
Then there exist
$\varepsilon_{\rm I}=\varepsilon_{\rm I}(D,\rho,\mathbf a_*,R)>0$ and
$C_{\rm I}=C_{\rm I}(D,\rho,\mathbf a_*,\kappa,R)>0$ such that whenever
$0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{\rm I}$,
$\mathbf a_\varepsilon\in B_\rho(\mathbf a_*)$, and a nonnegative
$\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\in L^\infty(D)$ satisfies
\[
  \int_D\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\,\mathrm d\mathbf x=\kappa,
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\omega_{\varepsilon,0}
  \subset B_{R\varepsilon}(\mathbf a_\varepsilon),
\]
one has
\begin{equation*}
  |\mathcal R(\omega_{\varepsilon,0})
  -\kappa^2H(\mathbf a_\varepsilon)|\leq C_{\rm I}\varepsilon.
\end{equation*}

Method: Sharp reinforcement threshold for WARM forests structural argument Result: At a positive equilibrium x, put s_v=sum_(e~v)x_e^alpha. The Hessian of the correctly rate-weighted Lyapunov function satisfies H[delta,delta]=(alpha-1)sum_e delta_e^2/x_e-alpha sum_v p_v/s_v^2 (sum_(e~v)x_e^(alpha-1)delta_e)^2. Along an even cycle choose alternating delta_e=+/-x_e^(1-alpha), zero elsewhere. Every vertex sum vanishes, giving a positive direction for alpha>1 and hence linear instability. Check: The equilibrium identity x_e=sum_(v~e)p_v x_e^alpha/s_v reduces the diagonal term. Multiplication by the positive diagonal x preserves the Hessian inertia of the linearized gradient flow. Obstruction: This eliminates even cycles, not odd cycles or all odd unicyclic supports. It does not improve the universal forest threshold by itself.

body: Define the Turing jump hierarchy above the empty set by 0^{(0)} equal to the empty set, and 0^{(n+1)} equal to the halting problem relative to an oracle for 0^{(n)}, so 0^{(1)} = 0' is the ordinary halting problem. Post's theorem states that a set B of natural numbers is definable by a Sigma^0_{n+1} formula of arithmetic if and only if B is computably enumerable relative to the oracle 0^{(n)}, and that 0^{(n+1)} has the same Turing degree as a complete Sigma^0_{n+1} set, and also as the set of true Sigma^0_{n+1} sentences. This aligns the syntactic arithmetical hierarchy with the effective Turing jump hierarchy. Proved by Emil Post.
title: Post's theorem

Method: Exact conditioning, spectral integral estimate, deterministic graph comparison or order-statistic asymptotics Result: The local-limit argument controls the fraction of vertices in components above a fixed size; it does not put those vertices in one component. To break that inference, compare one cycle of size n with a disjoint union of cycles of length floor(sqrt(n)), adjusting a negligible remainder. Both local weak limits are the bi-infinite path, which is infinite with probability one. The largest component fractions instead tend to one and zero. Thus the missing step for La-Kabkab is a genuine uniqueness/coalescence or sprinkling argument controlling dependencies among mutually preferred edges; local convergence alone cannot provide it. Check: For any fixed radius r, all vertices except a vanishing remainder in both examples have the same radius-r rooted path neighborhood once cycle lengths exceed 2r+1. The largest block sizes are n and O(sqrt(n)). Obstruction: This is a counterexample to a proposed proof implication on general graph sequences, not a counterexample within the La-Kabkab model.

body:
Let E be a family of subsets of a set X with the empty set in E and with X covered by countably many members of E, let rho : E -> [0, +infinity] satisfy rho(empty set) = 0, and define mu*(A) = inf { sum over k of rho(E_k) : E_k in E, A contained in the union of the E_k } for every subset A of X. Then mu* is an outer measure: mu*(empty set) = 0; A contained in B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B); and for EVERY countable family (A_n) of subsets of X, measurable or not, mu*(union of the A_n) <= sum of mu*(A_n). In particular Lebesgue outer measure on R^n is countably subadditive on all subsets of R^n, and finite subadditivity follows by padding the family with empty sets. WHERE THE INEQUALITY CANNOT BE IMPROVED: (a) equality fails in general even for pairwise DISJOINT sets. Let V be a Vitali set in [0,1] (one representative of each coset of the rationals) and let V_q = V + q for q in a countable enumeration of the rationals in [-1,1]. The V_q are pairwise disjoint, their union contains [0,1] and is contained in [-1,2], and by translation invariance all of them have the same Lebesgue outer measure; countable additivity would force that common value to be simultaneously 0 (giving outer measure 0 for [0,1]) and positive (to fill [0,1]), so the outer measure of the disjoint union is strictly less than the sum. Additivity is recovered exactly on the Caratheodory measurable sets. (b) Countable is sharp: the inequality does not extend to uncountable families - [0,1] is the union of its singletons, each of Lebesgue outer measure 0, while the union has outer measure 1. (c) No structure on rho is needed - rho need not be monotone, additive or a premeasure; that is why the construction is so robust, and also why mu* generally does not extend rho (mu*(E) <= rho(E) always, and equality for E in E requires rho to be a premeasure and E to be well behaved).
E contains the empty set and admits countable covers of X, so every subset has at least one admissible cover
rho : E -> [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0; nonnegativity is essential for the rearrangement of the double sum
the family (A_n) is countable; the sets need not be measurable, disjoint or nested
the conclusion is an inequality only; additivity requires the Caratheodory criterion

[Theorem 40 of arXiv:2511.13559, 'Asymptotic analysis of rare events in high dimensions'] Suppose $\g\in C^{2L}(\us(R\e)), \z \in C^{2L+2}(\us(R\e))$, $R^4d^2/\la\leq\CR$, $R\geq1$, and
\bs
\sup_{x\in\us(R\e)}\|\nabla^\ell\z(x)\|_H&\leq C_{k,\z} d^{\lceil \ell/2\rceil-2}\qquad\forall \ell=3,\dots,2L+2,\\
\sup_{x\in\us(R\e)}\|\nabla^\ell\g(x)\|_H&\leq C_{\ell,\g} d^{\lceil \ell/2\rceil}\qquad\forall \ell=0,\dots,2L.
\es
Then
\bs
\frac{1}{\mathcal Z}\int_{\us(R\e)}\g(x)e^{-\la \z (x)}\dd x = \sum_{k=0}^{L-1}\nu_k(\g)\la^{-k} + \Rem_L,
\es where
\bs
\max_{k=0,\dots,L-1}d^{-2k}|\nu_k(\g)|&\leq C_{L,\z,\g},\\
|\Rem_L|&\leq C_{L,\z,\g,R}\left((d^2/\la)^L+e^{-(R-1)^2d/4}\right).
\es Here, $C_{L,\z,\g}$ depends on $L$, on $C_{\ell,\z}$, $\ell=3,\dots,2L+2$, and on $C_{\ell,\g}$, $\ell=0,\dots,2L$. The constant $C_{L,\z,\g,R}$ is analogous and also depends on $\CR$. We have $\nu_0(\g)=\g(0_d)$, and the formula for $\nu_k(\g)$, $k\geq1$ is given by $A_{2k}$ in~\cite[(2.20)]{A24}.

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2606.09904, 'Non-explosion principles for branched rough differential equations with unbounded coeffici'] A path \(\mathbf{Y} : [0, T] \to \CH_{N - 1} = \bigoplus_{n = 0}^{N - 1} \CH_{(n)}\) is a 
  \(\mathbf{X}\)-controlled rough path for some \(\gamma\)-H\"older branched rough path \(\mathbf{X}\) if 
  \begin{equation}
    R^{Y, f}_{st} = R^f_{st} = \< f, \mathbf{Y}_t\> - \< \mathbf{X}_{st} \curvearrowright f, \mathbf{Y}_s\>
  \end{equation}
  satisfies 
  \[\sup_{s < t \in [0, T]} \frac{|R^f_{st}|}{|t - s|^{(N - |f|)\gamma}} < \infty\] 
  for all \(f \in \CF_{N - 1}\). We denote \(Y_t = \< \mathbf{1}, \mathbf{Y}_t\>\) for the 
  path component of \(\mathbf{Y}\) and furthermore, for \(f \in \CF_{N - 1}\), denote 
  \(\partial^f_X Y_t = \< f, \mathbf{Y}_t\>\). We call \(\partial^f_X Y_t\) the \(f\)-th Gubinelli 
  derivative of \(\mathbf{Y}\) against \(\mathbf{X}\).
title: Definition 7 of arXiv:2606.09904

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; depends on the companion memo on Problem 20.2] This is the negative part of the answer recorded for Svante Janson's Problem 20.4 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Problem 20.4 asks for a Gaussian extension of Theorem 7.12, the law of large numbers for fringe-subtree counts. Let T_n be the simply generated tree, equivalently the conditioned Galton-Watson tree, with n vertices. Let N_T be the number of vertices whose fringe subtree equals a fixed finite ordered rooted tree T, and let N_d be the number of vertices with d children. For the one-vertex tree bullet, N_bullet = N_0 exactly, since its occurrences are precisely the leaves. In both constructions of the companion memo on Problem 20.2, the subcritical law of its Theorem A (nu < 1) and the critical infinite-variance law of its Theorem B (nu = 1, sigma^2 = infinity), the bulk of the vertices has degree 0 or 1. Hence N_0 = n - N_1 + O(1), and N_bullet inherits the non-Gaussian limit of (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n): a two-point law in the first construction and a mixture of two Gaussians in the second. Assuming those two theorems, fringe-subtree counts are not asymptotically normal in general when nu < 1, nor when nu = 1 with sigma^2 = infinity. The finite-variance critical case is resolved in the literature by Janson (Random Structures Algorithms 48, 2016, Theorem 1.5) and is not included here as own work. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
T_n is an ordered rooted tree, and its one-vertex fringe subtrees are leaves.

body:
[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Fix $c > 0$ and let $Q_t$ be the birth-death process
  with
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $Q_0 \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(c)$;
    \item $n \mapsto n +1$ transitions of rate $c$; and
    \item $n \mapsto n - 1$ transitions of rate $n$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then the first hitting time of $0$,
  \[
    \tau_c \coloneqq \inf\{ t \geqslant 0 \mid Q_t = 0 \},
  \]
  has Laplace transform
  \[
    \E e^{-s\tau_c} = e^{-c}
    \left[1 - c\int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^{s} e^{-cx} \, dx
    \right]^{-1},
    \quad s \geqslant 0.
  \]
  \begin{proof}
    Fix $s > 0$. By total expectation,
    \[
      \E e^{-s \tau_c}
      = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty
      \E\left(e^{-s\tau_c} \middle| Q_0 = n\right)
      \PP(Q_0 = n)\\
      = e^{-c} \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \frac{c^n}{n!}\, \phi_n(s)
    \]
    where $\phi_n(s) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}(e^{-s\tau_c} \mid 
    Q_0 = n)$. So if $\Phi_s$ is defined on $[0, c]$ by
    \begin{equation}
      
      \Phi_s(y) \coloneqq \sum_{n=0}^\infty
      \phi_n(s) \, \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \quad \text{then} \quad
      \E(e^{-s\tau_c}) = e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c).
    \end{equation}
    Clearly $\phi_0(s) = 1$ and first-step analysis gives
    \[
      (c+n+s) \, \phi_n(s) = 
      n \, \phi_{n-1}(s) + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s),
      \quad n > 0.
    \]
    By taking a weighted sum of this recurrence,
    \[
      \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \left(c + n + s \right)
      \phi_n(s) = \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \left[ n \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s)\right].
    \]
    The left-hand side is
    \[
      (c+s) \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_n(s)
      + y \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_n(s)
      =
      (c+s)\left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
    \]
    while the right-hand side is
    \[
      y \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_{n+1}(s)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[ \Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s)\right].
    \]
    We are left with the differential equation
    \[
      (c+s) \left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[\Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s) \right]
    \]
    or equivalently,
    the initial value problem
    \begin{align}
      
      \left(c-y\right) \Phi_s'(y)
      + \left(- c + y - s\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= \overbrace{c \, \phi_1(s) - c - s}^{-K}\\ \notag
      \Phi_s'(y) + \left(-1-\frac{s}{c-y}\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= -\frac{K}{c-y}
    \end{align}
    with condition $\Phi_s(0) = 1$.
    Use the integrating factor $I_s(y) = e^{-y} \, (c-y)^s$ to write
    \begin{align*}
      \left[e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)\right]'
      &= \frac{-K}{c-y} \, e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s\\
      e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)
      - e^{-0} \left(c - 0\right)^s \Phi_s(0) 
      &= \int_0^y \frac{-K}{c-x} \, e^{-x} \left(c - x\right)^s \, dx
      \intertext{for any $y < c$. It's clear from \eqref{eq:Phi} that
      $\Phi_s$ is continuous, so take the $y \uparrow c$ limit:}
      \frac{c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}
      &= K.
    \end{align*}
    Finally, the $y \uparrow c$ limit of \eqref{eq:IVP}
    informs us $-s \, \Phi_s(c) = -K$, thus
    \begin{align*}
      \E e^{-s\tau_c}
      &= e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c)
      = \frac{e^{-c}\, c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \, s \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}\\
      &= \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^s dx}
      = \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^1 c \, e^{-cx} \left(c-c\,x\right)^s dx}\\
      &= e^{-c} \left[1 - c \int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^s e^{-cx}\, dx \right]^{-1}.
      \qedhere
    \end{align*}
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Primary-source dependency map, W719-T295-C011 v1, source audit pending. In Ma, Wang, Chi and Chen, Implicit Regularization in Nonconvex Statistical Estimation (arXiv:1711.10467v3), consider iid real Gaussian sensing, a fixed unit signal x_*, noiseless observations, quartic loss f(x)=(1/(4m)) sum_j ((a_j^T x)^2-(a_j^T x_*)^2)^2, and the source local induction in its absolute region of incoherence. The omitted-row loss keeps denominator m, and its iterate is z_t=x_t^(l). Appendix A.4, PDF pp51-52, splits Delta_next into a full-gradient secant term and omitted-row forcing evaluated at z_t. Under the source induction and Gaussian row/projection events, it bounds the forcing norm by an absolute constant times C4(C4+5)(C4+10) eta (n log n/m) sqrt(log n/n), then makes this at most c eta sqrt(log n/n) by sufficiently large m/(n log n). Full-gradient segment contraction 1-eta/2 closes the static gap C3 sqrt(log n/n) in equation106. At linear m=alpha n the displayed proof coefficient grows as log n/alpha, and reducing eta alone cannot improve its ratio to the contraction budget. Appendix A.6, p53 equation112, uses the same factor n log n/m to control spectral-initialization leave-one-out perturbations. Separately, the segment-contraction geometry assumes m>=c0 n log n. Lemma4 p26 and equations53-55 control an absolute gap and absolute maximum projection C2 sqrt(log n); they do not prove a projection bound proportional to the current error norm. These are limitations of the displayed proof estimates, not a lower bound on actual perturbations or a necessity theorem for log oversampling. No linear-sample GD convergence or nonconvergence is established.

[Corollary 49 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(k\) be a perfect field of characteristic \(p>0\), let \(C\) be a smooth projective curve over \(k\), and let
\[
\pi\colon Y \to  C
\]
be a smooth projective morphism of relative dimension \(n\).
Assume that, for every geometric point $\overline{c} \to  C$, one has
\[
H^i\left(
Y_{\overline{c}},
\Omega^j_{Y_{\overline{c}}}
\otimes\omega_{Y_{\overline{c}}}
\right)=0
\]
for every  \(i<n\) and \(0\leq j\leq n\).
Then \(Y\) is HT-split.

Status: proof draft, unaudited. Target 1 construction, not a nonlinear convergence theorem.

Let pi be the standard normal density, h_n=He_n/sqrt(n!) its normalized probabilists' Hermite polynomials. For b>1/4 define

q_b(x) = integral from 0 to 1 of b(1-u)^(b-1) phi_(1+u)(x) du,

where phi_v is the centered Gaussian density of variance v. This is a strictly positive probability density. For 0<epsilon<1 the density rho_0=(1-epsilon)pi+epsilon q_b is also strictly positive. It has mean zero and variance 1+epsilon/(b+1).

For all m>=0 its q_b Hermite coefficients are

a_(2m) = Gamma(b+1) sqrt((2m)!)/(2^m Gamma(m+b+1)),
a_(2m+1) = 0.

For X conditional on U=u distributed as N(0,1+u), the Hermite generating function gives

E exp(tX-t^2/2) = exp(u t^2/2).

Equating derivatives at zero yields E He_(2m)(X) = (2m)! u^m/(2^m m!), while odd moments vanish. Each fixed derivative is integrable over u in [0,1]; this also follows directly since each polynomial moment is bounded uniformly in the variance interval [1,2]. Integrating in u and using

E U^m = b B(m+1,b) = Gamma(b+1) Gamma(m+1)/Gamma(m+b+1)

proves the coefficient formula. Stirling's formula, equivalently the central binomial asymptotic and the Gamma ratio, gives

sqrt((2m)!)/(2^m m!) ~ (pi m)^(-1/4),
Gamma(m+1)/Gamma(m+b+1) ~ m^(-b).

Therefore a_(2m) ~ Gamma(b+1) pi^(-1/4) m^(-b-1/4). Every exponent s>1/2 is realized by b=s-1/4. Nonconstant coefficients of rho_0/pi are epsilon a_n. The odd coefficients vanish; the asserted profile is on the even sector.

To justify the L2 expansion rather than only formal moments, Tonelli's theorem and direct Gaussian integration give

integral phi_(1+u)(x) phi_(1+v)(x)/pi(x) dx = (1-uv)^(-1/2),

for 0<=u,v<1. Thus the squared L2(pi) norm of q_b/pi is the integral of (1-uv)^(-1/2) against the two independent Beta(1,b) mixing laws. Set a=1-u and c=1-v. Then 1-uv=a+c-ac lies between (a+c)/2 and a+c. Near (0,0) the integrand is comparable to a^(b-1)c^(b-1)(a+c)^(-1/2). With r=a+c, z=a/r, the radial exponent is 2b-3/2; the z integral is finite for b>0. Integrability is therefore equivalent to b>1/4. Away from that corner the integrand is integrable. Completeness of the Hermite basis now identifies the actual L2 coefficients and gives finite chi-square divergence and hence finite KL for b>1/4.

This construction resolves positivity and normalization of the requested initial profile. It does not identify coefficients in the Stein eigenbasis. The Hermite basis does not diagonalize the Stein operator, as the dossier's eigenvector diagnostics already show. No decay exponent transfers between these two bases without an additional comparison theorem.

# Characteristic KL diagnostic

For h=1 the exact mean-field velocity and its spatial derivative are

v(x) = integral exp(-(x-y)^2/2) [(x-y)-y] rho_t(y) dy,
v_x(x) = integral exp(-(x-y)^2/2) [1-(x-y)((x-y)-y)] rho_t(y) dy.

Along characteristics X_t(a), set L_t(a)=log(partial_a X_t(a)). Then dX/dt=v(X), dL/dt=v_x(X), L_0=0. Conservation of mass gives log rho_t(X_t(a))=log rho_0(a)-L_t(a), and therefore

KL(rho_t|pi) = E_(a~rho_0) [log rho_0(a)-L_t(a)+X_t(a)^2/2+log(2pi)/2].

The script approximates this expectation and velocity integrals with Gaussian-mixture product quadrature. Unlike a KL computed from an atomic empirical law, this formula is defined for the continuum density. Its numerical quadrature still requires resolution checks, and its finite-time fits are evidence only. The Stein-information kernel used as an additional diagnostic is k(x,y)[xy+1-2(x-y)^2].","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:18618181c1e55723453d3fd0280a04028682b29877205fda162197655ca2b74e","revision_digest":"sha256:1fddbb037ca02911702eb3fd1b185f588a56ed9680b05ba54e4a44e3dd76ca40","source_id":"owner-own-work:w722:T311:w722-positive-profile-v2","source_revision":"w722-positive-profile-v2","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Proposition 23 (Maximum principle for Einstein--Euler flows) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Let $(\Phi,\Psi)$ be a sufficiently regular Einstein--Euler areal flow on $[t_0,t_1]\times\Tbb^3$ with $\mu>0$ throughout.
Then, for every $t\in[t_0,t_1]$ and $m=2,3$,
\bel{equa-widetildemax}
\aligned
\inf_{\Sbb^1}\Gammaun_m(t_0,\cdot)&\leq\Gammaun_m(t,x)\leq\sup_{\Sbb^1}\Gammaun_m(t_0,\cdot),\\
\inf_{\Sbb^1}\Gammazero_m(t_0,\cdot)&\leq\Gammazero_m(t,x)\leq\sup_{\Sbb^1}\Gammazero_m(t_0,\cdot).
\endaligned
\ee
Then the range of $\Gammaunpar(t,\cdot)$, respectively $\Gammazero(t,\cdot)$, coincides with the range of the corresponding initial map, namely the range is an invariant set.
The statement about $\Gammazero$ extends to vacuum.
The bound on~$\Gammaun$ extends to vacuum as the statement that if $C_1\hNumb\leq\hNumb\Gammaun_m\leq C_2\hNumb$ at initial time $t=t_0$ for some constants $C_1,C_2\in\RR$ then these inequalities hold for all times.
As a result, the convex hull of the range of $\Gammaunpar(t,\cdot)$ coincides with that at initial time. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let X be a random variable with cumulant generating function psi(lambda) = log E[exp(lambda X)], finite on an interval containing 0 in its interior on the right. Then for every t, P(X >= t) <= exp(-psi^*(t)) where psi^*(t) = sup_{lambda >= 0} (lambda t - psi(lambda)) is the (one-sided) Legendre transform of psi. If X = sum_{i=1}^n X_i with the X_i independent and identically distributed with cumulant generating function psi_1, then psi = n psi_1 and P(X >= n t) <= exp(-n psi_1^*(t)): the exponent is LINEAR in n with rate psi_1^*(t), the Cramer rate function. Cramer's theorem says this exponential rate is exactly right, that is (1/n) log P(X >= n t) -> -psi_1^*(t) for t > E[X_1] under a finiteness condition on psi_1 near 0, so the Chernoff bound loses nothing at the level of the exponential rate although it can lose polynomial factors. The method requires SOME finite exponential moment: without it psi^* is identically 0 for t above the mean and the bound is vacuous, which is the correct behaviour for heavy-tailed laws. [standard; e.g. Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Chapter 2]
psi(lambda) = log E e^{lambda X} finite for some lambda > 0 (otherwise the bound is vacuous)
for the i.i.d. rate statement: independent and identically distributed summands

Let Y be finite with a distinguished always-true empty fact bot, let n>=1 and |Y|>n+1, and let p be any probability law on Y with p(bot)=0. Put F=supp(p) union{bot} and H=Y\F. Given n iid samples from p, let O be the observed symbols union{bot}, U=Y\O, and GT the fraction of sample positions whose symbol occurs exactly once. Both O and U are nonempty. Define g(y)=(1-GT)/|O| on O and g(y)=GT/|U| on U. Let B(g) be the partition into nonempty equal-g-probability level sets, let p^B be uniform within each level set with its original p mass, and define Mis_infinity(g,p)=TV(p^B,g). Deterministically, g(H)<=GT and Mis_infinity(g,p)<=|p(U)-GT|. Hence, for every delta in(0,1], Pr(g(H)<=GT and Mis_infinity(g,p)<=3*sqrt(log(4/delta)/n))>=1-delta. This is a deliberately inefficient matching construction in the source calibration notion. If factoids have a surjective document representation, choosing one representative document per factoid realizes g as a document generator. The zero empty-fact mass and alphabet-size assumptions here make all singleton and denominator conventions explicit; no claim for arbitrary non-iid corpora is included. If the two assigned per-symbol scores are distinct, Mis_infinity(g,p)=|p(U)-GT| exactly. If they coincide, g is uniform, its exact score partition has one bin, and Mis_infinity(g,p)=0; unconditional equality with |p(U)-GT| is not asserted.

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2605.20026, 'Quasihelix properties\\ of selected Volterra Gaussian processes'] \leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[1),left=5pt]
\item 
 \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item For any fixed $\lambda > 0$ and $\alpha\in(-1/2, 1/2)$ the process $U^{(1)}$ is a local $(\alpha+\frac12, 0, T)$-quasihelix for any $T>0$.
    \item Let $\alpha = 1/2$. Then for any fixed $\lambda > 0 $ and any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ the process $U^{(1)}$ is a  local $(1, 1 - \varepsilon, 0, T)$-generalized quasihelix for any $T>0$.  
    \item Let $\alpha > 1/2$. Then for any fixed $\lambda > 0$ the process $U^{(1)}$ is a local $(\alpha+\frac12, 1$, $0, T)$-generalized quasihelix  for any $T>0$ and $(1, T_1, T_2)$-quasihelix  for any  \mbox{$0 < T_1 < T_2$}.
\end{enumerate} 

\item 
For any $T > 0$, the   process $U^{(3)}$ is local $(1, \alpha, 0, T)$-generalized quasihelix in the case $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ and local $(\alpha, 1, 0, T)$-generalized quasihelix in the case $\alpha \in (1, 2)$. When $\alpha=1$, the process becomes standard Wiener process, and thus it is obviously a local $(\frac12, 0, T)$-quasihelix for all $T > 0$. For $\alpha \ge 2$ the process is a local $(\frac{\alpha}{2}, \frac12, 0, T)$-generalized quasihelix for any $T>0$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let (Omega, F, P) be a probability space and {X_i : i in I} a family of random variables. The family is uniformly integrable if and only if there exists a nondecreasing convex function G : [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) with G(t)/t -> infinity as t -> infinity such that sup_{i in I} E[G(|X_i|)] < infinity. The sufficiency direction is the one used in practice: a uniform bound on any superlinear moment, for example sup_i E[|X_i|^p] < infinity for a single p > 1, or sup_i E[|X_i| log^+ |X_i|] < infinity, forces uniform integrability. A uniform bound on the FIRST moment does not: on ([0,1], Lebesgue) the family X_n = n 1_{(0,1/n)} has E|X_n| = 1 for all n and is not uniformly integrable. [standard; e.g. Dellacherie and Meyer, Probabilities and Potential, or Williams, Probability with Martingales, Section 13.3]
a probability space (or a finite measure space)
G convex, nondecreasing, superlinear at infinity; the constant sup_i E[G(|X_i|)] must be uniform over the family

For a real random variable X and l >= 0 let Q(X; l) = sup_x P(x <= X <= x + l) (Levy's concentration function). There is an absolute constant C such that for independent X_1,...,X_n, S = X_1 + ... + X_n and any 0 < l_i <= l (i = 1,...,n): Q(S; l) <= C l (sum_i l_i^2 [1 - Q(X_i; l_i)])^{-1/2}. Also Q(X_1 + X_2; l) <= min(Q(X_1; l), Q(X_2; l)) for independent X_1, X_2. If X_i has density <= 1 then Q(X_i; l_i) <= l_i, so 1 - Q(X_i; l_i) >= 1 - l_i.

Assumes: independence; 0 < l_i <= l

Every finite nonempty S in the square lattice Z^2 has |boundary_E S|>=4sqrt(|S|), while the edge-Cheeger constant of Z^2 is zero. Indeed, if S occupies a columns and b rows then its edge boundary is at least 2a+2b>=4sqrt(ab)>=4sqrt(|S|); square boxes of side r have boundary/volume=4/r. Thus an IP_2 inequality cannot be substituted for the uniform positive-Cheeger hypothesis in the explicit threshold proof. This does not refute the conjecture that finite isoperimetric dimension greater than one ensures p_c<1.

The intake credits the dimension >4/Cayley results and leaves the non-Cayley intermediate regime unresolved. We give a self-contained stronger-hypothesis special case, not a new general resolution.

For an infinite connected graph of maximum degree D<infinity with edge-Cheeger constant h=inf_(finite nonempty S) |boundary_E S|/|S|>0, independent bond percolation satisfies

    1/(D-1) <= p_c <= 1/(1+h) < 1.

The lower bound is the union bound over at most D(D-1)^(r-1) simple paths of length r from a fixed vertex, for p(D-1)<1. To prove the upper bound, explore a cluster by testing only unrevealed edges from discovered vertices to undiscovered vertices. After s successful discoveries and f failures, the discovered set has s+1 vertices, and at least h(s+1)-f boundary edges remain untested. Thus the exploration cannot finish while Z=h+hs-f>0. The tests are an independent Bernoulli(p) sequence: each success adds h to Z and each failure subtracts 1. If p>1/(1+h), its drift is positive. For sufficiently small lambda>0, p exp(-lambda h)+(1-p) exp(lambda)<1. Then exp(-lambda Z), stopped at the first Z<=0, is a nonnegative supermartingale, and the probability ever reaching Z<=0 is at most exp(-lambda h)<1. With positive probability exploration never terminates, proving the upper bound. Critical equality itself is not decided by this drift argument. For the d-regular tree h=d-2, the upper bound matches its exact critical probability.

IP_(1+epsilon) does not supply a positive uniform h: the square lattice has a two-dimensional isoperimetric inequality but its square boxes have boundary/volume tending to zero. Fix -1<a<1 and sigma_a(t)=t for t>=0, sigma_a(t)=a*t for t<0, applied coordinatewise. A depth-L network has L affine layers, activation after the first L-1 layers, and an affine final output. Its squared parameter cost is sum_ell (||W_ell||_F^2+||b_ell||_2^2). For a function f and domain Omega, R_L is the infimum of this cost over all such finite-width networks equal to f on Omega; R_L=+infinity if the class is empty. Let Omega be a nonempty bounded open subset of R^d, and f:R^d->R^m a continuous function affine on each cell of a finite polyhedral decomposition. At every x in Omega at which f is differentiable, and for every integer L>=1, sum_(i=1)^rank(Jf(x)) s_i(Jf(x))^(2/L)<=R_L/L. The same lower bound applies if the hidden widths are prescribed, with their corresponding representation cost. It does not require the asymptotic cost to have a limit.

[Lemma 15 (Resonant skew-Hermitian endpoint identity) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $\Lambda\subset 2\pi\Q$ be finite and symmetric, and choose $m\geq1$ such that
\[
m\omega\in2\pi\Z
\qquad(\omega\in\Lambda).
\]
Let $\Gamma=\gamma^{*m}$ be the $m$-fold concatenation of $\gamma$, naturally parametrised on $[0,mT]$.
Fix $r\geq1$, frequencies $\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r\in\Lambda$, and real covectors $\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_r\in W^*$. No distinctness is assumed: the frequencies and covectors may repeat.
Choose real numbers $\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_r$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
\sigma_{j-1}-\sigma_j=\omega_j
\quad(1\leq j\leq r),
\qquad
m\sigma_j\in2\pi\Z
\quad(0\leq j\leq r).
\end{equation}
Set $D=i\diag(\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_r)$, write $I=I_{r+1}$, and, for $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_r)\in\R^r$, define
\begin{equation}
\rho_u(a)
 =\ell(a)D
  +\sum_{j=1}^r
   u_j\eta_j(a)(E_{j-1,j}-E_{j,j-1}),
\end{equation}
first as a real-linear map $V\to\uLie(r+1)$. Denote its complex-linear extension by
\[
\rho_{u,\C}:V_{\C}\longrightarrow M_{r+1}(\C).
\]
If $U^u$ is the right development
\[
\dd U_s^u=U_s^u\rho_u(\dd\Gamma_s),
\qquad U_0^u=I,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
U_{mT}^u=I
\qquad(u\in\R^r).
\end{equation}

[Lemma Monotonicity of arXiv:2606.13264, 'Interference Queueing Networks: A Replica Mean-Field Approach in the Symmetric Setting'] The Markov chain $Q$ is monotone with respect to the arrival rate, the initial condition, and the departure rate. More precisely:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the arrival rate.} If $\lambda_1 < \lambda_2$, then the chains $Q^{(1)}$ and $Q^{(2)}$ defined by \emph{(2)} with arrival rates $\lambda_1$, $\lambda_2$ and $Q^{(1)}(0)=Q^{(2)}(0)$ satisfy
    \[
    Q^{(1)} \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^{(2)}.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the initial condition.} If $x \leq y$, then the chains $Q^x$ and $Q^y$ defined by \emph{(2)} with initial conditions $Q^x(0)=x$ and $Q^y(0)=y$ satisfy
    \[
    Q^x \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^y.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Monotonicity in the departure rate.} If for all $i \in [1;N]$, $f \leq \mu_i$ (resp. $f \geq \mu_i$), and $Q^f(0)=Q(0)$, then the chain $Q^f$ defined by \emph{(2)} with departure rate $\mu_i = f$ for every $i$ satisfies
    \[
    Q \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q^f
    \qquad (\text{resp. } Q^f \leq_{\mathrm{st}} Q).
    \]
\end{itemize}

body:
[Lemma lem:anchor-taylor-debit of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix $L<\infty$.  Let $r\le L\log(n+2)$,
$0\le\Delta\le r$, and $0\le d\le r+B_0$.  For every physical
translation $a$ in a set of at most $m\le cN$ translations, let
$M(a)\in\{0,\ldots,m\}$ be its remaining gap budget, with distinct
translations giving distinct budgets, and let
\[
 \mathcal X_a^{(M(a))}=\sum_{q=0}^{M(a)}[z^q]\mathcal F_a(z).
\]
Suppose that, for one number $H\ge0$ independent of $a$,
\[
 \sup_{|z|=1}|\mathcal F_a(z)|\le Hn^{-\Delta}
\tag{3.2.10q$_{14}$}
\]
and, when $d\ge1$,
\[
 |[z^q]\mathcal F_a(z)|
 \le H\binom{q+d-1}{d-1}(1-\gamma_n)^q,
 \qquad q\ge0.
\tag{3.2.10q$_{15}$}
\]
For $d=0$ interpret $\mathcal F_a$ as constant.  Then
\[
 \boxed{
 \sum_a|\mathcal X_a^{(M(a))}|
 \le C_LcN Hn^{-\Delta}.}
\tag{3.2.10q$_{16}$}
\]
The conclusion is anchor-averaged: it does not assert a
dimension-free maximal-partial-sum estimate for one prescribed budget.
It remains valid for a final-scalar prescribed-gate contraction, provided
\crefrange{eq:3.2.10q-14}{eq:3.2.10q-15} hold after that contraction.

body:
[Lemma 14 (Multiscale block partial coloring) of arXiv:2606.16005, '\bfseries An Algebraic Matrix Spencer Theorem'] Let $A_1,\dots,A_n$ be self-adjoint satisfying $\|A_i\|\le1$ and which are block diagonal with respect to a fixed common block decomposition $H=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\mathcal B}H_\alpha$. Consider  block stratification as in Definition \ref{def:stratification} and let $(h_j,m_j,q_j,Q)$ be the associated parameters.
Then, for every active set \(S\subseteq[n]\), with \(s:=|S|\), and every shift $y\in(-1,1)^S$,
there exists an increment $x\in[-1,1]^S$
such that \(x+y\in[-1,1]^S\) and at least \(\Omega(s)\) coordinates of \(x+y\) lie in \(\{\pm1\}\), and
\[
\left\|
\sum_{i\in S}x_iA_i
\right\|
\le \Delta(s),
\]
where
\[
\Delta(s)
\le
\begin{cases}
O(\sqrt{s\log\!\left(e+\dfrac{Q}{s}\right)}), & s\ge J,\\[1.2em]
O(\sqrt{s\log\!\left(e+\dfrac{b_{\max}M}{s}\right)}), & s<J.
\end{cases}
\]
Moreover, if \(Q\le O(n)\), then
\[
b_{\max}\le O(\sqrt{n}),
\qquad
M\le O(n),
\qquad
b_{\max}M\le O(n^{3/2}).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Multiscale block partial coloring

body: A tree is a finite, simple, connected graph with no cycles; equivalently, a connected graph on n vertices with exactly n-1 edges. A forest is a graph every connected component of which is a tree, equivalently a graph with no cycles. A spanning tree of a connected graph G = (V,E) is a subgraph of G that is a tree and includes every vertex of V. [standard, e.g. Diestel, Graph Theory]
title: Tree, Forest, and Spanning Tree

On {-1, 1}^n (n >= 1) with the uniform probability measure mu, chi_S(x) = prod over i in S of x_i for S inside [n], and f^(S) = E[f chi_S] is the Walsh-Fourier coefficient of a real function f, so f = sum over S of f^(S) chi_S. Partition [n] = J u K and, for z in {-1, 1}^K, let f_{J|z}(y) = f(y, z) on {-1, 1}^J, its Walsh coefficients taken on {-1, 1}^J under that cube's uniform measure. For S inside J, f_{J|z}^(S) = sum over T inside K of f^(S u T) chi_T(z). If Z is uniform on {-1, 1}^K, then E_Z[f_{J|Z}^(S)] = f^(S), E_Z[f_{J|Z}^(S)^2] = sum over T inside K of f^(S u T)^2, and E_Z ||f_{J|Z}||_2^2 = ||f||_2^2, each norm under the uniform measure of its own cube. For one coordinate i, with f_+ and f_- the restrictions to x_i = 1 and x_i = -1 and S not containing i: f_+^(S) = f^(S) + f^(S u {i}) and f_-^(S) = f^(S) - f^(S u {i}), so f^(S) = (f_+^(S) + f_-^(S))/2 and f^(S u {i}) = (f_+^(S) - f_-^(S))/2.

Result: Theorem 4.8 gives lim X_n/n in {v, -cv} a.s. under a 0-1 law assumption for the directional events; on the non-transient event the walk returns to a bounded region infinitely often, so liminf |X_n|/n = 0 trivially along the return times, and the question is whether limsup X_n . l / n can be positive: the walk would have to make excursions of linear size and return. For Markovian RWRE the analogous statement (Zerner 2002) uses a regeneration argument; for excited walks the excursions of linear size would, on the non-transient event, be repeated infinitely often through the same (partially eaten) environment, and each long excursion in direction l has probability decaying exponentially in its length by a large deviation bound for the walk in a fixed (already modified) environment, IF the environment modification is bounded (bounded stacks) - so under (BD) the expected number of linear excursions from a bounded region is finite by Borel-Cantelli, giving the answer YES under (BD) plus a uniform large-deviation bound for excursions. Without (BD) (unbounded stacks under (EL) only) the modification of the environment can be unbounded and the large deviation bound is not uniform. Recorded: under (IID), (EL) and (BD) the answer is yes provided the uniform excursion large-deviation estimate holds (plausible from the elliptic Markov comparison since eaten cookies only change transition probabilities within [eps, 1-eps]); the general (EL) case without (BD) is the open part. Key identity: Linear excursions from a bounded region have exponentially small probability uniformly under (BD)+(UEL); Borel-Cantelli gives zero velocity on the recurrent event. [Lem 165 ($\by$ is Lipschitz) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Take $\by\equiv \by(q_{d+1})$ as in \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y}, so it is measurable with respect to $\cG(q_{d+1})$, as defined by \eqref{e:gaus.filt}. 
Conditional on $\cG(q_d)$,
the random vector $\by$ has mean zero, and is subgaussian with variance proxy $L^{O(1)}$.

\begin{proof} Let us abbreviate
	\[
	\bXi
	\equiv \bXi^{d+1}
	\equiv \frac{\bG(q_{d+1})
		-\bG(q_d)}{\sqrt{p_{d+1}-p_d}}\,,
	\]
so this is a gaussian independent of $\cG(q_d)$. Then we can express
	\begin{align*}
	\sqrt{\delta_d}\by
	&\stackrel{\eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y}}{=}
	\E\bigg[ \cA\Big(
		\bG(q_d)
		+(p_{d+1}-p_d)^{1/2}\bXi
		+ (1-p_{d+1})^{1/2} \bG'\Big)\,\bigg|\,\bG(q_d),\bXi
		\bigg]\\
	&\qquad-\E\bigg[ \cA\Big(
		\bG(q_d)
		+(p_{d+1}-p_d)^{1/2}\bXi
		+ (1-p_{d+1})^{1/2} \bG'\Big)\,\bigg|\,\bG(q_d)\bigg] \,.
	\end{align*}
Thus, conditional on $\cG(q_d)$,
the vector $\by$ has mean zero.
It follows by the assumption on $\cA$ together with assumption~\eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} that
 $\by$ is $L^{O(1)}$-Lipschitz in $\bXi$, so the subgaussian claim follows using Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: $\by$ is Lipschitz

body:
Let X be a topological space and T: X → X a map. A set A ⊂ X is (forward) invariant if T(A) ⊆ A. A minimal set is a nonempty closed invariant set M that contains no proper nonempty closed invariant subset. Some authors require T(M) = M (strict invariance); for a continuous T on a compact Hausdorff space a minimal set in the above sense automatically satisfies T(M) = M, since T(M) is then itself nonempty, closed (compact image) and invariant, hence equal to M. Characterization (T continuous): a nonempty closed invariant M is minimal if and only if for every x ∈ M the forward orbit {Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is dense in M. Proof of the equivalence: for x ∈ M the orbit closure cl{Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is nonempty, closed, contained in M, and invariant because continuity gives T(cl O) ⊆ cl T(O) ⊆ cl O; so minimality forces it to equal M; conversely, if every orbit in M is dense and N ⊂ M is nonempty closed invariant, any x ∈ N has its orbit inside N, so M = cl(orbit) ⊆ N. The system (X,T) itself is called minimal if X is a minimal set, i.e. every forward orbit is dense. Examples: a periodic orbit is a minimal set; an irrational rotation of the circle is minimal; the closure of a non-periodic orbit is in general NOT minimal (e.g. the orbit closure of a point of the doubling map whose orbit is dense contains the fixed point 0 as a smaller minimal set). Continuity is used in the orbit-closure characterization; the definition of a minimal set itself does not need it. For flows and group/semigroup actions the same definitions apply with 'orbit' read as the (semi)group orbit.
X is a topological space and T: X → X a map
for the orbit-closure characterization, T is continuous
title: Invariant sets and minimal sets of a topological dynamical system

Consider a finite Ising model: spins sigma_i in {-1, +1} for i in a finite set V, a Hamiltonian -H(sigma) = sum over finite subsets B of V of J_B sigma_B, where sigma_B = product of sigma_i over i in B, with all coupling constants J_B >= 0 (ferromagnetic; pair interactions J_{ij} >= 0 and external fields h_i >= 0 are the special case of B of size two and one), and the Gibbs expectation <f> = sum_sigma f(sigma) exp(-beta H(sigma)) / Z at inverse temperature beta >= 0. Then for all finite A, B contained in V: (GKS I) <sigma_A> >= 0, and (GKS II) <sigma_A sigma_B> >= <sigma_A> <sigma_B>. Equivalently, the derivative of <sigma_A> with respect to any coupling J_B is nonnegative: correlations are monotone increasing in every ferromagnetic coupling and in beta. Consequences: the magnetisation is increasing in the field and in the couplings; correlations in a finite box increase toward their infinite-volume limits under free boundary conditions, which makes the free-boundary limit exist and be monotone in the box; the Lee-Yang and FKG inequalities are its companions but not its corollaries (FKG holds for pair ferromagnetic couplings with an arbitrary, even signed, external field and gives positive association of all increasing functions, but it needs the lattice condition, which many-body couplings need not satisfy; GKS needs nonnegative fields, allows arbitrary many-body ferromagnetic couplings, and is specific to products of spins).
finite spin set V, spins +-1
all couplings J_B >= 0 (ferromagnetic), including any external field h_i >= 0
beta >= 0
no assumption on the graph structure: arbitrary many-body ferromagnetic interactions are allowed

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine the branching-process-with-migration proof and where i.i.d. is used. Result: The proof of Theorem 3.10 under (3.10) translates the walk into a branching process with migration whose offspring law at site k is determined by the cookie stack at k; under (IID) the branching process is homogeneous in space and the criterion delta > 1 is the criterion for the branching process to die out... under (SE) the process is a branching process in a stationary ergodic environment (BPRE with migration), whose survival criterion is governed by the Lyapunov exponent of the environment, i.e. by an ergodic average of log-means, not by the mean delta of the drift. So the natural (SE) analogue is NOT 'delta in [-1,1]' with delta = E sum_i (2 omega(0,i) - 1) but a criterion involving the annealed versus quenched growth rate of the associated BPRE; for i.i.d. environments the two coincide because the migration term is affine. I tested this on the simplest non-i.i.d. case: an environment alternating deterministically between two cookie stacks a and b (period 2, hence SE after a random shift): the branching process with migration is then periodic and its two-step transition is again a branching process with migration with delta_2 = delta_a + delta_b; the criterion becomes delta_a + delta_b > 2 for transience, i.e. the average delta > 1, consistent with the naive extension. For genuinely random ergodic environments a similar averaging holds if the migration is additive, which it is (the number of cookies eaten per visit adds). So the expected answer is YES for (SE) with the same delta, and the obstruction to a proof is that the branching-process comparison uses independence between the offspring at different sites when computing the extinction probability of the process with migration; with dependence one needs an ergodic theorem for the total progeny, available via the Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer approach only for i.i.d.. Recorded: periodic environments satisfy the naive extension; the general (SE) case reduces to an ergodic total-progeny theorem for branching with migration in stationary environments. Key identity: Periodic two-stack environment: transient iff delta_a + delta_b > 2, i.e. the averaged delta criterion holds. Obstruction: Ergodic total-progeny theorem for branching processes with migration in stationary environments.

body: In mathematics, Sard's theorem, also known as Sard's lemma or the Morse–Sard theorem, is a result in mathematical analysis that asserts that the set of critical values of a smooth function f from one Euclidean space or manifold to another is a null set, i.e., it has Lebesgue measure 0. This makes the set of critical values "small" in the sense of a generic property. The theorem is named for Anthony Morse and Arthur Sard.

  Let $(F,R, \rho)$ be a rooted compact resistance metric,

  and $\dot{\mu}$ be a Radon measure on $F \times \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$.
  Assume that

    \bigl( V_{G_{n}}, \alpha_{n}^{-1} R_{G_{n}}, \rho_{G_{n}}, \beta_{n}^{-1} \dot{\mu}^{\#}_{G_{n}}, (a_{i}^{(n)}, b_{i}^{(n)})_{i=1}^{N} \bigr) 
    \to
    \bigl( F, R, \rho, \dot{\mu}, (a_{i}, b_{i})_{i=1}^{N} \bigr)
  \end{equation}
  in the space $\mathfrak{M}_{c}(\markedfinMeasFunct{\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}} \times \tau^{2N \text{-}\mathrm{pts}})$,
  where $(\alpha_{n})_{n \geq 1}$ and $(\beta_{n})_{n \geq 1}$ are sequences of positive numbers 
  with $\alpha_{n} \wedge \beta_{n} \to \infty$.
  Then, it holds that 
  \begin{equation}
    \bigl( V_{\bar{G}_{n}}, \alpha_{n}^{-1} R_{\bar{G}_{n}}, \rho_{\bar{G}_{n}}, \beta_{n}^{-1} \dot{\mu}^{\#}_{\bar{G}_{n}} \bigr) 
    \to
    \bigl( \tilde{F}, \tilde{R}, \tilde{\rho}, \dot{\mu} \circ (\pi \times \id_{\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}})^{-1} \bigr)
  \end{equation}
  in the space $\mathfrak{M}_{c}(\markedfinMeasFunct{\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}})$,
  where $(\tilde{F}, \tilde{R})$ is the resistance metric space $(F, R)$ fused over $\{\{a_{i}, b_{i}\}\}_{i=1}^{N}$,
  $\pi: F \to \tilde{F}$ is the canonical map,
  and we set $\tilde{\rho} = \pi(\rho)$.

body:
Let X_1, X_2, ... be an INFINITE exchangeable sequence of random variables taking values in a Polish space S, meaning that for every n the law of (X_1, ..., X_n) is invariant under permutations of the n coordinates. Then there is a random probability measure Theta on S, measurable with respect to the exchangeable sigma-algebra, such that CONDITIONALLY on Theta the X_i are i.i.d. with common law Theta. Equivalently the law of the sequence is a MIXTURE of i.i.d. laws, and Theta is the almost sure limit of the empirical measures (1/n) sum_{i <= n} delta_{X_i}. The theorem is FALSE for finite exchangeable sequences. Counterexample with n = 2: let (X_1, X_2) be uniform on {(0,1), (1,0)}. This is exchangeable, but any mixture of i.i.d. Bernoulli sequences has Cov(X_1, X_2) = E[p^2] - (E p)^2 = Var(p) >= 0, whereas here E[X_1] = E[X_2] = 1/2 and E[X_1 X_2] = 0 give Cov = -1/4 < 0. Sampling without replacement is exactly the mechanism, and it produces the negative correlation that no mixture of i.i.d. can. What DOES survive in finite length is a quantitative approximation, due to Diaconis and Freedman: an exchangeable sequence of length n, restricted to k of its coordinates, is close in total variation to a mixture of i.i.d. sequences, with an error of order k/n. So infinite exchangeability is the hypothesis and it is not decorative; 'exchangeable' alone, applied to a finite sample, does not license treating the data as conditionally i.i.d. [de Finetti (1931); Hewitt and Savage (1955) for the general Polish case; Diaconis and Freedman (1980) for the finite version]

[Theorem thm:lb of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] In the setting of (thm:1 of the paper), fix $n\geq 1$ and $K>0$, let $\rho_n(x)$ be the maximum vertical distance of~$\mathfrak{L}_n$ above $x+(\frac{L}2,0)$ for $-N_n^{2/3} \leq x\leq N_n^{2/3}$,
and set $\sigma^2>0$ as per (def:sigma of the paper). 
Then every weak limit point $\mathbf{Y}_n(t)$ of the process $Y_n(t):=N_n^{-1/3}\rho_n(t N_n^{2/3})$ ($t\in[-K,K]$), as $L\to\infty$, satisfies
\[ \mathbf{Y}_n \succeq \mathsf{FS}_{\sigma}\,. \]
Moreover, for every fixed $m$, every weak limit point $({\ensuremath{\mathbf Y}}_n(t))_{n\leq m}$ of the processes $(Y_n(t))_{n\leq m}$ satisfies
\[ ({\ensuremath{\mathbf Y}}_n)_{n\leq m} \succeq \bigotimes_{n\leq m}\mathsf{FS}_{\sigma}\,.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); method obstruction only, no novelty or problem-impossibility claim. In the untagged paired prior N=5,d=2,K=3,r=2, observe factual samples (1,0),(1,1),(1,2),(2,0) without tags. Posterior atom i=(0,0) has mean factual density 1/15 and false risk 1/3, while j=(2,1) has density 7/120 and false risk 1/4. Merging these atoms in a uniform coarsening decreases the upper-risk event mass by 1/240. Thus the all-partitions density/risk tail-dominance lemma used by C009 cannot simply be carried to untagged data. This does not refute an untagged frontier or a narrower argument restricted to realizable score bins. Context 4 is known S, pairs are (0,1),(2,3), and a factual sample is uniform on contexts then true candidates. The four samples force context 1 to be S, but retain fair orientation for pair (2,3). The upper-risk event at threshold 1/3 is exactly all candidates in context 0. The demonstrated coarsening is arbitrary; no generator satisfying the original robust calibration budget is asserted to realize that partition.
Independent fair pair orientations; uniform independent 2-subset A supports; S has 3 truths; uniform factual context law
No partition tags or verifier; condition on the four specified actual factual observations
Coarsening merges exactly the two displayed atoms and leaves others singleton
