This refutes an attempted automatic extension of C009's LOWER-BOUND
METHOD. It is not a counterexample to any full untagged frontier theorem,
nor a proof that a different method cannot solve that problem.

Let N=5,d=2,K=3,r=2. Pairs are (0,1) and (2,3), each with one A and
one S, and context 4 is known S. A has a uniformly random 2-subset of
true candidates; S has all 3. Orientations are independent fair bits;
A supports are independent and uniform. A factual sample chooses a
context uniformly then a true candidate uniformly. Observe ONLY the
four factual samples

 (1,0), (1,1), (1,2), (2,0),

with NO partition tags and no verifier. Let mu be the posterior mean
factual law and s the posterior probability an atom is false.

All three candidates occurred in context 1, so it must be S and
context 0 must be A. The support in context 0 remains uniform and
unobserved, giving for i=(0,0)

 mu(i)=1/15,       s(i)=1/3.

The single sample (2,0) has the same marginal probability 1/15 under
either orientation of pair (2,3), so these orientations retain probability
1/2 each. If context 2 is A, its posterior support is uniform over
{0,1} and {0,2}. For j=(2,1), its conditional mean factual probability
in that branch is (1/2)*(1/10)=1/20 and false probability is 1/2.
If context 2 is S, the corresponding values are 1/15 and zero. Therefore

 mu(j)=(1/20+1/15)/2=7/120,       s(j)=1/4.

Thus s(i)>s(j) but mu(i)>mu(j): precisely the reverse of the ordering
needed by C009. The other two atoms in context 0 also have risk 1/3;
uncertified atoms in context 2 have risk 1/4, context 3 has risk 1/6,
and all remaining atoms have risk zero. Hence E={y:s(y)>=1/3} is exactly
the three candidates in context 0.

Let Pi merge just i and j and leave every other atom a singleton.
Uniform coarsening replaces their densities by
(1/15+7/120)/2=1/16. Consequently

 mu(E)-mu_Pi(E)=1/15-1/16=1/240>0.

So upper-risk event mass can DECREASE under coarsening after ordinary
untagged factual observations. The conditional finite triangle inequality
TV(mu_Pi,g)<=E[Mis(g,p)] remains valid; it is the next event-dominance
step that fails. These should not be conflated.

Verification in scripts/verify_tagged_factual_frontier.py enumerates all
36 original orientation/support worlds, weights each by the ACTUAL
four-sample factual likelihood, normalizes the posterior, and checks
both densities, both risks and the exact 1/240 event-mass drop using
Fraction. This is an exact negative control; no floating-point fit.

The partition Pi here is an arbitrary uniform coarsening; the example
does not assert that this Pi is the score partition of a generator
satisfying the original robust calibration budget. It diagnoses the
all-partitions dominance lemma used as a sufficient step in C009, and
does not alone invalidate a potentially narrower score-bin argument.
The elementary posterior computation is owner-own-work with no novelty
claim beyond the documented obstruction. [Corollary 9 (Sequence-independent endpoint topology) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Assume the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} with
\begin{equation}
 
 T=T_{\max}(F_0)<\infty
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 W(0)\leq8\pi.
\end{equation}
Then exactly one of the following mutually exclusive alternatives
holds:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
 \item $\Var_T=0$;
 \item $\Var_T\neq0$ and $\spt\Var_T$ is a closed embedded orientable
 Lipschitz surface of genus zero;
 \item $\Var_T\neq0$ and $\spt\Var_T$ is a closed embedded orientable
 Lipschitz surface of genus one.
\end{enumerate}
In the nonzero alternatives, $\Var_T$ has unit density.
The alternative and the limiting varifold are independent of the
sequence of times tending to $T$.

[Lemma lem:chung of arXiv:2605.26688, 'Absolute moment inequalities under quadratic-form positivity'] Let \(0<r<2\). Let
\[
   C_r=\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1-\cos u}{\left\lvert u\right\rvert^{r+1}}\,\mathrm{d} u\right)^{-1}
   =\frac{\Gamma(r+1)}{\pi}\sin\frac{\pi r}{2}.
\]
Then, for every \(z\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
   \left\lvert z\right\rvert^{r}=C_r\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{1-\cos(tz)}{\left\lvert t\right\rvert^{r+1}}\,\mathrm{d} t.
\]

body:
Let P be the transition matrix of an irreducible, reversible Markov chain on a finite state space with stationary distribution pi, and let gamma* = 1 - max{|lambda| : lambda an eigenvalue of P other than 1} be the absolute spectral gap, with relaxation time t_rel = 1/gamma*. Then for every epsilon in (0, 1/2) the total-variation mixing time satisfies (t_rel - 1) log(1/(2 epsilon)) <= t_mix(epsilon) <= t_rel log(1/(epsilon pi_min)), where pi_min is the smallest stationary probability (Levin, Peres, Wilmer, Theorems 12.4 and 12.5). Mixing time is therefore the relaxation time up to a factor between log(1/(2 epsilon)) and log(1/(epsilon pi_min)); on a state space of size N the gap between the two sides can be as large as log N, and neither side can be dropped in general. For a lazy chain (holding probability at least 1/2) all eigenvalues are nonnegative, so the absolute gap equals the ordinary gap 1 - lambda_2; a periodic chain (a simple random walk on a bipartite graph) has an eigenvalue -1, gamma* = 0, and never mixes.
the chain is reversible with respect to pi (real eigenvalues); the bounds are stated for the absolute spectral gap
aperiodicity (e.g. laziness) so that gamma* > 0
the upper bound carries the factor log(1/pi_min); the lower bound holds for epsilon < 1/2

Let lambda be a security parameter, lambda<=n(lambda)<=poly(lambda), and ell(lambda)<=poly(lambda). Let F_s:{0,1}^n->{0,1}, indexed by an ell-bit seed s, be efficiently evaluable, and fix q in[0,1/2). A noisy weak-PRF sample oracle chooses a fresh uniform X in{0,1}^n and an independent fresh Bernoulli(q) bit E at every call and returns(X,F_s(X) xor E), using one uniform seed s for the entire experiment. The ideal sample oracle returns(X,G(X)), with fresh uniform X at each call but one uniformly random function G:{0,1}^n->{0,1} fixed for the whole experiment. Noisy weak-PRF security means that every probabilistic polynomial-time sample-oracle adversary has an acceptance-probability difference negligible in lambda between these experiments. The oracle chooses the query inputs; the adversary cannot choose them. The ideal answers at repeated inputs are consistent, whereas the real oracle uses fresh noise. The family is tau-local when, for every seed s, there is a fixed set of at most tau input coordinates and a Boolean function on those coordinates representing F_s on every input. Assumption3.1 posits existence of such a secure family with tau(lambda)<=log n(lambda), polynomial seed and input lengths, and a fixed noise rate q<1/2. This is a computational assumption, not an unconditional existence theorem. The displayed definition uses adversary input1^n; the explicit lambda<=n<=poly(lambda) restriction here makes the two unary parameter lengths polynomially comparable.
The polynomially comparable parameter-length version is stated explicitly.
Efficient evaluation; one shared seed; independent uniform random sample inputs and fresh real-oracle noise.
The ideal experiment uses one shared random function, not independent labels on repeated inputs.

Then there is C depending only on n,q,r,q̃,r̃ such that: (i) homogeneous estimate ‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L^q_t L^r_x(R×R^n)} ≤ C‖f‖_{L²(R^n)}; (ii) dual estimate ‖∫_R e^{−isΔ}F(s) ds‖_{L²(R^n)} ≤ C‖F‖_{L^{q̃'}_t L^{r̃'}_x}; (iii) retarded estimate ‖∫_{s<t} e^{i(t−s)Δ}F(s) ds‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} ≤ C‖F‖_{L^{q̃'}_t L^{r̃'}_x}. Consequently, if u solves i∂_t u + Δu = F on I × R^n with 0 ∈ I and u(0) = u0, then ‖u‖_{L^q_t L^r_x(I×R^n)} + ‖u‖_{C(I;L²)} ≤ C( ‖u0‖_{L²} + ‖F‖_{L^{q̃'}_t L^{r̃'}_x(I×R^n)} ), with C independent of the interval I. [Proposition 15 of arXiv:2607.13401, 'Total variation cutoff for Kac's walk on the sphere'] Let \(t_n=\ceil{c n\log n}\) with \(c>3\).  Fix \(r>0\),
\(K<\infty\), and \(0<\delta<\delta_0\).  Whenever
\(\mb P(G_n(r,K,\delta))>0\), set
\[
        \mu_{n,G}:=
        \mb E\left[F_{A_t}\mid G_n(r,K,\delta)\right].
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
        \limsup_{n\to\infty}
        \chi^2(\mu_{n,G}\Vert\pi_n)
        \le
        e^{C\delta^2}-1,
\end{equation}
where \(C\) is universal.

[Defn 6 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] For every $\delta,\varsigma\in(0,1)$, let $\kappa_{d}^{\varsigma}:\mathbb{T}^{d}\to[0,\infty)$ and $\kappa_{1}^{\delta}:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)$ be standard convolution
kernels of scales $\varsigma$ and $\delta$ on $\mathbb{T}^{d}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ respectively, and let $\kappa^{\varsigma,\delta}$ be
\begin{align}
    \kappa^{\varsigma,\delta}(x,y,\xi,\eta):=\kappa_{d}^{\varsigma}(x-y)\kappa_{1}^{\delta}(\xi-\eta),\quad\text{for every }(x,y,\xi,\eta)\in(\mathbb{T}^{d})^{2}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}.
\end{align}
For every $\beta\in(0,1)$, let $\varphi_{\beta}\colon\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$
be the unique non-decreasing piecewise linear function that satisfies
\[
\varphi_{\beta}(\xi)=1\text{ if }\xi\geq\beta,\quad\varphi_{\beta}(\xi)=0\text{ if }\xi\leq\frac{\beta}{2},\quad\text{and}\quad\varphi_{\beta}^{\prime}(\xi)=\frac{2}{\beta}\mathbf{1}_{\{\beta/2\leq\xi\leq\beta\}},
\]
and for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\zeta_{N}\colon\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]$
be the unique non-increasing piecewise linear function that satisfies
\[
\zeta_{N}(\xi)=0\text{ if }\xi\geq N+1,\quad\zeta_{N}(\xi)=1\text{ if }\xi\leq N,\quad\text{and}\quad\zeta_{N}^{\prime}(\xi)=-\mathbf{1}_{\{N\leq\xi\leq N+1\}}.
\]

body: A statistic $T$ is sufficient for a family $\{P_\theta\}$ if the conditional law of the data given $T$ does not depend on $\theta$; by the factorization theorem this holds iff the density factors as $g_\theta(T(x))h(x)$, and Rao-Blackwellization over $T$ never increases the risk under a convex loss.

[Lemma lem:basic_concentration of arXiv:2507.10531, 'Quantitative central limit theorems for exponential random graphs'] There are constants $c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4 > 0$ such that the following holds.
Let $f$ be a function on $n$-vertex graphs with Lipschitz vector $\mathcal{L}$,
and let $\lambda > 0$ such that
$c_1 n^2 e^{-c_2 n} \leq \frac{\lambda}{\| \mathcal{L} \|_\infty} \leq c_3 n^{\frac{3}{2}}$.
Then
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{P}\mleft[ |f(X) - \mathbb{E}[f(X)]| > \lambda \mright] \leq 
    2 \Exp{- \frac{c_4 \lambda^2}{\| \mathcal{L} \|_\infty^2 n^2} }.
\end{equation}
title: Lemma lem:basic_concentration of arXiv:2507.10531

The unsmoothed teacher can have minimum separation 3R and component covariance condition number 1. metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:50899aca48b218362f95d98bd72b74ced8a9c9a32c2eb82fdc30b5593a4b8369","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/50/50899aca48b218362f95d98bd72b74ced8a9c9a32c2eb82fdc30b5593a4b8369.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:b5b65dd88f00db5725c385ec016c98fea8833c18cca3c9e9bdc667931aba59bb","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c06","bundle_id":"population.t309-transverse-tracking-and-spurious-ddpm-minimum-drafts","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability, Gaussian mixtures, score matching","draft":"w721/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:anisotropic-three-gaussian-ddpm-spurious-high-noise-minimum","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T309: an anisotropic triangle obstructs a global high-noise angular argument

T309-w721-C06 v1. Status: proof (unaudited), a counterexample to a fixed-high-noise landscape route. It does not refute Target 2, annealed GD, a high-probability guarantee for a specified initialization, or all polynomial-time learning algorithms. No novelty is asserted.

The exact obstruction is that the leading component-identifying tensor loss can itself have a nonglobal local minimum after mean and covariance matching. Thus a nonzero third-moment signal is not enough to obtain global angular convergence for arbitrary three-center geometry.

## Statement

Let u_j=(cos(2pi j/3),sin(2pi j/3)), j=0,1,2, and let A=diag(1,3). In dimension 2 define the teacher

    q_a=(1/3)sum_j N(a A u_j,I_2).

Use the equal-weight identity-covariance Eq. (9) score student, parameterized on centered triples M=(m_0,m_1,m_2), sum_j m_j=0. For every sufficiently small positive a, its exact population excess DDPM loss has a strict nonglobal local minimum at a centered triple

    M_a = -a A U + O(a^3),                                       (1)

up to permutation, where U has columns u_j. The loss at this minimum is

    (61/2) a^6+O(a^8)>0.                                        (2)

The same local minimum remains a strict local minimum in the full centered d-dimensional parameter space after embedding the teacher in a plane, for every d>=2, when a is sufficiently small. The small-radius cutoff can be chosen independently of d by the finite-span domination argument used below.

There is also a strict nonglobal local minimum for the unrestricted three-mean student, with the same leading locations and loss. Its centroid is O(a^5); it need not be exactly zero. Section 5 justifies this extension separately rather than assuming that centering is invariant under full GD.

These teachers arise by OU smoothing from well-separated spherical mixtures with original means R A u_j, component covariance I_d, equal weights 1/3, and minimum separation 3R, by choosing exp(-t)=a/R. In particular this example uses component covariance condition number 1, not a poorly conditioned component covariance. The covariance of the center locations has anisotropy; these are different quantities.

The planar block of the total mixture covariance has condition number at most 9: its eigenvalues are 1+R^2/2 and 1+9R^2/2. Any perpendicular eigenvalues of the full covariance are 1. In dimension 2 their ratio is at most 9. For d>2 the perpendicular eigenvalues 1 make the total condition number 1+9R^2/2, still an absolute constant when the well-separated radius R is fixed. Thus the component-covariance condition number is exactly 1 in every dimension, and no growing-conditioning claim is needed for this example.

## 1. General centered score expansion

For centered unit-scale locations v_j and a scalar a, let C=(1/3)sum_j v_j v_j^T and T=(1/3)sum_j v_j tensor v_j tensor v_j. Put tr T for the vector with entries sum_k T_{i,k,k}. Expanding the posterior mean in the score gives

    b(a,x)=a^2 Cx+(a^3/2)(T[x,x]-tr T)+O(a^4).                 (3)

Here the trace term is essential because the transformed triangle no longer has equal-radius vertices. It comes from differentiating the -a^2||v_j||^2/2 terms in the logits. Equivalently, the order-three density correction is a contraction with the third Gaussian Hermite tensor, whose gradient gives the quadratic Hermite term in (3).

If two centered triples have the same covariance C, their score difference starts at order a^3, and Gaussian Hermite orthogonality gives

    F_a=(a^6/2)||T_student-T_teacher||_F^2+O(a^8).              (4)

To check the coefficient, write D=T_student-T_teacher. Wick's formula gives E||D[G,G]-tr D||^2=2||D||_F^2 for any symmetric third tensor D, even when tr D is nonzero. The score coefficient is 1/2, so its squared coefficient is 1/4, producing (4). Parity under (a,x)->(-a,-x) removes odd orders. The same finite-mixture softmax domination as in C01 proves a uniform remainder with every fixed finite number of location derivatives on bounded sets. This is an integrated expansion, not a pointwise approximation assumed to survive expectation.

## 2. The covariance-matched angular potential

Consider v_j(theta)=A R_theta u_j. Every theta has center covariance C_*=AA^T/2. More generally for A=diag(p,q), the independent entries of its third tensor are

    T_xxx=p^3 cos(3theta)/4,
    T_xxy=p^2 q sin(3theta)/4,
    T_xyy=-p q^2 cos(3theta)/4,
    T_yyy=-q^3 sin(3theta)/4.

Taking multiplicities 1,3,3,1, define

    Qc=(p^6+3p^2 q^4)/16,     Qs=(3p^4 q^2+q^6)/16.

The leading angular risk divided by a^6 is

    H(theta)=(1/2)[Qc(cos(3theta)-1)^2+Qs sin^2(3theta)].       (5)

If Qs>2Qc, then theta=pi/3 is a strict local minimum of H with positive value. Indeed

    H(pi/3)=2Qc,
    H''(pi/3)=9(Qs-2Qc)>0,
    H(0)=0.

For p=1,q=3 the coefficients are exactly

    Qc=61/4,    Qs=189/4,    H(pi/3)=61/2,
    H''(pi/3)=603/4.

The other critical angles separating the two minima satisfy cos(3theta)=-61/128 and are local maxima. In the equilateral case p=q=1, by contrast, (5) reduces to (1-cos(3theta))/4, consistent with corrected C01 v3. This cross-check catches the tensor multiplicity factor that was wrong in C01 v1/v2.

The angle pi/3 gives the negative of the teacher's set of vertices, because rotation by pi/3 and multiplication by -1 differ by a cyclic permutation of the equilateral reference. A is applied after that permutation, so the identity remains true for the stretched triangle.

## 3. A constrained minimum is not enough: normal relaxation

We now verify that the bad angular minimum persists in the full centered parameter space; we do not infer full GD behavior from a loss restricted to a curve.

In dimension 2, every centered rank-two three-column matrix sufficiently near A R_{pi/3}U can be uniquely parameterized locally by its positive-definite center covariance C and an angle theta, on a fixed orientation branch:

    V(C,theta)=sqrt(2C) R_theta U.

This follows directly by choosing orthonormal coordinates on 1-perpendicular in the three-column index space and taking the ordinary polar decomposition of the resulting invertible 2-by-2 factor. The covariance is C, and the orthogonal polar factor on the selected determinant branch has a unique local angle. Thus (C,theta) are actual local coordinates for all centered perturbations, not just an ansatz.

Uniformly with sufficiently many derivatives near (C_*,pi/3), the exact loss satisfies

    F_a(C,theta)=a^4||C-C_*||_F^2+a^6 K(C,theta)+O(a^8),        (6)

where K(C_*,theta)=H(theta). The leading covariance term follows from the order-a^2 part of (3). Smoothness, parity, and dominated differentiation justify division by the vanishing powers of a and extension to a=0. For off-diagonal covariance coordinates the Frobenius metric includes its usual factor two; its normal Hessian is still strictly positive and invertible.

Apply the implicit function theorem to a^(-4) partial_C F_a=0 at a=0, C=C_*. The normal Hessian is that of ||C-C_*||_F^2 and is invertible. It supplies a smooth normal critical section

    C_a(theta)=C_*+O(a^2).

For theta in a neighborhood of pi/3, substituting the section gives the reduced loss

    F_a(C_a(theta),theta)=a^6 H(theta)+O_{C^2(theta)}(a^8).      (7)

This follows because the covariance displacement is O(a^2), so its squared leading penalty is O(a^8); the change in K contributes the same order. Higher location smoothness supplies the required differentiated remainders and the C^2 section; all Gaussian moments involved are finite.

Apply the implicit function theorem again to a^(-6) times the derivative of (7). The nonzero derivative H''(pi/3)=603/4 yields a critical angle theta_a=pi/3+O(a^2) with positive reduced second derivative. The covariance block of the full Hessian is positive definite of order a^4. The reduced second derivative is its Schur complement, positive of order a^6. Hence the full centered-coordinate Hessian is positive definite. This proves a strict local minimum. Its value follows from (7), and its mean locations satisfy (1) by smoothness of sqrt(2C) and the angle parameterization. Since the teacher itself attains loss zero, the local minimum is nonglobal.

## 4. Extra ambient directions

Embed the construction in a fixed plane in R^d. Reflection in its perpendicular complement fixes the teacher and every planar student. Thus all perpendicular gradient components vanish at the planar critical point, and mixed planar/perpendicular Hessian blocks vanish there as well.

For a centered perpendicular perturbation D, the leading covariance variation is (DV^T+VD^T)/3. It has a strictly positive squared norm for every nonzero such D because the two-column planar factor of V is invertible with singular values bounded away from zero. Concretely the two off-diagonal covariance blocks are transposes, and their Frobenius norm controls ||D||_F through the smallest singular value of that factor. At C=C_* their leading covariance Hessian is 2 times this squared norm. At C_a=C_*+O(a^2), the additional covariance-residual term and the higher-order score terms change the normalized Hessian by O(a^2). They cannot remove its positivity for sufficiently small a. Changing from unit-scale locations to physical means multiplies the leading Hessian by a^2, preserving its sign.

This establishes strict positivity also in every additional centered perpendicular direction. Uniform constants follow from the same finite-span Gaussian projection used in C05: for any pair of unit perturbation directions, all integrated derivatives involve at most twelve Gaussian coordinates. No estimate of a growing ambient Gaussian norm is used.

## 5. Releasing the centroid in the unrestricted student

Write the unit-scale student locations as b+v_j, with sum_j v_j=0. The physical centroid is a b. If b_V(a,x) denotes the centered posterior mean correction from (3), the unrestricted correction is exactly

    a b+b_V(a,x-a b).

Let C_V be the center covariance of V and C_* that of the centered teacher. Expanding through order four in a, while keeping b as a variable, gives

    F_a(b,V)=a^2||b||^2
        +a^4[||C_V-C_*||_F^2-2 b^T C_V b]+O(a^6).             (8)

Here the remainder is smooth with the needed b,V derivatives. To verify that no term linear in b was dropped at order four, the score difference through order three is

    a b+a^2(C_V-C_*)x
        +a^3[(T_V-T_*):H_2(x)/2-C_V b]+O(a^4).

The Gaussian expectation of H_2 is zero, and the teacher has mean zero. The order-two teacher density correction has integral zero as well, so multiplying it by a^2||b||^2 gives no order-four contribution. Squaring the displayed score difference therefore gives exactly (8) at order four. Parity removes all odd powers. In particular partial_b F_a(0,V)=O(a^6) with the same derivative bounds; it is not merely O(a^4).

The equation a^(-2) partial_b F_a=0 has derivative 2I+O(a^2) in b near zero. By the implicit function theorem it has a smooth solution b_a(V)=O(a^4). Its b Hessian is positive definite. Substitution into the loss changes F_a(0,V) only by O(a^10), with its needed V derivatives: its linear term is O(a^6) times a displacement O(a^4), and its quadratic term is O(a^2) times the square of that displacement. The corresponding derivatives of b_a are also O(a^4), as follows by differentiating the implicit equation.

Apply the covariance and angular reductions of Section 3 to this mean-reduced loss. The leading angular term and its positive bad curvature are unchanged. Positivity of the eliminated mean block and of the reduced Hessian gives positivity of the full unrestricted Hessian by the same Schur-complement argument. Thus a strict bad local minimum persists for ordinary unrestricted mean GD. Its physical centroid is a b_a=O(a^5), while its shape displacement is O(a^3).

The argument is uniform in ambient dimension: the mean Hessian is uniformly 2I+O(a^2) after division by a^2, and the directional derivative bounds follow by projecting onto the fixed finite span of the student, teacher, and differentiation directions. Perpendicular criticality and centered shape curvature follow as in Section 4. This is an additional analytic step; centered-network and unrestricted-mean claims are not being conflated.

## 6. Relation to well-separated original laws and GD

For A=diag(1,3), the teacher's pairwise center distances at unit scale are 3,3,3sqrt(3). Thus the unsmoothed mixture with means R A u_j is well-separated at minimum distance 3R. OU smoothing preserves component covariance I and scales all means by exp(-t), giving precisely q_a when exp(-t)=a/R.

The reflected set -R A U has minimum cross-distance R from R A U. After choosing a sufficiently small absolute a, the spurious means obtained from (1), rescaled by R/a, remain within R/4 of that reflected set. For d=2, take the union of radius-R/4 balls around the true centers. Under the true mixture its probability is at least 1-exp(-R^2/32), using the exact two-dimensional Gaussian radial tail. Under the bad mixture every such ball is at least R/2 from each bad center, after the stated perturbation bound; the weaker distance R/4 is enough to bound its probability by 3exp(-R^2/32). Therefore the TV distance between the original law and this rescaled bad law is at least

    1-4exp(-R^2/32).

For any fixed sufficiently large R this is bounded far away from zero, while its training landscape still has the strict bad local minimum at every sufficiently high noise level as above. The bad student is not rendered harmless by having small high-noise score error.

A strict nondegenerate local minimum has an open attracting neighborhood for sufficiently small-step centered GD, and also for sufficiently small-step unrestricted mean GD at the unrestricted minimum, by local strong convexity and smoothness. Thus an initialization with full support gives some positive probability of attraction to a bad point. This statement alone gives no useful lower bound on that probability for the specific small Gaussian initialization or on its dependence on d. It does not rule out random restarts, a carefully chosen initialization, or an annealing schedule which later changes the objective. Those are exactly the distinctions needed to avoid promoting a landscape obstruction into a false negative answer to Target 2.

## Checks and remaining questions

The exact symbolic script checks (4)--(5), the constants 61/4 and 189/4, the positive bad curvature 603/4, and the equilateral limiting formula. The persistence in the exact objective is an analytic implicit-function argument, not a numerical optimization certificate. Independent review should focus on the normal-coordinate reduction, the ambient-direction Hessian extension, and the separate centroid elimination in Section 5. No conclusion about the probability of reaching the bad basin from the target's specified initialization is supplied.

Biane semicircular density parametrization. Let mu be any Borel probability measure on R, let t>0, and let mu_t=mu free-additive-convolved with the centered semicircle of variance t. Set U_t={u: integral (u-y)^(-2) mu(dy)>1/t}, with the integral allowed to be infinite, and v_t(u)=inf{v>=0: integral ((u-y)^2+v^2)^(-1) mu(dy)<=1/t}. Then v_t is continuous, is positive exactly on U_t, and is real analytic there. Define psi_t(u)=u+t integral (u-y)/((u-y)^2+v_t(u)^2) mu(dy). At boundary points where numerator and denominator both vanish, use the continuous Cauchy-transform extension, equivalently the integrable boundary limit. The map psi_t is an increasing homeomorphism R to R, and mu_t has a continuous density p_t satisfying p_t(psi_t(u))=v_t(u)/(pi*t). In particular p_t is real analytic wherever positive, and 0<=p_t<=1/(pi*sqrt(t)). No moment, initial density, or compact-support assumption on mu is required. This is Biane1997 Lemma2, Lemma4 and Corollary3, with analyticity from Lemma5 and Corollary4, not a new result.
Arbitrary Borel probability measure mu on R; t>0 is the semicircular variance, not its standard deviation.

PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. In a rooted binary tree whose edges between levels k-1 and k are replaced by paths of integer length ell_k>=1 and unit conductance, resistance from the root to infinity equals sum_{k>=1} ell_k/2^k. Equal current splitting attains this energy and Cauchy-Schwarz on each level gives the matching lower bound. Thus ell_k=k is transient with resistance two, while ell_k=2^k is recurrent. An infinite binary branching topology alone does not guarantee transience after stretching.
Exactly a level-subdivided rooted binary tree
Integer positive corridor lengths
Unit edge conductances

[Prop LDP_321_pi_intro of arXiv:2604.23751, 'Large deviation principles for pattern-avoiding permutations, and limit shapes for constra'] Let $H^{321}: \mathcal D \rightarrow [0,\infty]$ be defined as follows:
\[
        H^{321}(\pi_1, \pi_2) := \int_0^1 \!\! \left( \rho_1 \log \rho_1 + (1\!-\!\rho_1) \log (1\!-\!\rho_1)
                + \rho_2 \log \rho_2 + (1\!-\!\rho_2) \log (1\!-\!\rho_2) + 2 \log 2 \right) \mathrm{dLeb} ,
    \]
     where $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ are the densities of $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure\footnote{
     These densities do exist since elements of $\mathcal D$ are pairs of subuniform measures.
     }.

	For all $n \geq 1$, let $\sigma_{n, 321}$ be a random permutation chosen uniformly among $321$-avoiding permutations of size~$n$.
	Then, the associated pairs $\left( \pi_1^{\sigma_{n, 321}}, \pi_2^{\sigma_{n, 321}} \right)$ of measures
    satisfy a large deviation principle on $\mathcal D$ at speed $n$ with rate function $H^{321}.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop LDP_321_pi_intro of arXiv:2604.23751

body: Universal approximation theorems: for suitable activations, feedforward networks are dense in the continuous functions ON COMPACT SUBSETS of R^n in the uniform norm - given compact K, continuous f, and eps > 0, some network is within eps of f uniformly on K. The one-hidden-layer, arbitrary-width version holds precisely when the activation is continuous and non-polynomial (Cybenko, Hornik, Leshno-Lin-Pinkus-Schocken); bounded-width arbitrary-depth versions also exist. These are existence results only: they bound neither network size nor learnability, and no finite network approximates a nonperiodic-behaved function like sin uniformly on ALL of R.
title: Universal approximation theorem

\[
A_m^N(t)=
\frac{1}{(m-1)!}\sum_{i=0}^{t+1}(m+i-1)!\binom{N-m}{i}\genfrac{\{}{\}}{0pt}{}{m+t+1}{m+i}.
\]
Then, it holds that
\[
\sum_{t\geq -1} A_m^N(t)x^{t+1}
=
\prod_{q=N-m+1}^{N}\frac{1}{1-qx}.
\]

Let theta_hat_n be a maximizer over Theta of the log-likelihood L_n(theta) = sum_{i=1}^n log f(X_i;theta). Then theta_hat_n converges in probability to theta_0 as n -> infinity.

body: The modularity theorem, formerly the Taniyama-Shimura-Weil conjecture, states that every elliptic curve defined over the rational numbers is modular: its L-function agrees with the L-function of a weight-2 modular form for a congruence subgroup Gamma_0(N), equivalently the curve admits a nonconstant morphism from the modular curve X_0(N), where N is its conductor. Andrew Wiles, with Richard Taylor, proved the semistable case in 1994-95, which via the Frey curve and Ribet's theorem implied Fermat's Last Theorem; Breuil, Conrad, Diamond, and Taylor completed the full theorem for all rational elliptic curves in 2001.
title: Modularity theorem

body: [Lem 89 of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Consider any adapted sequence of random variables $(M_n)_{n\ge 0}$ defined on any filtered probability space $(\Omega, (\mathcal F_r)_{r\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}}, P),$ with $M_0=0$. Suppose that the increments of the process $M$ satisfy $\mathcal G(M,\lambda):=\sup_{r\ge 0} \|E[e^{2\lambda (M_{r+1}-M_r)}|\mathcal F_r]\|_{L^\infty(\Omega,\mathcal F_r,P)}<\infty.$ Then $E[e^{\lambda M_r}]\leq e^{\frac12 r\log \mathcal G(M,\lambda)}$ for all $r\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$.

Fix d>=2 and the normalized zonal basis P_l for S^(d-1). Positive definite means nonnegative P_l coefficients; strictly positive definite means all coefficients through the degree are positive. For a nonconstant polynomial g with all roots in [-1,1), call g conductive when its Hermite interpolant H(a,g) is positive definite for every absolutely monotonic a on [-1,1), and strictly conductive when additionally, for every strictly absolutely monotonic a, H(a,g) has degree deg(g)-1 and strictly positive coefficients. Absolute monotonicity includes the zeroth derivative; strict absolute monotonicity requires every derivative positive in (-1,1). If g1 and g2 are conductive and g1 is positive definite, then g1 g2 is conductive. If g1 is conductive and strictly positive definite and g2 is strictly conductive, then g1 g2 is strictly conductive. All roots of g1 and g2 must lie in [-1,1). Common roots are allowed and their multiplicities add.
fixed d>=2 and its zonal-coefficient positivity convention
g1,g2 nonconstant real polynomials; all roots in [-1,1)
ordinary branch: g1,g2 conductive and g1 positive definite
strict branch: g1 conductive and strictly positive definite; g2 strictly conductive

body: [Theorem thm:wp of arXiv:2609.00672, 'Deciding superellipticity and computing the Weierstrass normal form'] Let $C: y^n=h(x)$ with $h$ separable of degree $m\ge 2$ and $g\ge 2$, and let $P$ lie above a root of $h$. Then $P$ is a Weierstrass point of $C$ if and only if $m\ge 3$. If $m=2$, the vanishing sequence at $P$ is $(0,1,\dots,g-1)$.

body: Let Z be a nonnegative random variable with 0 < E[Z^2] < infinity. Then for every theta in [0,1], P(Z > theta E[Z]) >= (1 - theta)^2 (E[Z])^2 / E[Z^2]. This second-moment anti-concentration bound gives a lower bound on the probability that Z is not much smaller than its mean, complementing upper-tail concentration inequalities. [standard, e.g. Alon and Spencer, The Probabilistic Method]
title: Paley-Zygmund Inequality

body:
[Theorem lem:8 of arXiv:2510.13572, 'Coalescence in Markov chains'] \mbox{\hfil}
\begin{letlist}
\item
We have that $1\in K(P)$ if and only if $P\in\mathcal{P}_S$ is aperiodic. 
In this case, $k(\mu_{\text{\rm ind}})=1$.
\item
If $P\in\mathcal{P}_S$ has period $d$, then the coalescence classes of $\mu_{\text{\rm ind}}$
are a.s.\ the cyclic classes of $P$ and therefore  $k(\mu_{\text{\rm ind}})=d$.
Hence, $d\in K(P)$, and moreover $d\le k$ for all $k\in K(P)$. 
\end{letlist} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem lem:8 of arXiv:2510.13572

For f in L^1(R^n) define the Fourier transform F f (xi) = integral over R^n of f(x) exp(-2 pi i x . xi) dx, a bounded continuous function vanishing at infinity. If F f is also in L^1(R^n), then f(x) = integral over R^n of F f (xi) exp(2 pi i x . xi) d xi for almost every x; in particular f agrees almost everywhere with a continuous function, and the identity holds at every point of continuity of f. With this normalisation no constant appears; with the convention exp(-i x . xi) the inverse carries the factor (2 pi)^{-n}.
f in L^1(R^n)
the transform F f is in L^1(R^n) (this is the hypothesis that fails for, say, the indicator of an interval)

[Definition 8 of arXiv:2511.16973, '2511.16973'] (Pathwise uniqueness)
The solution of SDE \eqref{ii1.5} is said to be pathwise unique if, for any two solutions $X$ and $\tilde{X}$ satisfying \eqref{ii1.5} with the same initial value $X_0=\tilde{X}_0$, it holds that
$$
\mathbf{P}\left(X_t=\tilde{X}_t,~~\text{for~all}~ t\in[0,\tau\wedge\tilde{\tau}]\right)=1,
$$
where $\tau$ is the stopping time defined as in Definition \ref{Def of weak solu} for $X$, and $\tilde{\tau}$ is defined analogously for $\tilde{X}$.
title: Definition 8 of arXiv:2511.16973

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; T419-C021 v1, proof (unaudited), no novelty claimed. Let Delta=u w^T be a real m-by-p nonzero rank-one target, ||u||=1, w nonzero. Let X be p-by-n full row rank, and let Z=Delta X exactly, without label noise. Set C=XX^T/n, lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op. Initialize b0=0 and any finite a0 in R^p with g0=w^T C a0 nonzero. Put

 q0=w^T C w/2>0,
 J=||a0||^2+1,
 R=||Delta||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=J+2R,
 ell=||Delta C||op=||C w||.

Choose one constant step

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/(6Kc+ell)}.

Then simultaneous empirical factor GD has, for every t>=1,

 q_t:=||(b_t a_t^T-Delta) C^(1/2)||F^2/2
 <=q0 exp[-eta^3 lambda g0^4(t-1)/(8q0 cK)],

and therefore

 ||b_t a_t^T-Delta||F^2
 <=(2q0/lambda)exp[-eta^3 lambda g0^4(t-1)/(8q0 cK)].

This is fitting from the prescribed zero output factor at arbitrary input-factor scale; it does not require near-identity covariance or a spectral initializer. Moreover, let x_i iid N(0,I_p), z_i=Delta x_i with zero label noise, and independently a0~N(0,s^2 I_p), s>0. The design is full row rank and g0 is nonzero almost surely when n>=p. Choosing a measurable safe constant step from the displayed bounds gives almost-sure product convergence. If n>p+3, a data-only integrable bound from Gaussian inverse-covariance moments gives lim_(t->infinity) E||b_t a_t^T-Delta||F^2=0, matching rank-one reduced-rank regression exactly. This includes genuine input/output rank-one bottlenecks m,p>=2 but only the noiseless infinite-iteration boundary; it does not establish positive-noise risk, a finite statistical stopping rule, or an initializer-independent step.
Nonzero rank-one target and exactly noiseless labels; full-row-rank design
Nonzero initial sample-gradient projection, automatic almost surely for independent nondegenerate Gaussian input-factor initialization
Measurable constant step chosen from the data and realized initializer and meeting both displayed bounds
For expectation: independent standard Gaussian inputs, n>p+3; comparison is a limit of expected risks with the zero RRR benchmark

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:a517dfacbe854900793b396a41507cb858c54b4ae19e9e9d120170b81523d3c1","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/a5/a517dfacbe854900793b396a41507cb858c54b4ae19e9e9d120170b81523d3c1.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:eea7b56f6d534a3fb9ffe2ae8cebd9697697adad861140d4d084e21f5b7966f5","bundle_entry_key":"noiseless-risk","bundle_id":"population.t419-rank-one-fixed-step-margin-and-noiseless-risk-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"LoRA rank-one convergence and deficiency margins","draft":"w705/bundle_010.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.lowrank:lora-rank-one-noiseless-empirical-gd-all-scales-expected-risk","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T419-C021 v1: proper rank-one noiseless empirical GD, all scales and limiting expected risk

Kind: narrowed. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.
This is a genuine input/output rank-one bottleneck when m,p>=2, but it is the zero-label-noise boundary of Target 2 and an infinite-iteration risk statement. Positive label noise remains open. The step depends on the realized initialization and data. The known deficiency-margin method and zero-output invariant subspace are credited in C020; the boundedness proof is C014, and integrable Gaussian covariance moments are proved in C018.

## Deterministic statement with arbitrary full-row-rank design

Let Delta=u w^T be a real m-by-p nonzero rank-one target, ||u||=1, w nonzero. Let X be p-by-n full row rank, and let Z=Delta X exactly, without label noise. Set C=XX^T/n, lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op. Initialize b0=0 and any finite a0 in R^p with g0=w^T C a0 nonzero. Put

 q0=w^T C w/2>0,
 J=||a0||^2+1,
 R=||Delta||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=J+2R,
 ell=||Delta C||op=||C w||.

Choose one constant step

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/(6Kc+ell)}.

Then simultaneous empirical factor GD has, for every t>=1,

 q_t:=||(b_t a_t^T-Delta) C^(1/2)||F^2/2
 <=q0 exp[-eta^3 lambda g0^4(t-1)/(8q0 cK)],

and therefore

 ||b_t a_t^T-Delta||F^2
 <=(2q0/lambda)exp[-eta^3 lambda g0^4(t-1)/(8q0 cK)].

This is fitting from the prescribed zero output factor at arbitrary input-factor scale; it does not require near-identity covariance or a spectral initializer.

## Deterministic proof

C014 applies to this covariance quadratic, with W=Delta and r=1. It gives loss descent, q_t<=q0 and ||b_t||^2+||a_t||^2<=K at every step. The output-space invariant gives b_t=beta_t u. The squared initial gradient norm is g0^2, so

 q1<=q0-(eta/2)g0^2<q0.

Write h=sqrt(2q0)=||w C^(1/2)||. The nonnegative first-step loss also implies eta g0^2<=h^2. For all t>=1, monotonic loss and the reverse triangle inequality in the C norm give

 ||beta_t a_t C^(1/2)||
 >=h-sqrt(2q_t)>=h-sqrt(h^2-eta g0^2)
 >=eta g0^2/(2h).

Since ||a_t C^(1/2)||^2<=cK, this implies

 beta_t^2>=eta^2 g0^4/(8q0 cK)=:b_lower^2>0.

Furthermore grad_a q=beta_t C(beta_t a_t-w), and C^2>=lambda C. Consequently ||grad q_t||F^2>=2 lambda beta_t^2 q_t. Descent gives q_(t+1)<=(1-eta lambda b_lower^2)q_t. The multiplier is nonnegative because b_lower^2<=beta_t^2<=K and eta lambda K<=1/6. Iteration proves the stated bound. This does not require singular values of a rectangular a_t to bound every residual; instead the scalar output coefficient is bounded below by the first-step margin.

## Gaussian zero-noise consequence and the comparator

Let x_i iid N(0,I_p), let z_i=Delta x_i exactly, and independently a0~N(0,s^2 I_p), s>0. If n>=p, the design has full row rank almost surely; conditional on X, g0=w^T C a0 is a nondegenerate Gaussian scalar because C w is nonzero. Thus g0 is nonzero almost surely. A measurable safe step can be chosen from the displayed quantities, and the deterministic theorem proves product convergence to Delta almost surely.

For the expected-risk assertion assume n>p+3. The data-only bound from C014 is

 ||b_t a_t^T-Delta||F^2<=2R^2+2||Delta||F^2,

where q0 and R do not depend on a0. Since q0<=c||Delta||F^2/2,

 R<=||Delta||F(1+sqrt(c/lambda)),
 2R^2+2||Delta||F^2
 <=||Delta||F^2[6+4||C||op||C^(-1)||op].

C018's elementary Gaussian column-distance proof gives

 E||C^(-1)||op^2<=n^2p^2/[(n-p-1)(n-p-3)],
 E||C||op^2<=p^2+2p/n.

Cauchy-Schwarz makes the envelope integrable. Dominated convergence on the joint data/initializer space now gives

 lim_(t->infinity) E||b_t a_t^T-Delta||F^2=0.

The unique unconstrained empirical coefficient product is Delta because X has full row rank. Since Delta has rank one, it is also the rank-one reduced-rank-regression product, whose population excess risk is zero. Thus limiting expected risk matches the rank-one RRR benchmark exactly in this noiseless proper-bottleneck family. The statement includes arbitrarily large samples satisfying n>=C0(p+m) for every fixed proposed constant C0, with signal condition number one.

## Limits and attribution

This proves the zero-noise boundary, not any positive-noise interval: positive noise breaks the exact rank-one output subspace and the scalar factor argument. A zero benchmark requires an infinite-iteration comparison; no finite-step exact recovery is claimed, consistently with C006. The safe step is initialization-dependent, consistently with C013. The Gaussian covariance second-moment condition is sufficient and is not claimed sharp. The method is an elementary combination of published margin/invariance ideas and the saved boundedness estimate; specialist-level novelty and independent audit are unresolved.


Full deterministic C014 component:
# T419-C014 v1: empirical GD boundedness with an initialization-dependent step

Kind: bound. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.
This is an explicit anisotropic version of the published Gram-imbalance/descent method, not a solution of Target 2. It proves a trajectory component without assuming the iterates are bounded. The prior source is Du-Hu-Lee, arXiv:1806.00900, Theorem 2.2 and Appendix B, Claim B.1; its full convergence theorems have different initialization/step hypotheses. C009 already identifies the exact covariance metric and C010 the positive-noise empirical landscape.

## Statement

Let C be any real positive definite p-by-p matrix, D any real m-by-p matrix, and r>=1. Put lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op, ell=||D||op, W=D C^(-1), and

 q(B,A)=(1/2)||(BA-W) C^(1/2)||F^2,

with B m-by-r and A r-by-p. This is the empirical regression objective up to a constant when C=XX^T/n and D=ZX^T/n. Initialize at any finite deterministic factors B0,A0, and define

 q0=q(B0,A0), J=||A0 A0^T-B0^T B0||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R), L=6Kc+ell.

For any fixed

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/L},

simultaneous ordinary factor GD satisfies, for every integer t>=0,

 q_t<=q0,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=K,
 ||(A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t)-(A0 A0^T-B0^T B0)||F<=2eta q0<1,
 sum_(t>=0) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/eta.

In particular the gradient tends to zero, every accumulation point is critical, and for every integer T>=1,

 min_(0<=t<T) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/(eta T).

All constants are finite and computable from C,D and the initialization. There is no Gaussian assumption and no low-rank assumption on W. No iterate-convergence, saddle-avoidance or statistical-risk assertion is included.

## Exact identities and product/factor bounds

Let G=BA C-D. The two factor gradients are G_B=G A^T and G_A=B^T G. With E_t=A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t the first-order cross terms cancel exactly, giving

 E_(t+1)-E_t=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B),
 ||E_(t+1)-E_t||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2).

This cancellation only uses dependence on BA and does not require isotropic C. Also

 (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2
 <=r [||AA^T-B^TB||F^2+4||BA||F^2].

To verify it, write P=B^TB,Q=AA^T. Scalar trace Cauchy-Schwarz gives (tr(P+Q))^2<=r tr((P+Q)^2), and cyclicity of trace gives tr((P+Q)^2)=||P-Q||F^2+4 tr(PQ), tr(PQ)=||BA||F^2. No commutation is assumed.

When q<=q0, positivity of C gives ||BA-W||F<=sqrt(2q0/lambda), hence ||BA||F<=R. If additionally ||E-E0||F<=1, then ||E||F<=J, so the preceding trace bound implies

 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2<=sqrt(r) sqrt(J^2+4R^2)<=K.

The initialization meets these conditions and therefore has pair norm at most sqrt(K).

## Descent established before closing the boundedness induction

Suppose at the current iterate the pair norm is at most sqrt(K), and preceding steps have valid descent inequalities. Then

 ||grad q||F<=||BA C-D||op sqrt(||B||F^2+||A||F^2)
             <=(Kc/2+ell)sqrt(K).

Because eta<=1/(6Kc+ell), the proposed next point has pair norm at most 2sqrt(K). The connecting segment also lies in that ball. On that ball the Hessian quadratic form in a perturbation (dB,dA) is

 ||(dB A+B dA) C^(1/2)||F^2+2<BA C-D,dB dA>.

Its absolute value is at most

 [c(||A||op^2+||B||op^2)+||BA C-D||op]
 times (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2)
 <=[4Kc+(2Kc+ell)] (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2).

Here the first summand uses Cauchy-Schwarz on dB A+B dA; the cross term uses |<G,dB dA>|<=||G||op||dB||F||dA||F. Thus the Hessian operator norm on the segment is at most L. Taylor's theorem along that segment proves

 q_next<=q-eta||grad q||F^2+(L eta^2/2)||grad q||F^2
        <=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2.

In particular q_next<=q0. Telescoping the descent inequalities, including the proposed step, and using q>=0 yields

 sum_(j=0)^t eta^2||grad q_j||F^2<=2eta q0
 <=2q0/(1+2q0)<1.

Summing the imbalance increments now proves ||E_next-E0||F<=2eta q0<1. The product/factor bound therefore puts the endpoint back in the smaller ball of pair radius sqrt(K). This closes the induction without assuming a bound before proving descent on the required larger segment. The q0=0 case is included: both gradients vanish, the sequence is constant, and all inequalities still hold.

## Consequences and exact remaining gap

Telescoping for every finite horizon gives the infinite summability bound. A nonnegative summable sequence tends to zero, so the gradients vanish. Bounded finite-dimensional factor pairs have convergent subsequences; gradient continuity makes every subsequential limit critical. The running-minimum bound follows by averaging the finite sum. These statements do not require that the entire sequence converges to one point.

For B0=0 and a Gaussian A0, this provides an allowed positive step after observing the initialization, conditional on every full-row-rank design. It does not supply a single positive step independent of the unbounded Gaussian initializer. C013 shows that unconditional expected-limit risk with such an initialization-independent fixed step can diverge even at rank one.

Combining this bound with the already verified empirical strict-saddle landscape C010 is insufficient to conclude global optimization. One must additionally show that the specified zero/Gaussian initialization does not approach a nonglobal critical point, with all hypotheses of a saddle-avoidance theorem checked for its lower-dimensional initial support and step rule. Vanishing gradients do not establish that. Even convergence almost surely would not by itself justify passing to expected population risk; a failure-tail/integrability or finite-stopping argument is separately required. The usual full-ambient absolutely-continuous random-initialization theorem cannot simply be cited for the plane B0=0.

Independent reviewer audit and any novelty assessment remain pending. This is a deterministic bound recorded as a component, not an advertised new theorem or a completed target.


Gaussian covariance moment proof from C018:

Let G=X^T be the n-by-p standard Gaussian design. For each column j let d_j be its distance from the span of the other p-1 columns. Almost surely these spans have dimension p-1. The j-th row of the left pseudoinverse G^+ has squared norm d_j^(-2): it is the normalized residual vector of column j after orthogonal projection onto the other columns. Consequently

 sigma_min(G)^(-2)<=||G^+||F^2=sum_j d_j^(-2),
 sigma_min(G)^(-4)<=p sum_j d_j^(-4).

Conditional on the other columns, d_j^2 is chi-squared with k=n-p+1 degrees of freedom, by Gaussian orthogonal projection. Its density is t^(k/2-1)e^(-t/2)/(2^(k/2) Gamma(k/2)). Direct integration gives, for k>4,

 E[d_j^(-4)]=1/[(k-2)(k-4)].

No independence between different d_j is assumed. Therefore

 E||C^(-1)||op^2
 <= n^2 p^2/[(n-p-1)(n-p-3)]<infinity.

Also ||C||op<=tr C and the sum of np independent squared standard Gaussians gives

 E||C||op^2<=E[(tr C)^2]=p^2+2p/n.

Cauchy-Schwarz now proves E[||C||op||C^(-1)||op]<infinity. The first inverse moments are finite by the second-moment bound, and tr(C^(-1))<=p||C^(-1)||op. This proves that the data-only dominating variable 2R^2+2||Delta||F^2 is integrable, including in the zero-noise case.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:31df2697a2e9485bb0f8e5639b0c673923bc78174d5c4524ff753358cd6cc4ab","revision_digest":"sha256:21c6842180ec6ca8f1000ef2b6555029537399fe396caf4bb9b4cf553b55014c","source_id":"owner-work:w705:T419-C021:v1","source_revision":"as-read-2026-10-20","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: In mathematics, specifically in real analysis, the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem, named after Bernard Bolzano and Karl Weierstrass, is a fundamental result about convergence in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space . The theorem states that each infinite bounded sequence in has a convergent subsequence. An equivalent formulation is that a subset of is sequentially compact if and only if it is closed and bounded. The theorem is sometimes called the sequential compactness theorem.
title: Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem

Let P be a finite poset, R a nonzero commutative ring with 1, Q a subset with the induced order and T_P f(x) = sum over y <=_P x of f(y). Then res_Q(T_P f) = T_Q(res_Q f) for every f: P -> R if and only if Q is a down-set of P. Consequently Moebius inversion inside Q applied to the restricted global transform returns res_Q f for every f exactly for down-sets. The top element of a two-element chain is order-convex but not a down-set and fails.
P finite
R a nonzero commutative ring with 1

Then E X=0, E X^2=1 and E X^4=9/5, but E exp(zX)=infinity for every real z!=0. Thus isotropy and finite fourth moments alone do not define an exponential tilt average near zero. Let (X,nu) and (Omega,tau) be probability spaces and sigma in L2(nu times tau). Let H(x,xprime)=E_theta~tau sigma(x,theta)sigma(xprime,theta) be the input kernel, U(theta,thetaprime)=E_x~nu sigma(x,theta)sigma(x,thetaprime) the feature kernel, and mu_j>=0 their ordered common nonzero eigenvalues with input eigenfunctions psi_j. Let D be the spectral target space spanned by the psi_j, and fix a deterministic f in D and a cutoff M>=0. Write g=P_>M f and h(theta)=E_x~nu[g(x)sigma(x,theta)]. Then E_theta~tau h(theta)^2=<g,Hg>=sum_(j>M) mu_j|<f,psi_j>|^2<=mu_(M+1)||g||_2^2=||U_>M||_op||g||_2^2. Interpret mu_(M+1)=0 beyond a finite spectrum. For independent theta_i drawn from tau and Vtail_i=h(theta_i), E||Vtail||_2^2<=N mu_(M+1)||g||_2^2. The target is fixed independently of the sampled features; no spectral-gap or asymptotic feature-count condition is needed for this expectation identity.

body: In set theory, the constructible universe, denoted by is a particular class of sets that can be described entirely in terms of simpler sets. is the union of the constructible hierarchy . It was introduced by Kurt Gödel in 1938, who proved that the constructible universe is an inner model of ZF set theory, and also that the axiom of choice and the generalized continuum hypothesis are true in the constructible universe. This shows that both propositions are consistent with the basic axioms of set theory, if ZF itself is consistent. Since many other theorems only hold in systems in which one or both of the propositions is true, their consistency is an important result.
title: Constructible universe

[Proposition eq:cutoff-event of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:quenched-cutoff}
Fix \(0\le\varepsilon<1/2\) and a Borel set \(B\subset\mathbb R\), with no
independence, identical-distribution, density, or genericity condition.
Set
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon}
 =\left\{\max_{I\in[N]^p}|J_I|
 \le N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\right\},\qquad
 \delta_{N,\varepsilon}
 =\mathbb P(\mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon}^c),
\end{equation}
and, whenever the conditioning event has positive probability, write
\(\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}
:=\mathbb P(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon})\).  If merely
\(\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1)\), then the event has positive probability
for all sufficiently large \(N\), and
\[
 \left\lVert\nu-\nu'\right\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
 :=\sup_A\left\lvert\nu(A)-\nu'(A)\right\rvert
\]
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \left\|
 \mathcal L_{\mathbb P}\bigl(Q_N^J(B)\bigr)
 -\mathcal L_{\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}}
 \bigl(Q_N^J(B)\bigr)
 \right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le\delta_{N,\varepsilon}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every deterministic sequence \(a_N\), every
\(\eta>0\), and every bounded measurable
\(\varphi:[0,\infty]\to\mathbb R\),
\begin{align}
 &\left|
 \mathbb P\bigl(\left\lvertQ_N^J(B)-a_N\right\rvert>\eta\bigr)
 -\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}
  \bigl(\left\lvertQ_N^J(B)-a_N\right\rvert>\eta\bigr)
 \right|
 \le\delta_{N,\varepsilon},\\
 &\left|\mathbb E\varphi(Q_N^J(B))
 -\mathbb E_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}\varphi(Q_N^J(B))\right|
 \le2\left\lVert\varphi\right\rVert_\infty\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1).
 
\end{align}
In particular, convergence of \(Q_N^J(B)\) in probability to a
deterministic limit is equivalent under the original and conditioned
laws.

The hypothesis \(\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1)\) follows, for example,
from the marginal bound
\[
 \sup_{I\in[N]^p}\mathbb E\exp(J_I^2/K^2)\le2,
\]
which requires no independence and gives
\begin{equation}
 \delta_{N,\varepsilon}
 \le2N^p\exp\{-K^{-2}N^{1-2\varepsilon}\}=o(1).
\end{equation}
Mean comparison needs only a separate integrability input.  In
particular, if \(0\le Q_N^J(B)\le M_N\) almost surely and
\(M_N\delta_{N,\varepsilon}\to0\), then
\begin{equation}
 \left|\mathbb E Q_N^J(B)
 -\mathbb E_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}Q_N^J(B)\right|
 \le M_N\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1).
\end{equation}
The critical-count ceiling \({\rm(CC)}_p\) is sufficient, with
\[
 M_N=\frac1N\log(1+D_{N,p})=O(1).
\]
Algebraic genericity gives the explicit \(N\)-independent choice
\begin{equation}
 M_N=M_p:=
 \log(p-1)+\log\left(1+\frac2{p-2}\right).
\end{equation}

[Definition The distributions $\wishart$ and $\gaussmat$ of arXiv:2602.11129, 'Information-Theoretic Thresholds for Bipartite Latent-Space Graphs Under Noisy Observation'] We let $\mathbb{W}(n, m, p, d)$ be the distribution over $n \times m$ matrices with entries in $\{0,1\}$ obtained as follows. Sample independent random vectors $ \mathbf{X}_{\text{R}}  = (\mathbf{x}_{u})_{u \in R}$ and $ \mathbf{X}_{\text{L}}  = (\mathbf{x}_{u})_{u \in L}$ from the standard $d$-dimensional Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I}_d)$.
    Define further the threshold $\tau = \tau(d, p)$ such that for any $u \in L, v \in R$, we have $
        \Prnop{d^{-1/2}\langle \mathbf{x}_u, \mathbf{x}_v \rangle \le \tau} = p.
    $
    Then, after drawing $(\mathbf{x}_{u})_{u \in R}$ and $(\mathbf{x}_{u})_{u \in L}$,  determine each entry of $W\sim \mathbb{W}(n, m, p, d)$ by thresholding\footnote{Instead of thresholding using the indicator $d^{-1/2}\langle \mathbf{x}_u, \mathbf{x}_v \rangle \le \tau$, we could also use $d^{-1/2}\langle \mathbf{x}_u, \mathbf{x}_v \rangle \ge \tau$ instead and our results would remain valid, up to some flipped signs. } $$
        W_{u, v} \coloneqq \mathds{1}( d^{-1/2} \langle \mathbf{x}_u, \mathbf{x}_v \rangle \le \tau).
    $$
    Moreover, we define $\ \mathbb{M}(n, m, p)$ as as the distribution over $n \times m$ matrices with entries in $\{0,1\}$ where each entry is an i.i.d. sample from the $\mathsf{Bern}(p)$ distribution.
title: The distributions $\wishart$ and $\gaussmat$

CAMPAIGN RESULT [independently checked proof; E0095-CYCLE v2; no novelty claim]. For even n>=8, among new-edge perfect matchings on C_n, the score tr(P_E L_M), where E is the original two-dimensional Fiedler eigenspace, is uniquely maximized by antipodal edges. The resulting ordinary SRW gap is (2-2cos(4pi/n))/3. Its absolute gap is zero for n=2 mod4 and (2-2cos(2pi/n))/3 for n=0 mod4. Both heuristic-to-optimal spectral-gap ratios tend to zero along even cycles, since admissible random matchings supply a uniformly positive absolute gap with high probability. This refutes relying only on original slow modes; it does not refute adaptive mode methods.

[Theorem thm:level-line-contains-Wulff of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Fix any $L$ and $n \geq 1$, and consider the \ensuremath{\mathbb Z\textsc{gff}}\xspace on an $L \times L$ box.\footnote{Here, we do not require that $L\notin {\ensuremath{\mathscr B}}$.} Recall that $H = H(L) := \max\{ h : {\widehat\pi}_\infty(\phi_o\geq h) \geq 5\beta / L\}$ and $N_n = N_n(L) := 1/ {\widehat\pi}_\infty(\phi_o \geq H+1-n)$. Then, w.h.p., we have
		\[\ensuremath{\mathcal E}_n(L{\ensuremath{\mathscr L}}(\ell_n^*(1+(\log L)^{-5/3}), -(H+1-n)\kappa_{n,15}))\,.\]
		In particular, if $x$ is a point on the bottom boundary of $\Lambda$ at distance at least, say, $L/10$ from the corners, then 
		\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
			\item  the vertical distance of $\mathfrak{L}_{n}$, the $(H+1-n)$ level line, from $x$ is at most $N_n^{1/3} (\log L)^{16}$;
			\item by the upper bound of (eq:LD-ratio of the paper), the analogous distance of $\mathfrak{L}_{n+1}$ is at most \[N_{n+1}^{1/3}(\log L)^{16} \leq N_n^{1/3} \exp\Big(-c \sqrt{\beta\tfrac{\log L}{\log\log L}}\Big)\,.\]
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:surface-tension-properties of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] The above limits for $\tau = \tau_{\beta, n}$ or $\tau_\beta$ exist and satisfy the following properties:
		\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
			\item The convergence of the limit is uniform over all unit vectors ${\vec{\mathsf{n}}}$.
			
			\item $\tau$ is analytic as a function from $\mathbb R^2$ to $\mathbb R^2$
			
			\item $\tau$ is strictly convex, i.e., for any two vectors ${\ensuremath{\mathsf u}}, \mathsf v$ pointing in different directions, 
			\[\tau({\ensuremath{\mathsf u}}) + \tau(\mathsf v) > \tau({\ensuremath{\mathsf u}} + \mathsf v)\,.\]
			
			\item $\tau$ is symmetric under rotations by $\pi/4$, reflections across the $x,y$ axes and diagonals $y = \pm x$.
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2606.11271, '\LARGE The $K$-th nearest neighbor random walk on a Poisson point process gets trapped'] Assume that Assumption (BS) holds.
Let $(X_n)_{n \ge 1}$ be a $K$-th nearest neighbor random walk in dimension $d=1$. 
Then there exists a constant $\kappa_0 \in (0,+\infty)$, depending only on $M$, such that for any $k \in \N^\ast$,
\[
\P \big[ \sup_{n \ge 0} |X_n| \ge k \big] \le 2 e^{-\kappa_0 k}.
\]

[Proposition prop:shared of arXiv:2608.28007, 'Exact Risk Ratios for Weighted Data Selection in Linear Regression'] In the two-block case, suppose cross gradients occur and all cross types
share an endpoint, that is, all use the same $a_i$ or all use the same
$c_j$. Suppose also that no four gradients form a rank-$3$ positive circuit
and no five gradients positively span. Then a five-point strictly convex
selection achieves $\lVert \hat q\rVert^2\le1$.

[Lem distrib of arXiv:2412.09535, 'Local limit theorem for joint subgraph counts'] Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a downwards closed set of graphs, $n$ be a positive integer, and $\mathcal{F}$ be an $(\mathcal{H}, n, \eta)$-IFS. If we let $\eps > 0$ and $I_\eps = \prod_{H \in \mathcal{H}} [-n^{-v(H)/2+\eps}, n^{-v(H)/2+\eps}]$, then for $\bm{t} \in I_\eps$ we have
\[\abs{\varphi^\mathcal{F}_X(\bm{t}) - \varphi^\mathcal{F}_Z(\bm{t})} \lsim_{\lambda,\ell,\eps,\eta} n^{-1/2+4\eps}.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lemma lem:normal of arXiv:2503.21737, 'High-intensity Voronoi percolation on manifolds'] Assume that all sectional curvatures of \(M\) lie in \([-K,K]\), where \(K\) is a positive constant.
    Let \(x_0 \in M\) and \(\varphi \in \pazocal{E}(x_0,r)\) where
    \begin{equation}
    
        0 < r \leq \min\left\{\frac{r_\text{inj}(M)}{2} , \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{K}} \right\}.
    \end{equation}
    Then the following holds:
    \begin{enumerate}[(1)]
        \item \(\varphi_* \mathrm{d}_M(0,x) = \mathrm{d}_{\mathbb{R}^d}(0,x)\), for all \(x \in B_{\mathbb R^d}(0,r)\),
        \item \((1-Kr^2) \mathrm{d}_{\mathbb{R}^d}(x,y) \leq \varphi_* \mathrm{d}_M(x,y) \leq (1+Kr^2) \mathrm{d}_{\mathbb{R}^d}(x,y)\), for all \(x,y \in B_{\mathbb R^d}(0,r)\),
        \item \((1-Kr^2)^{d/2} |A| \leq \varphi_*\mu_M(A) \leq (1+Kr^2)^{d/2} |A|\), for all measurable \(A \subset B_{\mathbb R^d}(0,r)\), where \(|A|\) denotes the Lebesgue
        measure of \(A\).
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:normal of arXiv:2503.21737

body: Publication record. V. Vu conjectured (Conjecture 9.5 in Recent progress in combinatorial random matrix theory) that the probability that an n x n random sign matrix M_n has all its eigenvalues in the Gaussian integers Z[i] is 2^{-(1+o(1))n^2}. Y. Shmalo, Gaussian-integer spectra of random sign matrices (2026) constructs for every n >= 1 a family F_n of sign matrices with eigenvalues in Z[i] and |F_n| = 2^{ceil(n^2/2)} 3^{floor(n/2)}, so P(Spec(M_n) in Z[i]) >= 3^{floor(n/2)} 2^{-floor(n^2/2)}, which contradicts Conjecture 9.5. A matching upper bound remains open, and the adjacent conjecture for symmetric sign matrices is not settled. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/gaussian-integer-spectra (commit ab366902fb67). Not refereed.
title: Vu's Conjecture 9.5 contradicted: an n x n random sign matrix has all eigenvalues in the Gaussian integers with probability at least 3^floor(n/2) 2^-floor(n^2/2) (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/gaussian-integer-spectra)

Let d>=2 and N>=2 be integers, f:(0,4]->R any real-valued function, and C a set of N distinct points on S^(d-1). Let P_l^(d)(t) be the normalized real zonal spherical-harmonic polynomial of degree l, with P_l^(d)(1)=1 and P_0^(d)=1. For d>=3 these are the Gegenbauer polynomials of parameter (d-2)/2 normalized at1; for d=2 they are the Chebyshev polynomials T_l. Suppose h(t)=sum_(l=0)^L a_l P_l^(d)(t) is a polynomial with a_l>=0 for every l, and h(t)<=f(2-2t) for every -1<=t<1. For the ordered-pair energy E_f(C)=sum_(x,y in C,x!=y)f(||x-y||_2^2), one has E_f(C)>=N^2 a_0-N h(1). Equality holds exactly when every off-diagonal pair attains the minorant equality and, for each l>=1 with a_l>0, sum_(x,y in C)P_l^(d)(<x,y>)=0. This is the energy linear-programming bound in Proposition4.1, printedpp119-120/PDFpp21-22, of math/0607446v2, expressed using normalized zonal polynomials. No smoothness or monotonicity of f is needed for this bound itself.

[Theorem 21 of arXiv:2609.00448, 'Equivariant formality and representation theory'] Let $G$ be a compact connected Lie group of rank $n$, $S$ a torus subgroup of dimension being $n-1$, $T$ a maximal torus of $G$ containing $S$, $\mu\in \chi(T)$ a primitive character of $T$ such that $S=\text{ker }\mu$, $L$ a primitive weight in the weight lattice $\mathfrak{t}^*_\mathbb{Z}$ corresponding to $\mu$ after exponentiation, and $W$ the Weyl group of $G$. Define
	\[\Phi_L:=\left(\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}} wL\right)^{n(L)}\in \text{Sym}^*(\mathfrak{t}^*)^W,\]
	where $W_{[L]}$ is the stabilizer of $[L]:=\{\pm L\}\in \mathfrak{t}^*/\{\pm 1\}$, $n(L)=1$ or 2 depending on whether $\displaystyle\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}}wL$ is $W$-invariant or $W$-anti-invariant, i.e. 
	\[\displaystyle w'(\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}}wL)=\text{sgn}(w')\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}}wL\text{ for all }w'\in W.\] 
	Then $(G, S)$ is isotropy formal if and only if $\Phi_L\notin (f_1, \cdots, f_n)^2$, where $f_1, \cdots, f_n$ are the fundamental $W$-invariant homogeneous polynomials on $\mathfrak{t}$, i.e. $\text{Sym}^*(\mathfrak{t}^*)^W=\mathbb{R}[f_1, \cdots, f_n]$.
title: Theorem 21 of arXiv:2609.00448

Let n >= 5 and let K = Q(a_0, ..., a_{n-1}) be the field of rational functions in independent indeterminates. The general polynomial x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + ... + a_1 x + a_0 over K is not solvable by radicals: no root of it lies in any radical extension of K (a tower K = K_0 < K_1 < ... < K_m in which each K_{i+1} = K_i(r) with r^{k} in K_i for some k >= 1). The reason is Galois' criterion: a polynomial is solvable by radicals exactly when its Galois group is a solvable group, and the general polynomial has Galois group the full symmetric group S_n over K, which is not solvable for n >= 5. For n <= 4 such formulas exist.

[Theorem 35 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(Z\) be a connected normal complex space whose dense analytic
regular locus \(\cR\) carries a K\"ahler structure \((g,J)\).  Assume
that the analytic and metric topologies agree, that \(d|_{\cR}\) is the
intrinsic length distance, and that \((Z,d)\) is a complete locally
compact length space equal to the metric completion of \((\cR,g)\).
Assume also that \(Z\) is klt, that \(\omega_g\) extends locally as a
positive current with bounded potential, and that every point has a
local closed holomorphic embedding
\(V\hookrightarrow\Omega_V\subset\C^L\) for which
\begin{equation}
                     \omega_g\ge c_V\omega_{\C^L}
                     \quad\text{on }V\cap\cR.
\end{equation}
Let $G:Z\to\C^r$ be continuous and holomorphic, and
assume on $\cR$ that
\begin{equation}
 \nabla dG^a=0,\qquad
 \left[\langle dG^a,d\overline{G^b}\rangle_{g^{-1}}\right]_{a,b=1}^r
 \text{ is positive definite}.
\end{equation}
Then, after composing \(G\) with an element of
\(\mathrm{GL}(r,\C)\), without translating the target, there is a global
biholomorphic isometry
\begin{equation}
                         Z\cong\C^r\times Z'
\end{equation}
under which $G$ is the projection.  The factor $Z'$ is connected, complete,
normal, and klt; write \(g'\) for its induced regular K\"ahler metric.
It inherits the bounded-local-potential K\"ahler current
and the local ambient metric lower bound of $Z$, and
\begin{equation}
                         \Sing Z=\C^r\times\Sing Z'.
\end{equation}

If, in addition, $f$ is locally Lipschitz on $Z$, smooth on $\cR$, and
satisfies \(\Rc+\nabla^2f=g/2\) on $\cR$, then
\[
                 f(z,y)=\frac{|z|^2}{4}+\ell(z)+f'(y),
\]
where $\ell$ is real affine-linear and $f'$ is locally Lipschitz; if $f$
is proper, then $f'$ is proper.  If also
\begin{equation}
                         \int_{\cR}e^{-f}\,dV_g<\infty,
\end{equation}
then \(\int_{\Reg Z'}e^{-f'}\,dV_{g'}<\infty\).  Finally, assume that
the flow of \(\nabla f\) is complete and preserves \(\cR\), and that its
canonical self-similar maps extend to the metric completions.  Then the
same Euclidean factor is static on every negative-time slice in that
canonical gauge. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 35 of arXiv:2609.02878

PRIVATE MECHANISM NOTE, author-recorded. On the torus T_{n,d} with volume V, a critical cluster of size V^{2/3} has intrinsic geometry of a critical tree embedded four-dimensionally, so its Euclidean diameter is of order (V^{2/3})^{1/4} = V^{1/6}, while the torus side is V^{1/d}. Since V^{1/6} > V^{1/d} iff d > 6, above six dimensions the window clusters wrap around the torus many times and see the torus uniformly; this is why the exploration process should have the same global (mass-proportional) depletion as in G(n,p), which is what the multiplicative-coalescent scaling limit (Heydenreich-van der Hofstad Open Problems 13.3 and 13.5) needs. The torus plateau theorem (Hutchcroft-Michta-Slade) is the two-point version of this uniformity; the open step is the exploration-level (higher-point) version. Same reason makes eps >> V^{-1/3} lie above the correlation-length crossover eps >> V^{-2/d} for d > 6 (Open Problem 13.2).
Bernoulli percolation on the discrete torus, d > 6
Mean-field cluster geometry (intrinsic diameter m^{1/2}, Euclidean diameter m^{1/4})
title: Critical percolation clusters on the torus wrap around it exactly when d > 6, which is the mechanism behind mean-field (Erdos-Renyi-like) depletion

body: [Proposition 2.4.3 (Euler 1736) of arXiv:2308.04512, 'An introduction to graph theory'] Let G be a simple graph. Then, the sum of the degrees of all vertices of G equals twice the number of edges of G. In other words, ∑ v∈V(G) deg v = 2 · |E (G)| .

[Corollary 6 of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] Suppose that the hypotheses in Theorem \ref{Theorem: Main}
hold, and that $\msf T_0(t)$ has the asymptotic expansion in \eqref{Equation: Smooth Heat Trace}.
Let $t_1>t_2>\cdots>0$ be a vanishing sequence of positive numbers.
The following holds for any fixed $\ka>0$:
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item If $t_n\leq cn^{-1/2-\eps}$ for some fixed $c,\eps>0$, then
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}2\pi t_n\,\msf T_\ka(t_n)=\msf{A}(D)\qquad\text{almost surely}.\]
\item If $t_n\leq cn^{-1-\eps}$ for some fixed $c,\eps>0$, then
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}4\sqrt{2\pi t_n}\left(\tfrac{\msf{A}(D)}{2\pi}t_n^{-1}-\msf T_\ka(t_n)\right)=\msf{L}(\partial D)\qquad\text{almost surely}.\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 6 of arXiv:2507.06186

[Theorem thm:cox2charac of arXiv:2412.04589, 'Inverting the Markovian projection for pure jump processes'] Let $X$, $\mathbb{G}$, $(J_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}^*}$, $(\tau_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ and $(\lambda^k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}^*}$ be given by Theorem~(thm:cox of the paper). Furthermore, suppose that each $\lambda^k$ is predictable with respect to $\mathbb{G}$. Let $h: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a truncation function. Then, $X$ is a $\mathbb{G}$-It\^o semimartingale whose differential characteristics associated with $h$ are
	\begin{equation*}
		\beta_t = \mathbb{E}[h(J_1)] \lambda_t,\quad
		\alpha_t = 0,\quad
		\kappa_t(d\xi) = \lambda_t \nu(d\xi),
	\end{equation*}
	where $\nu$ is the law of $J_1$ and $\lambda_t \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^\infty \bm{1}_{\{\tau_{k-1} < t \leq \tau_k\}} \lambda^k_t$.
title: Theorem thm:cox2charac of arXiv:2412.04589

body:
[Theorem main of arXiv:2411.07737, 'On Asymptotic Behavior of Extinction Moment of Critical Bisexual Branching Process in Rand'] Let $N_n$ be a critical BBPRE with $N_0 = N$ pairs satisfying Conditions~(cond:mating-superadditive of the paper)~--~(cond:bbpre-criticality of the paper).
    Then, the extinction moment 
    $
        \tau = \min\{ n \in \mathbb{N} \ \left| \ N_n = 0 \right. \}
    $
    satisfies the relation
    \[
        \frac{ \tau }{ \ln^2 N } \xrightarrow[N \rightarrow \infty]{\mathrm{D}} \chi,
    \]
    where $\chi$ is a r.v. with the density
    \[
        p_{\chi}(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2 t^3}} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2 \sigma^2 t} \right) I\{ t \geq 0 \}.
    \]

body: In linear algebra, a QR decomposition, also known as a QR factorization or QU factorization, is a decomposition of a matrix A into a product A = QR of an orthonormal matrix Q and an upper triangular matrix R. QR decomposition is often used to solve the linear least squares (LLS) problem and is the basis for a particular eigenvalue algorithm, the QR algorithm.

[Author-checked campaign proof; blind audit pending w346.] For a two-state irreducible discrete-time chain with prescribed stationary law (p,q), p,q>0 and p+q=1, the minimum expected cover time from stationarity is (p^2+q^2)/min(p,q). The initial state is counted at time zero. The unique optimizer has conductance kappa=min(p,q), with P(0,1)=kappa/p and P(1,0)=kappa/q.
Two states
Discrete time
Initial state visited at time zero
Prescribed p,q>0

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT, independently checked proof, T326-w697-C03 v1; reviewer claude-738954b6 PASS on this exact version recorded in AUDITS_FROM_REVIEWER.tsv. Let C be a finite p by p positive semidefinite matrix, J a fixed m by p matrix, and L(v,U)=||(vU-J)C^(1/2)||_F^2/2. Train the scalar v and matrix U by Euclidean gradient flow with v_0>0 and delta=v_0^2-||U_0||_F^2. Assume delta>0, or delta=0 with the strict loss gap L(v_0,U_0)<L(0,0). If P projects onto range C and Q=I-P, put D=delta+||U_0Q||_F^2 and A=||JP||_F^2. Then the flow is global and converges to zero loss with v_infinity=sqrt((D+sqrt(D^2+4A))/2) and effective map G_infinity=JP+v_infinity U_0Q. The case C=0 is constant flow with the same formula. The invariants are v^2-||U||_F^2=delta and UQ=U_0Q. When delta=0, the strict loss gap Delta gives v^2>=Delta/||JC||_F>0; a PL estimate on the positive spectrum of C then proves exponential loss decay. In the square proxy J=I_d, z(w)=w, or augmented proxy J=[I_d,0], z(w)=(w,||w||^2/d+rho), C=(1/M)sum z(w_i)z(w_i)^T, use balanced isotropic initialization v_0=epsilon, U_0=epsilon J/sqrt(d), 0<epsilon<1. The initial effective map is epsilon^2 J/sqrt(d), giving the strict loss gap almost surely for iid Gaussian tasks. The selected map is JP+a_eff JQ, where a_eff=(epsilon/sqrt(d))*sqrt((D+sqrt(D^2+4A))/2), D=epsilon^2(1-A/d). For fixed epsilon and rho>=0, with Gaussian tasks and an independent fresh Gaussian task, M/d->kappa yields normalized new-task excess risk ->(1-kappa)_+; the small-epsilon limit is taken after training. Exactly zero factors are stationary. Balanced factors alone do not ensure convergence: for C=J=1, v_0=epsilon>0 and U_0=-epsilon, the invariant line U=-v gives v'=-v(1+v^2) and converges to the zero saddle. This is a scalar-times-matrix parameterization, not a claim about unrestricted raw K,Q,V training. The proof applies prior balanced-flow ideas and has 413 exact-rational checks plus 31 rational root brackets; no Lean certificate or broad novelty claim is asserted.
Finite-dimensional PSD C; stated Euclidean scalar and matrix coordinates
v_0>0; either positive delta, or balanced delta=0 and a strict initial loss gap
For the task-diversity law: fixed epsilon in (0,1), fixed rho>=0, iid Gaussian task pool and independent fresh Gaussian task, infinite context
Training time tends to infinity before dimension or vanishing initialization

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Explicit model calculation, comparison identities and remaining hypothesis obstruction Result: A necessary condition follows by comparing a finite lag with the infinite-lag independent limit: Cov(g(X0),h(Xt))>=0 for every bounded increasing g,h and every t>=0. A simple nonmonotone candidate fails decisively. For the stationary clockwise three-cycle with rate-one jumps and state values0,1,2, the centered state observable has covariance (2/3)*exp(-3t/2)*cos(sqrt3*t/2). At t=2pi/sqrt3 this is negative, so that chain cannot be the desired example. Check: The two nonconstant eigenvalues of the three-cycle generator are -3/2 plus or minus i*sqrt3/2. The centered observable has variance2/3 and equal conjugate Fourier weights; this independently yields the displayed covariance and sign. Obstruction: Positive pairwise association would still be weaker than the required all-dimensional supermodular order. No nonmonotone chain satisfying the full order, or proof that none exists, has been found. Reset chains do satisfy the order but are already stochastically monotone and therefore do not answer the source question.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0291-a-nonmonotone-markov-intensity-with-supermodular-time-ordering
No independent review

[Theorem thm:phase-transition of arXiv:2509.16541, 'Two-stage Bootstrap Percolation'] For the standard variant, if $q \ll p^2/(\log(1/p))^2$, then
    \[
    \mathbb{P}(\text{the origin is eventually in state 2}\, ) \to 1,
    \]
    and if $q\gg p^2$, then
    \[
    \mathbb{P}(\text{the origin remains forever in state 0}\, ) \to 1.
    \]
    For the modified variant, if $q \ll p^2/(\log(1/p))^2$, then
    \[
    \mathbb{P}(\text{the origin is eventually in state 1}\, ) \to 1,
    \]
    and if $q\gg p^2/\log(1/p)$, then
    \[
    \mathbb{P}(\text{the origin remains forever in state 0}\, ) \to 1.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:phase-transition of arXiv:2509.16541

   \begin{align}
   &\int_\mathcal{D} \mathcal{N}(\phi, \psi) z = - \int \mathcal{N}(\phi, z) \psi,    \\
   & \int_\mathcal{D} \mathcal{N}(\phi, \psi) \phi  =0,  \\
     &\int_\mathcal{D} \mathcal{N}(\phi, \Delta \phi) z = \int_D \nabla^\perp \phi \otimes \nabla^\perp \phi : \nabla \nabla^\perp z. 
    \end{align}
    By density, the bilinear operator $\mathcal{N}$ can be extended as an operator $\mathcal{N}:(W^{1,4}\cap V)\times L^4 \rightarrow V'$ so that (equation N-properties 3 of the paper) holds for all $\psi\in L^4, \phi \in W^{1,4}$. 
    Define also the operator $\mathcal{N}(\phi):= \mathcal{N}(\phi, \Delta \phi)$. Then continuously $\mathcal{N}: V^2\rightarrow V^{-2}$.

[Lemma lem:dgt4-weighted-last-visits of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Let $X$ be simple random walk started at the origin. For integers
	$0\leq i\leq j$, let
	\[
		I_{i,j}(X)
		\coloneqq
	\mathbf{1}_{\{X_i\ne X_r\text{ for every }r\text{ with }i<r\leq j\}}\, .
	\]
	Then, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, as $n\to\infty$,
	\[
		\max_{0\leq j\leq\lfloor(1-\varepsilon)n\rfloor}
		\mathbf E_0\left|
		G(0,0)\sum_{i=0}^j\frac{I_{i,j}(X)}{n-i}
		+\log\left(1-\frac jn\right)
		\right|\longrightarrow0\, .
	\]

[Lemma 4 (Graph-dependent input bound) of arXiv:2608.16701, 'Order-Sensitive Fast-Synapse Limits in Sparse Excitatory--Inhibitory Threshold--Reset Netw'] Let $M_1,\dots,M_N$ be arbitrary firing counts satisfying
\eqref{eq:firing-bound} through $T$, and set
$H_j=k_{\tau(q_j^N)}*dM_j$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\int_0^T
 \left|
 \sum_{j=1}^N J_{\tau(q_j^N)}
 \left(\frac{a_{ij}^N}{\lambda_N}-\frac1N\right)H_j(t)
 \right|dt
 \le C_{T,\mathrm{data}}\Delta_N,
 
\end{equation}
where the constant may depend on the fixed class, kernel, coupling, and
refractory data, but is independent of the graph and firing histories.
