Choose a bounded finite-rank operator F that vanishes on (ker T)^⊥ and maps ker T ONTO ker T* = (range T)^⊥ (possible because dim ker T ≥ dim ker T*); F is compact, so T + F = I − (K − F) is again identity minus compact. [Lemma 27 (Grand coupling for almost uniform measures) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Let $\epsilon>0$ and consider the set $\calM$
    of probability measures $\mu$ on $[0,1]$ such that
    $\mu\geq (1-\epsilon)\cdot\diffi x$ (the Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$)
    as measures.
    Then all distributions in $\calM$ can be coupled together in such a way that:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If $\mu$ is stochastically dominated by $\nu$, then $X_\mu\leq X_\nu$,
        \item With probability $1-\epsilon$, all the random variables $(X_\mu)_{\mu\in\calM}$ are equal.

[Theorem 4 (Non-equilibrium fluctuations) of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] Assume that the initial distributions
 	\(\{\mu^n\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}\) satisfy Assumptions
 	\ref{ass1}--\ref{ass4}.
 	Then the sequence \(\{\mathbb Q_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N} }\) is tight in
 	\( \mathcal D([0,T],(\mathscr S^\dagger)')\). Moreover, every limit point \(\mathbb Q\) is
 	concentrated on paths \(\{\bm Y_t:0\le t\le T\}\) satisfying the following
 	property.
 	
 	For every \(\bm f\in\mathscr S^\dagger\) and every \(t\in[0,T]\),
 	\[
 	\bm Y_t(\bm f)
 	=
 	\bm Y_0(S_t\bm f)
 	+
 	\mathcal W_t(\bm f),
 	\]
 	where \((S_t)_{t\ge0}\) is the semigroup generated by $ \mathcal A^\dagger =\Delta \mathrm I_2+M^\top $
    on \(\mathscr S^\dagger \), and $ \mathcal W_t(\bm f) $ is a mean zero Gaussian variable of variance
    \[
    \int_0^t
    Q_r\left(
    S_{t-r}\bm f,
    S_{t-r}\bm f
    \right)\,dr.
    \]
 	Moreover, $ \bm Y_0 $ and $ \mathcal W_t $ are uncorrelated in the sense that $ \mathbb{E}  \left[ \bm Y_0(\bm f)\mathcal W_t(\bm g)  \right] = 0 $ for all $ \bm f,\bm g \in \mathscr{S}^{\dagger } $. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: The variance of X is Var(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2] = E[X^2] - E[X]^2, the mean squared deviation; its square root is the standard deviation. Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X). The covariance Cov(X,Y) = E[(X-EX)(Y-EY)] = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] measures joint variation; Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X,Y), so variances add for uncorrelated (in particular independent) variables. The correlation is Cov(X,Y)/(sd(X) sd(Y)) in [-1, 1].

body:
Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks (version 19 August 2026), Question 17.18 (p. 575) asks whether a consistent equivariant flow rule admitting a stationary measure EQUIVALENT to Galton-Watson measure must induce an ergodic Markov chain; their Proposition 17.17 proves it when all child weights are strictly positive, and Exercise 17.22 gives a non-ergodic example whose stationary measure is only absolutely continuous, so equivalence is the point of the question. Our result (id P0033, 2026-09-08): NO. Take Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5 (mean 12/5) and an isomorphism-invariant colour in {0,1} defined by AND at two-child vertices and OR at three-child vertices; both preserve unanimity, so every vertex has at least one child of its own colour, and the flow chooses uniformly among those. Galton-Watson measure is stationary, the root colour is invariant along the chain and takes each value with probability 1/2 - a non-constant invariant function, hence no ergodicity - and the stationary measure equals Galton-Watson measure, trivially equivalent to it. The colour exists because F(p) = (3/5) p^2 + (2/5)[1 - (1-p)^3] fixes 1/2, and r_n = E[q_n^2] satisfies r_{n+1} = 3/10 + (3/5) r^2 + (2/5) r^3 whose increment factors as (r - 1/2)[(2/5) r^2 + (4/5) r - 3/5], driving r_n from r_0 = 1/4 up to 1/2 and giving E[q(1-q)] = 0. Verification as the source words it: the step the proof leaves implicit, and which was checked, is that Galton-Watson really is stationary - it holds because, conditioned on the children's colours, the child subtrees are independent, each distributed as Galton-Watson conditioned on its own colour, so the chosen subtree is exactly GW given colour = c, the uniform choice adds no bias, and mixing over c returns GW. Prior art unchecked; the tree-automaton and factor-of-iid literature is where to look.
Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5
consistent equivariant flow rule choosing uniformly among same-coloured children

[Lem lemma:free-energy-random-ferro of arXiv:2608.06500, 'Free energy of Ising models under a spectral condition'] Let $G_N^{(r)}=(\text{\boldmath $A$}_N^{(r)},{\boldsymbol 0})$ be a sequence of random
$k$-regular graphs ($k\ge 3$) distributed according to the
configuration model, with constant edge weight $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$, and let
$F^{(r)}_N(\gamma)$ be the free energy density of the shifted graph
$G_N^{(r)}(\gamma)$. If $|\beta|<1/(4\sqrt{k-1})$, then there exists
$\eta=\eta(\beta,k)>0$ such that

\begin{align}
|\gamma-k\beta|<\eta\;\; \Rightarrow\;\;
\lim_{N\to\infty}F^{(r)}_{N}(\gamma)= \phi(\beta) \mbox{ a.s.}\, .
\end{align}

If $\beta\ge0$, then we may take $\eta=1/(4\sqrt{k-1})$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In mathematics, the concept of a measure is a generalization and formalization of geometrical measures and other common notions, such as magnitude, mass, and probability of events. These seemingly distinct concepts have many similarities and can often be treated together in a single mathematical context. Measures are foundational in probability theory, integration theory, and can be generalized to assume negative values, as with electrical charge. Far-reaching generalizations of measure are widely used in quantum physics and physics in general.

[Lemma decay greens function of arXiv:2411.14350, 'Randomized Geodesic Flow on Hyperbolic Groups'] For $n\in \mathbb{N}$ big enough, there exist $\varepsilon,r >0$ such that for all $a,b\in G$ with $d_{{\mathcal G}}(a,o),d_{{\mathcal G}}(b,o)\geq n$ we have
\[{\mathcal G}(a,b;B_{n}^{{\mathcal G}}(o))\leq \exp\big[- rn \alpha {\rm e} ^{\varepsilon n}\big] {\mathcal G}(b,b^n)\]
where $b^n$ is a point on $[o,b)$ with $\lfloor d_{{\mathcal G}}(b^n,0)\rfloor =n$ and $\alpha= \angle([0,\psi(a)[0,\psi(b))$ is the angle between $[0,\psi(a))$ and $[0,\psi(b))$ in $\mathbb{H}^d$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma decay greens function of arXiv:2411.14350

body: In mathematics, the Gershgorin circle theorem may be used to bound the spectrum of a square matrix. It was first published by the Soviet mathematician Semyon Aronovich Gershgorin in 1931. Gershgorin's name has been transliterated in several different ways, including Geršgorin, Gerschgorin, Gershgorin, Hershhorn, and Hirschhorn.
title: Gershgorin circle theorem

body:
In the category of harmonic spectra $\mathcal{H} = L_{\bigoplus K(p,n)} \operatorname{Sp}$, there exist cohomological Bousfield classes that are not homological. Consequently, the category of harmonic spectra is not homologically stratified by its chromatic Balmer spectrum.
\mathcal{H} is the category of harmonic spectra
Localization is with respect to the sum of all Morava K-theories

body: [Definition 27 of arXiv:2609.02197, '2609.02197'] A space-time white noise is a family $($\gls{sto1}$_\varphi)_{\varphi \in L^2\left(\mathbb{R}_+\times \mathbb{T}^d\right)}$ of real random variables such that for every $h \in L^2\left(\mathbb{R}_+\times \mathbb{T}^d\right),\xi_h$ is normally distributed, $\mathds{E}\left[\xi_h\right]=0,$ and $\mathds{E}\left[\xi_h^2\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}_+\times \mathbb{T}^d}\left|h\left(q,x\right)\right|^2\,\mathrm{d}q\,\mathrm{d}x.$

[Corollary cor:one-dimensional-induced-space of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] The family $(Q_z)_{z\in Z}$ is Borel, $\Gamma$-equivariant and
uniformly Delone. It satisfies
\[
    \widehat{\delta}_{Q_z}
    =
    \frac{4}{a}\delta_0
    \qquad\text{on }
    \left(-\frac1a,\frac1a\right),
\]
and
\[
    Q_w=Q_z-u
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    u\in\Gamma
    \ \text{ and }\
    w=u.z.
\]
Consequently, $(\operatorname{Ind}_{\Gamma}^{\mathbb R}(Z),\mu_{\Gamma,Z})$
admits a generating stealthy Delone cross-section.

[Corollary 46 (Score-density sufficient condition) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Assume \(f\in L^4(\nu)\), \(\E_\nu f=0\),
\(\E_\nu f^2=1\), and that \(p\) is twice weakly differentiable.  In the
weighted norms
\[
        \|u\|_{f,1}:=\E_\nu |f(\zeta)|\,|u(\zeta)|,
        \qquad
        \|u\|_{f^2,1}:=\E_\nu |f(\zeta)|^2|u(\zeta)|,
\]
one has
\[
        \left\|\frac{p(\cdot-s)}{p(\cdot)}-1+s\frac{p'}{p}\right\|_{f,1}=o(|s|)
\]
and
\[
        \left\|\frac{p(\cdot-s)}{p(\cdot)}-1+s\frac{p'}{p}-\frac{s^2}{2}\frac{p''}{p}\right\|_{f^2,1}=o(s^2).
\]
Assume also \(\sup_{|s|\le s_0}\int |f(y)|^4p(y-s)\,dy<\infty\), with uniform integrability as \(s\to0\).  Then the weighted likelihood-ratio criterion applies with
\[
        \ell_1=-\frac{p'}{p},\qquad \ell_2=\frac{p''}{p}.
\]
For the Gaussian density, \(\ell_1(y)=y\) and \(\ell_2(y)=y^2-1\).

In a bounded Jordan domain with smooth marked boundary neighborhoods, assume curve tightness with simple interior limits, all fixed-buffer critical endpoint partition ratios equal to the normalized boundary conformal derivative to power 5/8, and convergence of that derivative along the actual buffer hulls. Finite restriction and positive outer-buffer transfer then give the smooth-hull avoidance law used by LSW Proposition 3.3 and Theorem 6.1 to identify SLE(8/3). None of the SAW tightness or ratio inputs is proved here. This is a distinct ensemble from P0003.
Curve metric is uniform modulo increasing reparameterization
Every subsequential limit is simple, connects the fixed marks, and otherwise lies in the domain
Closed buffers satisfy the two-sided positive metric neighborhood inclusions and preserve simple connectivity
For each fixed buffer, the critical two-endpoint partition-ratio limit exists and is the stated 5/8 derivative
Actual buffer derivatives converge
After mapping to H, traces are connected, unbounded, meet R only at 0, and have connected complement in C
The standard measurable passage from oriented simple traces to curve classes needs referee confirmation

Let A be a real m x n matrix and b a vector in R^m. Exactly one of the following holds: (i) there is x in R^n with x >= 0 (componentwise) and A x = b; (ii) there is y in R^m with A^T y >= 0 (componentwise) and b^T y < 0. Equivalent form: b lies in the cone C = { A x : x >= 0 } if and only if b^T y >= 0 for every y with A^T y >= 0. The lemma is the finite-dimensional theorem of the alternative behind linear-programming duality; the nontrivial ingredient is that a finitely generated cone in R^m is closed.

body:
[Defn Local sets of arXiv:2602.06011, 'Excursion decomposition of the XOR-Ising model'] A coupling $(\phi,A,\phi_A)$ between a GFF $\phi$ in $D$, a random closed set $A \subset \bar{D}$ and a distribution $\phi_A$ is called a \emph{local set (coupling)} if
\begin{itemize}
    \item the restriction of $\phi_A$ to $D\setminus A$ is almost surely harmonic,
    \item conditionally on $\mathcal F_A := \sigma(A,\phi_A)$, the field
    \[
        \phi^A := \phi - \phi_A
    \]
    is a GFF with zero boundary conditions in $D \setminus A$.
\end{itemize}
title: Local sets

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2606.11994, 'Sample Path Properties of the\\ Fractional Wiener--Weierstrass Bridge II'] Let $L\in\N$ be such that $\beta=b^L\ge3$.  Put
$     D_L=\{1,2,\ldots,\beta-2\}
$,
and
\[     S_L=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\xi_i \beta^{-i}:     \xi_i\in D_L\text{ for every }i\ge1\right\}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}     S_L\subset T_{2L},     
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}     \dimH S_L=\frac{\log(\beta-2)}{\log \beta}.     
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every
\begin{equation}     0<\eta<\frac{\log(\beta-2)}{\log \beta},     
\end{equation}
there is an atomless Borel probability measure $\mu_L$ supported on $S_L$
such that
\begin{equation}     \iint |t-s|^{-\eta}\,\mu_L(\dd t)\mu_L(\dd s)<\infty.     
\end{equation}

body: [Defn Matrix domination of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Let $A$ be a $n\times n$ matrix with real and positive entries and $B$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with complex entries. Then we say that $A$ \emph{dominates} $\lvert B \rvert$, denoted by $A \geq \lvert B\rvert$ (or $\lvert B \rvert \leq A$), if each entry of $A$ is  at least the modulus of the corresponding entry of $B$.
title: Matrix domination

body: Let P be the transition matrix of an irreducible, aperiodic Markov chain on a finite state space S. Then P has a unique stationary distribution pi, pi(x) > 0 for every x in S, and there exist constants C > 0 and rho in (0,1) such that max_{x in S} ||P^n(x, .) - pi||_TV <= C rho^n for every n >= 1; in particular P^n(x,y) converges to pi(y) as n tends to infinity for every x, y in S, regardless of the initial distribution. [Levin and Peres, Markov Chains and Mixing Times]
title: Convergence Theorem for Irreducible Aperiodic Finite Markov Chains

[Lemma lem:subcriticalproj of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Define the families of truncated decorated trees $\left(\mathbb{T}_H,o,i_{-}^{H},i_{+}^{H}\right)_{H \geq 0}$ as follows:
    Sample $(\mathbb{T},o)$ an unweighted Bienaymé-Galton-Watson tree of reproduction law $\pi$, set $\mathbb{T}_H=B_H(\mathbb{T},o)$ and   $(i_{-}^{H})(u,v)=0$ for every edge of $\mathbb{T}_H$ pointing towards the $H-$boundary. Then use Recursion~(equation eq:systemrecursionzoombis of the paper) to define $i_{-}^{H}$ on the remainder of $\mathbb{T}_H$. Proceed similarly for $i_{+}^{H}$ by setting $i_{+}^{H}=1$ on the boundary instead of $0$.

    Then under assuming that $t \mapsto \hat{\phi}(1-\hat{\phi}(1-t))$ possesses a unique fixed point, both families $(i_{+}^{H}(o,v))_{v \sim o}$ and $(i_{-}^{H}(o,v))_{v \sim o}$ converges almost surely to a family $(i_l)_{l \leq N}$ where $(i_l)$ have i.i.d distribution $\gamma\delta_0+(1-\gamma)\delta_1$ and independent of $N$ of distribution $\pi$.

Let $p_1(x) = P(Y(1)=1 \mid X=x)$ and $p_0(x) = P(Y(0)=1 \mid X=x)$. For any fixed impression budget constraint $P(\pi(X)=1) \le B$, the policy maximizing incremental consumption per impression under monotonicity ($Y(1) \ge Y(0)$) is a level set of the uplift ratio $\frac{p_1(x) - p_0(x)}{c(x)}$, and the dual-threshold policy $\pi(x) = \mathbb{I}(p_1(x) \ge \theta_1 \land p_0(x) \le \theta_0)$ forms a conservative, robust approximation that provably purges always-takers whose $p_0(x) > \theta_0$.
Outcomes are binary
Cost per impression is positive and uniform
p_1(x) and p_0(x) are well-calibrated

Let k be an algebraically closed field and R = k[x_1, ..., x_n]. Weak form: every proper ideal of R has a common zero in k^n; equivalently, every maximal ideal of R is (x_1 - a_1, ..., x_n - a_n) for some a in k^n. Strong form: for every ideal I of R, the ideal of polynomials vanishing on V(I) is the radical of I, I(V(I)) = sqrt(I). Hence V and I are inclusion-reversing inverse bijections between the radical ideals of R and the algebraic subsets of k^n. Algebraic closure is needed: over the reals x^2 + 1 has no zero.

SETTING: X a compact metric space; T : X -> X a continuous, topologically exact map which is a local homeomorphism with finite fibres (so that the operator below sends continuous functions to continuous functions); w : X -> (0, infinity) a continuous weight. Define the transfer (Ruelle) operator on complex continuous functions by (L f)(x) = the sum of w(y) f(y) over the finitely many y with T(y) = x; L is a bounded positive operator on C(X). Assume the Perron data exist: a number lambda > 0 and a strictly positive h in C(X) with L h = lambda h, together with a Borel probability measure nu with L* nu = lambda nu, i.e. the integral of L f with respect to nu equals lambda times the integral of f with respect to nu for all f in C(X). CONCLUSION: (1) if f in C(X) is complex-valued and L f = z f with |z| = lambda, then z = lambda and f is a constant multiple of h - so lambda is the only eigenvalue of modulus lambda in C(X) and its eigenspace is one dimensional; (2) lambda is ALGEBRAICALLY simple: there is no f in C(X) with L f - lambda f = h, hence no Jordan block at lambda. WHERE THE HYPOTHESES BITE: (i) exactness cannot be weakened to minimality, unique ergodicity or transitivity. Take X the circle, T an irrational rotation and w identically 1, so that L f = f composed with T^{-1}: every character exp(2 pi i n x) is an eigenfunction with an eigenvalue of modulus 1, so the peripheral spectrum is infinite - and the system is minimal and uniquely ergodic but not exact (it is invertible, hence never exact). (ii) Strict positivity of the weight is essential. If w may vanish, the irreducibility can become periodic: in the finite-state model, where L is a nonnegative matrix, the statement above is the PRIMITIVE case of the Perron-Frobenius theorem, and an irreducible matrix of period p > 1 has exactly p eigenvalues of modulus equal to its spectral radius, so simplicity of the peripheral eigenvalue genuinely fails. (iii) The conclusion concerns the peripheral eigenvalue only and gives NO spectral gap: to place the rest of the spectrum in a strictly smaller disc one needs quasi-compactness (a Lasota-Yorke or Ionescu-Tulcea-Marinescu inequality on a Holder or bounded-variation space), a separate hypothesis on the regularity of w and the expansion of T. (iv) The existence of h and nu is assumed here, not proved; producing them is the other half of the Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius theorem and needs its own hypotheses.
X compact metric, T continuous and topologically exact
T is a local homeomorphism with finite fibres, so that L maps C(X) into C(X)
the weight w is continuous and strictly positive everywhere
there exist lambda > 0 and h in C(X) with h > 0 everywhere and L h = lambda h
there exists a Borel probability measure nu with L* nu = lambda nu (used only for algebraic simplicity)
the conclusion is about the eigenvalues of L acting on C(X); no Banach space of Holder or bounded-variation functions and no quasi-compactness is assumed

Let A be a finite subset of R^n with N = |A| >= 2 elements, and let r = max_{a in A} ||a||_2. Let sigma_1, ..., sigma_n be independent Rademacher signs (uniform on {-1, +1}). Then E_sigma [ max_{a in A} sum_{i=1}^{n} sigma_i a_i ] <= r sqrt(2 log N), and consequently E_sigma [ max_{a in A} (1/n) sum_i sigma_i a_i ] <= r sqrt(2 log N) / n. Two consequences used constantly in learning theory: (1) for a finite class F of functions bounded by B on a sample x_1, ..., x_n, the empirical Rademacher complexity satisfies R_hat_S(F) = E_sigma sup_{f in F} (1/n) sum_i sigma_i f(x_i) <= B sqrt(2 log |F| / n), since each vector (f(x_1), ..., f(x_n)) has Euclidean norm at most B sqrt(n); (2) for a class C of sets of VC dimension d, restricting to the sample leaves at most s(C, n) <= (e n / d)^d distinct indicator vectors (Sauer-Shelah), each of norm at most sqrt(n), so R_hat_S(C) <= sqrt(2 d log(e n / d) / n) for n >= d. The logarithm cannot be removed at this generality: for A = {-1, +1}^n (N = 2^n, r = sqrt(n)) the maximum is exactly n while the bound reads n sqrt(2 log 2), so the lemma is sharp up to the constant sqrt(2 log 2) = 1.18; for VC classes Dudley's chaining removes the logarithm, R_hat_S(C) <= C sqrt(d / n).
A finite with at least two elements (for N = 1 the maximum has mean 0)
the signs are independent and symmetric; the bound is on the expectation over the signs only, the vectors are fixed

[Theorem thm:G0 of arXiv:2412.05503, 'Critical scaling profile for trees and connected subgraphs \\ on the complete graph'] For both trees and connected subgraphs, for all $s \ge 0$, and for all sequences
$p_V$ with $p_V \le 1+sV^{-1/2}$ and $\lim_{V\to\infty}p_V=p\in [0,1]$,
\begin{align}

    \lim_{V\to\infty} G_{V,0}(p_V)
    &=
    \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{ n^{n-1} }{n!} \Big( \frac{p}{e} \Big)^{n-1}
    =
    -\frac{e}{p}W_0\Big(\!\!-\frac{p}{e} \Big)
    .
\end{align}
In particular, if $p=1$ then
$\lim_{V\to\infty} G_{V,0}(p_V) = e$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In any bipartite graph, the maximum size of a matching (a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint) equals the minimum size of a vertex cover (a set of vertices meeting every edge). Both can be computed efficiently, and a minimum vertex cover can be extracted from a maximum matching via alternating paths from unmatched vertices. The equality can fail in non-bipartite graphs, where the minimum vertex cover can strictly exceed the maximum matching, for instance in an odd cycle. Proved by Denes Konig in 1931; equivalent to Hall's marriage theorem and a special case of the max-flow min-cut theorem.
title: Konig's theorem

body: [Corollary 1 (Overfitting implies a robust gap) of arXiv:2602.20971, 'Does Order Matter : Connecting The Law of Robustness to Robust Generaliz'] If $0<\varepsilon<\sigma^{2}$ and $\widehat{R}_{0}(f)\leq\sigma^{2}-\varepsilon,$ then $\operatorname{Gap}_{\rho}(f)\geq\Gamma_{\rho}(\varepsilon,L)$ where $\Gamma_{\rho}(\epsilon,L):=\sigma^{2}-\left(\sqrt{\sigma^{2}-\varepsilon}+L\rho\right)^{2}=\varepsilon-2L\rho\sqrt{\sigma^{2}-\varepsilon}-L^{2}\rho^{2}$. In particular, the lower bound is positive whenever $L\rho<\sigma-\sqrt{\sigma^{2}-\varepsilon}$.

[Lemma 73 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Suppose that Assumptions~\ref{Assumptions_Theta}, \ref{Assumptions_basic} and \ref{Assumptions_offcrit}
 hold. Assume that $h = H$ and $\mathfrak{b} = +\infty$. Take an arbitrary $\mathfrak{a}$ such that
$[\mathfrak{a},+\infty)$ is included in a void. Then, for any $c>0$ there exists an interval $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2) \subseteq \amsmathbb{R}_{> 0}$ and $\eps > 0$ such that
\[
\forall x \in ( \mathfrak{a}+\zeta_2,+\infty) \qquad V^{\textnormal{eff}}_H(x) - V^{\textnormal{eff}}_H(\mathfrak{a}+\zeta_1)> c + \eps \log\big(1 + |x|\big),
\]
and
\[
 V^{\textnormal{eff}}_H(\mathfrak{a}+\zeta_1)=\inf_{x\in [\mathfrak{a}+\zeta_1,+\infty)} V^{\textnormal{eff}}_H(x).
\]
There exists $C>0$ depending only on $\mathfrak{a},c$ and the constants in the assumptions, such that the choice of $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2)$ can be made to obey $\zeta_2<C$ and $\zeta_2-\zeta_1> \frac{1}{C}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In probability theory, Chebyshev's inequality (also called the Bienaymé–Chebyshev inequality) provides an upper bound on the probability of deviation of a random variable (with finite variance) from its mean. More specifically, the probability that a random variable deviates from its mean by more than $k\sigma$ is at most $1/k^{2}$, where $k$ is any positive constant and $\sigma$ is the standard deviation (the square root of the variance).

The multi-season epidemic process is a discrete-time Markov chain on S_r subset Delta^{r-1} x [0, 1]^{r-1} with effective dimension 2r - 3. The state transition (p^{(k)}, iota^{(k)}) -> (p^{(k+1)}, iota^{(k+1)}) driven by (delta_k, tau_k) satisfies: p_1^{(k+1)} = z^{(k)}; p_j^{(k+1)} = p_{j-1}^{(k)} (1 - z_{j-1}^{(k)}) for 2 <= j < r; p_r^{(k+1)} = p_r^{(k)} (1 - z_r^{(k)}) + p_{r-1}^{(k)} (1 - z_{r-1}^{(k)}); iota_1^{(k+1)} = 1; and iota_j^{(k+1)} = iota_{j-1}^{(k)} (1 - delta_k) for 2 <= j < r.
Cutoff r >= 2
Shocks (delta_k, tau_k) are i.i.d.

body:
Let f be the pointwise limit of a sequence of continuous real functions on a metric space X (such an f is said to be of Baire class one). Then: (i) f is Borel measurable, indeed for every real a the set {f > a} is an F-sigma set; (ii) if X is completely metrizable, the set of points of continuity of f is a dense G-delta set, so f is continuous on a comeagre set. In particular a derivative, being a pointwise limit of continuous difference quotients, is Baire class one and is continuous on a comeagre set - the derivative of a differentiable function cannot be discontinuous everywhere.
Pointwise, not uniform, convergence;
completeness of X is needed only for the comeagre-continuity half.
Baire class one is strictly larger than the continuous functions and strictly smaller than the Borel functions.

body: In mathematical analysis, the Weierstrass approximation theorem states that every continuous function defined on a closed interval [a, b] can be uniformly approximated as closely as desired by a polynomial function. Because polynomials are among the simplest functions, and because computers can directly evaluate polynomials, this theorem has both practical and theoretical relevance, especially in polynomial interpolation. The original version of this result was established by Karl Weierstrass in 1885 using the Weierstrass transform.
title: Stone–Weierstrass theorem

\norm{u}_{\varepsilon,n}\leq\norm{u}_{\alpha,n}\leq\norm{u}_{\pi,n}
\qquad (u\in V_{\C}^{\otimes n}),

body: [Theorem 3 of arXiv:2110.07472, 'Capacity of Group-invariant Linear Readouts from Equivariant Representations: How Many Obj'] Suppose a code which is equivariant to a finite group G is pooled to a new code which is equivariant to a finite subgroup H ⊆G. Suppose the number of trivial dimensions in the original G-equivariant code is N0. Then the fraction of linearly separable dichotomies on the G-invariant problem for the pooled code is at least f(P, ⌊N0/k⌋) where k = |G/H|. Similarly the fraction is at most f(P, N0).
title: Theorem 3 of arXiv:2110.07472: Capacity of Group-invariant Linear Readouts from Equivariant Representations: How Many Obj

body: In mathematics, random graph is the general term to refer to probability distributions over graphs. Random graphs may be described simply by a probability distribution, or by a random process which generates them. The theory of random graphs lies at the intersection between graph theory and probability theory. From a mathematical perspective, random graphs are used to answer questions about the properties of typical graphs. Its practical applications are found in all areas in which complex networks need to be modeled – many random graph models are thus known, mirroring the diverse types of complex networks encountered in different areas. In a mathematical context, random graph refers almost exclusively to the Erdős–Rényi random graph model. In other contexts, any graph model may be referred to as a random graph.
title: Random graph

Its spectrum $\la_1(H_{\ka,\eps})\leq\la_2(H_{\ka,\eps})\leq\cdots$ is purely discrete, bounded below, and has no accumulation point.

\begin{align}

\end{align}

In a finite bipartite graph the maximum size of a matching equals the minimum size of a vertex cover (a set of vertices meeting every edge). The inequality maximum matching <= minimum vertex cover holds in every graph; equality is special to bipartite graphs and fails already for a triangle (matching 1, cover 2). Equivalent to Hall's marriage theorem and to the max-flow min-cut theorem on the corresponding unit-capacity network; the dual statement (Konig's edge-colouring theorem) says a bipartite graph of maximum degree D can be properly edge-coloured with D colours.
G finite and bipartite
a vertex cover meets every edge; a matching is a set of pairwise disjoint edges

body:
[Theorem 7 (Hardness of exact quantile and lower-buffered quantile evaluation) of arXiv:2608.22227, '\fontsize{18pt}{20pt}\selectfont \bf Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning with Smoothed Q'] The following decision problems are PP-hard under polynomial-time Turing
reductions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item exact finite-horizon QMDP evaluation, i.e., deciding whether
    \(Q_\tau(R^\pi)\le c\) for the return \(R^\pi\) of a fixed deterministic
    policy;
    \item exact lower-buffered quantile evaluation, i.e., deciding whether
    \(Q_\tau^\beta(R^\pi)\le c\) for the return \(R^\pi\) of a fixed
    deterministic policy.
\end{enumerate}
The hardness holds even for finite-horizon MDPs with two states, one action,
binary transition probabilities, and deterministic rational rewards in
\([0,1]\). Consequently, the corresponding exact planning problems are also
PP-hard under polynomial-time Turing
reductions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Hardness of exact quantile and lower-buffered quantile evaluation

body: [Corollary 3.7 of arXiv:2603.27659, 'Operator Norm Bounds for Multi-leg Matrix Tensors and Applications to Random Matrix Theory'] Let $m,N,a,b\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal{P}([m])$ be any permutations. With $M(\sigma,\tau;a,b)$ and $C(\sigma,\tau;a,b)$ as defined above, we have $\displaystyle N^{M(\sigma,\tau;a,b)}\leq\max_{\|A_{1}\|,\ldots,\|A_{m}\|\leq 1}\left|\left(\mathrm{Tr}_{\sigma}\otimes\mathrm{Tr}_{\tau}\right)\left(A_{1},\ldots,A_{m}\right)\right|\leq N^{C(\sigma,\tau;a,b)}.$ Here, for the graph $G_{\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k}}$ of the permutations, $M(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k})$ is the maximum over blue-edge configurations of the number of directed cycles, and $C(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k})=\min_{G^{\prime}}R_{G^{\prime}}$, the minimum over full simple partial graphs $G^{\prime}$ (partial graphs keeping every rectangle and containing no directed cycle for any blue-edge configuration) of the number $R_{G^{\prime}}$ of colored edges removed to obtain $G^{\prime}$ (Definition 2.1).

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2604.25769, 'The conformal dimension of the Brownian tree is one'] Condition~\eqref{eq:admissibility} is satisfied: Let $n \in \BN$ and $y, x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_N \in \SCT$ such that
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $B_{\alpha^{n - 1}}(y; d_\SCT) \cap B_{4\alpha^n}(x_0; d_\SCT) \neq \emptyset$,
        \item $B_{4\alpha^n}(x_{j - 1}; d_\SCT) \cap B_{4\alpha^n}(x_j; d_\SCT) \neq \emptyset$ for all $j \in [1, N]_\BZ$, and 
        \item $(\SCT \setminus B_{2\alpha^{n - 1}}(y; d_\SCT)) \cap B_{4\alpha^n}(x_N; d_\SCT) \neq \emptyset$. 
    \end{itemize}
    Then $\sum_{j = 0}^N \sigma(x_j, n) \ge 1$.

body: [Theorem 2.2 of arXiv:2110.09034, 'On the construction of cospectral nonisomorphic bipartite graphs'] [7, Lemma 3] Let A, B and C be (0, 1)-matrices. Let C be a non-zero matrix and A be a square matrix with no zero rows. Then, the matrices C ⊗A and C ⊗B are permutationally equivalent if and only if A and B are permutationally equivalent. Similarly, the matrices A ⊗C and B ⊗C are permutationally equivalent if and only if A and B are permutationally equivalent.
title: Theorem 2.2 of arXiv:2110.09034: On the construction of cospectral nonisomorphic bipartite graphs

body:
[Proposition 49 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Suppose $u: \T^d \to \R^d$ is continuous, $\nabla \cdot u =0$, and for almost every $y \in \T^d$, the ODE
    \[\begin{cases}
    \dot \Phi_t(y) = u(\Phi_t(y)),\\
    \Phi_0(y) = y,
    \end{cases}\]
    admits a unique solution on $(-\infty,\infty)$. Then for any $f \in L^1(\T^d)$ with $f \geq 0$, the continuity equation
    \begin{equation}
    
    \begin{cases}
        \partial_t \phi + \nabla \cdot (u \phi) = 0,\\
        \phi(0,\cdot) = f(\cdot),
    \end{cases}\end{equation}
    admits a unique distributional solution on $(-\infty,\infty) \times \T^d$ such that $\phi \geq 0$ and for all $T>0,$ $\phi \in \mathcal{C}^0([-T,T],L^1(\T^d))$. Further
    \[\phi(t,\cdot) = (\Phi_t)_* f = f \circ \Phi_{-t},\]
    where $(\Phi_t)_* f$ denotes the pushforward of $f$ as a measure density with respect to Lebesgue, and hence $\phi$ is a renormalized solution in the DiPerna--Lions sense: that is, for all $\beta : \R \to \R$ such that $\beta \in C^1_b(\R)$, $\beta(\phi)$ is also a distributional solution to~\eqref{eq:continuity abstract} with initial data $\beta(f)$.

[Thm THM52 of arXiv:2608.16170, '\bf On hitting time distributions of Markov processes with sub-Gaussian heat kernel bounds'] Let $X$ be a Borel right process on $(E,d)$ that satisfies (AC), (H2a) and (H2b).

 Further assume that $X$ admits the following short-time heat kernel lower bound at a fixed point $x\in E$: For some $T>0, \alpha>0,\beta>1$, there exist constants $C_1,C_2>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
p(t,x,y)\ge \frac{C_1}{t^{\alpha/\beta}}\exp\left\{-C_2\left(\frac{d(x,y)}{t^{1/\beta}}\right)^{\beta/(\beta -1)}\right\}, \quad \forall t\in (0, T], \, y\in E.
\end{equation}
Let $B\subset E$ be a nearly Borel set with compact closure $\overline{B}$. 
Then for any $\delta,\rho>0$ and any $\lambda>0$ ($\lambda\geq 0$ if $X$ is transient),
 \[
        \mathbb{P}^x[\sigma_B\leq t]\geq \frac{\nu^{(\lambda)}_{B_{x,\delta}}(\overline{B}_{x,\delta})}{\mathrm{e}^{\lambda T}}\cdot \frac{C_1C_3}{ t^{(\alpha-\beta)/\beta}}\exp\left\{-(1+\rho)C_2\left( \frac{\widetilde{d}(x,B)+\delta}{t^{1/\beta}}\right)^{\beta/(\beta-1)}\right\},\quad 0<t\leq T,
    \]
    where  $B_{x,\delta}:=\{y\in B:d(y,x)\leq \widetilde{d}(x,B)+\delta\}$, $\nu^{(\lambda)}_{B_{x,\delta}}$ is the measure obtained in Lemma~(LM51 of the paper), $C_1$ and $C_2$ are as in (equation eq:55 of the paper), and $C_3=(\beta-1)\rho\cdot \min\{(1+\rho)^{\alpha-\beta-\alpha/\beta}, 1\}>0$ is a constant depending on $\alpha, \beta,\rho$.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Integrator-authored exact special-case argument and failure analysis after checking the incoming source Result: The coordinate-diagonal case is a sum of binary entropies, whose second derivatives are -1/[q(1-q)]. There is also an explicit non-diagonal line: for Q(c)=[[1/2,c],[c,1/2]], |c|<1/2, the empty and doubleton probabilities are a=1/4-c^2 and the two singleton probabilities are b=1/4+c^2. Hence H(c)=-2*a*log(a)-2*b*log(b), and Hsecond(c)=4*log(a/b)-8*c^2*(1/a+1/b)<=0. Continuity includes c=+-1/2. This verifies concavity on this affine kernel line. In general the determinant probabilities depend nonlinearly on Q, so concavity of Shannon entropy in a probability vector cannot be applied directly to an arithmetic kernel midpoint. Check: Inclusion-exclusion gives p11=det(Q), p10=Q11-det(Q), p01=Q22-det(Q), p00=det(I-Q); these are a,b,b,a and sum to one. Differentiating H first gives 4*c*log(a/b), independently confirming the second derivative and its sign. Obstruction: No joint concavity proof, no extension to arbitrary off-diagonal or noncommuting kernels, and no numerical trials treated as certification.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0461-entropy-concavity-for-determinantal-kernels

Let X >= 0 with mu = E[X] > 0 and finite second moment, 0 <= theta < 1, t = theta mu and Y = (X - t)_+. Then P(X > t) >= E[Y]^2/E[Y^2] >= (mu - t)^2/E[X^2] = (1 - theta)^2 mu^2/E[X^2]. The two coefficients agree at theta = 0, and for 0 < theta < 1 the first is strictly larger.

[Theorem Theorem_optimal_stopping_times of arXiv:2608.08299, 'Non-linear optimal stopping with Bermudan strategies: the infinite horizon case'] \begin{enumerate}
    \item Assume that $\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty} \xi(\theta_n) <+\infty$.
    We assume that: if $\eta \in L^+_0(\mathcal{F}_{\infty})$, if 
  $(\tau_k)$ $\in \Theta^{\mathbb{N}}$ non-decreasing such that $\lim_{k \rightarrow +\infty} \tau_k  = +\infty$, then
  \[
  \limsup_{n \rightarrow +\infty} \limsup_{k \rightarrow +\infty} \rho_{\theta_n, \tau_k} [\eta] =  \eta.\]
    Let $\varepsilon >0 $. For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$, we define: 
    \begin{equation}
    A_k^{\varepsilon}:=\{\tau \in \Theta_{\theta_k} : V(\tau) < \xi(\tau)+\varepsilon \,\,\, a.s. \}
   \,\,\,\, \text{and} \,\,\,\,
    \nu_k^{\varepsilon}:= \essinf A_k^{\varepsilon}.
   \end{equation}
    Then, $\nu_k^{\varepsilon}$ is a.s. finite and 
    \[
 V(\theta_k) \leq  \rho_{\theta_k, \nu_k^{\varepsilon}} [\xi(\nu_k^{\varepsilon})]+C\varepsilon,
    \]
    where $C>0$ is a positive constant (depending on $\rho$ only).
    \item
    Let us define: 
    \begin{equation}
    A_k:=\{\tau \in \Theta_{\theta_k} : V(\tau) = \xi(\tau) \,\,\, a.s. \}
   \,\,\,\, \text{and} \,\,\,\,
    \nu_k:= \essinf A_k,
   \end{equation}
    with the convention that $\essinf A_k = + \infty$ if $A_k=\emptyset$.
   It holds: \\ $\nu_k$ is optimal for the problem with value $V(\theta_k)$, if and only if, $\nu_k < +\infty$ a.s.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Fix finitely many inputs x^1,...,x^m in R^n_in and a finite T>0. For clarity restrict to a positive definite input Gram matrix V_0^{alpha beta}=<x^alpha,x^beta>/n_in. All layers have width n, zero biases, and mutually independent standard Gaussian weight entries. Equivalently, start from this deterministic V_0 and, conditional on V_l, draw n independent Gaussian m-vectors G_i with covariance V_l; update V_{l+1}^{alpha beta}=(c_n/n) sum_i phi_n(G_i^alpha)phi_n(G_i^beta). This is the covariance Markov chain of the Gaussian network, up to the harmless first-layer index shift. Let d_n/n tend to T. Let phi in C^4(R) satisfy phi(0)=0, phi′(0)=1 and |phi^(4)(x)|<=C(1+|x|^p) for some C,p>0. Fix a>0, put s=a sqrt(n), phi_n(x)=s phi(x/s), and c_n=(E[phi_n(g)^2])^(-1) for standard Gaussian g. The upper-triangular covariance process V_{floor(nt)} converges locally in distribution in the Skorohod topology to dV=b(V)dt+Sigma(V)^(1/2)dB, started at V_0, where Sigma_{alpha beta,gamma delta}(V)=V^{alpha gamma}V^{beta delta}+V^{alpha delta}V^{beta gamma} and b_{alpha beta}(V)=phi′′(0)^2/(4a^2) [V^{alpha alpha}V^{beta beta}+V^{alpha beta}(2V^{alpha beta}-3)] + phi′′′(0)/(2a^2) V^{alpha beta}(V^{alpha alpha}+V^{beta beta}-2). Local convergence means convergence of the processes stopped when the Euclidean norm of their upper-triangular vector first reaches any fixed finite radius, as in Definition 3.8. A global finite covariance limit is not asserted when explosion can occur. When the terminal covariance V_T is finite, the source describes the limiting scalar readout vector conditionally on V_T as centered Gaussian with covariance V_T; the output law is undefined on paths that explode before T.
A fixed finite collection of inputs with positive definite normalized Gram matrix (explicit restriction of the source)
Independent iid N(0,1) weights, no biases, constant width n
phi is C^4, phi(0)=0, phi′(0)=1 and the fourth derivative has polynomial growth
Fixed a>0 and s=a sqrt(n), exact Gaussian normalization, depth/width tends to finite T
Only locally stopped convergence is claimed in general

Let (X_n)_{n=1}^\infty be i.i.d. random variables with \mathbb{E}[X_1] = 0 and \text{Var}(X_1) = 1. Define the linearly interpolated partial sum process S_t on [0, \infty), and for each n \ge 3, let \zeta_n(t) = \frac{S_{nt}}{\sqrt{2 n \log \log n}} for t \in [0, 1]. Then almost surely, the sequence of functions (\zeta_n)_{n \ge 3} in C([0, 1]) is relatively compact, and its set of limit points equals the Strassen compact set K = \{f \in C([0, 1]) : f(0) = 0, f \text{ is absolutely continuous}, \int_0^1 (f'(t))^2 dt \le 1\}.

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT C015 v1, proof (unaudited); no novelty or independent-review claim. For finite d>=1 let Sigma and Gamma be PSD d-by-d matrices with traces at most one. Take two independent samples of m iid pairs with common product law a~N(0,1), w~N(0,Gamma). For rho((a,w),(aprime,wprime))=|a-aprime|+||Sigma^(1/2)(w-wprime)||, the expected minimum mean permutation cost is at most r_G(m)=inf over R>0 and positive integers k,q of [4R/q+2R/sqrt(k+1)+2sqrt(2)R*sqrt(q^(k+1)/m)+16exp(-R^2/8)]. In particular r_G(m)=O(log log m/sqrt(log m)), uniformly over dimension and admissible covariances. The Gaussian integral gives E exp(||w||^2/4)<=sqrt(2), using product_j(1-lambda_j/2)>=1-sum_j lambda_j/2>=1/2; the same applies to a. Thus norm clipping at radius R costs at most 8exp(-R^2/8) per pair, and C004 v2 covariance matching applies to the clipped pairs. Choosing R=sqrt(32 log log(m+exp(exp(1)))) proves the rate. This is an initial matching bound, not a trained-SGD theorem. The trace restriction excludes unscaled N(0,I_d) uniformly in growing d. C004 v2 is an unaudited dependency; all constants and the proof appear in proofs/C015_gaussian_covariance_matching.md.
Common independent iid product Gaussian pair samples; PSD Sigma,Gamma with trace <=1
d is finite and may vary with m under these trace constraints; matching uses the covariance pseudometric in the statement

body: A Jordan normal form of a linear operator T on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field K is a block-diagonal matrix of Jordan blocks (equal eigenvalue down each block's diagonal, ones on the superdiagonal) representing T in some basis. Such a basis exists if and only if the characteristic polynomial of T splits into linear factors over K - automatic when K is algebraically closed, e.g. C, and false in general over R (a plane rotation by 90 degrees has no real Jordan form) - and the form is then unique up to the order of the blocks.
title: Jordan normal form

[Lemma general_order of arXiv:2604.05921, 'Simplicity of random hypergraphs'] Let $r \in [\delta_1], t \in [\delta_2]$. For any functions $f_1^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N},f_2^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N}$ and $w \in \mathds{N}$, if
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\delta_1, \delta_2 \in O(1)$
    \item $\forall (\vb*{y}, \vb*{z}) \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}\times \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} iy_i \leq \delta_1,  \sum_{j=1}^{\delta_2} jz_j \leq \delta_2$ and $ \|\vb*{y}\|_0 + \|\vb*{z}\|_0 \ge 2$:
    $$\mathds{E}[\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_1} (f_1^{(i)}(U))^{y_i}\prod_{j=1}^{\delta_2} (f_2^{(j)}(U))^{z_i}] \in o(n)$$
    \item $\forall k \in [\delta_1], \forall l \in [\delta_2]:$
    $$\mathds{E}[(f_1^{(k)}(U))^{\lfloor \frac{\delta_1}{k} \rfloor}],\mathds{E}[(f_2^{(l)}(U))^{\lfloor \frac{\delta_2}{l} \rfloor}] \in o(n)$$
    \item $\forall k \in [\delta_1]$ s.t. $\exists v \in V: f_1^{(k)}(v) > 0 $ and $ \forall l \in [\delta_2] $ s.t. $\exists v \in V: f_2^{(l)}(v) > 0 :\\
    \exists c>0 \textnormal{ s.t. }  \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}  \mathds{P}(f_1^{(k)}(U) \geq 1), \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \mathds{P}(f_2^{(l)}(U) \geq 1) \geq c$
\end{enumerate}
then
\begin{align*}
 &\sum_{\substack{\vb*{a} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}:\\\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} ia_i = \delta_1 }} \sum_{\substack{\vb*{b} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}:\\\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_2} ib_i = \delta_2}} \sum_{\gamma(\cdot) \in \hat{R}(\vb*{a},\vb*{b})} \hat{H}(\vb*{a},\vb*{b},\gamma(\cdot)) \\
 &= (\delta_1!\delta_2!)^w (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U) ])^{\delta_1} (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U) ])^{\delta_2} \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{0.5cm}+ \Big( -\frac{1}{2} \frac{\delta_1!^{1+w}\delta_2!^w}{(\delta_1-2)!}(n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_1-2} n\mathds{E}[(f_1^{(1)}(U))^2] (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_2} \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{1.15cm} -\frac{1}{2} \frac{\delta_1!^w \delta_2!^{1+w}}{(\delta_2-2)!} (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_1} (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_2-2} n\mathds{E}[(f_2^{(1)}(U))^2] \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{1.15cm} - \frac{(\delta_1!\delta_2!)^{1+w}}{(\delta_1-1)!(\delta_2-1)!}  (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_1-1} (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_2-1} n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)f_2^{(1)}(U)] \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{1.15cm} + \frac{1}{2^{1+w}} \frac{\delta_1!^{1+w}\delta_2!^w}{(\delta_1-2)!} (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_1-2} n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(2)}(U)] (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_2} \nonumber\\
 &\hspace{1.15cm}+ \frac{1}{2^{1+w}} \frac{\delta_1!^w \delta_2!^{1+w}}{(\delta_2-2)!} (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_1} (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U)])^{\delta_2-2} n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(2)}(U)] \Big) (1+o(1))\\
   &= (\delta_1!\delta_2!)^w (n\mathds{E}[f_1^{(1)}(U) ])^{\delta_1} (n\mathds{E}[f_2^{(1)}(U) ])^{\delta_2}(1+o(1)).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma general_order of arXiv:2604.05921

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT: proof (unaudited); independent mathematical and novelty review pending. Balanced four-point frozen-model spectral interpolation only; actual nonlinear transfer remains open.

# C017 v1: rescaled noise restores two roots in the iid-head frozen precursor
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: bound. Target:1. Novelty unestablished.
A supporting frozen-model result, not full Target1 and not yet a nonlinear-network result.

## 1. Model and precise limit
For 0<e<1/4 set D=1+e^2+e^4 and x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D), s,t=+/-1.
Use the uniform four-point population and teacher direction
u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2). The letter u_e denotes this direction, not
nu, the fixed readout magnitude in (0,1]. Set c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)),
alpha=c_e/2, g(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2. Its Walsh coefficients in modes
0,s,t,st are (0,alpha,alpha,alpha).
Initialize independent neurons with W_j~N(0,I_3) and heads independently +/-nu.
First take width to infinity at every fixed e, obtaining initial Gaussian
Walsh coefficients Z_(e,h). This is the ordinary fixed-width CLT of C016.
Then train the FROZEN deterministic full kernel
 H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z]
with discrete step1/2. Write b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2) for the normalized
four-point eigenvalues lambda_h. Use the settled clock premises
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi), b_0 bounded away from0.
Thus eta=(b_t+b_st)/b_s~e and b_t/(b_t+b_st)->1/2.

For fixed kappa>0 choose effective Walsh noise variance alpha^2 rho_e,
 rho_e=kappa/sqrt(e).
Four independent errors +/-sigma_e with sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(rho_e)
realize exactly this variance. In particular sigma_e~sqrt(kappa)e^(7/4),
so label noise remains <=1 for small e, but is not fixed as e decreases.
The noise-averaged clean risk conditional on initialization, in real-time
spectral interpolation of discrete GD, is
 Q_e(t)=sum_h [exp(-2b_h t)(Z_(e,h)-theta_h)^2
             +alpha^2 rho_e(1-exp(-b_h t))^2].             (1)
At integer t this is exactly discrete kernel GD. Real t is used only to
locate extrema of its spectral interpolation; no GD-to-flow limit is taken.

## 2. Joint initial-output covariance, on the relevant scales
Let phi_h(W)=(1/4)sum_(s,t) h(s,t) ReLU(W.x_(s,t)), and
lambda_h^RF=E phi_h(W)^2. The initial covariance is diagonal in Walsh modes,
Var(Z_(e,h))=nu^2 lambda_h^RF, by Gaussian coordinate sign symmetry.
In the Gaussian limit these modes are therefore independent.
C016 establishes lambda_s^RF/e^2->1/2 and the bounds
|phi_t|,|phi_st|<=e^2|W_2|/sqrt(D).
For W_0!=0, all four preactivations eventually have its sign. Consequently
phi_t/e^2 -> W_2 1{W_0>0}, and phi_st/e^2 ->0 almost surely.
Dominated convergence with the preceding bounds gives
 lambda_t^RF/e^4->1/2, lambda_st^RF/e^4->0.                (2)
On one probability space take independent standard normals G_0,G_s,G_t,G_st
and set Z_(e,h)=nu sqrt(lambda_h^RF)G_h for every e. This coupling has exactly
the required Gaussian law at each e. Since alpha~e^2/2, writing
A_(e,h)=(Z_(e,h)/alpha-theta_h/alpha)^2, we get almost surely
 e^2 A_(e,s)->a=2nu^2 G_s^2,
 A_(e,t)->(sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2, A_(e,st)->1.                (3)
Define B=((sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2+1)/2 >=1/2.
Here a>0 almost surely and a is independent of B. Independence is used only
after the joint Gaussian limit, not for finite-width output coefficients.

## 3. The new central derivative limit
For real s in a fixed compact interval set
 t_e(s)=((3/2)log(1/e)+s)/b_s, z=exp(-s).
Then q_s=exp(-b_s t_e(s))=e^(3/2)z exactly.
Normalize the risk derivative by 2alpha^2(b_t+b_st). Its fast contribution is
 [rho_e q_s-(A_(e,s)+rho_e)q_s^2]/eta
 =kappa(e/eta)z-[(e^2 A_(e,s))(e/eta)+kappa e^(5/2)/eta]z^2
 -> kappa z-a z^2.                                      (4)
For each slow mode q_h=1-O(e log(1/e)) uniformly on the compact interval.
Thus rho_e q_h(1-q_h)=O(sqrt(e)log(1/e))->0, while A_(e,h)q_h^2
has the limits in (3). The rate weights tend to1/2, giving their combined
contribution -B. The constant-mode contribution vanishes: its exponent
decays faster than every power of e and Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.
The same calculation after differentiating in s is valid: slow terms gain
a factor b_h/b_s=O(e), and even rho_e times that factor tends to0;
constant-mode exponentials dominate the additional polynomial factors.
Hence, almost surely in this coupling, uniformly on each compact s interval,

 Q'_e(t_e(s))/(2alpha^2(b_t+b_st)) -> H_kappa(s)
                                      =kappa exp(-s)-a exp(-2s)-B,
 and the derivatives in s converge too.                  (5)

## 4. Two-root criterion and peak time
On the event Delta=kappa^2-4aB>0 define
 z_+=(kappa+sqrt(Delta))/(2a), z_-=(kappa-sqrt(Delta))/(2a).
Both are positive and z_+>z_-. The classification is the elementary quadratic
criterion already used in C012, now with random coefficients a and B.
As s increases, H is negative, positive, then negative across
 s_min=-log z_+ and s_max=-log z_-.
The roots are simple. Uniform C1 convergence in (5) gives, for every such
fixed Gaussian realization, one nearby minimum and one nearby maximum of
the frozen interpolation for all sufficiently small e, converging to these
locations. Derivative convergence also gives strict decrease immediately
after the maximum. Thus there are two descents separated by a rise.
More precisely the peak satisfies
 b_s t_peak-(3/2)log(1/e) -> -log z_-,
 t_peak~(6pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e).                         (6)
The statements are pathwise in the coupling, on Delta>0. Random compact
neighborhoods are allowed: convergence on every integer-sized compact set
holds on one probability-one event. No deterministic width rate is asserted.
On Delta<0, H is negative on every compact s interval; this only addresses
this particular time window, not global absence of DD. Delta=0 is not treated.

For value-based nonlinear transfer, a useful additional consequence is this:
 d/ds [Q_e(t_e(s))/(2alpha^2 eta)] converges to H_kappa(s).
Therefore differences of the normalized risks converge to differences of
 V(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(a/2)exp(-2s)-Bs.
Values across the two simple extrema have strict gaps of order alpha^2 eta.
An o(alpha^2 eta) uniform risk error over a containing compact interval would
preserve appropriately chosen decrease/rise/decrease witnesses and interval
peak localization. Such a nonlinear error is NOT supplied in this claim.

## 5. A tunable probability lower bound
The Gaussian independence in Section2 gives E a=2nu^2 and E B=1+nu^2,
so E[4aB]=8nu^2(1+nu^2). Markov's inequality yields
 P(Delta>0) >= 1-8nu^2(1+nu^2)/kappa^2.                   (7)
Choose kappa^2>8nu^2(1+nu^2)/delta for any prescribed delta in (0,1).
Then the frozen limiting construction has two simple central extrema with
probability greater than1-delta. The noise amplitude still tends to zero.
This is an initialization probability bound, with risk already averaged over
labels; it is not concentration for one realized label vector.
For fixed kappa the exact event probability need not equal this lower bound.

## 6. Scope and next unpaid step
C016's failed rho~1 route is avoided by changing BOTH noise scale and time
center; fixed nu and the unit-norm single-index teacher are retained.
This lemma concerns the balanced four-point frozen precursor only. It does
not yet prove the result for actual nonlinear GD, continuous iid input laws,
fixed label-noise amplitude, macroscopic feature learning, or full Target1.
The next step is a uniform-in-time risk transfer at order o(alpha^2 eta),
with nonzero iid initial output retained. C009's finite-horizon strategy is
a candidate; C015's zero-output paired argument cannot simply be substituted.
Independent mathematical and novelty review is pending. No paper-level
priority claim is made. Sources: own C009 clocks, C012 quadratic-root tool,
C016 Gaussian covariance and exact risk formula; the added slow-mode limits
and derivative scaling are proved above.
Every definition and fixed-nu spectral clock premise in the statement
Balanced four-point frozen full-kernel GD with independent Gaussian hidden weights and iid readouts +/-nu; fixed0<nu<=1
Width limit precedes e->0; unit-norm single-index teacher, noise-averaged risk with rho_e=kappa/sqrt(e)
Simple-root event kappa^2>4aB; peak location refers to real spectral interpolation of discrete GD
No claim of nonlinear transfer, continuous iid-input extension, fixed label-noise amplitude or full Target1 closure

[Lemma lem:toric of arXiv:2609.03448, 'Prime-power Diophantine tuples'] Let
\[
 D_0=24^4=331776.
\]
There exists a nonconstant polynomial
\[
 Q(T_1,\ldots,T_5)\in\mathbb Z[T_1,\ldots,T_5]
\]
with
\begin{equation}
 1\le q:=\deg Q\le5D_0<2^{21},
\end{equation}
and polynomials
\[
 G_i\in\mathbb Z[t_1,\ldots,t_4,T_1,\ldots,T_5]\qquad(1\le i\le5)
\]
such that
\begin{equation}
 (t_1t_2t_3t_4)^{12D_0}Q(T)
 =\sum_{i=1}^5G_i(t,T)\bigl(A_i(t)-T_iB_i(t)\bigr).
\end{equation}
The same polynomial $Q$ may be chosen so that
\begin{equation}
 \log_2 \bigl(h(Q)64^q\bigr)<2^{116}.
\end{equation}
Consequently every reduced labelled quintuple satisfying~(equation eq:AiBi of the paper)
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 Q(64\Lambda_1,\ldots,64\Lambda_5)\equiv0\pmod N.
\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:isometric-conjugacy of arXiv:2609.00794, 'On operators whose adjoints or second adjoints attain their norms'] Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces, and let
\[
U\colon \ell_1\to X^*,
\qquad
V\colon \ell_1\to Y^*
\]
be surjective linear isometries. Given $T\in\mathcal L(X,Y)$, put $S:=U^{-1}T^*V\in\mathcal L(\ell_1,\ell_1)$.
    \begin{equation*}
    \begin{tikzcd}
	{Y^* } && {X^*} \\
	{\ell_1} && {\ell_1}
	\arrow["{T^*}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{U^{-1}}", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["V", from=2-1, to=1-1]
	\arrow["S"', from=2-1, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}    
    \end{equation*}
Then $\|S\|=\|T\|$, and $T \in \operatorname{NA}_2 (X,Y)$ if and only if $S^* \in \operatorname{NA} (\ell_\infty,\ell_\infty)$.

[Defn of arXiv:2411.06571, 'Moment-based approach for two erratic KPZ scaling limits'] Define $\theta:= 1-\|\varphi\|_{L^2(\Bbb R)}^2 = 1-\varphi *\varphi (0)>0$, where $\varphi$ is as in Theorem (mr3 of the paper). Define the following second-order elliptic operator on $C^2(\Bbb R^n)$: $$L^{(n,\epsilon)}_{\mathrm{Cen}}f(y_1,...,y_n):= \frac12 \sum_{i,j=1}^n \big( \theta \delta_{i,j}+\epsilon \Phi_\epsilon(y_i-y_j)\big)\cdot (\partial_{ij}f)(y_1,...,y_n).$$ 
    Denote by $ \mathbf E^{(x_1,...,x_n)}_{\mathrm{Cen}(\epsilon)}$ the expectation with respect to the Markov process $X$ on $\Bbb R^n$ with generator $L^{(n,\epsilon)}_{\mathrm{Cen}}$.
title: Unnumbered defn of arXiv:2411.06571, 'Moment-based approach for two erratic KPZ scaling limits'

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT, independently checked proof, T326-w697-C04 v1; reviewer claude-738954b6 PASS on this exact version recorded in AUDITS_FROM_REVIEWER.tsv. In the Lu et al. reduced linear-attention model, hold v21=0 fixed and train v=v22 and the independent raw block U=[M11^T,m21] by Euclidean gradient flow with no ridge. The effective matrix is Gamma=vUR, R=diag(I_d/d,1); M is a directly trained block, not further factored into K^TQ. In exactly infinite context, fix a pool of M iid N(0,I_d) tasks w_i; z(w)=(w,||w||^2/d+rho), rho>=0, J=[I_d,0]. Let P_R project onto the span of {Rz(w_i)}, Q_R=I-P_R, r=rank P_R, q=(Q_R)_(d+1,d+1), A_0=r-1+q. For balanced raw initialization v_0=epsilon, U_0=epsilon J/sqrt(d), 0<epsilon<1, define D=epsilon^2(1-A_0/d), z_*=(D+sqrt(D^2+4d^2 A_0))/2 and a_raw=epsilon sqrt(z_*)/(d sqrt(d)). The global zero-loss limit is Gamma_infinity=J+(a_raw-1)dJ Q_R R. For an independent fresh standard Gaussian task and query N(0,I_d/d), its normalized excess prediction risk equals (1-a_raw)^2 B_d,M, where B_d,M=[d+1-r-q+(d^2 eta-1)q(1-q)]/d and eta=(1+rho)^2+2/d. The scaling d^2 eta is essential. If M>=d+1 the risk is zero. If M<=d, W=[w_1,...,w_M], G=W^TW, s=(||w_i||^2/d+rho)_i and beta=s^T G^(-1)s give q=1/(1+d^2 beta). For any 0<delta<1, with probability at least 1-delta-8/(dM), 0<=B_d,M-(d-M)/d<=1/d+4sqrt(3)eta/sqrt(M delta). This follows from E tr G=dM, Var tr G=2dM, E tr G^2=dM(d+M+1), Chebyshev, Markov and a union bound; no independence between the two concentration events is assumed. Thus at fixed epsilon,rho, every sequence M->infinity with M/d->kappa has conditional fresh-task risk ->(1-kappa)_+ in probability over the task pool. If M instead stays a fixed positive integer, G/d->I_M and s->(1+rho)1_M give d beta->M(1+rho)^2 and d q->1/[M(1+rho)^2], so the risk tends to 1+1/M. A single task therefore gives limit 2, while a diverging sublinear pool gives limit 1, although both have M/d->0. These are in-probability limits, not expectation-over-pool claims. Exact finite identities passed 1456 rational assertions over 99 cases; the general probability statement rests on the written proof. No Lean certificate or general K,Q,V result is claimed.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:d89b9f9730df61ec17959fa9b292442425633dc4dfbc0612adf0326eebcc064e","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/d8/d89b9f9730df61ec17959fa9b292442425633dc4dfbc0612adf0326eebcc064e.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:3c4cc058c5748c636fa8601f5bbca68af3f2c81921ab94afb77b5a5eeb01e852","bundle_entry_key":"phase-retrieval-angular-transfer","bundle_id":"population.t321-radial-angular-transfer-unaudited","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability and statistical learning","draft":"w724/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.functional.inequalities:t321-phase-retrieval-angular-transfer-w724-draft","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# A uniform radial gap and an explicit angular reduction

Status: proofs (unaudited) of two lemmas toward Target 2. Neither lemma is a polynomial upper bound for the full empirical sign quotient. No scored frontier move is claimed.

## 1. Conditional radial Poincare bound

For an integer d>=2, a>0, beta>0 and any real b, let rho have density

    p(r)=Z^{-1} r^{d-1} exp(-beta(a r^4-2b r^2)), r>0.

Then, with the ordinary radial derivative as energy,

    C_P(rho) <= pi/(2 sqrt(beta a(d-1))).                 (1)

This is uniform in b; it does not require global convexity of minus log p.

**Proof.** Put k=d-1>0, tau=beta a>0 and q=b/a. For V(r)=tau r^4-2 tau q r^2-k log r, let z>0 and -s<0 be the two roots of t^2-q t-k/(4tau)=0. Thus z s=k/(4tau), z-s=q, s>0. Set r_*=sqrt(z). Direct factorization gives, for every r>0,

    V'(r)=(r-r_*) A(r),
    A(r)=4tau (r+r_*)(r^2+s)/r
         >=8tau r_* sqrt(s)=4sqrt(tau k)=:kappa.        (2)

The inequality uses r+r_*>=r_* and r+s/r>=2sqrt(s). It is valid also for negative q. At r=r_* the factored identity still holds; no division by r-r_* is performed.

For r>=r_*, V'(r)>=kappa(r-r_*). For r<=r_*, multiplication by the negative factor reverses the comparison: V'(r)<=kappa(r-r_*). Integrating outward from any r>=r_* therefore gives

    V(r+u)-V(r)>=kappa u^2/2, u>=0.

Similarly for r<=r_* and 0<=u<r,

    V(r-u)-V(r)>=kappa u^2/2.

Let F(r)=rho((0,r]). The Gaussian integral consequently yields

    (1-F(r))/p(r)<=sqrt(pi/(2kappa))       if r>=r_*,
    F(r)/p(r)<=sqrt(pi/(2kappa))           if r<=r_*.

Since min(F,1-F) is no larger than either of these tails, for every r>0,

    p(r)/min(F(r),1-F(r))>=sqrt(2kappa/pi)=:h.           (3)

Here is the full Poincare implication of (3), so no external Cheeger convention is needed. Let m be the unique median, F(m)=1/2, and take a locally absolutely continuous f with finite weighted H1 norm. Put g=f-f(m), so g(m)=0. Integrate the bound |g(r)|^2<= integral between m and r of 2|g g'|. Tonelli, first over each side of m, gives

    integral g^2 p <=2 integral_0^m |g g'| F
                       +2 integral_m^infty |g g'|(1-F)
                  <=(2/h) integral |g g'| p
                  <=(2/h)(integral g^2 p)^(1/2)
                          (integral |g'|^2 p)^(1/2).

All integrands before applying Cauchy-Schwarz are nonnegative; no unproved interchange of signed integrals is used. Weighted H1 functions have a locally absolutely continuous representative because p is strictly positive on every compact subinterval. The finite H1 norm makes g square-integrable. If its norm is zero the conclusion is immediate; otherwise divide by its positive norm and square. Since Var(f)<=integral g^2 p, we obtain C_P<=4/h^2=2pi/kappa, which is (1). Normalization is finite because d>0 at zero and tau>0 controls the quartic tail.

## 2. Polar disintegration of the empirical loss

For a fixed sample a_1,...,a_m and a unit teacher v, define on the unit sphere

    A(u)=m^{-1}sum (a_i.u)^4,
    B(u)=m^{-1}sum (a_i.v)^2(a_i.u)^2,
    B0=m^{-1}sum (a_i.v)^4.

Then L(ru)=A(u)r^4-2B(u)r^2+B0. If the sample covariance S satisfies S>=lambda I with lambda>0, Cauchy-Schwarz gives A(u)>=(u^T S u)^2>=lambda^2 for every u. Let nu be the spherical marginal, with surface density proportional to

    Z(u)=integral_0^infty r^{d-1}
                   exp(-beta(A(u)r^4-2B(u)r^2)) dr.

Its radial conditional rho_u is the measure of Section 1 with a=A(u), b=B(u). Let a0 be any positive lower bound on A, and set

    C_r=pi/(2sqrt(beta a0(d-1))).

Simultaneously for every u, C_P(rho_u)<=C_r. For the sample event used in C003, lambda=1/2 and a0=1/4, so C_r=pi/sqrt(beta(d-1)). This uses a fourth-moment LOWER bound only; the known failure of a dimension-free uniform fourth-moment UPPER bound is irrelevant.

For a smooth compactly supported even f, write f_r(u)=f(ru) and g(u)=E_{rho_u} f_r(u). Exact variance disintegration gives

    Var_mu f <= C_r E_mu |partial_r f|^2 + Var_nu g.     (4)

Both the conditional law and nu are invariant under u -> -u, and g is even. Thus the second term is on the real projective sphere. This is the term not yet bounded polynomially.

## 3. A quantitative transfer bound if the angular gap is supplied

Assume, in addition to A>=a0>0, the deterministic spherical bounds

    0<=B<=b0, |grad_S A|<=a1, |grad_S B|<=b1.

Let C_nu be the Poincare constant of nu restricted to even functions, using the ordinary round-sphere gradient. Define the following finite constants:

    q0=b0/a0, e0=d/(4beta a0),
    U2=1+q0+e0,
    U4=e0+q0 U2,
    U6=(d+2)U2/(4beta a0)+q0 U4,
    T=32(a1^2 U6+b1^2 U2).

Then the full even-function Poincare constant obeys

    C_even(mu) <= C_r+2C_nu(U2+beta^2 C_r^2 T).          (5)

If C_nu is infinite this is understood only as a conditional statement; it does not assert a finite useful bound. For finite C_nu the proof is as follows.

Radial integration by parts, whose boundary terms r^{d+j}exp(-beta(Ar^4-2Br^2)) vanish at both endpoints for j=0,2, gives

    4beta A E r^4=d+4beta B E r^2,
    4beta A E r^6=(d+2) E r^2+4beta B E r^4.

Jensen gives (E r^2)^2<=E r^4. Solving the resulting quadratic inequality yields

    E r^2<=B/A+sqrt(d/(4beta A))<=q0+sqrt(e0)<=U2.

The same identities give E r^4<=U4 and E r^6<=U6. All these estimates are uniform in u.

Differentiate the normalized conditional expectation at fixed radius:

    grad_S g=E grad_S f_r-beta Cov(f_r,H),
    H=r^4 grad_S A-2r^2 grad_S B.                       (6)

Differentiation under the radial integral is justified by the uniform lower bound A>=a0 and finite smooth spherical coefficient bounds: every derivative is dominated by a polynomial in r times exp(-beta a0 r^4+2beta b0 r^2), integrable against r^{d-1}dr. The same domination applies to the compactly supported smooth f and its derivatives. The normalizer is positive and has a positive minimum on the compact sphere.

Weighted Cauchy-Schwarz gives

    |E grad_S f_r|^2<=U2 E(r^{-2}|grad_S f_r|^2).

At a fixed u use an orthonormal tangent basis. Scalar radial Poincare for each component of H gives

    E|H-EH|^2<=C_r E|partial_r H|^2<=C_r T,

since |partial_r H|^2=|4r^3 grad_S A-4r grad_S B|^2
<=32(r^6 a1^2+r^2 b1^2). Vector Cauchy-Schwarz and radial Poincare for f give

    |Cov(f_r,H)|^2<=Var(f_r) E|H-EH|^2
                       <=C_r^2 T E|partial_r f|^2.

Consequently (6) and |x+y|^2<=2|x|^2+2|y|^2 imply

    |grad_S g|^2<=2U2 E(r^{-2}|grad_S f_r|^2)
                 +2beta^2 C_r^2 T E|partial_r f|^2.

Apply the even-function spherical Poincare inequality to g, integrate over u, and use (4). The Euclidean polar identity

    |grad f|^2=|partial_r f|^2+r^{-2}|grad_S f_r|^2

shows that the resulting constant is at most the right side of (5). Smooth even functions are sufficient for this variational inequality and extend by closure to the even weighted Sobolev domain. Alternatively (5) may be read first on this smooth core; the Gibbs density is positive smooth and coercive, so symmetric mollification and smooth radial cutoffs give the usual weighted H1 approximation.

## 4. The comparison coefficients are polynomial on the existing sample event

The C003 event includes

    S>=I/2,
    m^{-1}sum (a_i.v)^2|a_i|^2<=4d,
    m^{-1}sum |a_i|^4<=2d(d+2).

Therefore one may use

    a0=1/4, b0=4d, a1=8d(d+2), b1=8d.

For example |grad_S A| is at most the full ambient gradient norm, bounded by 4m^{-1}sum |a_i.u|^3|a_i|<=4m^{-1}sum |a_i|^4. Similarly B and its gradient are bounded by the trace of m^{-1}sum (a_i.v)^2 a_i a_i^T and twice that trace. These are crude polynomial bounds; no dimension-free directional upper bound is asserted.

Thus every coefficient in (5) is bounded polynomially in d, beta and beta^{-1} (square roots can be bounded by 1 plus their arguments). In a specified polynomial beta(d,epsilon) regime, a polynomial C_nu would imply the desired polynomial C_even. The remaining unpaid step is precisely a polynomial Poincare bound for the even spherical marginal nu, whose density is the explicit radial integral Z(u). Ordinary compactness gives only finiteness; a generic density-oscillation comparison can cost exp(O(beta)) and does not close Target 2.

## Checks and limits of the claim

Equation (2), the direction reversal below r_*, the two Gaussian-tail integrations, and the median argument are separate load-bearing steps. The radial result requires d>1 and beta a>0; b need not be nonnegative. The empirical transfer uses B>=0, the uniform coefficient bounds, and a specified finite angular constant. No independence of radial and angular variables is asserted. Equation (4) is conditional variance, and (6) includes the conditional score covariance that would be lost by treating the variables as independent. [Lemma 20 of arXiv:2511.13559, 'Asymptotic analysis of rare events in high dimensions'] The derivative bounds~\eqref{forq},~\eqref{forw} of Proposition~\ref{prop:main} imply 
\begin{align}
\sup_{x\in\us(R\e)}\|\nabla_x^\ell\z(x,0)\|_H&\leq C_{\z}d^{\lceil\ell/2\rceil-2},\quad\ell=3,\dots,2N+2,\\
\sup_{x\in\us(R\e)}\|\nabla_x^\ell\g_k(x)\|_H&\leq C_{\z,\g}d^{\lceil\ell/2\rceil},\quad \ell=0,\dots,2(N+1-k),\;k=1,\dots,N,\\
\sup_{x\in \us(R\e),y\in[0, (R\e)^2]}|D_{\z}^{k-1}\g(x,y)|&\leq C_{\z,\g},\quad k=1,\dots,N+1.
\end{align} The constant $C_{\z}$ depends on $C_{\z,\ell}$, $\ell=0,\dots,2N+2$ from~\eqref{forw}. The constant $C_{\z,\g}$ is similar and also depends on $C_{\g,\ell}$, $\ell=0,\dots,2N$ from~\eqref{forq}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let Gamma have terminals a_0,a_1,..., joining a_{n-1} to a_n by n^2 2^{n+1} internally disjoint length-(n+1) paths, with all internal vertices distinct across paths and blocks. Independent Bernoulli bond percolation has p_c=1/2 and theta_Gamma(1/2)>3/5. For A_N={a_0 connects to a_N}, for every fixed t>=0 the conditional exponential moment E_{1/2}[exp(t N_{A_N})|A_N] is bounded uniformly in N; the conditional mean is less than 3. Yet for every 0<a<1/2 its integrated conditional pivotal cost from a to 1/2 tends to infinity. There is almost surely one infinite critical cluster. [Dfn 175 (discrete drift processes) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We let $\vD(s)$ and $\vD^\frozen(s)$ be the processes which start from 
 $\vD(q_0)= \vY(q_0)$
and $\vD^\frozen(q_0)= \vY^\frozen(q_0)$, 
are linear on each interval $q_d \le s \le q_{d+1}$, and have increments defined by
	\begin{align}
	
	\Delta\vD(q_d) 
	&= \bE\Big[ \vY(q_{d+1})
		\,\Big|\,\cG(q_d)\Big] 
		- \vY(q_d)
	=\bE\Big[ \Delta\vY(q_d) 
	\,\Big|\,\cG(q_d)\Big]
	\,,\\
	\Delta\vD^\frozen(q_d) 
	&= \bE\Big[ \vY^\frozen(q_{d+1})
		\,\Big|\,\cG(q_d)\Big] 
		- \vY^\frozen(q_d)
	=\bE\Big[ \Delta\vY^\frozen(q_d) 
	\,\Big|\,\cG(q_d)\Big]
	\,,
	
	\end{align}
with $\cG(q_d)$ as in \eqref{e:gaus.filt}.

Dominated extension form: let V be a real vector space, p : V -> R a sublinear functional (p(x + y) <= p(x) + p(y) and p(t x) = t p(x) for t >= 0), U a linear subspace of V, and f : U -> R a linear functional with f(u) <= p(u) for all u in U. Then there is a linear functional F : V -> R extending f with F(x) <= p(x) for all x in V. Normed form: if X is a real or complex normed space, U a subspace, and f a bounded linear functional on U, then f extends to a bounded linear functional on X with the same norm. Consequently, for every nonzero x in X there is a functional of norm one with F(x) = ||x||, so the dual separates points.
p sublinear (real case); in the complex case dominate |f| by a seminorm
the proof uses Zorn's lemma / the axiom of choice in general; no choice is needed for separable spaces

[Cor 11 of arXiv:2604.25964, 'Strong convergence rate of Euler-Maruyama approximations in temporal-spatial H\"older-norm'] Let $p \ge 2,$ 
    
    $T\in (0, \infty),$ $\mu, \sigma, \gamma  \in C^2(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R})$, $(\Om, \mf, \pr, (\mathcal{F})_{t\in [0, T]})$ be a filtered probability space which satisfies the usual conditions. 
    For every $n \in \mathbb{N}, x\in \mathbb{R}$, let $Y^{n,x} = \left(Y^{n, x}_t \right)_{t\in [0, T]}: [0, T] \times \Om \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy for all $k \in \{0, \dots, n-1\},$ $t\in \left( \frac{kT}{n}, \frac{(k+1)T}{n} \right]$ that $Y_0^{n, x}=x$ and 
    $$Y_{t}^{n, x} = Y_{\frac{kT}{n}}^{n, x}+\mu \left(Y_\frac{kT}{n}^{n, x}\right) \left (t- \frac{kT}{n} \right) +\sigma \left(Y_\frac{kT}{n}^{n, x}\right) \left(W_{t}- W_{\frac{kT}{n}}\right) +  \gamma (Y_\frac{kT}{n}^{n, x})\left(Z_{t}- Z_{\frac{kT}{n}}\right).$$ 
    Then for 
    every $x\in \mathbb{R}$, there exists an uniqueness adapted stochastic process with c\`adl\`ag sample paths $(X_t^x)_{t\in [0, T]}: [0, T]\times \Om \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $t\in [0, T]$, it holds a.s that $$X_t^x=x+\int^t_0\mu(X^x_s)ds+\int^t_0\sigma(X^x_s)dW_s + \int^t_0 \int_{\bR_0} \gamma (X^x_{s-})z \widetilde{N}(d s, d z),$$ and 
    for any $p \geq 2$ and $m > 1$, there exists a constant $C> 0$ such that for all $n\in \mathbb{N},$  $x \in \mathbb{R},$ $y\in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{x\}$, $t\in [0, T]$, it holds that 
        \begin{align*}
        &  \dfrac{\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\left|X^x_{t}-X^{y}_{t}\right|^p\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}}{|x-y| n^{\frac{1}{mp}}} 
        + \frac{\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\left|Y^{n,x}_{t}-Y^{n,y}_{t}\right|^p\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}}{|x-y| n^{\frac{1}{mp}}}\\
&+\dfrac{\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\left|X^x_{t}-Y^{n, x}_t\right|^p\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}}{1+|x|}+\dfrac{\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\left(X^x_{t}-Y^{n, x}_t\right)-\left(X^y_{t}-Y^{n, y}_t\right)\right|^p\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}}{|x-y|(1+|x|+|y|)} \leq \dfrac{C}{n^{\frac{1}{mp}}}.
        \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem construction of Gmp from coding functions and binomial pointset of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{[Berry_Broutin_Goldschmidt_12_The_continuum]}] 
  Fix $p \in (0,1)$.
  Let $\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}$ to be a tilted tree as defined above
  and $\mathcal{Q}^{p}$ be a binomial pointset of intensity $p$, independent of $\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}$.
  Let $v_{0}, v_{1}, \ldots, v_{m-1}$ be the vertices of $\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}$ in depth-first order.
  Write $\mathscr{T}(\mathcal{Q}^{p}, X_{\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}}) = \{(x_{i}, y_{i}) : 1 \leq i \leq s \}$
  (recall its definition from (equation eq: def of time markers from excursion and pointset of the paper)).
  We define a graph $G(\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}, \mathcal{Q}^{p})$
  by attaching an edge between $v_{x_{i}}$ and $v_{y_{i}}$ on $\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}$.
  (If $\mathscr{T}(\mathcal{Q}^{p}, X_{\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}})$ is empty, we define $G(\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}, \mathcal{Q}^{p}) \coloneqq  \tilde{T}_{m}^{p}$.)
  Then, $G(\tilde{T}_{m}^{p}, \mathcal{Q}^{p})$ has the same distribution as $G_{m}^{p}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Homomorphisms constructed with its help are generally called connecting homomorphisms.

[Lemma 25 of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] Let $t>0$ and $x\in\mbb R^2$ be fixed. For every $\eps>0$ and $A\subset[0,t]^2$,
\[\be^{\eps}_A(B^{x,x}_t)\deq t\,\be^{\eps/t}_{A/t}(B^{0,0}_1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\be^{\eps}_{A}(B^x)\deq t\,\be^{\eps/t}_{A/t}(B^0).\]
In particular, if $A=[a,b]^2_{\leq}$ for $0\leq a<b\leq t$, then by Theorem \ref{Theorem: Existence of SILT}-(2),
\[\ga_A(B^{x,x}_t)\deq t\,\ga_{A/t}(B^{0,0}_1)
\qquad
\text{and}
\qquad
\ga_{A}(B^x)\deq t\,\ga_{A/t}(B^0).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In linear algebra, eigendecomposition (also known as eigenvalue decomposition or EVD) is a factorization of a matrix $A$ into a canonical form given by $A=QDQ^{\mathsf {-1}}$, where $D$ is a diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues of $A$ on the diagonal, and $Q$ is a matrix whose columns are the corresponding eigenvectors of $A$. Only diagonalizable matrices can be factorized in this way. When the matrix being factorized is a normal or real symmetric matrix, the decomposition is called "spectral decomposition", derived from the spectral theorem.

[Lem 20 of arXiv:2607.06242, 'Exponential mixing and Freidlin--Wentzell large deviation principle for Markov cocycles'] Suppose for any $M>0$, there is a finite measurable $C_M:\Sigma\to \mathbb R_+$ such that for any $t>0$, any controlled path $u
       =\Phi^{\varphi_u}_{0,\cdot, \xi}u_0
       $ satisfying 
       \[
      {\frac 12} \int_0^t
      \|\varphi_u (s)\|^2 ds  \leq M, \quad d(u_0, \mathcal{A}(\xi))<1,\]
      and any $v_0 \in \mathcal{A}(\xi)$, there is a controlled path $v
      =\Phi^{\varphi_v}_{0,\cdot, \xi}v_0
      $ such that 
      \begin{align}
        \sup _{0 \leq s \leq t}\|u(s)-v(s)\|^2 \leq C_M(\xi)\left\|u_0-v_0\right\|^2
      \end{align}
      and 
      \begin{align}
        \int_0^t\left\|\varphi_u(s)-\varphi_v(s)\right\|^2 d s \leq C_M(\xi)\left\|u_0-v_0\right\|^2. 
      \end{align}
      Then \eqref{e.072701} is true.

Let G be a finite undirected loopless multigraph on n vertices with positive edge weights w_e, L its weighted Laplacian, and t > 0. A spanning rooted forest is a spanning forest with one chosen root in each tree; its weight is t^|E(F)| prod_{e in F} w_e (so an unrooted forest with trees T_1, ..., T_k counts prod |T_i| times). Z(t) is the total weight of spanning rooted forests, and Q_t = (I + tL)^-1. If i and j lie in the same connected component, t (e_i - e_j)^T Q_t (e_i - e_j) tends to the effective resistance R(i, j) = (e_i - e_j)^T L^+ (e_i - e_j) as t -> infinity (conductances w_e). If they lie in different components, the quantity tends to infinity.

Consider the realizable two-dimensional least-squares distribution of Kidambi-Netrapalli-Jain-Kakade: independently on each iteration choose a=sigma_1*z*e_1 or sigma_2*z*e_2 with probabilities1/2 each, where sigma_1>sigma_2>0, E z^2=2 and E z^4=2c with c>=2; the label is b=<a,w_star>. Use fresh IID samples and the Heavy Ball recursion w_(k+1)=w_k-delta*a_(k+1)*<a_(k+1),w_k-w_star>+alpha*(w_k-w_(k-1)), with delta>0, alpha in[0,1], and initial pair independent of the samples with finite second moments. Fix coordinate j, put x=delta*sigma_j^2 and h=1+alpha-x. For e_k=w_k^(j)-w_star^(j), form m_k=E[(e_k^2,e_k*e_(k-1),e_(k-1)*e_k,e_(k-1)^2)^T]. Then m_(k+1)=B*m_k, where B=[[h^2+(c-1)*x^2,-alpha*h,-alpha*h,alpha^2],[h,0,-alpha,0],[h,-alpha,0,0],[1,0,0,0]]. Its characteristic polynomial det(z*I_4-B) is D(z)=z^4-[h^2+(c-1)*x^2]*z^3+(2*alpha*h^2-2*alpha^2)*z^2+alpha^2*[-h^2+(c-1)*x^2]*z+alpha^4. These are raw second moments, with no zero-mean assumption on the error. An eigenvalue of B alone does not assert a matching lower bound for every particular initial pair.
The stated IID realizable two-axis distribution and fourth moment c>=2.

Let A_1, ..., A_n be events with S = sum_i P(A_i) > 0 and let N = 1_{A_1} + ... + 1_{A_n} be the number that occur. Then P(A_1 or ... or A_n) >= S^2 / sum_{i,j} P(A_i and A_j) (Chung and Erdős, 1952). The sum runs over all ordered pairs, i = j included, so the denominator is E[N^2] = S + sum over i != j of P(A_i and A_j), which is at least S > 0. Equality holds if and only if N is almost surely constant on the event {N > 0}. No independence is assumed.

body: In combinatorics, Ramsey's theorem, in one of its graph-theoretic forms, states that one will find monochromatic cliques in any edge labelling, with a fixed finite number of colours, of a sufficiently large complete graph. Precisely: for all positive integers r and c there exists a positive integer N = R_c(r) such that every labelling of the edges of a complete graph on at least N vertices with at most c colours contains a set of r vertices all of whose connecting edges carry the same colour. The finiteness of the number of colours is essential: with unboundedly many colours available (for example, a fresh colour on every edge) no monochromatic clique on 3 or more vertices need appear, however large the graph.
title: In combinatorics, Ramsey's theorem, in one of its graph-theoretic forms, states that one will find monochromatic cliques

body: In abstract algebra, a composition series provides a way to break up an algebraic structure, such as a group or a module, into simple pieces. The need for considering composition series in the context of modules arises from the fact that many naturally occurring modules are not semisimple, hence cannot be decomposed into a direct sum of simple modules. A composition series of a module M is a finite increasing filtration of M by submodules such that the successive quotients are simple and serves as a replacement of the direct sum decomposition of M into its simple constituents.
title: Composition series

body: In mathematics, specifically in differential topology, Morse theory enables one to analyze the topology of a manifold by studying differentiable functions on that manifold. According to the basic insights of Marston Morse, a typical differentiable function on a manifold will reflect the topology quite directly. Morse theory allows one to find CW structures and handle decompositions on manifolds and to obtain substantial information about their homology.
title: Morse theory

\]
and let \(\mu\) be the corresponding scalar dyadic Mandelbrot cascade measure
on \([0,1]\).  Set \(M=\mu([0,1])\).  Then, almost surely on \(\{M>0\}\),
\begin{equation}
    \dim_{\mathrm F}(\mu)
    =
    \dim_{\mathrm E}(\mu)
    =
    \dim_2(\mu)
    =
    D^+(W),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
D^+(W)
=
\sup_{1<q<2}
\max\left\{
0,\,
2-\frac2q\bigl(1+\log_2\mathbb{E}[W^q]\bigr)
\right\},
\end{equation}
with the convention that the corresponding term is interpreted as \(0\)
whenever \(\mathbb{E}[W^q]=\infty\).  In particular, on the same event, if
\(D^+(W)>0\), then for every \(0<\sigma<D^+(W)\) there are finite random
constants \(C_\sigma(\omega),R_\sigma(\omega)<\infty\) such that
\begin{equation}
    |\widehat{\mu}(\xi)|
    \le
    C_\sigma(\omega)|\xi|^{-\sigma/2}
    \qquad (|\xi|\ge R_\sigma(\omega)).
\end{equation}
If \(D^+(W)=0\), the decay assertion is vacuous.
