body: In mathematics, Tychonoff's theorem states that the product of any collection of compact topological spaces is compact with respect to the product topology. The theorem is named after Andrey Nikolayevich Tikhonov, who proved it first in 1930 for powers of the closed unit interval and in 1935 stated the full theorem along with the remark that its proof was the same as for the special case. The earliest known published proof is contained in a 1935 article by Tychonoff, "Über einen Funktionenraum".
title: Tychonoff's theorem

body: Let (M,g) be a connected Riemannian manifold with induced geodesic distance d. The Hopf-Rinow theorem states the following are equivalent: (1) (M,d) is a complete metric space; (2) M is geodesically complete, i.e. every geodesic extends to be defined on all of R (equivalently the exponential map at some, hence every, point is defined on the whole tangent space); (3) every closed bounded subset of M is compact. If these hold, any two points of M can be joined by a minimizing geodesic whose length realizes the distance d between them. Due to Heinz Hopf and Willi Rinow.
title: Hopf-Rinow theorem

[Defn 24 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] Fix $\omega\in\Omega_{0}$. We construct a legal
path $\omega_{0}=\omega,\omega_{1}=\omega_{0}^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}},\dots,\omega_{2n+1}=\omega_{2n}^{x_{2n}-1,x_{2n}}=\omega^{-1,0}$
(with $n$ depending on $\omega$). We do it in three phases:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Begin with a path $\omega_{0}=\omega,\omega_{1}=\omega_{0}^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}},\dots,\omega_{n}=\omega_{n-1}^{x_{n-1}-1,x_{n-1}}$,
whose last configuration satisfies $c(-1,0,\omega_{n})\neq0$ (here
$c=c^{\land}$ by Observation \ref{obs:D_and}). Recall Lemma \ref{lem:and_move_0},
and that $(k+1)F_{l(\omega)}(\omega)<l(\omega)$. If $c(-1,0,\omega)\neq0$
we are done (taking $n=0$). Otherwise, there exists $x\in[2,l(\omega)]$
with $\omega(x)=0,\ \omega(x-1)=1,\ c(x-1,x,\omega)=1$. Set $x_{0}$
to be the minimal such $x$, and $\omega_{1}=\omega^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}}$.

Continue by induction: assume that we constructed $\omega_{m}$. If
$c(-1,0,\omega)\neq0$ we move to phase 2. Otherwise, set $x_{m}$
to be the minimal $x\in[2,l(\omega)]$ such that $\omega_{m}(x)=0,\ \omega_{m}(x-1)=1,\ c(x-1,x,\omega_{m})=1$,
and $\omega_{m+1}=\omega_{m}^{x_{m}-1,x_{m}}$.

This procedure is valid, since we only exchange sites in $[1,l(\omega)]$,
so the condition $(k+1)F_{l(\omega)}(\omega_{m})<l(\omega)$ holds
for all $m$. Moreover, it must end: at each step the center of mass
$\sum_{x=1}^{l(\omega)}x\eta(x)$ increases by $1$, and it cannot
exceed $\sum_{x=1}^{l(\omega)}x\cdot1\le l(\omega)^{2}.$
\item Next, exchange $-1$ and $0$, choosing $x_{n}=0$ and $\omega_{n+1}=\omega_{n}^{-1,0}$.
\item Finally, wind back the path of phase 1: for $m\in\{n+1,\dots2n\}$
we set $x_{m}=x_{2n-m}$, and $\omega_{m+1}=\omega_{m}^{x_{m}-1,x_{m}}$.
Since all these transitions are in $[1,L]$ they do not depend on
the configuration at $-1$ and $0$, hence they are all legal and
end at $\omega_{2n+1}=\omega^{-1,0}$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Definition 24 of arXiv:2608.13208

[Definition Edge-rooted unimodularity of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Let $\hat{\mu}$ be a probability measure on decorated edge-rooted graphs.
    Let $(\mathbb{G},(\mathbf{o}_-,\mathbf{o}_+))$ be a random edge-weighted decorated graph with law $\hat \mu$. Let $\overset{\rightarrow}{e}_1$ be a uniformly picked directed edge of the form $(\mathbf{o}_+,\mathbf{v})$ for $\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{o}_-$. 
    We say that $\hat{\mu}$ is:
    \begin{itemize}
    \item stationary if $(\mathbb{G},(\mathbf{o}_-,\mathbf{o}_+))\overset{\mathcal{L}}{=}(\mathbb{G},\overset{\rightarrow}{e}_1)$
    \item revertible if $(\mathbb{G},(\mathbf{o}_-,\mathbf{o}_+))\overset{\mathcal{L}}{=}(\mathbb{G},(\mathbf{o}_+,\mathbf{o}_-))$ 
    \item unimodular if it is both revertible and stationary.
    \end{itemize}
    The subspace of unimodular laws on edge-rooted graphs will be noted $\mathcal{L}_U(\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{\star})$
title: Edge-rooted unimodularity

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2607.20714, 'High Minima of Gaussian Processes: Overshoots and Minimizer Locations'] The probability measure
\(\mu\in\cM(K)\) is optimal
if and only if

\[
        k_\mu(t)\ge \mathcal E_R(\mu),
        \qquad t\in K.
\]

Moreover, if \(\mu\) is optimal, then
\[
        k_\mu(t)=\mathcal E_R(\mu),
        \qquad t\in\supp(\mu).
\]

In particular, if \(k_\mu\) is constant on \(K\), then \(\mu\) is
optimal. If, in addition,
\[
        \mathcal E_R(\eta)>0
\]
for every nonzero finite signed measure \(\eta\) on \(K\) satisfying
\(\eta(K)=0\), then the optimal measure is unique.

Consequently, if \(\supp(\mu)=K\), then \(\mu\) is optimal if and only if
\(k_\mu\) is constant on \(K\).

body: [Theorem 3.4 of arXiv:2607.29403, 'Strong invariants and Tverberg numbers in convexity spaces'] Let $(X,\mathcal{C})$ be a convexity space with generator family $\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$. The following are equivalent. 1. $\textup{VC}(\mathcal{C})\leq d$. 2. Every subset of $X$ in convex position has size at most $d$. 3. The comatching number of $\mathcal{C}$ is at most $d$. 4. Every finite $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ has a subfamily $\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ of size at most $d$ with $\bigcap\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\bigcap\mathcal{F}$. 5. Every finite $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{G}$ has a subfamily $\mathcal{F}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ of size at most $d$ with $\bigcap\mathcal{F}^{\prime}=\bigcap\mathcal{F}$. 6. Every $(d+1)$ -element set $S\subseteq X$ has a nontrivial partition $S=S_{1}\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}S_{2}$ such that $\operatorname{conv}(S_{1})\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(S_{2})$. 7. Every finite $S\subseteq X$ has a subset $S^{\prime}\subseteq S$ of size at most $d$ with $\operatorname{conv}(S^{\prime})=\operatorname{conv}(S)$. 8. Every finite $Y\subseteq X$ has a partition into nonempty blocks $Y=Y_{1}\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}\cdots\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}Y_{t}$, each of size at most $d$, such that $\operatorname{conv}(Y_{1})\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(Y_{t}).$ 9. Every finite $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{G}$ has a partition into nonempty blocks $\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}_{1}\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}\cdots\mathbin{\dot{\cup}}\mathcal{F}_{t}$, each of size at most $d$, such that $\bigcap\mathcal{F}_{1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\bigcap\mathcal{F}_{t}.$ 10. The same statement as in 9 holds for every finite $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$.

Method: Fixed-degree random Cayley graphs with optimal spectral gap structural calculation Result: Abelian groups cannot supply even a uniform fixed-degree gap in a basic test case. For arbitrary r generators a_i of Z/pZ, divide the r-dimensional phase cube into M^r boxes with M^r<p. Two of the p points k*(a_1,...,a_r)/p fall in one box. Their nonzero difference k gives a nontrivial character for which all generator phases have distance at most2*pi/M from zero. Hence its adjacency eigenvalue is at least2r-4*pi^2*r/M^2. Check: Use cos(x)>=1-x^2/2 in the eigenvalue2*sum_i cos(2*pi*k*a_i/p). Taking M tending to infinity at order p^(1/r) forces the gap to0, regardless of how the generators were chosen. Obstruction: The argument identifies a structural obstruction to abelian candidates but supplies no optimal bound for the nonabelian special-linear families.

[Corollary cor:LRPexplicit of arXiv:2608.25279, 'Provable Non-Acceleration of Standard Strang\\ Splittings of Kinetic Langevin Dynamics'] Set
\begin{equation}
 h_\star=\frac{2}{\sqrt{26}},\qquad
 \beta_\star=\frac49,\qquad
 \gamma_\star=-\frac1{h_\star}\log\frac49.
\end{equation}
There exist a potential $U\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$1\le U''\le25$ and a constant $C>0$ such that the following holds
for every $R\ge1$. Let
\[
 U_R(x)=R^2U(x/R),
 \qquad
 Q_R=Q_{h_\star,\gamma_\star}^{U_R}.
\]
Then $U_R\in\mathcal U_{25}^1$, $Q_R$ has a unique invariant law $\pi_R$, and at least one of
the two explicit initial states defined in Section~(sec:LRP of the paper),
denoted by $z_R$, satisfies
\begin{equation}
 W_2(\delta_{z_R},\pi_R)\le CR,
 \qquad
 \norm{\delta_{z_R}Q_R^n-\pi_R}_{\mathrm{TV}}\ge\frac38,
 \qquad
 0\le n\le
 \left\lfloor\frac1{16}e^{R^2/8000}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Method: Check which steps of the DGFF proof use only the covariance asymptotics and which use the Gibbs-Markov property of the DGFF specifically. Result: The intermediate-level-set moment calculations (Theorem 2.7) use only the two-point Gaussian densities, which are determined by the covariance asymptotics, plus a coarse Gibbs-Markov decoupling at one scale used to identify the limit as unique; for a general field the decoupling can be replaced by the comparison of the field with the DGFF plus an independent bounded-variance field via Kahane-type interpolation, provided the covariance difference is bounded uniformly. Under the hypothesis (16.12) with an additional uniform bound sup |C_N(x,y) - G_N(x,y)| < infinity this gives the Theorem 2.7 analogue by a Gaussian comparison of the exponential moments. The extremal-process part is harder: the cluster law at the maximum depends on the local covariance limit (16.12) and is model-dependent, so universality can only be of the form: same Poisson structure, model-dependent cluster law and constant, which is what the DRZ maximum result already indicates. Obstruction: Without uniform boundedness of C_N - G_N the interpolation fails; with it, the level-set statement follows but the cluster law remains model-dependent.

CAMPAIGN RESULT [independently checked proof; E0095-HC v2; no novelty claim]. On Q_d, d>=2, adding a perfect matching of new edges has optimal ordinary SRW gap 4/(d+1), uniquely attained by antipodal pairs. The optimal non-lazy absolute gap is 2/(d+1), attained exactly by matchings whose edges preserve bit parity. If d is even, antipodes attain both optima; if d is odd, the unique ordinary optimizer is bipartite and has absolute gap zero. Half-lazy ordinary gaps are half the stated ordinary gaps. These claims concern spectral objectives, not minimum total-variation mixing time.

body: The abc conjecture (also known as the Oesterlé–Masser conjecture) is a conjecture in number theory that arose out of a discussion of Joseph Oesterlé and David Masser in 1985. It is stated in terms of three positive integers $a,b$ and $c$ (hence the name) that are relatively prime and satisfy $a+b=c$. The conjecture essentially states that the product of the distinct prime factors of $abc$ cannot often be much smaller than $c$. A number of famous conjectures and theorems in number theory would follow immediately from the abc conjecture or its versions. Mathematician Dorian Goldfeld described the abc conjecture as "The most important unsolved problem in Diophantine analysis".

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check what the random-current and infrared bounds give and where each half of the conjecture sits. Result: Upper bound: the infrared bound gives <sigma_0 sigma_x> <= C |x|^{-(d-2)} = C|x|^{-1} in d = 3, and improving to |x|^{-(1+eps)} is the statement eta > 0 (anomalous dimension), known numerically eta = 0.036; an argument would need to show the two-point function is strictly smaller than the Gaussian one in a scale-invariant way, e.g. via the random-current intersection probabilities (the same quantity that gives non-triviality, C0052): if two independent currents from 0 to x and from y to z intersect with probability bounded below uniformly, one gets a strict improvement of Simon-Lieb at every scale which iterates to a power gain. Lower bound: Simon-Lieb / Lebowitz give <sigma_0 sigma_x> >= c |x|^{-(d-1)} = c|x|^{-2} in d = 3 (the source's Theorem 4.8), and improving the exponent below 2 needs a lower bound on the two-point function from the connectivity of the random-current clusters better than the trivial one-path bound. Whether the one-path bound can give better than d - 1 was not settled: the self-avoiding-path bound gives only tanh(beta_c) >= 1/mu_SAW, not equality, so the series of self-avoiding paths weighted by tanh(beta_c)^n is not known to be balanced at Ising criticality, and the view that the improvement must come from multi-path (cluster) contributions is a heuristic. No quantitative result. Obstruction: Both halves need scale-invariant intersection estimates for random currents in d = 3, which are not available.

PROOF (UNAUDITED), w741-T422-C02 v1. Not independently checked.
# T422 Target 1: explicit constants for the optimal constant step

Status: candidate proof; independent review pending. The theorem concerns expected
risk. Its first hitting index is deterministic, not a pathwise stopping time.

## Model and statement

Use the exact Gaussian second-moment recurrence established in the row diagnostics.
The covariance eigenvalues are h_j=j^(-alpha), alpha>1. The initial mode energies
are h_j a_j(0)=j^(-gamma), gamma>1. Labels have independent, mean-zero noise with
variance sigma2>=0. Each step uses B independent fresh examples, B a positive
integer. The batch gradient is their average. Put

    v_t = sum_j h_j a_j(t) = twice expected excess risk,
    Z_r = zeta(r),  v_0=Z_gamma,
    p=(gamma-1)/alpha >0, q=(2alpha-1)/alpha in (1,2).

This follows the existing diagnostics' gamma convention. If the target exponent
beta specifies a_j(0)=j^(-beta), then gamma=alpha+beta. If beta specifies the
risk mode energy h_j a_j(0)=j^(-beta), then gamma=beta. The two conventions must
not be interchanged. In Wang et al.'s Assumption 3.3, alpha is their beta and
p is their source exponent s.

Let S*(B,epsilon) be the minimum first hitting index of v_t<=epsilon v_0 over
ALL constant steps eta>0. No stability restriction is imposed on that minimum.
Define E*=B S*. For delta=epsilon Z_gamma, set

    eta_eff = min( 2B/Z_alpha, 2/(1+1/B), 4 delta B/(sigma2 Z_alpha) ),

where the third entry is omitted if sigma2=0, and

    Phi_1=epsilon^(-1/p)/eta_eff,
    Phi_2=(B epsilon)^(-1/q) eta_eff^(-(1-1/q)),
    Phi=max(Phi_1,Phi_2).

Here are explicit constants, all depending only on alpha,gamma:

    d=2^(-gamma-1-p)/(gamma-1),
    k=2^(-2alpha-1-q)/(2alpha-1),
    N=ceil(max(1, [2/((alpha-1) Z_alpha)]^(1/(alpha-1)))),
    T=N^alpha/2,
    epsilon_0=min(1/(8 Z_gamma), d/(2 Z_gamma T^p)).

For r>1 write s_r=(r-1)/alpha and define

    C(r)=2^s_r max( Z_r,
                   Gamma(s_r)/alpha + 2 [r/(e alpha)]^(r/alpha) ).
    C_D=C(gamma), C_K=C(2alpha).

If p<=q, define

    H=1+1/(1-p)                 if 0<p<1,
    H=1+1/(e(q-1))              if p=1,
    H=1+1/(p-1)                 if 1<p<=q,
    kappa=ceil(max(32, 1+4*2^p, 8*2^q C_K H/Z_alpha)),
    U=kappa (8 C_D/Z_gamma)^(1/p).

If p>q, define

    kappa=ceil(max(32, 1+4*2^p)),
    A=2^(q+4) C_K Z_(gamma-alpha),
    U=max( kappa (8 C_D/Z_gamma)^(1/p),
           kappa^(1-1/q) (A/Z_gamma)^(1/q) ).

Finally set

    c_minus=min( (d/Z_gamma)^(1/p)/4,
                 (k/(4 Z_gamma))^(1/q) 4^(-(1-1/q)) ),
    c_plus=2+U.

For every B>=1, sigma2>=0, and 0<epsilon<=epsilon_0, the claimed bounds are

    c_minus Phi <= S*(B,epsilon) <= c_plus Phi,
    c_minus B Phi <= E*(B,epsilon) <= c_plus B Phi.              (THEOREM)

The upper bound is achieved to these constants by the explicit stable choice
eta=eta_eff/kappa. The lower bound covers even a step that reaches the target
before subsequently diverging. Constants are deliberately conservative.



Model convention: the full gamma>1 range uses finite-risk Gaussian L2 series predictions, or the exact nonnegative second-moment recurrence. If the target coefficient sequence must belong to ordinary l2, impose gamma>alpha+1. The theorem does not assert an ordinary l2 target outside that range.

Status: candidate proof; independent review pending. The theorem concerns expected
risk. Its first hitting index is deterministic, not a pathwise stopping time.

## Model and statement

Use the exact Gaussian second-moment recurrence established in the row diagnostics.
The covariance eigenvalues are h_j=j^(-alpha), alpha>1. The initial mode energies
are h_j a_j(0)=j^(-gamma), gamma>1. Labels have independent, mean-zero noise with
variance sigma2>=0. Each step uses B independent fresh examples, B a positive
integer. The batch gradient is their average. Put

    v_t = sum_j h_j a_j(t) = twice expected excess risk,
    Z_r = zeta(r),  v_0=Z_gamma,
    p=(gamma-1)/alpha >0, q=(2alpha-1)/alpha in (1,2).

This follows the existing diagnostics' gamma convention. If the target exponent
beta specifies a_j(0)=j^(-beta), then gamma=alpha+beta. If beta specifies the
risk mode energy h_j a_j(0)=j^(-beta), then gamma=beta. The two conventions must
not be interchanged. In Wang et al.'s Assumption 3.3, alpha is their beta and
p is their source exponent s.

Let S*(B,epsilon) be the minimum first hitting index of v_t<=epsilon v_0 over
ALL constant steps eta>0. No stability restriction is imposed on that minimum.
Define E*=B S*. For delta=epsilon Z_gamma, set

    eta_eff = min( 2B/Z_alpha, 2/(1+1/B), 4 delta B/(sigma2 Z_alpha) ),

where the third entry is omitted if sigma2=0, and

    Phi_1=epsilon^(-1/p)/eta_eff,
    Phi_2=(B epsilon)^(-1/q) eta_eff^(-(1-1/q)),
    Phi=max(Phi_1,Phi_2).

Here are explicit constants, all depending only on alpha,gamma:

    d=2^(-gamma-1-p)/(gamma-1),
    k=2^(-2alpha-1-q)/(2alpha-1),
    N=ceil(max(1, [2/((alpha-1) Z_alpha)]^(1/(alpha-1)))),
    T=N^alpha/2,
    epsilon_0=min(1/(8 Z_gamma), d/(2 Z_gamma T^p)).

For r>1 write s_r=(r-1)/alpha and define

    C(r)=2^s_r max( Z_r,
                   Gamma(s_r)/alpha + 2 [r/(e alpha)]^(r/alpha) ).
    C_D=C(gamma), C_K=C(2alpha).

If p<=q, define

    H=1+1/(1-p)                 if 0<p<1,
    H=1+1/(e(q-1))              if p=1,
    H=1+1/(p-1)                 if 1<p<=q,
    kappa=ceil(max(32, 1+4*2^p, 8*2^q C_K H/Z_alpha)),
    U=kappa (8 C_D/Z_gamma)^(1/p).

If p>q, define

    kappa=ceil(max(32, 1+4*2^p)),
    A=2^(q+4) C_K Z_(gamma-alpha),
    U=max( kappa (8 C_D/Z_gamma)^(1/p),
           kappa^(1-1/q) (A/Z_gamma)^(1/q) ).

Finally set

    c_minus=min( (d/Z_gamma)^(1/p)/4,
                 (k/(4 Z_gamma))^(1/q) 4^(-(1-1/q)) ),
    c_plus=2+U.

For every B>=1, sigma2>=0, and 0<epsilon<=epsilon_0, the claimed bounds are

    c_minus Phi <= S*(B,epsilon) <= c_plus Phi,
    c_minus B Phi <= E*(B,epsilon) <= c_plus B Phi.              (THEOREM)

The upper bound is achieved to these constants by the explicit stable choice
eta=eta_eff/kappa. The lower bound covers even a step that reaches the target
before subsequently diverging. Constants are deliberately conservative.

## Exact recurrence and positivity

Set lambda=eta^2/B and g_j=(1-eta h_j)^2+lambda h_j^2. The row's Gaussian
fourth-moment identity gives

    a_j(t+1)=g_j a_j(t)+lambda h_j(v_t+sigma2).

Iteration gives, for finite integer t,

    D_t=sum_j j^(-gamma)g_j^t,
    K_u=sum_j h_j^2 g_j^u,
    v_t=D_t+lambda sum_(s=0)^(t-1) K_(t-1-s)v_s
             +lambda sigma2 sum_(u=0)^(t-1)K_u.                (1)

Every summand is nonnegative. All finite-time quantities are finite: h_j<=1,
g_j is uniformly bounded for fixed eta, sum j^(-gamma)<infinity, and
sum h_j^2<infinity. Tonelli justifies rearrangements of these nonnegative sums.

## Lower bound: a first-hit step cap without a stability hypothesis

Take any eta whose first hit t exists, and write tau=eta t. Since delta<1,
g_1>=1 would give v_t>=D_t>=1>delta. Consequently

    eta<2/(1+1/B),  and 0<=g_j<1 for every j.                 (2)

If tau<=1/2, Bernoulli's inequality gives
v_t>=g_1^t>=(1-eta)^(2t)>=(1-t eta)^2>=1/4, contradicting
delta<=1/8. Thus tau>1/2.

For j>=J=ceil((2tau)^(1/alpha)), eta h_j<=1/(2t), so Bernoulli
again gives g_j^t>=(1-t eta h_j)^2>=1/4. Since
J<=2(2tau)^(1/alpha), comparison with the decreasing tail integral yields

    D_t >= (1/4) sum_(j>=J) j^(-gamma)
        >= (1/4) J^(1-gamma)/(gamma-1)
        >= d tau^(-p).                                      (3)

In particular delta>=d tau^(-p), so epsilon<=epsilon_0 forces tau>=T.
The same argument with exponent 2alpha, using g_j^(t-1)>=g_j^t, gives

    K_(t-1)>=k tau^(-q).                                    (4)

We use the following elementary finite geometric bound:

    y>0, z>=max(0,1-y) implies
    sum_(u=0)^(t-1) z^u >= t/(1+ty).                        (5)

For 0<y<=1, the inequality (1-y)^t(1+ty)<=1 proves (5) by summing
the geometric series. The product decreases with t because its successive
difference is -(t+1)y^2(1-y)^t. For y>1, the left side is at least 1 and
the right side is below 1. In particular, applying (5) with y=2eta h_j
and z=g_j gives at least 1/(4eta h_j) whenever eta h_j t>=1/2.

The integer N above satisfies

    sum_(j>N) h_j <= N^(1-alpha)/(alpha-1) <= Z_alpha/2.

Because tau>=N^alpha/2, all j<=N are resolved in the sense of (5).
Therefore the truncated renewal mass obeys

    M_t=lambda sum_(u<t)K_u
       >= (eta/(4B)) sum_(j<=N)h_j
       >= eta Z_alpha/(8B).                                (6)

At a FIRST hit all v_s>delta for s<t, so (1), including D_t>0, gives
delta>=v_t>delta M_t. Thus M_t<1 and

    eta<8B/Z_alpha.                                        (7)

Also (1) gives v_t>=sigma2 M_t, so when sigma2>0,

    eta<=8delta B/(sigma2 Z_alpha).                         (8)

Combining (2), (7), (8) gives eta<=4 eta_eff. This argument does not
assume risk stability or monotonicity before the hit. It uses only the fact
that none of the earlier EXPECTED risks has crossed delta.

One further lower bound captures the intrinsic SGD noise tail. Removing
the label source and substituting v_s>=D_s in (1), monotonicity of K_u
from (2) gives

    v_t>=lambda K_(t-1) sum_(s<t)D_s.

The first initial mode has energy 1, and (5) with h_1=1 and tau>1/2
gives sum_(s<t)D_s>=1/(4eta). With (3), (4) we obtain

    t>=(d/delta)^(1/p)/eta,
    t>=(k/(4Bdelta))^(1/q) eta^(-(1-1/q)).                   (9)

Since both right sides decrease with eta, substituting eta<=4eta_eff
proves S*>=c_minus Phi. The argument holds for every hitting step, so it
also holds for the optimum over all positive constant steps.

## Upper bound: elementary spectral envelopes

Choose eta=eta_eff/kappa. Then eta<=1 and

    1-g_j=eta h_j[2-eta h_j(1+1/B)]>=eta h_j,
    S=lambda sum_j h_j^2/(1-g_j)
      <=eta Z_alpha/[2B(1-1/kappa)]<=1/(kappa-1).             (10)

Thus g_j<=exp(-eta h_j). Define f_r(t)=(1+eta t)^(-r).
We claim

    D_t<=C_D f_p(t),  K_t<=C_K f_q(t).                      (11)

For completeness, the continuous function x^(-r)exp(-tau x^(-alpha))
on x>0 is unimodal, has integral Gamma((r-1)/alpha) tau^(-(r-1)/alpha)/alpha,
and maximum [r/(e alpha tau)]^(r/alpha). Its sum at positive integers
is at most its integral plus twice its maximum. One justification is
to compare each integer value with its integral on [j,j+1]; the total
error is bounded by the integral of the absolute derivative, at most
twice the maximum. For tau>=1 this proves the second entry in C(r),
using r/alpha>(r-1)/alpha and (1+tau)<=2tau. For 0<=tau<1 use
sum_j j^(-r)g_j^t<=Z_r and (1+tau)^(-s_r)>=2^(-s_r).
This proves (11), including t=0. All integrals converge since r>1.

Separate the solution into v_det from the initial condition and v_sig
from the constant label-noise source. Linearity and nonnegative coefficients
justify this decomposition. We first bound v_det.

## Upper bound for 0<p<=q, including p=1

For x>=0, let I_p(x)=integral_0^x (1+u)^(-p)du. The three definitions
of H above give

    (1+x)^(p-q)[1+I_p(x)]<=H.                              (12)

For p<1 use I_p(x)<= (1+x)^(1-p)/(1-p) and q>1. For p>1 use
I_p(x)<=1/(p-1) and p<=q. For p=1 use
sup_(y>=1) y^(-(q-1))log y=1/(e(q-1)), obtained by differentiation.

Split a convolution at m=floor(t/2). If s>=m and s<t, then eta<=1
implies 1+eta s>=(1+eta t)/2. If s<m, the index u=t-1-s is at least m,
and 1+eta u>=(1+eta t)/2. The latter assertion is only needed when
the early sum is nonempty; t=1 has no early sum. Hence

    lambda sum_(s<t)K_(t-1-s) f_p(s)
    <=2^p S f_p(t)
       +lambda 2^q C_K f_q(t) sum_(s<m)f_p(s).

Monotonicity and an integral comparison give
sum_(s<m)f_p(s)<=1+I_p(eta t)/eta<=[1+I_p(eta t)]/eta.
Using (12), the convolution is at most

    [2^p/(kappa-1) + 2^(q+1) C_K H/(kappa Z_alpha)] f_p(t)
    <= (1/2) f_p(t),                                      (13)

by the definition of kappa. Equation (1) with sigma2=0 and induction
on t now gives

    v_det(t)<=2 C_D f_p(t).                                (14)

This supplies explicit constants even at p=1; no logarithmic loss in the
leading risk rate is required.

## Upper bound for p>q

Here gamma-alpha>1. By (10) and Tonelli,

    sum_t D_t=sum_j j^(-gamma)/(1-g_j)
             <=Z_(gamma-alpha)/eta.

For every finite cutoff L, (1) and positivity give
sum_(t<L)v_det(t)<=sum_t D_t+S sum_(t<L)v_det(t).
Thus

    sum_t v_det(t)<= Z_(gamma-alpha)/[eta(1-S)]
                  <=2 Z_(gamma-alpha)/eta.                 (15)

Split (1) again at m=floor(t/2). The early part is at most

    (eta/B) 2^(q+1) C_K Z_(gamma-alpha) f_q(t).

Put F(t)=C_D f_p(t)+(eta/B)2^(q+1)C_K Z_(gamma-alpha)f_q(t).
For the late part, induction v_det(s)<=2F(s), the inequalities
F(s)<=2^pF(t) for s>=m, and 2^pS<=1/4 give at most F(t)/2.
Adding D_t and the early part gives at most 3F(t)/2<=2F(t).
The initial case holds since C_D>=Z_gamma. Therefore

    v_det(t)<=2C_D f_p(t)
              +(eta/B)2^(q+2) C_K Z_(gamma-alpha) f_q(t).    (16)

No divergent mass is used: (15) is invoked only when p>q>1.

## Label-noise response and the hitting upper bound

At the chosen eta, the nonnegative linear update for a_sig is driven
by lambda sigma2 h. It increases coordinatewise from zero. Its stationary
solution has v_inf=sigma2 S/(1-S); alternatively, finite-time partial
sums and (10) directly give v_sig(t)<=sigma2 S/(1-S). Since kappa>=32,
S<=1/(kappa-1)<1/2 and S<=eta Z_alpha/B. If sigma2>0 the definition
of eta_eff consequently gives

    v_sig(t)<=2sigma2 eta Z_alpha/B<=8delta/kappa<=delta/4.  (17)

For sigma2=0 it is zero. No exchange of signed series or unproved
stationarity assumption is needed.

For p<=q choose t=ceil((8C_D/delta)^(1/p)/eta). Equation (14) gives
v_det(t)<=delta/4, so a hit has occurred by that index. For p>q choose

    t=ceil(max( (8C_D/delta)^(1/p)/eta,
                [2^(q+4)C_K Z_(gamma-alpha)/(Bdelta)]^(1/q)
                 eta^(-(1-1/q)) )).

Each term on the right side of (16) is then at most delta/4, and (17)
gives total v_t<=3delta/4. These are sufficient hitting times, not claims
that the optimal step equals eta_eff/kappa.

Substitute eta=eta_eff/kappa and delta=epsilon Z_gamma. The displayed
choice of U gives t<=1+U Phi. Finally eta_eff<=2 and epsilon<1 imply
Phi>=Phi_1>=1/2, so 1+U Phi<=(2+U)Phi=c_plus Phi.
Multiplying by B proves the example-complexity statement.

## Provenance, limitations, and checks

The exact moment recurrence is settled ground from the row's THEORY_DRAFT.md.
Wang, Huang, Li, Wu, arXiv:2609.02728v1, Section 3.1 Assumptions 3.1--3.3,
Section 4 Definitions 4.1--4.2, Section 5 equation (12), and Section 6
Definition 6.2 give the Gaussian power-law setting, risk-stable admissible
steps, and scaling-law comparison. They do not supply the constants above.
No priority claim is made beyond this inspected source comparison.

McCandlish et al., arXiv:1812.06162, equations (2.8)--(2.9), distinguish
Hessian-weighted B_noise from B_simple. This theorem does not settle their
calibration at the hitting iterate; that is Target 2.

The theorem uses exact power laws with unit coefficients, the same family
as the row diagnostics. Comparable power laws with nonunit envelopes need
additional constants. A finite truncation needs its own lower-tail cutoff.
The theorem concerns a last iterate and a fixed step, not iterate averaging
or a decaying schedule. These qualifications delimit the statement.

Checks to run before recording status as proof (unaudited): exact rational
geometric and finite-recurrence checks; a negative control removing FIRST
from the hitting hypothesis; inspect the p=1, p=q, sigma2=0 and B=1 cases;
verify every sum uses positivity or a summable envelope. A Lean check of
the finite geometric product is recorded separately and certifies that
product only, not this entire theorem.


## Review supplement: model scope and verification status
# Finite-risk Gaussian targets

The full gamma>1 range uses targets defined by Gaussian L2 series. If the
target coefficient sequence itself must lie in ordinary l2, impose gamma>alpha+1.

For c with sum_j h_j c_j^2<infinity, define its prediction as the L2 limit
of sum_(j<=n)c_j x_j. Independent centered Gaussian coordinates give tail
variance sum_(j>n)h_j c_j^2, which tends to zero. The same construction
applies conditionally to errors independent of the next fresh batch when
E sum_j h_j e_j^2<infinity. The weighted norm is finite almost surely.

Since tr H<infinity, x lies in l2 almost surely. The stochastic gradient
x(r(e,x)-xi) lies in l2 and its conditional expected squared norm equals

    (tr H)(e'He+sigma2)+2 e'H^2e.

This has finite expectation because e'H^2e<=e'He. Mini-batch averages have
finite second moments. Adding their l2 increments preserves finite expected
H-weighted error norm because H is bounded. Induction defines every finite
iterate and its risk. Thus an l2 predictor can train against an L2 Gaussian
target whose coefficient sequence does not itself belong to l2.

For h_j a_j(0)=j^-gamma the weighted norm is zeta(gamma), finite for gamma>1.
The unweighted coefficient norm sum_j j^(alpha-gamma) is finite exactly
when gamma>alpha+1. The core proofs also apply directly to the exact
nonnegative second-moment recurrence. They assert no ordinary l2 target
in the range where that norm diverges.

[Defn of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] For $\bm{x}\in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $1 \leq k \leq n$, we define the standard positive and negative quadrants at $\bm{x}$ in the $k$-first coordinates as
\begin{align*}
    C_k^+(\bm{x}) &\coloneqq [x_1,+\infty)\times\dots\times [x_k,+\infty) \times \{(x_{k+1}, \dots ,x_n)\} , \\
    C_k^-(\bm{x}) &\coloneqq (-\infty, x_1] \times \dots \times (-\infty,  x_k] \times \{(x_{k+1}, \dots ,x_n)\}.
\end{align*}

Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a closed set. A point $\bm{x}\in A$ is an \textbf{upper extremal point} in the $k$ first coordinates if $$C^+_k(\bm{x})\cap A = \{\bm{x}\},$$
and it is a \textbf{lower extremal point} in these coordinates if 
$$C^-_k(\bm{x})\cap A = \{\bm{x}\}.$$

[Theorem 1 (Exact common-center geometry for empirical energy-form FullCP) of arXiv:2608.24964, 'Common-Center Geometry and Certified Radial Reconstruction for Energy-Form Full Conformal '] Let $m\ge1$, $d\ge1$, and $y_1,\ldots,y_m\in\mathbb R^d$, with scores defined above.  For
\[
d_j=\sum_{i\ne j}\rho(y_j,y_i),
\]
assume first that $\rho$ is symmetric and has constant diagonal
\[
\rho(x,x)=q.
\]
Then, for every $j=1,\ldots,m$ and every candidate $t$,
\[
\alpha_j(t)-\alpha(t)
=
\frac{m+1}{m^2}
\left[
 d_j-\sum_{i\ne j}\rho(t,y_i)
\right].
\]
Consequently,
\[
I_j
=
\left\{
 t:\sum_{i\ne j}\rho(t,y_i)\le d_j
\right\}.
\]

Now additionally assume
\[
\rho(x,y)\ge q
\qquad\forall x,y,
\]
and that
\[
F(t)=\sum_{i=1}^m\rho(t,y_i)
\]
attains a global minimizer
\[
c\in\arg\min_t F(t).
\]
Then
\[
c\in I_j
\qquad\forall j.
\]
If, additionally, every $I_j$ is convex, then for every $0\le\varepsilon<1$ with
\[
1\le k=\lfloor(m+1)\varepsilon\rfloor\le m,
\]
the exact conformal prediction region
\[
\Gamma^\varepsilon
=
\{t:p(t)>\varepsilon\}
=
\{t:N(t)\ge k\}
\]
is star-shaped about $c$.

The endpoint conventions are
\[
k=0\Longrightarrow\Gamma^\varepsilon=\mathbb R^d,
\qquad
\varepsilon=1\Longrightarrow\Gamma^1=\varnothing.
\]
Score ties $\alpha_j(t)=\alpha(t)$ are included in $I_j$ and count as votes.

body: [Proposition 6 (Volterra criterion for an admissible diagonal) of arXiv:2606.16662, '2606.16662'] Assume Assumption~\ref{ass:diag} for \(\tau=(i;j,k)\), and let \(s<\Delta_\tau-10\eps\). Let (X, Sigma, mu) be any measure space and f, g in L^p(mu). (a) For 2 <= p < infinity: ||(f+g)/2||_p^p + ||(f-g)/2||_p^p <= (||f||_p^p + ||g||_p^p)/2. (b) For 1 < p <= 2 with q = p/(p-1): ||(f+g)/2||_p^q + ||(f-g)/2||_p^q <= ( (||f||_p^p + ||g||_p^p)/2 )^{q-1}. Consequently L^p(mu) is uniformly convex for every 1 < p < infinity: for 2 <= p < infinity, if ||f||_p = ||g||_p = 1 and ||f-g||_p >= epsilon, then ||(f+g)/2||_p <= (1 - (epsilon/2)^p)^{1/p} < 1. By the Milman-Pettis theorem, L^p is reflexive for 1 < p < infinity, and closed convex subsets have unique nearest points. L^1 and L^infinity are not uniformly convex (and not reflexive) on a nonatomic space such as [0,1].

[Lemma lem:regularise of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] Let $\rho$ be a probability measure with finite second moment and let $v>0$. Then
$\nu=\rho\boxplus\gamma_{v}$ has a bounded continuous density $\psi_{\nu}$ with
$\norm{\psi_{\nu}}_{\infty}\le(\pi\sqrt v)^{-1}$, and
\begin{equation}
  \Phi^{*}(\nu)\le\frac{1}{v}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for the forward flow (equation eq:marginal of the paper) and every $t>0$,
\[
  \Phi^{*}(\mu_{t})\le\frac{1}{1-\alpha_{t}}<\infty,
  \qquad \Xi_{t}=\xi_{\mu_{t}}(X_{t})\in L^{2}(\tau),
  \qquad I(\mu_{t}\Vert\gamma)<\infty .
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Instantaneous regularisation

[Corollary 6 of arXiv:2605.20026, 'Quasihelix properties\\ of selected Volterra Gaussian processes'] Let $0<T_1<T_2$ and $\gamma\in[0,1)$.
Comparing the properties of the process $U^{(2)}$ from Theorem \ref{theor1-1b} and of  process $V$ from Theorem \ref{theor1-2},  we can state the respective properties of the process $U^{(6)}$.
\begin{enumerate}[$(i)$]
\item
If $\alpha\in(-1/2,1/2)$, then $U^{(6)}$ is a local
$(\alpha+\frac12,T_1,T_2)$-quasihelix.

\item
If $\alpha=1/2$, then $U^{(6)}$ is a local
$(1,1-\varepsilon,T_1,T_2)$-generalized quasihelix for any
$\varepsilon\in(0,1)$.

\item
If $\alpha\in(1/2,1/2+\gamma/2)$, then $U^{(6)}$ is a local
$(1,T_1,T_2)$-quasihelix.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 6 of arXiv:2605.20026

For constants k ≥1 and K ≥0, we say a map f : X →Y is a (k, K)–quasiisometric embedding if, for all points x1, x2 ∈X 1 kdX(x1, x2) −K ≤dY �f(x1), f(x2)  ≤k dX(x1, x2) + K. If, in addition, every point in Y lies in the K–neighbourhood of the image of f, then f is called a (k, K)–quasi-isometry. When such a map exists, X and Y are said to be quasi-isometric.

Then there exists a sequence of weights $\{a_n(\theta)\}_{n\ge 1}\in{\mathbb{R}}$ with $a_n(\theta)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty,$ such that 
$$\varphi_\theta (z) \, =\, \exp \left[ \sum_{n\ge 1}\, \frac{a_n(\theta)}{n} \, z^n\right]$$
for all $z\in [-1,1].$ If $\theta \in (-1,0)$ one has $a_2(\theta) = - a_2(1/\theta) > 0.$ The sequence $\{p_n(\theta)\}_{n\ge 0}$ is never log-convex. body: Banach fixed-point theorem: if (X, d) is a nonempty complete metric space and T : X -> X satisfies d(T x, T y) <= q d(x, y) for all x, y with a fixed q in [0, 1), then T has exactly one fixed point x*, and from any start the Picard iterates x_{n+1} = T x_n converge to x* with d(x_n, x*) <= q^n d(x_1, x_0) / (1 - q). Completeness and q < 1 are both essential (x -> x + 1 on R shows q = 1 fails).
title: Banach fixed-point theorem

On {-1, 1}^n (n >= 1) with the uniform probability measure mu, chi_S(x) = prod over i in S of x_i for S inside [n], and f^(S) = E[f chi_S] is the Walsh-Fourier coefficient of a real function f, so f = sum over S of f^(S) chi_S. Let R_1, ..., R_r be subsets of [n] whose incidence vectors are linearly independent over F_2, let eps_1, ..., eps_r be signs and A = {x : chi_{R_j}(x) = eps_j for every j}. Then 1_A = 2^(-r) prod over j of (1 + eps_j chi_{R_j}) = 2^(-r) sum over u in F_2^r of (prod over j with u_j = 1 of eps_j) chi_{R(u)}, where R(u) is the symmetric difference of the R_j with u_j = 1, and u -> R(u) is injective. Hence mu(A) = 2^(-r) and |A| = 2^(n-r); 1_A^(R(u)) = 2^(-r) prod over j with u_j = 1 of eps_j on the span L = {R(u)}, 1_A^(S) = 0 for S outside L, and sum over S of 1_A^(S)^2 = 2^r 4^(-r) = mu(A), as Parseval requires of an indicator. For one constraint, 1_A = (1 + eps chi_R)/2, with coefficient 1/2 at the empty set and eps/2 at R. The signed encoding sigma_A = 2 1_A - 1 has sigma_A^(empty) = 2^(1-r) - 1 and sigma_A^(S) = 2 1_A^(S) for nonempty S, of magnitude 2^(1-r) on the nonempty part of L and 0 off it; for r = 1, sigma_A = eps chi_R.

body: [Thm ent of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] The Hilbert entropy strictly increases in a bending fiber of any Hitchin representation $\rho_0$. That is, if $\rho:\pi_1(S) \to \mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ is a quasi-Hitchin representation in the bending fiber of $\rho_0$, then $H(\rho) \geq H(\rho_0)$ and equality holds only if $\rho=\rho_0$. Moreover, the same is true for the translation length entropy in a bending fiber of an $n$-Fuchsian representation $\rho_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Entropy rigidity for bending

	    let $\eta_p$ be the trace of the curve after hitting $p$, and let 
	    $U \subset \mathbb{H}$ be the unbounded connected component of $\mathbb{H} \backslash \eta_p$. body: [Lemma Compactness of minimizing sequences for $I_\gamma$ of arXiv:2609.00324, 'Quantitative Stability for Fractional Yamabe minimizers'] Let $(M^n , [\hat{h}])$ be the conformal infinity of an asymptotically hyperbolic manifold $(X^{n+1},g^+ )$ such that $\Lambda_{\gamma} (M,[\hat{h}]) < \Lambda_{\gamma} (\mathbb{S}^n ,[h_{0}])$. Let $(w_k)_{k\in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{B}$ be a minimizing sequence, i.e. $I_{\gamma} [w_k,\hat{h}] \to \Lambda_{\gamma} (M,[\hat{h}])$. Then, up to subsequence, $(w_k)_{k\in \mathbb{N}}$ converges strongly in $H^{\gamma}(M)$ to some $w_* \in \mathcal{M}_1$.
title: Compactness of minimizing sequences for $I_\gamma$

    \begin{equation} g(s,p)= g(0,0) \det (I -sA_1 + p(A_1+A_2)(A_1-A_2)).\end{equation}
    In addition, $g(s,p)$ is without roots in $\overline{\mathbb G}$ if and only if there exists a strict real contraction \eqref{contr3} so that 
    \eqref{gh} holds.

Let (X, mu) be a measure space and A, A_1, A_2, ... measurable sets with 1(A_n) -> 1(A) mu-almost everywhere. If all A_n lie in one set B with mu(B) < infinity, then mu(A_n symmetric-difference A) -> 0. Without the finite envelope this fails: on the real line with Lebesgue measure, A_n = [n, n + 1] converges to the empty set pointwise, but mu(A_n symmetric-difference empty set) = 1 for every n.

[Lemma 19 (Fiber-inequivalent small fibers force small diameter) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Fix \(B\geq1\).  There is a constant \(C_{\mathrm{fib}}=C_{\mathrm{fib}}(B)\) with the
following property.  Let \(h\) be a metric on a closed three-manifold \(M\).
Suppose that \(M\) has two torus fibrations
\[
        \pi_i:M\to S^1_i,\qquad i=0,1,
\]
and invariant comparison metrics \(h_i\), with quotient metrics
\(h_{S^1,i}\), such that
\[
        B^{-1}h_i\leq h\leq B h_i,
        \qquad i=0,1.
\]
Suppose also that, for some \(d_f>0\), every fiber of each \(\pi_i\) has
\(h\)-diameter at most \(d_f\).  If \(\pi_0\) and \(\pi_1\) are fiber-inequivalent, then
\[
        \diam(M,h)\leq C_{\mathrm{fib}}d_f.
\]

Version 1, Target 1, kind moved; proof (unaudited), 20 October 2026.
This completes the local calculation left open in C030. It is not a
finite-horizon rate from the entrance. Fix 0<d0<K and u in [d0,K], put
theta=1/(nu), and a=1/(3pi), b=1/(6pi^2)=3a^2/2.

For a bounded C^5 test f with bounded derivatives, the explicitly regularized
Gaussian/ReLU transition below satisfies uniformly on that compact

    n(P_n f-f)(u)=A f(u)+(1/n)B f(u)+O_(f,d0,K)(n^(-3/2)),
    A f=(2u+a)f'+u^2 f'',
    B f=(10u+6a/5+b/u)f'
         +(11u^2+12au/5+a^2/2)f''
         +(4u^3+au^2)f'''+(u^4/2)f''''.               (1)

The same bounded-test expansion holds for the exact transition killed at
degeneracy, since its scaled-kernel discrepancy is exponentially small.
It does not assert a finite mean for that exact transition (C003/C028).

## 1. Nonsingular normalized Gram coordinates

For independent Gaussian rows (alpha_i,g_i), let x_i=(alpha_i)_+,
y_i=(cos(theta)alpha_i+sin(theta)g_i)_+. Define row variables

    s=x^2+y^2, r=(x-y)^2, h=x^2-y^2,
    Z_theta=(s,r/theta^2,h/theta).

Their sample averages are (A0,B0,C0). Here A0 is a coordinate, distinct
from the generator A. Their mean is

    mu_theta=(1,m_theta,0),
    m_theta=(1-kappa(theta))/theta^2
            =1/2-a theta-theta^2/24+O(theta^3).

Write D=2A0 B0-C0^2. On a fixed small box around mu_0=(1,1/2,0),
all required denominators are bounded away from zero and the output angle
alpha is positive and less than pi/2. The exact Gram identity gives

    sin(alpha)^2/theta^2
       =(2A0 B0-C0^2-theta^2 B0^2)/(A0^2-theta^2 C0^2).

Consequently the reciprocal multiplier T_theta=theta/alpha has the uniform
smooth expansion, together with its first five coordinate derivatives,

    T_theta=T0+theta^2 H+O(theta^4),
    T0=A0/sqrt(D),
    H=T0[B0^2/(2D)-C0^2/(2A0^2)-D/(6A0^2)].          (2)

In particular H(mu_0)=-1/24. Define G_theta as this fixed small box for
the sample averages (centered at mu_theta), and use U'=u T_theta on G_theta,
U'=u off it. The normalized rows have exponential moments uniformly for
small theta: r/theta^2 is bounded by C(g^2+theta^2 alpha^2), and s and
|h|/theta by C(alpha^2+g^2). Chernoff bounds give P(G_theta^c)<=C exp(-cn).
On this box U'/u is bounded above and below. Bounded tests therefore
transfer to the killed exact kernel with error O(n exp(-cn)).

## 2. Covariance and its one-sided variation at theta=0

At zero the row limit is (2alpha^2 I,g^2 I,-2alpha g I), I=1_(alpha>0).
Its covariance and first theta variation are

    Sigma0 = [[5,1/2,0],[1/2,5/4,0],[0,0,2]],
    Sigma1 = [[0,a,0],[a,-31a/5,0],[0,0,0]],
    Sigma_theta=Sigma0+theta Sigma1+O(theta^2).        (3)

For a check with exact polar moments, let m31=E x^3 y, m22=E x^2 y^2.
C020 gives their integrals and closed forms. Their relevant expansions are

    m31=3/2-3theta^2/4+theta^4/16+theta^5/(5pi)+O(theta^6),
    m22=3/2-theta^2+theta^4/3-2theta^5/(15pi)+O(theta^6).

Thus E(sr)/theta^2=1+O(theta^2), whereas E r/theta^2=1/2-a theta+O(theta^2).
This gives the +a in Sigma1's off-diagonal entry. Also

    E r^2/theta^4=3/2-12theta/(5pi)+O(theta^2),

so subtracting m_theta^2 gives Sigma1_BB=a-12/(5pi)=-31a/5.
The s-h and r-h covariances vanish exactly by exchanging x and y.
E h^2/theta^2=(3-2m22)/theta^2=2+O(theta^2), proving the remaining entries.

All fixed normalized row moments are uniformly bounded. Their third and
fourth joint moments converge at least at rate O(sqrt(theta)): the normalized
r variable differs in L2 from g^2 I by O(sqrt(theta)), using the sign-flip
strip |alpha|<=C theta |g|, and ordinary Taylor bounds off that strip.
The s and normalized h variables converge in L2 at least this fast as well.
Products are controlled by Holder with higher Gaussian moments; alternatively
each mixed row moment is a polar integral whose flip-sector contribution is
O(theta). Either gives the rate needed below.

## 3. Fourth-order sample-average expansion

Set Phi_theta(z)=f(u T_theta(z)). Taylor expand in the centered sample
average through order four on the good box. Its remainder in expectation
is O(n^(-5/2)), uniformly on the compact: normalized row moments bound the
fifth absolute moment, and deletions off the box cost exponentially small
terms by higher moments and Holder. The exact index partitions give

    E Phi_theta(Zbar)
      =Phi_theta(mu_theta)
       +(1/(2n)) Sigma_theta:D^2 Phi_theta(mu_theta)
       +(1/(6n^2)) kappa3_theta:D^3 Phi_theta(mu_theta)
       +(1/(8n^2)) (Sigma_theta tensor Sigma_theta):D^4 Phi_theta(mu_theta)
       +O(n^(-5/2)).                                 (4)

The tensor contractions sum over all coordinates; the factor 1/8 includes
the three pairings of the symmetric fourth derivative. The fourth cumulant
of one row enters only at n^(-3), below the required order. Since
theta=1/(nu), replace the n^(-2) coefficient in (4) by its value at zero,
at cost O_(d0,K)(n^(-5/2)). The theta^2 difference in coordinate derivatives
in (2) is also below the required order in the covariance term.

At theta=0, T0(Zbar) is exactly sqrt(S/R), with conditional chi-square
degrees k and k-1. Hence C030 supplies all n^(-2) baseline terms, including
the baseline contribution from the covariance Hessian. It remains to compute
the change in the deterministic and covariance terms of (4).

The deterministic value is exactly u theta/F(theta), so C029 gives

    n[Phi_theta(mu_theta)-f(u)]
       =a f'+(1/n)[(b/u)f'+(a^2/2)f'']+O(n^-2).       (5)

For the covariance term put Q(theta)=Sigma_theta:D^2[f(u T0)](mu_theta)/2.
At zero Q(0)=2u f'+u^2 f''. Since mu'_0=(0,-a,0), direct differentiation gives

    Q'(0)=(6a/5)u f'+(12a/5)u^2 f''+a u^3 f'''.      (6)

For transparent arithmetic, at mu0 the first derivatives of T0 are
(1/2,-1,0), and its diagonal Hessian entries are (-1/4,3,1), with
T_AB=-1/2. The needed contractions are

    Sigma0:T_ij=4,        Sigma0:T_i T_j=2,
    Sigma0:partial_B T_ij=-22,
    Sigma0:partial_B(T_i T_j)=-8,
    Sigma1:T_ij=-98a/5,   Sigma1:T_i T_j=-36a/5.

Combining them with mu'_B=-a and differentiating f' and f'' gives (6).
In the scaled generator, theta Q'(0)=Q'(0)/(nu).
Combining (5), (6), and the baseline correction of C030 proves (1).

Hardest remaining global step: (1) is uniform only away from zero. Its b/u
term is singular at the entrance. A finite-horizon error cannot be obtained

body:
On an infinite connected locally finite network whose underlying graph is a tree and whose edge conductances are positive, the free uniform spanning forest contains every edge almost surely and has exactly one component. Every finite connected induced exhaustion is itself a tree with a unique spanning tree; the free weak limit therefore fixes every edge as present. This is a boundary case of component-count determinism, not an argument for arbitrary networks.

title: FUSF on a tree is the whole connected tree

body: In calculus, Taylor's theorem gives an approximation of a k-times differentiable function around a given point by a polynomial of degree at most k, called the k-th-order Taylor polynomial. For a smooth function, the Taylor polynomial is the truncation at the order k of the Taylor series of the function. The first-order Taylor polynomial is the linear approximation of the function, and the second-order Taylor polynomial is often referred to as the quadratic approximation. There are several versions of Taylor's theorem, some giving explicit estimates of the approximation error of the function by its Taylor polynomial.
title: In calculus, Taylor's theorem gives an approximation of a k-times differentiable function around a given point by a poly

For a real matrix D in R^(m by n), and an integer r>=rank(D), the nuclear norm satisfies ||D||_* = min_{U in R^(m by r), V in R^(n by r), UV^T=D} (||U||_F^2+||V||_F^2)/2. The minimum is attained by balanced square-root singular-value factors, with zero columns if necessary. Let H and K be Hilbert spaces and T: H -> K a compact operator. Then T*T is a compact positive self-adjoint operator on H, and |T| = (T*T)^{1/2} is compact and positive. The singular values (s-numbers) s_1(T) >= s_2(T) >= ... >= 0 of T are the eigenvalues of |T| (equivalently, the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of T*T), listed in nonincreasing order and repeated according to multiplicity; if |T| has only finitely many nonzero eigenvalues the list is completed by zeros. Each nonzero singular value has finite multiplicity and s_n(T) -> 0. Basic facts: s_1(T) = ||T||; s_n(T*) = s_n(T); s_n(A T B) <= ||A|| s_n(T) ||B|| for bounded A, B; and for every n >= 0, s_{n+1}(T) = min{ ||T - F|| : F bounded, rank F <= n } (approximation numbers; the minimum is attained by a truncated Schmidt decomposition). If H = K and T is normal, the singular values are the absolute values of the eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity; for non-normal T they generally differ from the moduli of the eigenvalues.
H and K are Hilbert spaces
T: H -> K is a compact linear operator
title: Singular Values of a Compact Operator

Status: proof (unaudited). C007 v1. Novelty unestablished.

Use the adapted unbiased-gradient-oracle model of C006, now with arbitrary
deterministic u_0 in R^d and v_0 in R^q. Explicitly, H is constant SPD,
0<m<=lambda(H)<=M, sigma,D>=0, 0<rho<2, 0<eta<=rho/M, B=I-eta H,
and, for adapted states and filtration F_k,

    u_{k+1}=u_k-eta xi_k^u,
    v_{k+1}=Bv_k-eta xi_k^v,
    E[xi_k^u|F_k]=0, E[xi_k^v|F_k]=0,
    E[xi_k^v (xi_k^v)^T|F_k]<=sigma^2 H,
    E[|xi_k^u|^2|F_k]<=sigma^2 D^2 |v_k|^2.             (1)

Dimensions d,q are finite and positive. Matrix inequality means Loewner
order. The noise components may be dependent, past-dependent and
nonstationary; no symmetry or higher moments are required. The oracle
is unbiased for grad L, L(u,v)=v^T H v/2. Representation as gradients
of individual random sample losses is not claimed for every such oracle.

For F in C_b^2(R^{d+q}) set global block derivative bounds

    F_uu=sup_{u,v} ||D_u^2 F(u,v)||,
    F_uv=sup_{u,v} ||D_u D_v F(u,v)||,
    F_vv=sup_{u,v} ||D_v^2 F(u,v)||,
    c=sigma^2 q/(2-rho), gamma=min{m,M(2-rho)/rho},
    R_T=sigma^2 D^2 (|v_0|^2/gamma+T c).

Then, for every T>=0,

    sup_{integer 0<=K<=T/eta^2}
      |E F(u_K,v_K)-F(u_0,B^K v_0)| <= eta C(T,v_0),
    C(T,v_0)=F_uu R_T/2+F_uv sqrt(c R_T)+F_vv c/2.      (2)

This is a uniform weak-order-one estimate with the deterministic normal
initial layer retained, including K=0 and every fixed off-manifold start.
It does not claim uniform O(eta) comparison with F(u_0,0) at K=0.

For the target's covariance-proportional-on-manifold subclass, additionally
assume normal conditional covariance equals sigma^2 H when v_k=0.
Equation (1) forces tangent noise to vanish there, so full covariance on
the minimizing manifold is sigma^2 diag(0,H). The estimate uses only the
domination in (1); no global proportionality is asserted.
All C006 adapted unbiased-oracle conditional second-moment bounds; constant SPD H
Deterministic arbitrary u0,v0; sigma,D>=0; 0<rho<2; 0<eta<=rho/M
F in C_b^2 with global Fuu,Fuv,Fvv bounds on all ambient space
Comparison is F(u0,(I-eta H)^K v0), retaining the deterministic normal initial layer
For proportional covariance on the minimizing manifold additionally require normal covariance equality there; per-sample loss representation not asserted

Claim w730-T355-C007 v1. Kind: narrowed. Target: 1.
Status: proof (unaudited). Independent review and priority unresolved.

## Statement

Use the adapted unbiased-gradient-oracle model of C006, now with arbitrary
deterministic u_0 in R^d and v_0 in R^q. Explicitly, H is constant SPD,
0<m<=lambda(H)<=M, sigma,D>=0, 0<rho<2, 0<eta<=rho/M, B=I-eta H,
and, for adapted states and filtration F_k,

    u_{k+1}=u_k-eta xi_k^u,
    v_{k+1}=Bv_k-eta xi_k^v,
    E[xi_k^u|F_k]=0, E[xi_k^v|F_k]=0,
    E[xi_k^v (xi_k^v)^T|F_k]<=sigma^2 H,
    E[|xi_k^u|^2|F_k]<=sigma^2 D^2 |v_k|^2.             (1)

Dimensions d,q are finite and positive. Matrix inequality means Loewner
order. The noise components may be dependent, past-dependent and
nonstationary; no symmetry or higher moments are required. The oracle
is unbiased for grad L, L(u,v)=v^T H v/2. Representation as gradients
of individual random sample losses is not claimed for every such oracle.

For F in C_b^2(R^{d+q}) set global block derivative bounds

    F_uu=sup_{u,v} ||D_u^2 F(u,v)||,
    F_uv=sup_{u,v} ||D_u D_v F(u,v)||,
    F_vv=sup_{u,v} ||D_v^2 F(u,v)||,
    c=sigma^2 q/(2-rho), gamma=min{m,M(2-rho)/rho},
    R_T=sigma^2 D^2 (|v_0|^2/gamma+T c).

Then, for every T>=0,

    sup_{integer 0<=K<=T/eta^2}
      |E F(u_K,v_K)-F(u_0,B^K v_0)| <= eta C(T,v_0),
    C(T,v_0)=F_uu R_T/2+F_uv sqrt(c R_T)+F_vv c/2.      (2)

This is a uniform weak-order-one estimate with the deterministic normal
initial layer retained, including K=0 and every fixed off-manifold start.
It does not claim uniform O(eta) comparison with F(u_0,0) at K=0.

For the target's covariance-proportional-on-manifold subclass, additionally
assume normal conditional covariance equals sigma^2 H when v_k=0.
Equation (1) forces tangent noise to vanish there, so full covariance on
the minimizing manifold is sigma^2 diag(0,H). The estimate uses only the
domination in (1); no global proportionality is asserted.

## Proof

Let b_k=B^k v_0 and w_k=v_k-b_k. Then w_0=0 and

    w_{k+1}=Bw_k-eta xi_k^v, E w_k=0.                  (3)

The last identity follows by conditioning each fresh increment on F_k,
not by assuming independence. Its second moment is finite by induction.
With Q_k=E[w_k w_k^T], conditional centering in (1) gives

    Q_{k+1}<=BQ_kB+eta^2 sigma^2 H, Q_0=0.

Congruence preserves Loewner order. Comparing with the equality recurrence
and diagonalizing H gives

    Q_k<=eta sigma^2(I-B^{2k})(2I-eta H)^{-1},
    E|w_k|^2<=eta c.                                  (4)

Indeed the comparison matrix has eigenvalues
eta sigma^2[1-(1-eta lambda)^{2k}]/(2-eta lambda), between zero and
eta sigma^2/(2-rho). Q_k need not commute with H. Since b_k is
deterministic and E w_k=0,

    E|v_k|^2=|b_k|^2+E|w_k|^2<=r^{2k}|v_0|^2+eta c,  (5)

where r=||B||<1. For every eigenvalue lambda,

    1-|1-eta lambda|=min{eta lambda,2-eta lambda}
      >=min{eta m,2-rho}>=eta gamma.

Consequently 1-r^2>=1-r>=eta gamma>0.

The tangent process u_k-u_0 is a square-integrable martingale. For j<k,
the earlier increment h_j=u_{j+1}-u_j is F_k-measurable, and
E[h_k|F_k]=0. Thus E[h_j dot h_k]=0 by conditional expectation.
Pythagoras for this finite martingale sum and (1), (5) yield

    E|u_K-u_0|^2=sum_{j=0}^{K-1} E|h_j|^2
      <=eta^2 sigma^2 D^2 sum_{j=0}^{K-1}
                           (r^{2j}|v_0|^2+eta c)
      <=eta^2 sigma^2 D^2 |v_0|^2/(1-r^2)
                           +K eta^3 sigma^2 D^2 c
      <=eta R_T,                                     (6)

for K eta^2<=T. Finiteness of all terms follows from (4)-(5), which
also justifies the square-integrable martingale calculation. No product
of conditional probability bounds is used. In particular E[u_K-u_0]=0.

Fix any such K. Its deterministic b=b_K is kept fixed throughout the
following Taylor estimates. Put f_b(u)=F(u,b), a_b(u)=D_v F(u,b).
Taylor's theorem and (6), with E[u_K-u_0]=0, give

    |E f_b(u_K)-f_b(u_0)|<=F_uu eta R_T/2.             (7)

The normal Taylor expansion gives

    |F(u_K,b+w_K)-f_b(u_K)-a_b(u_K) dot w_K|
                                      <=F_vv |w_K|^2/2.

Since E w_K=0, subtract the deterministic a_b(u_0) before estimating
the linear term. The global mixed derivative bound implies

    |E[a_b(u_K) dot w_K]|
      =|E[(a_b(u_K)-a_b(u_0)) dot w_K]|
      <=F_uv E[|u_K-u_0| |w_K|]
      <=F_uv sqrt(E|u_K-u_0|^2 E|w_K|^2)
      <=eta F_uv sqrt(R_T c).                         (8)

This is unconditional Cauchy-Schwarz; u_K and w_K may be correlated.
Combining (4), (7), (8) proves (2) for every K with the same C(T,v_0).
The empty sums give K=0. Sigma=0, D=0 and T=0 cause no division by
zero; gamma>0 depends only on the positive spectral and stability data.

## What this adds and what remains open

C006 imposed v_0=0. Equation (2) supplies an explicit comparison from
every deterministic off-manifold start in the same oracle class by
retaining the normal initial layer. Its bound scales at most linearly
in T plus a square-root term. This does not settle general curved
manifolds or unshifted uniform comparison at zero from a fixed v_0!=0.

Initial-layer correction is known in the qualitative framework of
Li-Wang-Arora, arXiv:2110.06914v4, p.6. That contextual source does not
by itself certify the quantitative claim here. Priority is unestablished.
The step trusted least for independent review is the global tangent
martingale variance identity (6) and its use in the mixed term (8).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:072747cc9a49b568099c2691ca48f9a1653088163e5c28ea375935c5b5b22d8e","revision_digest":"sha256:2690f2c8332adc4eb3aade57eec4ee9110ca03a351b0acf2125296e49939500d","source_id":"owner-own-work:w730:T355:w730-T355-C007:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1-unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: [Definition 2.7 of arXiv:2603.24423, 'First passage percolation preserves sublinearly Morse boundaries'] Let (X, dX) be a proper geodesic metric space and Z ⊆X a closed subset, and let κ be a concave sublinear function. A map πZ : X →P(Z) is a κ-projection if there exist constants D1, D2, depending only on Z and κ, such that for any points x ∈X and z ∈Z, diamX({z} ∪πZ(x)) ≤D1 · dX(x, z) + D2 · κ(x). A κ-projection differs from a nearest point projection by a uniform multiplicative error and a sublinear additive error.

[Cor 196 (subsequential limits for piecewise constant processes) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Analogously to $\mu_{\bG^N}$ and $\Q_N$, let $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$ denote the law of the piecewise constant processes
	\[\Big(
	\Gamma^{\bullet,N},\Upsilon^{\bullet,N},\mathcal{E}^{\bullet,N}
	\Big)\]
conditional on $\bG^N$, and let $\Q_{\bullet,N}$ denote the law of $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$. Suppose $\Q_N\to\Q$ along an integer subsequence $N\to\infty$, as guaranteed by Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}. Then $\Q_{\bullet,N}\Rightarrow\Q$ along the same subsequence. The ``$\frozen$'' variant of the statement also holds.

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}, for any sequence of integers $N\to\infty$, there exists a further subsequence along which $\Q_N$ converges weakly to $\Q$, with $\mathcal{E}^N$ converging almost surely to the zero path. Take any such subsequence:
to simplify notation, we can assume (by re-indexing) that it is the entire sequence of integers $N\ge1$. 
This means there exists a Skorohod coupling of the disorder matrices $\bG^N$ for which, with probability one over $(\bG^N)_{N\ge0}$, we have $\mu_{\bG^N}\Rightarrow\mu$ along the same subsequence, where $\mu_{\bG^N}$ is the law of the process $(\Gamma^N,\Upsilon^N,\mathcal{E}^N)$ conditional on $\bG^N$. Moreover $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges almost surely to the zero path, which implies
that $\mathcal{E}^{\bullet,N}$ does also.

Now abbreviate $\Xi^N\equiv(\Gamma^N,\Upsilon^N)$
and $\Xi\equiv(\Gamma,\Upsilon)$.
 Let $L^\infty([0,1],\R^8)$ denote the space of (not necessarily continuous) functions $[0,1]\to\R^8$, equipped with the uniform metric. If $\Phi$ is a bounded Lipschitz functional on this space, then we have
	\beq
	\lim_{N\to\infty} 
	\bE_{\bG^N} \Phi(\Xi^N)
	=\bE \Phi(\Xi)
	\eeq
almost surely (along the subsequence, under the Skorohod coupling).
Let $\Xi^{\bullet,N}$ be the piecewise constant variant of $\Xi^N$, and let $\mu_{\bG_\bullet,N}$ be the law of $\Xi^{\bullet,N}$. To conclude the result, it suffices to show that
	\[
	\lim_{N\to\infty} 
	\bE_{\bG^N} \Phi(\Xi^{\bullet,N})
	=\bE \Phi(\Xi)
	\]
almost surely for all bounded Lipschitz functionals $\Phi$, possibly after passing to a further subsequence of integers $N_k\to\infty$, as long as the subsequence does not depend on $\Phi$. In light of \eqref{e:observable.a.s.conv}, it suffices to show that
	\[\lim_{N\to\infty} 
	\bE_{\bG^N} \Big[
	\Phi(\Xi^N)
	-\Phi(\Xi^{\bullet,N})
	\Big]=0
	\]
almost surely along the subsequence $N_k$, for all bounded Lipschitz functionals $\Phi$.

Recall the proof of Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}. For any sequence $\epsilon_N\to0$, for each $N$ we have a compact set
 $\mathcal{K}_N=\mathcal{K}((H_{N,k})_{k\ge0})$ defined by \eqref{e:compact.K}, such that $\Q_N(\mathcal{K}_N^c) \le \epsilon_N$ for all $N \ge N_0$. We can take $\epsilon_N\to0$ slowly enough so that $H_{N,1} \delta^\gamma \to0$, where $\gamma=1/5$ is the H\"older exponent from the proof of Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}. We then have
 	\begin{align*}
	&\bigg|\bE_{\bG^N} \Big[
	\Phi(\Xi^N)
	-\Phi(\Xi^{\bullet,N})
	\Big] \bigg|
	\le
	2\|\Phi\|_\infty \ind\{ (\mathcal{K}_N)^c\}
	+\ind\{\mathcal{K}_N\}
	\bigg|
	\bE_{\bG^N} \Big[
	\Phi(\Xi^N)
	-\Phi(\Xi^{\bullet,N})
	\Big] 
	\bigg| \\
	&\qquad\le
	2\|\Phi\|_\infty \ind\{ (\mathcal{K}_N)^c\}
	+\ind\{\mathcal{K}_N\}\bigg\{
	2\|\Phi\|_\infty \mu( A(H_{N,1}))
	+ \|\Phi\|_{\textup{Lip}}
	\bE_{\bG^N}\Big[
	\|\Xi^N-\Xi^{\bullet,N}\|_\infty
	; A(H_{N,1})^c
	\Big]
	\bigg\} \\
	&\qquad\le
	2\|\Phi\|_\infty \ind\{ (\mathcal{K}_N)^c\}
	+\bigg\{
	2\|\Phi\|_\infty \frac{17\mathscr{C}}{H_{N,1}}
	+ \|\Phi\|_{\textup{Lip}} O(1) H_{N,1} \delta^\gamma
	\bigg\}\,.
	\end{align*}
If we now take a subsequence $N_k\to\infty$ such that $\epsilon_{N,k}$ is summable, then the above converges to zero almost surely along this subsequence. This concludes the proof of the non-``$\frozen$'' version of the statement. The ``$\frozen$'' variant follows by the same argument, since all the preceding results of this section were also proved for this setting. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $S$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. Gaussian rows in $\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $\Sigma = \sigma^2 (I_p + \theta u u^T)$, $\|u\| = 1$, $\theta > 0$, in the regime $p/n \to \gamma \in (0, 1]$. Let $\hat\lambda$ be the largest eigenvalue of $S$ and $\hat u$ its unit eigenvector. THEOREM (Baik, Ben Arous, Peche 2005 for the eigenvalue in the complex case; Paul 2007 for real Gaussian data, eigenvalue and eigenvector; Baik-Silverstein 2006 in general). (i) If $\theta \le \sqrt{\gamma}$ then $\hat\lambda \to \sigma^2 (1 + \sqrt{\gamma})^2$ almost surely, the bulk edge of the Marchenko-Pastur law, and $|\langle \hat u, u \rangle|^2 \to 0$: the spike is invisible. (ii) If $\theta > \sqrt{\gamma}$ then $\hat\lambda \to \sigma^2 (1 + \theta)(1 + \gamma / \theta)$, which exceeds the bulk edge, and $|\langle \hat u, u \rangle|^2 \to \frac{1 - \gamma / \theta^2}{1 + \gamma / \theta}$. The limit $\sigma^2 (1 + \theta)(1 + \gamma/\theta) = \sigma^2 (1 + \theta + \gamma + \gamma/\theta)$ is strictly larger than the population eigenvalue $\sigma^2 (1 + \theta)$: a detected sample spike always overstates its population value, by $\sigma^2 \gamma (1 + 1/\theta)$. The same statements hold spike by spike for $r$ fixed spikes with distinct $\theta_k$, each compared with the threshold $\sqrt{\gamma}$.
rows are i.i.d. Gaussian with covariance sigma^2 (I + theta u u^T)
p/n -> gamma in (0, 1]
the spike rank r is fixed as p, n -> infinity

Let f ∈ C(R; R^n) be the flux and u0 ∈ L^∞(R^n). A function u ∈ L^∞(R^n × (0,∞)) is a weak (integral) solution of the Cauchy problem u_t + div_x f(u) = 0 in R^n × (0,∞), u(·,0) = u0, if for every test function φ ∈ C_c^1(R^n × [0,∞)) (compactly supported, but NOT required to vanish at t = 0): ∫_0^∞ ∫_{R^n} ( u φ_t + f(u)·∇_x φ ) dx dt + ∫_{R^n} u0(x) φ(x,0) dx = 0. Equivalently, u_t + div f(u) = 0 in the sense of distributions on R^n × (0,∞) together with the attainment of the initial datum encoded by the boundary term. Every classical (C^1) solution is a weak solution, and a weak solution that is C^1 on an open set is a classical solution there. Weak solutions are in general NOT unique: an additional admissibility (entropy) condition is required.

\begin{equation*}
\E_{\nu^{(p)}_{n,m}}[N_1(\pi)]
=\sum_{r=1}^{n}m^{1-r}\bigl(p^r-(-q)^r\bigr)
=\frac{p(1-(p/m)^n)}{1-p/m}+\frac{q(1-(-q/m)^n)}{1+q/m}.

\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Expected number of fixed points

body: [Definition 4 of arXiv:2608.30875, 'A Decomposition Theorem for Topological Semi-small Maps'] Let $f:X \longrightarrow Y$ be an almost covering where $X$ is a closed $n$-manifold, $Y$ is a closed $n$-pseudomanifold. Let the filtration $Y \supset Y_{n_{R}}(=R) \supset Y_{n_{R}-1} \supset \cdots$ be the refined stratification on $Y$ obtained by Proposition~\ref{RefinedStra}, where $R$ is the fibered set and $n_{R}:= \dim(R)$. The almost covering $f:X \longrightarrow Y$ is called a \textbf{topologically semi-small map} if for each point $r \in S_{k}(:=Y_{k} \setminus Y_{k-1})$ and for each $0 \leq k \leq n_{R}$, the condition $2 \dim(f^{-1}(r))+\dim(S_{k}) \leq n$ is satisfied. Furthermore, we the set $R_{\operatorname{rel}}:=\{S_{k} \ \vert \  2 \dim(f^{-1}(r))+\dim(S_{k}) = n \ \forall \ r \in f^{-1}(S_{k})\}$ is referred to as the set of relevant strata.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.04045, 'Heat content and spectrum for subordinated sub-Laplacians'] We study heat content and spectral properties of subordinated sub-Laplacians on arbitrary Carnot groups. We consider restrictions of such operators to bounded open sets with zero Dirichlet boundary condition and study their spectral properties. In particular, for a large class of subordinators we give explicit eigenvalue estimates in terms of the subordinator and the eigenvalues of the sub-Laplacian. We also provide large-time asymptotics of the heat content for the subordinated sub-Laplacian in terms of its spectral gap. For fractional sub-Laplacians we prove short-time asymptotics for the corresponding heat content and relative heat content. Our approach combines semigroup methods, probabilistic techniques, geometric measure theory, and heat kernel estimates.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.04045: Heat content and spectrum for subordinated sub-Laplacians

body: A square matrix with strictly positive entries has a unique eigenvalue of largest modulus; that eigenvalue is real, positive, simple, and possesses strictly positive left and right eigenvectors (Perron). For irreducible nonnegative matrices the largest eigenvalue is still positive and simple with positive eigenvectors, though other eigenvalues may share its modulus when the matrix is periodic (Frobenius). It governs stationary distributions of Markov chains, spectral ranking, and population models.
title: Perron-Frobenius Theorem

PROOF (UNAUDITED); novelty unverified. For each n>=2 and Z~N(0,1), let f_n(z)=min(1,max(0,z-n)), c_n^2=E[(1+f_n(Z))^2], and X_n(z)=(1,(1+f_n(z))/c_n)^T. The uncentered Gram G_n=E[X_nX_n^T] is positive definite with unit diagonal; each feature coordinate is bounded by 2 and 1-Lipschitz. For the empirical Gram S_n of n iid rows, let s be the second-coordinate Schur complement given the first. Then E[(sqrt(s(S_n)/s(G_n))-1)^2]>=1-1/n. The relative mean-square error is at least 1-1/n. Thus bounded Lipschitz Gaussian-derived features and unit marginal moments do not alone yield a uniform relative Schur sampling rate or a uniform kappa bound in the companion lemma. The feature threshold varies with n and the population conditional variance may vanish: this is not failure of a fixed program or a theorem with a uniform innovation floor.
Z standard normal; n independent rows; n>=2
Uncentered empirical Gram; Schur complement given the first constant coordinate
Feature threshold varies with n; population conditional variance need not be uniformly bounded below
No failure for a fixed activation, fixed program or realized critical-chain rate is claimed

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:dfc750496e9b0835124f4835970e1cf00845295a1bc65b9db93e2e19c848cf8d","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/df/dfc750496e9b0835124f4835970e1cf00845295a1bc65b9db93e2e19c848cf8d.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e37ea246d8a43361dab3862a47b126ef9570527b470c6d99080fa47cb3c834c5","bundle_entry_key":"t250_w712_c026","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c025-c026-relative-schur-and-rare-features","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability and Gaussian conditioning","draft":"w712/bundle_019.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:rare-gaussian-features-relative-schur-sampling-obstruction","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C026 v1: bounded Gaussian features do not give uniform relative Gram control

Kind: route-failure. Target: 4. Status: proof (unaudited); novelty unverified.
This is an exact obstruction to omitting the whitened-moment hypothesis of C025, not a fixed-program Tensor Program counterexample.

## Feature family and conclusion
For each integer n>=2, let Z be standard normal and define

f_n(z)=min(1,max(0,z-n)),
c_n^2=E[(1+f_n(Z))^2],
X_n(z)=(1,(1+f_n(z))/c_n)^T.

Take n iid rows X_n(Z_i), the uncentered empirical Gram S_n=n^(-1) sum X_n(Z_i)X_n(Z_i)^T, and G_n=E[X_n(Z)X_n(Z)^T]. Let s denote the Schur complement in the second coordinate given the first. Then

G_n is positive definite with both diagonal entries 1;
each feature coordinate is bounded in absolute value by 2 and is 1-Lipschitz (or better);
E[(sqrt(s(S_n)/s(G_n))-1)^2] >= 1-1/n.             (1)

In particular no uniform O(n^(-1/2)) relative square-root-Schur rate follows over this family from bounded Lipschitz feature coordinates, unit marginal second moments and Gaussian base rows alone. The empirical matrix can be singular; excluding that event without a probability bound would discard the obstruction.

## Proof
Write F=f_n(Z), mu=E F, and v=Var(F). We have 0<=F<=1 and 1<=c_n<=2. The positive Gaussian probability of Z<=n gives F=0 with positive probability, and the positive probability of n<Z<n+1 gives F>0 with positive probability. Thus v>0. Directly,

G_n=[[1,(1+mu)/c_n],[(1+mu)/c_n,1]],
s(G_n)=1-(1+mu)^2/c_n^2=v/c_n^2>0.

This proves positive definiteness and the stated diagonal entries. The first feature is constant. The clipped hinge f_n is 1-Lipschitz, so the second feature is 1/c_n-Lipschitz, at most 1; both coordinates are bounded by 2. These bounds do not depend on n. They also imply uniform bounded coordinate fourth moments, a fact that does not control whitened moments.

Let A_n be the event that all Z_i<=n. On A_n, every F_i=0 and

S_n=[[1,1/c_n],[1/c_n,1/c_n^2]].

Therefore S_n has rank one and s(S_n)=0. The random variable inside the expectation in (1) equals one on A_n. Since E Z^2=1, Markov's inequality gives P(Z>n)<=P(Z^2>=n^2)<=1/n^2. The union bound yields P(A_n)>=1-n/n^2=1-1/n. Nonnegativity on its complement proves (1).

## The exact unpaid implication
C025 controls relative Schur sampling through kappa=E[(X^TG^(-1)X)^2]. If a uniform kappa bound followed from the coordinate bounds just verified, C025 with d=2 would force the left side of (1) to tend to zero. Therefore that implication is false. This use does not refute C025; it locates the missing hypothesis. A rare transverse feature direction can have a much larger normalized fourth moment than the individual coordinates suggest.

The population conditional variance s(G_n) can tend to zero; no uniform lower bound for it is claimed. Thus this example also does not rule out a theorem with a separate uniform conditional-innovation lower bound. The threshold n changes with the sample size: it is a uniform-over-feature-families counterexample, NOT failure of convergence for a fixed activation or fixed program. It supplies no depth-to-width law, no realized growing-depth architecture lower bound, and no contradiction to arXiv:2607.06290, whose structural constants may depend on the activation and the Gram point.

## Strongest reason this might not obstruct the desired theorem
The actual critical chains may have additional analytic structure that prevents such rare standardized contrast directions, or an absolute-output coupling may remain accurate as s(G_n) tends to zero even while its relative error is large. Those alternatives remain open. A concrete check needed before extending this obstruction to the full target would be to realize comparable features in the stated fixed-activation critical chain with controlled stability constants; no such realization is supplied here.

The proof is analytic and uses only Gaussian positive density, E Z^2=1, Markov's inequality and a union bound. No Gaussian tail numerics or quadrature are used. The threshold-normalizing constant is an expectation defined exactly, not a floating estimate. C025 is an unaudited companion claim; equation (1) and the failure of uniform relative Schur control are proved independently above.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:aaabc5c893bde2a01d827bbf2481dfb9d080c5192eebb6167cd15af366f3bf1a","revision_digest":"sha256:2713a94d271ac41bb68aea63cf4fc481ed69431db0b826641b69a43eab17a95f","source_id":"owner-own-work:T250-w712-C026:v1","source_revision":"C026 v1; proof (unaudited); source context Section 4.2 (4.9), not a claim that the paper states this result","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: Theorem (campaign status: conditional): S9 verdict. There is a rigorous linear-in-defect theorem for the part of the high-corank problem in which the weighted two-shadow batching has bounded entropy-normalized exposure congestion kappa. It is conditional, works on affine boundary fibres, uses the conditional defect that the dense-witness exchange leaves unused, and controls ALL unselected rows. In the original junction basis the constant is 2*kappa+1. If selected witnesses have private support at most s then kappa <= (s-1)/beta with beta = log_2(4/3), giving new quotient residual rank <= (1 + 2(s-1)/beta)*L (tag 1); insisting on the triangularly exchanged witness basis raises the constant by only beta^{-1}, to (1 + (2s-1)/beta)*L (tag 2). Notes: S9: 'This is a genuine residual-compression result, not the false inference that one residual direction is enough per selected witness.' Conditional on bounded kappa, which is precisely what the residual class (congestion >~ log n in every useful basis) denies.

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item almost surely, $U \in C^{\alpha-}(\T^d)$,
        \item and $\limsup_{r \to 0} \sup_{x \in \T^d} r^{-\gamma d} \P( |U(x)| \leq r)<\infty$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then almost surely, if $Z := \{ x \in \T^d : U(x) =0\}$, for any $\rho < \gamma \alpha$, 
    \[\lim_{r \to 0} r^{-\rho d} |\{x \in \T^d : d_{\T^d}(x,Z) \leq r\}| =0.\]

Fix -1<a<1 and sigma_a(t)=t for t>=0, sigma_a(t)=a*t for t<0, applied coordinatewise. A depth-L network has L affine layers, activation after the first L-1 layers, and an affine final output. Its squared parameter cost is sum_ell (||W_ell||_F^2+||b_ell||_2^2). For a function f and domain Omega, R_L is the infimum of this cost over all such finite-width networks equal to f on Omega; R_L=+infinity if the class is empty. Let Omega be a nonempty bounded open subset of R^d and f:R^d->R^m continuous finite piecewise-affine. Define rank_J(f;Omega)=max_(x in Omega, f differentiable at x) rank(Jf(x)). Define rank_BN(f;Omega) as the least integer k>=0 for which f=g composed with h on Omega with both h:R^d->R^k and g:R^k->R^m continuous finite piecewise-affine; k=0 means constant. Then rank_J(f;Omega)<=liminf_(L->infinity) R_L/L<=limsup_(L->infinity) R_L/L<=rank_BN(f;Omega). If the two ranks agree, the ordinary normalized-cost limit exists and equals their common value. If that ordinary limit exists in any other case, it lies between the two ranks. This card does not assert existence of the ordinary limit for every f solely from these two estimates.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Efron-Stein: for f(X_1,...,X_n) with independent coordinates, Var f <= (1/2) sum_i E[(f(X) - f(X^{(i)}))^2], where X^{(i)} resamples coordinate i; for a Boolean function under a product measure the right side is a constant times the total influence sum_i I_i(f). This bounds variance by total influence and needs no monotonicity. Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm (1999): if f_n : {0,1}^{m_n} -> {0,1} satisfy sum_i I_i(f_n)^2 -> 0 then (f_n) is noise sensitive, i.e. Cov(f_n(omega), f_n(omega^eps)) -> 0 for every fixed noise level eps > 0; for monotone functions the converse also holds. The quantitative engine is Talagrand's inequality Var f <= C sum_i I_i(f)/log(e/I_i(f)) (hypercontractivity), which for functions with all influences at most n^{-a} improves Efron-Stein by a factor log n; the same mechanism gives the BKS sublinear variance bound Var(first-passage time to distance n) <= C n/log n for first-passage percolation with suitable edge weights. What these do NOT give: a lower bound on any individual influence (that is Kahn-Kalai-Linial: max_i I_i >= c Var(f) log n / n), or a power improvement n^{1-eps} on the variance, which remains open outside integrable models. Typical failure: Using the plain Efron-Stein variance bound and mistaking it for the BKS lower bound on the maximal individual influence, which is a distinct and much sharper statement requiring monotonicity and a total-influence hypothesis; conflating the two leads to claiming individual-coordinate sensitivity conclusions, needed for noise-sensitivity theorems, from a tool that in its basic form only controls the aggregate variance. Canonical reference: Efron and Stein, 1981, The Annals of Statistics; Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm, 1999, Publications Mathematiques de l'IHES.
Independent coordinates (product measure)
BKS noise sensitivity criterion: sum of squared influences tends to zero
Talagrand's logarithmic improvement needs hypercontractivity of the product measure

body: Lemma (campaign status: proved): One supported relation already uses one dimension of the rank-three global row space. By coordinate-fullness a genuinely new local full-dual form is represented by a displayed coordinate outside the forest endpoints; its equality with the local form gives a global row with a unique nonzero outside coordinate, so distinct extras give independent rows modulo the supported relation unless two local forms coincide on the global atom. Such a coincidence would be a second supported relation on the endpoints, which is excluded, so at most two local extras are possible. Notes: Exclusion of the second supported relation: with four or five endpoints, projective simplicity fails after two independent supported relations, so the only possible profile is six forms of rank four; normalizing $h=(1,1,1,1)$, the five old restrictions mod $h$ are five distinct nonzero vertices of $\{0,1\}^3$, any five of which contain two collinear signed pair differences, giving $d_{\rm geo}\le2$ and contradicting the standing $d_{\rm geo}=3$ hypothesis. S3 stresses the DEHOMOGENIZED reading: the relevant vectors are classes modulo $\mathbb Rh$, not the six sign rows in the unreduced four-space. This completes the bridge from the finite local table to the balanced support-four/six row.

Let d,n>=1 be integers, lambda>0, and tau=n/d^2. Let H_mu be arbitrary real d by (d+1) matrices and y_mu arbitrary real labels, for mu=1,...,n. Set m=d(d+1), h_mu=vec_row(H_mu) in R^m, where vec_row stacks rows. The unique minimizer Gamma_star of sum_mu(y_mu-<Gamma,H_mu>_F)^2+(n/d)lambda||Gamma||_F^2 satisfies vec_row(Gamma_star)=G(0)v/d, where v=sum_mu y_mu h_mu. For a symmetric positive semidefinite m-square matrix Pi and pi>=0, define G(pi)=[sum_mu h_mu h_mu^T/d+pi Pi+tau lambda I_m]^(-1), q(pi)=G(pi)v/(d sqrt(d)), z_mu=[y_mu/d;h_mu/sqrt(d)], Pi_e=diag(0,Pi), and G_e(pi)=[sum_mu z_mu z_mu^T+pi Pi_e+tau lambda I_(m+1)]^(-1). Let c(pi) be the first diagonal entry of G_e(pi); it is strictly positive. Then 1/c(pi)=sum_mu y_mu^2/d^2+tau lambda-v^T G(pi)v/d^3, and G_e(pi) has blocks [[c,-c q^T],[-c q,G+c q q^T]].
