[Theorem 12 (Probability-generating function) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The \textsc{pgf} of $T_{m,p}$ is
  \[
    G_{T_{m,p}}(z)
    \coloneqq \sum_{n=0}^\infty \PP \left(T_{m,p} = n\right) z^n
    = \left[
        \sum_{\ell=0}^m
        \binom{m-m/z}{\ell}
        (-1)^\ell
        \left(\frac{1}{1-p}\right)^\ell
      \right]^{-1}.
  \]
  As an analytic expression,
  both sides agree on an open ball around the origin
  with radius (strictly) greater than $1$,
  upon defining $G_{T_{m,p}}(0)$ by its limit $0$.
  \begin{proof}
    By Proposition \ref{thm:concatenation}, Remark \ref{rem:lgf is pgf},
    Lemma \ref{thm:H ogf} and Lemma \ref{thm:G ogf},
    \begin{align*}
      G_{T_{m,p}}(z) =
      \phi_J(z) = \frac{\phi_H(z)}{\phi_G(z)}
      &= \left(1-p\right)^m \binom{m/z - 1}{m}^{-1}
        \left[\sum_{\ell=0}^m \binom{m}{\ell} 
        \binom{m/z-1}{\ell}^{-1} \left(1-p\right)^\ell\right]^{-1} \\
      &= \left(1-p\right)^m
        \left[ \sum_{\ell=0}^m
        \binom{m/z - 1}{m}
        \binom{m}{\ell} 
        \binom{m/z-1}{\ell}^{-1} \left(1-p\right)^\ell\right]^{-1} \\
      &= (1-p)^m
        \left[
        \sum_{\ell=0}^m
        \frac{\left(m/z-1\right)^{\underline{m}} m^{\underline{\ell}}
        }{
          m! \left(m/z-1\right)^{\underline{\ell}}}
          \left(1-p\right)^\ell\right]^{-1}\\
      &= (1-p)^m
        \left[
        \sum_{\ell=0}^m
        \binom{m/z - \ell - 1}{m - \ell}
        \left(1-p\right)^\ell\right]^{-1}.
    \end{align*}
    Reverse the summation order via $\ell \mapsto m - \ell$
    then use $\binom{-\nu}{\ell} = (-1)^\ell \binom{\nu + \ell - 1}{\ell}$.
    This concludes the formal result.

    Let $E_k$ be the event that coupons
    $1, 2, \dots, m$ are collected on
    the days $k\,m + 1, k\,m+ 2, \dots, k\,m + m$ respectively.
    Then $\{ E_k \}_{k \geqslant 0}$ is a collection of
    independent events, each with positive probability $q = ((1-p)/m)^m$.
    The random variable $G = \inf_{k \geqslant 0} \1_{E_k}$
    is geometric with parameter $q$ and thus
    \[
      \PP(T_{m, p} = n) \leq \PP(T_{m, p} \geq n)
      \leq \PP(m\,G + m \geq n)
      = (1-q)^{\left\lceil\frac{n-m}{m}\right\rceil}.
    \]
    The radius of convergence is no less than $(1-q)^{-1/m} > 1$.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Probability-generating function

[Lemma asymptotics of arXiv:2609.02871, 'Estimating the number of real zeros of linear combinations of radicals of polynomials'] Let $\beta>-\frac{1}{2}$ and let $d\mu$ be the length measure on $\partial \mathbb{D}$. Then
\begin{itemize}
    \item  \begin{equation} 
u(z)
:= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\partial\mathbb{D}}
\left(\frac{|z-\zeta|^2}{1-|z|^2}\right)^{\beta} \, d\mu(\zeta)
\end{equation}
is the unique radial solution to $\Delta_\mathbb{D} u-\beta(\beta+1)u = 0$ in $\mathbb{D}$ such that $u(0)=1$. As $|z|\to 1-$ the function $u$ has the following asymptotic properties (for $\beta > -1/2$):
\[
u(z)
= C_1(\beta)\,(1 - |z|^2)^{-\beta}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr),
\]
where $C_1(\beta)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\partial\mathbb{D}}
|1-\zeta|^{2\beta} \, d\mu(\zeta)$ is a positive numerical constant.
   
    \item A function 
    \begin{equation} 
    g(z)= g(|z|)= \frac{u(|z|)}{2\pi}\int
    \limits_{|z|}^{1}\frac{1}{u^2(r)r}dr
    \end{equation}
      is radial fundamental solution to
    $\Delta_\mathbb{D} g+\lambda g = -\delta_0$
    in $\mathbb{D}$ (see (equation eq:distributions of the paper) in Appendix for the precise meaning).  As $|z|\to +0$ $$g(z)= \frac{-\log|z|}{2\pi}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr)$$
    and as $|z|\to 1-$ 
\[
g(z)
= C_2(\beta)\,(1 - |z|^2)^{\beta+1}\bigl(1+o(1)\bigr), \quad C_2(\beta) >0.
\]
    
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

What the lemma says: $f\in L^1$ implies $\hat f(n)\to0$ (on $\mathbb T$) or $\hat f(\xi)\to0$ as $|\xi|\to\infty$ (on $\mathbb R^d$), with $\hat f$ continuous and bounded by $\|f\|_1$. What it does not say. (i) No rate is implied: for every even sequence $(a_n)$ of nonnegative reals with $a_n\to0$ that is convex for $n\ge1$ ($a_{n-1}+a_{n+1}-2a_n\ge0$), there is a nonnegative $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ with $\hat f(n)=a_n$ for all $n$; taking $a_n=1/\log(|n|+e)$ shows the decay can be as slow as one likes. So an estimate like $|\hat f(n)|\le Cn^{-\alpha}$ must come from extra regularity: e.g. $\alpha$-Holder continuity gives $|\hat f(n)|\le\frac{C}{2}(2|n|)^{-\alpha}$ via $\hat f(n)=\frac12\int(f(x)-f(x+\tfrac1{2n}))e^{-2\pi inx}dx$, and bounded variation gives $|\hat f(n)|\le V(f)/(2\pi|n|)$. (ii) The converse fails: not every null sequence is the sequence of Fourier coefficients of an $L^1$ function. For odd $f\in L^1(\mathbb T)$ with sine coefficients $b_n$, the series $\sum_nb_n/n$ must converge; since $\sum_{n\ge2}\frac1{n\log n}=\infty$, the everywhere-convergent series $\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\sin(2\pi nx)}{\log n}$ is not the Fourier series of any integrable function. (iii) Consequently 'the coefficients tend to 0' is never evidence that a given trigonometric series is a Fourier series, and never by itself a convergence statement.

[Definition of arXiv:2411.19255, 'Moderate, large and super large deviations principles for Poisson process with uniform cat'] A family of random variables $\xi_T(1)$ satisfies local large deviation principle (LLDP)  in  $\mathbb{R}$ with a rate function
	$I = I(x): \mathbb{R} \rightarrow [0,\infty]$ and the normalizing function
	$\psi(T)$, such that $\lim\limits_{T\rightarrow\infty}\psi(T) = \infty$,
	if the following equality holds for any  $x \in  \mathbb{R}$,
	$$
	\lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}\limsup_{T\rightarrow \infty}\frac{1}{\psi(T)}
	\ln\mathbf{P}(\xi_T(1)\in U_\varepsilon(x))
	=\lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}\liminf_{T\rightarrow \infty}\frac{1}{\psi(T)}
	\ln\mathbf{P}(\xi_T(1)\in U_\varepsilon(x))=-I(x),
	$$
	where
	$
	U_\varepsilon(x):=\{y\in \mathbb{R}: \ |x-y|<\varepsilon\}.
	$

Owner-own-work research draft; status proof (unaudited), independent review and novelty assessment pending. Let k>=2, D>=1, F:[0,1]^k -> R^D extend C2 to a neighborhood of the cube, sup ||DF||_op<=L, sup ||D2F||_bilinear<=M, and let f>=0 integrate to one with Euclidean Lipschitz constant <=H. Define beta=2/(2k-1), C=L*(sqrt(k-1)+sqrt(k))/2+L*H/4+M/8 and K=8*C+L*sqrt(k). For every N>=1 there is a continuous N-piece affine generator of one-dimensional uniform noise with W1 error <=K*N^(-beta) to F_#(f dx). Use n^(2(k-1)) transverse rows spaced n^(-2), n chords per row, and positive-time connectors; zero-mass chords are omitted. For an (a,b)-bi-Lipschitz C2 chart, uniform surface law is covered with L=b and H=k*b^(k-1)*M/a^k through the area Jacobian. On F_k(x)=(x,|x|^2), b_k=sqrt(1+4k), A_k=8^k+2^k*sqrt(2*(1+8*sqrt(k))). Uniform parameter law has error >=(1/2)*(2*A_k*N)^(-beta); uniform surface law has the same bound with A_k replaced by b_k*A_k. Both have matching upper exponent beta. Thus the suggested universal curved-image exponent 2/(k+1) fails when k>2, although it agrees at k=2. This is a worst-case rate for the stated controlled C2/Lipschitz-density class, not a lower bound for every image. Merely upper/lower bounded densities are not covered by the upper construction, and no claim of originality or sharp unrestricted-deep rate is made.
k>=2; C2 chart with finite uniform derivative bounds L,M; nonnegative probability density with finite Lipschitz constant H; scalar uniform source; all positive-time connectors counted. Surface law additionally requires a>0 bi-Lipschitz chart.

[Corollary 38 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(k\) be a perfect field of characteristic \(p>0\).
For \(i=1,2\), let \(X_i\) be a smooth qcqs \(k\)-scheme and let
\(D_i\) be a simple normal crossings divisor on \(X_i\).
Assume that both pairs
\[
(X_1,D_1)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(X_2,D_2)
\]
are log HT-split.
Then the pair
\[
\left(
X_1\times_k X_2,\,
\pr_1^*D_1+\pr_2^*D_2
\right)
\]
is log HT-split.

body: [Definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] A stochastic process $(X_{g})_{g \in G}$ is \textbf{$k$-dependent} if for any subsets $ A, B \subset V$ with $d(A, B) > k$, the restrictions $X_{A} = (X_g)_{g \in A}$ and $X_B = (X_g)_{g \in B}$ are independent. A process $(X_g)_{g \in G}$ is \textbf{finitely dependent} if it is $k$-dependent for some $k \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}$.

[OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT: T407-WEDGE-008 v2, proof (unaudited); not independently checked; priority unestablished.] For independent Gaussian a,b in R^d and wedges where sign((exp(tG)a) dot b) differs from sign(a dot b), a coordinate-plane tangent has probability c_d t+o(t), c_d=Gamma(d/2)/(2sqrt(pi)Gamma((d+1)/2)). For d>=3 the distinct orthogonal tangents G12,G13 have pair intersection (1-1/sqrt(2))c_d t+o(t); for d>=4 the disjoint-coordinate tangents G12,G34 have intersection (c_d/4)t+o(t). Thus their overlaps are Theta_d(t), not O_d(t^2). In d=2 a single rotation wedge has probability t/pi exactly, but there is only one tangent direction. In d=4 the disjoint-plane intersection is exactly cot(t/2)[1-(t/2)cot(t/2)]/pi for 0<t<pi, with small-t coefficient 1/(6pi). These are coordinate-route obstruction results, not a sample-complexity lower theorem.
Fixed integer d>=3 or d>=4 as specified, t downarrow0, noiseless bilinear Gaussian classifiers; standard coordinate-plane generators with unit operator norm; no dimension-uniform remainder asserted.
For the exact d4 formula additionally 0<t<pi.
No independent reviewer PASS has been received.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:38196447624834cd27390838109fb9fda0f3887f3c2188a08c3b5c0a58eae29b","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/38/38196447624834cd27390838109fb9fda0f3887f3c2188a08c3b5c0a58eae29b.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:5296891cc5bad0156b818849cecfa00ca13472b6195781899d7f5f52bde564e2","bundle_entry_key":"gaussian-bilinear-tangent-overlap","bundle_id":"population.t407-draft-gaussian-tangent-wedge-overlap","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"statistical learning theory","draft":"w693/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.sample_complexity:draft-gaussian-bilinear-tangent-wedges-linear-overlap","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"Definitions and exact Gaussian identity


Let a,b be independent N(0,I_d). Put h_0(a,b)=sign(a dot b), h_i(t)(a,b)=sign((R_i(t)a) dot b), with R_i(t)=exp(t G_i) and G_i skew-symmetric. These are members of {sign(a^T U b): U in O(d)} because U=R_i(t)^T. Let W_i(t)={h_i(t)!=h_0}. The sign convention at zero is immaterial: each relevant nonzero linear form in b has zero Gaussian probability of vanishing, for a!=0, and a=0 is null.

For any two nonzero deterministic normals v,w and standard Gaussian b,
  P_b(sign(v dot b)!=sign(w dot b))=angle(v,w)/pi.
Proof: project b to the plane of the normals. Its angle is uniform on a circle; the two disagreement sectors have total angle 2 angle(v,w). Divide by 2pi. Collinear cases have angle zero or pi and satisfy the same identity.

Consequently, with u=a/||a|| uniform on S^(d-1),
  P(W_i(t))=E_u angle(u,R_i(t)u)/pi.
For ANY three binary classifiers, pointwise
  1_(W_1 intersection W_2)=(1_(W_1)+1_(W_2)-1_(h_1!=h_2))/2.
If exactly one wedge occurs, the last disagreement indicator is one; if both occur, h_1=h_2 is opposite to h_0; if neither occurs, all agree. Therefore
  P(W_1 intersection W_2)
   =E_u[angle(u,R_1u)+angle(u,R_2u)-angle(R_1u,R_2u)]/(2pi).       (A)
This is an exact probability identity with shared Gaussian b, not an independence assumption.

## 1. d=2: requested first diagnostic and exact answer

For the planar rotation R(t) and 0<=t<=pi,
  P(W(t))=t/pi,
because the angle of every nonzero normal and its rotation is t. For 0<=t<=pi/2, identity (A) gives
  P(W(t) intersection W(-t))=0,
  P(W(t) intersection W(2t))=t/pi.
There is only one tangent direction in O(2), since its local dimension is one. Opposite signs of that direction are not two independent tangent directions.


Tangent first variations and shared-coordinate pair


For a skew G and unit u,
  lim_(t downarrow0) angle(u,exp(tG)u)/t=||G u||.
Indeed exp(tG)u=u+tGu+O(t^2), Gu is perpendicular to u, and angle=2 arcsin(chord/2) for unit vectors. The same chord identity gives
  lim_(t downarrow0) angle(exp(tG_1)u,exp(tG_2)u)/t
    =||(G_1-G_2)u||.
For coordinate-plane generators below ||G_i||op=1. The curve exp(sG_i)u has speed ||G_i exp(sG_i)u||<=1, so its spherical angular distance from u is at most t. The angle between the two rotated normals is at most 2t by the triangle inequality. In particular each scaled term has a uniform integrable bound, and the nonnegative overlap integrand in (A), divided by t, is at most 1/pi. Dominated convergence is therefore justified:
  lim P(W_i(t))/t = E||G_i u||/pi,
  lim P(W_1(t) intersection W_2(t))/t
   =[E||G_1u||+E||G_2u||-E||(G_1-G_2)u||]/(2pi).                (B)
No exchange of an unbounded derivative and expectation is used.

## 3. Distinct Frobenius-orthogonal tangents sharing a coordinate

For d>=3 choose G_1=G_12=e_1 e_2^T-e_2 e_1^T and
G_2=G_13=e_1 e_3^T-e_3 e_1^T. Their Frobenius inner product is zero and each has operator norm one. Set
  c_d=Gamma(d/2)/(2 sqrt(pi) Gamma((d+1)/2))>0.
Then E||G_12 u||=pi c_d. To see this, ||G_12u||=sqrt(u_1^2+u_2^2); for d>2 the squared quantity has Beta(1,(d-2)/2) distribution. The beta integral gives its mean square root as
  Gamma(3/2) Gamma(d/2)/Gamma((d+1)/2)=pi c_d.
This beta distribution follows by writing u=g/||g|| for independent standard Gaussian coordinates: the first-two sum of squares and remaining sum are independent chi-squares. In d=2 the quantity equals one and c_2=1/pi, consistent with the formula.

Now G_12-G_13=e_1(e_2-e_3)^T-(e_2-e_3)e_1^T is orthogonally conjugate to sqrt(2) G_12. Uniform-sphere rotation invariance gives
  E||(G_12-G_13)u||=sqrt(2) pi c_d.
Substitution into (B) proves
  P(W_i(t))=c_d t+o(t),
  P(W_12(t) intersection W_13(t))=(1-1/sqrt(2)) c_d t+o(t).    (C)
The coefficient is strictly positive. Thus the intersection is Theta_d(t) and is NOT O_d(t^2). The subscript d means that d is fixed in the t limit; no dimension-uniform remainder is asserted.

In d=3, c_3=1/4. One can avoid gamma functions entirely: u_3 is uniform on [-1,1], and E sqrt(1-u_3^2)=pi/4 is a semicircle integral. Thus
  lim_(t downarrow0) P(W_12 intersection W_13)/t=(2-sqrt(2))/8.
This is approximately .0732233, a positive constant.


Disjoint-coordinate pair


For d>=4 instead take G_1=G_12 and G_2=G_34. These tangent matrices act on disjoint coordinates and are Frobenius-orthogonal. Pointwise,
  ||(G_12-G_34)u||=sqrt(u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2+u_4^2).
Its expectation is (3/2) pi c_d: for d>4 use Beta(2,(d-4)/2) and Gamma(5/2)/Gamma(2)=3sqrt(pi)/4; in d=4 the quantity is one, and pi c_4=2/3 gives the same ratio. Equation (B) now yields
  P(W_12(t) intersection W_34(t))=(c_d/4)t+o(t).               (D)
In d=4 the coefficient is 1/(6pi)>0. Disjoint coordinates in the perturbations do not make the events independent: both wedges concern the same base decision boundary a dot b=0.



## 5. Exact intersection formula for disjoint planes in d=4

For d=4, G_1=G_12 and G_2=G_34, there is also an exact finite-angle expression. Put z=t/2 with 0<t<pi. Then
  P(W_12(t) intersection W_34(t))=cot(z)(1-z cot(z))/pi.        (E)

Proof: for u uniform on S^3, S=u_1^2+u_2^2 is uniform on [0,1]. For the first plane rotation,
  angle(u,R_12(t)u)=2 arcsin(sin(z) sqrt(S)).
The conditional single-wedge probability is this angle divided by pi. Writing alpha=sin(z) and integrating over S gives
  E angle =4 integral_0^1 v arcsin(alpha v) dv
          =2z-z csc(z)^2+cot(z).
For completeness, integration by parts gives
  integral_0^1 v arcsin(alpha v)dv
   =z/2-[z-alpha sqrt(1-alpha^2)]/(4alpha^2),
which proves the evaluated expression. Symmetry gives the same expectation for the second plane. On the other hand,
  (R_12(t)u) dot (R_34(t)u)=cos(t)||u||^2=cos(t),
so the angle between those normals is exactly t. Equation (A) therefore makes the intersection equal to the single-wedge probability minus t/(2pi). Using csc(z)^2=1+cot(z)^2 gives (E).

For 0<z<pi/2, tan(z)>z, by integrating derivative sec(z)^2>1 from zero. Thus 0<z cot(z)<1 and the exact overlap in (E) is strictly positive. Finally cot(z)=1/z-z/3+O(z^3) yields
  P(W_12 intersection W_34)=t/(6pi)+O(t^3).
The displayed expansion is an analytic Taylor expansion at zero of smooth trigonometric quotients after their removable singularities are canceled; it is not a floating-point estimate. This exact formula strengthens the same overlap obstruction and makes no sample-complexity claim.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:84c6ed35e6d39ff33b26530b4fb31b1a0ec3838f775ec6c4cdd5752b45b2e677","revision_digest":"sha256:2bfbe9f5ac9b892595ae02a14536ccf15fa76fa102dbfd11dc7f313f881c1c05","source_id":"owner-own-work:w693:T407-WEDGE-008:v2","source_revision":"2026-10-20T11:46:47.545360+03:00; v2; proof unaudited; no priority established","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

         + \mathbb{E} \biggl[  \int_{\mathbb{X}} \Delta_E f_h(\Xi, \Sigma) \Delta\kappa(\Xi,x)  \boldsymbol{\lambda}_1(dx)  \biggr].

body: Let G = (V, E) and H = (W, F) be graphs. A graph homomorphism from G to H is a function phi: V -> W such that {u,v} in E implies {phi(u), phi(v)} in F, that is, phi maps adjacent vertices to adjacent vertices. A graph G has a homomorphism to the complete graph K_k if and only if G is properly k-colorable, so graph homomorphisms to K_k generalize proper colorings. [standard, e.g. Hell and Nesetril, Graphs and Homomorphisms]

Let $t_0 < T$, and let $a, x : [t_0, T] \to [0,\infty)$ and
$\delta : [t_0, T] \to [t_0, T]$ be measurable functions such that
$\delta(t) \le t$ for all $t \in [t_0, T]$. Assume that, for some
constants $c_\star > 0$ and $p \ge 1$,
\[
x(t) \le a(t) + \left( \int_{t_0}^t |c_\star x(\delta(s))|^p \, ds \right)^{1/p}
< \infty, \quad t \in [t_0, T].
\]
Then, for all $t \in [t_0, T]$, it holds that
\[
x(t) \le 2^{1-\frac{1}{p}}
\left( \sup_{s \in [t_0, t]} a(s) \right)
\exp\left( \frac{2^{p-1} c_\star^p (t - t_0)}{p} \right).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

OWNER-OWN-WORK; CONJECTURE, not a theorem; novelty UNCHECKED. For iid finite nonnegative teeth with tail C*t^(-1/3)*(log t)^kappa, the predicted backbone-collision threshold for two independent walks started together is kappa=2/3: infinite for kappa<=2/3, including equality, and finite for kappa>2/3. The heuristic balanced rectangle has height h_R of order R^(3/2)*(log R)^(3kappa/4), volume V_R of order R^2*(log R)^(3kappa/2), and time t_R of order R^3*(log R)^(3kappa/2). Inverting yields R(t) of order t^(1/3)*(log t)^(-kappa/2) and V(t) of order t^(2/3)*(log t)^(kappa/2). Reciprocal-volume kernel and horizontal-range predictions give squared backbone return sum density of order 1/[t*(log t)^(3kappa/2)], so the logarithmic exponent is 3kappa/2. At equality the expected return sum grows like log log T, and the predicted geometric-scale collision chances are of order 1/(m log m). These quenched estimates are unproved. Summability of backbone returns cannot establish finite total collisions in the teeth; a separate tooth-cluster bound is necessary. The full calculation and source estimates requiring revision are in I0012-H1 v1.

[Theorem thm:critical-toppling-d4 of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Fix $\nu_{0}>0$, $\theta_{0}>0$, and $K_{0}<\infty$. There are
			constants $c=c(\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})>0$,
			$C=C(\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})<\infty$, and
			$t_0=t_0(\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})<\infty$ such that, for every mean-zero i.i.d.\ field
			$(\zeta(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^4}$ satisfying
			\[
				\Var(\zeta(0))\geq\nu_{0}^2\, ,
				\qquad
				\mathbb{E} e^{\theta_{0}|\zeta(0)|}\leq K_{0}\, ,
			\]
			and every $t\geq t_0$,
			\begin{equation}
				c\log t\leq \mathbb{E} u_t(0)\leq C\log t\, .
			\end{equation}
			Moreover, for every $x\in\mathbb{Z}^4$, $t\geq2$, and $s\geq0$,
			\begin{equation}
				\mathbb{P}\left(|u_t(x)-\mathbb{E} u_t(0)|>s\right)
				\leq
				C\exp\left\{
					-c\min\left(\frac{s^2}{\log t},s\right)
				\right\}\, .
			\end{equation}
			Consequently,
			\[
				\frac{u_t(x)}{\mathbb{E} u_t(0)}\longrightarrow1
				\qquad\textup{in $L^2$ and almost surely}
			\]
			for every fixed $x$.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4cc2b444b9203a7b4b86107759b34f9a87614f875be8942194ce8b1d648ad8f0","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4c/4cc2b444b9203a7b4b86107759b34f9a87614f875be8942194ce8b1d648ad8f0.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:26ccb837dbba6c98e5cddc0e0c215c36f68708f1bc45cd1754c64b87d2b36f37","bundle_entry_key":"rie-oracle-bayes-conditional-variance-gap-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-square-calibration-and-oracle-gap-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:rie-oracle-bayes-conditional-variance-gap-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Oracle coefficients and Bayes risk: the missing conditional variance

Target 2 source obstruction; proof draft, unaudited. This is a standard
conditional-expectation identity and a counterexample to a literal finite-size
argument, not a refutation of an asymptotic formula or a novelty claim.

## Corrected finite-dimensional identity

Let S be a square-integrable random real matrix and Y an observation. Let
B_1(Y),...,B_k(Y) be a Y-measurable Frobenius-orthonormal family. Set
a_j=<S,B_j(Y)> and O=sum_j a_j B_j(Y). Suppose E[S|Y] lies in their span.
For any positive deterministic normalization c, put
R_B=E||S-E[S|Y]||_F^2/c and R_O=E||S-O||_F^2/c. Then

    R_B - R_O = sum_j E Var(a_j|Y)/c >= 0.             (1)

Indeed <E[S|Y],B_j>=E[a_j|Y], by measurability and conditional
expectation (localize if the observation-dependent coefficients are used).
Pointwise orthogonal projection gives
||S-O||^2=||S||^2-sum_j a_j^2. The assumed span condition and the
L2 projection identity give
E||S-E[S|Y]||^2=E||S||^2-sum_j E(E[a_j|Y]^2).
Subtract. All terms are integrable since sum_j a_j^2<=||S||^2.

Thus an oracle using the true coefficients is not an observation-only
competitor in the definition of Bayes risk. Asymptotic equality requires
the normalized conditional-variance sum in (1) to vanish; equivariance alone
does not prove this. For a biorthogonally invariant prior and isotropic
Gaussian noise the posterior mean is equivariant. At an observation with
distinct positive singular values, its stabilizers force the posterior mean
to lie in the observed singular-vector span, so (1) applies there. Gaussian
convolution makes the exceptional algebraic set of repeated or zero
singular values null. Formula (1) itself needs only the stated span condition.

## Exact scalar counterexample to the finite-size conclusion

Take N=P=1, S,Z independent standard normal, and Y=S+Z. The prior is
invariant under the left and right groups O(1). If Y=u sigma v is a real
singular value decomposition, u,v are signs. The oracle coefficient in
equation (4) of the source is a=u S v. Its reconstructed matrix is
u a v=S, so its squared error is zero almost surely.

The posterior density of S given Y=y is proportional to
exp(-(x^2+(y-x)^2)/2)=exp(-(x-y/2)^2-y^2/4).
It is N(y/2,1/2), hence the Bayes estimator is Y/2 and its MSE is 1/2.
The risk gap equals Var(a|Y) averaged, namely 1/2, in agreement with (1).
This example uses signal variance one and SNR one; all moments are finite.

The conclusion also fails with bounded signal: let S be uniform on {-1,1}.
The same oracle still returns S. Both posterior weights are positive for
every finite y, E[S|Y=y]=tanh(y), and Var(S|Y=y)=sech(y)^2>0.
Consequently Bayes MSE is strictly positive while oracle risk is zero.

## Primary-source locator and exact scope

Pourkamali and Macris, *Rectangular Rotational Invariant Estimator for
High-Rank Matrix Estimation*, arXiv:2403.04615v1 (7 March 2024), equation
(4), and Section 2.3, PDF page 4. The page says:

> Therefore, the oracle estimator is Bayes-optimal under bi-rotational invariant prior and achieves the MMSE.

The displayed comparison on that page treats the truth-dependent oracle
as a Bayes competitor. The rendered PDF page was visually checked, rather
than inferring the inequality direction from text extraction; evidence:
papers/2403_oracle_claim_page.png. The counterexample disproves that literal
finite-size sentence and identifies the missing step in its proof.

It does not disprove asymptotic Statements 1 or 3. Those require a separate
vanishing-conditional-variance argument or another direct proof. In
particular this note cannot be used to conclude that the source's limiting
RIE formula is false, or that Target 2 has been decided asymptotically.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:f91ebbe6b88f8d0da76d7a95800245ceda66ac687a4f50d4d4c01642933be55d","revision_digest":"sha256:2c2d1720e1ab3cebeb067b73fc07e9934756624c7beb71a7d27404b5d0a3b87e","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:rie-oracle-bayes-conditional-variance-gap-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21 claim w718-T287-018 version1, proof unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. real random variables with distribution function F, and let F_n(x) = (1/n) sum_{i <= n} 1{X_i <= x} be the empirical distribution function. Then sup_{x in R} | F_n(x) - F(x) | -> 0 almost surely. NO regularity of F is assumed: F may have atoms, may be singular, may be anything. The strong law alone gives only F_n(x) -> F(x) almost surely for each FIXED x, with a null set depending on x, and the union over uncountably many x of those null sets need not be null; the content of the theorem is that monotonicity upgrades pointwise convergence to UNIFORM convergence with a single null set. The quantitative companion is the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality, P( sup_x |F_n(x) - F(x)| > t ) <= 2 exp(-2 n t^2) with Massart's sharp constant 2, valid for every n and t. The abstract generalisation replaces the class of half-lines by a general class of sets or functions, and then a combinatorial condition such as finite Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension is required - uniform convergence over an ARBITRARY class of sets is false. [Glivenko and Cantelli (1933); Massart (1990) for the sharp DKW constant; see van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 19.1]
i.i.d. real observations
no assumption whatsoever on F
the uniformity is over half-lines; for a general class of sets a complexity condition is required

body: Consider $D$ related regressions whose coefficient vectors $w_d \in \mathbb{R}^p$ are modelled hierarchically, $w_d = w_0 + \delta_d$ with $\delta_d \sim N(0, T)$ independent across $d$, observed through $\hat w_d = w_d + z_d$ with known noise $z_d \sim N(0, \Sigma_d)$ (the sampling covariance of row $d$'s least-squares estimate). The posterior mean of $w_d$ given $\hat w_d$ is the matrix shrinkage $$\tilde w_d = w_0 + T\,(T + \Sigma_d)^{-1}(\hat w_d - w_0),$$ which shrinks fully in the directions where the prior spread $T$ is small relative to the noise and not at all where it is large. Empirical Bayes estimates the unknowns from the rows themselves: $w_0$ by the row mean (or by a pooled fit such as the global convex weights of a stacking problem), and $T$ from the row covariance of the residuals $\hat w_d - w_0$, whose expectation is $T + \bar\Sigma$: with a common noise covariance one whitens by $\bar\Sigma^{-1/2}$, forms the $p \times p$ residual covariance $\hat R = \frac{1}{D}\sum_d r_d r_d^T$ of the whitened rows, and takes $\hat T = (\hat R - I)_+$ (eigenvalues below one set to zero - the same 'subtract the noise level, keep the positive part' as the spiked-covariance debiasing, now at the aspect ratio $p/D$ of the row covariance, which is a random-matrix problem in its own right). The scalar positive-part James-Stein rule toward $w_0$ is the special case $T \propto \Sigma$. Two facts decide whether the construction helps in practice: the noise model $\Sigma_d$ must be right (under heteroscedastic residuals the homoscedastic $\sigma_d^2 (X_d^T X_d)^{-1}$ can understate the noise by a large factor in the ill-conditioned directions, making the estimated amount of shrinkage collapse to zero where cross-validation would shrink substantially - the sandwich covariance is the repair), and the gain is a variance reduction only, so it is largest when the rows are noisy relative to their spread, i.e. at small calibration sizes.

body: In computational complexity theory, the Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem states that nondeterministic space complexity classes are closed under complementation. It was proven independently by Neil Immerman and Róbert Szelepcsényi in 1987, for which they shared the 1995 Gödel Prize. In its general form the theorem states that NSPACE(s(n)) = co-NSPACE(s(n)) for any function s(n) ≥ log n. The result is equivalently stated as NL = co-NL; although this is the special case when s(n) = log n, it implies the general theorem by a standard padding argument. The result solved the second LBA problem.
title: Immerman–Szelepcsényi theorem

Train all original Euclidean mean-field parameters of a exp(b+w.x), with square loss against a fixed target of L2 norm <=Y, Y>=1, from a=b=0 and a rotation-invariant probability law of p. Assume an existing characteristic solution satisfies |a|,|b|,||p||<=K uniformly in time and dimension, K>=1. Then ||p_t.u||_L2 <=s_d(t)=K/sqrt(d)+B_K Y t/d, B_K=3^(1/4) K exp(K+2K^2). The actual degree-1 output coefficient is at most K exp(K+K^2/2)s_d(t). Any axial exponential approximant with coefficients bounded by C to Z with a fixed L2 error delta in [0,1), independent of d must have C>=(1-delta)exp(-K^2/2)/s_d(t). Thus a t=o(d) phase with one fixed K cannot generate the dimension-uniform bounded-coefficient or fixed interval-density handoff used by the prepared-axis C11-C13 proofs. This uses only initial rotational invariance, not later invariance, and allows off-axis neurons. Uniform parameter control is assumed, not derived; longer phases or dimension-growing parameters remain open. This is not an unrestricted learning-time lower bound or a refutation of Target 3. No novelty or independent audit is asserted.

	$N=|Q|\geq2$. For $F=(F_z)_{z\in Q}$, set
	\[
		L_Q(F)\coloneqq
		\max_{\Gamma}
		\min_{z\in\Gamma}F_z\, ,
	\]

	$Q$ from the left to the right. For every
	$\beta\geq1$ there is a $C^\infty$ function $L_{Q,\beta}$ of the

		|\partial_{z_1}\cdots\partial_{z_k}L_{Q,\beta}(F)|
		\leq C\beta^{k-1}(\log N)^{k-1} \, . 
	\end{equation}

Let 1<=k<=d, S subset {1,...,d} with |S|=k, and X have independent {-1,1} coordinates of common mean mu in (0,1). Put Y=chi_S(X)=product_{i in S} X_i and L_mu=mu^(k-1)-mu^(k+1). Then E[Y]=mu^k. For every fixed b in [-1,1], E[(Y-b)X_j]=mu^(k-1)-b*mu when j is in S, and mu^(k+1)-b*mu otherwise. In particular, b=mu^k gives L_mu on S and zero off S. If b is the mean of B>=1 iid labels from independent D_mu inputs, then P(|b-mu^k|>=zeta)<=2 exp(-B*zeta^2/2) for every zeta>0. Conditional on this independent centering batch, take a fresh X with the stated product law. On the event |b-mu^k|<=zeta, all its centered coordinate moments simultaneously differ from L_mu on S, or zero off S, by at most mu*zeta. For 0<delta<1, B>=2 log(2/delta)/zeta^2 makes that event have probability at least1-delta. This is the algebraic content of the source first-layer drift calculation; no assertion about jointly moving ReLU gates or batch-one training follows.
Independent product inputs with common mean0<mu<1; a fixed nonempty parity support.
For the probabilistic centering consequence, the B centering samples are iid and independent of the fresh input.
This is not a conditional-iid claim after arbitrary data-dependent filtering or sample reuse.

Partition Efron-Stein tensorization needs independence. Let X_1=X_2=B with B~Bernoulli(1/2), use the singleton partition {{1},{2}}, and let f(x_1,x_2)=x_1+x_2. Then Var(f)=1 but E Var(f|X_2)+E Var(f|X_1)=0. In the replace-one form, with each X_i resampled independently from its own law, (1/2)(E[(f - f^(1))^2] + E[(f - f^(2))^2]) = 1/2, since f - f^(i) = B - B' with B' an independent copy of B; so the classical Efron-Stein inequality Var(f) <= (1/2) sum_i E[(f - f^(i))^2] fails as well, 1 against 1/2. Thus the nontrivial partition tensorization inequality can fail completely without product-law independence, and the replace-one form fails by a factor of two.

Method: Explicit model calculation and hypothesis obstruction Result: A diagnostic linear calculation shows why a naive time-difference argument is insufficient. For du_k+lambda_k*u_k dt=x_k dW, a time increment includes fresh noise integral_t^(t+h) exp[-lambda_k*(t+h-s)]x_k dW_s. Its A^(1/2)-weighted second moment is (1/2)sum |x_k|^2*(1-exp[-2lambda_k*h]). Integrating h^(-1-2alpha) over h gives a term comparable to sum lambda_k^(2alpha)|x_k|^2. Thus even a constant-in-time coefficient needs additional spatial regularity to give W^(alpha,2) time regularity in D(A^(1/2)). Check: The change of variables z=lambda_k*h gives the lambda_k^(2alpha) factor, and the integral near zero is finite exactly when alpha<1/2. Agresti-Veraar2026, arXiv2509.07803, proves this precise obstruction for the linear problem. Obstruction: This known obstruction is not a counterexample to the full nonlinear bootstrap theorem, whose diffusion mapping assumptions may supply the missing spatial input. [Theorem 5 of arXiv:2608.27569, 'Laplace and Dolbeault operators on Sasakian manifolds'] Let $(M^{2n+1},g,\xi )$ be a compact Sasakian manifold. Let $m\in \{0,\ldots, 2n+1\}$. Then 
\begin{itemize} 
\item If $m>n+1$ we have $\mathcal{H}_{\overline\partial,P}^{m}(0)=0$,   and $\mathcal{H}_{\overline\partial,P}^{n+1}(0)\subset H^{n+1}(M)$. 
\item If $\mathcal{H}_{\overline\partial,P}^{m}(0)$ is nonzero

for some $m<n$, the first positive eigenvalue $\lambda_{1,m+1}$  satisfies
$$\lambda_{1,m+1}<4(n-m+1).$$
Also, we have 
$$\lambda_{1,m+2b}< 4(b+1)(n-m-b+1),$$
for any $0<b\leq\frac{n-m}{2}$. 
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Cor 9 of arXiv:2604.24189, 'Malliavin calculus and densities for chaos-driven stochastic differential equations'] Let $q \in \N$ and $f \in \mathfrak{H}^{\odot  q}$ be fixed, and set $F=I_q(f)$. For every $h \in \mathfrak{H}$, there exists an event $\Omega_h$ with $\mathbb{P}(\Omega_h)=1$ such that, for every $\omega \in \Omega_h$ and $0 \leq \ell \leq q$,
\[D^\ell F(\omega + j(h)) = \sum_{k=0}^{q-\ell} \frac{1}{k!} \langle D^{k+\ell} F(\omega),h^{\otimes k} \rangle_{\mathfrak{H}^{\otimes k}}. \]

body:
Fix a finite Netsor program. Its inputs are fixed real vectors of fixed dimensions and independent matrix variables W of shape n by m with independent N(0,1/m) entries. Its only instructions are MatMul g=W h and coordinatewise NonLin h=phi(h_1,...,h_k), with matching dimensions; a matrix variable may be reused, but transposition is not an instruction. Let n_hidden be the program collection of dimensions internal to chains of matrix contractions, and n_output the output dimensions; input dimensions remain fixed. Write h^ell in R^(n_ell) for the finite-width variable on line ell and bar_h^ell for the infinite-width execution. In the latter, every MatMul variable bar_g is centered Gaussian, all MatMul variables are jointly Gaussian, different matrix variables have zero cross-covariance, and two products using the same W, with parent variables bar_h,bar_h_prime in R^m, have cross-covariance [E(bar_h^T bar_h_prime)/m] I_n. NonLin instructions apply the same functions coordinatewise to this Gaussian execution. Assume every function phi used in a NonLin instruction is globally Lipschitz. For every p>=1 there is c<infinity depending only on p and the structural constants of the fixed program such that W_p((h^ell/sqrt(n_ell))_(ell=1)^L, (bar_h^ell/sqrt(n_ell))_(ell=1)^L) <= c sum_(m in n_hidden) m^(-1/2). W_p uses the Euclidean norm on the concatenated vector of all line variables. Structural constants include the fixed input vectors, input dimensions and activation functions; c is uniform in the hidden widths. The theorem does not give a polynomial dependence of c on program length L, and does not cover transpose instructions or arbitrary non-Lipschitz activations.

body:
For the population loss (1/2)||BA-Delta||_F^2 with Delta an m-by-n rank-r matrix, rotate the two factors by the left and right singular vectors of Delta. Write R,T for the r-by-r principal blocks of the rotated B and A transpose, and J,K for the complementary blocks. Define S=(R+T)/2 and D=(R-T)/2, P=Sigma-SS^T+DD^T, and Q=SD^T-DS^T, with Sigma the positive diagonal r-by-r singular-value matrix. Then the principal error is P+Q, P is symmetric, Q is skew-symmetric, and its squared Frobenius norm is ||P||_F^2+||Q||_F^2. Ye and Du's proof grows the smallest singular value of S while controlling D,J,K in a warm-up phase, then uses a local geometric convergence phase. Their Theorem 1.1 assumes nondegenerate independent Gaussian entries in both factor matrices; its theorem statement does not directly cover B0=0. This is an optimization symmetrization of factor matrices, distinct from empirical-process symmetrization. Source: arXiv:2106.14289, sections 2.1-2.3 and 3.1-3.3.
Population squared Frobenius factorization loss
Exact rank-r target and matching factor rank
title: Ye-Du asymmetric matrix factorization symmetrization

[Proposition prop:born-binomial-starts of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] Suppose the symmetric urn starts from $\mathrm{Binomial}(n,p_0)$, where
$p_0=\cos^{2}(\theta_0/2)$ and $\theta_0\in[0,\pi]$. Then its law at time $t$ is the
Born distribution of the coherent state

\begin{equation}
e^{-i\theta(t)J_x}\lvert m=+\tfrac n2\rangle,\qquad
\theta(t)=\arccos\bigl(\cos\theta_0\,e^{-2t}\bigr).

\end{equation}

Equivalently, the initial coherent state at angle $\theta_0$ is rotated through
the additional angle $\theta(t)-\theta_0$ about the same axis.

body:
[Lem 20 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $C$ be as in \eqref{e:wishart.bound.repeated}.
    Fix any realization of $\bG$ satisfying
    \beq
    
    \max\bigg\{
       \frac{ \|\bG\|_{\op}}{C},
       \frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|}{2}
      \bigg\} \le N^{1/2}\,.
    \eeq
For such $\bG$, we have the following:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item  Under the additional constraint that $\bXi$ satisfies
        \beq
            
            \frac{\|\bXi\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}}
             \le C\,,
        \eeq
        the function
$\by \mapsto F^{\ri}(\bG,\bXi,\by)$,
        restricted to the domain $\{\|\by\| \le 2 N^{1/2}\}$, is $O(N^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz.
        \item 
Restricted to the (convex) domain \eqref{e:fp-F-kirszbraun-bXi-event},
the function
        \beq
        
            \bXi \mapsto F^{\ri}(\bG,\bXi,\ytrunc(\bG,\bXi))\,,
        \eeq
         is $O(N^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz.
    \end{enumerate}
Consequently, for any realization of $\bG$ satisfying \eqref{e:fp-F-kirszbraun-bG-event}, there exists a function $\tilde{F}(\bXi;\bG)$ which is $O(N^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz in $\bXi$, and agrees with the function
\eqref{e:fp-F-kirszbraun-fn-bXi} on the set of $\bXi$ satisfying \eqref{e:fp-F-kirszbraun-bXi-event}.

\begin{proof}
Fix $\bG$, $\bXi$ satisfying \eqref{e:fp-F-kirszbraun-bG-event}, \eqref{e:fp-F-kirszbraun-bXi-event}. Recalling \eqref{e:F.B}--\eqref{e:F.w}, we calculate
    \begin{align*}
    \nabla_\by F_B(\bG,\bXi,\by)
    &=
    \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{2\hB_j}{MN|B_j|}
        \bigg(\sum_{a\in B_j} \bmeta^a, \by \bigg)
        \bigg(\sum_{a\in B_j} \bmeta^a \bigg)\,,\\
            \nabla_\by F_v(\bG,\bXi,\by)
    &=\sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{2\hv_j}{M}
        \sum_{a\in B_j}
        \frac{(\barbg^a,\by) \barbg^a}{N}
    \\
            \nabla_\by F_U(\bG,\bXi,\by)
    &=
    \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{2\hU_j}{M|B_j|}
        \bigg(
            \sum_{a\in B_j}
            \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})(\barbg^a,\by)}{N}
        \bigg)\bigg(
            \sum_{a\in B_j}
            \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})\barbg^a}{N}
        \bigg)\\
            \nabla_\by F_w(\by)
    &=\sum_{j=1}^s\frac{2\hw_j}{N} \Pi_j \by\,.
    \end{align*}
Let $\bG^{B_j} \in \R^{B_j\times N}$ denote the restriction of $\bG$ to the rows indexed by $B_j$, and similarly denote $\bXi^{B_j}$.
Let $\ind_{B_j}\in\R^M$ denote the indicator of the $B_j$ coordinates.
Then we can bound
    \begin{align*}
    \Big| \nabla_\by F_B(\bG,\bXi,\by) \Big|
    &= \bigg| \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{2\hB_j}{MN|B_j|}
    (\ind_{B_j})^\st \bXi \by
    \cdot \bXi^\st\ind_{B_j} \bigg|
    \le  \bigg| \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{2\hB_j}{MN}
            (\|\bXi\|_\op)^2 \|\by\|  \bigg|
    \lesssim \frac{1}{N^{1/2}}\,,\\
    \Big| \nabla_\by F_v(\bG,\bXi,\by) \Big|
    &=\bigg| \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{2\hv_j}{MN}
        (\bG^{B_j})^\st\bG^{B_j} \by \bigg|
            \le
    \bigg|\sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{2\hv_j}{MN}
    (\|\bG\|_\op)^2 \|\by\|
    \bigg|\lesssim \frac{1}{N^{1/2}}\,,\\
    \Big| \nabla_\by F_U(\bG,\bXi,\by) \Big|
    &=\bigg|\sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{2\hU_j}{MN^2|B_j|}
        (\bXi^{B_j}\bar{\bx},\bG^{B_j}\by)
        \cdot
            (\bG^{B_j})^\st \bXi^{B_j}\bar{\bx}\bigg| \\
    &\le \bigg|\sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{2\hU_j}{MN^2|B_j|}
        (\|\bXi\|_\op\|\bG\|_\op)^2
        \|\bar{\bx}\|^2 \|\by\|
        \bigg|
        \lesssim \frac{1}{N^{1/2}}\,,\\
        \bigg|\nabla_\by F_w(\by)\bigg|
    &\le \bigg|
    \sum_{j=1}^s\frac{2\hw_j}{N} \|\by\|\bigg|
           \lesssim \frac{1}{N^{1/2}}\,.
    \end{align*}
Here, all factors of $\hB_j, \hv_j, \hU_j, \hw_j$ can be absorbed in the $\lesssim$ notation, as indicated by Remark~\ref{r:fp-implicit-constants}. Combining these estimates proves part \eqref{i:fp-F-kirszbraun-yLip}.

[Definition def:ncP of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] A non-commutative probability space consists of a unital algebra
  $\mathcal{A}$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and a linear functional $\varphi :
  \mathcal{A} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$, such that $\varphi (1_{\mathcal{A}}) =
  1$. The elements of $\mathcal{A}$ are called non-commutative random
  variables. The non-commutative distribution of $a \in \mathcal{A}$ is the
  linear functional $\mu_a : \mathbb{C} \langle \mathbf{x} \rangle \rightarrow
  \mathbb{C}$, defined by
  \[ \mu_a (P) := \varphi (P (a)) \text{, \quad for every ploynomial } P \in
     \mathbb{C} \langle \mathbf{x} \rangle . \]
  For $(a_1, \ldots, a_n) \in \mathcal{A}^n$ the values $\varphi (a_1 \ldots
  a_n)$ are called moments.

Let (G_n)_{n >= 0} be a DECREASING family of sub-sigma-algebras, G_0 containing G_1 containing G_2 and so on, and let G_infinity be their intersection. For Y in L^1, E[Y | G_n] converges almost surely and in L^1 to E[Y | G_infinity]. More generally a BACKWARD MARTINGALE, a family (X_n) with X_n G_n-measurable and E[X_n | G_{n+1}] = X_{n+1}, converges almost surely and in L^1 - and unlike the forward case NO extra hypothesis is required, because a backward martingale is automatically uniformly integrable: X_n = E[X_0 | G_n] is a family of conditional expectations of one integrable variable. This asymmetry with the forward theorem is the point: forward martingales need an L^1 bound for almost sure convergence and uniform integrability for L^1 convergence, backward martingales need neither. The classical application is the strong law of large numbers: with S_n the partial sums of an i.i.d. integrable sequence and G_n the exchangeable sigma-algebra generated by S_n, S_{n+1}, ..., one has E[X_1 | G_n] = S_n/n, so S_n/n converges almost surely and in L^1, and the Hewitt-Savage 0-1 law identifies the limit as E[X_1]. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.6.1]

[Thm main of arXiv:2608.30847, 'An Almgren-type formula for planar $p$-harmonic functions'] Let $u$ be a nonconstant $p$-harmonic function in a planar domain $\Omega$, and let $x_0\in\Omega$.  Put $v=u-u(x_0)$.  For all sufficiently small $r>0$, define
$$
  D(x_0,r)=\int_{B_r(x_0)} |D u|^p\,dx,
\quad 
  H(x_0,r)=\int_{\partial B_r(x_0)} |D u|^{p-2}v^2\,dS,
$$
and
$$
  N_*(x_0,r)=\frac{rD(x_0,r)}{H(x_0,r)}.
$$
If $u$ is not locally constant near $x_0$, then $H(x_0,r)>0$ for all sufficiently small $r$ and the limit
$$
  N_*(x_0,0+)=\lim_{r\to0}N_*(x_0,r)
$$
exists.

If $D u(x_0)\ne0$, then $ N_*(x_0,0+)=1.$
If $D u(x_0)=0$ and the Aronsson order of $x_0$ is $N\ge1$, then
$$
  N_*(x_0,0+)=\lambda_N(p),
$$
where
$$
  \lambda_N(p)=\frac{\beta_{N+1}(p)}{\beta_{N+1}(p)-1}
$$
and
$$
  \beta_{N+1}(p)
  =
  \frac{\sqrt{(p-2)^2+4(p-1)((N+1)/N)^2}-(p-2)}{2}.
$$
Moreover, in both cases there are constants $C>0$, $\delta>0$, and $r_0>0$ such that
$$
  |N_*(x_0,r)-N_*(x_0,0+)|\le Cr^\delta
  \qquad 0<r<r_0.
$$

In addition, the obstruction $\Theta$ defined as (equation eq:theta-defn of the paper) in Proposition~(thm:exact-identity of the paper) belongs to $L^1(0,r_0)$, and the gauge-corrected frequency (equation eq:gauge-frequency of the paper) in Corollary (cor:gauge-formal of the paper) is nondecreasing. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 6 (Dirichlet bounds) of arXiv:2604.00642, 'Quantitative central limit theorem for an integrated periodogram via the fourth moment the'] There exists $C<\infty$ such that for all $n\ge1$ and $\lambda\in(-\pi,\pi)$, we have
\[
\abs{D_n(\lambda)}\le C\min\Big(\sqrt n,\frac{1}{\sqrt n\,\abs{\lambda}}\Big)
\le C H_n(\lambda),
\qquad
\Phi_n(\lambda):=\abs{D_n(\lambda)}^2 \le H_n^2(\lambda).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\Phi_n(\lambda)\dd\lambda=1,
\qquad
\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}D_n(\lambda-\omega)D_n(\omega-\mu)\dd\omega
=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{n}}\,D_n(\lambda-\mu),
\]
\begin{align*}
\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|D_n(\lambda-\omega)D_n(\omega-\mu)|\dd\omega \leq C\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|H_n(\lambda-\omega)H_n(\omega-\mu)|\dd\omega \leq C_{\eta}n^{\eta-1/2}H_n(\lambda-\mu).
\end{align*}

[Df 27 of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] Let $m, r$ be positive integers. Let $\eta$ be a primitive $m$-th root of unity. The \textbf{cyclic Dowling arrangement} of order $m$ and rank $r$, denoted $Q_r(m)$, is the arrangement in $\mathbb{C}^r$
    \[
        Q_r(m) = \{ x_i \mid 1 \leq i \leq r\} \cup \{x_i - \eta^k x_j \mid 1 \leq i < j \leq r, \; 0 \leq k < m\}.
    \]
    The \textbf{cyclic Dowling geometry} of order $m$ and rank $r$ is the matroid $MQ_r(m) \deq M(Q_r(m))$.
    For a subset $Z$ of $\{1,\dots,m\}$, the \textbf{Dowling subarrangement} induced by $Z$ is the subarrangement 
    \[
        Q_Z(m) \deq \{x_i \mid i \in Z\} \cup \{x_i - \eta^k x_j \mid i, j \in Z,\; i < j,\; 0 \leq k < m\}.
    \]
    The corresponding submatroid $MQ_Z(m) \deq M(Q_Z(m))$ of $MQ_r(m)$ is the \textbf{Dowling subgeometry} induced by $Z$. It is isomorphic to 
    $Q_{\abs{Z}}(m)$ and its ground set is a flat of $Q_r(m)$. We also call ``Dowling subgeometry'' the flat $E(M(Q_Z(m )))$ of any submatroid of $MQ_r(m)$ containing it.

body:
Let A_1, ..., A_m be pairwise independent with S = sum_i P(A_i) > 0. Then P(A_1 or ... or A_m) >= S/(1 + S(1 - 1/m)), with equality if and only if all P(A_i) are equal and the number N of events that occur is constant on the union. If every P(A_i) = p > 0 the bound reads mp/(1 + (m - 1)p), with equality if and only if N takes only the values 0 and r = 1 + (m - 1)p; so equality is impossible unless 1 + (m - 1)p is an integer. For the three even-parity events on {000, 011, 101, 110}, p = 1/2, r = 2 and the bound 3/4 is attained.

[Definition 21 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Let $F$ be a non-empty set.  A pair $(\CE,\CF)$ is called a \emph{resistance form} if the following are true:
\begin{enumerate}[(RF1)]
\item $\CF$ is a linear subspace of the space of $\R$-valued functions on $F$ that contains the constant functions, and $\CE$ is a non-negative symmetric quadratic form on $\CF$.  Moreover, $\CE(f,f) = 0$ if and only if $f \in \CF$ is a constant function.
\item Let $\sim$ be the equivalence relation on $\CF$ given by $f \sim g$ if and only if $f-g$ is constant.  Then $(\CF/{\sim}, \CE)$ is a Hilbert space.
\item For each $x \neq y$ there exists $f \in \CF$ such that $f(x) \neq f(y)$.
\item For each $x,y \in F$, we have
\begin{equation}
 R(x,y) \defeq \sup \left\{ \frac{| f(x) - f(y)|^2}{\CE(f,f)} : f \in \CF,\, \CE(f,f) > 0 \right\} < \infty .
\end{equation}
\item We have $\ol{f} \in \CF$ and $\CE(\ol{f},\ol{f}) \leq \CE(f,f)$ for each $f \in \CF$ where $\ol{f} = (f \vee 0) \wedge 1$.
\end{enumerate}

[Proposition prop:wheel-geodesics of arXiv:2609.02544, 'A finiteness theorem for geodesic Leech wheels'] Every geodesic of $W_{m+1}$ belongs to exactly one of the following four classes.
\begin{align*}
&uv_i, &&\text{weight }a_i;\\
&v_iv_{i+1}, &&\text{weight }b_i;\\
&v_iv_{i+1}v_{i+2}, &&\text{weight }b_i+b_{i+1};\\
&v_i u v_j\quad(0\le i<j<m,\ \{i,j\}\notin E(C_m)),
&&\text{weight }a_i+a_j.
\end{align*}
Consequently
\[
  t_{gp}(W_{m+1})=\frac{m(m+3)}2.
\]
Equivalently, for $n\ge5$,
\[
  t_{gp}(W_n)=\frac{(n-1)(n+2)}2.
\]

[Corollary multilinear reursion of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] Let ${\bf x} = \{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequences of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. Let $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n}$ be multi-indexed sequences of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define a degree-$D$ multilinear polynomial random matrix as
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{d=1}^D ~ \sum_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right).
$$
Suppose ${\bf F}^{=d}({\bf x})$ is permutation symmetric for $1\leq d \leq D$. Let $a,b,c\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $d = a+b+c$. Then for $2 \leq t \leq \infty,$
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf F}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf F}({\bf x})}_{4t}^{4t} ~\leq~ \sum_{d=1}^D  D^{4t} (48dt)^{4dt} \left( \sum_{\substack{a,b,c: \\a+b+c=d }} L^{4ct} \norm{{\bf F}_{a,b,c}^{=d}}_{4t}^{4t} \right).
$$

[Dfn 202 (buckets for spherical perceptron) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We now define $\vX^\trunc$ and $\vX^\frozen$, which may be regarded as the processes $\vX^\trstar$ and $\vX^\frstar$ with \textbf{small spatial buckets frozen}. For the spherical perceptron, initialize $\vX^\trunc(q_0)\equiv\vX^\trstar(q_0)$
and $\vX^\frozen(q_0)\equiv\vX^\frstar(q_0)$, and suppose inductively that $\vX^\trunc(q_\ell)$
and $\vX^\frozen(q_\ell)$
have been defined for $0\le\ell\le d$. Then let
    \begin{align}
    B(q_d, J(q_{0:d})) 
    &\equiv \Big\{ a\in[M]:
    \vX^\trunc(q_\ell,a)
    \in J(q_\ell)
    \textup{ for each }0\le\ell\le d
    \Big\}\,,\\
    B^\frozen(q_d, J(q_{0:d})) 
    &\equiv \Big\{ a\in[M^\frozen]:
    \vX^\frozen(q_\ell,a)
    \in J(q_\ell)
    \textup{ for each }0\le\ell\le d
    \Big\}\,.\end{align}
We emphasize that in both \eqref{e:bucket} and \eqref{e:bucket.fr}, the $J$ blocks are restricted to within $[-\trK,\trK)^3$. We then let
    \begin{align*}
    B(q_d,a)
    &= \begin{cases}
    B(q_d, J(q_{0:d}))
    &\textup{if $a\in B(q_d, J(q_{0:d}))$,}\\
    \{a\}
    &\textup{otherwise, meaning 
    $\vX^\trunc(q_d, a)
    \notin[-\trK,\trK)^3$;}
    \end{cases} \\
    B^\frozen(q_d,a)
    &= \begin{cases}
    B^\frozen(q_d, J(q_{0:d}))
    &\textup{if }a\in B(q_d, J(q_{0:d}))\,,\\
    \{a\}
    &\textup{otherwise, meaning }\vX^\frozen(q_d, a)\notin[-\trK,\trK)^3\,.
    \end{cases}
    \end{align*}
The sets $\mathcal{B}(q_d)\equiv\{B(q_d,a) : a\in[M]\}$ partition $[M]$, and the partition is progressive in the sense that each $\mathcal{B}(q_{d+1})$ refines the previous partition $\mathcal{B}(q_d)$.  Similarly, the sets
$\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)\equiv\{B^\frozen(q_d,a) : a\in[M^\frozen]\}$ progressively partition $[M^\frozen]$. In either case we call these the \textbf{buckets} at time $q_d$.  We define the quantity
    \beq
    \BUCKETS
    \equiv \bigg(\frac{8\trK}{\eta}\bigg)^{6\dmax}\,,\eeq
so that $\BUCKETS$ upper bounds the total number of buckets within $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ over all times. We then let
    \begin{align}
    
    \vX^\trunc(q_{d+1},a)
    &=\begin{cases}
    \vX^\trstar(q_{d+1},a)
    &\textup{if } |B(q_d,a)| 
        \ge M/\BUCKETS^2\,,\\
    \vX^\trunc(q_d,a)
    &\textup{otherwise}\,.
    \end{cases}\\
    
    \vX^\frozen(q_{d+1},a)
    &=\begin{cases}
    \vX^\frstar(q_{d+1},a)
    &\textup{if } |B^\frozen(q_d,a)  \cap[M]  | 
        \ge M/\BUCKETS^2\,,\\
    \vX^\frozen(q_d,a)
    &\textup{otherwise}\,.
    \end{cases}
    \end{align}
Note that because the partitions $\mathcal{B}(q_d)$ and $\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$ are progressive, particles that are frozen in step $d+1$ (i.e. such that the second case of \eqref{e:small-bucket-freezing-trunc} or \eqref{e:small-bucket-freezing-frozen} holds) stay frozen in all future steps. Note also that when determining whether buckets for the $\vX^\frozen$ process are too small we only look at particle indices in $[M]$, that is, we ignore the added particles from Definition~\ref{d:froze} when determining bucket size. With this definition, one can verify by induction that the set of buckets $B\in \mathcal{B}(q_d)$ can be obtained by taking $B=B^\frozen\cap[M]$ for each $B^\frozen\in\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$.
title: buckets for spherical perceptron

body: Maximum modulus principle: Let D be a nonempty connected open subset of C (a domain) and let f be holomorphic on D. If |f| attains a local maximum at some point of D, then f is constant on D. Equivalently, if f is holomorphic and non-constant on D, then |f| has no local maximum at any point of D. Consequently, if D is bounded and f is continuous on the closure of D and holomorphic on D, then the maximum of |f| over the closure of D is attained on the boundary of D.
title: Maximum modulus principle

body: The interlacement (crossing) graph G_x(pi) of a pair partition pi does not determine the Toeplitz moment-polytope volume p_T(pi). Through order 8 every graph class carries one volume (K_3 gives 1/2, K_4 gives 2/5, matching p_T(w_r) = 2/(r+1) for G_x(w_r) = K_r; the empty graph gives 1). At order 10 exactly one of 34 classes is impure: the graph on five vertices with two disjoint edges and an isolated vertex carries 9/20 (aabcbcdede) and 4/9 (ababcdedec). Connected graphs are pure through order 10, but not at order 12: of 110 connected classes, 42 are realised by more than one inequivalent diagram and 10 of those are impure, every split being 19/90 against 22/105 (abacdbefcdfe and abacdecbfdef, two diagrams of the connected graph {01,02,03,04,12,13,14,25}). Adding the nesting number does not repair it (8 of the 10 still collide, both witnesses having nesting number 1), and the crossing number does not either. Exact rational arithmetic; orders 6, 8 and 10 enumerated completely.

PRIVATE REDUCTION, author-recorded. For a filled-in peeling exploration of the infinite Boltzmann map with critical weight sequence q, every boundary vertex is eventually swallowed almost surely iff sum_n q_{S_n} = infinity a.s., where S_n is the half-perimeter process (an h-transform of the step walk with law nu) and q_l is the probability that a peeling step at perimeter l swallows at least half of the boundary on a given side. For type a in [3/2, 5/2] the source proves divergence from q_l asymp l^{1-a} and the scaling limit S_n asymp n^{1/(a-1)}. Without a type, the criterion is a recurrence-type statement for the positive test function q along the h-transformed walk; it holds whenever liminf n q_{S_n} is bounded below in probability, so the question reduces to the growth of the h-transformed perimeter walk for non-regularly-varying critical nu. The reduction is rigorous (conditional Borel-Cantelli); the growth control is the open part.

body: Lemma (campaign status: audited-pass): psi(u) = min{3/4, 2^{1-u}*C(u, floor(u/2))} <= min{3/4, 2/sqrt(u)} (tag 12). For u = 2 the 3/4 bound is the nondegenerate-parallelogram bound; for u >= 3 it is the ordinary two-atom Littlewood-Offord bound. Over F_p invoke the finite-group one-point Littlewood-Offord theorem: when u < p and all coefficients are nonzero, each atom is at most the central-binomial mass; a union bound over the two targets gives the same psi. Notes: The bound must be uniform in the target center b, in the coefficients, and in all earlier block values - all three quantifiers are used by the reverse-exposure argument.

Let X,W be n by n and a in R^n, with X_ij iid N(0,1/n), W_ij and a_j iid N(0,1), jointly independent of X and each other. Let H=ReLU(XW), G_ij=1{(XW)_ij>0}, S=XX^T and D=S elementwise-multiplied by (G diag(a_j^2)G^T/n). For the bias-free scalar network f(x)=n^(-1/2) sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j dot x), its all-weights empirical NTK is K=HH^T/n+D. Hence K has all its ordered eigenvalues within o_P(1) of HH^T/n+S/4+I_n/4+(1/(2pi))1_n1_n^T/n. The proof combines conditional matrix Bernstein after truncating Gaussian output squares with El Karoui's quadratic-kernel approximation and uniform row-radius control. It retains the quadratic rank-one term. It does not establish a full NTK bulk law, a bounded spectral edge, anisotropic resolvent limits, or a Marchenko-Pastur bulk. Independent review is pending.

[Lemma le:mixture-given-beta-I of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] Let $\Lambda=I\cup J$ be finite with $I\cap J=\emptyset$, $\rho\in J$, and
  $W\in[0,\infty)^{\Lambda\times\Lambda}$. 
  For $\beta=(\beta_I,\beta_J)\in{\mathbb R}^\Lambda$ such that $[H_\beta^W]_{\Lambda_-\Lambda_-}$
  is positive definite, let 
  $e^{u_{\Lambda_-}(\beta)}=([H_\beta^W]_{\Lambda_-\Lambda_-})^{-1}W_{\Lambda_-\rho}$
  and $u_\rho(\beta)=0$.
  Let $H_{\beta_J}^{W^J(\beta_I)}$ and $H_{\beta^{J\neq}}^{W^{J\neq}(\beta_I)}$
  denote the $J\times J$ matrices obtained
  from $H_\beta^W$ defined in (equation eq:def-H-beta of the paper) with $(\beta,W)$
  replaced by $(\beta_J,W^J(\beta_I))$ and $(\beta^{J\neq},W^{J\neq}(\beta_I))$,
  respectively, with $\beta^{J\neq}:=(\beta_j-\frac12W^J_{jj}(\beta_I))_{j\in J}$,
  $W^J(\beta_I)$ from (equation def:W-J of the paper), and 
  $W^{J\neq}(\beta_I)$ from (equation eq:def-W-J-neq of the paper). 
  Then, one has the following restriction property
  \begin{align}
    
    e^{u_{J_-}(\beta)}=([H_{\beta_J}^{W^J(\beta_I)}]_{J_-J_-})^{-1}W_{J_-\rho}^J(\beta_I)
    =([H_{\beta^{J\neq}}^{W^{J\neq}(\beta_I)}]_{J_-J_-})^{-1}W_{J_-\rho}^{J\neq}(\beta_I). 
  \end{align}
  As a consequence, $u_{J_-}(\beta)$ depends only on $W^J(\beta_I)$ and $\beta_J$.
  We write $u_J(W^J(\beta_I),\beta_J)=u_J(W^{J\neq}(\beta_I),\beta^{J\neq})$
  instead of $u_J(\beta)$.
  
  As an application of (equation eq:exp-u-J-in-volume-J of the paper) for fixed $\beta_I$, 
  vrjp on $J$ with parameters $W^J(\beta_I)$ and $W^{J\neq}(\beta_I)$, respectively, are
  mixtures of reversible Markov jump processes with weights 
  \begin{align}
    
     C^J_{ij}(\beta_I,e^{u_J})
    =W^J_{ij}(\beta_I)e^{u_i+u_j} \quad\text{and}\quad
    C^{J\neq}_{ij}(\beta_I,e^{u_J})
    =W^{J\neq}_{ij}(\beta_I)e^{u_i+u_j}, 
    \quad i,j\in J,
  \end{align}
  and the same reversible measure $\pi(u_J)=(2e^{2u_i})_{i\in J}$ 
  with $u_J=u_J(W^J(\beta_I),\beta_J)$ in both cases, where
  $\beta_J$ is a $\nu_J^{W^J(\beta_I)}$-distributed random variable.
  In other words, for any event $A\subseteq J^{{\mathbb N}_0}\times{\mathbb R}_+^{{\mathbb N}_0}$, one has
  \begin{align}
    
  P_\rho^{W^{J\neq}(\beta_I),J}((X,T)\in A)=&
  \int_{{\mathbb R}^J}Q^{C^{J\neq}(\beta_I,e^{u_J(W^{J\neq}(\beta_I),\tilde\beta_J)}),J}_{\rho,\pi(u_J(W^{J\neq}(\beta_I),\tilde\beta_J))}((X,T)\in A)\,
  \nu_J^{W^{J\neq}(\beta_I)}(d\tilde\beta_J)
  \end{align}
  and the same formula with ``$J{\neq}$'' replaced by ``$J$'' at all five
  occurrences. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let $X \sim N(\theta, \sigma^2 I_k)$ in $\mathbb{R}^k$ with $k \ge 3$ and $\sigma^2$ known, and let $\mu_0 \in \mathbb{R}^k$ be any fixed target. Define $$\hat\theta_{\mathrm{JS}} = \mu_0 + \Big(1 - \frac{(k - 2)\sigma^2}{\|X - \mu_0\|^2}\Big)(X - \mu_0), \qquad \hat\theta_{\mathrm{JS}+} = \mu_0 + \Big(1 - \frac{(k-2)\sigma^2}{\|X - \mu_0\|^2}\Big)_+ (X - \mu_0).$$ Then for every $\theta$: (i) $E\|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{JS}} - \theta\|^2 = k\sigma^2 - (k-2)^2\sigma^4\, E\big[\|X - \mu_0\|^{-2}\big] < k\sigma^2 = E\|X - \theta\|^2$, so the shrunk estimator strictly dominates the observation itself in total squared error, with the largest gain when $\theta$ is near $\mu_0$ (risk $\to 2\sigma^2$ at $\theta = \mu_0$); (ii) the positive-part version dominates the plain one, $E\|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{JS}+} - \theta\|^2 \le E\|\hat\theta_{\mathrm{JS}} - \theta\|^2$ with strict inequality. The shrinkage amount $s = (k-2)\sigma^2/\|X - \mu_0\|^2$ is the ratio of the expected squared noise norm to the observed squared distance from the target; it is small exactly when the observation sits far from the target relative to its noise. When the noise covariance is a known $\Sigma$ rather than $\sigma^2 I$, apply the lemma to $\Sigma^{-1/2}(X - \mu_0)$ (so $s = (k - 2)/\big((X - \mu_0)^T \Sigma^{-1}(X - \mu_0)\big)$) - the Mahalanobis form; a mis-specified $\Sigma$ that understates the noise gives an $s$ that is too small.
Gaussian observation with known noise covariance
k >= 3
the target mu_0 is fixed (not data-chosen)

Stein's lemma: for $X \\sim N(\\theta, I)$ and $g$ almost differentiable with $E\\|\\nabla g\\| < \\infty$, $E[(X - \\theta)^T g(X)] = E[\\nabla \\cdot g(X)]$ (integration by parts against the Gaussian density coordinate by coordinate; $g$ is almost differentiable for $k \\ge 3$ because $\\|X\\|^{-2}$ is integrable near the origin in dimension at least three). Compute $\\nabla \\cdot g = (k-2)\\big( \\frac{k}{\\|X\\|^2} - \\frac{2}{\\|X\\|^2}\\big) = \\frac{(k-2)^2}{\\|X\\|^2}$ and $\\|g\\|^2 = \\frac{(k-2)^2}{\\|X\\|^2}$. Part (ii): on the event $\\|X\\|^2 < k - 2$ the plain estimator overshoots the target (its coefficient $1 - (k-2)/\\|X\\|^2$ is negative, so $\\hat\\theta_{\\mathrm{JS}}$ points away from $X$ through $\\mu_0$), and replacing it by $\\mu_0$ on that event reduces the squared error conditionally on $X$ whenever $\\theta^T X$ and the overshoot have the geometry implied by $\\theta$ - the standard argument (Baranchik 1964; Efron and Morris 1973) shows the positive-part rule has risk pointwise no larger and strictly smaller for every $\\theta$.   Let $h$ be a whole-plane GFF. Fix $\nu>0$ and $0 < \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 \leq \lambda_3 \leq \lambda_4 < \lambda_5$. Then there exists $\mathbbm{p} \in (0,1)$ such that the following is true.  Suppose that for each $z\in \mathbb{C},r>0$, we have events $E_r(z) \in \sigma(h)$ and additionally for any points $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z} ,  \text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w} \in \mathbb{C}$, and any simple path $\eta$ from $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z}$ to $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}$, we have events $\mathfrak{C}_r^{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w},\eta}(z) \in \sigma(h)$, satisfying, for a deterministic constant $\Lambda > 1$, the following properties.

\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item 
  For all $z \in \mathbb{C}$ and all $r >0$,  the event $E_r(z)$ is determined by $(h-h_{\lambda_5 r}(z))|_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}A}_{\lambda_1 r ,  \lambda_4 r}(z)}$,  and for all $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w} \in \mathbb{C}$,  the event $\mathfrak{C}_r^{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w},\eta}(z)$ is determined by $h|_{B_{\lambda_4 r}(z)}$ and the path $\eta$ stopped at the last time that it exits $B_{\lambda_4 r}(z)$.
\item 
For all $z \in \mathbb{C}$ and all $r >0$, we have $\mathbb{P}(E_r(z)) \geq \mathbbm{p}$.
\item 
For all points $z \in \mathbb{C},r >0$ and $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}$ satisfying $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}\notin B_{\lambda_4 r}(z)$, we have
\begin{align*}
\Lambda^{-1} \mathbb{P}(E_r(z) \cap \{\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}} \cap B_{\lambda_2 r}(z) \neq \emptyset\} \lvert h|_{\mathbb{C} \setminus B_{\lambda_3r}(z)}) \leq \mathbb{P}(\mathfrak{C}_r^{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w},\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}}}(z) \cap \{\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}} \cap B_{\lambda_2 r}(z) \neq \emptyset\} \lvert h|_{\mathbb{C} \setminus B_{\lambda_3r}(z)}).

\end{enumerate}

Under the above hypotheses, for all $q>0,  \ell \in (0,1)$,  and for each bounded open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$,  it holds with probability tending to $1$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$,  at a rate depending only on $U,q,\ell,\nu,  \{\lambda_i\}_{i=1,\cdots,5},  \Lambda$,  that for all $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w} \in (\varepsilon^q \mathbb{Z}^2) \cap U$ with $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}\notin \mathcal{B}_{\tau_{4\ell}(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})}^\bullet(\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z})$,  there exist $z \in \mathbb{C},  r \in [\varepsilon^{1+\nu} ,  \varepsilon]$ such that $\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}} \cap B_{\lambda_2 r}(z) \neq \emptyset$ and $\mathfrak{C}_r^{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w},\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}}}(z)$ occurs. [Defn 7 of arXiv:2605.25762, 'Brownian Convergence of Planar Domains and Stability of the Planar Skorokhod Embedding Pro'] Let $f$ be analytic on the unit disc $\mathbb{D}$ and $p>0$. The
$p$-th Hardy norm of $f$ is 
\begin{equation}
\Vert f\Vert_{\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})}:=\sup_{0\le r<1}\Big\{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int^{2\pi}_{0}\big|f(re^{i\theta})\big|^{p}\,d\theta\Big\}^{\frac{1}{p}}.
\end{equation}
The supremum is well-defined\cite{Rudin2001}. The Hardy space, denoted
by $\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})$, consists of analytic $f$ with $\Vert f\Vert_{\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})}<+\infty$.
A key fact of Hardy spaces is the boundary trace: if $\Vert f\Vert_{\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})}<+\infty$,
then the radial boundary values $f^{*}(e^{i\theta}):=\lim_{r\to1}f(re^{i\theta})$
exists a.e.\ on $\mathbb{S}$. Moreover 
\[
\|f^{*}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{S})}=\Vert f\Vert_{\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})}.
\]
When $p>1$, $\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})$ identifies with $L^{p}_{2\pi}$
in the following way: if $\xi\in L^{p}_{2\pi}$ then the map
\begin{equation}
\Psi(re^{\theta i})=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int^{2\pi}_{0}\frac{1+re^{(\theta-t)i}}{1-re^{(\theta-t)i}}\xi(t)dt
\end{equation}
belongs to $\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})$ and $\Re(\Psi^{*})=\xi$.
When $p=1$, $\Psi$ is analytic in the unit disc but not necessarily
an element of $\mathbf{H}^{1}(\mathbb{D})$. We recommend \cite{duren2000theory,butzer1971hilbert,king2009hilbert,mcgovern1980hilbert,pandey2011hilbert}
for a concise background on Hardy spaces as well as their connections
with the Hilbert transform. The following result illustrates a deep
connection between Hardy spaces and planar Brownian motion.

[Definition 1 of arXiv:2609.03495, 'Spectral Characteristics of Autoencoder Parameters as a Vector Representation of Data'] Let the sets of vectors ${\mathbf{X}_a \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}}$ and ${\mathbf{X}_b \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}}$ be given. Define mixing as the concatenation of vectors from $\mathbf{X}_a$ and $\mathbf{X}_b$ to obtain ${\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{a|b} \in \mathbb{R}^{(n + m) \times d}}$.

$\alpha$-mixing is defined as the concatenation of $\mathbf{X}_a$ and ${\lfloor\alpha m\rfloor, ~ \alpha \in [0; 1]}$ vectors from $\mathbf{X}_b$ to obtain ${\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{a|b} \in \mathbb{R}^{(n + \lfloor\alpha m\rfloor) \times d}}$.

Own-work C012 v1, proof (unaudited), novelty unestablished. Literal leaky ReLU phi(v)=max(v,lambda*v), 0<lambda<1, f=m^-1 sum_j a_j phi(w_j.x), both-layer simultaneous GD with actual step m*eta, average logistic loss L and G=average (1+exp(y_i*f_i))^-1. Finite data ||x_i||<=1, z_i=y_i*x_i, z_i.z_l>=kappa>0, rank>=2, and a unit u with u.z_i>=gamma>0. Suppose one neuron initially has a and every w.z_i nonzero of the same sign. Put c=lambda*sqrt(kappa), 0<eta<=c, h0=min(|a0|,min_i|w0.z_i|/sqrt(kappa)), B=h0^2/m, r0=||theta0||^2/m, zeta=2*eta*c/(1+eta*c)-eta^2>0. Then for every T>=1, sum_{t<T}G_t<=log((r0+4*eta*T)/B)/zeta. This follows by comparing r_T>=B*exp(2*eta*c*sum G/(1+eta*c)) from a persistent aligned neuron against r_T<=(r0+4*eta*T)*exp(eta^2*sum G), using the exact degree-two Euler identity. If Q_T=log((r0+4*eta*T)/B)/(zeta*T) and n*Q_T<1, some s<T satisfies L_s<=Q_T/(1-n*Q_T). Thus liminf loss is zero and best-iterate loss is O(log T/T); no last-iterate rate or permanent burn-in is claimed. For epsilon>0, q=zeta*epsilon/(1+n*epsilon), H=max(1,(r0+4*eta)/B), T=ceil(max(1,2*log(H)/q,4/q^2)) is a sufficient epsilon-hitting horizon. For iid coordinate N(0,sigma^2), define b=(gamma/sqrt(2*pi*d))^d exp(-(1+gamma/2)^2/2), p=2*exp(-2)*b/sqrt(2*pi). At width m>=log(2/delta)/p, with probability >=1-delta one can replace B by (sigma^2/m)*min(1,gamma^2/(4*kappa)) and r0 by 2*(d+1)*sigma^2/delta, uniformly in T and 0<eta<=c. This uses independent neuron initializations plus a union bound with the initial energy event, not independent trajectory events. Constants may be poor in dimension. Exact finite controls passed 9939 assertions but do not certify the full theorem; no independent audit or Lean certificate. The Euler identity is specific to positively homogeneous literal leaky ReLU; C011 smooth centered activations generally fail it. The remaining TARGET is permanent trained-output burn-in and arbitrary large steps.
Literal positively homogeneous leaky ReLU, mean-field scaling, actual GD step m*eta, no biases.
Strict signed-Gram positivity, normalized bounded data and rank>=2; one aligned neuron, or stated Gaussian sufficient-width event.
0<eta<=lambda*sqrt(kappa); best iterate and finite first entry only, not permanent burn-in.
Own unaudited work; novelty unestablished.

[Corollary cor:edgeprob of arXiv:2607.17764, 'Non-vanishing uniqueness threshold for\\hyperbolic Poisson-Voronoi percolation\\in dimensi'] There exist $K=K(d), c=c(d), \delta=\delta(d) > 0$ such that, 
for all $0<\lambda\leq 1$, all $0 < p \leq 1/2$, all $z, w \in \ensuremath{{\mathbb H}}^d$, all $n$ and all 
$z_1,\dots,z_n, w_1,\dots,w_n \in \ensuremath{{\mathbb H}}^d$ 
satisfying 

$$\mu\left( \ensuremath{B_{\text{Gab}}}(z,w) \cap \left( \bigcup_{i=1}^n \ensuremath{B_{\text{Gab}}}(z_i,w_i) \right) \right) < 
\delta \cdot \mu\left( \ensuremath{B_{\text{Gab}}}(z,w) \right), $$ 

\noindent
we have 

$$ \ensuremath{{\mathbb P}}_{p,\lambda}( E(z,w) | E(z_1,w_1) \cap \dots \cap E(z_n,w_n) ) \leq 
K \cdot \exp\left[ -c \cdot \lambda \cdot e^{\left(\frac{d-1}{2}\right)\cdot\dist(z,w)}\right]. $$

    Given any $0 < \sigma < 1$, let further $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ with CDFs $\Phi$ and $\Phi_\sigma$, respectively. Then for every $x \in \mathbb{R}, x \neq 0$, and assuming that $|1 - \sigma^2|$ is small enough (as a function of $x$), there are constants $c, C > 0$ independent on $\sigma$ (but dependent on $x$) such that
    $$
        c \ \mathrm{sgn}(x) \cdot (1 - \sigma^2) \le \Phi_\sigma(x) -  \Phi(x) \le C \ \mathrm{sgn}(x) \cdot (1 - \sigma^2).
    $$

body: Let (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}) be a probability space. A double sequence of random variables (X_{n, k})_{1 \le k \le k_n, n \ge 1} together with nested sub-\sigma-algebras \mathcal{F}_{n, 0} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{n, 1} \subseteq \dots \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{n, k_n} \subseteq \mathcal{F} is called a martingale difference array if for every n \ge 1 and every 1 \le k \le k_n: (1) X_{n, k} is \mathcal{F}_{n, k}-measurable; (2) \mathbb{E}[|X_{n, k}|] < \infty; and (3) \mathbb{E}[X_{n, k} \mid \mathcal{F}_{n, k-1}] = 0 almost surely.
title: Martingale Difference Array

[Lemma 68 of arXiv:2607.18104, '2607.18104'] Fix some $M,K\in \N$ and let  $n\in \N$. Assume that for all $i\in \lbr M\rbr$ and $\varepsilon>0$, we have some $\hfix^{\per,(i),\varepsilon}_0$ in $\UCp$ so that the associated particle configurations satisfy \eqref{eq:DominationAssumption} at time $0$, and such that the rescaled height functions $\hfix^{\textup{patch},n^{-1},\varepsilon}(\hfix^{\per,(i),\varepsilon}_0;\cdot,0)$ of the $(n^{-1},N)$-patched ASEP at time $0$ converge to $\hfix^{\per,(i)}_0 \colon \mathbb{T}\rightarrow \R$ as $\varepsilon \rightarrow 0$ with respect to the UC topology. 
Then there exist $c,C>0$, not depending on $n$ or $\varepsilon$,  such that for any $ t_1 <t_2<\dots<t_{K}$ in $\mathcal{T}$,
with probability $1-C \exp(-c n^{1/2})$, we find a coupling between $\hfix^{\textup{patch},n^{-1},\varepsilon}$ and $\hfixpa$ so that
\begin{equation}
  \max_{i \in \lbr M \rbr} \max_{\ell \in \lbr K \rbr}  \sup_{y\in \mathbb{T}} \left|\hfix^{\textup{patch},n^{-1},\varepsilon}(\mathfrak{h}^{\per,(i),\varepsilon}_0;y,t_\ell)- \hfixpa(\mathfrak{h}^{\per,(i)}_0;y,t_\ell) \right|   \leq (2n+1) 2^{-n}
\end{equation} for all $\varepsilon>0$ sufficiently small.
Here, the functions on the left-hand side are coupled according to the patched coupling $\Ppatch$ for the underlying ASEPs in the definition of the patched ASEPs, while the functions on the right-hand side are coupled as in Definition~\ref{def:PeriodicKPZfixed} with respect to the same patched directed landscape $\Lpa$, taking values in $\mathcal{T}$ for the time component.

body: [Theorem 3.2 of arXiv:1908.07093, 'Uniform Reliability of Self-Join-Free Conjunctive Queries'] Let Q be a CQ without self-joins. If Q is hierarchical, then UR(Q) is solvable in polynomial time. Otherwise, UR(Q) is #P-complete. As said above, the hardness side of Theorem 3.2 is essentially the statement that when Q is non-hierarchical, PQE(Q) is #P-hard even when every fact has the probability 1 2, and this is what we need to prove.
title: Theorem 3.2 of arXiv:1908.07093: Uniform Reliability of Self-Join-Free Conjunctive Queries

[Definition 14 (Interlacing \cite{Brouwer-Haemers}) of arXiv:2609.01114, 'Unbalanced spectral Tur\'an problem for color-critical graphs with prescribed large maximu'] Let $\theta_1\ge\cdots\ge\theta_n$ and
	$\eta_1\ge\cdots\ge\eta_m$ be real sequences with $m<n$.  We say that
	$(\eta_j)_{j=1}^m$ interlaces $(\theta_i)_{i=1}^n$ if
	\begin{equation*}
		\theta_i\ge\eta_i\ge\theta_{n-m+i}
		\quad
		\text{for all } i\in[m].
	\end{equation*}
	The interlacing is tight if there exists $k\in\{0,1,\dots,m\}$ such that
	$\eta_i=\theta_i$ for $i\le k$ and
	$\eta_i=\theta_{n-m+i}$ for $i>k$.
title: Interlacing \cite{Brouwer-Haemers}

body:
[Lem 12 of arXiv:2606.04636, 'A Thomson-type variational principle for diffusion coefficients'] For almost any $\omega\in\Omega$, $\omega(0)\neq\omega(1)$,
there exists a path $\omega_{1},\dots,\omega_{N}$, for $N=N(\omega)\in2\N$,
and a sequence of sites $x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1}$ in $[0,X(\omega)]$,
such that $\omega_{N}=\omega^{0,1}$, $\omega_{i+1}=\omega_{i}^{x_{i},x_{i}+1}\neq\omega_{i}$,
and $c(x_{i},x_{i+1};\omega_{i})=1$ for any $i\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$.
Moreover, the following properties are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x_{1},\dots,x_{N/2-1}$ are all in $[2,X(\omega)],$ $x_{N/2}=0$,
and $x_{i}=x_{N-i}$ for any $i\ge N/2+1$.
\item $\omega_{j}(0)-\omega_{j}(1)=\omega(0)-\omega(1)$ for $j\le N/2$
and $\omega_{j}(0)-\omega_{j}(1)=\omega(1)-\omega(0)$ for $j>N/2$.
\item For all $i\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$, $\omega_{i}(x)=\omega(x)$ if $x\notin[0,X(\omega)+1]$.
\item For all $i\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$, $X_{-}(\omega)=X_{-}(\omega_{i})$.
\item For all $i\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$, $X_{+}(\omega)\le\min\{x\ge x_{i}+4:\omega_{i}(x)=\omega_{i}(x+1)=0\}$.
\item Let $\eta\in\Omega$, and assume that there exists $i\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$
such that $\tau_{x_{i}}\eta=\omega_{i}$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $X_{-}(\omega)=X_{-}(\eta)+x_{i}$;
\item $X_{+}(\omega)\le X_{4}(\eta)+x_{i}\le X_{4}(\eta)-X_{-}(\eta)$.
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $\eta\in\Omega$, $x,x'\in\Z$, $\zeta=\pm1$. Then there is at
most one possible configuration $\omega$ and one possible $i\in\{1,\dots,N(\omega)\}$
such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x=x_{i}$ and $\eta=\eta_{i}$,
\item $X(\omega)=x'$, and
\item $\omega(0)-\omega(1)=\zeta$.
\end{enumerate}
\item For $\omega'=\omega^{0,1}$, the path $\omega'_{1},\dots,\omega_{N}'$
beginning with $\omega'$ is given by the reversed path $\omega'_{k}=\omega_{N-k}$;
and the associated sites $x_{1}',\dots,x_{N-1}'$ are the same as
$x_{N-1},\dots,x_{1}$, which are also the same as $x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1}$.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:dirty-evacuation of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix a fresh plane $i$ and let $\mathbb T_i$ be its coordinate circle.
Let
$\mathcal S_i(\mathbf X):V_{\rm in}\to V_{\rm out}$ be a complete
same-time physical supernode made from current deposits, their centered
pure-Weyl gates, normalized Brauer maps, and physical root/pass maps, with
all non-current pieces retained once as typed gaps
$X_j:V_j^-\to V_j^+$.  Put
\[
 \delta_iX_j=d\rho_{V_j^+}(a_i)X_j-X_jd\rho_{V_j^-}(a_i).
\]
Then the exact identity
\[
 \boxed{
 d\rho_{V_{\rm out}}(a_i)\mathcal S_i(\mathbf X)
 -\mathcal S_i(\mathbf X)d\rho_{V_{\rm in}}(a_i)
 =\sum_j\mathcal S_i(X_1,\ldots,\delta_iX_j,\ldots,X_g)}
\tag{3.3.1u}
\]
holds before the plane sum and before either replica is estimated.
Therefore a marked action entering the supernode exits at one named
external leg or gap, or vanishes at $a_i$ or after complete scalar
closure; it is never duplicated.  If it passes immediately through
$W_i^\circ$, it acquires the exact scalar
\[
 b_n=-\frac{n-3}{(n-1)(n-2)},
 \qquad
 A_iW_i^\circ=W_i^\circ A_i=b_nA_i.
\tag{3.3.1v}
\]
The identity is stable under every gap substitution allowed by
(lem:bridge-consequences of the paper).
