body: Every symmetric positive semidefinite kernel k on a set X is the reproducing kernel of a unique RKHS of functions on X: the space is built as the completion of finite linear combinations of the functions k(x, .) under the inner product determined by <k(x, .), k(y, .)> = k(x, y). Kernels and RKHSs are thus in one-to-one correspondence.
title: Moore-Aronszajn Theorem

body:
The load-bearing hypothesis in uniqueness for the Cauchy problem $u_t=\Delta u$ on $\mathbb R^n\times(0,T)$, $u(\cdot,0)=g$, is the growth bound $|u(x,t)|\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ with $A,a$ independent of $t$ (the Tychonoff class); smoothness of $u$ and continuity down to $t=0$ are not enough. Tychonoff's counterexample ($n=1$): let $g(t)=e^{-t^{-2}}$ for $t>0$, $g(0)=0$, and $u(x,t)=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{g^{(k)}(t)}{(2k)!}x^{2k}$. The Cauchy estimates for $g$ ($|g^{(k)}(t)|\le k!\,(\theta t)^{-k}e^{-\frac12t^{-2}}$ for some $\theta>0$) make the series converge locally uniformly together with all its derivatives, and termwise differentiation gives $u_{xx}=u_t$; $u$ is continuous on $\mathbb R\times[0,\infty)$ with $u(x,0)\equiv0$, yet $u\not\equiv0$. So the zero initial datum admits the two distinct solutions $0$ and $u$, and by the uniqueness theorem $u$ cannot satisfy any uniform bound $|u|\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ on a strip. Two corollaries an auditor should apply: (1) a solution of the heat equation is not determined by its initial data unless a class is specified -- 'the' solution of a Cauchy problem is meaningless without one; (2) the Tychonoff solution necessarily changes sign, because nonnegative solutions with zero initial data are unique by Widder's theorem, so one-sided bounds are an alternative (and weaker) substitute for the growth class. The class is essentially sharp: the counterexample family with $g(t)=e^{-t^{-\alpha}}$, $\alpha>1$, shows uniqueness fails as soon as growth $e^{a|x|^{2+\varepsilon}}$ is allowed, while $|u|\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ suffices.
The growth bound must be uniform in t on the time strip
Continuity at t = 0 and smoothness for t > 0 do not substitute for it
Nonnegativity (Widder) is an alternative hypothesis
title: Pitfall: Uniqueness for the Heat Cauchy Problem needs a growth condition (Tychonoff)

Let $(X, \mathcal{A}, \mu)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{B}, 
u)$ be $\sigma$-FINITE measure spaces and let $f: X	imes Y 	o [0, \infty]$ be measurable with respect to the product $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}$ (the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the measurable rectangles $A	imes B$). Then: (i) for every $x \in X$ the section $y \mapsto f(x,y)$ is $\mathcal{B}$-measurable and for every $y$ the section $x \mapsto f(x,y)$ is $\mathcal{A}$-measurable; (ii) the functions $x \mapsto \int_Y f(x,y)\,d
u(y)$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)$ (with values in $[0,\infty]$) are $\mathcal{A}$- resp. $\mathcal{B}$-measurable; (iii) $\int_{X	imes Y} f\,d(\mu	imes
u) = \int_X\Big(\int_Y f(x,y)\,d
u(y)\Big)d\mu(x) = \int_Y\Big(\int_X f(x,y)\,d\mu(x)\Big)d
u(y)$, all three possibly $= +\infty$, where $\mu	imes
u$ is the (unique, by $\sigma$-finiteness) product measure with $(\mu	imes
u)(A	imes B) = \mu(A)
u(B)$. Fubini's theorem is the companion for signed/complex $f$: if $f \in L^1(\mu	imes
u)$ - which by Tonelli applied to $|f|$ can be checked by ONE iterated integral of $|f|$ - then the sections are integrable for a.e. $x$ (resp. $y$), the partial integrals are integrable, and the three integrals agree as finite numbers. Sharp edges: (1) $\sigma$-finiteness cannot be dropped: $X = Y = [0,1]$, $\mu$ = Lebesgue, $
u$ = counting measure, $f = \mathbf{1}_{\{x = y\}}$ (measurable for the product $\sigma$-algebra since the diagonal is closed hence Borel); then $\int_X\int_Y f\,d
u\,d\mu = 1$ while $\int_Y\int_X f\,d\mu\,d
u = 0$; (2) nonnegativity (or integrability) cannot be dropped: $f(x,y) = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2$ on $(0,1)^2$ has iterated integrals $\pi/4$ and $-\pi/4$, and $f(x,y) = \mathbf{1}_{\{x = y\}} - \mathbf{1}_{\{x = y+1\}}$ on $\mathbb{N}	imes\mathbb{N}$ with counting measures has iterated sums $1$ and $0$ - in both $\int|f| = \infty$; (3) joint measurability cannot be dropped: assuming the continuum hypothesis there is a set $S \subset [0,1]^2$ (Sierpinski) with every vertical section countable and every horizontal section co-countable, so the iterated integrals of $\mathbf{1}_S$ are $0$ and $1$ - $S$ is not Lebesgue measurable in the plane; (4) for the COMPLETED product (Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ is the completion of $\mathcal{L}^m\otimes\mathcal{L}^n$) the sections are measurable only for a.e. $x$ and the partial integral is defined a.e.; the equalities in (iii) still hold with this proviso; (5) the theorem gives equality of the iterated integrals with the DOUBLE integral - the existence and equality of the two iterated integrals of a signed function does not by itself imply integrability (example (2) reversed: symmetrise to make both iterated integrals 0).
both measure spaces are sigma-finite
f is nonnegative (values in [0, infinity]) and measurable for the product sigma-algebra A (x) B
the product measure is the one determined by mu(A) nu(B) on rectangles (unique under sigma-finiteness)

There is no continuous retraction of the closed n-ball D^n onto its boundary sphere S^{n-1}; that is, no continuous r : D^n -> S^{n-1} with r(x) = x for all x in S^{n-1}. This is equivalent to Brouwer's fixed-point theorem.

Biane density-cube regularity. For any Borel probability measure mu on R and any t>0, let p_t be the continuous density of mu free-additive-convolved with the centered semicircle of variance t. At every x with p_t(x)>0, its ordinary derivative exists and |p_t(x)^2*p_t_prime(x)|<=1/(4*pi^3*t^2). Consequently the globally continuous function x maps to p_t(x)^3 is Lipschitz on R with Lipschitz constant at most 3/(4*pi^3*t^2). The derivative bound is sharp: for mu a point mass at zero, equality holds at x=plus or minus sqrt(2*t). Neither compact support nor an initial density or finite moment is assumed. The derivative is asserted only on the positive-density set; the global cube-Lipschitz conclusion uses continuity through the zero set. This is Biane1997 Proposition4 and its elementary global consequence, not an entropy-differentiability or matrix mutual-information theorem.
Arbitrary Borel probability measure mu on R; t>0 is the semicircular variance, not its standard deviation.

	$$\begin{array}{llll}
	u_0 = (0,0), & u_1 = (1,0), & u_2 = (1,1), & u_3 = (2,1),\\
	u_4 = (2,2), & u_5 = (1,2), & u_6 = (1,3), & u_7 = (0,3),\\
	u_8 = (0,2), & u_9 = (-1,2), &&
	\end{array}

body: In computational complexity theory, Savitch's theorem, proved by Walter Savitch in 1970, gives a relationship between deterministic and non-deterministic space complexity. It states that for any space-constructable function $f\in \Omega (\log(n))$, $${\mathsf {NSPACE}}\left(f\left(n\right)\right)\subseteq {\mathsf {DSPACE}}\left(f\left(n\right)^{2}\right).$$

\begin{itemize}
    \item If $\lambda_1 < n-M$, then $\widehat{\xi_M}(\lambda) = 0$.

body:
[Corollary cor:endpoint-acm-type-two of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $k\geq4$.  The lower bound in (equation eq:endpoint-local of the paper) already counts
distinct degree-$h$ Hilbert values of arithmetically Cohen--Macaulay
projective monomial curves in $\mathbb P^{k-1}$ of Cohen--Macaulay type two.
More precisely, for $t=k-4$ and with $\xi$ recording homological degree, the
witnesses have graded Betti polynomial
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 \mathcal B_{A_t}(\xi,z)
 ={}&\bigl(
  1+\xi(z^p+z^{q+s}+z^{r+s})
  +\xi^2(z^{p+s}+z^{q+r+s})
 \bigr)\\
 &\hspace{18mm}\cdot
 \prod_{i=1}^t(1+\xi z^{\ell_i}).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Writing $\beta_i(A_t)=\sum_j\beta^{A_t}_{i,j}$, their total Betti polynomial
depends only on $k$:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  \sum_{i=0}^{k-2}\beta_i(A_t)\xi^i
  &=\mathcal B_{A_t}(\xi,1)=(1+2\xi)(1+\xi)^{k-3},\\
  \beta_i(A_t)&=\binom{k-3}{i}+2\binom{k-3}{i-1}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here out-of-range binomial coefficients are zero.  In particular, the
homogeneous prime toric ideal $I_{A_t}$ has
\[
 \operatorname{ht}I_{A_t}=k-2,
 \qquad
 \mu(I_{A_t})=k-1=\operatorname{ht}I_{A_t}+1,
\]
so it is an almost complete intersection.  Thus the witnesses have ACM
coordinate rings of type two.  Their defining ideals are prime toric almost
complete intersections, all with the same total Betti format.  As
$h\to\infty$, they realize $h^{k-1+o_k(1)}$ distinct degree-$h$ Hilbert
values; at $k=4$, they realize a positive proportion of the ambient interval.
The internal degree shifts in
(equation eq:endpoint-betti-tower of the paper) vary with the parameters.
Their Hilbert numerator is obtained by setting $\xi=-1$ in
(equation eq:endpoint-betti-tower of the paper); equivalently,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{HS}_{R_{A_t}}(z)=
 \frac{
  (1-z^p-z^{q+s}-z^{r+s}+z^{p+s}+z^{q+r+s})
  \prod_{i=1}^t(1-z^{\ell_i})}
 {(1-z)^k}.
\end{equation}

For all integers n >= 0 and k >= 0, binom(n, k)^2 = sum_{j=0}^k c(k, j) binom(n, 2k - j), where c(k, j) = (2k - j)!/(j! ((k - j)!)^2) = binom(2k - j, j) binom(2k - 2j, k - j) and binom(n, r) = 0 for r > n. Hence E[binom(N, k)^2] = sum_{j=0}^k c(k, j) E[binom(N, 2k - j)] for any random variable N with values in the nonnegative integers.

body: [Theorem 1.1 (Main Theorem, Informal) of arXiv:2304.07612, 'A Cheeger Inequality for Small Set Expansion'] Let G = (V, E) be a finite, undirected, degree-regular graph, and δ, ǫ ∈ (0, 1/4). Suppose G is such that sets of density up to δ have expansion at least ǫ. Then, let V1−ǫ denote the direct sum of eigenspaces of G with eigenvalue at least 1 −ǫ. For any 2 ≤p ≤q ≤∞, the p →q norm of the eigenspace of G, ∥V1−ǫ∥p→q ≤ 1 √ δ. Our main theorem describes the “hard direction” (combinatorial to algebraic) of the equivalence.

[Thm theta-n-L1-nondegenerate of arXiv:2608.30847, 'An Almgren-type formula for planar $p$-harmonic functions'] Let $u$ be $p$-harmonic in $B_R(x_0)\subset \mathbb R^n$, $n\ge 3$, and assume
that $Du(x_0)=0$. Suppose that $u$ has a nondegenerate homogeneous tangent
$P$ of degree $\lambda>1$ at $x_0$, with rate $\delta>0$, in the sense of
Definition~(def:nondegenerate-homogeneous-tangent of the paper). Then, for all sufficiently
small $r>0$, $H(r)>0$, $N_\ast(r)$ is well-defined, and
$$
N_\ast(r)=\lambda+O(r^\delta).
$$
Moreover, $  \Theta(r)=O(r^{-1+\delta}). $
Consequently,
$  \Theta\in L^1(0,r_0) $
for some $r_0>0$, and the gauge-corrected frequency
$$  r\mapsto  \exp\left(\int_{r_0}^r \Theta(s)\,ds\right)N_\ast(r)
$$
is nondecreasing on $(0,r_0)$.

body:
Fix a finite Netsor program. Its inputs are fixed real vectors of fixed dimensions and independent matrix variables W of shape n by m with independent N(0,1/m) entries. Its only instructions are MatMul g=W h and coordinatewise NonLin h=phi(h_1,...,h_k), with matching dimensions; a matrix variable may be reused, but transposition is not an instruction. Let n_hidden be the program collection of dimensions internal to chains of matrix contractions, and n_output the output dimensions; input dimensions remain fixed. Fix one matrix variable W of shape n by m. Let F_(ell-1) be the sigma-algebra generated by all vector variables constructed before line ell. Stack the parent vectors previously multiplied by this W as columns of H, and their observed products W h as the corresponding columns of G. If line ell is g=W h, then h is F_(ell-1)-measurable and the conditional law of g given F_(ell-1) is Gaussian with mean G H^+ h and covariance [h^T(I_m-H H^+)h/m] I_n. Here H^+ is the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. H H^+ is the orthogonal projector onto the span of H, so R=I_m-H H^+ is a projector with operator norm at most one. If h lies in that span, the conditional covariance is zero and the product is determined by the previous products. Empty H,G give mean zero and covariance (|h|^2/m) I_n. The claim allows rank-deficient histories and causal reuse of W; it does not assert a formula for programs using W^T.

fixed input vectors; only causal Netsor MatMul and NonLin instructions
F_(ell-1) includes the full vector transcript before the new product

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Let $\mathcal B$ be a field of characteristic $0$. Let $\mathcal C$ be a $\mathcal B[G]$-module.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} We say that $\mathcal C$ is rational if it is definable over $\mathbb Q$, i.e., there exists a $\mathbb Q[G]$-module $\mathcal C_{\mathbb Q}$ whose extension $\mathcal C_{\mathbb Q}\otimes_{\mathbb Q} \mathcal B$ to $\mathcal B$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal C$.

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} Suppose that $\mathcal B$ contains a primitive $m$-th root of unity $\zeta_m$ (e.g., $\mathcal B$ contains $B_0$). We say that $\mathcal C$ is almost rational if it is definable over $\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)$, i.e., there exists a $\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)[G]$-module $\mathcal C_{\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)}$ whose extension $\mathcal C_{\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)}\otimes_{\mathbb Q(\zeta_m)} \mathcal B$ to $\mathcal B$ is isomorphic to $\mathcal C$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} A lift $\mathcal V$ of a $k[G]$-module $V$ to $R$ is called rational (resp.\ almost rational) if the $B[G]$-module $\mathcal V\otimes_R B$ is rational (resp.\ almost rational).

[Theorem thm:convbls2 of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] For $z_1, \dots, z_n \in D$ distinct points, and 
$\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n > 0$, let 
$D_{\varepsilon_1,\dots, \varepsilon_n}(z_1, \dots, z_n)$ be the 
$n+1$-connected domain 
$D \setminus \bigcup_{j = 1}^n \overline{\mathbb{D}(z_j,\varepsilon_j)}$. 
Let $\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}$ be the corresponding approximating metric graphs.

In these domains consider the Brownian loop soup 
$\mathcal{L}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\dots, \varepsilon_n}(z_1, \dots, z_n)}$ at the critical intensity, and the metric graph loop soup 
$\widetilde \mathcal{L}_{\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}}$, also at the critical intensity. 
Let 
$\widetilde \Xi^a_{\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}}$ denote the PPP of Brownian boundary to boundary excursions of intensity equal to $a \geq 0$ on the outer boundary and equal to $0$ on the inner boundaries on the metric graph 
$\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}$. 
We let $\Xi_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\dots, \varepsilon_n}(z_1, \dots, z_n)}^a$ denote the corresponding PPP of Brownian boundary to boundary excursions in the continuum.

Finally, let 
$(\widetilde C_k^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n, m})_{k \geq 1}$ 
be the clusters of 
$\widetilde \Xi^a_{\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}} 
\cup \widetilde \mathcal{L}_{\widetilde D^m_{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}}$, 
and $(C_k^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n})_{k \geq 1}$ the clusters of $\Xi_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\dots, \varepsilon_n}(z_1, \dots, z_n)}^a 
\cup \mathcal{L}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\dots, \varepsilon_n}(z_1, \dots, z_n)}$,  
listed say by the order of decreasing diameter. 
Let $\widetilde \gamma, \gamma$ denote closed paths on the metric graph and in the continuum respectively.

Then we have that the probabilities
$$\tilde p^{\rm mult}_{a,m} := \mathbb{P}\left(\nexists \widetilde C_i^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n, m}\text{ with }\widetilde \gamma \in \widetilde C_i^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n, m}\text{ such that} \sum_{j=1}^{n}
\indx_{\widetilde \gamma}(z_j)
\text{ odd}
\right),$$ 
converge, as $m \to \infty$, to 
$$p^{\rm mult}_a := \mathbb{P}\left(\nexists C_i^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}\text{ with }\gamma \in C_i^{\varepsilon_1, \dots, \varepsilon_n}\text{ such that} \sum_{j=1}^{n}
\indx_{\gamma}(z_j)
\text{ odd}\right).$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:oracle of arXiv:2608.30072, 'Learning Representations through Token Prediction: \\ Geometry, Approximation, and Downstr'] Suppose $\mathcal K$ has the form $\mathcal K(\Theta_j(X),E_v)=\exp\left(E_v^T\Theta_j(X)\right)$ and $\mathcal S_j(X)$ is the support of $p_j(X)$. Then, 
	$$
	\inf_{\Theta\in \mathcal R^L(\mathcal G, \mathcal R^0), E} \mathbb{E}_{X,j}\left[L\left(p_j(X);\hat{p}_{E}(\Theta_j(X))\right)\right]\le \inf_{\Theta^\ast,E^\ast}\left[\mathbb{E}_{X,j}\left[L\left(p_j(X);\hat{p}_{E^\ast}(\Theta^\ast_j(X))\right)\right]+\mathcal A(E^\ast,\Theta^\ast)\right],
	$$
	where the approximation error $\mathcal A(E^\ast,\Theta^\ast)$ is defined as
	$$
	\mathcal A(E^\ast,\Theta^\ast)=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{v\in\mathcal S_j(X),v'\in\mathcal V}\left\|E^\ast_v-E^\ast_{v'}\right\|^2\right]\inf_{\tilde{\Theta}\in \mathcal R^L(\mathcal G, \mathcal R^0) }\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\tilde{\Theta}_j(X)-\Theta^\ast_j(X)\right\|^2\right]}.
	$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 36 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(q\in Y^{\rm rv}\), choose a relatively compact holomorphic
coordinate neighbourhood \(U\Subset Y^{\rm rv}\), coordinates
\(a=(a^1,\ldots,a^m):U\to\C^m\) with \(a(q)=0\), and
\[
                         q\in U_0\Subset U_1\Subset U.
\]
Let \(\xi=(\mu_t)_{t<T}\) be a fixed limiting point based at \(q\),
and let \(\tau_i\searrow0\) realize a tangent space at \(\xi\), whose
time-\((-1)\) model is
\((Z,d,\cR,g,J,f,\mathfrak m)\).  On \(\pi^{-1}(U)\), set
\begin{equation}
                             F_i=\tau_i^{-1/2}a\circ\pi.
\end{equation}
Assume $(\mathrm S)_U$.  After passing to a further subsequence still
realizing the same tangent space, the maps $F_i$ converge
smoothly on every compact time-$(-1)$ regular chart to a holomorphic map
\begin{equation}
                              F:\cR\longrightarrow\C^m.
\end{equation}
The limit \(F\) has bounded differential and therefore extends uniquely
to a globally Lipschitz map \(F:Z\to\C^m\).  This extension is
holomorphic on the normal complex space \(Z\).

If $(\mathrm Q)_U$ also holds, then on $\cR$
\begin{equation}
 cI_m\le
 \left[\langle dF^\alpha,d\overline{F^\beta}\rangle_{g^{-1}}
 \right]_{\alpha,\beta=1}^m
 \le CI_m.
\end{equation}

[Proposition prop:randomcluster-Ising of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected graph. Let $\Omega:=\{0,1\}^E$ be the space of bond configurations and $\Sigma:=\{-1,+1\}^V$ be the space of spin configurations. Define $f:\Omega\to 2^{\Sigma}$ by 
$
      f(\omega) = \{ \sigma \in \Sigma \mid \omega_e = 0, \forall e \not \in S(\sigma) \}.
$ 
For any $A\subset V$ with $|A|$ even, let
	\[\rho[\omega] \propto 1\! \!1[\omega\in\mathcal{F}_A]\mathbb{P}_p[\omega],~\forall \omega\in\Omega,~\gamma[\sigma]\propto 1, ~\forall \sigma\in \Sigma,\]
    where $p=(1-e^{-2J_e})_{e\in E}$.
	Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(a)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$ is $\mu^A$ defined by
		$\mu^A[\sigma] \propto \mu[\sigma] \mathbb{P}_{S(\sigma),p}[\mathcal{F}_A].$
		 For each $\omega\in\Omega$ with $\omega\in\mathcal{F}_A$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega]$ on $\Sigma$ is realized by tossing independent fair coins to get $\pm$ for each open cluster.
		\item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$ is $\phi_p[\;\cdot \mid \mathcal{F}_A]$.  For each $\sigma\in\Sigma$ with $S(\sigma)\in\mathcal{F}_A$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \sigma]$ on $\Omega$ is the independent Bernoulli percolation on $S(\sigma)$ with parameter $p$ conditioned on $\mathcal{F}_A$,  $\mathbb{P}_{S(\sigma),p}[\;\cdot \mid \mathcal{F}_A]$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

    there exists $U : [0,1] \times \T^d \to \R^d$ with decomposition $U = \sum_{j=0}^\infty u^j$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)]  $U = \sum_{j=0}^\infty u^j$ satisfies Assumption~\ref{asmp:main for refreshing} for $\beta,d$.
        \item[(ii)] For all $n \in \N, \ep>0$, there exists $K(d,n,\alpha,\beta,\ep)>0$ such that for all $j \in \N, p \geq 1$,
        \[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega \continuous^0_{t,x}} \leq K \sqrt{p}2^{(n-\alpha+\ep)j}.\]
        \item[(iii)] For all $j \in \N, \nabla \cdot u^j =0.$
    \end{enumerate}
    However, 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item  For all $y \in \T^d$ and $h\in (0,1]$,
        \[\P\big(\text{\eqref{eq:main refreshing ODE 0} has a unique solution on } [0,h]\big) = 0.\]
        Further, for all $y \in \T^d$ and for all $\ep>0$ sufficiently small, almost surely in $U$, 
        \[\limsup_{t\to 0} t^{-\frac{1}{2 -2\alpha - \beta -\ep}} \mathrm{diam}\{X_t : X \text{ is a solution to~\eqref{eq:main refreshing ODE 0}}\} = \infty.\]
        \item 
        
        Almost surely, $U$ admits nonunique bounded solutions on $[0,1]$ to~\eqref{eq:continuity} for some bounded initial data.

The following is an archival copy of the reviewed v1 text. Its old draft/status and scoring labels are historical; the scope and status above govern this v2 edition.

## Reviewed v1 proof text

# Linear hardness with bounded covariance condition number

Status: proof (unaudited). Target 2, endpoint-qualified result.
The hardest step is transferring the distributional score guarantee under
contamination; its complete argument is in clipped_oracle_transfer.md.

## Precise model and conclusion

Fix a polynomial per-round query budget P(d) and inverse-polynomial
0<e(d)<=1. The oracle is a fixed jointly measurable field satisfying
E_{Q*Gaussian(sigma^2 I)}||f_sigma-s_{Q,sigma}||^2<=e^2/sigma^2
for EVERY sigma>0. Queries may use arbitrary points and positive noise
levels, and the algorithm has no hidden-instance information beyond the
oracle and public parameters. No pointwise-error or Lipschitz promise is
imposed. The result below does not assert an absolute error bound uniform
over sigma.

There is a family Q^theta in R^d with E||Y||^2<=2 and
kappa(Cov(Q^theta))<=3, with such legal fixed oracles, so every randomized
algorithm using fewer than d adaptive rounds has TV error at least
0.9-eta on at least 0.9 of the hidden instances. Here
B=4(d+1)/e and eta=e^2/[4(B+d)^2]. Thus eta is inverse polynomial,
eta<=1/(2d), and eta<1/4 (indeed <=1/324 for d>=1).

The same lower bound, less 1/200, holds for sampling the Gaussian-smoothed
law Q^theta*Gaussian(tau^2 I) whenever 0<tau<=h_d/(100d).
This is exponentially fine smoothing, with
log(1/tau)=O(d log q + log(Md)) for tau chosen at the displayed boundary.
For these smoothed laws the second moment is at most 3 and condition
number at most 3. This is NOT a fixed-smoothing dimensional lower bound.

## Construction and proof

1. Invoke Kou--Wang, arXiv:2610.09166v1, Theorem 4.1, with original
score tolerance e0=e/4 and query budget P(d). Their fixed public box
parameters (Appendix B.1, (61)--(62)) are
M=ceil(100(dP+1)), q=100Md/e0, a_i=q^{-(i-1)}/4,
h_i=a_i/(100M), and centers a_i+(k-1/2)a_i/M. Write P^theta for the
uniform box law and a^theta for their fixed legal oracle.

The supplied theorem says: for every randomized algorithm using fewer
than d rounds, TV(output,P^theta)>=0.9 on a set of theta of probability
at least 0.9. Public parameters and oracles are independent of the sampler.
This theorem is used as settled ground, not re-proved.

2. Their Lemma B.1 gives support in the unit ball and
Cov(P^theta)=diag(h_i^2/3). In particular
||Cov(P^theta)||op=h_1^2/3=1/(480000 M^2)<=1/d,
since M>=100d for integer P>=1. Let H=N(0,I/(eta d)), public and
independent of theta, and Q^theta=(1-eta)P^theta+eta H.

Writing mu=E P^theta and Sigma=Cov(P^theta), the covariance identity is
Cov(Q^theta)=I/d+(1-eta)Sigma+eta(1-eta)mu mu^T.
It follows in quadratic form order that I/d<=Cov(Q^theta)<=3I/d.
Also E_Q||Y||^2=(1-eta)E_P||Y||^2+1<=2.

3. Supply f^theta_sigma=projection_{ball(B/sigma)} a^theta_sigma.
The clipping-transfer lemma gives score error at most e^2/(2sigma^2),
hence the requested e^2/sigma^2 guarantee. All parameters are public,
and f is fixed and jointly measurable. A batch of queries to f is
simulated by exactly the same batch to a, then deterministic clipping.
No extra information, extra adaptive round, or hidden density is used.

4. Given any sampler for Q using f, simulate it using a as just described.
Its output law L^theta is exactly the same. Theorem 4.1 gives
TV(L^theta,P^theta)>=0.9 on at least 0.9 of theta. As
TV(P^theta,Q^theta)<=eta, triangle inequality yields
TV(L^theta,Q^theta)>=0.9-eta there. This proves the unsmoothed conclusion.
For sequential samplers, at least d rounds implies at least d queries.

5. For a one-dimensional uniform law U on an interval of half-width h,
TV(U,U+z)=min(1,|z|/(2h)). Convexity under mixtures gives
TV(U,U+tau Z)<=tau E|Z|/(2h)<=tau/(2h).
For products, the telescoping product bound (or independent coupling)
gives TV(P^theta,P^theta*Gaussian(tau^2 I))
<=sum_i tau/(2h_i)<=d*tau/(2h_d)<=1/200.
This uses no false multiplication of conditional query probabilities.
Therefore TV(Q^theta*Gaussian(tau^2 I),P^theta)<=eta+1/200.
The same simulated output lower bound is now 0.9-eta-1/200.
Adding tau^2 I to a positive covariance can only reduce its condition
number, and the second moment increases by d*tau^2<=1.

6. If one treats R^theta=Q^theta*Gaussian(tau^2 I) as the base target,
its legal oracle at additional noise sigma is f^theta_{sqrt(tau^2+sigma^2)}.
Its squared error is at most e^2/[2(tau^2+sigma^2)]<=e^2/sigma^2.
Again one original query suffices. Thus the construction also yields
smooth positive densities, with intrinsic smoothing tau exponentially small.

7. For the OU convention X_t=e^{-t}Y+sqrt(1-e^{-2t})Z, set
sigma=sqrt(e^{2t}-1). Its score is
e^t s_{Q,sigma}(e^t x), and the corresponding oracle is
e^t f_sigma(e^t x). Its error bound is e^2/(1-e^{-2t}).
To target the OU endpoint at time t, rescale the sampler's output by e^t.
The Gaussian endpoint argument applies when sqrt(e^{2t}-1)<=h_d/(100d).
Any stronger OU error normalization requires an additional argument.

## What this moves, and what remains open

Covariance conditioning alone does not prevent the linear box mechanism:
rare public mass repairs it while clipped approximate oracles preserve
hardness. The targets are neither log-concave nor uniform convex-body laws;
this does not answer the source paper's near-isotropic convex-body question.
Their fourth moments grow as eta decreases; bounded second moment is the
only tail assumption used here.

The fixed or inverse-polynomial smoothing endpoint is the unpaid step.
The box coordinates below that smoothing scale can be discarded in TV,
so this construction does not close T306's dimension exponent at that
endpoint. It is a complete lower bound for unsmoothed targets and for the
explicit fine endpoint above. The reviewer must decide how Target 2's
unstated endpoint dependence should be scored; the row must not be closed
on the strength of this qualified result.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:02ed4e3e9471762e0c7b668ebd062aacf59e2c7858ef371bcde0c00af522059d","revision_digest":"sha256:2e56818e86f2f7ad5ae3c3fb468643d4d7ae566a5992507c769ae33bb5e065ac","source_id":"owner-own-work:w720-T306-C03","source_revision":"C03 v2; scope-only clarification, proof (unaudited); v1 PASS by claude-5693aca3; 2026-10-20","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Definition 10 of arXiv:2608.26084, 'Localic Esakia Duality\\via Conic Frames'] The \emph{source} and \emph{target maps} of a localic relation $r\colon R\rightarrowtail X\times X$ are defined as the maps $s,t\colon R\to X$ given by $s:=\pr_1\circ r$ and $t:=\pr_2\circ r$, where~$\pr_i\colon X\times X\to X$ are the product projections. For~$U,V\in \Opens X$ we get in particular that~(\cref{lemma:coproduct structure}):
	\begin{gather*}
		r^{-1}(U\tensor V) = s^{-1}(U)\wedge t^{-1}(V),\\
		s^{-1}(U) = r^{-1}(U\tensor \top)
		\qquad\text{and}\qquad
		t^{-1}(V) = r^{-1}(\top\tensor V).
	\end{gather*}

Write h_2(a)=-a log_2 a-(1-a)log_2(1-a), with endpoint values zero. The global Fourier entropy-influence conjecture asks for one finite absolute C with H(f)<=C sum_i I_i(f) for every Boolean f in every dimension; none of the accompanying local drafts asserts that conjecture is proved.

[Proposition 5 (Minimization over equivariant fields) of arXiv:2608.26961, 'Gromov--Monge Flow Matching for Equivariant Graph Generation'] Let $\pi\in\mathrm{c}_{\R^D}(\mu,\nu)$ be arbitrary. Then the
field $v^{\pi^G}$ associated with $\pi^G$ minimizes $J_\pi$ over all
$G$-equivariant fields:
\[
v^{\pi^G}\in
\argmin_{\substack{v:I\times\R^D\to\R^D\ \mathrm{jointly\ Borel}\\
v_t(gx)=gv_t(x)\ \forall\,t,g,x}}
J_\pi(v).
\]
In particular, the constrained problem is the ordinary
flow-matching problem for the diagonally symmetrized coupling $\pi^G$.

[Lemma lem:h_inverse of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] The characteristic sub-gamma function $h(u) = 1 + u - \sqrt{1+2u}$ 
is a strictly increasing
function from $[0,\infty)$ onto $[0,\infty)$ with inverse
\begin{align}
  h^{-1}(v) = v + \sqrt{2v},
  \qquad 
  v\geq 0.
  
\end{align}
Consequently, for any $v \geq 0$,
$h(u) \geq v$ if and only if $u \geq v + \sqrt{2v}$.

body: Let (M,g) be a complete Riemannian manifold of dimension n with Ricci curvature Ric >= (n-1) K for a constant K, and let M_K be the complete simply connected model space of constant sectional curvature K. For p in M, let V(p,r) be the volume of the geodesic ball of radius r about p, and V_K(r) the volume of a radius-r ball in M_K. The Bishop-Gromov inequality states that the ratio V(p,r)/V_K(r) is a nonincreasing function of r > 0 (if K > 0, for 0 < r <= pi/sqrt(K), the diameter of M_K, which by Bonnet-Myers also bounds the diameter of M), with limit 1 as r -> 0; consequently V(p,r) <= V_K(r) for every such r. Due to Richard Bishop and Mikhail Gromov.
title: Bishop-Gromov inequality

body:
[Theorem thm:mPAM of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] For each $\epsilon>0$, we take $d_\epsilon>0$, such that $d_\epsilon\epsilon^{1/2}|\log(\epsilon)|\to 0$ as $\epsilon\to 0$.
Then consider the following function defined on $\mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$:
\begin{equation}   
\mathcal{M}^{\rho,\epsilon}(x, s; y, t):= -\epsilon^{1/2}H_{d_\epsilon}^-(\lfloor 2\epsilon^{-1}x \rfloor, 2\epsilon^{-3/2}s;  \lfloor 2\epsilon^{-1}y \rfloor, 2\epsilon^{-3/2}t) + \epsilon^{-1}(t-s),
\end{equation}
where either (1) fixed $\alpha\ge \frac{1}{2}$ and $\rho=-\infty$, or (2) $\alpha = \frac{1}{2}-\rho\epsilon^{1/2}/2$ for some $\rho\in\mathbb{R}$.
Then as $\epsilon\to 0$, the above function converges to $\mathcal{L}^\rho$, weakly under the uniform-on-compact topology.

[Proposition 11 of arXiv:2608.27156, 'Traveling Waves in Equity Markets with\\Rank-Based Entry and Exit'] In the setting of Theorem~\ref{thm:wave}, let $\alpha$ be the tail exponent \eqref{eq:alpha-main} of Corollary~\ref{cor:tail}, and let $0 \leq p < \alpha$. Then
\begin{equation}
    G^p \;=\; c \;+\; (1 - p)\, G^p_* \;+\; \Big\langle \frac{\tilde f}{g},\, \bar\Pi^p \Big\rangle \;-\; \big\langle \lambda_d,\, \bar\Pi^p \big\rangle,
    \qquad
    G^p_* \;:=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\, \langle \sigma^2, \bar\Pi^p \rangle,
\end{equation}
where $G^p_*$ is the portfolio's excess growth rate. With $\tilde f = 0$ this is the reduction formula of \cite[Proposition 5.5]{jourdain_capital_2015}.

body: [Cor prop:implication of arXiv:2605.10908, 'On Talagrand's Convexity Conjecture'] Suppose that for any $n\geq 1$, any random vector in $\mathbb{R}^n$ which is dominated in convex order by a standard Gaussian random vector is the sum of three standard Gaussian vectors. Let $b, c \in (0, 1)$ satisfy $2b +c \leq 1$. Then for any closed set $A \subset \mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $\gamma_{n}(A) > \frac{5}{6}$, the set $b^{-1}(A+A+A)$ contains a symmetric convex body $K$ with $\gamma_{n}(K) \geq c$.

body:
[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $P$ be the transition matrix of a reversible Markov chain; That is, $P$ satisfies,
   \[\pi(x) P(x,y) = \pi(y)P(y,x),\quad \forall x,y\in \Omega\]
   where $\pi$ is the stationary distribution. Then,
   \[\langle Pf,g\rangle_\pi = \langle f,Pg\rangle_\pi,\quad \forall f,g \in \mathbb{R}^\Omega\]
   \begin{proof}
     \begin{align*}
      \langle Pf, g\rangle_\pi &= \sum_{x\in \Omega}(Pf)(x)g(x)\pi(x)\\
      &= \sum_{x\in \Omega}\sum_{y\in \Omega}P(x,y)f(y)g(x)\pi(x)\\
      &= \sum_{x\in \Omega}\sum_{y\in \Omega}P(x,y)f(y)g(x)\pi(x)\\
      &= \sum_{y\in \Omega}\sum_{x\in \Omega}P(y,x)g(x)f(y)\pi(y)\tag{By reversibility}\\
      &= \sum_{y\in \Omega}(Pg)(y)f(y)\pi(y)\\
      &=  \langle f, Pg\rangle_\pi
     \end{align*} 
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Maintheorem 3 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] There is a probability law \(\mu_H\) on
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal Y
  :=\mathbb R_+^2\times C_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R_+)^2
  
\end{equation}
equipped with its product topology, with local uniform convergence in each
path coordinate,
such that
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal L_{\widehat{\PP}_a}
  (U_a,V_a,\overline L_a,\overline R_a)
  \Longrightarrow \mu_H.
  
\end{equation}
Let \((U,V,\overline L,R)\) denote the coordinate random element under
\(\mu_H\).
The left horizon \(U\) is finite almost surely, whereas \(R\) is defined on
the whole half-line.  The path \(\overline L\) is constant on
\([U,\infty)\) almost surely.  Write \(L\) for the restriction of the
constant-extended path \(\overline L\) to \([0,U]\).  Moreover,
\begin{equation}
  J_\infty
  :=\int_0^Ue^{-L(s)}\,\mathrm ds
    +\int_0^\infty e^{-R(s)}\,\mathrm ds
  
\end{equation}
satisfies \(0<J_\infty<\infty\) almost surely and
\begin{equation}
  J_a\Longrightarrow J_\infty,
  \qquad
  \widehat{\EE}_a[J_a^{-1}]
  \longrightarrow
  D_H:=\EE_{\mu_H}[J_\infty^{-1}]\in(0,\infty).
  
\end{equation}
Finally, the persistence probability satisfies
\begin{equation}
  \lim_{T\to\infty}{T^{1-H}}{\PP\bigl(B_t\leq1\text{ for every }0\leq t\leq T\bigr)} = \mathsf C_H,
  
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
  \mathsf C_H
  =\frac{H\,\EE[M]}{\Gamma(1/H)D_H}.
  
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Maintheorem 1 (Stationary product limit and avalanche sharpness) of arXiv:2608.10992, '2608.10992'] For each $\gamma\in\{\mathrm{os},\mathrm{iso}\}$,
\[
        t_{\mathrm d}^\gamma
        =t_{\mathrm{sus}}^\gamma
        =t_\infty^\gamma
        =:t_c^\gamma.
\]

The critical values satisfy
\[
        1\leq t_c^{\mathrm{os}}\leq2\log2,
        \qquad
        \frac13\leq t_c^{\mathrm{iso}}
        \leq t_c^{\mathrm{os}}.
\]
Moreover, for every fixed collection of distinct sites
$x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\in\mathbb Z$, viewed as elements of $\Lambda_N$ for sufficiently large $N$,
\[
        \bigl(
        F_{N,x_1}^\gamma,\ldots,F_{N,x_\ell}^\gamma
        \bigr)
        \xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{\mathrm d}
        \nu_{t_c^\gamma}^{\otimes\ell}.
\]
Equivalently, in the original uniform parametrisation, the limiting
fitnesses are independent and uniform on $[q_c^\gamma,1]$, where
$q_c^\gamma:=1-e^{-t_c^\gamma}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Stationary product limit and avalanche sharpness

[Lem 100 (comparison of Fokker--Planck equations) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let
$\hvY(t) = \vY(t-\sss)+\xxx$
where $(\sss,\xxx)\sim\varphi$.
Let $\hvX$ be the SDE solution from Definition~\ref{d:intro.SDE.coefs}.
Assume the coefficients $B^i$ and $\Sigma^{ij}$ of \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv} are bounded and Lipschitz. Then the processes $\hvX$ and $\hvY$ satisfy the same Fokker--Planck equations. Consequently, for each fixed $t$, the marginal law of $\hvX(t)$ agrees with the marginal law of\/ $\hvY(t)$.

\begin{proof}
Abbreviate $\rho\equiv\rho_{\vY}$ for the occupation density of $\vY$, and recall from Lemma~\ref{l:ideal.smoothed.occ.msr} that $\hvY$ has occupation density $\nu\equiv\rho_{\vY}*\varphi$.
Let $\mu$ denote the occupation density of $\hvX$.
 Let $f:\R^d\to\R$ be a smooth compactly supported test function. 
\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{Fokker--Planck equations for $\hvY(t) = \vY(t-\sss)+\xxx$.} We will calculate
	\[
	\bE\Big[ f(\vY(T))-f(\vY(0))\Big]
	= \int_{s,x} \varphi(s,x)
	\bE\Big[ f(Y(T-s)+x)
	-f(Y(-s)+x)\Big]
	\,ds\,dx
	=\textup{(dr)}+\textup{(qv)}
	\]
where $\textup{(dr)}$
and $\textup{(qv)}$
denote the contributions from the drift and covariation respectively:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(dr)}
	&= \sum_{i=1}^d \textup{(dr)}^i
	= \sum_{i=1}^d
	\int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{-s}^{T-s}
	\partial_i f(Y(t)+x)\,dD^i(t)
	\,ds\,dx \,,\\
	\textup{(qv)}
	&= \sum_{i,j=1}^d \textup{(qv)}^{ij}
	= \frac12
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{-s}^{T-s}
	\partial_i\partial_j
	f(Y(t)+x)\,dQ^{ij}(t)
	\,ds\,dx\,.
	\end{align*}
Abbreviate $I_T(s)\equiv \ind\{s\in[0,T]\}$. The above can be further simplified as follows:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(dr)}^i
	&= \int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{t,y} I_T(t+s)
	\partial_i f(y+x)
	\,\rho_{D^i}(dt\,dy)\,ds\,dx \\
	&=
	\int_{s',x'}
	I_T(s')\partial_i f(x')
	\bigg\{\int_{t,y} 
	\varphi(s'-t,x'-y)
	\,\rho_{D^i}(dt\,dy)
	\bigg\}\,ds'\,dx'\\
	&=
	\int_{t,y}
	I_T(t)\partial_i f(y)
	\frac{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi(t,y)}
	{\rho*\varphi(t,y)}
	\nu(dt\,dy)\,,
	\end{align*}
recalling at the last step that $\nu=\rho*\varphi$ is the occupation density of $\hvY$.\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{Fokker--Planck equations for SDE solution $\hvX$.}
 If $f:\R^d\to\R$ is a smooth compactly supported test function, define
	\[
	L_t f(x)
	= \sum_{i=1}^d
	B^i(t,x)
	\partial_i f(x)
	+\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	A^{ij}(t,x)
	\partial_i\partial_j f(x)
	\]
Then, by It\=o's formula, the process
	\[
	N(t)
	= f(\hvX(t))-f(\hvX(0)) - \int_0^t L_s f(\hvX(s))\,ds
	\]
is a local martingale. Since we assumed the coefficients are bounded, we can conclude that $N$ is a true martingale, and the optional stopping theorem gives
	\[
	\bE\Big[ f(\hvX(T))-f(\hvX(0))\Big]
	= \bE \int_0^T L_t f(\hvX(s))\,ds
	= \textup{(Dr)}+\textup{(QV)}\,,
	\]
where $\textup{(Dr)}$ and $\textup{(QV)}$ denote the contributions from the drift and covariation respectively:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(Dr)}
	&= \sum_{i=1}^d \textup{(Dr)}^i
	=\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bE \int_0^T \partial_i f(\hvX(t))
	B^i(t,\hvX(t))\,dt\,,\\
	\textup{(QV)}
	&= \sum_{i,j=1}^d \textup{(QV)}^{ij}
	=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bE \int_0^T 
	\partial_i\partial_j f(\hvX(t))
	A^{ij}(t,\hvX(t))\,dt\,.
	\end{align*}
Again abbreviate $I_T(s)\equiv \ind\{s\in[0,T]\}$. The above can be further simplified as
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(Dr)}^i
	&= \int I_T(t)
	\partial_i f(y) 
	\frac{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi(t,x)}
		{\rho*\varphi(t,x)}
	\mu(dt\,dy)\,,\\
	\textup{(QV)}^{ij}
	&= \int I_T(t)
	\partial_i\partial_j f(y) 
	\frac{\rho_{Q^{ij}}*\varphi(t,x)}
		{\rho*\varphi(t,x)}
	\mu(dt\,dy)
	\end{align*}
recalling that $\mu$ is the occupation density of $\hvX$, and using the definitions \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv} of $B^i$ and $A^{ij}$.

Comparing the expressions for $\hvX$ and $\hvY$ shows that $\mu$ and $\nu$ satisfy the same Fokker--Planck equations. We now apply \cite[Lem.~2.3]{MR2375067}: this is a general result applying to $\R^d$-valued stochastic differential equations
such as \eqref{e:abstract.sde}, with a given law fo (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $n,k,d\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge k$, and $d\ge2$. There exists a constant
$C(k,d,n)>0$, depending only on $k,d,n$, such that, for every isotropic
log-concave measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^n$, every
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\in\mathcal P_d(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^k)$, and every
$\psi\in C_0^\infty(\mathbb R^k)$ with $0\le \psi\le1$, one has
\[
\biggl(\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Delta_f\,d\mu\biggr)^{\frac{1}{2(k(d-1)+1)}}
\biggl(\int_{\mathbb R^n}\psi(f)\,d\mu\biggr)
\le
C(k,d,n)
\|\psi\|_{L^1(\mathbb R^k)}^{\frac{1}{k(d-1)+1}}.
\]

Let eta be a probability measure on [0,R], R>0, with a Lebesgue density
bounded by C<infinity. Necessarily C>0. Let F be its distribution function,
and for n>=2 set x_i=F^(-1)((i-1/2)/n), 1<=i<=n, with the left quantile
convention. Put

    V_n(x)=n^(-2) sum_(i<j) log|x_j^2-x_i^2|,
    nu=(eta+reflection(eta))/2,
    Sigma(nu)=integral integral log|u-v| nu(du)nu(dv).

The conclusions are:

1. x_i>0, x_j-x_i >= (j-i)/(Cn), and x_i>=(i-1/2)/(Cn).
2. For every 0<d<1,

   n^(-2) sum_(i<j: x_j-x_i<d) log(1/(x_j-x_i))
       <= C*d*(1+log(1/d)).                           (1)

3. V_n(x)->Sigma(nu), a finite number.
4. Let delta_n=1/(4Cn^3). Every y with |y_i-x_i|<=delta_n is positive
   and increasing, and

   product_(i<j)(y_j^2-y_i^2)
     >= (1-1/(2n^2))^(n(n-1)) product_(i<j)(x_j^2-x_i^2),
   V_n(y) >= V_n(x)-1/n^2.                            (2)

   The corresponding product box has volume (1/(2Cn^3))^n, whose
   logarithm divided by n^2 tends to zero.
5. For any positive profiles z^(n) in a fixed [0,R'] with empirical

       limsup_n V_n(z^(n)) <= Sigma(nu).              (3)

   Coincident coordinates give V_n=-infinity and do not cause an exception.

## Proof of spacing and the uniform logarithmic tail

Absolute continuity makes F continuous, and F(x_i)=(i-1/2)/n, including
when F has flat intervals. The density bound gives
F(v)-F(u)<=C(v-u). Apply this to two quantiles and to zero and x_i to get
conclusion 1. The empirical quantile laws converge weakly to eta; bounded
support also gives convergence of all bounded continuous kernels below.

Write k=j-i. If x_j-x_i<d, then k<Cnd and
log(1/(x_j-x_i))<=log(Cn/k). There are at most n pairs for each k. Let
K=min(n-1,floor(Cnd)); including an endpoint pair only increases this
upper bound. If K=0 the sum is empty. Otherwise

    left side of (1) <= (1/n) sum_(k=1)^K log(Cn/k)
      <= (1/n) integral_0^K log(Cn/u) du
      = (K/n)[1+log(Cn/K)].

The integral is finite at zero, and the sum bound uses a decreasing
integrand on each unit interval. Put a=K/(Cn). Since 0<a<=d<1, the function
a*(1+log(1/a)) is increasing on (0,1]. This proves (1).

For the second logarithm, x_i+x_j>=x_j-x_i>0. Thus the analogous negative
log tail for x_i+x_j<d is bounded by the same right side of (1). This also
handles quantiles approaching zero; no hard-edge gap is assumed.

## Convergence of the energy, with the cutoff paid

For a fixed d>0, the kernels log(max(|u-v|,d)) and
log(max(u+v,d)) are bounded continuous on [0,R]^2. Their double empirical
integrals converge to the corresponding double eta integrals. The
diagonal terms are bounded by a constant depending on d,R divided by n,
so half of each double empirical sum equals its i<j sum up to o(1).

Replacing the truncated pair logs by the true logs changes the normalized
sums by at most C*d*(1+log(1/d)) for each kernel, by (1). The continuum
negative log tails tend to zero too: the bounded density gives uniform
local integrability of log|u-v|, while log(u+v)>=log|u-v| controls the
other negative tail. Positive parts are bounded on the compact square.
Take n->infinity first, then d->0. This proves

    V_n(x)->(1/2) integral integral
           [log|u-v|+log(u+v)] eta(du)eta(dv).

For u,v>=0 off the null singular set, |u^2-v^2|=|u-v|(u+v).
Expanding the four quadrants of the symmetrization shows that the last
display equals Sigma(nu). All involved logs are integrable, so these
identities are not a cancellation of undefined infinities.

## Stability throughout the boxes

If |y_i-x_i|<=delta_n, each positive difference x_j-x_i and each sum
x_i+x_j changes by at most 2delta_n. Conclusion 1 bounds each of these
original quantities below by 1/(Cn). Hence each new difference or sum
is at least (1-1/(2n^2)) times its old value. Also
y_1>=1/(2Cn)-1/(4Cn^3)>0. The squared differences factor into these
positive sums and differences. Multiply their bounds over n(n-1)/2
pairs to obtain the first part of (2). With u=1/(2n^2)<=1/2, the
elementary inequality log(1-u)>=-2u gives a total log loss at most
n(n-1)/n^2<=1. Dividing this log loss by n^2 proves the second part of
(2). The box is inside the ordered positive chamber, and its stated
volume and subexponential logarithmic scale follow directly.

## Upper bound for arbitrary nearby profiles

Truncate both logarithmic kernels below as above. The untruncated pair
sums are no larger than the truncated ones. For fixed cutoff, weak
convergence on [0,R'] gives their limit, with diagonal corrections O(1/n).
Then decrease the cutoff to zero. Integrability under eta identifies the
limiting energy, proving (3). The same argument gives a uniform upper
bound in a sufficiently small weak neighborhood of eta for all large n:
fix the cutoff first, use continuity of its bounded double integral,
and only then remove it. This is the form used in the Laplace argument.

The proof is analytic. The accompanying Fraction script checks the
polynomial box inequality on finite rational profiles and all their
corners, and detects a collision in a deliberately oversized box. Those
finite checks do not certify the general convergence argument.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:f91ebbe6b88f8d0da76d7a95800245ceda66ac687a4f50d4d4c01642933be55d","revision_digest":"sha256:2ecfea7de06b18284b31dd76bb8e4c02ca3e283bd8b91f83cf7e9d2571d78496","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:bounded-density-quantile-vandermonde-boxes-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21 claim w718-T287-017 version1, proof unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma L:two-point-TASEP of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Fix $\alpha_0 \in \mathbb{R}$. 
There are constants $C_0, c > 0$ depending only on $\alpha_0$ such that the following holds. Take $0 < t_1 \le t_2 < \alpha_0 t_1$, and $x_1, x_2, y \in \II{0, \alpha_0 t_1^{2/3}}$, and $\alpha \ge 1/2 - \alpha_0 t_1^{1/3}$.  Then 
\begin{align*}
	\mathbb{P}\Big(|\bar h^\alpha(x_1, t_1; \delta_y) - \bar h^\alpha(x_2, t_2; \delta_y)| \ge a (|x_1 - x_2|^{1/2} + |t_2 - t_1|^{1/3})\Big) &\le 2\exp(-c a^{1/2}),
\end{align*}    
for any $a > 0$ satisfying
$$
C_0\log^2 \left( \frac{t_1^{1/3}}{|x_1 - x_2|^{1/2} + |t_2 - t_1|^{1/3}}\right) < a < t_1^{1/4}.
$$

body: Blum's speedup theorem, from machine-independent complexity theory, produces computable functions with no best program. For any total computable function r, there is a computable 0-1 valued function h such that for every program P1 computing h with complexity Phi_1, there exists another program P2 also computing h whose complexity Phi_2 is so much smaller that r(Phi_2(x)) <= Phi_1(x) for all but finitely many inputs x. So for h, any candidate optimal program is beaten, by an arbitrarily large computable factor r, by another program that is itself beatable the same way, with no program ever asymptotically optimal. Proved by Manuel Blum in 1967 from the Blum axioms for complexity measures.
title: Blum's speedup theorem

Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random elements and let F be a countable class of measurable real functions (countability, or a suitable separability/measurability condition, is needed so the suprema are measurable). Let eps_1, ..., eps_n be independent Rademacher signs, independent of the X_i. Then E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) | <= 2 E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n eps_i f(X_i) |, and in the other direction E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n eps_i ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) | <= 2 E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) |. The constant 2 in the first inequality is the standard one and is not claimed sharp. Symmetrization is what allows one to work CONDITIONALLY on the data, replacing an empirical process by a Rademacher process whose conditional law is sub-Gaussian with an explicit variance proxy, which is the entry point for chaining bounds and Rademacher complexity. The X_i need not be identically distributed. Note the direction of the useful inequality: it bounds the centred empirical process by the Rademacher process, which is the one that can be chained. [standard; e.g. van der Vaart and Wellner, Weak Convergence and Empirical Processes, Lemma 2.3.1]
X_i independent (not necessarily identically distributed)
F countable, or measurable in the sense that the suprema are measurable
eps_i Rademacher, independent of the sample

[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Denote by \(\ParaHoelder{\alpha}([0,1]\times\R)\) the parabolic H\"older space.
The following hold.
\begin{enumerate}
  \item 
  The map \(\bm{\Psi}:\Opendenseset_\alpha \rightarrow \ParaHoelder{\alpha}([0,1]\times\mathbb R)\) defined by
  \[
  \bm{\Psi}(\gamma)(s,x)=\Psi^\gamma(s,x)-\log\cosh x,
  \qquad (s,x)\in [0,1]\times \R,
  \]
  is \(C^2\) in the Fr\'echet sense.
  \item 
  Fix $\gamma\in \Opendenseset_\alpha$ and $h\in \Hoelder{\alpha/2}([0,1])$. 
  Then, for all $s\in [0,1)$,
  \[
  D^2\Psi^\gamma[h,h](s,0)\leq 0.
  \]
  \item 
  Fix $\gamma\in\Opendenseset_\alpha$ and fix $h_1,h_2\in \Hoelder{\alpha/2}([0,1])$ where $h_1\geq 0$ and $h_2\geq 0$.
  Then, for all $s\in [0,1)$,
  \[
  D^2\Psi^\gamma[h_1,h_2](s,0)\leq 0.
  \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 5 of arXiv:2606.15432

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: ‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L^∞} ≤ (4π|t|)^{−n/2}‖f‖_{L¹} measures the data in L¹ (or in L^{p'} with p' ≤ 2 for the interpolated version). It does not say that the solution of a Schrödinger equation with L² data becomes small in L^∞ as time passes. Concrete counterexample: fix any t ≠ 0, pick g ∈ L²(R^n) \ L^∞(R^n), and set f = e^{−itΔ}g. Then ‖f‖_{L²} = ‖g‖_{L²} < ∞, while e^{itΔ}f = g ∉ L^∞ — so e^{itΔ} is not even a bounded operator from L² to L^∞, at any time, let alone a decaying one. Since the group is unitary, ‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L²} = ‖f‖_{L²} for all t: no norm decay occurs in L²; dispersion is a spreading of a fixed amount of mass, and it can only be seen in norms that punish spreading. Related traps: (i) the decay factor is |t|^{−n/2} pointwise in t and is not integrable near t = 0 for n ≥ 2, so it cannot be used naively inside a Duhamel integral — that is exactly the role of Hardy–Littlewood–Sobolev in the Strichartz proof; (ii) the wave analogue ‖e^{it|∇|}f‖_{L^∞} ≲ |t|^{−(n−1)/2}‖f‖_{L¹} is false without frequency localization (or a loss of (n+1)/2 derivatives), because the wave kernel is a measure on the light cone; (iii) with a potential, decay estimates require spectral hypotheses (no zero-energy eigenvalue or resonance), not just decay of the potential.
title: Pitfall: The Dispersive Decay Estimate Needs L¹ Data — There Is No L² → L^∞ Decay

T250-w712-C003 v1. Target 1. Status: proof (unaudited).

The depth dependence is polynomial whenever the following scalar conditions hold. No claim about a general covariance-matrix recursion follows from these conditions.

Let n>=1, c>0, kappa>0, and let (Q_l,F_l) be an adapted process taking values in [0,1], with Q_0=q_0 deterministic in (0,1]. Suppose F:[0,1]->[0,1] is increasing and concave, F(0)=0, and F(q)>0 for q>0. Assume, throughout [0,1],

    F(q) <= q-c q^2,
    E[Q_(l+1)|F_l] = F(Q_l),
    Var(Q_(l+1)|F_l) <= (kappa/n) F(Q_l)^2.

Write s_0=q_0 and s_(l+1)=F(s_l). Then, for every integer l>=0,

    E(sqrt(Q_l)-sqrt(s_l))^2 <= 4 kappa/(c n).       (1)

This is an abstract stability lemma, not an assumption of independent layers. Only conditional moments are used.

Proof. All s_l are strictly positive. Put R_l=Q_l/s_l, S_l=F(Q_l)/F(s_l), and v_l=E(R_l-1)^2. These moments are finite since R_l<=1/s_l at each fixed l.

Concavity with F(0)=0 and monotonicity imply that S_l lies between R_l and 1: for Q_l<=s_l, Q_l/s_l<=F(Q_l)/F(s_l)<=1; for Q_l>=s_l, the inequalities reverse. Consequently

    (S_l-1)^2 <= (R_l-1)^2,
    S_l^2 <= 2(S_l-1)^2+2.

The second inequality follows because its right side minus its left side is (S_l-2)^2. Conditional centering, rather than independence, gives

    v_(l+1) = E(S_l-1)^2 + E Var(R_(l+1)|F_l)
             <= (1+2 kappa/n)v_l + 2 kappa/n.

Starting at v_0=0, induction gives v_l<=(1+2 kappa/n)^l-1. If 2 kappa l/n<=1, then log(1+x)<=x and exp(x)-1<=2x on [0,1] give v_l<=4 kappa l/n.

Let mu_l=E Q_l. Taking the conditional mean and using the drift assumption and Jensen for the square gives

    mu_(l+1) <= mu_l-c mu_l^2.

The same inequality holds for s_l. The assumptions imply c a<1 at every positive deterministic iterate; for a positive mean with positive next mean the drift inequality likewise implies c a<1. Hence reciprocal comparison is legitimate:

    1/[a(1-c a)] >= 1/a+c.

If a next mean is zero, all subsequent Q values vanish almost surely, because F(0)=0 and the conditional mean is nonnegative. In either case the resulting upper bounds remain valid:

    mu_l, s_l <= 1/(q_0^(-1)+c l) <= 1/(c l), l>=1.

For 1<=l<=n/(2 kappa), |sqrt(r)-1|<=|r-1| for r>=0 yields

    E(sqrt(Q_l)-sqrt(s_l))^2 <= s_l v_l
                  <= (1/(c l))(4 kappa l/n).

For l>n/(2 kappa), use (sqrt(a)-sqrt(b))^2<=a+b to bound the same expression by mu_l+s_l<=2/(c l)<4 kappa/(c n). At l=0 it is zero. These ranges cover integer depths even when n/(2 kappa)<1. This proves (1).

Gaussian chain corollary. If the process is driven by successive fresh standard Gaussian vectors g_j, the finite preactivation is h_j=sqrt(Q_(j-1))g_j, and the deterministic comparison is hbar_j=sqrt(s_(j-1))g_j, then the same fresh Gaussian vectors couple the complete trajectories. With the product Euclidean metric on the vectors normalized by sqrt(n),

    W2((h_j/sqrt(n))_(j=1)^L,
       (hbar_j/sqrt(n))_(j=1)^L)^2 <= 4 kappa L/(c n).

Here Q_(j-1) must depend only on preceding innovations, so g_j is independent of it. This requirement is explicit; arbitrary post hoc Gaussian vectors do not establish the original network's joint law.

Application. The critical one-input tanh chain satisfies c=1/6 and kappa=48, as proved in tanh_depth_uniform.md. Thus the abstract bound is 1152/n, and the joint bound is 1152 L/n. The only ingredients involving tanh are concavity, quadratic signal decay, and bounded conditional relative variance; this pinpoints what a different scalar activation or stable chain must supply.

Limits. The ratio contraction is scalar. A matrix analogue does not follow by applying concavity entrywise, nor by replacing conditional centering with marginal variance bounds. The unpaid step for several inputs is a covariance/shape stability statement that remains uniform as the deterministic signal decays.

Verification. Every denominator is positive where inverted; Q=0 is included in the ratio contraction, while q_0=0 is the separate identically-zero case. body: In computational complexity, problems that are in the complexity class NP but are neither in the class P nor NP-complete are called NP-intermediate, and the class of such problems is called NPI. Ladner's theorem, shown in 1975 by Richard E. Ladner, is a result asserting that, if P ≠ NP, then NPI is not empty; that is, NP contains problems that are neither in P nor NP-complete. Since it is also true that if NPI problems exist, then P ≠ NP, it follows that P = NP if and only if NPI is empty.
title: NP-intermediate

# C020 v2: a shifted peak for ONE realized label vector
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Novelty unestablished.
General T267 remains open. This is a restricted four-atom width-first theorem.

## 1. Model and precise probability statement
For 0<e<1/4 put D=1+e^2+e^4, x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D),
s,t in {-1,1}. The population is uniform on these four atoms and the
training set contains one observation at each atom (stratified, not iid).
Set u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2), c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)), alpha_e=c_e/2,
and g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2. Thus ||u_e||=1 and its four Walsh
coefficients (0,s,t,st) are (0,alpha_e,alpha_e,alpha_e).
Fix 0<nu<=1 and kappa>0. Independently draw four noise signs xi_(s,t),
each uniform {-1,1}, and label y_i=g_e(x_i)+sigma_e xi_i, where
 sigma_e=2alpha_e sqrt(kappa/sqrt(e))~sqrt(kappa)e^(7/4).
Initialize f_m(x)=m^(-1/2)sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j.x), with iid w_j~N(0,I_3)
and independent iid a_j uniform {-nu,nu}. Both layers undergo simultaneous
GD with step gamma=1/2 on loss (1/8)sum_i(f_m(x_i)-y_i)^2, using gate
derivative zero at zero. The individual clean risk is
 R_(e,m,xi)(k)=(1/4)sum_i(f_(m,xi)(x_i;k)-g_e(x_i))^2.
There is NO noise average anywhere in the claim.

Let H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z], and let
lambda_h be the Walsh eigenvalues of H(X,X)/4, b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2),
eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s. C009's clock premises are
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi), eta_e~e,
with b_0 bounded away from zero.
For epsilon>0 let E_(e,m,xi)(epsilon) mean that there exist integer
k0<k1<k2<k3 with k0>=0, satisfying
 R(k0)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k3),                   (1)
 |k1/((3pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e))-1|<epsilon,
 |k2/((9pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e))-1|<epsilon,
and k2 is an interior maximum on a nontrivial integer interval [l,k3]
with k1<l<k2<k3 and both endpoint risks strictly below R(k2).
Ties between interior maximizing indices are allowed. The claim is
 liminf_(e downarrow0) liminf_(m to infinity)
 P_(xi,initialization)(E_(e,m,xi)(epsilon)) >= 1/16.       (2)
For each fixed chi in {-1,1}, conditional on xi_(s,t)=chi*s, the lower
bound over initialization alone is 1/2. The time k1 is a low-risk
cancellation WITNESS, not a claimed uniquely located stationary minimum.
The time k2 is an interval peak, not a unique stationary point theorem.
Equation (1) is the finite-witness meaning of two descents separated by a rise;
no monotonicity of every intervening nonlinear GD step is asserted.

## 2. Gaussian-width precursor and its exact unaveraged risk
C016/C017 supply, after the fixed-e width limit, independent Gaussian
Walsh initial outputs Z_(e,h) with covariance nu^2 lambda_h^RF. Couple them
for all e using independent standard G_0,G_s,G_t,G_st. Set
 U_(e,h)=Z_(e,h)/alpha_e-theta_h/alpha_e.
Then almost surely
 e U_(e,s)->L=sqrt(2)nu G_s,
 U_(e,t)->L_t=sqrt(2)nu G_t-1, U_(e,st)->-1.
These convergences are uniform when the four Gaussian coordinates range
over a fixed bounded set; the scalar variance coefficients are deterministic.
The constant initial output Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.

Fix the single label branch xi_(s,t)=chi*s. Its only nonzero normalized
noise Walsh coefficient is N_s=d e^(-1/4), d=2sqrt(kappa)chi;
N_0=N_t=N_st=0. Write N=N_s. The exact frozen clean risk is
 Q_(e,chi)(t)=alpha_e^2 sum_h [q_h U_(e,h)+(1-q_h)N_h]^2,
 q_h=exp(-b_h t).                                       (3)
At integer times this is discrete kernel GD, not gradient flow. In real
time it is only the spectral interpolation used to select integer witnesses.
Use the favorable initialization event chi*L<0, of probability1/2.
Every assertion below first refers to a fixed Gaussian realization in
this event, then is made probabilistic through compact exhaustion.

## 3. Early cancellation and two large value gaps
For small e, N and U_(e,s) have opposite signs. Thus
 q_*=-N/(U_(e,s)-N) belongs to (0,1),
 q_*~(-d/L)e^(3/4).
The fast residual N+q_*(U_(e,s)-N) is EXACTLY zero. Define
 t_1=-log(q_*)/b_s, t_0=-log(2q_*)/b_s.
Both are nonnegative for small e, t_0<t_1, and
 b_s t_1=(3/4)log(1/e)-log(-d/L)+o(1).                 (4)
Round these to nearest integers k0,k1. Their separation is (log2)/b_s,
which tends to infinity, so rounding preserves their order. A time change
of at most1/2 multiplies q_s by exp(O(b_s))=1+O(e). The residual error at
k1 is therefore O(|N|e)=O(e^(3/4)); at k0 it is -N+O(|N|e).
Slow-mode q_h tend to1 at both times and their U_h stay bounded. The
constant-mode residual is negligible faster than every power of e because
its initial normalized coefficient is O(e^(-2)) and b_0 is positive.
It follows that
 Q(k1)/alpha_e^2 -> L_t^2+1=2B,
 Q(k0)/(alpha_e^2 e^(-1/2)) -> d^2=4kappa,
where B=(L_t^2+1)/2>=1/2. In particular Q(k0)>Q(k1).
This proves the first descent witness and its leading clock; no derivative
argument or minimum uniqueness is needed.

## 4. The later single-label peak
Set t_e(v)=((9/4)log(1/e)+v)/b_s and z=exp(-v). Then q_s=e^(9/4)z.
Differentiate (3), using the exact derivative identity of C019:
 Q'(t_e(v))/(2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st))
 =sum_h [b_h/(b_t+b_st)]
   [q_h N_h(N_h-U_h)-q_h^2(U_h-N_h)^2].                 (5)
The fast term -q_s N U_s/eta_e converges to -dL z=A z,
with A=-dL>0. Its other four expansion terms vanish uniformly on bounded
v intervals. Their orders are respectively e^(3/4), e^(3/2), e^(9/4), e^3,
for q_s N^2/eta_e, q_s^2 U_s^2/eta_e, q_s^2 U_s N/eta_e,
and q_s^2 N^2/eta_e. The slow terms, with N_t=N_st=0, tend to -B,
since their weights tend to1/2 and q_t,q_st=1-O(e log(1/e)).
The constant term is again exponentially negligible. Hence locally uniformly
 Q'(t_e(v))/(2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st)) -> A exp(-v)-B.         (6)
Integration on bounded intervals gives convergence of centered risk differences:
 [Q(t_e(v))-Q(t_e(0))]/(2alpha_e^2 eta_e)
 -> V(v)-V(0), V(v)=-A exp(-v)-Bv.                     (7)
The function V is strictly concave, with its unique maximum at
 v_*=log(A/B), and has strict value gaps to either endpoint of any compact
interval containing v_* in its interior. Also, uniformly on compact v sets,
 Q(t_e(v))/(alpha_e^2 e^(-1/2)) -> d^2=4kappa.            (8)
Indeed q_s U_s=O(e^(5/4)) is negligible relative to N=O(e^(-1/4));
slow risk is O(alpha_e^2) and the constant-mode risk is negligible.
Equations (8) and Section3 give the second strict gap Q(peak)>Q(k1).
Equation (7) gives the third strict gap to a later time, now of order
alpha_e^2 eta_e. It is much smaller than the two early value gaps.

Round all central t_e(v) to the integer grid. The mesh in v is b_s->0,
so (7) remains uniform on the grid. On a fixed compact interval containing
v_* inside, an integer maximizing index is interior and its v coordinate
tends to v_*. This uses the positive gap between V(v_*) and the compact
complement of any neighborhood of v_*, not derivatives of nonlinear GD.
The central maximizing time consequently has leading term
 (9pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e).                              (9)
The early cancellation witness (4) precedes the entire central interval,
since their b_s-scaled time separation is (3/2)log(1/e)+O(1).
This completes the Gaussian frozen-array witness construction.

## 5. Probability and transfer to the actual BOTH-layer nonlinear updates
For an integer M>=1 restrict to the compact Gaussian event
 K_M={chi L<=-1/M, |G_0|,|G_s|,|G_t|,|G_st|<=M}.
These increasing events exhaust {chi L<0}. On K_M, A is bounded above
and away from zero and B is bounded above and below. Thus v_*, the offset
in (4), and all coefficients used above lie in deterministic bounded sets.
All estimates in Sections3-4 are uniform on K_M: the U limits have deterministic
coefficients linear in bounded G, the denominator L is bounded away from0,
and the exponentially small constant-mode bounds are uniform as well.
Choose a deterministic central v interval [-J,J] whose interior contains
all possible v_* on K_M, with a margin of at least1. Strict concavity and
compactness give uniform positive endpoint gaps for V. The two large early
gaps are also uniform. For small e, the entire central grid interval lies
inside the relative time tolerance epsilon in (2), and the cancellation
indices lie inside the stated earlier relative tolerance.

For each fixed e choose a finite integer horizon T_e(M) containing the
central grid interval and the possible earlier witnesses. C009 Section3,
as applied in C018 Section3, gives joint weak convergence of all actual
individual risks through that finite horizon to (3) when m tends to infinity.
The proof retains the actual nonzero initial output and controls both-layer
motion and gate-crossing remainders. The finite sixteen-label family is
covered, although here only the fixed single branch is used. Risk squaring
is continuous on the finite array, and the prediction arrays are tight.
No finite-width Gaussian-mode independence or e-uniform width bound is used.

For clarity about maxima and weak convergence, take the deterministic
central interval just specified. The event that there exist k0<k1 before
it and a grid index j in its interior, with the two early witness gaps
strictly positive and R(j) strictly above BOTH central endpoint values,
is open in the finite risk array: it is a finite union of finite intersections
of strict inequalities. Restrict k1 to its required relative time band.
The frozen arrays on K_M satisfy this open event for sufficiently small e.
Any maximum k2 over that central interval then lies in its interior;
replacing j by k2 only increases the witness gaps. The right endpoint is
k3, and k1 precedes the central interval. The entire central interval is
already in the required peak-time band, so all maximizers qualify.
The open-set Portmanteau inequality transfers the LOWER probability bound
to actual nonlinear risk arrays for each fixed e. Thus the two ordered
liminf limits have conditional probability at least P(K_M). Let M increase
to infinity to obtain the conditional lower bound1/2. This argument sends
width to infinity separately at every e and finite horizon, before e tends
to zero. No infinite-horizon NTK statement or interchange of limits occurs.

Finally the two noise events xi=+s and xi=-s are disjoint and each has
probability1/16 under the original four independent sign errors. Noise is
independent of initialization. Summing their conditional lower bounds gives
(1/16)(1/2)+(1/16)(1/2)=1/16, proving (2). Other sign patterns might add
probability, but they are not analyzed or counted in this claim.

## 6. Limits and unresolved piece
This is a single REALIZED label vector result, unlike C017/C018. It is
consistent with C019: its peak is at the later (9/4)log(1/e) clock, while
C019 addresses bounded offsets around (3/2)log(1/e).
The four input atoms cluster as e decreases; training inputs are stratified,
noise amplitude shrinks, width is taken first, and only a positive-probability
noise/initialization event is proved. No full typical-data theorem, macroscopic
feature learning, fixed-noise theorem, unique stationary points or complete
noise window is claimed. The hardest unpaid step is a general single-dataset
result beyond this shrinking four-atom, positive-probability construction.
Dependencies C009,C016,C017,C018,C019 and this claim all remain unaudited.
Independent correctness and novelty review are pending; no priority claim
is made. Sources: the named own proof files; the full ReLU kernel and clock
premises come from C009, with Heckel-Yilmaz 2007.10099v2 Section3 as its
primary kernel source. No new external literature result is claimed here.
Exact stratified four-point shrinking-input model and finite-witness meaning in proofs/SINGLE_LABEL_SHIFTED_PEAK.md

Fixed0<nu<=1 and kappa>0; iid Gaussian hidden weights and independent iid signed heads; both layers trained by simultaneous step1/2 GD
Width tends to infinity at each fixed e and finite horizon before e decreases

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Try to derive the tail exponent from the Gibbs-Markov fixed-point equation as for smoothing transforms (Durrett-Liggett classification). Result: The Gibbs-Markov property along dyadic square partitions gives a fixed-point equation of smoothing type Z^D =_d sum_i e^{alpha Phi_i} Z^{D_i} with Gaussian binding field Phi and 4 pieces; Durrett-Liggett gives, for such equations, that non-trivial solutions have tails whose exponent is the root of a structure equation, here forcing E[Z^D(A)^s] finite iff s < 1. This yields the correct tail EXPONENT (P(Z^D(A) > t) decays like t^{-1} up to slowly varying factors) but not the precise Laplace asymptotic E e^{-lambda Z} = 1 - c lambda log(1/lambda)(1+o(1)) demanded by property (5); the slowly varying factor is exactly the content of the conjecture and the Durrett-Liggett theory does not fix it. Obstruction: Smoothing-transform theory fixes the power in the tail but not the logarithmic correction; the log factor is what (5) asserts.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0003-bypassing-the-laplace-transform-tail-condition-for-the-dgff-extremal-m

body: In topology, a discipline within mathematics, the Jordan curve theorem (JCT), formulated by Camille Jordan in 1887, asserts that every Jordan curve divides the plane into two regions: the interior, bounded by the curve, and an unbounded exterior, containing all of the nearby and faraway exterior points. Every continuous path connecting a point of one region to a point of the other intersects with the curve somewhere.

[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $\beta >0$ and $\alpha \in (0,1)$ such that $\alpha + \beta/2 > 1$. Suppose $U:[0,1] \times \T^d \to\R^d$ is a $C^0([0,1],C^{\alpha-}(\T^d))$ multiscale finite range random velocity field; that is, $U$ satisfies Assumption~\ref{asmp:main for refreshing}, and \eqref{eq:refreshing theorem hypothesis} holds for some $p >\frac{ \beta}{\alpha + \beta/2-1} \lor \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$.
    
    Then almost surely:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item  for all $y \in \T^d$ and $s \in [0,1]$, the ODE~\eqref{eq:main refreshing ODE s} admits a unique solution on $[0,1]$, and thus the two-parameter flow $\Phi_{s,t}$ given by~\eqref{eq:main refreshing flow} is uniquely defined,
        \item  $\Phi_{s,t}$ is uniformly-in-time Lipschitz-in-space, $\sup_{0 \leq s,t \leq 1} \|\Phi_{s,t}\|_{W^{1,\infty}_y} < \infty$,
        \item  and the continuity equation~\eqref{eq:continuity} admits unique positive measure-valued solutions, that is, if $\phi \in TV(\T^d)$ is a positive measure, then there exists a unique distributional solution to~\eqref{eq:continuity} such that for all $t \in [0,1], f(t,\cdot) \in TV(\T^d)$ is a positive measure.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 7 of arXiv:2608.05931

by $S\cap T$, the two normal lines $\mathbb{F} u_S$ and $\mathbb{F} u_T$ are independent Haar-distributed lines in the

phase-invariant events one may take $u_S,u_T$ to be independent Haar unit vectors in $E^\perp$.

body:
Let X_1, X_2, ... be INDEPENDENT AND IDENTICALLY DISTRIBUTED. Call an event A EXCHANGEABLE if it is invariant under every permutation of finitely many indices, that is A is unchanged when the values of any finite set of coordinates are permuted. Then P(A) is 0 or 1 for every exchangeable A. This is strictly stronger than Kolmogorov's 0-1 law, which applies to TAIL events: every tail event is exchangeable, but not conversely. The standard separating example is A = { S_n = 0 for infinitely many n } for a simple random walk, which is exchangeable but NOT a tail event, since changing X_1 changes every partial sum. Identical distribution is essential and cannot be relaxed to mere independence. Minimal counterexample: let X_1 be Bernoulli(1/2) and let X_n = 0 deterministically for every n >= 2. These are independent but not identically distributed, and the event A = { x : x_n = 1 for some n } is invariant under every finite permutation of the coordinates, hence exchangeable, yet P(A) = P(X_1 = 1) = 1/2. The proof below breaks exactly where one needs it to: the permutation swapping the first n coordinates with the next n is not measure preserving unless the coordinates share a law. A standard use: for an i.i.d. sequence the events {limsup S_n = + infinity} and {liminf S_n = - infinity} are exchangeable, because permuting finitely many summands changes S_n for only finitely many n, so each has probability 0 or 1; for a non-degenerate mean-zero law a short further argument then shows both probabilities are 1, but that conclusion is NOT delivered by the 0-1 law alone. [Hewitt and Savage (1955); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.1.1]

body: Let Sigma be a p by p positive semidefinite matrix and n >= 1 an integer, and let X be a p by n random matrix whose n columns are independent and identically distributed as the p-dimensional Gaussian N(0, Sigma). The Wishart distribution W_p(Sigma, n) is the probability distribution of the p by p random matrix X X^T. When Sigma is positive definite and n >= p, a matrix distributed as W_p(Sigma, n) is almost surely positive definite (invertible). [standard, e.g. Muirhead, Aspects of Multivariate Statistical Theory]

body: [Definition 4.5 (VC Dimension) of arXiv:2502.03023, 'Parametric Scaling Law of Tuning Bias in Conformal Prediction'] Let F be a class of Boolean functions defined on a domain Ω, f : Ω→{0, 1} for all f ∈F. A subset Ω′ ⊆Ωis said to be shattered by F if any function g : Ω′ →{0, 1} can be obtained by restricting some function f ∈F onto Ω′. The VC dimension of F, denoted by VC(F), is the size of the largest subset Ω′ ⊆Ω that can be shattered by F.

body:
Aldous and Fill, Open Problem 4.30 (p. 137) asks whether there is an explicit function psi(b,s) tending to 0 as s tends to infinity, not depending on the chain, with sup_x |P(S_t/(sigma sqrt t) <= x) - P(Z <= x)| <= psi(||g||_inf, t/tau2) for standardized g and continuous-time reversible chains. Our result (id P0209, 2026-09-08): NO such psi exists. Take two independent reversible chains: Y two-state with rates epsilon and 1 - epsilon (spectral gap exactly 1) and Z a fair sign flip at rate R/2; set epsilon = s^-2, R = s^4, A = 2 epsilon + sqrt((1-epsilon)(1-4 epsilon)), B = (2-A)/(1-epsilon) and g = A Z + B (Y - epsilon). Then exactly, at every s: E g = 0, E g^2 = 1, ||g||_inf = 2 and tau2 = 1. Taking t = s sends t/tau2 to infinity with the sup norm pinned at 2, yet normality fails: S_t is compound Poisson with vanishing intensity (the mean number of visits to the rare state is epsilon t = 1/s, tending to 0), so with probability 1 - O(1/s) no visit occurs and S_t sits near the deterministic value -B epsilon t while the whole variance is carried by one rare excursion. Verification as the source words it: the identities were checked to seven decimals at every s, and the measured Kolmogorov distance to N(0,1) is 0.478, 0.505, 0.509, 0.506 at s = 30, 100, 300, 1000 - flat at about 1/2, not decreasing, while t/tau2 rises from 30 to 1000. Prior art not cleared.

\[
\mathcal{L}^p_{k}(\Rr^d) = W^{k, p}(\Rr^d).
\]

body: In mathematical analysis, a function of bounded variation, also known as BV function, is a real-valued function whose total variation is bounded (finite): the graph of a function having this property is well behaved in a precise sense. For a continuous function of a single variable, being of bounded variation means that the distance along the direction of the y-axis, neglecting the contribution of motion along x-axis, traveled by a point moving along the graph has a finite value. For a continuous function of several variables, the meaning of the definition is the same, except for the fact that the continuous path to be considered cannot be the whole graph of the given function, but can be every intersection of the graph itself with a hyperplane parallel to a fixed x-axis and to the y-axis.
title: Bounded variation

body:
[Definition def:above_below_waterfall of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] Denote by $\mathcal{W}^{\pm}$ the regions above and below the waterfall, that is,
	\begin{equation*}
		\mathcal{W}^{+}\coloneqq
		\begin{cases}
			\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
			\mathsf{x}>\mathsf{N}+(\mathsf{t}-\mathsf{T}+\mathsf{S})^+\},&\textnormal{if $\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{T}$};\\
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
			\mathsf{t}_l<\mathsf{t}<\mathsf{t}_r,\ \mathsf{x}>\tfrac12(\mathsf{S+\mathsf{t}+\mathsf{N}})
		\}\\\hspace{20pt}
			\cup
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
					\mathsf{t}\le \mathsf{t}_l,\
					\mathsf{x}>\mathsf{N}
			\}\mathbf{1}_{\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{S}}
			\\\hspace{20pt}
			\cup
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
					\mathsf{t}\ge \mathsf{t}_r,\
					\mathsf{x}>\mathsf{S}+\mathsf{N}+\mathsf{t}-\mathsf{T}
				\}\mathbf{1}_{\mathsf{S}+\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{T}}
		,
		&\textnormal{if $\mathsf{N}<\mathsf{T}$},\\
		\end{cases}
	\end{equation*}
	and
	\begin{multline*}
		\mathcal{W}^{-}\coloneqq
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
			\mathsf{t}_l<\mathsf{t}<\mathsf{t}_r,\ \mathsf{x}<\tfrac12(\mathsf{S+\mathsf{t}-\mathsf{N}})
		\}
			\\
			\cup
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
					\mathsf{t}\le \mathsf{t}_l,\
					\mathsf{x}<\mathsf{t}
			\}\mathbf{1}_{\mathsf{N}<\mathsf{S}}
			\cup
				\{(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})\in \mathcal{H}\colon
					\mathsf{t}\ge \mathsf{t}_r,\
					\mathsf{x}<\mathsf{S}
				\}\mathbf{1}_{\mathsf{S}+\mathsf{N}<\mathsf{T}}.
	\end{multline*}
	Here the indicator $\mathbf{1}_{\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{S}}$ means that the
	subset in the union is present only if $\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{S}$, and similarly for all
	other indicators.
	In the samples in (fig:waterfall_region of the paper), right,
	the regions $\mathcal{W}^{\pm}$ are the lighter-colored ones. They consist solely of the horizontal lozenges
	\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline = (current bounding
		box.south),scale=.25]
	\draw[thick] (0,0)--++(1,1)--++(1,0)--++(-1,-1)--cycle;
	\end{tikzpicture}.\footnote{The below region $\mathcal{W}^-$ exists only if
	$\mathsf{N}<\mathsf{T}$. In (sec:asymptotic_clustering_of_nonintersecting_paths of the paper) below,
	we show that for
	$\mathsf{N}>\mathsf{T}$, the nonintersecting paths stay
	as low as they can: First, they go straight with
	slope $0$ until $\mathsf{t}=\mathsf{T}-\mathsf{S}$, and then
	continue diagonally with slope $1$.}

	Also denote $\mathcal{P}\coloneqq \mathcal{H}\setminus(\mathcal{W}^+\cup \mathcal{W}^-)$,
	this is the region inside the hexagon where we expect the nonintersecting paths to cluster together.
	We call $\mathcal{P}$ the \emph{saturation band}. It has constant width~$\mathsf{N}$
	and includes the waterfall region.
title: Definition def:above_below_waterfall of arXiv:2507.22011

body:
[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $\beta>0$, $\lambda>0$, $p\geq 1$ and let, for all $j\geq 0$, $u^j$ be defined by~\eqref{eq:refreshing poisson}. Suppose there exists $M\geq 1$ such that for all $j\geq 0$, $n\in\{0,1,2\}$, and $s\in[0,1]$,
\[\|\nabla^n f^j_s\|_{L^p_\omega C^0_{t,x}}\leq M 2^{(n-\alpha-\beta /p)j}.\]
Then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item the $u^j$ are mutually independent with $\E u^j =0$,
\item for each $j\geq 1$, $u^j$ has a finite temporal range of dependence $2^{-\beta j}$,
\item and there exists a constant $C>0$ such that for all $j\geq 0$ and $n\in\{0,1,2\}$,
\[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega C^0_{t,x}}\leq CM(\lambda+p)2^{(n-\alpha)j}.\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
