body:
Let A0,A1 be real Hurwitz 2x2 matrices. Fix lambda in (0,1) such that Alambda=(1-lambda)A0+lambda A1 has real eigenvalues -lambda_minus<0<lambda_plus. For beta>0 let I switch 0->1 at rate beta*lambda and 1->0 at rate beta*(1-lambda), and let Xdot=AI X. For every initial probability law assigning no mass to X=0, t^-1 log||Xt|| converges almost surely to an initial-law-independent real chi(beta). There exist 0<beta1<=beta2<infinity such that chi(beta)<0 for beta<beta1 and chi(beta)>0 for beta>beta2. Consequently the norm tends respectively to zero or infinity. The theorem does not assert beta1=beta2, monotonicity, or a single instability interval. Source: Benaim, Le Borgne, Malrieu and Zitt, arXiv:1204.1921, Section 1 standing Hurwitz assumption, Assumption 1.1, rates preceding Theorem 1.6, Theorem 1.6, PDF pp.1-2.

lambda in (0,1)

[Lemma Planar two-disk logarithmic capacity and
boundary-layer profile, \(d = 2\) of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] For
\(0 < \varepsilon \ll \delta\) the logarithmic capacity of the
union of two disks of radius \(\varepsilon\) whose centers are at
distance \(2\delta\) is
\(\operatorname{cap}_{\log} = \sqrt{2\varepsilon\delta}\,\left( 1 + o(1) \right)\).
Consequently, writing
\(\delta_{\varepsilon} = \operatorname{dist}\left( x_{\varepsilon},\partial M \right)\)
and assuming
\(\log\delta_{\varepsilon}/\log\varepsilon \rightarrow \theta \in \lbrack 0,1\rbrack\),
the reflected half-plane condenser energy of
\(B\left( x_{\varepsilon},\varepsilon \right) \cap M\) is
\(E_{H} = B(\theta)\, E_{0}\,\left( 1 + o(1) \right)\) with the
planar profile

\[B(\theta) = \frac{1}{1 + \theta},\quad\quad B(1) = \frac{1}{2},\quad B(0) = 1.\]

body: The hairy ball theorem of algebraic topology (formally, the Sphere Vector Field Theory, sometimes called the hedgehog theorem) states that there is no non-vanishing continuous tangent vector field on even-dimensional n-spheres. For the ordinary sphere, or 2‑sphere, if f is a continuous function that assigns a vector in ℝ3 to every point p on a sphere such that f(p) is always tangent to the sphere at p, then there is at least one pole, a point where the field vanishes (a p such that f(p) = 0).

The unique strictly positive finite entrance has u0=0 and q(0+)=1/c^2; u0>0 gives q(0+)=0 and q_t/t^2->1/(2u0^2). For ReLU c=sqrt(2)/(3pi), the positive entrance is 9pi^2/2. {"artifact_digest":"sha256:54b935f5d04384f98388cd26f184cb32669870fae035922a848f9c6aa7dd7ba2","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/54/54b935f5d04384f98388cd26f184cb32669870fae035922a848f9c6aa7dd7ba2.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:958669126e19ce594fff359e2a92cd1f563c764945b59c8336f694e1baf7968d","bundle_entry_key":"rescaled-correlation-entrances","bundle_id":"population.t244-rescaled-correlation-sde-entrances-006","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; stochastic differential equations; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_006.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:rescaled-correlation-sde-positive-entrance-linear-transform","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"REVIEW STATUS: exact claim version 1 PASS by claude-738954b6; original author draft below retains its drafting-time labels.

# Positive entrances for the rescaled-correlation SDE

Status: proof draft (unaudited), Target1 architecture step. This is a theorem about a specified SDE, not a correction to Li-Nica Theorem4.1 and not a proof of finite-width network convergence. The result includes both disputed constant drifts, so it does not require deciding C012's source correction.

Let c>0, gamma be real, and B be standard Brownian motion on [0,T] with B_0=0 on a usual filtered probability space. Consider finite, continuous, adapted processes q_t>0 for t>0 satisfying on every compact positive-time interval

    dq_t = 2q_t[(1-c sqrt(q_t))/t+gamma]dt+2sqrt(2)q_t dB_t.   (Q)

Put a=c/sqrt(2), b=3-gamma. Every such solution corresponds to a finite nonnegative F_0-measurable variable u_0 through

    E_t=exp((b-1)t-sqrt(2)B_t),
    U_t=E_t[u_0+a integral_0^t E_s^(-1)ds],
    q_t=t^2/(2U_t^2), t>0.                                  (R)

Conversely every finite u_0>=0 in F_0 gives a strictly positive solution on positive times by (R). For u_0=0 its unique continuous entrance is q_0=1/c^2. For u_0>0 its continuous entrance is q_0=0, and q_t/t^2->1/(2u_0^2). Thus the unique solution having a strictly positive finite entrance value has necessarily q_0=1/c^2 and is pathwise unique for a given B. Merely assigning the value q_0=0 does not select a unique positive solution.

For the ReLU coefficient c=sqrt(2)/(3pi), the positive entrance is q_0=9pi^2/2. The source's displayed Eq4.7 has gamma=-1 (b=4); its displayed log equation4.8 corresponds to gamma=+1 (b=2). The entrance classification above applies separately to both. C004's checked compact generator selects gamma=+1 in its coordinate transformation, but the source-theorem correction remains for the Claude reviewer.

## Reciprocal transformation and classification

For t>0 define U=t/sqrt(2q). Its derivatives are U_t=U/t, U_q=-U/(2q), U_qq=3U/(4q^2). Ito's formula gives

    dU=[U/t-U((1-c sqrt(q))/t+gamma)+3U]dt-sqrt(2)U dB
       =[a+bU]dt-sqrt(2)U dB.                                (U)

The constant term uses U c sqrt(q)/t=c/sqrt(2)=a. The coefficients of (U) are globally Lipschitz, and its integrating factor is E_t as above. On any positive-time interval the variation-of-constants identity says E_t^-1 U_t-a integral_0^t E_s^-1 ds is constant in t. Evaluating at one positive time shows that this constant u_0 is finite. Since E is continuous, positive, and E_0=1, it follows that U_t->u_0 as t decreases to zero. Positivity of U at every positive time forces u_0>=0. Its measurability at zero follows from the usual right-continuity of the filtration and adaptedness of U_t. This proves that every positive solution must have representation (R).

Conversely the representation solves (U), is positive at every t>0 since a>0, and is finite on every finite interval. Applying Ito to t^2/(2U^2) away from t=0 proves (Q). Thus the representation covers exactly the positive solutions.

If u_0>0, U_t->u_0 immediately gives the stated q_t/t^2 limit. If u_0=0, continuity of B implies uniformly for 0<=s<=t that E_t/E_s->1 as t->0. Consequently

    U_t/(a t)=(1/t) integral_0^t E_t/E_s ds ->1 almost surely,
    q_t ->1/(2a^2)=1/c^2 almost surely.

This also proves continuity and strict positivity at the canonical entrance. Uniqueness follows from the integrating-factor formula, with no choice of an initial Brownian correlation or independent marginal limits.

## Integral interpretation through the singular time

The canonical extension also satisfies the integral SDE from time0; its singular drift is locally integrable. To see this directly without an unstated regularity assumption, set M_t=sup_(s<=t)|B_s|. On a fixed Brownian path and finite T, the exponential-ratio estimate gives

    |U_t/(at)-1| <= C(omega)(t+M_t)

near zero. Since the ratio tends to1, it follows that |q_t-1/c^2|<=C(omega)(t+M_t). The function q(1-c sqrt(q)) is locally Lipschitz and vanishes at 1/c^2, so the absolute singular drift is bounded by C(omega)(1+M_t/t). Doob's L2 inequality gives E M_t<=2sqrt(t), and therefore

    E integral_0^T M_t/t dt <=4sqrt(T)<infinity.

Tonelli's theorem makes the latter integral finite almost surely. The remaining drift is continuous and the noise coefficient q is bounded near zero on each path. Localize by these path bounds and let the lower integration endpoint decrease to zero; the stochastic integral has a continuous extension. Thus the integral equation is well defined with q_0=1/c^2. For u_0>0, q_t=O(t^2), making the drift integrable even more directly.

## Why this is not a full q-chain convergence statement at time0

For the network observable q_l=l^2(1-rho_l), the literal value at l=0 is0. The canonical positive-time limit instead has continuous extension 1/c^2>0. Hence the unmodified q_floor(nt) paths cannot converge in the usual Skorohod topology on [0,T] to that continuous extension: evaluation at0 preserves the value0 under Skorohod convergence. Changing only the value at the first time point also does not address the whole shrinking initial layer.

The natural continuous entrance variable is U_n=1/(n theta_floor(nt)), whose initial value tends to0. Once its network convergence is established, q_t=t^2/(2U_t^2) on positive times selects u_0=0 and thus the canonical q entrance. C005-C006 attempt precisely that network step but remain unaudited. The theorem above resolves the SDE entrance classification, while keeping this separate finite-width obligation explicit.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:bbfefc84f0aff1c56b907affa58118298696f5d8fa98c4a718e5143fbbc07351","revision_digest":"sha256:2fa51fbd0025d4dc64b7f47ed1cef1245d82a4ba78081dcc6205e9fbc7e5b21e","source_id":"owner-own-work:T244-w691-C014:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1-unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: In the random recursive tree, the layer of a vertex is the number of rounds of leaf-stripping until it is a leaf, and l_k is the limiting fraction of vertices at layer k. Conjecture 1 of arXiv:2608.04303, l_k = exp[-k/e - (3/(2e)) log k - O(1)], holds: the paper's recursion s_0 = 1, s_i(y) = 1 - exp(-int_0^y s_{i-1}) is exactly the Poisson product formula P(M_i <= y) for the generation-i minimum M_i of the branching random walk on the Poisson-weighted infinite tree, so lbar_k = E[e^{-M_k}], and the velocity 1/e with the (3/(2e)) log k correction is Addario-Berry and Ford (Ann. Appl. Probab. 2013, Theorem 1.1). With Aidekon (2013) the O(1) is a genuine limit: lbar_k e^{k/e} k^{3/(2e)} -> C* ~ 1.42 and l_k / lbar_k -> 1 - e^{-1/e} ~ 0.3078. The layer half of Conjecture 2 also holds: the maximum layer is floor(diameter/2), so L_n = e log n - 1.5 log log n + O_P(1).

[Lemma lem:moment_bound of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\bm{X}$ be a L\'evy process with 
generating triplet $(\bm{\gamma_X},\bm{\Sigma_X}\bm{\Sigma_X}^{\scalebox{0.6}{$\top$}},\nu_{\bm{X}})$.
 Recall the Blumenthal--Getoor index $\beta$ from~(equation eq:BG of the paper) and the associated quantity $\beta_+\in [\beta,2]$. Assume that, for some $p>0$, we have
$\int_{\mathbb{R}^d\setminus B_{\bm{0}}(1)}|\bm{w}|^p\nu_{\bm{X}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})<\infty$.
 Then there exist constants $C_i\in[0,\infty)$, $i=1,\ldots,4$, such that
\[
\mathds{E}\bigg[\sup_{s\in[0,t]}|\bm{X}_s|^p\bigg]
\leqslant \1_{\{\bm{\Sigma_X}\neq\bm{0}\}}C_1 t^{p/2} 
+C_2 t^p + C_3 t^{\min\{1,p/\beta_+\}},
\quad \text{ for } t\in[0,1].
\]
If $\int_{B_{\bm{0}}(1)\setminus\{\bm{0}\}}|\bm{w}|\nu_{\bm{X}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})< \infty$ and $\bm{X}$ has zero natural drift, i.e. $\bm{\gamma_X}=\int_{B_{\bm{0}}(1)\setminus\{\bm{0}\}}\bm{w}\nu_{\bm{X}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})$, then $C_2=0$ in the inequality above. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:fourier of arXiv:2607.12564, 'Power-law and log-periodic degree tails for a family of probability generating function eq'] Let $\chi:=2\pi/\log\lambda$, $s_m:=\rho+1+i\chi m$, and
$\mathcal{M}_j(s):=\int_0^\infty w_j(x)x^{s-1}dx=\mathbb{E}[V_j^{\,s-1}]$, finite and analytic for
$\operatorname{Re}s>1$. Then the continuous period-$1$ function $\Psi_j$ has Fourier coefficients
\begin{equation}
  \widehat\Psi_j(m):=\int_0^1\Psi_j(u)e^{2\pi i m u}\,du=\frac{2p}{a\log\lambda}\,\mathcal{M}_j(s_m).
\end{equation}
In particular $\widehat\Psi_j(0)=\overline\Psi_j=\frac{2p}{a\log\lambda}\mathbb{E}[V_j^{\,\rho}]>0$.

body:
[Lem 159 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-chaotic}, in the limiting regime \eqref{eq:eta-delta-eps} we have
  \[
    \sup_{\upp \in [0,1]}
    \lt|
      \lim_{N\to\infty} \chi_{\breve{\cA}_N}(\upp) - \plim_{N\to\infty} \frac{(\hat{\by}^{\ubl},\tilde{\by}^{\ubl})}{N}
    \rt| \le \iota'\,,
  \]
  where $\hat{\by}^{\ubl},\tilde{\by}^{\ubl}$ are the outputs of $\IAMP_{\chaos,N}(p,\sigma,b,w,\delta,\eta)$ on $\upp$-correlated $\bz, \tilde{\bz}$.
\begin{proof}
  For each $\upp \in [0,1]$, we have
  \[
    \chi_{\breve{\cA}_N}(\upp)
    = \frac{\bbE (\breve{\cA}_N(\bz), \breve{\cA}_N(\tilde \bz) )}{N}
    = \frac{N}{\bbE_{\bz'}[\|\bar\cA_N(\bz')\|^2]} \cdot \frac{\bbE (\bar{\cA}_N(\bz), \bar{\cA}_N(\tilde \bz) )}{N}\,.
  \]
  As argued in the \hyperlink{proof:t.IAMP.main.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}},
  \[
    \bigg|\frac{N}{\bbE_{\bz'}[\|\bar\cA_N(\bz')\|^2]} - 1\bigg| \le \iota'\,.
  \]
  We can write
  \[
    \frac{(\bar{\cA}_N(\bz), \bar{\cA}_N(\tilde \bz))}{N}
    = \frac{\|\bar{\cA}_N(\bz) + \bar{\cA}_N(\tilde \bz)\|^2}{2N} 
    - \frac{\|\bar{\cA}_N(\bz)\|^2}{2N} 
    - \frac{\|\bar{\cA}_N(\tilde\bz)\|^2}{2N}
  \]
  Since $\bar{\cA}$ is a $C(L,\epsilon)$-Lipschitz function of standard gaussians, each of the terms on the right-hand side has variance $O(1/N)$.
  Thus $(\bar{\cA}_N(\bz), \bar{\cA}_N(\tilde \bz)) / N$ has variance $O(1/N)$, which implies
  \[
    \lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{\bbE (\bar{\cA}_N(\bz), \bar{\cA}_N(\tilde \bz) )}{N}
    = \plim_{N\to\infty} \frac{(\bar{\cA}_N(\bz), \bar{\cA}_N(\tilde \bz) )}{N}\,.
  \]
  Finally, because $\bar{\cA}_N(\bz)$ agrees with $\tilde{\cA}_N(\bz)$ with probability $1-e^{-cN}$,
  \[
    \plim_{N\to\infty} \frac{(\bar{\cA}_N(\bz), \bar{\cA}_N(\tilde \bz) )}{N}
    = \plim_{N\to\infty} \frac{(\tilde{\cA}_N(\bz), \tilde{\cA}_N(\tilde \bz) )}{N}
    = \plim_{N\to\infty} \frac{(\hat{\by}^{\ubl},\tilde{\by}^{\ubl})}{N}\,. 
  \]
  This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 159 of arXiv:2608.29416

Method: Exact tree identity, source-specific recurrence or explicit limiting obstruction Result: The bounded test f(j)=1 when j is a power of2 and0 otherwise has finite limiting sum S because a(2^r)=O(r*2^-r). Along n=2^K, the certain root visit contributes1 in addition to every fixed initial set of terms tending to S. Thus the liminf is at least S+1, contradicting the proposed limit S. The test g(j)=j*f(j) separately refutes the divergent-series clause: the actual sum is at least2^K whereas the proposed truncated sum is of order K^2. Check: Both constructions use the exact root identity a(n,n)=1, nonnegativity and the established pointwise formula. No computed rate is needed. The stronger dyadic occupation bound in P0340 proves validity for suitable uniformly decreasing tails and explains why it does not cover these sparse root-sensitive tests. A comprehensive sharp two-parameter error theory and the best admissible class of tests remain unresolved here; therefore the broader numbered problem is only partly answered.

[Prop rodl1995threshold of arXiv:2609.02588, 'Ramsey-type results for Maker-Breaker games'] Let $r\geq 2$ and let $H$ be a graph with a cycle. Then there exist a constant $C$ such that for $m=Cn^{2-1/m_2(G)}$ and any $t\geq 0$ the random graph $G(n,m)$ contains a subgraph $F'$ that satisfies the following with probability tending to $1$ as $n$ tends to infinity:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Every subgraph $G\subseteq F'$ with $v(G)\leq t$ satisfies $m_2(G)\leq m_2(H)$
        \item $F'\rightarrow_r H$
    \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let M>=1 finite linear-regression tasks have matrices X_m in R^(n_m by d) and labels y_m. Suppose X_m*w_star=y_m for every m, put R=max_m||X_m||_2>0, and define L(w;m)=||X_m*w-y_m||^2/2 and L(w)=M^(-1)*sum_m L(w;m). Initialize w_0=0 and sample tau_1,...,tau_k independently and uniformly from{1,...,M}, with replacement. Scheme1 performs the exact update w_t=argmin_w {L(w;tau_t)+(lambda_t/2)*||w-w_(t-1)||^2}. Write D2=||w_0-w_star||^2. For a known integer horizon k>=2, use lambda_t=(13*R^2/3)*(k+1)/(k-t+2), t=1,...,k. Then E L(w_k)<=20*D2*R^2/(k+1). The regularizer penalizes movement from the preceding iterate; its coefficient grows through the run. The bound concerns the full-collection population loss L defined above.
Finite jointly realizable linear tasks; R is the largest task-matrix operator norm and R>0.

body:
[Prop 7 of arXiv:2606.30349, 'Attenuated Poisson Dirichlet approximations for divisibility configurations'] Let $\vec{C}(n)=(\alpha_p(H_n):p\le n)$ and $\vec{\xi}(n)=(\xi_p:p\le n)$. Then for all $n\geq  21$
\begin{align}
\PP[A_n]
  &=
\mathfrak{l}_n\prod_{p\le n}(1-p^{-1})\ge \frac12 , 
\\
\mathcal{L}(\vec{C}(n))
  &=\mathcal{L}(\vec{\xi}(n)\mid A_n).

\end{align}
In particular, for any additive arithmetic function $\psi$,
\begin{align}
\mathcal{L}(\psi(H_n))
=
\mathcal{L}\big(
\sum_{p\le n}\psi(p^{\xi_p}) \,\big|\, A_n
\big).
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop 7 of arXiv:2606.30349

[Lemma lem:phase-pair of arXiv:2609.02544, 'A finiteness theorem for geodesic Leech wheels'] Let $\alpha,\beta,\Gamma,V>0$ with $\Gamma>V$, and set
\[
  \tau=\frac{\alpha}{2\sqrt{\Gamma-V}}.
\]
Assume also
\[
  0<\tau<\beta,
  \qquad
  \Gamma(\beta-\tau)\ge V(2\beta-\tau).
\]
If complex numbers $z,w$ satisfy
\[
  |z^2-w|\le \Gamma,
  \qquad
  |w|\le V,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
  \alpha\operatorname{Im}z+
  \beta\operatorname{Re}w
  \le
  \alpha\sqrt{\Gamma-V}+\beta V.
\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:Afbound of arXiv:2608.29657, 'Hypocoercivity of Tempered Bouncy Particle Samplers for Heavy-Tailed Targets'] Let~(ass:wpi of the paper), (ass:sigmabounds of the paper),~(ass:curvature of the paper) hold.
    For $f \in C^2_c({\mathbb R}^d \times {\mathbb R}^d)$, the following inequalities hold:
    \begin{align}
        \|{\mathcal A} f\|_{L^2(\mu_\sigma)} &\leq \frac{1}{2\sqrt m } \|f\|_{L^2(\mu_\sigma)}, \\
         \|{\mathcal L}_{\mathrm{tr}}{\mathcal A} f\|_{L^2(\mu_\sigma)} &\leq  \|f\|_{L^2(\mu_\sigma)}.

body:
[Lem 72 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have 
\begin{align*}
\sM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0) 
&\subseteq \sM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)\,,\\
\sM^{\six}(\alpha,q_0) 
&\subseteq \sM^{\sidealast}(\alpha,q_0)\,.
\end{align*}

\begin{proof}
We repeat the most relevant part of Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification} for this proof:
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tabular}[h]{r|cccccccc}
	\MSRheader\\
	\hline
	\PRFTWOdefn\\
	\PRFFOURdefn\\
	\PRFONEHALFdefn\\
	\SUPERPERFECTASTdefn
	\end{tabular}
	\end{center}
The classes only differ in the conditions on the function $p$.

    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$ where $\epsilon < 1/2$. 
    Then $\mu$ is of the form $\mu = \mu(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,p,\zeta = \delta_0)$ for some $(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta = \delta_0,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$.
    Since $p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1}, $p$ is twice differentiable and therefore continuous, and further satisfies $p(q_0) \le \epsilon$.
    So we can find $q' \in (q_0,1)$ such that $p(q') = 2\epsilon$, and define $\tilde p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ by
    \[
        \tilde p(t) = \begin{cases}
            2\epsilon (t - q_0) / (q' - q_0) & t \in [q_0,q')\,, \\
            p(t) & t \in [q',1]\,.
        \end{cases}
    \]
    In particular $\tilde p(q_0) = 0$, so $\tilde p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.5withzero}, as required for the $\sxii$ class.
    Since $p$ and $\tilde p$ agree on $[q',1]$, we have
    \[
        \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1
        = \int_{q_0}^{q'} |p'(t) - \tilde p'(t)|\,dt
        \le \int_{q_0}^{q'} (p'(t) + \tilde p'(t))\,dt
        \le p(q') + \tilde p(q')
        = 4\epsilon\,.
    \]
Recalling Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}, we have $\mu \in \cM(q_0;p,f)$ for budget function
$f(t) = (\E w_t)^2 / \alpha$. Applying
    Proposition~\ref{p:continuity.in.p} gives the existence of a measure
    \[
        \tilde\mu \in \cM(q_0;\tilde p,f)
        \subseteq \cM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)
    \]
    with $\bbW_2(\mu,\tilde \mu)^2 \le 6(1+1/\alpha) \cdot 4\epsilon$.
    Since this holds for all $\mu \in \cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$ with $\epsilon < 1/2$, we conclude
    \[
        \cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cB_{\tilde\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)\Big)
    \]
    for some $\tilde\epsilon$ tending to $0$ with $\epsilon$.
    By adjusting $\tilde\epsilon$ we can also ensure
    \[
        \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big) \subseteq \cB_{\tilde\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)\Big)\,.
    \]
 Recall \eqref{e:measure.classes.simplification.without.L0}: taking a union over $L$ and an intersection over $\epsilon$ proves the first assertion, $\sM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)$.

    The proof of the second assertion $\sM^{\six}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\sidealast}(\alpha,q_0)$ is very similar, so we only describe the differences.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\six}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$ where $\epsilon < 1/2$, realized by controls $(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta = \delta_0,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\six}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$.
    In this case $p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1concave}, so $p$ is concave in addition to the properties of condition~\ref{it:3.1} used above.
    Let $q'$ and $\tilde p$ be defined as above.
    Since $p(q_0) \ge 0$ and $p(q') = 2\epsilon$, the concavity of $p$ implies $p(t) \ge \tilde p(t)$ for all $t\in [0,q']$.
    Thus $\tilde p$ is also concave, and in particular satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.3}, as required for the $\sidealast$ class.
Then, arguing identically as above completes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 72 of arXiv:2608.29416

 \(v:=|2r-1|\).

 \item If \(\E(\eta)<\infty\) and
 \[
   \Gamma(1/\gamma)v\,
   \limsup_{n\to\infty} L(n^\gamma)
   <
   \frac{1}{2\E(\eta)},
 \]

 \item If \(\Pbb(\eta=0)<1\) and
 \[
   \Gamma(1/\gamma)v\,
   \liminf_{n\to\infty} L(n^\gamma)
   >
   \frac{1}{\E(\eta)},
 \]

 with positive probability in the direction of the drift. More precisely, the
 survival occurs to the right if \(r>1/2\), and to the left if \(r<1/2\).
 \end{enumerate}

[Theorem thm:main-simple of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] Let $D$ be a simply-connected domain and $z_1 \neq z_2 \in D$. Let $E^{\rm simp}_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)$ denote the event that the  CLE$_4$ gasket comes $\varepsilon_1$-close to $z_1$ and $\varepsilon_2$-close to $z_2$. Then we have
$$
\lim_{\max(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)\to 0}
\varepsilon_1^{-1/8}\varepsilon_2^{-1/8}
\mathbb{P}(E^{\rm simp}_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2))
=
C_1\CR(z_1,D)^{-1/8}\CR(z_2,D)^{-1/8}
\sqrt{\frac{\theta_3(q^{1/4})}{\theta_2(q^{1/4})}},
$$
where $C_1$ is an absolute constant, and the nome $q$ is uniquely determined by
$$
\exp\!\left(\pi G_D(z_1,z_2)\right)
=
\frac{\theta_3(q^{1/2})}{\theta_2(q^{1/2})}.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Two-point correlations of the simple CLE$_4$

body: [Theorem 5 of arXiv:2609.00448, 'Equivariant formality and representation theory'] Let $G$ be a compact connected Lie group and $S$ a torus subgroup, and $\pi: G/S\to\text{pt}$ be the collapsing map. Denote by $A$ the subring of $K_S^*(G/S)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ generated by $S$-equivariant line bundles $G\times_S\mathbb{C}_\mu$ where $\mu\in\mathfrak{s}^*$. Define $\mathcal{L}_S$ to be the $R(S; \mathbb{Q})$-submodule of $K_S^*(G/S)\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ generated by the odd equivariant $K$-theory classes of $G/S$ defined by the $\delta$-construction (see Definitions \ref{deltaconstruction} and \ref{equivsamelson}). Then $(G, S)$ is isotropy formal if and only if there exist $a\in A$ and $b\in\bigwedge\nolimits_{R(S; \mathbb{Q})}^{\text{rank }G-\text{rank }S}\mathcal{L}_S$ such that $\pi_*(ab)\notin I(S; \mathbb{Q})$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 5 of arXiv:2609.00448

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Let $\mathcal B$ be a field of characteristic $0$. Let $\mathcal C$ be a $\mathcal B[H]$-module. Then the following statement are equivalent.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} The  $\mathcal B[H]$-module $\mathcal C$ is rational.

\smallskip
{\bf (2)} The monic characteristic polynomial of the $\mathcal B$-linear map $\tau:\mathcal C\rightarrow \mathcal C$ belongs to $\mathbb Q[x]$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} For each $i\in\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket$, the trace of  the $\mathcal B$-linear map $\tau^i:\mathcal C\rightarrow \mathcal C$ is a rational number.

\smallskip
{\bf (4)} For each $i\in\llbracket1,p^s-1\rrbracket$, the trace of  the $\mathcal B$-linear map $\tau^i:\mathcal C\rightarrow \mathcal C$ is a rational number.

body: A function f : U -> C on an open set U in C is holomorphic if the complex derivative f'(z) = lim_{h->0} (f(z+h) - f(z))/h exists at every z in U (the limit taken over complex h). Writing f = u + iv, differentiability at z implies the Cauchy-Riemann equations u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x; conversely continuous partials satisfying Cauchy-Riemann on U give holomorphy.

body:
[Theorem 224 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider the master Riemann--Hilbert problem with sources $(D_h(z))_{h = 1}^H$. In addition, choose $\boldsymbol{\kappa} \in \amsmathbb{C}$ and rational functions $(L_h(z))_{h=1}^H$ that can have poles at $z = \alpha_h,\beta_h$ and such that $L_h(z) = O(\frac{1}{z})$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$ for each $h\in[H]$.

Then there exists a unique solution $(F_h(z))_{h = 1}^H$ to the master Riemann--Hilbert problem such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\displaystyle \left(F_h(z) - \sigma_h^{-1}(z) L_h(z) - \frac{1}{2\theta_{h,h}}D_h(z)\right)_{h = 1}^H$ is tame with exponent $1$; and
\item $\displaystyle\oint_{\gamma_h} \frac{\dd z}{2\ii\pi}\,F_h(z) = \kappa_h$ for all $h\in[H]$.
\end{enumerate}
The solution is given by the formula:
\[
F_h(z) = \sum_{g = 1}^H \big(\kappa_g \mathfrak{c}^{\textnormal{1st}}_{h;g}(z) - r(\alpha_g)\mathfrak{c}_{h;g}^{\textnormal{3rd}}(z;\alpha_g) - r(\beta_g)\mathfrak{c}^{\textnormal{3rd}}_{h;g}(\z;\beta_g)\big) - \sum_{\textnormal{J} \in \{\textnormal{I},\textnormal{II},\textnormal{III}\}} \mathfrak{F}_h^{\textnormal{J}}[\boldsymbol{f}^{\textnormal{J}}](z).
\]
The $H$-tuple of functions $\boldsymbol{f}^{\textnormal{J}}$ and the constants $(r(\alpha_g),r(\beta_g))_{g = 1}^{H}$ are determined by
\[
\forall g \in [H]\qquad f_g^{\textnormal{II}}(z) = \frac{2}{\sigma_g(z)} \int_{z}^{\infty} \frac{L_g(\zeta)}{\sigma_g(\zeta)}\dd \zeta,
\]
and the (unique up to addition of a constant to $f^{\textnormal{I}}_g$) decomposition of the source
\begin{equation}

\forall g \in [H]\qquad D_g(z) = \partial_z f^{\textnormal{I}}_g(z) + \frac{r(\alpha_g)}{z - \alpha_g} + \frac{r(\beta_g)}{z -\beta_g} + \partial_z f^{\textnormal{III}}_g(z),
\end{equation}
where the function $f_g^{\textnormal{I}}(z)$ is holomorphic in a complex neighborhood of $\overline{\amsmathbb{B}}_g$ and $f^{\textnormal{III}}_g(z)$ is a rational function with possible poles at $\alpha_g,\beta_g$ and such that $f^{\textnormal{III}}_g(z) = O(\frac{1}{z})$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 224 of arXiv:2601.16377

\[
        \varphi_p(x):=|x|^{p-2}x,
        \qquad
        \ell_p:=p\,\mb E[B^{p-1}(1-B)] .
\]
There exists \(K_p<\infty\) such that, for all \(a,b\in\mb R\),
\begin{equation*}
        \mb E|Ba+(1-B)b|^p
        \le
        \frac{m(p)}2(|a|^p+|b|^p)
        +
        \ell_p\{\varphi_p(a)b+\varphi_p(b)a\}
        +
        K_p|ab|^{p/2}.
\end{equation*}

[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2609.03875, 'Measure theory without infinities'] Let $\mathcal Q$ be a $\delta$-ring. Then the following statements hold:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item [(i)] Let $B\in\mathcal Q$ and $\mb A\colon I\to \mathcal Q$ be a countable family such that $\mb A(i)\subset B$ for all $i\in I$. Then $\bigcup_{i\in I} \mb A(i) \in \mathcal Q$.
  \item [(ii)] $\sigma(\mathcal Q) = \sigma_0(\mathcal{Q})$.
  \item [(iii)] If $A\in \sigma(\mathcal Q)$ and $A\subset B$ for some $B\in \mathcal Q$, then $A\in \mathcal Q$.
  \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Prop log-concave of arXiv:2605.10908, 'On Talagrand's Convexity Conjecture'] Let $\mu=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{m} p_i \delta_{x_i}$ be a finitely supported centered probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $\nu$ be a centered  probability measure  on $\mathbb{R}^n$ absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, and with finite first moments. Assume that $\mu\preceq_{\text{cx}}\nu$.
    Then there exists a natural bijection between the set of martingale couplings $(X,Y)$ of $\mu$ and $\nu$, and the collection $\mathcal{C}$ of tuples of nonnegative functions $(f_1,\ldots, f_m)$ (defined up to $\nu$-null sets) where the $f_{i} \colon \mathbb{R}^{n} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $$ \sum\limits_{i=1}^{m}p_if_i(x)=1,\ \mathbb{E}\left[f_i(Y)\right]=1,\ \mathbb{E} \left[Yf_i(Y)\right]=x_i.$$ 

 Moreover, we have $X\preceq_{\text{cx}}(1-\varepsilon) Y$ for some $\varepsilon>0$ if and only if there exist $(f_1^*,\ldots, f_m^*)$ in $\mathcal{C}$ such that each $f_i^*$ is of the form
 $$f_i^*(x)=\dfrac{e^{U_i+\langle V_i,x\rangle}}{\sum\limits_{j=1}^{m} p_j e^{U_j+\langle V_j,x\rangle}}$$
 for some $U_i\in \mathbb{R},\ V_i\in \mathbb{R}^n$. Note that each $f_i^*$ is log-concave. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Prop 2 of arXiv:2411.06571, 'Moment-based approach for two erratic KPZ scaling limits'] Let $\tilde Z_{s,t}(x,y)$ be the continuous modification from Proposition (mr0 of the paper). Fix some $x,s\in \Bbb R$. Then for all $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\Bbb R)$ the process $$M_t(\phi) := (\tilde Z_{s,t}(x,\bullet),\phi)_{L^2(\Bbb R)}-\frac12 \int_s^t (\tilde Z_{s,u}(x,\bullet),\phi'')_{L^2(\Bbb R)}du,\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; t\ge s$$ is a continuous martingale in the filtration $(\mathcal F_{s,t})_{t\ge s}$ where $\mathcal F_{s,t}:=\sigma(\tilde Z_{a,b}(x,y): s<a<b<t,x,y\in\Bbb R\}$. The quadratic variations are furthermore given by $$\langle M(\phi)\rangle_t = \int_s^t (\tilde Z_{s,u}(x,\bullet)^2 , \phi^2)_{L^2(\Bbb R)} du.$$

body: TYPEWRITER (L^p convergence does not imply almost-everywhere convergence). On [0,1] write n = 2^k + j with 0 <= j < 2^k and let f_n be the indicator of [j 2^{-k}, (j+1) 2^{-k}). Then ||f_n||_p^p = 2^{-k} -> 0, so f_n -> 0 in L^p for every p < infinity and in measure. But for every x in [0,1) and every k there is exactly one j with f_{2^k + j}(x) = 1, so f_n(x) equals 1 for infinitely many n and 0 for infinitely many n: the sequence converges at NO point. This is why one extracts an a.e. convergent subsequence rather than hoping for the full sequence. SLIDING BUMP (pointwise convergence does not imply L^1 convergence). On [0,1] let g_n = n 1_{(0, 1/n)}. Then g_n(x) -> 0 for every x in (0,1], indeed the convergence is pointwise everywhere on (0,1], yet integral g_n = 1 for every n. The mass does not disappear, it concentrates. The dominated convergence theorem excludes exactly this: no integrable g dominates all g_n, since any such g would satisfy g >= n on (0,1/n) for every n, forcing integral_{(0,1/n)} g >= 1 for all n and contradicting absolute continuity of the integral. ESCAPING MASS is the third, distinct failure and lives on infinite measure spaces: h_n = 1_{[n, n+1]} on R is uniformly bounded, converges to 0 everywhere, and has ||h_n||_1 = 1. Three different mechanisms, three different repairs: a subsequence, a dominating function, and a tightness condition. [standard; the typewriter sequence is sometimes attributed to Kolmogorov]

For complex matrices A (n by n) and B (m by m), S(X) = AX - XB on n by m matrices X, and the Frobenius separation is sep_F(A, B) = min over ||X||_F = 1 of ||AX - XB||_F. If A and B are normal, sep_F(A, B) = min over lambda in spec A and mu in spec B of |lambda - mu|. Repeated eigenvalues within A or within B are allowed; only overlap between the two spectra makes the separation vanish.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: For a stationary occupation field with covariance c(z), $\mathrm{Var}(S_B)=\sum_z c(z)|B\cap(B-z)|$. If $\sum_z c(z)=0$ and $\sum_z |z|_1|c(z)|<\infty$, a cube of side L satisfies $\mathrm{Var}(S_B)\le C_d L^{d-1}\sum_z|z|_1|c(z)|$. Subtract |B| times the zero sum, then bound the lost overlap by $C_d L^{d-1}\min(|z|_1,L)$. This would give the desired exponent d-1, including bounded variance when d=1. Check: Expand the variance as a double sum of covariances and count ordered pairs with displacement z. For a cube the overlap equals the product of (L-|z_i|)_+, verifying the geometric bound directly. Obstruction: Neither the infinite-volume covariance cancellation nor the weighted absolute summability is proved for ARW. Finite-torus conservation gives a zero sum at each size but does not justify interchanging that sum with the infinite-volume limit.

[Theorem thm:dependency_encoding of arXiv:2604.18558, 'Uniform analyticity of local observables in FK-percolation and analyticity of the Ising sp'] Let $(d,p,q) \in \mathcal G_{\mathsf{FK}}$. 
Then there exists $L_0 > 0$ such that for any $L \geq L_0$, there exists a probability measure $\mathbb P$ on $  \{0,1\}^{E(\mathbb T_N)} \times (\mathsf{P}^L_N)^{\mathbb T_N^L}$ satisfying the following properties.
When $(\omega, (\mathcal C_x)_{x \in \mathbb T_N^L})  \sim \mathbb P$, then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\omega$ is distributed according to $\phi_{\mathbb T_N,p}$.
\item For any $x\in\mathbb T_N^L$, $\mathcal C_x$ contains $x$. 
\item For any $\Delta_1, \Delta_2 \subset \mathbb T_N^L$, any $F,G$ functions of $\omega$ supported on $\Delta_1$ and $\Delta_2$ respectively and any $C_1 \supset \Delta_1, C_2 \supset \Delta_2$ such that $C_1 \cap C_2 = \emptyset$, then
\[
\mathbb P[F(\omega)G(\omega) \ind{\mathcal C_{\Delta_1} = C_1} \ind{\mathcal C_{\Delta_2 = C_2}} ] = \mathbb P[F(\omega)\ind{\mathcal C_{\Delta_1} = C_1} ] \mathbb P[G(\omega)\ind{\mathcal C_{\Delta_2 = C_2}} ],
\]
where we call $\mathcal C_\Delta \coloneqq  \bigcup_{x\in\Delta}\mathcal C_x$. 
\item There exist two sequences $\tilde c_L, c_L > 0$ going to infinity when $L$ goes to infinity such that, for any $x \in \mathbb T_N^L$ and any $n \in \mathbb Z_{> 0}$, 
\[  \mathbb P[|\mathcal C_x| \geq n] \leq \tilde c_L\exp(-c_L n). \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In statistics, Gibbs sampling or a Gibbs sampler, also known in statistical mechanics as the heat bath algorithm, is a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm for sampling from a specified multivariate probability distribution when direct sampling from the joint distribution is difficult, but sampling from the conditional distribution is more practical. This sequence can be used to approximate the joint distribution ; to approximate the marginal distribution of one of the variables, or some subset of the variables ; or to compute an integral. Typically, some of the variables correspond to observations whose values are known, and hence do not need to be sampled.

A spanning rooted forest is a spanning forest with one chosen root in each tree; its weight is t^|E(F)| prod_{e in F} w_e (so an unrooted forest with trees T_1, ..., T_k counts prod |T_i| times). Z(t) is the total weight of spanning rooted forests, and Q_t = (I + tL)^-1. Draw a spanning rooted forest with probability proportional to its weight. Let X be a normed space with dual X* carrying the weak-star topology sigma(X*, X). Then the closed unit ball B of X* is metrizable in the relative weak-star topology if and only if X is separable; in that case every bounded subset of X* is weak-star metrizable, and a compatible metric is d(f,g) = sum over n of 2^(-n) min(1, |f(x_n) - g(x_n)|) for any dense sequence (x_n) of the unit sphere of X. Combined with Banach-Alaoglu (B is weak-star compact), separability of X gives that B is weak-star compact and metrizable, hence weak-star SEQUENTIALLY compact: every bounded sequence in X* has a weak-star convergent subsequence. The dual statement also holds: for a Banach space X, the closed unit ball of X is metrizable in the weak topology sigma(X, X*) if and only if X* is separable. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) 'bounded' is essential - the weak-star topology on ALL of X* is metrizable only when X is finite dimensional; indeed if it were metrizable with countable base (U_m) at 0 and X is infinite dimensional, each U_m contains a nonzero subspace (it is cut out by finitely many functionals), so one can pick f_m in U_m with ||f_m|| >= m, and then f_m converges weak-star to 0 while being unbounded, contradicting the uniform boundedness principle; (b) the two directions are not interchangeable - separability of X does not imply separability of X*: X = l^1 is separable, so B of (l^1)* = l^infinity is weak-star metrizable, but (l^1)* = l^infinity is not separable, so the unit ball of l^1 is NOT weakly metrizable; (c) the metric above is not translation-invariantly compatible on the whole of X* and the equivalence is genuinely a statement about the relative topology on bounded sets; (d) for X = l^infinity, which is not separable, the unit ball of (l^infinity)* is weak-star compact but not weak-star metrizable, and weak-star compactness there is not sequential compactness.
X is a normed space (Banach for the uniform boundedness step in the failure remark and for the dual statement)
X* is the topological dual with the weak-star topology sigma(X*, X)
B is the closed unit ball of X*, or any bounded weak-star closed subset - the equivalence concerns bounded sets only
for the dual statement (weak metrizability of the ball of X iff X* separable), X is Banach

[Theorem 2 (Sampling active subspaces~\protect{\cite[Thm.~3.7) of arXiv:2604.27119, '\Large Applied Random Matrix Theory\relatedversion'] {Con15:Active-Subspaces}}]
Let $f : \R^d \to \R$ be $L$-Lipschitz and differentiable.
As in~\cref{eqn:sensitivity-matrix,eqn:empirical-sensitivity},
consider the sensitivity matrix $\mtx{\Sigma} \in \Sym_d(\R)$
and the empirical approximation $\widehat{\mtx{\Sigma}}_n \in \Sym_d(\R)$
determined by $n$ gradient samples.  The expectation of the relative approximation error satisfies
\[
\Expect\left[ \frac{ \norm{ \widehat{\mtx{\Sigma}}_n - \mtx{\Sigma} }}{\norm{\mtx{\Sigma}}} \right]
	\leq \sqrt{2\beta_n} + \frac{1}{3} \beta_n
	\quad\text{where}\quad
	\beta_n \coloneqq \frac{L^2 \log(2d)}{\norm{\mtx{\Sigma}}} \cdot \frac{1}{n}.

\]
For $\eps \in (0,1)$, the sample complexity $n \geq 4\eps^{-2} L^2 \log(2d) / \norm{\mtx{\Sigma}}$
results in expected relative error at most $\eps$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2606.02036, 'Self-intersection local times for Volterra Gaussian processes in stochastic flows with int'] A centred Gaussian process $\{u(t) : t\in[0,1]\}$ is called a Volterra Gaussian process, if  it admits the representation
$
u(t) = 

\int^t_0k(t,s)\differential{w(s)},
$ for each $t\in(0,1]$, 
where $k\in L^2([0,1]^2)$ is a Volterra kernel, i.e., 
$k(t,s)=0$  for all $s>t$, and 
$
\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\int^t_0k(t,s)^2 \differential{s}<\infty. 
$
title: Definition 5 of arXiv:2606.02036

body: A probability distribution \mu with characteristic function \phi is said to be self-decomposable (or belonging to Lévy's class L) if for every c \in (0, 1), there exists a characteristic function \phi_c such that \phi(t) = \phi(ct) \phi_c(t) for all t \in \mathbb{R}. body:
[Lem 149 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $(b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered}. 
Fix any vectors $\bx^{\dagger,0},\prxbx^{\dagger,0}\in\bbR^M$, and let $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ be the centered IAMP specified by Definition~\ref{d:centered.iamp}. 
Then, for $C\equiv C(L,\epsilon,\delta)$, 
there exists a $C$-Lipschitz map $\cA^\dagger$ which agrees
with $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ with probability $1-\exp(-cN)$, and satisfies
	    \[
    \cA(-\bG,-\bg^\aux)
    =
    -\cA(\bG,\bg^\aux)\,.
    \]
In particular, it follows that $\bbE[\cA(\bG,\bg^{\aux})~|~\bx^{\dagger,0},\prxbx^{\dagger,0}]=\bzero\in\bbR^N$.
\begin{proof}
    Let $(\hat\by^{\dagger,k},\hat\prxby^{\dagger,k},\hat\bx^{\dagger,k},\hat\prxbx^{\dagger,k})$ be the IAMP iterates corresponding to $(-\bG,- \bg^{\aux})$.
    We claim that for all $0\leq k\leq \ubl$ we have
    \begin{align*}
    (\hat\prxby,\hat\by,\hat\bu,\hat\bw)^{\dagger,k}
    &=
    (-\prxby,-\by,-\bu,\bw)^{\dagger,k}
      \,\\
    (\hat\prxbx,\hat\bx,\hat\bv,
    \hat\bm,\hat\bsig,\hat\bb)^{\dagger,k}
    &=
    (\prxbx,\bx,\bv,
    \bm,\bsig,\bb)^{\dagger,k}\,.
    \end{align*}
Indeed, the base case for the first statement above holds easily since
$w$ is even by the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} \eqref{i:IAMP-main-centered}, the functions
 $\psi$ and $\prxpsi$ are odd (Lemma~\ref{lem:even-manual-init}), 
the vectors $(\by,\prxby,\hat{\by},\hat{\prxby})^{\dagger,0}$ are defined by \eqref{eq:mean-0-initialization},  and  we defined $\bu^{\dagger,0}=\hat{\bu}^{\dagger,0}=\bzero\in\R^M$.
The remaining statements follow by 
induction, using the formulas \eqref{eq:proxy-y-amp-def}--\eqref{eq:x-amp-def}. 

The above shows the desired symmetry for the mapping $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$, and we must now transfer it to $\cA^\dagger$. This proceeds similarly as in the \hyperlink{proof:t.IAMP.main.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}}, using the Kirzsbraun extension theorem, except that we now need to ensure that the symmetry requirement is satisfied. 
First, we have by easy induction that $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ is $C$-Lipschitz on a subset $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}\subseteq \bbR^{MN+N_{\aux}}$, similarly to the \hyperlink{proof:t.IAMP.main.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}}. To be precise, 
    \[\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}
    =\bigg\{
    \begin{array}{c}
    (\bG,\bg^\aux) : 
    \textup{$\bG_\circ$
    satisfies \eqref{eq:Brownian-bridge-condition},
    $\|\bG\|_\textup{op}\le C_0
    (M^{1/2}+N^{1/2})$,}\\
    \textup{$\|\bar\bg^{\ell}\|\leq 2\sqrt{N}$
    for all $0\le\ell\le\ubl$, and
    $\|\bar\bg^{\init}\|\leq 2\sqrt{N}$}
    \end{array}
    \bigg\}\,.
    \]
In particular, this choice of $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}$ is origin-symmetric. 
(Again, see e.g.\ the discussion on ``standard optimization algorithms'' in \cite{HuangSellke2021} for the Lipschitz bound on such a domain.)

Thus, let $S=\{\bg_1,\bg_2,\dots\}$ be a countable dense set in $\bbR^{MN+N_{\aux}}$.
    For each $\bg_i$, we assume $\tilde\cA^{\dagger}$ has been extended to a $C$-Lipschitz function on $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}\equiv \mathcal{U}^{\dagger}\cup \{\bg_1,-\bg_1,\dots,\bg_i,-\bg_i\}$.
    Then by the Kirzsbraun extension theorem, there exists a $C$-Lipschitz extension to $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}\cup \{\bg_{i+1}\}$.
    Since 
  $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}$ is symmetric,  
the unique odd extension to $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i+1}$ is still $C$-Lipschitz. Continuing in this way yields a $C$-Lipschitz extension to $ \mathcal{U}^\dagger\cup S\cup -S$. This set is dense by definition of $S$, so the result follows by continuously extending to all of $\R^{MN+N_{\aux}}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 149 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Proposition prop_prop_SL of arXiv:2603.26307, '\LARGE The incompressible Navier--Stokes--Fourier system with thermal noise'] Let Assumption (Ass:noise of the paper) hold, $(\Omega,\mathfrak{A},\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space equipped with a filtration $\mathscr{F}$ satisfying the usual conditions and $3$-dimensional standard $\mathscr{F}$-Brownian motions $(W_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$ and $3\times 3$-matrix valued $\mathscr{F}$-Brownian motions $(B_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$ with covariance structure (equation Eq_noise_matrix_covariation of the paper) be independent. Moreover, we let  $U\colon [0,\tau ) \to C^1(\mathbb{T}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ and $\Psi\colon [0,\tau )\to  C^1(\mathbb{T}^3)$ be continuous, adapted processes, defined up to a stopping time $\tau>0$, such that for a strictly increasing localizing sequence $0\le \tau_j\nearrow \tau $ properties (equation Item_pos_Phi of the paper) and (equation Item_U_eq of the paper) of Definition (defi_strong_sol of the paper) holds. 
	Then, $(U,\Psi)$ is a local strong solution to (equation Eq_new_var of the paper), 
	iff the temperature $\Theta = \Psi^2/2$ satisfies the following for any $j\in \mathbb N$:
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)']
		\setcounter{enumi}{2}
		\item 
		For every $\eta\in C^{{\infty}}( \mathbb{T}^3)$ it holds
		\begin{align}\begin{split}
				&
				\int_{\mathbb{T}^3} \Theta_t \eta \, \mathrm{d} x \,-\, \int_{\mathbb{T}^3} \Theta_0 \eta \, \mathrm{d} x \,=\, \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3}\eta \bigl((1+F_1/2)
				|\nabla_\mathrm{sym} U|^2 - F_1|\nabla \sqrt{\Theta}|^2\bigr) \, \mathrm{d} x \,\mathrm{d} s
				\\&\qquad+\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3} - \bigl(1+ {F_1}/2 +G_1/2\bigr)  \nabla \Theta \cdot \nabla  \eta \,+\,\Theta U\cdot \nabla \eta \,-\, F_2 \Theta \eta \,\mathrm{d} x\,\mathrm{d} s
				\\&\qquad + \sum_{i=1}^3
				\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}^3}\int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{T}^3} 
				\Theta g_n \partial_i \eta  
				\,\mathrm{d} x \, \mathrm{d} W_{n,s}^i
				\,-\, \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}^3}\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb{T}^3}\eta f_n \sqrt{\Theta} \nabla U\,\mathrm{d} x :\mathrm{d} B_{n,s},
			\end{split}
		\end{align} for all $t\in [0,\tau_j ]$, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely.
	\end{enumerate}

[Definition 16 of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] A \textbf{Navier--Stokes triple} \((\mathscr F,\chi,\mathscr B)\) is called \textbf{admissible} provided the following \textbf{invariant-domain property} holds for each of the two associated Einstein--Navier--Stokes models 
\eqref{eq:pot-production-system} and \eqref{eq:pot-dissipated-system}, as follows. 

Let \(\{\Sigma_t\}_{t_0\leq t<t_1}\) be a spacelike foliation of a compact spacetime slab, and let \((g,\beta,\zeta)\) be a regular solution of the corresponding hyperbolic evolution-constraint system\footnote{A gauge must be chosen to deal with the spacetime metric and formulate a well-posed initial value problem; this is a standard topic, not reviewed here \cite{Choquet-book}.} on \([t_0,t_1)\). Assume that
\be
\zeta(t_0,\Sigma_{t_0})\subset\mathcal K_0
\qquad\text{for some closed fiber subset }\mathcal K_0\Subset\mathscr F.
\ee
Then one has
\be
\zeta(t,\Sigma_t)\subset\mathscr F
\qquad\text{for every }t_0\leq t<t_1.
\ee
Moreover, if the fields admit a continuous limit in the ambient bundles as \(t\uparrow t_1\), while the nonsingular coefficients in the equation for~\(\zeta\) remain bounded, then the terminal relaxing field satisfies
\be
\zeta(t_1,\Sigma_{t_1})\subset\mathscr F,
\ee
rather than merely taking its values in~\(\overline{\mathscr F}\). Equivalently, the constitutive boundary~\(\del\mathscr F\) cannot be the first cause of breakdown of a regular solution.

body: [Theorem 3.6 of arXiv:2210.03711, 'Matrix tree theorem for the net Laplacian matrix of a signed graph'] Let G be a simple connected signed graph on n ≥2 vertices 1, 2, . . . , n with the net Laplacian matrix L±. Then for each i = 1, 2, . . . , n, det(L±(i)) is the number of positive spanning trees minus the number of negative spanning trees of G.

[Theorem 14 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider an off-critical ensemble \eqref{eq_measure_general_intro} with fixed filling fractions. There exists functions $\mathcal{F}_{h_1,h_2}(z_1,z_2)$ indexed by $h_1,h_2 \in [H]$ depending only on $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ and the endpoints of the bands, and having the following properties. First $\mathcal{F}_{h_1,h_2}(z_1,z_2) = \mathcal{F}_{h_2,h_1}(z_2,z_1)$. Second, for any $h_1,h_2 \in [H]$, any $x_1$ in bands of $[\hat{a}_{h_1},\hat{b}_{h_1}]$ and $z_2$ away from bands, we have
\[
\theta_{h_1,h_1}\big(\mathcal{F}_{h_1,h_2}(x_1^+,z_2) + \mathcal{F}_{h_1,h_2}(x_1^-,z_2)\big) + \sum_{g \neq h_1} 2\theta_{h_1,g}\,\mathcal{F}_{g,h_2}(x_1,z_2) = - \frac{\delta_{h_1,h_2}}{(x_1 - z_2)^2}.
\]
Third, for an analytic function $f$ near the bands, we have as $\N \rightarrow \infty$
\[
\amsmathbb{E}\big[(\Delta\textnormal{\textsf{Lin}}[f])^2\big] = \sum_{h_1,h_2 = 1}^{H} \oint_{\gamma_{h_1}}\oint_{\gamma_{h_2}} \frac{\dd z_1 \dd z_2}{(2\ii\pi)^2} \,\mathcal{F}_{h_1,h_2}(z_1,z_2)\,f(z_1)f(z_2) + o(1).
\]
where the contour $\gamma_h$ surrounds the $h$-th band. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 14 of arXiv:2601.16377

Let Omega in R^n be open and u in L^1_loc(Omega) satisfy integral_Omega u (Laplacian of phi) dx = 0 for every phi in C_c^infinity(Omega). Then u agrees almost everywhere with a function that is harmonic, hence real-analytic, in Omega. More generally, if P is a linear differential operator with smooth coefficients that is elliptic (nonvanishing principal symbol), then every distributional solution of Pu = f with f smooth is smooth; ellipticity, not any a priori regularity of u, is what does the work.
Omega open in R^n
u in L^1_loc(Omega)
integral u times Laplacian of phi vanishes for all phi in C_c^infinity(Omega) (u is harmonic in the sense of distributions)

Let U subset R^d be an open set and let {K_n}_{n=1}^infinity be an increasing sequence of closed subsets of U with Union_{n} K_n = U, such that for each n there exists an open precompact set K_tilde_n with K_n subset K_tilde_n subset U. Consider the autonomous SDE dX_t = mu(X_t) dt + sigma(X_t) dW_t where mu, sigma are locally Lipschitz on U. For example, with Bayes' theorem, the probability that a patient has a disease given that they tested positive for that disease can be found using the probability that the test yields a positive result when the disease is present. The theorem was developed in the 18th century by Bayes and independently by Pierre-Simon Laplace.

[Corollary 5 (Time-uniform probability estimate for the mixed example) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] In the setting of Proposition~\ref{prop:mixed-brownian-error}, assume $x_0=\wt x_0$ and $\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}<1$. Then, for every $h>0$,
\[
  \mathbb P\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-\wt X_t|>h\right)
  \le
  \frac{C}{h^{\alpha-1}}
  \|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  \mathbb P\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}>h\right)
  \le
  \frac{C}{h}
  \|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}}.
\]
The constant is independent of $h$ and $r$; for $0<\lambda<1$ it can be chosen uniformly in $\lambda$.

For iid Exp(1) edge weights on undirected nearest-neighbor Z^2, let T_n be the passage time from (0,0) to (n,0), n>=1, and sigma_n^2=Var(T_n)>0. Enumerate all edges, let F_k be the first-k-edge sigma-field with trivial F_0, M_{n,k}=E[T_n|F_k]-E T_n, D_{n,k}=M_{n,k}-M_{n,k-1}, and Q_{n,k}=sum_{j<=k} D_{n,j}^2. Uniform boundedness of E|T_n-E T_n|^4/sigma_n^4 is equivalent up to factor 81 to uniform boundedness of E Q_{n,k}^2/sigma_n^4 over n,k. If V_{n,k}=sum_{j<=k} E[D_{n,j}^2|F_{j-1}] satisfies E V_{n,k}^2<=a sigma_n^4 and sum_{j<=k} E D_{n,j}^4<=b sigma_n^4 uniformly for finite a,b>=0, then E|T_n-E T_n|^4<=81(sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))^2 sigma_n^4. These lattice estimates are hypotheses, not established facts.

Exact remaining lattice condition and a predictable criterion

In the original specialization, T_n is the undirected nearest-neighbor passage time from (0,0) to (n,0) in Z^2 with iid Exp(1) edge weights. Enumerate the countably many edges, let F_k be the sigma-field generated by the first k weights, and set

    M_{n,k}=E[T_n | F_k]-E T_n,
    D_{n,k}=M_{n,k}-M_{n,k-1},
    sigma_n^2=Var(T_n),
    Q_{n,k}=sum_{j<=k} D_{n,j}^2.

Use a trivial F_0. T_n has finite fourth moment, since it is nonnegative and bounded above by the weight of the straight n-edge path. Its variance is positive: the minimum of the four weights incident to the starting vertex is a lower bound with unbounded support, while the straight-path upper bound is finite. Thus T_n cannot be almost surely constant. The endpoint is distinct for n>=1.

The following two conditions are equivalent up to universal constants:

    G: sup_n E|T_n-E T_n|^4 / sigma_n^4 < infinity;
    Q: sup_{n,k} E Q_{n,k}^2 / sigma_n^4 < infinity.

If G holds with constant K, conditional Jensen and the reverse inequality in L6 give Q with constant 81K. If Q holds with constant C, the forward inequality in L6 gives E M_{n,k}^4<=81C sigma_n^4. Moreover M_{n,k} converges to T_n-E T_n in the L^4 norm. To justify this step, cylinder random variables measurable with respect to some F_j are dense in L^4(F_infinity); conditional expectation is an L^4 contraction. Approximating T_n-E T_n by such a variable X gives, for k>=j,

    ||E[T_n-E T_n | F_k]-(T_n-E T_n)||_4
      <= 2 ||X-(T_n-E T_n)||_4.

T_n is F_infinity-measurable because it is an infimum over a countable collection of finite-path sums. The displayed approximation therefore proves the asserted convergence. Taking k to infinity yields G with constant 81C.

For a concrete sufficient criterion put

    v_{n,j}=E[D_{n,j}^2 | F_{j-1}],
    V_{n,k}=sum_{j<=k} v_{n,j}.

Suppose fixed finite constants a,b>=0 satisfy, uniformly in n,k,

    E V_{n,k}^2 <= a sigma_n^4,
    sum_{j<=k} E D_{n,j}^4 <= b sigma_n^4.

Then G holds with constant 81(sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))^2. Proof: the differences D_{n,j}^2-v_{n,j} form an L^2 martingale difference sequence. Orthogonality and conditional expectation give the exact identity

    E(Q_{n,k}-V_{n,k})^2
      = sum_{j<=k} (E D_{n,j}^4-E v_{n,j}^2)
      <= sum_{j<=k} E D_{n,j}^4.

Minkowski now bounds ||Q_{n,k}||_2 by ||V_{n,k}||_2 plus the square root of the jump-fourth-moment sum. Apply L6 and L^4 convergence. All uses of orthogonality concern actual martingale differences; no conditional probabilities are multiplied.

This criterion has not been verified for lattice FPP. The comparison Q<=>G is a reformulation of the missing moment estimate, not a proof that it holds. Unconditional identities E Q_{n,k}=E V_{n,k}=E M_{n,k}^2<=sigma_n^2 are insufficient to bound the required second moments of Q or V. The variance denominator here is that of the full T_n, not that of a truncated martingale.

## Counterexample to replacing the square-function second moment by its mean

Let 0<p<=1, B be Bernoulli(p), and epsilon be an independent symmetric sign. Use F_0 trivial, F_1=sigma(B), F_2=sigma(B,epsilon), and M_0=M_1=0, M_2=B epsilon/sqrt(p). This is a martingale with variance 1. Nonetheless

    Q_2=V_2=B/p,
    E Q_2=E V_2=1,
    E Q_2^2=E V_2^2=E M_2^4=1/p.

Thus the needed bound can fail arbitrarily badly even for two independent input variables and a two-step Doob martingale. Independence of the inputs does not make the conditional variance budget deterministic. [Lemma prop:geodesics_intersect of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] It is almost surely the case that the following is true. Let $P_n\colon [0,T_n]\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a sequence of $D_h$-geodesics converging to some $D_h$-geodesic $P \colon [ 0 , T]\rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ as $n \to \infty$ in the Hausdorff sense with respect to $D_h$. Let $0<s<t<T$. Then, given $\varepsilon>0$, for all $n$ large enough, we have at least one of the following:
  \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
  \item  $d_H^1(P\lvert_{[s,t]},P_n\lvert_{[s,t]})\leq \varepsilon$,
  \item  $P\lvert_{[s,t]}\cap P_n\lvert_{[s,t]} \neq \emptyset$.
  \end{enumerate}
title: Lemma prop:geodesics_intersect of arXiv:2512.09219

[Proposition 28 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] For any $r > 0$, the tail event $\{ T_{m, p} \geq r \}$ has the following
  upper bound:
  \begin{align*}
      \PP(T_{m, p} \geq r)
      &\leq 2 - 2 
      \binom{m\exp(1/r)}{m}^{-1}
      (1-p)^m\\
      &\phantom{{} \leq 2 - 2} \times
      \left[
      1 - \int_0^1 p \, m
      \left(1-x\right)^{m\exp(1/r)-m}
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx
      \right]^{-1}.
  \end{align*}
  \begin{proof}
    Since $T_{m, p}$ is non-negative,
    we can invoke a common bound from \cite[p.~126]{kallenberg2021probability},
    namely $\PP(T_{m,p} \geq r) \leq 2\left(1 - M_{T_{m,p}}(-1/r)\right)$.
    Substitute Lemma \ref{thm:factored mgf}.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 16 (Full convergence of a fixed anchored finite-time Hopf profile) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Under the hypotheses of Corollary~\ref{cor:hopf}, fix the oriented
normal gauge and the material anchor introduced above, and let
\(\widetilde\gamma_t\) be the anchored constant-speed profile
\eqref{eq:anchored-gauge}.  Set
\begin{equation}
 
 C_{\mathrm g}:=\left(\frac2\pi+64\right)^{1/2}.
\end{equation}
Then, for \(0\leq s<t<T\),
\begin{equation}
 
 \|\widetilde\gamma_t-\widetilde\gamma_s\|_{L^2(\Sph^1)}
 \leq
 \frac{C_{\mathrm g}}{\sqrt\pi}
 \sqrt{(t-s)\bigl(W(s)-W(t)\bigr)} .
\end{equation}
There are an embedded regular constant-speed curve
\(\gamma_T\in W^{2,2}(\Sph^1,\Sph^2)\cap C^1(\Sph^1,\Sph^2)\)
and a number \(L_T\in[\pi,8]\) such that, as \(t\nearrow T\),
\begin{align}
 \widetilde\gamma_t&\rightharpoonup\gamma_T
 &&\text{weakly in }W^{2,2}(\Sph^1,\R^3),\\
 \widetilde\gamma_t&\longrightarrow\gamma_T
 &&\text{strongly in }W^{1,2}(\Sph^1,\R^3),\\
 \widetilde\gamma_t&\longrightarrow\gamma_T
 &&\text{strongly in }C^{1,\alpha}(\Sph^1,\R^3),
   \quad 0<\alpha<\tfrac12,\\
 L(\widetilde\gamma_t)&\longrightarrow L_T=L(\gamma_T),
 \qquad |\partial_x\gamma_T|=L_T .
\end{align}
The trace of \(\gamma_T\) is the embedded \(C^1\) profile
\(\pi(\spt\Var_T)\) of the unique limiting Hopf torus.
title: Full convergence of a fixed anchored finite-time Hopf profile

body:
Suppose one-way functions exist. For any measurement count m>d^0.01, Gupta et al. establish a family of 10-well-modeled distributions over R^d and normalized linear measurement models Y=A X+eta with m measurements, ||A||_op<=1 and independent eta~N(0,beta^2 I_m), beta=Theta(1/(log d)^2), for which (1/10,1/10)-posterior sampling requires superpolynomial time in d. Well-modeled and posterior sampling have exactly the meanings of the two companion definition cards. In particular the approximation guarantee is a typical-measurement coupling guarantee; the shrinking noise parameter is a standard deviation, not a variance. The result supplies priors with efficient approximate smoothed-score representations despite computationally hard posterior sampling. It does not assert this lower bound under a dimension-independent noise level or under log-concavity, and gives no general unit-cost exact-score-oracle lower bound.
Existence of one-way functions in the standard asymptotic computational sense
m>d^0.01 and sufficiently large dimension d
10-well-modeled prior; normalized linear observation as in the source
posterior approximation and its two failure levels as in Definitions1.2 and1.5

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT. Status: proof (unaudited), C023 v2; independent audit and novelty assessment pending. Gaussian input, unit teacher u, fixed positive outer weights, activation sigma=sqrt(A)He2/sqrt(2)+sqrt(B)He3/sqrt(6), and zero temperature. For d>=4, 1/2<=a<1, 0<=p<1, define n=d-1, ell=1-p, q=1-a^2, J=n(1+a^3)-3aq, D=aJ+q, A=3D/(3D+2dq), B=1-A, s=q/J. The law rho*=p delta_u+ell times the uniform latitude u.w=-a has an attracting basin among axial laws with fixed pole mass p. Put W=-na(1+a^2+4a^3-2a^5)+6a^2q^2, Lf=ell*q*(6BJ/n)*(s-a), Lc=ell*(6B/n)*W, gamma=min(-Lf,-Lc)>0. For initial ring overlap -a+h, set N0=|Eh|+||h-Eh||infinity. If N0<=min((1-a)/2,gamma/(3072ell)), then Nt<=N0 exp(-gamma*t/2), and the spherical laws converge in W2 to rho*. The collective rate Lc includes the changing moment feedback; Lf is only the frozen-field rate. The exact factorization W=-(n-3)a(1+a^2+4a^3-2a^5)-3a[(1-a)^2+4a^3(2-a^2)] proves negativity. A polynomial Frechet remainder gives Dini derivative N'<=-gamma*N+1536ell*N^2. This is a local zero-temperature basin with fixed pole mass. It supplies neither uniform-start reachability nor a noisy escape-time lower bound, and does not assert a local risk minimum in unrestricted W2 topology. Exact algebra checks are supplemental; the Lean attempt is runtime-unverified.

Let (X_n)_{n=1}^\infty be i.i.d. strictly positive inter-arrival times with finite mean \mu = \mathbb{E}[X_1] \in (0, \infty). Let S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n X_k with S_0 = 0, and define the renewal counting process N(t) = \sup\{n \ge 0 : S_n \le t\}. Let m(t) = \mathbb{E}[N(t)] be the renewal function. Then \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{m(t)}{t} = \frac{1}{\mu}.
(X_n) i.i.d., X_n > 0

body: FIRES WHEN a paper states a clean iff and credits it to an earlier short note, especially one in another language, and you are about to record the problem as resolved in the literature. WHAT HAPPENED: Ganikhodjaev and Zanin, arXiv:1205.3841 (2012, Russian), state as Theorem 1 that the Volterra operator on S^2 is non-ergodic if and only if a, b, c are nonzero and of one sign, attributing the condition to their 2004 note (Russian Math. Surveys 59:3, 571-572) whose TITLE announces only a necessary condition. An intermediate pass of this campaign recorded the problem as RESOLVED IN THE LITERATURE on that basis. Reading the 2004 note in full (Mathnet) shows it proves ONLY the necessary condition; the sufficiency was not there and had to be proved - see the E0061 result node. CONDITION OF FAILURE: an attribution chain read from the citing paper rather than from the cited one. The circumstantial warning was already visible and was not acted on: the 2009 source POSED the question five years AFTER the note it is attributed to, which is close to impossible if the note contained the answer.

body: In probability theory, statistics and related fields, a Poisson point process is a type of mathematical object that consists of points randomly located on a mathematical space with the essential feature that the points occur independently of one another. The process's name derives from the fact that the number of points in any given finite region follows a Poisson distribution. The process and the distribution are named after French mathematician Siméon Denis Poisson. The process itself was discovered independently and repeatedly in several settings, including experiments on radioactive decay, telephone call arrivals and actuarial science.

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Blockage.}

    For $\landsc$ a landscape and $(x, y)\in \Half$ a point, we call (first) blocking building of $(x, y)$ in $\landsc$ the following quantity when it is well defined:
    \[\tau(x, y, \landsc) = (x_b, y_b) := \underset{\substack{(a, b) \in \landsc \\a>x}}{\text{argmax}} \frac{b-y}{a-x}.\]
    When the blocking building of $(x, y)$ is well defined, we further introduce its blockage angle as:
    \[\theta(x, y, \landsc): = \arctan\left(\frac{y_b - y}{x_b-x}\right).\]
    In the following, when the involved landscape is unequivocal, we will simply write $\tau(x, y)$.

body: In mathematics, Schur's lemma is an elementary but useful statement in representation theory of groups and algebras. In the group case it says that if M and N are two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G and φ is a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group, then either φ is invertible, or φ = 0. An important special case occurs when M = N, i.e. φ is a self-map; in particular, for representations over an algebraically closed field, any element of the center of a group must act as a scalar operator on M. The lemma is named after Issai Schur who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations and develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. Schur's lemma admits generalisations to Lie groups and Lie algebras, the most common of which are due to Jacques Dixmier and Daniel Quillen.
title: Schur's lemma

Iterating the path coupling yields an N*log N bound with constant proportional to(q-Delta)/(q-2*Delta). Obstruction: The denominator degenerates before the source threshold. Exploiting local color availability or multi-vertex moves is necessary; the failed bound is not a counterexample to rapid mixing.

[Lem polyhom of arXiv:2608.06500, 'Free energy of Ising models under a spectral condition'] Let $p\in\mathbb{R}[x]$ be a polynomial. For all test graphs $X$, there
    exist test graphs $X_1,\ldots,X_r$ and constants
    $c_1,\ldots,c_r\in\mathbb{R}$ (depending on $p$ and $X$)
    such that for all weighted graphs
    $G=(\text{\boldmath $A$},\text{\boldmath $h$})$, we have that

    \begin{align*}
t(X,(p(\text{\boldmath $A$}),\text{\boldmath $h$}))=\sum_{i=1}^rc_it(X_i,G).
\end{align*}

    In other words, weighted homomorphism densities into the graph
    defined by a polynomial of the adjacency matrix of $G$ can be
    written as \emph{fixed} linear combinations of other weighted
    homomorphism densities into $G$. Consequently, local functions of
    $(p(\text{\boldmath $A$}),\text{\boldmath $h$})$ are also local functions of $G$.

body: Fitting a per-output affine stack directly in the per-sample relative metric - weighted least squares with case weights $1/\|y_i\|^2$, or a per-output simplex fit with the same weights - overfits badly: the weights concentrate the effective sample on the handful of smallest-norm cases and $M + 1$ coefficients fitted to them are unusable out of sample (measured on the EMIT pool, seed 101: 0.1236 against 0.0465 for ordinary least squares on Y1, 0.1591 against 0.1292 on Y2; cross-validation on the weighted fit chooses to discard it entirely). The same objective becomes the best available estimator when it is reached through the error covariance rather than through the regression: form the error covariance in the relative metric, replace its sample eigenvalues by the Ledoit-Peche nonlinear-shrinkage values (floored at a small fraction of the bulk level), and take the sum-to-one minimum-variance weights with the intercept closing the weighted mean error, with no cross-validation anywhere. Measured on the same three cells (Y1, Y2, Y4): 0.0451 / 0.1190 / 1.799 against ordinary least squares 0.0465 / 0.1292 / 1.898 (+3.0 / +7.9 / +5.2 percent), matching the cross-validated best heuristic of the pool twice and beating it once; with the residual shrink toward the pooled simplex weights on top (cross-validated amount 0.2-0.4) it is the best estimator on all three cells, +4.1 / +11.7 / +6.7 percent over least squares and +3.4 to +3.9 percent over the pool's best. Two ingredients do the work: the nonlinear shrinkage tames the heavy-tailed spectrum that the small-norm cases create, and the sum-to-one constraint removes the scale and intercept freedom those cases exploit. In this metric the random-matrix cleaning is not a small correction on top of least squares; it is the difference between an unusable fit and the best one. Three cells of one seed at the time of writing; the seventy-cell population test on both corpora was running.

body:
[Corollary cor:Bernoulli-Bartlett-component of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $\Gamma\leq\mathbb R^d$ be a lattice and let $(Z,\nu)$ be a
nontrivial Bernoulli $\Gamma$-space. Then the induced space
$\smash{\operatorname{Ind}_\Gamma^{\mathbb R^d}(Z)}$ admits a generating
stealthy Delone cross-section $Y$ whose Bartlett spectrum has the
form
\[
    \sigma_Y
    =
    \sigma_Y^{\mathrm{tor}}
    +
    h\,d\lambda_d,
    \qquad
    \operatorname{supp}\sigma_Y^{\mathrm{tor}}
    \subset\Gamma^*\setminus\{0\},
\]
where $h\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d)$ is nonnegative and
not identically zero. Moreover, $h$ vanishes almost everywhere on
a neighborhood of the origin.

body: An inner product space is a vector space H over the real or complex numbers with an inner product <x, y> that is linear in its first argument, conjugate-symmetric (<y, x> equals the complex conjugate of <x, y>; symmetric in the real case), and positive definite (<x, x> > 0 for x nonzero). The inner product induces the norm ||x|| = sqrt(<x, x>), and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality |<x, y>| <= ||x|| ||y|| holds. A Hilbert space is an inner product space that is complete with respect to this norm; in particular every Hilbert space is a Banach space. Vectors x and y are orthogonal when <x, y> = 0. Examples: R^n and C^n with the dot product, l^2, and L^2 spaces.
title: Hilbert space

Even Bernstein polynomial, including coefficient control

Subtract phi(0). Set h(t)=phi(|t|)-phi(0) on [-1,1] and g(u)=h(2u-1) on [0,1]. Then |h|<=1, h is even and 1-Lipschitz, and g is 2-Lipschitz and satisfies g(u)=g(1-u).

Put n=2k and define

    P(t)=2^(-n) sum_{v=0}^n g(v/n) binom(n,v) (1+t)^v(1-t)^(n-v).

For t=2u-1 and X~Binomial(n,u), this is E[g(X/n)]. The Lipschitz inequality followed by Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the error above:

    |P(t)-h(t)| <= 2 E|X/n-u|
                 <= 2 sqrt(Var(X/n))
                 = 2 sqrt(u(1-u)/n) <= 1/sqrt(n) <= epsilon/2.

This uses only the binomial variance and Cauchy-Schwarz, not a Bernstein tail inequality. All expectations are finite sums; endpoints u=0,1 have zero variance. The last inequality uses n=2 ceil(2 epsilon^-2)>=4 epsilon^-2.

Replacing v by n-v gives P(-t)=P(t), so P(t)=sum_{j=0}^k a_j t^(2j). For a polynomial q write ||q||_coeff,1 for the sum of the absolute values of its monomial coefficients. Triangle inequality and submultiplicativity give

    ||(1+t)^v(1-t)^(n-v)||_coeff,1 <= 2^v 2^(n-v)=2^n.

Since |g(v/n)|<=1,

    A := sum_{j=0}^k |a_j| <= 2^(-n) sum_v binom(n,v) 2^n = 2^n=4^k.  (2)

The offset subtraction is essential for this bound; an arbitrary additive target constant is restored only at the final affine output.

## 2. Polarization with repeated coordinates

For integer r>=1 and real y_1,...,y_r,

    product_l y_l = [2^r r!]^-1 sum_{s in {-1,1}^r}
                     (product_l s_l) (sum_l s_l y_l)^r.             (3)

To verify (3), expand each r-th power. For a multi-index alpha with sum alpha_l=r, its sign sum is product_l sum_{s_l=+-1} s_l^(alpha_l+1). This vanishes unless every alpha_l is odd. There are r nonnegative odd exponents with sum r; hence each is 1. This term has multinomial coefficient r! and sign factor 2^r. Division is valid because 2^r r!>0. The identity holds before variables are identified, so repeated coordinates and zero coordinates do not change it.

For j>=1, expand (sum_i x_i^2)^j over all ordered tuples in [d]^j. Each of its d^j terms is a product of 2j coordinate variables, allowing repetitions. Apply (3) to each with r=2j. Each linear form is ell(x)=sum_{l=1}^{2j} s_l x_{i_l}; its Euclidean coefficient norm is at most 2j by triangle inequality. On the unit ball Cauchy-Schwarz therefore gives |ell(x)|<=2j.

Define the globally continuous function

    G_j(t)=(t/(2j))^(2j) if |t|<=2j, and G_j(t)=1 otherwise.

Inside the interval the derivative has absolute value at most 1; outside it is zero, and the endpoint values match. Splitting intervals at the two endpoints proves global 1-Lipschitz continuity. It is constant outside [-2j,2j], as required by Assumption 1. On the ball ell(x)^(2j)=(2j)^(2j) G_j(ell(x)).

Consequently the nonconstant part of P(||x||) is a finite sum of scalar ridge profiles, with at most

    T=sum_{j=1}^k d^j 2^(2j) <= k(4d)^k                           (4)

terms. A valid total absolute coefficient budget is

    B=sum_{j=1}^k |a_j| d^j (2j)^(2j)/(2j)!
      <= sum_{j=1}^k |a_j| (d e^2)^j
      <= A(d e^2)^k <= (4d e^2)^k.                                (5)

The factorial estimate follows from sum_{i=1}^r log i >= integral_1^r log t dt = r log r-r+1 >= r log r-r. Thus r^r/r!<=e^r. This also holds for r=1; here r>=2. The budget includes all unmerged terms, so it remains valid if zero terms or repeated directions are removed. Its use does not assume cancellation or independence.

## 3. Scalar conversion: the coefficient budget is paid

If B=0, all nonconstant a_j vanish, and the affine output phi(0)+a_0 already achieves error <=epsilon/2. Otherwise B>0 and delta=epsilon/(2B)>0. For each ridge G_j, Assumption 1 with R=2j and L=1 supplies global uniform error <=delta using at most

    c_sigma (2j)/delta = 4 c_sigma j B/epsilon
                        <= 4 c_sigma k B/epsilon                 (6)

sigma units. Its scalar parameters are finite real numbers supplied by that assumption. Replacing its input by ell(x) changes each hidden affine form into an affine form in x and introduces no hidden layer. Sum these finitely many ridge networks with their original coefficients, combine the affine output constants, and add phi(0)+a_0.

with shift $\theta\in\R$.
 Assume that, for some
$\eps\in(0,\frac12]$,

\noi
\begin{align}
 \eps\leq p_k\leq1-\eps
 \qquad
 \text{for every $k$ with $\Inf_k(F) > 0$}.
 
\end{align}
Then every  coordinate  $k$ with positive influence
satisfies

\noi
\begin{align}
 d\,d!\Inf_k(F)
 \geq\eps^d(1-\eps),
 
\end{align}
and $F$ depends on at most
$
 \frac{d\,m_2(F)}
 {\eps^d(1-\eps)}
 $
coordinates.  In the symmetric case,
$
 \Inf_k(F)\geq \frac{2^{-(d+1)}}{d\,d!}
$
for every   coordinate $k$ with positive influence.  

Consequently, no sequence of integer-valued shifts
$F_n+\theta_n$ satisfying \eqref{bias_compact}, with fixed $d$,
a common $\eps>0$, and uniformly bounded variances, can converge to a

Proof (unaudited), standard criterion derived locally. Let s_t take finitely many states, a_t finitely many actions, and e_t in R^d obey e_{t+1}=B(i,a,j)e_t. Given all past variables and s_t=i, assume (a_t,s_{t+1}) has fixed law mu(a|i)P(j|i,a), with deterministic finite matrices B. On tuples of real symmetric matrices define (L X)_j=sum_{i,a} mu(a|i)P(j|i,a) B(i,a,j)X_i B(i,a,j)^T. Then E||e_t||^2 tends to zero for every initial joint law of (s_0,e_0) with finite second moment iff the ordinary spectral radius of L is less than one. This is not an arbitrary-switching joint-spectral-radius condition.

The following table classifies the isotropy formality of $(G, S)$ in terms of $L$. Here $\omega_i$ is the $i$-th fundamental weight of the relevant simple Lie group following the Bourbaki convention.
		\begin{center}
		\begin{tabular}{|c|c|}
		\hline
		$G$&$L$\\
		\hline
		$A_n, n\geq 2, n\neq 3$& $L\in W\cdot \omega_1$\\
		\hline
		$A_3$&$L\in W\cdot \omega_1\cup W\cdot \omega_2$\\
		\hline
		$B_2, C_2$&$\text{Any primitive weight}$\\
		\hline
		$B_n, C_n, n=3, 4$&$L\in W\cdot \omega_1\cup W\cdot \omega_n$\\

body: Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold with Levi-Civita connection nabla. A smooth curve gamma: I -> M on an interval I subset R is a geodesic if its velocity field is parallel along itself: nabla_{gamma'(t)} gamma'(t) = 0 for every t in I. Equivalently, in local coordinates x^1,...,x^n a curve gamma(t) = (x^1(t),...,x^n(t)) is a geodesic iff it satisfies the second-order ODE system d^2x^k/dt^2 + sum_{i,j} Gamma^k_{ij}(gamma(t)) (dx^i/dt)(dx^j/dt) = 0 for k=1,...,n, where Gamma^k_{ij} are the Christoffel symbols of g. Geodesics are the critical points of the energy functional among curves with fixed endpoints, and, when locally minimizing, are the locally shortest paths between nearby points.
title: Geodesic

 Then, upon fixing the notation $\mc{L}n_0(x)= \ln \big( x  \wedge 1\big) $ for $x \geq 0$, one has that the $N$-fold integral

body: In mathematics, Schur's lemma is an elementary but useful statement in representation theory of groups and algebras. In the group case it says that if M and N are two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G and φ is a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group, then either φ is invertible, or φ = 0. An important special case occurs when M = N, i.e. φ is a self-map; in particular, for representations over an algebraically closed field (e.g. $\mathbb {C}$), any element of the center of a group must act as a scalar operator (a scalar multiple of the identity) on M. The lemma is named after Issai Schur who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations and develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. Schur's lemma admits generalisations to Lie groups and Lie algebras, the most common of which are due to Jacques Dixmier and Daniel Quillen.

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2609.02017, 'Optimal girth-dependent bounds for the Bethe approximation of the permanent'] Let $g\geq4$ be even, and let
$A\in\R_{\geq0}^{n\times n}$ be a nonnegative matrix whose support
graph has girth at least $g$. Then
\[
  \on{Bethe}(A)
  \leq\on{per}(A)
  \leq2^{2n/g}\on{Bethe}(A).
\]
Moreover, whenever $g\mid2n$, the upper bound is attained by the
$0$--$1$ matrices whose support graphs are disjoint unions of cycles
of length $g$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 2 of arXiv:2609.02017

[Lemma 3.3 of arXiv:2110.05374, 'When Janson meets McDiarmid: Bounded difference inequalities under graph-dependence'] (A step in the proof of Theorem 2.1; setting as in Lemma 3.2.) For i ∈ [n−1] let Ω-valued random vectors Y^{(i)}, Z^{(i)} be jointly distributed so that (C1) Y^{(i)}_{[i]} = x_{[i]}; (C2) Y^{(i)}_{[i+1,n]} has the conditional law of X_{[i+1,n]} given X_{[i]} = x_{[i]}; (C3) Z^{(i)}_{[i]} = x^{(i)}_{[i]} and Z^{(i)}_{S_i} = Y^{(i)}_{S_i}; (C4) given Z^{(i)}_{S_i} = ω_{S_i}, Z^{(i)}_{p_i} has the conditional law of X_{p_i} given X_{[i]} = x^{(i)}_{[i]} and X_{S_i} = ω_{S_i}. Then for every i ∈ [n−1] and ω_{[i+1,n]} ∈ Ω_{[i+1,n]}: (A1) P(Y^{(i)}_{[i+1,n]} = ω_{[i+1,n]}) = P(X_{[i+1,n]} = ω_{[i+1,n]} | X_{[i]} = x_{[i]}); (A2) P(Z^{(i)}_{[i+1,n]} = ω_{[i+1,n]}) = P(X_{[i+1,n]} = ω_{[i+1,n]} | X_{[i]} = x^{(i)}_{[i]}). So (Y^{(i)}, Z^{(i)}) is a coupling (Marton-type) of the two conditional laws of X in which the two vectors differ at most in coordinates i and p_i; (A2) uses Lemma 3.2.
G-dependent (Definition 1.3 of the paper): X = (X_i)_{i∈V(G)} is G-dependent when for all disjoint S, T ⊂ V(G) with no edge of G between S and T, the families (X_i)_{i∈S} and (X_j)_{j∈T} are independent; this is stronger than pairwise independence of non-adjacent coordinates.
Proof setting (Section 3 of the paper): G is a dependency tree on [n] that is Rooted (rooted at vertex n, with c_n = c_min) and Ordered (j is a descendant of i only if j < i), which a topological sort always provides; p_i is the parent of a non-root vertex i, S_i := [i+1, n] \ {p_i}, and for x ∈ Ω and x'_i ∈ Ω_i, x^{(i)} := (x_1, ..., x_{i−1}, x'_i, x_{i+1}, ..., x_n). The paper writes conditional probabilities of point events; for non-discrete Ω_i read them as conditional distributions.
