[Corollary 21 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] Assume that the Dirichlet form $(\form, \dom)$ is transient. The following hold$:$
\begin{itemize}
\item[\sf (1)]
If a smooth measure $\mu$ satisfies $R\mu \in L^\infty(E;m)$ and $\mu(E)<\infty$, then $\mu$ belongs to ${\cal S}_0^{(0)}$.

\item[\sf (2)] {\rm({\it cf.} \cite[Theorem 2.4.2]{FOT11})}
 If $\mu$ is a smooth measure such that $R\mu \in L^\infty(E;m)$, then
$$
\int_E \tilde{u}(x)^2 \mu(dx) \le \| R\mu\|_\infty \form(u,u)<\infty, \quad u \in \dom_e.
$$
In particular, this implies that the embedding $\tilde{\dom}_e \subset L^2(E;\mu)$ is continuous, where $\tilde{\dom}_e$ is the set of all quasi-continuous modifications of functions 
in $\dom_e$.

\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Proposition prop:twodir of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] Suppose the atoms take exactly two directions. Then the directions are
antipodal, each class has total weight $\frac12$ and zero conditional mean,
and $C(q)=\frac12(|m_+|^2+|m_-|^2)$ where $m_\pm$ are the conditional means
of the selected weights. Consequently
\[
  \inf_{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le4}C\le\frac E4,\qquad
  \inf_{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le3}C\le\frac{5E}8 ,
\]
and both constants are attained: for six equally weighted atoms with
$z$-values the cube roots of unity over each direction, the three-point
optimum is exactly $\frac{5E}8$ and the four-point optimum exactly
$\frac E4$. Equality at $\frac{5E}8$ forces both classes to have equal
energy, conditional weights $\frac13$ each, and equilateral $z$-triangles of
equal radius. Furthermore, for five-atom two-direction systems the sharp
constant at three points is $\frac47<\frac58$ (attained by an equilateral
triple against an antipodal pair with energy ratio $4{:}3$).

body:
[Definition def:sections of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Given $\tau \in \mathfrak{T}$, we define $\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau] \subset \prod_{\underline{\tau} \in \tau} \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ 
by setting 
\begin{equs}
\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]
\eqdef
\big\{ 
\big(F_{\underline{\tau}}\in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}] : \underline{\tau} \in \tau\big): \enskip 
\forall \underline{\tau}, \underline{\tau}' \in \tau\;\text{and}\; f \in \mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')\,,\; \mathbf{f} F_{\underline{\tau}} =  F_{\underline{\tau}'}
\big\}\,.
\end{equs}
We define $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\tau]\subset \prod_{\underline{\tau} \in \tau} \text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ analogously. 

Moreover, for $\underline{\tau} \in \tau \in \mathfrak{T}$, let $\iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}: \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau] \rightarrow \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ be the ``fiber'' map $\big(F_{\underline{\tau}'}\in\mathcal{H}^{\underline{\tau}'} : \underline{\tau}' \in \tau\big) \mapsto F_{\underline{\tau}}$. 
Observe that $\iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ has a left inverse given by the ``section'' map $\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}: \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}] \rightarrow \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]$ defined by setting
\[
\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]\ni F_{\underline{\tau}}\mapsto\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}F_{\underline{\tau}}\eqdef\Big(\frac{1}{|\mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')|}
\sum_{f \in \mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')} \text{$\mathbf{f}$} F_{\underline{\tau}} : \underline{\tau}'\in\tau\Big)\in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]
\,.
\] 
We use the same notation for the analogous maps between $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ and $\text{${\mcb{C}}$}[\tau]$. 

Note that $|\mathrm{Iso}(\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}')|$ actually does not depend on the choice of $\underline{\tau},\underline{\tau}'\in\tau$. In the sequel, we therefore just write $|\mathrm{Aut}(\tau)|\eqdef |\mathrm{Aut}(\underline{\tau})|$ for any $\underline{\tau}\in\tau$.

Finally, for $\underline{\tau} \in \tau$ we sometimes write $\iota_{\underline{\tau}} \eqdef \iota_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ and $\pi_{\underline{\tau}} \eqdef \pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}}$ to lighten subscripts.

body: In mathematical analysis, Lipschitz continuity is a regularity property of functions between metric spaces that is stronger than uniform continuity, and hence also stronger than continuity. Intuitively, a Lipschitz continuous function is limited in how fast it can change: there exists a real number such that, for every pair of points on the graph of this function, the absolute value of the slope of the line connecting them is not greater than this real number; the smallest such bound is called the Lipschitz constant of the function. For instance, every function that is defined on an interval and has a bounded first derivative is Lipschitz continuous.

OWNER OWN WORK, proof draft UNAUDITED; novelty unestablished. Let N,P>=2 and M>=1 be integers. Independent factor arrays U and V
have iid centered real entries of variance one within each array,
with finite fourth moments u4=E u^4 and v4=E v^4. No symmetry or
vanishing third moment is assumed. Let Z be independent standard
Gaussian noise, X=UV^T/sqrt(N), Y=sqrt(s)X+Z, and d=NP. Define

 beta=M/N, c=(N-1)(P-1)/N^2,
 a=(N+u4-3)/N, b=(P+v4-3)/N, v(s)=1+beta s,
 Q(s)=v(s)^3+beta(a+b)v(s)s^2+beta*a*b*s^3,
 D(s)=v(s)^2 Q(s),
 i_N(s)=I(X;Y)/d, B_N(s)=log(v(s))/2-i_N(s),
 m_N(s)=E||X-E[X|Y]||F^2/d, g(s)=beta/v(s).

Since u4,v4>=1, a,b>=0. For every s>=0,

 g(s)-m_N(s)>=beta^2 c s^3/D(s),                      (1)
 B_N(s)>=(beta^2 c/2) integral_0^s t^3/D(t) dt
       >=beta^2 c s^4/[8 D(s)].                      (2)

An explicit one-sided quartic remainder, for 0<=s<=1, is

 B_N(s)>=beta^2 c s^4/8-beta^2 c C_N s^5/10,
 C_N=D(1)-1.                                         (3)

These are finite-dimensional inequalities, not formal expansions.
With bounded positive aspect ratios, C_N is bounded uniformly for
fixed factor fourth moments. If P/N->alpha>0, M/N->beta0>0, then
every limiting information function satisfies

 log(1+beta0 s)/2-i(s)
 >=alpha beta0^2 s^4/[8 D_infty(s)],
 D_infty(s)=(1+beta0 s)^2[(1+beta0 s)^3
       +beta0(1+alpha)(1+beta0 s)s^2+beta0 alpha s^3].  (4)

Consequently the lower limiting quartic coefficient is at least
alpha beta0^2/8. No matching upper coefficient is proved here.

Claim w718-T287-038 v2, Target1 partial result, proof (unaudited).
Novelty unestablished. This proves the one-sided quartic bound, not
the requested sharp two-sided quartic expansion.

Prior-work scope: Semerjian, arXiv:2402.16719v2, abstract, treats
symmetric orthogonally invariant matrix denoising and conjectures
an extension beyond that class. Its Eq(108) gives scalar cubic
polynomial-estimator normal equations. Polynomial least squares
is therefore not a new method here. The finite-N rectangular UV^T
identity and its conditioned-mixture KL consequence are written
out separately below; absence of an identical literature bound
has not been established.

## 1. Statement and exact finite-size constants

Let N,P>=2 and M>=1 be integers. Independent factor arrays U and V
have iid centered real entries of variance one within each array,
with finite fourth moments u4=E u^4 and v4=E v^4. No symmetry or
vanishing third moment is assumed. Let Z be independent standard
Gaussian noise, X=UV^T/sqrt(N), Y=sqrt(s)X+Z, and d=NP. Define

 beta=M/N, c=(N-1)(P-1)/N^2,
 a=(N+u4-3)/N, b=(P+v4-3)/N, v(s)=1+beta s,
 Q(s)=v(s)^3+beta(a+b)v(s)s^2+beta*a*b*s^3,
 D(s)=v(s)^2 Q(s),
 i_N(s)=I(X;Y)/d, B_N(s)=log(v(s))/2-i_N(s),
 m_N(s)=E||X-E[X|Y]||F^2/d, g(s)=beta/v(s).

Since u4,v4>=1, a,b>=0. For every s>=0,

 g(s)-m_N(s)>=beta^2 c s^3/D(s),                      (1)
 B_N(s)>=(beta^2 c/2) integral_0^s t^3/D(t) dt
       >=beta^2 c s^4/[8 D(s)].                      (2)

An explicit one-sided quartic remainder, for 0<=s<=1, is

 B_N(s)>=beta^2 c s^4/8-beta^2 c C_N s^5/10,
 C_N=D(1)-1.                                         (3)

These are finite-dimensional inequalities, not formal expansions.
With bounded positive aspect ratios, C_N is bounded uniformly for
fixed factor fourth moments. If P/N->alpha>0, M/N->beta0>0, then
every limiting information function satisfies

 log(1+beta0 s)/2-i(s)
 >=alpha beta0^2 s^4/[8 D_infty(s)],
 D_infty(s)=(1+beta0 s)^2[(1+beta0 s)^3
       +beta0(1+alpha)(1+beta0 s)s^2+beta0 alpha s^3].  (4)

Consequently the lower limiting quartic coefficient is at least
alpha beta0^2/8. No matching upper coefficient is proved here.

## 2. A leave-one-out cubic statistic and its exact norm

For a matrix y define

 tau_ij(y)=(1/N) sum_(k!=i,l!=j) y_il y_kj y_kl.

The omitted row/column coincidences ensure
partial_(y_ij) tau_ij=0, hence div tau=0. All terms in
E||tau(Y)||^2 have at most fourth powers of any individual factor
entry: across two three-edge L-shapes every row and column occurs
at most four times. Thus finite fourth moments, not sixth moments
of u or v, suffice for the integrations below.

The exact sixth mixed-moment identity is

 E||tau(Y)||^2/d=c Q(s).                              (5)

Here is a direct derivation. Fix i,j, and classify the two triples
in tau_ij^2 according to whether k=k' and l=l'. Divide their counts
by (N-1)(P-1). The relative counts are respectively

 1, P-2, N-2, (N-2)(P-2).

For the pure-signal sixfold products in these four cases, the
expectations are, in the same order,

 beta^3+beta^2(u4+v4-2)/N+beta(u4-1)(v4-1)/N^2,
 beta^2/N+beta(u4-1)/N^2,
 beta^2/N+beta(v4-1)/N^2,
 beta/N^2.                                           (6)

To verify each expression, expand hidden indices, partition the six
positions according to their equal hidden index, and use independence
of factor entries. A block with a singleton row or column vanishes
by centering. Every surviving row/column multiplicity is two or four;
the number of assignments to r distinct hidden blocks is (M)_r.
This proves (6) without presuming Gaussian or symmetric entries.

For mixed Gaussian-noise terms, only identical matrix positions can
pair, and each position occurs at most twice. The coefficients of
s^0,s^1,s^2,s^3 in (5), after division by c, are respectively

 1,
 3 beta,
 3 beta^2+beta(a+b),
 beta(beta+a)(beta+b).

The last line follows from (6); the s^2 line also includes one
noise pair times the four-corner rectangle moment beta/N in the
same-k/different-l and different-k/same-l cases. Expanding Q gives
exactly these four coefficients.

The independent finite verifier enumerates all hidden-index
partitions and all eligible Gaussian noise pairings, then clears
denominators by N^5 and compares every integer polynomial
coefficient in N,P,M,u4,v4. This is a formal coefficient identity,
not evidence from substitutions. See scripts/certify_rectangle_sixth_moment.py
and logs/rectangle_sixth_moment_certificate.json. It certifies only
the finite moment algebra.

## 3. Direct polynomial-estimator proof of the risk bound

The initially derived score projection has an equivalent elementary
proof that removes any need for score integration by parts. The
centered output covariance is v(s) I_d. Put

 l(Y)=sqrt(s)beta Y/v(s).

Its risk is g(s). The exact four-corner rectangle moments give

 E[X dot tau(Y)]/d=beta c s^(3/2),
 E[Y dot tau(Y)]/d=beta c s^2,
 E[(X-l(Y)) dot tau(Y)]/d=beta c s^(3/2)/v(s).         (7)

Indeed for distinct i,k and j,l,
E[X_ij X_il X_kj X_kl]=beta/N. The four factors use each row
and each column twice, so only a common hidden index survives.
In the first line of (7), all three Y factors must supply their
signal part; in the second line all four must do so. Noise terms
vanish because the matrix positions are distinct. These are finite
sums of absolutely integrable terms; no Fubini or limiting argument
is required. Cauchy-Schwarz also gives integrability directly from
the finite second moments of X,Y and the finite norm (5).

Consider the explicit degree-three estimator

 Xhat(Y)=l(Y)+b_s tau(Y),
 b_s=beta s^(3/2)/[v(s)Q(s)].

Expanding its squared error using (5) and (7) yields exactly

 E||X-Xhat(Y)||^2/d=g(s)-beta^2 c s^3/D(s).            (8)

The Bayes conditional mean minimizes squared error among measurable
estimators. Therefore m_N(s) is at most (8), proving (1). This
direction supplies a KL lower bound after I-MMSE; it cannot give
the matching upper bound. No regularity theorem for a Gaussian
mixture density is used in this direct proof.

## 4. Integrating the risk improvement with an explicit remainder

I-MMSE for finite-second-moment inputs gives
B_N'(s)=[g(s)-m_N(s)]/2 and B_N(0)=0. Integrating (1) proves the
first bound in (2). D has nonnegative polynomial coefficients and
D(0)=1, so D(t)<=D(s) for 0<=t<=s. This proves the second bound.

For 0<=t<=1, D(t)-1<=t[D(1)-1]=C_N t. Since D(t)>=1,
1/D(t)>=1-[D(t)-1]>=1-C_N t. Integrate t^3(1-C_N t) to obtain
(3), including its denominators8 and10. No inequality involving
the derivative of a pointwise information bound is being asserted.

For convergent positive aspects, a->1,b->alpha,c->alpha. Passing
through the explicit finite inequalities gives (4), without
interchanging SNR differentiation with the dimension limit.

## 5. The conditioned Gaussian mixture requested in NEXT

Specialize to sub-Gaussian U and Gaussian V as in034. Condition U
on E={||U||op<=L sqrt(N)} and call the resulting output density p_E.
Let q_v=N(0,v(s)I_d). Define the normalized conditioned KL
K_E,N(s)=D(p_E||q_v)/d. Retain034's explicit q_N,J,delta_N and set

 H_N(s)=sqrt(s)delta_N+s[beta_*q_N+J sqrt(q_N)]/v(s).

The exact conditional trace/entropy identity and034's paid coupling
and energy errors give

 |K_E,N(s)-B_N(s)|<=H_N(s).

Therefore (2) gives the explicit conditioned-mixture lower bound

 K_E,N(s)>=beta^2 c s^4/[8D(s)]-H_N(s).              (9)

Meanwhile034 gives only K_E,N(s)<=A s^4+2q_N/(NP). Thus the
lower coefficient in the limiting mixture is alpha beta0^2/8;
the upper coefficient is not yet matched. The conditioning error
vanishes exponentially with N at each fixed positive SNR and was
not discarded as a mere small event probability.

## 6. Exact remaining obstruction: a nonlinear projection residual

Let l(Y)=sqrt(s)beta Y/v(s) and

 b_s=beta s^(3/2)/[v(s)Q(s)],
 R_N(s)=E||E[X|Y]-l(Y)-b_s tau(Y)||^2/d.

Equation(7) implies that the bracketed residual is orthogonal to
tau in L^2. Consequently, for s>0, the exact decomposition is

 g(s)-m_N(s)=beta^2 c s^3/D(s)+R_N(s), R_N(s)>=0,
 B_N(s)=(beta^2 c/2) integral_0^s t^3/D(t)dt
                  +(1/2) integral_0^s R_N(t)dt.      (10)

No claim is made that tau is itself orthogonal to the linear
observations. Orthogonality to tau in this single projection is
enough for (10); the residual includes any needed linear cancellation.

To finish a limiting sharp quartic expansion one must additionally
prove that the limiting upper envelope of the integrated residual
is o(s^4). For an explicit O(s^5) remainder, a sufficient NEW input
would be R_N(t)<=epsilon_N t^2+C t^4 for a dimension-independent C
and epsilon_N->0, on a fixed SNR interval. Neither034's second
moment bound nor032's nonuniform finite Taylor bound proves this.
This residual estimate is the FIRST unproved step in extending
the present argument to the full requested quartic expansion.

Least trusted new steps for independent review: the sixth mixed
moment algebra and its finite-fourth-moment scope, followed by the
conditioning transfer in (9). The direct proof needs no score
integration by parts. All analytic steps remain independently

body: For observed data x under two hypotheses, the likelihood ratio is Lambda(x) = L(theta_0; x) / L(theta_1; x), the ratio of the likelihood under the null to that under the alternative. The Neyman-Pearson lemma shows that the most powerful test of a simple null against a simple alternative at a given size rejects exactly when Lambda is below a threshold. A family with monotone likelihood ratio in a statistic T admits uniformly most powerful one-sided tests, and the generalized likelihood-ratio statistic -2 log Lambda has an asymptotic chi-squared distribution (Wilks' theorem).

CAMPAIGN RESULT [independently checked proof; E0095-BIP v1; no novelty claim]. Let G be a finite connected bipartite unweighted d-regular graph, d>=2, with both bipartition classes of even size and lambda_2(L_G)>=2. Among perfect matchings of new edges, the optimal non-lazy absolute SRW gap on the (d+1)-regular augmentation is 2/(d+1). A matching attains it if and only if every matching edge lies within a bipartition class. This includes Q_d for d>=2 and K_{m,m} for even m>=2. It does not assert total-variation mixing-time optimality, and the spectral threshold is needed for the sufficiency argument.

body:
Consider i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d with weight law F. EXISTENCE of a finite geodesic between every pair of vertices, almost surely and simultaneously over all pairs, is known in each of the following cases, and the case division matters. (a) d = 2 and F ARBITRARY: Wierman and Reh proved that for any passage time distribution, with probability one there is a geodesic between any two points of Z^2. (b) Any d, with F(0) < p_c(d): existence follows from standard subcritical estimates. (c) Any d, with F(0) > p_c(d) and E[tau_e] < infinity: existence was proved by Zhang. (d) The remaining case F(0) = p_c(d) with d > 2 is STILL UNRESOLVED in general, though existence is known for distributions with F(0) = F(delta) = p_c for some delta > 0 in sufficiently high dimensions. So it is WRONG to say that geodesics need F(0) < p_c; that condition is sufficient and convenient, not necessary, and supercritical zero-weight percolation does not by itself destroy existence. UNIQUENESS is a separate matter: a continuous F is a SUFFICIENT condition for the model to be uniquely geodesic, since two distinct finite paths then have equal passage time with probability zero and there are countably many pairs of paths. With atoms - a two-valued weight law, say - ties are genuine and multiple geodesics occur with positive probability. All of the above is about FINITE geodesics; the existence, direction, uniqueness and coalescence of semi-infinite geodesics is a separate and largely open subject whose known results require differentiability or curvature assumptions on the limit shape. [Wierman and Reh (1978); Kesten, Aspects of First Passage Percolation, (9.23); Zhang; verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 4.1]
i.i.d. nonnegative weights on Z^d
existence holds in case (a) d=2 with no hypothesis, case (b) F(0) < p_c, case (c) F(0) > p_c with E tau_e < infinity; case (d) F(0) = p_c with d > 2 is OPEN
F continuous is a SUFFICIENT condition for uniqueness
the statement is about FINITE geodesics only

[Lemma lem:expectation-taylor of arXiv:2608.23742, 'Second-order fusion asymptotics for $\Sine_\beta$ correlation functions'] Let $d\ge1$, $\gamma>0$, and put $D=d\gamma$. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be compact. Suppose that real random variables $X,Y,M$ satisfy, for some $p,q$,
\begin{equation}
p>\max\{2,D\},\qquad q>\max\{1,D\},\qquad
2q\left(1-\frac1p\right)>1,
\end{equation}
and $X\in L^p$, $Y,M\in L^q$. Suppose, uniformly for $b\in K$ and $1\le j\le d$,
\begin{equation}
U_j(t,b)=tb_jX+\frac{t^2b_j^2}{2}Y+R_j(t,b),
\qquad |R_j(t,b)|\le C_K|t|^3M.
\end{equation}
Then, with
\[
F(u):=\prod_{j=1}^d|1+u_j|^\gamma,
\qquad A(b):=\sum_jb_j,
\qquad B(b):=\sum_jb_j^2,
\]
one has, uniformly for $b\in K$,
\begin{align}
\mathbb E F(U(t,b))
&=1+\gamma tA(b)\mathbb E X\\
&\quad+\frac{t^2}{2}\left\{\gamma B(b)\mathbb E Y+
\left[\gamma(\gamma-1)B(b)+\gamma^2(A(b)^2-B(b))\right]\mathbb E X^2\right\}
+o(t^2).\notag
\end{align}

body:
[Lemma 23 (Cone of influence; pathwise echo decay) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Assume the saturated regime and $\kappa<1$. Couple the true system $s$ and the directed system $\tilde s$ (all back-reaction and non-genealogical couplings replaced by their saturated idealisations) synchronously, edge by edge, using the same Brownian motions. Let $D^{(v)}_t:=s^{(v)}_t-\tilde s^{(v)}_t$. Then, pathwise,
\[
\sup_{t\le\tau}\big|D^{(v)}_t\big|\le\frac{\gamma_{\max}\,\varepsilon(\delta)}{\alpha_{\min}(1-\kappa)}\sum_{u\in S_\tau}\kappa^{d(u,v)},
\]
where $S_\tau$ is the set of vertices failed by time $\tau$ and $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ is graph distance: the influence of an echo source decays geometrically, at rate $\kappa$, in graph distance.

body:
[Corollary 4 (Basis-independent geometric quantities) of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] Let $U\in \mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$ be constant and $f\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}^m)$. Then

\[
\langle Uf,Uf\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}
=U\,\langle f,f\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\,U^{\top}.
\]

If $U\in O(m)$, then $\langle f,f\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}$ and $\langle Uf,Uf\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}$ have the same spectrum, and hence
\[
\mathrm{tr}\big(\langle Uf,Uf\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\big)
=\mathrm{tr}\big(\langle f,f\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\big).
\]

body: [Lemma lem:XYsample of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Let $\Omega'$, $\Omega''$ be  Polish spaces and $\mathcal{F}$ be the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega'\times\Omega''$. On a measurable space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$, suppose $(X,Y)\to\Omega'\times\Omega''$ are random variables with distribution $m_x(dy)\mu_X(dx)$, where $\mu_X$ is a $\sigma$-finite measure and for each $x\in\Omega'$, $m_x$ is a probability measure on $(\Omega'',\mathcal{F})$. Further assume that $m_x$ is a kernel, in the sense that for any measurable set $A\subset \Omega''$, the function $x\mapsto m_x(A)$ is measurable on $\Omega'$. Then there exist $\sigma$-finite measures $(\tilde m_y)_{y\in\Omega''}, \nu$ (which are not necessarily finite), such that $(X,Y)$ can be sampled from the measure $\tilde m_y(dx)\nu(dy)$.

[Lemma 2 of arXiv:2604.04848, '\bf Addendum to:\\ Bounds for survival probabilities in \\ supercritical Galton-Watson pro'] The following representation holds:
\begin{equation}
	\tilde g_{\rm NB}(u;r,\ze) = \sum_{k=1}^{r-1}\sum_{n=0}^{2r-3-k} u^k \ze^n \cgt(r,k,n) \,,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{subnumcases}
	{\cgt(r,k,n)  = } \textstyle
		k \binom{n+k+2}{k+2}  & if $0\le n \le r-1-k$\,, \vspace{2mm}  \\
		\textstyle
		\binom{r}{k+1}\frac{(2r-k)(k+1)-(n+1)(k+2)}{k+2} & if $r-k \le n \le r-1$\,, \vspace{2mm}  \\
		\textstyle
		\binom{r}{k+1}\frac{(2r-k)(k+1)-(n+1)(k+2)}{k+2} \vspace{2mm} \notag \\
		\textstyle

[Lemma lem:stayin of arXiv:2608.05089, 'Correlation decay in area-tilted line ensembles'] If $\mathbf{W}_1, \mathbf{W}_2 \in \mathcal{W}_N$, then $\mathbf{W}_1 \wedge \mathbf{W}_2, \mathbf{W}_1 \vee \mathbf{W}_2 \in \mathcal{W}_N$ as well.
Moreover, we also have
\begin{equation}
    \widetilde{\mathbf{W}_1 \wedge \mathbf{W}_2} = \widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_1 \wedge \widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_2
    \qquad \text{and}  \qquad
    \widetilde{\mathbf{W}_1 \vee \mathbf{W}_2} = \widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_1 \vee \widetilde{\mathbf{W}}_2,
\end{equation}
i.e.\ the maximum or minimum can be taken before or after linear interpolation.

Here the polynomial size and bounds are in d with C fixed. The definition asserts approximability at each smoothing level; it does not equate this with efficient posterior sampling or impose log-concavity.

Method: Source-specific calculation, conditional implication or exact obstruction Result: Conditional on a stationary unit-density process with an integrable truncated pair density h satisfying integral h=-1, Var N(B_R)=-integral h(z)*(|B_R|-|B_R intersect(B_R-z)|)dz. For a ball, the intersection deficit is of order R^(d-1)*min(|z|,R). If h has a noncanceling negative tail of order |z|^(-(2d-s)), the contribution from1<|z|<R is of order R^(d-1)*integral_1^R r^(s-d)dr, yielding exactly the three predicted powers. Check: The variance identity follows by expanding the second factorial moment and using the sum rule. The tail beyond R contributes order R^s and is subleading in the surface regime; at equality the integral is logarithmic. Obstruction: This is a conditional calculation, not a proof that a Gibbs state satisfies the required sum rule, signed tail, uniform bounds or positive surface coefficient. Oscillatory tails may require cancellation rather than absolute comparisons. These unresolved hypotheses carry the probabilistic content.

body:
[Ppn 216 (constraints on $(\bbb,\vvv,\uuu,\rrr,\www)^{\frozen,\coarse,N}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For the coefficients defined by \eqref{e:b.plus.coarse}--\eqref{e:w.plus.coarse},
with high probability,
the following hold simultaneously for all $0\leq d\leq d_{\max}-1$:
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
\item 
     
    The ``domain constraint'': for all 
    $B^{\frozen,\coarse} \in \mathcal{C}^\frozen(q_d)$,
    \beq
    \vvv^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d,B^{\frozen,\coarse}) 
    \ge 
    q_d p'(q_d)
    \frac{\uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d,B^{\frozen,\coarse})^2 }
    {\rrr^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d,B^{\frozen,\coarse})}
    - \frac{\eta^2}{2}\,.
    \eeq
(If $\uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}$ and $\rrr^{\frozen,\coarse,N}$ are both zero, we interpret the ratio on the right-hand side as zero.)
 \item
 
The ``budget constraint'' for the spherical perceptron:
    \beq
    
    \bE_{\bG^N}
    \bigg[ \Cost\Big(
        \bbb^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
        \vvv^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
            \uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)
        \Big) \bigg]
    \le \frac{1}{\alpha} 
    + \epsilon^\circ
 .
    \eeq
\item 
The ``budget constraint'' for the Ising perceptron:
    \beq
    
    \bE_{\bG^N}\bigg[ \Cost\Big(
        \bbb^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
        \vvv^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d),
        \uuu^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)
        \Big) \bigg]
    \le \frac{\bE_{\bG^N}[
    \www^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)^{1/2}]^2}{\alpha} 
    + \epsilon^\circ\,.
    \eeq
\item  The ``diffusivity'' for the Ising perceptron:
    \[\Big|\bE(\www^{\frozen,\coarse,N}(q_d)) -1\Big|
    \le\epsilon^\circ\,.\]
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
Assertions
\eqref{it:spherical-budget-constraint-plus-coarse}--\eqref{it:Ising-w-constraint-plus-coarse} follow straightforwardly from Jensen's inequality. For assertion \eqref{it:domain-constraint-plus-coarse}, note 
from \eqref{e:indicator.qd.less.than.qT},
 \eqref{e:def.r}, and \eqref{e:P.plus.hist}
that Proposition~\ref{p:budget-constraints-HIST}\ref{it:domain-constraint-plus-HIST} can be rewritten as
	\[
	\vvv^{\frozen,N}(q_d,B^\frozen) 
    \ge  q_d p'(q_d) 
    I(B^\frozen)
	\frac{\uuu^{\frozen,N}(q_d,B^\frozen)^2}
		{\rrr^{\frozen,N}(q_d,B^\frozen)}
    - \frac{\eta^2}{2}\,,
	\]
where we again interpret a $0/0$ ratio as zero, and
	\[I(B^\frozen)\equiv \ind\bigg\{|B^\frozen \cap[M]| \ge 
		\frac{M}{\BUCKETS^2}
		\bigg\}\,.\]
If $I(B^\frozen)=0$ for all $B^\frozen\in B^{\frozen,\coarse}$,
then the bound \eqref{e:domain.plus.coarse} follows.
Otherwise, consider a discrete probability measure $\pi$, and random variables $v_j,u_j,r_j$ which are zero on a set of indices $Z$, and otherwise satisfy
	\[
	v_j \ge A' \frac{(u_j)^2}{r_j} - a'\]
Assume $\pi_+ \equiv 1-\pi(Z)\in(0,1]$. Then Jensen's inequality gives
	\[
	\frac{\sum_j \pi_j v_j}{\pi_+}
	\ge \frac{1}{\pi_+}
	\sum_{j\notin Z} \pi_j \bigg\{
	A' \frac{(u_j)^2}{r_j} - a'\bigg\}
	\ge A'
	\bigg(\frac{1}{\pi_+}\sum_j \pi_j u_j\bigg)^2\bigg/
	\bigg(
	\frac{1}{\pi_+}\sum_j \pi_j r_j
	\bigg) - a'
	\]
and rearranging gives
	\[
	\sum_j \pi_j v_j
	\ge
	A' \bigg(\sum_j \pi_j u_j\bigg)^2\bigg/
	\bigg(\sum_j \pi_j r_j
	\bigg)
	-a'\pi_+\,.
	\]
If we apply the above inequality with the probability measure $\pi$
over buckets $B^\frozen\in B^{\frozen,\coarse}$ with probabilities 
$\pi(B^\frozen)=|B^\frozen|/|B^{\frozen,\coarse}|$, then we obtain the desired conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary eq:B5 of arXiv:2608.16170, '\bf On hitting time distributions of Markov processes with sub-Gaussian heat kernel bounds'] For any $t>0,x\in E$,
\[
    \int_E p(t,x,y)f(y)\mu(\mathrm{d} y)=\int_E p_\sigma(t,x,y)f(y)\mu(\mathrm{d} y),\quad \forall f\in \mathrm{b} \mathscr{B}(E)
\]
where $p_\sigma(t,x,y)=p^+_\sigma(t,x,y)+p^-_\sigma(t,x,y)$. In particular, for any $t>0$ and $x\in E$,
\begin{equation}
p(t,x,\cdot)=p_\sigma(t,x,\cdot),\quad \mu\text{-a.e.}
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Corollary 2 (Admissible coefficient errors) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Assume Assumptions~\ref{ass:baseline} and~\ref{ass:perturbed}, and let $X$ solve \eqref{eq:X}. Suppose that there exist measurable functions
\[
  h_b\in L^1(0,T),\qquad h_a\in L^2(0,T),\qquad h_\sigma\in L^\alpha(0,T)
\]
and exponents
\[
  \theta_b\in[0,1],\qquad \theta_a\in[0,\alpha/2),\qquad \theta_\sigma\in[0,1)
\]
such that, for all $(s,y)$,
\begin{align*}
|b(s,y)-\wt b(s,y)|&\le h_b(s)(1+|y|^{\theta_b}),\\
|a(s,y)-\wt a(s,y)|&\le h_a(s)(1+|y|^{\theta_a}),\\
|\sigma(s,y)-\wt\sigma(s,y)|&\le h_\sigma(s)(1+|y|^{\theta_\sigma}).
\end{align*}
Then $B,A,S<\infty$. More precisely, if $m_r:=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t|^r$ for $r<\alpha$, then
\[
B\le \|h_b\|_{L^1(0,T)}(1+m_{\theta_b}),\quad
A^2\le 2\|h_a\|_{L^2(0,T)}^2(1+m_{2\theta_a}),\quad
S^\alpha\le 2^{\alpha-1}\|h_\sigma\|_{L^\alpha(0,T)}^\alpha(1+m_{\alpha\theta_\sigma}).
\]

For the critical random-cluster model with cluster weight q <= 4 on Dobrushin domains, the exploration path converges to SLE(kappa) with kappa = 4 pi / (pi - arccos(sqrt q / 2)); known for q = 2 (Smirnov, Chelkak et al.) and, for q = 1 site percolation, on the triangular lattice only. [Lem L2 of arXiv:2609.01350, 'New classes of trace-form permutation polynomials and their compositional inverses'] Let $q=2^m$ and define $H:\mathbb F_{q^2}\setminus\mathbb F_2\to\mathbb F_q$ by
\[
  H(z)={\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\!\left(\frac{z^{2q}+z}{z^2+z}\right).
\]
Then $\mathrm{Im}(H)=\mathbb F_q\setminus\{1\}$.
title: Lem L2 of arXiv:2609.01350

[Theorem thm:coercivity of arXiv:2608.29657, 'Hypocoercivity of Tempered Bouncy Particle Samplers for Heavy-Tailed Targets'] Let~(ass:wpi of the paper), (ass:sigmabounds of the paper) and (ass:curvature of the paper) hold.  Let $K_0$ be as in~(equation eq:defconstants of the paper).
    Set $$\delta_\ast^{-1} \coloneqq{\lambda_{\mathrm r}}^{-1}\left({4 + \left(2\sqrt{K_0} + \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm r}}{2\sqrt{m}}\right)^2}\right),$$
    where $m$ is the Poincar\'e constant in~(ass:wpi of the paper) and $\lambda_{\mathrm r}>0$ the refresh intensity of~(equation eq:TBP of the paper).
    Then for $f \in C_c^1({\mathbb R}^d \times {\mathbb R}^d)$ with $ \mu_\sigma(f) = 0$,
    \begin{equation}{\mathcal E}_{\delta_\ast} (f) \geq \frac{\delta_\ast}{4} \|f\|_{L^2(\mu_\sigma)}^2.\end{equation}
    Also, for $g \in L^2(\mu_\sigma)$ 
    \begin{equation}\frac{1}{4}\|g\|_{L^2(\mu_\sigma)}^2 \leq {\mathcal V}_{\delta_\ast}(g) \leq \frac{3}{4}\|g\|_{L^2(\mu_\sigma)}^2 . \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem thm:endpoint-spectrum of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] For every fixed integer $k\geq4$, there are constants
$0<\alpha_k<\beta_k$ such that, as $h\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \left|\mathcal R(h,k)\cap
 [\alpha_kh^{k-1},\beta_kh^{k-1}]\right|
 \geq
 h^{k-1}\exp\!\left(
  -O_k\!\left(\frac{\log h}{\log\log h}\right)\right).
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{h\to\infty}\frac{\log|\mathcal R(h,k)|}{\log h}=k-1,
 \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
 |\mathcal R(h,k)|=h^{k-1+o_k(1)}.
\end{equation}
Here $o_k(1)\to0$ as $h\to\infty$; the subscript records that $k$ is fixed.
Together with the elementary cases, the complete fixed-cardinality exponent
law is
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{h\to\infty}\frac{\log|\mathcal R(h,k)|}{\log h}=
 \begin{cases}
  0,&k=1,2,\\
  1,&k=3,\\
  k-1,&k\geq4.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Complete fixed-cardinality exponent law

$$\mathbb{E}(A_\ell(s),\Omega_p)=\beta_{\mathrm{MP}_y,\ell}+O_\ell\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),$$
where $A_\ell(s)$ is the $\ell$-th moment of $\mu_{\mathcal{G}_s}$.

This means
$$\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{i=1}^p \lambda_i^\ell,\Omega_p\right)=p\beta_{\mathrm{MP}_y,\ell}+O_\ell(1).$$

Also C=B-vv^T=H0(I_m-1_m 1_m^T/m)H0^T/m+D is PSD and K=C+(mu+v)(mu+v)^T. Therefore at most one eigenvalue of K exceeds the largest eigenvalue of C, and at most one exceeds the largest eigenvalue of B. For a bias-free two-layer scalar Gaussian ReLU NTK, H=ReLU(XW), mu_i=||x_i||/sqrt(2pi), and D is the PSD hidden-weight derivative Gram. The exact spike vectors depend on the centered bulk, so replacing their matrix-valued resolvent by its normalized trace is an additional unproved isotropy assumption. This statement does not extend Fan-Wang to ReLU.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For one-dimensional nearest-neighbor random walk in an i.i.d. random environment in the subballistic or intermediate regime, parametrized by an index kappa solving E[rho^kappa]=1 for rho the local odds ratio of the environment, hitting times of successive integers admit a classical Kesten construction as a branching process with migration: individuals reproduce according to an environment-dependent offspring law with an added immigration/emigration term reflecting the local environment. The Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer theorem shows that for kappa in the relevant range below 2, the hitting time of level n, normalized by n^{1/kappa}, converges to a kappa-stable distribution, via a result on the total population size of the associated branching-with-migration process, which itself has heavy-tailed, stable-scaling behavior. This gives the precise non-Gaussian scaling limits characterizing anomalous, subdiffusive or index-dependent, behavior in one-dimensional random walk in random environment, a phenomenon absent for simple random walk. It does not extend to higher dimensions, since the explicit branching correspondence is a genuinely one-dimensional, nearest-neighbor phenomenon, and it requires the environment to be i.i.d. with a moment condition admitting a solution kappa in the relevant range. Typical failure: Extending the branching-process-with-migration correspondence and its kappa-stable scaling conclusion to multi-dimensional random walk in random environment, or to environments with dependence rather than i.i.d. structure, where no analogous exact combinatorial bijection to a branching process is known; the Kesten construction is a special, essentially exact identity in one dimension that does not generalize by analogy, so claiming kappa-stable scaling outside the one-dimensional i.i.d. setting requires an entirely separate justification. Canonical reference: Kesten, Kozlov and Spitzer, 1975, Compositio Mathematica.
one-dimensional, nearest-neighbor random walk in an i.i.d. random environment
existence of kappa in (0,2) solving E[rho^kappa]=1 for the environment's local odds ratio rho
transience of the walk, or the appropriate directional condition for the regime under study
technical non-lattice or non-degeneracy conditions on the environment law needed for the stable-law convergence

CLAIM (Janson, Conjecture 18.4): if m = o(n) then Y(1) = o_p(log n). Quantitatively, for m <= n/4, with gamma = min(1, w_1/w_0) and any r < rho, Y(1) <= (1 + delta) log n / log(gamma r n / (2m)) with high probability, i.e. Y(1) = O_p(log n / log(n/m)). The case w_1 = 0 (span 1) follows by the same comparison, writing j as a fixed sum of parts from a finite allowed set F by Frobenius, with constant max F / log(gamma_F r^{max F} n / (2m)); span d > 1 reduces to span 1 by dividing box counts by d. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: the finer multinomial asymptotics log n / log(n log n / m) of Gonnet and of Raab and Steger have no general-weight analogue here.

body: FIRES WHEN you plan to prove a balls-in-boxes statement by adding one ball and coupling B_{m,n} to B_{m+1,n}. THE ROUTE: for the multinomial weights w_k = 1/k! a ball-by-ball coupling shows the largest occupancy Y(1) is stochastically nondecreasing in m, and the monotonicity then sandwiches m/n -> 0 below every fixed lambda. WHY IT FAILS FOR A GENERAL WEIGHT SEQUENCE: there is no coupling of B_{m,n} and B_{m+1,n} that moves only one ball, because the conditional law of the extra ball's box depends on the WHOLE configuration through the ratios w_{Y_i + 1}/w_{Y_i}. With multinomial weights that ratio is 1/(Y_i + 1) and the dependence collapses; with any other weight sequence it does not. CONDITION OF FAILURE: w_{k+1}/w_k not of the multinomial form. The source itself names this as the missing piece. What worked instead was a direct partition-function comparison, which uses no coupling at all - see the F0055 result node.

[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2608.12804, 'Scaling Limits for Ising Models on Inhomogeneous Random Graphs and Applications'] Suppose that the entries of $\bs \coloneqq (\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_N)$ are i.i.d. Rademacher with mean $0$. Let $K:[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and Riemann
integrable, and suppose that
\(
    \|T_{|K|}\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1.
\)
    Then there exists $\delta >0$ such that
    \begin{equation}
        \limsup_{N \to \infty} \E \left[\exp\left(\frac{1+\delta}{2N}\sum_{i\neq j}K\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{j}{N}\right)\sigma_i \sigma_j\right)\right] < \infty.
    \end{equation}
    Consequently,
    \[
        \exp \left(\frac{1}{2 N} \sum_{i \neq j} K\left(\frac{i}{N}, \frac{j}{N}\right) \sigma_{i} \sigma_j\right)
    \]
    is uniformly integrable.
title: Lemma 18 of arXiv:2608.12804

body:
[Corollary 9 of arXiv:2609.01166, 'Nonparametric inference for density-dependent McKean--Vlasov diffusions'] The rates above can be transferred to the case of finite-time observations, provided that exponential ergodicity holds.
To observe that, let \(\V\) be a potential for which the corresponding nonlinear dynamics satisfy
\begin{equation}
\chi^2(P_t\Vert\Pi_0)
\leq
\eta_t
:=
C_{t_0}e^{-\rho_\chi(t-t_0)},
\qquad t\geq t_0,
\end{equation}
for some \(t_0\geq0\), \(C_{t_0}<\infty\), and \(\rho_\chi>0\), where \(P_t\) and \(\Pi_0\) denote the laws with densities \(p_t\) and \(\pi_0\), respectively. For the OU potential~\eqref{eq:ou-potential}, the inequality~\eqref{eq:chi2-transfer-assumption} holds under the assumptions of~\cite{belomestny-morozova-ou}, with
\(
C_{t_0}=\chi^2(P_{t_0}\Vert\Pi_0).
\)
Let \(X_1^{T_n},\ldots,X_n^{T_n}\) be independent observations from \(P_{T_n}\) for some \(T_n>0\), and let \(G_{M_n}\) be the event on which~\eqref{eq:full-mle-oracle-transfer} holds. Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:oracle}, it holds that
\[
P_{T_n}^{\otimes n}(G_{M_n}^c)
\leq
\delta+n\tau_0(M_n)
+
\frac12\sqrt{(1+\eta_{T_n})^n-1}.
\]
Indeed,
\[
1+\chi^2(P_t^{\otimes n}\Vert\Pi_0^{\otimes n})
=
\left(1+\chi^2(P_t\Vert\Pi_0)\right)^{n}
\leq
(1+\eta_t)^n,
\]
and therefore
\(
\TV(P_t^{\otimes n},\Pi_0^{\otimes n})
\leq
0.5\sqrt{(1+\eta_t)^n-1}.
\)
The claimed bound follows from
\(
P_{T_n}^{\otimes n}(G_{M_n}^c)
\leq
\Pi_0^{\otimes n}(G_{M_n}^c)
+
\TV(P_{T_n}^{\otimes n},\Pi_0^{\otimes n})
\)
and
\(
\Pi_0^{\otimes n}(G_{M_n}^c)
\leq\delta+n\tau_0(M_n).
\)
Consequently, if
\(
n\eta_{T_n}\longrightarrow0
\)
and
\(
n\tau_0(M_n)\longrightarrow0,
\)
then the stationary oracle inequality and the rates in~\eqref{eq:kl-rate} remain valid for observations from \(P_{T_n}\). Under~\eqref{eq:chi2-transfer-assumption}, it is sufficient to choose, for any \(\varepsilon>0\),
\(
T_n
\geq
t_0+(1+\varepsilon)\rho_\chi^{-1}\log n,
\)
which guarantees
\(
n\eta_{T_n}
\leq
C_{t_0}n^{-\varepsilon}
\longrightarrow0
\)
as \(n\to\infty\).
Since by Lemma~\ref{lem:explicit-tails}
it holds that
\(
\tau_0(M)\lesssim e^{-c_a(M-v_\star)},
\)
taking
\(
M_n=v_\star+C_{\mathrm{tr}}\log n
\)
with \(c_aC_{\mathrm{tr}}>1\) yields the overall error \(\delta+o(1)\) and hence the desired rate. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:main_event_high_prob of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] We can choose the parameters $\delta,\Delta,\zeta,\alpha \in (0,\frac{\delta_3\rho}{4A^2}),\theta \in (0,\zeta/100),M,\Lambda_0 , B>1$ in a manner depending only on $b,\mathbbm{p},\delta_1,\delta_2,\delta_3,A$ and $\rho$ in such a way that the following hold.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item 
    We have $\mathbb{P}(E_r(0)) \geq \mathbbm{p}$ for all $r>0$.
  \item The event $E_r(0)$ is measurable with respect to $\sigma( (h - h_{5r}(0))\lvert_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}A}_{r/4,4r}(0)})$.
  \item 
   For all $x,y\in \partial B_{2r}(0)$ with $|x-y|\geq \delta r$, and any $z\in J_{x,y}\cap \mathcal{Z}$, the corresponding sets $\mathcal{A}_{u_+},\mathcal{A}_{u_-},\mathcal{M},\mathcal{A}_{v_-},\mathcal{A}_{v_+}$ and tubes $\mathcal{D}_u,\mathcal{D}_v$  have the following properties.  
Set $\mathcal{C} = B_{2 \zeta r}(U_r^{x,y} \cup W_r^x \cup W_r^y)$ and suppose that $z = z_k$ for some $k \in [\![k_x ,  k_y]\!]$.  Then the following conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item 
Any path in $\mathcal{C}$ connecting $B_{2 \zeta r}(L_k)$ to $B_{2\zeta r}(L_{k+1})$ has to intersect all of the sets $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{D}_u),  B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{D}_v)$ and $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{M} \setminus (S_u \cup S_v))$. 
\item 
Any path in $\mathcal{C}$ from $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{D}_u)$ to $B_{2\zeta  r}(\mathcal{A}_{u_+} \cup \mathcal{A}_{u_-})$ (resp.\  $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{D}_v)$ to $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{v_+} \cup \mathcal{A}_{v_-})$) has to intersect $B_{2\zeta r}(S_u)$ (resp.\  $B_{2\zeta r}(S_v)$).
\item 
Any path in $\mathcal{C}$ from $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{D}_u)$ to $B_{2\zeta r}(V_{\rho r / A^2}(z) \setminus (\mathcal{A}_{u_+} \cup S_u \cup \mathcal{A}_{u_-}))$ (resp.\  $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{D}_v)$ to $B_{2\zeta r}(V_{\rho r / A^2}(z) \setminus (\mathcal{A}_{v_+} \cup S_v \cup \mathcal{A}_{v_-}))$) has to intersect $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{u_+} \cup \mathcal{A}_{u_-})$ (resp.\  $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{v_+} \cup \mathcal{A}_{v_-})$). 
\item 
  Any path in $\mathcal{C}$ from $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{u_+} \cup \mathcal{A}_{u_-})$ to $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{M} \setminus S_u)$ (resp.\  $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{v_+} \cup \mathcal{A}_{v_-})$ to $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{M} \setminus S_v)$) has to intersect $B_{2\zeta r}(S_u)$ (resp.\  $B_{2\zeta r}(S_v)$).
    \item  
    Any path in $\mathcal{C}$ from $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{u_+}\cup \mathcal{A}_{u_-})$ (resp.\ $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{v_+}\cup \mathcal{A}_{v_-}))$ to $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{v_+}\cup S_v\cup \mathcal{A}_{v_-})$ (resp.\ $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{u_+}\cup S_u\cup \mathcal{A}_{u_-})$) necessarily intersects $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{M}\setminus S_u)$ (resp.\ $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{M}\setminus S_v)$).
    \item 
    Any path in $\mathcal{C}$ from $B_{2\zeta r}(L_k)$ (resp.\ $B_{2\zeta r}(L_{k+1})$) to $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{u_+} \cup \mathcal{A}_{u_-})$ (resp.\ $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{v_+} \cup \mathcal{A}_{v_-})$) intersects $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{D}_u)$ (resp.\ $B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{D}_v)$).
\end{enumerate}     
  \item 
    We have $B_{\frac{b\rho r}{2A^2}}(\{u_-,u_+\})\cap B_{2\zeta r}(U_r^{x,y}\cup W_r^x \cup W_r^y) = B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{u_-}\cup\mathcal{A}_{u_+}) \cap B_{\frac{b\rho r}{2A^2}}(\{u_-,u_+\})$.
  \item 
    We have $B_{\frac{b\rho r}{2A^2}}(\{v_-,v_+\})\cap B_{2\zeta r}(U_r^{x,y}\cup W_r^x \cup W_r^y) = B_{2\zeta r}(\mathcal{A}_{v_-}\cup\mathcal{A}_{v_+}) \cap B_{\frac{b\rho r}{2A^2}}(\{v_-,v_+\})$. 
  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Lagrange's theorem (group theory): If G is a finite group and H is a subgroup of G, then the order |H| divides the order |G|. More precisely, |G| = [G : H] |H|, where the index [G : H] is the number of distinct left cosets of H in G; this follows because the left cosets of H partition G and each has exactly |H| elements. In particular, the order of every element of G (the order of the cyclic subgroup it generates) divides |G|.

Owner-own-work draft, proof (unaudited), claim T280-w716-C1 v2; independent review pending. For d>=3, uniform probability inputs on S^(d-1), square loss and all-parameter characteristic mean-field gradient flow of f_t(x)=E[a_t ReLU(w_t.x+b_t)], assume continuous L2 residual and locally integrable second parameter moments. Let the initial law be invariant under (a,w,b)->(a,Qw,b) for every Q in O(d), S0=sqrt(a0^2+|w0|^2+b0^2), |w0|>0 almost surely, M2=E[S0^2]<infinity, Mgate=E[a0^2 S0/|w0|]<infinity. For r_t=f_t-y (or centered output minus y), R=||r_0||2>0, c=sqrt(2)R, Cd=Gamma(d/2)/(sqrt(pi)Gamma((d-1)/2)), and initial tangent operator K0, the draft proves ||r_t-exp(-tK0)r_0||2 <= (R/c)[4M2(exp(ct)-1)^2+8sqrt(2)Cd Mgate(exp(ct)-1-ct)] on every finite interval where the characteristic flow exists. The same bound holds for ||P_k r_t-exp(-mu_k t)P_k r_0||2 in each harmonic degree, since K0 is rotationally invariant. The error is O(t^2). For nonzero initial components and mu_j>mu_k it yields strict ordering of their normalized residual norms on an explicit positive short interval. It does not imply ordered half-energy hitting times or settle long-time feature learning. R=0 gives stationary flow. Gaussian a,b,w with nondegenerate isotropic w satisfy the moments. Core step: E[a0^2 |1_{w_t.x+b_t>0}-1_{w0.x+b0>0}|] <=2sqrt(2)Cd Mgate(exp(ct)-1), uniformly in unit x. The bound conditions on initial a,b,|w|; later trajectories need not remain isotropic. No novelty, PDE existence/uniqueness, Lean certification or independent audit is asserted.

[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Within our coupling of the collection times (Definition~\ref{def:coupling}),
  $T_{m,0}$ is independent of $T_{m,p} - T_{m,0}$ and this difference
  has \textsc{mgf}
  \[
    M_{T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}}(t) = I_{m, p}(t), \quad t \leqslant 0.
  \]
  \begin{proof}
    If $T_{m, 0} = k$, then the value of $T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}$
    is a deterministic function of the initial clumsiness $\{ U_{L(i,k)} \}_{i \in [m]}$,
    the future updates $\{ C_n \}_{n > k}$,
    and the future clumsiness $\{ U_n \}_{n > k}$. Call this function $f$.
    We will make $f$ explicit. Consider an initial clumsiness vector
    $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_m)^\top \in [0, 1]^m$,
    coupon updates $\mathbf{y} = (y_n)_{n > 0} \in [m]^\mathbb{N}$,
    and future clumsiness $\mathbf{z} = (z_n)_{n > 0} \in [0, 1]^\mathbb{N}$.
    Then define
    $L'(i, n; \mathbf{y})$ as the most recent update of coupon $i$
    no later than $n$,
    \[
      L'(i, n; \mathbf{y}) \coloneqq
      \sup\{ k \leqslant n \mid y_k = i \}, \quad
      i \in [m], \quad n \geqslant 0,
    \]
    where naturally $\sup\emptyset = -\infty$ and $L'(i, 0; \mathbf{y}) = -\infty$.
    Define
    \begin{align*}
      f(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{y}; \mathbf{z})
      \coloneqq \inf \{ n \geqslant 0 \mid {} &\text{for all $i \in [m]$,}\\
          &\text{if $x_i > 1-p$ or $L'(i, n; \mathbf{y}) > 0$,}\\
          &\text{then $L'(i, n; \mathbf{y}) > 0$
          and $z_{L'(i, n; \mathbf{y})} \leq 1-p$}
          \}.
    \end{align*}
    Thus, for any integers $\ell \geqslant m$ and $x \geqslant 0$,
    \begin{align*}
      \PP\left( T_{m,p} - T_{m,0} = x \right)
      &= \sum_{k \geqslant m}
        \PP\left( T_{m,p} - T_{m,0} = x \mid T_{m,0} = k\right)
        \PP(T_{m,0} = k)\\
      &= \sum_{k \geqslant m} \PP\left(f(U_{L(1, k)}, \dots, U_{L(m, k)};
      C_{k+1}, C_{k+2}, \dots;
      U_{k+1}, U_{k+2}, \dots) = x\right)\\
      &\qquad \qquad \qquad \times \PP\left(T_{m,0} = k\right)\\
      &= \sum_{k \geqslant m} \PP\left(f(U_{L(1, \ell)}, \dots, U_{L(m, \ell)};
      C_{\ell+1}, C_{\ell+2}, \dots;
      U_{\ell+1}, U_{\ell+2}, \dots) = x\right)\\
      &\qquad \qquad \qquad \times \PP\left(T_{m,0} = k\right)\\
      &= \PP\left(f(U_{L(1, \ell)}, \dots, U_{L(m, \ell)};
      C_{\ell+1}, C_{\ell+2}, \dots;
      U_{\ell+1}, U_{\ell+2}, \dots) = x\right)\\
      &\qquad \qquad \qquad \times \underbrace{
        \sum_{k \geqslant m} \PP\left(T_{m,0} = k\right)
      }_1\\
      &= \PP\left(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0} = x \mid T_{m,0} = \ell\right).
    \end{align*}
    The third line uses our i.i.d.~assumptions from
    Definition~\ref{def:coupling}.
    This proves the independence of $T_{m,0}$ and $T_{m,p} - T_{m, 0}$.
    Hence the factorisation
    $M_{T_{m,0}}(t)\,M_{T_{m,p} - T_{m,0}}(t) = M_{T_{m,0}}\,I_{m,p}(t)$.
    These quantities are non-zero; divide both sides to conclude the proof.
    
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 19 of arXiv:2605.14206

For broad parametric function classes with p parameters bounded polynomially in n and d, any function fitting n noisy generic data points below the noise floor has Lipschitz constant at least of order sqrt(n d / p), with high probability. For two-layer networks with p of order m d parameters this gives the sqrt(n/m) law, but ONLY under the polynomial parameter bound; a depth-three construction with unbounded weights violates the law, so boundedness cannot be dropped in general.

Let n >= 2 and Omega in R^n open, and let Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + sum b^i D_i u + c u with a^{ij} = a^{ji} merely measurable and lambda|xi|^2 <= sum a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j <= Lambda|xi|^2 a.e. (0 < lambda <= Lambda), and |b| + |c| <= K. Let u in W^{2,n}_loc(Omega) satisfy Lu = 0 a.e. and u >= 0 in Omega. Then for every ball with B_{2R}(y) contained in Omega and R <= R_0, sup over B_R(y) of u <= C inf over B_R(y) of u, with C depending only on n, Lambda/lambda, K/lambda and R_0 (and only on n and Lambda/lambda when b = c = 0). Consequently strong solutions of Lu = 0 with measurable uniformly elliptic coefficients are locally Hoelder continuous, with the corresponding interior estimate; for b = c = 0 the exponent is alpha = alpha(n, Lambda/lambda), and in general it depends in addition on K/lambda and on the scale R_0. This is the nondivergence-form counterpart of the De Giorgi-Nash-Moser theory; neither theorem implies the other, because a nondivergence operator with measurable coefficients has no variational structure.

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2604.01978, 'Homogenized Transformers'] Fix $i,j\in[n]^2$ and define
\(
R_{ij}(t)\coloneqq \langle x_i(t),x_j(t)\rangle.
\)
We have
\begin{equation}
\de R_{ij}(t)
=
\de M_{ij}(t)
+
\cD_{ij}(t)\,\de t,
\end{equation}
where the local martingale part is
\begin{equation}
\de M_{ij}(t)
=
\int_\Uptheta
\left(\langle G_i(t,\bm{\theta}),x_j(t)\rangle+\langle x_i(t),G_j(t,\bm{\theta})\rangle\right)
\,\mathsf{W}(\de\bm{\theta},\de t),
\end{equation}
and the drift is
\begin{align}
\cD_{ij}(t)
&=
\frac1d\left(d-2+R_{ij}(t)^2\right)\,s_{\mu(t)}(x_i(t),x_j(t))\nonumber\\
&-
\frac{(d-1)}{2d}\,R_{ij}(t)\left(s_{\mu(t)}(x_i(t))+s_{\mu(t)}(x_j(t))\right),
\end{align} 
where $\mu(t) = \mu_{X(t)}$ and 
\begin{align*}
s_\mu(x)&\coloneqq \E\left\|\mathsf{m}_{\upbeta,\bA}[\mu](x)\right\|^2,\nonumber\\
s_\mu(x,x')&\coloneqq \E\left\langle \mathsf{m}_{\upbeta,\bA}[\mu](x),\mathsf{m}_{\upbeta,\bA}[\mu](x')\right\rangle.
\end{align*}

Consider the coexistence equilibrium K_3 = (N*, P*) with m > c and k*(m - c) > c. The Jacobian matrix J(K_3) has positive determinant. Its trace satisfies (1 + N*)*Trace(J(K_3)) = (2*N*/k)*((k - 1)/2 - N*). Consequently, K_3 is a locally asymptotically stable sink if k < (m + c)/(m - c), undergoes a supercritical Hopf bifurcation at k = (m + c)/(m - c), and becomes an unstable source surrounded by a unique stable limit cycle for k > (m + c)/(m - c).
m > c and k*(m - c) > c

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Fluctuations of shortest routes in Poisson proximity networks structural calculation Result: A deterministic route of length D connecting points at distance r and reaching perpendicular deviation T must satisfy D>=sqrt(r^2+4*T^2). To see this, split at a point of maximal deviation and minimize the sum of its distances to the two endpoints over the longitudinal coordinate; the minimum occurs above the midpoint. Hence T<=sqrt(D^2-r^2)/2. Check: When D/r tends to a stretch constant mu>1, the bound gives only T/r<=sqrt(mu^2-1)/2 asymptotically. It does not force sublinear wandering. This explicitly explains why the existing route-length shape theorem does not already identify a transversal exponent. Obstruction: A KPZ-type prediction needs estimates for centered route excess and correlations of competing near-geodesics. The deterministic Euclidean inequality leaves an order-r allowance whenever the limiting stretch exceeds1.

For n>=3, let A_n={(a,b_1,...,b_n) in {-1,1}^{n+1}: a+b_i+b_(i+1) is in {-1,1} for every cyclic index i}, with b_(n+1)=b_1. Choose an independent dominating vertex set U of C_n with d=|U|=ceil(n/3) and every cyclic gap between consecutive vertices of U of length 2 or 3 (the singleton case n=3 has gap length 3). For u in U define L_u(a,b)=a+b_u and Z_u=1_{L_u!=0}. For z in {0,1}^U write (A_n)_z={x in A_n: Z(x)=z} and |z|=sum_u z_u. Then |(A_n)_z|<=2^(n+1-d-|z|) for every z. Consequently |A_n|/2^(n+1)<=(3/4)^d and, defining ell(A_n)=n+1-log_2|A_n|, d<=ell(A_n)/log_2(4/3). This is the activation-cell estimate for this particular certificate, not for an arbitrary vertex set U. On a=1, the vertices with b_i=1 form an independent set; gap lengths 2 and 3 have completion counts (2,1,1) and (3,2,1) according to the endpoint sum (0,1,2), each at most 2^(g-1-(s+t)/2). Antipodality supplies the factor 2.

[Lemma eq:expdecay of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Fix $t_0\in[0,1]$, $N\in\N$, and consider $\lambda\in C^\infty(\R)$ with $\mathrm{supp} \,\lambda\subset[t_0-c\mu,t_0]$ for some universal constant $c>0$. Then, the following holds uniformly in $t_0\in[0,1]$ and $\mu\in[0,1]$:
   \begin{equs}
         \norm{K_{N,\mu}\lambda}_{L^p}&\lesssim_c  \mu^{1/p} \norm{K_{N,\mu}\lambda}_{L^\infty}\;\;\text{for every}\;p\in[1,\infty]\,,\\         
       \norm{(t_0-)K_{N,\mu}\lambda}_{L^1}&\lesssim_c  \mu \norm{K_{N,\mu}\lambda}_{L^1}\,. 
   \end{equs} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Fix beta in(0,1/2], n>=1 and a deterministic nonzero x in R^n. Let a_1,...,a_m be independent N(0,I_n) vectors. Define gamma_beta(t)=|t| when |t|>beta, and gamma_beta(t)=t^2/(2 beta)+beta/2 when |t|<=beta. On the probability-one event that a_i^T x!=0 for every i, set F_beta(z)=(1/(2m))sum_i |a_i^T x|^2(gamma_beta((a_i^T z)/(a_i^T x))-1)^2. There are positive C_beta,c_beta,delta_beta depending only on beta such that, if m>=C_beta n, with probability at least1-c_beta exp(-delta_beta m), every local minimum of F_beta is global and every critical point that is not a global minimum has a unit direction v with D_v^2 F_beta(z)<0. Here D_v h(z)=lim_{t down to0}(h(z+t v)-h(z))/t and D_v^2 h=D_v(D_v h), when the limits exist. F_beta is C1 and this is the one-sided directional-curvature convention of the source. This is Theorem1.1 p4 of2101.03540, a geometric result for the stated smoothed amplitude loss.

body:
[Theorem maintheorem2 of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Let $G_n=(V_n,E_n)$ be a sequence of random graphs and choose a root $\overset{\rightarrow}{o}_n$ uniformly among the vertices.
    Suppose that the sequence of rooted weighted random graphs $(G_n,o_n)$ converges locally to an (vertex-rooted) Unimodular Bienaymé-Galton-Watson (UBGW) tree $(\mathbb{T},o)$ with reproduction law $\pi$. Assume further that the ratio $\frac{2|E_n|}{|V_n|}$ converges in probability to the expectation of $\pi$ and that the hypothesis of Theorem~(maintheorem of the paper) holds on the UBGW tree. Now assign i.i.d weights $(w_n(e))_{e \in E(G_n)}$ of distribution $\omega$ on the edges of $G_n$. We have
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item There exists a sequence $(M_n)_n$ of matchings of $G_n$ such that $(G_n,o_n,M_n)$ converges locally to $(\mathbb{T},{o},\mathbb{M}_{\mathrm{opt}})$ given by Theorem~(maintheorem of the paper).
        In particular, we have that:

         \[
        \lim_{n \to \infty} 
        \left(  \mathbb{P}\left( \exists v \sim o_n, \{o_n,v\} \in M_n\right),\mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{v\sim o_n}w_n(o_n,v)\mathbbm{1}_{\{o_n,v\} \in M_n}\right]\right) = \perfE(\mathbb{T},o,\mathbb{M}_{\mathrm{opt}}),
        \]
        
        \item Reciprocally, for any sequence $(M_n)_n$ of matchings of $G_n$, take $(a,b)$ to be any subsequential limit of
        \[ \left(  \mathbb{P}\left( \exists v \sim o_n, \{o_n,v\} \in M_n\right),\mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{v\sim o_n}w_n(o_n,v)\mathbbm{1}_{\{o_n,v\} \in M_n}\right]\right) ,\]
        then we must have that 
        \[ (a,b)\overset{\mathrm{lex}}{\leq} \perfE(\mathbb{T},o,\mathbb{M}_{\mathrm{opt}}).
        \]
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem maintheorem2 of arXiv:2601.20502

\begin{itemize}
\item $\exists i \in \llbracket i_0 + 1,i_0 + \# I - 1\rrbracket\qquad \ell_i < p < p +\theta_{h,h} \leq \ell_{i + 1}\quad \textnormal{and} \quad p - \ell_i \in \amsmathbb{Z}_{> 0}$.
\item $\exists m \in \amsmathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} \qquad p=\ell_{i_0+1}-\theta_{h,h}-m\quad \textnormal{and} \quad p\geq \max\big(\N\mathfrak a-\theta_{h,h}, a_h, \ell_{i_0}+1\big)$.
\item $\exists m \in \amsmathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} \qquad p=\ell_{i_0+\#I}+m \quad \textnormal{and} \quad p\leq \max\big(\N \mathfrak b +1,b_h,\ell_{i_0+\#I+1}-\theta_{h,h}\big)$.
\end{itemize}
If $i_0=0$ or $i_0+\# I+1=N$, then the corresponding inequalities are ignored.

For the spherical perceptron, the process $\vX^\frstar\equiv\vX^{\frstar,\RomI:\RomIII}$ is defined on the augmented space
    \[[M^\frozen]

    \bigg[ M\bigg(1 + \frac1{\trK^6}\bigg)\bigg]\,.

For $a\in[M]$ we set
$\vX^\frstar(q_d,a)\equiv\vX^\trstar(q_d,a)$.
The remaining particles

    \[[N^\frozen] 
    \equiv
    \bigg[ N\bigg(1 + \frac1{\trK^3}\bigg)\bigg]\,,
    \]
such that the added particles are spaced evenly over $[-2\trK,2\trK]$ and frozen for all time. We then denote $\vX^\frstar\equiv(\vX^{\frstar,\RomI:\RomIII},X^{\frstar,\Ising})$.

AUTHOR-CHECKED; independent w346 audit PENDING. Unconditional convergence, even almost sure convergence, and an exact
survival probability of order 1/n do not suffice for a conditioned scaling limit.
For U uniform on (0,1), let A_n={U<=1/n} and Z_n=a_n*1_{A_n}, with a_n=1
for even n and 2 for odd n. Then Z_n->0 almost surely and n*P(A_n)=1 exactly,
but Law(Z_n|A_n) alternates between point masses at one and two.
A valid sufficient replacement on a Polish state space is: n*P(A_n)->c>0
and n*E[f(Z_n)*1_{A_n}]->c*integral f dnu for every bounded continuous f;
then Law(Z_n|A_n) converges weakly to nu.
Rare events have positive probability
Polish state space for weak-convergence criterion
No assertion that the toy process is percolation

Does the noisy voter model on $G^{(n)}$, for every fixed $\theta\in(0,1)$ and $q\geq 2$, and every sequence of initial conditions $\mathsf{x}_0^{(n)}$, satisfy $t_\textsc{mix}^{\mathsf{x}_0}(\varepsilon)-t_\textsc{mix}^{\mathsf{x}_0}(1-\varepsilon) = O(1)$ with an implicit constant depending on $\varepsilon$? (Stated as a question by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)

body: The Malliavin-Stein quantity $\langle DF, -DL^{-1}F\rangle_{\mathfrak H}$, which equals $\Gamma(F, -L^{-1}F)$ for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck generator $L$ (where $\Gamma(f, g) = \langle Df, Dg\rangle_{\mathfrak H}$), is an infinite-dimensional realization of the Bakry-Émery carré du champ operator $\Gamma(f, g) = \frac{1}{2}(L(f g) - f L g - g L f)$ extended to Hilbert-valued diffusion generators. The f2GPI bounds can be viewed as quantitative curvature bounds controlling the second carré du champ operator $\Gamma_2$.

body:
[Proposition NA1-NA2-general of arXiv:2609.00794, 'On operators whose adjoints or second adjoints attain their norms'] Let $X$ and $Y$ be Banach spaces, and let $T \in \mathcal{L}(X,Y^*)$. \begin{enumerate}
        \itemsep0.25em
        \item If $T^\top \in \operatorname{NA}(Y,X^*)$, then $T \in \operatorname{NA}_1 (X,Y^*)$. In other words,
\[
    (\Xi_{X,Y})^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{NA}(Y,X^*)\bigr)
    \subseteq \operatorname{NA}_1(X,Y^*).
\]
\item If $T^\top \in \operatorname{NA}_1(Y,X^*)$, then $T \in \operatorname{NA}_2 (X,Y^*)$. In other words,
\[
(\Xi_{X,Y})^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{NA}_1(Y,X^*)\bigr)
    \subseteq \operatorname{NA}_2(X,Y^*).
\]
\end{enumerate}
If $Y$ is reflexive, then both inclusions are equalities.

Let mu be full-dimensional log-concave with finite K=C_P(mu). Define Y=X+sqrt(t)G, nu_t=Law(Y), and T_t f(y)=E[f(X)|Y=y] using independent G~N(0,I). If integral |grad T_t f|^2 dnu_t <= q integral |grad f|^2 dmu for all finite-energy tests, where t>0 and 0<=q<1, then K<=t(1+q)/(1-q). Conversely, K<=C implies this contraction with q=C/t whenever t>C. Thus fixed numerical t,q valid for all regular isotropic log-concave measures yield KLS by regular approximation; KLS itself yields such constants. The uniform strict nonlinear contraction is an assumption, not a proved conclusion in this draft.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The smallest eigenvalue of the NTK of a deep tanh network in the ordered phase (November 2026), shows that for a fully connected tanh network of depth L in the infinite-width limit with bias variance sigma_b^2 > 0, in the ordered phase chi_1 < 1, and n distinct inputs on the fixed-point sphere, lambda_min(Theta_L) = (q* + B T*/chi_1) lambda_perp_min(-A) L chi_1^L (1 + O(1/L)), where q* is the fixed-point variance, T* = q*/(1 - chi_1), B = chi'(1) and A is the matrix of limiting rescaled correlation gaps. The order L chi_1^L is due to Xiao, Pennington and Schoenholz (ICML 2020); the paper adds the constant, a proof that lambda_perp_min(-A) > 0 for any distinct inputs (every Taylor coefficient of the limiting gap profile is strictly positive, so the Schoenberg and Chen-Menegatto-Sun criterion applies), and the same form for inputs of unequal norm when lambda_perp_min(-A) > 0. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/ntk-smallest-eigenvalue-ordered-phase (commit 73fda1d4e515). Not refereed.
title: Smallest eigenvalue of the NTK of a deep tanh network in the ordered phase: the constant, and attainment for any distinct inputs (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/ntk-smallest-eigenvalue-ordered-phase)

[Defin 9 of arXiv:2609.00974, 'On Algebraic Integrability\\ of Vector Fields \\ with Rational Function Coefficients\\ tha'] A \textbf{generic point of a curve} is a field $K$ of positive characteristic $p>0$ such that the extension $K/k$, where $k=\bigcap_{n\ge 1} K^{p^n}$, is a finitely generated field extension of transcendental degree $1$.
    
    Concretely, it is equivalent to $K$ being isomorphic to the following construction: take a perfect field $k$, take rational functions in one variable over $k$, i.e., $k(x)$, take a finite separable extension $K/k(x)$. Any choice of such $x$ is called a coordinate for $K$.
title: Definition 9 of arXiv:2609.00974

[Theorem FK rep of arXiv:2411.09614, 'Moment estimates for the stochastic heat equation on Cartan-Hadamard manifolds'] Let $p\geq 2$, $\set{B^{x,j}}_{1\leq j\leq p}$ be Brownian motions starting at $x$ independent of $W$ and each other. The following Feynman-Kac formula for the $p$-th moment of $u(t,x)$ holds if $u_0\in L^\infty(M)$: $$\mathbb{E}[\abs{u(t,x)}^p]=\mathbb{E}_x\left[\prod_{j=1}^p u_0(B^{x,j}_t)\exp\left\{\beta^2 \sum_{1\leq i,k \leq p,i\neq k}\int_0^t G_{2\alpha}(B^{x,i}_s,B^{x,k}_s)ds\right\}\right].$$
    Here $\mathbb{E}_x$ is the expectation with respect to the Brownian motions $(B^{x,j})_{1\leq j\leq p}$.

body: A (left) action of a group G on a set X is a map G x X -> X, (g, x) -> g.x, with e.x = x and g.(h.x) = (gh).x; equivalently a homomorphism G -> Sym(X). The orbit of x is G.x = {g.x : g in G}; orbits partition X. The stabilizer G_x = {g : g.x = x} is a subgroup, and the orbit-stabilizer theorem gives |G.x| = [G : G_x]. Actions are the bridge from abstract groups to concrete symmetry (Cayley, Sylow, Burnside all run through them).
title: Group Action

\begin{enumerate}
\item $f \in T^{s,\alpha}_{p,q}B(\mathbb{R}^2)$,
\item $ (c_{\bar{j},\bar{k}} )\in t^{s,\alpha}_{p,q}b $.

Let F_q be the finite field with q = p^m elements (p prime) and let f_1, ..., f_r be polynomials in F_q[x_1, ..., x_n] with sum_i deg f_i < n. WARNING (1935): the number N of common zeros of f_1, ..., f_r in F_q^n is divisible by p. CHEVALLEY (1935): if in addition every f_i has zero constant term (so 0 is a common zero), then there is another common zero; in particular a homogeneous form of degree d in more than d variables has a nontrivial zero over F_q, so finite fields are quasi-algebraically closed (C_1 fields). Strengthenings: Ax (1964) showed q^b divides N with b = ceil((n - sum deg f_i) / max deg f_i) (Ax-Katz); the theorem gives the Erdos-Ginzburg-Ziv theorem (among 2n - 1 integers some n have sum divisible by n) by applying it to two forms of degree p - 1 in 2p - 1 variables.
F_q finite with q = p^m
sum_i deg f_i < n (total degrees); the bound is sharp, as the norm form shows
Chevalley's form needs the f_i to vanish at the origin

For beta>=0, q>=2 and m crossing bonds, D(gamma_b||gamma_f)<=beta*m and D(gamma_f||gamma_b)<=beta*m. Every mixture rho of the exterior-boundary laws has D(rho||gamma_f)<=beta*m. For n^d lattice boxes this gives D(rho||gamma_f)/n^d<=2*d*beta/n, at every temperature. It does not give an energy gap. Pinning variable sites in only one law would violate the common-support hypothesis.

# Moitra-Risteski: relevant decomposition, uncovered phase-retrieval hypotheses

T321 Target 2. Literature applicability finding, not a new proof of Target 2.
Source: Fast Convergence for Langevin Diffusion with Manifold Structure,
arXiv:2002.05576, primary PDF saved under papers/.

Section 2, PDF page 3, requires the matrix-sensing operator to satisfy
(19/20)||M||_F^2 <= ||A(M)||_2^2 <= (21/20)||M||_F^2
for every matrix M of rank at most 2k. This is an operator-wide assumption,
not concentration for a fixed deterministic M.

For phase retrieval take k=1 and A_ph(M)_j=(a_j^T M a_j)/sqrt(m), so the
squared residual is precisely the normalized empirical quartic loss.
For every nonzero measurement a_i, set u=a_i/||a_i|| and M=uu^T. Then
rank(M)=1, ||M||_F=1 and

 ||A_ph(M)||_2^2=(1/m)sum_j(a_j.u)^4 >= ||a_i||^4/m.

Thus the upper RIP inequality would force
m >= (20/21)max_i||a_i||^4. The witness is allowed to depend on the sample,
because RIP quantifies over EVERY rank-one matrix. This is the exact
deterministic fourth-moment obstruction already relevant to this row,
applied to the paper's stated hypothesis; it is not presented as new.
For Gaussian measurements, ||a_1||^2/d tends to 1 in probability. Therefore
for m=C d log^3 d with fixed C, this necessary inequality fails with
probability tending to 1 as d grows. Multiplication by any fixed scalar
normalization of A_ph does not remove the growing d/log^3 d obstruction.
No claim is made here about operators obtained by data-dependent weighting,
truncation or a changed loss; those require their own arguments.

Section 4.1, Theorem 4, PDF page 7, is nevertheless a relevant generic
decomposition framework: along-level and across-level Poincare control,
control of changing conditional density/Jacobian, and finite-time retention
near the minimizer manifold combine into convergence to a restricted law.
These are hypotheses to establish, not consequences of benign landscape
alone. Our C007 is a different polar decomposition with the same unresolved
need for one conditional spectral-gap estimate.

Section 4.2, Theorem 5, PDF pages 7-8, assumes the matrix measurement
conditions above, a sufficiently large beta, and an absolutely continuous
initial law supported near one minimizer component. The target p_i is
defined just before the theorem as the Gibbs law restricted to points
closer to component E_i than the other component. The theorem's displayed
TV error includes an additive epsilon, as well as a decaying chi-square
term. It is not a statement of the full unrestricted even Poincare constant
for the empirical rank-one measurement model at beta~d/epsilon_loss.
The TV accuracy epsilon in the paper must not be identified silently with
the row's optimization/loss tolerance epsilon_loss.

The discussion on PDF page 9 explicitly leaves reaching the prescribed
initialization by unmodified Langevin for future work, while explaining
that optimization can supply such an initialization in the stated models.
Even if a warm-start sampling guarantee were imported, an additive-error
TV guarantee alone is not a variational Poincare inequality for the full law.

NEXT: adapt the near-well decomposition and retention estimates using the
actual rank-one measurement geometry, without imposing false global RIP;
then control the rest of the quotient to obtain the full polynomial gap.
No claim of a solved parameter range or a scored frontier move is made.
The rank-one diagnostic is analytic and unaudited, not a numerical bound
or a Lean-certified assertion.
Primary-source scope record, not a new polynomial-gap theorem

[Theorem l.CLT-Cumulants of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $(\mathfrak{m}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$  be a sequence of purely
 atomic random signed measures and assume they admit  correlation functions $m^{\bk k1{p}}(\bk x1{p})= m^{\bk k1{p}}(\bk x1{p};n)$ defined as at (equation eqn:mixedmoment-general of the paper).   Assume  there exist fast decreasing functions $\tilde\phi_{k}$,
 and constants $M_{k}$,	$\tilde C_k$, 
 such that for all $p\ge 2$, $k_1,\ldots,k_p\in \mathbb{N}$, $k_1+\ldots+k_p=k$
 \begin{equation}
   \sup_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\sup_{\bk x1p\in\mathbb{R}^{dp}}m^{\bk k1{p}}(\bk x1{p};n)\le M_{k}<\infty
 \end{equation}
 and statement (i) of Lemma~(l.moments-cumulants of the paper) holds for
 the functions $\tilde\phi =\tilde\phi_k$ and constants  $\tilde C=\tilde C_k$ (uniformly in $n \in \mathbb{N}$).
 If the sequence  $(g_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of real-valued, measurable functions on $ \mathbb{R}^d$, 
 is uniformly  bounded in $n$ (i.e., $\sup_{n \geq 1}  \|g_n\|_\infty\le M<\infty$) and  satisfies
$\|g_n\|_1 := \int_{\mathbb{R}^d}|g_n(x)|\,\mathrm{d} x=O(n^\kappa)$ for some $\kappa<\infty$, and
  ${\rm Var}[\langle g_n,\mathfrak{m}_n\rangle] = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$, then

$$
({\rm Var}[\langle g_n,\mathfrak{m}_n\rangle])^{-1/2} ( \langle g_n,\mathfrak{m}_n\rangle - \mathbb {E} [\langle g_n,\mathfrak{m}_n\rangle]) \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z
$$
where $Z$ denotes a standard normal random variable.

body:
[Definition def:BESQflow of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] Let $\delta \in {\mathbb R}$.  We call ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow  driven by $\mathcal W$ a collection ${\mathcal S}$ of continuous processes $({\mathcal S}_{r,x}(a),\, x\ge r)_{r\in {\mathbb R},a\ge 0}$ such that: 
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item
for each $(a,r)\in {\mathbb R}_+\times {\mathbb R}$, the process $({\mathcal S}_{r,x}(a),\, x\ge r)$ is almost surely the strong solution of the following SDE  
\begin{equation}
{\mathcal S}_{r,x}(a) = 
a + 2 \int_r^x  {\mathcal W}([0,{\mathcal S}_{r,s}(a)], \, \mathrm{d} s) + 
\delta (x-r) 
,\, x\ge r
\end{equation}
 and which, in the case $\delta<0$, is absorbed when hitting $0$.
 \item Almost surely,
 \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
 \item for all $r\in {\mathbb R}$ and $a\ge 0$, $ {\mathcal S}_{r,r}(a)=a$,
 \item for all $r\le x$, $a\mapsto  {\mathcal S}_{r,x}(a)$ is c\`adl\`ag,
 \item (Perfect flow property) for any $r\le x \le y$ and $a\ge 0$, $\mathcal S_{r,y}(a)=\mathcal S_{x,y}\circ \mathcal S_{r,x}(a)$. 
\end{enumerate} 
\end{enumerate}

We call killed ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow driven by $\mathcal W$ the flow obtained from the ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow by absorbing at $0$ the flow line $\mathcal S_{r,\cdot}(a)$ at time $\inf\{x>r\,:\,\mathcal S_{r,x}(a)=0\}$. 

We call general ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow  a  ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow or a  killed ${\rm BESQ}^\delta$ flow.

[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2609.03958, '2609.03958'] Let \(G\in L^\infty(B_1;\mathbb R^n)\), \(E\in L^\infty(B_1)\) and
let \(\mathbb A=(a^{ij})\) satisfy
\[
\lambda_0 I\leq\mathbb A\leq\Lambda_0I.
\]
Suppose that \(v\in W^{1,2}(B_1)\) satisfies
\[
\operatorname{div}(\mathbb A Dv)
\geq \operatorname{div}G-E
\qquad\text{in }B_1.
\]
Then
\begin{equation*}
 \sup_{B_{1/2}}u
 \le C\left(1+\|v_+\|_{L^1(B_1)}
 +\|G\|_{L^\infty(B_1)}+\|E\|_{L^\infty(B_1)}\right),
\end{equation*}
where $C>0$ depends only on $n$, $\lambda_0$ and $\Lambda_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem th:sec-order-main of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $A$ be a random Hermitian matrix of size $N$ and assume that for every
  finite $r$ one has
  \begin{equation} 
  \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^2 \left( \frac{1}{N} \log \mathbb{E}[H
     \text{} C (x_1, \ldots, x_r, 0^{N - r} ; \lambda_1 (A), \ldots, \lambda_N
     (A))] - \sum_{i = 1}^r \Psi (x_i) - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i = 1}^r \Phi (x_i)
     \right) = \sum_{i = 1}^r \mathrm{T} (x_i), 
     \end{equation} 
  where $\Psi, \Phi, \mathrm{T}$ are smooth functions in a complex neighborhood of $0$ and
  the above convergence is uniform in a complex neighborhood of $0^r$. Then the $1 /
  N^2$ correction of the average empirical distribution of $N^{- 1} \cdot A$
  is given by
  \[ \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^2 \left( \frac{1}{N^{k + 1}}
     \mathbb{E}[\ensuremath{\operatorname{Tr}} (A^k)] -\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k - \frac{1}{N}
     \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'_k \right) =\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}''_k
     +\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\nu}}''_k, \]
  where $(\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}, (\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}'_k)_{k \in
  \mathbb{N}}$ are given by ((topg of the paper)),((G of the paper)) respectively. The sequences
  $(\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}''_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}, (\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\nu}}''_k)_{k \in
  \mathbb{N}}$ are given by
  \[ \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}''_k = \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 1} \frac{k!}{m! (m + 1) ! (k -
     m - 1) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi' (x))^{k - m - 1}
     \mathrm{T}' (x)) \right|_{x = 0} \]
  \begin{equation}
    \text{{\hspace{10em}}} + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 2} \frac{k!}{m! (m
    + 1) ! (k - m - 2) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
    (x))^{k - m - 2} (\Phi' (x))^2) \right|_{x = 0} 
  \end{equation}
  and
  \[ \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\nu}}''_k = \frac{1}{24} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 3} \frac{k!}{m! (m
     + 1) ! (k - m - 3) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
     (x))^{k - m - 3} \Psi''' (x)) \right|_{x = 0} \]
  \[ \text{{\hspace{4em}}} + \frac{1}{12} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 3} \frac{k!}{m! (m
     + 2) ! (k - m - 3) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
     (x))^{k - m - 3} \Psi''' (x)) \right|_{x = 0} \]
  \begin{equation}
    \text{{\hspace{10em}}} + \frac{1}{12} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - 4} \frac{k!}{m! (m
    + 2) ! (k - m - 4) !}  \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'
    (x))^{k - m - 4} (\Psi'' (x))^2) \right|_{x = 0} . 
  \end{equation}

[Lemma p:mppmixcl_double of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Fix $p,q \in \mathbb{N}$ and $r \in (0, \infty)$.
Assume that we are given
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt,partopsep=0pt,topsep=0pt,parsep=0pt]
\item  a marking function $\xi: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \to \mathbb{K}'$, and
\item  
a marked point process $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{K}$ having  $\mathbb{B} $-mixing  correlations
as in  Definition (B-omega-mixing of the paper)(Bmixing of the paper)
with correlation decay functions $\omega_{k}(s) = C_k  \phi(s)$, $k \in \mathbb{N}$, 
where $(C_k)_{k \geq 1}$ is a non-decreasing sequence such that for some fixed $\epsilon \in (0,1)$, we have

\begin{equation}  
\sum_{l = 1}^{\infty}  \frac{ ({w}_0(1 + \epsilon)\kappa_0^{1 + \epsilon})^l }{l!} C_{l + p + q}  < \infty,
\end{equation}

with  ${w}_0= 4(p+q)\theta_d r^d$ and where $\kappa_0 = \max\{1, \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}\rho^{(1)}(x)\}$ is related to the ground process $\mathcal{P}$.
\end{enumerate}

\vskip.2cm
Then for  all $f \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^p),$   $g \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^q)$ and for almost all $\bk x1{p+q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d(p+q)}$ such that $s:=d(\bk x1p,\bk x{p+1}{p+q}) >4r$ we have

\begin{align} \nonumber
& \Big| \mathbb {E} _{\bk x1{p+q}}[f(\bk{{\xi}^{\cup(r)}}{1}{p}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))g(\bk{{\xi}^{\cup(r)}}{p+1}{p+q}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))]\rho^{(p+q)}(\bk x1{p+q})  \\
&  \qquad - \,
\mathbb {E} _{\bk x1p}[f(\bk{{\xi}^{\cup(r)}}{1}{p}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))] \rho^{(p)}(\bk x1{p}) \; \mathbb {E} _{\bk x{p+1}{p+q}}[g(\bk{{\xi}^{\cup(r)}}{p+1}{p+q}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}))]\rho^{(q)}(\bk x{p+1}{p+q}) \Big|  \nonumber \\
& \le 
\phi( \frac{s}{2})\sum_{l=1}^\infty \frac{w_0^l}{l!}  C_{l+p+q}
=:\phi( \frac{s}{2})\hat{C}_{p+q}<\infty.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: A mixing correlation bound for union-restricted marks

Let M>=1 finite linear-regression tasks have matrices X_m in R^(n_m by d) and labels y_m. Suppose X_m*w_star=y_m for every m, put R=max_m||X_m||_2>0, and define L(w;m)=||X_m*w-y_m||^2/2 and L(w)=M^(-1)*sum_m L(w;m). Initialize w_0=0 and sample tau_1,...,tau_k independently and uniformly from{1,...,M}, with replacement. Scheme1 performs the exact update w_t=argmin_w {L(w;tau_t)+(lambda_t/2)*||w-w_(t-1)||^2}. Write D2=||w_0-w_star||^2. Use the same coefficient lambda_t=lambda>0 in every round, and set a=R^2/(R^2+lambda), so0<a<1. For each integer k>=1, E L(w_k)<=e*D2*R^2/[2*a*(2-a)*k^(1-a*(1-a/4))]. The expectation is over the random task ordering and the loss averages over the full collection of M tasks.
Finite jointly realizable linear tasks; R is the largest task-matrix operator norm and R>0.
Independent uniform task indices sampled with replacement; exact Scheme1 updates; w_0=0.
The coefficient lambda>0 stays fixed within the entire run.
