For theta=(1-p)/p>0 let h_{L+1}(theta) be the unrestricted constant-word WHOLE no-cut coefficient, summing theta^B2^(L+1-R) over all L-step nearest-neighbor paths without an upward cut. Then limsup over even L of h_{L+1}^(1/L)>=4sqrt(theta). Confined loops starting and ending at zero have no upward cut; on [-K,K] their count is >=[2cos(pi/(2K+2))]^L/(K+1) for even L. Their contribution gives h_{L+1}>=2^(-2K)[4sqrt(theta)cos(pi/(2K+2))]^L/(K+1). Hence raw geometric activity decay with any finite prefactor is impossible for p<=16/17, and raw activities grow exponentially for p<16/17. This limits a raw-activity proof of the conjectured good interval 4/5<p<=16/17, not the RWRS model itself. No summability claim is made at exactly p=16/17; normalization by competing blocks can matter.

body: In the mathematical discipline of group theory, Cayley's theorem, named in honour of Arthur Cayley, states that every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of a symmetric group. More specifically, G is isomorphic to a subgroup of the symmetric group Sym(G) whose elements are the permutations of the underlying set of G. Explicitly, for each g in G, the left-multiplication-by-g map L_g : G -> G sending each element x to gx is a permutation of G, and the map L : G -> Sym(G) sending each element g to L_g is an injective homomorphism, so it defines an isomorphism from G onto a subgroup of Sym(G).

Thus every term retained in $\mathcal C_{k,{\rm R}}^{(0,+)}$ contains
at least one nonroot monomer.  Let
$\mathcal C_{k,{\rm R}}^{(0,{\rm hard})}$ be its subfamily in which the
Ricci residual component contains an ordinary hard resource in the sense
of (lem:ricci-internal-hard of the paper), and put
\[
 \mathcal C_{k,{\rm R}}^{(0,{\rm soft})}
 :=\mathcal C_{k,{\rm R}}^{(0,+)}-
   \mathcal C_{k,{\rm R}}^{(0,{\rm hard})}.
\]
Resolve the internal full-centered hard blocks of this last family as in
(lem:ricci-soft-threshold of the paper).  Route every all-Weyl child and,
by (lem:ricci-mixed-closed-hard of the paper), every nonzero mixed child
back into $\mathcal C_{k,{\rm R}}^{(0,{\rm hard})}$; one-box mixed
children vanish.  Thus the residual soft family has $u=0$.  Let
$\mathcal C_{k,{\rm R}}^{(0,{\rm low})}$ be the restored sum of exactly
those resolved children for which
\[
 \Delta_0=o+\frac v2<f_R.
\]
Denote the restored sum of the complementary soft children with
$\Delta_0\ge f_R$ by
$\mathcal C_{k,{\rm R}}^{(0,{\rm soft},\ge)}$; it is covered by
(lem:ricci-soft-threshold of the paper) and is not part of the low family.
Resources in different Haar-separated components do not enter this
classification.

For every fixed $L$ there are $A_L,C_L<\infty$ and a numerical $B$ such
that, for $m\le cN$, $c\ge1$, and $k\le L\log n$,
\[
 \boxed{
 \|\mathcal C_{k,{\rm R}}^{(0,{\rm low})}\|_2^2
 \le C_L n c^{k+1}(k+1)^B A_L^{2k}.}
\tag{3.3.1w$_{12k}$}
\]
The assertion is only about this intact physical low-debit sum: the complete term
has at least one nonroot monomer, while its Ricci component has no internal
ordinary hard resource.  The Ricci component may itself be all-dimer when
the monomer lies behind a Haar separator; that exterior resource remains
owned by its own component.  It makes no
termwise estimate after fixing a ribbon, status, Green coefficient, or
Weingarten pairing.

STATUS: proof (unaudited). For the exact iid Gaussian zero-bias width-n ReLU angle chain started at any theta0 in (0,pi], killed at zero norm or angle and embedded as angle0 after killing, each fixed positive integer p and T<infinity admit constants C_(p,T),c,n0, uniform in theta0, with E[theta_k^p;alive]<=C_(p,T)/(k+1)^p for0<=k<=Tn and n>=n0. For0<eta<=pi and0<=m<=N<=Tn, P(max_(m<=k<=N)theta_k>=eta)<=C_(p,T)/(eta^p(m+1)^p)+C_T n exp(-cn). A specified hybrid normalized/ordinary Gram self-loop kernel satisfies both estimates without the exponential maximal-error term. Assumptions: Independent Gaussian rows across coordinates and layers; zero-bias ReLU and width n sufficiently large; constants depend on fixed p,T and good-box choices. Inverse-U moments are interpreted only on alive states, U=1/(n theta). The hybrid kernel uses normalized difference coordinates below a fixed small angle threshold and ordinary Gram coordinates above it, with fixed concentration boxes and self-loop off the selected box. The angle transition uses n independent row pairs x=max(g,0), y=max(cos(theta)g+sin(theta)h,0), g,h iid standard Gaussians, independent across layers, and the angle between the resulting vectors. Kill at zero norm or zero angle. For the hybrid kernel use a fixed small concentration box for (mean(x^2+y^2),mean((x-y)^2)/theta^2,mean(x^2-y^2)/theta) at small theta, and ordinary Gram averages at larger theta, each centered at its expectation; self-loop on failure. Limit: New global localization proof awaits reviewer audit. This is moment decay and rare-return control, not the sharp asymptotic E theta_k~3pi/k or a finite-width weak-rate theorem. Literature novelty not asserted.

Inverse-U moments are interpreted only on alive states, U=1/(n theta). {"artifact_digest":"sha256:d217043545da2a40987c42088792bfbac5c0890229369c9694436297afecd9b8","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/d2/d217043545da2a40987c42088792bfbac5c0890229369c9694436297afecd9b8.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:af0b975c427f642f8aec1205def6bc54a1a3515149422f6182a41c5f8c3dc067","bundle_entry_key":"relu-global-angle-moments","bundle_id":"population.t244-logarithmic-bounded-weak-rate-015","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_015.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-relu-global-angle-moments","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C039: global angle moment decay and rare late returns

Version 1, 20 October 2026. Target 1, kind moved, proof (unaudited).
This removes the small-angle stopping restriction from C037 by specifying
a global hybrid regularization. No novelty relative to the literature is
asserted. Its purpose is quantitative entrance localization for the rate.

## Statement

Let the width-n Gaussian, zero-bias ReLU angle chain start at any
theta0 in (0,pi]. Set the angle to zero and absorb when either layer vector
vanishes or its angle is exactly zero. For every fixed positive integer p
and finite T there are C_(p,T),c>0 and n0 such that for n>=n0,

    E[theta_k^p; alive at k] <= C_(p,T)/(k+1)^p,
                              0<=k<=floor(Tn).                (1)

For 0<eta<=pi and integers 0<=m<=N<=floor(Tn),

    P(max_(m<=k<=N) theta_k >= eta)
       <= C_(p,T)/(eta^p (m+1)^p)+C_T n exp(-cn).              (2)

The same estimates hold for the hybrid regularized chain below; its
exponential error term in (2) is unnecessary. These constants are uniform
in the initial angle. The alive indicator excludes any cemetery inverse
moments; on alive states U_k=1/(n theta_k) and (1) gives
E[U_k^(-p);alive]<=C_(p,T)n^p/(k+1)^p.

In particular, for any delta>0, r>0, fixed eta>0, and p with delta*p>r,
the probability of any return to theta>=eta between ceil(n^delta) and Tn
is o(n^(-r)). Here delta<1 ensures a nonempty interval eventually.

## 1. Hybrid concentration event, uniform over all angles

For independent standard Gaussians g_i,h_i write

    x_i=(g_i)_+, y_i=(cos(theta)g_i+sin(theta)h_i)_+.

Fix a sufficiently small angle threshold theta_*>0. When theta<=theta_*,
use C032's fixed small concentration box for the averages of

    (x^2+y^2, (x-y)^2/theta^2, (x^2-y^2)/theta)

about their population mean. On it the output angle divided by theta
is bounded above and below by positive constants; it is a smooth function
of those averages with uniformly bounded first and second derivatives.
These facts follow directly from C032's positive Gram determinant and
uniform normalized angle formula, not from a reciprocal raw moment.

When theta>theta_*, use the ordinary Gram averages

    (A,B,C)=(mean x^2, mean y^2, mean xy).

Their mean is (1/2,1/2,kappa(theta)/2), where

    kappa(theta)=[sin(theta)+(pi-theta)cos(theta)]/pi.

Since kappa(theta)<=kappa(theta_*)<1, a fixed sufficiently small box
about these means ensures A,B bounded away from zero and
C/sqrt(AB) in a compact subinterval of (-1,1), uniformly in this angle
range. This is valid also at theta=pi, where the population cross term
is zero. On the box

    alpha=arccos(C/sqrt(AB))

and (alpha/theta)^p have uniformly bounded first and second coordinate
derivatives, and alpha/theta is bounded above and below by positive
constants. The artificial part of the box with C<0 only supplies a smooth
extension; every realized ReLU cross term is nonnegative.

Both sets of row coordinates have uniformly bounded moments and a common
positive neighborhood of exponential integrability. For the normalized
rows this is the Gaussian quadratic-form domination in C032; for the
ordinary rows it follows from |xy|<=(x^2+y^2)/2 and Gaussian squares.
Chernoff bounds give a uniform good-event failure probability C exp(-cn).
Uniform row second moments also imply E|Zbar-EZ|^2<=C/n.

Define the global regularized transition to use the actual angle on its
appropriate good event and self-loop off it. Its angle stays in (0,pi]
and its angle ratio is bounded above and below uniformly. Piecewise choice
at theta_* is measurable; no differentiability of this kernel in theta is
used.

## 2. A global one-step nonlinear drift

Let F(theta)=arccos(kappa(theta)). The second-order sample-average Taylor
argument used in C037, now applied to each of the two boxes, gives

    E[(theta_next/theta)^p]
        <= [F(theta)/theta]^p+C_p/n,
                          uniformly for 0<theta<=pi.          (3)

For small theta use the normalized angular ratio test; for larger theta
divide the ordinary angle test by theta^p, whose denominator is bounded
below by theta_*^p. Centered linear terms have zero mean before truncation
and exponentially small deleted expectation. Quadratic remainders are
O(1/n). Off-box self-loops and bounded deterministic test values add only
exponentially small errors. Thus (3) does not divide an absolute angular
error by an arbitrarily small theta.

For theta>0, kappa(theta)-cos(theta)=(sin(theta)-theta cos(theta))/pi>0:
the numerator has derivative theta sin(theta)>0 on (0,pi) and starts at0.
Hence 0<F(theta)<theta. At zero F(theta)/theta=1-a theta+O(theta^2),
a=1/(3pi). The continuous function

    [1-(F(theta)/theta)^p]/theta

is therefore strictly positive on the compact interval [0,pi], with
limiting value p*a at zero. Choose c_p>0 below its minimum and small enough
that c_p*pi<=1/2. Equation (3) then implies

    E[theta_next^p | theta]
           <= (1+C_p/n)theta^p-c_p theta^(p+1).                (4)

## 3. Moment decay and the maximal bound

With m_k=E theta_k^p, Jensen transforms (4) into

    m_(k+1)<=rho m_k-c_p m_k^(1+1/p), rho=1+C_p/n.

The discrete nonlinear comparison in C037 applies on [0,pi] too: put
v_k=rho^(-k)m_k, decrease c_p if necessary so (c_p/rho)v_k^(1/p)<=1/2,
and use (1-z)^(-1/p)>=1+z/p. It gives v_k<=C_p/(k+1)^p, uniformly in
m0<=pi^p. Multiplication by rho^k<=exp(C_p T) proves (1) for the
regularized chain.

By (4) without its negative term, rho^(-k)theta_k^p is a nonnegative
supermartingale. Apply its conditional maximal inequality starting at m:

    P(max_(m<=k<=N)theta_k>=eta)
       <=rho^(N-m) E theta_m^p/eta^p
       <=C_(p,T)/(eta^p(m+1)^p).

This proves (2) for the regularized chain.

## 4. Transfer to the exact chain

Use identical Gaussian rows until the first hybrid good-event failure.
Its probability by time N is at most C N exp(-cn), uniformly over the
entire state range, by conditioning on the past at each layer. Until then
both chains are nondegenerate and have identical angles. Killed exact
angles lie in [0,pi]. Their pth moments thus differ at time k by at most
C pi^p k exp(-cn); their late-return event probabilities differ by at most
C N exp(-cn). For k<=Tn the moment error can be absorbed in C_(p,T)/(k+1)^p,
since (Tn+1)^(p+1) exp(-cn) is uniformly bounded. This proves (1)-(2).

## Remaining matching problem

These estimates allow a polynomial burn-in followed by small-angle
localization with an arbitrarily high fixed polynomial confidence level.
They do not determine the coefficient of the singular occupation sum.
In particular, an upper bound E theta_k<=C/(k+1) is not the asymptotic
E theta_k~3pi/k needed to identify the logarithmic bias coefficient.
That sharp mesoscopic statement and the associated weak-error matching
remain separate steps.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:48d5412d05f2566420246d906fe5e2cb5ea63da0a7aee9e2d7460ec5d88ae3f3","revision_digest":"sha256:3fa83ce44fb574362f46b2a57b62c0857f8fe7e4bc8ae34f8b6d54ca52943321","source_id":"owner-own-work:T244-w691-C039:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Proposition prop:limit_of_difference_operator_intro of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] \begin{enumerate}[$\bullet$]
		\item
			If $(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})$ is above or below $\mathcal{W}$, we have $d(\Delta x)=0$ and $a(\Delta x)=-1$, that is, the
			limiting difference operator is the negative identity $(-Id)$;
		\item If $(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})$ lies on the upper boundary of $\mathcal{W}$,
			then
			\begin{equation*}
				d(\Delta x)=-\kappa^{2} q^{2\Delta x+1/2},
				\qquad
				a(\Delta x)=-1-\kappa^{2}(1+q)q^{2\Delta x+1}.
			\end{equation*}
			On the lower boundary of $\mathcal{W}$, 
			one has to 
			replace the powers of $(q,\kappa)$ with those of
			$(q^{-1},\kappa^{-1})$, while the factor $1+q$ is kept
			the same.
		\item 
			Inside $\mathcal{W}$ but away
			from its center line $\lfloor
			L\hspace{1pt}\mathsf{x}\rfloor=\tfrac12(S+t)$, the
			coefficients in the upper half are
			\begin{equation*}
				d(\Delta x)=-\kappa^{2} q^{2\Delta x+1/2},
				\qquad 
				a(\Delta x)=-\kappa^{2}(1+q)q^{2\Delta x+1}.

Fix an irrational theta and reduced rationals p_j/q_j tending to theta with q_j tending to infinity. The clock/shift pairs U_j,V_j from the nilpotent construction, with omega_j=exp(2*pi*i*p_j/q_j) and c_j=exp(pi*i/q_j), converge in all star-moments and in the norms of every fixed matrix-valued star-polynomial to the canonical irrational rotation pair u,v. This uses simplicity and the faithful canonical trace of the irrational rotation C*-algebra. The cached Fang--Jiang--Lin--Xu paper, arXiv:1210.4771v1, Theorem 12.2, identifies the Brown measure of u+v in this canonical tracial representation as Haar measure on the unit circle. Every finite sum U_j+V_j has empirical eigenvalue measure delta_0. This gives a candidate counterexample to the implication from arbitrary strong convergence to Brown-measure convergence, pending independent review and with no novelty claim. It does not address independent Ginibre ensembles or a free limiting family.

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] For any $n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 3}$ and $d\in \mathbb{Z}_{ \geq 2}$, let   $\Omega,\Omega_*$, $P,P_*$ and $\pi,\pi_*$ be the state space, transition matrix and stationary distribution of the standard Rook's walk and the RWBD chains resp. each with parameters $n$ and $d$. Also, let $x\in \Omega_*$. Then,
  \[\Vert P_*^t(x,\cdot) - \pi_*(\cdot) \Vert_\text{TV} = \Vert (P^t \mu_x)(\cdot) - \pi(\cdot) \Vert_\text{TV}\]
  where $\mu_x$ is a distribution of $\Omega$ with probabilities uniformly distributed over $H_x$. That is,
   \[\mu_x(h) = \begin{cases}
      \frac{1}{\varphi(x)}, \quad &h\in H_x\\
      0, \quad &h\not\in H_x
   \end{cases}\]
   for all $h\in \Omega$, where $\varphi(x) = {d \choose i}(n-1)^i$ as in Definition \ref{defphi}.
   \begin{proof}
      \begin{align*}
         \Vert P_*^t(x,\cdot) - \pi_*(\cdot) \Vert_\text{TV} &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{y\in \Omega_*}|P^t_*(x,y) -\pi_*(y)|\\
         &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{y\in \Omega_*}|(P^t \mu_x)(H_y) -\pi(H_y)| \tag{By Def. \ref{BDRW}}\\
         &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{y\in \Omega_*}\sum_{h_y\in H_y}|(P^t \mu_x)(h_y) -\pi(h_y)|\\
         &= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{z\in \Omega}|(P^t \mu_x)(z) -\pi(z)|\\
         &= \Vert (P^t \mu_x)(\cdot) - \pi(\cdot) \Vert_\text{TV}
      \end{align*}
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 8 of arXiv:2604.07478

[Theorem 24 (see \cite{FrGue}) of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $K$ be a compact convex set in $\mathbb R^n$, let
$p\in\mathbb N$, and let
\[
u_j\colon K\to\mathbb R,
\quad j=1,\ldots,p,
\]
be continuous functions. Let $P_{u_1,\ldots,u_p}(K)\ne\emptyset$ be the set of all
log-concave measures $\nu$ supported in $K$ such that
\[
\int_K u_j\,d\nu\ge0,
\quad j=1,\ldots,p.
\]
Let
\[
\Phi\colon P(K)\to\mathbb R
\]
be a convex continuous functional, where $P(K)$ is the space of all Borel
probability measures on $K$, equipped with the weak topology. Then
\[
\sup_{\nu\in P_{u_1,\ldots,u_p}(K)} \Phi(\nu)
\]
is attained at a log-concave measure $\nu\in P_{u_1,\ldots,u_p}(K)$ such that
the affine span $S(\nu)$ of $\operatorname{supp}(\nu)$ satisfies
\[
\dim S(\nu)\le p.
\]
Consequently,
\[

body:
Let $T: X \to X$ be a continuous map of a compact metric space $(X, d)$. For $n \ge 1$ define the dynamical metric $d_n(x, y) = \max_{0 \le k < n} d(T^k x, T^k y)$. A set $E \subset X$ is $(n, \varepsilon)$-separated if $d_n(x, y) > \varepsilon$ for all distinct $x, y \in E$; let $s(n, \varepsilon)$ be the maximal cardinality of such a set (finite by compactness). A set $F$ is $(n, \varepsilon)$-spanning if every $x \in X$ has $d_n(x, y) \le \varepsilon$ for some $y \in F$; let $r(n, \varepsilon)$ be the minimal cardinality. The topological entropy is
$$h_{top}(T) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log s(n, \varepsilon) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} \log r(n, \varepsilon) \in [0, \infty],$$
using $r(n,\varepsilon) \le s(n,\varepsilon) \le r(n, \varepsilon/2)$; the limit in $\varepsilon$ exists by monotonicity, and replacing the $\limsup$ in $n$ by a $\liminf$ gives the same value. The value is independent of the compatible metric (this uses compactness) and coincides with the open-cover definition $h_{top}(T) = \sup_{\mathcal{U}} \lim_n \frac1n \log N(\mathcal{U}^n_0)$ where $N$ counts the minimal subcover of the join $\mathcal{U}^n_0 = \bigvee_{k<n} T^{-k}\mathcal{U}$. Basic properties: $h_{top}(T^m) = m\, h_{top}(T)$ for $m \ge 1$; $h_{top}(T^{-1}) = h_{top}(T)$ for homeomorphisms; $h_{top}$ is an invariant of topological conjugacy; a Lipschitz map of a compact metric space of finite box dimension has finite entropy, but a continuous map of a compact metric space can have $h_{top} = \infty$. On a NON-compact space the separated-set quantity depends on the metric, not merely on the topology, and the equalities above can fail.
X is a compact metric space and T is continuous
the metric enters only through the compact topology

[Lemma 42 (Difference equation for two Ricci--DeTurck solutions) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(s(t)\) be a Ricci-flow background and let \(v_0(t)\) and \(v_1(t)\)
be two positive definite solutions of the Ricci--DeTurck equation relative to
\(s(t)\) on the same time interval.  Put
\[
        U=v_1-v_0,
        \qquad v_\vartheta=v_0+\vartheta(v_1-v_0),
        \quad 0\leq\vartheta\leq1,
\]
and assume that every \(v_\vartheta\) is positive definite.  With \(\nabla\)
the connection of \(s(t)\), the difference satisfies a homogeneous linear
system
\begin{equation}
        \partial_tU-P^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qU
        =B^p\nabla_pU+CU,
\end{equation}
where the second-order part is diagonal in the tensor components: in a fixed
frame, every component \(U^A\) is acted on by the same operator
\(P^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_q\), and no second derivative of a different component
occurs.  More precisely, for
\[
        \mathcal Q_s(v)=-2\Ric(v)+\Lie_{W(v,s)}v,
\]
one has the structural formula
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \mathcal Q_s(v)
        ={}&v^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qv
        +v^{-1}*v^{-1}*\nabla v*\nabla v \\
        &\quad+\mathcal R(\Rm(s),v,v^{-1}),
\end{split}
\end{equation}
and the mean-value identity
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \partial_tU
        &=\mathcal Q_s(v_1)-\mathcal Q_s(v_0)\\
        &=\int_0^1D\mathcal Q_s|_{v_\vartheta}[U] \,d\vartheta.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Differentiating \eqref{eq:rdt-structural-form} gives
\begin{equation}
        D\mathcal Q_s|_{v_\vartheta}[Z]
        =v_\vartheta^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qZ
          +\mathcal B_\vartheta^p\nabla_pZ+\mathcal C_\vartheta Z,
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \mathcal B_\vartheta
        &=v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*\nabla v_\vartheta,\\
        \mathcal C_\vartheta
        &=v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*\nabla^2v_\vartheta
          +v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}
             *\nabla v_\vartheta*\nabla v_\vartheta\\
        &\qquad+\mathcal R_1(\Rm(s),v_\vartheta,v_\vartheta^{-1}).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Here \(*\) denotes universal tensor contractions, and \(\mathcal R\) and
\(\mathcal R_1\) are algebraic in the displayed arguments; in particular,
\(\mathcal R_1\) contains no derivatives of \(v_\vartheta\).  The
coefficients in \eqref{eq:rdt-difference-system} are
\[
 P^{pq}=\int_0^1v_\vartheta^{pq}\,d\vartheta,
 \qquad B^p=\int_0^1\mathcal B_\vartheta^p\,d\vartheta,
 \qquad C=\int_0^1\mathcal C_\vartheta\,d\vartheta.
\]
Consequently, uniform metric equivalence and finite-order bounds for
\(v_0,v_1\), and \(s\) give the corresponding ellipticity and H\"older bounds
for \(P,B,C\).

[Corollary cor:conjugate-constant-poc of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let $X_i^N(0)$ be i.i.d. with law $\mu_0$, and set $Y_i^N(0):=A(X_i^N(0))$.  If
\[
        \mathbb E\left\|A(X(0))\right\|^2<\infty,
\]
then the matrix-SVGD flow for $(\pi_A,K_A^{(1)})$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
        \mathbb E\left[\sup_{t\ge0}\, d_{A,1}^2(\mu_t^N,\mu_t)\right]
        \le
        \frac{\operatorname{Tr}\operatorname{Cov}(A(X(0)))}{N}.
\end{equation}
The same estimate holds with $\mu_t^N,\mu_t$ replaced by their time averages.

body: Consider a parametric model with parameter theta in an open subset of R^d, satisfying standard regularity (identifiability, smoothness, nonsingular Fisher information, true parameter interior to the space), and a null hypothesis restricting theta to a smooth submodel of codimension k. Let Lambda_n be the likelihood ratio: the supremum of the likelihood over the full model divided by its supremum over the null submodel, from n iid observations. Wilks' theorem states that under the null hypothesis, as n -> infinity, 2 log Lambda_n converges in distribution to a chi-squared distribution with k degrees of freedom, justifying the asymptotic chi-squared likelihood-ratio test. Due to Samuel S. Wilks.
title: Wilks' theorem

[Thm 6 (CLT for the normalized traces) of arXiv:2604.26499, 'Spectrum of Random Matrices with Exploding Moments'] Let $M$ be the matrix same as in Condition \ref{cond:matrixcond_1_NonHer} with $\alpha=1$. For any partition $\pi\in\bigcup_{k}\mathcal{P}(k)$, let $Z_N(T_\pi)$ be defined similar as in \eqref{eq:centered and normalized random variables Z_N} for matrix $M$.
Then the family
$
\big(Z_N(T_\pi)\big)_{\pi\in\bigcup_{k}\mathcal{P}(k)}
$
converges, as $N\to\infty$, to a centered Gaussian process
$\big(z(T_\pi)\big)_{\pi\in\bigcup_{k}\mathcal{P}(k)}$.
Moreover, for any two partitions $\pi_1,\pi_2$,
$$
\mathrm{Cov}\left(z(T_{\pi_1}),z(T_{\pi_2})\right)
=
\sum_{T\in\mathcal P^{\#}(T_{\pi_1},T_{\pi_2})}
\tau^{nh}[T],
$$
where $\mathcal{P}^{\#}(T_{\pi_1},T_{\pi_2})$ denotes the collection of graphs obtained by disjoint copies of the graphs $T_{\pi_1}$ and $T_{\pi_2}$ and gluing them with at least one common edge, and where $\tau^{nh}[T]$ is same as defined in the Theorem \ref{thm:Convergence of normalized trace for non-Hermitian matrices with independent exploding entries}.

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: finite speed of propagation and the domain-of-dependence cone are properties of the wave equation (and of symmetric hyperbolic systems), proved by a local energy identity on the cone. The Schrödinger equation has no such identity and propagates instantaneously. Concrete counterexample: let f ∈ L¹(R^n) be nonzero and compactly supported and let t ≠ 0. By the kernel formula, e^{itΔ}f(x) = (4πit)^{−n/2} e^{i|x|²/(4t)} · G(x/(2t)) where G is the Fourier transform of the compactly supported integrable function y ↦ e^{i|y|²/(4t)}f(y). By the Paley–Wiener theorem G extends to an entire function on C^n, and it is not identically zero, so its zero set contains no nonempty open set. Hence e^{itΔ}f is nonzero almost everywhere on every open subset of R^n at every t ≠ 0: compactly supported data instantly become globally supported. The same phenomenon rules out any cone-shaped domain of dependence, and the heat equation behaves the same way. What survives for Schrödinger are local smoothing, dispersive decay and (pseudo)locality statements about wave packets moving at velocity ≈ 2ξ, not a finite propagation speed; the wave equation's finite-speed argument must never be transplanted to a dispersive or parabolic equation.
title: Pitfall: Finite Speed of Propagation Is Hyperbolic, Not Dispersive — It Fails for Schrödinger

body: [Lemma 2.8 (Borel–Cantelli) of arXiv:2512.05720, 'First-passage percolation, non-positive curvature, and radial maps'] Let $(A_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ be a sequence of events in a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$. (1) If $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(A_{n})<\infty$, then $\mathbb{P}\bigl(A_{n}\text{ i.o.}\bigr)=\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\limsup_{n\to\infty}A_{n}\Bigr)=0.$ (2) If the events $(A_{n})$ are independent and $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(A_{n})=\infty$, then $\mathbb{P}\bigl(A_{n}\text{ i.o.}\bigr)=1.$

body: In vector calculus, Green's theorem relates a line integral around a simple closed curve C to a double integral over the plane region D (surface in $\mathbb {R} ^{2}$) bounded by C. It is the two-dimensional special case of Stokes' theorem (surface in $\mathbb {R} ^{3}$). In one dimension, it is equivalent to the fundamental theorem of calculus. In two dimensions, it is equivalent to the divergence theorem.

body:
Let T be a MINIMAL homeomorphism of a compact metric space X and let f be a continuous real function on X. Then the following are equivalent: (i) the Birkhoff sums S_n f(x) = sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(T^k x) are uniformly bounded in n for SOME point x; (ii) the Birkhoff sums are uniformly bounded in n and in x; (iii) f is a continuous coboundary, that is f = g composed with T minus g for some continuous g on X. In particular a cohomological equation with continuous data is solvable continuously precisely when its Birkhoff sums stay bounded at a single point - a striking upgrade from one orbit to the whole space, which is where minimality is used.
MINIMALITY of T and CONTINUITY of f.
Without minimality the equivalence fails;
with merely measurable data the corresponding statement is the Gottschalk-Hedlund analogue for measurable coboundaries and is different.

For m>=5 and q>=2, the arc-transitive graph C_m[empty_q] has mq vertices and degree 2q. Its mean hitting time from a target twin is mq, and from fiber j!=0 is j(m-j)+m(q-1). Its maximal commute time is 2 floor(m^2/4)+2m(q-1), its stationary mean hitting time is (m^2-1)/6+m(q-1), and its rate-one continuous-time relaxation time is 1/(1-cos(2*pi/m)). For fixed q their maximal-commute to twice stationary-hitting ratio tends to 3/2.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Status: proof written by w336, independent KEEP pending. This extends the recorded q=2 campaign counterexample; it is not a new literature priority claim. The source's tau_star is a maximal commute time, not a maximal one-way hitting time. Relaxation here uses the rate-one continuous-time generator P-I.

Let m>=5, q>=2 and G=C_m[empty_q]. Its vertices are (i,a), with i modulo m and 1<=a<=q; two vertices are adjacent precisely when their first coordinates differ by one modulo m. G is simple, connected, 2q-regular, has n=mq vertices, and is not a cycle. Rotations, reflection of C_m and independent permutations inside each fiber act transitively on directed edges, so G is arc-transitive.

Fix target (0,1). Let a be the mean hitting time from a different vertex in fiber 0. Every visit to fiber 0 from elsewhere chooses a uniformly distributed vertex. If h_j is the mean from fiber j!=0, the quotient cycle's hitting-time equation gives

    h_j = j(m-j) + ((q-1)/q)a.

The identity j(m-j)=1+[(j-1)(m-j+1)+(j+1)(m-j-1)]/2 verifies that equation away from 0. From a twin of the target, a=1+h_1=m+((q-1)/q)a, so a=mq and h_j=j(m-j)+m(q-1). These values solve all first-step equations. A finite connected chain hits the target with finite mean, so uniqueness of the killed-chain linear system identifies them with the actual hitting times.

The graph automorphisms exchange any two vertices of a specified fiber separation, so hitting times are symmetric. For m>=5, floor(m^2/4)>m, hence the largest one-way hitting time is floor(m^2/4)+m(q-1), larger than the twin value mq. Consequently

    tau_star = 2 floor(m^2/4) + 2m(q-1),
    tau_0 = (m^2-1)/6 + m(q-1).

The second formula is the stationary mean hitting time of the fixed target, including its zero self-hitting time: sum_{j=1}^{m-1}j(m-j)=m(m^2-1)/6, and the remaining constant terms sum to m(q-1). A neighbor has mean hitting time m-1+m(q-1)=n-1.

P equals (A(C_m)/2) tensor (J_q/q). The fiber-constant subspace has eigenvalues cos(2*pi*k/m), 0<=k<m; its orthogonal complement has m(q-1) zero eigenvalues. Since cos(2*pi/m)>0 for m>=5, tau_2=1/(1-cos(2*pi/m)). This is the continuous-time relaxation time; for even m the non-lazy discrete-time absolute spectral gap vanishes, which is a different parameter.

For each fixed q>=2 and m tending to infinity,

    tau_star/n^2 -> 1/(2q^2),
    tau_2/n^2 -> 1/(2*pi^2*q^2),
    tau_star/(2*tau_0) -> 3/2.

Thus the same family refutes the three bounds recorded for Aldous-Fill Problem 7.27: O(n log n), O(n), and ratio 1+o(1). This statement relies on the cached problem's parameter definitions and does not establish whether the refutation was previously published.

Checks: scripts/check_p0208.py solves the full hitting-time systems, compares the full transition spectrum, checks the directed-edge orbit, and tests the stationary sum and neighbor identity. Method: Maximal stationary antivoter variance structural calculation Result: On the complete graph all distinct-pair correlations equal c. At stationarity, the generator applied to eta_i*eta_j gives c=-(1+(n-2)c)/(n-1), hence c=-1/(2n-3). Therefore Var(S)=n+n(n-1)c=n(n-2)/(2n-3). The general source inequality Var(S)<n/2 has the same leading term but leaves the exact gap n/[2(2n-3)]. Check: The correlation equation can also be obtained by conditioning on which member of the pair updates and whether it samples its partner. Each route gives the same c. In particular merely proving Var(S)<=n/2 cannot resolve the proposed finite-n optimizer. Obstruction: A sharp bound on the return-parity expression for the meeting chain, or on averaged spin correlations, is missing. Pairwise correlations need not all be bounded by the complete-graph value.

[Lemma 32 of arXiv:2608.12804, 'Scaling Limits for Ising Models on Inhomogeneous Random Graphs and Applications'] Let
\(
    K,K':[0,1]^2\rightarrow\mathbb R
\)
be symmetric, Riemann-integrable kernels, and suppose that
$\{\sigma_i\}_{i\geq1}$ and $\{\tau_i\}_{i\geq1}$ are two independent
sequences of i.i.d. Rademacher random variables. Let
$\{\lambda_r(K)\}_{r\geq1}$ and
$\{\lambda_r(K')\}_{r\geq1}$ denote the nonzero eigenvalues of
$T_K$ and $T_{K'}$, respectively, repeated according to
multiplicity. Then, we have:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle
\frac{1}{2N}
\sum_{1\leq i\neq j\leq N}
K\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{j}{N}\right)
\bigl(\sigma_i\sigma_j+\tau_i\tau_j\bigr)
\\[4mm]
\displaystyle
\frac{1}{2N}
\sum_{1\leq i\neq j\leq N}
K'\left(\frac{i}{N},\frac{j}{N}\right)
\sigma_i\tau_i\sigma_j\tau_j
\end{pmatrix}
\xrightarrow{d}
\begin{pmatrix}
\displaystyle
\frac12\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}
\lambda_r(K)(X_r^2-1)
+
\frac12\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}
\lambda_r(K)(Y_r^2-1)
\\[4mm]
\displaystyle
\frac12\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}
\lambda_r(K')(Z_r^2-1)
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where
$\{X_r\}_{r\geq1}$,
$\{Y_r\}_{r\geq1}$, and
$\{Z_r\}_{r\geq1}$ are mutually independent sequences of
i.i.d. standard Gaussian random variables.
All three infinite series appearing in the distributional limit converge in $L^2$ and almost surely.

[Theorem 8 (Error bound for the realised volatility classifier) of arXiv:2609.00402, '2609.00402'] Suppose Assumption~\ref{ass:volatility} holds. Fix \(\alpha_V\in(0,1)\), define \(a_{V,\alpha_V}=U^2\sqrt{n\log(1/\alpha_V)/2}\), and set \(\lambda_{V,\alpha_V}=n\nu_0+a_{V,\alpha_V}\). Then the exact classifier \(h_{V,\lambda_{V,\alpha_V}}(\bm X)=\mathbb I\{V(\bm X)>\lambda_{V,\alpha_V}\}\) satisfies \(\mathbb P\{h_{V,\lambda_{V,\alpha_V}}(\bm X)=1\mid Y=0\}\leq\alpha_V\) and
\[
\mathbb P\{h_{V,\lambda_{V,\alpha_V}}(\bm X)=0\mid Y=1\}
\leq
\exp\left\{-\frac{2(n\kappa_V-a_{V,\alpha_V})_+^2}{nU^4}\right\}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{err}(h_{V,\lambda_{V,\alpha_V}})
\leq\pi_0\alpha_V+
\pi_1\exp\left\{-\frac{2(n\kappa_V-a_{V,\alpha_V})_+^2}{nU^4}\right\}.
\]

Now fix \(M>0\) and \(\epsilon_V>0\), and suppose that \(\sup_{\bm x\in\mathcal X_M}\lvert f_{\epsilon_V,M}^{RV}(\bm x)-V(\bm x)\rvert\leq\epsilon_V\). Define the clipped neural classifier $\overline h_V(\bm X)=\mathbb I\left\{f_{\epsilon_V,M}^{RV}(\operatorname{clip}_M(\bm X))>\lambda_{V,\alpha_V}+\epsilon_V\right\}.$ Then
\[
\operatorname{err}(\overline h_V)
\leq\pi_0\{\alpha_V+\tau_0(M)\}
+\pi_1\left[\exp\left\{-\frac{2(n\kappa_V-a_{V,\alpha_V}-2\epsilon_V)_+^2}{nU^4}\right\}+\tau_1(M)\right]
=:\mathfrak B_V(\alpha_V,\epsilon_V,M).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Error bound for the realised volatility classifier

[Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] There is an absolute constant $c>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large
$h$,
\begin{equation}
 \left|\left\{|hA|:A\subset\mathbb Z,\ |A|=4,
 \ \operatorname{ndiam} A<\frac{13}{20}h^2\right\}\right|\geq ch^3.
\end{equation}
More locally,
\begin{equation}
 \left|\mathcal R(h,4)\cap
 \left[\binom{h+3}{3}-\frac{h^3}{250},
       \binom{h+3}{3}-\frac{h^3}{400}\right]\right|\geq ch^3,
\end{equation}
where the endpoints may be rounded to integers.  Consequently
\[
 \boxed{|\mathcal R(h,4)|=\Theta(h^3)},
 \qquad
 \liminf_{h\to\infty}
 \frac{|\mathcal R(h,4)|}{|[3h+1,\binom{h+3}{3}]\cap\mathbb Z|}>0.
\]
The values counted in (equation eq:localmain of the paper) may be chosen with primitive
representatives having two independent homogeneous relations of degree at
most $h$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Positive-density four-point spectrum

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $n,d,k\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge k$, and let $\mu$ be an isotropic
log-concave measure on $\mathbb R^n$. Let
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\in \mathcal P_d(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^k)$
and assume that
\[
\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f_j)>0,
\quad \forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.
\]
Then
\[
\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Delta_{\hat f}\,d\mu=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\det \Sigma_\mu^d(f)=0.
\]

\begin{aligned}

of total dimension $8$.

body:
[Definition 20 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] For a function $g : X \to Y$, where $X = \T^d$ or $\R^d$ and $Y$ is a Banach space, we define for $s \geq 0$ the (semi)norm space $\mathcal{C}^s$ as follows. For $s=0$, we let
    \[\|g\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(X) Y} := \sup_{x \in X} \|g(x)\|_Y.\]
    For $s \in (0,\infty)$---letting $s = n + r$ where $r \in (0,1]$ and $n \in \N$---we define $\mathcal{C}^s(X)$ as a seminorm on a subspace of $C^n(X)$ by
    \[\|g\|_{\mathcal{C}^s(X) Y} := \sup_{x,x' \in X, x \ne x'} \frac{\|\nabla^n g(x) - \nabla^ng(x')\|_Y}{|x-x'|^r}.\]
    We note in particular that $\mathcal{C}^1$ is the Lipschitz seminorm and that $\mathcal{C}^0$ is the natural norm on the space of bounded functions---rather than $C^1$ and $C^0$ which have additional qualitative regularity hypotheses that we do not want to require, as we will frequently be working with Lipschitz functions that are not $C^1$.

    We also consider for $p \in [1,\infty), s\geq 0$ the fractional Sobolev (semi)norm spaces $W^{s,p}$. For $s \in \N$, we just let $\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(X)Y} := \|\nabla^s g\|_{L^p(X)Y}$, and for $s>0$ and $s \not \in \N$, we again write $s = n+r$ where $r \in (0,1)$ and $n \in \N$ and define
    \[\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(X) Y} := \Big(\int_X \int_X \frac{\|\nabla^n g(x) - \nabla^n g(x')\|^p_Y}{|x-x'|^{d + rp}}\,dx\,dx'\Big)^{1/p}.\]

body: The halting problem is undecidable: there is no Turing machine H that, given as input an encoding of an arbitrary Turing machine M together with an input string w, always halts and correctly reports whether M halts on w. The halting set {(M, w) : M halts on w} is, however, computably enumerable (recognizable): a universal machine can simulate M on w and accept if the simulation halts.

body:
[Lemma Polynomial basis identity of arXiv:2602.07920, 'On the position matrix of single-shelf shuffle and card guessing'] Let $N, m$ be a fixed positive integer. Then, 
    \[(N-x)^{\underline{m}} = \sum_{k=0}^{m}c_{N}(k, m) x^{\underline{k}},\]
    where \[c_N(k, m) = (-1)^{k}(N-k)^{\underline{m-k}}\binom{m}{k} = (-1)^{k}\frac{(N-k)!}{(N-m)!}\binom{m}{k},\qquad 0\leq k\leq m\;.\]
    In particular, $c_{N}(m, m)=(-1)^{m}$ and $ c_N(0, m)=N^{\underline{m}}$ for all $m$. Furthermore, $c_N(k, m)=0$ for $k>m$.
title: Lemma Polynomial basis identity of arXiv:2602.07920

[Theorem 7 (van den Berg) of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] Suppose that $D$ is simply connected and that $\partial D$ is Minkowski nondegenerate with
Minkowski dimension $\msf d_M(\partial D)\in[1,2)$. That is,
\[0<\liminf_{r\to0}\frac{\msf{A}(\partial D_r)}{r^{2-\msf d_M(\partial D)}}\leq
\limsup_{r\to0}\frac{\msf{A}(\partial D_r)}{r^{2-\msf d_M(\partial D)}}<\infty,\]
where we define
\[\partial D_r=\left\{x\in\mbb R^2:\inf_{y\in\partial D}|x-y|<r\right\}.\]
There exists constants $c\in(1,\infty)$ and $\th>0$ such that
\begin{align}

c^{-1}t^{1-\msf d_M(\partial D)/2}\leq\msf{A}(D)-\msf M_0(t)\leq ct^{1-\msf d_M(\partial D)/2},\qquad t\in(0,\th).
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

exist at most $2d-1$ indices and strictly positive weights whose objective
$G(q)=\sum\alpha_i(\ip{q}{\xi_i}-\eta_i)^2$ is strictly convex with unique
minimizer $\hat q$ satisfying
\[
1+\lVert \hat q\rVert^2\;\le\;1+\frac1d .
\]

[Lemma 13 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $\varrho\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ be a nonnegative, integrable,
unimodal function on $\mathbb R$. Then, for every $d\in\mathbb N$ and every
$f\in \mathcal P_d(\mathbb R)\cap L^1(\varrho\,ds)$, one has
\[
\int_{\mathbb R}|f(s)|\,|\varrho'(s)|\,ds
\le
2\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}|f(s)\varrho(s)|
+
\int_{\mathbb R}|f'(s)|\varrho(s)\,ds.

body:
[Corollary Two centered radial initial vortices of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Under the assumptions of (thm:two-vortex of the paper), suppose in addition that, for
$i=1,2$,
\[
  \mathbf a_{i,\varepsilon}=\mathbf a_{*,i},
  \qquad
  \zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}(\mathbf x)
  =\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}^*
  (\mathbf x-\mathbf a_{*,i}).
\]
Then, for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$,
\begin{equation*}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\left\{
  \sum_{i=1}^2\mathcal D(\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,t})
  +\sup_{(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)\in
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{1,\varepsilon,t})\times
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{2,\varepsilon,t})}
  \Bigl[W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)
  -W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}
  (\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})\Bigr]\right\}
  \leq C\varepsilon,
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation*}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\sum_{i=1}^2
  \mathcal A(\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,t})
  \leq C\varepsilon^{1/2}.
\end{equation*}
If the Hessian of $W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}$ at
$(\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})$ is positive definite, then, after
possibly decreasing $\rho$,
\begin{equation*}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\ \sup_{(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)\in
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{1,\varepsilon,t})\times
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{2,\varepsilon,t})}
  |(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)
  -(\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})|
  \leq C\varepsilon^{1/2}.
\end{equation*}
Here $C>0$ depends only on
$D,\rho$, and $\mathbf a_{*,i},\kappa_i,M_i,R_i$, $i=1,2$.

[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $m,n,\ell\in\Nsf$, let $U\subseteq\Rsf^m$ be an open convex set, and let $\phi:U\to\Rsf^\ell$ be a smooth function. Let $p\in [1,3)$, let $\omega$ be a control function on interval $[S,T]$, and let $X=(X^\tau)$ be an $n$-dimensional branched rough path on interval $[S,T]$ with regularity $p$ and control $\omega$. Let $Y: [S,T]\to U$ be a continuous curve in $U$ and let $f_\tau^i:U\to\Rsf$ (for $\tau\in\Fcal_n^2$ and $i\in\llbracket 1,m \rrbracket$) be smooth functions. Assume that there exists $C\in (0,\infty)$ such that the inequality 
	\begin{equation}
	
		\bigg| 
			Y^i(t) - Y^i(s) 
			- f_{\ta}^i(Y(s)) X^{\ta}(s,t) 
			- \frac{1}{2} f_{\tab}^i(Y(s)) X^{\tab}(s,t) 
			- f_{\tc}^i(Y(s)) X^{\tc}(s,t) 
		\bigg| 
		\leq C \omega(s,t)^\frac{3}{p}
	\end{equation}
holds for every $i\in\llbracket 1,m \rrbracket$ and $(s,t)\in\Delta[S,T]$. Then there is a constant $\widetilde{C}\in (0,\infty)$ such that 
	\[
		\bigg|
			\phi^i(Y(t)) - \phi^i(Y(s)) 
			- g^i_{\ta}(Y(s))X^{\ta}(s,t) 
			- \frac{1}{2} g^i_{\tab}(Y(s)) X^{\tab}(s,t) 
			- g^i_{\tc}(Y(s))X^{\tc}(s,t) 
		\bigg| 
		\leq \widetilde{C}\omega(s,t)^\frac{3}{p},
	\]
where 
	\[
		g^i_{\ta} := \frac{\partial\phi^i}{\partial y^j}f_{\ta}^j, 
			\quad 
		g_{\tab}^i := \frac{\partial\phi^i}{\partial y^j}f_{\tab}^j + \frac{\partial^2 \phi^i}{\partial y^j\partial y^k} f_{\ta}^jf_{\tb}^k, 
			\quad\mbox{and}\quad  
		g_{\tc}^i := \frac{\partial\phi^i}{\partial y^j}f_{\tc}^j,
	\]
holds for every $i\in \llbracket 1,\ell \rrbracket$ and $(s,t)\in\Delta[S,T]$.
title: Lemma 3 of arXiv:2609.01190

In population dynamics, a Holling Type II functional response (or Michaelis-Menten / Monod saturation kinetics) is a per-predator consumption rate function h(N) = (s*N) / (1 + s*tau*N), where N is the prey density, s > 0 is the search / attack rate, and tau > 0 is the handling time per captured prey item. As N -> infinity, h(N) asymptotically saturates to the maximal kill rate 1/tau.
Prey density N >= 0
Attack rate s > 0 and handling time tau > 0
title: Holling Type II Functional Response

body: Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple undirected graph with V = {1, ..., n}. The adjacency matrix of G is the n by n matrix A with A_{ij} = 1 if {i,j} is in E and A_{ij} = 0 otherwise, including A_{ii} = 0 for all i. The (combinatorial) graph Laplacian is L = D - A, where D is the diagonal matrix of vertex degrees, D_{ii} = deg(i) = number of edges incident to vertex i. L is symmetric positive semidefinite, and its smallest eigenvalue is 0 with eigenvector the all-ones vector. [standard, e.g. Godsil and Royle, Algebraic Graph Theory]
title: Adjacency Matrix and Graph Laplacian

Fix a finite irreducible row-stochastic Q with stationary probability pi, p in [0,1]^d, c>0, f=cr^2 and 0<r with r+f<=1. For Z in the state space [0,1]^d, let X_i be conditionally independent Bernoulli((QZ)_i), and update Z prime=(1-r-f)Z+rX+fp. Put pbar=pi.p and K=sum pi_i^2. For 0<pbar<1, as r->0 the unique joint stationary law converges weakly to Y times the all-ones vector, where Y has Beta(2c*pbar/K,2c*(1-pbar)/K) law. At pbar=0 or 1 the stationary law is the corresponding point mass. This concerns stationary laws only; a functional diffusion limit and initial-layer analysis are not asserted.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Status: proof written; w346 KEEP pending. This proves a full stationary-law limit, stationary moments and a scalar generator limit under conditional independence. It does not prove the general network's functional diffusion limit or its initial layer.

Assume a fixed finite irreducible row-stochastic Q, its stationary probability row vector pi, p in [0,1]^d, c>0, r>0, f=c*r^2 and r+f<=1. Update

    Z'=(1-r-f)Z+r X+f p,

with conditionally independent X_i given Z, and P(X_i=1|Z)=(QZ)_i. There is a unique stationary law on [0,1]^d. Its mean is z*=f*((r+f)I-rQ)^(-1)p. Write pbar=pi.p and K=sum pi_i^2. As r decreases to zero, its stationary covariance satisfies

    Cov(Z) -> [K*pbar*(1-pbar)/(2c+K)]*1*1^T.

Proof of existence/uniqueness: the transition is Feller on a compact cube. Couple two states using the same independent uniforms for their Bernoulli coordinates. Because 1-r-f>=0, the weighted L1 distance has expected next value at most (1-f) times its present value; use pi Q=pi. Thus stationary laws are unique and the transition contracts in this Wasserstein distance. Taking expectations yields the displayed mean; the matrix is invertible because its eigenvalues have positive real part.

For synchronization, let D=diag(pi), S=pi.Z, and E_Q(z)=z^T D(I-Q)z=(1/2)sum pi_i Q_ij(z_i-z_j)^2. At stationarity, with Delta=r(X-Z)+f(p-Z),

    2r E[E_Q(Z)] = 2f E[<Z,p-Z>_D] + E[||Delta||_D^2]
                   <= 2f+(r+f)^2 = O(r^2).

Irreducibility makes E_Q(z)>=gamma*||z-1*(pi.z)||_D^2 for some fixed gamma>0: the finite symmetric quadratic form has kernel precisely the constants. Hence E||Z-1*S||_D^2=O(r). Also E[S]=pbar exactly, so z*_i tends to pbar.

The martingale innovation for S has conditional variance r^2 sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i); conditional independence is used exactly here. Total variance at stationarity gives

    (2f-f^2) Var(S)=r^2 sum pi_i^2 E[(QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i)].

Synchronization shows (QZ)_i-S tends to zero in L2. The variables are bounded, so for any subsequential limit V of Var(S), division by r^2 gives 2c V=K*(pbar*(1-pbar)-V). Its solution is unique. Every subsequence has that limit, and synchronization gives the full covariance limit.

For the scalar case Q=(1), stationarity gives the exact variance

    Var(Z)=r^2*p*(1-p)/(2f-f^2+r^2)
          =p*(1-p)/(1+2c-c^2*r^2).

For h in C^3([0,1]), the one-step scalar generator divided by r^2 converges uniformly to

    Lh(z)=c(p-z)h'(z)+(1/2)z(1-z)h''(z).

Indeed E[Delta]=c*r^2(p-z), E[Delta^2]=r^2*z(1-z)+c^2*r^4(p-z)^2, and |Delta|<=r+cr^2. Taylor's remainder, divided by r^2, is bounded by ||h'''||_infinity*r*(1+cr)^3/6, with the additional second-order drift term O(r^2). This identifies the candidate Wright-Fisher generator; path tightness and martingale-problem uniqueness are further steps.

Theorem (full stationary law). Under the same fixed-network assumptions and 0<pbar<1, the joint stationary law of Z converges weakly to Y*1, where

    Y ~ Beta(2c*pbar/K, 2c*(1-pbar)/K).

Proof: write S'=S+f*(pbar-S)+r*eta, where eta=pi.(X-QZ), E[eta|Z]=0, |eta|<=1 and E[eta^2|Z]=sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i). For every polynomial h, the stationary Taylor identity divided by r^2 gives

    0=c E[(pbar-S)h'(S)]
      +(1/2)E[sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i)*h''(S)] + O(r).

The drift-square contribution is O(r^2), and the third-order remainder is uniformly O(r). The proved L2 synchronization implies that the sum inside the second term differs from K*S*(1-S) by a quantity tending to zero in L1. Every subsequence has a further weakly convergent subsequence of S because [0,1] is compact. If its limiting moments are mu_k, use h(s)=s^k, k>=1, to obtain

    [2c+K*(k-1)]*mu_k = [2c*pbar+K*(k-1)]*mu_(k-1), mu_0=1.

These are exactly the moments of the displayed beta law: iterating gives the product of (2c*pbar/K+j)/(2c/K+j) for j=0,...,k-1, which also follows by integrating the beta density. A probability law on [0,1] is determined by its moments, since polynomials approximate continuous functions uniformly. Hence all subsequential limits agree and S converges weakly. Synchronization gives Z-S*1 tending to zero in probability, so the joint law converges to Y*1. If pbar=0 or 1, positivity of pi forces every p_i to be that endpoint and the unique stationary law is the corresponding point mass.

This proof uses all polynomial moments, not an inference from the first two moments. It proves convergence of stationary laws, not a limit for trajectories begun away from synchronization. Without conditional independence, the innovation variance changes. For example, Q=J_d/d, constant p, and one shared Bernoulli coin across all coordinates preserve a synchronized state and give the scalar beta parameters 2cp and 2c(1-p), rather than 2cdp and 2cd(1-p).

For reproducible finite checks, the exact covariance identity is

    V=B V B^T+r^2*diag(s*(1-s)-diag(Q V Q^T)),
    B=(1-r-f)I+rQ, s=Q z*.

Checks: the scalar exact formula; first four scalar stationary moments; exact polynomial generators; finite-network covariance systems; first four moments of the exact consensus Markov chain for Q=J_d/d at d=2,3,5; a common-coin control that changes the beta variance. [Lemma 12 of arXiv:2608.07365, 'A pathwise Ito formula \\for weakly differentiable functions'] For any path $\omega\in Q_{\pi}([0, T], \Rr^d)$ the sequence $\mathcal{L}^{\pi_n}_{\omega}$ converges weakly to the weighted occupation  measure $\mu^T_{\omega}$ defined by 
\[
\forall A\in {\cal B}(\mathbb{R}^d),\qquad \mu^T_{\omega}(A):= {\rm tr}\int_0^T 1_A(\omega(t)) \d [\omega]_{\pi} (t).
\]
\begin{align*}\forall \phi\in C_c(\Rr^d),\qquad 
\int_{\Rr^d} \phi(x) \mathcal{L}^{\pi_n}_{\omega}(x) \d x  \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} \int_{\Rr^d} \phi(x) d\mu^T_{\omega}(x)
= {\rm tr}\int_0^T (\phi\circ\omega\,) \d[\omega]_{\pi}.
\end{align*}
title: Lemma 12 of arXiv:2608.07365

OWNER-OWN-WORK METHOD DRAFT; proof (unaudited), attributed to w737 T385-C13 v1; no independent PASS or novelty claim. Fix L>0 and eta>0. For each n let X be a deterministic real n by n matrix with operator norm at most L, and w_1,...,w_n independent N(0,I_n) vectors. Put h_j=ReLU(Xw_j), mu=E h_j, z_j=h_j-mu, Phi=E[h_j h_j^T], and Sigma=E[z_j z_j^T]. Let R_j be real symmetric, measurable in X and the columns w_k with k!=j (and optionally auxiliary randomness independent of all feature weights), with operator norm at most 1/eta almost surely. The recorded unaudited derivation gives, for each fixed epsilon>0, P(max_j |z_j^T R_j z_j/n-Tr(Sigma R_j)/n|>epsilon)<=C n exp[-c n min(epsilon^2,epsilon)], with C,c depending only on L,eta. The centering step uses the exact identity z^T R z-Tr(Sigma R)=h^T R h-Tr(Phi R)-2 mu^T R(h-mu) for deterministic symmetric R. Louart-Liao-Couillet quadratic-form concentration controls the raw term. Gaussian Lipschitz concentration controls the mean correction. Indeed mu_i=||x_i||/sqrt(2 pi), ||mu||^2<=n L^2/(2 pi), and w->mu^T R ReLU(Xw) is Lipschitz with constant at most sqrt(n/(2 pi))*L^2/eta. Condition on all columns except j before applying those bounds; integrate and take a union bound, without asserting independence between deviation events. Thus the method allows correlations among coordinates within each feature column, but R_j must exclude the tested column. For X=I and eta=1, taking the same-column R=zz^T/||z||^2 makes z^T R z/n tend to kappa=1/2-1/(2 pi)>0 while Tr(Sigma R)/n=kappa/n, illustrating failure if this independence hypothesis is removed. For random X independent of all w_j with tight operator norm, conditioning first on ||X||<=L and then letting L grow gives convergence in probability, rather than a uniform unconditional exponential rate. This is a fixed-positive-ridge concentration ingredient; it supplies neither an edge law nor a justification for a ridge tending to zero. The underlying source-based proof draft and all proposed uses remain subject to independent review.
Fixed L>0 and eta>0; deterministic square X with operator norm at most L.
Independent standard Gaussian feature-weight vectors; coordinates of the resulting ReLU column need not be independent.
Each symmetric R_j excludes w_j from its measurability and has norm at most 1/eta.
Any auxiliary randomness is independent of all Gaussian feature weights.
Random-input extension requires independence from feature weights and a tight input norm; only convergence in probability is claimed there.
Owner-work proof (unaudited), w737 T385-C13 v1; no independent PASS or novelty claim.

Internal demographic noise in continuous population models refers to stochastic fluctuations arising endogenously from the discrete, probabilistic birth, death, and predation interactions of individual agents. In the diffusion approximation, the infinitesimal diffusion matrix has entries whose magnitudes scale proportionally to the square root of the interaction rates (i.e., variance linear in the population state), distinct from external environmental noise where diffusion coefficients are proportional to the state itself.
Continuous diffusion approximation of discrete branching / birth-death processes
No fluctuating exogenous environmental drivers
title: Internal Demographic Noise in Population Models

[Lemma 34 (Fourier recovery) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $\beta^{(1)}:[0,T_1]\to V$ and $\beta^{(2)}:[0,T_2]\to V$ be continuous bounded-variation paths, translated to start at zero, with the same nonzero increment $v$.
Fix one functional $\ell\in V^*$ with $\ell(v)=1$, put $W=\ker\ell$, and write
\[
\beta_t^{(k)}=x_t^{(k)}v+X_t^{(k)},
\qquad x_t^{(k)}=\ell(\beta_t^{(k)}),
\qquad X_t^{(k)}\in W
\quad(k=1,2).
\]
Equip $W$ with an auxiliary Euclidean norm, define the decorated paths by \cref{eq:decorated-path}, and define the measures by \cref{eq:pushforward-measure}.
If
\[
S(B^{\Lambda}(\beta^{(1)}))
 =S(B^{\Lambda}(\beta^{(2)}))
\]
for every finite symmetric $\Lambda\subset 2\pi\Q$, then
\[
\mu_{\beta^{(1)}}^{\eta}
 =\mu_{\beta^{(2)}}^{\eta}
\]
for every $r\geq1$ and every tuple $\eta=(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_r)\in(W^*)^r$.
title: Fourier recovery

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Reduce the intrinsic limit to a renewal-type statement for the branching-process comparison. Result: The intrinsic one-arm probability is bounded above and below by constants over n (Kozma-Nachmias), and the comparison object is the survival probability of a critical branching process with finite variance, for which n P(survive n generations) -> 2/sigma^2 (Kolmogorov). For the intrinsic arm event the analogous statement would be n P(intrinsic radius >= n) -> a_in where a_in should be 2/V with V the variance of the offspring distribution of the effective branching structure (the cluster explored by intrinsic distance is a branching process with dependent offspring). Existence of the limit therefore reduces to a Kolmogorov-type limit theorem for the intrinsic exploration, which needs the mean-field two-point asymptotics at the level of an exact constant (the lace expansion gives tau_{p_c}(x) ~ A/|x|^{d-2} with an exact constant A, Hara 2008), plus an exact constant for the 'variance' of the exploration, which is the sum of the three-point function's connected part, computable from the lace expansion in principle. The extrinsic limit is harder because the extrinsic arm event mixes intrinsic distance and Euclidean displacement; its bounded-ratio form comes from a second-moment argument that does not give constants. I could not complete either constant. Obstruction: Exact constants for the intrinsic branching structure require second-order lace expansion information.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0066-sharp-intrinsic-and-extrinsic-one-arm-exponents-in-high-dimensions
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

Let $A(x,t)$ be real measurable on $\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R$ and uniformly parabolic with constants $0<\lambda\le\Lambda<\infty$, and consider $\partial_tu=\mathrm{div}(A(x,t)\nabla u)$. The equation has a weak fundamental solution $\Gamma(x,t;y,s)$, defined for $s<t$, nonnegative, with $\int\Gamma(x,t;y,s)dx=1$ (conservation of mass; no symmetry of $A$ is needed, since constants solve the adjoint equation), and there is $C=C(n,\lambda,\Lambda)\ge1$ with $\frac{1}{C\,(t-s)^{n/2}}\exp\Big(-\frac{C|x-y|^2}{t-s}\Big)\ \le\ \Gamma(x,t;y,s)\ \le\ \frac{C}{(t-s)^{n/2}}\exp\Big(-\frac{|x-y|^2}{C(t-s)}\Big)$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and all $s<t$. The constants depend only on $n,\lambda,\Lambda$ and never on any modulus of continuity of $A$; in particular the bounds are stable under homogenization and rough coefficients. If bounded lower-order terms are present, or the equation is posed only for $0<t-s\le T$, the same two-sided bounds hold with $C$ depending in addition on $T$ and the bounds on those terms.
A measurable, uniformly parabolic with constants lambda, Lambda (no continuity assumed)
divergence form (the analogous statement for nondivergence form with merely measurable coefficients is a different theory)
s < t; for equations with lower-order terms or on a finite time interval, constants also depend on T and those bounds

TECHNIQUE CARD. The alteration method, in Zhao's words: first make a random construction, and then fix the blemishes. A random object is shown to have few defects in expectation, the defects are removed or repaired deterministically, and the cost of the repair is bounded by the same expectation, often through Markov's inequality. Zhao, Chapter 3 (Alterations). Theorem 3.1.1: every graph on n vertices with minimum degree δ > 1 has a dominating set of size at most ((log(δ+1) + 1)/(δ+1)) n; the proof puts each vertex in X independently with probability p, adds the set Y of vertices that are neither in X nor adjacent to X, so that X ∪ Y dominates and E|X ∪ Y| ≤ (p + e^{−p(1+δ)}) n, and takes p = log(δ+1)/(δ+1). Theorem 3.4.1 (Erdős 1959): for all k and ℓ there is a graph with girth greater than ℓ and chromatic number greater than k; the proof takes a random graph G(n,p), uses Markov's inequality to make the number of cycles of length at most ℓ small, bounds the independence number, and deletes one vertex from each short cycle.
a random construction whose expected number of defects, or expected repair cost, can be computed

For a fixed real beta, let N=ceil(8(1+abs(beta))), B_n=floor(n/2+beta*log_2(1+n/N)), and let T_beta be the rooted tree with 2^(B_(n+1)-B_n) children at each vertex at depth n. Contract unary corridors to the rooted binary branching skeleton. Each corridor and the initial stem have length at most 4; the resulting surjection pi obeys d_binary(pi(u),pi(v))<=d_T(u,v)<=4*d_binary(pi(u),pi(v))+8. Hence every T_beta is quasi-isometric to the rooted binary tree. T_0 and T_2 have equal critical probability 1/sqrt(2), yet only T_0 has critical extinction. Critical extinction is not a quasi-isometry invariant for arbitrary bounded-degree graphs, even with equal critical parameters. No claim is made about invariance within quasi-transitive graphs.

STATUS: proof (unaudited). For the exact critical unshaped Gaussian tanh scalar chain with fixed K0>0, let Y=2L*K_L,t=L/n. For each fixed order k and c<infinity, uniformly n>=n0 and 1<=L<=cn, E Y^j=m_j(t)+(5j/12)J_j(t)*log(L)/L+O(1/L), 1<=j<=k. Here m_j=E A_t^(-j), J_j=E[H_t A_t^(-j-1)] using the same Brownian path, A_t=int_0^1 exp(tr+sqrt(2t)B_r)dr,H_t=exp(t+sqrt(2t)B_1). Therefore kappa_k(Y)=F_k(t)+(5/12)G_k(t)*log(L)/L+O(1/L), F_k=P_k(m), G_k=sum_j j J_j partial_j P_k(m). Both coefficient functions have arbitrary finite small-t Taylor expansions with explicit Gaussian-integral remainder bounds. At fixed t>0 this supplies the first log(n)/n width term and an O_t(1/n) remainder. Assumptions: Zero bias; independent standard Gaussian rows/layers; weight variance exactly1/n, no activation shaping or normalizer; K0>0 fixed; fixed cumulant order and finite positive depth-ratio cap c. Constants depend on k,K0,c; threshold n0 large enough for the stated inverse moments. Scope: First logarithmic finite-width order only; the full all-orders 1/n expansion of C019 is NOT proved. The uniform O(1/L) constant is finite but not given as a numerical closed form. Analytic proof and dependencies C044-C046 await independent audit. Higher-order printed Hanin constants disagree with the Brownian-functional coefficients; explicit discrepancy retained for reviewer, not used as a premise.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4bd7b04b5b7a94864afcf30d797a4508ad77fe7cff0f25ee6d83ed613ba54a6c","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4b/4bd7b04b5b7a94864afcf30d797a4508ad77fe7cff0f25ee6d83ed613ba54a6c.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:3033abec3bbdad34b43d0cf2aa8e4236a3ecee64ec1b67ecc4466b1444830e88","bundle_entry_key":"tanh-cumulant-first-logarithmic-double-expansion","bundle_id":"population.t244-tanh-cumulant-first-logarithmic-double-expansion-019","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_019.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-tanh-cumulant-first-logarithmic-double-expansion","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C053: a uniform tanh double expansion, through the first logarithmic width term

20 October 2026. Target 3. Proof draft, unaudited. No novelty asserted.
This proves a first finite-width correction and arbitrary finite small-t
Taylor order. It does NOT prove the all-orders inverse-width expansion
available for the exactly multiplicative ReLU chain in C019.

## Statement

Use the exact unshaped critical tanh chain
K_(j+1)=n^(-1)sum_i tanh(sqrt(K_j)Z_(j,i))^2, K_0>0 fixed,
with independent Gaussian rows/layers, zero bias and weight variance 1/n.
Fix an integer k>=1 and c<infinity. For integers 1<=L<=cn put t=L/n,
Y=2L K_L, and, using ONE Brownian path B,

    A_t=integral_0^1 exp(tr+sqrt(2t)B_r)dr,
    H_t=exp(t+sqrt(2t)B_1),
    m_j(t)=E A_t^(-j),
    J_j(t)=E[H_t A_t^(-j-1)],             m_0=1.

There exist finite C=C(k,K_0,c) and n_0 such that, for every n>=n_0,
uniformly over all those L,

    |E Y^j - m_j(t) -(5j/12)J_j(t)log(L)/L| <= C/L,
                                                 1<=j<=k.       (1)

In particular the logarithm is log L, not a log n term asserted uniformly
down to L=1. At fixed t>0 this is a log n/n correction with O_t(1/n)
remainder. The unspecified finite constant in (1) is uniform; no numerical
closed form for it has been optimized or supplied here.

Let P_k(x_1,...,x_k)=sum_(pi in Pi_k) (|pi|-1)!(-1)^(|pi|-1)
product_(D in pi) x_|D| be the moment-cumulant polynomial. Define

    F_k(t)=P_k(m_1(t),...,m_k(t)),
    G_k(t)=sum_(j=1)^k j J_j(t) (partial_j P_k)(m_1(t),...,m_k(t)).

Then

    |kappa_k(Y)-F_k(t)-(5/12)G_k(t)log(L)/L| <= C'/L.        (2)

For an independent final Gaussian readout R=sqrt(2L)z_out, its conditional
variance is Y and
kappa_(2k)(R)=[(2k)!/(2^k k!)]kappa_k(Y); multiply (2) by this factor.
Odd cumulants vanish by conditional Gaussian symmetry.

For every integer M>=0 these functions have computable Taylor coefficients
f_(k,r),g_(k,r) at zero, with an explicit finite Gaussian-integral bound
C_(k,M,c) described below, such that

 |kappa_k(Y)-sum_(r=0)^M f_(k,r)t^r
              -(5/12)(log L/L)sum_(r=0)^M g_(k,r)t^r|
 <= C_(k,M,c)t^(M+1)(1+log L/L)+C'/L.                    (3)

First coefficients are

    m_j(t)=1+j(j-2)t/3+O(t^2),
    J_j(t)=1+(j-1)(j-2)t/3+O(t^2).

Consequently F_2(t)=2t/3+O(t^2), G_2(t)=2t/3+O(t^2).
Thus Var(Y)=2t/3+(5/18)t log(L)/L
+O_(K0,c)(t^2(1+log L/L)+1/L). This is an absolute uniform
remainder, not a relative error in a regime where 1/L dominates t.

## 1. Rescaling keeps the entrance uniform in L/n

Let epsilon=1/L and W_j=1/(L K_j). The diffusion reference, on the unit
time interval, is

    dW=(2tW+2)ds+sqrt(2t)W dB_s,        W(0)=0,
    A^(t)=(2tw+2)D+tw^2 D^2.

Its terminal value is 2 A_t in law, jointly with its affine initial-state
slope H_t. Write P_s^(t) for its semigroup, f(w)=(2/w)^j and
g_s(w)=P_(1-s)^(t) f(w). The true starting state is W_0=1/(LK_0).
In particular P_1^(t)f(0)=m_j(t) and

    D_j(t):=(P_1^(t)f)'(0)=-(j/2)J_j(t).                  (4)

The joint identity in (4) uses time reversal of the Brownian increments
and preserves the endpoint B_1: H and A are not made independent.

## 2. Backward tests and the terminal singularity

The reference transition is affine, W_s(w)=H_s w+I_s, with
H_s=exp(ts+sqrt(2t)B_s), I_s=2int_0^s exp(t(s-r)+sqrt(2t)(B_s-B_r))dr.
For M_B=sup_(0<=r<=1)|B_r|, these give, uniformly 0<=t<=c,
H_s and its inverse <=exp(c+sqrt(2c)M_B), and
I_s>=2s exp(-c-2sqrt(2c)M_B). Differentiation in w and Gaussian
integrability of exp(a M_B) therefore give, for each fixed derivative r,

 |g_s^(r)(w)|<=C_r(1+w)^(-j-r),             s<=1/2,
 |g_s^(r)(w)|<=C_r w^(-j-r),               s>=1/2.         (5)

All needed time derivatives on s<=1/2 satisfy analogous bounds by applying
A^(t). In particular |g_s'(w)-D_j(t)|<=C(s+w) there. Constants depend
only on j,r,c. The Gaussian supremum bounds below make them finite
and computable; no differentiation at a singular initial value is used.

C027, now reviewer PASS, implies for every fixed p,

    E W_j^(-p)=L^p E K_j^p<=C_p[L/(j+1)]^p,              (6)

including j=0 with a K_0-dependent constant. Thus every derivative bound
in (5), even at the terminal test s=1, is integrable along the second
half of the exact chain, uniformly in L,n. This is the terminal-tail
control missing from a bare application of weak convergence.

## 3. The next one-step operator

Conditionally on K_j=q, W_j=w, put S=n^(-1)sum_i Y_q(Z_i),
Y_q=tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2/q. Then W'=w/S, q=epsilon/w, n^(-1)=t epsilon.
The scalar expansions needed are

 E Y_q=1-2q+(17/3)q^2+O(q^3),
 Var(Y_q)=2-16q+O(q^2),  kappa_3(Y_q)=8+O(q).

Writing delta=S-1, the retained terms, in powers of (q,h), h=1/n, are

 E delta=-2q+(17/3)q^2,
 E delta^2=2h+4q^2-16qh,
 E delta^3=-12qh+8h^2,
 E delta^4=12h^2.

Each omitted term is bounded by C(q^3+q^2 h+q h^2+h^(5/2)) on a fixed
small interval q<=eta. This follows from the centered iid sample moment
identities and their fifth/sixth moment bounds. Taylor expansion of
(S^-1-1)^r, for 1<=r<=4, yields respectively

 2q+2h-(5/3)q^2-4qh+4h^2;
 2h+4q^2+8qh+20h^2;
 12qh+28h^2;
 12h^2.

C044 removes the inverse-sample tails at exponentially small cost,
uniformly in q<=max(1,K_0), for n above a fixed threshold depending
on the derivative/moment orders. The positive sample tails are bounded
using Y_q<=Z^2. Thus the expansion applies to these unbounded tests.

For Q_n the exact one-step kernel this identifies

 Q_n g = g+epsilon A^(t)g+epsilon^2 B^(t)g+remainder,

 B^(t)g=(4t^2w-4t-5/(3w))g'
       +(10t^2w^2+4tw+2)g''
       +((14/3)t^2w^3+2tw^2)g'''+(t^2w^4/2)g''''.

Subtract the reference semigroup expansion. The defect operator is

 C^(t)=B^(t)-(A^(t))^2/2
      =(2t^2w-6t-5/(3w))D
        +(3t^2w^2-2tw)D^2+(2/3)t^2w^3 D^3.             (7)

Only the 1/w coefficient is singular at the entrance.

## 4. Summed remainder bound (the uniformity step)

For q<=eta and s<=1/2, (5) and the previous moment estimates bound the
one-step remainder after subtracting epsilon^2 C^(t) by

 C[epsilon^3(w^-2+w^-1+1)+epsilon^(5/2)+exp(-a n)].      (8)

For example the worst q^3 term is w q^3=epsilon^3/w^2;
h^(5/2)w^r |g^(r)|<=C epsilon^(5/2), since t<=c. The fifth Taylor
remainder has the same bound. The third semigroup remainder is bounded
by C epsilon^3 through A^3 g. For s>=1/2 the counterpart of (8) is
bounded by a finite sum of these quantities multiplied by powers of
w^-1, which are integrable uniformly by (6).

In the first half, summing the worst term uses

 epsilon^3 sum E W_j^-2 =epsilon sum E K_j^2<=C epsilon,
 epsilon^3 sum E W_j^-1 =epsilon^2 sum E K_j<=C epsilon.

Both follow from C027; the remaining sums in (8) are O(epsilon).
In the second half, (6) bounds the sum by O(epsilon^(3/2)+epsilon^2).
Exponential tails sum to O(1/L), since L<=cn; constants may depend on c.

On q>eta do not use the small-q series. In the first half, w<=epsilon/eta
and C044 gives E W'<=C w, so the bounded Lipschitz test changes by
O(epsilon); the reference step and epsilon^2 Cg have the same bound.
The expected number of these visits is bounded by
eta^-2 sum E K_j^2<=C. In the second half, (5)-(6), with two additional
positive K moments, bound each such visit's expected defect by
O(epsilon^2): use 1_(q>eta)<= (epsilon/(eta w))^p, p sufficiently large.
Its sum is O(epsilon). This establishes, with no unstated localization,

 sum_(j=0)^(L-1) E |Q_n g_((j+1)/L)(W_j)
             -P_epsilon^(t)g_((j+1)/L)(W_j)
             -epsilon^2 C^(t)g_((j+1)/L)(W_j)| <= C/L.    (9)

The nonsingular terms of (7), summed with epsilon^2, are also O(1/L),
using (5) before the midpoint and (6) after it.

## 5. Entrance occupation gives the logarithm

C046 gives, uniformly L<=cn,

    sum_(j=0)^(L-1) E K_j=(1/2)log L+O_(K0,c)(1).         (10)

Indeed its error divided by j sums as j^-3/2+(nj)^-1/2, whose sum is
bounded by C(1+sqrt(L/n)). For the weighted version, before the midpoint
use (5), E K_j<=C/(j+1), and the EXACT identity K_j W_j=1/L:

 sum E[K_j |g_((j+1)/L)'(W_j)-D_j(t)|] <= C.

After the midpoint |g'|<=C W^-j-1, so (6) bounds each summand by C/L.
(The exponent j in this sentence denotes the fixed test moment order,
not the summation index.) Thus

 sum E[K_i g_((i+1)/L)'(W_i)]
       =(D_j(t)/2)log L+O(1).                            (11)

The singular part of (7) contributes -(5/(3L)) times (11). By (4) this
is +(5j/12)J_j(t)log L/L+O(1/L). Exact backward-semigroup telescoping,
(9), and |P_1f(W_0)-P_1f(0)|<=C/(LK_0) prove (1).
No independent products of conditional bounds have been used.

## 6. Cumulants and small-t remainders

Apply the finite polynomial P_k to the k moment estimates (1). Its
linear correction is exactly G_k. Moments and coefficients are bounded
for t<=c by Brownian supremum exponential moments. Quadratic correction
terms are O((log L/L)^2)=O(1/L), because sup_(L>=1)(log L)^2/L<infinity.
This proves (2), including k=1.

For explicit small-t remainder construction put z=sqrt(t),
a(z)=int_0^1 exp(z^2r+sqrt(2)zB_r)dr and h(z)=exp(z^2+sqrt(2)zB_1).
The expectations of a(z)^(-j) and h(z)a(z)^(-j-1) are even smooth
functions of real z, by B -> -B. Their derivatives can be passed under
the expectation: with M_B=sup|B|, they are bounded by a polynomial in
M_B times exp(C sqrt(c)M_B+C c).

More explicitly let Z_c=2(2sqrt(c)+sqrt(2)M_B+1), D_0(j)=1 and

 D_N(j)=sum_(r=1)^N ((j)_r/r!) binom(N-1,r-1), N>=1.

Normalized derivatives of a satisfy |a^(r)|/r!<=a Z_c^r. The reciprocal
power composition formula therefore gives

 |(a^-j)^(N)|/N! <= D_N(j) Z_c^N exp(j sqrt(2c)M_B),
 |(h a^-j-1)^(N)|/N!
   <= [sum_(r=0)^N D_r(j+1)] Z_c^N exp(c+(j+2)sqrt(2c)M_B).

These expectations are explicit finite Gaussian-integral constants.
For a fully numerical bound use P(M_B>x)<=min(1,4exp(-x^2/2)) and
E F(M_B)=F(0)+int_0^infinity F'(x)P(M_B>x)dx for increasing F.
Taylor at z=0 through degree 2M+1, with N=2M+2, gives the stated
O(t^(M+1)) remainders. The coefficients are finite Gaussian polynomial
moments, computable by Wick pairings and integrals of min(r,s), hence
rational. Finite polynomial substitution gives (3) with an explicit
finite sum of these bounds and derivatives of P_k on the bounded
moment box.

Finally E int B=0, E(int B)^2=1/3, and E[B_1 int B]=1/2 give the first
coefficients displayed in the statement. In particular the small-t
limiting variance is 2t/3. This is a check on the model normalization;
it is NOT a transfer to a non-Gaussian weight universality class.

## Limits and remaining scope

For the bounded depths L<=4, enlarge the constant directly using
K_L<=1, the finite diffusion inverse moments, and bounded J_j on [0,c];
the midpoint arguments above are needed only for L>=5.
All finite-chain estimates above are simultaneous for n>=n0 and
1<=L<=cn; no L->infinity limit is hidden in the O(1/L) statement.
At fixed t, log L/L=log n/(nt)+log t/(nt). The last term belongs to
the unknown order-1/n coefficient. Determining that coefficient, or
arbitrary powers of 1/n and their boundary logarithms, requires a
finer entrance matching calculation and is NOT proved here.

## Exact coefficient artifact and source discrepancy

scripts/tanh_series_exact.py computes the Taylor coefficients by exact
rational integration over ordered Gaussian times. For j>=0,

 E A_t^j = j! int_(0<=r1<=...<=rj<=1)
                 exp(2t sum_i (j-i+1)r_i) dr,
 E[H_t A_t^j] = exp(2t) j! int_ordered
                 exp(2t sum_i (j-i+2)r_i) dr.

Expanding (A-1)^r by binomial inversion, for 0<=r<=2M, gives all
Taylor coefficients through t^M of the required inverse moments.
The script is finite exact Fraction arithmetic; it checks coefficients,
not the analytic finite-width remainder. Through t^3 it gives

 F_1=1-t/3+t^2/15-4t^3/315,
 F_2=2t/3-14t^2/45+2t^3/21,
 F_3=16t^2/15-568t^3/945,
 F_4=96t^3/35,
 G_1=1-t^2/15+8t^3/315,
 G_2=2t/3-2t^3/21, G_3=16t^2/15, G_4=96t^3/35,

each with its own O(t^4) Taylor remainder. These F_k are cumulants of
the normalized VARIANCE mixture variable Y, not ordinary cumulants of
the final Gaussian-mixture output.

The 2/3 variance coefficient agrees with Roberts-Yaida-Hanin, book
arXiv:2106.10165, printed p.142 (PDF p.150), Eq.(5.131), and Hanin
arXiv:2204.01058, Corollary4.1, Eq.(4.12), C4=2/3. However that latter
source prints C6=28/15 and C8=8756/315, which do NOT equal our F3 and
F4 leading coefficients after the apparent normalization Eq.(3.12).
This higher-order source/normalization discrepancy is OPEN FOR REVIEW;
neither printed number is used in this proof. An independent Wick
check of our F3 coefficient is:

 a=sqrt(2)int_0^1 B_r dr, b=int_0^1(r+B_r^2)dr,
 Y=1-sqrt(t)a+t(a^2-b)+O_in_moments(t^(3/2)),
 [t^2]kappa_3(Y)=3[Var(a^2)-Cov(a^2,b)]
                 =3[8/9-4 int_0^1(r-r^2/2)^2dr]=16/15.

We have checked the covariance and joint-cumulant definitions in
Hanin Eq.(3.12); a referee should inspect the remaining large-depth
coefficient derivation before declaring the source wrong. No claim
of a universality transfer is being made.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:264fa0bbae6ae6bec60290e4dcbc49d7f357d91989213f1c1fa3d50aa536ab4d","revision_digest":"sha256:412e5279d1e420d9da6610ad5affaf7fa0d62280c0a63506abfb3b20c914f221","source_id":"owner-own-work:T244-w691-C053:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20T14:12:29.483033","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma 19 (Main partial coloring of Bansal--Jiang--Meka ---  slightly adapted) of arXiv:2606.16005, '\bfseries An Algebraic Matrix Spencer Theorem'] There are universal constants \(c,\eta,C>0\) with the following property. Let
\(L_1,\ldots,L_n\) be self-adjoint matrices satisfying
\[
\|L_i\|\le 1,
\qquad
\|L_i\|_F^2\le \frac{n}{\log^3(en)}
\]
for every \(i\in[n]\). Let \(S\subseteq[n]\), with \(s:=|S|\) be arbitrary and let $t_L(s):=
C\left(\sqrt{s}+n^{1/4}s^{1/4}\right)$.
Then there exist a subspace $H_S\subseteq \mathbb R^S$ with $\dim H_S\ge (1-\eta)s$ such that the  discrepancy body   $K_L(S):=\{z\in H_S:\left\|
\sum_{i\in S}z_iL_i
\right\|
\le
t_L(s)\}$  relative to this subspace satisfies
\[
\gamma_{H_S}\bigl(K_L(S)\bigr)\ge \exp(-\eta s).
\]
Consequently, for every point \(y\in(-1,1)^S\), there exists a partial coloring increment \(z\in\mathbb R^S\) such that $y+z\in[-1,1]^S$ and $|\{i\in S: |y_i+z_i|=1\}|\ge cs$ satisfying

\[
\left\|
\sum_{i\in S}z_iL_i
\right\|
\le
C\,t_L(s).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

We call $B\subset T$ a {\it branch}

A branch $L$ of order $\vartheta(L)=1$ is 
called a {\it leaf} of $T$.

body: A family {X_i : i in I} of random variables on a probability space is uniformly integrable if sup_{i in I} E[|X_i| 1(|X_i| > K)] tends to 0 as K tends to infinity; equivalently, for every epsilon > 0 there exists K such that E[|X_i| 1(|X_i| > K)] < epsilon for every i in I simultaneously. Uniform integrability of a family bounded in L^1 is the exact extra condition needed to upgrade almost-sure or in-probability convergence to convergence in L^1. [standard, e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales]
title: Uniformly Integrable Family of Random Variables

[Definition 19 of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] [Liquid and frozen region, arctic boundary]
  Given any open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, we call a function $F : \overline{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ \emph{admissible} if $F$ is $1$-Lipschitz and satisfies $\nabla F (z) \in \overline{\mathcal{T}}$ for Lebesgue almost every $z \in \Omega$. Let $\Adm (\Omega)$ denote the set of admissible functions $F : \overline{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and, for any function $f : \partial \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, let $\Adm (\Omega; f)$ denote the set of $F \in \Adm (\Omega)$ satisfying $F |_{\partial \Omega} = f$.  Define the \emph{liquid region} $\mathfrak{L}_F \subseteq \Omega$ associated with an admissible height function $F \in \Adm (\Omega)$ by 
         \begin{flalign*}
         	\mathfrak{L}_F = \big\{ z \in \Omega : \nabla F(z) \in \mathcal{T} \big\},
         \end{flalign*}
         where the condition $\nabla F(z) \in \mathcal{T}$ in particular implies that $\nabla F(z)$ exists.

         In particular, we define the liquid region of $\cH_{q;a,b,c}$ as
         \[\mL_{q;a,b,c}:=\mL_{\cH_{q;a,b,c}}.\] The  boundary
        $\mathfrak A_{q;a,b,c}:=\partial\mL_{q;a,b,c}$ is called the
        \emph{arctic boundary} and the interior of
        $\mX_{a,b,c}\setminus\mL_{q;a,b,c}$ is called the \emph{frozen
        region}.
title: Definition 19 of arXiv:2605.26664

Let $\Phi(x,t)=(4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4t)}$ and $e^{t\Delta}g=\Phi(\cdot,t)*g$ for $t>0$. For $1\le p\le q\le\infty$ and $g\in L^p(\mathbb R^n)$: $\|e^{t\Delta}g\|_{L^q(\mathbb R^n)}\le(4\pi t)^{-\frac n2(\frac1p-\frac1q)}\|g\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}$, and $\|\nabla e^{t\Delta}g\|_{L^p}\le C_nt^{-1/2}\|g\|_{L^p}$ with $C_n=\|\nabla\Phi(\cdot,1)\|_{L^1}$. In particular $e^{t\Delta}$ is a contraction on every $L^p$ ($p=q$), maps $L^1$ into $L^\infty$ with norm $(4\pi t)^{-n/2}$, and $e^{t\Delta}g\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ for $t>0$ with all derivatives bounded: the heat semigroup is instantaneously smoothing and has infinite propagation speed ($e^{t\Delta}g>0$ everywhere for $t>0$ whenever $g\ge0$, $g\not\equiv0$). The restriction $p\le q$ is essential.
