[Proposition 3 (Uniform-in-time weak expansion) of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Assume that Assumptions \ref{ass:smooth}, \ref{ass:flow-smothness} and
\ref{ass:coeff-level-new} hold. Let $\varphi \in C_b^7\left(\R^d\right)$ and let
$\Phi_1,\Phi_2\colon\Ptwo\to\R$ be defined above. Then,
there exist measurable functions $\beta_\ell \colon \left[ 0,\infty
\right) \to \R$, $\ell \in \left\{ 1,2 \right\}$, and constants $ C_\ell, C_\ell' > 0 $ such that, for every $ t \ge 0 $ and every $ N \ge 1 $,
\begin{equation}

\E\left( \Phi_\ell\left( \mu_t^N \right) \right)
=
\Phi_\ell\left( \mu_t \right)
+
\frac{\beta_\ell\left( t \right)}{N}
+
\frac{1}{N}
\int_0^t \Gamma P_{t-s}\Phi_\ell \left( \mu_s \right) ds
+
R_{\ell,N}\left( t \right),
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}

\abs{\beta_\ell\left( t \right)} \le C_\ell e^{-\omega t}\quad\mbox{and}\quad
\abs{\Gamma P_r\Phi_\ell \left( \mu \right)} \le C_\ell e^{-\omega r},
\end{equation}
for all $ t,r \ge 0 $ and $ \mu \in \Ptwo $, and with
\begin{equation}

\sup_{t \ge 0} \abs{R_{\ell,N}\left( t \right)} \le \frac{C_\ell'}{N^2}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Uniform-in-time weak expansion

body: Let M be a smooth manifold and p a point of M. The tangent space T_pM is the real vector space of derivations at p: linear maps v from the algebra of smooth real-valued functions defined near p to R that satisfy the Leibniz rule v(fg) = f(p)v(g) + g(p)v(f) for all smooth f, g. Equivalently, in a coordinate chart (U, phi) around p with coordinates x^1,...,x^n, T_pM is the n-dimensional real vector space spanned by the partial derivative operators d/dx^1|_p ,..., d/dx^n|_p, and a tangent vector may also be identified with an equivalence class of smooth curves through p under the relation of having equal velocity at p.
title: Tangent Space

body: C = (c_1, ..., c_m) in R^{3 x m}, S_t = {x in {\pm 1}^m : Cx = t}, W = ker C, old coordinate forms f_i = x_i|_W. Homogenize: C-hat = [C | -t], W-hat = ker C-hat, h = the last coordinate form. Antipodal homogenized fibre A-hat_t = {(x,1) : x in S_t} \cup {(-x,-1) : x in S_t} = W-hat \cap {\pm 1}^{m+1}. Row rank three gives dim W-hat = m-2 = dim W + 1. Notes: Extraction glyphs 'bC', 'cW', 'bAt' are hats (C-hat, W-hat, A-hat). Agresti and Veraar (journal version 2025, p. 130), Problem 5 asks: if u_0^n tends to u_0 in L^2(Omega; H), does u^n tend to u in L^2(Omega; L^2(0,T;V) intersect C([0,T];H))? Our result (id P0267, 2026-09-08): NO, from the same critical Allen-Cahn example as P0266. Take u_0^n = 1/n tending to 0; the limit solution is identically zero, and convergence in L^2(Omega; C([0,T];H)) would require E sup ||u^n||^2 to tend to 0, but that quantity is infinite for every n by the P0266 result (the constant-data solution's supremum has tail index one, coming from a four-dimensional Bessel process's capacity estimate). Verification as the source words it: uses the same construction and checks as Problem 4; of the six problems attacked in that session the memo states these two have the best odds of being genuinely new, since the source is a year old. Prior art not cleared.

Let n, m ≥ 1 and T > 0. Consider ∂_t u + Σ_{j=1}^n A_j(t,x) ∂_j u + B(t,x) u = F(t,x) for u : [0,T]×R^n → C^m, where each A_j is Hermitian (real symmetric in the real case) at every (t,x), A_j ∈ C¹ with A_j and ∂_{x_j}A_j bounded on [0,T]×R^n, B continuous and bounded, and F ∈ C([0,T];L²). Let u ∈ C¹([0,T]×R^n;C^m) be a solution with u(t,·) supported in a fixed compact set for all t (or u ∈ C([0,T];H¹) ∩ C¹([0,T];L²)). Put K = (1/2) sup |Σ_j ∂_j A_j| + sup |B| (matrix operator norms). Then for 0 ≤ t ≤ T, ‖u(t)‖_{L²} ≤ e^{Kt} ( ‖u(0)‖_{L²} + ∫_0^t ‖F(s)‖_{L²} ds ). (2) The Codazzi equation implies $\nabla_i h_{jk} - \nabla_j h_{ik} = W(e_0, e_k, e_i, e_j)$; contracting yields $\operatorname{div}_g h - \nabla_g H = 0$.

Under uniform ellipticity kappa, a shortest path gives q(x)>=kappa^{|x-y|_1}q(y); the bound depends on distance.

Consequently exactly one of the following holds: q is identically zero; q is identically one; or 0<q(x)<1 at every site and inf_x q(x)=0, sup_x q(x)=1. In the third case L1 rules out a positive infimum; L1 applied to the complementary event rules out a supremum below one.

Suppose that the pair $(Z_1,Z_2)$ is either $({_1}B^{x_1},{_2}B^{x_2})$
or $({_1}B^{x_1,x_1}_t,{_2}B^{x_2,x_2}_t)$.
For any Borel measurable $A_1,A_2\subset[0,t]$,
there exists a random variable $\al_{A_1\times A_2}(Z_1,Z_2)$ such that
\[\al_{A_1\times A_2}(Z_1,Z_2)=\lim_{\eps\to0}\al^\eps_{A_1\times A_2}(Z_1,Z_2)\qquad\text{in probability}.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

title: Current best upper bound on the NON-RANDOM fluctuation in first-passage percolation: if F(0) < p_c and E[Y^2] < infinity, where Y is the minimum of d i.i.d. copies of tau_e, then there is C = C(F,d) with mu(x) <= E T(0,x) <= mu(x) + C (|x| log |x|)^{1/2} for every x in Z^d with |x| > 1. [Thm 2 of arXiv:2604.11489, '2604.11489'] Assume that the function $g:[0,1] \to \rr$ is differentiable and its derivative $g'$ is $\beta$-H\"{o}lder
continuous for some $\beta \in (0,1]$. Let
\beq
\sigma^2_n=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_{n,i}\left(g'\left( p_{n,i}\right)\right)^2-\left(\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_{n,i}g'\left( p_{n,i}\right)\right)^2
\deq
and
\beq
\gamma=
\begin{cases}
\beta/2 \ \ &\text{if}\ \ \beta\in (0,0.5]\\
\beta-0.5 \ \ &\text{if}\ \ \beta\in (0.5,1]
\end{cases}.
\deq
If
\begin{enumerate}[$(1)$]
\item $\beta\in (0.5,1]$ or
\item $\beta\in (0,0.5]$ and
\beq
\sup_{n}\sum_{i=1}^\infty p_{n,i}^{(\beta+1)/2}<\infty,
\deq
\end{enumerate}
then we have
\beq
\sup_x\left|\pp\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma_n}(\hat \theta_n-\theta_n)\le x\right)-\Phi(x)\right|\le\frac{C}{n^{\gamma/2} \sigma_n^{1/2}},
\deq
where $\Phi$ denotes the standard normal distribution function. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 2 of arXiv:2604.11489

[Defi 3 of arXiv:2609.02261, 'Quantization and process'] For each $h>0$,  the space 
  $D_h ( \R^{2 n })$  stands for the set of   functions $F$ on $\R^{2 n }$ such that there exists an analytic  function $ (X,Y)\rightarrow F^{\rm ext} (X , Y)$ on   $\C^{2n }$ 
  having the following properties.
  
  i)  $F^{\rm ext}$ satisfies for any $(X,Y)\in\R^{4n}$,

    \be   (\partial _{x_j } + i \partial _{\xi_j }) 
   F^{\rm ext} (X , Y) = 0 ,\quad
     (\partial _{y_j } - i \partial _{\eta_j })
      F^{\rm ext}    (X , Y) = 0,\ee 
      
  ii) We have $$F^{\rm ext}(X , X) = F(X).$$ 
  
 iii) There is 
a function $\psi_F \in L^1(\R^{2n}) \cap L^{\infty}(\R^{2n})$ verifying the estimate for all $(X,Y)\in\R^{4n}$,
       
       $$ | F^{\rm ext}(X , Y)| \leq e^{ \frac { 1 }  { 4h } |X-Y|^2  } 
       \psi_F (X - Y) .$$
       
When the conditions i) ii) and iii) are fulfilled, we set,

$$ \Vert F \Vert _{D_h( \R^{2n})}  =  \Vert \Psi_F  \Vert _{L^1 (\R^{2n})} + 
 \Vert \Psi_F \Vert _{L^{\infty } (\R^{2n})}.  $$

[Lem AnaLem of arXiv:2506.18207, 'Cartan's Path Development, the Logarithmic Signature and a Conjecture of Lyons-Sidorova'] Let $N\geqslant2$ be a given fixed integer. Suppose
that $S_{n}(a_{1},\cdots,a_{n})=0$ for all $n\leqslant N-1$ and
all non-degenerate sequences $(a_{1},\cdots,a_{n})$ with $a_{j}\in2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$.
Let $(b_{1}^{*},\cdots,b_{N}^{*})$ be a fixed non-degenerate sequence
with $b_{j}\in2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$. Given $w\in\mathbb{C}$, we define
the path development $F_{w}:\mathbb{C}^{2}\rightarrow\mathfrak{sl}_{N+1}(\mathbb{C})$
by 
\begin{equation}
F_{w}({\rm e}_{1})\triangleq A_{w},\ F_{w}({\rm e}_{2})\triangleq E_{12}+\cdots+E_{N,N+1},
\end{equation}
where $A_{w}\in\mathfrak{h}$ is chosen to satisfy 
\begin{equation}
[A_{w},E_{k,k+1}]=(b_{k}^{*}+w)E_{k,k+1}\ \ \ (k=1,\cdots,N).
\end{equation}
Then for any vector $K=(k_{1},\cdots,k_{n})$ satisfying $|K|=N,n\geqslant2$ or $|K|\leqslant N-1,n\geqslant1$ and any $j=1,\cdots,N,$ there exists a meromorphic function $\Psi_{K,j}:\mathbb{C}^{|K|}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$
(i.e. the quotient of two holomorphic functions) in $|K|$ complex variables,
such that 
\[
\hat{F}_{w}(H_{K})=\sum_{j}\Psi_{K,j}(b_{j}^{*}+w,\cdots,b_{j+|K|-1}^{*}+w)E_{j,j+|K|}
\]
and the function $w\mapsto\Psi_{K,j}(b_{j}^{*}+w,\cdots,b_{j+|K|-1}^{*}+w)$
is analytic in a neighbourhood of $w=0$ for all $(K,j)$. Here $\hat{F}_{w}$
is the induced Lie homomorphism on ${\cal L}((\mathbb{C}^{2}))$ (cf.
((eq:HatF of the paper))). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem AnaLem of arXiv:2506.18207

\]

[Definition 13 of arXiv:2609.02755, 'The Sharp Rate of Probabilistically Strong Convergence to the KPZ Equation'] Given a rooted tree $\tau$, we say that $C \subset E_+(\tau)$ is a cut of $\tau$ if any path in $E(\tau)$ with the root of $\tau$ as an endpoint contains at most one edge in $C$. We denote by $\mathbb{C}[\tau]$ the set of all cuts of $\tau$.
	We recall that for a rooted tree $\tau$, there is a natural partial ordering on $E(\tau)$ in which $e \ge e^\prime$ iff $e^\prime$ lies on the unique path from $e$ to the root.
	
	 We write $\tau_{\ng C}$ for the subgraph consisting of those edges $e \in E(\tau)$ such that there does not exist $\tilde{e} \in C$ with $e \ge \tilde{e}$.

body: [Lemma lem:cox_J of arXiv:2412.04589, 'Inverting the Markovian projection for pure jump processes'] Let $\lambda$, $\Lambda$, $E$ and $\tau$ be given by Lemma~(lem:cox of the paper). Furthermore, suppose that $\Omega$ supports a non-vanishing integrable random variable $J$ which is independent of $\mathcal{F}_\infty \lor \sigma(E)$. Define the filtration $\widetilde{\mathbb{A}} = (\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_t)_{t \geq 0}$ by $\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}_t \coloneqq \sigma(J\bm{1}_{\{\tau \leq s\}}; s \leq t)$. Let $\widetilde{\mathbb{G}} \coloneqq \mathbb{F} \newtriangledown \widetilde{\mathbb{A}}$. Then, the process $(J\bm{1}_{\{\tau \leq t\}} - \mathbb{E}[J]\Lambda_{\tau \land t})_{t \geq 0}$ is a $\widetilde{\mathbb{G}}$-martingale, and we have $\mathbb{F} \hookrightarrow \widetilde{\mathbb{G}}$.

[Theorem thm:max_lh of arXiv:2607.22291, 'Rare subtree patterns in size-conditioned Bienaymé trees: Poisson approximation and declum'] Assume that $\mu$ is critical and belongs to the domain of attraction of a stable law.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)]  Assume that $\mu_{1}>0$. There exists a constant $C_{\mu}>0$ such that the following holds. Set
$$k^*_{n} =  \frac{1}{\log(1/\mu_{1})}\log n +  \frac{1}{\log(1/\mu_{1})} \log\bigl((1-\mu_1)C_{\mu}\bigr).$$
Then for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$ we have
\[
\P\bigl(\lambda(\mathcal{T}^n) \leq \lfloor k^*_{n} + t\rfloor\bigr) - \exp\bigl(-\mu_1^{t+1 - \{k^*_{n} + t\}}\bigr) \to 0.
\]
\item[(ii)] Assume that $\mu_{1}=0$. Set $\kappa = \min\{i \geq 2 : \mu_i > 0\}$. There exists a constant $D_{\mu} \in (0,1)$ such that the following holds. Set
$$
k_{n}^{**} \coloneqq  \log_\kappa \log n - \log_\kappa \log(1/D_{\mu}).
$$
 Write $m_n=\lfloor k_n^{**}\rfloor$ and
$\theta_n=\{k_n^{**}\}$, and define
$$
  J_n=
  \begin{cases}
    \{m_n-1,m_n\},&\theta_n\le\tfrac12,\\
    \{m_n,m_n+1\},&\theta_n>\tfrac12.
  \end{cases}
$$
Then $\P(\lambda(\mathcal T^n)\in J_n)\longrightarrow1$. In addition, if $\liminf_n\min(\theta_n,1-\theta_n)>0$, then
$\P(\lambda(\mathcal T^n)=m_n)\to1$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:max_lh of arXiv:2607.22291

 Let $X_1, X_2, \cdots, X_n$ be independent and not necessarily identically distributed random variables with zero means and finite variances. Define $W=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and assume that $Var(W)=1$. body: A graph G = (V, E) is a finite set V of vertices together with a set E of edges, each an unordered pair of vertices; G is simple if it has no loops or repeated edges. A subgraph uses a subset of the vertices and edges. The degree of a vertex is the number of incident edges, and the handshake lemma gives sum of degrees = 2|E|. A walk is a vertex-edge alternation; a path has distinct vertices, a cycle is a closed path, and G is connected if every two vertices are joined by a path. Standard families: the complete graph K_n (all pairs adjacent), a tree (connected and acyclic, with |V|-1 edges), and a bipartite graph (vertices two-colorable so every edge crosses, equivalently no odd cycle). The vertex connectivity kappa(G) and edge connectivity lambda(G) are the least numbers of vertices, respectively edges, whose deletion disconnects G (or reduces it to a single vertex), and kappa(G) <= lambda(G) <= min-degree.
title: Graph, Subgraph, and Basic Invariants

Let X, Y be Banach spaces and T: D(T) ⊂ X → Y a linear operator defined on a linear subspace D(T). Its graph is G(T) = {(x, Tx) : x ∈ D(T)} ⊂ X × Y. T is closed if G(T) is closed in X × Y; equivalently, whenever x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → x in X and Tx_n → y in Y, then x ∈ D(T) and Tx = y. Equivalently, D(T) is complete under the graph norm ‖x‖_T = ‖x‖ + ‖Tx‖. S is an extension of T (written T ⊂ S) if D(T) ⊂ D(S) and Sx = Tx for x ∈ D(T). T is closable if it has a closed extension; equivalently, x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → 0 and Tx_n → y imply y = 0; equivalently, the closure of G(T) is the graph of an operator, called the closure T̄ (the smallest closed extension). If T is closed, a subspace D_0 ⊂ D(T) is a core for T if D_0 is dense in D(T) for the graph norm, i.e. the closure of T restricted to D_0 equals T. A closed operator need not be bounded, and being closed says nothing about D(T) being dense; by the closed graph theorem a closed operator with D(T) = X is bounded.
X and Y are Banach spaces
T is linear on a linear subspace D(T) of X
title: Closed Operator, Closable Operator, and Core

Theorem C: sigma_t is not ⊠-strongly log-unimodal for any t > 0. [Theorem 7 (Error bound for the slope change classifier) of arXiv:2609.00402, '2609.00402'] Suppose Assumption~\ref{ass:slope} holds. Let \(T\geq5\), \(\mathcal I=\{3,\ldots,T-2\}\), and \(m_T=\lvert\mathcal I\rvert=T-4\). For \(\tau\in\mathcal I\), define \(v_\tau=1/D_L(\tau)+1/D_R(\tau)\), \(v_T^{\max}=\max_{\tau\in\mathcal I}v_\tau\), and, for \(\alpha_S\in(0,1)\), \(\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}=\sigma_S\sqrt{2v_T^{\max}\log(2m_T/\alpha_S)}\). Then \(h_{S,\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}}(\bm X)=\mathbb I\{S(\bm X)>\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}\}\) satisfies \(\mathbb P\{h_{S,\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}}(\bm X)=1\mid Y=0\}\leq\alpha_S\) and
\[
\mathbb P\{h_{S,\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}}(\bm X)=0\mid Y=1\}
\leq
\exp\left\{-\frac{(\kappa_S-\lambda_{S,\alpha_S})_+^2}{2\sigma_S^2v_T^{\max}}\right\},
\]
where \(x_+=\max\{x,0\}\). Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{err}(h_{S,\lambda_{S,\alpha_S}})
\leq\pi_0\alpha_S+
\pi_1\exp\left\{-\frac{(\kappa_S-\lambda_{S,\alpha_S})_+^2}{2\sigma_S^2v_T^{\max}}\right\}
=:\mathfrak B_S(\alpha_S).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Error bound for the slope change classifier

[Lem 171 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let indices $a(q_d),a^\frozen(q_d)$
be sampled as in Definition~\ref{d:rerand}, and let
indices $i(q_d),i^\frozen(q_d)$
be sampled as in Definition~\ref{d:rerand.Ising}. 
For $N$ large enough, we have
	\[\max_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}}
	\E\bigg[
	\max_{r\in[s,t]} 
	\bigg|
	\sum_{\ell=s}^{r-1}
	\Delta X^\sigma(q_\ell,a(q_{\ell+1}))
	\bigg|^8
	\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_t-q_s)^4
	\]
for all $0\le s\le t\le \dmax$.
The same bound holds
	with $\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$
	or $\Delta X^{\frozen,\sigma}(q_d,a^\frozen(q_{d+1}))$
	in place of $\Delta X^\sigma(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$.
We also have
	\[
	\E \left[
	\max_{r\in[s,t]}
	\left|
	\sum_{\ell=s}^{r-1}
	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_\ell,i(q_{\ell+1}))
	\right|^8
	\right]
	\le L^{O(1)}(q_t-q_s)^4\,,
	\]
and likewise with $\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_\ell,i(q_{\ell+1}))$ or $\Delta X^{\Isplus}(q_\ell,i^\frozen(q_{\ell+1}))$ in place of $\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_\ell,i(q_{\ell+1}))$.

\begin{proof}
This follows by a very similar argument as for Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising}. We will describe the proof for $X^\RomII$. A key difference is that in Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising} we considered $X^\RomII(q_d,a)$ as a process indexed by time $q_d$ for a fixed index $a\in[M]$, with respect to the filtration $\cG(t)$. Here, we instead consider the process $X^\RomII(q_d,a(q_d))$, with respect to the filtration $\cFt(t)$ defined by \eqref{e:gaus.filt.plus}. With this change, repeating the argument of
Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising} gives the conclusion for $X^\RomII$ (cf.\ \eqref{e:martingale.X.holder.estimate}). The conclusions for $X^\RomIII$ and $X^\Ising$ follow similarly. It is straightforward to verify that the same bounds hold for the modified processes 
$X^{\trunc,\sigma}$ and $X^{\frozen,\sigma}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 171 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Lemma 8 of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] There exist constants \(C>0\) and \(\kappa>0\) such that, for every
		\(\bm f\in \mathcal L^2((0,1);\mathbb R^2)\),
		\[
		\|T_t\bm f\|_{\mathcal L^2}
		\le
		Ce^{-\kappa t}\|\bm f\|_{\mathcal L^2},
		\qquad t\ge0.
		\]
		Consequently, the adjoint semigroup also satisfies
		\[
		\|S_t\bm f\|_{\mathcal  L^2}
		\le
		Ce^{-\kappa t}\|\bm f\|_{\mathcal L^2},
		\qquad t\ge0.
		\]
		In particular,
		\[
		\lim_{t\to\infty}T_t\bm f=0,
		\qquad
		\lim_{t\to\infty}S_t\bm f=0
		\]
		in \(\mathcal  L^2((0,1);\mathbb R^2)\).

body:
[Thm conv-DL-zero of arXiv:2411.16376, 'Higher order approximations in arcsine laws for subordinators'] Under the assumption of Theorem $(Thm:potential-zero of the paper)$ with $\beta_0=\beta\in(0,1]$,  let us define a function $\varepsilon_2:(0,+\infty)\to\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ by 
\begin{align}
    \Pi((x,+\infty))=
    \frac{c_0 x^{-\beta}}{\Gamma(1-\beta)}+\varepsilon_2(x),
    \quad
   0<x<+\infty.	
\end{align}
Set 
\begin{align}
 \varepsilon_3(s,x)
   =
   s\Pi((s-sx,+\infty))\varepsilon_1(sx),
   \quad 0<s, x<+\infty.	
\end{align}
Then, for $s\in(0,+\infty)$, the finite measure 
\begin{align}
\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}\bigg(\frac{X_{T(s)-}}{s}\in dx,\; 0<\frac{X_{T(s)-}}{s}<1\bigg),
\quad 0<x<1,
\end{align}
 admits a density expressed in the form
\begin{align}
   s\Pi((s-sx,&+\infty))u(sx)
   \\
   =\,&
   \frac{\sin(\pi\beta)}{\pi}x^{-1+\beta}(1-x)^{-\beta}
   +
   \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{c_0 s^{\beta_k-\beta}}{c_k\Gamma(\beta_k)\Gamma(1-\beta)}
   x^{-1+\beta_k}(1-x)^{-\beta}
   \\
   &+
   \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{s^{\beta_k}}{c_k\Gamma(\beta_k)}
   x^{-1+\beta_k}\varepsilon_2(s-sx)
   +
   O(\varepsilon_3(s,x)),
   \quad
   \text{as $s\to0+$,}	
\end{align}
uniformly in $x\in I$ for any closed interval $I\subset (0,1)$. 
Therefore, for any closed interval $I\subset (0,1)$,
\begin{align}
	&\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}\bigg(\frac{X_{T(s)-}}{s}\in I\bigg)
	\\
	=\,&
	 \frac{\sin(\pi\beta)}{\pi}
	 \int_I x^{-1+\beta}(1-x)^{-\beta}\,dx
	 +
	 \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{c_0 s^{\beta_k-\beta}}{c_k\Gamma(\beta_k)\Gamma(1-\beta)}
   \int_I x^{-1+\beta_k}(1-x)^{-\beta}\,dx 
   \\	
   &+
   \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{s^{\beta_k}}{c_k\Gamma(\beta_k)}
   \int_I
   x^{-1+\beta_k}\varepsilon_2(s-sx)\,dx
   + 
   O\bigg(\sup_{x\in I}\varepsilon_3(s,x)\bigg),
   \quad
   \text{as $s\to0+$}.
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

  written as  $\Phi = \Phi _1  +  \Phi _2 $.  
 Suppose that  the function $\Phi_1 $ is the symbol of a bounded operator in  $L^{\infty } (\R^{4n} )$  commuting with  translations. 
Assume that the function $\Phi_2 \in C^{\infty } (\R^{4n} )$ and that, for any $\alpha\in \N^{4n}$,
   there exists a real number $A_{\alpha }$ such that, for every  $u\in\R^{4n}$,
  
   \be | \partial ^{\alpha }\Phi_2 (u) | \leq A_{\alpha } (|u|^2 +1).
  \ee
  
Also suppose that there exists $m  \in \R$  such that,  for any $u\in\R^{4n}$ large enough,
  
      \be  {\rm Re} \,\Phi_2 (u) \leq  m |u|^2 .\ee
   
  
   
Set  $\lambda >0 $ and  $\mu >0$ satisfying,
   
   \be   m < \lambda,\quad 
   0 < \mu <  4 ( \lambda -m) . \ee 
   
Then, there exists an operator  $T$ bounded from $ D_{\lambda h}(\R^{4n})$ 
  into $ D_{\mu h}(\R^{4n})$ which is commuting with  translations and with  symbol equals to

[Theorem thm:reverse of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] Let $(X_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}$ solve (equation eq:forward of the paper) and let $\varepsilon\in(0,T)$. On
$[0,T-\varepsilon]$ set $Y_{s}:=X_{T-s}$. Then there exists a free Brownian motion
$(\bar S_{s})$, adapted to the filtration generated by $(Y_{r})_{r\le s}$, such that
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{d} Y_{s}=\Big(\tfrac12\beta(T-s)\,Y_{s}-\beta(T-s)\,\xi_{\mu_{T-s}}(Y_{s})\Big)\mathrm{d} s
  +\sqrt{\beta(T-s)}\;\mathrm{d}\bar S_{s},
\end{equation}
where $\xi_{\mu_{t}}=2H\mu_{t}$ is well defined in $L^{2}$ for $t\ge\varepsilon$ by
Lemma~(lem:regularise of the paper). The spectral law of $Y_{s}$ is $\mu_{T-s}$; in particular
$\mu_{Y_{T-\varepsilon}}=\mu_{\varepsilon}\to\mu_{0}$ weakly as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$.

body:
Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]

For every neighborhood U of 0 in X, its polar U^circ = {phi in X^*: |phi(u)| <= 1 for every u in U} is weak-* compact. Here X^* is the continuous dual and the weak-* topology is pointwise convergence on X; neither completeness nor separability of X is needed.
X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed
for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable
Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case

body: Every n by n complex matrix A can be written as A = U P, where U is unitary and P is positive semidefinite Hermitian, specifically P = (A* A)^{1/2}. [Lemma 20 of arXiv:2512.19517, 'Spiking and Resetting'] Suppose $(h^\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ and $h$ are non-negative continuous non-increasing functions from $[0,\infty)$ into $\mathbb R$ uniformly bounded by a constant $M>0$. If
\[
\forall \sigma>0, \quad \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \int_0^\infty e^{-\sigma s} h^\varepsilon (s) \, ds = \int_0^\infty e^{-\sigma s} h (s) \, ds \ ,
\]
then $(h^\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon> 0}$ converges to $h$ uniformly on compact subsets of $[0,\infty)$.

body: [Theorem 1.5 of arXiv:2607.02272, 'The case of equality in BK'] For any pair of increasing events A, B in Ω, we have P(A ◦B) ≤P ⊗P(A ⊠B) . (1.1) This theorem immediately implies the BK inequality. Indeed, the disjoint testimony A ⊠B is a subset of A × B, thus P(A ◦B) ≤P ⊗P(A ⊠B) ≤P ⊗P(A × B) = P(A)P(B) . In their recent paper [2], Radhakrishnan and Tassion say that this inequality is known (see [2], formula (13) in remark 7).
title: Theorem 1.5 of arXiv:2607.02272: The case of equality in BK

body: Events A_1, ..., A_n are independent if for every subset S of indices, P(intersection of A_i for i in S) = product of P(A_i) over i in S. Random variables are independent if the sigma-algebras they generate are independent, equivalently their joint distribution is the product of the marginals. An infinite family is independent if every finite subfamily is.
title: Independence of Events and Random Variables

body: Let N = 2n with n >= 4 and 1 = lambda_1 = lambda_2 < lambda_3 = lambda_4 < ... < lambda_{N-1} = lambda_N, write |x|^2 = sum_l x_l^2, |x|_{-1}^2 = sum_l x_l^2/lambda_l, mu_i = lambda_{2i} (1 <= i <= n) and C = {(u,v): 0 <= v <= u <= lambda_N v}. The functions q_l on C, regular versions of the conditional expectations under the Gaussian measure mu of x_l^2 given |x|^2 = u and |x|_{-1}^2 = v, satisfy u = sum_l q_l(u,v) and v = sum_l q_l(u,v)/lambda_l on C, and q_{2i} = q_{2i-1}; write qhat_i = q_{2i} + q_{2i-1}. Then (1 - 1/mu_i) qhat_i(u,v) is non-decreasing in i for 2 <= i <= n and (u,v) in C, and qhat_i(u,v) <= [(n - i + 1)(1 - 1/mu_i)]^{-1} (u - v) for 2 <= i <= n and (u,v) in C.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, Entropy and singularity of spectral and pivotal sets in planar percolation (arXiv:2609.15388, September 2026) proves that for crossings of critical bond percolation on the square lattice, and of site percolation on the triangular lattice with critical or inhomogeneous near-critical parameters, the Shannon entropies of the spectral sample and of the pivotal set are both comparable to the total influence, of order R^2 alpha_4(R). This answers Question 1 in Section 11 of C. Garban, G. Pete and O. Schramm, The Fourier spectrum of critical percolation (Acta Math. 205, 2010, 19-104), and proves both bounds of Conjecture 8 in G. Kalai, Three puzzles on mathematics, computation, and games (Proc. ICM 2018), for these crossings; the spectral bound is the percolation case of the Friedgut-Kalai Fourier entropy-influence conjecture. For critical triangular-site square crossings the two laws are asymptotically mutually singular. Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/percolation-crossing-entropy (commit 29a39246dc9c); ResearchGate record 414266816. Not refereed.
title: Garban-Pete-Schramm Section 11 Question 1 answered and Kalai's Conjecture 8 (ICM 2018) proved for planar percolation crossings: entropy of the spectral sample and the pivotal set (Shmalo 2026, arXiv:2609.15388, repository yspennstate/percolation-crossing-entropy)

  + (1-p) \sum_{m \ge 1} \binom{k}{m} \frac{(1- \varepsilon )^{k-m}  \varepsilon ^m}{k-m+1} \left( \sum_{(\tau,i) \in {\mathcal D}_m(\pi)}  d _\tau^o(\mu)  \right).
\end{multline}

body: Over the abelian group G = Z2 x Z6 (element k written as (k div 6, k mod 6)), the squares L_i(x, y) = x + theta_i(y) are Latin whenever theta_i permutes G, and L_i is orthogonal to L_j exactly when theta_i - theta_j is a bijection. With theta_1 the identity, theta_2 = [0, 2, 1, 6, 8, 7, 5, 10, 3, 11, 4, 9] and theta_3 = [0, 3, 7, 9, 6, 4, 1, 5, 11, 10, 8, 2] give three pairwise orthogonal Latin squares of order 12, and the resulting orthogonal array OA(12, 5) with 144 rows covers every ordered pair exactly once in each of its ten coordinate pairs (strength 2, index 1). The cyclic group Z12 admits no such linear construction, since differences of units mod 12 are even; Z2 x Z6 satisfies the Hall-Paige condition for complete mappings. All three squares have 108 intercalates.

On P_2(R^d), let F=G+tau H be convex under linear mixing, where tau>0 and H(mu)=integral log(dmu/dx) dmu for absolutely continuous mu, and +infinity otherwise. For every mu, G admits a first variation G_prime[mu] in C^1(R^d) of the form G_prime[mu](x)=a|x|^2/2+V[mu](x), with a,L>0 independent of mu and |grad V[mu](x)|<=L for every mu,x. A Wasserstein gradient flow here means a P_2-continuous distributional solution partial_t mu_t=div(mu_t grad G_prime[mu_t])+tau Delta mu_t, positive for t>0, which satisfies F(mu_t2)-F(mu_t1)=-integral_t1^t2 integral |grad G_prime[mu_s]+tau grad log(mu_s)|^2 dmu_s ds. Suppose there exist sigma_1,sigma_2,m,M>0 such that m gamma_1(x)<=mu_t(x)<=M gamma_2(x) for every t>=0 and almost every x, where gamma_i is the density of N(0,sigma_i^2 I_d). Assume 0<sigma_1<=sigma_2<sqrt(2) sigma_1 and finite initial gap h_0=F(mu_0)-inf F. Set r=sigma_2^2/sigma_1^2 and C=(2r-r^2)^(-d/2). Then for every t>=0, F(mu_t)-inf F <= [h_0^(-1)+m^2 t/(4 C M^2 sigma_1^2)]^(-1). If h_0=0 the right side means zero. In particular the result requires linear convexity of F, without requiring a log-Sobolev inequality for mu_t. The Gaussian-comparison factor C can grow exponentially with d when r>1 is fixed.

STATEMENT
Fix b=9/10,d=999/1000,nu=1-d,c=1/19,gamma=9/19 and constant
0<=e<1/2. Let (y_t,z_t,V_t,q_t), t in all integers, satisfy
 V>=0, s=sqrt(V)+e, q*s=z, V>=nu*z^2,
 V'=d*V+nu*y^2, z'=y, q'*s'=y,

Assume sup_t V_t<infinity. Retain both branch labels at s=1:
L is permitted when s>=1; H when s<=1.
Let Gamma(V)=8*gamma*min(sqrt(V),1-e)^3/3, and define
 phi_L=-c*(y-z)^2/2-Gamma(V),
 phi_H=(y^2-b*z^2)/(1+b)-(y+q-z)^2/2-Gamma(V).
On every edge put Psi=phi'-phi-[(q')^2-2*y*q'].
Assume Psi=0 on EVERY edge. Finally assume F3 explicitly:
on every regular edge with source H label, w=1/s'>c.
Regular here means s>0 and s'>0; on regular edges p=1/s.

Then the entire PHYSICAL STATE history is either the origin
(y,z,V,q)=(0,0,0,0), or the exact alternating two-cycle
 (y_t,z_t,V_t,q_t)=(sigma_t*a,-sigma_t*a,a^2,-2*sigma_t*a),
 a=1/2-e>0, sigma_(t+1)=-sigma_t in {+1,-1}.
At e=0 the origin may have arbitrary permitted edge decorations u_t;
this statement does not assert uniqueness of those decorations.
Conversely both listed physical histories admit zero-dissipation
labeled full histories satisfying these hypotheses.

1. ANY ZERO VARIANCE FORCES THE ENTIRE ORIGIN HISTORY
Apply the explicit argument079, whose hypotheses are precisely the
nonnegative variance recursion, full negative history, the displayed
edge equations, and zero Psi. For completeness, the only singular
calculation it uses can be reconstructed directly from our definitions.
When e=0 and y=z=V=0, V'=z'=0, y'=-(1+b)*q'. Both labels are H.
The source potential is -q^2/2; substitution in the target potential
and subtracting (q')^2 gives
 Psi=b*(2-b)*(q')^2/2+q^2/2=99*(q')^2/200+q^2/2.
Thus zero Psi forces q=q'=0 and y'=0. Backwards variance induction
first gives y_j=V_j=z_j=0 for j<0; this identity gives q_j=0 and
propagates the origin forward. At e>0 the constraints instead give
q=0 when z=V=0, and the position equation propagates the origin.
This is proof079's full-history argument; a one-sided V0=0 start is
insufficient. No independent audit of079 is being asserted.

It remains to consider histories with V_t>0 for all t. Then all edges
are regular, including at e=0, so p,w are well-defined and positive.

2. POSITIVE PURE VARIANCE IS EXCLUDED
If at any time y=z=q=0,V>0, the predecessor has y=0,V_old=V/d>0.
Since u=s/s'>0, its position equation forces z_old=0 and then q_old=0.
Inductively V_(-k)=V*d^(-k), contradicting bounded variance.
This is the argument069; it uses b>0,d in(0,1), not a potential.
It excludes isolated equality alternatives only because a full bounded
negative-time history is assumed.

3. THRESHOLD LABELS ARE COVERED BEFORE THE OPEN BRANCHES
If s=1 or s'=1, equivalently p=1 or w=1, apply the labeled table074.
It covers both source labels at p=1 and both target labels at w=1.
All margins are positive, except for the low-source target-threshold
pure-variance edge y=z=q=0,V=(1-e)^2/d, excluded by Section2.
Its F3 requirement w>=c is implied by our strict F3 assumption for
source H labels. Its e_max can be taken equal to our fixed e<1/2.
Thus no threshold state or threshold edge can occur on this history.
The double-threshold cases also lie in that table (and were checked070).

4. OPEN BRANCHES FORCE THE CYCLE
Away from thresholds, use086's reconstructed equality table:
LL forces y=z=0, hence q=0 because s>0, excluded by Section2;
LH and HL are strictly positive, the latter using F3;
HH has equality only at the origin or exact two-cycle by084-085.
The origin has V=0, ruled out in the present case. Hence every state
is a cycle phase with a=1/2-e. On these phases s=s'=1/2,
u=1,q'=2*y, and the position equation gives y'=-y.
So the signs alternate for all integers; no switching phase or physical
jump is available. This proves the stated classification.

5. CONVERSE AND DEPENDENCY BOUNDARY
The origin satisfies every physical equation with u=1 (for e>0);
for e=0 any allowed u works, with q=q'=0. It has H labels since e<1/2.
At a cycle, s=1/2, u=1, both labels are H, Gamma(V')=Gamma(V),
and direct substitution gives Psi=0. F3 holds since w=2>c.
The variance bound holds for both histories.

This theorem assumes a full zero-Psi history and F3. It does NOT show
that an arbitrary corrected Adam path generates such a history, that
its omega-limit set is confined to these histories, or that nearby paths
enter cycle tubes. Compact limiting relations, bias-error control, and
transversality/null basins are still separate global021 obligations.

conditional dependency has been disguised as an independent PASS.

w=up>1, U=1/p in(0,1). The denominator 3u(1-du^2) is

coefficient, to compare with an UPPER bound on the square-completion cost.
There is no probability, independence hypothesis, variance proxy,
concentration inequality or asymptotic rate in this calculation.

1. Direct interval certificate.
Since d*(1001/1000)^2>1, we have u<1001/1000. Put
 N(u)=3du^2(u+1)-nu(2u+1)-(9/2)u^2
     =u^2*[3d(u+1)-9/2]-nu(2u+1).
On this interval the bracket is at least
 3d*(19/10)-9/2=11943/10000>0.
Therefore multiplying lower bounds for the two positive factors, and
using an upper bound in the term with a negative sign, gives
 N(u)>= (81/100)*(11943/10000)-(1/1000)*(1501/500)
      =964381/1000000>0.
This is an interval inequality; equality at every factor bound is not
asserted. In fact the upper endpoint for u is strict.

Consequently for the exact function in084,
 T(u)=[3du^2(u+1)-nu(2u+1)]/[3u(1-du^2)],
 T(u)-(3/2)*u/(1-du^2)=N(u)/[3u(1-du^2)]>0.
This proves the lower bound for T on the whole required interval
without a polynomial-basis conversion or sampled substitutions.

2. Carrying constants to the Schur remainder.
We have 0<1-du^2<=1-d*b^2=19081/100000<1/5 and gamma>=9/20.
Thus the available coefficient satisfies
 8gamma U T(u)>=12gamma U u/(1-du^2)
                  >=60gamma U u >=(243/10)U.
All denominators are positive; their reciprocals reverse their order.
The weak inequalities displayed are sufficient although some are strict.

For completeness the cost upper bound from084 uses A/p^2<=1/2,
|F1|/p<=1/2, F2<1 and det>=6w^2/25>0. These follow from
 A=p^2/2-p+(1/2+gamma+ku^2),
 F1/p=1/2-(1/2+chi*u^2)/p, F2=chi*u^2+1/2,
 1/2+gamma+k/d<1, chi/d<1/2,
and det=chi*w^2/2+gamma*F2*(1-u^2).
For u<=1 the determinant bound follows from chi/2>6/25.
For u>1 use w>1,F2<1,u^2<1/d and
 chi/2-6/25-gamma*(1/d-1)>0.
The cost is then bounded by
 gamma^2*(10u^2+6u+1)/[(6/25)w^2]
 <=75/(4w^2)=75U^2/(4u^2)<=625U^2/27.
Here 10u^2+6u+1<18 because u<1001/1000, and gamma<1/2.
Hence the remaining coefficient is at least
 (243/10)U-(625/27)U^2
 >=[(243/10)-(625/27)]U=(311/270)U>0.
The last step uses U^2<=U; no lower bound away from zero for U is needed.

Fan and Wang (arXiv:2005.11879, Assumption 3.2(b), PDF p.5) assume a twice differentiable activation with globally bounded first and second derivatives, E sigma(Z)=0 and E[(sigma(Z))^2]=1 for standard Gaussian Z. Theorem 3.7 retains Assumption 3.2: fixed depth; independent standard Gaussian weights; approximately pairwise orthogonal input columns with deviations epsilon_n n^(1/4) tending to zero, bounded input norm and total squared norm deviations; a limiting input Gram empirical distribution; and positive finite limiting sample-to-hidden-width ratios. Together with Lemma 3.5 it describes the limiting empirical NTK eigenvalue distribution through conjugate-kernel matrices. Section 2.2 footnote 2 (p.4) explicitly distinguishes this weak empirical convergence from convergence of extreme eigenvalues. Raw ReLU has Gaussian mean 1/sqrt(2pi), second moment 1/2 and a corner at zero. Centering and dividing by sqrt(1/2-1/(2pi)) repairs its moments but not differentiability. Thus neither raw nor centered normalized ReLU is directly covered by the stated theorem. A separate nonsmooth approximation argument, and a separate outlier argument, are needed. This is a source-coverage note, not a claimed extension.
Use of the theorem as stated; no unproved extension by approximation
title: Fan--Wang activation assumptions: centered ReLU is still outside the stated NTK bulk theorem

Let R be a commutative ring with 1, let I be an ideal contained in the Jacobson radical J(R) (the intersection of all maximal ideals), and let M be a finitely generated R-module. If I M = M then M = 0. Consequences: if N is a submodule with M = N + I M then M = N; and if elements m_1, ..., m_k of M have images generating M / I M, then they generate M. For a local ring (R, m) and finitely generated M this reads: M = m M implies M = 0, and a subset of M generates M if and only if its image spans the k-vector space M / m M, k = R / m.
M finitely generated (the lemma fails for infinitely generated modules, e.g. M = Q over the localisation of Z at a prime)
I inside the Jacobson radical; for a local ring any proper ideal qualifies

$$

[Lemma 22 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(k:(0,\infty)^2\to\mathbb C\) be measurable. Assume that, for almost every
\(\eta>0\), the map \(\xi\mapsto k(\xi,\eta)\) is locally absolutely continuous
on \((0,\infty)\), satisfies \(\lim_{\xi\to\infty}k(\xi,\eta)=0\), and
\[
        A:=
        \int_0^\infty
        \sqrt u
        \left(
        \int_0^\infty |\partial_1 k(u,\eta)|^2\,\mathrm d\eta
        \right)^{1/2}
        \,\mathrm du
        <\infty .
\]
Then the integral operator \(K\) on \(L^2(0,\infty)\) with kernel \(k\) is trace
class, and \(\|K\|_1\le A\).

Let X_n converge in distribution to a real random variable X and let Y_n converge in probability to a real constant c. Then (X_n,Y_n) converges jointly in distribution to (X,c). Consequently X_n+Y_n converges in distribution to X+c, X_n Y_n converges in distribution to cX, and, if c!=0, X_n/Y_n converges in distribution to X/c. For the quotient, define its value arbitrarily on {Y_n=0} when necessary; that event has probability tending to zero. Convergence Y_n=>c in distribution is equivalent to convergence Y_n->c in probability, so either hypothesis gives the same conclusion for a constant target. With a nonconstant target, separate marginal convergence alone does not identify the joint limit: if X is a nondegenerate symmetric random variable, X_n=X and Y_n=-X, then both marginal laws converge to the law of X, but X_n+Y_n=0 does not converge to the law of 2X. A random second limit is allowed when joint convergence (X_n,Y_n)=>(X,Y) is supplied; the continuous mapping theorem then gives the corresponding sum and product limits, and the quotient limit if P(Y=0)=0. [Re-derived local source, M9; textbook cross-reference: van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 2.8.]

[Theorem thm: connected cutsets of arXiv:2503.21737, 'High-intensity Voronoi percolation on manifolds'] Let $M$ be simply connected. Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph such that $V\subset M$. Assume that to each $x\in V$ we can associate an open connected set $O(x)\subset M$ containing $x$ such that
\begin{enumerate}[i)]
\item $\bigcup_{x\in V}O(x)=M$,
\item $O(x)\cap O(y)\ne \emptyset $ if and only if $\{x,y\}\in E$ (for $x\neq y$).
\end{enumerate}
    Then for all $x,y\in V$, any minimal cutset separating $x$ from $y$ is connected in $G$.
    
    If we further assume that $G$ is one-ended and locally finite\footnote{We call a graph $G=(V,E)$ \emph{one-ended} if for any finite set $\Gamma\subset V$ the induced subgraph on $V\setminus \Gamma$ has a unique infinite connected component.
    We call \(G\) \emph{locally finite} when each of its vertices has finite degree.}
    (which holds, for instance, if $M$ itself is one-ended, the sets $O(x)$ are all bounded and any bounded set \(B \subset M\) intersects at most finitely many of the sets \(O(x)\)), then any minimal cutset separating $x$ from infinity is connected in $G$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2608.24356, 'Another solvable population dynamic\\ with uniform ancestral memory'] The following assertions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)]
The function $\Lambda$ is $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ and convex on $\R^S$. Its gradient  $\nabla \Lambda$, viewed as a row vector,  takes values in the subspace  of probability measures on $S$ with full support.
\item[(ii)] The Fenchel--Legendre transform $\Lambda^* $ is a strictly convex function. 

\item[(iii)] For any $\boldsymbol{\rho}\in \mathcal{P}_S$ with full support, there exists $\blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}\in \R^S$ such that
\[\nabla \Lambda(\blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}})=\boldsymbol{\rho} \quad \text{and} \quad \Lambda^*(\boldsymbol{\rho} )=\boldsymbol{\rho}  \blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}} - \Lambda(\blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}). \]
Moreover, for any $\boldsymbol{\rho}'\in \mathcal{P}_S$ different from $\boldsymbol{\rho}$, there is the strict inequality
\[ \Lambda^*(\boldsymbol{\rho}' )- \boldsymbol{\rho}'  \blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}}  > \Lambda^*(\boldsymbol{\rho} )-  \boldsymbol{\rho} \blambda_{\boldsymbol{\rho}} . \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theo 3 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Assume that $0<\alpha<1$, $|\Omega^+|>0$, $|\Omega^-|>0$, and
$m\in L^\infty(\Omega)$. Suppose that there exist $\rho_0>0$ and $m_{\rho_0}^-$ such that
\begin{equation}
	\mathcal C_{\rho_0}\subset\Omega^-
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
	-m(x)\geq m_{\rho_0}^-
	\qquad\text{for a.e. }x\in\mathcal C_{\rho_0}.
\end{equation}
Let $u_\lambda^+$ be the non-negative weak solution of \eqref{Eq1} given by
Theorem~\ref{thm1}. Then there exists $\sigma<0$ such that, for every
$\lambda<\sigma$, the solution $u_\lambda^+$ has compact support in
$\Omega$.

More precisely, there exists $\rho\in(0,\rho_0)$, independent of all
sufficiently negative $\lambda$, such that
$u_\lambda^+=0$ in $\mathcal C_\rho$. Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{supp}u_\lambda^+
\subset
\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)\geq\rho\}
\Subset\Omega.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem Main 2 of arXiv:2609.02871, 'Estimating the number of real zeros of linear combinations of radicals of polynomials'] Let $a_k, b_k$ and $c_k$ be real numbers.  Let $\alpha \in (-\infty, -1/2]$. If the function
\[
f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}c_{k}[(x-a_{k})^{2}+b_{k}^{2}]^{\alpha}
\]
is not identically zero, then it has no more than $2(n-1)$ distinct real roots on $\mathbb{R}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In probability theory, a Lévy process, named after the French mathematician Paul Lévy, is a stochastic process with independent, stationary increments: it represents the motion of a point whose successive displacements are random, in which displacements in pairwise disjoint time intervals are independent, and displacements in different time intervals of the same length have identical probability distributions. A Lévy process may thus be viewed as the continuous-time analog of a random walk.

[Theorem thm:introduction-continuous-spectrum of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $\Gamma\leq\mathbb R^d$ be a full-rank lattice and let
$(Z,\nu)$ be a nontrivial weakly mixing
probability-preserving Borel $\Gamma$-space. Then $\smash{\operatorname{Ind}_{\Gamma}^{\mathbb R^d}(Z)}$
admits a generating stealthy Delone cross-section $Y$. Writing
\[
    \sigma_Y
    :=
    \sigma_{Y,\mu_{\Gamma,Z}}
    =
    \sigma_{(\kappa_Y)_*\mu_{\Gamma,Z}},
\]
one has a decomposition
\[
    \sigma_Y
    =
    \sigma_Y^{\mathrm{tor}}
    +
    \sigma_Y^Z,
\]
where
\[
    \operatorname{supp}\sigma_Y^{\mathrm{tor}}
    \subset
    \Gamma^*\setminus\{0\},
    \qquad
    0\neq\sigma_Y^Z
    \ll
    \widetilde{\mathfrak m}_{Z,\nu}^0.
\]
In particular, $\sigma_Y$ has a nonzero continuous component. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In topology, a covering or covering projection is a map between topological spaces that, intuitively, locally acts like a projection of multiple copies of a space onto itself. In particular, coverings are special types of local homeomorphisms. If $p:{\tilde {X}}\to X$ is a covering, $({\tilde {X}},p)$ is said to be a covering space or cover of $X$, and $X$ is said to be the base of the covering, or simply the base. By abuse of terminology, ${\tilde {X}}$ and $p$ may sometimes be called covering spaces as well. Since coverings are local homeomorphisms, a covering space is a special kind of étalé space.

[Definition def:chemical of arXiv:2607.02367, 'Flux solutions for stochastic chemical systems with sources and sinks'] Assume that $\mathcal R$ is a set of bidirectional chemical reactions between elements of $\Omega $, i.e. 
 $\mathcal R := \{ S_\rho \}_{\rho=1}^r \cup  \{ S_{- \rho }\}_{\rho=1}^r $ where $S_{\rho_1} \neq - S_{\rho_2 } $ for every $\rho_1 \neq \rho_2 $. Assume that $ \mathcal R_s $ is a set of sources and sinks, i.e.  $\mathcal R_s := \{e_k \}_{k \in \Omega_c}  \cup  \{ - e_{ k  }\}_{\Omega_c }  $ with $ \Omega_c \subset \Omega$.  
 Assume that $\mathcal K := \{ R_\rho  \}_{ \rho =1 }^r \cup \{ R_{-\rho}\}_{\rho=1}^r  $ is the set of kinetics associated with the chemical reactions $S_\rho, S_{- \rho } \in \mathcal R $ and $\mathcal K_s := \{ \alpha_k  \}_{ k \in \Omega_c }  \cup \{ \beta_k  \}_{ k \in \Omega_c } $ is the set of the chemical rates associated with the sources and sinks. 
 We say that  $(\Omega, \mathcal R,  \mathcal R_s , \mathcal K, \mathcal K_s )$ is a chemical system. Moreover 
 \begin{itemize}
\item if $ \Omega_c \neq \emptyset $, then we say that $(\Omega, \mathcal R,  \mathcal R_s , \mathcal K, \mathcal K_s )$ is a chemical system with sources and sinks. 
\item If $ \Omega_c = \emptyset $, then we say that $(\Omega, \mathcal R,  \mathcal R_s , \mathcal K, \mathcal K_s )$ is a chemical system without sources and sinks. We denote it with $(\Omega, \mathcal R,  \mathcal K)$. 
\end{itemize}
title: Chemical system

The source exponential-moment assumption yields the asymptotic expansion mode(t)=m-mu_3/(2*t)+(mu_5-6*mu_2*mu_3)/(8*t^2)+O(t^-3). We say that $\partial \Omega$ is completely non-characteristic if it does not have any characteristic points.

Let f: {0, 1}^n -> {0, 1}, n >= 2, under the uniform measure, q_j(f) = P(f(X) != f(X with bit j flipped)) and I_flip(f) = sum_j q_j(f). Fix a coordinate i and let f_0, f_1 be the restrictions x_i = 0, 1 on the remaining (n - 1)-cube. Then q_j(f) = (q_j(f_0) + q_j(f_1))/2 for j != i, q_i(f) = E[(f_1 - f_0)^2], and so I_flip(f) = q_i(f) + (I_flip(f_0) + I_flip(f_1))/2. Also Var(f) = (Var f_0 + Var f_1)/2 + (a_1 - a_0)^2/4 with a_b = E f_b, and the Poincare defect D(f) = I_flip(f) - 4 Var(f) satisfies D(f) = (D(f_0) + D(f_1))/2 + Var(f_1 - f_0).
uniform measure on {0, 1}^n, n >= 2
f Boolean

For a finite graph G with inherited positive edge weights, C_m(G;v) is the sum of product weights over simple paths of exactly m edges starting at v, with a free terminal vertex; C_0(G;v)=1 for a retained v. In a uniform n-step origin-started SAW law, a realized k-edge prefix eta has a suffix law on G_eta with exact remaining length n-k, where G_eta deletes earlier prefix vertices and retains its tip. Obstacle avoidance therefore uses C_(n-k)(G_eta minus A;tip)/C_(n-k)(G_eta;tip), multiplied by the prefix-avoidance indicator. An all-length partition sum defines a different conditional law.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.03793, 'Typical martingale diverges on a co-$\sigma$-porous set'] We consider the space of $L^p$-bounded martingales on the Cantor space for $p\in[1,\infty]$. Equipping the Cantor space with two standard metrics, we show that under both, a typical martingale diverges at a typical point. By a ``typical martingale'', we mean an element of a co-$\sigma$-porous set when $p\in[1,\infty)$ and of a co-porous set when $p=\infty$. Specifically, we show that while a typical martingale diverges on a co-$\sigma$-porous set with respect to the first metric, no martingale diverges on a co-$\sigma$-porous set with respect to the second metric. Finally, we investigate the key factors determining whether the divergence set can be co-$\sigma$-porous.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.03793: Typical martingale diverges on a co-$\sigma$-porous set

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine whether the moment condition controls the back-and-forth trap time and hence the regeneration-time tail. Result: The quantity 1/(1 - omega(0,e) omega(0,-e)) is the expected number of returns of the two-site back-and-forth excursion between 0 and e, so the moment condition bounds the expected holding time in two-site traps but not in larger traps (a trap of k sites in a line has holding time controlled by products of k such ratios, whose expectation is not bounded by the first-moment condition). Proposition 2.21 of the source shows the condition is necessary; sufficiency would need a bound on the expected time spent in traps of every size, i.e. on E[tau_1 | D = infinity]. A natural sufficient strengthening is a moment condition on the exit time from every finite box, which is implied by the two-site condition only under an additional assumption on the transition probabilities to move away. I therefore see the question as open in the sense that the two-site condition is strictly weaker than what the regeneration argument needs, and the Dirichlet case works because of the specific reversal identity of Dirichlet environments (Sabot's exit-time integrability). No new result. Obstruction: Two-site moment condition does not control larger traps; the Dirichlet argument uses a special reversal identity.

Let $E = \frac{1}{n} X^T X$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\mathbb{R}^p$ with population covariance $C$ (rows $C^{1/2} z_i$ with $z_i$ having i.i.d. entries of mean zero, variance one and finite twelfth moment), in the regime $p, n \to \infty$ with $q = p/n \to q_0 \in (0, \infty)$, and assume the spectral distribution of $C$ converges to a limit with bounded support. Let $\lambda_k, u_k$ be the sample eigenvalues and eigenvectors and let $g_E(z) = \frac{1}{p}\operatorname{tr}(z I - E)^{-1}$ be the Stieltjes transform of the sample spectrum, and $g(z) = \int (z - x)^{-1} F(dx)$ that of its almost-sure limit $F$, the limiting sample spectral distribution, with $g(\lambda - i0) := \lim_{\eta \downarrow 0} g(\lambda - i\eta)$ inside the bulk (the finite-sample $g_E(\lambda - i\eta)$ has no useful limit as $\eta \downarrow 0$: it diverges at each sample eigenvalue and is real between them). THEOREM (Ledoit and Peche, 2011, Theorem 4; in the form of Bun, Bouchaud and Potters 2017). The oracle eigenvalues $\xi_k^{\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$, as the weighted measure $\frac{1}{p}\sum_k \xi_k^{\mathrm{or}} \delta_{\lambda_k}$, converge almost surely to $\xi(\lambda) F(d\lambda)$ on $(0, \infty)$, where $$\xi(\lambda) = \frac{\lambda}{\big|\, 1 - q_0 + q_0\, \lambda\, g(\lambda - i0) \,\big|^2};$$ informally $\xi_k^{\mathrm{or}} \approx \xi(\lambda_k)$ for sample eigenvalues inside the bulk (the theorem is about the weighted measure, not a limit for each $k$). This limit depends on the population covariance $C$ only through the observable sample spectrum, so it is a consistent, computable estimator (the rotationally invariant estimator, RIE, or nonlinear shrinkage): replace each sample eigenvalue by $\xi(\lambda_k)$, keep the sample eigenvectors. In practice $g_E$ is evaluated at $\lambda_k - i\eta$ with a small $\eta$ of order $n^{-1/2}$ times the eigenvalue scale, and the result is floored at a small positive fraction of the bulk level. When $C = \sigma^2 I$ the formula returns $\sigma^2$ for every eigenvalue (the Marchenko-Pastur spread is entirely removed); for a spike above the bulk it returns approximately the debiased population spike. Applying the formula to a matrix whose largest eigenvalue is a signal one is trying to keep, and flooring relative to that top eigenvalue, destroys the small eigenvalues that the inverse depends on.

OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; status: proof (unaudited), w714-T272-C002 version 2; independent review and priority determination pending. Let d>=1 and f_theta(x)=m^-1 sum_j a_j sigma(m^-1 sum_i B_ji sigma(w_i dot x)), with |sigma|, |sigma prime|, |sigma double prime|<=1 and sigma in C2. Assume ||x||<=1, |y|<=1; independently initialize both networks with identical iid laws for w_i in [-1,1]^d, a_j in [-1,1], and B_ji in [-1,1], with the three arrays independent. Train every array on half squared loss by fresh conditionally unbiased SGD, with deterministic nonnegative base steps eta_k, multipliers m on a,w and m^2 on B, and sum eta_k<=T<infinity. The two runs may use independent minibatch sequences. There exist consistent permutations of both hidden layers, chosen from the initial boundary weights, for which the expected supremum positive excess of population half-squared loss along parameter interpolation over the endpoint loss chord is <=C(d,T)[m^(-1/(d+2))+sqrt(sum eta_k^2)]. Therefore eta_max<=m^(-2/(d+2)) gives expected barrier O_{d,T}(m^(-1/(d+2))). The method uses the established cut-norm/operator inequality for correlated middle edges, deterministic all-layer SGD stability in boundary-L1 plus middle-cut norm, and a normalized-Hilbert martingale comparison to population-gradient Euler dynamics. This does not cover ReLU, unbounded Gaussian initialization, fixed nonzero SGD step in the width limit, or training horizon tending to infinity. Finite exact sublemma checks pass; the full proof has no independent PASS and the Lean sublemma attempt returned runtime unverified.

Let V be an affine algebraic set and p in V. If H_1, ..., H_d are general hyperplanes through p such that p is an isolated point of V intersect H_1 intersect ... intersect H_d, then dim_p(V) <= d. Furthermore, if d is minimal, then dim_p(V) = d.

[Defn def:nondegenerate-homogeneous-tangent of arXiv:2608.30847, 'An Almgren-type formula for planar $p$-harmonic functions'] Let $u$ be $p$-harmonic in $B_R(x_0)\subset \mathbb R^n$, and set
$ v=u-u(x_0).$
Assume $Du(x_0)=0$. We say that $u$ has a nondegenerate homogeneous tangent
of degree $\lambda>1$ at $x_0$, with rate $\delta>0$, if there exists a nonzero
homogeneous $p$-harmonic function $P$ of degree $\lambda$, namely
$$
 P(r\theta)=r^\lambda P(\theta),
 \qquad r>0,\quad \theta\in S^{n-1},
$$
such that $\inf_{\theta\in S^{n-1}} |DP(\theta)|>0,$
and, for some constant $C_0>0$,
$$
\sum_{j=0}^2 r^j   \left|D^j v(x_0+r\theta)-D^jP(r\theta)\right| \le  C_0 r^{\lambda+\delta}
$$
for every $\theta\in S^{n-1}$ and every sufficiently small $r>0$.
Here $D^0 f=f$.

Method: Integrator-authored exact restricted calculation or proof-obstruction analysis after primary-source comparison Result: To test a naive bounded-perturbation argument, add one independent Gaussian W to every DGFF site. The covariance changes by the bounded constant Var(W), yet the centered maximum changes exactly by W. Intermediate threshold counts are also shifted in height, giving a random multiplicative change of their limiting spatial intensity rather than an identical limit. This does not refute the stated conjecture: the added constant changes the macroscopic covariance and so violates its prescribed continuum Green limit. It does show why comparison inequalities using only a uniform covariance error cannot identify the same extremal law. Microscopic perturbations can likewise change cluster decorations even when macroscopic behavior agrees. Check: For every sample, max_x(h_x+W)=max_x h_x+W. Conditional on W, an exceedance at threshold a is exactly an original exceedance at a-W. These exact identities require no asymptotic covariance comparison. Obstruction: No general comparison theorem proving the full source process convergence; the restricted rapidly decaying Gaussian perturbation case is already discussed in the source.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Check the branching-process-with-migration proof for its dependence on bounded stacks. Result: Under (BD) the branching process with migration has bounded migration per generation, and the criterion delta > 2 comes from the tail of the total progeny of a critical branching process with migration delta: P(total progeny > n) ≍ n^{-delta/2}... the speed is positive iff the expected total progeny (expected excursion time) is finite iff delta > 2. With unbounded stacks under (POS1) the migration is unbounded but positive; the total progeny tail is then governed by the same exponent if the migration has finite mean, and the natural conjecture is that the criterion persists as long as the expected total drift delta = E sum_i (2 omega(0,i) - 1) is finite, with additional conditions on the tail of the stack size (as in the source's assumption (6.2) with the exponential-moment-type condition on the number of cookies far from 1/2). A partial result: under (POS1), (IID), (UEL) and E[sup{i : omega(0,i) not 1/2}] < infinity (the condition in (6.2)), the branching process with migration has migration with finite mean, and the Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer-type tail analysis for branching processes with migration of finite mean gives the same exponent delta/2 for the total progeny, hence the same criterion delta > 2 for positive speed; the source proves the recurrence/transience part under (6.2) for the functional CLT in the recurrent regime, so the ballisticity part appears to follow the same route. I did not verify the tail analysis under unbounded migration with finite mean; recorded as the expected answer with the condition from (6.2). Key identity: Total progeny tail exponent delta/2 depends on the mean migration, not on its boundedness, if the migration has finite mean. Obstruction: Tail analysis of branching with unbounded finite-mean migration not verified.

[Lemma lem:md-ledger of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Put $X_0=D_m-(\gamma+1)I$.  For every $s\ge0$,
\[
 Q_s(D_m)=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak T_s}
 (-\gamma)^{a(\pi)}X_0^{r(\pi)},
 \qquad 2a(\pi)+r(\pi)=s,
\tag{3.2.10i}
\]
where $\mathfrak T_s$ is the set of monomer--dimer tilings of an interval;
in particular $|\mathfrak T_s|\le2^s$.  In a term of the squared
degree-$k$ differentiated shell, let $a$ be the total number of dimers
and let $r$ count all nonconstant slots, including in each replica the
differentiated deposit and the endpoint root.  Then
\[
 a+\frac r2=k+1.
\tag{3.2.10j}
\]

Fix one ribbon contraction and let $p$ be its number of centered
pairing-connected packet components, including the single paired root
component.  Every such component contains at least two nonconstant slots,
so
\[
p\le r/2,\qquad a+p\le k+1.
\tag{3.2.10k}
\]
All constants in these statements are independent of $c\ge1$.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Reduce to tightness plus a characterisation of subsequential limits through the Gibbs-Markov property, uniformly in lambda; try to replace the moment method of Theorem 2.7 by a single martingale approximation of the exponential of a Gaussian field. Result: Partial reduction only. For any finite set of lambdas the vector of point measures is tight (each coordinate is), and any subsequential limit satisfies the Gibbs-Markov property coordinatewise; the coupling question is therefore whether the joint limit is the image of one CGFF under the map lambda -> e^{alpha lambda h} dx with the Seneta-Heyde normalisation. A direct route is to prove the joint limit of the truncated exponentials of the circle-average field at scale epsilon N, whose lambda-dependence is explicit, and then let epsilon -> 0; the missing input is an estimate for the joint contribution of the truncated region uniform in lambda near 1, where the second moment of the measure diverges. Key identity: Z^D_lambda(dx) = lim_eps eps^{lambda^2 alpha^2 g/2} e^{alpha lambda h_eps(x)} dx would identify all Z^D_lambda through one field h. Obstruction: Second moments of Z^D_lambda blow up as lambda -> 1/sqrt2 in the moment method; the uniform-in-lambda control needed for a joint limit up to lambda -> 1 is not available from moment calculations.

body: [Defn of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] A \emph{weighted planar network} $(\Gamma, \omega)$  is a finite acyclic directed planar graph $\Gamma$, with $n$ sources on the left boundary and $n$ sinks on the right boundary, and with a weight function $\omega:\mathcal{E} \to \mathbb{C}$ defined on the set of directed edges. The \emph{weight matrix} $\mathcal{W}(\Gamma, \omega)$ of such a network is the $n\times n$ matrix whose $(i,j)$--entry is the sum of the weights of all directed paths from source $i$ to sink $j$, where the weight of a path is the product of the weights of its edges.

Let sigma be a translation-invariant mean-zero +/-1 field on Z^3 or a finite abelian group, with 0<=G(x)=E[sigma_0 sigma_x]<=1 and finite chi=sum_x G(x). Put B=sum_x G(x)^2. For the ordered triples D such that (0,x2,x3,x4) has at least two equal sites, sum_D[-U4(0,x2,x3,x4)]=12chi^2-16chi-6B+12, between 0 and 12chi^2. Here U4 is the mean-zero fourth cumulant. For any xi>0 the contact contribution normalized by chi^2 xi^3 is at most 12/xi^3, and therefore vanishes if xi diverges. Since B<=chi, the unnormalized contact mass divided by chi^2 tends to 12 when chi diverges. The coefficient is sharp over the stated class, as N perfectly correlated spins on a cyclic group give 12N^2-22N+12. Exact coincident tuples only are controlled; the distinct-site mass required for C0052 is not lower-bounded.

At a fixed common Bernoulli bond parameter p define a_n(R)=P_p(o connects in G_n to ambient graph distance at least R). [Defi 42 of arXiv:2608.28148, 'Flows and homotopies of Banach Lie algebroids'] Consider a manifold $M$ and a subset $\mathcal{S} \subseteq C^0(M,\R)$ of continuous functions. We say that $M$ 
\begin{enumerate}
\item admits $\mathcal{S}$-bump functions or is ($\mathcal{S}$ -regular) if for every $x\in M$ and every open $x-$neighborhood $U \subseteq M$ there exists $\chi \in \mathcal{S}$ such that $\chi (M) \subseteq [0,1], U = \chi^{-1} (]0, 1])$ and $\chi (x) = 1$.
\item is $\mathcal{S}$-paracompact if every open cover $(U_i)_{i \in I}$ of $M$ admits a subordinate partition
of unity $(\chi_i)_{i\in I}$ of functions $\chi_i \in \mathcal{S}, i \in I$.
\end{enumerate}
If $\mathcal{S} = C^k(M, \R)$ for some $k\in \N_0 \cup \{\infty\}$, we shorten the notation and say that $M$ admits $C^k$-bump functions or is $C^k$
-paracompact. Note that $C^0$-paracompactness is equivalent to the usual topological notion of paracompactness.
title: Definition 42 of arXiv:2608.28148

PROOF OF A SPECIAL CASE; independent audit pending. Fix a,b in [0,1] and let K(z)=[[a,z],[conjugate(z),b]]. On the disk |z|^2<=min(ab,(1-a)(1-b)), the Shannon entropy of the determinantal subset measure with kernel K(z) is concave as a function of the complex number z. Its four atom probabilities are ab-|z|^2, (1-a)(1-b)-|z|^2, a(1-b)+|z|^2, and (1-a)b+|z|^2. This covers all two-site Hermitian positive contractions with common diagonals, including boundary kernels, but does not settle jointly varying diagonals or larger kernels.
Exactly two sites
Hermitian positive contractions
The two diagonal entries are held fixed

A predictor $\hat{p}(X) \in [0, 1]$ is perfectly calibrated for binary outcome $Y \in \{0, 1\}$ if $P(Y = 1 \mid \hat{p}(X) = p) = p$ for all $p \in [0, 1]$. The Expected Calibration Error (ECE) partitions predictions into $M$ bins $B_m$ and computes the weighted average difference $\text{ECE} = \sum_{m=1}^M \frac{|B_m|}{N} |\operatorname{acc}(B_m) - \operatorname{conf}(B_m)|$.
Y \in {0, 1} is a binary label
B_m partitions the probability interval [0, 1]
title: Probability Calibration and Expected Calibration Error (ECE)

body: Let u and beta be continuous, nonnegative real-valued functions on [a,b], and let C >= 0 be a constant such that u(t) <= C + integral from a to t of beta(s) u(s) ds for every t in [a,b]. Then u(t) <= C exp(integral from a to t of beta(s) ds) for every t in [a,b]. When C = 0, this forces u to be identically 0 on [a,b]. [standard, e.g. Evans, Partial Differential Equations]

Let X be a centered real random variable (E[X] = 0). The following properties are equivalent up to universal multiplicative constants: (1) Tail bound: P(|X| >= t) <= 2 * exp(-c1 * t^2) for all t >= 0; (2) Moment bound: (E[|X|^p])^{1/p} <= c2 * sqrt(p) for all p >= 1; (3) MGF bound: E[exp(lambda * X)] <= exp(c3 * lambda^2) for all lambda in R; (4) Orlicz norm: ||X||_{psi_2} <= c4.

[Lemma lem:KP_vec of arXiv:2604.28068, 'Mean-square Stability and Bifurcations for Dissipative SDEs'] Let $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ be real matrices.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item If the matrices $A+B$ and $C+D$ exist, then 
    $$(A+B)\otimes (C+D)=A\otimes C+A\otimes D+B\otimes C+B\otimes D.$$ 
    \item  If $A$, $B$, $C$ are three matrices, such that the matrix product $ABC$ exists, then $$\mathrm{vec}(ABC)=(C^T\otimes A)\mathrm{vec}(B).$$
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Definition 172 (Gluing of trapezoids) of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Take trapezoids $\mathcal{T}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{T}_m$ with long bases $\llbracket D_i,U_i\rrbracket$, $i\in[m]$, equipped with type maps \eqref{eq:typemap} and containing a total of $2H$ (maximal) blue segments. We say that the trapezoids are glued into a domain $\mathcal D$, if for each trapezoid $\mathcal T_i$ and each of its blue segment $\llbracket A_h,B_h\rrbracket\subset \llbracket D_i,U_i\rrbracket$ there exists exactly one other trapezoid $\mathcal T_{i'}$, $i'\neq i$ and a blue segment in it $\llbracket A_{h'},B_{h'}\rrbracket\subset \llbracket D_{i'},U_{i'}\rrbracket$, such that $\llbracket A_{h'},B_{h'}\rrbracket$ coincides with $\llbracket A_{h},B_{h}\rrbracket$. In this situation, the trapezoids $\mathcal T_i$ and $\mathcal{T}_{i'}$ are \emph{adjacent}, and we identify indices $h$ and $h'$. We require the gluing to be connected: any two trapezoids can be linked by a chain of adjacent ones.

body: When one ensemble of $M$ members predicts $D$ output coordinates (spectral bands, pixels, reduced coefficients) and a separate affine stack is fitted per output, the $D$ least-squares weight vectors form a matrix $\hat W \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times (M+1)}$ with $\hat W = W + Z$: row $d$ of the noise $Z$ has covariance $\sigma_d^2 (X_d^T X_d)^{-1}$, $X_d$ the calibration design of output $d$ and $\sigma_d^2$ its residual variance, while the true $W$ has low effective rank whenever the optimal weighting varies smoothly across outputs (neighbouring bands weight the same members similarly). The relevant random-matrix ratio is then $\beta = (M+1)/D$ - not $M/n_{\mathrm{cal}}$ - and the problem is low-rank matrix denoising: after scaling row $d$ by $1/\sigma_d$ (and, when the designs $X_d$ are nearly common across outputs, right-whitening by $\bar G^{1/2}\sqrt{n}$ with $\bar G$ the average of $X_d^T X_d / n$), the Gavish-Donoho optimal singular-value shrinkage selects the rank as the number of singular values above the Marchenko-Pastur edge $1 + \sqrt\beta$ and debiases each retained singular value, with no cross-validation. Shrinking every row toward one global weight vector by a cross-validated scalar - the best heuristic found on the EMIT/OCO-2 pools, beating per-output least squares on 69 of 70 cells by 3.1 percent - is the rank-one special case of this estimator with the direction fixed and the amount tuned by hand. For EMIT ($M = 23$, $D = 285$) $\beta = 0.084$; for OCO-2 ($M = 18$, $D = 40$) $\beta = 0.475$, a wide bulk in which only strong structure clears the edge.

[campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed, prior art searched but not cleared] Let f_R be the plus/minus-one indicator of the left-right crossing of the square [0,R]^2, for critical bond percolation on Z^2 or critical site percolation on the triangular lattice. Let S(f_R) be its spectral sample and P(f_R) its pivotal set, and I(f_R) = E|P(f_R)| the total influence. CLAIM: there is a constant C depending only on the lattice such that for every R >= 2, H(S(f_R)) <= C I(f_R) and H(P(f_R)) <= C I(f_R); equivalently Ent(f_R) = O(R^2 alpha_4(R)). This is Kalai, Three puzzles on mathematics, computation and games, ICM 2018, arXiv:1801.02602, Section 3.3.2, Conjecture 8, and the first open problem of Garban, Pete and Schramm, The Fourier spectrum of critical percolation, Acta Mathematica 205 (2010), Section 11. The general entropy-influence conjecture for arbitrary Boolean functions is NOT claimed; this is the percolation crossing case only. The general principle the argument isolates: the inequality holds for every Boolean function on a planar array whose spectral sample satisfies sum_{k>=1} E|S_{2^k}| = O(E|S|), i.e. whose spectral sample is a fractal of dimension strictly below two.

The decoder always knows how many bits to read, so the code is uniquely decodable and Shannon source coding gives H(A) <= 1 + 4 sum_{k=1..K} E|A_{2^k}| + C_0 E|A_1|. Since E|A| = I(f_R) for both S and P, the finest term is a multiple of the influence and everything rests on the coarser scales. For d >= 2r and D >= 8d the four-arm event from B forces four alternating arms from B to radius d/2 and three alternating half-plane arms from 2d to D/2, on disjoint bits, so alpha_box(B,Q_R) <= alpha_4(r,d/2) alpha_3^+(2d,D/2) <= C alpha_4(r,d) (d/D)^2. At most C (d/r)(D/r) squares have d and D in given dyadic ranges, so E|A_r| <= C (R/r)^2 alpha_4(r,R) + C. Inserting this and using (R/r)^2 alpha_4(r,R) <= C R^2 alpha_4(1,R) r^{-eps} makes the scale sum geometric, and I(f_R) >= c R^2 alpha_4(1,R) absorbs the additive logarithm. Let d>=2 and let the iid undirected nearest-neighbor weights on Z^d have a nondegenerate law supported in [r,R] with 0<r<=R<infinity. Put mu=E t_e. Choose separated positive-mass support intervals with low upper bound a, high lower bound b>a, and k>=1 with k*b>(k+2)*a. Let S be the sum of k axial weights, H the sum of the k+2 edges of its disjoint height-one detour, and delta=E[(S-H)_+]>0. Then E T(0,n*e1)<=n*mu-floor(n/(k+1))*delta and almost surely limsup_n T(0,n*e1)/n<=mu-delta/(k+1). The coordinate-monotone axial sum divided by n tends to mu, so its raw same-environment difference from unrestricted FPP has asymptotic liminf at least delta/(k+1)>0. This does not compare centered fluctuations or exponents.

[Proposition 4 (Stability near a compact family of flat metrics) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(M\) be a fixed torus and let \(\mathcal F\) be a compact set of
flat metrics on \(M\) (not modulo diffeomorphisms).  For a fixed
\(\rho\in(0,1)\), there is a uniform
\(h^{2+\rho}\)-neighborhood of \(\mathcal F\), measured using one fixed smooth
reference metric on \(M\), such that the Ricci flow starting from any
metric in this neighborhood exists for all future time and, without applying a
time-dependent pullback, converges exponentially as a tensor field on \(M\) to
a flat metric.  Here \(h^{2+\rho}\) is the little H\"older space, namely the
closure of smooth metrics in the \(C^{2,\rho}\)-norm.  The exponential rate and
the constants may be chosen uniformly on \(\mathcal F\), and parabolic
bootstrapping gives convergence in every fixed \(C^m\)-norm.

Let A generate a C_0-semigroup (T(t)) on a Banach space X with ‖T(t)‖ ≤ M e^{ωt}, and let B ∈ B(X) be bounded and everywhere defined. Then A + B with domain D(A + B) = D(A) generates a C_0-semigroup (S(t)) satisfying ‖S(t)‖ ≤ M e^{(ω + M‖B‖)t}. The perturbed semigroup solves the variation-of-constants equation S(t)x = T(t)x + ∫_0^t T(t − s) B S(s)x ds for all x ∈ X, and is given by the Dyson-Phillips series S(t) = Σ_{n ≥ 0} S_n(t) with S_0(t) = T(t) and S_{n+1}(t)x = ∫_0^t T(t − s)B S_n(s)x ds, converging in operator norm uniformly on compact time intervals. In particular boundedness of the perturbation is enough; no relative-boundedness smallness is needed, and D(A) is unchanged.
X is a Banach space
A generates a C_0-semigroup
B is bounded and defined on all of X

Let k>=0 be an integer. A sample compression scheme maps a finite labeled sample S to a subset kappa(S) of at most k observations and reconstructs a classifier h_S. Assume stability: whenever kappa(S) is contained in S_prime and S_prime is contained in S, reconstruction on S_prime equals h_S. For any input-label distribution P, n>2k IID observations S, and 0<delta<1, with probability at least 1-delta the following implication holds: if h_S has zero empirical classification error on S, then its population error is at most 2[k ln4+ln(1/delta)]/(n-2k). The bound is distribution-free and contains no extra log n factor.

Let N=N(n) with N/n->c in (0,infinity). For all n,i,j let X_ij^(n) be real independent identically distributed random variables with mean zero, variance one, and E|X_ij^(n)|^(4+epsilon)<infinity for some epsilon>0. Let sigma_ij(n) be deterministic real numbers uniformly bounded in absolute value. Let A_n be deterministic real N-by-n matrices whose row Euclidean norms and column Euclidean norms are uniformly bounded over all n and all rows and columns. Put (Y_n)_ij=sigma_ij(n) X_ij^(n)/sqrt(n) and Sigma_n=Y_n+A_n. For the relevant N,n, write A=A_n and sigma_ij=sigma_ij(n), D_j=diag(sigma_1j^2,...,sigma_Nj^2), and Dtilde_i=diag(sigma_i1^2,...,sigma_in^2). Let S_plus consist of the functions z->integral_[0,infinity) (lambda-z)^(-1) nu(dlambda) for probability measures nu on [0,infinity), analytically continued to C minus [0,infinity). Define the unique S_plus-valued solution psi_i,psitilde_j by psi_i(z)=-1/[z(1+tr(Dtilde_i Ttilde(z))/n)] and psitilde_j(z)=-1/[z(1+tr(D_j T(z))/n)], where Psi=diag(psi_i), Psitilde=diag(psitilde_j), T(z)=[Psi(z)^(-1)-z A Psitilde(z) A^T]^(-1), and Ttilde(z)=[Psitilde(z)^(-1)-z A^T Psi(z) A]^(-1). Both trace terms in these canonical equations use division by n. Set Q_n(z)=(Sigma_n Sigma_n^T-z I_N)^(-1) and Qtilde_n(z)=(Sigma_n^T Sigma_n-z I_n)^(-1). Almost surely, for every z in C minus [0,infinity), tr(Q_n(z)-T_n(z))/N->0 and tr(Qtilde_n(z)-Ttilde_n(z))/n->0 as n->infinity. The conclusion is for normalized unweighted resolvent traces of this independent-entry variance-profile model. The canonical measures can vary with n; convergence of the variance profiles to a limiting distribution is not an assumption.

[Theorem eq:conditional-remainder-cost of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:one-spike}
Assume that \(J_{1\cdots1}\) has law \(\mu\).  Fix \(M<\infty\),
\(a>2M\), and \(\eta>0\).  Assume that the spike event below has
positive probability for all sufficiently large \(N\) and that
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N
 \log\mathbb P\left(
 \left.\left\lVertR_N\right\rVert_\infty\le M\,\right|\,
 \frac{J_{1\cdots1}}{\sqrt N}\in[a,a+\eta]\right)=0.
\end{equation}
No assumptions of independence, centering, identical distribution, or
existence of a density are needed beyond this conditional-rate
hypothesis.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^J([a-M,a+\eta+M])
 \ge-\overline I_\mu(a,\eta).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_N^J([a-M,a+\eta+M])
 \ge-\overline I_\mu(a,\eta).
\end{equation}

[Lemma 18 (Stable generator identity) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\mathcal S(\R)$ denote the Schwartz space and let $\mathcal S'(\R)$ denote the space of tempered distributions. Let $L^\alpha$ be the generator of the one-dimensional symmetric $\alpha$-stable process, with sign convention
\[
L^\alpha f(x)=\int_{\R\setminus\{0\}}\left(f(x+z)-f(x)-\1_{\{|z|\le1\}}zf'(x)\right)c_\alpha |z|^{-1-\alpha}\dd z.
\]
Then
\[
  L^\alpha u_{\delta,\eps}(x)=C_\alpha\psi_{\delta,\eps}(x)
\]
in the sense of distributions and pointwise for the mollified function, for some constant $C_\alpha>0$. Consequently, for a scale parameter $\gamma\in\R$,
\[
  L^\alpha_\gamma u_{\delta,\eps}(x)=C_\alpha |\gamma|^\alpha\psi_{\delta,\eps}(x),
\]
where
\[
L^\alpha_\gamma f(x):=\int_{\R\setminus\{0\}}\left(f(x+\gamma z)-f(x)-\1_{\{|z|\le1\}}\gamma z f'(x)\right)\nu(\md z).
\]

Fix alpha>0, rho>0 and lambda>0, all independent of the positive integer N. For each N let M_N=floor(exp(alpha N)), and let epsilon_(1,N),...,epsilon_(M_N,N) be independent centered Gaussian variables, each of variance rho^2/N. Define phi_N=(1/(lambda N)) log(sum_(mu=1)^(M_N) exp(lambda N epsilon_(mu,N))). On any common probability space for these arrays, phi_N converges almost surely to alpha/lambda+lambda rho^2/2 when lambda<=lambda_c=sqrt(2alpha)/rho, and to rho sqrt(2alpha) when lambda>=lambda_c. The two expressions agree at lambda_c. Independence is required within each N; no independence across different N is needed. Equivalently, for independent Gaussian patterns xi_mu~N(0,I_N) and a state x_N of norm rho sqrt(N), chosen independently of these patterns, one may take epsilon_(mu,N)=<x_N,xi_mu>/N. The result applies to that fixed state or independently chosen state sequence. It does not assert a uniform limit over pattern-dependent states or along an adaptive retrieval trajectory. This is the classical Gaussian random energy model condensation formula, used as a noise free-energy computation, not a retrieval or basin theorem. Source: Lucibello--Mezard, arXiv:2304.14964v4, equations (4)--(5), PDF p2; variational derivation Appendix A, PDF pp7--9. The exponentially large count may equally be exp(alpha N)-1 with the usual integer rounding, since its logarithmic rate is unchanged.
alpha,rho,lambda are fixed strictly positive real numbers
M_N=floor(exp(alpha N)); the energies within each N are independent N(0,rho^2/N)
All arrays are on a common probability space; arbitrary dependence across different N is permitted
For the pattern interpretation, x_N has norm rho sqrt(N) and is independent of every competing Gaussian pattern

[Proposition 27 of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(u\in[0,1]\) and \(\theta>0\). Define
\[
C_\theta:=
\begin{cases}
1, & \theta=1,\\[1ex]
\dfrac{\theta |\log \theta|}{|\theta-1|}, & \theta\neq 1.
\end{cases}
\]

Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with \(|V|=n\), and assume that for some \(\eta,\varepsilon>0\),
\[
e_G(S)\le (1+\varepsilon)|S|
\qquad\text{for every }S\subset V\text{ with }|S|\le \eta n.
\]
Assume moreover that
\[
\frac{|E|}{n}\in [m_-,m_+]
\]
for some \(m_-,m_+>0\).
Then for every \(a\ge 0\) and every \(s>0\),
\[
\frac1s\int_a^{a+s}\Pbb^G_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\,\dd t
\ge
\frac{
m_- - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)-C_\theta/s
}{
(1+\theta)m_+ - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)
},
\]
