Two distributions on a Euclidean space are (tau,delta)-close if they admit a coupling (X,X_hat) such that Pr(||X-X_hat||_2>tau)<delta. For a joint distribution of (X,Y), an algorithm taking y and outputting law p_hat_(.|y) is a (tau,delta)-posterior sampler if, with probability at least 1-delta over Y, its output law and the true conditional law p(.|Y) are (tau,delta)-close in this coupling sense. There are two failure probabilities: the exceptional-measurement probability delta, and the conditional coupling-failure probability delta on good measurements. The definition is not a TV-error bound or an every-fixed-observation guarantee. In the paper's linear model Y=A X+eta, ||A||_op<=1 and eta is independent N(0,beta^2 I_m); beta is the noise standard deviation.

body:
The alternative 'injective implies surjective' for operators of the form lambda I - K is carried entirely by two hypotheses: K is compact, and lambda is nonzero. (1) Compactness is load-bearing. On l^2 the unilateral shift S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) is bounded and injective but not surjective, and S = I - K with K = I - S bounded but not compact; its index is -1, not 0. So for a general bounded perturbation of the identity the two alternatives can both fail to be the right dichotomy: the equation x - K x = y can be uniquely solvable for some y and unsolvable for others, with no finite-dimensional solvability condition of equal dimensions on the two sides. What actually powers the alternative is that the index is 0, which compactness guarantees; a Fredholm operator of nonzero index (like S) is a counterexample to the dichotomy but not to Fredholm theory. (2) lambda nonzero is load-bearing. Take K = diag(1, 1/2, 1/3, ...) on l^2, which is compact and injective, with dense but proper range (the sequence (1/n) is not in ran K, since it would need preimage (1, 1, 1, ...)). So for lambda = 0, 'injective' does not give 'surjective', the range is not closed, and 0 is in the spectrum of every compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space. (3) In the Hilbert-space version the solvability condition uses the conjugate: lambda x - K x = y is solvable exactly when y is orthogonal to ker(conjugate of lambda times I - K*), not to ker(lambda I - K*); forgetting the conjugation is a common slip for complex lambda. (4) The dimension identity dim ker(lambda - K) = dim ker(lambda - K') is an identity of the two kernels, not a claim that the kernels correspond naturally, and it fails for non-compact perturbations (for S, ker S = 0 while ker S' is one-dimensional).
the perturbation K is compact
lambda is a nonzero scalar
the ambient space is a Banach space (Hilbert space for the adjoint form with conjugated lambda)
title: Pitfall: The Fredholm Alternative Needs a Compact Perturbation and a Nonzero lambda

[Cor 5 of arXiv:2609.01101, '2609.01101'] Let $K_1,\ldots,K_r$ be fixed number fields, and let $L$ be the compositum
of their Galois closures over $\Q$.  Let
$$
G=\Gal(L/\Q),\qquad
H_j=\Gal(L/K_j),\qquad
\rho_{K_j}=|H_j\backslash G/H_j|.
$$
Assume GRH for $\zeta_L$, and let
$V_j\asymp\sqrt{\log\log T}$.  Then
\begin{align*}
\frac1T\operatorname{meas}\Bigg\{
t\in[T,2T]:
\log\left|\zeta_{K_j}\left(\frac12+it\right)\right|
\ge
V_j\sqrt{\frac{\rho_{K_j}}2\log\log T},
\ 1\le j\le r
\Bigg\}
\\
\asymp_{K_1,\ldots,K_r}
\exp\left(
-(1+o(1))
\frac{V_1^2+\cdots+V_r^2}{2}
\right).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
DEFINITIONS. For a class C of subsets of X and points x_1, ..., x_n, the number of distinct traces |{ A intersect {x_1, ..., x_n} : A in C }| is at most 2^n; the growth (shatter) function is s(C, n) = max over all n-point sets of this number; the VC dimension d = VC(C) is the largest n with s(C, n) = 2^n (infinite if s(C, n) = 2^n for all n). Sauer-Shelah: if d < infinity then s(C, n) <= sum_{i <= d} binom(n, i) <= (e n / d)^d for n >= d. THEOREM (Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1971). Let X_1, ..., X_n be i.i.d. from P and P_n the empirical measure. For every eps > 0 and n >= 2 / eps^2, P( sup_{A in C} |P_n(A) - P(A)| > eps ) <= 4 s(C, 2n) exp( -n eps^2 / 8 ); a form valid for all n is P( sup_{A in C} |P_n(A) - P(A)| > eps ) <= 8 s(C, n) exp( -n eps^2 / 32 ). COROLLARIES. If VC(C) = d < infinity, then sup_A |P_n(A) - P(A)| -> 0 almost surely for EVERY P (C is a uniform Glivenko-Cantelli class), with E sup_A |P_n(A) - P(A)| <= C_0 sqrt(d / n) for an absolute constant C_0 (Talagrand's sharpening of the log-free bound); the sample size n = O( (d log(1/eps) + log(1/delta)) / eps^2 ) makes the sup at most eps with probability 1 - delta; and the condition is also necessary: if VC(C) = infinity there is a distribution P for which the sup does not converge to 0 in probability (Vapnik-Chervonenkis; Assouad; Dudley). In learning: for a class of classifiers of VC dimension d, every classifier's true error is within eps of its training error simultaneously once n is of order d / eps^2 (up to logarithms), so empirical risk minimisation is consistent exactly for finite VC dimension (the fundamental theorem of statistical learning, PAC learnability iff finite VC dimension).
C a class of measurable sets (or of {0,1}-valued functions); the suprema are assumed measurable (a countable class, or the standard measurability conditions)
i.i.d. sampling from an arbitrary P on X
the constants 4, 8 and 8, 32 are the classical ones; several textbooks state slightly different constants from the same proof

For integer L>=2 on T_L=(R/LZ)^3, let X={0,...,L-1}^3 and Y=X+(1/2,0,0). For any translation-invariant configuration energy E and any 0<delta<1/2, E(Y)-E(X)=0 although all L^3 points of Y have distance greater than delta from the fixed reference X. Thus E(Y)-E(X)>=c times that fixed-reference bad-point count cannot hold for every configuration with any c>0. This says nothing about a phase-fitted or boundary-pinned estimate.

body: [Definition 253 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] A \emph{connectoid} is a symmetric $H \times H$ positive semi-definite matrix $\boldsymbol{\Theta}$ with entries in $\{0,\frac{1}{2},1\}$ and having the following connectedness property: for any $h,h' \in [H]$ there exists a finite sequence $h_0,\ldots,h_s$ with $h_0 = h$, $h_d = h'$ and for any $c \in [d]$ we have $\theta_{h_{c - 1},h_c} \neq 0$. A connectoid is \emph{realizable} if it comes from a graph $\mathsf{G}$ as in \eqref{ThetaGeq}; we can also ask for bipartite or non-bipartite realizability.

It is used in the proof of results in many areas of analysis and geometry, including some of the fundamental theorems of functional analysis.

Let $A$ be measurable and uniformly parabolic with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$ and let $u\ge0$ be a local weak solution of $\partial_tu=\mathrm{div}(A\nabla u)$ in $B_{2r}(x_0)\times(t_0-4r^2,t_0)$. Set $Q^-=B_r(x_0)\times(t_0-3r^2,t_0-2r^2)$ and $Q^+=B_r(x_0)\times(t_0-r^2,t_0)$. Then $\sup_{Q^-}u\ \le\ C\,\inf_{Q^+}u$ with $C=C(n,\lambda,\Lambda)$. The time lag is essential and so is the direction: the past cylinder's supremum is controlled by the future cylinder's infimum, never the reverse, and no inequality of this form holds on a single time slice. Nonnegativity on the whole cylinder $B_{2r}\times(t_0-4r^2,t_0)$ is required. Consequences: interior Holder continuity of solutions, the near-diagonal lower bound for the fundamental solution, and (through chaining) Aronson's Gaussian lower bound; the inequality is equivalent to the conjunction of the volume doubling property and a Poincare inequality in the Grigor'yan-Saloff-Coste characterization on manifolds and graphs.
A measurable, uniformly parabolic with constants lambda, Lambda; divergence form
u >= 0 and a local weak solution on the whole cylinder B_{2r} x (t_0 - 4r^2, t_0)
the two cylinders are separated in time, with Q^- earlier than Q^+

[Corollary cor:growth-bound-partition-functions of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] For any $A', B'$ in $Q$, we have
		\begin{equation*}
			Z^n_{Q, \mathbb Z^2; F, \mu}(A', B') = \sum_{\gamma \in \ensuremath{\mathcal P}_Q(A', B')} q^n_{\mathbb Z^2; F, \mu}(\gamma) \leq \exp({\ensuremath{\mathscr G}}^n_\mu(\ell_{A', B'}, \theta_{A', B'}) + O((\log L)^{2a}))\,.
		\end{equation*}
		Let $W$ be any region containing the infinite vertical strip between the lines $x = A'_1 + (\log L)^2$ and $x = B'_1 - (\log L)^2$. The same bound holds if we replace the weight $q^n_{\mathbb Z^2; F, \mu}(\gamma)$ with $q^n_{W; F, \mu}(\gamma)$, or with

		uniformly over all $\gamma_{\mathsf{left}} \in \ensuremath{\mathcal P}_Q(A, A')$, with $\Delta\mathfrak{I}_W(\gamma, \gamma_\mathsf{left})$ defined as in (eq:correction-term of the paper).

body: [Lemma compatible sequence of arXiv:2605.03151, 'Giants through Higher-Order paths in Random Simplicial Complexes'] Let $\left( (X_r, \sigma_r) \right)_{r \geq 0}$ be a sequence of $(k+1)$-connected $k$-rooted simplicial complexes locally finite above dimension $k$. Assume that the sequence $\left( (X_r, \sigma_r) \right)_{r \geq 0}$ is compatible in the sense that $B_{X_s}(\sigma_s; r) \cong (X_r, \sigma_r)$ for all $s \geq r$. Then there exists a $(k+1)$-connected $k$-rooted simplicial complex $(X, \sigma)$ that is locally finite above dimension $k$ and $(X_r, \sigma_r) \cong B_X(\sigma; r)$ for every $r \geq 0$. Moreover, $(X, \sigma)$ is unique up to isomorphisms.

    \begin{enumerate}[label = (\alph*)]
        \item If $\mu >p$, then $\mathfrak{J} \geq e^{cn}$ w.h.p.\ for some $c = c(\mu,p)>0$.

        \item If $\mu <p$, then $\mathfrak{J} \leq C n$ w.h.p.\ for some
        $C = C(\mu,p)< \infty$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let 1 <= p < infinity and let Omega be a bounded connected open subset of R^n with Lipschitz boundary. Poincare-Wirtinger form: there is a constant C depending only on p and Omega such that ||u - u_Omega||_{L^p(Omega)} <= C ||grad u||_{L^p(Omega)} for every u in W^{1,p}(Omega), where u_Omega denotes the average of u over Omega. Zero-boundary form: for u in W_0^{1,p}(Omega), with Omega merely bounded in one direction, ||u||_{L^p(Omega)} <= C ||grad u||_{L^p(Omega)}, so the gradient term alone is an equivalent norm on W_0^{1,p}(Omega). The inequality says a Sobolev function is controlled by its gradient once its mean (or boundary value) is pinned; it is the engine behind coercivity of variational problems, spectral gaps for the Laplacian, and compactness arguments.
title: Poincare inequality

[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2609.01166, 'Nonparametric inference for density-dependent McKean--Vlasov diffusions'] For every candidate $\xi$, and \(M>v_\star\),
\begin{eqnarray}
 \KL(\pi_0\Vert\pi_\xi)
 &=& (1-\tau_0(M))\KL(\pi_0^M\Vert\pi_\xi^M) + (1-\tau_0(M))\log\frac{1-\tau_0(M)}{1-\tau_\xi(M)} + R_\xi(M)\\
 &\leq& \KL(\pi_0^M\Vert\pi_\xi^M)+d_m(M)+\bar R_m(M),
\end{eqnarray}
where $R_\xi(M):=\int_{A_M^c}\pi_0(x) \log(\pi_0(x)/\pi_\xi(x))\,\dd x$. Moreover, 
\begin{equation}
\KL(\pi_0^M\Vert\pi_\xi^M)
\leq \frac{1}{c_M}\left(
\KL(\pi_0\Vert\pi_\xi)+d_m(M)+\bar R_m(M)
\right)
\end{equation}
with \(c_M:=\int_{A_M} e^{-K(V(x)-v_\star)}\,dx\left(\int_{\R^d} e^{-\kappa(V(x)-v_\star)}\,dx\right)^{-1}\in(0,1)\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 5 of arXiv:2609.01166

body: [Lemma 50 of arXiv:2608.27630, 'Oriented planar maps and \\ annular mating of trees'] Let $(\cA_\tau,\phi,\eta,-i,\eta') {/}{\sim_\gamma}$ be the embedding of an LQG surface from $\MA^{1,0,\dagger}(a,b)$. Let $x$ be a point on $C_0 = \partial\bbD$ sampled according to the probability measure proportional to $\cL^\phi_0$. Let $\wh\phi(\cdot) = \phi(x\cdot)$, and $\wh \eta$ be $(-i)x^{-1}$ times the west-going flow line started from $x$. Let $(-i)x^{-1}\eta'(\cdot+\tau_x)$ be defined via $\eta'$ and $x$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:ig-curve-resample}. Then the law of $(\cA_\tau,\wh\phi,\wh\eta,-i,(-i)x^{-1}\eta'(\cdot+\tau_x)) {/}{\sim_\gamma}$ is still $\MA^{1,0,\dagger}(a,b)$.

body:
Hanin-Nica, Finite Depth and Width Corrections to the Neural Tangent Kernel, arXiv1909.05989v1, Section2 and Theorem1 (PDFp4), is a source for initialization moments of the diagonal NTK of a fully connected ReLU network. Its setting uses a scalar output, zero-initialized but trainable biases, independent identically distributed raw weights with a Lebesgue density, symmetry about zero, variance one and finite fourth moment. Its Theorem1 gives an exact first-moment formula and a two-sided comparison for the second moment, including an exponential factor in a sum of inverse widths and a multiplicative error involving a sum of inverse squared widths. A comparison E[K^2] comparable to (E[K])^2 exp(5 beta) does not by itself establish Var(K)=O(1/n), even if beta tends to zero: the unspecified comparison constants prevent subtracting (E[K])^2 to obtain that rate. This comparison is also not a quantitative theorem for arbitrary smooth activations or transposed/reused-matrix Tensor Programs. Before using the exact formulas, resolve these printed-v1 conventions: Section2 prose says the output is linear but Eq2 applies ReLU for i=1,...,d; Eq3 prints reciprocal square-root normalization factors; beta is defined by a sum through d while n_d=1 is specified, whereas the equal-hidden-width consequence writes beta=d/n. These are unresolved source-interpretation questions, not a refutation of the authors intended theorem. This card records source scope and the limitation of a second-moment comparison; it does not assert a corrected NTK theorem or an NTK nonconcentration inference from moments alone.
Source-v1 scope note; intended endpoint and normalization conventions remain for independent source review.

body: Lemma (campaign status: proved): For twelve nonzero coefficients, an affine atom which is not the central atom of twelve equal magnitudes has size at most $792$. Unequal-magnitude case: reorient positively and condition on an unequal pair; its four signed sums are distinct, and the ten-coordinate subsets hitting one of the four required targets form a four-Sperner family, so their total is at most $\binom{10}{5}+2\binom{10}{4}+\binom{10}{3}=252+210+210+120=792$. Equal magnitudes with noncentral target: largest noncentral layer is $\binom{12}{5}=792$. A three-sign affine atom has size three only for three equal magnitudes at a one-minority target; otherwise at most two. Notes: VERIFIED: $252+420+120=792$. Consequence: more than $2592$ joint states forces both own-layer rows to be equimodular, since otherwise the joint count is at most $3\cdot792=2376$ or $2\cdot924=1848$. The four-Sperner step is the reusable device.

[Corollary Ball-like certificates of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] There exist
constants \(C > 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{0} > 0\), depending
only on the geometric and analytic data of \(M\), such that the
following holds. Let \(0 < \varepsilon < \varepsilon_{0}\) and
let
\(\mathcal{A = \{}B_{M}\left( y_{1},\varepsilon \right),\ldots,B_{M}\left( y_{m},\varepsilon \right)\}\)
be a degree-\(q\), radius-\(r\) homological
certificate for \(M\). Then, for every \(z \in M\) and
\(\delta \in (0,1)\),

\begin{multline*}
\mathbb{P}_{z}\left( H_{q}\left( \Gamma_{T}^{r} \right) \cong H_{q}(M) \right) \geq 1 - \delta\\
\text{whenever}\quad T \geq C\left( s_{0} + \kappa_{d}(\varepsilon)^{- 1}\left( \log m + \log\tfrac{1}{\delta} \right) \right).
\end{multline*}

If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a full certificate, the same
condition gives simultaneous recovery of all homology groups.

Let n ≥ 1 and F ∈ C^{⌊n/2⌋+1}([0,∞)×R^n). For each s ≥ 0 let v(·,·;s) be the solution of ∂_t²v − Δv = 0 on {t > s} with v(s,·;s) = 0 and ∂_t v(s,·;s) = F(s,·). Then u(t,x) := ∫_0^t v(t,x;s) ds is C² on [0,∞)×R^n and solves ∂_t²u − Δu = F, u(0,·) = 0, ∂_t u(0,·) = 0. In semigroup notation u(t) = ∫_0^t ( sin((t−s)|∇|)/|∇| ) F(s) ds. For n = 3 this is the retarded potential u(t,x) = (1/4π) ∫_{B(x,t)} F(t − |y−x|, y) |y−x|^{−1} dy. Adding the solution of the homogeneous problem with data (u0,u1) solves the general Cauchy problem.
n ≥ 1
F ∈ C^{⌊n/2⌋+1}([0,∞)×R^n) (enough regularity for the homogeneous solution operator to produce C² solutions)

[Definition 21 of arXiv:2606.02036, 'Self-intersection local times for Volterra Gaussian processes in stochastic flows with int'] A family of random maps $\{\phi_{s,t}:\mbR^d\times\Omega\to\mbR^d,\ 0\leqslant s\leqslant t<\infty\}$ is called a stochastic flow of homeomorphisms if for $\prob$-almost all $\omega\in\Omega:$  
 \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
 \item $\phi_{s,t}(\omega)=\phi_{r,t}(\omega)\circ\phi_{s,r,}(\omega)\ \text{holds for all}\ s\leqslant r\leqslant t.$ 
 \item $\phi_{s,s}(\omega)$ is the identity map for all $s\geqslant 0.$
 \item $\phi_{s,t}(\omega):\mbR^d\to\mbR^d$ is a homeomorphism for all $s\leqslant t.$ 
 \end{enumerate}
 If additionally, the mapping  $\phi_{s,t}(\omega):\mbR^d\to\mbR^d$ is $k$-times continuously differentiable for all $s\leqslant t,$ then $\phi$ is a stochastic flow of $C^k$-diffeomorphisms.
title: Definition 21 of arXiv:2606.02036

[Defi defn:higher-order-path of arXiv:2605.03151, 'Giants through Higher-Order paths in Random Simplicial Complexes'] For any pair of $(d-1)$-dimensional simplices $\sigma, \sigma' \in S_{d-1}(X)$, we say that they are \textit{adjacent} if there exists a $d$-dimensional simplex $\tau \in S_d(X)$ such that $\sigma \subseteq \tau$ and $\sigma' \subseteq \tau$.  
For any pair of $(d-1)$-dimensional simplices $\sigma_1, \sigma_2 \in S_{d-1}(X)$, we say that they are \textit{adjacent} if there exists a $d$-dimensional simplex $\tau \in S_d(X)$ such that $\sigma_1 \subseteq \tau$ and $\sigma_2 \subseteq \tau$. Also, we say that $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$ are connected through a \textit{$d$-dimensional path}, denoted by $\sigma \overset{\scriptscriptstyle d}{\longleftrightarrow} \sigma'$ if there exist distinct elements $(\sigma_i)_{i=0}^m\subseteq S_{d-1}(X)$ with $\sigma_0 = \sigma$ and $\sigma_m = \sigma'$ such that $\sigma_{i-1}$ and $\sigma_{i}$ are adjacent for all $i = 1, \dots, m$.

The smallest simplicial complex containing all $d$-dimensional simplices $\{\tau_i\}_{i=1}^m$ each of which defines the adjacency $\sigma_{i-1} \sim \sigma_i$ is called a $d$-dimensional path of length $m$ connecting $\sigma = \sigma_0$ and $\sigma' = \sigma_m$. The length of the shortest path between $\sigma,\sigma' \in S_{d-1}(X)$ is the minimum value of $m$ such that there exists a $d$-dimensional path between $\sigma,\sigma'$ of length $m$.
title: $d$-dimensional paths

body: In information theory, the entropy of a random variable quantifies the average level of uncertainty or information associated with the variable's potential states or possible outcomes. This measures the expected amount of information needed to describe the state of the variable, considering the distribution of probabilities across all potential states. Given a discrete random variable $X$, which may be any member $x$ within the set ${\mathcal {X}}$ and is distributed according to $p\colon {\mathcal {X}}\to [0,1]$, the entropy is $\mathrm {H} (X):=-\sum _{x\in {\mathcal {X}}}p(x)\log p(x),$ where $\Sigma$ denotes the sum over the variable's possible values. The choice of base for $\log$, the logarithm, varies for different applications. Base 2 gives the unit of bits (or "shannons"), while base e gives "natural units" nat, and base 10 gives units of "dits", "bans", or "hartleys". An equivalent definition of entropy is the expected value of the self-information of a variable.

body: [Definition def:marked_GUE of arXiv:2603.27906, 'Marked GUE-corners process in doubly periodic dimer models'] Let~$\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{GUE}}$ be the GUE-corners process defined on~$\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\times \mathbb{R}$. For a measurable function~$\theta:\Lambda\to [0,1]$, the \emph{marked GUE-corners process}~$\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{GUE}}^\theta$ is the point process on~$\Lambda_{\{0,1\}}=\Lambda \times \{0,1\}$ obtained by assigning to each point in a given realization from~$\mathbb{P}_{\operatorname{GUE}}$ an independent mark~$m\sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta(t,\mu))$, where~$(t,\mu)\in \Lambda$ is the location of the point. We denote its corresponding point configurations ~$(\xi_{s,j}^t)_{1\leq s\leq t}$.

\(m_0, H_1<\infty\) 
such that, for every \(m\geq m_0\), there exists a candidate \(\xi_m \in \cX_m\)

 \int_{J_{j,m}}\left(

\|\mathcal A(\xi_m-\Xi_0)\|_{L^2(\nu_0)}

\end{equation}
with
\(
C_{\mathrm{app}}
=C_{\mathrm{app}}(\beta,H,U,\kappa,K,\vartheta),
\)
and
\(
C_{\mathrm{fwd}}
=C_{\mathrm{fwd}}
(\beta,H,U,\kappa,K,\vartheta,r_0,\alpha,C_\nu)

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Second Ray-Knight isomorphism to transfer the DGFF level-set result to local times. Result: By the second Ray-Knight theorem the local time at level theta of the walk is, in law, (1/2)(h + sqrt(2 theta ...))^2 for an independent DGFF-type field h; level sets of the local time at height eta times the cover-time scale correspond to DGFF level sets at height lambda log N with lambda determined by eta and theta, giving eta < 1 + (1/2) sqrt(theta)... in the notation of the notes exactly the range where the corresponding DGFF lambda is below 1. The transfer is rigorous for the part of the level set where the sign of h + constant is positive; the difficulty is the negative branch, where the square masks the sign and the point measures of the two branches are dependent. For eta near the upper endpoint the negative branch contributes a lower-order but not negligible set; separating it needs a joint limit of the two branches, which is again Problem 16.1 in disguise. Obstruction: Sign ambiguity in the isomorphism couples two DGFF level sets; no joint limit is available.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0011-scaling-limit-of-local-time-level-sets-of-planar-random-walk-in-the-fu
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Infinitely many planar FPP geodesic rays for continuous laws structural argument Result: Finite geodesic existence and finite lattice degree yield at least one ray: among geodesics to points tending to infinity, choose an infinite subsequence with a common first edge, then a common second edge, and continue. Every finite segment of the diagonal limit is minimizing. Check: At each stage finitely many choices ensure an infinite subsequence. Path lengths tend to infinity, and any shortcut of a limiting finite segment would contradict minimization in all sufficiently long selected paths. Obstruction: This compactness proof gives one ray, not many eventually disjoint rays. Endpoint sequences in different directions could still share the same limiting tail without additional shape information.

[Theorem thm:gradphi-large-deviations of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] There exists a constant $C=C(p)>0$ such that the following holds for any domain $V$ that contains $\ensuremath{\mathcal B}_R(o)$, where $R = Ch^{p-1}$ for $1 < p < 2$ and $R = Ch$ for $2 < p < \infty$. Let $z$ be such that $\ensuremath{\mathcal B}_{R+1}(z) \subset V$. Then there exist absolute constants $c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4>0$ such that
    \begin{align}
		\exp\Big[-c_0 \beta h^{(p-1)\,\wedge\, 1}\Big] \leq \frac{{\widehat\pi}^{(p)}_V(\phi_o = h)}{{\widehat\pi}^{(p)}_V(\phi_o = h-1)} &\leq \exp\Big[-c_1 \beta h^{(p-1)\,\wedge\, 1}\Big]\,,\\
		\exp\Big[-c_2 \beta h^{p \,\wedge\, 2}\Big] \leq {\widehat\pi}^{(p)}_V(\phi_o = h) &\leq \exp\Big[-c_3\beta h^{p \,\wedge\, 2}\Big]\,,\\        
		{\widehat\pi}^{(p)}_V(\phi_z = h \mid \phi_o = h) &\leq \exp\Big[-c_4 \beta h^{p\,\wedge\,\frac{p}{p-1}}\Big]\,.
	\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

STATUS: proof (unaudited). For fixed Q>0, positive integer p, Y_q(Z)=tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2/q, and S_(n,q) the average of n iid copies, sup_(0<q<=Q,n>=4p) E S_(n,q)^(-p)<infinity. Its deviations outside any fixed sufficiently small interval about E Y_q have probability <=C exp(-cn), uniformly in q; E[S^(-p);bad]<=C exp(-cn/2) for n>=8p. These exact negative moments justify deletion of inverse tails for critical tanh. Assumptions: Standard Gaussian iid rows, fixed finite Q>0 and moment order p. Constants may depend on Q,p and concentration-box radius; all sample averages are positive almost surely. Model: K_(j+1)=n^-1 sum_(i=1)^n tanh(sqrt(K_j)Z_(j,i))^2, with independent standard Gaussian rows and layers, K0>0 fixed, no bias, Gaussian weight variance exactly1/n, and no width-dependent normalizer. Write Y_q=tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2/q, S_(n,q)=n^-1 sum_i Y_q(Z_i), q=K_j, v=1/(nq), V_next=1/(nK_(j+1)). Limit: Unaudited analytic proof; no novelty claim. Provides inverse-tail control, not a cumulant expansion.
Standard Gaussian iid rows, fixed finite Q>0 and moment order p. Constants may depend on Q,p and concentration-box radius; all sample averages are positive almost surely.

Write Y_q=tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2/q for q>0 and Z standard Gaussian, and
S_(n,q)=n^(-1)sum_(i=1)^n Y_q(Z_i), with iid rows.

## C044: uniform inverse sample moments and deleted tails

For every fixed Q<infinity and positive integer p, there is a finite
C_(Q,p) such that

    sup_(0<q<=Q, n>=4p) E[S_(n,q)^(-p)] <= C_(Q,p).            (1)

For any fixed sufficiently small eta>0, with m(q)=E Y_q and
G_(n,q)={|S_(n,q)-m(q)|<=eta},

    P(G_(n,q)^c)<=C_Q exp(-c_Q n),
    E[S_(n,q)^(-p);G_(n,q)^c]<=C_(Q,p)exp(-c_Q n/2), n>=8p.   (2)

Constants can be made explicit from the Gaussian expectations in the
proof. The sample mean is strictly positive almost surely. These are
exact-chain inverse moment estimates, in contrast with the ReLU atom and
near-collinearity obstruction.

Proof. tanh(x)/x decreases for x>0: tanh(x)-x sech(x)^2 has derivative
2x sech(x)^2 tanh(x)>0 and value0 at zero. Therefore Y_q>=Y_Q for q<=Q,
and Y_q<=Z^2. Let H=Y_Q>0 and phi(s)=E exp(-sH). For small y>0,

    P(H<=y)=P(|Z|<=arctanh(sqrt(Qy))/sqrt(Q))<=C sqrt(y),

using arctanh(w)<=2w for w<=1/2 and the bounded Gaussian density.
Increasing C_Q extends P(H<=y)<=C_Q sqrt(y) to every y>0.
Integration by parts gives phi(s)<=C'_Q s^(-1/2). Also for0<=s<=1,

    phi(s)<=1-c_Q s<=exp(-c_Q s), c_Q=E[H exp(-H)]>0,

and rho_Q=phi(1)<1. The Gamma identity and independence yield

    E[(n^(-1)sum_i H_i)^(-p)]
       =n^p/Gamma(p) integral_0^infinity s^(p-1)phi(s)^n ds.    (3)

Choose s0>=max(1,(2C'_Q)^2). On [0,1], (3) is bounded by c_Q^(-p).
On [1,s0], use rho_Q^n, giving at most
n^p s0^p rho_Q^n/(p Gamma(p)), uniformly bounded in n. On [s0,infinity),
for n>=4p,

    integral_(s0)^infinity s^(p-1)(C'_Q/sqrt(s))^n ds
      <= s0^p 2^(-n)/(n/2-p).

After multiplication by n^p/Gamma(p), this is uniformly bounded too.
This proves (1), since S_(n,q)>=n^(-1)sum H_i under the common-row coupling.

Uniform exponential integrability follows from0<=Y_q<=Z^2; m(q)>=E H>0.
Centered exponential-moment bounds and Chernoff give the first part of(2),
uniformly in q. Choose eta< E H/2 so G also stays uniformly away from zero.
Cauchy-Schwarz, (1) at order2p and the first bound in(2) prove its second
bound. All integrations use nonnegative integrands, so Tonelli applies.

## C045: full next drift of the exact reciprocal

Consider the exact scalar critical chain K_next=q S_(n,q) and
v=1/(nq), V_next=1/(n K_next). There are epsilon>0,C,c,n0 such that for
0<q<=epsilon and n>=n0,

    E(V_next-v)
      =(2v+2)/n + [4v-4-5/(3v)]/n^2+r_n(v),
    |r_n(v)|<=C[v/n^(5/2)+(1+1/v+1/v^2)/n^3+v exp(-cn)].     (4)

The exact inverse moments in C044 justify this unbounded observable.
In particular the singular next correction is negative. On any fixed
0<q<=Q, the following coarser estimates hold uniformly for sufficiently
large n (depending on Q and the indicated moment orders):

    E[(V_next/v)^j]<=1+C_(Q,j)(q+1/n), j=1,2,
    E[(V_next-v)^2]<=C_Q(v^2/n+1/n^2),                        (5)
    |E(V_next-v)-(2v+2)/n|
                         <=C_Q[q/n+1/n^2+v/n^(3/2)].         (6)

Proof of(4). Global Taylor inequalities for tanh, using boundedness on
|x|<=1 and polynomial domination on |x|>=1, imply

    m(q)=1-2q+(17/3)q^2+O(q^3),
    Var(Y_q)=2-16q+O(q^2),
    kappa_3(Y_q)=8+O(q).

For example tanh(x)^2=x^2-(2/3)x^4+(17/45)x^6+O(x^8), with a global
remainder bound C|x|^8. Similarly E Y_q^2=3-20q+O(q^2). Every fixed
positive row moment is bounded; its first variation is O(q) since
|Y_q-Z^2|<=Cq Z^4.

Taylor expand 1/S about m(q) through order four on G. The fifth absolute
sample-average moment is O(n^(-5/2)); it follows, for instance, from the
sixth moment bound for centered iid sample sums and Holder. The exact
sample-mean third moment is kappa_3(Y_q)/n^2, and its fourth moment is
3 Var(Y_q)^2/n^2+O(n^-3). Deleted inverse tails are exponentially small
by C044. Therefore uniformly on0<q<=epsilon,

    E S^(-1)=m^(-1)+Var(Y_q)/(n m^3)
              +[-kappa_3(Y_q)/m^4+3 Var(Y_q)^2/m^5]/n^2
              +O(n^(-5/2))+O(exp(-cn))
      =1+2q-(5/3)q^2+(2-4q)/n+4/n^2
              +O(q^3+q^2/n+q/n^2+n^(-5/2)+exp(-cn)).         (7)

Multiply by v, subtract v, and use vq=1/n. This gives(4).

For(5), the same good-event Taylor expansion through order two applied
to S^(-j), with C044 for the deleted tails, gives
E S^(-j)=m(q)^(-j)+O_(Q,j)(1/n). The function
[m(q)^(-j)-1]/q stays bounded on0<q<=Q, so its first assertion follows.
The Lipschitz estimate for1/S on G, and C044 off G, give
E(S^(-1)-m(q)^(-1))^2<=C_Q/n. Since m(q)^(-1)-1=O_Q(q), the second
assertion follows by v^2 q^2=1/n^2.

For(6), the second-order centered Taylor expansion has remainder
O(n^(-3/2)), and Var(Y_q)/m(q)^3=2+O(q). This yields
E S^(-1)=1+2q+2/n+O(q^2+q/n+n^(-3/2)) for small q, which gives(6).
On epsilon<=q<=Q, v<=1/(n epsilon); the error is O_Q(1/n), absorbable
in C_Q q/n. This completes the global extension.

[Lemma 11 (Finite, possibly inflated, offspring variance) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] In the saturated regime, $N\,|\,(\text{types})\sim\mathrm{Bin}(\text{children},p_{d,d'})$ and
\[
\sigma^2_{\mathrm{off}}=\underbrace{\E[(\deg-1)]\,\bar p(1-\bar p)}_{\text{Bernoulli}}+\underbrace{\Var(\deg-1)\,\bar p^{\,2}}_{\text{degree fluctuation}}<\infty,
\]
where $\bar p$ is the $\pi$-averaged transmission probability and $\deg-1$ the offspring count. In the sensitive regime an additional Cox term $\E[(\deg-1)(\deg-2)]\Var_A(p(A))$ appears; it is also finite since $p(\cdot)\in[0,1]$. Both expressions are finite under the standing assumption $\E[\deg^2]<\infty$ ($\Leftrightarrow g''(1)<\infty$).

[Theorem thm:2DNSE of arXiv:2412.01381, 'Ergodicity and mixing for locally monotone stochastic evolution equations'] Assume that $B\in L_2(U,W^{1,2}_{0,\,\operatorname{sol}}({\mathcal O}))$. Assume that for some $\lambda\in (0,1)$,
\[\|B\|^2_{L_2(U,H)}\le\frac{1}{4}\lambda\nu^3 c_0^2,\]
and
\[\|B\|^2_{L_2(U,H)}\le(1-\lambda)\nu c_0^2.\]
Then the Markovian Feller semigroup $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ of the stochastic incompressible 2D Navier-Stokes equations~(equation eq:2DNSE of the paper) with degenerate additive Wiener noise possesses a unique invariant measure $\mu_\ast$ with second moments in $V$.

Furthermore, if there exists $\gamma\in (0,\nu c_0^2]$ and $\lambda\in (0,1)$ such that
\[\|B\|^2_{L_2(U,H)}\le\frac{1}{4}\lambda(\nu^3 c_0^2-\nu^2\gamma),\]
and
\[\|B\|^2_{L_2(U,H)}\le(1-\lambda)\nu c_0^2,\]
then $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ is exponentially mixing and exponentially ergodic, and we have the following upper bound for the $\varepsilon$-mixing time
\[\tau^x_{\textup{\textsf{mix}}}(\varepsilon)\leq 
\frac{2}{\gamma}\left[\frac{1}{\lambda \nu^2 }\|x\|^{2}_H+\log\left(\|x\|_H+\frac{\|B\|_{L_2(U,H)}}{\sqrt{2\lambda \nu}c_0}\right)+\log\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)\right].\]

[Prop max_concave of arXiv:2604.23751, 'Large deviation principles for pattern-avoiding permutations, and limit shapes for constra'] Let $E$ be a topological vector space and $K \subset E$ compact and convex, and let $f:K \to \mathbb{R}$ be lower semicontinuous and strictly convex.
    Then $f$ has a minimum which is attained at exactly one point $x_0 \in K$.
    Moreover, if $x \in K$ is such that for any $y \in V_x(K)$, we have
    \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\Big|_{t=0^+} f(x+ty)=0 ,\]
    then $x=x_0$.

[Lem 13 of arXiv:2605.30779, '2605.30779'] Let \(U\subset\mathbb C\) be an open set, let \(x_0\in U\cap\mathbb R\), and assume that \(\{f_N\}_{N=1}^\infty\xrightarrow{\mathrm{mer}} f\) on \(U\). Suppose that \(x_0\) is not a pole of \(f\), and
  \begin{align*}
    f(x_0)= {}& 0, & f'(x_0) \neq {}& 0 .
  \end{align*}
  Then there exists \(\delta>0\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(N\), \(f_N\) has exactly one zero \(z_N\) in the disc \(\{z:|z-x_0|<\delta\}\), and \(z_N\to x_0\). Moreover,
  \[
    f_N'(z_N)\to f'(x_0).
  \]
  If, in addition, \(f_N(\overline z)=\overline{f_N(z)}\) on this disc, then \(z_N\in\mathbb R\).

Let d>=2 and let phi_d:[-1,1]->R be 1-Lipschitz with |phi_d(t)|<=1. For ReLU activation, or another activation satisfying Assumption 1 of Venturi-Jelassi-Ozuch-Bruna, the radial function f_d(x)=phi_d(||x||_2) on the Euclidean unit ball admits, for every 0<epsilon<1, uniform approximation by a one-hidden-layer neural network with N <= exp(O(epsilon^(-5) log(d/epsilon))) neurons. The maximum parameter magnitude can also be bounded at this exponential scale in the normalized setting. The constants are independent of d and epsilon and may depend on the fixed activation. This is depth 2 when the affine output is counted as a layer. For a general 1-Lipschitz radial profile on [0,1], subtract its value at zero, extend evenly, apply the normalized width result, and restore the value as an affine output constant; the bound on the restored bias must then include that offset. Corollary 13 already improves the earlier Safran-Eldan-Shamir exponent 9 to 5; neither optimality of 5 nor a joint polynomial-in-(d,1/epsilon) bound is asserted. The later paper's quantitative activation hypothesis must not be replaced by the earlier paper's weaker activation hypothesis.
d>=2; 0<epsilon<1
Normalized 1-Lipschitz radial profile with uniform absolute value <=1
Fixed ReLU activation, or the source's Assumption 1
Uniform approximation on the Euclidean unit ball; one hidden layer and affine output

CONSTANT DEPENDENCE: C_1 and C_2 depend on the weight law F and on d only. They do not depend on x, on ||x||, or on the direction of x. The bound is direction-uniform.
METHOD: Kesten introduced the method of bounded differences to FPP; the survey sketches the argument through the Efron-Stein inequality, consuming E #Geo(0,x) <= C||x||_1 and the one-edge resampling bound T_i(0,x) - T(0,x) <= tau'_{e_i}.
EARLIER, WEAKER BOUND, same author: Kesten, 'Aspects of first passage percolation' (Saint-Flour XIV, Lecture Notes in Math. 1180, 1986), Theorem 5.16, gave Var T(0,ne_1) <= C(n / log^{1/p} n)^2 with p = 9d + 3 - only a logarithmic improvement on the trivial n^2 for bounded weights. Do not cite that for the linear bound.
NOTE ON C_1: the lower half of the sandwich is a CONSTANT, not a growing bound. The growing lower bound is Newman-Piza's B log n and it holds only in d = 2 and only under an extra atom condition - see the Newman-Piza node.
SOURCE: Kesten, 'On the speed of convergence in first-passage percolation', Ann. Appl. Probab. 3 (1993), 296-338. Statement read in Auffinger-Damron-Hanson, '50 years of first passage percolation', arXiv:1511.03262v2 (AMS University Lecture Series 68, 2017), theorem 'thm: kesten_variance', tex lines 1072-1082. Independently corroborated by the authors of arXiv:2604.01214, whose abstract attributes the O(n) variance upper bound to 'Kesten's O(n) upper bound (Ann. Appl. Probab., 1993)'.
VERIFICATION STATUS: survey-claim. Lane P4 did not read Kesten (1993) itself.
title: Kesten (1993): for i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d, if E[tau_e^2] < infinity, P(tau_e = 0) < p_c(d), and the weight law is not concentrated at a single point, then there exist constants C_1, C_2 > 0 with C_1 <= Var T(0,x) <= C_2 ||x||_1 for every nonzero x in Z^d. The linear upper bound is what gives the fluctuation-exponent bound 0 <= chi(d) <= 1/2 in every dimension, and that upper bound on chi is still the best known unconditionally.

Draft counterexample awaiting independent review: on the graph with a common root and n disjoint branches of n-1 vertices with iid standard Gaussian weights, the maximum n-vertex path sum is convex and sqrt(n)-Lipschitz, with path-indicator gradient of squared norm n. It has normalized expected overlap tending to zero at Ornstein-Uhlenbeck time u_n=16 log(log n)/log n, yet Var(M_n)>=c n/log n for all sufficiently large n and some c>0. Thus these structural facts alone do not yield a power bound. The growing-degree fan is not Z^2; fixed lattice geometry may provide the missing quantitative premise.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Try to derive transience from the quenched invariance principle route used for balanced walks, in the general case. Result: For balanced environments Lawler's argument uses the invariant measure of the environment process (from the maximum principle) to get a quenched CLT and then transience via the Green function decay; for general elliptic i.i.d. environments no invariant measure absolutely continuous with respect to P is known to exist (its existence is Open question 2.19's territory), so the route fails at the first step. An alternative is the Lyapunov-exponent route: transience follows if the quenched Green function G_omega(0,0) is finite a.s., which for a random walk with bounded-range transitions in d >= 3 follows from a lower bound on the spectral gap of the walk killed outside large boxes; in a random environment the killed walk's Perron eigenvalue could be arbitrarily close to 1 if the environment contains near-recurrent regions, and under (E) alone such regions exist at all scales with small probability. A quantitative bound needs the density of such traps to decay fast enough with their size, which is a large-deviation statement about the i.i.d. environment that I could not verify without (UE). Under (UE) the trap analysis of Bolthausen-Sznitman-Zeitouni suggests transience should hold but no proof exists. No result. Obstruction: No invariant measure for the environment process; trap density under mere ellipticity uncontrolled.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0043-transience-of-i-i-d-elliptic-rwre-in-dimensions-d-3

Bounded-spectrum specialization of Pourkamali-Macris Theorem4. Let N,M tend to infinity with N<=M, N/M->alpha in(0,1], and M/N bounded. Let S_N=U_N*Sigma_N*V_N^T be a real N by M biorthogonally invariant signal, where U_N,V_N are independent Haar orthogonal matrices independent of the singular values in Sigma_N. Assume a deterministic K<infinity bounds ||S_N||_op almost surely for every N. Suppose the empirical singular-value probability laws converge almost surely weakly to a deterministic probability density mu on[0,K]. Let bar_mu be its symmetrization to R. Require integral integral log|x-y| dbar_mu(x)dbar_mu(y)>-infinity and integral log|x| dbar_mu(x)>-infinity; the second moment is finite. For fixed lambda>0 observe Y_N=sqrt(lambda)*S_N+Z_N, where the entries of Z_N are iid N(0,1/N), independently of S_N. Define I_{N,M}(A,B)=E_{U,V} exp(N*Tr(A^T*U*B*V^T)) with independent normalized Haar U,V. Let J_lambda be the deterministic limiting value of log I_{N,M}(sqrt(lambda)*S_N,Y_N)/(N*M), supplied by the rectangular spherical-integral asymptotics for these limiting spectral laws. Then lim I(S_N;Y_N)/(N*M)=lambda*alpha*integral x^2 mu(x)dx-J_lambda, with mutual information in nats. The uniform operator-norm cap is an explicit additional restriction of this card, implying source Assumption3 and making the spectral approximation uniformly integrable. Source Assumption2, including density and logarithmic integrability, is retained. This card does not supply an extension to limiting spectral atoms or general non-rotationally-invariant factor priors.

 			\]

body: [Prop 21 (Members with exact moment generating function domain) of arXiv:2609.02398, '\textbf{Convex Order Comparisons for Sub-Gamma Random Variables}'] For every $a > 0$ there exists $X \in \SE(1,a)$, symmetric, with $M_X(\lambda) = \infty$ for all $|\lambda| > 1/a$. Consequently, any integrable random variable $W$ with $X' \lecx W$ for all $X' \in \SE(1,a)$ satisfies $M_W(\lambda) = \infty$ for $|\lambda| > 1/a$; in particular $c\Lap$ requires $1/c \le 1/a$, i.e.\ $c \ge a$.
title: Members with exact moment generating function domain

body:
[Lemma eq:positive-time-local-density-equivalence of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Under Assumption~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper), there is a function
$\varrho\in C((0,T]\times\mathbb R^d)$, locally H\"older continuous on $Q$, such
that
\begin{equation*}
 \mu_t(\,\mathrm d x)=\varrho(t,x)\,\mathrm d x,
 \qquad \varrho(t,x)>0,
 \qquad (t,x)\in(0,T]\times\mathbb R^d.
\end{equation*}
For every $0<\varepsilon<T$ and $K\Subset\mathbb R^d$,
\begin{equation}
 0<\inf_{(t,x)\in[\varepsilon,T]\times K}\varrho(t,x)
 \leq\sup_{(t,x)\in[\varepsilon,T]\times K}\varrho(t,x)<\infty.
 
\end{equation}
Consequently, Lebesgue measure and the occupation measure $\mathfrak m$ are

body:
Let (Z_n) be a Galton-Watson branching process with Z_0 = 1 and offspring distribution (p_k)_{k >= 0} having generating function f(s) = sum_k p_k s^k and mean m = sum_k k p_k, assumed finite. Let q = P( Z_n = 0 for some n ) be the extinction probability. Then q is the SMALLEST root in [0,1] of the equation f(s) = s, and: if m < 1 (subcritical) then q = 1; if m = 1 (critical) then q = 1 UNLESS p_1 = 1, in which case the process is deterministic and never dies; if m > 1 (supercritical) then q < 1. The critical case is the one that gets misquoted: a critical branching process dies out almost surely even though E[Z_n] = 1 for every n, so the population is not uniformly integrable and the mean survives while the process does not. Excluding the degenerate p_1 = 1 is necessary. A second standard trap: q < 1 does not mean the process survives with probability 1 - it survives with probability exactly 1 - q, and conditioned on survival Z_n grows geometrically at rate m. [standard; e.g. Athreya and Ney, Branching Processes, Chapter I, or Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Section 4.3.3]

In a Hilbert space H a sequence (x_n) converges weakly to x, written x_n ⇀ x, if ⟨x_n, y⟩ → ⟨x, y⟩ for every y ∈ H; by the Riesz representation theorem this is convergence against every bounded linear functional. The weak topology on H is the coarsest topology making every functional x ↦ ⟨x, y⟩ continuous. Norm convergence implies weak convergence; the converse fails in infinite dimensions (an orthonormal sequence e_n converges weakly to 0 while ||e_n|| = 1). Weak limits are unique; weakly convergent sequences are norm-bounded (Banach–Steinhaus); the norm is weakly lower semicontinuous (||x|| ≤ liminf ||x_n|| when x_n ⇀ x); norm-closed convex sets are weakly closed (Mazur), and in infinite dimensions the weak closure of the unit sphere is the closed unit ball. If x_n ⇀ x and ||x_n|| → ||x|| then x_n → x in norm (Radon–Riesz property of Hilbert spaces). Bounded operators preserve weak convergence; compact operators turn weak convergence into norm convergence.

In a general normed space X the weak topology is the coarsest topology making every f ∈ X* continuous, and the weak-* topology on X* is the coarsest making every evaluation f ↦ f(x), x ∈ X, continuous. The weak-* topology on X* is in general coarser than the weak topology of X* (which is induced by X**); the two coincide when X is reflexive. In a Hilbert space, after identifying H* with H, weak and weak-* convergence are the same notion.
H a real or complex Hilbert space; X a normed space for the general remarks
title: Weak convergence and the weak / weak-* topologies

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2604.24664, 'Absolute continuity of Rosenblatt measures'] Let $(B_t)_{t \in [0, T]}$ be an $\FctT$-Wiener process. Let $\phi: [0, T] \times \Omega \to \Rbb$ be an $\FctT$-progressively measurable process such that $\phi \in L^2([0, T])$ almost surely and assume that the process $(Z_t)_{t\in [0,T]}$ defined by
	\begin{equation}
		
		Z_t = \exp\left( - \int_0^t \phi_s \d{B_s} - \frac12 \int_0^t \phi^2_s \d{s} \right), \quad t \in [0, T],
	\end{equation}
	is an $\FctT$-martingale. Let $\tilde{\Pbb}$ be the probability measure on $(\Omega, \Fcal)$ defined by $\d{\tilde{\Pbb}} = Z_T \d{\Pbb}$. Then the process $(\tilde{B}_t)_{t \in [0, T]}$ defined by
	\[
		\tilde{B}_t = B_t + \int_0^t \phi_s \d{s}, \quad t \in [0, T],
	\]
	is an $\FctT$-Wiener process with respect to $\tilde{\Pbb}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:e767be6490ac7e0dd22a85699dc9939b70e59a554202d4911951f5a4708c9abc","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/e7/e767be6490ac7e0dd22a85699dc9939b70e59a554202d4911951f5a4708c9abc.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:bd43de8dcb06f799c171e84b491fd3ed96f16a4aa79c15e2b93e64bffef0ad46","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c03","bundle_id":"population.t309-equilateral-ddpm-symmetry-breaking-drafts","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability, score matching, Gaussian mixture learning","draft":"w721/bundle_001.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:equilateral-gaussian-population-ddpm-random-angle","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T309: a population GD symmetry-breaking step for equilateral triples

T309-w721-C02 v1 (invariance) and C03 v2 (population convergence).
Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim. The general empirical Target 2 remains open.

The next unpaid step is to reach this invariant family from a generic random triple in an unknown plane, or to replace exact population equivariance with an empirical argument. The initialization here is random in angle, has known radius and plane, and is exactly equilateral. These are substantive extra assumptions. It can be outside every componentwise warm-start basin.

## The population statement

Let the target be an equal-weight mixture N(a u_j,I_d), j=0,1,2, where u_j are the unit equilateral vectors in a known plane, centered at zero. Its orientation in that plane need not be known. Assume 0<a<=a_0 for a sufficiently small absolute constant. Parameterize the student by three unrestricted mean vectors m_j in R^d, using exactly Eq. (9) of Shah--Chen--Klivans. Train on the population DDPM objective at this fixed noise level, with all three means updated by ordinary Euclidean GD with the same step h.

Initialize m_j=a R_Theta u_j, where Theta is uniform on the circle, independently of the target orientation. There are absolute h_0,c,C>0 such that for 0<h<=h_0/a^2 the following hold:

1. Every iterate has m_j=a r_n R_{theta_n}u_j, with 1/2<r_n<2.
2. Except at the three exact unstable initial angles (a probability-zero event), the iterates converge to the true mean triple up to permutation.
3. If the initial angle is at distance at least delta from every unstable angle, then for 0<delta,eta<=1/10, after at most

       C/(h a^4) [1+log(1/delta)+log(1/eta)]

   iterations, the matched mean error is at most C a eta. Consequently the probability statement can be made 1-p by taking delta=pi p/3, or a smaller delta<=1/10. The dependence on d is absent at population level. This does not yet establish polynomial sample complexity or arbitrary random initialization.

The same statement applies to the high-noise training stage of a well-separated original mixture with center radius R: choose t so that R exp(-t)=a. Rescaling the recovered means multiplies the error by R/a. Learning to an arbitrary original mean error therefore requires eta of the corresponding order. This observation does not remove the known-plane and known-radius initialization assumptions.

## 1. The invariant family under unrestricted mean updates

Let Q be rotation by 2pi/3 in the target plane and identity on its orthogonal complement. The target law and population DDPM loss are invariant under Q. The objective is also invariant under permutations of the three student labels. Combining the rotation with the inverse cyclic label permutation gives an orthogonal linear action on the whole parameter space which fixes every configuration satisfying m_{j+1}=Q m_j (indices modulo 3).

For a differentiable function L invariant under an orthogonal map A, differentiating L(Ax)=L(x) gives grad L(Ax)=A grad L(x). If Ax=x, then A grad L(x)=grad L(x). Both a GD step and the gradient flow therefore preserve its fixed-point subspace.

There is another exact symmetry: reflection S which is identity on the target plane and minus identity on its orthogonal complement. At a planar configuration, every parameter is fixed by S, so the gradient is planar. Intersecting the two fixed-point subspaces leaves precisely

    m_j=Q^j z,    z in the target plane.

For z nonzero write z=a r R_theta u_0. This is the full radius-angle equilateral family. Its invariance is exact, holds for every a, and concerns the unrestricted population objective. In particular its proof does not assume that two spaces of the same dimension coincide: it explicitly solves the fixed-point equations. For d=2 the perpendicular reflection is unnecessary.

The radius-one angular circle alone is generally not invariant. Section 2 below gives F_r(1,theta)=(3a^6/4)(1-cos(3theta))+O(a^8), which is nonzero away from the aligned angles for sufficiently small a.

## 2. Uniform expansion with a variable radius

Let F_a(r,theta) denote the population excess score loss between this student and the target. Uniformly for r in [1/4,3], and with every fixed finite number of r,theta derivatives needed below,

    F_a(r,theta)=a^4 A4(r)+a^6 A6(r,theta)+O(a^8),                    (1)
    A4(r)=(r^2-1)^2/2,
    A6(r,theta)=(r^6+1-2r^3 cos(3theta))/8
                 -(r^2-1)(r^4-1)/2+(r^2-1)^2/4.                   (2)

The proof uses the same dominated Taylor argument as angular_landscape.md. In that argument the logit has magnitude at most 3|a| ||y|| instead of |a| ||y||. This still has Gaussian-integrable domination. It supplies any fixed derivative order, not merely a pointwise remainder.

For completeness, the score expansions through order four are

    b_student = a^2 r^2 y/2 + a^3 r^3 T_theta[y,y]/2
                  -a^4 r^4 y||y||^2/16 + O(a^5),
    b_target  = a^2 y/2 + a^3 T_0[y,y]/2
                  -a^4 y||y||^2/16 + O(a^5).

The teacher density relative to phi_2 is 1+a^2(||y||^2/4-1/2)+O(a^3). Squaring the score difference and integrating gives (1)--(2): the order-six contributions are the squared order-three term, the cross term between orders two and four, and the order-two teacher-density correction multiplying the squared order-two term. Their expectations respectively are

    (r^6+1-2r^3 cos(3theta))/8,
    -(r^2-1)(r^4-1)/2,
    (r^2-1)^2/4.

Odd powers again vanish by the exact a -> -a, y -> -y symmetry. The script scripts/check_angular.py verifies these Gaussian polynomial identities with exact symbolic arithmetic. It is not used to prove the domination.

Periodicity and reflection give, by the zero-preserving remainder argument in angular_landscape.md, uniformly on 1/2<=r<=2,

    F_theta(r,theta)=a^6 k_a(r,theta) sin(3theta),
    c <= k_a(r,theta) <= C.                                       (3)

Here the leading coefficient is 3r^3/4, bounded above and below on this annulus. Bounds on the remainder after two theta derivatives force its first derivative to vanish linearly at each n pi/3. This justifies the uniform division by the sine, including near its zeros.

Near r=1, the expansion and the exact identity F_r(1,0)=0 give

    F_r(r,0)=a^4 g_a(r)(r-1),       c<=g_a(r)<=C,                   (4)
    |F_r(r,theta)-F_r(r,0)|<=C a^6 theta^2                        (5)

for |r-1|<=1/10 and |theta|<=pi/3, interpreting theta relative to the nearest minimum. To check (4), F_rr(r,0)=2a^4(3r^2-1)+O(a^6) is positive throughout this radial neighborhood; apply the mean value theorem. For (5), the a^4 term is independent of theta, the mixed derivative F_{r theta theta} is O(a^6), and F_{r theta}(r,0)=0 by exact evenness; integrate twice in theta. All constants are absolute.

## 3. The exact discrete update

At an equilateral configuration, the symmetry from Section 1 implies that every gradient is the same linear combination of its own radial and tangential unit vectors v_j=R_theta u_j and Jv_j. Differentiating with respect to r and theta fixes the coefficients:

    grad_{m_j} L = F_r v_j/(3a) + F_theta Jv_j/(3ar).

Set

    A = r-h F_r/(3a^2),     B=-h F_theta/(3a^2 r).

Then ordinary GD on the three means gives the exact update

    r_next=sqrt(A^2+B^2),    theta_next=theta+atan2(B,A).             (6)

The Euclidean gradient is not the coordinate gradient of F in (r,theta). Formula (6) accounts for the induced metric and for the discrete tangential step's second-order radial effect.

## 4. Radial confinement and descent

On r in [1/4,3], the gradient in the z-coordinate of the invariant linear subspace is O(a^3), and its Hessian is O(a^2), by (1) and the chain rule away from z=0. The three-mean Euclidean metric on this subspace is 3 times the metric of z, which only changes absolute constants. Choose h_0 sufficiently small to satisfy the descent bound h<=1/(L a^2) and to make the largest possible one-step radial displacement from r in [0.9,1.1] less than 0.1. Both choices use uniform bounds on the larger annulus.

Initially r=1 and F_a=O(a^6). Suppose an iterate lies in [0.9,1.1] and has F_a<=C_0 a^6, where C_0 is an absolute bound for all initial angles. The step segment stays in [1/2,2] by the displacement bound, so the descent lemma applies along that segment. It gives F_next<=F_current. Equation (1) then implies

    (r_next^2-1)^2 <= C a^2,

because A6 and the remainder are uniformly bounded on the annulus. Thus |r_next-1|<=C' a. Decrease a_0 until C' a_0<0.1. This proves the induction and confinement. It also proves monotone descent. No assumption about a sublevel barrier preventing a discrete jump is needed; the step-segment bound was established first.

## 5. Angular convergence and rate

Confinement implies A is bounded above and below by positive absolute constants after further decreasing h_0 if needed. By (3) and (6), the angular displacement has the opposite sign to sin(3theta), and its absolute value lies between

    c h a^4 |sin(3theta)|    and    C h a^4 |sin(3theta)|.           (7)

Indeed |B/A|<=C h a^4<=C h_0 a^2, so arctan(|B/A|) is between |B/A|/2 and |B/A|. Make a_0 small enough that 3C h a^4<1/2. Since |sin(3theta)| is at most three times the distance to either neighboring zero of the sine, no step can cross a minimum or maximum. Every open angular basin is invariant.

The same geometric-growth and geometric-decay argument as in angular_landscape.md, now using h a^4 rather than h a^6, proves that the angle reaches distance eta from its basin's minimum in at most

    C/(h a^4) [1+log(1/delta)+log(1/eta)]

steps. It remains there and continues toward zero. An exact maximum is stationary in angle; it is excluded. There are exactly three such initial angles modulo 2pi, and their delta-neighborhood has probability 3delta/pi under a uniform angle.

## 6. Radius follows the angular convergence

Write e=r-1, and let theta be measured relative to the basin's minimum. From (4)--(5),

    F_r=a^4 g_a(r)e+f,       |f|<=C a^6 theta^2.

The relation sqrt(A^2+B^2)-A=B^2/(sqrt(A^2+B^2)+A) and A>=c>0 bound the radial correction by C h^2 a^8 theta^2. Since h a^2<=h_0, it is bounded by C h a^4 theta^2 (after adjusting an absolute constant). Shrinking h_0 so the radial linear factor is nonnegative, (6) gives

    |e_next| <= (1-c h a^2)|e| + C h a^4 theta^2.                  (8)

After the angular stage makes |theta|<=eta, iteration of (8) yields

    |e_{n+k}| <= (1-c h a^2)^k |e_n| + C' a^2 eta^2.

An additional C/(h a^2)[1+log(1/eta)] steps therefore makes |e|<=C'' eta. This is bounded by the iteration order asserted in the theorem since a<=a_0<1. The matched mean error is at most a(|e|+r |theta|)<=C a eta. Letting eta tend to zero proves convergence, and using the rate at a fixed eta proves the finite-time claim.

## Checks and scope

The proof uses equal weights, exact equilateral geometry, known centering and plane, and a population objective. Removing any of them breaks the fixed-point argument or the single-angle landscape reduction. At a=0 every student center in this initialization is zero and there is no angular signal, so the strict requirement a>0 is necessary. At an exact antipodal angle the gradient cannot choose a component labeling; this is why a measure-zero exception and a distance-from-saddles parameter appear. The dimension-independent reduction does not apply to an arbitrary initial triple with perpendicular components.

For an empirical objective, an individual sample set usually lacks the target's rotational invariance. Orbit augmentation by the known 120-degree rotation could preserve the invariant family, but the needed uniform gradient estimates and the resulting finite-sample convergence theorem are not supplied here. For an unknown plane, estimating and entering the plane is also unpaid.   Q_{\mathrm{gate}}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(t+1)})
  \geq Q_{\mathrm{gate}}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}^{(t)})
\]
for all~$t$. Hence, the resulting optimization procedure defines a valid generalized EM
algorithm [wu1983].

Independently checked proof (PASS w667 and w668): C004 v1. Partition compactly supported F into finite measurable cells, with exact masses b_j and enclosing coordinate boxes of maximum width h. Enumerate n-label multisets whose box-sum intervals contain n*mean(F), and form occupancy columns A_(j,a)=count of j divided by n. If F is n-CM then A lambda=b has a nonnegative solution. Conversely, feasible solutions along h tending to zero give couplings with exact marginals F and sum error at most n*h in each coordinate; compactness yields an exact n-mix. An exact dual vector with y^T A>=0 and y^T b<0 disproves continuous n-CM. Floating solver failures and inner point-grid infeasibility are not certificates. Finite outer-LP successes are numerical evidence only.

[Lemma lem: estimate of Kostka of arXiv:2604.23890, 'The Cutoff Profile for Random Transpositions on Repeated Cards in the Full Range of Parame'] Let $\lambda\vdash n$, and $r:=n-\lambda_1,r':=n-\lambda_1'$. Then, we have
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $\lambda_1'>m$, then $K_{\lambda,(l^m)}=0$.
\item $K_{\lambda,(l^m)}\le m^r$. 
\item $K_{\lambda,(l^m)}\le\binom{n}{r}K_{\lambda^*,(\lfloor r/m\rfloor+1,\ldots,\lfloor r/m\rfloor+1,\lfloor r/m\rfloor,\ldots,\lfloor r/m\rfloor)}$. Here and from now on, for the partition $(\lfloor r/m\rfloor+1,\ldots,\lfloor r/m\rfloor+1,\lfloor r/m\rfloor,\ldots,\lfloor r/m\rfloor)$, there are $r-m\lfloor r/m\rfloor$ parts of size $\lfloor r/m\rfloor+1$, and $m\lfloor r/m\rfloor+m-r$ parts of size $\lfloor r/m\rfloor$.
\item $K_{\lambda,(l^m)}\le\binom{n}{r'}K_{\lambda^\bullet,(\lfloor r'/m\rfloor+1,\ldots,\lfloor r'/m\rfloor+1,\lfloor r'/m\rfloor,\ldots,\lfloor r'/m\rfloor)}$. Here and from now on, for the partition $(\lfloor r'/m\rfloor+1,\ldots,\lfloor r'/m\rfloor+1,\lfloor r'/m\rfloor,\ldots,\lfloor r'/m\rfloor)$, there are $r'-m\lfloor r'/m\rfloor$ parts of size $\lfloor r'/m\rfloor+1$, and $m\lfloor r'/m\rfloor+m-r'$ parts of size $\lfloor r'/m\rfloor$.
\end{enumerate}

Let x be uniform on {-1,1}^n, A an n x n symmetric matrix of complex numbers and L an arbitrary linear form. (Thm 6) If every row of A has at least r nonzero entries, r >= exp((ln n)^{1/4}), then for every fixed delta > 0: sup_c P(x^T A x = L(x) + c) = O_delta(r^{-1/2+delta}). (Cor 1) The same with r replaced by m if A has at least mn nonzero entries and m >= 3 exp((ln n)^{1/4}); the exponent 1/2 is sharp, see (x_1+...+x_n)(x_1+...+x_m). (Thm 4) If at least r rows of an m x n array A each have at least r nonzero entries and x, y are independent uniform sign vectors, sup_c P(x^T A y = c) = O(r^{-1/2}). (Thm 5) If every row has >= r nonzero entries, r and m are large and P(x^T A y = f(y)) >= r^{-1+eps}, then A has a rank-one submatrix of size at least (m - O_eps(r/log^6 r)) x (n - O_eps(r/log^6 r)).

Assumes: x uniform on {-1,1}^n (Thm 5 also allows lazy {0,+-1} entries in y); many nonzero coefficients per row (Thm 6) or in total (Cor 1)

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Exact integral manipulation, Palm calculus, mass transport, limiting obstruction or conditional construction Result: Uniform probability measures on finite approximating cells do not automatically pass to invariant probability kernels on the limiting classes. The elementary sequence uniform[-n,n] on Z has mass 1/(2n+1) at each included point; every coordinate tends to zero, so its pointwise limit is the zero measure, not a probability measure. For the Voronoi limit, a proof must retain an appropriate Reiter or hyperfinite approximation with a uniform error bound, rather than taking an unqualified limit of the finite-cell averages. Check: Sum each finite kernel to obtain one, but sum its pointwise limit to obtain zero. This directly demonstrates failure of the needed exchange of infinite summation and limit. Obstruction: No Voronoi-specific uniform amenability estimate is proved. Conversely, the known arbitrary finite-relation counterexamples need not arise from low-density Voronoi cells.

[Proposition 9 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] For the grids of Proposition~\ref{prop:dyadic-grid-diagonal}, define
\begin{equation}
  \Lambda_{n,k}:=\{h_n(j-k):0\leq j\leq M_n\},
  \qquad 0\leq k\leq M_n,
  
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
  Q_{n,k}:=\mathcal L\left(
    B\,\middle|\, B_t\leq0\text{ for every }t\in\Lambda_{n,k}
  \right),
  \qquad
  p_{n,k}:=\PP(B_t\leq0:t\in\Lambda_{n,k}).
  
\end{equation}
Then
\(p_{n,k}=\PP(K_n=k)>0\),
\(\sum_{k=0}^{M_n}p_{n,k}=1\), and
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal L(\Xi_n^{\mathrm{grid}})
  =\sum_{k=0}^{M_n}p_{n,k}Q_{n,k}.
  
\end{equation}
Write
\begin{equation}
  L_{n,k}^-=h_nk,
  \qquad L_{n,k}^+=h_n(M_n-k).
  
\end{equation}
For \(0<k<M_n\), the component \(Q_{n,k}\) is
\(Q_{h_n,L_{n,k}^-,L_{n,k}^+}\) from \eqref{eq:pure-wall-law}.  The endpoint
components \(k=0,M_n\) retain their direct conditional definitions in
\eqref{eq:mixture-components}; they are full-path laws constrained on only
one side of the pin and are not covered by the positive-two-horizon
definition \eqref{eq:pure-wall-law}.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Transform asymptotics, exact special case, coupling reduction or identifiability check Result: Take two servers and two simultaneously present jobs with identical replica durations a<=b across servers. Replicating the shorter job on both servers first gives completion times a and a+b, with mean a+b/2. Assigning one job to each server immediately gives completion times a and b, with mean (a+b)/2. The second policy improves the mean by a/2. Therefore a proof based on always assigning every free server to the currently shortest job cannot be valid across the correlated-copy model class. Check: List the two completion epochs directly; at a=b=1 the means are 3/2 versus 1. This is a two-job scheduling example, not a stationary optimality theorem. Obstruction: Need a dynamic rule and a stochastic comparison or control proof for the full arriving system. Finite-workload preference need not identify a steady-state optimizer.

[Lemma 45 (Local one-derivative gain for Ricci--DeTurck systems) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Fix an integer \(k\geq2\) and \(\sigma\in(0,1)\).  Let \(Q\) and \(Q'\) be
concentric coordinate cylinders in a fixed spatial chart, with \(Q'\) having
smaller spatial radius and a positive time gap from the lower time face of
\(Q\); the two cylinders may share their upper time face.  Let \(r(t)\) be a
smooth reference metric on \(Q\), and let \(q(t)\) be a smooth positive
definite solution of the Ricci--DeTurck equation relative to \(r(t)\).  In a
fixed tensor frame this equation has the scalar-principal form
\begin{equation}
 \partial_tq^A-q^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jq^A
 =\mathcal F^A\bigl(x,t,q,q^{-1},\partial q;
                 r,\partial r,\partial^2r\bigr),
\end{equation}
where \(\mathcal F\) is a universal smooth expression and contains no second
spatial derivatives of \(q\).  Suppose, in the fixed coordinates, that
\[
 \lambda I\leq(q_{ij})\leq\Lambda I,
 \qquad
 \|q\|_{C^{k+\sigma,(k+\sigma)/2}(Q)}
 +\|r\|_{C^{k+1+\sigma,(k+1+\sigma)/2}(Q)}\leq A.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \|q\|_{C^{k+1+\sigma,(k+1+\sigma)/2}(Q')}
 \leq C,
\end{equation}
where \(C\) depends only on the displayed bounds, the rank and dimension, and
the fixed spatial and lower-time separations between \(Q'\) and \(Q\).
Consequently, the estimate is uniform in any bounded-geometry atlas with fixed
nested-cylinder ratios.

\begin{enumerate}
    \item The space $(X,\mu)$ satisfies the metric-Santal\'o inequality induced by $2\cdot\Theta$ on the domain $(\mathcal{B}(X),\mathcal{B}(X))$.

    \item Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal D\subset \mathcal{B}(X)$ be sub-collections
    satisfying $\mu(A\cap D)=0$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $D\in\mathcal D$. Then $(X,\mu)$ satisfies
    the sharper metric-Santal\'o inequality induced by $\Theta$ on the domain $(\mathcal A,\mathcal D)$.
\end{enumerate}

body: In mathematics, the Poincaré inequality is a result in the theory of Sobolev spaces, named after the French mathematician Henri Poincaré. The inequality allows one to obtain bounds on a function using bounds on its derivatives and the geometry of its domain of definition. Such bounds are of great importance in the modern, direct methods of the calculus of variations. A very closely related result is Friedrichs' inequality.
title: Poincaré inequality

Let G be a finite undirected loopless multigraph on n vertices with positive edge weights w_e, L its weighted Laplacian, and t > 0. A spanning rooted forest is a spanning forest with one chosen root in each tree; its weight is t^|E(F)| prod_{e in F} w_e (so an unrooted forest with trees T_1, ..., T_k counts prod |T_i| times). Z(t) is the total weight of spanning rooted forests, and Q_t = (I + tL)^-1. For all vertices i and j, (Q_t)_ij = f_ij(t) / Z(t), where f_ij(t) is the total weight of spanning rooted forests in which i belongs to the tree rooted at j. In particular Q_t is symmetric, entrywise nonnegative and doubly stochastic.
G is a finite undirected loopless multigraph with positive edge weights
t > 0

[Definition def:admissible_classes of arXiv:2607.04514, 'Boundary-layer asymptotics for Gaussian-smoothed singular measures'] Let \(\ell\in\mathbb N\) and \(\omega>0\). Fix \(A,\sigma_0>0\) and \(R\in(0,\infty]\).

  \begin{enumerate}
    \item A function \(B:\overline{\mathbb B}_A\times \mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}\times (0,\sigma_0]\to\mathbb
    R\) belongs to \(\mathfrak B_\ell\) if its pullback \( B(a,\varphi (\theta),\sigma)\) is
    \(C^\ell\) in \((a,\theta, \sigma)\) and, for every \(\gamma\) with \(|\gamma| \leqslant \ell\),
    \begin{equation*}
      \sup_{{\mathcal D}_{A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},\sigma_0}} \bigl| \partial_{a,\theta,\sigma}^{\gamma}
      B(a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma) \bigr|<\infty.
    \end{equation*}

    \item A function \(E:\overline{\mathbb B}_A \times\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}\times (0,\sigma_0]\to\mathbb
    R\) belongs to \(\mathfrak E_\ell^\omega\) if its pullback \( E(a, \varphi (\theta),\sigma)\) is
    \(C^\ell\) in \((a, \theta, \sigma)\), and there exists \(c>0\) such that, for every \(\gamma\)
    with \(|\gamma|\leqslant\ell\), there is a constant \(C_\gamma>0\) satisfying
    \begin{equation*}
      \bigl|\partial_{a,\theta,\sigma}^{ \gamma} E(a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma) \bigr|
      \leqslant C_\gamma e^{-c/\sigma^{\omega}},\quad
      \forall (a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma)\in {\mathcal D}_{A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0}.
    \end{equation*}

    \item A function \(P: \mathcal D_{R, A, \mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0} \to\mathbb R\) belongs to
    \(\mathfrak P_\ell \) if it is measurable in \(\zeta\) and its pullback
    \(P(\zeta;a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma)\) is \(C^\ell\) in the
    parameter variables \((a,\theta, \sigma)\), for every fixed \(\zeta\), and there exists
    \(n\geqslant 0\) such that
    \begin{equation*}
      \bigl| \partial_{a,\theta,\sigma}^{\gamma} P(\zeta; a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma) \bigr|
      \leqslant C_\gamma \bigl(1 + \|\zeta\|^n\bigr)
    \end{equation*}
    for every \(\gamma\) with \(|\gamma|\leqslant\ell\), uniformly on \(\mathcal D_{R, A,
    \mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0} \).

    \item A function \(G: \mathcal D_{R, A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0} \to\mathbb R\) belongs to
    \(\mathfrak G_\ell\) if it is measurable in \(\zeta\) and its pullback
    \(G(\zeta;a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma)\) is \(C^\ell\) in the
    parameter variables \((a,\theta,\sigma) \), for every fixed \(\zeta\), and there exist \(c_0>0,
    n\geqslant 0\) such that
    \begin{equation*}
      \bigl| \partial_{a,\theta,\sigma}^{\gamma} G(\zeta;a,\varphi(\theta),\sigma) \bigr|
      \leqslant C_\gamma\bigl(1+\|\zeta\|^n\bigr)\Gamma_{c_0}(\zeta;a)
    \end{equation*}
    for every \(\gamma\) with \(|\gamma|\leqslant\ell\), uniformly on \({\mathcal
    D}_{R,A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}},\sigma_0}\).
  \end{enumerate}
title: Admissible classes

\bel{Tchi-DEC}
|T_\chi^{mn}| \leq T_\chi^{00} , \qquad
-4 T_\chi^{00} \leq \eta_{mn} T_\chi^{mn} \leq 2 T_\chi^{00} .
\ee
The Euler stress-tensor with pressure law satisfying~\eqref{hyperbolic-eos-zero} admits the stronger trace bound
\bel{TrTE-lower}
- T_{\rm E}^{00} \leq \eta_{mn} T_{\rm E}^{mn} \leq 2 T_{\rm E}^{00} .
\ee

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT, C009 version 1, proof (unaudited); dependencies C004 v2 and C006 v2 also await independent review, and priority is not established. Fix any L>=3 and T<infinity, set H=L-1, and use equal hidden widths m with h1_i=sigma(w_i dot x), hl_j=sigma(m^(-1)sum_i B^l_ji h(l-1)_i) for 2<=l<=H, and f=m^(-1)sum_j a_j hH_j. Assume a globally C2 activation with absolute values of sigma and its first two derivatives at most one, data ||X||<=1 and |Y|<=1, and population half-squared risk. Two runs are independently initialized from the same laws: w_i iid with Euclidean norm <=1, a_i iid with |a_i|<=1, and iid entries in [-1,1] in each middle matrix; all named arrays are mutually independent. Layer entry laws can differ and need not be centered. Train all parameters simultaneously by fresh-iid SGD or finite minibatch averages, with multipliers m on w,a and m^2 on every middle matrix, using common deterministic nonnegative steps of total at most T. The runs may see independent data. Put S2=sum eta_k^2, A=2exp(T), M_l=1+2A^2 T product_{s=l+1}^H M_s backwards from l=H to 2, W=1+2A^2 T product_{s=2}^H M_s, R=max(1,A,W,M_2,...,M_H), and kappa=64L^2 R^(2L). For r_cov(m)=inf_{k,q positive integers}[4/q+2/sqrt(k+1)+2sqrt(2)sqrt(q^(k+1)/m)], an initialization-selected compatible tuple of hidden permutations gives expected population loss-chord barrier <=8R^L exp(kappa T)[r_cov(m)+6(L-2)/sqrt(m)+4LR^L sqrt(S2)]. Thus eta_max<=1/log(m) yields O_{L,T}(sqrt(log(log(m)+e)/log(m))) uniformly in input dimension, including dimensions growing arbitrarily with width, provided the stated Euclidean bounds hold uniformly. The proof matches initial boundary pairs using |delta a|+||Sigma^(1/2)delta w|| for Sigma=E[XX^T], propagates the cut-norm estimates in L2 of the input distribution for population gradients only, and compares SGD to population Euler in the full normalized Hilbert norm. Singular Sigma is allowed; no inverse covariance or teacher model is assumed. This does not assert samplewise covariance stability, a ReLU result, unbounded initialization, a fixed independent-data step result, low-risk endpoints, uniform growing-depth control, an independent audit, or novelty.
All bounded C2 activation, bounded iid independent initialization and fresh-sample SGD hypotheses in the statement
Uniform Euclidean input/initial-weight norm bounds, not just coordinate bounds; fixed L and T; shrinking steps for a vanishing barrier

[Theorem 77 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Suppose that Assumptions~\ref{Assumptions_Theta}, \ref{Assumptions_basic} and \ref{Assumptions_offcrit} hold. Take $h \in [H]$ and a saturated interval $(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}) \subseteq [\hat{a}_h,\hat{b}_h]$ of the equilibrium measure $\boldsymbol{\mu}$. Assume that $\mathfrak{a}$ is a
point separating a saturation from a band, but $\mathfrak{b}$ is not.\footnote{As the equilibrium measure has finite mass, this situation requires $\mathfrak{b}$ to be finite.} Then for each $\eps>0$ there exists $C>0$ depending only on $\eps$ and the constants in the assumptions, such that
\[
\P\big[\textnormal{There are no holes in}\, [\mathfrak{a}+\eps,\mathfrak{b}]\big]\geq 1- C\exp\bigg(-\frac{\N}{C}\bigg).
\]
Similarly, if $\mathfrak{b}$ is a point separating a saturation from a band, but $\mathfrak{a}$
is not, then
\[
\P\big[\textnormal{There are no holes in}\, [\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}-\eps]\big] \geq 1- C\exp\bigg(-\frac{\N}{C}\bigg).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In mathematical logic, the lambda calculus is a formal system for expressing computation based on function abstraction and application using variable binding and substitution. Untyped lambda calculus, the topic of this article, is a universal machine, i.e. a model of computation that can be used to simulate any Turing machine. It was introduced by the mathematician Alonzo Church in the 1930s as part of his research into the foundations of mathematics. In 1936, Church found a formulation which was logically consistent, and documented it in 1940.

[Lemma lem:purntbd of arXiv:2606.02472, 'Correlated uniform attachment trees'] [Lemma~3 of [Pekoz2017]]
Let $R_m$ be the number of red balls in a standard P\'olya urn  started with $r\in\mathbb{N}$ red balls and $b\in \mathbb{N}$ blue balls after $m$ draws and replacements. Then there is a coupling of $R_m$ and  $B_{r,b}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(r,b)$ such that
\[
|R_m - m B_{r,b}| \leq 2(b\wedge r) (r+b), 
\]
and consequently

\begin{align*}
	\mathbb{P}(R_m \geq t) &\geq  \mathbb{P}(m B_{r,b} \geq t + 2(b\wedge r) (r+b)).
\end{align*}

The chain is positive recurrent with an invariant probability measure $\pi$ satisfying
$\int_{\sf X} h(x)\pi(dx)< \infty$ for a non-negative function $h$ if and only if there is

[Defn 3 of arXiv:2609.02879, 'On the cut locus of Hamilton--Jacobi equations I: structure and propagation via the touchi'] Let \( \Omega \subset \R^n \) be an open convex subset and $\phi\in\text{\rm SCL}\,(\Omega)$.
	\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
		\item We define the \emph{differentiability set} of \( \phi \) as 
		\[
		\text{Diff}\,(\phi)= \{ x \in \Omega : \phi \text{ is differentiable at } x \},
		\]
		and the \emph{singular set} of $\phi$ as $\sing(\phi)=\Omega\setminus\text{Diff}\,(\phi)$.
		\item We denote by \( \text{Alex}\,(\phi) \) the set of points in \( \Omega \) where \( \phi \) is twice differentiable, i.e.,
		\begin{align*}
			\text{Alex}\,(\phi)= \big\{ x \in \Omega :\ & \text{there exists }D\phi(x)\text{ and }D^2\phi(x) \text{ such that} \\
			& \phi(y) = \phi(x) + \langle D\phi(x), y-x \rangle + \frac{1}{2} \langle D^2\phi(x)(y-x), y-x \rangle + o(|y-x|^2) \big\}.
		\end{align*}
	\end{enumerate}

$G$ in the $t$th round of the $H$-dynamics. 
For each $e\in E(\langle W^{(e)} \rangle_H)=\bigcup_{t\geqslant0}E_t$, 
we define $W^{(e)}$ as follows. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $e\in E_0$, we simply put $W^{(e)}=e$. 
\item Otherwise, if $e\in E_t$, for some $t\geqslant1$, 
we select a copy $H^{(e)}$ of $H$, for which 
$E(H^{(e)}\setminus e)\subset \bigcup_{s<t}E_s$, 
and put 
\begin{equation}
W^{(e)}=\bigcup_{f\in E(H^{(e)}\setminus e)} W^{(f)}. 
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

body: [Theorem mainv2 of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Suppose $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Z}$ are smooth separated Deligne--Mumford surfaces, and there is a contraction $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Z}$ whose exceptional $\mathcal{C}$ is a smooth stacky curve (not necessarily irreducible). Moreover, suppose that there is a closed reduced substack $\mathcal{Y}\subseteq \mathcal{Z}$ of dimension 0 such that $f(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{Y}$ set theoretically and $f : \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{C} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{Z} \setminus \mathcal{Y}$ is an isomorphism. Then $f$ is a regular weighted blowup with reduced center $\mathcal{Y}$, in particular $f|_\mathcal{C} : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is a weighted projective bundle, and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathcal{C})|_{\mathcal{C}} \simeq \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{C}}(-1) \otimes f^*\mathcal{L}$ for some line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ on $\mathcal{Y}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem mainv2 of arXiv:2609.04023

body:
[Definition 12 (Block stratification) of arXiv:2606.16005, '\bfseries An Algebraic Matrix Spencer Theorem'] Let
\[
H=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\mathcal B}H_\alpha
\]
be a fixed common block decomposition, and write $b_\alpha:=\dim H_\alpha .$ A \emph{block stratification} is a partition
\[
\mathcal B=\mathcal P_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup \mathcal P_J
\]
of the block index set into nonempty groups, called strata. For a stratum $\mathcal P_j$, define
\[
\cH_{\mathcal P_j}:=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\mathcal P_j}\cH_\alpha,
\qquad
h_j:=\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal P_j} b_\alpha,
\qquad
m_j:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal P_j} b_\alpha,
\]
and $q_j:=h_jm_j$. The total stratified block complexity is $Q(\mathcal P):=\sum_{j=1}^J q_j= \sum_{j=1}^J h_jm_j$.

We also write
\[
\cH_{\max}:=\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal B}b_\alpha,
\qquad
M:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal B}b_\alpha,
\]
for the largest block size and total ambient dimension of the compressed block system.
title: Block stratification

For data uniform on the sphere (dimension d >= 3) or Gaussian, labels with independent noise, and ANY width-m two-layer network with a continuous piecewise-linear activation (ReLU included), arbitrary unbounded weights, bias, and skip connection: fitting eps below the noise floor forces Lip(f) at least of order eps sqrt(n / (m log(C m n d / eps))) with high probability. This proves the Bubeck-Li-Nagaraj conjectured lower bound up to one logarithmic factor for the piecewise-linear class, removing the boundedness assumption; depth two is the critical case since the law fails at depth three with unbounded weights. The fully log-free, every-activation conjecture remains open.
