Method: Diameter-squared upper bound for transitive mixing explicit structural calculation Result: The cycle illustrates the missing spectral information. On the N-cycle, lazy eigenvalues are1-sin^2(pi*k/N). Since sin(pi*k/N)>=2*k/N for k<=N/2, the chi-square bound from a point is at most2*sum_(k>=1) exp(-8*t*k^2/N^2). At t=C*N^2 this sum is as small as desired for a universal C, proving the proposed diameter-squared order in this case without a log N penalty. Check: Use symmetry k versus N-k and(1-x)^(2t)<=exp(-2tx). The Gaussian series converges and tends to0 as C increases. The cycle diameter is floor(N/2) and its degree is2. Obstruction: For a general transitive graph, the gap alone bounds all N-1 modes by the same exponential and introduces log N. A uniform bound on low-frequency multiplicities or spectral mass strong enough to remove that factor is missing.

[Definition def:discrete_continuous_coupling of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let $X(t) = (x(t), (\sigma^1(t), \sigma^2(t)))$ be a continuous
  process as defined in definition
  (def:continuous_process_min_max_construction of the paper), with fixed
  parameters $\omega$ (resp. $\alpha$ and $\beta$) and $\ell$, and
  $\sigma^1(t)$ and
  $\sigma^2(t)$ two independent Markov jump
  processes with the transition rates of figure
  (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2016 of the paper)
  (resp. (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2017 of the paper)). Denote
  by $0 = T_0 < T_1 < \cdots$ the jump times of the couple
  $(\sigma^1, \sigma^2)$. For $L \ge 2$, let $N_1^L$ and $N_2^L$ be
  two independent Poisson processes with parameter
  $\gamma_L = (L - 1)/\ell$ independent of the $\sigma^i$.

  Recursively define $y^L$ by setting
\[
y^L(0) = \left\lfloor (L-1)x(0)/\ell\right\rfloor+ 1 \ \text{and}\  	z^L(t) := y^L(T_k) + \sum_{i = 1, 2} (-1)^i \sigma^i(T_k)
  \left[ N^L_i(t) - N^L_i(T_k) \right],
\]
  \begin{itemize}    
  \item if $(\sigma^1(T_k), \sigma^2(T_k)) \neq \pm (1, 1)$
$$
y^L(t) = \max \left[1,  \min \left[ L, z^L(t)  \right] \right] \text{ for } t \in [T_k, T_{k+1}],
$$
\item if $(\sigma^1(T_k), \sigma^2(T_k)) = \pm (1, 1)$
$$
y^L(t) = p_L \left( z^L(t) \right) \text{ for } t \in
[T_k, T_{k+1}]
$$
where $p_L : \mathbb Z \rightarrow \{1, \ldots, L\}$ is given by
$$
p_L(k + 2 m L) =
\left\{
\begin{array}{cl}
k &\text{ for } m \in \mathbb Z \text{ and } 1 \le k \le L, \\
2L + 1 - k &\text{ for } m \in \mathbb Z \text{ and } L + 1 \le k \le 2L.
\end{array}
\right.
$$
\end{itemize}

Finally, set $Y^L(t) = (y^L(t), (\sigma^1(t), \sigma^2(t)))$.

body: For an elliptic curve E over a number field K, the group E(K) of K-rational points is finitely generated: E(K) is isomorphic to a finite torsion group times Z^r, where r is the rank. The proof combines the weak Mordell-Weil theorem (E(K)/mE(K) finite, via Kummer theory and finiteness of class and unit groups) with a descent using height functions. Ranks are computable in practice but no general algorithm is proven; the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture ties r to the order of vanishing of the L-function at s = 1.

For each n let A_n,Phi_n be real symmetric n-by-n matrices with Phi_n positive semidefinite. Fix gamma>0,Im(z)>0,and nonzero alpha with Im(alpha)<=0. Define S_n(s)=(A_n+s^(-1)*Phi_n-zI)^(-1) and f_n(s)=alpha^(-1)+gamma*tr(S_n(s)Phi_n),tr=Tr/n. Suppose the empirical eigenvalue distributions of A_n and Phi_n converge weakly to deterministic probability measures,the limit for Phi_n is not delta_0,and f_n(s)->f(s) for every s in the open upper half-plane. Then s=f(s) has at most one solution with Im(s)>0. Existence is not part of this assertion. No uniform operator-norm bound on A_n or Phi_n is required by this source corollary. Draft,independent review pending.
The matrices,parameters and pointwise limits are as specified;gamma,alpha,z are fixed across n.
Weak spectral limits are probability measures and the covariance limit is not the point mass at0.
tr is normalized trace and compared roots lie strictly in the upper half-plane.

[Proposition prop:green-potential-L2-Cb of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] Fix $x\in\Omega_{\rm Fr}\cap\Omega_{\rm op}$.  For
$\theta\in L^2(M_x)$, define
\[
 u_\theta(z):=\int_DG_D(z,w)\theta(w)\,M_x(dw),
 \qquad z\in D.
\]
Then $u_\theta\in C_b(D)$ and
\begin{equation}
 [u_\theta]_{M_x}=G_x\theta,
 \qquad
 \|u_\theta\|_\infty
 \le K_G(x)^{1/2}\|\theta\|_{L^2(M_x)}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, the continuous representative is unique:
\[
 v\in C_b(D),\quad [v]_{M_x}=G_x\theta
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 v=u_\theta\quad\text{on }D.
\]

[Proposition prop:L2-thin of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] The coupling $(\bm{D}^{\bm{X},\kappa},\bm{D}^{\bm{Y},\kappa},\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa},\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa})$ defined in~(equation eq:comp_Poisson_measures of the paper) and~(equation eq:thining_coupling_defn of the paper) satisfies
\begin{equation}

\mathds{E}\bigg[\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\big|\bm{D}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_t-\bm{D}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_t\big|^2\bigg]
\leqslant 4\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\1_{B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})|\bm{w}|^2|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|
    \mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}).
\end{equation}
Moreover, if $\nu_{\bm{X}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})$ and $\nu_{\bm{Y}}(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})$ have a finite second moment, then 
\begin{gather*}
\mathds{E}\bigg[\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\big|\bm{D}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_t+\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_t-(\bm{D}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_t+\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_t)-\bm{m}_\kappa t\big|^2\bigg]
\leqslant 4\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}|\bm{w}|^2|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|
    \mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\quad\text{and}\\
\mathcal{W}_2(\bm{X},\bm{Y})
\leqslant |\bm{\gamma}_{\bm{X},\kappa}-\bm{\gamma}_{\bm{Y},\kappa}+\bm{m}_\kappa|
    + 2 d^{1/2} |\bm{\Sigma_X}-\bm{\Sigma_Y}|
    + 2\bigg(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}|\bm{w}|^2|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|
    \mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\bigg)^{1/2},
\end{gather*}
where the mean $\bm{m}_\kappa:=\mathds{E}[\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_1-\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_1]
=\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\bm{w}\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})

[Thm 3.1 of arXiv:2606.16237, 'The Backward Stochastic Partial Differential Integral Equations: Solvability and Compariso'] Assume that Assumptions (ass:b1 of the paper)--(mz4 of the paper) hold. If
$f_0 \in \mathbb{H}^{-1}$ and $\varphi \in L^2_{\mathscr{F}_T}(\Omega; L^2)$,
then BSPDIE (equation eq:2.1 of the paper) admits a unique weak solution $(u,q,r) \in \mathbb{S}^2(H^0) \cap \mathbb{H}^1 \times \mathbb{H}^0 \times \mathbb{H}^{\nu,0}$ satisfying
\[
\mathbb{E} \left[\sup_{0 \leq t \leq T} \|u(t)\|_0^2 \right] + |||u|||_1^2 + |||q|||_0^2 + |||r|||_{\nu,0}^2 \leq C \left( |||f_0|||_{-1}^2 + \mathbb{E}[\|\varphi\|_0^2] \right),
\]
where $C = C(L, \kappa, \alpha, \delta, T)$ is a positive constant.

body: [Proposition 8 of arXiv:2609.03070, 'Variants of order semicontinuity in Banach lattices'] Assume that $F$ is a vector lattice with PPP and let $Q\subset F_{+}$ and $e\in F$ be such that $e=\bigvee Q$. Then, for every $0\le r<1$ there is a disjoint $D\subset F_{+}$ such that $\bigvee D=re$ and for every $d\in D$ there is $q\in Q$ such that $d\le q$. Moreover, if $Q$ is countable then $D$ can also be chosen to be countable.

[Lemma lem_decode of arXiv:2608.15344, 'A Harris recurrent continuous-time Markov process without wide-sense regenerative structur'] There exists a Borel measurable function $c:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}$ with the following property. Let
\[
p=(p_0,p_1,\dots,p_m),\;\;\;\;q=(q_0,q_1,\dots,q_n)
\]
be two finite simple directed paths (no vertex is visited more than once) with the same initial vertex ($p_0=q_0$) and the same terminal vertex ($p_m=q_n$). If
\[
d=\sum_{i=1}^ml(p_{i-1},p_i)-\sum_{i=1}^nl(q_{i-1},q_i)\neq0,
\]
then $c(d)$ is a non-initial vertex occurring in both $p$ and $q$, i.e., 
\[
c(d)\in\{p_1,\dots,p_m\}\cap\{q_1,\dots,q_n\}.
\]

[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2608.29855, 'Growth of Simple Closed Geodesics in closed Hyperbolic $3$-Manifolds'] For every $0<\varepsilon<1$ there exist a finite set
$S\subset\Gamma^+$, an open spherical disk
$D\subset\partial\hts$, and constants $\alpha,R>0$ such that,
with
$$
U_S\coloneqq \max_{s\in S}d(o,so),
$$
the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $s(\overline D)\subset D$ for every $s\in S$, and the sets
$s(\overline D)$ are pairwise disjoint;
\item the positive semigroup on $S$ is free;
\item for every bi-infinite sequence $(s_j)_{j\in\Z}$ with
$s_j\in S$, if $P_0=e$, $P_{j+1}=P_js_{j+1}$, and $x_j=P_jo$, then
\begin{equation}
    \alpha|p-q|
\le
d(x_p,x_q)
\le
U_S|p-q|
\qquad(p,q\in\Z);
\end{equation}
\item every periodic positive $S$-word corresponds to a loxodromic element of $\Gamma^+$ and has a periodic broken geodesic at Hausdorff distance at most $R$ from its axis;
\item
$$
\frac{\log|S|}{U_S}>2-\varepsilon.
$$
\end{enumerate}

[Definition 12 (\cite{xia1996vector}) of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] We say that $\Phi$ is a scaling function for a vector-valued multiresolution analysis $\{V_j\}_{j\in \mathbb{Z}}$ of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}^m)$ if the sequence $\{V_j\}_{j\in \mathbb{Z}}$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(VMRA\arabic*)}]
\item $V_{j}\subset V_{j+1}$ for all $j\in \mathbb{Z}$.
\item $\bigcap_{j\in\mathbb{Z}} V_j=\{0\}$ and $\bigcup_{j\in \mathbb{Z}} V_j$ is dense in $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}^m)$.
\item $h\in V_j$ if and only if $h(A\cdot)\in V_{j+1}$ for all $j\in\mathbb{Z}$.
\item $h\in V_j$ if and only if $h(\cdot-k)\in V_{j}$ for all $j\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $k\in\mathbb{Z}^d$.
\item The sequence $\{\Phi(\cdot-k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V_0$.
\end{enumerate}

Let Delta be a real d-by-k matrix of rank r_star>=1, C a positive definite d-by-d matrix and G=C Delta. Let A be d-by-h, B h-by-k with h>=r_star. Consider simultaneous factor GD A_next=A-eta C(AB-Delta)B^T and B_next=B-eta A^T C(AB-Delta), at any finite steps eta, initialized at arbitrary A_0 and B_0=0. Then row(B_t) is contained in row(Delta)=row(G) at every integer t>=0, equivalently B_t(I-P)=0 for the orthogonal projector P onto row(Delta). This inclusion version of the known zero-factor alignment component is the content used from Zhang-Liu-Chen, LoRA-One, arXiv:2502.01235, Theorem 3.1 and Appendix C.1 Theorem C.10 (printed pp.26-27). It does not imply that A_t has aligned, that B_t has full rank, or that the product has fitted Delta. The induction applies to the noiseless quadratic C-metric loss; with additive noise the sample gradient generally has larger rank, so a rank-r_star invariant signal subspace no longer follows.
Real exact-rank-r_star target; positive definite input covariance; h>=r_star
Zero initial output-side factor, arbitrary input-side factor; simultaneous ordinary GD on the noiseless covariance quadratic
Conclusion is a row-space inclusion, not rank equality or residual convergence

[Proposition 18 of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] The family $\{\mathbf{V}_j\}_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}$ is an MRA of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with dyadic dilation $2$ and integer
translations. Moreover, for each $j\in\mathbb{Z}$ one has the orthogonal decomposition
\[
\mathbf{V}_{j+1}
=
\mathbf{V}_j\ \oplus\ \bigoplus_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d\setminus\{0\}} \mathbf{W}_j^{(\epsilon)},
\]
where
\[
\mathbf{W}_j^{(\epsilon)}
=
\bigotimes_{\ell=1}^d X_{j}^{(\epsilon_\ell)},
\qquad
X_{j}^{(0)}=V_j,\ \ X_{j}^{(1)}=W_j.
\]
In particular,
\[
L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)
=
\mathbf{V}_0\ \oplus\ \bigoplus_{j\ge 0}\ \bigoplus_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^d\setminus\{0\}} \mathbf{W}_j^{(\epsilon)},
\]
and the associated orthonormal wavelet basis consists of the usual $2^d-1$ wavelet types (one for each
$\epsilon\neq 0$), obtained by tensoring the scalar scaling functions and mother wavelets componentwise.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: Finite-volume stationarity gives pi_V*K_v,V=pi_V for addition at v. To pass this identity through a local limit, truncate the avalanche at a radius r. If its influence on an observed window leaves that ball with probability at most epsilon_r, uniformly in outer V, then for each bounded local test f the discrepancy between the full and truncated expectations is at most 2*||f||_infinity*epsilon_r. The truncated operator is local and continuous, so subsequential limits inherit addition invariance if epsilon_r tends to zero. Check: Use the same stacks up to the exit from the radius-r ball. On the no-exit event the two evaluations agree, giving the bound directly. This requires a uniform probability estimate; finite-volume almost-sure stabilization alone is not enough. Obstruction: Uniform localization is missing and may fail for critical avalanches. Even inherited addition invariance would still need a uniqueness theorem to identify all subsequential limits.

    E V_j<=C_(K0,T)(j+1)/n,
    E V_j^2<=C_(K0,T)(j+1)^2/n^2.                            (3)

Indeed, conditionally on K_j=q and V_j=v,
E V_(j+1)^p <=(1+C/n)v^p+(C/n)v^(p-1) for p=1,2.
Sum first for p=1, then for p=2, starting at V0=1/(nK0). All moments
are finite: conditional inverse sample moments are uniformly finite by
C044 on0<q<=Q, and iteration through finitely many layers preserves this.

Let M_k be the martingale of centered reciprocal increments. C045(5)
and (3) imply

    ||M_k||_2<=C[sqrt(k^3/n^3)+sqrt(k)/n].

The drift estimate C045(6), (2)-(3), and Minkowski give

    ||V_k-V0-2k/n-M_k||_2
        <=C[k(k+1)/n^2+log(k+1)/n+k/n^2
                                      +k(k+1)/n^(5/2)].

This is the C040 martingale argument with K replacing theta and a=2.
It uses no independence between the current state and its conditional
drift; only orthogonality of martingale differences across layers.
Consequently for Z_k=nV_k/k,

    ||Z_k-2||_2<=C[k^(-1/2)+sqrt(k/n)].

Since 1/Z_k=kK_k has a uniformly bounded second moment by (2), inversion
is controlled exactly as in C040: on Z_k>=1 the inverse map is Lipschitz;
on its complement Chebyshev and Cauchy-Schwarz bound the L1 contribution
by C||Z_k-2||_2. This proves(1).

In particular, for fixed t>0 and N=floor(nt),

    sum_(k=1)^(N-1) E K_k=(1/2)log(n)+O_(K0,t)(1),            (4)

because the absolute error term in E K_k is bounded by
C[k^(-3/2)+1/sqrt(nk)], whose sum is bounded through N<=tn.

## C047: a logarithmic bias for the exact reciprocal mean

For every fixed K0>0 and t>0,

    E[1/(nK_floor(nt))]
      = exp(2t)-1 -(5/6)exp(2t)log(n)/n+O_(K0,t)(1/n).        (5)

The limiting mean exp(2t)-1 is the mean of the reciprocal SDE
dV=(2V+2)dt+sqrt(2)VdW,V0=0. This numerical coefficient identifies the
leading logarithmic correction, not the coefficient of the remaining1/n
term. The statement concerns an exact integrable raw reciprocal mean,
unlike the ReLU angle reciprocal.

Proof. Write h=1/n. The exact conditional mean of the limiting linear
diffusion after time h from v is

    L_h(v)=(v+1)exp(2h)-1.

C045(4), subtracting the h^2 coefficient2v+2 of L_h(v)-v, gives on
K=q<=epsilon

    E[V_next | v]-L_h(v)
      =[2v-6-5/(3v)]/n^2+rho_n(v),
    |rho_n(v)|<=C[v/n^(5/2)
                   +(1+v+1/v+1/v^2)/n^3+v exp(-cn)].        (6)

On epsilon<q<=Q, v<=1/(n epsilon). The global inverse sample moment
bound gives E V_next<=C_Q v<=C/n. Both L_h(v)-v and the displayed main
correction in(6) are also O(1/n), since1/v=nq<=nQ. Hence the remaining
defect is bounded by C_Q/n on this large-variance range.

Along the exact chain, the expected number of large-variance visits is
bounded by epsilon^(-2)sum E K_k^2<=C_(K0,T), by (2). On the small range,
use (2)-(3) and1/V_k=nK_k in(6). Summation through N<=Tn yields

    sum_(k=0)^(N-1) E|rho_n(V_k)|<=C_(K0,T)/n.               (7)

For clarity, the inverse-square contribution is at most
n^(-1)sum E K_k^2=O(1/n); the inverse first-power contribution is
O(log(n+1)/n^2); the v/n^(5/2) term sums to O(n^(-3/2)); all remaining
terms are smaller or O(1/n). The large-variance bound was included
separately, so(7) does not apply the small-q Taylor series globally.

Let w_k=exp(2(t_n-(k+1)/n)), t_n=N/n. The affine nature of L_h makes
conditional-mean telescoping exact:

    E V_N - [(V0+1)exp(2t_n)-1]
      =sum_(k=0)^(N-1) w_k E[E(V_(k+1)|V_k)-L_h(V_k)].       (8)

All expectations are legitimate by (3). The weighted sum of the errors
in(7) remains O(1/n). The nonsingular correction2V_k-6 in(6) contributes
O(1/n), using (3). The singular correction contributes

    -(5/(3n)) sum_(k=0)^(N-1) w_k E K_k.

The k=0 term is O_(K0,t)(1/n). For k>=1,
|w_k-exp(2t)|<=C_t(k+1)/n, so (2) bounds the total weighted occupation
error by a constant. Equation(4) therefore gives

    sum_(k=1)^(N-1) w_k E K_k
                        =(exp(2t)/2)log(n)+O_(K0,t)(1).

Insert this into(8), and use V0=1/(nK0), |t_n-t|<=1/n. The initial-state
and fractional-layer effects are O(1/n). This proves(5).

## Scope

C047 is a first finite-width correction for an exactly critical unshaped
tanh scalar observable; it does not prove Target3's all-order uniform
finite-width cumulant expansion. Its proof does not require C026 and
never replaces the model by the shaped tanh model in Li-Nica-Roy.
Independent review is required for C044's inverse-tail deletion, the
coefficient -5/3 in C045, and the global summation of the small-q remainder.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:33310ec7d7ee9992c8f2862dbcd7608afde5016da91276ffa01336685b6b5ff6","revision_digest":"sha256:515fe058a5192e3ef08957c4adfba4362dd6ba75e9ef9800f5baddd34aefb3eb","source_id":"owner-own-work:T244-w691-C047:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma lem:comXs of arXiv:2510.26724, 'Sharp Fuss-Catalan thresholds in graph bootstrap percolation'] Suppose that $S$ is a 
partial TWG for a given edge $e$, 
with 
\begin{itemize}
\item $\sigma=\sigma(S)$ many vertices not in $e$; and 
\item edge efficiency $\mathcal E=\mathcal E(S)$. 
\end{itemize}
Suppose also that $V$ 
is a vertex set of size $(r-2)k+2$
that contains 
\begin{itemize}
\item all vertices in $S$; 
\item the edge $e$; and 
\item an additional 
$\sigma'=(r-2)k-\sigma$
other vertices.
\end{itemize}
Then the number of $k$-TWGs $T$ for $e$ 
on $V$  
such that $S\subsetneq T$ is at most
\[
k^{c(\mathcal E+1)}\gamma^{\sigma'}\sigma'!,
\]
for some constants $c$ 
depending only on $r$.

Let f be twice continuously differentiable on [a,b]. For the composite trapezoidal rule with n equal subintervals of width h = (b-a)/n and nodes x_k = a + k*h, approximating the integral by T_n = h * ( f(x_0)/2 + f(x_1) + ... + f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)/2 ), the error satisfies integral_a^b f(x) dx - T_n = -( (b-a) * h^2 / 12 ) * f''(xi) for some xi in (a,b). In particular, | integral_a^b f(x) dx - T_n | <= ( (b-a) * h^2 / 12 ) * max_{x in [a,b]} |f''(x)|, so the error shrinks quadratically in h (equivalently as 1/n^2) as the number of subintervals grows.

[Lemma lem:metric-solver-detailed of arXiv:2609.00556, 'Higgs--Demailly System and Positivity of Higgs Bundles'] Let $f$ range in a bounded subset of $C^{2,\gamma}(M)$.  There is a unique
positive determinant-one endomorphism $V$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \sqrt{-1}\Lambda_\omega\left(
 R^0_{h_{\rm ref}}+\bar\partial(V^{-1}\partial^{h_{\rm ref}}V)
 +[\theta,V^{-1}\theta_{h_{\rm ref}}^*V]
 \right)=-e^f\log V.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $V$ is bounded in $C^{4,\gamma}$ on bounded sets of $f$ and

[Corollary 14 (First and second variation equations) of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Let \(\gamma\in\Opendenseset_\alpha\) and
\(h,h_1,h_2\in\Hoelder{\alpha/2}([0,1])\). Then
\(V_h^\gamma\in\mathcal X_1\) is the unique solution of
\begin{equation}

\begin{cases}
-\partial_s V_h^\gamma
=
\gamma(s)L_s^\gamma V_h^\gamma
+
\dfrac12h(s)v^\gamma,
& (s,x)\in[0,1)\times\R,
\\[0.6ex]
V_h^\gamma(1,x)=0,
& x\in\R,
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
where \(v^\gamma\) is the quantity fixed in Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}.
Moreover, \(W_{h_1,h_2}^\gamma\in\mathcal X_1\) is the unique solution of
\begin{equation}

\begin{cases}
\begin{aligned}
-\partial_s W_{h_1,h_2}^\gamma
={}&
\gamma(s)L_s^\gamma W_{h_1,h_2}^\gamma
+
h_1(s)L_s^\gamma V_{h_2}^\gamma
+
h_2(s)L_s^\gamma V_{h_1}^\gamma
\\
&+
\gamma(s)s\,\partial_xV_{h_1}^\gamma\,\partial_xV_{h_2}^\gamma,
\end{aligned}
& (s,x)\in[0,1)\times\R,
\\[0.6ex]
W_{h_1,h_2}^\gamma(1,x)=0,
& x\in\R.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
The map \(h\mapsto V_h^\gamma\) is linear, and
\((h_1,h_2)\mapsto W_{h_1,h_2}^\gamma\) is symmetric bilinear.

  Let $A=(A_{t})_{t \geq 0}$ be a PCAF and let $\nu$ be the associated smooth measure.
  Let $F \colon (0,\infty) \times \Omega \to [0,\infty]$ be 
  $\mathcal{B}((0,\infty)) \otimes \EuScript{F}_{\infty}$-measurable, set
  $F_{t}(\omega) \coloneqq F(t, \omega)$ for $(t, \omega) \in (0,\infty) \times \Omega$,
  and assume that the following conditions are satisfied:
  \begin{enumerate} [label = \textup{(\roman*)}]
    \item  
    there exists a set $\Lambda \in \EuScript{F}_{\infty}$ with $P_x(\Lambda) = 1$ for all $x \in M$ such that
    the function $(0,\infty) \times \Omega \ni (t, \omega) \mapsto 1_{\Lambda}(\omega) F_{t} \circ \theta_{t}(\omega) = 1_{\Lambda}(\omega) F_{t}(\theta_{t}\omega)$ is 
    $\mathcal{B}((0,\infty)) \otimes \EuScript{F}_{\infty}$-measurable;
    \item  
      the function $(0,\infty) \times M \ni (t, x) \mapsto E_{x}[F_{t}]$ is Borel measurable.
  \end{enumerate}

  \begin{equation} 
    E_{x}\biggl[ \int_{0}^{t} F_s \circ \theta_{s}\, dA_{s} \biggr]
    =

DRAFT proof (unaudited), T421-W706-005 v1. The common-fixed-point conclusion of Theorem 1 as printed on p.7 of Bock-Weiss arXiv:2210.02070v1 does not follow from its hypotheses. On the closed set X=[0,2], the maps T(t,x)=x/2+2^(-t), t>=0, map X to X, contract uniformly by 1/2, and satisfy |T(t+1,x)-T(t,x)|=2^(-t-1). But their individual fixed points 2^(1-t) are different, so they have no common fixed point. The trajectories do converge to 0, the fixed point of the limiting map; common-fixed-point and limiting-fixed-point statements must be distinguished. This checks the printed statement only, not the validity of the paper as a whole.

[Lemma 10 of arXiv:2604.09248, '\bfseries Limit laws for longest edges in empty region graphs'] Assume that {$S$ is as in \eqref{eq:SetswithoutRot} with a compact and star-shaped set $K\subset\RR^d$} and let $c>0$. Let $x,y,u,v \in \RR^d$ be such that $\lVert x-y \rVert \ge \lVert u-v \rVert$. Then,
\[
\vol(S(x,y)\setminus S(u,v)) \ge {1\over c+1}{\vol(K)\over {\rm diam}(K)} \Big\lVert \frac{x+y}{2} - \frac{u+v}{2} \Big\rVert \lVert x-y \rVert^{d-1},
\]
whenever {$\lVert \frac{x+y}{2} - \frac{u+v}{2} \rVert\leq c\,{\rm diam}(K) \lVert x-y \rVert$.}

    $\psi$ is regularly varying of index $\alpha\in (0,2)$ at zero, i.e.,

    \begin{equation}
       p_\lambda(t,x,y) \sim \frac{\mathcal{A}_{d,\alpha}}{\lambda} |y|^{-d} \psi(|y|^{-1}).
    \end{equation}

[Theorem BEBT! of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] Let $A$ be a random Hermitian matrix of size $N$ and assume
  that for every $r \in \mathbb{N}$ one has
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \log \mathbb{E} [H \text{} C (x_1, \ldots,
    x_r, 0^{N - r} ; \lambda_1 (A), \ldots, \lambda_N (A))] = \sum_{i = 1}^r
    \Psi (x_i), 
  \end{equation}
  where $\Psi$ is a smooth function in a neighborhood of $0$ and the above
  convergence is uniform in a neighborhood of $0^r$. Then for every $k \in
  \mathbb{N}$, the $k$-th moment of the random measure $\sum_{i = 1}^N
  \delta \left( N^{- 1} \lambda_i (A) \right)$ converges as $N \rightarrow \infty$ in
  probability to $\Psi^{(k)} (0) / (k - 1) !$.
title: Theorem BEBT! of arXiv:2412.09290

so $\ket{\sqrt{\pi_t}}=\mathcal{E}\ket{\psi_{\theta(t)}}$ and

  \\\displaystyle

\end{array}\right.

Then, for all $p\geq 1$, the unique solution of the markovian BSDE in ((fbsde of the paper)) is such that
\[
 \Vert Y-Y^n\Vert _{{\cal S}^p}+\Vert Z-Z^n\Vert_{{\cal M}^p}\rightarrow 0 \qquad \text{as }n\rightarrow \infty.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Test the d = 3 analogue of the Apollonian structure on the simplest candidates (diagonal matrices). Result: Gamma(Z^d) is the set of symmetric matrices A for which there is an integer-valued function on Z^d whose discrete Laplacian is at most the constant ... with quadratic growth A: g(x) = (1/2) x^T A x + (lower order) integer-valued superharmonic. Diagonal A = diag(a_1,...,a_d): g(x) = sum_i (1/2) a_i x_i^2 rounded is integer-valued; the discrete Laplacian of x -> ceil(a x^2 / 2) in one dimension is at most a + 1 ... in one dimension the maximal a with an integer superharmonic quadratic of curvature a is determined by the 1D odometer; for diagonal matrices the problem separates into d one-dimensional problems and the maximal diagonal elements are rational (the 1D maximal curvatures are rational, e.g. the 1D sandpile has only finitely many patterns). This gives rational maximal elements on the diagonal slice, but maximality in Gamma(Z^d) (not just among diagonal matrices) is not implied: a diagonal A might be dominated by a non-diagonal B. In d = 2 the LPS classification shows the maximal elements are dense in the boundary and rational; for d = 3 the analogue of the Apollonian packing would be a packing by spheres of a slab, whose tangency structure has more degrees of freedom (a sphere touching four others is not determined by rational data in general: Descartes-type relations in 3D involve a quadratic form on curvatures with generic irrational solutions unless the initial spheres are chosen integrally). This suggests that rationality may FAIL in d = 3 unless the initial configuration forces integrality via the Soddy-Gosset relation with integer curvatures; the analogue of the band packing in d = 3 has initial curvatures determined by the lattice (integer), and integral Apollonian-type packings in 3D do have all curvatures integral when the initial ones are (Soddy-Gosset gives a quadratic recursion preserving integrality). So rationality is plausible in d = 3 if the correspondence to packings persists, and isolation would be false (packings are dense in the boundary). Recorded as a conjectural picture with the Soddy-Gosset integrality argument as the reason to expect rational entries. Key identity: If the d = 3 maximal elements correspond to a sphere packing generated from integer initial curvatures, Soddy-Gosset integrality gives rational entries. Obstruction: No d = 3 analogue of the LPS correspondence between Gamma(Z^d) and packings.

[Thm 7 of arXiv:2604.11489, '2604.11489'] Let $\{X_n, n\ge 1\}$ be a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables with common nonuniform distribution $\{p_i, i\ge 1\}$ satisfying $\ee|\ln p(X_1)|^{2+\delta} < \infty$. Assume that there exists an integer valued function $K(n)$ such that, for some $0< \delta<\frac{1}{2}$,
\beq
K(n)\le n^{\frac{1}{2}-\delta},\ \ n^{\frac{1}{2}+\delta}\ln n\sum_{i=K(n)}^{\infty}p_i \leq C
\ \ \text{and}\ \ -n^{\frac{1}{2}+\delta}\sum_{i=K(n)}^{\infty}p_i\ln p_i\leq C.
\deq
If there exists an $\epsilon \in (1/2, 1)$ with
\beq
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}p_{i}^{1-\epsilon}<\infty,
\deq
then we have
\beq
\sup_x\left|\pp\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}(\hat H_{JK}-H)\le x\right)-\Phi(x)\right|\le
Cn^{-\frac{\delta}{2}}+Cn^{\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\epsilon}{2}},
\deq
where $\Phi$ denotes the standard normal distribution function and $\sigma^2=Var(\ln p(X_1))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm 7 of arXiv:2604.11489

body: [Definition 1.1 (Connective constants) of arXiv:2604.02746, 'Zero-Freeness of the Hard-Core Model with Bounded Connective Constant'] For a family H of finite graphs, the k-depth connective constant of H for a fixed k, denoted by µk(H), is supG∈H µk(G). The lower connective constant of H, denoted by µinf(H), is infk≥1 µk(H). For an infinite graph G, let HG denote the set of all finite subgraphs of G. We establish the following relationship: for any infinite graph G with connective constant σ(G), µinf(HG) ≤σ(G).
title: Definition 1.1 (Connective constants) of arXiv:2604.02746: Zero-Freeness of the Hard-Core Model with Bounded Connective Constant

body: [Theorem 4.4 of arXiv:2510.05566, 'Domain-Shift-Aware Conformal Prediction for Large Language Models'] shows that the same discrepancy term governing the lower bound also governs possible over-coverage. The only additional term is E[πn+1], which is the expected mass assigned to the point at infinity. This term appears because the empirical score distribution used by DS-CP includes the regularization mass λ, and hence the resulting quantile can be inflated relative to the oracle exchangeable benchmark.

body: For an m by n real or complex matrix A with entries a_{ij} and singular values sigma_1 >= ... >= sigma_{min(m,n)} >= 0, the Frobenius norm is ||A||_F = sqrt(sum_{i,j} |a_{ij}|^2) = sqrt(trace(A* A)) = sqrt(sum_i sigma_i^2). The Frobenius norm is the norm induced by the trace inner product <A,B> = trace(A* B) on the space of m by n matrices, and it is submultiplicative: ||AB||_F <= ||A||_F ||B||_F whenever the product is defined. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Matrix Analysis]
title: Frobenius (Hilbert-Schmidt) Norm of a Matrix

[Theorem 2.4 of arXiv:2110.05374, 'When Janson meets McDiarmid: Bounded difference inequalities under graph-dependence'] Let the Ω-valued random vector X be G-dependent and let f : Ω → R be forest-decomposable c-Lipschitz with respect to G. Then for every t > 0, P(f(X) − E[f(X)] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−2t²/D(G, c)), where D(G, c) := min over {(F_k, w_k)}_k ∈ FFC(G) of ( Σ_k w_k √( Σ_{{i,j}∈E(G[F_k])} (c_i + c_j)² + Σ_{T∈T(F_k)} c_{min,k,T}² ) )², with c_{min,k,T} := min{c_i : i ∈ T} for T ∈ T(F_k). By Remark 2.5 of the paper, D(G, c) ≤ χ_f(G)‖c‖₂², the denominator of Janson's inequality (take a fractional independent vertex cover).
c-Lipschitz (Definition 1.1 of the paper): Ω = Ω_1 × ... × Ω_n is a product of Polish spaces, c = (c_1, ..., c_n) ∈ R_+^n, and f : Ω → R is c-Lipschitz when |f(x) − f(x')| ≤ Σ_{i=1}^n c_i 1{x_i ≠ x'_i} for all x, x' ∈ Ω (Lipschitz for the c-weighted Hamming distance).
G-dependent (Definition 1.3 of the paper): X = (X_i)_{i∈V(G)} is G-dependent when for all disjoint S, T ⊂ V(G) with no edge of G between S and T, the families (X_i)_{i∈S} and (X_j)_{j∈T} are independent; this is stronger than pairwise independence of non-adjacent coordinates.
Fractional forest vertex cover: a family {(F_k, w_k)}_k with F_k ⊆ V(G), w_k ∈ [0, 1] and Σ_{k: v∈F_k} w_k = 1 for every v ∈ V(G), such that each F_k induces a forest G[F_k]; T(F_k) is the set of vertex sets of the trees of G[F_k], and FFC(G) is the set of all fractional forest vertex covers of G.
Forest-decomposable c-Lipschitz with respect to G (Section 2.2 of the paper): for every {(F_k, w_k)}_k ∈ FFC(G) there are (c_i)_{i∈F_k}-Lipschitz functions f_k : Ω_{F_k} → R with f(x) = Σ_k w_k f_k(x_{F_k}) for all x ∈ Ω. The paper's sentence puts 'for all x' before 'there exist f_k'; the f_k cannot depend on x, since constant f_k would then make every f decomposable.

Let X = (X_1,...,X_n) have independent real coordinates. (Thm 1.1) If each X_i has density <= K a.e., then for every orthogonal projection P onto a d-dimensional subspace, PX has density <= (CK)^d a.e., C absolute. (Thm 1.2) For d = 1 the optimal constant is sqrt(2): if sum a_j^2 = 1, sum a_jX_j has density <= sqrt(2)K, attained by (X_1+X_2)/sqrt(2) with X_i uniform on [-1/(2K),1/(2K)]. (Cor 1.4) With L(Z,t) = sup_u P(||Z-u||_2 <= t): if L(X_i,t) <= p for all i, then L(PX, t sqrt(d)) <= (Cp)^d. (Thm 1.5) For every m x n matrix A and delta in (0,1), L(AX, t||A||_HS) <= (C_delta p)^{(1-delta) r(A)}, where r(A) = ||A||_HS^2/||A||^2 is the stable rank and C_delta depends only on delta; with densities <= K this reads L(AX, t||A||_HS) <= (C_delta K t)^{(1-delta) r(A)}.

Assumes: independent real coordinates; densities bounded by K a.e. (Thms 1.1-1.2) or L(X_i,t) <= p (Cor 1.4, Thm 1.5); P an orthogonal projection of rank d; A arbitrary in Thm 1.5

body: [Theorem 1.2 (The Power of Few for sparse graphs) of arXiv:2302.05605, 'The "Power of Few" Phenomenon: The Sparse Case'] Consider a set V of n vertices with an arbitrary partition V = R ∪B where |R| = n/2 + ∆, then draw a G(n, p) random graph over V . If n −10 ≥pn ≥(1 + λ) log n and p∆≥10, where λ > 0 is a constant, then majority dynamics on G with initial coloring (R, B) achieves a Red unanimity within time O(logpn n) with probability at least 1 −O  1 min{n, p∆2} + n−λ/2  .
title: Theorem 1.2 (The Power of Few for sparse graphs) of arXiv:2302.05605: The "Power of Few" Phenomenon: The Sparse Case

body:
Let p be a prime, f a polynomial with coefficients in the p-adic integers Z_p (in particular any polynomial with integer coefficients), and a in Z_p with f(a) congruent to 0 modulo p and f'(a) not congruent to 0 modulo p. Then there is a unique alpha in Z_p with f(alpha) = 0 and alpha congruent to a modulo p. Concretely: a simple root of f modulo p lifts to a unique root modulo p^k for every k, and these lifts converge p-adically to the root alpha. The general form replaces the hypothesis by |f(a)|_p < |f'(a)|_p^2, which allows f'(a) to be divisible by p.
p prime, f in Z_p[x], a in Z_p
f(a) congruent to 0 mod p
f'(a) a p-adic unit (a SIMPLE root modulo p); the double-root case needs the general form |f(a)|_p < |f'(a)|_p^2

body: The set R of real numbers is uncountable: there is no surjection from N onto R, hence no bijection between N and R. Equivalently, for every sequence x_1, x_2, x_3, ... of real numbers there is a real number different from every x_n.

Let x_1, x_2, ... be any sequence in [0,1]. Choose for each x_n a decimal expansion x_n = 0.d(n,1) d(n,2) d(n,3) ... (each digit d(n,k) in {0, ..., 9}). Define a new number x = 0.b_1 b_2 b_3 ... by the diagonal rule: b_n = 5 if d(n,n) is not 5, and b_n = 6 if d(n,n) = 5. Then x lies in [0,1], and its expansion differs from the chosen expansion of x_n in the n-th digit for every n. Because all digits of x lie in {5, 6}, its expansion contains no infinite tail of 0s or of 9s, and a real number can have two distinct decimal expansions only when one ends in all 9s and the other in all 0s; hence x has exactly one decimal expansion. If x were equal to some x_n as a real number, the chosen expansion of x_n would be a decimal expansion of x differing from x's unique expansion (they differ in digit n), which is impossible. So x differs from every x_n, and no sequence lists all of [0,1]. Since [0,1] is a subset of R, no sequence lists R, so R is uncountable.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:81845b66a64fd9e8baa9830788af1d24ccfa7255e76ef65a7c1032858629b23b","revision_digest":"sha256:5217c7a5ca26073bea088c4a23a842fa0dd29c9f47c16b42b319b5cc59055627","source_id":"wikipedia:Cantor's_diagonal_argument","source_revision":"as-read-2026-08-02","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}
title: Uncountability of the real numbers (Cantor's diagonal argument)

[Definition def:decograph of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Let $(G,o,w)$ be a vertex-rooted (resp.\ edge-rooted) weighted graph. Fix $I$ an integer and $(f_i)_{i \in \{1,...,I\}}$ some functions from $\overset{\rightarrow}{E}$ to $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$. We then say that
    $(G,o,w,(f_i)_{i \in \{1,...,I\}})$ is a \emph{decorated} vertex-rooted (resp.\ edge-rooted) weighted graph.  If $f_i$ is symmetrical then we will identify it with a map from $E$ to $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$.

[Lemma lem:ricci-removal of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $P_z$ be the rank-one projector onto a unit decomposable bivector and
$C_z=P_z-N^{-1}I_W$.  If $L_z=-2z_{\rm mat}^2$ is the orthogonal
projector onto the plane of $z$, put
\[
 B_z=\frac{L_z-(2/n)I_H}{n-2}.
\tag{2.6.2}
\]
Then the orthogonal curvature decomposition is
\[
 C_z=W_z+X_{B_z},\qquad W_z\in\mathcal W,
 \qquad X_B(u\wedge v)=Bu\wedge v+u\wedge Bv,
\tag{2.6.3}
\]
with no scalar or $\Lambda^4H$ summand, and
\[
 \|B_z\|_\mathrm{op}=\frac1n,\qquad
 \|B_z\|_F^2=\frac{2}{n(n-2)},\qquad
 \|X_B\|_2^2=(n-2)\|B\|_F^2,\qquad
 \|X_B\|_\mathrm{op}\le2\|B\|_\mathrm{op}.
\tag{2.6.4}
\]

In the cumulative moving frame the transported $B_z$ are reverse
martingale differences.  If $\mathfrak B_r$ is their sum, then
\[
 \mathbb E\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^2=\frac{2r}{n(n-2)},\qquad
 \mathbb E\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^4
 \le C\frac{r^2}{n^2(n-2)^2},
\tag{2.6.5}
\]
and, for fixed $c$, uniformly over $r\le cN$,
\[
 \max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_\mathrm{op}=o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\tag{2.6.6}
\]
More quantitatively, for every fixed $L$ and $1\le p\le L\log n$,
\[
 \left(\mathbb E\max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_\mathrm{op}^p\right)^{1/p}
 \le C_{c,L}\left(
 \sqrt{\frac{p+\log n}{n}}+\frac{p+\log n}{n}
 \right)=o(1).
\tag{2.6.6a}
\]
The same martingale satisfies the dimension-free Frobenius estimate
\[
 \left(\mathbb E\max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^p\right)^{1/p}
 \le C_c\sqrt p,
 \qquad 2\le p\le L\log n.
\tag{2.6.6b}
\]

Finally let $A_i=\operatorname{ad}_{a_i}$.  For traceless symmetric $B$
on $H$ and arbitrary $Z\in\operatorname{End}(W)$, define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R_i(B,Z)&=\{X_B,[A_i,Z]\}a_i,&
 U_i(B,Z)&=\{X_B,Z\}a_i,\\
 E_i(B,Z)&=\{X_{[a_i,B]},Z\}a_i,&
 \bar E(B,Z)&=N^{-1}\sum_iE_i(B,Z).
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.6.7}
\]
Put $\Psi(T)=\sum_jA_jTa_j$ and
$H_B(Z)=-N^{-1}X_B\Psi(Z)$.  Then the exact two-gradient decomposition is
\[
 \boxed{\mathcal R_i=A_iU_i-(E_i-\bar E)
 -\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j-H_B(Z)},
 \qquad
 \bar E=\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j+H_B(Z),\qquad V_j=X_BZa_j,
\tag{2.6.8}
\]
and its star-normalized square functions obey
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac1N\sum_i\|U_i\|^2
 &\le\frac{4(n-2)}N\|B\|_F^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_j\|V_j\|^2
 &\le\frac{n-2}N\|B\|_F^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_i\|E_i-\bar E\|^2
 &\le\frac{64}{n-1}\|B\|_F^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.6.9}
\]
The residue obeys
\[
 \|H_B(Z)\|
 \le\frac{2\sqrt{n-2}}N\|B\|_\mathrm{op}\|Z\|_2.
\tag{2.6.9a}
\]

[Lem 21 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\tilde{F}$ be the function from the statement of Lemma~\ref{l:fp-F-kirszbraun}. We then have
    \[\Big|F^{\ri}(\bG,\bXi,\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)) - \E [\tilde{F}(\bXi;\bG) | \bG]
    \Big| \le
    \frac{\epsilon'}{15}\]
with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$.

\begin{proof}
    By Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc} and
    \eqref{e:wishart.bound.repeated}, it holds with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$ that $\bG$ satisifes \eqref{e:fp-F-kirszbraun-bG-event}, $\bXi$ satisfies \eqref{e:fp-F-kirszbraun-bXi-event}, and $\hat{\by} = \ytrunc$.
    On this event, $F^{\ri}(\bG,\bXi,\hat{\by}(\bG,\bXi)) = \tilde{F}(\bXi;\bG)$. It follows by gaussian concentration of measure (Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}) that
        \[\Big|\tilde{F}(\bXi;\bG) - \E [\tilde{F}(\bXi;\bG)
    \,|\,\bG] \Big| \le \frac{\epsilon'}{15}\]
with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$, so the claim follows.
\end{proof}

OWNER OWN WORK method record, proof (unaudited), W719-T295-C016 v1; no specialist novelty asserted. Given a conditional Gaussian vector X with predictable mean mu and PSD covariance Sigma, predictable real vectors g,w, v_i=Sigma_ii and ell_i=3mu_i^2+3v_i-g_i^2, S=sum_i w_i(X_i^3-g_i^2 X_i) has conditional mean sum_i w_i[mu_i^3+(3v_i-g_i^2)mu_i] and variance (w*ell)^T Sigma(w*ell)+18(w*mu)^T Sigma^{circ 2}(w*mu)+6w^T Sigma^{circ 3}w. Here * and circ denote entrywise product and power. If Sigma<=sigma^2 I, the variance is at most sigma^2||w*ell||^2+18sigma^4||w*mu||^2+6sigma^6||w||^2. For the C015 phase-retrieval forward law, w=g/m gives centered signal-gradient innovations D_t with conditional mean zero in the post-backward-query filtration. Stop before any predictable budget sigma_t<=s, sum g_i^2/m<=G0, sum g_i^2 mu_(t,i)^2/m<=G1 or sum g_i^2 ell_(t,i)^2/m<=G2 fails. Then N_n=-eta sum_(t<n)1_(t<tau)D_t satisfies P(max_(n<=T)|N_n|>=u)<=T eta^2(s^2G2+18s^4G1+6s^6G0)/(m u^2). With s=K eta, eta=c/log d<=1, m=ceil(alpha*d), T<=C log^2 d and fixed budget constants, max|N_n|=O(1/sqrt(d log d)) with probability at least 1-1/log d. This is stopped unamplified fresh-noise control only; actual-path budgets and positive drift remain unproved. Proof: expand the centered coordinate polynomial as ell_i Z_i+3mu_i(Z_i^2-Sigma_ii)+(Z_i^3-3Sigma_ii Z_i). Gaussian mgf differentiation makes the three degrees orthogonal with covariances Sigma_ij, 2Sigma_ij^2 and 6Sigma_ij^3. Schur-product positivity bounds the entrywise covariance powers. Predictable stopping and conditional mean zero give orthogonal martingale increments; the squared-martingale maximal inequality yields the cumulative bound. No product of conditional characteristic functions or iid stopped Gaussian list is used. No actual-path budget survival, memory-dependent positive drift, amplified-noise bound, overlap growth or convergence follows from this conditional record.

body: In topology, two continuous functions from one topological space to another are called homotopic if one can be "continuously deformed" into the other, such a deformation being called a homotopy between the two functions. A notable use of homotopy is the definition of homotopy groups and cohomotopy groups, important invariants in algebraic topology.

Let a finite nonempty deterministic path family visit exactly one site in each of finitely many layers t. In layer t there are m_t independent N(0,sigma_t^2) weights, and all layers are independent. For deterministic positive a_p and finite beta, put F=log(sum_p a_p exp(beta sum_t omega(t,p_t))). If A_t is the layer mean and R(t,x)=omega(t,x)-A_t, then Var(F)=beta^2 sum_t sigma_t^2/m_t+Var(F(R)). For M=max_p sum_t omega(t,p_t), Var(M)=sum_t sigma_t^2/m_t+Var(M(R)). In the unrestricted n-vertex up/right model with unit Gaussian weights, this gives Var(M_n)>=H_n; in any n-layer width-W family it gives Var(M)>=n/W.
Finite nonempty deterministic path family
One selected site per layer
Independent centered Gaussian weights with common variance within each layer
Deterministic positive coefficients for F
Finite beta for F

		\\
		H_{\<bs(2)0>; \eps, \delta}^{z, g}(z') =& \partial_x K \ast g_\eps(z') \<s(1)0> + \eps^{-1/2} \partial_x K \ast g_{\eps, \delta}(z') \<b1>,

		\\
		H_{X^k; \eps, \delta}^{z, g}(z') =& 0

	alongside the recursive relations
	\begin{align*}
		H_{\tau \bar{\tau}; \eps, \delta}^{z, g}(z') =& H_{\tau; \eps, \delta}^{z, g}(z') \tilde\Gamma_{z'z}^{\eps, \delta} \bar{\tau} + \tilde \Gamma_{z'z}^{\eps, \delta} \tau H_{\bar{\tau}; \eps, \delta}^{z, g}(z'),

[Corollary cor:recover-liu-wasserstein-poc of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Consider the affine Gaussian kernel (equation eq:affine-kernel of the paper) and the
standard Gaussian target on $\mathbb R^d$.  Assume that
\[
        \widetilde\mu_0=N(m_0,\Sigma_0),
        \qquad \Sigma_0>0,
\]
and let $Y_1(0),\ldots,Y_N(0)$ be i.i.d. with law $\widetilde\mu_0$.  Let
$\widetilde\mu_t$ denote the mean-field solution and let
\[
        \widetilde\mu_t^N:=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{Y_i(t)}
\]
be the empirical measure of the particle system.  Then there is a constant
$C=C(d,m_0,\Sigma_0)<\infty$ such that, for all $N$ sufficiently large,
\begin{equation}
        \mathbb E \left[\sup_{t\ge0}\, W_2^2(\widetilde\mu_t^N,\widetilde\mu_t)\right]
        \le
        C r_d(N),
\end{equation}
where
\[
        r_d(N):=
        \begin{cases}
        N^{-1}\log\log N, & d=1,\\
        N^{-1}(\log N)^2, & d=2,\\
        N^{-2/d}, & d\ge3.
        \end{cases}
\]
Moreover, for fixed \(k\ge1\), writing $\mathcal L(Y_1^N(t),\ldots,Y_k^N(t))$ for the joint law of $Y_1^N(t),\ldots,Y_k^N(t)$,
\begin{equation}
        \sup_{t\ge0}
        W_2^{(k)}\left(\mathcal L(Y_1^N(t),\ldots,Y_k^N(t)),\widetilde\mu_t^{\otimes k}\right)^2
        \le
        C'\left(k r_d(N)+\frac{k^2(k-1)}{N}\right),
\end{equation}
for some constant
$C'=C'(d,m_0,\Sigma_0)<\infty$.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: For a stabilizable stationary system, mass transport preserves the mean particle density: send one unit from every initial particle to its final sleeping site. Thus any local subsequential limit of the bounded occupation indicators has one-site mean zeta_c. This still does not imply almost-sure density. To see the precise gap, fill consecutive blocks of length m with iid Bernoulli(rho) values, constant within a block, and randomize the block origin uniformly. Each resulting process is stationary ergodic with density rho. As m tends to infinity its local law converges to the mixture rho*delta_all_ones+(1-rho)*delta_all_zeros, whose density is random. Check: A fixed window crosses a block boundary with probability at most its diameter/m. Away from a boundary it sees a single Bernoulli variable. Ergodicity of each finite-block process follows by iid block ergodicity and the cyclic action on the random phase. Obstruction: Need control of correlations or ergodic components that is uniform near criticality, together with uniqueness and independence from the initial law. Conservation of mean does not supply any of these.

[Proposition 18 (Nine-component two-point correlation equation) of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] For every \((x,y)\in V_n\), the nine-component correlation function
	\(\bm\varphi^{n,t}(x,y)\) satisfies
	\begin{equation}
		\partial_t\bm\varphi^{n,t}(x,y)
		=
		\mathcal L_n^\ast\bm\varphi^{n,t}(x,y)
		+
		\bm G^{n,t}(x,y),
	\end{equation}
	where
	\begin{align}
		\mathcal L_n^\ast
		={}&
		n^2\mathscr A_n \mathrm I_9
		+
		n^2\mathbf 1_{\{y=x+1\}}\mathsf P
		+
		\mathbf 1_{\{2\le x\le n-2\}}(Q\otimes \mathrm I_3)
		\nonumber\\
		&+
		\mathbf 1_{\{2\le y\le n-2\}}(\mathrm I_3\otimes Q)
		+
		n\mathbf 1_{\{x=1\}}(R^\alpha\otimes \mathrm I_3)
		+
		n\mathbf 1_{\{y=n-1\}}(\mathrm I_3\otimes R^\beta).
	\end{align}
	The source term \(\bm G^{n,t}\) is supported on the discrete diagonal $ D_n=\{(x,y)\in V_n:\ y=x+1\} $ and for \(a,b\in E\),
	\begin{equation}
		G_{ab}^{n,t}(x,y)
		=
		-n^2
		\left(
		\rho_a^{n,t}(x+1)-\rho_a^{n,t}(x)
		\right)
		\left(
		\rho_b^{n,t}(x+1)-\rho_b^{n,t}(x)

[Lemma Spherical curvature approximation of arXiv:2608.27248, 'Optimal Transport and the ABP Method in Higher Codimension'] Let $U$ be a geodesically convex body contained in an open hemisphere of
$\mathbb{S}^3$.  The local spherical Steiner formula uniquely defines a
nonnegative finite Borel measure $M_1(U,\cdot)$ on $\partial U$, called the
first spherical curvature measure.  It has the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item on every $C^2$ part $W$ of $\partial U$,
\[
 M_1(U,W)=\int_W H_{\mathbb{S}^3}\,\mathrm dA;
\]
\item if $\mathsf d_{\mathrm H}(U_j,U)\to0$, with all bodies contained in a
fixed open hemisphere, then $M_1(U_j,\cdot)$ converges weakly to
$M_1(U,\cdot)$ and $|U_j|\to|U|$.
\end{enumerate}

[Lemma lem:jw-degree-law of arXiv:2607.00731, 'Sharp Asymptotics for the Largest Component in the Subcritical Regime of Preferential Atta'] Let $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be i.i.d.\ random variables with
\[
\mathbb P(Y_i=k)=\binom{\alpha+k-1}{k}(1-p_n)^{\alpha}p_n^k,
\]
where $$p_n=\frac{2m}{\alpha n+2m}=\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\alpha+2-\varepsilon}.$$
Then
\[
d\bigl(G_{n,m}^{\alpha,\ast}\bigr)\overset{d}= (Y_1,\dots,Y_n)\,\big|\,\{Y_1+\cdots+Y_n=2m\}.
\]
In particular, if $Y^{(n)}\sim\operatorname{NBin}(\alpha,p_n)$, then for every fixed integer $k\ge 0$ and every fixed integer $r\ge 1$,
\[
\pi_k(d)=\mathbb P\bigl(Y^{(n)}=k\bigr)+O_p(n^{-1/2}),
\]
and
$$\mu_r(d)=\mathbb E\bigl[(Y^{(n)})^r\bigr]+O_p(n^{-1/2}).$$
For each fixed $r\ge 1$ one also has $\mathbb E\bigl[(Y^{(n)})^r\bigr]=O(1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$$
\psi_{n,\delta}(R)<\frac{\varepsilon}{4}.

Equivalently, because $\gamma(R)=0$, it is sufficient that
$$
 m_R>
 \frac{32\sigma_{\KSD}^2}{\varepsilon^2}
 \log\!\left(\frac{2nL_n}{\delta}\right).
$$
Then every $\tau_i(\varepsilon,\delta)$ is finite and belongs to $\{1,\ldots,R\}$.  If
\begin{equation}
 B_{\mathrm{eff}} \geq \eta L_n \max _{2 \leq i \leq n} i\left(1+\tau_i(\varepsilon, \delta)\right),
\end{equation}
then the output $\widehat{i}$ of KSD-SuccessiveHalving satisfies
$$
 \nu_{\widehat{i}}-\nu_1\le\frac{\varepsilon}{2}
$$
with probability at least $1-\delta$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem Main 3 of arXiv:2609.02871, 'Estimating the number of real zeros of linear combinations of radicals of polynomials'] Let $P_k$, $k=1,\dots,n$ be real polynomials of one variable of degree at most $d$ and assume that each $P_k$ is positive on an interval $I=(a,b)$, where $a,b \in \mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty,-\infty\}$. Let $\alpha_k$ be arbitrary real numbers. If $P_k^{\alpha_k}$ are linearly independent on $I$, $c_k$ are real and not all zero, then $$f=\sum_{k=1}^{n} c_k P_k^{\alpha_k}$$
has no more than $4n^3d+n$ distinct roots on $I$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma eq:moment-matrix of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[lemma]{lem:moment-interior}
Let
\[
 m_k=\mathbb E G^{2k}=(2k-1)!!,
 \qquad k=0,\ldots,q.
\]
There exist symmetric, compactly supported \(C^\infty\) probability densities
\(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_q\) and positive weights \(w_0,\ldots,w_q\) such that the matrix
\begin{equation}
 B_{kj}=\int x^{2k}\phi_j(x)\,\mathrm d x,
 \qquad 0\le k,j\le q,
\end{equation}
is invertible and
\begin{equation}
 m_k=\sum_{j=0}^q w_jB_{kj},
 \qquad k=0,\ldots,q.
\end{equation}
Moreover, all moment vectors sufficiently close to \((m_0,\ldots,m_q)\) in the affine hyperplane with zeroth moment equal to one admit such a representation with strictly positive weights summing to one.
title: Interior moment representation by smooth bumps

For biorthogonally invariant real n by n signals S_n with ||S_n||op<=C almost surely and E||S_n||_F^2/n->a, observe Y_n=sqrt(s)S_n+Z_n, with independent iid Gaussian noise variance1/n and fixed s>=0. If its empirical positive singular law converges in expected squared W2 to a deterministic compact bounded-density law eta, then I(S_n;Y_n)/n^2->Sigma(sym eta)-Sigma(semicircle_1). Input singular profiles may be random, atomic or rank deficient. The exact mixture partition function includes its input quadratic weight, so the finite MI identity is s*E||S_n||_F^2/(2n)-E Q_n(Y_n). A uniform spectral Lipschitz estimate, lemma017 quantile boxes and the signal-independent calibration019 identify every subsequential limit. No prior MI-limit assumption or unitary-to-real asymptotic-freeness extension is used. Novelty of this standard density argument is unestablished.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:3b08fdae3bb7ff924ea3e4896262836456507449bcf8a19f7bed47185bf1cc63","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/3b/3b08fdae3bb7ff924ea3e4896262836456507449bcf8a19f7bed47185bf1cc63.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:f7ee46a2e3388a11ce13fc89ccd7a2a712259b34ba37615dbe0afe0e0398d634","bundle_entry_key":"random-profile-square-mi-calibration-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-near-square-c1-and-finite-variance-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_008.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:random-profile-square-mi-calibration-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Square invariant signals with random singular profiles: spectral calibration

Target 2 supporting lemma, proof draft, unaudited. Standard density
normalization argument; novelty unestablished. This removes the
deterministic-profile restriction from claim019. No generic real/complex
asymptotic freeness theorem is assumed.

Let S_n be biorthogonally invariant real n by n signals, independent of
Z_n whose entries are iid N(0,1/n). Suppose ||S_n||op<=C almost surely
for one constant C, and a_n=E||S_n||_F^2/n -> a. Fix s>=0 and put
Y_n=sqrt(s)S_n+Z_n. Assume its empirical positive singular law eta_n
satisfies E W2(eta_n,eta)^2->0 for a deterministic compact bounded-density
probability law eta on [0,infinity). Then

    I(S_n;Y_n)/n^2 -> Sigma(sym eta)-Sigma(sigma_1).    (1)

Here sigma_1 is the variance-one semicircle law and all logarithms are
natural. The input singular profiles may be random, atomic or rank
deficient. Output regularity is an explicit assumption, not a conclusion.

## Exact partition function and its Lipschitz bound

For a deterministic matrix T define

 Q_n(T)=n^-2 log E_S exp[n sqrt(s)<S,T>-n*s*||S||_F^2/2].

The expectation is with respect to a fresh sample from the signal prior.
This includes its quadratic input weight. Biorthogonal invariance makes
Q_n a function of the singular values of T. Since ||S||_F<=C sqrt(n),
uniform exponent comparison gives

 |Q_n(T)-Q_n(T')|<=C sqrt(s) ||T-T'||_F/sqrt(n).

After optimally aligning the singular frames,

 |Q_n(T)-Q_n(T')|<=C sqrt(s) W2(eta_T,eta_T').         (2)

The absolute bounds at a profile y are

 -s C^2/2-C sqrt(s*m2(eta_y)) <= Q_n(diag y)
                          <= C sqrt(s*m2(eta_y)).    (3)

These inequalities follow pointwise in the prior signal before taking
expectation and logarithm. No independence of singular values is used.

The Gaussian mixture density and the real square SVD Jacobian give the
exact ordered singular-value density

 p_n(y)=C_n exp[n^2(-m2(eta_y)/2+Q_n(diag y)+V_n(y))],               (4)
 V_n(y)=n^-2 sum_(i<j)log|y_j^2-y_i^2|.

C_n is the same signal-independent constant calibrated in claim019,
using the real Jacobian of arXiv:2203.07752 Section2.1 equation(15):

    n^-2 log C_n -> 1/2-Sigma(sigma_1).              (5)

The exact likelihood-ratio calculation now gives

    i_n(s)=s*a_n/2-E Q_n(Y_n).                       (6)

The factor1/2 differs from the fixed-profile formula for J_n in claim019,
because Q_n already contains -n*s*||S||_F^2/2. Indeed the conditional
log-density has Gaussian quadratic -n||Z||_F^2/2, while the marginal
has -n||Y||_F^2/2+n^2 Q_n(Y). Their expected difference divided by n^2
is (s/2)E||S||_F^2/n-E Q_n(Y), as asserted.

## Subsequential calibration, with all limit premises explicit

Let q_n be the midpoint-quantile profile of eta. It has bounded entries.
By (3), K_n=Q_n(diag q_n) is bounded. Along any subsequence with K_n->K,
(2), the assumed expected W2 convergence and deterministic quantile
W2 convergence imply

    E|Q_n(Y_n)-K_n|->0.                             (7)

The same expected W2 convergence implies m2(eta)=1+s*a, because
E m2(eta_n)=1+s*a_n and the square roots of second moments differ by
at most W2. This passage uses Cauchy-Schwarz to pass the squared norms;
it does not replace weak convergence by moment convergence.

For a fixed large R, P(||Y_n||op<=R)->1. This follows from
||Y||op<=sqrt(s)C+||Z||op and the Gaussian net estimate in claim019.
Thus the observed profile lies with high probability in [0,R] and in
any given small W2 neighborhood of eta. In that neighborhood, the
quadratic term and Q_n are uniformly close to their respective limits,
by bounded support and (2). The V_n uniform upper bound of claim017
then bounds the exponent in (4) above by

    c -(1+s*a)/2 +K+Sigma(sym eta)+epsilon,

where c is the limit in (5). The neighborhood volume is at most R^n.
Its probability tends to one; consequently the displayed expression
without epsilon must be nonnegative.

For the opposite direction, integrate (4) on the product boxes of radius
1/(4C_eta n^3) around q_n, where C_eta is a finite density bound of eta.
Claim017 gives their log volume o(n^2) and matching uniform energy lower
bound. Their W2 distance to q_n is O(n^-3), so (2) and the quadratic
term give the matching lower exponent. Its integral is at most one,
so that same limiting expression must be nonpositive. Therefore

    0=c -(1+s*a)/2+K+Sigma(sym eta),
    K=s*a/2+Sigma(sigma_1)-Sigma(sym eta).            (8)

Every convergent subsequence of the bounded K_n has the same limit.
Hence K_n converges, and (6)-(8) prove (1) along the full sequence.
No existence assumption for the information limit is needed.

[Theorem thm:kpoint of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] Let $z_i\in\mathbb{R}^M$ carry weights $p_i>0$, $\sum_ip_i=1$, with
$\sum_ip_iz_i=0$, and $E=\sum_ip_i\lVert z_i\rVert^2$. For every
$1\le k\le M+1$ there is a convex combination $\delta$ of at most $k$ of the
points with
\[
  \lVert \delta\rVert^2\ \le\ E\cdot\frac{M+1-k}{kM}.
\]
The constant is sharp: for the uniformly weighted regular $M$-simplex, every
convex combination supported on $k$ points has squared norm at least
$E\frac{M+1-k}{kM}$, with equality for $k$ vertices at equal weights. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: $k$-point mean lemma

body: [Theorem 4 (Large deviations of the density of the infinite cluster [39]) of arXiv:2404.19583, 'Catalan percolation'] For any p > poc, there exist ε, c > 0 such that, for any integer n ≥1 and finite set A ⊂Z+, we have that Pp (|{a ∈A : (a, a) →L−n}| ≤ε|A|) ≤e−c|A|. Strictly speaking, [39] proves this result with {(a, a) : a ∈A} replaced by an interval of the form {(a, 0) : a ∈{1, . . . , |A|}}, but the same proof works. As noted in [39], the proof applies to oriented percolation, in addition to the contact process.

[Ppn 194 (subsequential limits) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $N\to\infty$ with parameters satisfying Assumption~\ref{a:params}. Then the measures $\Q_N$, as defined by \eqref{e:pm.on.pm.over.paths.Gamma}, are tight. Moreover, for any subsequential limit $\Q$, if $\mu\sim\Q$ and $(\Gamma,\Upsilon,\mathcal{E})\sim\mu$, then $\mathcal{E}\equiv0$. The ``$\frozen$'' variant of the statement also holds. 

\begin{proof}
Write $\E_N$ for expectation with respect to $\Q_N$. We use Assumption~\ref{a:params} throughout. We will argue that $\Gamma^N$ and $\Upsilon^N$ are asymptotically equivalent to
	\[
	\bar{\Gamma}^N
	\equiv \Big(
	\bar{D}^{\RomI},
	Q^{\RomII},Q^{\RomII,\RomIII},C^{\RomIII}, Q^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,,\quad
	\bar{\Upsilon}^N
	\equiv\Big( 
	Y^{\RomII},Y^{\RomIII},Y^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,.
	\]
For the purposes of this proof, it is more convenient to treat $\bar{D}^{\RomI}$ separately, and group together the remaining processes as
	\[
	\bar{f}^N
	\equiv
	\Big(
	Q^{\RomII},Q^{\RomII,\RomIII},C^{\RomIII}, Q^{\Ising},
		Y^{\RomII},Y^{\RomIII},Y^{\Ising}
	\Big)
	\,.\]
By Proposition~\ref{p:drift.kolmogorov}, for $N$ large enough we have
	\beq
	\frac{\E_N[\|
		\bar{D}^{\RomI,N}(t) -
		\bar{D}^{\RomI,N}(s)
		\|^2]}{(t-s)^2}
	\le L^{O(1)}
	\le \mathscr{C}\,.
	\eeq
Meanwhile, by Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}, together with \eqref{e:Q.naive.kolmogorov} and the definition~\eqref{e:def.r} of $C^{\RomIII}$, for $N$ large enough we also have 
	\beq
	\frac{\E_N[\|\bar{f}^N(t)-
		\bar{f}^N
		(s)\|^4]}{(t-s)^2}
	\le L^{O(1)}
	\le \mathscr{C}
	\eeq
for $N$ large enough. We next address the error terms, using Assumption~\ref{a:params}. For any function $f$ on $[0,1]$
we use $\|f\|_\infty$ to denote the supremum norm.
\begin{itemize}
\item It follows by the bound \eqref{e:Q.I.small} from Proposition~\ref{p:qv.kolmogorov}, combined with Doob's $L^2$
martingale inequality, that we have
	\[
	\E_N\bigg[ \Big( \| Z^{\RomI}\|_\infty \Big)^2\bigg]
	\le 4 \E_N[Z^{\RomI}(1)^2]
	= 4\E_N Q^{\RomI}(1)
	\le L^{O(1)} \delta
	\ll1\,,
	\]
recalling that we assumed $\delta\to0$ as $N\to\infty$.
\item It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:D.barD.discrep} that
	\[
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
	\Big\|D^\sigma-\bar{D}^\sigma\Big\|_\infty
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\eta}{\delta}\ll1\,,
	\]
recalling that we assumed $\eta\ll\delta$.
\item It follows by the bound \eqref{e:bar.D.notI.unif} from Proposition~\ref{p:drift.kolmogorov}
that 
	\[
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
	\E_N \| \bar{D}^\sigma\|_\infty
	\ll 1\,,
	\]
using that $\BUCKETS \ll N\delta$.
\item It follows by the bounds \eqref{e:Q.Ising.cross.small},
\eqref{e:qv.error.unif.bound}, and \eqref{e:tildeE.III.unif}
from Proposition~\ref{p:qv.kolmogorov}
that
	\[
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}}
		\E_N\|\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\Ising}\|_\infty
	+\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
		\E_N\|E^{\sigma,\tau}\|_\infty
	+ \E_N\|\tilde{E}^{\RomIII}\|_\infty\ll1\,,
	\]
using that $\eta\ll \delta\ll \delta^{1/2}$ and 
$\BUCKETS \ll N\delta \ll N$.
\end{itemize}
Altogether this proves that $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges in probability to the zero path. By passing to a subsequence we can assume that $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges almost surely to the zero path.
 
Now let $J_n(H)$
be the event that $\bar{D}^{\RomI}$
fails to be $\gamma$-H\"older with constant $H$ at dyadic scale $2^{-n}$, and similarly $F_n(H)$ for the process $\bar{f}$:
	\begin{align*}
	J_n(H)
	&\equiv
	\bigg\{
	\bigg\|
	\bar{D}^{\RomI}
	\bigg(\frac{i}{2^n}\bigg)
	-\bar{D}^{\RomI}
	\bigg(\frac{i-1}{2^n}\bigg)
	\bigg\|
	> \frac{H}{(2^n)^\gamma}
	\textup{ for some }
	1\le i\le 2^n
	\bigg\}\,,\\
	F_n(H)
	&\equiv 
	\bigg\{
	\bigg\|
	\bar{f}
	\bigg(\frac{i}{2^n}\bigg)
	-\bar{f}
	\bigg(\frac{i-1}{2^n}\bigg)
	\bigg\|
	> \frac{H}{(2^n)^\gamma}
	\textup{ for some }
	1\le i\le 2^n
	\bigg\}\,.
	\end{align*}
Finally, the moment estimates above give
\[
	\E_N\big[|Y^{\Ising}(0)|^2\big]\le \mathscr{C}\,.
\]
Let $I(H):=\{|Y^{\Ising}(0)|>H\}$. Then $\P_N(I(H))\le \mathscr{C}/H^2$.

body:
[Lem 6 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the definition of $\Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)$ from the statement of Proposition~\ref{p:convex.body.polytope.bound.new}. 
Recall $\cD_+$ from \eqref{e:cD-plus}.
Given any $\mu$, define 
    \[
        \cD_{+,\mu}(2) \equiv \Big\{
            \YY = (\BBb,\vvv,\UUu,\www) \in \cD_+ : (\mu, \www) \le 2
        \Big\}\,,
    \]
For $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$ and $\dot{\YY}, \ddot{\YY} \in \cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, we have
    \[\Big|\Surplus(\dot{\YY};\lambda,\mu) - \Surplus(\ddot{\YY};\lambda,\mu)\Big|
        \le
        \frac{4\|\Delta\YY\|_2
            +  6\|\Delta\YY\|_2^{1/2}}{\iota \min\{1,\alpha\}}\,,
    \]
where we abbreviate $\Delta\YY \equiv \dot{\YY} - \ddot{\YY}$. 
That is, $\YY \mapsto \Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)$ is uniformly continuous in $\cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, uniformly in $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$.

\begin{proof}
We will bound separately the differences 
	\baln
	\Delta\Cost
	& \equiv\Cost(\dot{\YY};\lambda) - \Cost(\ddot{\YY};\lambda)\,,\\
	\Delta\Budget
	& \equiv\Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu) - \Budget(\ddot{\YY};\mu)\,.
	\ealn
Note that for any $\xxxx \in \bbR^r$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
    \[
        \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j |\xxxx_j|
        \le \bigg(\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j |\xxxx_j|^2\bigg)^{1/2}
        \le \|\xxxx\|_2\,.
    \]
    Thus, abbreviating $\Delta\YY
    \equiv(\Delta\vBBb,\Delta\vvvv,\Delta\vUUu,\Delta\vwww)
    \equiv\dot{\YY}-\ddot{\YY}$, we have
    \baln
        |\Delta\Cost|
        &\le \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j \bigg\{
            |\Delta\vBBb_j|
            + |\Delta\vUUu_j|
            + \Big|
            (\dot{\vvvv}_j-\dot{\vUUu}_j)_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}_j-\ddot{\vUUu}_j)_+
            \Big| 
            + 2 \Big|(\dot{\vvvv}_j-\dot{\vUUu}_j)_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}_j-\ddot{\vUUu}_j)_+^{1/2} 
            \Big|
        \bigg\} \\
        &\le \|\Delta\vBBb\|_2
        + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2
        + \Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+
        	\Big\|_2 
        + 2\Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2}
        \Big\|_2\,,
    \ealn
    where the operations $x\mapsto x_+$ and $x\mapsto (x_+)^{1/2}$ are applied entrywise.
    Since $x\mapsto x_+$ is a contraction,
    \[
        \|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+\|_2
        \le \|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu}) - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})\|_2
        \le \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2 + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2\,.
    \]
Furthermore, since $|a^{1/2}-b^{1/2}| \le |a-b|^{1/2}$ for all $a,b\ge0$, for any vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b}\in[0,\infty)^r$ we can bound
	\[
	\Big(\|\vec{a}^{1/2}-\vec{b}^{1/2}\|_2\Big)^2
	=\sum_{j=1}^r \Big((a_j)^{1/2}-(b_j)^{1/2}\Big)^2
	\le \sum_{j=1}^r |a_j-b_j| = \|\vec{a}-\vec{b}\|_1\,.
	\]
Applying this estimate gives 
    \baln
        &\bigg(\Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2}\Big\|_2\bigg)^2
        \le 
        \Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+
        \Big\|_1 \\
        &\qquad \le 
            \|\Delta\vvvv\|_1
            + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_1 
            \le r^{1/2} \Big(
            \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2
            + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2
        \Big)\,.
    \ealn
    Finally, crudely upper bounding 
$\|\Delta\vBBb\|_2,
        \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2,
        \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2$ by $\|\Delta\YY\|_2$,
    we obtain
    \[
        |\Delta\Cost|
        \le 4 \|\Delta\YY\|_2
        + 2
        \Big(2 r^{1/2} \|\Delta\YY\|_2 \Big)^{1/2} \,.
    \]
This gives a continuity estimate for the $\Cost$ function.

We next turn to the $\Budget$ function.
    For all $\YY  \in \cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, we have
    \[
        0\le \alpha \cdot \Budget(\YY;\mu) \le (\mu,\vwww) \le 2\,,
    \]
    where the intermediate step is by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality.
    Therefore,
    \baln
        \alpha |\Delta\Budget| 
        &= \alpha^{1/2} \Big|
        \Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2} + 
        \Budget(\ddot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2}\Big| 
        \cdot 
        \alpha^{1/2} \Big|
        \Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2}

Cauchy-Schwarz implies Im F_eta(z)>=Im z, strictly for a non-point-mass law. The standard free-additive subordination theorem supplies upper-half-plane omega_lambda,omega_kappa satisfying F_lambda(omega_lambda)=F_kappa(omega_kappa)=F_lambda_boxplus_kappa(z) and omega_lambda+omega_kappa=z+F_lambda_boxplus_kappa(z). These equations have at most one upper-half-plane pair: with h_eta=F_eta-id, omega_kappa is a fixed point of T_z(v)=z+h_lambda(z+h_kappa(v)); this self-map cannot be the identity because its image has imaginary part at least Im z. Schwarz's lemma excludes two distinct interior fixed points.

Fix non-point-mass mu and let lambda_epsilon=D_epsilon mu. Dominated convergence gives F_lambda_epsilon->id locally uniformly on the upper half-plane, including derivatives. For any bounded disk D with closure in the lower half-plane, U={1/w:w in closure(D)} is compact in the upper half-plane. Choose a bounded convex V with closure in that half-plane containing U with positive boundary distance. For small epsilon, |F_lambda_epsilon'-1|<1/2 on V, which proves injectivity by integrating along segments. Rouche's theorem on fixed small circles about points of U gives an analytic inverse H_epsilon on a neighborhood of U, with H_epsilon(u)->u uniformly. Therefore R_epsilon(w)=H_epsilon(1/w)-1/w is analytic on D, tends uniformly to zero, and has strictly negative imaginary part by the strict F inequality. No moments or global inverse branch are used.

Set p=1/100, q=99/100 and kappa=p delta_0+q U[0,1], unimodal with mode 0. Put x_1=p, x_2=1/4, c=pi q, g(x)=p/x+q log(x/(1-x)), and w_j=g(x_j)-ic. Its Cauchy transform has local analytic continuation A(z)=p/z+q[Log z-Log(1-z)-i pi] near either point. Take b=g(x_2)-10i, r=99/10, and D={|w-b|<r}. This closed disk lies strictly in the lower half-plane. The bounds 3<pi<4 imply 2.97<c<3.96. Also d=g(x_1)-g(x_2)=24/25-(99/100)log 33 satisfies |d|<3. Hence both w_j belong to D. Write Delta=r^2-(10-c)^2>48.5891. Then 2r/Delta<5/12. Their disk pseudohyperbolic distance satisfies rho=r|d|/|r^2-(w_1-b)conjugate(w_2-b)|<=r|d|/Delta<2/3.

Apply the inverse construction on D. Let a_epsilon=Re R_epsilon(w_2), B_epsilon=R_epsilon-a_epsilon and t_epsilon=-Im R_epsilon(w_2)>0. Then t_epsilon->0, B_epsilon maps D into the lower half-plane, and B_epsilon(w_2)=-it_epsilon. Schwarz-Pick applied to (B_epsilon+it_epsilon)/(B_epsilon-it_epsilon) gives uniform O(t_epsilon) bounds for B_epsilon and all fixed-order derivatives on compact subsets of D. With K_epsilon=-Im B_epsilon and real-direction derivative K_epsilon', it gives K_epsilon(w_1)>t_epsilon/5, K_epsilon(w_2)=t_epsilon and |K_epsilon'(w_2)|<=|B_epsilon'(w_2)|<=t_epsilon 2r/Delta<(5/12)t_epsilon. These bounds follow respectively from (1-rho)/(1+rho) and the derivative form of Schwarz-Pick; the factor 2r is retained.

Let lambda_tilde_epsilon be lambda_epsilon translated by -a_epsilon and sigma_epsilon=lambda_tilde_epsilon boxplus kappa. On fixed small complex neighborhoods of x_j, the equation W_epsilon=A(z-B_epsilon(W_epsilon)) has a unique holomorphic solution near A. The O(t_epsilon) bounds make its right side a contraction mapping an O(t_epsilon)-ball about A(z) into itself. Thus W_epsilon=A+O(t_epsilon), uniformly, with values in D. For upper-half-plane z in either neighborhood, put u=1/W_epsilon(z), omega_lambda=H_epsilon(u)-a_epsilon=u+B_epsilon(W_epsilon(z)), and omega_kappa=z-B_epsilon(W_epsilon(z)). Both are in the upper half-plane. They satisfy the subordination equations by the inverse construction and the defining equation for W_epsilon. The uniqueness proved above identifies W_epsilon=G_sigma_epsilon. Consequently Stieltjes inversion gives real-analytic local density f_epsilon=-Im W_epsilon/pi, positive for small epsilon.

Taylor expansion, using the uniform bounds and writing t=t_epsilon, gives W_epsilon(z)=A(z)-A'(z)B_epsilon(A(z))+O(t^2) on fixed complex neighborhoods. Cauchy's estimates give the same error order after differentiation on smaller neighborhoods. Therefore f_epsilon'(x)=-[g''(x)K_epsilon(g(x)-ic)+(g'(x))^2K_epsilon'(g(x)-ic)]/pi+O(t^2), with constants independent of epsilon. Direct differentiation yields g'(x)=(x-p)/(x^2(1-x)), g''(x)=2p/x^3+q[-1/x^2+1/(1-x)^2], hence g'(x_1)=0, g''(x_1)=1000000/99, g'(x_2)=128/25 and g''(x_2)=-64/5. Thus f_epsilon'(x_1)<=-[200000/(99pi)]t+O(t^2)<0, whereas f_epsilon'(x_2)>=[64/5-(128/25)^2(5/12)]t/pi-O(t^2)=[704/(375pi)]t-O(t^2)>0 for sufficiently small epsilon. These signs at x_1<x_2 contradict unimodality: the first forces any mode to lie at or left of x_1, after which the second is impossible.

Finally, set L=1/epsilon and nu_L=p delta_0+q U[0,L]. D_epsilon(mu boxplus nu_L)=lambda_epsilon boxplus kappa, whose translation by -a_epsilon is the nonunimodal sigma_epsilon. Since translation and positive dilation preserve unimodality, mu boxplus nu_L is nonunimodal for every sufficiently large L. Each nu_L is unimodal. Conversely delta_a boxplus nu is a translation of nu, so point masses are freely strongly unimodal. This completes the proof. [Prop gbf of arXiv:2411.06571, 'Moment-based approach for two erratic KPZ scaling limits'] Consider a two-variable process $(G_{s,t})_{-\infty <s\le t<\infty}$ with $s,t\in \Bbb Q$, defined on some complete probability space, and satisfying 
\begin{enumerate}
        \item $G_{s_j,t_j}$ are independent if $(s_j,t_j)$ are disjoint intervals.

        \item $G_{s,t}G_{t,u}= G_{s,u}$ whenever $s<t<u$.

        \item For $n=1,2,3,4,5,6$, we have that $\Bbb E\big[ G_{s,t}^n \big] = e^{\frac{n^2}2(t-s)}.$
\end{enumerate}
These three conditions uniquely determine the finite-dimensional distributions of the process $(G_{s,t})_{s<t}$ as being the same as those of $(e^{B(t)-B(s)})_{s<t}$  for a standard Brownian motion $B$, and moreover $B$ can be defined on the same space so that the relation holds pathwise on $\Bbb Q^2$.

[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2608.27569, 'Laplace and Dolbeault operators on Sasakian manifolds'] Let $(M^{2n+1},g,\xi)$ be a compact Sasakian manifold. Let $f$ be an eigenfunction of the ${\overline\partial}$-Laplacian associated with an eigenvalue $q$ of the Lie derivative, that is, $\Delta_{\overline\partial} f=\lambda f$ and  $\xi(f)=iqf$. Let $m\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. 
Then there exist four linear combinations of the forms
$\alpha_m:=L^mf$, $\eta\wedge \overline\partial^*\alpha_m$, 
$\eta\wedge \partial^*\alpha_m$, and 
$\overline\partial\partial\alpha_{m-1}$ that are
eigenforms of degree $2m$ of the Hodge Laplacian corresponding 
to eigenvalues
$$\Theta_0(q,\lambda)=2\lambda-4m^2+4mn+2nq+q^2,$$
and/or 
$$\Theta_\pm(q,\lambda)=2\lambda-4m^2+4mn+4m+2nq-2n+q^2\pm 2\sqrt{2\lambda+(n+q)^2}.$$
When all of the forms $\overline\partial^*\alpha_m$, 
$\eta\wedge \partial^*\alpha_m$, and 
$\overline\partial\partial\alpha_{m-1}$ are nonzero, 
$\Theta_0(q,\lambda)$ has multiplicity two, and 
each $\Theta_\pm(q,\lambda)$ has multiplicity one. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:equivariant-families of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] The set $Y_P$ is a Borel cross-section, and
\[
    (Y_P)_{[t,z]}=P_z-t,
    \qquad
    \kappa_{Y_P}([t,z])=\delta_{P_z-t}.
\]
If the family $(P_z)_{z\in Z}$ is uniformly Delone, then $Y_P$ is
a Delone cross-section and
\[
    \bigl(
        \operatorname{Ind}_{\Gamma}^{\mathbb R^d}(Z),
        \mu_{\Gamma,Z},
        Y_P
    \bigr)
\]
is a cross-section system.

Suppose, moreover, that there is a $\Gamma$-invariant conull
Borel set $Z_0\subset Z$ such that
\[
    P_{z'}=P_z-u
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    u\in\Gamma
    \ \text{ and }\
    z'=u.z
\]
for all $z,z'\in Z_0$ and $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Then $Y_P$ is
generating.

body: Let G be a d-regular graph on n vertices with adjacency matrix eigenvalues d = lambda_1 >= lambda_2 >= ... >= lambda_n, and let lambda = max(|lambda_2|, |lambda_n|). For subsets S, T of the vertex set, let e(S,T) = sum_{i in S, j in T} A_{ij}, where A is the adjacency matrix. Then |e(S,T) - d|S||T|/n| <= lambda sqrt(|S||T|). [standard, e.g. Hoory, Linial and Wigderson, Expander Graphs and Their Applications]
title: Expander Mixing Lemma

body: Let X_n be an n by n random matrix whose entries are independent and identically distributed standard complex Gaussian random variables, meaning each entry has independent real and imaginary parts distributed N(0, 1/2), so that E[|X_{jk}|^2] = 1. Let M_n = X_n / sqrt(n). Then, almost surely, the empirical spectral distribution of the eigenvalues of M_n converges weakly, as n tends to infinity, to the uniform probability distribution on the unit disk {z in C : |z| <= 1}. [Ginibre (1965), Mehta; see Bai and Silverstein, Spectral Analysis of Large Dimensional Random Matrices]
title: Circular Law for the Complex Ginibre Ensemble

		\tbg^a = \begin{cases}
			\bg^a & a \not\in S\,, \\
			\hat\bg^a & a\in S\,.

That is to say, $\tbG$ uses the rows of $\hat{\bG}$ indexed by $S$, and the rows of $\bG$ indexed by $[M]\setminus S$.

[Proposition 56 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] If Assumptions~\ref{Assumptions_Theta} and \ref{Assumptions_basic} hold, then for $\N$ large enough (compared to the constants in the assumptions), the partition function
\[
\Z_{\N} := \sum_{\boldsymbol{\ell} \in \amsmathbb{W}_{\N}} \prod_{1 \leq i < j \leq N} \frac{1}{\N^{2\theta_{h(i),h(j)}}}\cdot \frac{\Gamma\big(\ell_j - \ell_i + 1\big)\cdot\Gamma\big(\ell_j - \ell_i + \theta_{h(i),h(j)}\big)}{\Gamma\big(\ell_j - \ell_i\big)\cdot\Gamma\big(\ell_j - \ell_i + 1 - \theta_{h(i),h(j)}\big)} \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^{N} w_{h(i)}(\ell_i)
\]
is finite. Hence
\begin{equation}
 \amsmathbb{P}_{\N}(\boldsymbol{\ell}) := \frac{1}{\Z_{\N}} \prod_{1 \leq i < j \leq N} \frac{1}{\N^{2\theta_{h(i),h(j)}}}\cdot\frac{\Gamma\big(\ell_j - \ell_i + 1\big)\cdot\Gamma\big(\ell_j - \ell_i + \theta_{h(i),h(j)}\big)}{\Gamma\big(\ell_j - \ell_i\big)\cdot\Gamma\big(\ell_j - \ell_i + 1 - \theta_{h(i),h(j)}\big)} \cdot \prod_{i = 1}^{N} w_{h(i)}(\ell_i)
\end{equation}
is a well-defined probability measure on the configuration set $\amsmathbb{W}_{\N}$.
title: Proposition 56 of arXiv:2601.16377

[Lemma 56 (No mass at chaos degree infinity) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $\mathcal U$ be a free ultrafilter and put
\[
 \cH_q=(H_n^{\odot q},\ip{\cdot}{\cdot})_{\mathcal U}.
\]
Here the factorial normalization has already been absorbed into
$x_{n,a,q}=\sqrt{q!}\,f_{n,a,q}$.
All tensor norms below are the ordinary tensor norms of these scaled coordinates.  The
product transported by the primitive--Fock unitary is the normalized product
\begin{equation}
 u\wtensor_{\mathrm{nor}}v
 =
 \sqrt{\frac{q!}{p!(q-p)!}}\,
 \Sym(u\otimes v),
 \qquad
 u\in H^{\odot p},\quad v\in H^{\odot(q-p)}.
 
\end{equation}
The raw contractions of Section~\ref{all:sec:infinite-feedback} are ordinary
Hilbert tensor contractions of the scaled coordinates.  The dictionary
between the two normalisations used in this paper is therefore
\[
 \underbrace{(H_n^{\odot q},q!\ip{\cdot}{\cdot})_{\mathcal U}}
 _{\text{Parts II--IV, kernels }f_{n,a,q}}
 \;\xrightarrow{\ f\,\mapsto\,x=\sqrt{q!}f\ }\;
 \underbrace{(H_n^{\odot q},\ip{\cdot}{\cdot})_{\mathcal U}}
 _{\text{Parts V--VI, coordinates }x_{n,a,q}},
\]
an isometry which carries $\wtensor$ to $\wtensor_{\mathrm{nor}}$ and
multiplies an $s$-fold contraction of a weight-$p$ by a weight-$q$ coordinate
by $\sqrt{p!\,q!/(p+q-2s)!}$.  No statement below depends on the choice, but
all displayed constants refer to the scaled coordinates.
Under $\mathrm{QT}_2$, the represented coordinates
$x_{a,q}=[x_{n,a,q}]_{\mathcal U}$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{a,q}\norm{x_{a,q}}_{\cH_q}^2
 =
 \lim_{\mathcal U}\sum_{a,q}\norm{x_{n,a,q}}^2.
 
\end{equation}
Consequently the represented packet belongs to
$\bigoplus_{q\ge1}\cH_q$ and has no additional component at an infinite chaos grade.

[Lemma 33 (Series law) of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] The following holds almost surely. Let g be the cutoff planar Gaussian increment field, m=6, h=2pi/m, and U,V independent uniforms in [0,h), independent of g. Set q(x)=h floor((g(x)+V)/h), theta=U+q. The field q has stationary increments. With v=Var[g(x)-g(y)], v<=Var[q(x)-q(y)]<=v+h^2/4, so its variance grows logarithmically with bounded error. However E exp[i6(theta(x)-theta(y))]=1 identically and E exp(i6theta(x))=0. This disproves a variance-only inference for periodic order, not the existence of a hexatic Riesz Gibbs phase.
