ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Express rho^D through the extremal measure and look for a conformal-covariance functional equation that pins it. Result: rho^D(dx) = E[Z^D(dx)/Z^D(D)] where Z^D is the (random) extremal measure; conformal covariance of Z^D gives rho^{f(D)}(f(x)) |f'(x)|^2 = E[ r_D(x)^2 |f'(x)|^{2} ... ] only for the intensity E Z^D(dx) = c r_D(x)^2 dx, not for the ratio, because the normalisation Z^D(D) is not covariant. On the unit disk, rotation invariance gives rho^D radial; a PDE characterisation would need the joint law of (Z^D(dx), Z^D(D)), which is the object Problem 16.1 asks for. Computed check: the naive guess rho^D proportional to r_D(x)^2 fails to integrate to the correct mixture (it equals E Z^D(dx)/E Z^D(D), which is a different density unless Z^D(D) is a.s. constant, which it is not). Obstruction: rho^D is a ratio expectation; without the law of the total mass Z^D(D) no closed form or PDE is available.

body:
Aldous and Fill, Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, Open Problem 7.27 (Chapter 7, p. 259) asks whether, over arc-transitive graphs excluding the n-cycles, tau* = O(n log n), tau2 = O(n) and tau*/(2 tau0) = 1 + o(1). Our result (id P0208, 2026-09-08): all three claims are FALSE. The counterexample is the lexicographic product C_m[Kbar_2] for odd m >= 5 - the m-cycle with every vertex split into two non-adjacent twins - which is connected, 4-regular, arc-transitive and not a cycle, on n = 2m vertices. With g(j) = j(m-j) + m the mean hitting time at cycle-distance j and 2m the twin hitting time: tau* = 2*floor(m^2/4) + 2m ~ n^2/8 (quadratic, not O(n log n)); tau2 = 1/(1 - cos(2 pi/m)) ~ n^2/(8 pi^2), because A(C_m[Kbar_2]) = A(C_m) tensor J_2 so the relaxation time is the m-cycle's own; and tau*/(2 tau0) tends to 3/2, not 1 + o(1). Verification, as the source words it: exact hitting times by linear algebra at m = 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 21 (all five formulas exact at every size); arc-transitivity checked mechanically at m = 5, 7, 9 (the group generated by the rotation, one reflection and one fibre swap has order 2^m * 2m and its orbit of one arc is all 8m arcs); and a Lean file P0208.lean with nine theorems, no sorry, axioms propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound only. Not formalised: uniqueness of the solution of (I-P)h = 1 and the tensor eigenvalue computation, both standard and checked numerically. Prior art not cleared.

[Lemma 12 (Quantile representation of \(W_1\) on the real line) of arXiv:2608.22227, '\fontsize{18pt}{20pt}\selectfont \bf Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning with Smoothed Q'] Let \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) be probability measures on \(\mathbb R\) with finite first
moments. Let $F_\mu(x)\coloneqq \mu((-\infty,x])$, and $F_\nu(x)\coloneqq \nu((-\infty,x])$ be their CDFs, and define their left-continuous generalized inverses by $F_\mu^{-1}(u)\coloneqq \inf\{x\in\mathbb R:F_\mu(x)\ge u\}$, $F_\nu^{-1}(u)\coloneqq \inf\{x\in\mathbb R:F_\nu(x)\ge u\}$, for all $u\in(0,1)$. Equivalently, \(F_\mu^{-1}(u)=Q_u(\mu)\) and
\(F_\nu^{-1}(u)=Q_u(\nu)\). Then $W_1(\mu,\nu)
=
\int_0^1
\left|
F_\mu^{-1}(u)-F_\nu^{-1}(u)
\right|\,du
=
\int_0^1
\left|
Q_u(\mu)-Q_u(\nu)
\right|\,du$.

Let X be a compact metric space, F a closed subset of X x X, and U a closed subset with F(U) contained in the interior of U relative to X. For a set C, F(C) consists of all targets of edges whose source lies in C, and F^(-1)(C) is the image under the inverse relation. Put A=intersection over n>=0 of F^n(U) and B=intersection over n>=0 of F^(-n)(X minus interior(U)). Then every chain-recurrent point of F belongs to A union B. Here a point is chain recurrent if for every epsilon>0 a finite chain of F-edges and jumps of size less than epsilon returns it to itself. F need not be a single-valued map or invertible. A is the attractor associated to the inward set U and B its dual repeller.

[Lemma gradient TAP of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Recall $\mathrm{TAP}$ from (equation def:TAPmu of the paper) and $k_\zeta$ from~(equation def:kqm of the paper).
		Fix $\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N$ and set $q=\frac{1}{N}\Vert \mathbf{m}\Vert^2$.
		Let $\zeta$ be a probability measure on $[q,1]$. Then for every $i\in[N]$:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item (\emph{Exact gradient at the minimizer}) If $\zeta_\mathbf{m}$ is the minimizer in Definition~(def:zetam of the paper), then
			\begin{equation}
				\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})})=-\frac{1}{N}k_{\zeta_\mathbf{m}}(q,m_i).
			\end{equation}
			
			\item (\emph{Exact defect formula and explicit boundary stability}) One has
			\begin{equation}
				-N\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})},\zeta)
				=
				k_\zeta(q,m_i)-m_i\,\xi''(q)\,\Delta_\zeta^{\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})}},
			\end{equation}
			where $\Delta_\zeta^{\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})}}$ is defined in (equation eq:def-Delta of the paper).
			Consequently, if
			\[
			\max_{j\in[N]}|m_j|\le 1-\delta
			\qquad\text{for some }\delta\in(0,1),
			\]
			and
			\[
			\zeta(\{q\})\ge u_0>0,
			\]
			then there exists $C=C(\xi,u_0)<\infty$ such that
			\begin{equation}
				\Bigl|\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})},\zeta)+\frac{1}{N}k_{\zeta}(q,m_i)\Bigr|
				\le \frac{C}{N\delta}\,\mathrm{dist}(\zeta_\mathbf{m},\zeta).
			\end{equation}
		\end{enumerate}

$U\in\cC_j^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$ and

\end{align}

Let $H=\sum_{j=1}^rH_j$, with
$H_j\in\cC_j^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$, and let $H_t$ be obtained
from the thinning coupling when $\mathsf{S}=\mathsf{P}$ and from the
coordinate-refresh coupling when $\mathsf{S}=\mathsf{R}$.  Without
any lattice assumption,
\noi
\begin{align}
 \cJ_r(H)
 =\lim_{t\downarrow0}
 \frac{\E[(H_t-H)^2\{(H_t-H)^2-1\}]}
 {1-e^{-rt}}.
 
\end{align}
If $H$ satisfies the lattice condition \eqref{cond_La} with shift
$\theta>0$, then $\cJ_r(H)\geq0$.

If $F\in\cC_r^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$ and
$B=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}B_j$, with
$B_j\in\cC_j^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$, then
\noi
\begin{align}
 \abs{\cJ_r(F+B)-\cJ_r(F)}
 \leq84\bigl(1+\norm{F}_4+\eps\bigr)^3\eps,
 
\end{align}
where
$\eps:=\sum_{1\leq j<r}\norm{B_j}_4$.

Assume that a nonnegative quantity $\rho(F)$ satisfies
\eqref{top_rho}, and put
$\mathfrak d(F):=\abs{\cD(F)}+\rho(F)$ as in
\eqref{frak_d}.  Then, without any lattice assumption,
\noi
\begin{align}
 \cJ_r(F)
 \leq4\sqrt{m_2(F)\mathfrak d(F)}+12\mathfrak d(F)
 
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}
 |\cJ_r(F)|
 \leq
 4\sqrt{m_2(F)\mathfrak d(F)}
 +16\mathfrak d(F).
 
\end{align}

In the Poisson setting, one has the sharper estimates
\noi
\begin{align}
 \cJ_r(F)
 &\leq4\sqrt{m_2(F)\cP(F)}+8\cP(F).
 
\end{align}

body: A sequence (x_n) in a metric space (X, d) is Cauchy if for every epsilon > 0 there is an index N such that d(x_m, x_n) < epsilon for all m, n >= N. The metric space (X, d) is complete if every Cauchy sequence in X converges to a point of X. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy, but not conversely in general: the rationals with the usual distance are not complete, while the real line R and Euclidean space R^n are complete. A closed subset of a complete metric space is complete, and a complete subspace of any metric space is closed in it.
title: Complete metric space

body: Let (mu_n) be a sequence of probability measures on R with characteristic functions phi_n(t) = integral of exp(i t x) d mu_n(x). If phi_n(t) converges pointwise, for every real t, to a limit phi(t) that is continuous at t = 0, then phi is the characteristic function of a probability measure mu, and mu_n converges weakly to mu. Conversely, if mu_n converges weakly to a probability measure mu, then phi_n converges to the characteristic function of mu, uniformly on compact sets. [Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples]
title: Levy's Continuity Theorem

body:
Define the heat kernel Phi: R^n x (0,infinity) -> R by Phi(x,t) = (4 pi t)^{-n/2} exp(-|x|^2/(4t)). Then Phi is smooth and satisfies partial Phi/partial t = Delta_x Phi for all x in R^n, t>0. For every bounded uniformly continuous g: R^n -> R, u(x,t) = integral_{R^n} Phi(x-y,t) g(y) dy is smooth on R^n x (0,infinity), solves partial u/partial t = Delta u there, and u(x,t) -> g(x) uniformly on R^n as t -> 0+. Moreover Phi(.,t) is an approximate identity: integral_{R^n} Phi(x,t) dx = 1 for every t>0.
Phi is the explicit Gaussian kernel on R^n x (0,infinity) given above
g is bounded and uniformly continuous on R^n (for the convolution/initial-value statement)

Let Ω ⊂ ℝⁿ be open and F: Ω × ℝ × ℝⁿ → ℝ continuous; consider the equation F(x, u(x), Du(x)) = 0 in Ω. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity SUBsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every point x₀ ∈ Ω at which u − φ has a local maximum, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity SUPERsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every local minimum point x₀ of u − φ, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. (Equivalent reformulations: replace 'local' by 'strict local' or 'global' max/min, or use C^∞ test functions, or use super-/subdifferentials D⁺u(x₀) and D⁻u(x₀): the conditions read F(x₀, u, p) ≤ 0 for all p ∈ D⁺u(x₀) and ≥ 0 for all p ∈ D⁻u(x₀).) Every classical C¹ solution is a viscosity solution, and a viscosity solution that is differentiable at x₀ satisfies the equation pointwise there. For time-dependent equations u_t + H(x, Du) = 0 on Ω × (0,T) apply the same definition with the gradient variable (u_t, Du) and test functions of (x,t). SHARP EDGE — the sign of F matters: writing the same equation as −F = 0 interchanges the roles of sub- and supersolutions, so the two forms have DIFFERENT viscosity solutions. Example: on (−1,1) with boundary values u(±1) = 0, the function 1 − |x| is a viscosity solution of |u'| − 1 = 0 but NOT of 1 − |u'| = 0, while |x| − 1 is a viscosity solution of 1 − |u'| = 0 but not of |u'| − 1 = 0 (at the kink x = 0, a concave kink admits only test functions touching from above, and a convex kink only test functions touching from below). Viscosity solutions are in general only continuous, are stable under uniform limits, and for convex H coincide with Lipschitz solutions that are semiconcave; the notion is designed so that comparison/uniqueness theorems hold where classical and a.e. solutions are non-unique.
F is continuous
u is continuous on Ω
the equation is written in the form F = 0 with a fixed sign convention

[Theorem result of arXiv:2607.01463, 'Two Multi--Draw Coupon Collector models with different retention rules'] Consider the  $d$ coupon collector's problem (d--CCP), where in each run we keep \textbf{all} the new observed coupons. Let $T_{N,d}$ be the number of trials until all $N$ different types of coupons, which are uniformly distributed, are collected (at least once). Then, as $N\rightarrow \infty$
\begin{equation}
\mathbb {E}\left[T_{N,d}\right]=
\frac{N}{d}\log N
+\frac{\gamma N}{d}
-\frac{d-1}{2d}\log N
+\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{d-1}{2d}\gamma\right)
+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\log N}{N}\right).

\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem result of arXiv:2607.01463

body: Over connected unweighted graphs on n vertices with simple random walk, max_G tau_0(G) = n^3/54 + O(n^{19/7}), settling the Kemeny half of Aldous-Fill Open Problem 6.13. The balanced barbell attains n^3/54 + 0.056 n^2 + o(n^2), so the maximum's second-order term is positive and of order n^2 and the n^{19/7} is the upper bound's looseness. Ingredients: the bridge-tree identity, a deletion comparison, the mass-capacity inequality A <= gamma (s+a_n)^2 / (2 P S^2), a distance budget, a Rayleigh test function, a stability squeeze, and the Alev-Anari-Lau-Oveis Gharan cut/resistance-diameter theorem (balance 3-a = 1+6a, a = 2/7). Exhaustively for n <= 7 every maximizer is a barbell; the optimal block fraction is 1/3 at n = 60, 120, 240.

Joint Gaussianity, stationarity, and zero mean

Cov(X_1,X_{1+h}) tends to zero
rho is fixed and finite

[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2607.29536, 'Multi-hop visibility through the vacant set of Poissonian obstacles'] Let $\rho>0$. For any line $\ell$ and $y,y'\in\R^d$ with $d(y',\ell)\geq d(y,\ell)$,
\[
\lambda_d\big(B([y,y'],\rho)\setminus B(\ell,\rho)\big)\geq 
c\rho^{d-2}\min(\rho,1)\, \|y-y'\| \min\big(d(y',\ell),1\big),
\]
for some $c=c(d)>0$.

body: [Theorem 3 of arXiv:2609.01114, 'Unbalanced spectral Tur\'an problem for color-critical graphs with prescribed large maximu'] Let $F$ be a connected color-critical graph with $\chi(F)=r+1\ge4$. There is a constant $s_F\in [0,1)$ such that, for all sufficiently large $n$, every $F$-free graph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta$ satisfying $\left\lceil(r-1)n/r\right\rceil \le \Delta\le n-\Theta(n^{s_F})$ satisfies $\rho(G)\le\rho(S_{n,\Delta}^{(r)})$. Equality holds if and only if $G\cong S_{n,\Delta}^{(r)}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Lem 162 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $I$ be a finite, nonempty index set. Let 
  \[
    \lt(\Theta, 
    \vec{\hat{Z}}\equiv
    (\hat Z_i)_{i\in I},
    \vec{\tilde{Z}}
    \equiv(\tilde Z_i)_{i\in I}\rt)
  \]
  be a random variable where
  $(\vec{\hat{Z}},\vec{\tilde{Z}})$
  are centered, jointly gaussian, and independent of $\Theta$. 
  Assume that $\vec{\hat{Z}}$ and $\vec{\tilde{Z}}$ are equidistributed,
 and that, for distinct $i,k\in I$,
  \[
    \bbE[\hat Z_i\hat Z_k]
    =\bbE[\tilde Z_i\tilde Z_k]
    =\bbE[\hat Z_i\tilde Z_k]=0.
  \]
Let $F$ and $G$ be measurable functions
such that $F(\Theta,\hat Z)$ and 
$G(\Theta,\hat Z)$ have finite variance, and such that
	\beq
    \bbE\Big[F(\Theta,\hat Z) 
    	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big] = 0 = 
    \bbE\Big[G(\Theta,\tilde Z) 
    	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]\,,
    \eeq
  $\Theta$-almost surely.
Then the covariance between $F(\Theta,\hat{Z})$ and $G(\Theta,\tilde{Z})$ is bounded by
  \beq
    \lt| \bbE[F(\Theta,\hat Z) G(\Theta,\tilde Z)] \rt|
    \le
    \rho_{\max} \cdot
    \bbE[F(\Theta,\hat Z)^2]^{1/2}
    \bbE[G(\Theta,\tilde Z)^2]^{1/2}\,, 
    
  \eeq
where $\rho_i\in[-1,+1]$ denotes the correlation between $\hat{Z}_i$ and $\tilde{Z}_i$, and 
$\rho_{\max} 
   \equiv\max\{|\rho_i|: i\in i\}$.
 
\begin{proof}
Let $\sigma_i$ denote the standard deviation of $\hat{Z}_i$, and denote
  \[
    \hat W_i \equiv 
    \frac{\hat Z_i}{\sigma_i}\,, \quad
    \tilde W_i 
    \equiv \frac{\tilde Z_i}{\sigma_i}\,,
  \]
which are marginally standard gaussians. It follows from the assumptions that
$(\hat W_i,\tilde W_i)$ are independent over $i\in I$, and $\bbE[\hat W_i\tilde W_i]=\rho_i$.
Let $(h_m)_{m\geq 0}$ denote the orthonormal Hermite polynomials for the
one-dimensional standard gaussian measure. We note that if $W$ and $\tilde{W}$ are marginally standard gaussians, and $(W,\tilde{W})$ is jointly gaussian and $\rho$-correlated, then it is straightforward to verify that
	\beq
	\E[ h_n(W) h_m(\tilde{W})]
	= \ind\{n=m\} \rho^n\,.\eeq
 For a multi-index $\vec n=(n_i)_{i\in I}\in\bbZ_{\ge 0}^I$, define the multivariate Hermite polynomial
  \[
    H_{\vec n}(w)
    \equiv\prod_{i\in I}h_{n_i}(w_i).
  \]
  We expand $F,G$ in the Hermite bases of $\hat W$ and $\tilde W$ respectively, conditional on $\Theta$, to obtain Hermite coefficients $a_{\vec n}(\Theta)$ and $b_{\vec n}(\Theta)$ such that
  \begin{align*}
    F(\Theta,\hat Z)
    &= \sum_{\vec n}a_{\vec n}(\Theta)
        H_{\vec n}(\hat W)\,, \\
    G(\Theta,\tilde Z)
    &= \sum_{\vec n}b_{\vec n}(\Theta)
        H_{\vec n}(\tilde W)\,.
  \end{align*}
  The assumption \eqref{e:conditional-centering} ensures $a_{\vec 0}(\Theta)=b_{\vec 0}(\Theta)=0$, $\Theta$-almost surely.
  Consequently, expanding in the Hermite bases and applying \eqref{e:hermite.corr.ip} gives
  \begin{align*}
    &\bigg|
      \bbE\Big[
        F(\Theta,\hat Z)G(\Theta,\tilde Z) \,\Big|\, \Theta
      \Big]
    \bigg|
    \le
      \sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
         |a_{\vec n}(\Theta)b_{\vec n}(\Theta)|
         \prod_{i\in I}|\rho_i|^{n_i}\\
    &\qquad\le
      \rho_{\max}
      \bigg(\sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
        a_{\vec n}(\Theta)^2
        \bigg)^{1/2}
      \bigg(\sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
        b_{\vec n}(\Theta)^2
        \bigg)^{1/2}
    =\rho_{\max}
      \bbE\Big[F(\Theta,\hat Z)^2 
      	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]^{1/2}
      \bbE\Big[G(\Theta,\tilde Z)^2 
      	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]^{1/2}\,.
  \end{align*}
  Taking expectation over $\Theta$ and again applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality proves the conclusion.
\end{proof}

body:
[Theorem th:Foster-Liapunov of arXiv:2603.20078, '\bf \Large Gated Infinite Server Queues in Light Traffic'] Suppose 
	that a Markov Chain with countable state space, say $\mathbb{Z}_+$, and transition
	probability matrix $P_{ij}$ is irreducible and let $N$ be a given natural
	number. If $V:\mathbb{Z}_+\to \mathbb{R}_+$, is a non-negative and $h:\mathbb{Z}_+\to \mathbb{R}_+$ a
	strictly positive function on the state space such that
	\begin{eqnarray}
		\sum_{j\in \mathbb{Z}_+} P_{ij}V(j) &\leq  & b,\hspace{1.14in}i \leq  N,
		 \\
		\sum_{j\in \mathbb{Z}_+} P_{ij}V(j) &\leq  & V(i)-h(i) ,\hspace{0.4in} i>N,  
	\end{eqnarray}
	where $b>0$, then the Markov Chain is positive recurrent and its (unique, 
	due to its irreducibility) stationary distribution, $\pi$, satisfies $\sum_j\pi(j) h(j) <\infty$. 
	Furthermore we have 
	$\sum_{j}P_{ij}^n h(j) \rightarrow \sum_j \pi_j h(j)$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 30 (Scaling) of arXiv:2607.24561, 'Range convergence and sharp one-arm asymptotics\\for the critical percolation cluster in h'] For $\lambda>0$ define $\Phi_\lambda:\cM\to\cM$ by
$(\Phi_\lambda\mu)(A):=\lambda^{-4}\mu(\lambda A)$. Then
\[
\bN\circ\bigl(\mu\mapsto\Phi_\lambda\mu\bigr)^{-1}
\;=\;\lambda^{-2}\,\bN
\qquad\text{as measures on }\cM .
\]
In particular $\supp(\Phi_\lambda\mu)=\lambda^{-1}\Ran$, so  the family
$K\mapsto\bN(\Ran\not\subset\overline B_K)$ scales as $K^{-2}$; see
Proposition~\ref{prop:range}.

[Proposition 3 of arXiv:2608.12839, 'Spiking Neural Networks with Elephant Reinforcement'] Let \(\boldsymbol\mu(t)\) be a solution of the nonlinear RMF equation. Then, for
all \((v,s,k)\in E\), the coordinate probabilities are absolutely continuous
in time and satisfy the following equations for almost every \(t\geq0\).

For \(v\geq1\),
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dt}p_i(t;v,s,k)
=
a_i(t)p_i(t;v-1,s,k)

-
\bigl[a_i(t)+\gamma+\lambda(v,s,k)\bigr]
 p_i(t;v,s,k).
\end{align}

For \(v=0\),
\begin{align}
\frac{d}{dt}p_i(t;0,s,k)
=&
-a_i(t)p_i(t;0,s,k)

+
\gamma\sum_{u\geq1}p_i(t;u,s,k)
\\
&+
q^{+}(s-1,k-1)
\sum_{u\geq0}
\lambda(u,s-1,k-1)
 p_i(t;u,s-1,k-1)
\nonumber\\
&+
q^{-}(s+1,k-1)
\sum_{u\geq0}
\lambda(u,s+1,k-1)
 p_i(t;u,s+1,k-1).
\nonumber
\end{align}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}

\beta_i(t)
=
\sum_{(v,s,k)\in E}
\lambda(v,s,k)p_i(t;v,s,k).
\end{equation}
For the hard-threshold intensity,
\begin{equation}

\beta_i(t)
=
\sum_{s,k}
\sum_{v>\alpha s^+}
p_i(t;v,s,k).
\end{equation}

body:
Let Omega be a bounded open set in R^n with C^1 boundary and outward unit normal nu, and let F be a vector field in C^1(closure of Omega) (or in W^{1,1}(Omega) with an integrable trace). Then the integral over Omega of the divergence of F equals the boundary integral of F dotted with nu with respect to (n-1)-dimensional surface measure. Two standard consequences: integration by parts, the integral over Omega of u_{x_i} v = minus the integral of u v_{x_i} plus the boundary integral of u v nu_i; and Green's identities, for instance the integral over Omega of ( u Laplacian v - v Laplacian u ) equals the boundary integral of ( u times the normal derivative of v minus v times the normal derivative of u ). The theorem extends to Lipschitz domains, where the normal exists at almost every boundary point, and to sets of finite perimeter with the reduced boundary and measure-theoretic normal in place of the classical ones.
Boundary regularity (C^1, or Lipschitz, or finite perimeter) and enough integrability of the field and its derivative up to the boundary.
On an arbitrary bounded open set the statement is false - the boundary can be too wild to carry a normal.

[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] For $n\in \mathbb{N}$, fix $1\leq k<n$ and $T\geq0$. Then fix a function $f= f_{n}$ with $f \, : \: \So{n} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ of the form 
\[
f(X) = \prod_{r=1}^{k} X[i_{r},j_{r}].
\]

Let $C > 0$ be the constant appearing in the statement of Theorem \ref{LemmaMainContractionEstimate} and let 
\be 
\omega_{n} = C_{\mathrm{diam}}\,k\, n^{- \left\lfloor \frac{T}{C n (k+\log(n))\log(n)} \right\rfloor}
\ee 
be the upper bound obtained in that theorem.\footnote{Here we replace $D(X,Y)$ with the upper bound $C_{\mathrm{diam}} \, k$, where $C_{\mathrm{diam}}$ is a universal constant chosen so that the diameter of $\mathrm{St}(n,k)$ with respect to the Riemannian distance $D$ is at most $C_{\mathrm{diam}}k$.}

There exists some universal constant $N_{0}$ so that, for all $n > N_{0}$ and all $x \in \So{n}$,
\be 
| \kacdist_{n,T,x}(f) - \haarOdist_{n}(f) | \leq 2\sqrt{2k\,\omega_{n}}.
\ee

[Lemma convexity of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Let $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be $C^2$ with $g''\ge \kappa$ for some $\kappa\in\mathbb{R}$, and let
		$\Phi_\zeta$ be the solution of the Parisi PDE run backward on $[t,1]$ with terminal
		condition $\Phi_\zeta(1,\cdot)=g$, where $\xi''\ge 0$ and $\zeta\ge 0$.
		Then for every $s\in[t,1]$,
		\[
		\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\,\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(s,x)
		\;\ge\;
		\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\,g''(x)
		\;\ge\;
		\kappa.
		\]
		In particular, $x\mapsto\Phi_\zeta(s,x)$ is everywhere at least as convex as $g$.

Let gamma be the standard normal probability measure on R and g be a real function in L^2(gamma). Use the orthonormal probabilists Hermite basis H_k=He_k/sqrt(k!) and coefficients a_k=E[g(Z)*H_k(Z)], Z~gamma. For jointly standard normal X,Y with correlation q in (-1,1), define C_g(q)=Cov(g(X),g(Y)) and V=Var_gamma(g). Then C_g(q)=sum_(k>=1) a_k^2*q^k and V=sum_(k>=1) a_k^2. In particular, lim_(q up to 1) [V-C_g(q)]/(1-q)=sum_(k>=1) k*a_k^2, allowing the value +infinity. This sum is finite exactly when g has a weak derivative g_prime in L^2(gamma), that is, g belongs to H^1(gamma); weak derivative means the usual distributional derivative with respect to Lebesgue measure. In that case ||g_prime||_(L^2(gamma))^2=sum_(k>=1) k*a_k^2 and V-C_g(q)=||g_prime||_(L^2(gamma))^2*(1-q)+o(1-q). These are Gaussian analytic identities used in the authors' activation-smoothness calculation. They do not require the replica ansatz and do not assert a rigorous storage-capacity threshold.
Real g in L^2 of the standard Gaussian measure; orthonormal probabilists Hermite convention.
For the finite-energy first-order expansion, also g in H^1(gamma).

Let (D,d) be a Polish metric space and let mu_i,nu_i be Borel probability measures with finite second moments, for i=1,...,k with finite k>=1. Let t_i>=0 and sum_i t_i=1. Then W_2(sum_i t_i mu_i,sum_i t_i nu_i)^2<=sum_i t_i W_2(mu_i,nu_i)^2. The same weights occur on both sides of the coupling. In particular, for r in [0,1] and mu,nu,tau in P_2(D), W_2((1-r)mu+r tau,(1-r)nu+r tau)^2<=(1-r)W_2(mu,nu)^2. Thus the corresponding contraction factor for W_2 itself is sqrt(1-r). Joint convexity is asserted for the squared distance. The unsquared version is false: on R take mu_1=mu_2=nu_2=delta_0, nu_1=delta_1, and weights r,1-r with 0<r<1; the distance between mixtures is sqrt(r), whereas the weighted sum of the two unsquared distances is r. Source: Ambrosio--Stra--Trevisan, A PDE approach to a 2-dimensional matching problem, Section 2.1, equation (2.4).
Polish metric space (complete and separable)
Finite collection of probability-measure pairs, each with finite second moment

body: In probability theory, if a large number of events are all independent of one another and each has probability less than 1, then there is a positive probability that none of the events will occur. The Lovász local lemma allows a slight relaxation of the independence condition: As long as the events are "mostly" independent from one another and aren't individually too likely, then there will still be a positive probability that none of them occurs. This lemma is most commonly used in the probabilistic method, in particular to give existence proofs.

body: [Corollary 4 of arXiv:2609.03070, 'Variants of order semicontinuity in Banach lattices'] Let $E\subset F$ be an order dense sublattice and let $B\subset E$ be solid in $E$. Then, the order and uo adherences of $B$ in $F$ and the order and uo adherences of $\Sol_{F} B$ all coincide. This set is always solid, and it is convex whenever $B$ is. $f\in F$ belongs to this set if and only if there is $Q\subset B_{+}$ with $Q\uparrow\left|f\right|$.

body:
Load-bearing hypothesis: 'take the closure of T' presupposes that T is closable, i.e. that x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → 0 and Tx_n → y force y = 0; equivalently (in a Hilbert space) that D(T*) is dense. What fails: without closability the closure of the graph is not a graph, and 'the smallest closed extension' does not exist. Counterexample: H = ℓ², D(T) = finitely supported sequences, T x = (Σ_n x_n) e_1. T is densely defined and linear. Take x^{(k)} = (1/k, ..., 1/k, 0, 0, ...) with k entries: ‖x^{(k)}‖ = 1/√k → 0 while T x^{(k)} = e_1 for every k, so the graph closure contains both (0,0) and (0, e_1) and T is not closable. Consistently, ⟨Tx, y⟩ = (Σ x_n) conj(y_1) is ℓ²-bounded in x only if y_1 = 0, so D(T*) = {y : y_1 = 0} is not dense - exactly the criterion. The same phenomenon occurs for pointwise evaluation f ↦ f(0)g on L²(ℝ) restricted to continuous L² functions. Related traps: (i) an operator can be closable while its closure has strictly larger domain on which a defining formula no longer holds pointwise, so identities proved on D(T) must be re-derived by continuity in the graph norm; (ii) symmetry rescues closability (a symmetric operator is always closable, since T ⊂ T* and T* is closed), which is why this pitfall bites mainly for non-symmetric operators such as first order operators with unbalanced boundary conditions or multiplication-composition operators; (iii) a core argument ('it suffices to verify on a dense subspace') is valid only if the subspace is dense in the graph norm of the closed operator, not merely dense in the ambient space.
the operator is densely defined but not assumed symmetric or closed
a closure or a core argument is being invoked
title: Pitfall: A Densely Defined Operator Need Not Be Closable (and Closures Can Destroy Formulas)

body: In probability theory, the de Moivre–Laplace theorem, which is a special case of the central limit theorem, states that the normal distribution may be used as an approximation to the binomial distribution under certain conditions. In particular, the theorem shows that the probability mass function of the random number of "successes" observed in a series of $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, each having probability $p$ of success (a binomial distribution with $n$ trials), converges to the probability density function of the normal distribution with expectation $np$ and standard deviation ${\textstyle {\sqrt {np(1-p)}}}$, as $n$ grows large, assuming $p$ is not $0$ or $1$.

body: [Definition 1 (Asymmetric shelf-shuffle) of arXiv:2606.18047, 'Analysis of the asymmetric shelf shuffle'] Let $m\in \mathbb{N}$ be a natural number and $p\in (0, 1)$. An $(m, p)$-shelf shuffler has $m$ labelled shelves. A deck of cards labelled $1, \ldots, n$ is dealt from the bottom sequentially and assigned a shelf independently and uniformly at random. Each card is placed at the top or bottom of the existing pile, on the assigned shelf, with probability $p$ and $1-p$, respectively, independently of everything else. The shuffled deck is then formed by joining the piles in shelf order.
title: Asymmetric shelf-shuffle

[Theorem 16 (Kac's walk applied to the Johnson--Lindenstrauss transform) of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] There is a universal constant $C_{\mathrm{JL}}<\infty$ such that the following holds. Let $n\geq 2$, let $x\in\So{n}$, and let $M\sim\kacdist_{n,T,x}$ be the endpoint of $T$ steps of Kac's walk started from $x$. Let $\mathcal X\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ have $N\geq2$ points, and let $0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2$. Set
\be 
r=\left\lceil \log\frac{N}{\delta}\right\rceil,
\ee
and assume $4r<n$. Let $\ell$ be an integer satisfying
\be 
C_{\mathrm{JL}}\varepsilon^{-2}r\leq \ell<n.
\ee

If
\be 
T\geq
C_{\mathrm{JL}}\,n(4r+\log n)\left(r\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}+\log\frac{N}{\delta}\right),
\ee
then, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $M\sim\kacdist_{n,T,x}$,
\be 
(1-\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\leq
\|A_M(x_i-x_j)\|_2^2
\leq
(1+\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\ee
for every pair $1\leq i<j\leq N$.

In particular, for fixed $\varepsilon$ and $N/\delta\leq n^A$, with $A<\infty$ fixed, the usual Johnson--Lindenstrauss target dimension $\ell=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(N/\delta))=O_A(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ \vnote{Isn't the JL target dimension $\epsilon^{-2}\log N$? EDIT: Ah, I see what's going on, $N$ is set to polynomial in $n$. But see below.} is achieved by taking $T\geq C_A n\log^3 n$. \vnote{I am worried that this is not the best illustration of our bound. In particular, when $N$ is polynomial in $n$, the JL embedding dimension $\ell$ is already $O(\log n)$ and so applying the matrix already only costs $O(n\log n)$. Shouldn't we be thinking about very large point sets of size, say $2^{n^{\epsilon'}}$ for some constant $0 < \epsilon' < 1$.} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Kac's walk applied to the Johnson--Lindenstrauss transform

body: Let dx/dt = f(x) be a C^1 vector field on R^n with an equilibrium x_0 (f(x_0) = 0) that is hyperbolic, meaning the Jacobian Df(x_0) has no eigenvalue with zero real part. The Hartman-Grobman theorem states that there is a neighborhood U of x_0 and a homeomorphism h: U -> R^n with h(x_0) = 0 conjugating the nonlinear flow near x_0 to the linear flow generated by Df(x_0): h(phi_t(x)) = exp(t Df(x_0)) h(x) whenever both sides are defined. So near a hyperbolic equilibrium the qualitative behavior of the nonlinear system matches its linearization; an analogous statement holds for hyperbolic fixed points of diffeomorphisms.
title: Hartman-Grobman theorem

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2608.19396, '\bf Penalisation of Two-Dimensional Brownian Motion'] Let $(F_{t})_{t \geq 0}$ denote an $(\mathcal{F}_t)$-adapted, nonnegative process. We shall say that this process belongs to the class $\mathcal{C}$ if and only if the following conditions hold:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item  $(F_{t})_{t \geq 0}$ is a nonnegative and nonincreasing process. In particular, since $0 \leq F_{t} \leq F_{0}$ and $F_{0}$ is a.s. constant ($\mathcal{F}_0$ is trivial), this process is $W^{(2)}$-almost surely bounded by a constant $C = F_{0}$.
     \item 
    There exists $a>0$ such that for every $t \geq \sigma_a$, where $
    \sigma_a := \sup \{ t \geq 0 :  |X_{t}|\le a \}$, 
    we have $$F_{t} = F_{\sigma_a} = F_{\infty} := \underset{s \rightarrow \infty}{\lim} F_s.$$
    \item We have

    \end{enumerate}

[Theorem thm:abstract-square-transversality of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] Let $\nu_{\rm ref}$ be a sigma-finite positive Radon measure on $S$, and let
$(\Lambda_i,\phi_i)_{i=1}^M$ be real eigenpairs of $A_\mu$ with continuous
representatives.  Assume that the following three conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt,topsep=0.35em,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item The eigenpairs satisfy
\begin{equation}
 A_\mu\phi_i=\Lambda_i\phi_i,
 \qquad
 \Lambda_i>0,
 \qquad
 \Lambda_i\ne\Lambda_j\ (i\ne j),
 \qquad
 \left\|\phi_i\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=1.
 
\end{equation}
\item The measures satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \mu\perp\nu_{\rm ref},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{supp}\mu=S,
 \qquad
 \rho=0\ \text{or}\ \rho\ll\nu_{\rm ref}.
 
\end{equation}
\item There exist $c_0>0$, finite signed measures $b_i\ll\nu_{\rm ref}$, and a
linear map
\begin{equation}
 L:
 \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{\phi_1^2,\ldots,\phi_M^2\}
 \longrightarrow\mathcal M_{\rm fin}(S),
 
\end{equation}
such that
\begin{equation}
 L(\phi_i^2)
 =c_0\Lambda_i\phi_i^2\mu-b_i,
 \qquad 1\le i\le M.
 
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Then, for every $a\in\mathbb R^M$,
\begin{align}
 \sum_{i=1}^Ma_i\Theta_\mu(\phi_i,\phi_i)=0
 &\Longrightarrow a=0,
 \\
 \sum_{i=1}^Ma_i\Lambda_i\Theta_\mu(\phi_i,\phi_i)=0
 &\Longrightarrow a=0.
 
\end{align}

[Proposition 5 (Continuity / Cauchy--Schwarz) of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] Fix $f\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}^m)$. The map
\[
T_f:\ L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}^m)\to \mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R}),\qquad
T_f(g):=\langle f,g\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})},
\]
is linear and bounded. More precisely, for any matrix norm $\|\cdot\|$ on $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$,
there exists a constant $C_m>0$ (depending only on $m$ and on the chosen norm) such that
\[
\|\langle f,g\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\|
\le C_m\,\|f\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}^m)}\,\|g\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}^m)}
\qquad\forall\,g\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^d,\mathbb{R}^m).
\]
In particular, $T_f$ is continuous.

[Corollary cor:inverse-weight-linear-dynamics of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Let $0\leq\alpha<1$ and assume
Assumption~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper).  Let
\begin{equation*}
 F\in L_\alpha^2,\qquad \psi\in L^2(\mu_T),\qquad u=\mathcal U(F,\psi),
\end{equation*}
and put $Y=u(\cdot,X)$ and $P=D_xu(\cdot,X)$.  There exists a universal numerical
constant $C>0$ such that
$Y\in\mathbb S^2(\mathbb R)$, $P^\top\in\mathbb H^2(\mathsf M^X;\mathbb R)$,
\begin{equation}
 Y_t=\psi(X_T)+\int_t^TF(s,X_s)\,\mathrm d s
      -\int_t^TP_s^\top\,\mathrm d\mathsf M_s^X,
 
\end{equation}
The accompanying estimate is
\begin{equation}
 \left\lVert Y\right\rVert_{\mathbb S^2(\mathbb R)}^2
 +\left\lVert P^\top\right\rVert_{\mathbb H^2(\mathsf M^X;\mathbb R)}^2
 \leq C\left(
   \norm\psi_{L^2(\mu_T)}^2
   +\frac{T^{1-\alpha}}{1-\alpha}\left\lVert F\right\rVert_\alpha^2\right).
 
\end{equation}
If, in addition, Assumption~(ass:drift-multiplier of the paper) holds,
$F\in H_{x,\alpha}^1$, and $\psi\in H^1(\mu_T)$, set
\begin{equation*}
 \mathsf H=D_x^2u(\cdot,X),\qquad
 \mathfrak A_t=-\int_0^t\mathfrak g[u,F](s,X_s)\,\mathrm d s.
\end{equation*}
Then $P\in\mathbb S^2(\mathbb R^d)$,
$\mathsf H\in\mathbb H^2(\mathsf M^X;\mathbb R^d)$, and
$\mathfrak A\in\mathbb V^2(\mathbb R^d)$, with
\begin{equation}
 P_t=P_0+\mathfrak A_t
       +\int_0^t\mathsf H_s\,\mathrm d\mathsf M_s^X,
 \qquad
 P_T=D_x\psi(X_T).
 
\end{equation}
The gradient processes satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \left\lVert P\right\rVert_{\mathbb S^2(\mathbb R^d)}^2
 +\left\lVert \mathsf H\right\rVert_{\mathbb H^2(\mathsf M^X;\mathbb R^d)}^2
 +\left\lVert \mathfrak A\right\rVert_{\mathbb V^2(\mathbb R^d)}^2
 \leq C\left(
   \left\lVert D_x\psi\right\rVert_{L^2(\mu_T)}^2
   +\frac{T^{1-\alpha}}{1-\alpha}
       \left\lVert \mathfrak g[u,F]\right\rVert_\alpha^2\right).
 
\end{equation}

Method: Optimal limited independence for Gaussian polynomial thresholds exact calculation or structural obstruction Result: Take n=k+1 signs uniformly distributed subject to product_i sign_i=1, independent of n independent absolute standard Gaussians R_i. Then X_i=sign_i*R_i has k-wise independent standard-Gaussian coordinates. Yet product_i X_i>0 almost surely, while the same product for fully independent Gaussians is positive with probability1/2. Check: Every assignment of any k signs has exactly one extension satisfying the parity constraint, so its probability is2^-k. Independent magnitudes then yield independent Gaussian marginals on that subset. The distinguishing polynomial has degree k+1. Obstruction: For epsilon<1/2 this proves the necessary bound k>=d. It is weaker than known quantitative lower bounds and supplies no sharp dependence on epsilon.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0170-optimal-limited-independence-for-gaussian-polynomial-thresholds

body: Tonelli's theorem needs BOTH measures sigma-finite and the integrand nonnegative and product-measurable; it then asserts that the double integral and both iterated integrals agree in [0, infinity], with no integrability assumption. Fubini's theorem needs both measures sigma-finite and f in L^1(mu tensor nu); it then asserts the same equality with all three quantities finite. Two failure modes are standard and are NOT the same failure. (1) Integrability dropped, sigma-finiteness kept: on (0,1)^2 with Lebesgue measure take f(x,y) = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2 + y^2)^2. Since d/dy [ y/(x^2+y^2) ] = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2, the inner integral over y in (0,1) is 1/(1+x^2), so integrating in x afterwards gives pi/4; f is antisymmetric under swapping x and y, so the other order gives -pi/4. Both iterated integrals exist and are finite and they differ, so f cannot be in L^1 of the product. (2) sigma-finiteness dropped, nonnegativity kept: let mu be Lebesgue measure on [0,1], nu counting measure on [0,1], and f the indicator of the diagonal. Then integral over x of (integral over y of f dnu) dmu = integral 1 dmu = 1, while integral over y of (integral over x of f dmu) dnu = integral 0 dnu = 0. Tonelli's conclusion fails although f >= 0, because nu is not sigma-finite. A third, quieter caveat: for COMPLETE measure spaces the correct statement is that ALMOST every section is measurable, not every section, since a null set in the product can have non-measurable sections; the theorem for the completed product measure is stated that way. In practice the usable recipe is: apply Tonelli to |f| first to decide integrability, then apply Fubini to f. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorems 2.37 and 2.39]

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Review the failure of perturbation theory and test a restricted version on a tree-like subgraph. Result: On the Bethe lattice a.c. spectrum is known (Klein; Aizenman-Warzel) because the self-consistent equation for the Green function has a stable solution; on Z^3 the corresponding equation is not closed. A known partial statement is that the rescaled disorder-averaged Wigner distribution evolves diffusively up to times lambda^{-2-kappa} for a small kappa > 0 (Erdos-Salmhofer-Yau), beyond the kinetic time scale lambda^{-2} but still finite, so it does not reach the infinite-time statement. I tested the possibility of transferring the tree result through a spanning tree of Z^3: the operator restricted to a spanning tree is not the operator on Z^3, and removing the edges changes the spectrum non-perturbatively, so no transfer. No result; the problem is recorded as attempted with the explicit obstruction that the only tools proving a.c. spectrum are tree-specific. Obstruction: Absence of a closed self-consistency equation on Z^3; kinetic-regime results stop at finite times.

body: [Theorem 1 (Perron-Frobenius Perron (1907) of arXiv:2503.19927, 'Fully personalized PageRank and algebraic methods to distribute a random walker'] Let A ∈RN×N be a non-negative, irreducible square matrix. Then the following statements are true: 1. ρ(A) ∈σ(A) and its algebraic multiplicity is 1. 2. There exists a vector c ∈Rn with c > 0 such that it is an eigenvector of A associated to the eigenvalue ρ(A). 3. The eigenvector c is unique up to scaling. The eigenvector c is sometimes referred to as the Perron eigenvector of A.

[Definition 12 ($\ivgff$) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Fix $d=2$ and $\beta \in \R_{>0}$. For any domain $\Lambda$ and any $\zeta: \Z^2 \mapsto \Z$, the \emph{two-dimensional lattice integer-valued Gaussian free field} (2D IV-GFF) --- also known as \emph{discrete Gaussian model} --- on $\Lambda$ with boundary conditions $\zeta$ at inverse temperature $\beta$ is the probability measure on $\phi: \Z^2 \mapsto \Z$ given by 
\[ \mu^\zeta_{\ivgff, \Lambda, \beta} [\phi =f ]  = \frac{1}{Z_{\ivgff, \Lambda, \beta}^\zeta} \e^{- \beta H^\zeta_{\ivgff, \Lambda}(f)}, \]
where $Z^\zeta_{\ivgff, \Lambda, \beta}$ is the normalising constant and 
\[ H^\zeta_{\ivgff, \Lambda}(f) = \sum_{\substack{\{x,y\}\subset \Lambda \\ x \sim y}}(f_x - f_y)^2 + \sum_{\substack{x \in \Lambda, y \in \Lambda^c \\ x \sim y}}(f_x - \zeta_y)^2.  \]

body:
[Defn of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Let $X$ be a marked hyperbolic structure on $S$, let
$\rho_0:\pi_1(S)\to\mathrm{PSL}(2,\mathbb R)$ be its holonomy, and identify
$\widetilde X$ with $\mathbb{H}^2$. Given a representation
$\rho:\pi_1(S)\to\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$, a \emph{$\rho$-equivariant pleated plane}
is a continuous map  $\Psi:\widetilde X\longrightarrow \mathbb{H}^3$
such that
\[
        \Psi\bigl(\gamma \cdot x\bigr)
        =\rho(\gamma)\Psi(x)
        \qquad
        \text{for every $\gamma\in\pi_1(S)$ and $x\in\widetilde X$,}
\]
and with the following properties:

(i) There is a geodesic lamination $\lambda$ on $X$ such that $\Psi$ is a totally-geodesic embedding on the closure of every complementary component of its lift $\tilde{\lambda} \subset \tilde{X}$. Such a component $P$ is called a \textit{plaque} and its $\Psi$-image lies on a totally-geodesic copy of the hyperbolic plane $H_P \subset \mathbb{H}^3$, called the \emph{support plane} of $P$.

(ii) $\Psi$ is path-isometric: for every rectifiable arc
$a\subset\widetilde X$, $\ell_{\mathbb{H}^3}(\Psi(a))
        =\ell_{X}(a)$, 
where the length on the left is the length of the parametrized
image. The smallest geodesic lamination for which these properties
hold is the \emph{pleating locus}.

(iii) The pleating locus is equipped with a transverse measure recording
the bending angles. More precisely, if a leaf $\ell\subset \widetilde\lambda$, of weight
$\theta\in(0,\pi]$ separates two plaques $P_-$ and $P_+$, the support plane $H_{P_+}$ is obtained from
$H_{P_-}$ by an elliptic rotation about the geodesic
$\Psi(\ell)$ through angle $\theta$; the direction of rotation is
determined by the chosen orientations.

More generally, let $a$ be an oriented arc transverse to
$\widetilde\lambda$, with endpoints in plaques $P$ and $Q$.
Approximating the measured lamination in a neighborhood of $a$ by
finitely many weighted leaves, one may compose, in their order along
$a$, the rotations through the corresponding bending angles about
the successive images of their leaves. The convergence theorem for
quakebend cocycles (see
[EpsteinMarden], and also
[BonShear]) implies that these ordered products converge in
$\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ to an isometry  $B_{\widetilde\lambda}(P,Q)\in\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$. 
The limit is independent of the finite approximation and satisfies
\begin{equation*} 
    B_{\widetilde\lambda}(P,R)
        =
                B_{\widetilde\lambda}(P,Q) 
        B_{\widetilde\lambda}(Q,R)
\end{equation*} 
where the composition is from left to right. This $B_{\widetilde\lambda}$ is the
\emph{bending cocycle} (see also [Dumas]). 
The rotation-angle component of the bending defines a transverse measure  on $\widetilde\lambda$; from the equivariance it descends to a measured
geodesic lamination $\lambda$ on $X$ that we call the \textit{bending lamination}. Moreover, 

the \emph{straightening} of $\Psi$ is obtained by replacing the bending cocycle by the trivial cocycle; its intrinsic hyperbolic structure is $X$.
title: Unnumbered defn of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'

[Proposition identity1 of arXiv:2411.05534, 'Inverse problems for stochastic partial differential equations'] Assume that $u$ is an $H^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$-valued
continuous It\^o process. Put $v=\theta u$ (with $\theta$ given by (weight1-1 of the paper)). Then,
\begin{align}
\notag
& \quad-\theta\Big[ \sum_{j,k=1}^n (b^{jk}v_{x_j})_{x_k}+s\lambda\varphi \psi_t v
\Big]\Big[ du - \sum_{j,k=1}^n (b^{jk}u_{x_j})_{x_k}dt \Big]
\\ \notag
& \quad+
\frac{1}{4}\lambda\theta v \Big[du - \sum_{j,k=1}^n
(b^{jk}u_{x_j})_{x_k}dt\Big]
\\ \notag
& = - \!\sum_{j,k=1}^n\! \Big(b^{jk}v_{x_j} dv\! +\!
\frac{1}{4}b^{jk}v_{x_j} vdt\Big)_{x_k}  \!
+ \frac{1}{2}d\Big(
\sum_{j,k=1}^n b^{jk}v_{x_j} v_{x_k}\! -\!
s\lambda\varphi\psi_t v^2\! + \!\frac{1}{8}\lambda v^2 \Big)
\\ \notag
& \quad + \Big(\frac{1}{4}\lambda
\sum_{j,k=1}^n b^{jk}v_{x_j} v_{x_k} dt - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j,k=1}^n b^{jk}dv_{x_j}
dv_{x_k}
\Big) + \frac{1}{2}s\lambda^2\varphi \psi_t^2 v^2 dt
\\ \notag
& \quad
+ \frac{1}{2}   s\lambda\varphi\psi_{tt} v^2dt
- \frac{1}{4}s\lambda^2\psi_t \varphi v^2 dt
+ \frac{1}{2}s\lambda\varphi\psi_t (dv)^2
- \frac{1}{8}\lambda (dv)^2
\\
&  \quad
+ \Big[ \sum_{j,k=1}^n (b^{jk}v_{x_j})_{x_k}

body:
Let {X_{m,n} : 0 <= m < n} satisfy: (L1) X_{0,n} <= X_{0,m} + X_{m,n} for every 0 < m < n; (L2) for each m >= 1 the sequence {X_{nm, (n+1)m} : n >= 1} is STATIONARY; (L3) the distribution of the row {X_{m, m+k} : k >= 1} does not depend on m; (L4) E[X_{0,1}^+] < infinity and E[X_{0,n}] >= -c_0 n for every n, for some finite c_0. Then: (a) gamma = lim_n E[X_{0,n}]/n = inf_n E[X_{0,n}]/n exists in [-c_0, infinity); (b) X = lim_n X_{0,n}/n exists almost surely and in L^1, with E[X] = gamma; (c) if in addition all the stationary sequences in (L2) are ERGODIC then X = gamma almost surely. The difference from Kingman is that (L2) and (L3) together are strictly WEAKER than joint stationarity of the whole array: they demand stationarity only along each fixed block length and equality of the row laws, not invariance of the full joint distribution. That weakening is what lets the theorem apply to models where the array is not generated by a single measure-preserving transformation. Note also that (L4) asks only for the POSITIVE part of X_{0,1} to be integrable, weaker than Kingman's E|X_{0,1}| < infinity. Quoting Kingman's hypotheses when using Liggett's conclusion, or the reverse, is the standard misquotation here. [Liggett (1985), 'An improved subadditive ergodic theorem', Ann. Probab. 13, 1279-1285; textbook form in Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 6.6.1]
(L1) subadditivity
(L2) stationarity of the sequence of blocks of each fixed length
(L3) the row law does not depend on the starting index
(L4) E[X_{0,1}^+] finite and a linear lower bound on E[X_{0,n}]
ergodicity of the block sequences is needed only for a constant limit

Let Omega in R^n be a bounded open set and let Lu = sum a^{ij} D_{ij}u + sum b^i D_i u + c u with a^{ij} = a^{ji} and (a^{ij}(x)) positive definite for every x in Omega, with smallest eigenvalue lambda(x) > 0, and with sup over Omega of |b(x)|/lambda(x) finite. No continuity of the coefficients is needed. Let u be in C^2(Omega) intersect C^0(closure of Omega). (a) If c = 0 in Omega and Lu >= 0, then max over the closure of u = max over the boundary of u. (b) If c <= 0 in Omega (and sup |c|/lambda finite) and Lu >= 0, then max over the closure of u <= max over the boundary of u^+, where u^+ = max(u,0). The reversed statements hold for supersolutions (Lu <= 0) with min and -u^-. Consequences: comparison (if Lu >= Lv in Omega, c <= 0, and u <= v on the boundary, then u <= v in Omega) and uniqueness of the classical Dirichlet problem when c <= 0.

c = 0 for (a); c <= 0 with |c|/lambda bounded for (b)

body: In the field of mathematics known as functional analysis, the invariant subspace problem is a partially unresolved problem asking whether every bounded operator on a complex Banach space sends some non-trivial closed subspace to itself. Many variants of the problem have been solved, by restricting the class of bounded operators considered or by specifying a particular class of Banach spaces. The problem is still open for separable Hilbert spaces.

body:
Let f be a predictor fitted on a calibration sample, evaluated at design points x with targets y = mu(x) + e, where e has mean zero and variance sigma^2(x) and is independent of the sample. For a weighted average over a set of evaluation points E and the same average over the calibration points C (weights w_x summing to one on each set), write R_E = sum_E w_x E(y - f(x))^2 for the expected weighted risk on E, R_C the same on C, V_S = sum_S w_x Var f(x) for the average estimation variance on a set S, B_S = sum_S w_x (mu(x) - E f(x))^2 for the average squared bias, and N_S = sum_S w_x sigma^2(x) for the average noise. Then R_E = R_C + (V_E - V_C) + (B_E - B_C) + (N_E - N_C). Consequently, for a family of predictors f_t indexed by t (for instance a blend that is linear in t between two fitted bases), the minimiser over t of R_E(t) is the minimiser of R_C(t) + [V_E(t) - V_C(t)] + [B_E(t) - B_C(t)], the noise difference being free of t. A label-free criterion that replaces R_C(t) by the cross-validated risk on the calibration rows and V_E(t), V_C(t) by pairs-bootstrap estimates - the transductive covariance penalty used to choose the amount of simplex constraint at the scored rows - is this identity with the bias-shift term dropped; its single assumption is that the squared bias of the family shifts between the two point sets by an amount that does not depend on t, or does so less than the variance shift. What it cannot see is exactly the bias shift, which needs the targets at the new points; that is why such a criterion recovers only part of the hindsight-best t and errs toward the endpoint the calibration rows favour.
targets at every design point are mean plus noise with the noise independent of the calibration sample (so Cov(e, f(x)) = 0)
the weights on each point set sum to one; the family f_t is any family of fitted predictors (linearity in t is not needed for the identity, only for the cheap computation of the blend's cross-validated and bootstrap predictions)

Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables with E[X_i] = 0 and X_i <= b almost surely for every i - a ONE-SIDED bound suffices for the upper tail - and let v = sum_{i=1}^n E[X_i^2]. Then for every t > 0, P( sum_i X_i >= t ) <= exp( - (v/b^2) h(bt/v) ) where h(u) = (1+u) log(1+u) - u. Bennett's inequality implies Bernstein's inequality through h(u) >= u^2/(2(1 + u/3)), which gives the familiar P(sum X_i >= t) <= exp(-t^2/(2(v + bt/3))), and it is strictly sharper in the large-deviation regime bt/v large, where Bennett decays like exp(-(t/b) log(bt/v)) - a Poisson tail - while Bernstein decays only like exp(-3t/(2b)). This is the right inequality when the summands are bounded but their variance is much smaller than the square of the bound, the regime where Hoeffding's inequality is badly lossy. [Bennett (1962); see Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 2.9]
X_i independent with E[X_i] = 0
one-sided bound X_i <= b almost surely (no lower bound needed for the upper tail)
v = sum_i E[X_i^2] finite

body: [Theorem 3.3 (Adaptive wavelet estimation) in the first version of arXiv:2512.18592, 'Wavelet Latent Position Exponential Random Graphs'] Assume that conditional on observed latent positions $U_{1},\dots,U_{n}\in[0,1]$, the edges $\{A_{ij}:1\leq i<j\leq n\}$ are independent with $A_{ij}\mid(U_{k})_{k=1}^{n}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}\bigl(W(U_{i},U_{j})\bigr),$ for a symmetric graphon $W:[0,1]^{2}\to[0,1]$. Let $N_{n}:=\binom{n}{2}$ and assume $W\in\mathcal{F}^{s}_{p,q}(M)\cap[0,1],\qquad s>0,\quad 1\leq p\leq 2,\quad 0<q\leq\infty,$ where $\mathcal{F}^{s}_{p,q}(M)$ is the Besov ball from Definition 3.1. Let $\{\Psi_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda}$ be an orthonormal tensor-product wavelet basis of $L^{2}([0,1]^{2})$ of regularity $r>s$, and assume there exists $C_{\Psi}<\infty$ such that $\|\Psi_{\lambda}\|_{\infty}\leq C_{\Psi}\,2^{j(\lambda)}$ for all indices $\lambda$. Let $J_{n}$ and $\tau_{n}$ be chosen as $J_{n}:=\max\Bigl\{j\in\mathbb{N}:\ 2^{2j}\leq\frac{N_{n}}{\log N_{n}}\Bigr\},\qquad\tau_{n}:=\kappa\sqrt{\frac{\log N_{n}}{N_{n}}},$ and let $\widehat{W}_{n}$ be the hard-thresholded wavelet estimator from Definition 3.2. Fix a clipping level $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ and define the clipped estimator by $\widehat{W}_{n}^{\mathrm{clip}}(x,y):=\bigl(\widehat{W}_{n}(x,y)\vee\varepsilon\bigr)\wedge(1-\varepsilon).$ Then there exists $\kappa_{0}>0$ such that for all $\kappa\geq\kappa_{0}$ there exist constants $C_{1},C_{2}>0$ (depending only on $s,p,q,M,B$) with $\sup_{W\in\mathcal{F}^{s}_{p,q}(M)\cap[0,1]}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bigl\|\widehat{W}_{n}^{\mathrm{clip}}-W\bigr\|_{2}^{2}\,\bigm|\,U_{1},\dots,U_{n}\right]\;\leq\;C_{1}\,N_{n}^{-\frac{2s}{2s+2}}(\log N_{n})^{C_{2}}.$ Taking expectations over $(U_{i})$ yields the same bound for the unconditional risk. Moreover, since $(J_{n},\tau_{n})$ do not depend on $s$, the estimator is adaptive in $s$ over any compact interval $[s_{-},s_{+}]\subset(0,r)$ (with constants $C_{1},C_{2}$ chosen uniformly over $s\in[s_{-},s_{+}]$).

[Defn lengths of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Given a representation $\rho:\pi_1(S)\to \mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ and $\gamma\in\pi_1(S)$, let $A\in \mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ be a determinant-one  lift of $\rho(\gamma)$ and let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ be the eigenvalues of $A$ ordered so that $|\lambda_1|\le\cdots\le |\lambda_n|$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The \emph{Hilbert length} of $\gamma$ with respect to $\rho$ is
\[
\ell^H_{\rho}(\gamma):=\log\Bigg|\frac{\lambda_n}{\lambda_1}\Bigg|.
\]
\item The \emph{translation length} of $\gamma$ with respect to $\rho$ is the translation length of $\rho(\gamma)$ in the symmetric space $\mathbb{X}_n=\mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})/\mathrm{PSU}(n)$, namely
\[
\ell_{\rho}(\gamma):=\ell_{\mathbb{X}_n}(\rho(\gamma))
=\sqrt{2\big((\log|\lambda_1|)^2+\cdots+(\log|\lambda_n|)^2\big)}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
(These expressions are well-defined, i.e.\ independent of the choice of the determinant-one lift $A$; two such lifts differ by multiplication by an $n$-th root of unity.)

Suppose that $\lambda\in \Gamma_2$ satisfies $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\geq -K$ and $\sigma_2(\lambda)=f$ with $f_0\leq f\leq f_1$ for two constants $f_1\geq f_0>0$ and that $$\ell_i:=\sigma_1(\lambda)-\lambda_i,\ \ \ i=1,\ldots,n.$$
Then there exist  some constants $S_0>0$ and $J_0>0$ depending only on $n$, $K$, $f_0$ and $f_1$ such that
\begin{align}
 1-\left(1+(1+\theta)\frac{\ell_k}{\sigma_1(\lambda)}\right)R_k &\geq \frac{1-\theta}{6} &&\mbox{if}\ \ \sigma_1(\lambda )\geq S_0\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ k\geq2 ,\\
 1-\left(1+(1+\theta)\frac{\ell_1}{\sigma_1(\lambda)}\right)R_1
 &\geq\left(\frac13-\theta\right)\frac{\ell_1}{\sigma_1(\lambda)} &&\mbox{if}\ \ \sigma_1(\lambda )\geq S_0,  \\
  1-\left(1+(1+\theta)\frac{\ell_k}{\sigma_1(\lambda)+J_0}\right)R_k& \geq \frac{\delta}{2} &&\mbox{if}\ \ \sigma_1(\lambda )\leq S_0 \ \ \mbox{and}\ \ k\geq1,
  
\end{align}
where $\theta\in (0,1/3)$ and $\delta=2f_0/S_0^2\in(0,1)$.

body:
A set T of first-order sentences (in a language of arbitrary cardinality) has a model if and only if every finite subset of T has a model. Equivalently: if T semantically entails phi, then some finite subset of T already entails phi. Typical consequences: a theory with arbitrarily large finite models has an infinite model; nonstandard models of arithmetic exist.
T is a set of sentences of first-order logic

By the completeness theorem (model-existence form), T is then syntactically inconsistent: a contradiction is derivable from T. A formal derivation is a finite object and uses only finitely many sentences of T, so some finite subset of T is already inconsistent and, by soundness, has no model - contradicting the hypothesis. Alternative purely semantic proof via ultraproducts: let F be the set of finite subsets of T, choose a model M_S for each S in F, and take an ultrafilter U on F containing, for each sentence s in T, the set of finite subsets that include s (these sets have the finite intersection property, so such an ultrafilter exists by Zorn). By Los's theorem, the ultraproduct of the M_S over U satisfies every sentence of T. The nontrivial direction of compactness uses a weak form of choice (the Boolean prime ideal theorem suffices).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:81845b66a64fd9e8baa9830788af1d24ccfa7255e76ef65a7c1032858629b23b","revision_digest":"sha256:554e2fd418f4db4bcff8eb0f05079b002eb88adeffc7d43baa31b5323ec69a73","source_id":"wikipedia:Compactness_theorem","source_revision":"as-read-2026-08-02","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: [Definition def:hitting of arXiv:2606.14895, 'Effective Resistances and Commute Times in Sparse Random Geometric Graphs'] Define the hitting time $H_{uv}$ between nodes $u$ and $v$ to be the expected number of steps for a random walk started at $u$ to first reach $v$, i.e., $H_{uv} \equiv \mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\min\{t \ge 0 : X_t = v\} \,\middle|\, X_0 = u\right]$. Note that $H_{uu} = 0$.

body:
[Proposition 32 (Pointwise lower bound under sparsity, edge-density control, and log-convexity) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(u\in[0,1]\) and \(\theta\in\mathbb N\) with \(\theta>1\). Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph with \(|V|=n\), and assume that for some \(\eta,\varepsilon>0\),
\[
e_G(S)\le (1+\varepsilon)|S|
\qquad\text{for every }S\subset V\text{ with }|S|\le \eta n.
\]
Assume moreover that
\[
\frac{|E|}{n}\in [m_-,m_+]
\]
for some \(m_-,m_+>0\), and that
\[
m_->c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon).
\]
Then, for every
\[
t>
\frac{\theta\log\theta}{(\theta-1)\bigl(m_- - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)\bigr)},
\]
one has
\[
\Pbb^G_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)
\ge
\frac{
m_- - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)-\frac{\theta\log\theta}{(\theta-1)t}
}{
(1+\theta)m_+ - c_{\theta,u}(1+\varepsilon)
}.
\]
title: Pointwise lower bound under sparsity, edge-density control, and log-convexity

\forall S\subset[n]\text{ with }|S|\le \eta n:\ 
e_{G_n}(S)\le (1+\varepsilon)|S|
\Bigr)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
\]

body: In mathematical logic and descriptive set theory, the analytical hierarchy is an extension of the arithmetical hierarchy. The analytical hierarchy of formulas includes formulas in the language of second-order arithmetic, which can have quantifiers over both the set of natural numbers, $\mathbb {N}$, and over functions from $\mathbb {N}$ to $\mathbb {N}$. The analytical hierarchy of sets classifies sets by the formulas that can be used to define them; it is the lightface version of the projective hierarchy.

body:
[Dfn 106 (SDE coefficients with spatial smoothing
	and coordinate sum projection) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\sphicirc:\R\to[0,\infty)$ be a smooth nonnegative function that integrates to one and has support $[-1,1]$. We also assume that we have
$\sphicirc(\vx)\ge \Omega(1)$ for all $\vx\in[-1/2,1/2]$. With an abuse of notation, for $\vx\in\R^d$ for any $d\ge1$ we will denote
	\beq
	
	\sphicirc(\vx)
	= \prod_{i=1}^d
	\sphicirc(x^i)\,,\quad
	\sphi(\vx)\equiv 
	\frac{1}{\sep^d}
	\sphicirc\bigg(
	\frac{\vx}{\sep}\bigg)\,,
	\eeq
so that $\sphi$ also integrates to one and has support $[-\sep,\sep]^d$.
Recall from above that we use the abbreviation 
$\rho_t\equiv \rho_{\vY,N,t}$. It will also be convenient to factorize $\rho_t=\varrho_t\otimes\varsigma_t$ where $\varrho_t$ refers to the first three spatial coordinates while $\varsigma_t$ refers to the fourth spatial coordinate (cf.\ \eqref{e:a.i.factorization}). We then have $\rho_{D,t} = \varrho_{D,t}\otimes\varsigma_t$, etc., as well as $\rho_{\www,t}= \varrho_t\otimes\varsigma_{\www,t}$.
 Recall from Definition~\ref{d:projected.coeffs} the notation $\rho\mapsto\bar{\rho}$ for the coordinate sum projection.
Then, analogously to
\eqref{e:discrete.ratio.occ.B}--\eqref{e:discrete.ratio.occ.U}, we let
	\begin{align*}
	\sB^N(t,y)
	&\equiv
	\frac{\overline{\varrho_{D,N,t}*\sphi}(y)}
		{\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi}(y)}
	\equiv
	(p^N)'(t)^{1/2} \cdot \sbbb^N(t,y)\,,\\
	\sV^N(t,y)
	&\equiv
	\frac{\overline{\varrho_{V,N,t}*\sphi} (y)}
		{\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi} (y)}
	\equiv
	p^N(t) \cdot \svvv^N(t,y)\,,\\
	\sU^N(t,y)
	&\equiv
	\frac{\overline{\varrho_{U,N,t}*\sphi} (y)}
		{\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi} (y)}
	\equiv
	\Big[ p^N(t) \cdot 
	t (p^N)'(t) \Big]^{1/2}
		\cdot \suuu^N(t,y)\,.
	\end{align*}
Likewise, analogously to \eqref{e:discrete.ratio.occ.r.w}, we let
	\[
	\srrr^N(t,y)\equiv
	\frac{\overline{\varrho_{\rrr,N,t}*\sphi}(y)}
		{\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi}(y)}\,,\quad
	\swww^N(t,y^4)
	\equiv
	\frac{\varsigma_{\www,N,t}*\sphi(y^4)}
		{\varsigma_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi(y^4)}\,.
	\]
We emphasize again that we have combined spatial smoothing with coordinate sum projection in this definition, so the above coefficients are all functions on $\R^2$ rather than $\R^5$. Lastly, we shall abbreviate
$\sPsi^N\equiv(\sB,\sV,\sU)^N$ and $\sGam^N\equiv(\sbbb,\svvv,\suuu)^N$; these are variants of the quantities
$\Psi^N$ and $\Gamma^N$ from Definitions \ref{d:disc.coefficients} and \ref{d:disc.rescaled.coeffs}.
title:
SDE coefficients with spatial smoothing
	and coordinate sum projection

body:
[Theorem thm:gapclosing of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] Let $\mu_{0}$ be compactly supported and suppose $(\alpha_{-},\alpha_{+})$ is a bounded
gap of $\supp\mu_{0}$, that is a bounded interval disjoint from $\supp\mu_{0}$ with
mass on both sides. Put
\[
  T:=\min_{u\in(\alpha_{-},\alpha_{+})}\Theta_{\mu_{0}}(u)\in(0,\infty).
\]
Then along the forward flow (equation eq:marginal of the paper) the corresponding gap of
$\supp\mu_{t}$ persists precisely while
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_{t}>\frac{T}{1+T},
  \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
  \Lambda(t)<\Lambda^{*}:=\log\Big(1+\frac1T\Big),
\end{equation}
and closes at $\Lambda(t)=\Lambda^{*}$.

[Thm 12 of arXiv:2609.03054, 'The classes of bivariate Schur and Herglotz matrix-valued rational functions: realizations'] Let $p(z_1,z_2)$ be a symmetric polynomial of degree $(n, n)$ without roots in $\RHPtwo$. Then there exist a constant $c\neq 0$, complex matrices $\alpha_0, \alpha_1, \alpha_2$, with $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ positive semidefinite so that $\alpha_1+ \alpha_2 =I $, and 
$ {\rm Re}\ \alpha_0 = \frac{1}{2}(\alpha_0+\alpha_0^*) \ge 0$, an integer $0\le l \le n$, and a unitary involution $U$ so that 
$$ (z_1+1)^l(z_2+1)^l p(z_1, z_2)  = c\det( \alpha_0 + z_1\alpha_1 + z_2 \alpha_2 ) $$
and $U\alpha_0U=\alpha_0, U\alpha_1U=\alpha_2$.

In the case that $p(z_1,z_2)\in{\mathbb R}[z_1,z_2]$, the matrices $\alpha_0, \alpha_1$ and $U$ can be chosen to be real. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Dfn 114 (variants of temporal smoothing) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For comparison with Definition~\ref{d:t.smooth}, we define
$\TGam^N\equiv(\Tbbb,\Tvvv,\Tuuu)^N$ by directly convolving $\sGam^N$ with $\tphi$:
	\[\Tbbb^N(t,y)
	\equiv
	\int_{\R} 
        \tphi(s) 
        \sbbb^N(t-s,y)\,ds
	= \tE\Big[ \sbbb^N(t-\sss,y)\Big]
	= \tE\bigg[
	\frac{\sB^N(t-\sss,y)}{(p^N)'(t-\sss)}
	\bigg]\,,
	\]
and analogously $\Tvvv^N$ and $\Tuuu^N$. We abbreviate $\TGam^N\equiv(\Tbbb,\Tvvv,\Tuuu)^N$.
Recalling Definition~\ref{d:intro.SDE.coefs}, we also define the ``ideal'' smoothed coefficients 
	\[\iB^N(t,y)
	\equiv\frac{ \displaystyle
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s) \overline{\varrho_{D,N,s}*\sphi}(y)\,dy}
		{\displaystyle
		 \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s) \overline{\varrho_{N,s}*\sphi}(y)\,dy}\,,
	\]
and similarly $\iV$, $\iU$, $\ir$. We similarly define
	\[\iw^N(t,y)
	\equiv
	\frac{\displaystyle
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s) \varsigma_{\www,N,s}*\sphi(y)\,dy
	}{\displaystyle
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s) \varsigma_{N,s}*\sphi(y)\,dy
	}\,.
	\]
Recalling \eqref{e:sde.F.N}, \eqref{e:sp.smoothed.F.N}, and \eqref{e:temp.smoothed.F.N}, we let 
	\beq
	\iF^N(t,y)\equiv
	\Big\{ \iV^N+\iU^N+\ir^N\Big\}(t,y)
	+2\eta^{1/2}\,.\eeq
Note that $\iF^N$ is the ideal smoothing of $F^N$ from \eqref{e:sde.F.N}, and since $F^N\ge0$ we also have $\iF^N\ge0$.
title: variants of temporal smoothing

OWNER RESULT DRAFT, proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C015 v1. Under all C013 raw-input cube RBF hypotheses (d>=1,n>=0,ell,s,epsilon>0,B>=0, contexts of length <=n and labels bounded by B), the exact C004 cone encoder with feature bound 1, coordinate Lipschitz constant 1/ell and gating bound 2, followed by C002 Chebyshev attention at feature bound 2, has every Q,K,V, residual-MLP matrix and final selector entry bounded by W_star=(n+1)max(4,s,2/s,1/ell). The fixed parameter-independent input encoding has coordinate bound K_input=max(1,B,s). In the shared-register attention head, the combined coefficient beta-eta*s has absolute value at most 3, eta<=2/s, 0<=beta<=1, and there is no token-count factor in that head. Cone grid coefficients are at most one, individual slope entries are 1/ell, and role-gating entries are at most two. Thus this predictor belongs to C014 parameter cube with W=W_star, K0=K_input, A=5 and P=L(15D^2+2DH)+2D, for the fully counted D,H,L of C013. Conditional on C013 scalar error bounds, fixed clips mean [-U,U], U=nB/s+sqrt(s epsilon)+1, and variance [s,1+2s] leave the comparator unchanged. No KL monotonicity of variance clipping for other class members is asserted. C002 and C004 are accepted ground; C013 approximation composition, C014 cover and the present membership bridge remain unaudited. This is not the full prior-averaged ERM theorem, a finite-bit theorem or a novelty claim.
All C013 raw-input RBF hypotheses and counted encoder-plus-Chebyshev architecture
Entrywise coefficient bound, not an operator-norm or bit-complexity bound; fixed affine input placement excluded as in C004

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:fd3502bad36abbd92203b2cd72bf3b62af0f4fa0c92e72077c36e91abc4d0ef5","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/fd/fd3502bad36abbd92203b2cd72bf3b62af0f4fa0c92e72077c36e91abc4d0ef5.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:0f46a58b01ff5a7514ba5971c7348f809809fc95597fb843aabc40328056e327","bundle_entry_key":"t336-w727-c015","bundle_id":"population.w727-t336-comparator-parameter-bound-010","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Transformer approximation and generalization; Gaussian-process inference","draft":"w727/bundle_010.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:learning.transformers:draft-raw-rbf-transformer-comparator-parameter-bound","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C015 v1: explicit bounded-parameter membership of the raw-input RBF predictor

Kind: bound. Target: none. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim.

## 1. Statement and dependencies
Use exactly the hypotheses, dimensions D,H,L, grid and truncated Gaussian features of C013 v1: raw inputs in [0,1]^d, d>=1, n>=0, ell,s,epsilon>0, labels bounded by B>=0, and normalized bidirectional ReLU attention followed by tokenwise residual ReLU MLPs. The Gaussian kernel has diagonal one and noise variance s. Use the C004 v1 cone encoder with feature bound R=1, gating bound S=2, and coordinate Lipschitz constant K=1/ell, followed by the accepted C002 v1 Chebyshev solver with feature bound 2. Both accepted constructions are ground; the present task only bounds their displayed individual matrix entries. C013's approximation composition and C014's parameter cover remain unaudited.

Put N=n+1 and

    W_star = N max(4, s, 2/s, 1/ell),
    K_input = max(1,B,s),
    U = n B/s + sqrt(s epsilon) + 1,
    v0 = s,  v1 = 1+2s.

All trainable Q,K,V matrices, both MLP matrices and the final two-coordinate linear selector of this particular C013 predictor can be chosen entrywise in [-W_star,W_star]. Its fixed affine input placement is parameter independent and entrywise bounded by K_input. The construction therefore belongs to C014's bounded parameter class with A=5, W=W_star, K0=K_input and P=L(15D^2+2DH)+2D. Unused heads/MLP units are padded with zero weights.

Moreover, conditional on C013's stated approximation bounds, fixed output clipping to [-U,U] for the mean and [s,1+2s] for the variance leaves this comparator unchanged for every permitted context. This does not assert that variance clipping decreases KL for other predictors.

## 2. Encoder entries
C004 Section 4 lists every nonzero encoder operation. Gaussian feature projection has norm at most one, hence each grid coefficient phi_j(a) has absolute value at most one.

* Absolute-value layer: rows read x_r-a_r or a_r-x_r from raw coordinates and the preserved constant. Since 0<=a_r<=1, input entries have absolute value at most one. Output sums use entries one.
* Cone layer: the hidden map copies nonnegative absolute-value registers and the constant, with entries one. The output writes phi_j(a)+K sum_r |x_r-a_r|. Its individual entries are K or phi_j(a), bounded by max(1,K). The sum over d registers does not turn K into a matrix entry Kd.
* Minimum tournament: each hidden row reads u-v and the output subtracts its ReLU from the u register. All entries are zero or plus/minus one. Unused registers pass through the architecture's fixed identity residual.
* Role gating: ReLU(f+2(r-1))-ReLU(-f+2(r-1)) uses entries of absolute value at most two, including both the role coefficient and the coefficient on the constant register. Output entries are plus/minus one.

All encoder attention matrices can be zero, and all unneeded MLP entries are zero. Thus every encoder entry is bounded by max(2,1/ell). Counts J,p,d may grow but do not enlarge an individual entry.

## 3. Solver scalar coefficients
In C002 with the feature bound 2 and n_plus=max(1,n), set

    L_spec=s+4 n_plus, c=(L_spec+s)/2=s+2 n_plus,
    d_spec=(L_spec-s)/2=2 n_plus, a=c/d_spec>1.

Here L_spec is a spectral endpoint, not the network depth L. At the first solver step eta_0=1/c and beta_0=0. At all later steps C002 gives

    eta_j=2 C_j(a)/(d_spec C_(j+1)(a)),
    beta_j=C_(j-1)(a)/C_(j+1)(a),
    eta_j c = 1+beta_j.

For completeness, if t=log(a+sqrt(a^2-1))>0, the recurrence C_0=1,C_1=a,C_(j+1)=2a C_j-C_(j-1) gives C_j(a)=cosh(jt) by substitution and induction. These numbers are positive and nondecreasing with j. Consequently 0<=beta_j<=1, 0<eta_j<=2/c<=2/s and eta_j s<=2 for every step, including step zero.

## 4. Literal solver matrix entries
C002 Section 4 uses selector Q,K matrices: their entries are zero or plus/minus one. Its initial broadcast head has V entry N. In the solver's first four heads, each nonzero V entry is plus/minus N eta_j, hence at most 2N/s in absolute value.

The fifth head has Q=K=one and NO N factor in V. It writes

    beta(w-w_old)-eta s w          into w,
    beta(u-u_old)+eta(qbar-s u)    into u,
    w-w_old                      into w_old,
    u-u_old                      into u_old.

The combined coefficient on w (respectively u) is beta-eta s, not two different entries. Its absolute value is at most beta+eta s<=3. The other entries in this head are -beta, eta, one or minus one, bounded by max(3,2/s). The fixed residual identity is not a learned parameter. All vector coordinates are separate registers, so no additional merging of the displayed coefficients occurs.

The four readout heads use selector Q,K and V entries plus/minus one or plus/minus s. The final linear map selects mout and vout with entries zero or one. The initial vout=s is fixed input data; it is included in K_input. Solver MLP matrices can be zero, and zero extension into the encoder's larger register space introduces no new nonzero entries.

Combining Sections 2-4 bounds every matrix entry by

    max(2,1/ell,N,2N/s,3,2/s,s) <= W_star,

because N>=1. Also W_star>=4, as required by C014's W>=1 hypothesis. No operator norm bound or finite-bit description bound is asserted.

## 5. Fixed encoding and output clips
Input coordinates consist of raw x in [0,1]^d, labels of absolute value at most B, binary flags, the constant one, the initial variance s, and zeros. Their bound is K_input and does not depend on learned parameters. C014 is applied to the whole encoder-plus-solver class, so its fixed encoding does not silently include learned feature computation.

For an m-point context, m<=n, the exact Gaussian posterior mean is k_*^T(K+sI)^(-1)y. Positive semidefiniteness and unit diagonal imply |k_*(i)|<=1, hence ||k_*||_2<=sqrt(m), ||y||_2<=sqrt(m)B and ||(K+sI)^(-1)||_op<=1/s. Thus |mu|<=mB/s<=nB/s, including the empty context by mu=0. Its noisy variance satisfies s<=v<=s+1.

C013's separate scalar bounds are |muhat-mu|<=sqrt(s epsilon), vhat>=s, and |vhat-v|<=min(s/2,s sqrt(epsilon)). They imply |muhat|<U and s<=vhat<=1+3s/2<1+2s. The fixed interval clips therefore leave both comparator coordinates unchanged. For other members of the class the same clips enforce bounded outputs and are nonexpansive for the parameter-cover argument only.

## 6. What remains
This supplies an explicit comparator parameter radius and output ranges for the C014 deterministic cover. It is not the full prior-averaged ERM theorem. To obtain that theorem one must compose the appropriate task-law concentration argument with the original Gaussian context law, including context clipping and its bias, and retain all unbounded Gaussian query-tail terms. C006/C007, C013 and C014 still require their own independent review. ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Attainment of the optimal SIRSN length-stretch tradeoff structural attempt Result: Uniform expected length in every compact set supplies tightness for the unlabelled length measures: Markov bounds on an exhausting sequence of compact sets control local masses, and bounded-mass sets of Radon measures are vaguely relatively compact. However the prescribed feasible-route class is not closed under even uniform convergence with bounded lengths. Inscribed polygonal approximations to a semicircle are finite unions of straight segments with uniformly bounded length, while their limit is a smooth arc and is not a jagged route made of straight segments. Check: For the semicircle, no nontrivial subarc is a line segment; countably many straight segments lying in the arc can therefore cover only countably many points. The source itself discusses a possible extension from jagged to rectifiable routes. Obstruction: A compactness proof for length measures alone loses route labels, compatibility and the allowed-curve condition. One must choose a richer topology and prove closure or justify a relaxed model before claiming attainment.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0225-attainment-of-the-optimal-sirsn-length-stretch-tradeoff

body:
Let (X, B, mu, T) be an invertible measure-preserving system on a standard probability space with T ERGODIC. Let G be a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m, let phi : X -> G be measurable, and let T_phi(x, g) = (T x, phi(x) g) be the associated group extension of (X x G, mu x m). Then:

  T_phi is ergodic  <=>  for EVERY nontrivial irreducible unitary representation pi : G -> U(d_pi), the functional (transfer) equation
        F(T x) = pi(phi(x)) F(x)      for mu-a.e. x
  has no nonzero MEASURABLE solution F : X -> M_{d_pi}(C).

Equivalently, ergodicity fails exactly when some nontrivial pi admits such a nonzero F. A nonzero solution can always be normalized so that its Hilbert-Schmidt norm is constant, because ||F(x)||_HS is then a T-invariant function and T is ergodic.

Abelian case (the form most often used). If G is abelian, the irreducible representations are the characters chi in the dual group, and the criterion reads: T_phi is ergodic if and only if for every nontrivial character chi there is NO measurable h : X -> S^1 with h(T x) = chi(phi(x)) h(x); i.e. no nontrivial character of phi is a measurable multiplicative coboundary. For G = S^1 and phi written additively this is: for every nonzero integer n, the equation u(T x) - u(x) = n * phi(x) (mod 1) has no measurable solution u.

SHARP EDGES. (1) Ergodicity of the BASE T is a hypothesis, not a conclusion: if T is not ergodic then T_phi is not ergodic either (invariant sets of the base lift), and the displayed equivalence is false as stated without it. (2) Compactness of G is essential -- the proof uses the Haar PROBABILITY measure and the Peter-Weyl decomposition of L^2(G); for noncompact G (e.g. G = R, cylinder flows) the natural invariant measure is infinite and ergodicity is a genuinely different problem. (3) 'Measurable' cannot be weakened to 'continuous': a cocycle can be a measurable coboundary without being a continuous one, so verifying that the equation has no CONTINUOUS solution does not certify ergodicity. (4) Every nontrivial irreducible pi must be tested, not one convenient one. Example: G = S^1 and phi taking values in {+1, -1} with the induced two-point extension ergodic. Then for the character chi_1(z) = z the equation has no solution (that is exactly ergodicity of the two-point extension), yet chi_2(z) = z^2 satisfies chi_2(phi(x)) = 1, so h identically 1 solves the equation for chi_2 -- and indeed T_phi is not ergodic, since phi lives in the proper closed subgroup {+1,-1}.
(X, B, mu, T) is an invertible measure-preserving system on a standard (Lebesgue) probability space
T is ergodic with respect to mu
G is a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m
phi : X -> G is measurable and the extension is T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, phi(x) g) on mu x m
solutions F of the transfer equation are required only to be measurable (matrix-valued), not continuous
