[Theorem thm:dilation of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] The generator $K=\sigma^y\otimes A$ of (equation eq:K of the paper) satisfies

\begin{equation}
K^{T}=-K\qquad\text{and}\qquad K^{*}=K,

\end{equation}

that is, $K$ is antisymmetric for the transpose and Hermitian for the conjugate
transpose. For $z\in\mathbb{C}$ set $W_z:=e^{zK}$. Then $z\mapsto W_z$ is an entire
homomorphism from $(\mathbb{C},+)$ into $\OO(2M,\mathbb{C})$, with

\[
W_{z+w}=W_zW_w,\qquad W_0=\mathrm{I},\qquad W_z^{T}W_z=\mathrm{I},
\]

and it has the closed block form

\begin{equation}
W_z=\begin{pmatrix}\cosh(zA)&-i\sinh(zA)\\ i\sinh(zA)&\cosh(zA)\end{pmatrix}.

\end{equation}

[Lemma lem:rows of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] Write $w_j^\top$ for the $j$-th row of $W$ and $y_{ij}$ for the $j$-th entry
of $y_i$. Then
$F_c(W)=\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_ic_i(\langle w_j,x_i\rangle-y_{ij})^2$ and
$\lVert W\rVert_F^2=\sum_j\lVert w_j\rVert^2$. Hence the minimizer set of $F_c$ is the
Cartesian product over rows of scalar weighted least-squares solution sets,
and $A(F_c)$ consists of the minimal-$\ell_2$-norm scalar solutions row by
row --- \emph{with the single shared weight vector $c$}.

[Lemme 26 of arXiv:2604.00635, 'Large deviations of the periodic Toda chain'] Let $\mu$ be a probability measure such that $I[\mu] <+\infty$.
Then there exists a sequence of probability measures $(\mu_p)_{p\ge 1} $ so that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For every $p\in \mathbb{N}^*$, $d_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mu,\mu_p)\le 1/p$,
    \item For $p$ large enough, there exists $\kappa_p>0$
    \begin{align*}
        &1+\frac{2}{\ell}\int\ln|x-y|\mathrm{d}\mu_p(y)\ge \kappa_p \, , &  &\forall x\in \mathbb{R} \; .
    \end{align*}
    \item $\mu_p$ is compactly supported.
    \item If $\int x \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x)=0$, then $\int x \, \mathrm{d}\mu_p(x)=0$ for every integer number $p$.
    \item $\mu_p$ has bounded density with respect to Lebesgue measure.
    \item $I[\mu_p] \longrightarrow I[\mu]$ as $p \to +\infty$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

the resulting $6\times6$ Cassels matrix.  If $\Pf(C_{pqr})=1$, then $pqr$ is
noncongruent,
\[
\Sha(E_{pqr})[2^\infty]\cong(\Z/2\Z)^6,
\qquad
|\Sha(E_{pqr})[2^\infty]|=64,
\]
and
\[
r_a(pqr)\equiv h(-pqr)+64\pmod{128}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 43 (Glauber dynamic) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Consider the square lattice graph $\Z^d$ (also denoted $G=(V,E)$).
    Let $\mu$ denote a stationary measure on $\Pi_G$.
    For any $u\in V$, let $G_u$ denote the subgraph of $G$ induced by the vertices $V\setminus\{u\}$.
    A \emph{Glauber dynamic} for $\mu$ is a function
    \[
        R:\Pi_G\times V\times\Sigma \to \Pi_G,
    \]
    with the following properties.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item\textbf{Local update.}
        For any $\tau\in \Pi_G$, $u\in V$ and $\iota\in\Sigma$, we have $R(\tau,u,\iota)|_{G_u}=\tau|_{G_u}$.
        \item\textbf{Consistency.}
        For any $\tau\in \Pi_G$ and $u\in V$, the distribution of $R(\tau,u,\iota)$ in $\diff\iota$ is $\mu[\blank|\tau|_{G_u}]$.
        \item\textbf{Equivariance.}
        For any $\tau\in \Pi_G$, $u\in V$, $\iota\in\Sigma$ and $\theta\in\Theta$, we have $R(\tau,u,\iota)\circ\theta=R(\tau\circ\theta,u\circ\theta,\iota)$.
    \end{itemize}
    We shall also write $R_{u,\iota}:\Pi_G\to\Pi_G,\,\tau\mapsto R(\tau,u,\iota)$ for any $u\in V$ and $\iota\in\Sigma$.
title: Glauber dynamic

Let (Omega,tau) be a probability space and phi_1,...,phi_Z real orthonormal functions in L2(tau), with Z finite. Assume that for every fixed real q>=1 there is a finite C(q) such that ||f||_L2q(tau)<=C(q)||f||_L2(tau) for every f in their linear span. Let lambda_1,...,lambda_Z be real numbers and define the finite-rank positive kernel U(theta,theta_prime)=sum_k lambda_k^2 phi_k(theta)phi_k(theta_prime), using these same representatives on its diagonal. Then for every q>=1, ||U||_L2q(tau x tau)<=C(q)^2 ||U||_L2(tau x tau), and ||U(theta,theta)||_Lq(tau)<=C(q)^2 E_tau U(theta,theta). Here ||U||_L2(tau x tau)=(sum_k lambda_k^4)^(1/2), E_tau U(theta,theta)=sum_k lambda_k^2, and all noninteger moments use absolute values. If the assumed C(q) are uniform over a dimension-indexed family, these conclusions are uniform over that family. This is Lemma6, equations78-79, printed p36, of arXiv:2101.10588.

ATTEMPT RECORD (SUPERSEDING REVISION 2026-09-07 12:4x after the Codex holder's review), author-checked only. CORRECTION of C0004-A001. The sentence 'the naive guess rho^D proportional to r_D(x)^2 fails unless Z^D(D) is a.s. constant' is too strong: if Z^D = xi mu with xi a random scalar and mu deterministic, then Z^D(dx)/Z^D(D) = mu(dx)/mu(D) is deterministic and E[Z^D(dx)/Z^D(D)] = E Z^D(dx)/E Z^D(D) although Z^D(D) is random. The correct statement: since E Z^D(A) = E[M P(A)] with M = Z^D(D) and P(A) = Z^D(A)/Z^D(D), rho^D equals the normalised intensity E Z^D(dx)/E Z^D(D) (when E Z^D(D) is finite) exactly when M is uncorrelated with P(A) for every Borel set A; independence of the mass and the normalised measure is sufficient, not necessary. For the DGFF extremal measure the mass and the shape are coupled through the Gibbs-Markov structure, which suggests that rho^D is not r_D(x)^2 dx normalised, but nothing in A001 or here proves it and the question stands. Key identity: rho^D(A) = E[Z(A)/Z(D)] equals E Z(A)/E Z(D) for every A iff Cov(Z(D), Z(A)/Z(D)) = 0 for every A; independence of the total mass and the normalised measure, and a constant mass, are special cases. Standing obstruction: see the earlier attempt; the correction above replaces the flawed step only.

body: [Proposition 2.1 of arXiv:2110.09034, 'On the construction of cospectral nonisomorphic bipartite graphs'] Let Q and R be the matrices of the form I(Q1, Q2) and I(R1, R2), respectively. If M = U V W X  and H = A B C D  are 2 × 2 block matrices, then (Q⊗R)(M⊗H) = (QM)⊗(RH). The same holds true when the matrices Q and R are both of the form P(Q1, Q2) and P(R1, R2), respectively. Two matrices A and B are said to be equivalent, if there exists invertible matrices P and Q such that Q−1AP = B.

[Thm Inverse2 of arXiv:2609.01350, 'New classes of trace-form permutation polynomials and their compositional inverses'] Let $q=2^m$ with $m$ odd, and let $f_1$ be as above a permutation
polynomial of $\mathbb F_{q^2}$. By Theorem~(Result1 of the paper), one of the
following holds, and in each case the compositional inverse is:

\begin{equation}
f_1^{-1}(x)=
\begin{cases}
x, & \gamma=0,\\[8pt]
x+\left(\dfrac{h_1(x)}{{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2)}\right)^{q/2},
  & \gamma\in\mathbb F_q^{*},\ c_3=1,\ {\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2)\neq0,\\[12pt]
x+\dfrac{\gamma\,h_1(x)}{1+\gamma{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1)},
  & \gamma\in\mathbb F_q^{*},\ c_3=1,\ {\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2)=0,\\[12pt]
x+\dfrac{\gamma}{A}\Big(B(x)+\big(B(x)^{3}+A^{2}h_1(x)\big)^{1/3}\Big),
  & \begin{array}{@{}l@{}}
      \gamma\notin\mathbb F_q,\ A\neq0,\\[2pt]
      {\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(\gamma^{2})=(c_3\gamma+\gamma^{q})^{q+1},\\[2pt]
      A\big(1+{\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_1\gamma)\big)={\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_2^{2}\gamma^{4}),
    \end{array}
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
where $A={\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}(c_3\gamma^3+\gamma^{q+2})$,
$B(x)={\rm Tr}_q^{q^2}\big((c_2+c_3x+x^q)\gamma^2\big)$, and $(.)^{1/3}$ denotes
the unique cube root map of $\mathbb F_q$ (a bijection since $m$ is odd).

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Explicit model calculation, comparison identities and remaining hypothesis obstruction Result: Consider the reversible birth-death chain on states1,2,3 with symmetric edge rates1 on1-2 and2 on2-3. It is doubly stochastically monotone. Its slow nonzero eigenvalue is3-sqrt(3), with eigenvector (1,sqrt(3)-2,1-sqrt(3)). The last two components have the same sign, so P_t(2,3)>1/3 for sufficiently large t. Label intensities f(1)=1,f(2)=0,f(3)=2. For g=1{f>=1},h=1{f>=2}, covariance at lag t is -(P_t(2,3)-1/3)/3<0. Hence the image process does not satisfy the supermodular time-slowing order, whose infinite-lag limit would require this covariance nonnegative. Check: The eigenvector sums to zero and direct multiplication by the symmetric generator gives eigenvalue -(3-sqrt3). The remaining nonzero mode decays at rate3+sqrt3, so it cannot cancel the eventual positive transition overshoot. The covariance formula uses g=1-1{X=2} and h=1{X=3}. Obstruction: This blocks transferring the established sufficient supermodular-order argument through arbitrary f. It does not produce a queue-workload reversal. In fact same-observable covariance under a reversible environment is a nonnegative mixture of exponentials, so the simplest light-traffic coefficient remains monotone. Higher-order queue effects or a different comparison method are needed.

[Theorem 5 (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck limit) of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] Assume that the sequence of initial fluctuation fields $ \left\{\bm Y_0^n\right\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}} $
 	converges, as \(n\to\infty\), to a mean-zero Gaussian field \(\bm Y_0\) on
 	\( (\mathscr S^\dagger)'\), whose covariance is given by
 	\[
 	\lim_{n\to\infty}
 	\mathbb E_{\mu^n}^n
 	\left[
 	\bm Y_0^n(\bm f)\bm Y_0^n(\bm g)
 	\right]
 	=
 	\mathbb E
 	\left[
 	\bm Y_0(\bm f)\bm Y_0(\bm g)
 	\right]
 	=:
 	\sigma(\bm f,\bm g),
 	\qquad
 	\bm f,\bm g\in\mathscr S^\dagger.
 	\]
 	Then the sequence \(\{\mathbb Q_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N} }\) converges in
 	\(\mathcal D([0,T],(\mathscr S^\dagger)')\) to the generalized Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process \(\{\bm Y_t:0\le t\le T\}\) characterized by the
 	martingale problem
 	\[
 	\mathcal M_t(\bm f)
 	=
 	\bm Y_t(\bm f)-\bm Y_0(\bm f)
 	-
 	\int_0^t
 	\bm Y_s(\mathcal A^\dagger \bm f) \,\mathrm ds,
 	\qquad
 	\bm f\in\mathscr S^\dagger,
 	\]
 	where \(\mathcal M_t(\bm f)\) is a continuous centered Gaussian martingale with
 	quadratic covariation
 	\[
 	\left\langle
 	\mathcal M(\bm f),\mathcal M(\bm g)
 	\right\rangle_t
 	=
 	\int_0^t
 	Q_s(\bm f,\bm g) \,\mathrm ds.
 	\] 	
 	Equivalently, for every \(0\le s\le t\le T\) and every
 	\(\bm f,\bm g\in\mathscr S^\dagger\),
 	\[
 	\mathbb E\left[
 	\bm Y_t(\bm f)\bm Y_s(\bm g)
 	\right]
 	=
 	\sigma(S_t\bm f,S_s\bm g)
 	+
 	\int_0^s
 	Q_r\left(
 	S_{t-r}\bm f,
 	S_{s-r}\bm g
 	\right) \,\mathrm dr.
 	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 2 (Canonical solvability of the metric Hodge system) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $X:\Real_y^n\to\Real_x^n$ be an orientation-preserving global
bi-Lipschitz map with $d\mu=J dy$.  Fix $1<p<n$ and put
\[
 p^*:=\frac{np}{n-p}.
\]
For every $q\in L^p(\mu)$ there is a unique vector field $F=F^i\eframe_i$ along $X$, whose Cartesian components belong to
$L^{p^*}(\mu;\Rn)$, satisfying \eqref{eq:invdiv} in the conjugated
distributional sense: equivalently, $u:=F\circ X^{-1}$ satisfies
\[
 \partial_{x^i}u^j-\partial_{x^j}u^i=0,
 \qquad
 \partial_{x^i}u^i=q\circ X^{-1}
 \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real_x^n).
\]
The solution is
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal P_{\gmetric}q
 :=\mathcal C_X\nabla\Delta_x^{-1}\mathcal C_X^{-1}q, \qquad \mathcal{C}_Xf=f\circ X,
\end{equation}
and it satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \|\mathcal P_{\gmetric}q\|_{L^{p^*}(\mu)}
 \le C_{n,p}\|q\|_{L^p(\mu)}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for
\begin{equation}
    r_{\mathrm{HLS}}:=\frac{4n}{n+4},
\end{equation}
one has $1<r_{\mathrm{HLS}}<n$ for every $n\ge2$ and $r_{\mathrm{HLS}}^*=4$; hence
every $q\in L^{r_{\mathrm{HLS}}}(\mu)$ has a unique solution
$\mathcal P_{\gmetric}q\in L^4(\mu)$ which we refer to as the canonical Hodge vector field along $X$.

[Lemma 30 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] Let \(A\) be a trace-class operator. For \(|\theta|\) sufficiently small, define
\[
        H_A(\theta):=\log\det\left(\operatorname{Id}+(e^\theta-1)A\right),
\]
where the logarithm is the holomorphic branch near \(0\) normalized by
\(H_A(0)=0\). Then, for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\begin{equation}

        H_A^{(n)}(0)
        =
        \sum_{m=1}^n
        (-1)^{m+1}(m-1)!S(n,m)\operatorname{tr}(A^m),
\end{equation}
where \(S(n,m)\) is the Stirling number of the second kind. Consequently,
\begin{equation}

        F_{a,L}^{(n)}(0)
        =
        \sum_{m=1}^n
        (-1)^{m+1}(m-1)!S(n,m)
        \left(
        \operatorname{tr}(T_{a,L}^m)-\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde W_{a,L}^m)
        \right).
\end{equation}

body: [Lemma 2 of arXiv:2609.02392, 'Large values of cubic and quartic Dirichlet $L$-functions of prime moduli'] The primitive cubic Dirichlet characters of prime conductor $p$ co-prime to $3$ are induced by $\chi_{3, \varpi}$ for some prime $\varpi \in \mz[\omega]\setminus \mz$ with $N(\varpi) = p$.  The primitive quartic Dirichlet characters of prime conductor $p$ co-prime to $2$ such that their squares remain primitive are induced by $\chi_{4, \varpi}$ for some prime $\varpi \in \mz[i] \setminus \mz$ with $N(\varpi) = p$. body: For a positive finite Borel measure mu on R, its STIELTJES TRANSFORM (also Cauchy transform) is m_mu(z) = integral (x - z)^{-1} mu(dx) for z in the open upper half plane C^+. It is analytic on C^+, maps C^+ into C^+ when mu is positive, and satisfies the a priori bound |m_mu(z)| <= mu(R)/Im(z). INVERSION: for a < b continuity points of mu, mu( (a,b) ) = (1/pi) lim_{eta decreasing to 0} integral_a^b Im m_mu(x + i eta) dx, so the transform determines the measure. CONTINUITY: a sequence of probability measures mu_n converges weakly to a probability measure mu if and only if m_{mu_n}(z) -> m_mu(z) for every z in C^+; convergence on any set with an accumulation point in C^+ suffices, by analyticity plus a tightness argument. In random matrix theory the transform of the empirical spectral distribution of a Hermitian matrix H is m_n(z) = (1/n) tr ( H - z I )^{-1}, the normalised trace of the RESOLVENT, which is why resolvent methods and Stieltjes-transform methods are the same method. Sign conventions differ across the literature: some authors define the transform with (z - x)^{-1}, which flips the sign of the whole calculus; the convention must be checked before importing a formula. [standard; e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Section 2.4]

Then, for $\alpha\in(0,2)$
\begin{equation}
Q^{(\alpha)}_{D_1\cup D_{2}}(t)\geq Q^{(\alpha)}_{D_1}(t)+Q^{(\alpha)}_{D_2}(t).
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Theorem 1 (Uniform high order factorial bound) of arXiv:2608.04799, '2608.04799'] Fix \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), let \(p_n\) be given by
\eqref{eq:pn-intro}, and let \(\Xi_n\) be given by \eqref{eq:Xi-intro}.
For every compact \(K\Subset E\), there are constants
\(C_K,c_K>0\), depending only on \(K\) and \(\lambda\), such that
\begin{equation}
  \mathbb E[(\Xi_n(K))_q]
  \le C_K^q e^{-c_Kq^3},
  \qquad q\ge1,
\end{equation}
uniformly in every \(n\ge n_\lambda\).
Moreover, if \(|\lambda|\le L<\infty\), then \(n_L\) can be chosen so that
for every compact \(K\Subset E\) there are \(C_K,c_K>0\), depending only on
\(K\) and \(L\), for which \eqref{eq:main-uniform-bound} holds uniformly in
all \(n\ge n_L\) and all \(|\lambda|\le L\), with \(p_n\) and \(\Xi_n\)
carrying the parameter \(\lambda\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Uniform high order factorial bound

body:
[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2606.22656, 'Fluctuations of Point Vortex Ensembles\\ at Small Negative Inverse Temperature'] Fix $\beta_*<8\pi$.  There exists $C_{\beta_*}<\infty$ such that, for
all $\beta\leq \beta_*$, all $N\ge2$, and all $2\leq n\leq N$,
\begin{equation}
    B_{N,n}
    :=
    \binom Nn
    \sum_{\Gamma\in\ipi(n)}|A_N(\Gamma)|
    \leq 
    Cn^{-1/2}\rho^n,
    \qquad
    \rho:=C_{\beta_*}\beta.
\end{equation}
As a consequence, denoting by $\K_N$ the complete graph with $N$ vertices, if $\rho<1$,
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{N\ge2} \sum_{\Gamma\subseteq \K_N}|A_N(\Gamma)|
    \leq \exp\pa{C\sum_{n\ge2}n^{-1/2}\rho^n}<\infty.
\end{equation}

Let f: U -> R^n be C^r (r>=1) on an open set U subset R^n containing a hyperbolic equilibrium x* of y'=f(y), and let E^s, E^u be the stable and unstable subspaces of A=Df(x*) (generalized eigenspaces for eigenvalues of negative, respectively positive, real part), with R^n = E^s (+) E^u. Then there exist local stable and unstable manifolds W^s_loc(x*), W^u_loc(x*), each a C^r embedded disk through x* tangent to E^s, respectively E^u, at x*, of the same dimension as E^s, respectively E^u, invariant under the forward, respectively backward, flow near x*, with W^s_loc(x*) = {y in a neighborhood N of x* : the forward orbit of y stays in N for all t>=0 and phi_t(y) -> x* as t -> infinity} (and symmetrically for W^u_loc with t -> -infinity).
f is C^r, r>=1, near x*
x* is a hyperbolic equilibrium

[Lemma l:non-bdd-mppmixing of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $(\tilde\mathcal{P}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} = \bigl(\{(x_i,\xi_{i,n})\}\bigr)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$
be a family of marked point processes on $\mathbb{R}^d$ sharing the same ground
point process $\mathcal{P}$, and equipped with real-valued marks (scores)
$\xi_{i,n} \in \mathbb{R}$. Fix $p,q,k_1,\ldots,k_{p+q} \in \mathbb{N}$ with $K = k_1 + \ldots + k_{p+q}$. Assume that $(\tilde\mathcal{P}_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ satisfies the fast \textnormal{BL} \,mixing correlation condition~(equation e.mppmixing of the paper) for $p,q$ with fast decay function $\hat\omega_{p+q}$ (and replacing $U(x_i)$ with $\xi_{i,n}$ in (equation e.mppmixing of the paper)) and for all functions $f \in \textnormal{BL}(\mathbb{R}^p)$, $g \in \textnormal{BL}(\mathbb{R}^q)$.

For some $\epsilon>0$ we assume finiteness of the moment $\widetilde{M}_{K,\epsilon, p + q}$ as in (equation e.moment-cond-Lemma of the paper) associated to the marks $\xi_{i,n}$.  
Then there is a fast decreasing function $\tilde \omega_K$ such that
the  correlation functions $m^{\bk k1{p+q}}(\bk x1{p+q};n)$ of $\tilde\mathcal{P}_n$ satisfy~(equation dbtpptruncmixing of the paper) uniformly in $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\bk k1{p+q}$ given $k_1+\ldots+k_{p+q}=K$. The function $\tilde \omega_K$  depends on the value of $K$, the function $\hat\omega_{K}$,  and the constants  $M^\xi_{K+\epsilon}$, 
$C_K$, $\kappa_0$   related to $\xi$ and $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Limit constant for common random two-dimensional partial orders structural calculation Result: Partition each square into m-by-m cells, m=floor(n^(1/3)). Keep a label when its two points occupy the same cell, and retain it only if no other kept label shares that row or column. The retained labels have identical comparisons in both posets. For a fixed label the match probability is1/m^2; conditional on its cell, another label is a conflicting match with probability(2m-1)/m^4. Therefore the expected retained number is n/m^2*[1-(2m-1)/m^4]^(n-1), asymptotic to exp(-2)*n^(1/3). Check: Two retained labels have distinct row and column indices, so each of their coordinate orderings is determined by cell indices in both independent samples. Independence over labels gives the exact no-conflict probability. The bound is liminf E C_n/n^(1/3)>=exp(-2). Obstruction: The isolated-cell matching discards many usable labels and supplies no matching upper constant. Optimizing a local grid construction does not establish existence of the global optimal limit.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0216-limit-constant-for-common-random-two-dimensional-partial-orders
No independent review
title: Attempt on Limit constant for common random two-dimensional partial orders

body: For jointly distributed discrete random variables X and Y with joint pmf p(x,y) and marginal pmfs p(x), p(y), the mutual information is I(X;Y) = sum_{x,y} p(x,y) * log( p(x,y) / (p(x)*p(y)) ). Equivalently, I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X|Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) = H(X) + H(Y) - H(X,Y) = D( P_{X,Y} || P_X times P_Y ), the KL divergence between the joint distribution and the product of the marginals. I(X;Y) >= 0 always, by nonnegativity of KL divergence, with equality if and only if X and Y are independent.
title: Mutual Information

[Theorem 6 (Multi-group non-degenerate limit) of arXiv:2605.21155, 'Asymptotic Probabilities of Attaining the Maximum in Heterogeneous Gaussian Samples'] Assume that $n_k\to\infty$ for every $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$. Then \(\boldsymbol p_n\) converges to a non-degenerate limit \(\boldsymbol p=(p_1,\ldots,p_K)\in(0,1)^K\) if and only if
\[
\boldsymbol\beta_n\to\boldsymbol C=(C_1,\ldots,C_K)\in(0,\infty)^K.
\]
Under this condition, for each \(k=1,\ldots,K\),
\[
p_k
=
\mathbb P\!\left(\sigma_k^2(\Lambda_k-\kappa(C_k,\sigma_k)) > \sigma_j^2(\Lambda_j-\kappa(C_j,\sigma_j)),\ \forall j\neq k\right),
\]
where \(\Lambda_1,\ldots,\Lambda_K\) are independent Gumbel random variables, and  \(C_1=1\) and \(\kappa(C_1,\sigma_1)=0\). Equivalently,
\[
p_k
=
\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-\kappa(C_k,\sigma_k)}}{\sigma_k^2} x^{1/\sigma_k^2 - 1} \exp\left( - \sum_{j=1}^K e^{-\kappa(C_j, \sigma_j)} x^{1/\sigma_j^2} \right) \mathrm{d} x,
\qquad k=1,\ldots,K.
\]
title: Multi-group non-degenerate limit

On one uniform bit x in {-1, 1}, let 1 < p < q < infinity, rho in [-1, 1], T_rho the noise operator (T_rho x = rho x) and f_eps = 1 + eps x. Then log(||T_rho f_eps||_q/||f_eps||_p) = ((q - 1) rho^2 - (p - 1)) eps^2/2 + ((p - 1)(p^2 + p - 3) - (q - 1)(q^2 + q - 3) rho^4) eps^4/12 + O(eps^6) as eps -> 0. So if rho^2 > (p - 1)/(q - 1), small eps != 0 give ||T_rho f||_q > ||f||_p; if rho^2 < (p - 1)/(q - 1) the ratio is below 1 to second order; and at rho^2 = (p - 1)/(q - 1) the quartic coefficient equals (p - 1)(p - q)(pq - p - q + 2)/(12 (q - 1)) < 0, a strict local contraction.

\mathbf{P}\bigl(\mathrm{diam}_{\mathrm{ext}}(W_{1}(H))\ge R\bigr)
&=G(0,0)\,\mathbb{P}_{0}\bigl(\mathrm{diam}_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathfrak{T})\ge R\bigr),\\
\mathbf{P}\bigl(|W_{1}(H)|\ge n\bigr)
&=G(0,0)\,\mathbb{P}_{0}\bigl(|\mathfrak{T}|\ge n\bigr).
\end{align}
More generally, the same identity holds for every continuity event $\mathcal{A}$ of finite vertex sets such that every set in $\mathcal{A}$ contains a nearest neighbour of $0$.

[Proposition 37 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$ with $\alpha + \beta/2>1$. Suppose for some $K \geq 1$ and
        \[0 \leq \lambda < \frac{\beta}{2-\alpha} \land \Big( 1- \frac{1-\alpha}{\beta}\Big),\]
    we have that for all $j \in \N, n \in \{0,1,2\}, p \geq 1$,
    \[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega \mathcal{C}^0_{t,x}} \leq K p^\lambda 2^{(n-\alpha)j}.\]   
    Then there exists $\delta(\alpha,\beta,\lambda)>0$ and  $C(\alpha,\beta,\lambda)>0$ such that for all $N \in \N$, there exists a random field $M^N : \T^d \to [0,\infty)$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item
         For all $p \geq 1$ and $t \geq 2,$
        $\P(\|M^N\|_{\mathcal{C}^0_y} \geq t) \leq  C e^{C p^C K^C} (\log t)^{-p}$,
        \item 
        for all $p \geq 1$, $\|M^N\|_{L^p_\omega L^p_y} \leq C e^{Cp^C K^C}$,
        \item 
        
        and for any $y,z \in \T^d$, any $w \in \mathcal{C}^{1/2 + \delta}([0,1])$ with $w_0 =0$, if we let $X_t = \Phi^N_t(y)$, and take the solution $\tilde X$ to 
          \begin{equation}
         
         \tilde X_t=z+\int_0^t U^N(s,\tilde X_s)\,ds+w_t,\qquad t\in[0,1],
         \end{equation}
         then we have the stability estimate on the time interval $[0,1]$,
         \[\|X - \tilde X\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1/2 +\delta}_t} \leq M^N(y)\big(|y-z| + \|w\|_{\mathcal{C}^{1/2+\delta}_t}\big),\]
         and the expansion/compression estimate for all $t\in[0,1]$
         \[ \frac{1}{M^N(y)}|y-z|-\|w\|_{C^{1/2+\delta}_t}\leq |X_t-\tilde X_t|\leq M^N(y)\big(|y-z|+\|w\|_{C^{1/2+\delta}_t}\big).\]
    \end{enumerate}
title: Proposition 37 of arXiv:2608.05931

[Theorem 8 of arXiv:2608.08242, 'Bang--bang representation of $3\times 3$ embeddable stochastic matrices'] Let $A\in\mathcal M_+$.
	\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
		\item
		If $A$ has a zero entry, then 
		\[
		A\in\T\Longleftrightarrow G(A)\geq0.
		\]
		In that case $A\in R_5$, and $G(A)=0$ implies $A\in R_4$.
		
		\item
		If $A>0$, then $A\in\V$ if and only if $\max_{i,j}V_{ij}(A)\geq0$.
		More generally, if $A\in \mathcal M_+$, then
		\[
		A\in\T\cup\V
		\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
		\max_{i,j}V_{ij}(A)\geq0.
		\]
		
		\item
		If $A\notin\T\cup\V$, then $A\in\NH$ if and only if, for some
		ordered pair $(i,j)$ with $i\neq j$, the quadratic $q_{ij}^A$
		has a root in $[0,C_{ij}(A)]$.
	
		
		\item
		One has
		\[
		R_6=\T\cup\V\cup\NH.
		\]
	\end{enumerate}

body: Intermediate value theorem: Let f be a real-valued function that is continuous on the closed interval [a, b] with a < b, and let u be any number between f(a) and f(b). Then there exists a point c in [a, b] with f(c) = u; if u lies strictly between f(a) and f(b), then c may be taken in the open interval (a, b). Equivalently, the image f([a, b]) of an interval under a continuous real function is again an interval, and it contains every value between f(a) and f(b).
title: Intermediate value theorem

[Defn 12 of arXiv:2605.30779, '2605.30779'] Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb C\) be an open set, and let \( \{ f_N \}^{\infty}_{N = 1} \) and \(f\) be meromorphic functions on \(\Omega\). We write
  \[
    f_N\xrightarrow{\mathrm{mer}} f
    \qquad\text{on }\Omega
  \]
  if, for every compact set \(K\subset\Omega\) containing no pole of \(f\), there exists \(N_0=N_0(K)\) such that \(K\) contains no pole of \(f_N\) for all \(N\ge N_0\), and
\[
\sup_{z\in K}|f_N(z)-f(z)|\to0
\qquad\text{as }N\to\infty .
\]

body:
[Proposition 1 (Standard asymptotic characterization) of arXiv:2606.27774, 'Variational Formulas for the Spectrum of\\ Block Wishart Matrices'] Assume the rows $\bx_i\in\C^{p}$ are i.i.d., centered (i.e., $\E[\bx_i] =\bzero$), and isotropic
(i.e., $\E[\bx_i\bx_i^*] = \bI_p$). Assume further that there exists 
$\sfK \in (0,\infty)$
such that, for each $i\in[n]$, all deterministic $\bA\in \C^{p\times p}$, and all $t>0$,

\begin{equation}

   \P\Big( \big|\bx_i^*\bA \bx_i - \Tr(\bA)\big| \ge t \Big)
   \le
   2 \exp\bigg\{-c \min\bigg(\frac{t^2}{\sfK^4 \|\bA\|_\Fnorm^2},\, 
   \frac{t}{\sfK^2 \|\bA\|_\op}\bigg)\bigg\}\, ,
\end{equation}
for some universal constant $c>0$, where $\|\bA\|_\Fnorm$ and $\|\bA\|_\op$ denote 
the Frobenius and operator norms of $\bA$, respectively.
Fix integer $k\ge 1$, $\alpha \in (0,\infty)$ and
let $\nu\in\cuP_0(\sa{k}{\C})$.
Define
\begin{equation}

    \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS) := \int  \bT(\bI + \bS\bT)^{-1} \nu(\de \bT) - \frac1\alpha\bS^{-1},\quad\quad \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}:\C^{k\times k} \to\C^{k\times k}.
\end{equation}

For any $z \in\bbH_+$, there exists a unique 
solution 
$\bS_\up{\nu,\alpha}(z)$
to
\begin{equation}

    \bK_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS) = z\bI,\quad\quad \bS\in\bbH_+^k := \{\bB\in \C^{k\times k}: \Im(\bB) \succ\bzero\}.
\end{equation}
Furthermore,
    \begin{equation}
        s_\up{\nu,\alpha}(z) := 
         \frac{\alpha}{k} \Tr(\bS_\up{\alpha,\nu}(z))\quad\quad\textrm{for}\quad z\in\bbH_+
    \end{equation}
is the Stieltjes transform of a probability measure 
$\mu_\up{\alpha,\nu}\in\cuP(\R)$ such that, almost surely
\begin{equation}
    \hmu_{\bW_k} \Rightarrow \mu_\up{\alpha,\nu} \quad\quad \textrm{almost surely, as} \quad\quad n\to\infty,\;\frac{n}{p} \to\alpha,
\end{equation}
where $\hmu_{\bW_k}$ is the empirical spectral distribution of $\bW_k$ and $\Rightarrow$ denotes weak convergence of probability measures.

Finally, if $\dist(\{\bT_i:i\le n\},\supp(\nu))\to 0$ (with $\dist$ denoting
Hausdorff distance between sets in $(\reals^k,\|\,\cdot\,\|$), then,
almost surely,

\begin{align}
\dist\big(\supp(\hmu_{\bW_k}),\supp (\mu_\up{\alpha,\nu})\big) \to 0\, .
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Standard asymptotic characterization

[Proposition 38 (MTP for the marked Poisson point process) of arXiv:2504.02435, 'Poisson-Voronoi percolation in higher rank'] Let $G$ be a non-compact connected semisimple real Lie group and $(X,d_X)$ be its symmetric space.
Let ${\bf Y}^{(\lambda)}$ be the marked Poisson point process on $X$ with intensity $\lambda \, {\rm vol}$ for some $\lambda>0$.
Let ${\bf Y}^{(\lambda)}_o={\bf Y}^{(\lambda)} \cup \{\mathbf o\}$, where~$\mathbf o$ is equipped with an independent ${\rm Unif}[0,1]$-mark.
Then
\begin{equation*} 
\mathbb E \bigg[ \sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} F(o,Y^{(\lambda)}_i,{\bf Y}_o^{(\lambda)}) \bigg] = \mathbb E \bigg[ \sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} F(Y^{(\lambda)}_i,o,{\bf Y}_o^{(\lambda)}) \bigg]
\end{equation*}
for every measurable $F : X\times X\times \mathbf M(X\times[0,1]) \to [0,\infty]$ such that 
$$
F(\tau(x),\tau(y),\tau \circ \overline \eta) = F(x,y, \overline \eta)
$$
for every $\overline\eta \in\mathbf M(X\times[0,1])$ and every $x,y\in X$ and $\tau\in{\rm Isom}(X)$ which interchanges $x$ and $y$.

body: In mathematics, a self-avoiding walk (SAW) is a sequence of moves on a lattice that does not visit the same point more than once. This is a special case of the graph theoretical notion of a path. A self-avoiding polygon (SAP) is a closed self-avoiding walk on a lattice. Very little is known rigorously about the self-avoiding walk from a mathematical perspective, although physicists have provided numerous conjectures that are believed to be true and are strongly supported by numerical simulations.
title: Self-avoiding walk

Let tau be uniform on [T,2T], T>0, and let A and B be products of at most r prime factors each, all primes <=y, y>=2. For A=B, E exp(-i tau log(A/B))=1. For A!=B its modulus is at most min(1,2/(T |log(A/B)|))<=min(1,2 y^r/T). Independent Haar phases at the primes have the same expectation 1 when A=B and 0 otherwise. Thus for a finite polynomial in these phases and their conjugates with such monomials and coefficient absolute sum M, the time-average versus Haar moment error is at most 2 M y^r/T. This is a sufficient fixed-moment approximation window, not a necessary condition and not a decomposition theorem for log|zeta|.

[Lemma lem:internalcutpoint of arXiv:2608.23135, 'Graph distance and effective resistance of the random walk trace in four and five dimensio'] Let $(j,k)\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{RW}}$.  Suppose that
\[
   [u_{j-1},u_{j+2}]\subset I_a,
   \qquad [u_{k-2},u_{k+1}]\subset I_b.
\]
Let $\widetilde A_{j,k}$ be the event that there exist times
$L_j^+\in [u_{j+1},u_{j+2}]$ and $L_k^-\in [u_{k-3},u_{k-2}]$ such that
\begin{equation*}

        S[t_{a-1},L_j^+]\cap S[L_j^++1,t_a]=\emptyset,
        \qquad
        S[t_{b-1},L_k^-]\cap S[L_k^-+1,t_b]=\emptyset .
\end{equation*}
Equivalently, $L_j^+$ and $L_k^-$ are local cut times for the full macro blocks
$I_a=[t_{a-1},t_a]$ and $I_b=[t_{b-1},t_b]$, respectively.
Then
\begin{equation}

\mathbb{P}\bigl(\exists (j,k)\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{RW}}:\widetilde A_{j,k}^c\bigr)
\le C\frac{(\log\log n)^{C_0}}{\log n}.
\end{equation}

[Proposition 18 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $\lambda>0$, and $p\geq 1$, and let, for all $j\geq 0$, $u^j$ be defined by~\eqref{eq:autonomous poisson}. Suppose there exists $M\geq 1$ such that for all $j\geq 0$, $n\in\{0,1,2\}$, and $y\in\T^d,$
\[\|\nabla^n f^j_y\|_{L^p_\omega C^0_x}\leq M 2^{(n-\alpha-d/p)j}.\]
Then 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item the $u^j$ are mutually independent with $\E u^j =0$,
\item for each $j\geq 1$, $u^j$ has a finite spatial range of dependence $2^{-j}$,
\item and there exists a constant $C(d)>0$ such that for all $j\geq 0$ and $n\in\{0,1,2\}$,
\[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega C^0_x}\leq CM(\lambda+p)2^{(n-\alpha)j}.\]
\end{enumerate}
Letting $U:=\sum_{j= 0}^\infty u^j$, we further have that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] if for all $j\geq 0$ and $y\in\T^d$, $\nabla\cdot f^j_y=0$, then $\nabla\cdot U=0$,
    \item[(ii)] if there exists $r\in(0,1)$ and $C>0$ such that for all $j\geq 0$
    \begin{equation}
    \sup_{\substack{x,y\in\T^d\\d_{\T^d}(x,y)\leq 2^{-(j+2)}}}\bigg\|\frac{d\mu^j_{y,x}(z)}{dz}\bigg\|_{L^\infty(\R^d)}\leq Cr^j e^{\lambda j},
    \end{equation}
    then it almost surely holds that for all $\alpha'<\alpha$
    \[\lim_{\eps\rightarrow 0} \eps^{-\alpha'd}|Z_\eps|=0,\]
    where $Z_\eps$ is defined as in~\eqref{eq:zero sets}.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition 18 of arXiv:2608.05931

The inequality $\|\hat f\|_{p'}\le\|f\|_p$, $\frac1p+\frac1{p'}=1$, holds for $1\le p\le2$ (Riesz-Thorin interpolation between $\|\hat f\|_\infty\le\|f\|_1$ and Plancherel) - and only there. The restriction $p\le2$ is load-bearing: (i) On $\mathbb T$, $L^p\subset L^2$ for $p>2$, so the coefficients are automatically in $\ell^2$, but no better exponent is available: Carleman's example provides a continuous (hence in every $L^p$) function $f$ on $\mathbb T$ with $\sum_n|\hat f(n)|^q=\infty$ for every $q<2$. So no bound $\|\hat f\|_{\ell^{p'}}\le C\|f\|_{L^p}$ with $p'<2$ can hold for any $p>2$. (ii) On $\mathbb R^d$ and $p>2$, the Fourier transform of an $L^p$ function exists only as a tempered distribution and need not be representable by a locally integrable function, so the left-hand side of the inequality is not even defined in general. (iii) The direction matters too: the dual statement '$\hat f\in L^{p'}$ implies $f\in L^p$' is false in general; what is true is the companion inequality $\|f\|_{p'}\le\|\hat f\|_p$ for $1\le p\le2$. (iv) On $\mathbb R^d$ the constant $1$ is not sharp: Babenko-Beckner give $\|\hat f\|_{p'}\le\big(p^{1/p}/(p')^{1/p'}\big)^{d/2}\|f\|_p$ for $1<p<2$, attained by Gaussians, whereas on $\mathbb T$ and $\mathbb Z$ the constant $1$ is sharp.

[Proposition 7 of arXiv:2506.15159, 'Conditional central limit theorems for exponential random graphs'] For $W$ and $Y=\t E$ in \cref{20001}, 
    
    
    
    
    we have (recall \cref{eq:Mlpm})
    \begin{align}
       M_{0,\pm}(W,\t E)&=\t p\,\t q +R_{0,\pm},\\
     M_{1,+}(W,\t E)&=-\lambda \left( \alpha_+ W+R_{1,+}\right),\notag\\
      M_{1,-}(W,\t E)&=-\lambda \left( \alpha_- W+R_{1,-}\right),\notag\\
      M_{2,\pm}(W,\t E)&=\lambda(1+R_{2,\pm}),\notag
    \end{align}
where $\lambda=(2(1-2\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_ls_l\t p^{e_l-1}\t q))/N$, $\Delta W=O_r(n^{-1}),$
\begin{align*}
     a_+=&\frac{\t p-2\t q^2\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_l s_l\t p^{e_l-1}}{1-2\t q\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_ls_l\t p^{e_l-1}}, \quad a_{-}=\frac{\t q-2\t q\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_l s_l\t p^{e_l}}{1-2\t q\sum_{l=2}^m\beta_ls_l\t p^{e_l-1}},
     \\
     R_{0,\pm}=&O_{r}(n^{-1}),\quad R_{1,+}=O_{r}(n^{\frac{1}{2}}),\quad R_{1,-}=O_{r}(n^{\frac{1}{2}}),\quad
     R_{1,+}+R_{1,-}=O_{r}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}),\\
    \t R_{1,+}=&R_{1,+}-\E R_{1,+}=O(n^{-\frac{1}{2}})\t E+O_{r}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}),\\
    \t R_{1,-}=&R_{1,-}-\E R_{1,-}=O(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}) \t E+O_{r}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}),\\
     R_{2,+}=&O_{r}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}),\quad R_{2,-}=O_{r}(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}).
\end{align*}
Hereafter, for convenience, we use $O_{r}(h)$ in an unconventional way to denote some random variable $X$ such that the $L^r$ norm $\|X/h\|_r\leq C_r$ for any given $r\geq 1$ and a constant $C_r$ depending only on $r$ and the subset $B$ of the subcritical region considered in \cref{thm:twostar}. Status: proof (unaudited). Uses the Wang-Wang monotone-density joint mixability theorem; special case only. Novelty not asserted.

For 0<epsilon<1/2 and 0<p<1, let F=(1-p)Uniform[0,epsilon]+p Uniform[1-epsilon,1]. Then F is n-CM for every integer n>=ceil(2/epsilon), regardless of p. This covers a nonsymmetric disconnected-support family where the global density-floor theorem is unavailable.

External theorem used exactly: Wang-Wang joint monotone-density criterion, quoted in Wang arXiv:1411.6190v3 Section 2.2(e), equation (7), p.9, citing Wang and Wang, Joint Mixability, doi:10.1287/moor.2015.0755. If all n laws have increasing densities (or all have decreasing densities) on finite essential supports [a_i,b_i], with means mu_i, they are jointly mixable iff sum a_i+max_i(b_i-a_i)<=sum mu_i<=sum b_i-max_i(b_i-a_i). We use only this established theorem, not a new proof of it.

1. Put q=np. When q is integer, D0007-C005 gives a complete mix directly. Otherwise write k=floor(q), theta=q-k in (0,1), and w=1-theta. Let K=k with probability w and K=k+1 with probability theta, so E[K]=np. Think of K as the high-interval label count.

2. The probabilities of the K=k state conditional on a uniformly selected coordinate's low/high label must be

    t_L=(n-k)w/[n(1-p)],  t_H=k w/(np).

Both belong to [0,1]. Indeed the complementary probabilities are (n-k-1)theta/[n(1-p)] and (k+1)theta/(np), respectively, and each pair sums to one. If t_H=0 or t_L=1, the absent conditional label need not be defined; the present counterpart is just uniform.

3. On a component interval [a,a+epsilon], and for 0<t<1, define U^+_t=Uniform[a+(1-t)epsilon,a+epsilon] and U^-_t=Uniform[a,a+(1-t)epsilon]. Then t U^+_t+(1-t)U^-_t=Uniform[a,a+epsilon]. Relative to the full uniform center, their means are shifted by +(1-t)epsilon/2 and -t epsilon/2. The first lies at the upper end, the second at the lower end.

For each label j=L,H with t=t_j, conditional on K=k use distribution

    (1-tau) Uniform_j + tau U^+_t,

and conditional on K=k+1 use

    (1-tau) Uniform_j + tau U^-_t,

where tau in [0,1) is chosen below. The first has an increasing step density on the full component interval; the second a decreasing step density there. Their t/(1-t) mixture restores the full uniform marginal for that label. For t=0 use full uniform in the K=k+1 state; for t=1 use full uniform in the K=k state; the other state has no such label. The formulas for present means and densities follow by this convention.

4. Conditional on K=k the unperturbed sum of means is k(1-epsilon)+n epsilon/2. The target is n mu=q(1-epsilon)+n epsilon/2, so the required positive shift is theta(1-epsilon). The maximum shift coefficient at tau=1 is

    M=epsilon/2 * [(n-k)(1-t_L)+k(1-t_H)]
     =epsilon*theta/2 * [n - (1-theta)theta/(n p(1-p))].

To verify the second identity, (n-k)^2/[n(1-p)]+k^2/(np)=n+theta^2/[n p(1-p)]. Substituting the t values gives the displayed expression.

The correction d=(1-theta)theta/[n p(1-p)] is at most one. Indeed put l=n-k-1>=0. Since q=k+theta and n-q=l+(1-theta),

    q(n-q)-n theta(1-theta)
       =k*l+k*(1-theta)^2+l*theta^2 >=0.

Because n p(1-p)=q(n-q)/n, this proves d<=1. Consequently M>=epsilon*theta*(n-1)/2. Since n>=2/epsilon, epsilon*(n-1)/2>=1-epsilon/2>1-epsilon. Thus M>theta(1-epsilon), and

    tau=theta(1-epsilon)/M

belongs to (0,1). Conditional on K=k the perturbed sum of means equals n mu.

5. Conditional on K=k+1 its sum of means also equals n mu. Here is the exact averaging argument: the label-conditioned t mixtures restore both original component uniforms, and P(high)=E[K]/n=p, so a uniformly permuted coordinate has unconditional marginal F. Thus the unconditional expected total is n mu. The K=k state's total mean was just set equal to n mu; since the other state has positive probability theta, its total mean must also be n mu. This calculation concerns means only and does not assume a constant-sum coupling before it is built.

6. Joint mixes exist in each state. All conditional densities in the k state are increasing; all in the k+1 state are decreasing. Their essential interval widths are epsilon, since tau<1 keeps a positive uniform part. For a state with s high labels, the sum of support left endpoints is s(1-epsilon), and the sum of right endpoints is s(1-epsilon)+n epsilon. The monotone-density theorem requires the target to lie between s(1-epsilon)+epsilon and s(1-epsilon)+(n-1)epsilon.

For s=k its displacement above the unperturbed center is theta(1-epsilon); for s=k+1 the displacement below center is (1-theta)(1-epsilon). Both are <=1-epsilon. Since n>=2/epsilon,

    (n/2-1)epsilon >=1-epsilon.

Thus the target satisfies both support-mean inequalities in each state. The established theorem supplies a coupling of those n conditional laws with sum n mu almost surely.

7. Select the state K, use its joint mix, and uniformly permute all n coordinates. The sum is n mu in both states. The conditional label mixture from Steps 2-3 ensures every full marginal is exactly F. Therefore F is n-CM.

Scope and hardest piece: this proves a finite threshold for the indicated two equal-width uniform intervals. It neither claims the count condition of D0007-C005 is sufficient at smaller n nor solves arbitrary bounded absolutely continuous laws. Convention $\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}dx$. Let $W>0$ and let $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\hat f=0$ a.e. outside $[-W,W]$. Then $\hat f\in L^1$, so $f$ has a (unique) continuous representative $f(x)=\int_{-W}^{W}\hat f(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\xi}d\xi$, and for that representative $$f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}f\!\left(\frac{n}{2W}\right)\operatorname{sinc}(2Wx-n),\qquad \operatorname{sinc}(t)=\frac{\sin(\pi t)}{\pi t},$$ the series converging in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ and uniformly on $\mathbb R$. Moreover $\sum_n|f(n/2W)|^2=2W\|f\|_2^2$, so the samples determine $f$ isometrically. The sampling rate $2W$ (the Nyquist rate) is critical: functions bandlimited to $[-W,W]$ are in general not determined by samples at a slower rate, and the theorem's conclusion uses $f\in L^2$ - the distributionally bandlimited function $\sin(2\pi Wx)$ has all samples $f(n/2W)=0$ without being zero, and it is excluded only because it is not in $L^2$.

[Proposition lemma:Itildeinvariantsetfoundaftercountablymanysteps of arXiv:2506.10448, 'Hitting probabilities and the Ekstr\"om--Persson conjecture'] Let $\mu \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^d)$, let $\underline{V}$ be an admissible sequence of open sets and let 
$C\subseteq \spt \mu$ be compact. For all $t\ge 0$, define compact sets $C_t^{\gamma}$ for
each ordinal number $\gamma$ as follows: 
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[i)] Set $C_t^0:=C$.
  \item[ii)] If $C_t^{\gamma}$ has been defined, set 
             $C_t^{\gamma+1}:=\JmuVt(C_t^{\gamma})$.
  \item[iii)] If $\lambda$ is a nonzero limit ordinal and $C_t^{\gamma}$ has been defined for 
              every $\gamma<\lambda$, set 
        \[
        C_t^{\lambda}:=\bigcap_{\gamma<\lambda}C^{\gamma}_t.
        \]
\end{enumerate}        
Then there exists a countable ordinal $\beta_t$ for which $C_t^{\beta_t}$ is a fixed point of 
$\JmuVt$, i.e.,  $C_t^{\beta_t+1}=C_t^{\beta_t}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

PRIVATE STATUS NOTE from a bounded web search on 2026-09-07, not a re-read of the papers. Bourgade's ICM 2018 conjecture (0.2) for d = 1: bulk eigenvectors of N x N Hermitian band matrices with band width W are localised for W << N^{1/2} and delocalised with GUE statistics for W >> N^{1/2}. Yau and Yin (arXiv 2501.01718, 2025) proved, for W > N^{1/2+eps}, the local semicircle law down to scale N^{-1+eps}, simultaneous delocalisation of all bulk eigenvectors, quantum unique ergodicity and GUE bulk universality; arXiv 2508.05802 (2025) treats the localised side; together with Erdos-Riabov's delocalisation work the d = 1 transition is established. The d = 2 localisation side at fixed W (localisation length exp(W^2)) and the finite W_c in d = 3 remain open as far as the search found. A solver meeting the 1D conjecture should treat it as a theorem to cite, not a target.

    $ on $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^{d+1})$ 
    by
    \begin{align*} D_Nf(t,x) &= N \big[ f(t+N^{-1},x)-f(t,x)\big],\\
        L_N f(t,x) &= N\bigg[f(t+N^{-1},x-N^{-1}   d_N) -\int_I f(t,x-N^{-1/2}y) \mu^{   \varsigma_N} (\dr y)\bigg],\\
        K_N f(t,x) &= N^{-1}\sum_{s\in [0,T]\cap (N^{-1}\mathbb Z_{\ge 0})} \int_{I} f(t-s,x-N^{-1/2}y)p_N(Ns,\dr y).
    \end{align*}
    These equalities should be understood by integration against smooth functions $\varphi \in \mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d+1})$, and the convolutions need to be understood using the explanation after \eqref{eq:convPhi}.

[Defi 25 of arXiv:2603.27433, 'The $k$-cycle shuffling with repeated cards'] Let $n=ml$. We define the \emph{fixed point set} $F_{n,l}:\S_n\rightarrow 2^{[n]}$ as follows. For $\sigma\in\S_n$, let
$$F_{n,l}(\sigma):=\{i\in [n]:\ \sigma(i)\equiv i \pmod m\}.$$
The function $F_{n,l}$ naturally descends to a well-defined function on $\sim_l\backslash\S_n$, which we still denote by $F_{n,l}$. We say that an element $\sigma\in\S_n$ is \emph{clustered} if $|F_{n,l}(\sigma)\cap T_{i,l}|\ge 2$ for some $1\le i\le m$.

Let P be any fixed target-independent latent probability law, and G a nonempty class of measurable maps into R^D, D>=1. Targets are supported on [-B,B]^D, B>0. Suppose each coordinate of the clipped maps Pi_B o g has subgraph VC dimension at most an integer V>=1. For 0<t<=2BD the clipped output laws have an external W1 t-cover with at most (12eBD/t)^(2DV) laws. Coordinate centers may come from different network parameters: their tuple need not be a realizable network, because the target packing lower bound must permit arbitrary law centers. If every family of <=2^S laws has minimax target error >=c(S+1)^(-alpha), then the original generator minimax error is at least c[2DV*log2(12eBD/t)+1]^(-alpha)-t. Thus error <=epsilon<=2BD requires 2DV*log2(12eBD/epsilon)+1 >=[c/(2epsilon)]^(1/alpha). For a standard fixed ReLU architecture with W total affine coefficient slots, U>=1 units and L>=1 layers, put Wprime=W+5, Uprime=U+2, Lprime=L+1 and V=ceil[Lprime+Lprime*Wprime*log2(4e*Lprime*Uprime*log2(2e*Lprime*Uprime))]. Bartlett-Harvey-Liaw-Mehrabian Theorem 6 (arXiv:1703.02930v3, p.4), applied to (z,s)->g_j(z)-s with an optional dummy unit, justifies this V without any bound on weight magnitudes or precision. Count every affine slot, including tied and fixed slots; no bound in terms of distinct shared slots alone is asserted. Clipping improves error to targets in the box. A finite union of A0 architectures adds log2(A0) to the cover bit budget. A target-dependent latent law or uncounted architecture choices are excluded. The proof uses an elementary Sauer counting and random-separation argument; no general-method novelty or matching optimal upper rate is asserted.
Fixed latent law; measurable maps; targets in a fixed box; finite coordinate subgraph dimension; arbitrary external law centers; complete architecture/slot accounting.

Put u_i=a_i^T z and v_i=a_i^T x. The smoothed amplitude-flow loss is F_beta(z)=(1/(2m))sum_i L_beta(u_i,v_i), where L_beta(u,v)=v^2(gamma_beta(u/v)-1)^2 for v!=0 and L_beta(u,0)=u^2. Since gamma_beta is even, the nonzero-v expression also equals v^2(gamma_beta(|u|/|v|)-1)^2. The loss is continuously differentiable. The source uses D_v h(z)=lim_{t down to0}(h(z+t v)-h(z))/t, when this limit exists, and D_v^2 F(z)=D_v(D_v F)(z). For C1 F this second derivative is lim_{t down to0}<grad F(z+t v)-grad F(z),v>/t. [Theorem 3 (Variational formula for the logarithmic potential) of arXiv:2606.27774, 'Variational Formulas for the Spectrum of\\ Block Wishart Matrices'] Fix  $k \ge 1$ integer,
$\alpha \in (0,\infty)$, and $\nu\in\cuP_0(\sa{k}{\C})$.
For $u<\zeta_{-,\up{\alpha,\nu}}$,
set
\begin{equation}
    g_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS;u) := -\alpha u \Tr(\bS) + \alpha \int \log \det(\bI + \bT \bS) \nu(\de\bT) - \log|\det(\bS)| - k(\log \alpha +1 ).
\end{equation}
then we have (for $\cP_-$ defined as in Eq~\eqref{eq:P_def})
    \begin{equation}
  \Phi(u) := \int \log |\zeta - u| \, \mu_{\up{\alpha,\nu}}(\de \zeta) 
    =  \frac1k\inf_{\bS\in\cP_{-}} g_\up{\alpha,\nu}(\bS;u)\, .
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lem 239 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix any $\alpha,L > 0$, $\fq \in [1,2]$, and $\mu \in \cP_2(\R)$. 
	Then, for any $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$,
	\begin{align}
		(\E \bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu))^2
		&\ge \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^2 - o_N(1)\,,\\
	
		(\E \bbW_2(\EmpDist(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\cP(\{\pm 1\})))^2
		&\ge \bbW_2(\mu^\Ising(\cA_N),\cP(\{\pm 1\}))^2 - o_N(1)\,.
	\end{align}
where $o_N(1)$ denotes a term tending to $0$ as $N\to\infty$, which may depend on $\alpha,L,\mu$.

\begin{proof}
	Abbreviate $X = \bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu)$.
	By Jensen's inequality, we have
	\[
		\E[X^\fq]^{2/\fq} 
		\le \E[X^2] 
		= (\E X)^2 + \E[(X-\E X)^2] \stackrel{\eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var}}{=} (\E X)^2 + o_N(1)\,.
	\]
By convexity of $\bbW_\fq(\cdot,\cdot)^\fq$, we have
	\[
		\E[X^\fq] = \E [\bbW_\fq(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu)^\fq] \ge \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^\fq\,.
	\]
	Rearranging yields the first assertion \eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound}.
	The second assertion
	\eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound.ising} is proved in the same way, replacing $X$ with $J \equiv \bbW_2(\EmpDist(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\cP(\{\pm 1\}))$ in the above argument and using \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var.ising} from Lemma~\ref{l:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc} in place of \eqref{e:Wq.lip.to.fixed.msr.conc.var}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem 239 of arXiv:2608.29416

[Definition 1 (Stopping times and overshoot event) of arXiv:2604.23133, 'High-Precision Framework for Expected Hitting Times Analysis in the Dice-Sum Process'] Let $\mathcal{H} \subset \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ be a target set and $N \in \mathbb{N}$ a cutoff.  
Define
\[
T := \inf\{\, t \ge 0 : S_t \in \mathcal{H} \,\}, \qquad
\omega_N := \inf\{\, t \ge 0 : S_t > N \,\}, \qquad
A_N := \{\, \omega_N < T \,\},
\]
where $T$ is the first hitting time of the target set~$\mathcal{H}$,
$\omega_N$ is the first time the cumulative sum exceeds the cutoff~$N$,
and $A_N$ is the \emph{overshoot event}, corresponding to paths that cross~$N$
before reaching~$\mathcal{H}$.
title: Stopping times and overshoot event

body: A metric space is a pair (X, d) where X is a set and d is a function from X x X to the real numbers satisfying, for all x, y, z in X: (i) d(x,y) >= 0, with d(x,y) = 0 if and only if x = y; (ii) symmetry, d(x,y) = d(y,x); (iii) the triangle inequality, d(x,z) <= d(x,y) + d(y,z). The open ball of center x and radius r > 0 is B(x,r) = {y in X : d(x,y) < r}. The metric topology on X is the topology generated by the open balls as a basis: a set U is open exactly when for every point x of U some open ball B(x,r) is contained in U. Convergence of a sequence x_n to x means d(x_n, x) tends to 0.

Let X have joint density or pmf f(x;theta) for a scalar parameter theta in an open subset of R, satisfying regularity conditions under which differentiation with respect to theta may be passed under the integral/sum sign, both for the normalization condition and for computing E_theta[T(X)]. Let T(X) be any statistic with finite variance used to estimate g(theta) for a differentiable function g, and let b(theta) = E_theta[T(X)] - g(theta) be its bias, assumed differentiable in theta. Then Var_theta(T(X)) >= (g'(theta) + b'(theta))^2 / I(theta), where I(theta) = E_theta[ (d/dtheta log f(X;theta))^2 ] is the Fisher information, assumed finite and positive. In particular, if T is unbiased for theta itself (g(theta)=theta, b=0), then Var_theta(T(X)) >= 1/I(theta).

Standard approximation arguments in L^p silently use p < infinity. On R^n with Lebesgue measure: (1) DENSITY. Continuous compactly supported functions are dense in L^p for 1 <= p < infinity, but their closure in L^infinity is C_0(R^n) (continuous functions vanishing at infinity), a proper closed subspace; L^infinity(R^n) is not separable, while L^p(R^n) is for p < infinity. (Simple functions are dense in L^p for every p including infinity; simple functions with support of FINITE measure are dense only for p < infinity.) (2) MOLLIFICATION. If phi is an approximate identity then phi_eps * f -> f in L^p for 1 <= p < infinity, but not in L^infinity: for f = 1_{[0,infinity)} each phi_eps * f is continuous, and any continuous g satisfies ||g - f||_infinity >= 1/2, so the convergence fails; in L^infinity one only gets convergence at points of continuity (and weak-* convergence). (3) TRANSLATION. h -> f(. - h) is continuous from R^n to L^p for p < infinity; in L^infinity it is not: for f = 1_{[0,infinity)}, ||f(. - h) - f||_infinity = 1 for every h not equal to 0. Consequences for proofs: any argument that proves an estimate for nice functions and 'passes to the limit by density', or that uses continuity of translation (Riemann-Lebesgue, convolution identities, Lebesgue differentiation via density), must be carried out in L^p with p < infinity, or re-done by a separate weak-* / pointwise argument at p = infinity.

[Lemma 19 (Maximal moment estimate for stable stochastic integrals) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\gamma=(\gamma_s)_{0\le s\le T}$ be predictable and satisfy
\[
  \E\int_0^T |\gamma_s|^\alpha\dd s<\infty.
\]
Define
\[
  M_t:=\int_0^t\int_{\R\setminus\{0\}}\gamma_s z\,\wt N(\md s,\md z).
\]
Then, for every $p\in(0,\alpha)$, there is a constant $C_{p,\alpha}$ such that
\[
  \E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^p
  \le C_{p,\alpha}\left(\E\int_0^T |\gamma_s|^\alpha\dd s\right)^{p/\alpha}.
\]

[Thm 8 (CLT for the normalized traces) of arXiv:2604.26499, 'Spectrum of Random Matrices with Exploding Moments'] Let $M$ be the block diagonal matrix defined in 
\eqref{eqn: main definition of block matrix M} satisfying 
Condition \ref{cond: Correlated Block matrix} with $\alpha=1$. 
For any partition $\pi\in \bigcup_{k\ge1}\mathcal P(k)$, let $Z_N(T_{\pi})$ be defined as in \eqref{eq: Z_N T pi}. Then the family of random variables
$
\big(Z_N(T_\pi)\big)_{\pi\in\bigcup_{k}\mathcal{P}(k)}
$
converges to a centered Gaussian process $\big(z(T_\pi)\big)_{\pi\in\bigcup_{k}\mathcal{P}(k)}$ as $N \rightarrow \infty$. 
Moreover, for any two partitions $\pi_1,\pi_2$, the limiting covariance is given by
\begin{align}
\mathrm{Cov}\left(z(T_{\pi_1}),z(T_{\pi_2})\right)
&=
\sum_{r_1,r_2 \in \{1,2\}}\sum_{T \in\mathcal{P}^{\#}(T_{\pi_1}^{(r_1)},T_{\pi_2}^{(r_2)})} \tau^b[T],
\end{align}
where the expression of $\tau^b[T]$ is given in \eqref{eq:covariance kerne for block matrix model}. Here $\mathcal{P}^{\#}(T_{\pi_1}^{(r_1)}, T_{\pi_2}^{(r_2)})$ denotes the collection of graphs obtained by disjoint copies of the graphs $T_{\pi_1}^{(r_1)}$ and $T_{\pi_2}^{(r_2)}$ and gluing them with at least one common edge.

Let lambda* denote Lebesgue outer measure on R^d, defined by lambda*(E) = inf of sum of volumes of countably many open boxes covering E, let L be the sigma-algebra of Caratheodory-measurable (Lebesgue measurable) sets, and let lambda = lambda* restricted to L. Then: (1) OUTER REGULARITY, valid for EVERY set E contained in R^d, measurable or not: lambda*(E) = inf { lambda(U) : U open, U contains E }. (2) MEASURABILITY CRITERION: E is in L if and only if for every eps > 0 there is an open U containing E with lambda*(U \ E) < eps, if and only if there is a G_delta set G containing E with lambda(G \ E) = 0, if and only if there is an F_sigma set F contained in E with lambda(E \ F) = 0. (3) INNER REGULARITY by compact sets, valid for every E in L: lambda(E) = sup { lambda(K) : K compact, K contained in E } (both sides may be +infinity). Equivalently, for E in L with lambda(E) < infinity and eps > 0 there is a compact K contained in E with lambda(E \ K) < eps. Thus lambda is a Radon measure: it is finite on compacta, outer regular and inner regular. (4) COMPLETENESS: if lambda*(N) = 0 then N is in L and lambda(N) = 0, and hence every subset of a null set is measurable with measure zero. Equivalently, (R^d, L, lambda) is the completion of (R^d, Borel, lambda|Borel): L = { B union Z : B Borel, Z a subset of a Borel null set }. SHARP EDGES. (a) The Borel sigma-algebra itself is NOT complete: the Cantor set is Borel and null, it has 2^continuum subsets, all of them Lebesgue null and hence Lebesgue measurable, while there are only continuum many Borel sets; so L is strictly larger than the Borel sigma-algebra, and 'measurable' must never be silently upgraded to 'Borel'. (b) Regularity statements about the MEASURE are for measurable sets. Outer regularity in the form (1) does hold for arbitrary sets because it is the definition of the outer measure, but inner regularity fails badly for non-measurable sets: a Vitali set has inner measure 0 and positive outer measure, so the two approximations do not meet. It is exactly the meeting of the two that measurability expresses. (c) Completeness is what makes 'a.e. defined' harmless: if f = g almost everywhere and f is measurable then g is measurable. That inference is FALSE in the Borel sigma-algebra, and is a frequent silent error. (d) Regularity is not automatic for general Borel measures: on a non-sigma-compact or non-locally-compact space a finite Borel measure need not be inner regular by compact sets. Lebesgue measure is regular because R^d is sigma-compact, locally compact and second countable, and because lambda is finite on boxes. (e) Not every set is measurable: the existence of a non-measurable set uses the axiom of choice, and translation invariance plus countable additivity forbid extending lambda to all subsets of R^d.
the ambient space is R^d with Lebesgue outer measure defined by countable covers by boxes
L is the sigma-algebra of Caratheodory-measurable sets and lambda = lambda* restricted to L
R^d is sigma-compact, locally compact and second countable, and lambda is finite on bounded sets - this is what drives regularity
the axiom of choice is used only for the remark that non-measurable sets exist

Fix beta,a,b,Lambda,rho>0 and 0<s<2. In the stipulated planar Gaussian displacement-increment model with Fourier covariance beta^{-1}1_{0<|k|<=Lambda}[P_L(k)/(a|k|^s)+P_T(k)/(b|k|^2)] and inverse Fourier measure d^2k/(2pi)^2, let delta rho=-rho div u. Then Var(delta rho(0))=rho^2 Lambda^{4-s}/[2pi beta a(4-s)]>0; rho+delta rho is negative infinitely often on any fixed equally spaced ray almost surely. Therefore it cannot have the exact one-point law of a finite smoothing sum of any locally finite point configuration with a nonnegative kernel. This concerns only the auxiliary Gaussian model, not an actual Riesz Gibbs law or a controlled approximation.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the Ising model, or more generally ferromagnetic spin systems with finite-range or summable interactions, let G(x,y) = <sigma_x sigma_y> be the two-point function. The Simon-Lieb inequality bounds G(x,y) across any finite set Lambda separating x from y (x in Lambda, y outside Lambda) by G(x,y) <= sum_{u in Lambda, v not in Lambda, u~v} G(x,u) J_{uv} G(v,y), a one-step recursive bound relating the two-point function across a separating surface to the two-point function up to the boundary of Lambda times the coupling crossing it. Iterating the inequality over a sequence of nested separating sets, such as concentric boxes, yields exponential decay of G(x,y) once the associated generating function drops below its self-consistency threshold, giving a classical route, predating and complementary to the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, to sharpness of the phase transition and analyticity of the free energy in the high-temperature regime. It does not determine the exact critical temperature directly, only characterizing it implicitly through the inequality's self-consistency condition, and it applies specifically to ferromagnetic spin systems with a workable notion of finite separating surfaces; it does not transfer automatically to percolation, which uses combinatorially different, though philosophically related, inequalities. Typical failure: Iterating the Simon-Lieb inequality across many nested separating surfaces while implicitly assuming a geometric decay rate that has not actually been verified to be summable; turning the one-step recursive bound into exponential decay requires checking that the relevant generating function, summing G times J over the boundary, lies strictly below its self-consistency threshold, and this check is exactly where the difficulty of locating beta_c resides, so skipping it silently assumes the conclusion. Canonical reference: Simon, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Lieb, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics.
ferromagnetic pairwise interactions, finite-range or with summable coupling strengths
finite volume, or an infinite-volume Gibbs state for which the relevant correlation inequalities (e.g. Griffiths inequalities) hold
existence of a family of finite sets separating the two points of interest
the model's symmetry, such as spin-flip Z_2 symmetry, used in the classical derivation of the inequality

[4 10 of arXiv:2607.12303, 'Marginal Stationary Distributions and Convergence Rates of Higher Order Markov Chains'] Suppose that $\mathcal{W}$ is a joint stationary distribution of an $(m-1)$th order Markov chain  $\{X_t\}_{t=1}^{\infty}$ on state space $S$ with transition tensor $\mathcal{P}$ and $\pi$ is the  marginal stationary distribution defined by $\mathcal{W}$. If the chain starts with $Y_1=(X_{m-1}, \ldots, X_1)$ that has the joint distribution $\mathcal{Z}^{(1)}=\mathcal{W}$, then the joint distribution ${\cal Z}^{(t)}$ of $Y_t=(X_{t+m-2}, \ldots, X_t)$ satisfies
$$
\mathcal{Z}^{(t)} = \mathcal{W}
$$
for all $t \ge 1$. Furthermore, let $\beta^{(t)} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be the marginal distribution of $X_{t+m-2}$ in $Y_t$, that is, 
$$
\beta^{(t)}_i=\sum_{i_2, \ldots, i_{m-1} \in S} z^{(t)}_{i i_2 \ldots i_{m-1}}, \ \ i \in S.
$$
Then we have
$$
\beta^{(t)} = \pi, 
$$
for all $t \ge 1$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:max_string of arXiv:2607.22291, 'Rare subtree patterns in size-conditioned Bienaymé trees: Poisson approximation and declum'] Assume that $\mu$ is critical and belongs to the domain of attraction of a stable law.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] Assume that $\mu_{1}>0$.  Set
$$t_n^* = \frac{1}{\log(1/\mu_{1})} \log n + \frac{1}{\log(1/\mu_{1})} \log(1-\mu_1).$$
For every $t \in \mathbb{R}$ we have 
$$\P\bigl(H_{1} ( \mathcal{T}^{n})  \leq \lfloor t_n^* + t\rfloor\bigr) - \exp\bigl(-\mu_1^{t+1 - \{t_n^* + t\}}\bigr)   \quad \mathop{\longrightarrow}_{n \rightarrow \infty} \quad  0$$
\item[(ii)] Let $r\ge2$ be such that $\mu_r>0$, and set
$$
  t_n^{**}=\log_r\log n-
  \log_r\left(\frac{\log(1/\mu_r)}{r-1}\right).
$$
Write $m_n=\lfloor t_n^{**}\rfloor$ and
$\theta_n=\{t_n^{**}\}$, where $\{x\} = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$ is the fractional part, and define
$$
  J_n=
  \begin{cases}
    \{m_n-1,m_n\},&\theta_n\le\tfrac12,\\
    \{m_n,m_n+1\},&\theta_n>\tfrac12.
  \end{cases}
$$
Then $
  \P(H_r(\mathcal T^n)\in J_n)\longrightarrow1$.
Moreover, if $\liminf_n\min(\theta_n,1-\theta_n)>0$, then
$\P(H_r(\mathcal T^n)=m_n)\to1$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let n ≥ 3 be odd, put m = (n+1)/2, and let u0 ∈ C^{m+1}(R^n), u1 ∈ C^m(R^n) both vanish outside the closed ball B̄(0,R). Let u be the (unique) C² solution of ∂_t²u − Δu = 0 with these data. Then u(t,x) = 0 whenever |x| > t + R (finite speed) and also whenever |x| < t − R. Equivalently: u(t,x) depends only on the data on the sphere ∂B(x,t), not on the data inside the ball B(x,t); a compactly supported disturbance produces a signal supported in the spherical shell t − R ≤ |x| ≤ t + R, which passes and leaves no residue.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Try to control the finite-cluster susceptibility above p_c via the lace expansion with a cluster-size cutoff. Result: Above p_c the finite-cluster two-point function tau^f(x) = P(0 <-> x, |C(0)| < infinity) is not directly lace-expandable because the finite-cluster condition is not local; the standard route is through the h -> 0 limit of the magnetisation, whose derivatives in h at fixed p > p_c give the finite-cluster moments. The scaling relation gamma' = gamma follows if the magnetisation M(p,h) has a scaling form M ~ (p - p_c) f(h / (p - p_c)^Delta) with the same Delta on both sides, which is the mean-field prediction; the mean-field magnetisation satisfies M ~ (p-p_c) + sqrt(h) crossover, and the finite-cluster susceptibility above p_c would then be chi^f ~ (p - p_c)^{-1}, i.e. gamma' = 1. A rigorous one-sided bound is available: chi^f(p) >= c/(p - p_c) from the differential inequality of Aizenman-Barsky applied above p_c (since dtheta/dp is bounded by chi^f up to constants and theta ~ (p - p_c)); the matching upper bound needs the finite-cluster expansion. So gamma' >= 1 in the bounded-ratio sense is rigorous; gamma' <= 1 is the open half. Similarly nu' >= nu follows from the lower bound on the finite-cluster correlation length via the same inequality chain. Key identity: dtheta/dp <= C chi^f(p) and theta ~ (p - p_c) give chi^f(p) >= c/(p - p_c), i.e. gamma' >= 1 in the ratio sense. Obstruction: No expansion for finite-cluster quantities above p_c; only the lower bounds are rigorous.

Version 1, Target 1, kind bound; proofs (unaudited), 20 October 2026.

## C033: discrete-time semigroup subtraction

Let a=1/(3pi), b=1/(6pi^2), and A,B be the differential operators in C032.
One step of duration 1/n has P_n=I+A/n+B/n^2+O(n^(-5/2)) on positive
compacts. A diffusion step has exp(A/n)=I+A/n+A^2/(2n^2)+O(n^-3), for
sufficiently smooth local tests. Thus the local weak-error operator is

    C=B-A^2/2
     =(8u+a/5+b/u)D+(4u^2-3au/5)D^2.               (3)

This is an algebraic identity, not a global semigroup expansion at zero.
Direct differentiation gives

    A^2=(4u+2a)D+(14u^2+6au+a^2)D^2
                  +(8u^3+2au^2)D^3+u^4 D^4.

Subtracting half of this from C032's B proves (3); the third- and fourth-
derivative terms cancel exactly. Their inclusion before subtraction was
necessary. A global modified diffusion with this C is not asserted:
the drift b/u is singular and its second-order coefficient can be negative
near zero at finite n.

## C034: a rigorous logarithmic divergence of the limiting Duhamel functional

Use the reviewer-PASS C017 diffusion dU=(2U+a)ds+sqrt(2)U dW, U0=0,
and its semigroup P_s. Fix t>0 and f(u)=1-exp(-u). Define, for 0<epsilon<t,

    I_epsilon(t)=integral_epsilon^t E[(C P_(t-s)f)(U_s)] ds,
    D_t=(D P_t f)(0)=E[J_t exp(-U_t)],
    J_t=exp(t+sqrt(2)W_t).

Then 0<D_t<infinity, and there is a finite H_t such that

    I_epsilon(t)=(D_t/(2pi))log(1/epsilon)+H_t+O_t(sqrt(epsilon)). (4)

This statement concerns the specified cutoff integral for the limiting SDE.
It does not replace epsilon by 1/n inside a network weak-error theorem.

Proof of regularity. The solution from initial value u is U_v^u=U_v^0+uJ_v.
Consequently D^j P_v f(u)=E[J_v^j f^(j)(U_v^0+uJ_v)] for j>=1.
All these derivatives are bounded uniformly for 0<=v<=t, because Gaussian
exponentials J_v have every positive moment. Differentiation under expectation
is justified by these dominating moments. The time derivative of D P_v f
is bounded too: Af and (Af)' are bounded (polynomials times exp(-u)), and
the semigroup identity P_v f-f=integral_0^v P_r Af dr allows differentiation
in u. In particular, with h(s,u)=D P_(t-s) f(u),

    |h(s,u)-D_t|<=C_t(s+u), 0<=s<=t, u>=0.          (5)

The same bounded-derivative estimates apply to D^2 P_(t-s)f.

Proof of the entrance estimate. The explicit solution gives

    U_s=a integral_0^s exp((s-r)+sqrt(2)(W_s-W_r)) dr.

Let M_s=sup_(r<=s)|W_r| and H_s=s+2sqrt(2)M_s. Then
exp(-H_s)<=U_s/(as)<=exp(H_s). Brownian scaling and the Gaussian tail of
M_1 show, for each fixed t,

    E(1/U_s)<=C_t/s,
    E|1/U_s-1/(as)|<=C_t/sqrt(s), 0<s<=t.           (6)

For the second inequality use |1/(U_s/(as))-1|<=exp(H_s)-1 and
E(exp(H_s)-1)<=C_t sqrt(s). The moments of U_s of each fixed order are
O_t(s^j), by the same pathwise bound.

Equations (5)-(6) imply

    E[h(s,U_s)/U_s]=D_t/(as)+O_t(s^(-1/2))+O_t(1).

The nonsingular terms in C have bounded expectation near s=0, by the
derivative and U_s moment bounds. Therefore

    E[(C P_(t-s)f)(U_s)]= (b/a)D_t/s+O_t(s^(-1/2)). (7)

The difference between the integrand and (b/a)D_t/s is integrable at zero.
Integrating it proves (4), including its remainder. Finally b/a=1/(2pi).

## Consequence and the unpaid step

The natural candidate network leading correction for this bounded test is
(D_t/(2pi))log(n)/n, with a theta0-dependent constant/n at the next order.
This is a prediction, not proved network asymptotics. A proof still needs
uniform control while u approaches zero, a matching scale and remainder,
and the accumulated exact-to-regularized bounded-test comparison through
the entrance. A lower-cutoff contribution might alter or cancel a formal
coefficient unless controlled. C029's deterministic logarithmic offset is
compatible with this prediction but cannot supply that missing stochastic
matching theorem. [Definition 10 (Two-dimensional Coulomb gas) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Fix $d=2$ and $\beta\in\R_{\geq 0}$.
    The \emph{two-dimensional lattice Coulomb gas} on $\Lambda_n$ with free boundary conditions at inverse temperature $\beta$
    is the probability measure on $q\in\Z^{F(\Lambda_n)}$
    given by
    \begin{equation}
      
        \mu_{\Coulomb,\Lambda_n,\beta}^\free[\{q=Q\}] = \frac{1}{Z_{\Coulomb,\Lambda_n,\beta}^\free} \mathbf{1}\Big[\sum\nolimits_{f\in F(\Lambda_n)}Q(f)=0\Big]\cdot e^{-\frac{\beta(2\pi)^2}{2} \langle Q , -\Delta^{-1} Q \rangle}.
    \end{equation}
    Notice that, contrary to the XY model,
    the Hamiltonian of the Coulomb gas is non-local due to the presence of the inverse Laplacian.

Let $\mathcal{A} = \{A_i\}_{i \in I}$ be a finite collection of non-empty subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$. The nerve $N(\mathcal{A})$ of $\mathcal{A}$ is the simplicial complex with vertex set $I$ where a non-empty finite subset $\sigma \subseteq I$ forms a simplex in $N(\mathcal{A})$ if and only if $\bigcap_{i \in \sigma} A_i \neq \emptyset$. By the Nerve Theorem, if each $A_i$ and all finite non-empty intersections are contractible (e.g. convex sets), then the union $\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i$ is homotopy equivalent to the geometric realization of $N(\mathcal{A})$.
\mathcal{A} is a finite family of non-empty subsets in \mathbb{R}^d

For f_r=1-2*1_(x_1=...=x_r=0) on the uniform F_2^r cube, r>=2, its squared Fourier law S has Pr[i in S]=I_i(f_r)=a=2^(1-r) for every i. The first spectral-coordinate chain entropy increment in any deterministic ordering is h2(a), and h2(a)/I_i>=r-1. Thus no absolute C bounds every chain-rule increment H(1_(i in S)|previously exposed spectral coordinates) by C I_i(f) for all Boolean f. For distinct i,j and r>=3, Pr[i,j in S]=2^-r, whereas Pr[i in S]Pr[j in S]=2^(2-2r); spectral coordinates are dependent despite independent input bits. The assertion does not rule out adaptive or block entropy budgets.

[Definition def:Holder of arXiv:2606.02003, 'Higher-Order Multifractional Stable Motion:\\ Definition and Fundamental Properties'] For a stochastic process $\{X(t)\}_{t \in \mathbb{R}}$ and
$t_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, the \emph{pointwise H\"older exponent} at $t_0$
is
\[
\alpha_X(t_0)
:= \sup\!\left\{
\gamma \geq 0 :
\limsup_{h \to 0}
\frac{|X(t_0+h) - X(t_0)|}{|h|^\gamma} < \infty
\;\text{ a.s.}
\right\}.
\]
title: Pointwise H\"older exponent

[Lemma lem:real-freedman-rescaled of arXiv:2606.08683, 'Exact Fourier dimensions of dyadic Mandelbrot cascades under minimal integrability'] Let \((\mathcal H_j)_{j=0}^N\) be a filtration, and let \((M_j,\mathcal H_j)_{j=0}^N\) be a real-valued martingale with \(M_0=0\) and martingale differences \(\xi_j=M_j-M_{j-1}\).  Let \(R,V\in(0,\infty)\).  Assume that \(
\lvert \xi_j\rvert\le R\) for every \(j\) and
\[
\sum_{j=1}^N
\mathbb{E}\left(\xi_j^2\mid \mathcal H_{j-1}\right)
\le V
\]
almost surely.  Then, for every \(u>0\),
\[
\mathbb{P}\left(
\max_{0\le j\le N} M_j>u
\right)
\le
\exp\left(
-\frac{u^2}{2(V+Ru)}
\right).
\]

[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.06038, 'Efron type identities\\ for stopping sets and Poisson hulls'] Let $\eta$ be as in Theorem~\ref{t:spatMarkov}. Let $(Z_n)$ be a 
  sequence of $\eta$-finite stopping sets. 
  Assume that $Z\colon \bN\to\cX$ satisfies
  \begin{align}
    
    \lim_{n\to\infty}\I\{x\in Z_n(\mu)\}=\I\{x\in Z(\mu)\},
    \quad (x,\mu)\in\BX\times\bN.
  \end{align}
  Then $Z$ is a Markov set with respect to $\eta$.

[Theorem of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] (See also [Oue22:thesis] Theorem 7) Let ${\bf T} \in (\mathbb{R}^n)^{\otimes 3}$ be a random noise tensor with i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries. For $i,j \in [n]$, let $T_i$ and $T_j$ be the first-mode slices of ${\bf T}$. The pure noise matrix ${\bf M} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ associated to the melon graph has entries ${\bf M}[i,j] = \langle T_i, T_j \rangle$. Then
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf M} - {\mathbb E} {\bf M}}_{2t}^{2t} ~ \leq ~ {\mathcal O} (n^{3t}).
$$

[Corollary 5 of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Fix $q\geq2$.  For each $n$, let
$\big(N_{n,i,j}:1\leq i\leq m_n,  1\leq j\leq q\big)$
be independent random variables with $N_{n,i,j} \sim \Pois(\alpha_{n,i,j})$.  
Put

\noi
\begin{align}
 \beta_{n,i}
 :=\prod_{j=1}^q\alpha_{n,i,j},
 \quad
 X_n
 :=\sum_{i=1}^{m_n}
 \prod_{j=1}^qN_{n,i,j},
\AND
 \delta_n
 :=
 \max_{\substack{1\leq i\leq m_n\\1\leq j\leq q}}
 \alpha_{n,i,j}.
 
\end{align}
If
\noi
\begin{align}
 \delta_n\to0
 \AND
 \sum_{i=1}^{m_n}\beta_{n,i}\to\lambda>0,
\notag 
\end{align}
then $X_n$ converges to $\Pois(\lambda)$ in total variation, and its
first four moments converge to those of the limit.
 
Moreover, there exists a constant $C_{q,\lambda}$ depending only on $q$ and $\lambda$
 such that
 
 
\noi
\begin{align}
 \dTV\bigl( X_n, P_\lambda\bigr)
 \leq C_{q,\lambda} 
 \left(
 \left|\sum_{i=1}^{m_n}\beta_{n,i}-\lambda\right|
 +\sqrt{\delta_n}\right)
 
\end{align}
for all
sufficiently large $n$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary 5 of arXiv:2608.12451

[Corollary cor:farey-sixth-order of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] For each integer $N\geq1$, let $\mathrm{FV}(N)$ be the number of distinct
intersections of Farey lines of order $(N,N)$, and let $\mathrm{FR}(N)$ be
the number of connected regions into which those lines cut the open unit
square.  Then, as $N\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathrm{FV}(N)=\Theta(N^6),\qquad
 \mathrm{FR}(N)=\Theta(N^6).
\end{equation}
The lower bound for $\mathrm{FV}(N)$ already comes from intersections in
the open triangle $0<x<y<1$.

[Theorem main body of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Suppose $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Z}$ are smooth separated Deligne--Mumford surfaces, and there is a contraction $f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Z}$ where the exceptional $\mathcal{C}$ is a smooth irreducible stacky curve. 
    Moreover, suppose $f(\mathcal{C}) = p \in |\mathcal{Z}|$ and $f : \mathcal{X} \setminus \mathcal{C} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{Z} \setminus \mathcal{Y}$ is an isomorphism where $\mathcal{Y} := \mathcal{B}\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal{Z}}(p)$. 
    Then, $f$ is a regular weighted blowup of $\mathcal{Z}$ with reduced center $\mathcal{Y}$. In particular, $f|_\mathcal{C} : \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{Y}$ is a weighted projective bundle, and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathcal{C})|_{\mathcal{C}} \simeq \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{C}}(-1) \otimes f^*\mathcal{L}$ for some line bundle $\mathcal{L}$ on $\mathcal{Y}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem main body of arXiv:2609.04023

[Theorem 16 (finite-time weak convergence of the ULA scheme) of arXiv:2605.13648, 'Sticky CIR process with potential: invariant measure and exact sampling'] Suppose $G\in C^2([0,\infty))$ with $\|G'\|_\infty<\infty$, and \cref{ass:moment} holds.  Then, as $h\to 0$, for every $\varphi\in C_{\mathrm b}([0,\infty))$ and every $t>0$,
  \[
    \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_{n_h})\mid X_0=x]
      \;\to\;
      \mathbb{E}[\varphi(u_t)\mid u_0=x],
      \qquad n_h \coloneqq  \lfloor t/h\rfloor,
  \]
  uniformly for $x$ in compact subsets of $[0,\infty)$.

body: A linear map T between normed spaces is bounded if there is a constant C with ||Tx|| <= C ||x|| for all x; the least such C is the operator norm ||T||. For linear maps between normed spaces, bounded is equivalent to continuous, and to continuous at a single point. The bounded operators from X to a Banach space Y form a Banach space under the operator norm.

body:
Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a measure-preserving system on a probability space with $T$ invertible (a measure-preserving automorphism). A finite or countable measurable partition $\xi = \{A_1, A_2, \dots\}$ of $X$ is a (two-sided) generator if the smallest $\sigma$-algebra containing all the sets $T^{-n} A_i$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, coincides with $\mathcal{B}$ up to $\mu$-null sets; in join notation, $\bigvee_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} T^{-n}\xi = \mathcal{B}$ (mod $\mu$). For a non-invertible $T$ one uses the one-sided join $\bigvee_{n=0}^{\infty} T^{-n}\xi$ and speaks of a one-sided (strong) generator. Why it matters: by the Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem, if $\xi$ is a generator with finite entropy $H_\mu(\xi) < \infty$ then the measure-theoretic entropy of the system equals the entropy relative to $\xi$, $h_\mu(T) = h_\mu(T, \xi)$; no supremum over partitions is needed. Existence (Krieger): an ergodic automorphism of a Lebesgue probability space with $h_\mu(T) < \log k$ has a generator with $k$ atoms; a system with infinite entropy has no finite generator. Sharp edges: a partition may generate for one invariant measure and not another; the join over $n \geq 0$ alone need not generate for an automorphism (e.g. the time-zero partition of a two-sided shift does not generate one-sidedly); and 'generates' is a statement mod null sets, not about separating every pair of points, although separating points does imply generating (see the Walters entry).
(X, B, mu) is a probability space and T is measure-preserving
the partition is finite or countable and consists of measurable sets
for the two-sided join T must be invertible
title: Generator (generating partition) of a measure-preserving transformation

[Lemma lem:Aizenman-Lebowitz of arXiv:2509.16541, 'Two-stage Bootstrap Percolation'] Suppose that the initial configuration on a finite square box $B \subset {\mathbb Z}^2$ contains only $1$s and $2$s, and run the bootstrap percolation dynamics of $2$s on $1$s internal to $B$.
    Consider an arbitrary rectangle $S \subset B$ that is completely filled by $2$s in the final configuration of the internal dynamics on $B$.
    Then for every $j \in \mathbb{N}$ with $j \leq \operatorname{long}(S)$,

[Theorem 4 (Stability of the maximal EPI on compact groups) of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be a connected, compact and metrizable topological abelian group, 
equipped with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Let $X,Y$ be independent random

 h(X+Y) - h(Y) \geq \min{\Bigl\{\frac{1}{4},
