whose sum from1 toN-1 is bounded by C_(theta0,t). Consequently
sum E theta_k=(1/a)log(n)+O_(theta0,t)(1). Combining these facts and
|D_(t_n)-D_t|<=C_t/n proves (9). The killed exact chain has the same
estimates and the identity theta*U=1/n only on alive states, as required.

The singular drift term in C is b/u. In (10) its contribution is b/n
times (9), giving (b/a)D_t log(n)/n. The remaining terms are

    (8u+a/5) D P_v f+(4u^2-3au/5) D^2 P_v f.

Their expected absolute values are uniformly bounded using the bounded
derivatives and (4) through time t_n. Their n^-2 sum is therefore O(1/n).
Finally b/a=1/(2pi), proving (10).

The remaining global weak-rate step is a semigroup telescoping identity
whose accumulated local errors are O(1/n) for this unbounded reciprocal
state space and whose initial-layer contribution is also O(1/n).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:48d5412d05f2566420246d906fe5e2cb5ea63da0a7aee9e2d7460ec5d88ae3f3","revision_digest":"sha256:5dd8c87ca1986234f07df8c27b9999283f4a603a2d3d51680b9b8e5c4bf453e5","source_id":"owner-own-work:T244-w691-C040:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Sharp relaxation exponent for local tree rotations and triangulation flips structural attempt Result: A canonical-path construction that first rotates every tree to one fixed comb has exponential congestion, even if each route is short. Let N be the number of states and use uniform stationary mass1/N. Routing the all-pairs demand pi(x)*pi(y) through that comb sends total order1 flow through a vertex whose total stationary transition capacity is1/N. Some incident edge therefore has load-to-capacity ratio at least order N. For triangulations N is a Catalan number of order4^n/n^(3/2). Check: The total capacity through the chosen vertex is sum_y pi(v)P(v,y)=1/N. Pairs not starting or ending there have total demand(1-1/N)^2 and must cross it in the proposed construction. Summing their edge loads gives the claimed bottleneck independently of path length. Obstruction: A proof needs routes or transport flows distributed over many intermediate shapes. The comb normal form is useful for irreducibility but cannot furnish the conjectured polynomial relaxation bound.

Let X=(X_1,...,X_n) be a fixed finite tuple of bounded selfadjoint elements in a finite von Neumann algebra with faithful normal tracial state tau(1)=1. In a free extension, let S_1,...,S_n be centered semicircular elements with tau(S_j^2)=1, such that the algebra generated by X and the individual algebras generated by the S_j are freely independent. For a tuple Y, let Phi_star(Y) be conjugate-variable free Fisher information, the sum of squared L2 norms of its conjugate variables, with value +infinity if they do not all exist. Voiculescu defines non-microstates free entropy relative to C by chi_star(X)=(1/2)*integral_0^infinity [n/(1+t)-Phi_star(X_1+sqrt(t)*S_1,...,X_n+sqrt(t)*S_n)]dt+(n/2)*log(2*pi*e), using the improper-integral convention of the source. Logarithms are natural and the semicircular variance parameter is t. The integrand uses Phi_star, the sum of squared L2 norms of the conjugate variables. The notation chi_star distinguishes this construction from microstates free entropy chi; equality for arbitrary tuples is not asserted here. This card records the definition and its normalization, not a matrix mutual-information limit or an entropy differentiability theorem.
Fixed finite bounded selfadjoint tuple in a normalized tracial von Neumann setting.
Standard variance-one semicircular perturbations are mutually free and free from the input tuple.
Phi_star is conjugate-variable free Fisher information; logarithms are natural.

[Proposition 16 (The uniform-grid fixed-rate optimum is within-group flatness) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Writing $E=\sum_k v_k^2$ for the total energy over coordinate magnitudes $v_k$,
the objective \eqref{eq:fixedrate-D}, which is the group-maximum objective of
\Cref{prop:schur}(ii) rederived from the quantizer's own step rule, satisfies
\[
D_{\mathrm{fr}}=\sum_g M_g^2 \;\ge\; \frac1G\sum_k v_k^2 \;=\; \frac{E}{G},
\]
with equality iff every group is internally \emph{uniform}. Thus, at fixed $E$, $D_{\mathrm{fr}}$
is minimized precisely by driving every within-group crest factor to its floor;
the \emph{across}-group energy profile is irrelevant once each group is internally
balanced. No within-group concentration step lowers $D_{\mathrm{fr}}$, and any such step that
raises a group's peak $M_g$ raises it strictly; $D_{\mathrm{fr}}\le E$, with equality
when every group's mass sits on a single coordinate.

body: The fundamental group pi_1(X, x0) of a topological space X at a basepoint x0 is the set of homotopy classes of loops based at x0, with concatenation as the group operation, constant loop as identity, and reversal as inverse. For path-connected X the isomorphism class is basepoint-independent. pi_1 is a homotopy invariant and a functor: continuous maps induce homomorphisms.
title: Fundamental Group

body: Dominated convergence theorem: if measurable functions f_n converge pointwise almost everywhere to f on a measure space, and |f_n| <= g almost everywhere for a single integrable g, then f is integrable, the integrals of f_n converge to the integral of f, and in fact f_n converges to f in L^1. Domination is essential: f_n = n on (0, 1/n) converges pointwise to 0 while the integrals stay 1.
title: Dominated convergence theorem

[Corollary 4 (Certified finite-direction radial reconstruction for $1<\beta<2$) of arXiv:2608.24964, 'Common-Center Geometry and Certified Radial Reconstruction for Energy-Form Full Conformal '] Assume
\[
m\ge2,
\qquad
1<\beta<2.
\]
Fix
\[
0\le\varepsilon<1
\quad\text{such that}\quad
1\le k=\lfloor(m+1)\varepsilon\rfloor\le m.
\]
Let $c$ be the common center from Corollary~\ref{cor:power} and define the explicit constants
\[
\mu_{-j},r_j,H_j,D_{ij},M_j,\lambda_j,\ell_j,L
\]
as above.  Then
\[
\operatorname{Lip}(R_j)\le\ell_j,
\qquad
\operatorname{Lip}(R_\varepsilon)\le L,
\]
where Lipschitz constants on $\mathbb S^{d-1}$ are taken in chord distance.

Let
\[
\mathcal U=\{u_\ell\}_{\ell=1}^N\subset\mathbb S^{d-1}
\]
be a nonempty finite directional set.  Assume certified radial intervals
\[
a_\ell\le R_\varepsilon(u_\ell)\le b_\ell,
\qquad
b_\ell-a_\ell\le\delta.
\]
Define
\[
\underline R(u)
=
\max\left\{
0,
\max_\ell\left[a_\ell-L\|u-u_\ell\|\right]
\right\},
\]
and
\[
\overline R(u)
=
\min_\ell\left[b_\ell+L\|u-u_\ell\|\right].
\]
Then
\[
\underline R(u)\le R_\varepsilon(u)\le\overline R(u)
\qquad\forall u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}.
\]
Let
\[
h_{\mathcal U}
=
\sup_{u\in\mathbb S^{d-1}}
\min_\ell\|u-u_\ell\|.
\]
Then
\[
\|\overline R-\underline R\|_\infty
\le
\delta+2Lh_{\mathcal U}.
\]
Define
\[
\underline\Gamma
=
\{c+ru:u\in\mathbb S^{d-1},\ 0\le r\le\underline R(u)\},
\]
and
\[
\overline\Gamma
=
\{c+ru:u\in\mathbb S^{d-1},\ 0\le r\le\overline R(u)\}.
\]
Then
\[
\underline\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma^\varepsilon\subseteq\overline\Gamma.
\]
Moreover,
\[
d_H(\underline\Gamma,\Gamma^\varepsilon)
\le
\|R_\varepsilon-\underline R\|_\infty
\le
\delta+2Lh_{\mathcal U},
\]
\[
d_H(\Gamma^\varepsilon,\overline\Gamma)
\le
\|\overline R-R_\varepsilon\|_\infty
\le
\delta+2Lh_{\mathcal U},
\]
and directly
\[
d_H(\underline\Gamma,\overline\Gamma)
\le
\|\overline R-\underline R\|_\infty
\le
\delta+2Lh_{\mathcal U}.
\]

[Theorem 2 (Microscopic second-moment universality) of arXiv:2608.27641, 'Hard-Edge Determinant Fields and Second-Moment Universality for Random Matrix Ratios'] Under Assumption~\ref{ass:matrix-atoms}, the following statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item The rescaled spectrum converges to the infinite complex Ginibre process:
\[
\mathcal{Z}_n
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}
\qquad
\text{in }\mathcal{N}\left(\mathbb{C}\right).
\]

\item For every fixed \(k\geq 1\),
\[
\left(
\sqrt{n}R_{n,1},
\ldots,
\sqrt{n}R_{n,k}
\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\left(
R_1,\ldots,R_k
\right).
\]

\item For every fixed \(k\geq 1\),
\[
\left(
\frac{R_{n,n}}{\sqrt{n}},
\ldots,
\frac{R_{n,n-k+1}}{\sqrt{n}}
\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\left(
R_1^{-1},\ldots,R_k^{-1}
\right).
\]

\item In particular,
\[
\sqrt{n}\rho_{\min}\left(M_n\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
R_1,
\qquad
\frac{\rho_{\max}\left(M_n\right)}{\sqrt{n}}
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
R_1^{-1}.
\]

\item If \(D\subset\mathbb{C}\) is a bounded Borel set whose boundary has zero planar Lebesgue measure, then
\[
\mathcal{Z}_n\left(D\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{\rightarrow}
\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}\left(D\right).
\]
\end{enumerate}

More explicitly, let
\(\left(\Gamma_j\right)_{j\geq 1}\) be independent random variables satisfying
\[
\Gamma_j\sim\operatorname{Gamma}\left(j,1\right).
\]
The Kostlan representation gives the equality in distribution of unordered point configurations
\[
\left\{
\left|Z\right|^2:
Z\in\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}
\right\}
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}
\left\{
\Gamma_j:
j\geq 1
\right\};
\]
see \citet[Theorem~4.7.3 and Section~7.2]{HoughKrishnapurPeresVirag2009}.
Consequently, \(\left(R_1,\ldots,R_k\right)\) are the first \(k\) order statistics of
\[
\left\{
\sqrt{\Gamma_j}:
j\geq 1
\right\}.
\]

For \(a>0\), let
\[
D_a:=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\left|z\right|\leq a\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{Gin}_{\infty}\left(D_a\right)
\overset{\mathrm{d}}{=}
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}I_j\left(a\right),
\]
where the variables \(\left(I_j\left(a\right)\right)_{j\geq 1}\) are independent and
\[
I_j\left(a\right)
\sim
\operatorname{Bernoulli}\left(p_j\left(a\right)\right),
\qquad
p_j\left(a\right)
=
\Pr\left(\Gamma_j\leq a^2\right)
=
1-e^{-a^2}
\sum_{\ell=0}^{j-1}
\frac{a^{2\ell}}{\ell!}.
\]

body:
[Lemma le:law-restriction of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] \mbox{}\\
  Consider a reversible Markov jump process $(X,T)$ on the
  finite graph $G$. Assume that it starts in
  $\rho\in J$, has the reversible measure $\pi$ with 
  $\pi_i>0$ for all $i\in\Lambda$, and that the  
  jump rates are given by $q_{ij}=C_{ij}/\pi_i$ for $i,j\in\Lambda$. 
  Then, the processes $(X^{\neq},T^{\neq})$ and $(X^J,T^J)$ are
  again reversible Markov jump processes with rates $q^{\neq}$ and $q^J$, weights
  $C^{\neq}$ and $C^J$, transition probabilities $p^{\neq}$ and $p^J$, and
  reversible measures $\pi$ and $\pi|_J$, respectively. Applying both
  transformations successively, $(X^{J\neq},T^{J\neq})$ is also a reversible Markov jump process
  with rates $q^{J\neq}$, weights $C^{J\neq}$, transition probabilities $p^{J\neq}$, and
  reversible measure $\pi|_J$. 
  In particular, the restriction $X^{J\neq}$ of $X$ to $J$ with self-loops removed
  with starting point $X_0=\rho\in J$ has the same law as
  a random walk on the complete graph over $J$ endowed with the weights $C^{J\neq}$.
  In other words, $Q_{\rho}^{C,\Lambda}(X^{J\neq}\in\cdot)=Q_{\rho}^{C^{J\neq},J}$.

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The binary and ternary harmonic measures of the Cantor set are mutually singular (October 2026). For the middle-thirds Cantor set E and an integer b >= 2, the coding tree of E in base b has as vertices the b-adic intervals meeting E; simple random walk on it is transient, and the law of its limiting end pushed forward to E is a probability measure nu_b (nu_3 is the Cantor measure). Lyons and Peres (Probability on Trees and Networks, Question 16.7) asked whether nu_2 and nu_3 are mutually singular; the paper proves they are. The proof compares conditional splits of the two measures on dyadic cells through Hellinger affinities: at the dyadic cell [4/128, 5/128], whose intersection with E is the ternary cylinder [8/243, 9/243], the Cantor measure splits evenly while the harmonic measure, computed as an electrical current, gives the left half more than 0.507 of the mass, and a Fourier argument based on Stewart's theorem on digit changes in bases 2 and 3 shows that non-singularity would contradict the summability of the Hellinger losses. Exact rational checks and a Lean 4 file verify the numerical values. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/cantor-harmonic-codings-singular (commit 228666ba76c4). Not refereed.
title: The binary and ternary harmonic measures of the Cantor set are mutually singular, answering Lyons-Peres Question 16.7 (Shmalo 2026, repository yspennstate/cantor-harmonic-codings-singular)

body: In Riemannian geometry, the Cheeger isoperimetric constant of a compact Riemannian manifold M is a positive real number h(M) defined in terms of the minimal area of a hypersurface that divides M into two disjoint pieces. In 1971, Jeff Cheeger proved an inequality that related the first nontrivial eigenvalue of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on M to h(M). In 1982, Peter Buser proved a reverse version of this inequality, and the two inequalities put together are sometimes called the Cheeger-Buser inequality. These inequalities were highly influential not only in Riemannian geometry and global analysis, but also in the theory of Markov chains and in graph theory, where they have inspired the analogous Cheeger constant of a graph and the notion of conductance.
title: Cheeger constant

[Definition upper and lower incomplete gamma functions of arXiv:2411.09614, 'Moment estimates for the stochastic heat equation on Cartan-Hadamard manifolds'] For $s>0$, $x>0$, $\Gamma(s,x):=\int_x^{+\infty} t^{s-1}e^{-t}dt$ is the upper incomplete gamma function, and $\gamma(s,x):=\int_0^x t^{s-1}e^{-t}dt$ is the lower incomplete gamma function. For $s>0$ they satisfy $\Gamma(s)=\gamma(s,x)+\Gamma(s,x)$, where $\Gamma(s)$ is the well-known gamma function with domain $s>0$. The above additive relation tells us that for $s>0$,$$\sup_{x>0}\gamma(s,x)=\sup_{x>0}\Gamma(s,x)=\Gamma(s).$$
        If $s=0,$ the additive relation fails due to $\gamma(0,x)$ being undefined. However, we have $\Gamma(0,x)=-\text{Ei}(-x)$, where $\text{Ei}(z):=-\int_{-z}^{+\infty} \frac{e^{-t}}{t}dt$ is the exponential integral function. 
        The following asymptotic results follow from elementary calculus arguments.
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item For $s>0$, $\gamma(s,x)\sim_{x\downarrow 0}x^{s}.$
            \item For $s\geq 0$, $\Gamma(s,x)\sim_{x\uparrow+\infty}e^{-x}$.
            \item $-\text{Ei}(-x)\sim_{x\downarrow0}-\ln(x)$.
        \end{enumerate}
title: Some non-elementary functions

[Lem 88 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\mu \in \cP_2(\bbR_{\ge 0})$, the preimage
    \[
        \sym^{-1}(\mu) \equiv \Big\{
            \tilde \mu \in \cP_2(\bbR) : \sym(\tilde\mu) = \mu
        \Big\}
    \]
    is compact with respect to the $\bbW_2$ metric.

\begin{proof}
The set $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ is clearly closed. Therefore, it suffices to show that any sequence $(\tilde \mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ in $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ has a $\bbW_2$-convergent subsequence. The collection of measures $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ is clearly tight, since we have 
	\[
	\tilde{\mu}([-K,K])
	=\mu([0,K]) 
	\stackrel{K\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 1\,,
	\]
uniformly over all $\tilde{\mu}\in \sym^{-1}(\mu)$. 
    By Prohorov's theorem, any sequence $(\tilde \mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$ must have a subsequence $(\tilde \mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$ that converges weakly to some measure $\tilde{\mu}$, which is also clearly in $\sym^{-1}(\mu)$. 
By Skorokhod's theorem, we have can find random variables $X_n,X$ such that $X_n$ is distributed according to $\tilde{\mu}_{n_j}$, $X$ is distributed according to $\tilde{\mu}$, and $X_n$ converges to $X$ almost surely as $n\to\infty$. Then, for any finite $M$, we have
	\[
	\E\Big[
	(X_n-X)^2; \max\{|X_n|,|X|\} \le M
	\Big]
	\le \E\Big[\max\Big\{(X_n-X)^2
	; (2M)^2
	\Big\}
	\Big] \stackrel{n\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 0
	\]
by the bounded convergence theorem. On the other hand,	since $|X_n|$ and $|X|$ are distributed as samples from $\mu$, we have
	\begin{align*}
	&\E\Big[
	(X_n-X)^2; \max\{|X_n|,|X|\} 
		> M
	\Big]
	\le 2\Big\{
	\E[(X_n)^2;|X_n|>M]
	+\E[X^2;|X|>M]\Big\} \\
	&\qquad= 4 \E[X^2;|X|>M]
	\le o_M(1)\,.
	\end{align*}
By sending $M\to\infty$ we conclude $\tilde \mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \tilde \mu$ in $\bbW_2$, from which the compactness claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Define a {\bf Rook's Walk Birth-Death} (denoted RWBD) Markov chain over the state space $\Omega_* = \{0,\dots , d\}$ with a transition from $X_t \in \Omega_*$ to $X_{t+1}\in \Omega_*$ governed by parameter $n\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 3}$ as follows:
  \[X_{t+1}=\begin{cases}
   X_t, \quad&\text{w.p. } \mathbb{P}[Y_1 \in H_{X_t} \mid Y_0\in H_{X_t}] \\
   X_t-1, \quad&\text{w.p. } \mathbb{P}[Y_1 \in H_{X_t-1} \mid Y_0\in H_{X_t}]\\
   X_t+1, \quad&\text{w.p. } \mathbb{P}[Y_1 \in H_{X_t+1} \mid Y_0\in H_{X_t}] \\

Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon unbiased selection influence objective. Let X have a specified probability law. For fixed p>=1, let H be a deterministic symmetric positive-definite p-by-p matrix, Q a deterministic symmetric positive-semidefinite p-by-p matrix, and G(X) a measurable positive-semidefinite p-by-p matrix. Define Z(X)=Tr(G(X) H^(-1) Q H^(-1)), and assume E Z(X)<infinity. A nonnegative randomized selection weight S is unbiased when E[S|X]=1 almost surely. Its retention probability is pi(X)=P(S>0|X), and a fixed mean retention budget is E pi(X)=gamma. Define the influence objective J(S)=E[S^2 Z(X)], allowing infinity. An inverse-probability scheme draws I conditional on X as Bernoulli(pi(X)), and sets S=I/pi(X), for measurable pi(X)>0; then it is unbiased and J(S)=E[Z(X)/pi(X)]. In the source statistical application, G is the conditional score outer-product matrix and H is the population risk Hessian. Identifying J with an estimator asymptotic error requires the separate regularity hypotheses of source Proposition4.1; no estimator limit or exponential pruning law is asserted by this definition.
Fixed finite-dimensional positive-definite H, positive-semidefinite Q and measurable positive-semidefinite G; finite mean score.

Sharp two-quantile variance lower bound

Let X be a real square-integrable random variable. Suppose a < b, p,q > 0, P(X <= a) >= p, and P(X >= b) >= q. Necessarily p+q <= 1. Then

    Var(X) >= [pq/(p+q)] (b-a)^2.

Proof. Write mu=E X. If mu lies in [a,b], the two disjoint events give
Var(X) >= p(mu-a)^2 + q(b-mu)^2. Completing the square gives the claimed lower bound. If mu<a, the right event alone gives Var(X) >= q(b-mu)^2 >= q(b-a)^2, which is at least the claimed expression. The case mu>b is symmetric. Equality is attained by masses p at a, q at b, and 1-p-q at (pa+qb)/(p+q). The mean of this three-atom law is that middle location, so the computed variance is exactly the lower bound. This proves sharpness. No claim about independence of lattice events is used.

body: Burnside's lemma, sometimes also called Burnside's counting theorem, the Cauchy–Frobenius lemma, or the orbit-counting theorem, is a result in group theory that is often useful in taking account of symmetry when counting mathematical objects. It was discovered by Augustin Louis Cauchy and Ferdinand Georg Frobenius, and became well known after William Burnside quoted it. The result enumerates orbits of a symmetry group acting on some objects: that is, it counts distinct objects, considering objects symmetric to each other as the same; or counting distinct objects up to a symmetry equivalence relation; or counting only objects in canonical form. For example, in describing possible organic compounds of certain type, one considers them up to spatial rotation symmetry: different rotated drawings of a given molecule are chemically identical.
title: Burnside's lemma

body: [Proposition 3.3 of arXiv:2304.14793, 'Learning Graph Neural Networks using Exact Compression'] Let 𝐿be a GNN composed of𝑑∈N layers,𝑑≥1. If cr𝑑(𝐺)(𝑣) = cr𝑑(𝐻)(𝑤) then 𝐿(𝐺)(𝑣) = 𝐿(𝐻)(𝑤). In other words, 𝑑-layer GNNs cannot distinguish nodes that are assigned the same color by 𝑑steps of color refinement.

body:
[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The language $H$ admits a well-defined decomposition into primitive languages:
\begin{align*}
  H = \Big[\Big(\C_1^{\geqslant 0} \circ \D_1^{\geqslant 0}\Big).\C_1\Big]
  \circ \cdots \circ
  \Big[
    \Big(\C_m^{\geqslant 0} \circ \D_m^{\geqslant 0}\Big).\C_m
  \Big].
\end{align*}
Its exponential generating function is hence
\[
  \hat\phi_H(z) = \left(1-p\right)^m \left(e^{z/m} - 1\right)^m.
\]
\begin{proof}
It holds for all $i$ that
\[
  \hat\phi_{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z) = 
  e^{z(1-p)/m} \quad \text{and} \quad
  \hat\phi_{\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z) = 
  e^{zp/m} \quad \text{and} \quad 
  \phi_{\C_i}(z) = \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m}.
\]
Apply Proposition \ref{thm:shuffling} to find
\[
  \hat\phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}}(z)
  = \hat\phi_{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z) \,
    \hat\phi_{\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z)
  = e^{z/m},
\]
then take the Laplace--Borel transform:
\[
  \phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant 0}}}(x)
  = \int_0^\infty e^{xt/m}\, e^{-t} \, dt
  = \int_0^\infty e^{-\left(1-x/m\right)t} \, dt
  = \frac{1}{1-x/m}, \quad 0 < x < 1.
\]
Therefore
\[
  \phi_{\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant0}}\right).\C_i}(z)
    = \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m} \cdot \frac{1}{1-z/m}
  = \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{z}{m}\right)^n
  = (1-p) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(\frac{z}{m}\right)^n,
\]
so by introducing the $n!$ terms,
\[
  \hat\phi_{\left(\C_i^{\geqslant0} \circ \D_i^{\geqslant0}\right).\C_i}(z)
  = (1-p)\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(z/m)^n}{n!}
  = (1-p)\left(e^{z/m} - 1\right).
\]
We find $\hat\phi_H(z) = \prod_i 
\hat\phi_{\left(\C_i^{\geqslant0} \circ \D_i^{\geqslant0}\right).\C_i}(z)
= (1-p)^m\left(e^{z/m} - 1\right)^m$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 16 (Finite-free quotient) of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] Let $\cO$ be a complete DVR with uniformizer $\pi$, let $m\ge1$, let
$u_1,\ldots,u_m\in\pi\cO$, and put
\[
 g(U)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}(U-u_i)\in\cO[U].
\]
For every $F(U)\in\cO[[U]]$, there is a unique polynomial
$P(U)\in\cO[U]$ of degree $<m$ whose class in
$B=\cO[U]/(g)$ is the convergent value of the series $F(U)$.  Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 P(u_i)=F(u_i)\qquad(1\le i\le m).
\end{equation}

[Defn Slices of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $A \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\bm{t} \in \mathbb{R}^{n-k}$ for $0 \leq k \leq n-1$. 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item The \textbf{(right) $\bm{t}$-slice of $A$} is defined as
    $$Sl_{\vert \bm{t}}A \coloneqq \left(\mathbb{R}^{k} \times \{\bm{t}\}\right) \cap A.$$
    It can be naturally identified with a subset of $\mathbb{R}^k$.
        \item The set of \textbf{transversally interior points} in the (right) $\bm{t}$-slice $Sl_{\vert \bm{t}}A$, denoted by $Sl^\circ_{\vert\bm{t}} A$, is the set of $\bm s \in Sl_{\vert \bm{t}}A$ such that there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ satisfying 
        $$\{\bm{s}\} \times (\bm{t}-\bm{\varepsilon}, \bm{t} +\bm{\varepsilon}) \subset A.$$
    \end{itemize}

body: In combinatorics, the inclusion–exclusion principle is a counting technique which generalizes the familiar method of obtaining the number of elements in the union of two finite sets; symbolically expressed as where A and B are two finite sets and |S| indicates the cardinality of a set S. The formula expresses the fact that the sum of the sizes of the two sets may be too large since some elements may be counted twice. The double-counted elements are those in the intersection of the two sets and the count is corrected by subtracting the size of the intersection.
title: Inclusion–exclusion principle

[Lemma lem:lbm-abstract-direction-interface of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] The space $\mathcal Q_D$ has the following three properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt,topsep=0.35em,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item $\mathcal Q_D$ is a nonzero countable rational vector space contained in
$C_c^\infty(D)=H_{\mathrm{reg}}$.
\item It is dense in the Cameron--Martin space:
\[
 \overline{\mathcal Q_D}^{\,H_0^1(D)}=H_0^1(D).
\]
\item Its annihilator among finite signed measures is trivial:
\begin{equation}
 \int_Dq\,d\sigma=0\quad(q\in\mathcal Q_D)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \sigma=0,
 \qquad \sigma\in\mathcal M_{\rm fin}(D).
 
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

title: FPP chi=1/3 campaign, 2026-08-15 fire 8: rerouting FATTENS the per-block conditional fourth moment - the campaign's first positive measurement, pre-registered. THE DESIGN IS THE RESULT. Raw kappa4 cannot discriminate for (L2'): a sum of L iid centred uniforms has kurtosis exactly 3 - (6/5)/L, which CONVERGES to 3 as occupation grows, and (L2') holding also predicts a bounded kurtosis near 3 - null and alternative converge on the same number, so enlarging the blocks makes the experiment WEAKER, not stronger. The fix is PAIRING: each resample yields both Delta (rerouting allowed) and Delta_0 (no-reroute, summed over the ORIGINAL geodesic's edges inside the block) on the SAME weights with the SAME occupation, so Delta_0 is an EXACT empirical null and EXCESS := kappa4(Delta) - kappa4(Delta_0), bootstrapped by resampling PAIRS, cancels the occupation confound by construction. GENERAL FORM: when null and alternative converge on the same summary statistic, do not enlarge the experiment - find a statistic on which they diverge. MEASURED, reps sized from a measured first-pass CI half-width: at N=24, 106134 conditional samples, occupation 6.04, reroute fraction 0.383, kappa4 3.048 vs 2.992, excess +0.0557 with 95% CI [0.0263, 0.0843]; at N=40, 45345 samples, occupation 10.09, reroute 0.605, kappa4 3.106 vs 2.920, excess +0.1855 with CI [0.1290, 0.2403]. Both clear of zero and the excess more than triples. NOT A REVERSAL of the underpowered first pass - the N=40 estimate was +0.137 there with half-width 0.18 against +0.186 here with 0.056. HALF-EXPLAINED and flagged at the claim: the excess grows because kappa4(Delta) rises (+0.058) AND the null FALLS (-0.072), the latter against what the fixed-L formula predicts; the plausible cause is occupation VARIANCE differing by size, unmeasured. WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY: (L2') asks whether kappa4 stays BOUNDED, and kappa4 itself is 3.048 and 3.106 - bounded, near Gaussian, moving six hundredths over the whole range. Two points cannot establish a rate. NEXT: 3-4 more occupation points at matched sample counts plus a direct read of occupation variance per size; if the excess keeps climbing with the null controlled, that is the first real evidence AGAINST (L2'), which would take the 9.5 reduction with it. chi = 1/3 UNMOVED.

body: Bayesian inference is a method of statistical inference in which Bayes' theorem is used to calculate a probability of a hypothesis, given prior evidence, and update it as more information becomes available. Fundamentally, Bayesian inference uses a prior distribution to estimate posterior probabilities. Bayesian inference is an important technique in statistics, and especially in mathematical statistics. Bayesian updating is particularly important in the dynamic analysis of a sequence of data. Bayesian inference has found application in a wide range of activities, including science, engineering, philosophy, medicine, sport, psychology, and law. In the philosophy of decision theory, Bayesian inference is closely related to subjective probability, often called "Bayesian probability".

body:
Let P be a finite partially ordered set. The largest size of an antichain in P (a set of pairwise incomparable elements) equals the smallest number of chains (totally ordered subsets) whose union is P. The statement extends to infinite posets of finite width w: such a poset is a union of w chains. The dual statement (Mirsky's theorem) exchanges chains and antichains: the largest chain has size equal to the least number of antichains covering P.
P finite, or of finite width

Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent centered random variables such that each X_i is sub-exponential with parameters (sigma_i^2, b). Let v = sum_{i=1}^n sigma_i^2. Then for any t >= 0, P(sum_{i=1}^n X_i >= t) <= exp(- t^2 / (2 * (v + b * t))).

$ Y $ be an adapted continuous $ \R^d $-valued process satisfying
\begin{equation*}
Y_r
=
Y_s
+
\int_s^r
\left(
A_\ell Y_\ell + f_\ell
\right)
d\ell
+
\int_s^r
\left(
C_\ell\left[ Y_\ell \right] + g_\ell
\right)
dW_\ell,
\qquad
r \in [s,u],
\end{equation*}
where, for almost every $\ell \in [s,u] $, $ A_\ell$ is an $ \R^{d
  \times d}$-valued progressively measurable process, $ C_\ell $ is progressively measurable with values in the space of linear maps from
$ \R^d $ into $ \R^{d \times m} $, $ f_\ell $ is an $ \R^d $-valued
progressively measurable process, and $ g_\ell $ is an $ \R^{d \times
  m} $-valued progressively measurable process. Assume that, for all $ h \in \R^d $,
\begin{equation}

2 \left\langle h, A_\ell h \right\rangle
+
\left( p-1 \right)
\norm{C_\ell\left[ h \right]}^2
\le
-\kappa \abs{h}^2\quad\mbox{and}\quad
\norm{C_\ell\left[ h \right]}
\le
M \abs{h}.
\end{equation}
Assume also that
\begin{equation*}
\E\left( \abs{Y_s}^p \right)
+
\int_s^u
\E\left(
\abs{f_\ell}^p + \norm{g_\ell}^p
\right)
d\ell
<
\infty.
\end{equation*}
Then, it holds that
\begin{align}

\E\left(
\abs{Y_u}^p
\right)^{1/p}
\le
e^{-\kappa \left( u-s \right)/4}
\E\left(
\abs{Y_s}^p
\right)^{1/p}
+
\Lambda_{p,\kappa,M}
\left(
\int_s^u
e^{-p \kappa \left( u-r \right)/4}
\E\left(
\abs{f_r}^p + \norm{g_r}^p
\right)
dr
\right)^{1/p},
\end{align}
where $\Lambda_{p,\kappa,M}$ and $\Xi_{p,\kappa}$ are the quantities
defined in Assumption \ref{ass:first-malliavin-uniform}.

Established criterion stated by Ruodu Wang in arXiv:1411.6190v3 Section 2.2(e), equation (7), p.9, attributing Wang-Wang Joint Mixability (doi:10.1287/moor.2015.0755): Let n>=2, and let F_i all have increasing densities on finite essential intervals [a_i,b_i], or all have decreasing densities there, with means mu_i. The tuple is jointly mixable if and only if sum a_i+max_i(b_i-a_i)<=sum mu_i<=sum b_i-max_i(b_i-a_i). Increasing/decreasing is nonstrict and includes step densities and uniform laws. Joint mixability here means a coupling with marginals F_i and sum equal to sum mu_i almost surely. This card records the exact author-survey statement; it does not claim the original long proof has been independently checked. Publisher access to the original theorem was blocked in this round.
All densities monotone in the same direction on their finite essential intervals

a_i<b_i finite

[Definition of arXiv:2605.15066, 'The critical activation density in graph bootstrap percolation'] Let $S\subset F$ be graphs and suppose that 
$V(F)$ is ordered. 
Let $S'\subset F'\subseteq G$ be some other graphs, where $V(G)$ is ordered.  
Then we call $F'$ an {\it $(S,F)$-extension}
of $S'$ in $G$ if  there is an isomorphism of the graphs $F\setminus E(S)$
and $F'\setminus E(S')$ such that 
the $i$th largest vertex in $S$ is mapped to the $i$th 
largest vertex in $S'$, for each $1\leqslant i\leqslant v(S)$.

[Definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] Given a strongly irreducible subshift $X$, a cocycle $c$ and a configuration $x\in X$, the \textbf{slope} of $x$ in the direction $v$ for $c$ is given by
\[ \Phi(v) := \limsup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \frac{|c(x,nv)|}{n||v||_1}.\]
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'

Method: Explicit model calculation, comparison identities and remaining hypothesis obstruction Result: Finite-dimensional supermodular order cannot be reduced to pairwise correlation alone. Let three fair bits have the uniform even-parity law on000,011,101,110. Every pair is independent, exactly as for three iid fair bits, but the supermodular function phi(x)=x1*x2*x3 has expectations0 and1/8 respectively. The odd-parity law has the same pairwise distributions and expectation1/4. Thus identical pairwise data permits opposite comparisons for a legitimate supermodular test. Check: On the Boolean cube, each mixed second difference of the product function equals the remaining coordinate and is nonnegative, so phi is supermodular. Enumerating the four parity configurations verifies every pair marginal and the three distinct product expectations. Obstruction: These are static diagnostic laws, not a CTMC counterexample. A necessary-and-sufficient Markov generator condition must control the entire sequence of transition kernels at all lags and all supermodular test functions. Covariance inequalities and a spectral-gap calculation leave those higher-dimensional constraints unresolved.

body: [Mydef of arXiv:2411.08430, 'The Restricted Isometry Property of Block Diagonal Matrices Generated by $\varphi$-Sub-Gau'] A set \(\mathcal{S} = \{\mathcal{S}_1, \ldots, \mathcal{S}_G\}\) of subsets \(\mathcal{S}_i \subseteq [D] := \{1, \ldots, D\}\) is referred to as a group partition of \([D]\) if \(\mathcal{S}_i \cap \mathcal{S}_j = \emptyset\) for all \(i \neq j\), and \(\bigcup_{i=1}^G \mathcal{S}_i = [D]\). Obviously, the elements within $\mathcal{S}_i$ do not need to be consecutive indices, and it is not assumed that the sizes of the individual sets are uniform.

[Lem qsft of arXiv:2412.09535, 'Local limit theorem for joint subgraph counts'] Let $\mathcal{N}\colon \setr^d \to \setr$, given by $\mathcal{N}(\bm{x}) = (2\pi)^{-d/2} e^{-\Abs{\bm{x}}^2_2/2}$, be the standard multivariate normal probability density. Then for any $(d,a)$-quasishear $\Psi$,
\[\abs{\widehat{\mathcal{N} \circ \Psi}(\bm{t})} = \Abs{\bm{t}}_\infty^{-\omega_{d,a}(1)},\]
where the asymptotic is taken in the limit $\Abs{\bm{t}}_\infty \to \infty$.

body: In mathematics, the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture describes the set of rational solutions to equations defining an elliptic curve. It is an open problem in the field of number theory and is widely recognized as one of the most challenging mathematical problems. It is named after mathematicians Bryan John Birch and Sir Peter Swinnerton-Dyer, who formulated the conjecture in the 1960s with the help of machine computation. Only special cases of the conjecture have been proven.
title: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture

[Lem Varadhan of arXiv:2604.23751, 'Large deviation principles for pattern-avoiding permutations, and limit shapes for constra'] For any $n\ge 1,$ let $\mu_n$ denote the distribution of $X_n$ and assume that $(X_n)$ satisfies an LDP at speed $a_n$ with good rate function $I.$ Let $F:E \rightarrow \mathbb R$ be a bounded continuous function. Let the distribution $\nu_n$  be defined as follows:
 \[ \mathrm{d}\nu_n(x) := \frac{1}{Z_n} \textup{e}^{a_nF(x)} \mathrm{d}\mu_n(x),\]
 where $Z_n$ is a normalizing constant such that $\nu_n$ is a probability measure.
 Then we have
	\[ \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{a_n} \log Z_n = -  \inf_{y\in E} (I(y)- F(y)). \]
	Moreover, if we let $Y_n$ have distribution $\nu_n$,
the sequence $(Y_n)$ satisfies an LDP at speed $a_n$ with good rate function $J$
 given by
 \[ \forall x\in E, \quad J(x) = I(x) - F(x) - \inf_{y\in E} (I(y)- F(y)).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lem Varadhan of arXiv:2604.23751

[Propo oo of arXiv:2412.01673, 'Spatial SIR epidemic model with varying infectivity without movement of individuals'] The system of equations (equation sy of the paper) admits a unique solution  $\left\{\left(\overline{\mu}^S_t,\overline{\mu}_t^{\mathfrak{F}},\overline{\mu}_t^{I},\overline{\mu}_t^{R}\right),\ t\ge0\right\}$   which is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, with the densities\\ $\left\{\left(\overline{\mu}^S(t,.), \overline{\mu}^{\mathfrak{F}}(t,.), \overline{\mu}^{I}(t,.) ,\overline{\mu}^{R}(t,.)\right),\ t\ge0\right\}$ satisfying for all $(t,x)\in \mathbb{R}_+\times D$
	\begin{equation}
	
	\left\lbrace
	\begin{aligned}
	\overline{\mu}^{S}(t,x)&= \overline{\mu}^{S}(0,x)- \int_0^t\overline{\mu}^S(s,x)\int_DM(x,y)\overline{\mu}^{\mathfrak{F}}(s,y)dyds,\\
	\overline{\mu}^{\mathfrak{F}}(t,x) &=\overline{\lambda}^0(t)\mu^I(0,x)+\int_0^t\overline{\lambda}(t-s)\overline{\mu}^S(s,x)\int_DM(x,y)\overline{\mu}^{\mathfrak{F}}(s,y)dyds,\\
	\overline{\mu}^{I}(t,x)&= \mu^I(0,x)F_0^c(t)+\int_0^t F^c(t-s)\overline{\mu}^S(s,x)\int_DM(x,y)\overline{\mu}^{\mathfrak{F}}(s,y)dyds,\\
	\overline{\mu}^{R}(t,x)&= \overline{\mu}^R(0,x)+\overline{\mu}^I(0,x)F_0(t)+\int_0^tF(t-s) \overline{\mu}^S(s,x)\int_DM(x,y)\overline{\mu}^{\mathfrak{F}}(s,y)dyds,\\
	\overline{\mu}^{S}(0,x)&= \overline{S}(0)\pi_S(x),\ \overline{\mu}^{I}(0,x)= \overline{I}(0)\pi_I(x),\ \overline{\mu}^{R}(0,x)= \overline{R}(0)\pi_R(x),
	\\ \overline{\mu}(x)&=\overline{\mu}^S(t,x)+\overline{\mu}^{I}(t,x)+\overline{\mu}^{R}(t,x),\ \forall t\ge0.
	\end{aligned}
	\right.
	\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Propo oo of arXiv:2412.01673

$G(t)=\alpha_{t}^{-1/2}G_{0}(u)$ and
$z(t)=\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}u+(1-\alpha_{t})\alpha_{t}^{-1/2}G_{0}(u)$, so
(equation eq:burgers of the paper) has a unique solution in the class of Cauchy transforms of
probability measures with $\mu_{t}|_{t=0}=\mu_{0}$, namely (equation eq:marginal of the paper).

body: Theorem (campaign status: proved): For five-sign support with repeated planar types $A,A,B$, let $G$ be the graph on the five supported columns with $ij\in E$ when $u_i+u_j=2T$, $T\in\{\pm B,\pm2A\pm B\}$. Each edge contributes at most two solutions, so a total of at least fourteen implies $|E(G)|\ge7$; Mantel gives a triangle, and a disconnected graph on five vertices has at most six edges, so $G$ is connected. Relabelling a triangle $0,1,2$ with edge labels $a,b,c$ determines $u_0=a+b-c$, $u_1=a+c-b$, $u_2=b+c-a$ uniquely; a spanning tree to vertices $3,4$ has exactly two forms, giving the count $6^3\bigl((3\cdot6)^2+3\cdot6\cdot6\bigr)=93{,}312$. Notes: VERIFIED: $216\cdot(324+108)=216\cdot432=93312$. There is no remaining continuous parameter -- the triangle determines $u_0,u_1,u_2$ and every attachment equation determines the next $u_i$. Sorting the five $u_i$ quotients only by an allowed $S_5$-symmetry, so the reduction to $2{,}934$ multisets is LOSSLESS. This is the argument that upgrades a finite enumeration into a complete classification.

body:
[Theorem 22 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $n,d,k\in\mathbb N$ and assume that $n\ge k$. There exist two functions
\[
\alpha_{n,d,k}\colon(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\beta_{n,d,k}\colon(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty),
\]
with the following property.

Let $\mu$ be an isotropic log-concave measure on $\mathbb R^n$,
and let
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\in \mathcal P_d(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^k)$
be such that
\[
\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f_j)>0,
\quad
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.
\]
Then, for every $a>0$,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \Delta_{\hat{f}}\,d\mu\ge a
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\det \Sigma_\mu^d(f)\ge \beta_{n,d,k}(a),
\]
and, for every $b>0$,
\[
\det \Sigma_\mu^d(f)\ge b
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \Delta_{\hat{f}}\,d\mu\ge \alpha_{n,d,k}(b).
\]

[Proposition prop:VDC_conseq of arXiv:2609.04045, 'Heat content and spectrum for subordinated sub-Laplacians'] Suppose that $\Omega$ is an open set in $\mathbb{G}$.
    \begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
    \item If $\Omega$ satisfies the volume density condition then $\operatorname{Vol}(\partial\Omega)=0$.
    \item If $\Omega$ satisfies the intrinsic exterior cone condition and $\overline{\Omega}$ has finite volume, then it also satisfies the volume density condition. In particular, if $\Omega$ is open, bounded with $C^1$ boundary having no characteristic points, it satisfies the volume density condition.
    \end{enumerate}
title: Proposition prop:VDC_conseq of arXiv:2609.04045

[Theorem 14 (Frequency-envelope variant) of arXiv:2606.16662, '2606.16662'] Fix \(0<T\le T_0\) and a finite family \(\mathcal M\) of mixed labels.
Assume the Fourier-diagonal covariance model \eqref{eq:conv-cov} together with the envelope coefficient bounds \eqref{eq:env-K}--\eqref{eq:env-A-increment}.  Let \((\beta_\tau,\zeta_\tau,\sigma)\) be such that, for every \(\tau\in\mathcal M\), the two quantities \(\mathfrak S_{\tau,H}^{\eps}(\beta_\tau,\sigma)\) and \(\mathfrak S_{\tau,B}^{\eps}(\zeta_\tau,\sigma)\) in \eqref{eq:env-SH}--\eqref{eq:env-SB} are finite, with \(\eps>0\) leaving room for the time-lift absorption \eqref{eq:time-lift-absorb}.  Then, for every finite \(p\ge2\), the centered cutoff operators satisfy
\begin{equation}
        B_\Lambda^\tau\longrightarrow B^\tau
        \quad\hbox{in}\quad
        L^p\bigl(\Omega;\mathcal L(X_T^\sigma,Y_T^{\beta_\tau,\zeta_\tau})\bigr)
\end{equation}
and almost surely in the corresponding operator norm.  If, in addition, a deterministic diagonal resolution has been chosen so that the retained branches satisfy \eqref{eq:env-retained-bound}, the localized source-tail bound \eqref{eq:env-X-localized}, and fixed-block convergence in \(Y_T^{\beta_\tau,\zeta_\tau}\), then
\begin{equation}
        T_\Lambda^{\tau,\mathfrak P}=T_\Lambda^\tau-\Ctr^\tau_\Lambda
        \longrightarrow \Ret^\tau+B^\tau
        \quad\hbox{in}\quad
        \mathcal L(X_T^\sigma\cap\mathcal X_T,Y_T^{\beta_\tau,\zeta_\tau})
\end{equation}
almost surely and in \(L^p(\Omega)\).  Fully Wick-subtracted branches are obtained by setting \(\Ret^\tau_\Lambda=0\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Frequency-envelope variant

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2606.06193, 'Peng's Maximum Principle for McKean-Vlasov Stochastic Differential Equations with Common N'] If Assumption \ref{Assumption:C^{2,1}} holds, then, for any $k \geq 1$,
    \begin{align}
        &\mathbb{E}\left[\sup _{t \in[0, T]}\left\|\Delta X_t\right\|^{2 k}\right] \in O(\epsilon^k), \\
        &\mathbb{E}\left[\sup _{t \in[0, T]}\left\|Y_t\right\|^{2 k}\right] \in O(\epsilon^k), \\
        &\mathbb{E}\left[\sup _{t \in[0, T]}\left\|Z_t\right\|^{2 k}\right] \in O(\epsilon^{2k}),  \\
        &\mathbb{E}\left[\sup _{t \in[0, T]}\left\|\Delta X_t-Y_t\right\|^{2 k}\right] \in O(\epsilon^{2k}). 
    \end{align}

Everything is a function of (A_m, x_m); the bit is A_m mod 2 and the depth-k history is fixed by A_m mod 3^k, so the coupling is governed by whether A_m equidistributes mod 2x3^k - and A_m ranges over only about (3/2)^m consecutive integers. Hence the free window is exactly k < m log(3/2)/log 3 = 0.36907m (where 3^k still fits), and the full history needs 3^m residues against (3/2)^m available, a shortfall of 2^m = log 2 per step. Same number three ways, and log 2/log(4/3) = 2.4094 is the same 2.41 reported independently. ONE WALL, not three: the integer A_m is too small a register for the information the phase history carries. body: Lemma (campaign status: audited-pass): Let E_1,...,E_k be the selected witness rows in deletion order; choose one pivot coordinate p_s from each witness pair. The pivots are distinct and E_s contains no later pivot p_t (t>s), so the matrix (h_s(p_t))_{s,t=1..k} is triangular with nonzero diagonal. Consequently {h_1,...,h_k} united with {e_i : i not in {p_1,...,p_k}} is a coordinate basis, and k <= ell/log2(4/3). All selected dense witnesses can be inserted simultaneously after O(ell) exchanges. If an old selector used a removed pivot Q_{p_s}, select the witness Y_s and add the discrepancy e_s = Q_{p_s} - Y_s: at most one new direction per exchange. Under bounded congestion the exchanged-basis quotient rank remains linear. Notes: ell = entropy defect ell(A). What fails is the stronger hope that ALL remaining rows are paid solely by the number of selected witnesses - ruled out by the Walsh crosspolytope (p.43).

[Theorem 1 (Descent--Hochster decomposition; informal form) of arXiv:2609.01882, '\textbf{Coxeter Descents and Parabolic Homotopy Colimits}\\[2mm] \large A Hochster-type de'] For every finite Coxeter system $(W,S)$ and every simplicial complex $\mathcal K\subseteq 2^S$ there is a based chain decomposition
\[
  \BK_{\mathcal K}(W)
  \cong
  \bigoplus_{w\in W}
  \Sigma^{2\ell(w)} C_*(A_{\mathcal K},L_{\mathcal K,\DesR(w)};\Z),
\]
and each relative summand admits an explicit unit Morse reduction
\[
  C_*(A_{\mathcal K},L_{\mathcal K,D};\Z)
  \simeq
  \Sigma\wtC_*(\sd\mathcal K_D;\Z).
\]
Consequently
\[
  H_n(\BK_{\mathcal K}(W);\Z)
  \cong
  \bigoplus_{w\in W}
  \wtH_{n-2\ell(w)-1}(\mathcal K_{\DesR(w)};\Z).
\]
For Weyl groups, $\BK_{\mathcal K}(W)$ is the cellular chain complex of $\XK(G)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Descent--Hochster decomposition; informal form

For every integer N >= 2 let X be uniform on H_N = {x in {-1,1}^N : x_1 x_2 ... x_N = 1}. Then every family of at most N - 1 coordinates of X is mutually independent, each coordinate an unbiased sign: P(X_i = s_i for i in I) = 2^(-|I|) for every proper subset I of {1, ..., N} and all signs s_i. The whole family is not independent: X_1 X_2 ... X_N = 1 almost surely, whereas for N independent unbiased signs the product is itself an unbiased sign. In bits b_i = (1 - X_i)/2 this is the uniform law on the words of even parity; N = 3 gives the classical three pairwise independent but not mutually independent events.
N is an integer, N >= 2
X is uniform on the sign vectors whose product is 1

body:
[Definition D:prelandscapes of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] A random function $\mathcal{M}^\rho: \mathbb{Q}^4 \cap \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow \to \mathbb{R}$ is a \textbf{(half-space) pre-landscape} with parameter $\rho \in \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty\}$ if the following three conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item (Triangle inequality) For any $o = (x, s)$, $p = (y, r)$, $q = (z, t) \in \mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0} \times \mathbb{Q}$ with $s<r<t$, we have
				$\mathcal{M}^\rho(o; p) + \mathcal{M}^\rho(p; q) \le \mathcal{M}^\rho(o; q)$.
				\item (Independent increments) For any $s_1<s_2<\cdots<s_k \in \mathbb{Q}$, the increments $\mathcal{M}^\rho(\cdot, s_i; \cdot, s_{i+1}):\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}^2 \to \mathbb{R}, i\in\llbracket1, k-1 \rrbracket$ are independent.
                \item (KPZ fixed point marginals) Recall that $\NW_{+}$ is the set of all $f \in \operatorname{UC}_+$ such that $\text{supp}(f) = \{x : f(x) > -\infty\}$ is finite. Consider any function $f \in \NW_{+}$ with $\text{supp}(f) \subset \mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}$ and $f(\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{Q}\cup\{-\infty\}$.  Then for any $t, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, $s > 0$ and any finite set $Y \subset \mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}$ we have that
				\[
				 (f \diamond \mathcal{M}^\rho(\cdot, t; y, t + s) : y \in Y)
				\stackrel{d}{=} (\mathfrak{h}^\rho (t, y; f) : y \in Y).
				\]
                Here the right-hand side above is given by Theorem (T:half-space-fixed-point of the paper).
\end{enumerate}
Moving forward, we will use the notation $\mathcal{M}^\rho_{s, t}(\cdot, \cdot) = \mathcal{M}^\rho(\cdot, s; \cdot, t)$ for the increment in a pre-landscape from time $s$ to time $t$, and the notation $\mathfrak{h}^\rho_t f = \mathfrak{h}^\rho (t, \cdot; f)$, which will help emphasize the semigroup structure under metric composition.
title: Definition D:prelandscapes of arXiv:2604.10020

[Proposition SI_subshift_cocycle of arXiv:2605.02226, 'Finitely Dependent Processes on Subshifts'] Let $ X \subset \mathcal{A}^{\mathbb{Z}^d}$ be a strongly irreducible subshift for $ d \geq 2$. Let $G$ be a finitely generated group and $c:X\times \mathbb{Z}^d\to G$ be a continuous cocycle. For all $x\in X$, consider the map $c_x:\mathbb{Z}^d\to G$ given by $c_x(v)=c(x,v)$. Then there exists a constant $K$ such that
    \begin{enumerate}
            \item For all $x,y\in X$ and $u\in \mathbb{Z}^d$, there are group elements $g_1, g_2\in G$ such that $|g_1|, |g_2|<K$ and $c_x(u)=g_1c_y(u)g_2$.
        \item For all $x\in X$ and $v,w\in \mathbb{Z}^d$, there are group elements $g_1, g_2\in G$ such that $|g_1|, |g_2|<K$ such that $c_x(v+w)=c_x(v)g_1c_x(w)g_2$.
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 27 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Suppose that $X\rightarrow X/G$ is an HKG cover. Let
$$l_1<\cdots<l_s$$
be the lower jumps of the wild cyclic subgroup $H=C_{p^s}$ at the wild branch point. Then the following properties hold.

\medskip
\smallskip
{\bf (1) (Bleher--Chinburg--Kontogeorgis)} For each $b\in\llbracket0,p^s-1\rrbracket$, with the notation of Proposition \ref{P3}(4), we have
\begin{equation}
d_b=\left\lfloor \frac{N_{s,b}}{p^s}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor \frac{\sum_{i=1}^s p^{s-i}[p-1+(p-1-\delta_{i,b})l_i]}{p^s}\right\rfloor.
\end{equation}

{\bf (2)} The set $\{x^idx|i\in\llbracket0,d_b-2\rrbracket\}$ is a $k$-basis of $H^0\bigl(\mathbb P_k^1,\Omega_{\mathbb P_k^1}(D_b)\bigr)$. In particular, if $d_b\le 1$, then this $k$-vector space is $\{0\}$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} For $b\in\llbracket0,p^s-1\rrbracket$, we have $d_b=0$ if and only if $b=p^s-1$.

\smallskip
{\bf (4)} The sequence $(d_b)_{b\in\llbracket0,p^s\rrbracket}$ is non-increasing.

[Lemma 8 (Talagrand's inequality) of arXiv:2608.18557, 'Randomly Permuted Orthogonal Products and Fast Dimension Reduction'] Let \(\xi\in\{-1,1\}^d\) be a Rademacher vector, and let
	\(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz with
	respect to the Euclidean norm. If \(M_f\) is a median of \(f(\xi)\),
	then
	\[
	\Pp\left\{
	\left|f(\xi)-M_f\right|\ge t
	\right\}
	\le
	4\exp\left(
	-\frac{t^2}{8L^2}
	\right) \qquad \text{for } t\geq0.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Talagrand's inequality

Then, whenever N > 2n+1, Sard's theorem guarantees that almost every linear projection R^N -> R^{N-1}, restricted to the image of M, remains an injective immersion: the set of 'bad' projection directions along which injectivity or immersivity fails is a countable union of images of maps out of manifolds of dimension at most 2n < N-1, hence a measure-zero set of directions by Sard's theorem, so a direction avoiding it can be chosen. Iterating this projection step reduces the ambient dimension one step at a time down to 2n+1. [Definition def:discrete_process of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let $L$ be a positive integer,
  $y^L_0 \in \{ 1, \ldots, L \}$  and
  $\sigma^1_0, \sigma^2_0 \in \{-1, 1\}$ (resp.
  $\sigma^1_0, \sigma^2_0 \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$) . Let $\sigma^1$ and $\sigma^2$ be two
  independent Markov jump processes with the transition rates of
  figure (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2016 of the paper)
  (resp. (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2017 of the paper)) and respective initial states \( \sigma^1_0 \) and \( \sigma^2_0 \). Further let
  $N_1$ and $N_2$ be two independent Poisson clocks with rate $\gamma$
  independent of the $\sigma^i$. Recursively define $y^L(t)$ by $y^L(0) = y^L_0$ and,
\begin{itemize}
\item when $N_1$ rings at time $t$, $y^L(t)=\max(1,\min(L, y^L(t-) - \sigma^1(t-)))$.
\item when $N_2$ rings at time $t$, $y^L(t)=\max(1,\min(L, y^L(t-) + \sigma^2(t-)))$
\end{itemize}
title: Discrete process

[Corollary cor:multiplicative-type-diversity of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] For fixed $k\geq3$ and $0\leq r\leq k-2$, as $h\to\infty$, the number of weak
$h$-multiplication-table types of rank $r$ is
\[
 \Theta_{k,r}\!\left(h^{(k-1)r}\right).
\]
The total number of weak multiplication types, the total number of ordered
multiplication types, and the total number of generic multiplication types
are all
\begin{equation}
 \Theta_k\!\left(h^{(k-1)(k-2)}\right).
\end{equation}

Fix a unit vector x_star in R^n. Draw a_1,...,a_m independently from N(0,I_n), observe y_i=(a_i^T x_star)^2, and set f(x)=(1/(4m)) sum_i ((a_i^T x)^2-y_i)^2. Initialize x_0 independently from N(0,I_n/n), and iterate x_{t+1}=x_t-eta grad f(x_t), reusing the same samples, with eta=c for a sufficiently small positive absolute constant c. There is a sufficiently large absolute constant C such that m >= C n (log m)^13 suffices for the following event to have probability 1-o(1) as n tends to infinity: for some absolute constants gamma,rho in (0,1), there is an integer T_gamma=O(log n) with min(||x_t-x_star||_2,||x_t+x_star||_2) <= gamma(1-rho)^(t-T_gamma) for every t>=T_gamma. Thus the iteration count to error epsilon is O(log n+log(1/epsilon)). The exponent 13 is the sufficient sample condition explicitly recorded after Theorem 2, rather than an unspecified polylogarithm in Theorem 1.

body: Let C and D be categories and F: C -> D, G: D -> C be functors. F is left adjoint to G (equivalently G is right adjoint to F), written F -| G, if for all objects c in C and d in D there is a bijection Hom_D(F(c), d) <-> Hom_C(c, G(d)) that is natural in both c and d, meaning it is compatible with morphisms c -> c' in C and d -> d' in D via the actions of F and G on morphisms. Equivalently, an adjunction can be specified by a unit natural transformation eta: 1_C => G o F and a counit natural transformation epsilon: F o G => 1_D (where 'o' denotes composition of functors), satisfying the triangle identities: epsilon_{F(c)} o F(eta_c) = 1_{F(c)} for every object c of C, and G(epsilon_d) o eta_{G(d)} = 1_{G(d)} for every object d of D.
title: Adjoint Functors

[Lemma tech cond of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Suppose $f : X \to Z$ is a birational contraction morphism between two smooth separated schemes where $Z$ is quasi-projective. 
Suppose further that there is a smooth closed subscheme $Y \subseteq Z$ where $f$ defines an isomorphism away from $Y$. 
Let $\bar{Z}$ and $\bar{Y}$ be projective schemes containing $Z$ and $Y$ as schematically-dense open subschemes respectively where $\bar{Y} \subseteq \bar{Z}$ is closed.
Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a very ample line bundle on $\bar{Z}$, and let $f^*\mathcal{L}$ denote the pullback of the line bundle under the composition $X \xrightarrow{f} Z \hookrightarrow \bar{Z}.$

Then,
there exists $d \gg 0$ such that for $L := \mathcal{L}^{\otimes d}$ the finite-dimensional vector space $V := \operatorname{H}^0(\bar{Z}, L)$ satisfies the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(a)] The restriction map $\operatorname{H}^0(\bar{Z}, L) \to \operatorname{H}^0(\bar{Y}, L|_{\bar{Y}})$ is surjective.
    \item[(b)] If $V_Y := \operatorname{im}(\operatorname{H}^0(\bar{Z}, L) \to \operatorname{H}^0(Y, L|_Y))$, then $V_Y$ is naturally identified with $\operatorname{H}^0(\bar{Y}, L|_{\bar{Y}}).$ 
    In particular, for $d \gg 0$, $\dim V_Y > r:= \dim Y.$
    \item[(c)] The sections of $V := \operatorname{H}^0(\bar{Z}, L)$ generate $L|_Z$, and the image sections $V_Y$ generate $L|_Y$.
    Consequently, the pulled-back sections generate $f^*L$ on $X$ and generate $f^* L |_E$ on $E$.
\end{itemize}

[Proposition theorem_size_bias_coupling of arXiv:2606.03442, 'Stein's method in network analysis'] Let $X = \sum_{j=1}^m Y_j$ be a sum of non-negative random variables, with $0 < \mathbb{E} [X] < \infty$,
   and let $F_j(\cdot;y) = \mathcal{L}\bigl(\sum_{i, i \neq j} Y_i \,|\, Y_j = y\bigr)$. Let $J$ be a random index with values in $1, \ldots, m$, with $\mathbb{P}(J = j) = \mathbb{E}[Y_j] / \mathbb{E}[X]$.
   Given $J=j$, let~$Y_j^{(s)}$ be sampled from the size biased distribution of~$Y_j$; then, if $Y_j^{(s)} = y$,
    sample~$X_j^{\star}$ from $F_j(\cdot;y)$. Then $X^{(s)} = X_J^{\star} + Y_J^{(s)}$ has the size bias distribution of~$X$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A topological space X is path-connected if for every pair of points x and y in X there is a path from x to y, that is, a continuous map gamma from the interval [0,1] (with its standard topology) to X such that gamma(0) = x and gamma(1) = y. Every path-connected space is connected; the converse fails in general (the topologist's sine curve is connected but not path-connected).

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For two independent centered Gaussian fields X, Y indexed by a common finite (or suitably truncated) set T with covariance functions C_X, C_Y, Kahane's interpolation forms Z(t,u) = sqrt(u) X(t) + sqrt(1-u) Y(t) for u in [0,1] and computes d/du E[F(Z(.,u))] for a smooth test function F, obtaining, since Z(.,u) has covariance u C_X + (1-u) C_Y, d/du E[F(Z(.,u))] = (1/2) sum_{s,t in T} (C_X(s,t) - C_Y(s,t)) E[d_s d_t F(Z(.,u))]. When C_X <= C_Y pointwise (or the relevant difference has a consistent sign) and F is chosen with matching sign of mixed partials, this yields a comparison inequality between functionals of X and Y, an approach that both generalizes Slepian-type comparisons and, in the Gaussian multiplicative chaos literature, is used to show that different regularizations of a log-correlated field, such as the two-dimensional Gaussian free field, converge to the same limiting chaos measure regardless of the approximation scheme, a key technical step in constructing Liouville quantum gravity measures. It does not apply to non-Gaussian fields, the interpolation is built from independent copies of the two fields (always available, since only their laws are compared; a dependent coupling adds cross-covariance terms to the derivative), and the sign or convexity conditions on F needed to obtain a clean inequality must be verified case by case rather than assumed. Typical failure: Running the interpolation on a dependent coupling of the two fields while dropping the cross-covariance terms, or to a family of regularizations whose covariance difference does not have a consistent sign across the whole index set, which is common when comparing regularizations of a log-correlated field near its singular set; either error breaks the monotonicity the interpolation is meant to exploit, and the resulting comparison can go in the wrong direction with no explicit error term to control it. Canonical reference: Kahane, 1986, Annales des Sciences Mathematiques du Quebec; Robert and Vargas, 2010, Comptes Rendus Mathematique; Berestycki, 2017, Electronic Communications in Probability.
two independent centered Gaussian fields on a common finite or suitably truncated index set
existence and enough regularity of the covariance functions to differentiate the interpolated expectation under the integral

body: [Theorem 1.3 of arXiv:2512.17823, 'van den Berg-Kesten--type correlation inequalities for disjoint polymers in the KPZ univer'] There exist $C,c,L_{0}>0$ such that the following holds. Let $y\in\mathbb R$, $K\geq 0$, and $\mathsf{A}\subseteq\mathcal{C}([0,K],\mathbb R)$ be an increasing Borel measurable set. For any $t>0$, $L\geq L_{0}(t^{-1/6}\vee 1)$, and $M>C(L+y^{2})^{3/4}$, $\displaystyle\mathbb P\Bigl(\hat{\mathfrak{h}}_{t,2}|_{[y,y+K]}-Ct^{-1/3}\log M\in\mathsf{A}\ \Big|\ \hat{\mathfrak{h}}_{t,1}(y)=L\Bigr)$ $\displaystyle\leq\mathbb P\left(\hat{\mathfrak{h}}_{t,1}|_{[y,y+K]}\in\mathsf{A}\right)+3(K+1)t^{2/3}\exp(-cM^{2}).$ The same also holds when the conditioning is replaced by $\hat{\mathfrak{h}}_{t,1}(y)\geq L$. The same also holds under both conditionings when the processes are considered on $[y-K,y]$ rather than $[y,y+K]$.

body:
CAUTION ON THE NAME: 'Rosenblum's argument' is used for at least two different results of M. Rosenblum; this entry is the scattering-theory one, the Plancherel estimate that drives the Kato-Rosenblum theorem on trace class perturbations and the standard existence proofs for wave operators. STATEMENT: let A be a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space H with spectral measure E, let psi in H be a vector whose spectral measure mu_psi(S) = <psi, E(S) psi> is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure with density bounded by a constant M (that is, d mu_psi / d lambda <= M almost everywhere), and let K be a Hilbert-Schmidt operator on H. Then the map t -> K exp(-i t A) psi is square integrable on R as an H-valued function and the integral over R of the squared norm of K exp(-i t A) psi dt is at most 2 pi M times the square of the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of K. Consequently the quantity tends to 0 along a sequence of times, and combined with Cook's criterion this is what produces existence of wave operators for perturbations that factor through Hilbert-Schmidt operators; note that the bound is UNIFORM over all vectors psi with the same density bound M, which is how the estimate is bootstrapped from a dense set of vectors to the whole absolutely continuous subspace. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) the bounded density is essential. If psi has any point mass, for instance if psi is an eigenvector of A, then the norm of K exp(-i t A) psi equals the norm of K psi for all t and the time integral is infinite unless K psi = 0. The lemma is a statement about the absolutely continuous subspace with a locally bounded density, not about arbitrary vectors. (ii) 'Hilbert-Schmidt' cannot be relaxed to 'bounded': taking K the identity makes the left-hand side the integral of a positive constant over R, which diverges. (iii) The constant 2 pi is tied to the Fourier convention; with the kernel exp(-2 pi i t lambda) the constant is 1. (iv) Nothing is claimed about the pointwise decay of the norm of K exp(-i t A) psi in t; only its square integrability.
H is a complex Hilbert space and A is self-adjoint on it
psi lies in the absolutely continuous subspace of A and its spectral density is bounded by M almost everywhere
K is Hilbert-Schmidt (in particular compact); boundedness alone is not enough
the Fourier convention is exp(-i t lambda), which fixes the constant 2 pi
the estimate is uniform in psi given the density bound and in K given its Hilbert-Schmidt norm

\[ f^{321}_\beta(x) := \frac12 + \frac1\beta \log\left( \frac{\textup{e}^{\beta x} + \textup{e}^{\beta/2}}{1 + \textup{e}^{\beta/2} + \textup{e}^{\beta} - \textup{e}^{\beta x}} \right) \,.\]
Then, the random permutations $\tau^{\beta,321}_{n}$ converge almost surely in the sense of permutons to the deterministic permuton
\[ \mu^{321}_\beta := \big( (X,f^{321}_\beta(X))_\# + (f^{321}_\beta(X),X)_\#  \big) \frac{\textup{d} x}{1+\exp\left(\beta(\frac12-x) \right)} 
\]
if $\beta>0$,
and to the diagonal permuton if $\beta\le 0.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2606.14812, 'Joint convergence in Wiener chaos via transport hierarchy and Malliavin covariances'] Let $(X_N=I_p(f_N), N\geq 1)$, where $p\geq 2$ and $f_N\in H^{\odot p}$ 
	for each $N\geq 1$. Assume that $X_N$ satisfies \eqref{c1}. Consider a 
	$d$-dimensional random sequence $(\mathbb{Y}_N, N\geq 1)=((Y_{1,N},\ldots,
	Y_{d,N}), N\geq 1)$ such that for all $i=1,\ldots,d$,
	\begin{equation*}
		Y_{i,N} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty I_k(g_{k,N}^{(i)}), 
		\qquad g_{k,N}^{(i)}\in H^{\odot k} 
		\text{ for all } N,k\geq 1,\ i=1,\ldots,d.
	\end{equation*}
	Suppose that:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item There exists $\mathbb{Y}\in L^2(\Omega)$ such that 
		$\mathbb{Y}_N\to_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{Y}$ in $L^2(\Omega)$.
		\item For every $i=1,\ldots,d$, 
		$\mathbf{E}[X_NY_{i,N}]\to_{N\to\infty}\rho_i$.
		\item For every $i=1,\ldots,d$,
		\begin{equation}
			\sup_{N\geq 1}\sum_{k=M+1}^\infty k!\,
			\|g_{k,N}^{(i)}\|^2_{H^{\otimes k}} \to_{M\to\infty} 0.
		\end{equation}
	\end{enumerate}
	Then $(X_N,\mathbb{Y}_N)\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{(d)}(Z,\mathbb{Y})$, 
	where $Z\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ and the characteristic function of 
	$(Z,\mathbb{Y})$ is given by \eqref{phi}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: A parametric family of distributions {f(x;theta): theta in Theta subset R^k}, given as densities or pmfs with respect to a common sigma-finite dominating measure, is an exponential family if it can be written in the form f(x;theta) = h(x) * exp( sum_{i=1}^k eta_i(theta) * T_i(x) - A(theta) ), where h(x) >= 0 does not depend on theta, T_1,...,T_k are real-valued statistics not depending on theta, eta_1,...,eta_k are real-valued functions of theta called the natural parameters, and A(theta) = log( integral h(x) * exp( sum_{i=1}^k eta_i(theta) T_i(x) ) dx ) is the log-normalizing function that makes f integrate to 1. When theta is taken directly as the natural parameter (eta_i(theta) = theta_i), the family is said to be in canonical form.
title: Exponential Family

[Lemma 22 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] Put
\begin{equation}
  \Gamma_\rho(t,u)
  :=K_H(t,u)-\frac{K_H(t,\rho)K_H(u,\rho)}{|\rho|^\alpha}.
  
\end{equation}
Fix \(0<a<R<\infty\) and \(r_*>0\).  There are
\(\rho_0,C>0\) such that, if \(0<|\rho|\leq\rho_0\),
\(s,t\in[a,R]\), and \(u\notin\{0,\rho\}\), then
\begin{equation}
  |\Gamma_\rho(t,u)-\Gamma_\rho(s,u)|
  \leq C|t-s|^\alpha\Gamma_\rho(r_*,u).
  
\end{equation}
If instead \(r_*<0\), the reflected estimate holds for
\(s,t\in[-R,-a]\), with the same quantifiers.

If \(v=1/\rho\) and
\begin{equation}
  \overline\Gamma_v(t,u)
  :=K_H(t,u)-\frac{K_H(t,v)K_H(u,v)}{|v|^\alpha},
  
\end{equation}
then, for every \(\bar r_*>0\), there are \(v_0,C>0\) such that
\[
 |\overline\Gamma_v(t,u)-\overline\Gamma_v(s,u)|
 \leq C|t-s|^\alpha\overline\Gamma_v(\bar r_*,u)
\]
whenever \(|v|\geq v_0\), \(s,t\in[a,R]\), and
\(u\notin\{0,v\}\).  The reflected far-pin estimate holds for
\(\bar r_*<0\) and \(s,t\in[-R,-a]\).  Every reference kernel on the
right is strictly positive on its displayed domain.

[Definition 14 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] A weak solution of \eqreftag{eq:Fokker-planck-a} is a weak continuous flow
$
    (\P_t)_{t\ge0}\subset\Pc(\Xc\times\R^d),
$ 
$
    \P_0=\pi_0,
$
together with a Borel vector field
$
    \hat A:\R_+\times\R^d\longrightarrow\R^d,
$
such that the following conditions hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item 
    There exists \(p>1\) such that, for every \(T>0\),
    \[
    \int_0^T
    \int_{\Xc\times\R^d}
    \left|
    \hat A(t,y)
    -
    a\bigl(t,x,y,(\P_t)_x\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(y)
    \right|^p
    \P_t(dx,dy)\,dt
    <\infty.
    \]

    \item 
    For every \(t\ge0\) and every
    \(h\in C_b(\Xc\times\R^d; \R)\) such that
    \(h(x,\cdot)\in C_c^\infty(\R^d; \R)\) for all \(x\in\Xc\),
    \begin{align*}
    \E^{\P_t}[h]
    =&
    \E^{\P_0}[h] 
    +
    \int_0^t
    \E^{\P_s}\!\Big[
    \nabla_y h(X,Y)\cdot
    \big(
    \hat A(s,Y)
    -
    a\bigl(s,X,Y,(\P_s)_X\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(Y)
    \big)\Big]ds
    \\
    &+
    \int_0^t
    \E^{\P_s}\!\Big[ \Delta_y h(X,Y)
    \Big]ds .
\end{align*}

    \item[(iii)] 
    For a.e. \(t\ge0\),
    \[
    \hat A(t,y)
    =
    \E^{\P_t}\!\left[
        a\bigl(t,X,y,(\P_t)_X\bigr)
        \mid Y=y
    \right],
    \qquad
    \P_t\text{-a.s.}
    \]
\end{enumerate}

Let H be a complex Hilbert space and T: D(T) ⊂ H → H densely defined. Then: (a) T* is closed. (b) T is closable if and only if D(T*) is dense, and in that case T̄ = T**. (c) If T is closable, (T̄)* = T*. (d) ker T* = Ran(T)^⊥, and if T is closed also ker T = Ran(T*)^⊥ provided T* is densely defined (true for closed densely defined T). (e) If S ⊂ T (both densely defined) then T* ⊂ S*. (f) If B is bounded and everywhere defined, (T + B)* = T* + B*. In general only inclusions hold for sums and products: (S + T)* ⊃ S* + T* when S + T is densely defined, and (ST)* ⊃ T*S* when ST is densely defined; equality in (ST)* = T*S* holds if S is bounded and everywhere defined.

body: In abstract algebra, an abelian group (G, +) is called finitely generated if there exist finitely many elements x_1, x_2, ..., x_s in G such that every x in G can be written in the form x = n_1 x_1 + n_2 x_2 + ... + n_s x_s for some integers n_1, n_2, ..., n_s. In this case, we say that the set {x_1, x_2, ..., x_s} is a generating set of G or that x_1, ..., x_s generate G. So, finitely generated abelian groups can be thought of as a generalization of cyclic groups.

body:
[Proposition prop:8 of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] ([GM21])
  
  For a GFF plus a continuous function $\mathtt{h}$, there exists a unique (up to a deterministic multiplicative constant) random metric $D_{\mathtt{h}}$ on $\mathbb{C}$ which is measurable with respect to $\mathtt{h}$ and satisfies the following almost sure properties.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item 
 \textbf{Length space}: Almost surely, for all $u,v\in \mathbb{C}$, $D_\mathtt{h}(u,v)=\inf_{\eta}\ell(\eta;D_\mathtt{h})$, where the infimum is over all paths $\eta$ connecting $u,v$.
  \item 
   \textbf{Locality}: For any deterministic set $U\subseteq \mathbb{C}$, consider the induced metric $D_{\mathtt{h}}(\cdot,\cdot;U)$ defined by $D_{\mathtt{h}}(u,v;U)= \inf_{\eta\subseteq U} \ell(\eta; D_{\mathtt{h}})$,  where the infimum is taken over all paths contained in $U$. Then, for any fixed open set $U\subseteq \mathbb{C}$, the induced metric $D_{\mathtt{h}}(\cdot,\cdot;U)$ is measurable with respect to $\mathtt{h}\lvert_U$. 
  \item 
  \textbf{Weyl scaling}: For a continuous function $f\colon \mathbb{C}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, consider the metric $e^f\cdot D_h$ defined by $e^f\cdot D_h(u,v)=\inf_{\eta}\int_{0}^{\ell(\eta;D_h)}e^{f(\eta(t))}dt$, where the infimum is over all paths $\eta$ from $u$ to $v$. Then, for $\xi=\gamma/d_\gamma$, with $d_\gamma$ denoting the fractal dimension of $\gamma$-LQG as defined in [DG20], we a.s.\ have the equality $e^{\xi f}\cdot D_{\mathtt{h}}=D_{\mathtt{h}+f}$ simultaneously for every continuous function $f\colon \mathbb{C}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.
  \item 
   \textbf{Coordinate change formula}: Fix a deterministic $z\in \mathbb{C}$ and $r>0$. With $Q$ defined by $Q=\gamma/2+2/\gamma$ and the field $\mathtt{h}'$ defined by $\mathtt{h}'(\cdot)=\mathtt{h}(r\cdot+z)+Q\log r$, almost surely, for all $u,v\in \mathbb{C}$, we have $D_\mathtt{h}(ru+z,rv+z)=D_{\mathtt{h}'}(u,v)$.

  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition prop:8 of arXiv:2512.09219

body:
A Borel measure 
u on \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\} is called a Lévy measure if \int_{\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}} \min(1, x^2) d
u(x) < \infty. In particular, 
u can have infinite total mass near the origin (infinite activity of small jumps), but must assign finite measure to sets bounded away from zero (finite activity of jumps of size > \epsilon).
title: Lévy Measure

body: In mathematics, the Vitali covering lemma is a combinatorial and geometric result commonly used in measure theory of Euclidean spaces. [campaign result 2026-09-14, Author-checked only, no independent read.] This is the energy-flow extension of the restricted negative answer to the question in Chapter 4 of David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html), recorded as intake row I0024. That question asks whether the relaxation time can be characterized exactly as an infimum over flows. Let G be a finite connected undirected graph with positive rational conductances c_e on its edges and distinct vertices a,b. Orient the edges arbitrarily and minimize E(f)=sum_e f_e^2/c_e over real flows f with divergence +1 at a, -1 at b, and zero at all other vertices. The minimum is the effective resistance R_eff(a,b). It is rational, because the electrical-flow optimality equations are a rational linear system. More generally, the same rationality conclusion holds for attained convex quadratic flow programs with rational data whose optimizing point is determined by a rational linear system. Therefore these minimum-energy constructions cannot universally return the relaxation time tau_2=1/(1-lambda_2) on rational reversible chains, since the simple random walk on the six-vertex path has tau_2=3+sqrt(5). This is an unrefereed campaign result.
Positive rational conductances and a finite connected graph.
For the stated extension, the optimizer is determined by a rational linear system.

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked against a direct linear-algebra solve on twelve graphs, with the complete graph and the cycle as independent controls at the two extremes.] This is a sufficient-condition reduction of Open Problem 7.31 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html), which asks for tau_0=O(n) uniformly over distance-regular graphs other than cycles. Let G be a finite connected simple distance-regular graph with n>=2 vertices, valency k, and diameter d: for vertices at distance i, the numbers of neighbors one step closer to or farther from the target are constants c_i and b_i depending only on i. Use c_1=1, b_0=k, b_d=0. Let k_i be the number of vertices at distance i from a fixed vertex, so k_0=1, k_1=k, k_{i+1} c_{i+1}=k_i b_i, and n=sum_{i=0}^d k_i. For the simple random walk, let T_y be the first hitting time of y, measured in steps, and define tau_0=max_{x,y} E_x[T_y]; here tau_0 is the maximum mean hitting time, not the spectral Kemeny sum. Define the tail count T_i=sum_{j=i}^d k_j and u_i=k/(k_i c_i). The intersection recurrence gives u_1=1 and u_{i+1}=u_i c_i/b_i for 1<=i<d, hence tau_0/n=sum_{i=1}^d (T_i/n) product_{j=1}^{i-1}(c_j/b_j) <= sum_{i=1}^d product_{j=1}^{i-1}(c_j/b_j), where an empty product is one. A uniform bound on the last sum over noncycle distance-regular graphs would prove the requested O(n) estimate. The campaign does not prove this uniform bound, and the sufficient criterion is not asserted to be necessary. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The graph and intersection numbers satisfy the preceding definitions.
Only indices j<d occur in denominators b_j.

 \frac{d\vartheta}{d\tau}=\lambda\frac{\cos\vartheta}{\rho}.
\end{equation}
Along its solution through $(0,1,0)$,
\[
 \frac{d}{d\rho}\log(\cos\vartheta)=-\frac\lambda\rho,
 \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
 \cos\vartheta=\rho^{-\lambda}.
\]
Integration gives exactly \eqref{eq:limit-data}.  The limiting orbit on
$[0,\tau_*]$ satisfies
\[
 1\leq\rho\leq\rho_*,
 \qquad
 \cos\vartheta\geq \rho_*^{-\lambda}=:c_*>0.
\]

Let (Omega, F, P) be a probability space, G a sub-sigma-field of F, X a real random variable with E[X^2] < infinity, and m = E[X | G]. For every G-measurable real random variable A with E[A^2] < infinity, E[(X - A)^2] = E[(X - m)^2] + E[(m - A)^2], and all three terms are finite.
(Omega, F, P) is a probability space and G is a sub-sigma-field of F
X is a real random variable with E[X^2] < infinity
A is G-measurable and real valued with E[A^2] < infinity

Let tasks z_j be iid from a fixed law. For each task let C_z be a nonempty affine subspace of R^d, and assume a common point x* belongs to C_z almost surely. Start from a deterministic x_1 and set x_(j+1)=P_(C_(z_j))x_j by exact Euclidean projection. Then for every k>=1, E[(1/k) sum_(j=1)^k (1/2)dist(x_(k+1),C_(z_j))^2]<=10||x_1-x*||^2/k. The mean counts sampled occurrences, including repetitions, and includes factor 1/2. The bound holds for arbitrary affine task ranks and is independent of task count and dimension. It is not a statement about an adversarial ordering or a distinct-label mean.

nonempty affine solution sets in finite-dimensional real Euclidean space
one common solution almost surely
exact Euclidean projection at each update

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT. Status: proof (unaudited), T323-SMALLBETA-001 v2; no independent audit. Fix finite n>=1 and a symmetric real 3x3 V with eigenvalues lambda_1>=lambda_2>0>lambda_3. For the self-inclusive projected sphere attention flow on (S^2)^n with Q^T K=V, there exists epsilon(V,n)>0 such that for each 0<beta<epsilon, product-volume-almost every initial configuration converges to consensus at one unit vector in the top eigenspace of V. This covers normalized and unnormalized flows. Repeated largest eigenvalues are included. Epsilon is existential and need not be uniform in n or V. Arbitrary Q,K and arbitrary beta remain unresolved. Local consensus stability was already proved by Kuehn-Yoon; the candidate increment is the full small-beta almost-everywhere classification.
