body:
[Lem 19 of arXiv:2605.05986, '\bf Convergence rate of the occupation measure of { classes of ergodic processes toward th'] Let $p>0$,  $\b\!\in (0, 1/2]$. Let $t>0$ be fixed and let $L: (0, +\infty)\to \R_+$ be defined by 
\[
L_t(u):=\sum_{\ell\ge 0} 2^{-p\ell} \min\Big(u^{\frac{1}{2\b}}, \big(u/t)^{\frac 12}2^{d\ell(1-\b)}\Big).
\]

The function $L$ satisfies the following upper-bounds depending on $p$, $\b$ and the dimension $d$ where $C_{p,\b,d}>0$ denotes    a positive constant only depending on $p$, $\b$, $d$ that may vary from line to line.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $p>d(1-\b)$, then 
\[
L_t(u) \le C_{p, \b,d} \min\Big( u^{\frac{1}{2\b}}, \Big( \frac{u}{t}\Big)^{\frac 12}\Big).
\]

\item  If $p=d(1-\b)$ then
	\begin{align}
	 L_t(u) &\le C_{p,\b,d}
	
	 \Big(u^{\frac{1}{2\b}} \mbox{\bf 1}_{\{u\,t^{\frac{\b}{1-\b}}  \le 1\}}+ \Big(\frac ut\big)^{\frac 12} \big(1+\log(u\,t^{\frac{\b}{1-\b}})\big) \mbox{\bf 1}_{\{ut^{\frac{\b}{1-\b}}  \ge 1\}}\Big)\\
		 & \le C_{p,\b,d}
	
	\Big(\frac ut\Big)^{\frac 12} \big(1+\big(\log(u\,t^{\frac{\b}{1-\b}})\big)^+\big) 
	\end{align}
	

\item If $p < d(1-\b)$, then
$$
L(u) \le C_{p,\b,d} u^{\frac{1}{2\b}}\min\Big( 1,\big(ut^{\frac{\b}{1-\b}}\big)^{-\frac{p}{2\b d}}\Big).
$$
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let Omega be a compact region in R^n (bounded, equal to its own closure) whose boundary partial Omega is piecewise smooth, oriented by the outward-pointing unit normal vector field n. Let F be a continuously differentiable (C^1) vector field defined on an open set containing Omega. Then the integral over Omega of div F dV, where div F = sum_i partial F_i / partial x_i, equals the integral over partial Omega of F . n dS, the flux of F outward through the boundary. In R^3 this is also called Gauss's theorem.

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: in ∂_t u + Σ_j A_j ∂_j u = 0 the estimate ‖u(t)‖_{L²} ≤ e^{Kt}‖u(0)‖_{L²} comes from the Hermitian symmetry of the A_j (which makes u* A_j ∂_j u an exact divergence up to lower order). Real eigenvalues alone (weak hyperbolicity) are not enough. Concrete counterexample in n = 1, m = 2: take A = [[0,1],[0,0]], a Jordan block whose only eigenvalue is 0 (real, so the system is weakly hyperbolic) but which is not symmetrizable. The system ∂_t u1 + ∂_x u2 = 0, ∂_t u2 = 0 with data (f,g) has the solution u2(t,x) = g(x), u1(t,x) = f(x) − t g'(x). So ‖u(t)‖_{L²} ≥ t‖g'‖_{L²} − ‖f‖_{L²}, which is not bounded by any function of t times ‖(f,g)‖_{L²}: one derivative is lost per unit time, and the Cauchy problem is ill-posed in L² (and in every H^s). Consequences for auditing: (i) hyperbolicity claims must say symmetric, symmetrizable or strictly hyperbolic, never merely 'real eigenvalues'; (ii) the constant K in the energy estimate depends on sup|Σ_j ∂_j A_j| and sup|B|, so the argument needs the coefficients to be differentiable in x with bounded derivative — Lipschitz in x is enough (the derivative then exists a.e. and is bounded), but mere continuity is not, and for merely continuous, non-Lipschitz coefficients well-posedness can genuinely fail with a loss of derivatives; (iii) after an approximate symmetrization, the estimate holds with the symmetrizer's constants, not with 1.

[Prop intro of arXiv:2509.08659, 'Gap metrics for stationary point processes and quantitative convexity of the free energy'] Let $1<p<2$ and $\varphi(x)=|x|^{-s}$. Then, $(X^a_p,\mathscr W_{gap,p})$ is a complete geodesic metric space. The free energy $\mathcal F_\beta$ is weakly $\lambda$-geodesically convex on $(X^a_p,\mathscr W_{gap,p})$ with $\lambda=\beta a^{-\frac{2-p}{p}}>0$, i.e.\ for $\mathsf{P}_0,\mathsf{P}_1\in X^a_p$ there is a constant speed geodesic $(\mathsf{P}_t)_{t\in[0,1]}$ such that for any $0\leq t \leq 1$
    \begin{align*}
        \mathcal F_\beta(\mathsf{P}_t)\leq (1-t) \mathcal F_\beta(\mathsf{P}_0)+t \mathcal F_\beta(\mathsf{P}_1)-\lambda \frac{t(1-t)}{2} \mathscr W_p^2(\mathsf{P}_0,\mathsf{P}_1).
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop intro of arXiv:2509.08659

[Definition 21 (Property~\ref{prop:mono}: Monotonicity) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Suppose that $S$ is a partially ordered set.
    Then we call a Glauber dynamic $R$ \emph{monotone} if for any $u\in V$ and $\iota\in\Sigma$,
    the map $R_{u,\iota}:S^V\to S^V$ preserves the partial order at the spin $u$.
    This means that
    $R_{u,\iota}(\alpha)_u\preceq R_{u,\iota}(\alpha')_u$ for any $\alpha,\alpha'\in S^V$ such that $\alpha_v\preceq\alpha'_v$ for all $v\in V$.
title: Property~\ref{prop:mono}: Monotonicity

  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}|Z_T|\mathbf{1}(n\le T<\infty)=0.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Theorem (campaign status: proved): (S14 (23)-(26).) Z_u = 1{L_u != 0}; after conditioning on the root sign A this is the occupancy indicator of u in the corresponding stable set. Match every u_j to the FIRST vertex m_j of its following gap; the matched vertices are distinct and lie outside U. Fix an activation pattern z contained in U: the d signs on U are fixed and every active u in z forces its matched neighbour to be unoccupied. Hence, FOR EVERY fixed root value and every additional ancestor boundary value w, |(A_n)_{W=w, Z=z}| <= 2^{n-d-|z|}. Incompatible patterns give an empty cell; exactly, on the full rooted cycle the cell count is the number of independent sets of C_n[V \ (U u N(z))]. Summing, |supp(B_1,...,B_n | W=w)| <= 2^n (3/4)^d. Notes: TARGET-UNIFORM is the operative strengthening over S12 (2): the bound holds for every boundary value w, not just on the root marginal. So (14) is not merely a selector basis but a target-uniform CONDITIONAL activation-cell certificate.

body: In mathematics, a Sobolev space is a vector space of functions equipped with a norm that is a combination of Lp-norms of the function together with its derivatives up to a given order. The derivatives are understood in a suitable weak sense to make the space complete, i.e. a Banach space. Intuitively, a Sobolev space is a space of functions possessing sufficiently many derivatives for some application domain, such as partial differential equations, and equipped with a norm that measures both the size and regularity of a function.
title: Sobolev space

body: In probability theory, Lindeberg's condition is a sufficient condition for the central limit theorem (CLT) to hold for a sequence of independent random variables. Unlike the classical CLT, which requires that the random variables in question have finite variance and be both independent and identically distributed, Lindeberg's CLT only requires that they have finite variance, satisfy Lindeberg's condition, and be independent. It is named after the Finnish mathematician Jarl Waldemar Lindeberg.
title: Lindeberg's condition

PRIVATE OBSERVATION, author-recorded, used to reduce Heydenreich-van der Hofstad Open Problem 15.1. If random probability measures mu_n on R^d have r-point (moment) measures converging weakly to those of a random probability measure mu whose moment measures satisfy a Carleman-type determinacy condition (total masses of order r! K^r), then mu_n converges in distribution to mu: the law of a random probability measure is determined by its moment measures under such a condition, and tightness is automatic on the compact scaling window. Integrated super-Brownian excursion satisfies the condition. Consequently, for spread-out critical percolation in d > 6, Hara-Slade's convergence of the r-point functions conditioned on cluster size n (with the n^{-1/4} spatial scaling at fixed Fourier variable) implies the conditional-measure convergence to ISE asked in Open Problem 15.1, provided the r-point convergence gives weak convergence of the r-point measures (characteristic-function convergence at every bounded Fourier variable suffices). The nearest-neighbour case is not covered (no r-point expansion in d >= 11).

[Defn 2 of arXiv:2605.25762, 'Brownian Convergence of Planar Domains and Stability of the Planar Skorokhod Embedding Pro'] Let $U$ be planar domain and let $(U_{n})_{n}$ be
a sequence of planar domains, all containing a common point, say the
origin. For each $n$, let $(Z^{[n]}_{t})_{t\geq0}$ be a planar Brownian
motion started at $0$ and denote by $\tau_{n}$ its exit time from
$U_{n}$. Similarly, let $(Z_{t})_{t\geq0}$ be a planar Brownian
motion started at $0$ and denote by $\tau$ its exit time from $U$.
We say that $(U_{n})_{n}$ converges to a domain $U$ in the \textbf{$p$-Brownian
sense} if there exists a coupling of the laws of $(Z^{[n]}_{\tau_{n}},\tau_{n})$
and $(Z_{\tau},\tau)$ on a common probability space such that 
\[
\mathscr{C}_{1}:\begin{alignedat}{1}\mathbf{E}\left(\big|Z^{[n]}_{\tau_{n}}-Z_{\tau}\big|^{p}\right) & \underset{n\to+\infty}{\longrightarrow}0\end{alignedat}
\]
and 
\[
\mathscr{C}_{2}:\begin{alignedat}{1}\mathbf{E}\left(\big|\tau_{n}-\tau\big|^{\frac{p}{2}}\right) & \underset{n\to+\infty}{\longrightarrow}0\end{alignedat}
.
\]

This definition captures the geometric proximity of the domains in
terms of Brownian trajectories. More discussion of the \emph{$p$-Brownian
convergence }is presented in the last section. The main result of

body: In mathematics, and in particular linear algebra, the Moore–Penrose inverse $A^{+}$ of a matrix $A$, often called the pseudoinverse, is the most widely known generalization of the inverse matrix. It was independently described by E. H. Moore in 1920, Arne Bjerhammar in 1951, and Roger Penrose in 1955. Earlier, Erik Ivar Fredholm had introduced the concept of a pseudoinverse of integral operators in 1903. The terms pseudoinverse and generalized inverse are sometimes used as synonyms for the Moore–Penrose inverse of a matrix, but sometimes applied to other elements of algebraic structures which share some but not all properties expected for an inverse element.

body:
The Fejer kernel is K_N(t) = (1/(N+1)) sum_{n=0}^{N} D_n(t) = (1/(N+1)) ( sin((N+1)t/2) / sin(t/2) )^2 for t not a multiple of 2pi, with K_N(0) = N+1. It satisfies: (i) K_N(t) >= 0 for all t; (ii) (1/2pi) integral over [-pi,pi] of K_N = 1; (iii) for every delta in (0,pi), the supremum of K_N over delta <= |t| <= pi tends to 0 as N tends to infinity. These three properties are precisely the definition of a nonnegative approximate identity, and they are what drive Fejer's theorem. By contrast the Dirichlet kernel D_N has L^1 norms growing like log N and changes sign, which is why partial sums behave worse than Cesaro means.
Stated on the circle with the normalised measure dt/2pi.

body:
Setting: $N$ is a compact interval or the circle $S^1$, and $f: N \to N$ is a $C^2$ map. Write $\mathrm{Crit}(f) = \{x : Df(x) = 0\}$ for the critical set. A periodic point $p$ of period $k$ is hyperbolic repelling if $|Df^k(p)| > 1$.

Theorem (Mañé, 1985). Let $\Lambda \subset N$ be a compact set which is forward invariant ($f(\Lambda) \subset \Lambda$) and such that
  (i) $\Lambda$ contains no critical point of $f$, and
  (ii) every periodic point of $f$ lying in $\Lambda$ is hyperbolic repelling (so $\Lambda$ contains no attracting and no neutral / indifferent periodic point);
  (iii) if $N = S^1$, assume in addition that $f$ has at least one periodic point in $N$. (This excludes in particular every circle homeomorphism of irrational rotation number, for which the conclusion is false; the literature states the caveat as 'f is not a homeomorphism without periodic points', and the hypothesis given here is the safe, slightly stronger form. Interval maps always have a fixed point, so (iii) is automatic on an interval.)
Then $\Lambda$ is uniformly expanding (a hyperbolic repelling set): there exist constants $C > 0$ and $\lambda > 1$, depending only on $f$ and $\Lambda$, such that
  $|Df^n(x)| \ge C \lambda^n$ for every $x \in \Lambda$ and every $n \ge 0$.

Standard corollary (the form usually quoted as the uniform expansion criterion). Suppose every periodic orbit of $f$ is hyperbolic repelling (and, on the circle, $f$ has a periodic point). Let $U$ be any open neighbourhood of $\mathrm{Crit}(f)$ and let $\Lambda(U) = \{x \in N : f^n(x) \notin U \text{ for all } n \ge 0\}$ be the set of points whose forward orbit never enters $U$. Then $\Lambda(U)$ is compact, forward invariant, disjoint from the critical set, and hence uniformly expanding: $|Df^n(x)| \ge C_U \lambda_U^n$ on $\Lambda(U)$. In words: 'all periodic orbits repelling' forces uniform expansion on any piece of the phase space that stays a fixed distance away from the critical points. Consequently every point either accumulates on the critical set or is uniformly expanded.

Where it FAILS if a hypothesis is dropped. (a) Without (i) the conclusion is false trivially: $Df = 0$ at a critical point. (b) Without (ii): an attracting or neutral periodic point in $\Lambda$ has $|Df^{nk}(p)| \le 1$. Attracting periodic orbits may exist elsewhere in $N$; the theorem only asks that none lies in $\Lambda$. (c) Without (iii): an irrational rotation, or any $C^2$ circle diffeomorphism with irrational rotation number, has $\Lambda = S^1$, no critical points and no periodic points at all (so (ii) holds vacuously), yet the derivatives $|Df^n|$ do not grow exponentially (each $f^n$ is a diffeomorphism of a circle of length 1, so $\min_x |Df^n(x)| \le 1$ for all $n$). (d) Smoothness: the proof uses $C^2$ (bounded distortion of iterates away from critical points); do not quote it for maps that are merely $C^1$. (e) Only one-dimensional: this is a theorem about interval and circle maps; there is no analogue for higher-dimensional maps or for holomorphic maps without further hypotheses. Note also that the theorem does NOT assume non-flat critical points and does NOT need to assume the absence of wandering intervals: both are handled inside the proof, and in particular no wandering interval can lie in a set $\Lambda$ satisfying (i)-(iii).
N is a compact interval or the circle S^1 and f: N -> N is C^2 (not merely C^1)
Lambda is compact and forward invariant, f(Lambda) contained in Lambda
Lambda contains no critical point of f
every periodic point of f that lies in Lambda is hyperbolic repelling (no attracting or neutral periodic point in Lambda)
if N is the circle, f has at least one periodic point (excludes homeomorphisms of irrational rotation number, where the conclusion fails)

On the compact set $\Lambda$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $|Df| \ge \delta$ on a neighbourhood $V$ of $\Lambda$, and $\log |Df|$ is Lipschitz on $V$ because $f$ is $C^2$. Hence for an interval $J$ whose images $J, f(J), \dots, f^{n-1}(J)$ all lie in $V$ one has the distortion bound $\log \frac{|Df^n(x)|}{|Df^n(y)|} \le K \sum_{k<n} |f^k(J)|$ for $x, y \in J$. If in addition the intervals $f^k(J)$ are pairwise disjoint, the sum is at most $|N|$, so the distortion of $f^n$ on $J$ is bounded by a constant independent of $n$.

Step 1 (no point of $\Lambda$ has bounded derivative along its whole orbit unless it is trapped by a periodic orbit). Suppose $x \in \Lambda$ and $|Df^n(x)| \le M$ for infinitely many $n$. Pull back a small interval around $f^n(x)$ along the orbit; by Step 0 the pulled-back interval $J_n$ around $x$ has length comparable to $|Df^n(x)|^{-1}$, so the intervals $J_n$ have length bounded below. Using disjointness or a covering argument on the images one produces an interval $J$ around $x$ whose images stay in $V$ for all time and are either (a) pairwise disjoint (a wandering interval whose orbit avoids the critical set), or (b) eventually periodic in the sense that some $f^m(J)$ meets $J$. The circle hypothesis (iii) is used exactly here: for a circle homeomorphism without periodic points case (a) does occur (Denjoy-type behaviour) and nothing forbids it.

Step 2 (from pointwise to uniform). Step 1 gives: for every $x \in \Lambda$ there is $n(x)$ with $|Df^{n(x)}(x)| \ge 2$. By compactness and continuity of $Df^n$ a finite collection of such $n$ works for all of $\Lambda$ with a neighbourhood, and there is $n_0$ such that every $x \in \Lambda$ satisfies $|Df^{n}(x)| \ge 2$ for some $n \le n_0$. Let (X, d) be a nonempty complete metric space and let T from X to X be a contraction: there exists a constant q with 0 <= q < 1 such that d(T(x), T(y)) <= q d(x, y) for all x, y in X. Then T has exactly one fixed point x* in X (a point with T(x*) = x*). Moreover, for any starting point x_0 in X the iterates x_(n+1) = T(x_n) converge to x*, with the a priori error bound d(x_n, x*) <= q^n d(x_1, x_0) / (1 - q).

For m > n, the triangle inequality and the geometric series give d(x_m, x_n) <= (q^n + q^(n+1) + ... + q^(m-1)) d(x_1, x_0) <= q^n d(x_1, x_0) / (1 - q), which tends to 0 as n grows; hence (x_n) is Cauchy and, by completeness, converges to some x* in X. A contraction is Lipschitz, hence continuous, so T(x*) = lim T(x_n) = lim x_(n+1) = x*, and x* is a fixed point. Uniqueness: if x and y are both fixed points then d(x, y) = d(T(x), T(y)) <= q d(x, y), and since q < 1 this forces d(x, y) = 0, that is, x = y. Letting m tend to infinity in the displayed bound for d(x_m, x_n) yields d(x*, x_n) <= q^n d(x_1, x_0) / (1 - q).","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:81845b66a64fd9e8baa9830788af1d24ccfa7255e76ef65a7c1032858629b23b","revision_digest":"sha256:626f847ce40a84768e019fa3cdadd10e8d0b827e51626996fee08499fcf8c844","source_id":"wikipedia:Banach_fixed-point_theorem","source_revision":"as-read-2026-08-02","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Proposition prop:quadric of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] The real and imaginary parts of $\Phi=x+iy\in\mathcal{Q}$ satisfy
$|x|^{2}-|y|^{2}=1$ and $x\cdot y=0$, so $\mathcal{Q}$ is the set of pairs $(x,y)$ with
$x$ on a sphere of radius $|x|\ge1$ and $y$ tangent to it. After rescaling,
$\mathcal{Q}$ is the tangent bundle $TS^{N-1}$. On this quadric the imaginary slice
$W_{i\theta}$ acts as a real rotation of the base sphere, and the real slice
$W_s$ acts as a boost along the fibres, growing $|x|$ and $|y|$ without bound
while preserving $|x|^{2}-|y|^{2}=1$.

[Lemme 39 of arXiv:2604.00635, 'Large deviations of the periodic Toda chain'] Let  $\eta, \kappa, M_0, M_1, M_2,  M_3> 0$, and assume that  $\kappa < \frac{1}{2}$.
Fixing the notation $\mathbf{M}=(M_0,\dots, M_3)$, define the continuous and bounded function

$$f_{\kappa, \mathbf{M}}(x,y) \overset{\mathrm{def}}{=}

\max\Big\{   \ln_{M_0} |x - y| - \frac{\ell \kappa}{4M_1} V(x)  - \frac{\ell \kappa}{4M_1} V(y),

- M_{2} \Big\}  \, .$$

Next, given $\bs{\mf{r}} \, = \, (\eta, \kappa,\mathbf{M})$

define the functional $J_{\bs{\mf{r}}} : \mathcal{M}_1(\mathbb{R}) \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}$

\beqa

J_{\bs{\mf{r}}}[\mu]  &\overset{\mathrm{def}}{=} & \Int{\mathbb{R}}{}\ln_{M_1}\Big( 1+ \frac{2}{\ell}

\Int{\mathbb{R}}{} f_{\kappa, \mathbf{M}}(x,y) \, \mathrm{d}\mu (y)+ \eta \Big) \, \mathrm{d}\mu(x) \nonumber \\

 && \qquad + \Int{\mathbb{R}}{}\max\Big\{  -(1-\kappa) V(x)  + W(x),  - M_3\Big\} \,  \mathrm{d}\mu(x) \, .

\eeqa

Then $J_{\bs{\mf{r}}}$ is continuous with respect to the weak topology.

Let (X,d) be a compact metric space of diameter at most one, with covering numbers N(X,epsilon)<=epsilon^(-d_x) for 0<epsilon<=1, where d_x>0. Let P be a Borel probability measure, and W:X x X->[0,cmax] a measurable symmetric kernel with 0<cmin<=d_P(x)=integral W(x,y)dP(y) and cmax<=1. Assume there is ONE partition X=X_1 union ... union X_q into q>=1 measurable pieces such that |W(x,y)-W(xprime,y)|<=cLip d(x,xprime) for every y and every x,xprime in the same piece. Let x_1,...,x_n be independent samples from P, and fix 0<rho<=1/2. Define d_X(x)=n^(-1)sum_i W(x,x_i) and D_X(rho)=cmin^(-1)[cLip sqrt(d_x)+(cmax+cLip)sqrt(log(q/rho))]. For a universal sufficiently large C, n>=C D_X(rho)^2 implies P(inf_x d_X(x)>=cmin/2)>=1-rho. This is a common-partition restricted version of the source degree lemma; it is not a lower bound on the random Bernoulli graph degrees themselves.

[Lemma Nevanlinna of arXiv:2608.18320, 'Asymptotics for Beta-Splitting Trees via Homogeneous Fragmentations and Meromorphic Potent'] Let $f$ be a nonconstant complete Bernstein function which admits a
    meromorphic extension to $\mathbb C$. Then there exist $\gamma,\alpha\ge0$, a
    finite or infinite strictly increasing sequence
    \[
            0<b_1<b_2<\cdots,
    \]
    with $b_n\to\infty$ in the infinite case,
    and coefficients $B_n>0$ satisfying
    $\sum_n B_n/b_n^2<\infty$, such that
    \begin{equation}
            f(z)
            =
            \gamma+\alpha z
            +\sum_{n\ge1}B_n
            \left(
            \frac1{b_n}-\frac1{z+b_n}
            \right)
            =
            \gamma+\alpha z
            +\sum_{n\ge1}B_n
            \frac{z}{b_n(z+b_n)}.
    \end{equation}
    The series converges locally uniformly on
    $\mathbb C\setminus\{-b_n:n\ge1\}$. The poles of $f$ are real and simple. All zeros of $f$ are real and
    simple, and the zeros interlace with the poles.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Explicit model calculation or source-specific limiting obstruction Result: In a location-family submodel Y=m(X)+Z with known noise law and a reference matching Z, the conditional transport map is T_x(u)=m(x)+u. Thus estimating the map under integrated squared error is at least as hard as estimating the regression function m: the map difference is exactly the shift-estimation error for every reference point u. Check: Integrating |T_hat_x(u)-T_x(u)|^2 in the shift submodel over a unit-mass reference measure gives |m_hat(x)-m(x)|^2. For an arbitrary map estimator, averaging T_hat_x(u)-u over the reference law produces an estimator of m(x), whose squared error is bounded by the map loss by Jensen. Thus a uniformly faster map estimator would imply an equally faster regression estimator on that submodel. Obstruction: This reduction supplies a lower-bound route but no sharp rate for the general conditional map. One must combine covariate localization with the response-dimensional transport difficulty and prove a matching estimator under precisely specified regularity assumptions.

No independent review
title: Attempt on Minimax rates for conditional optimal-transport maps

[Corollary 5 (The Functional Sine-Santal\'o inequality) of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $n \geq 2$. For any non-negative measurable functions $f, g: \R^n \to \R_+$ and any non-increasing measurable function $\Omega: (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ satisfying the pointwise bound:
    $$f(x)g(y) \leq \Omega^2([x,y]) \quad \text{for all } x, y \in \R^n \text{ with } [x,y] > 0,$$
one has the inequality:
    $$\left(\int_{\R^n} f(x) dx \right) \left(\int_{\R^n} g(y) dy \right) \leq \left(\int_{\R^n} \Omega(|z|^2) dz \right)^2.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: The Functional Sine-Santal\'o inequality

body:
[Definition 28 of arXiv:2604.01978, 'Homogenized Transformers'] Let $B\in C^{1}((\S^{d-1})^{n};\mathsf{T}(\S^{d-1})^{n})$ and
$G:(\S^{d-1})^n\times\Uptheta\to \mathsf{T}(\S^{d-1})^n$ be such that for ${\uprho_*}$-a.e.\ $\theta$,
the map $X\mapsto G(X,\theta)$ is $C^2$.
A continuous $(\S^{d-1})^{n}$-valued adapted process $(X(t))_{t\ge 0}$ with $X(0)=x$ is called a solution to the Itô SDE 
    \begin{equation} 
        \de X(t)=B(X(t))\de t+\int_{\Uptheta}G(X(t),\bm{\theta})\mathsf{W}(\de \bm{\theta},\de t),
    \end{equation}
if for all $g\in C^{\infty}((\S^{d-1})^{n})$, we have
\begin{align*}
g(X(t))
= g(x)
&+ \int_{0}^{t} (Bg)(X(s))\,\de s \\
&+ \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\Uptheta} \Hess g(X(s))[G(X(s),\theta), G(X(s),\theta)]\,{\uprho_*}(\de \theta)\,\de s \\
&+ \int_{0}^{t}\int_{\Uptheta} (G(\cdot,\theta)g)(X(s))\,\mathsf{W}(\de \theta,\de s),
\end{align*}
where $Bg=\langle \grad g,B\rangle$, $G(\cdot,\theta)g=\langle \grad g, G(\cdot,\theta)\rangle$.
title: Definition 28 of arXiv:2604.01978

Let (X, mu) be a measure space and 0 < p < infinity. Let (f_n) be a sequence in L^p(mu) that is bounded in L^p norm and converges mu-almost everywhere to a function f. Then f is in L^p and lim_n ( ||f_n||_p^p - ||f_n - f||_p^p ) = ||f||_p^p. Equivalently the L^p norm splits asymptotically into the norm of the limit plus the norm of the vanishing part - a refinement of Fatou's lemma, which alone gives only ||f||_p <= liminf ||f_n||_p.
Uniform L^p boundedness AND almost-everywhere convergence.
Without the norm bound the conclusion fails;
no convergence in norm is assumed or concluded.

[Lem paley-zygmund of arXiv:2607.05097, 'Asymptotics of Lyapunov Exponents and Phase Transitions for Fluids with Degenerate Forcing'] Given $K \in \mathbb{N}_0$ and a sequence of elements $g_k \in \mathcal{H}^{\otimes_s k}$, let
    $X = \sum_{k=0}^K \tilde I_k(g_k)$.
Then, whenever $\|g_K\| \geq \delta$, one has
    $$\mathbb{P}\Big(|X| > \Big[\frac{K!}{2}\Big]^{1/2}\delta\Big) \geq \frac{3^{-2K}}{4} \,.$$

body:
ONE VARIABLE. Let $a, b: (t_0, t_1) \to \mathbb{R}$ be $C^1$ and let $F(x, t)$ and $\partial_t F(x, t)$ be continuous on an open set of $\mathbb{R}^2$ containing $\{(x,t) : t \in (t_0,t_1),\ x \text{ between } a(t) \text{ and } b(t)\}$. Then for $t \in (t_0, t_1)$
$$\frac{d}{dt} \int_{a(t)}^{b(t)} F(x,t)\,dx = \int_{a(t)}^{b(t)} \partial_t F(x,t)\,dx + F(b(t),t)\, b'(t) - F(a(t),t)\, a'(t).$$

SEVERAL VARIABLES. Let $v(x,t)$ be a $C^1$ velocity field on an open set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, $t \in (t_0, t_1)$, with flow $\varphi_t$ (so $\partial_t \varphi_t(y) = v(\varphi_t(y), t)$, $\varphi_{0} = \mathrm{id}$), and let $\Omega(t) = \varphi_t(\Omega_0)$ where $\Omega_0$ is a bounded open set with Lipschitz (e.g. piecewise $C^1$) boundary whose closure stays in $U$. Let $F(x,t)$ be $C^1$ on $U \times (t_0, t_1)$. Then
$$\frac{d}{dt} \int_{\Omega(t)} F\,dx = \int_{\Omega(t)} \partial_t F\,dx + \int_{\partial \Omega(t)} F\,(v \cdot \nu)\,dS = \int_{\Omega(t)} \big(\partial_t F + \nabla\cdot(F v)\big)\,dx,$$
where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal and $v \cdot \nu$ is the outward normal velocity of the boundary. Only the NORMAL component of the boundary velocity enters: two motions of the domain whose boundaries sweep the same sets (differing by a tangential reparametrisation) give the same derivative, so the formula can be stated with any $C^1$ boundary velocity having the correct normal component. The one-variable formula is the case $n = 1$, $\nu = \pm 1$ at $b$ and $a$.

WHERE IT FAILS OR NEEDS CARE. (1) $F$ must be continuous up to the moving boundary from inside; if $F$ jumps across $\partial\Omega(t)$ the boundary integrand is the one-sided limit from inside $\Omega(t)$. (2) $\partial_t F$ must be integrable over $\Omega(t)$ (continuity on a compact closure suffices); without domination, differentiation under the integral sign can fail. (3) The bounded-domain / Lipschitz-boundary hypothesis is what licenses the divergence theorem in the second equality; the first equality (Lagrangian form) needs only the change of variables. (4) If the domain is not transported by a $C^1$ flow but its boundary merely moves with a prescribed normal speed $w$, the same formula holds with $v \cdot \nu$ replaced by $w$, but the proof must build a flow with that normal speed.
F and its time derivative are continuous (F is C^1) on a neighbourhood of the closures of the moving domains
the domain is transported by a C^1 velocity field (one variable: the endpoints are C^1 functions of t)
the domain is bounded with Lipschitz boundary so that the divergence theorem applies
only the outward normal component of the boundary velocity enters the boundary term

Let G be a finite undirected loopless multigraph on n vertices with positive edge weights w_e, L its weighted Laplacian, and t > 0. A spanning rooted forest is a spanning forest with one chosen root in each tree; its weight is t^|E(F)| prod_{e in F} w_e (so an unrooted forest with trees T_1, ..., T_k counts prod |T_i| times). Z(t) is the total weight of spanning rooted forests, and Q_t = (I + tL)^-1. As t -> infinity, Q_t converges to the orthogonal projector onto ker L, which equals sum over the connected components C of G of 1_C 1_C^T / |C|.

For a finite undirected graph with labeled terminal vertices and a random open-edge configuration, its terminal partition puts two terminals in the same block exactly when an open path joins them inside the graph. The boundary-partition law is the probability distribution on these terminal partitions. When the graph attaches to an exterior only through those terminals, ordinary open-path connectivity in the union is determined by this partition and the exterior connectivity.

Let A,Phi be real symmetric n-by-n matrices with Phi positive semidefinite. Fix z with Im(z)>0,nonzero alpha with Im(alpha)<=0,and gamma>0. For s in the open upper half-plane let S(s)=(A+s^(-1)*Phi-zI)^(-1),f_n(s)=alpha^(-1)+gamma*tr(S(s)Phi),and tr=Tr/n. Then Im f_n(s)>=gamma*Im(z)*tr(S Phi S*)>=0. More precisely,Im f_n(s)=Im(alpha^(-1))+gamma*Im(s)/|s|^2*tr(S Phi S* Phi)+gamma*Im(z)*tr(S Phi S*). For s1,s2 in the upper half-plane,write S_j=S(s_j) and d_j=(Im f_n(s_j)-gamma*Im(z)*tr(S_j Phi S_j*))/Im(s_j)>=0. Then |f_n(s1)-f_n(s2)|<=|s1-s2|*sqrt(d_1*d_2). These are normalized-trace identities and inequalities for finite matrices;no simultaneous diagonalization of A and Phi is assumed. Draft,independent review pending.

body: The continuous (topological) dual X* of a normed space X is the space of bounded linear functionals f : X -> scalars, itself a Banach space under the operator norm ||f|| = sup_{||x||<=1} |f(x)|. The Hahn-Banach theorem guarantees X* is rich (functionals extend and separate points); the natural map X -> X** is an isometric embedding, and X is reflexive when it is onto.
title: Dual Space

[Definition Weibull tail index of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[definition]{def:stretched-tail}
For \(\alpha>0\), a real random variable \(\xi\) has Weibull tails of index \(\alpha\) if there is \(c_\xi\in(0,\infty)\) such that
\[
 \lim_{t\to\infty}t^{-\alpha}\log\mathbb P(\abs\xi>t)=-c_\xi.
\]
title: Weibull tail index

[Proposition 13 (\cref{sec:end-analysis}) of arXiv:2608.31008, 'Stability of gravitational instantons with a bounded Killing vector field'] Let $(M^4,g)$ be a complete Ricci-flat ALF manifold satisfying
\eqref{eq:intro-end}, and let $K$ be a nonzero bounded Killing field.
After multiplying $K$ by a nonzero constant, for every
$0<\varepsilon<\frac12$ one has, on the end,
\[
 |\nabla_b^j(K-T)|_b+|\nabla_b^j(V-1)|_b
   =\mathcal O(r^{-1-j}),\qquad \text{ and }\qquad
 |\nabla_b^jF|_b=\mathcal O(r^{-2-j}),\qquad \text{for }j\geqslant0.
\]
There are global functions $u$ and $\chi$ respectively satisfying 
 $\Delta u=V+2$ and $d\chi=\iota_K(*F)$ and for every $j\geqslant0$,
\[
 |\nabla_b^j(u+r^2/2)|_b=\mathcal O(r^{1+\varepsilon-j}),
 \qquad
 |\nabla_b^j\chi|_b=\mathcal O(r^{-1+\varepsilon-j}).
\]
The symmetric $2$-tensor
 $k_K=\nabla^2u-\kappa\otimes\kappa+\frac{V+1}{2}g$ satisfies
 $$|\nabla^jk_K|=\mathcal O(r^{-1+\varepsilon-j})\qquad \text{ for }0\leqslant j\leqslant2.$$ In particular, all of the integrals used below converge: for $M_R=\{r<R\}$, we have as $R\to+\infty$
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
 &\int_{\partial M_R}|k_K|\,|\nabla k_K|\,dA\longrightarrow0,\\
 &\int_{\partial M_R}
   |(F^+\circ F^-)(\nabla u,\nu)|\,dA\longrightarrow0,\\
 &\int_{\partial M_R}|1-V\pm\chi|\,
   |\partial_\nu(V\pm\chi)|\,dA\longrightarrow0.
\end{split}
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \cref{sec:end-analysis}

[Theorem thm:main-critical-level-percolation of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Let $d\geq2$ and let $\nu_{0}>0$, $\theta_{0}>0$, and $K_{0}<\infty$. There are $c=c(d,\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})>0$ and $t_0=t_0(d,\nu_{0},\theta_{0},K_{0})<\infty$ such that the following holds. Suppose $(\sigma(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ is an i.i.d.\ field with mean $\mathbb{E}\sigma(0)=1$, $\Var(\sigma(0))\geq\nu_{0}^2$, and $\mathbb{E} e^{\theta_{0}|\sigma(0)-1|}\leq K_{0}$. Then, for every integer $t\geq t_0$, the level set
\[
    \{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d:u_t(x)>c \, h(t)\}\, ,
    \qquad\text{where}\quad
    h(t)=
    \begin{cases}
    t^{(4-d)/4} & \text{if } d\in\{2,3\}\, ,\\
    \log t & \text{if } d=4\, ,\\
    (\log t)^{2/d} & \text{if } d\geq5\, ,
    \end{cases}
\]
contains an infinite nearest-neighbor component almost surely.

[Corollary cor:augment_stable of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Assume that $\bm{X}$ is an augmented $\alpha$-stable process and $\bm{Z}$ is an $\alpha$-stable process with $\alpha\in(0,2)\setminus\{1\}$ and fix any $q\in(0,1]\cap(0,\alpha)$ with $\mathds{E}[|\bm{X}_1|^q]<\infty$.
\begin{description}[leftmargin=0em, nosep]
\item[(a)]

Assume $|\mathcal{Q}(x,\bm{v})-c_\alpha| \leqslant K(1\wedge x)$ for  some $K>0$ and all $x>0$, $\bm{v}\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then, for $\bm{X}^t\coloneqq(\bm{X}_{st}/t^{1/\alpha})_{s\in[0,1]}$,  
\begin{equation*}
c_1 t^{1-q/\alpha}
\leqslant\mathcal{W}_q\big(\bm{X}^t_1,\bm{Z}_1\big)
\leqslant\mathcal{W}_q\big(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z}\big)\leqslant
c_2\big(t^{1-q/\alpha}\1_{\{\alpha<1\}} + t^{q(1-1/\alpha)}\1_{\{\alpha>1\}}\big),
\end{equation*}
for some $c_1,c_2>0$ and all sufficiently small $t>0$.

\item[(b)] Assume $\mathcal{Q}(x,\bm{v})\!=\! c_\alpha H(x)^\alpha$ for $x>0$, $\bm{v}\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ and some monotone $H\in\mbox{SV}_0\cap C^1$. Set $\varrho(x)\!\coloneqq \!\int_x^\infty H(y)^\alpha y^{-\alpha-1}\mathrm{d} y$ and let $\varrho^{\leftarrow}$ be its right-continuous inverse. Suppose $G(x)\coloneqq H(\varrho^{\leftarrow}(1/x))$ satisfies Assumption~(\nameref{asm:S}) for some function $G_2\in\mbox{SV}_0$. Then, for $g(t)\coloneqq t^{1/\alpha}G(t)$, $a(t)\coloneqq G(2t)/G(t)$ and $\bm{X}^t\coloneqq(\bm{X}_{st}/g(t))_{s\in[0,1]}$, we have
\[
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z})=\mathcal{O} ( G_2(t)^q),
\quad\text{as }t \downarrow 0,\quad\text{and}\quad
\max\big\{\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t_1,\bm{Z}_1)
,\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^{2t}_1,\bm{Z}_1)\big\}
\geqslant |1-a(t)^q|\mathds{E}\big[|\bm{Z}_1|^q\big]/3,
\]
for sufficiently small $t >0$. The function $t\mapsto|1-a(t)^q|$ is not upper bounded by any non-decreasing function $\phi$ with $\int_0^1\phi(t)t^{-1}\mathrm{d} t<\infty$, $G$ is $C^1$ with $t\mapsto t|G'(t)|\in\mbox{SV}_0$ and there exists some $\phi\in\mbox{SV}_0\cap\mbox{SV}_\infty$ satisfying the inequality $\phi(x)\geqslant\sup_{t>0,y\in[x\wedge 1,x\vee1]}yG'(yt)/G'(t)$ for all $x>0$. Moreover, defining  $L(t)\coloneqq t|G'(t)|/G(t)$, there exist constants $c_1,c_2>0$ such that for all sufficiently small $t>0$, we have
\[
c_2L(t)
\leqslant\max\{\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t_1,\bm{Z}_1)
,\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^{2t}_1,\bm{Z}_1)\}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}^t,\bm{Z})
\leqslant c_1L(t)^q.
\]

\end{description}
title: Corollary cor:augment_stable of arXiv:2411.03609

Let mu(dx) be proportional to exp(-V(x))dx with smooth convex V and a finite second moment. Let G~N(0,I) be independent of X~mu and t>0. For Y=X+sqrt(t)G, the posterior mu_y has density proportional to exp(-V(x)-|x-y|^2/(2t)). For smooth bounded f, grad_y E[f(X)|Y=y]=Cov_mu_y(f,X)/t. The strong-log-concavity Poincare bound gives C_P(mu_y)<=t and 0<=Cov(mu_y)<=tI. These assertions also hold for nonsmooth convex potentials by log-concave approximation; they do not assert C_P(mu)<=t.

t>0

body: In probability theory, the central limit theorem (CLT) states that, under appropriate conditions, the distribution of a normalized version of the sample mean converges to a standard normal distribution. This holds even if the original variables themselves are not normally distributed. There are several versions of the CLT, each applying in the context of different conditions.
title: Central limit theorem

body: A topological space X is connected if it cannot be written as the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets. Equivalently: the only subsets of X that are simultaneously open and closed are the empty set and X itself. A subset of a topological space is called connected if it is connected in the subspace topology. A pair (U, V) of disjoint nonempty open sets whose union is X is called a separation of X. The real interval [0,1] with its standard topology is connected (a consequence of the least-upper-bound property of the reals).
title: Connected space

body: A consistent first-order theory T is complete if for every sentence \sigma in the language of T, either T \vdash \sigma or T \vdash \neg \sigma.
title: Complete First-Order Theory

body:
[Thm reg_existence of arXiv:2506.01746, '\bf Optimal Bregman quantization: existence and uniqueness of optimal quantizers revisited'] Let $r>0$ and let $\|\cdot\|$ denote any norm on  $\mathbb{R}^d$.  Assume $\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\|\xi\|^{r}\mathbb{P}(\mathrm{d}\xi)< + \infty$.

\smallskip
\noindent $(a)$ For every $n\ge 1$, there exists at least one $L^r$-optimal quantizer $\Gamma^{(r,n)}$ of size at most $n$, solution to the minimization problem
\[
\inf_{\Gamma: |\Gamma|\leq n}  e_r(\Gamma,P,\|.\|)
\]
i.e. such that 
\[
e_r(\Gamma^{(r,n)},P,\|.\|)=  e_{r,n}(P,\|.\|).  
\]

\smallskip
\noindent $(b)$ If ${\rm card}\big({\rm supp}(P)\big) \ge n$, then any $L^r$-optimal quantizer $ \Gamma^{(r,n)}$ has full size $n$ and for every $a\!\in  \Gamma^{(r,n)}$, $P(C_a( \Gamma^{(r,n)}))>0$. Moreover, 

\smallskip
 $(i)$ if the norm $\|\cdot\|$ is smooth~(\footnote{that $\|\cdot\|$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{0\}$, like Euclidean norms or $\ell^p$-norms, $1<p<+\infty$.}) and strictly convex then {\em the boundary of the Voronoi partition is $P$-negligible}: for every $a\!\in \Gamma^{(r,n)}$, $P\big(\partial C_a(\Gamma^{(r,n)})\big)=0$

\smallskip
  $(ii)$ if   $r\ge 2$ and the norm $\|\cdot\|=|\cdot|_e$ is Euclidean then these quantizers are {\em $L^r$-stationarity}: for every $a\!\in \Gamma^{(r,n)}$,
\[
a = \frac{\int_{C_a(\Gamma^{(r,n)})}\xi|\xi-a|^{r-2}P(\mathrm{d}\xi)}{\int_{C_a(\Gamma^{(r,n)})}|\xi-a|^{r-2}P(\mathrm{d}\xi)}.
\]
\
\noindent $(c)$ When $d=1$  and $P=U([0,1])$, then for every $r>0$, the $L^r$-optimal quantizer is unique and 
\[
\Gamma^{(r,n)} = \Big\{\frac{2k-1}{2n},\; k=0,\ldots,n\Big\}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 18 (Uniform compactly supported half-space quasimodes) of arXiv:2608.30211, '2608.30211'] There are $R_0,C>0$ such that, for every $R\geq R_0$ and
$\varrho\in[0,1]$, one can find an $L^2$-normalized function
$\Psi_{\varrho,R}$ in the $\varrho$ form domain on $\Hh^d$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{supp}\Psi_{\varrho,R}\subset B_{3R}(0)\cap\overline{\Hh^d},
 \qquad
 Q_\varrho(\Psi_{\varrho,R})\leq\mu_\varrho+\frac{C}{R}.
\end{equation}
At the Dirichlet endpoint the quasimode has zero trace.

body: [Corollary 58 of arXiv:2609.03070, 'Variants of order semicontinuity in Banach lattices'] Let $E\subset F$ be a super order dense sublattice and let $B\subset E$ be solid in $E$. Then, the $\sigma$-order and $\mathrm{u\sigma o}$ adherences of $B$ in $F$ and the $\sigma$-order and $\mathrm{u\sigma o}$ adherences of $\Sol_{F} B$ all coincide. A sequence is Cauchy if for every epsilon > 0 there is N with |a_m - a_n| < epsilon for all m, n >= N. In R (and any complete metric space) a sequence converges if and only if it is Cauchy. The forward direction holds in any metric space; the converse is exactly completeness. This lets one prove convergence without knowing the limit.

[Definition of arXiv:2602.00853, 'Mixing times for the stochastic $p$-Laplace equation'] Let $p\in (1,2)$. We say that $\{X_t\}_{t\in [0,T]}$ is a \emph{stochastic variational inequality (SVI) solution} to (equation eq:pLaplace of the paper) for initial data $x_0\in L^2(U)$ if
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $X\in L^2([0,T]\times\Omega;L^2(U))$ such that
\[\operatorname{ess\,sup}\displaylimits_{t\in [0,T]}\mathbb{E}\int_0^T\int_U|\nabla X_s|^p\,\mathrm{d} z\,\mathrm{d} s<\infty,\]
\item for any $z_0\in L^2(U)$, every $Z\in L^2([0,T]\times\Omega;H^1_0(U))$, and every progressively measurable $G\in L^2([0,T]\times\Omega;L^2(U))$ such that
\[Z_t=z_0+\int_0^t G_s\,\mathrm{d} s+B\,W_t,\]
we have that for a.e. $t\in [0,T]$
\begin{align*}&\mathbb{E}\left[\|X_t-Z_t\|^2_{L^2(U)}\right]+\frac{2}{p}\mathbb{E}\int_0^t\int_U|\nabla X_s|^p\,\mathrm{d} z\,\mathrm{d} s\\
\le &\mathbb{E}\left[\|x_0-z_0\|^2_{L^2(U)}\right]+\frac{2}{p}\mathbb{E}\int_0^t\int_U|\nabla Z_s|^p\,\mathrm{d} z\,\mathrm{d} s-2\mathbb{E}\int_0^t\int_U G_s(X_s-Z_s)\,\mathrm{d} z\,\mathrm{d} s.\end{align*}
\end{enumerate}

[Definition 11 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] For \(p=[w]\in\PP^N\), define the ambient chord-square barrier
\begin{equation}
 \widehat\rho_p([z])
 :=1-\frac{|\langle z,w\rangle|^2}{|z|^2|w|^2}.
\end{equation}
It is a smooth nonnegative function, vanishes precisely at \(p\), and
the family \(\{\widehat\rho_p\}_{p\in\PP^N}\) has uniform first- and
second-derivative bounds.  Moreover, for uniform \(0<c<C<\infty\),
\begin{equation}
 c\,d_{\rm FS}(y,p)^2\le\widehat\rho_p(y)
 \le C\,d_{\rm FS}(y,p)^2,
 \qquad y,p\in\PP^N.
\end{equation}
Indeed, in the standard normalization
\(\widehat\rho_p=\sin^2d_{\rm FS}(\,\cdot\,,p)\), and the
Fubini--Study diameter is finite.

Now let \(q\in U_0\Subset U_1\Subset Y^{\rm rv}\).  Compose
\(\widehat\rho_{\iota(q)}|_Y\) with a smooth nondecreasing function
that is the identity near zero and is constant once its argument leaves
a sufficiently small sublevel set contained in \(U_1\).  The resulting
function \(\rho_q\) is called a \emph{localized squared-distance
barrier at \(q\)}.  It is the restriction of a smooth ambient function,
has zero set \(\{q\}\), is uniformly comparable to
\(d_\eta(\,\cdot\,,q)^2\) near \(q\), is bounded below on
\(Y\setminus U_0\), and has its first two derivatives supported in
\(U_1\).

body:
[Lem 79 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] On the time interval $[q_0,\gamma(1)]$ let $\tilde{Y}$, $\tilde{W}$, $\tilde{w}$, $\tilde{\cF}_Y$ be as given by Lemma~\ref{l:time.change}.
It is possible to extend these to the full time interval $[q_0,1]$ such that
$|\tilde Y(1)| = 1$ almost surely, and the same conditions as before are satisfied: $\tilde{W}$ is a standard Brownian motion,
$\tilde{w}$ is progressively measurable with respect to
    \[
    \tilde \cF_Y(t) = \sigma\Big(
        (\tilde W_s)_{s\in [q_0,t]}, U', \tilde Y(q_0)
    \Big)
\]
with $\bbE[(\tilde w_t)^2] = 1$ for all $t$,
and
 \[
        \tilde Y(t) = \tilde Y(\gamma(1))
            + \int_{\gamma(1)}^t \tilde w_s\,d\tilde{W}(s)\,.
    \]

\begin{proof} Abbreviate $t_1=\gamma(1)$.
Let $Z$ be a standard Brownian motion on the time interval $[t_1,{{\infty)}}$ with initialization $Z(t_1)=\tilde{Y}(t_1)$. Let
    \[
    \bar{\tau}
    \equiv\inf\Big\{t\ge t_1 : |Z(t)|\ge1\Big\}\,,
    \]
and define the stopped martingale
    \[\bar{Z}(t)\equiv Z(t\wedge\bar{\tau})
    =\tilde{Y}(t_1)+ \int_{q_0}^t \ind\{t\le\bar{\tau}\} \,dZ(t)\,.
    \]
Then, similarly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:time.change}, we define $\tilde{Y}$ to be the time change of $\bar{Z}$ satisfying the desired properties. Explicitly, let 
    \[
    \bar{\gamma}(t)
    = \E[\bar{Z}(t_1+t)^2] -\E[\bar{Z}(t_1)^2] 
    = \E \int_{t_1}^{t_1+t} \ind\{t\le\bar{\tau}\}\,dt\,,
    \]
and denote its generalized inverse $\bar{\lambda}$.
We then take $\tilde{Y}(t)=\bar{Z}(t_1+\bar{\lambda}(t-t_1))$, so that
$\E[\tilde{Y}(t)^2]=t$. As in Lemma~\ref{l:time.change}, we can express
    \[
    \tilde{Y}(t)
    = \tilde{Y}(t_1) + \int_{t_1}^t \tilde{w}_t\,d\tilde{W}(t)
    \]
where we can define explicitly    \begin{align*}
    \tilde{W}(t) 
    &=\int_{t_1}^{t_1+\bar{\lambda}(t-t_1)}
	\bar{\gamma}'(u-t_1)^{1/2}\,dZ(u)\,,\\
    \tilde{w}_t
    &= \frac{\ind\{t_1+\bar{\lambda}(t-t_1)\le\tau\}}
        {\bar{\gamma}'(\bar{\lambda}(t-t_1))^{1/2}}\,.
    \end{align*}
The claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Defn def:condLBSF of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] A flow $\Phi$ is \textbf{locally branched surface finite} (\textbf{LBSF}) if for every $p\in \mathbb{R}^n$, there is a neighborhood $U$ of $p$ and a finite collection of $\Phi$-horizontal branched surfaces $\Sigma_1,\dots, \Sigma_m$ such that, up to the action of flow preserving homeomorphisms of $(M,\Phi)$ rel boundary, every $\Phi$-horizontal foliation with generalized boundary multislope in $U$ is carried by some $\Sigma_i$. Here, a generalized boundary multislope is in $K$ if some substitution of its $\aleph$ components with real numbers lies in $K$.

Let $A$ be measurable and uniformly parabolic with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$ and let $u$ be a local weak solution of $\partial_tu=\mathrm{div}(A\nabla u)$ in the backward cylinder $Q_{2r}=Q_{2r}(x_0,t_0)$. Then: (a) local boundedness -- $\sup_{Q_r}|u|\le C\big(\frac{1}{|Q_{2r}|}\iint_{Q_{2r}}u^2\big)^{1/2}$; (b) interior Holder continuity -- there are $\alpha=\alpha(n,\lambda,\Lambda)\in(0,1)$ and $C=C(n,\lambda,\Lambda)$ such that $u$ has a continuous representative with $|u(x,t)-u(y,s)|\le C\Big(\frac{|x-y|+|t-s|^{1/2}}{r}\Big)^{\alpha}\sup_{Q_{2r}}|u|$ for $(x,t),(y,s)\in Q_r$. Both constants depend only on $n$ and the ellipticity constants, and on nothing else about $A$ -- this is exactly what makes the theorem the parabolic counterpart of De Giorgi's and Nash's solution of Hilbert's 19th problem and the engine behind Aronson's bounds. Estimates are interior in the parabolic sense: they hold up to the top time $t_0$ but require distance from the bottom and the lateral sides.
A measurable, uniformly parabolic with constants lambda, Lambda
divergence form, no lower-order terms (with bounded lower-order terms the same holds with constants depending on their bounds and on r)
u a local weak solution in Q_{2r} in the energy class L^infty_t L^2_x cap L^2_t H^1_x

[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2608.18557, 'Randomly Permuted Orthogonal Products and Fast Dimension Reduction'] Let \(b\in\R^d\) satisfy \(\sum_{k=1}^d b_k=0\), let
	\(X_1,\ldots,X_d\) be symmetric \(r\times r\) matrices, and let
	\(\pi\) be uniform on \(S_d\). Set
	\[
	\sigma^2
	=
	\frac{\norm{b}_2^2}{d}
	\left\|
	\sum_{j=1}^d X_j^2
	\right\|,
	\qquad
	M
	=
	\norm{b}_\infty\max_{j\in[d]}\norm{X_j}.
	\]
	Then
	\[
	\probb{\pi}{\norm{\sum_{j=1}^d b_{\pi(j)}X_j}\ge t}
	\le
	2r\exp\left(
	-\frac{t^2}
	{12\sigma^2+4\sqrt2\,Mt}
	\right)
	\qquad \text{for }t\geq0.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

The co-stability is then the expected co-margin S∗(g) := E[h∗ g(x)], and the normalized co-stability is accordingly defined as the expected normalized co-margin ¯S∗(g) := E[¯h∗ g(x)]. body: The Riemann zeta function is zeta(s) = sum over n >= 1 of n^{-s}, absolutely convergent for Re(s) > 1, extended by analytic continuation to a meromorphic function on C with a single simple pole at s = 1 of residue 1. It satisfies the functional equation relating zeta(s) and zeta(1 - s) through the completed function xi(s) = pi^{-s/2} Gamma(s/2) zeta(s), which is symmetric under s -> 1 - s. Its zeros in the critical strip 0 < Re(s) < 1 govern the distribution of primes; the Riemann hypothesis places them all on Re(s) = 1/2.
title: Riemann Zeta Function

[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2609.03238, 'Representation Defects and Cassels Pairings for Congruent Number Curves'] Let $p\ne q$ be odd primes and let $n\in\{pq,2pq\}$.  Then
\[
s_2(n)=4
\]
if and only if
\[
p\equiv q\equiv1\pmod8,
\qquad
\left(\frac qp\right)=1.
\]
For every other residue pattern one has only the general bound $s_2(n)\le3$; the value
$s_2(n)=3$ can occur.

For the population DDPM score loss of an equilateral three-Gaussian teacher of small noisy radius a, centered-network GD contracts shape and plane errors toward the two-dimensional equilateral subspace at rate 1-c h a^2, locally in a fixed relative tube whose projected radius lies in [0.9a,1.1a]. The exact transverse covariance Hessian has plane coefficient 2r^2-2/3 and perpendicular coefficient 2r^2/3. Constants are independent of ambient dimension. Scope limits: This is conditional local tracking only; random entry, radial tube preservation, centroid drift for free means, and long empirical perturbations are not settled.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:9079094046d8c0b1e0aa17c0424af5a5640169fa1327da97b27f9fdb7d4b6377","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/90/9079094046d8c0b1e0aa17c0424af5a5640169fa1327da97b27f9fdb7d4b6377.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:b5b65dd88f00db5725c385ec016c98fea8833c18cca3c9e9bdc667931aba59bb","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c05","bundle_id":"population.t309-transverse-tracking-and-spurious-ddpm-minimum-drafts","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability, Gaussian mixtures, score matching","draft":"w721/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:equilateral-gaussian-ddpm-transverse-tracking","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T309: transverse attraction toward the equilateral family

T309-w721-C05 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). This is a local population statement for a centered student parameterization, not a solution of Target 2. No novelty is asserted.

The point of this lemma is to control the previously unpaid shape and plane directions near the family used in C03. It does not establish entry into that neighborhood from a generic random initialization. It also does not treat centroid drift of the unrestricted three-mean parameterization or finite-sample errors over the ensuing long angular stage.

## 1. Setup and statement

Fix d>=2. Let u_j, j=0,1,2, be unit equilateral vectors in a plane P, and let Q rotate P by 2pi/3. The teacher is q_a=(1/3)sum_j N(a u_j,I_d), where a>0 is sufficiently small.

Let H be the linear space of d-by-3 mean matrices M whose columns sum to zero. Train the Eq. (9) score student with equal component weights and identity covariance, parameterized on H, using the population DDPM objective. Equivalently, choose any orthonormal coordinates on H and apply Euclidean GD in those coordinates. In the original three-column coordinates, this is the centered projection of the full gradient, not unrestricted three-mean GD. This distinction is part of the assumptions.

Let L be the two-dimensional linear subspace consisting of matrices with columns Q^j z for z in P. Write Pi_L for its orthogonal projection within H. For M=v+w, where v=Pi_L M and w is orthogonal to L within H, define r by ||v||_F=sqrt(3) a r.

There are absolute constants a_0,rho,c,C>0, independent of d, such that throughout the tube

    0<a<=a_0,    9/10<=r<=11/10,    ||w||_F<=rho a,

the following hold:

    <w, grad_H F_a(v+w)> >= c a^2 ||w||_F^2,                     (1)
    ||Pi_{L-perp} grad_H F_a(v+w)||_F <= C a^2 ||w||_F.          (2)

Here F_a is the exact population excess score loss, equal to the population excess DDPM objective. Consequently, for centered GD with 0<h<=c/(C^2 a^2),

    ||w_next||_F^2 <= (1-c h a^2)||w||_F^2,                     (3)

provided the current iterate lies in the tube. For the centered gradient flow, the corresponding squared distance decays at least as exp(-2c a^2 t) for as long as the projection radius remains in the indicated interval. These are conditional local tracking estimates; (3) alone is not a proof that a trajectory stays radially confined or enters the tube.

The plane and subspace L are used only to state and analyze the error. The centered gradient step itself does not require knowing P. Centering, however, is enforced in the student parameterization.

## 2. The high-noise loss expansion in all centered directions

For a centered matrix U with columns u'_j, write C(U)=UU^T/3. Let U_* be the teacher's unit-radius matrix. Uniformly on any fixed Frobenius ball ||U||_F<=B inside H,

    F_a(aU)=a^4 ||C(U)-C(U_*)||_F^2 + O_{C^2(U)}(a^6).         (4)

The C^2 bound is in operator norm with respect to the Frobenius metric, and its constant can be chosen independently of d. The teacher is fixed at a U_* while the student varies as aU.

For completeness, the posterior mean correction in the score is

    b_U(a,x)=a sum_j w_j u'_j,
    w_j proportional to exp(a u'_j dot x-a^2 ||u'_j||^2/2).

Since sum_j u'_j=0, expansion gives b_U(a,x)=a^2 C(U)x+O(a^3). Hence the squared difference between the student and teacher scores begins at a^4, and its Gaussian leading expectation is ||C(U)-C(U_*)||_F^2. The exact replacement (a,x)->(-a,-x) makes the risk an even function of a, so the next possible order is a^6.

The integrated Taylor remainder and its two U derivatives are justified by the softmax-weight domination argument used in C01. To check dimension independence rather than hiding it in an ambient Gaussian norm, fix unit Frobenius directions D,E when taking a mixed Hessian derivative. Every logit and every directional derivative depends on x only through the span of the columns of U,U_*,D,E. Its dimension is at most 12, independently of d. All norms of these four matrices are bounded, so the derivative envelopes are fixed polynomials in a Gaussian vector of dimension at most 12, times exp(C||G||) if a derivative of the teacher density is present. Their moments are bounded uniformly. Coordinates perpendicular to that span integrate to 1 and make identical score contributions for teacher and student. This proves a common bound for all unit D,E and hence the required operator-norm C^2 remainder.

## 3. Exact transverse Hessian of the covariance loss

Choose a 3-by-2 matrix A with orthonormal columns spanning 1-perpendicular, and let E be an orthonormal basis matrix for P. Right multiplication M->MA is an isometry on H because AA^T is the projection onto 1-perpendicular. Choose the orientation of E and A so the equilateral reference has factor

    U A=sqrt(3/2) r E.

At another angular position the same calculation holds after rotating E, which leaves the teacher covariance C(U_*)=P/2 unchanged. For a centered perturbation D write its two-column factor as

    D A=E X+E_perp Y,

where E_perp is an orthonormal basis for the perpendicular complement (absent if d=2). Orthogonality of D to L says that X is orthogonal to both I_2 and the 90-degree rotation J. Every real 2-by-2 matrix orthogonal to I_2 and J is symmetric with trace zero. This follows directly by writing its four entries: its two diagonal entries sum to zero and its two off-diagonal entries are equal.

Let G(U)=||C(U)-P/2||_F^2. Its Hessian in a direction D is

    Hess G(U)[D,D]=2||DC(U)[D]||_F^2
                   +2<C(U)-P/2,D^2C(U)[D,D]>,
    DC(U)[D]=(DU^T+UD^T)/3,    D^2C(U)[D,D]=2DD^T/3.

Using the factor sqrt(3/2)r E, symmetry and tracelessness of X, and orthogonality of P and P-perpendicular gives exactly

    ||DC(U)[D]||_F^2=(2r^2/3)||X||_F^2+(r^2/3)||Y||_F^2,
    Hess G(U)[D,D]=(2r^2-2/3)||X||_F^2+(2r^2/3)||Y||_F^2.       (5)

In particular, for 9/10<=r<=11/10,

    Hess G(U)[D,D] >= (27/50)||D||_F^2.                        (6)

Indeed the plane coefficient is at least 143/150 and the perpendicular coefficient is at least 27/50; also ||D||_F^2=||X||_F^2+||Y||_F^2. This is not a dimension-count argument: it identifies and computes the two normal blocks. The exact symbolic check in scripts/check_normal.py independently expands the 3-by-2 factor perturbation and verifies (5).

## 4. Transfer of the Hessian to the exact loss

Because (5) is a polynomial Hessian with dimension-independent Frobenius operator bounds on bounded balls, there is a sufficiently small absolute rho>0 such that (6), weakened to a lower bound 2/5, holds in the fixed directions D orthogonal to L also at U+W whenever ||W||_F<=rho. The perturbation W need not remain equilateral. This is continuity in operator norm on a bounded ball, with constants bounded by the covariance polynomial itself, so it does not introduce a dimension-dependent compactness argument.

By (4), after changing from U=M/a to physical means M, the Hessian of F_a is

    Hess_M F_a = a^2 Hess_U G + O_op(a^4)

on the centered space. Choose a_0 sufficiently small that the remainder leaves at least a^2/4 of normal curvature throughout the tube and its segments v+s w, 0<=s<=1. The same expansion gives a full centered Hessian upper bound C a^2 there. Thus one may take c=1/4 after adjusting the tube and the upper constant C.

The exact symmetry in C02 implies grad_H F_a(v) lies in L at every v in L. Therefore its normal projection is zero. Integrating the normal Hessian along v+s w proves (1), while its upper bound proves (2):

    Pi_{L-perp} grad_H F_a(v+w)
        =integral_0^1 Pi_{L-perp} Hess_H F_a(v+s w) w ds.

All projections here are orthogonal in the same Frobenius metric as the parameterization.

## 5. The tracking inequalities

For centered GD, w_next=w-h Pi_{L-perp} grad_H F_a(v+w). Expanding its squared norm and applying (1)--(2) gives

    ||w_next||^2 <= (1-2c h a^2+C^2 h^2 a^4)||w||^2.

For h<=c/(C^2 a^2) this is (3). For the flow, differentiating ||w||^2 gives -2<w,grad_H F_a>, yielding the exponential estimate by integration while the tube condition holds. No probability product, independence claim, or numerical integration bound is used.

## 6. The exact outstanding bridge

For a centered generic initial triple, the leading loss in (4) is a rank-two PSD covariance-factorization problem. Reaching the tube by that leading dynamics does not automatically prove that the exact DDPM trajectory does so. A successful random-entry argument needs quantitative control of the high-noise perturbation for the entire covariance-learning phase, anti-concentration of the inherited angular coordinate away from the three saddles, radial confinement during the subsequent phase, and a finite-sample perturbation estimate over its polynomially long duration if a shrinks with d.

The finite-horizon argument in C04 cannot simply be reused with a=d^(-c): it would generally raise inverse accuracy to an exponent growing with d. This is an exact limitation of that transfer route, not an SQ lower bound or a counterexample to Target 2. Centered-network GD also must not be silently substituted for unrestricted mean GD; centroid tracking is a separate step for that architecture.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:927c5b3c33a3e77790e962beb6c27b526ea19266a9216a8fffaa1f31512a5ffe","revision_digest":"sha256:6358af5f3329a32e1d2b356901f4f3070fb108844204377c1a6abd9890f04e4d","source_id":"owner-own-work:T309-w721-C05-v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20T20:39:18.089313","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Every such ray hits S_n, so sum_{x in S_n}q(x)=E|T_0 intersect S_n|>=P(T_0 nonempty). If a ray exists almost surely, the sum is at least 1 for every n and sup_{x in S_n}q(x)>=1/(8n). Thus vanishing raw forward-ray shell incidence and the uniform rate o(1/n) are impossible in this setting. This concerns forward rays and does not imply a bigeodesic exists.

and
$$\sup_{i> \kappa_2(P)}\|\widehat  W_{\kappa_2(P)}^{-1} \mathbb E_{i}(W^{-1/p}f)\|_{\mathbb C^d}\leq C_\gamma\mathbb E_{\kappa_2(P)}\|\widehat  W_{\kappa_2(P)}^{-1}W^{-\frac{1}{p}}f\|_{\mathbb C^d}\quad \mbox{on}\quad E(P).$$

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2506.16259, 'Two-dimensional Rademacher walk'] Let $a_n\in \R_+$,  $n=1,2,\dots$. We call the sequence $\{a_n\}$ {\em good}, if for each large~$n$ there is a positive integer $K_n$ such that
$$
\frac{K_n}{\log_2 a_n}\to 1\text{ as }n\to\infty,
$$
and a subset  of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$  with $K_n$ distinct elements, say $\{ i_1,i_2,\dots,i_{K_n}\}$, such that $i_{K_n}= n$ and $a_{i_{k+1}}\ge 2a_{i_{k}}$ for every $k=1,2,\dots,K_n-1$.

An affine algebraic set V is irreducible if it cannot be expressed as the union V = V_1 union V_2 of two proper algebraic subsets V_1, V_2 strictly contained in V. An algebraic set is irreducible if and only if its vanishing ideal I(V) is a prime ideal in the polynomial ring.
V is a non-empty affine algebraic set

body: [Lemma exclusion of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Suppose that $\Sigma$ contains two elements $\eta'\subset \eta$ with $\prod_{e\in \eta'} x_e<\prod_{e\in \eta} x_e$. Then, there exists \textit{no} measure $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega\times \Sigma$ such that the marginal $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta] \propto \prod_{e\in \eta} x_e$ and such that  the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega]$ is uniform on $\Sigma^{\downarrow}(\omega)$.

For any positive integers c and k_1, k_2, ..., k_c, there exists a least integer R(k_1, ..., k_c) such that every edge-coloring of the complete graph K_N with c colors, where N >= R(k_1, ..., k_c), contains a complete subgraph of size k_i monochromatic in color i for some i in {1, ..., c}.
c >= 2
k_i >= 2 for all 1 <= i <= c

body: Let A be an event depending on the states of a finite set of edges, and let omega be a configuration. The edge e is PIVOTAL for A at omega if the occurrence of A is decided by the state of e alone, that is if omega with e forced open lies in A and omega with e forced closed does not, or the reverse. Pivotality is a function of the states of the OTHER edges only, so the event {e is pivotal for A} is independent of the state of e - a fact used constantly and easy to forget. The INFLUENCE of e on A under P_p is I_e(A) = P_p( e is pivotal for A ). Under the uniform measure on the discrete cube this coincides with the usual influence P( f(X) != f(X with coordinate e flipped) ) for the indicator f of A. The total influence sum_e I_e(A) is, by Russo's formula, exactly the derivative of p -> P_p(A) for increasing A, which is why influences govern the sharpness of the phase transition; and by the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem the maximum influence of a balanced Boolean function on n coordinates is at least of order log n / n, which is the quantitative input behind sharp-threshold results. [standard; e.g. Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Section 2.4, and O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Chapter 2]

body:
Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system. For a finite (or countable, with finite entropy) measurable partition $\xi = \{A_1, \dots, A_k\}$ put $H_\mu(\xi) = -\sum_i \mu(A_i) \log \mu(A_i)$ (with $0 \log 0 = 0$), and $\xi^n_0 = \bigvee_{j=0}^{n-1} T^{-j}\xi$, the partition into sets $A_{i_0} \cap T^{-1}A_{i_1} \cap \dots \cap T^{-(n-1)}A_{i_{n-1}}$ (the $n$-step itineraries). The entropy of $T$ relative to $\xi$ is $h_\mu(T, \xi) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n H_\mu(\xi^n_0)$ (the limit exists because $n \mapsto H_\mu(\xi^n_0)$ is subadditive; it also equals $\inf_n \frac1n H_\mu(\xi^n_0)$ and $\lim_n H_\mu(\xi \mid \xi^n_1)$). The Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is $h_\mu(T) = \sup_\xi h_\mu(T, \xi)$ over finite partitions, in $[0, \infty]$. Facts used constantly: $h_\mu(T, \xi) \le H_\mu(\xi) \le \log k$; $h_\mu(T, \xi) \le h_\mu(T, \eta) + H_\mu(\xi \mid \eta)$ for partitions $\xi, \eta$; $h_\mu(T^m) = m\, h_\mu(T)$ for $m \ge 1$; the Kolmogorov-Sinai generator theorem: if $\xi$ is a generator ($\bigvee_{j \ge 0} T^{-j}\xi$ generates $\mathcal{B}$ mod $\mu$, or $\bigvee_{j\in\mathbb{Z}}$ for invertible $T$) then $h_\mu(T) = h_\mu(T, \xi)$; and if $\xi_m$ is an increasing sequence of partitions generating $\mathcal{B}$ then $h_\mu(T, \xi_m) \uparrow h_\mu(T)$. On a compact metric space, finite Borel partitions $\xi_m$ with $\mathrm{diam}(\xi_m) \to 0$ also give $h_\mu(T, \xi_m) \to h_\mu(T)$ (for every finite partition $\eta$, $H_\mu(\eta \mid \xi_m) \to 0$), but not monotonically in general, since such partitions need not refine one another. The map $\mu \mapsto h_\mu(T)$ on invariant measures is affine, but it is NOT in general continuous or even upper semicontinuous in the weak* topology; upper semicontinuity holds when $T$ is expansive (and for $C^\infty$ maps of compact manifolds by Newhouse), which is what guarantees measures of maximal entropy exist in those cases.
mu is a T-invariant probability measure
partitions are finite or have finite static entropy

 d=rho/2, a=d/(10r^(3/2)), b=sqrt(rp/d),
 Kbar=sqrt(r)(s^2 b^2+1+4sqrt(r)).

Initialize B0=0 and A0=sG where G is r-by-p with independent standard Gaussian entries. For any one fixed eta with

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:795b618bab79ffa26752a7159c4a514a6b84a9f0f8daa4357ff3ce683e0817bb","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/79/795b618bab79ffa26752a7159c4a514a6b84a9f0f8daa4357ff3ce683e0817bb.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:1c3267ea507d610faaf85368365c81870dd1924296569053b1524373ea4fe548","bundle_entry_key":"all-scale-flat","bundle_id":"population.t419-julia-dilation-operator-contraction-all-scale-flat-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"LoRA convergence and Julia operator dilation","draft":"w705/bundle_013.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.lowrank:lora-all-ranks-aspect-ratios-all-gaussian-scales-flat-spectrum-gd","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T419-C025 v1: every Gaussian scale, every rank and aspect ratio, flat spectrum

Kind:narrowed. Target:1. Status:proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.

This application depends on the new unaudited C024 operator-norm contraction proof and the unaudited explicit C014 discrete boundedness proof. Both are included in full in the queued card. The single hardest dependency is C024's exact nonlinear orthogonal-dilation compression; this application does not replace it by an assumption of spectral monotonicity from loss descent. Known output-span invariance is credited to Zhang-Liu-Chen, arXiv:2502.01235, Theorem3.1/C.10. The sufficient-margin idea for continuous flow is attributed to Min-Tarmoun-Vidal-Mallada, arXiv:2105.06351, Corollary5. The discrete imbalance method is due to Du-Hu-Lee, arXiv:1806.00900, AppendixB ClaimB.1. None of those citations alone proves the present zero/Gaussian GD statement; novelty remains unresolved.

## Statement

Let r>=1, m,p>=r be arbitrary integers and Delta any real m-by-p matrix of rank exactly r, with all nonzero singular values equal to1. Let any s>0 and 0<rho<1. Define

 d=rho/2, a=d/(10r^(3/2)), b=sqrt(rp/d),
 Kbar=sqrt(r)(s^2 b^2+1+4sqrt(r)).

Initialize B0=0 and A0=sG where G is r-by-p with independent standard Gaussian entries. For any one fixed eta with

 0<eta<=1/(6Kbar+1),

ordinary simultaneous GD on ||BA-Delta||F^2/2 satisfies, with probability at least1-rho, for every integer t>=1,

 ||B_t A_t-Delta||F <=sqrt(r) exp[-eta^3 s^4 a^4(t-1)/(8Kbar)].

For every 0<eps<sqrt(r), a sufficient time is

 1+ceil[(8Kbar/(eta^3 s^4 a^4))log(sqrt(r)/eps)].

The success event and the fixed step are independent of requested accuracy. This covers every positive Gaussian scale, every rank and every input/output aspect ratio, including all proper bottlenecks m,p>r. It covers condition number1, not arbitrary target spectra. No expected-risk or finite-sample claim is included. The rate is deliberately conservative; independent proof audit and any novelty judgment remain pending.

## 1. Gaussian event

Write Delta=U V^T with orthonormal columns in U m-by-r and V p-by-r. By Gaussian rotation invariance H=G V has independent standard Gaussian entries. The event

 sigma_min(H)>=a, ||G||F<=b

has probability at least1-rho. For completeness, H is nonsingular almost surely. If sigma_min(H)<a then ||H^{-1}||F>1/a; at least one row has norm >1/(a sqrt(r)). Its reciprocal is the distance of the corresponding Gaussian column from the span of the remaining r-1 columns. Conditional on those columns that distance has distribution |N(0,1)|. A union bound and the normal density bound give probability at most r sqrt(2/pi)a sqrt(r)<d. Markov gives Pr[||G||F>b]<=rp/b^2=d. A union bound, without assuming the two events independent, proves the stated success probability. Fix any G on this event below.

## 2. Descent, bounded factors, and applicability of C024

Apply C014 with C=I, D=W=Delta, q0=r/2, J=||A0 A0^T||F+1<=s^2 b^2+1, R=2sqrt(r), K=sqrt(r)(J+2R)<=Kbar. The step condition in the statement implies eta<=1/(6K+1) and eta<=1/(1+r), since Kbar>=4r. Hence C014 proves, before invoking C024,

 q_next<=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=Kbar,
 ||E_t||F<=sqrt(r), E_t=B_t A_t-Delta.

At every iterate, h_t=||B_t||op^2+||A_t||op^2<=Kbar and e_t=||E_t||op<=sqrt(r)<=Kbar/4. Therefore

 eta(e_t+h_t)<= (5Kbar/4)/(6Kbar+1)<1/2.

C024 applies at every iterate and proves ||E_(t+1)||op<=||E_t||op. This is a consequence of its explicit small-step contraction lemma, not a consequence of Frobenius loss descent alone. The factor bounds used to apply it were established independently of any margin or operator-norm monotonicity.

## 3. First-step margin and a uniformly nonsingular output factor

Because B0=0, A1=A0 and B1=eta Delta A0^T. Let L=A0^T A0. The initial factor bound gives eta||L||op<=1. Then

 E1=Delta(eta L-I),
 U^T E1 E1^T U=V^T(I-2eta L+eta^2 L^2)V
                  <=I-eta V^T L V
                  <=(1-eta s^2 a^2)I.

Here eta^2 L^2<=eta L is a scalar spectral inequality for the PSD matrix L, and V^T L V=(A0 V)^T(A0 V)>=s^2 a^2 I. The scalar eta s^2 a^2 is in (0,1), since a<=b and eta s^2 b^2<1. As col(E1) is contained in col(U),

 ||E1||op<=sqrt(1-eta s^2 a^2)<=1-eta s^2 a^2/2.

Put delta0=eta s^2 a^2/2>0. Section2 makes this margin persist for all t>=1. By the known invariant output span, B_t=U R_t for a square r-by-r R_t. Hence E_t=U(R_t A_t-V^T), and Weyl gives sigma_min(R_t A_t)>=1-||E_t||op>=delta0. Also

 sigma_min(R_t A_t)<=sigma_min(R_t)||A_t||op,

by testing the transposed product on a left minimum-singular vector of R_t. The factor bound therefore yields sigma_min(R_t)>=delta0/sqrt(Kbar). This deduction does not assume A_t has full input rank, and remains valid for p>r.

## 4. Frobenius contraction with the same step forever

The A gradient is R_t^T(R_t A_t-V^T), so

 ||grad q_t||F^2>=delta0^2 ||E_t||F^2/Kbar.

Together with section2 this gives

 ||E_(t+1)||F^2 <=[1-eta delta0^2/Kbar]||E_t||F^2.

The multiplier is in (0,1) under the displayed bounds. Iteration from t=1, using ||E1||F<=sqrt(r), and sqrt(1-x)<=exp(-x/2), gives the rate in the statement because eta delta0^2/(2Kbar)=eta^3 s^4 a^4/(8Kbar). No step change or accuracy-dependent safe step is used.

## Nonempty spectral interval and general scale normalization

The same argument also covers normalized rank-r targets Delta=U Lambda V^T with sigma1=1 and mu=sigmar satisfying mu>1-delta0, with all constants above unchanged. The first-step Loewner estimate becomes

 U^T E1 E1^T U <=(1-eta s^2 a^2)Lambda^2<=(1-eta s^2 a^2)I,

and needs no commutation of Lambda with V^T L V. q0<=r/2 gives the same factor and operator-contraction bounds. Set beta=mu-1+delta0>0; then for all t>=1 the Frobenius residual is bounded by sqrt(r)exp[-eta beta^2(t-1)/(2Kbar)]. Thus at each s>0 there is a nonempty condition-number interval 1<=kappa<1/(1-delta0), although its width may be very small. This does not prove arbitrary condition number at every scale.

For a flat target with nonzero singular value alpha>0, let s'=s/sqrt(alpha), Kbar'=sqrt(r)((s')^2 b^2+1+4sqrt(r)), and choose original eta<=1/[alpha(6Kbar'+1)]. Normalizing both factors by sqrt(alpha) and Delta by alpha gives step eta'=alpha eta. Consequently

 ||B_t A_t-Delta||F<=alpha sqrt(r)exp[-alpha eta^3 s^4 a^4(t-1)/(8Kbar')].

The nonnormalized formula is a change of variables, not a new algorithm. The main unresolved population range is arbitrary condition number across all scales. Positive-noise proper-bottleneck empirical optimization and statistical stopping remain separate gaps. This application and its C024 dependency are unaudited; prior work may already imply some or all of the stated family.

# T419-C014 v1: empirical GD boundedness with an initialization-dependent step

Kind: bound. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.
This is an explicit anisotropic version of the published Gram-imbalance/descent method, not a solution of Target 2. It proves a trajectory component without assuming the iterates are bounded. The prior source is Du-Hu-Lee, arXiv:1806.00900, Theorem 2.2 and Appendix B, Claim B.1; its full convergence theorems have different initialization/step hypotheses. C009 already identifies the exact covariance metric and C010 the positive-noise empirical landscape.

## Statement

Let C be any real positive definite p-by-p matrix, D any real m-by-p matrix, and r>=1. Put lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op, ell=||D||op, W=D C^(-1), and

 q(B,A)=(1/2)||(BA-W) C^(1/2)||F^2,

with B m-by-r and A r-by-p. This is the empirical regression objective up to a constant when C=XX^T/n and D=ZX^T/n. Initialize at any finite deterministic factors B0,A0, and define

 q0=q(B0,A0), J=||A0 A0^T-B0^T B0||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R), L=6Kc+ell.

For any fixed

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/L},

simultaneous ordinary factor GD satisfies, for every integer t>=0,

 q_t<=q0,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=K,
 ||(A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t)-(A0 A0^T-B0^T B0)||F<=2eta q0<1,
 sum_(t>=0) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/eta.

In particular the gradient tends to zero, every accumulation point is critical, and for every integer T>=1,

 min_(0<=t<T) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/(eta T).

All constants are finite and computable from C,D and the initialization. There is no Gaussian assumption and no low-rank assumption on W. No iterate-convergence, saddle-avoidance or statistical-risk assertion is included.

## Exact identities and product/factor bounds

Let G=BA C-D. The two factor gradients are G_B=G A^T and G_A=B^T G. With E_t=A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t the first-order cross terms cancel exactly, giving

 E_(t+1)-E_t=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B),
 ||E_(t+1)-E_t||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2).

This cancellation only uses dependence on BA and does not require isotropic C. Also

 (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2
 <=r [||AA^T-B^TB||F^2+4||BA||F^2].

To verify it, write P=B^TB,Q=AA^T. Scalar trace Cauchy-Schwarz gives (tr(P+Q))^2<=r tr((P+Q)^2), and cyclicity of trace gives tr((P+Q)^2)=||P-Q||F^2+4 tr(PQ), tr(PQ)=||BA||F^2. No commutation is assumed.

When q<=q0, positivity of C gives ||BA-W||F<=sqrt(2q0/lambda), hence ||BA||F<=R. If additionally ||E-E0||F<=1, then ||E||F<=J, so the preceding trace bound implies

 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2<=sqrt(r) sqrt(J^2+4R^2)<=K.

The initialization meets these conditions and therefore has pair norm at most sqrt(K).

## Descent established before closing the boundedness induction

Suppose at the current iterate the pair norm is at most sqrt(K), and preceding steps have valid descent inequalities. Then

 ||grad q||F<=||BA C-D||op sqrt(||B||F^2+||A||F^2)
             <=(Kc/2+ell)sqrt(K).

Because eta<=1/(6Kc+ell), the proposed next point has pair norm at most 2sqrt(K). The connecting segment also lies in that ball. On that ball the Hessian quadratic form in a perturbation (dB,dA) is

 ||(dB A+B dA) C^(1/2)||F^2+2<BA C-D,dB dA>.

Its absolute value is at most

 [c(||A||op^2+||B||op^2)+||BA C-D||op]
 times (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2)
 <=[4Kc+(2Kc+ell)] (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2).

Here the first summand uses Cauchy-Schwarz on dB A+B dA; the cross term uses |<G,dB dA>|<=||G||op||dB||F||dA||F. Thus the Hessian operator norm on the segment is at most L. Taylor's theorem along that segment proves

 q_next<=q-eta||grad q||F^2+(L eta^2/2)||grad q||F^2
        <=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2.

In particular q_next<=q0. Telescoping the descent inequalities, including the proposed step, and using q>=0 yields

 sum_(j=0)^t eta^2||grad q_j||F^2<=2eta q0
 <=2q0/(1+2q0)<1.

Summing the imbalance increments now proves ||E_next-E0||F<=2eta q0<1. The product/factor bound therefore puts the endpoint back in the smaller ball of pair radius sqrt(K). This closes the induction without assuming a bound before proving descent on the required larger segment. The q0=0 case is included: both gradients vanish, the sequence is constant, and all inequalities still hold.

## Consequences and exact remaining gap

Telescoping for every finite horizon gives the infinite summability bound. A nonnegative summable sequence tends to zero, so the gradients vanish. Bounded finite-dimensional factor pairs have convergent subsequences; gradient continuity makes every subsequential limit critical. The running-minimum bound follows by averaging the finite sum. These statements do not require that the entire sequence converges to one point.

For B0=0 and a Gaussian A0, this provides an allowed positive step after observing the initialization, conditional on every full-row-rank design. It does not supply a single positive step independent of the unbounded Gaussian initializer. C013 shows that unconditional expected-limit risk with such an initialization-independent fixed step can diverge even at rank one.

Combining this bound with the already verified empirical strict-saddle landscape C010 is insufficient to conclude global optimization. One must additionally show that the specified zero/Gaussian initialization does not approach a nonglobal critical point, with all hypotheses of a saddle-avoidance theorem checked for its lower-dimensional initial support and step rule. Vanishing gradients do not establish that. Even convergence almost surely would not by itself justify passing to expected population risk; a failure-tail/integrability or finite-stopping argument is separately required. The usual full-ambient absolutely-continuous random-initialization theorem cannot simply be cited for the plane B0=0.

Independent reviewer audit and any novelty assessment remain pending. This is a deterministic bound recorded as a component, not an advertised new theorem or a completed target.
