body: [Definition notation:binom of arXiv:2511.15893, 'On a Class of Dynamical Poisson-Voronoi Tessellations'] For $l,r,k\in \{1,2\}$ with $l\neq r$, we say that an intersection is of type $\binom{k}{l,r}$, if it is the $k$-th intersection between the radial birds of type $l$ and $r$. \!\!\! In the combinatorial like notation $\binom{k}{l,r}$, the fact that the position of $l$ is on the \textbf{left} means that the head of the bird of type $l$ is on the left of the head of the bird of type $r$, which is on the \textbf{right}. The two values of $k$ refer to the two intersections, as in ((eq:HOs of the paper)), of radial birds of two different types, where $k=1$ means the left intersection and $k=2$ means the right intersection. We call intersections of these type \textbf{mixed intersections} and the handovers given by these intersections as \textbf{mixed handovers}.

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.03902, 'Bundles of Probability Schemes'] For any bundle $\pi \colon \gv{\Omega,\pr} \to \gv{\Omega',\pr'}$,
  \begin{enumerate}[i.]
    \item $\pi_{\flat}\pi^{\sharp}$ is the identity map on $\Rr^{\Omega'}$.
      
    \item Both $\pi^{\sharp}$ and $\pi_{\flat}$ preserve expectation.
      
    \item $\pi_{\flat}$ is an $\Rr^{\Omega'}$-module map. 
    \item The operators $\pi^{\sharp}$ and $\pi_{\flat}$ form an adjoint pair.
      
    \item $\E_{\pi}:=\pi^{\sharp}\pi_{\flat}$ is the orthogonal projection of
      $\Rr^{\Omega}$ to $\cA_{\pi}$. 
    \item $\pi^{\sharp}$ is an isometry. 
  \end{enumerate}

body: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space on a set X is a Hilbert space H of functions f : X -> R (or C) in which every evaluation functional f -> f(x) is bounded. By Riesz representation there is then a unique kernel k(x, .) in H with the reproducing property f(x) = <f, k(x, .)> for all f in H; the function k(x, y) = <k(y, .), k(x, .)> is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
title: Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space

body:
Let (a_n)_{n >= 1} be a sequence of reals with a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m, n >= 1. Then lim_{n -> infinity} a_n / n exists in [-infinity, +infinity) and equals inf_{n >= 1} a_n / n. In particular the limit is finite if and only if a_n / n is bounded below. The SUPERadditive version, a_{m+n} >= a_m + a_n, gives lim a_n/n = sup_n a_n/n in (-infinity, +infinity]. The lemma requires nothing beyond subadditivity - no monotonicity, no positivity, no continuity - and the limit can be minus infinity, as with a_n = -n^2. Fekete's lemma is the deterministic skeleton of Kingman's subadditive ergodic theorem: applying it to a_n = E[X_{0,n}] gives the existence of the constant that the ergodic theorem then identifies as the almost sure limit. [Fekete (1923); standard, e.g. Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, Chapter 1]
a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m, n >= 1
nothing else; the limit may be -infinity

[Thm 1 of arXiv:2605.31300, 'Cone-Additive Functions for Random Walks on Free Products of Graphs'] Let $f:\Pi \to \mathbb{R}$ be a cone-additive function such that $|f(\pi)|$ grows at most polynomially in the length of $\pi\in \Pi$. Furthermore, assume that the power series $G(o,o|z)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\P[X_n=o]\cdot z^n$ has radius of convergence strictly bigger than $1$.
Then there exists some constant $\mathfrak{c}\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n f\bigl([X_0,\ldots,X_n]\bigr) = 
\mathfrak{c}\quad \textrm{almost surely}.
$$    
Moreover, if $f$ is strictly positive  then $\mathfrak{c}>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: The Paris-Harrington theorem strengthens the finite Ramsey theorem. Call a finite set Y of positive integers relatively large if its size is at least as large as its minimum element. The strengthened statement asserts: for all positive integers n, k, m there is an N such that for every coloring of the k-element subsets of {1,...,N} with m colors, some relatively large subset Y of {1,...,N} with at least n elements is homogeneous, meaning every k-element subset of Y receives the same color. This statement is true, provable in second-order arithmetic, but Paris and Harrington proved in 1977 it is not provable in first-order Peano arithmetic, a natural combinatorial example of incompleteness.
title: Paris-Harrington theorem

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a centered, almost surely bounded Gaussian process (X_t)_{t in T}, let M = sup_t X_t and sigma^2 = sup_t Var(X_t). The Borell-TIS inequality states P(|M - E[M]| >= u) <= 2 exp(-u^2/(2 sigma^2)) for all u >= 0, giving Gaussian concentration of the supremum around its mean at the scale of the process's maximal pointwise variance, regardless of the cardinality or geometry of the index set. Separately, Slepian's inequality compares two centered Gaussian processes on the same index set with equal marginal variances: if E[(X_s-X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2] for all s,t, then E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], and in its classical strong form also gives a tail comparison, typically under an additional nonnegative-correlation condition. The Sudakov-Fernique inequality removes the equal-variance requirement, needing only the pointwise increment domination, but concludes only the expectation comparison E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], not the stronger distributional comparison. Together these tools reduce bounding E[sup] of a complicated Gaussian field to bounding it for a simpler, dominating comparison field. Borell-TIS does not give the value of E[M] itself, which requires a separate chaining or Dudley-integral bound, and Sudakov-Fernique is strictly weaker in conclusion than the classical Slepian inequality even when both sets of hypotheses happen to hold. Typical failure: Invoking the classical Slepian inequality's tail or distributional comparison after only verifying the weaker Sudakov-Fernique hypotheses, namely increment domination without equal variances or a correlation-sign condition; Sudakov-Fernique licenses comparing E[sup X] to E[sup Y] only, and treating the two comparison theorems as interchangeable overstates what has actually been proven. Canonical reference: Borell, 1975, Inventiones Mathematicae; Tsirelson, Ibragimov and Sudakov, 1976, in Proceedings of the School-Seminar on Random Processes; Slepian, 1962, Bell System Technical Journal; Fernique, 1975, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.
a centered Gaussian process, almost surely bounded on the index set, for Borell-TIS
for Slepian/Sudakov-Fernique: two Gaussian processes on the same index set with pointwise increment-variance domination E[(X_s-X_t)^2]<=E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2]
for the classical Slepian tail comparison specifically: equal marginal variances or a nonnegative-correlation condition, beyond the plain increment domination Sudakov-Fernique needs
measurability and separability of the process so the supremum is well defined

[Dfn 113 (temporal smoothing) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the spatially smoothed quantities specified by Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth}. Recall the function $\sphicirc$ from Definition~\ref{d:sp.smooth}, and let
	\[\tphi(t)
	\equiv
	\frac{2}{\tep}
	\sphicirc\lt(\frac{2
		t}{\tep}-1\rt)\,,\] so that $\tphi$ integrates to one and has support $[0,\tep]$. We define temporally smoothed coefficients by simply convolving with $\tphi$ in the time coordinate:
	\[\tB^N(t,y)
	\equiv\int_{\R} 
        \tphi(s) 
        \sB^N(t-s,y)\,ds
	= \tE\Big[ \sB^N(t-\sss,y)\Big]	\,,\]
where $\tE$ refers to expectation over the law of the random variable $\sss$ sampled from density $\tphi$. We define analogously $\tV^N$, $\tU^N$, $\trrr^N$,and $\twww^N$.  Recalling \eqref{e:qbar.and.qstar}, we will view all these quantities as being defined only for $t\in [q_*,1]$, so its definition only involves the values $\sbbb^N(t-s)$ for $t-s\in [\bar q,1]$, thus avoiding any temporal boundary issues. We then define 
	\begin{align*}
	\tbbb^N(t,y)
	&\equiv\frac{\tB^N(t,y)}{(p^N)'(t)^{1/2} }\,,\\
	\tvvv^N(t,y)
	&\equiv \frac{\tV^N(t,y)}{p^N(t) } 
	\,,\\
	\tuuu^N(t,y)
	&\equiv
	\frac{\tU^N(t,y)}{[ p^N(t)
		\cdot t (p^N)'(t)]^{1/2}} \,.
	\end{align*}
We abbreviate $\tGam^N\equiv(\tbbb,\tvvv,\tuuu)^N$. Recalling \eqref{e:sp.smoothed.F.N} we let
	\beq
	\tF^N(t,y)
\equiv\Big\{ \tV^N+2\tU^N+\trrr^N
\Big\}(t,y)+2\eta^{1/2}\,,
	\eeq
and we note that $\tF^N$ can be obtained by convolving $\sF^N$ with $\tphi$ in the time coordinate. In particular, since $\sF^N\ge0$, it follows that $\tF^N\ge0$ also.
title: temporal smoothing

body: A finite normal-form (strategic-form) game is a tuple (N, (S_i)_{i in N}, (u_i)_{i in N}) where N = {1,...,n} is a finite, nonempty set of players; for each player i, S_i is a finite, nonempty set of pure strategies; and for each player i, u_i: S_1 x S_2 x ... x S_n -> R is a payoff function assigning a real number to every strategy profile s = (s_1,...,s_n), one strategy per player. A mixed strategy for player i is a probability distribution sigma_i over S_i, and the expected payoff to player i under a profile of mixed strategies sigma = (sigma_1,...,sigma_n), with players randomizing independently, is the expectation of u_i(s_1,...,s_n) over s_i drawn from sigma_i for each i.
title: Finite Normal-Form Game

lossless lift of a reversible chain started from the random law $\pi^{(\ell)}$
with probability $w_\ell$. The weights are constants of the motion.
title: Mixtures evolve as mixtures, with frozen weights

body:
[Thm Weak Convergence of Approximate Tridiagonal Entries of arXiv:2411.01633, 'On the Limit of the Tridiagonal Model \\for $\beta$-Dyson Brownian Motion'] Fix a $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $T>0$ and define a vector of approximated tridiagonal entry processes,
\begin{equation*}
    \Tilde{E}_n(t):=\left(\Tilde{a}_1(t),\dots ,\Tilde{a}_k(t), \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(\Tilde{b}_1(t)^2-n),\dots ,\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(\Tilde{b}_k(t)^2-n)\right).
\end{equation*} Then, $\Tilde{E}_n(t)$ converges weakly in $C[0,T]$ to a vector process $E(t)=(A_1(t),\dots ,A_k(t),B_1(t),\dots,B_k(t))$, distributed as $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}E(t) \sim \mathbf{OU}_{2k}(1,3,\dots ,2k-1,2,4,\dots ,2k)$. More explicitly, the components $A_j(t) \in C[0,T]$ and $B_j(t) \in C[0,T]$ are jointly-independent centered Ornstein--Uhlenbeck processes with covariances $\mathrm{Cov}(A_j(t),A_j(s))=2e^{-(2j-1)|t-s|}$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(B_j(t),B_j(s))=2e^{-2j|t-s|}$, for $j=1,\dots ,k$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Weak Convergence of Approximate Tridiagonal Entries

body: Let F, G: C -> D be functors between the same two categories. A natural transformation eta: F => G assigns to every object c of C a morphism eta_c: F(c) -> G(c) in D, called the component of eta at c, such that for every morphism f: c -> c' in C, the naturality square commutes: G(f) o eta_c = eta_{c'} o F(f), both sides being morphisms F(c) -> G(c') in D. If every component eta_c is an isomorphism in D, eta is called a natural isomorphism, and F, G are said to be naturally isomorphic.
title: Natural Transformation

body:
[Proposition p:difference of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] In the setting of Definition (def:vary of the paper), let $\overline{\delta_0}, \overline{\delta_1}$, $\overline{\delta_2}$ be deterministic drift functions such that $\overline{\delta_0}(x)>0$ on ${\mathbb R}$.  Let $r_0\in {\mathbb R}$ be a constant and $r_1\ge r_0$ be an $\mathcal F$-stopping time. We write $Y=(Y_x,\, x\ge r_0)$ for the ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta_0}\,|_{r_1}\, \overline{\delta_1})$ flow line  starting at $(0,r_0)$ and we let $\mathcal S$ be the ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta_2})$ flow, both driven by $\mathcal W$. Let $\mathcal W^-_Y$ and $\mathcal W^+_Y$ defined as in (equation eq:W- of the paper) and (equation eq:W+ of the paper) from $(\mathcal W,Y)$ in place of $(\mathcal W,S)$. We extend $Y$ to ${\mathbb R}$ by setting $Y_x=0$ when $x<r_0$.  Consider the collection of processes 
 \begin{align*}
\mathcal S^+_{r,x}(a) &:=\mathcal S_{r,x}(a+ Y_r)- Y_x, &&  a\ge 0,\,  t(Y)>x\ge r, \\
\mathcal S^-_{r,x}(a) &:=  \mathcal S_{r,x}(a), && a\le Y_r,\, t(Y)>x\ge r\ge r_0
\end{align*}

\noindent where $t(Y):=\inf\{x\ge r_1\,:\, Y_x=0 \hbox{ and } \overline{\delta_1}(x)< 0\}$. We impose that 
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal S^+_{r,x}(a)=0  \mbox{ \rm if } x\ge \varphi_+(a,r), \qquad \mathcal S^-_{r,x}(a)=Y_x \mbox{ \rm if } x\ge \varphi_-(a,r),
\end{equation}

\noindent where, for any $a$ and $r$, 
\begin{align}
 \varphi_+(a,r) & :=\inf\{y> r\,:\, \mathcal S_{r,y}(a+ Y_r)\le Y_y  
\hbox{ and }  \overline{\delta_2}(y)\le  (\overline{\delta_0}\,|_{r_1}\, \overline{\delta_1})(y)\},\\
\varphi_-(a,r) & :=\inf\{y> r\,:\, \mathcal S_{r,y}(a)\ge Y_y\hbox{ and } \overline{\delta_2}(y) \ge (\overline{\delta_0}\,|_{r_1}\, \overline{\delta_1})(y)\}. \nonumber 
\end{align}

\noindent See Figure (fig:decomp of the paper). Then
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item  $\mathcal S^+$ is a ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta_2}\,|_{r_0}\,\overline{\delta_2} - \overline{\delta_0}\,|_{r_1}\, \overline{\delta_2} -\overline{\delta_1})$ flow driven by the white noise $\mathcal W^+_Y$ killed on $\{\overline{\delta_2} \le (\overline{\delta_0}\,|_{r_1}\, \overline{\delta_1})\}$ and restricted to $(-\infty,t(Y))$.
\item  The noise  $\mathcal W$ driving the SDEs of $Y$ and $\mathcal S^-$ can be replaced with $\mathcal W^-_Y$. In particular, $Y$ and $\mathcal S^-$ are measurable with respect to $\mathcal W^-_Y$ and $r_1$.
\item If $Y$ is a $\ominus$-flow line, then $\mathcal W^+_Y$ is a white noise on ${\mathbb R}_+ \times {\mathbb R}$  independent of $\mathcal W^-_Y$. 
\item Let $b\in {\mathbb R}$ and $\overline{\delta'}:= (\overline{\delta_0} \,|_b\, \overline{\delta_1})$. If $Y$ is a $\oplus$-flow line, then conditionally on 
$r_1=b$, $\mathcal W^-_Y$ is independent of $\mathcal W^+_Y$ and has the law of $\mathcal W^-$ associated by (equation eq:W- of the paper) to  the ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta'})$ flow line starting at $(0,r_0)$. 
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Proposition p:difference of arXiv:2411.04773

body:
[Proposition 5 (Structure of the first-order formulation: hyperbolicity and quadratic nonlinearities) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Consider the Einstein--Euler system under $\Tbb^2$ symmetry on $\Tbb^3$ for a general equation of state  satisfying~\eqref{hyperbolic-eos-zero}. After expressing the spacetime metric in areal gauge~\eqref{metric:areal}, consider the metric unknowns~$\amdeux, \Omega, P, Q, G, H$, together with the fluid unknowns $\mu, u$ entering the stress-energy tensor~\eqref{eq:Einsframe}. Assume furthermore that the solutions under consideration are sufficiently regular.
\bei

\item \emph{Hyperbolicity.}

\bei

\item \emph{Under the non-vacuum condition $- \Jbb \cdot \Jbb>0$,} in terms of $(\amdeux, \Omega)$ and of the unknowns $(\Jbb, \Kpar, \Lbb)$ defined in~\eqref{eq:definevar-KL} and \eqref{Jdef}, subjected to the causality inequalities~\eqref{eq:causal}, the evolution system consisting of~\eqref{eq:T2-1234-def},~\eqref{eq:T2-Euler-perp-def}, and~\eqref{eq:T2-all-suite-def} is a first-order hyperbolic system of $12$ nonlinear balance laws, supplemented with the $3$ constraints~\eqref{eq:theconstraints-def}. In addition, the wave equation for the lapse~\eqref{eq:waveconffac}, below, follows from this set of equations; in vacuum, it is a consequence of the geometry equations alone.

\hfuzz=0.3pt
\item At every non-zero null state, the two acoustic speeds and the (double) matter speed coalesce. Thus the diagonalization established on the timelike cone \emph{does not extend} uniformly to its null boundary; at $\Jbb=0$, the fluid direction is undefined.

\item If $p'(0)=0$, the limiting equations displayed in~\eqref{equa-Euler-Minko-trivial} have an explicit nontrivial Jordan structure at every non-zero null state; this is a degenerate, weakly hyperbolic regime. 

\eei 

\item \emph{Nonlinearities.}

\bei

\item The double characteristic family associated with the speed ${-\amdeux^{-1}\frac{J_1}{J_0}}$ is \emph{linearly degenerate} (even on the vacuum).  The other two nonlinear wave speeds are distinct away from the vacuum. If $p(\mu)/\mu$ tends to zero with $\mu$ tends to zero, these two nonlinear wave speeds coincide on the vacuum on which hyperbolicity is lost.  If $p(\mu)/\mu$ tends to a constant in $(0,1)$ (isothermal limit), these two nonlinear wave speeds remain distinct even on the vacuum and strict hyperbolicity holds. 

\item The metric evolution equations~\eqref{eq:T2-1234-def} and~\eqref{eq:T2-all-suite-def} and the fluid evolution equations~\eqref{eq:T2-Euler-perp-def} contain only terms that are quadratic in $(\Jbb,\Kpar,\Lbb)$, except that the fluid quadratic forms are multiplied by the bounded state-dependent coefficient $q_\Jbb$. 
They are all exactly quadratic in the isothermal case, since $q_\Jbb$ is then a constant.
\item With the exception of the lapse equations in~\eqref{eq:T2-567-def} and~\eqref{eq:evollambda-def}, all quadratic source terms involving only the variables $\Jperp, \Lbb$ are null forms\footnote{This is not the case for nonlinearities involving the variables $\Jpar, \Kpar$.}.

\eei
\eei

[Cor Cor_strong_alpha_convex of arXiv:2606.22183, 'Expected loss of quasi-arithmetic means of exchangeable random variables'] Let $I\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be a nonempty open interval, $\alpha:(I-I)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ be an even function,
 and $L:I\to \mathbb{R}$ be a strongly $\alpha$-convex function.
Then
 \begin{align*}
   L\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^n t_ix_i\bigg)
   \leqslant \sum_{i=1}^n t_iL(x_i)
        -\sum_{i=1}^n t_i\alpha\bigg(x_i-\sum_{j=1}^n t_jx_j\bigg)
 \end{align*}
 for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in I$ and $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in[0,1]$ satisfying $t_1+\cdots +t_n=1$.
title: Cor Cor_strong_alpha_convex of arXiv:2606.22183

RESOLVED IN THE LITERATURE (status recorded by a bounded search or recall on 2026-09-07, verify before citing). The ancestral partition process of the N-particle branching Brownian motion with selection (Brunet-Derrida model), sped up by (log N)^3, converges to the Bolthausen-Sznitman coalescent. Resolution: Schweinsberg 2017 (EJP); Berestycki-Berestycki-Schweinsberg 2013. Notes: Berestycki, Berestycki and Schweinsberg (Ann. Probab. 2013) proved it for branching Brownian motion with absorption at a near-critical drift; Schweinsberg, 'Rigorous results for a population model with selection II: genealogy of the population' (Electron. J. Probab. 2017), proved the conjecture for the N-particle model itself. Bounded recall. Source posing it: Berestycki: Recent progress in coalescent theory, Ensaios Matematicos 2009, with open problems, Conjecture 6.1, p. 178.
Posed as open in Berestycki: Recent progress in coalescent theory, Ensaios Matematicos 2009, with open problems

[Proposition 16 of arXiv:2609.02444, 'The Hasse norm principle for $A_4$-quartic extensions of global function fields'] Let \(H \subset H(n_1,n_2)_{\CC}\) be a connected component.
  The pre-image of \(H\) in \(\widetilde H^{\rm fail}(n_1,n_2)_{\CC}\) has at most two connected components.
   Furthermore, the action of \(S_{n_2}\) on this preimage preserves the connected components.

[Thm 4 (Main theorem for $n=2$) of arXiv:2609.00974, 'On Algebraic Integrability\\ of Vector Fields \\ with Rational Function Coefficients\\ tha'] Let $f,g\in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}(X)$ be nonzero rational functions.
    Let $PFD(\frac{1}{f})=P_1+L_1+H_1$ and $PFD(\frac{1}{g})=P_2+L_2+H_2$ be partial fraction decompositions over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, see Theorem \ref{thm: PFD}, where $L_i=\sum_{j=1}^{d_i}\frac{c_{i,j}}{X-\alpha_{i,j}}$ for $i=1,2$.
    Let $D=f(x)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}+g(y)\frac{\partial}{\partial y}$ be a derivation.

    Then the following are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For almost all primes, the derivation $D$ modulo $p$ is $p$-closed.
        \item One of the following is true:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item We have $L_1=L_2=0$.
        \item We have $P_1=P_2=H_1=H_2=0$, and 
        
        there exists $\eta\in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, $\eta\ne 0$, such that for all $i,j$ we have $\eta c_{i,j}\in {\mathbb{Q}}$.
    \end{enumerate}
        \item There exists a non-constant $F\in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}(x,y)$ such that $D(F)=0$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Moreover, we can write explicit formulas for the killed element:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item (2a) We can take: $F\coloneqq \int \frac{dx}{f}-\int \frac{dy}{g}$.
        \item (2b) We can take: $G \coloneqq \op{exp}\left(N\eta \left(\int \frac{dx}{f}-\int \frac{dy}{g}\right)\right)$, where $N\ne 0$ is any integer such that $N\eta c_{i,j}\in \mathbb{Z}$.
    \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Main theorem for $n=2$

[Definition Kk:(K1 K2) of arXiv:2605.16963, 'Stochastic Euler Equations with Pseudo-differential Noise: Continuous and Discontinuous Pe'] Let $d, m \ge 1$ and $s\in\mathbb R$. A subset $\mathscr O\subset {\mathrm{OP}}\mathfrak M^{s}$ is said to be bounded if
		$
		\big\{\mathscr{p}: {\mathrm{OP}}(\mathscr{p})\in \mathscr O\big\}\subset \mathfrak M^{s}
		$
		is bounded with respect to the seminorms in (equation OPM seminorms of the paper). Let $\varsigma \ge 0$.
		We define
		\[
		\mathbb{M}^{\varsigma} \triangleq \left\{\mathcal K:\
		\text{there exist }\mathcal H={\mathrm{diag}}(\mathcal H_{1},\cdots ,\mathcal H_{m})\in\mathrm{OP}\mathfrak M^{\varsigma}
		\text{ and }\mathcal E\in\mathrm{OP}\mathfrak M^0\text{ such that }
		\mathcal K=\mathcal H+\mathcal E
		\text{ and  (Kk:(K1 K2) of the paper)  holds} \right\},
		\]
		where condition (Kk:(K1 K2) of the paper) is specified as follows:
		\begin{enumerate}[label={$(\mathbf{K}^{\varsigma})$},leftmargin=0.79cm]

Let a target width-D ReLU FNN have depth q>=1, weights A_i and biases a_i, i=1,...,q. Let the frozen width-D ReLU FNN have depth L>=q, weights W_l, and let every adapted bias be freely trainable. All weights are real D-by-D matrices; every layer, including the output layer, applies ReLU. Let X subset R^D be bounded, M=floor(L/q), and partition the frozen layers into consecutive blocks P_i={(i-1)M+1,...,iM} for i<q and P_q={(q-1)M+1,...,L}. Define B_i as the ordered product of W_l in P_i (later layers on the left), and E_i=A_i-B_i. For fixed integer 1<=R<=D, assume every W_l and every B_i+LR_j(E_i) for i=1,...,q and integers 0<=j<=R(M-1) are nonsingular, with fixed nested SVD truncations for each E_i. If R>=ceil(max_i rank(E_i)/M), then there exist rank-at-most-R additive weight updates at every frozen layer and choices of all biases such that the adapted FNN equals the target FNN at every x in X. This is an existence/expressivity statement; it provides no guarantee for gradient descent, fixed or zero biases, an unbounded input domain, or bounded-bit parameters.
Target depth q>=1 and frozen depth L>=q, equal square width D
Bounded input set and ReLU at every layer
All biases are trainable without size constraints
Assumption1: frozen weights and every stated partial low-rank correction are nonsingular
Rank threshold at least ceil(maximum block error rank /floor(L/q))
No claim about learnability or finite-sample excess risk

[Lemma le:martingale of arXiv:2604.21142, 'Gaussian fluctuations for Internal DLA on cylinders'] Let $\psi : {\ensuremath{\mathbb G}} _N \to {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}} $ be a discrete harmonic function with the zero horizontal average property~(equation eq:zero_average of the paper) and exponential decay as $y \to -\infty$, let $(A(t))_{t \geq 0}$ be an IDLA process on ${\ensuremath{\mathbb G}} _N$ with $A(0) = R_0$, and let
	\[ M(t) \coloneqq \frac{1}{N}\,\langle \! \langle D_t, \psi\rangle \! \rangle = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{(x,y) \in A_+(t)} \psi(x, y) \qquad (t \geq 0)\,. \]
Then $(M(t))_{t \geq 0}$ is a martingale with respect to the natural filtration of the IDLA process.

body: In graph theory, Kuratowski's theorem is a mathematical forbidden graph characterization of planar graphs, named after Kazimierz Kuratowski. It states that a finite graph is planar if and only if it does not contain a subgraph that is a subdivision of K_5 (the complete graph on five vertices) nor of K_{3,3} (the complete bipartite graph on six vertices with parts of size three, the utility graph).

body: Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables with E[X_i] = 0 and Var(X_i) < infinity for each i, and let S_k = X_1 + ... + X_k. Then for every lambda > 0, P(max_{1 <= k <= n} |S_k| >= lambda) <= Var(S_n) / lambda^2 = (sum_{i=1}^n Var(X_i)) / lambda^2. This strengthens Chebyshev's inequality applied to S_n alone into a bound on the whole running maximum. [Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples]

STATUS: proof (unaudited), owner-own-work draft. For the coupled scalar two-token joint-head factored-attention logistic gradient flow, every nonzero-imbalance leaf k^2-q^2=C has a unique reduced saddle and two escaping basins. In full R^3 almost every initialization escapes with kq,v of matching infinite sign, factors O(sqrt(log |v|)), head-normalized limit +/-e_v and margin Gamma_+ or Gamma_-. The finite saddle-stable set plus balanced planes is null. Balanced k=-q, v>0 and max root<kq<0 instead collapse to uniform attention and margin min a_i, showing an actual third fate on a null surface.

# Target 1: almost-everywhere full-space factored gradient-flow classification

Version 1, proof unaudited. Owner own work; novelty unestablished.
This concerns continuous gradient flow, not arbitrary-step GD.

## Statement

For n>=2, b_i,kappa_i>0, 0<a_i<b_i, set
h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s) and
L(v,k,q)=mean_i log(1+exp(-v h_i(kq))).
Let p_bar be the unique zero of mean_i h_i. For every initial point with
C=k^2-q^2!=0, the Euclidean gradient flow exists globally forward and has
exactly one of these outcomes:

1. convergence to a finite point on the stationary curve v=0,kq=p_bar;
2. v,kq->+infinity, loss->0, normalized direction (v,k,q)/norm ->(1,0,0);
3. v,kq->-infinity, loss->0, normalized direction ->(-1,0,0).

The set in outcome 1, together with the excluded balanced surfaces C=0,
has three-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Hence almost every finite
initialization belongs to one of the two escaping basins. Both basins
are open in the FULL parameter space, are nonempty, and have respective
normalized minimum margins Gamma_+=min_i(a_i+b_i) and Gamma_-=min_i(b_i-a_i).
The second is strictly inferior, as in claim 010. The known imbalance
invariant is used for reduction, not claimed as a new result.

We do not classify trajectories on C=0 in this theorem. They really allow
another fate: on k=q=0, v solves v_dot=mean_i a_i/(1+exp(v a_i))>0,
so v->infinity and L->0 while attention stays uniform. In fact a relatively
open subset of the balanced plane has this fate: if k=-q!=0, v>0 and
R<kq<0, where R=max_i rho_i<0, then v increases, s increases toward zero,
and k,q tend to zero. To check this, all h_i(s)>=c>0, forcing v->infinity.
If s tended to a strictly negative limit, alpha=2|s| and all h_i' would
be bounded below there; ds/dv>=c_1 v would contradict bounded s. Thus
s->0 and both factors vanish. Its normalized margin is min_i a_i.
These null sets demonstrate why the almost-everywhere qualification
must not be omitted.

## Reduction and global existence

Put s=kq, F=mean_i g_i h_i(s), G=mean_i g_i h_i'(s)>0,
g_i=(1+exp(v h_i(s)))^-1. Flow equations are

 v_dot=F, k_dot=vqG, q_dot=vkG.

Differentiating gives d(k^2-q^2)/dt=0. Also
(k^2+q^2)^2=C^2+4s^2. Thus on a fixed nonzero-C leaf,

 v_dot=F(v,s), s_dot=alpha_C(s) vG(v,s),
 alpha_C(s)=sqrt(C^2+4s^2)>0.

If H=max_i(a_i+b_i), M=max_i b_i kappa_i, then |v_dot|<=H.
On any finite time interval v is bounded, and
|k_dot|+|q_dot|<=M|v|(|k|+|q|). Gronwall gives finite factors on that
interval. The smooth full flow therefore has no finite-time blow-up,
in either time direction. Nonzero-C leaf coordinates are global charts on
each sheet: for C>0 fix sign k, solve
k=sign(k)sqrt((alpha_C(s)+C)/2), q=s/k;
for C<0 instead fix sign q and use the symmetric formula.

-A<=F_v<=0, F_0 strictly increases with unique zero p_bar, and G>0.

on each sheet. With u=s-p_bar, the two good quadrants v,u>0 and v,u<0
are forward invariant: s_dot has sign v; on the boundary v=0 the vector
field F_0(s) points into the respective quadrant. More explicitly, in
the positive quadrant v_dot>=-A v, so a strictly positive v cannot hit zero
in finite time, and u increases. Reflection treats the negative quadrant.

Both coordinates move monotonically toward their axes until one axis is
crossed or the orbit stays forever. Crossing an axis enters a good quadrant;
uniqueness excludes hitting the equilibrium in finite time. If the orbit
stays in the bad quadrant, it has a finite limit. Continuity and monotonicity
force F=alpha_C vG=0 at that limit, hence it is the saddle.
The other bad quadrant is handled by the reflected links -h_i(-s).
Nonstationary points on an axis enter a good quadrant immediately.

## Escape from good quadrants

Consider the positive quadrant. Then s increases from s_0>p_bar.
Suppose s tends to finite P. If v is bounded, compactness and
alpha_C G>0 imply integral_0^infinity v(t)dt<infinity.
Since |v_dot|<=H, the nonnegative function v is uniformly continuous;
the elementary disjoint-triangle argument gives v->0. But then
v_dot->F_0(P)>0, contradiction.

       >=|C| d v/H,

bounded below. Therefore v->infinity. Reflection proves negative escape.

alpha_C(s)<=|C|+2s and

zero-loss limits follow. By fixed C and |s|->infinity, both |k| and |q|
also tend to infinity (their squared difference is constant).

 [[-A_s,B_s],[alpha_C(p_bar) B_s,0]],

the limiting condition using countable thresholds and integer times.

body: [Lemma 6 (Conformal factor comparison) of arXiv:2608.26619, 'Uniqueness of Positively Curved Ancient Ricci Flows on Surfaces with Boundary'] Suppose we are given a solution to the (not necessarily rotationally symmetric) Ricci flow with boundary $u(\psi,\theta,t)$ starting from initial data $u_0 = u_0(\psi,\theta)$. If for a time-slice $U_1(-T)$ (resp. $U_2(-T)$) of the spherical cap supersolution $U_1$ (resp. subsolution $U_2$) one has $u_0\leq U_1(-T)$  (resp. $\geq$), then $u(t) \leq U_1(t-T)$ (resp. $\geq$) for all $t>0$ for which the flows are defined.

body:
[Proposition 34 (Bulk confinement and one-outlier alternative) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let \(M_N\) denote either \(M_N^{(4)}\) or \(M_N^f\).  For every fixed
\(\delta>0\), all but possibly one eigenvalue of \(M_N\) lie in
\([-2-\delta,2+\delta]\) with probability \(1-o(1)\).  More precisely:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item if \(|\theta|\le1\), then
\(\spec(M_N)\subset[-2-\delta,2+\delta]\) with probability \(1-o(1)\);
\item if \(|\theta|>1\), then there is one eigenvalue on the side determined
by \(\theta\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \lambda_{\rm out}(M_N)\longrightarrow
 \rho_\theta=\theta+\theta^{-1}.
\end{equation}
All remaining eigenvalues lie in \([-2-\delta,2+\delta]\).  In particular,
if \(0<\delta<|\rho_\theta|-2\), the outlier is the unique eigenvalue outside
that interval with probability \(1-o(1)\).
\end{enumerate}

body:
Fix -1<a<1 and sigma_a(t)=t for t>=0, sigma_a(t)=a*t for t<0, applied coordinatewise. A depth-L network has L affine layers, activation after the first L-1 layers, and an affine final output. Its squared parameter cost is sum_ell (||W_ell||_F^2+||b_ell||_2^2). For a function f and domain Omega, R_L is the infimum of this cost over all such finite-width networks equal to f on Omega; R_L=+infinity if the class is empty. Let Omega be a nonempty bounded open subset of R^d. Suppose f=g composed with h on Omega, where h:R^d->R^k and g:R^k->R^m are continuous finite piecewise-affine functions and k>=1. Translate h by a constant vector so h(Omega) lies in the strictly positive orthant, and compensate the input of g. There exist fixed finite depths L_h,L_g and finite constant B, independent of L, such that for every integer L>=L_h+L_g, R_L<=B+k*(L-L_h-L_g). Here B is the total squared parameter cost of fixed networks realizing the translated factors. Hence limsup_(L->infinity) R_L/L<=k. For k=0, the corresponding factorization means f is constant on Omega; using zero weights and the final output bias gives R_L<=||f||_2^2 for every L. A prescribed-width version requires widths sufficient for the fixed end subnetworks and width at least k in the middle; arbitrary narrow architectures are excluded.

body:
A homogeneous linear equation c_1 x_1 + c_2 x_2 + ... + c_k x_k = 0 with integer coefficients is partition regular over the positive integers if for every finite coloring of the positive integers N, there exists a solution (x_1, ..., x_k) in N^k where all x_i have the same color.
c_1, ..., c_k are non-zero integers
k >= 2
title: Partition Regular Linear Equation

body: [Example 2.7 of arXiv:2110.05374, 'When Janson meets McDiarmid: Bounded difference inequalities under graph-dependence'] Let (X_1, X_2, X_3) be dependent random variables with K_3 as their dependency graph, and let (X_i)_{4≤i≤9} be independent random variables that are also independent of (X_1, X_2, X_3). Then the vertex-disjoint union G of K_3 and 6 copies of K_1 is a dependency graph for (X_i)_{i∈[9]}. If every X_i takes values in a real interval of length c ≥ 0, then for every t > 0 Janson's inequality (Theorem 1.4 of the paper, with χ_f(G) = 3) gives P(Σ_{i∈[9]} X_i − E[Σ_{i∈[9]} X_i] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−2t²/(27c²)), while Corollary 2.6 gives the better bound P(Σ_{i∈[9]} X_i − E[Σ_{i∈[9]} X_i] ≥ t) ≤ exp(−8t²/(81c²)). The second bound uses the fractional forest vertex cover with weight 1/2 on each of F_1 = {1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7}, F_2 = {1, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9} and F_3 = {2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9}: each G[F_k] is K_2 plus 4 copies of K_1, so (Σ_k w_k √(Σ_{{i,j}∈E(G[F_k])} (c_i + c_j)² + Σ_{T∈T(F_k)} c_{min,k,T}²))² = ((3c/2)·√(2² + 1 + 4))² = 81c²/4.

body: Lemma 23 (Rakhlin et al. (2015)). Let z be a Z-valued binary tree, F a class of functions Z -> {0, 1, ..., m}, z_0 the root of the tree, and F_j = {f in F | f(z_0) = j}. Let r >= 1 be an integer. If j, j' in {0, ..., m} are such that fat_r(F_j) = fat_r(F_j') = fat_r(F), then |j - j'| < r. In particular, there can be at most r values of j such that fat_r(F_j) = fat_r(F). Here fat_r(F) is the sequential fat-shattering dimension of F at scale r: the maximal depth of a tree that F shatters at scale r.

body: [Defn def:NW of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\Phi = (\varphi_t)$ be a (topological) flow on $M$. OPEN per arXiv:2609.02820v1 (Theorems 1.5–1.6, PDF pp.5–6); bounded later-work check found no settlement. In the critical iid particle–hole model on Z^4, particles take synchronous discrete-time simple random-walk steps and settle permanently into stationary holes. After immediate cancellation the iid integer-valued excess η is nonconstant, has mean zero and an exponential moment. Does P(the origin is strictly closer in ℓ1 distance to an unfilled hole than to an active particle at time t) tend to zero for every such law? The source proves yes for d≤3 and exhibits counterexamples for d≥5 with P(η=1)=P(η=−1)=p and P(η=0)=1−2p. It explicitly says simulations suggest this counterexample extends to d=4. This general particle–hole question is distinct from the original binary one-car-or-one-spot parking initial law. Novelty: KNOWN source gap; current openness not certified by zero indexed citations.

Eη=0; Eexp(θ|η|)<∞ for some θ>0

body: For any integers r, s >= 1, every sequence of more than (r-1)(s-1) distinct real numbers contains either an increasing subsequence of length r or a decreasing subsequence of length s. The bound is sharp: there exist sequences of exactly (r-1)(s-1) distinct reals with no increasing subsequence of length r and no decreasing subsequence of length s. [Erdos and Szekeres (1935); see Bollobas, Combinatorics]
title: Erdos-Szekeres Theorem (Monotone Subsequences)

[Lem taylor-expansion of arXiv:2607.05097, 'Asymptotics of Lyapunov Exponents and Phase Transitions for Fluids with Degenerate Forcing'] Let $K \in \mathbb{N}$, $m \in \mathbb{N}_0$, $M \geq \delta > 0$, and $f:\Delta^K(1) \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be smooth and such that
    $$\|D^m f(0)\| \geq \delta \quad \text{and} \quad \sup_{t \in \Delta^K(1)} \|D^{m+1} f(t)\| \leq M\,.$$
    
    Then there is some $C(K,m)$ (independent of $f$) such that
    $$\|f\|_{L^2(\Delta^K(1))} \geq C(K,m)\delta^{K/2+m+1}M^{-K/2-m} \,.$$

body: [Defn of arXiv:2412.09535, 'Local limit theorem for joint subgraph counts'] For an integer $n$, let $\mathcal{R}_n = \mathcal{R}/(\gamma_\kone - n)$ and for downwards closed $\mathcal{H}$ let $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{H},n} = \mathcal{R}_\mathcal{H}/(\gamma_\kone - n)$. Note that the intersection of the ideal $(\gamma_\kone - n) \subseteq \mathcal{R}$ with $\mathcal{R}_\mathcal{H}$ is the ideal generated $(\gamma_\kone - n)$ in $\mathcal{R}_\mathcal{H}$, so we may treat $\mathcal{R}_{\mathcal{H},n}$ as a subalgebra of $\mathcal{R}_n$.

body: PROVED (separable case of the bounded-density quadratic-form conjecture, 2026-09-22). If Q(X)=sum_j lambda_j X_j^2 is diagonal in the independent coordinates X_j (densities <=1) and has at least three eigenvalues with |lambda_j|>=1, then Q(X) has a density bounded by pi, and pi is attained (X1^2+X2^2, uniforms). Proof: among three eigenvalues of modulus >=1, two share a sign (pigeonhole); each squared term lambda X^2 has density <= y^{-1/2}; two same-sign terms convolve to a density <= B(1/2,1/2)=pi (Beta integral); convolving the remaining independent terms cannot increase the sup (Young). Sharpness: one large eigenvalue gives density y^{-1/2} (unbounded); two opposite-sign give a logarithmic singularity (unbounded). The GENERAL non-separable case remains OPEN: it reduces to a uniform L1 bound on the characteristic function, but the per-direction oscillatory decay integral e^{isx^2}f dx = O(|s|^{-1/2}) is NOT uniform over densities <=1 (for each s there is an admissible f with |integral|>=1/2), so the coupled case needs the joint oscillatory-integral analysis (resolution of singularities). Paper: Downloads/Quadratic_Form_Bounded_Density_paper.pdf.

for all $x\in X$.
Then, for all $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $r\geq 1\vee r_0$, and $U\subset B(r)$ satisfying $m(U)\geq \varepsilon m(B(r))$, we have 
\[
\lambda(U)
\geq 
\frac{C_n'}{r^{2+\varepsilon}}
\left(
\frac{m(B(r))}{m(U)}\right)^{\frac{2}{N}}\left[1\wedge \frac{1}{m(B(r))}\right] ^{\frac{1}{C_n'q(r^2)}}
\]
where $C_n'=C_n'(C,n)>0$ and 
\[
N\geq n\frac{q(r^2)}{q(r^2)-1}+ \frac{\ln \frac{1}{\varepsilon}}{\varepsilon}\frac{1}{\ln r}+\frac{1}{q(r^2)-1}\ln(1\vee m(B(r)))
\]

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). A probability measure mu on R is moment-determinate if it is the unique probability measure sharing its full sequence of moments (m_k)_{k>=0}. The Carleman condition gives a simple sufficient criterion: if sum_{k=1}^infinity m_{2k}^{-1/(2k)} = infinity, then mu is moment-determinate. In practice this is most often invoked via a stronger, easier-to-check sub-condition, such as subgaussian or lighter tails, for instance P(|X|>t) <= C exp(-ct^2), which implies the even moments grow at most at Gaussian rate and hence satisfy Carleman's sum divergence; a common proof strategy in random matrix theory and random measure convergence is to show convergence of all moments to those of a known moment-determinate limit, such as the compactly supported semicircle law, and then invoke Carleman's condition, or compact support directly, to upgrade moment convergence to convergence in distribution. It does not hold automatically for every measure with finite moments of all orders: the classical log-normal distribution is the standard counterexample, having finite moments of every order yet failing to be moment-determinate, so other measures share its entire moment sequence, meaning that verifying Carleman's sum diverges, or invoking compact support, is a genuinely necessary step, not a formality. Typical failure: Assuming that finiteness of all moments, or even termwise convergence of a sequence's moments to a limit's moments, is sufficient to conclude convergence in distribution, without checking that the limit measure is itself moment-determinate; the log-normal-type failure of moment determinacy is the standard cautionary example, and in random matrix or random measure contexts, using the method of moments toward a limit whose determinacy has not been separately established, as happens for some heavy-tailed spectral limits, can produce a plausible-looking but invalid convergence claim. Canonical reference: Carleman, 1926, Les Fonctions Quasi Analytiques, Gauthier-Villars; Akhiezer, The Classical Moment Problem, 1965, Hafner Publishing; Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, 2010, Cambridge University Press.

body:
[Theorem thm:introduction-lattice-induction of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] The following assertions hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item
For every $d\geq 1$, each lattice-induced
probability-preserving Borel $\mathbb R^d$-space admits a
generating stealthy Delone cross-section.

\item
Let $\eta$ be an ergodic translation-invariant point process on
$\mathbb R$ with positive intensity and local second moments. If
\[
    \int_{0<|\xi|<1}
    \frac{1}{\xi^2}\,d\sigma_\eta(\xi)
    <
    \infty,
\]
then the translation action on its configuration space has a
nonzero eigenvalue and is lattice-induced.
\end{enumerate}

Consequently, an ergodic probability-preserving Borel
$\mathbb R$-space is lattice-induced if and only if it admits a
generating stealthy Delone cross-section. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Stealthy cross-sections and lattice induction

body:
Load-bearing hypothesis: the equivalence 'admissible shock ⇔ Lax inequalities f'(u_-) ≥ σ ≥ f'(u_+)' requires the flux to be convex (genuinely nonlinear) on the range of the data. For a nonconvex flux one must use Oleinik's full chord condition, which involves f at every intermediate state, not only the two endpoint derivatives. Counterexample: f(u) = u^4 - 5u^2 (so f'(u) = 4u^3 - 10u), left state u_- = 2, right state u_+ = -2. Since f(2) = f(-2) = -4, Rankine-Hugoniot gives the stationary shock σ = 0, and the Lax inequalities hold strictly: f'(2) = 12 > 0 > f'(-2) = -12. Yet the shock is NOT admissible: the chord joining (-2,-4) and (2,-4) is the constant -4, while f(0) = 0 lies ABOVE it, so Oleinik's condition fails; equivalently the Kruzhkov inequality with k = 0 requires σ(k - u_-) ≥ f(k) - f(u_-), i.e. 0 ≥ 4, which is false. The correct entropy solution of this Riemann problem is read off the least concave majorant of f on [-2,2] (the hull construction for a decreasing jump u_l > u_r): a shock from u_- = 2 down to u* = (√7 - 2)/3 ≈ 0.2153, the point at which the line through (2, f(2)) is tangent to the graph of f, then an attached rarefaction from u* down to -u*, then, by symmetry, a shock from -u* to u_+ = -2. The two shock speeds are -(16 + 14u*)/9 ≈ -2.113 and +(16 + 14u*)/9 ≈ +2.113, and the rarefaction sweeps the speeds between them. Auditor's check: whenever a proof calls a jump admissible using only characteristic speeds, verify convexity of the flux on the interval spanned by the two states; otherwise test the whole chord.
Counterexample flux f(u) = u^4 - 5u^2 with states u_- = 2, u_+ = -2, shock speed σ = 0
Lax inequalities compare σ only with f'(u_-) and f'(u_+)
Oleinik's condition requires the graph of f between the two states to lie on the correct side of the chord at EVERY intermediate value
For nonconvex flux the Riemann solution is generally a composite of shocks and rarefactions given by the convex (or concave) hull construction
title: Pitfall: Lax's Shock Inequalities Are Not Sufficient When the Flux Is Not Convex

body: Theorem (campaign status: audited-pass): Under affine spanning, projective simplicity, and coordinate-full homogenization, an affine fibre of density greater than 27/512 cannot have old geometric distance three. Structure: homogeneous compression yields an optimal residual plane; if it descends with any slack the old distance is ≤ 2; otherwise it has the saturated shared-h pattern, the balanced local relation reduces the old support to three or five coordinates, and long directions, flag estimates, planar spectra, the m = 8 exact normal forms, and the m ≤ 7 intrinsic enumeration cover every possible effective size. In each case either the density is ≤ 27/512 or an old rank-two residual certificate contradicts distance three. Notes: Quantifier: under the distance-three hypothesis EVERY optimal homogenized plane must be exceptional, so excluding any selected one suffices. Density threshold 27/512 ~ 0.0527. Finite components certified per p.27; this is a deterministic local theorem, not the determinant conjecture.

For a probability space of absolutely continuous characteristic paths theta=(a,b,w), assume finite integrated squared Euclidean speed, original w learning rate one, nonnegative loss with integral_0^t E||theta_prime||^2 <= L0-Lt, L0<=E, and rotationally invariant p0=w0/sqrt(d) with E||p0||^2<=R^2. For fixed unit u and gamma_t=<w_t,u>/sqrt(d), ||gamma_t||_2 <= (R+sqrt(t*(L0-Lt)))/sqrt(d) <= (R+sqrt(t E))/sqrt(d). If P(|gamma_t|>=h)>=m>0, necessarily t E >= [sqrt(d)*h*sqrt(m)-R]_+^2. If Law(gamma_t)>=ell Lebesgue on [l,r], then replace h sqrt(m) with sqrt(ell*(r^3-l^3)/3). Hence bounded initial loss and normalized second moment exclude fixed positive unweighted mass of order-one scales in t=o(d), without pointwise bounds on parameters. This standard action-displacement application does not control amplitude-weighted exponential features, does not rule out an O(d) alignment phase, and does not prove Target 3. Concrete smooth flows need the explicitly stated differentiation and energy hypotheses; global existence is not asserted.

For a connected finite plane honeycomb graph with f bounded faces and compatible prescribed boundary midpoint values, the homogeneous vertex-relation kernel has complex dimension f. Fewer than f additional complex linear conditions cannot determine interior midpoint values uniquely. Exactly f suffice: orient each internal edge, put J_e=(v-u)F(p_e)/2, and impose c_i^T J=0 on the real signed cycle vectors of the bounded faces. These constraints give a unique solution to the algebraic boundary problem; they are not claimed to hold for the actual SAW observable or to prove a scaling limit. This is an author-proved auxiliary result, pending full independent review.

Let mu be a nonnegative Borel measure on R such that every polynomial is absolutely integrable and integral q(t)^2 dmu(t)>0 for every nonzero real polynomial q. Let p_k be its degree-k monic orthogonal polynomials, with p_0=1. Fix n>=1 and alpha in R, and write r_1<...<r_n for the n distinct real roots of p_n+alpha p_(n-1). There are strictly positive real numbers lambda_1,...,lambda_n such that integral f(t)dmu(t)=sum_(i=1)^n lambda_i f(r_i) for every real polynomial f of degree<=2n-2. These weights are unique. The parameter alpha is arbitrary real; no support-location restriction on the roots is added. The asserted exactness degree is2n-2, not2n-1 for arbitrary alpha. This is Lemma3.6 of Cohn-Kumar.
mu nonnegative; every nonzero polynomial has positive squared norm; all polynomial absolute moments finite
p_k monic orthogonal; n>=1; alpha any real number
the n roots are real and distinct, as in the source Section3 setup

[Corollary of arXiv:2605.15066, 'The critical activation density in graph bootstrap percolation'] Let $A$ be a graph. 
Consider the graphs $F_e$ in 
Lemma (L_Fs of the paper). Suppose that, for some $e$ in $\langle A\rangle_H\setminus A$, 
we have $v(F_e)>v(H)e(H)$. 
Then, for some $f$ that is added to $A$ before $e$ during the WGA, 
we have 
\[
v(F_e)/e(H)
\leqslant v(F_f)<v(F_e).
\]

[Proposition 2 (Probabilistic representation and error decomposition) of arXiv:2604.23133, 'High-Precision Framework for Expected Hitting Times Analysis in the Dice-Sum Process'] For every \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(s \ge 0\), define
\[
F(s) := \mathbb{E}_s\big[\min(T,\omega_N)\big].
\]
Then, \(F\) satisfies the same recursion and boundary conditions as~\eqref{eq:ENdef}, and hence provides a solution of the truncated recursion.
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
E(s) - F(s)
\;=\;
\mathbb{E}_s\!\big[(T - \omega_N)\,\mathbf{1}_{\{\omega_N < T\}}\big].
\end{equation}
In words, \(\min(T,\omega_N)\) represents the truncated stopping time, and
\((T-\omega_N)\mathbf{1}_{\{\omega_N<T\}}\) is the additional waiting time incurred along paths that overshoot the cutoff \(N\) before hitting the target set~\(\mathcal{H}\).

	\begin{equation}
		\|  y \|_{Y_\alpha}\,\le\, \|  y \|_{Y_0}^{1-\alpha} \|  y \|_{Y_1}^\alpha
	\end{equation}
	holds for some $\alpha \in (0,1)$. Let $(X_\epsilon)_{\epsilon\in (0,1)}$ be a family of $Y_\alpha$-valued random variables  that is uniformly tight in $ Y_0$ and has uniform tail estimates in $Y_1$, i.e., 
	\[\biggl(\sup_{\epsilon\in (0,1)} \mathbb{P} ( \|X_\epsilon \|_{Y_1} \ge N) \biggr)\,\to\, 0,
	\]
	as $N\to\infty$. Then $(X_\epsilon)_{\epsilon\in (0,1)}$ is also tight in $Y_\alpha$.

[Theorem 2.7 (van den Berg) of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] Suppose that $D$ is simply connected and that $\partial D$ is Minkowski nondegenerate with
Minkowski dimension $\msf d_M(\partial D)\in[1,2)$. That is,
\[0<\liminf_{r\to0}\frac{\msf{A}(\partial D_r)}{r^{2-\msf d_M(\partial D)}}\leq
\limsup_{r\to0}\frac{\msf{A}(\partial D_r)}{r^{2-\msf d_M(\partial D)}}<\infty,\]
where we define
\[\partial D_r=\left\{x\in\mbb R^2:\inf_{y\in\partial D}|x-y|<r\right\}.\]
There exists constants $c\in(1,\infty)$ and $\th>0$ such that
\begin{align}

c^{-1}t^{1-\msf d_M(\partial D)/2}\leq\msf{A}(D)-\msf M_0(t)\leq ct^{1-\msf d_M(\partial D)/2},\qquad t\in(0,\th).

[Lemma lem:d_P_bound of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] \noindent{\nf(a)} Let $\bm\xi$ be a random vector in $L^q$, i.e. $\mathds{E}[|\bm\xi|^q]<\infty$, for some $q\in(0,1]$. Then, 
$$\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{\xi},a\bm{\xi})\geqslant |1-a^q|\mathds{E}\big[|\bm\xi|^q\big] \quad \text{ for any constant }a \in(0,\infty).$$

\noindent{\nf(b)} Assume that the random vectors
$\bm\xi_1, \bm\xi_2, \bm\zeta_1, \bm\zeta_2$ are in $L^q$, for some $q\in(0,1]$, and that 
$(\bm{\xi}_1,\bm{\zeta}_1)$ and $(\bm{\xi}_2, \bm{\zeta}_2)$ are independent. Then the following inequality holds:
\begin{equation*}
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{\xi}_1+\bm{\xi}_2,\bm{\zeta}_1+\bm{\zeta}_2)
\leqslant \mathcal{W}_q(\bm{\xi}_1,\bm{\zeta}_1) + \mathcal{W}_q(\bm{\xi}_2,\bm{\zeta}_2).
\end{equation*}

body:
PROOF (UNAUDITED); novelty unverified. For deterministic x in R^d with d>=1 and s=||x||^2/d in (0,1], take independent standard Gaussian U(n by d), W(n by n), v(n), with n>=1. Define h=Ux/sqrt(d), a=tanh(h), H=Wa/sqrt(n), f=v^T tanh(H)/sqrt(n). With all raw U,W,v trainable and no biases, the diagonal NTK Theta_n=||grad_U f||_F^2+||grad_W f||_F^2+||grad_v f||^2 satisfies ||Theta_n-Theta_infty||_2<=37/sqrt(n). Here F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2, R(q)=E sech(sqrt(q)Z)^4 and Theta_infty=F(F(s))+(F(s)+s R(s))R(F(s)). This is also a W2 bound to the deterministic NTK point mass.
Two hidden layers of common width n; one fixed nonzero input, normalized squared norm <=1; independent Gaussian initialization; tanh; raw-parameter NTK scaling as stated; no trainable biases. Uses unaudited C021 and reviewed C002 v2 scalar kernel shape.
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:2e54f669559ce1276dfe40f4e7ccfcb607ea68e74c8a28015756a0133b6fdbad","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/2e/2e54f669559ce1276dfe40f4e7ccfcb607ea68e74c8a28015756a0133b6fdbad.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:e2e1bc637816e6b944341d984f919970cfde3f7ed1aa1e1b29dfda4fadb928db","bundle_entry_key":"t250_w712_c022","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c021-c022-transpose-tanh-ntk","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Tensor Programs and Gaussian shared-weight conditioning","draft":"w712/bundle_016.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:two-hidden-tanh-diagonal-ntk-rate","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C022 v1: n^(-1/2) rate for one initial two-hidden-layer tanh NTK program

Kind: narrowed. Target: 2, one transpose-using program.
Status: proof (unaudited). Novelty unverified. This is a one-input
diagonal NTK result, not the entire NTK matrix on multiple inputs or
a quantitative Master Theorem for arbitrary transpose programs.

## Model and statement

Let x in R^d be deterministic, with d>=1 and s=||x||^2/d in (0,1].
Let U in R^(n by d), W in R^(n by n) and v in R^n have independent
standard Gaussian entries, mutually independent, with n>=1. Define

    h=Ux/sqrt(d), a=tanh(h), H=Wa/sqrt(n),
    f(x)=v^T tanh(H)/sqrt(n).

All nonlinearities are coordinatewise. Train the raw parameters U,W,v
with the displayed scaling retained in the computational graph; there
are no bias parameters. The scalar diagonal empirical NTK is

    Theta_n(x,x)=||grad_U f||_F^2+||grad_W f||_F^2+||grad_v f||^2.

For Z standard Gaussian put

    F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2,
    R(q)=E sech(sqrt(q)Z)^4,
    q1=F(s), q2=F(q1), r1=R(s), r2=R(q1),
    Theta_infty=q2+(q1+s r1)r2.

Then, for all n>=1,

    ||Theta_n(x,x)-Theta_infty||_2 <=37/sqrt(n).     (1)

Equivalently, W2(Law(Theta_n(x,x)),delta_(Theta_infty)) is at most
37/sqrt(n), since coupling to a deterministic point has exactly that
L2 cost. The constant is universal on 0<s<=1 and deliberately loose.
The program genuinely uses W and W^T together; the quantitative shared-
weight step is C021, not an independent-backward-weight replacement.

## 1. Differentiate the exact finite-width program

Set qhat=||a||^2/n, D=diag(sech(h_i)^4), rhat=tr(D)/n,
g_j=sech(H_j)^2, b_j=v_j g_j and Rhat=||b||^2/n. Direct differentiation
with respect to the raw parameters in the stated parametrization gives

    ||grad_v f||^2 = Qhat2:=mean_j tanh(H_j)^2,
    ||grad_W f||_F^2 = qhat Rhat,
    ||grad_U f||_F^2 = s T,
    T=b^T W D W^T b/n^2.

For the last line grad_(U_ik) f=x_k sech(h_i)^2(W^Tb)_i/(n sqrt(d));
summing its square over i,k supplies exactly s, not an additional n.
Hence

    Theta_n=Qhat2+qhat Rhat+s T.                    (2)

Conditional on h, a,D are fixed with 0<=D<=I, and a!=0 almost surely
because s>0 and tanh vanishes only at zero. W,v are still fresh independent
Gaussians. C021 with g(t)=sech(t)^2 therefore gives, conditionally and
then unconditionally,

    ||T-rhat Rhat||_2<=9/sqrt(n).                   (3)

This is the only new transpose-conditioning input, and is unaudited.

## 2. Scalar forward and derivative moments

The h_i are iid N(0,s). Since tanh^2 and sech^4 lie in [0,1],

    ||qhat-q1||_2<=1/sqrt(n),
    ||rhat-r1||_2<=1/sqrt(n).                       (4)

Given h, the H_j are iid N(0,qhat). Thus

    ||Qhat2-F(qhat)||_2<=1/sqrt(n).

The independently reviewed C002 establishes that F is increasing and
concave, with F(0)=0 and F'(0+)=1. Consequently it is 1-Lipschitz on
[0,1]. Equations (4) give

    ||Qhat2-q2||_2<=2/sqrt(n).                      (5)

Given h, the pairs (H_j,v_j) are iid and E Rhat=R(qhat). Their individual
second moment is E[v_j^4 sech(H_j)^8]<=3. Conditional variance and total
expectation therefore give

    ||Rhat-R(qhat)||_2<=sqrt(3)/sqrt(n).             (6)

We also need a Lipschitz bound for R, proved here without an inverse
variance denominator. Let psi(t)=sech(t)^4. Its second derivative is

    psi''(t)=16 sech(t)^4 tanh(t)^2-4 sech(t)^6,

so |psi''|<=20 on R. If 0<=p<=q, take independent standard Gaussians
Z,Z'. The random variable sqrt(p)Z+sqrt(q-p)Z' has variance q. Taylor's
theorem, with a pointwise remainder at most 10(q-p)(Z')^2, and conditional
centering of the first-order term in Z', show

    |R(q)-R(p)|<=10(q-p).                          (7)

All expectations of the remainder are finite; psi' is bounded, so the
centered linear term is integrable. This includes p=0 and does not move
an uncontrolled derivative or limit through an integral.

## 3. Assemble the NTK rate without factoring dependent errors

Put Ahat=qhat+s rhat and A=q1+s r1. Both lie in [0,2]. From (2)--(3),

    ||Theta_n-[Qhat2+Ahat Rhat]||_2<=9/sqrt(n).      (8)

Expand the remaining product in the following exact order:

    Ahat Rhat-A r2
       =Ahat[Rhat-R(qhat)]
        +Ahat[R(qhat)-R(q1)]+(Ahat-A)r2.

Bounding Ahat pointwise by 2, r2 by 1, and using (4), (6), (7),

    ||Ahat Rhat-A r2||_2
       <=[2sqrt(3)+20+2]/sqrt(n).                  (9)

Neither Ahat nor qhat is assumed independent of Rhat. Triangle
inequalities with pointwise bounds suffice. Combine (5), (8), (9):

    ||Theta_n-Theta_infty||_2
       <=[33+2sqrt(3)]/sqrt(n)<37/sqrt(n),

using sqrt(3)<2. This proves (1).

## Scope, prior work, and remaining question

This is an explicit bounded-smooth-activation, diagonal, single-input
example of Target2. It does not control the NTK at two distinct inputs,
the full backward row distribution, growing depth, or reuse in a general
Tensor Program. The next mathematical extension is the off-diagonal
kernel: joint forward conditioning then has rank two and may become
ill-conditioned when the input features align.

Primary-source prior-work check: Hanin--Nica, arXiv:1909.05989v1,
Theorem1, PDF page4, treats ReLU diagonal NTK moments with zero-initialized
but trainable biases and two-sided second-moment comparability. That
comparability alone is insufficient to subtract the squared mean and
deduce a variance O(1/n); no such inference is used here. This is not a
claim that an n^(-1/2) tanh NTK rate is new in the literature. Independent
novelty assessment remains pending. The elementary Gaussian conditioning
mechanism itself is standard and is not claimed new.

Load-bearing checks: the precise raw-parameter normalization in section1;
the conditional independence required by C021; qhat>0 almost surely;
bounded derivatives for (6)--(7); and pointwise rather than independence
estimates in (9). At n=1 the conditioning still includes the rank-one
term, and (1) remains valid. There is no s=0 cancellation in the proof;
that case is outside the stated range. All checks are author checks only.
Formalization remains UNVERIFIED; no independently checked proof or

There exists a strongly continuous semigroup (T(t))_{t >= 0} of bounded linear operators on X with ||T(t)|| <= 1 for every t >= 0 (a contraction semigroup) whose infinitesimal generator is A if and only if: (i) A is closed and D(A) is dense in X; and (ii) every lambda > 0 lies in the resolvent set of A, with ||(lambda I - A)^{-1}|| <= 1/lambda for every lambda > 0. [Theorem thm:explicit_current_1 of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let $(X_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be an ergodic diffusion with invariant measure $\mu$ whose
symmetric part $\mathcal{L}_S$ satisfies the Poincar\'e inequality~(equation eq:poincare of the paper)
with spectral gap $\lambda_\mathrm{gap}>0$ (Assumptions~(ass:dynamics of the paper)). 
Let $\overline{J}_t(U)$ denote the empirical current according to Definition~(def:empirical_current of the paper)
with ergodic mean $\E^\mu[\overline{J}_t(U)]=\E^\mu[v_{\textrm{s}}\cdot U]= \E^\mu[W]$,
and let $\nu\ll\mu$ with $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu\in L^2(\mu)$.
Then for all $t > 0$ and $a > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{J}_t(U) - \E^\mu[\overline{J}_t] \geq a\right)
  \leq
  \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}
  \exp\left[-t\frac{\tilde\sigma_{J,1}^2}{c_{J,1}^2}h\left(\frac{c_{J,1} a}{\tilde\sigma_{J,1}^2}\right)\right],
  
\end{align}
where $h(u) \equiv 1 + u - \sqrt{1+2u}$ and we define
\begin{align}
  \tilde\sigma_{J,1}^2 \equiv
  \frac{2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(W)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}} + 2\|Q\|_{L^\infty(\mu)},
  \qquad 
  c_{J,1} \equiv \frac{\|W-\E^\mu[W]\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}}.
\end{align}

body: Theorem (campaign status: audited-pass): Choose an independent dominating set U in C_n of size d = ceil(n/3) whose cyclic gaps have (edge-)length two or three. Put L_u = A + B_u and R = span{L_u : u in U}; the L_u are independent. Orient the cycle: in a length-two gap u-v-u' take basis forms B_v, C_v; in a length-three gap u-v-w-u' take B_v, C_v, C_w. Together with A these are exactly n+1 full-dual forms, linearly independent by backward substitution through each gap. Modulo R: B_u = -A, C_u = B_v, B_w = C_w in the relevant gap cases, so every full-dual form has a signed basis representative with residual in R. Hence dcb(A_n) = dgeo(A_n) = ceil(n/3). Notes: Explicit optimal certificate, not just an existence bound. Form count checks: sum of gap lengths = n edges, so d gaps contribute n forms, plus A = n+1.

[Theorem intro-fredi of arXiv:2412.09290, 'Asymptotics of Harish-Chandra transform and infinitesimal freeness'] (Theorem (fredi of the paper))
  
  Let $n$ be a fixed integer. Let $A$ be a random Hermitian matrix of size $N$ and assume
  that for every finite $r$ one has
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^{n \varepsilon} \left( \frac{1}{N} \log
    \mathbb{E}[H \text{} C (x_1, \ldots, x_r, 0^{N - r} ; \lambda_1 (A),
    \ldots, \lambda_n (A))] - \sum_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \sum_{i = 0}^r
    \frac{1}{N^{j \varepsilon}} \Psi_j (x_i) \right) = \sum_{i = 1}^r \Psi_n
    (x_i), 
  \end{equation}
  where $\Psi_0, \ldots, \Psi_n$ are smooth functions in a complex neighborhood of
  $0$, the above convergence is uniform in a complex neighborhood of $0^r$, and $0 <
  \varepsilon < n^{- 1}$. Then the $1 / N^{n \varepsilon}$ correction of the
  average empirical distribution of $N^{- 1} A$ is given by
  \begin{equation}
    \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} N^{n \varepsilon} \left( \frac{1}{N^{k + 1}}
    \mathbb{E}[\ensuremath{\operatorname{Tr}} (A^k)] - \sum_{j = 0}^{n - 1} \frac{1}{N^{j
    \varepsilon}} \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(j)}_k \right) =\ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_k^{(n)},
    
  \end{equation}
  where for every $j \in \{0, \ldots, n\}$
  \[ \ensuremath{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{(j)}_k := \sum_{b_1 + 2 b_2 + \cdots + j \text{} b_j
     = j} \sum_{m = 0}^{k - b_1 - \cdots - b_j} \frac{k!}{m! (m + 1) ! (k - m
     - b_1 - \cdots - b_j) !b_1 ! \ldots b_j !} \text{{\hspace{8em}}} \]
  \begin{equation}
    \text{{\hspace{14em}}} \times \left. \frac{\mathrm{d}^m}{\mathrm{d} x^m} ((\Psi'_0
    (x))^{k - m - b_1 - \cdots - b_j} (\Psi'_1 (x))^{b_1} \ldots (\Psi'_j
    (x))^{b_j}) \right|_{x = 0} . 
  \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem thm: main dual of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] The process $(V(-r)+r,\, r\ge 0)$ is a homogeneous Feller process starting from $0$. For any $r>0$, $\frac{V(-r)+r}{r}$ has distribution ${\mathcal B}(\frac{\widehat{\delta}}{2},\frac{\delta}{2})$. [Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.12839, 'Spiking Neural Networks with Elephant Reinforcement'] Let \(N<\infty\). Consider the process
\[
Y_t=(V_t,S_t,K_t)
\in \mathbb N^N\times\mathbb Z^N\times\mathbb N^N.
\]
Assume that site \(i\) fires with rate
\[
\lambda_i(V,S,K)
=
\mathbf 1_{\{V_i>\alpha S_i^+\}},
\qquad
S_i^+=\max\{S_i,0\},
\]
and leaks with rate
\[
\gamma\mathbf 1_{\{V_i>0\}},
\qquad \gamma>0.
\]
When site \(i\) fires, \(V_i\) is reset to \(0\), its two neighbours receive
one unit of potential, and
\[
S_i\mapsto S_i+\xi_i,
\qquad
K_i\mapsto K_i+1.
\]
Then the process is non-explosive. More precisely, if \(N_t\) denotes the
number of events up to time \(t\), then
\[
\mathbb E[N_t]\leq (\gamma+1)Nt<\infty.
\]

DRAFT concept backed by an author derivation, not a promoted theorem. Let mu_omega be random probability Borel measures, I a bounded open interval, 1<p<infinity, and eta_n>0 a deterministic sequence tending to zero. Set F_n(omega,E)=integral eta_n/((t-E)^2+eta_n^2) dmu_omega(t), jointly measurable. If sup_n E integral_I F_n^p <= C<infinity, then almost surely mu_omega|I=rho_omega dE with rho_omega in Lp(I), and E integral_I rho_omega^p <= C/pi^p. For 0<p<=1, integral_I F_eta^p <= |I|^(1-p)pi^p holds for every probability measure, including atoms; those power bounds alone cannot imply ac. p>1 is sufficient, not necessary for ac, and the criterion may yield zero mass on I.

[Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.18834, 'The Parabolic Anderson Model's Total Mass at Small Times: Geometry, Fluctuations, and Reno'] Suppose that Assumption \ref{Assumption} holds,
and let $\ka>0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $H_0>1/2$ or $\partial D$ is sufficiently irregular, then the deterministic
heat diffusion mechanism dominates $u_\ka$'s total mass asymptotics. More specifically:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $H_0>1/2$ and \eqref{Equation: Regular Heat Content} holds, then
\[\lim_{t\to0} t^{-1/2}\big(|D|-\msf M_\ka(t)\big)=\frac{\sqrt{2}|\partial D|}{\sqrt{\pi}}\qquad\text{in probability}.\]
\item If \eqref{Equation: Fractal Heat Content} holds for any $\msf m\in(d-1,d)$, then
\[\lim_{t\to0}\frac{1}{\log t}\log\big||D|-\msf M_\ka(t)\big|=\frac{d-\msf m}{2}\qquad\text{in probability}.\]
\end{enumerate}
\item If $H_0=1/2$ and \eqref{Equation: Regular Heat Content} holds, then as $t\to0$, one has
\[\mbf E\big[|D|-\msf M_\ka(t)\big]\sim\frac{\sqrt{2}|\partial D|}{\sqrt{\pi}}t^{1/2}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sqrt{\mbf{Var}\big[|D|-\msf M_\ka(t)\big]}\sim\ka\mf c\,t^{1/2}.\]
In particular, the noise now has an impact on the first-order total mass asymptotic via $\ka$ and the constant $\mf c$ in \eqref{Equation: c Constant}.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Analyse M(1,1) on Z^2 through the range of the first-coordinate walk. Result: In M(1,1) the first coordinate moves only at first visits and the second at later visits; the set of visited vertices is the range, and the first-coordinate process is a simple random walk on Z run at the rate of new visits. Recurrence of M(1,1) would follow if the walk returns to the origin infinitely often; since the second coordinate performs a simple random walk on the column above the current first coordinate whenever the vertex was visited before, the walk behaves in each column like a 1D random walk (recurrent) until it hits an unvisited vertex, at which time the first coordinate steps. The number of new visits up to time n is the range R_n; the first coordinate after n steps is a simple random walk at time R_n, so |X^1_n| is of order sqrt(R_n), and the range of a planar walk-like process is at most n, giving |X^1_n| <= sqrt n; a return to the origin requires both coordinates to vanish. A heuristic: if R_n ≍ n/log n as for planar simple random walk then the first coordinate is diffusive at the slower clock, and the walk is 'more recurrent' than planar simple random walk, supporting the conjecture; but the range of M(1,1) is not that of simple random walk because the exploration is column-wise. A rigorous partial fact: M(1,1) is recurrent if and only if the first coordinate returns to 0 infinitely often at times when the second coordinate is 0; since within a column the second coordinate is a recurrent 1D walk that keeps returning to 0 until it finds a new vertex, and new vertices in a column are found at the ends of the visited interval, the question is whether the first-coordinate walk (which is a simple random walk in the clock of new visits) visits 0 infinitely often, which it does a.s. (1D recurrence), and whether at those visits the second coordinate is 0 - not automatic. So recurrence of M(1,1) reduces to: at the (infinitely many) times the first coordinate is 0, the second coordinate, which then performs a 1D walk in the column of 0 with the visited interval of that column, returns to height 0 before finding a new vertex - which has probability bounded below by a constant each time if the visited interval around height 0 in column 0 has length bounded... the visited interval in column 0 grows, and the probability of returning to 0 from the boundary of an interval of length L before exiting is of order 1/L... summing over the visits to column 0 gives a divergent series only if the interval lengths grow slowly enough. This is the crux and I did not settle it; the reduction is recorded. Key identity: M(1,1) recurrent iff, at the infinitely many returns of the first coordinate to 0, the second coordinate returns to 0 in column 0 before finding a new vertex; the return probability is of order 1/(visited interval length). Obstruction: Growth rate of the visited interval in column 0 not controlled.

Method: Centered fourth-moment diameter inequality and reweighted Cauchy-profile critical points Result: Candidate sharp answer C=1. For any centered law Q of support diameter D, with a=E X^2 and b=E X^4, a<=D^2/4 and b+3a^2<=D^2*a. Reweighting mu by ((x-u)^2+R^2)^(-2) at a stationary Cauchy profile gives y=R^2<=3a when the second derivative is nonnegative, and 1/F=(b+2ay+y^2)/(a+y)<=D^2. Equality forces symmetric endpoint Bernoulli and a strict fourth-order maximum. Thus no local minimum has F<=1/D^2; each level 1/t for t>=D^2 has at most two roots. Biane parametrization and the source level-set lemma imply unimodality. Symmetric Bernoulli gives sharpness. Check: Second analytic route differentiates v_t directly at critical points. The centered moment inequality follows independently from E[(X-Xprime)^4]<=D^2*E[(X-Xprime)^2]. These are same-author checks, not independent review. Let A be a linear operator on a Banach space X, and let M ≥ 1, ω ∈ ℝ. The following are equivalent: (a) A generates a C_0-semigroup (T(t))_{t ≥ 0} with ‖T(t)‖ ≤ M e^{ωt} for all t ≥ 0; (b) A is closed, densely defined, every real λ > ω lies in ρ(A), and ‖(λ − A)^{-n}‖ ≤ M/(λ − ω)^n for all λ > ω and all n ≥ 1; (c) A is closed, densely defined, every λ with Re λ > ω lies in ρ(A), and ‖(λ − A)^{-n}‖ ≤ M/(Re λ − ω)^n for all such λ and all n ≥ 1. Contraction case (M = 1, ω = 0): A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup iff A is closed, densely defined, (0, ∞) ⊂ ρ(A) and ‖(λ − A)^{-1}‖ ≤ 1/λ for all λ > 0; here the single power n = 1 suffices. When M > 1 the estimates on all powers n cannot be dropped: the n = 1 bound alone is a strictly weaker (Kreiss-type) condition.
X is a Banach space
A is a linear operator, closed and densely defined in (b),(c)

[Definition 14 (Square well model (SWM)) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Fix $d\in\Z_{\geq 1}$ and $\beta\in\R_{\geq 0}$.
    For any domain $\Lambda$ and $\zeta:\Z^d\to[-1,1]$,
    the \emph{square well model} (SWM) on $\Lambda$ with boundary condition $\zeta$
    at inverse temperature $\beta$ is the probability measure  on $\alpha\in[-1,1]^\Lambda$ given by
    \[
        \diff\mu_{\SWM,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta(\alpha) = \frac1{Z_{\SWM,\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta} e^{-\beta H_{\SWM,\Lambda}^\zeta(\alpha)} \diff\alpha,
    \]
    where $Z_{\Lambda,\beta}^\zeta$ is the normalising constant,
    $\diff\alpha$ the Lebesgue measure, and
    \[
        H_{\SWM,\Lambda}^\zeta(\alpha) := \sum_{\substack{\{x,y\}\subset\Lambda\\x\sim y}} (\alpha_x-\alpha_y)^2 + \sum_{\substack{x\in\Lambda,\,y\in\Lambda^c\\x\sim y}} (\alpha_x-\zeta_y)^2.
    \]
    The label $\SWM$ is omitted when no confusion is likely to arise.
title: Square well model (SWM)

[Thm 5 of arXiv:2606.07194, 'Survival Probability of Markov Linear Reccurence Sequence in a Random Environment: Subcrit'] Let $\{Y_n\}$ be a strongly subcritical positive zero-absorbing MRSRE with $\rho\in (0,1)$. Assume that~(\ref{BnCond}) and ${\bf E}^{(h)}\kappa<\infty$ holds for some $h>h^*_+$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item \begin{equation}

{\bf P}(Y_n>0|Y_0=i)\sim f^*_i \rho^n,\quad {\bf P}(Y_n=k|Y_n>0)\to p_k^*,\ n\to\infty,
\end{equation}
where $\{p_k^*\}$ is a distribution, and $\{f^*_i\}$ is a bounded sequence such that
$$
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} p_{i,j} f^*_j=\rho f^*_i,\ i>0,\
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} p_i^* p_{i,j}=\rho p^*_i,\ j>0,\
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} p_i^* f^*_i=1;
$$
\item for any $h>h^*_+$ 
$$
{\bf P}(Y_n>0|Y_0=i)\le c i^h \rho^n,\ i>0,
$$
where $c=c(h)$ is some constant.
\item For any positive $h$ such that $R(h)<\rho$ and~(\ref{BnCond}) holds, the distribution $\{p_k^*\}$ has a finite $h$-th moment.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
For unit vectors v,w in C^n, let P=vv* and Q=ww*. Their determinantal laws are single-site laws with probabilities |v_i|^2 and |w_i|^2. The optimal coupling cost for normalized Hamming distance on subsets of {1,...,n} equals (1/n)sum_i ||v_i|^2-|w_i|^2| and is at most trace|P-Q|/n. If both laws are invariant under a finite permutation group, averaging yields an invariant coupling of the same cost. This is a finite rank-one result, with no general equivariant approximation theorem asserted.

body:
[Prop P:properties-elpp of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Fix $\rho \in \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty\}$, and let $\mathcal{Q}^\rho$ be a subsequential limit in law of $\mathcal{Q}_n^{\rho_n}$ along a sequence $\rho_n \to \rho$. Then $\mathcal{Q}^\rho$ satisfies the following properties. In what follows, $c> 0$ are universal constants, and we define
		$\mathcal{G}^\rho(x, s; y, t) = \mathcal{Q}^\rho(x, s; y, t) + \frac{(x-y)^2}{(t-s)}$ for any $(x,s;y,t)\in \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item \textup{(Independent increments)} For any disjoint collection of time intervals $(s_i, t_i), i\in\llbracket1, k \rrbracket$, the increments
		$\mathcal{Q}^\rho(\cdot, s_i; \cdot, t_i)$
		are independent.
		\item \textup{(Metric composition)} For any fixed $r < s < t$ and $x, y \ge 0$, we have
		$$
		\mathcal{Q}^\rho(x, s; y, t) = \max_{z \ge 0} \mathcal{Q}^\rho(x, s; z, r) + \mathcal{Q}^\rho(z, r; y, t).
		$$
		\item \textup{(KPZ scaling)} Fix $q > 0$, and consider the rescaled field
		$$
		\mathcal{Q}^{\rho, q}(x, s; y, t) := q^{-1} \mathcal{Q}^\rho(q^2x, q^3 s; q^2 y, q^3 t).
		$$
		Then $\mathcal{Q}^{\rho, q}$ is a subsequential limit of the sequence $\mathcal{Q}^{q \rho_n}_n$.
		\item \textup{(One-point tail bounds)} For $u = (x, s; y, s + t) \in \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$, and all $a > 0$,
		\begin{align*}
			\mathbb{P}( \mathcal{G}^\rho(u)< - a t^{1/3}) &\le 2\exp(-c a^3), \\
			\mathbb{P}( \mathcal{G}^\rho(u) > a t^{1/3} + t (\rho\vee 0)^2) &\le 2\exp\left(-c a^{3/2} \left(1 \wedge \frac{\sqrt{a}}{(\rho \vee 0) t^{1/3}}\right)\right).
		\end{align*}
		Furthermore, for $u = (0, s; 0, s + t)$ on the diagonal, we have the following Gaussian lower bound: for all $0 < a < t (\rho\vee 0)^2$,
		\begin{align*}
			\mathbb{P}( \mathcal{G}^\rho(u) < -a + t (\rho\vee 0)^2) &\le 2\exp\left(- \frac{ca^2}{(\rho\vee 0)t}\right).
		\end{align*}
		\item \textup{(Two-point spatial tail bound)} 
        There is a universal constant $C_0>0$, such that for any $u = (x, s; y, s+t), u' = (x, s; y + z, s+t)  \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$, and 
        $a>C_0\max(z^{3/2}/t, \sqrt{z}|x-y|/t, \sqrt{z} (\rho\vee 0))$,
        we have:
		\begin{equation}
			
\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{G}^\rho(u) - \mathcal{G}^\rho(u')| \ge a\sqrt{z}) \le 2 \exp(- c a^2).
		\end{equation}
		\item \textup{(Two-point temporal tail bound)} There is a universal constant $C_0>0$, such that for any $u = (x, s; y, s + t), u' = (x, s; y', s+t + r)  \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$, where $0<r<t$ and $(x, s), (y, s+t), (y', s + t + r)$ are all collinear, and $a > C_0\max(r^{2/3}(x-y)^2/t^2, r^{2/3}(\rho\vee 0)^2)$, we have:
		\begin{equation*}
			\mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{G}^\rho(u) - \mathcal{G}^\rho(u')| \ge a r^{1/3}) \le 2 \exp(- c a^{3/2}).
		\end{equation*}
		\item \textup{(Basic parabolic shape estimate)} For any $(x, s; y, s + t) \in \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$ and $a, \delta > 0$ we have:
		\begin{equation*}
            \begin{split}
                \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}^\rho(x, s; y + z, s+ t) &\le t(\rho\vee 0)^2  + a t^{1/3} + \delta z^2 \text{ for all } z \in [-y, \infty)) \\
                &\ge 1 - 2\exp\left(-c_\delta a^{3/2} \left(1\wedge \frac{\sqrt{a}}{(\rho\vee 0) t^{1/3}}\right)\right),
            \end{split}
		\end{equation*}
        where $c_\delta$ is a constant depending on $\delta$.
		\item \textup{(Time stationarity and reversal)} For any $r \in \mathbb{R}$, we have
        $$
\mathcal{Q}^\rho(x, s; y, t) \stackrel{d}{=} \mathcal{Q}^\rho(x, s + r; y, t + r) \stackrel{d}{=} \mathcal{Q}^\rho(y, -t; x, -s),
        $$
        where the equality in law is as continuous functions on $\mathbb H^2_\uparrow$. 

        \item \textup{(Quadrangle inequality)} For any $s < t$, and  $x_1 \le x_2$ and $y_1 \le y_2$, we have
        $$

[Corollary cor:sharp of arXiv:2608.25279, 'Provable Non-Acceleration of Standard Strang\\ Splittings of Kinetic Langevin Dynamics'] \begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm(i)] For the tuning
\begin{equation*}
 h=\frac1{4\sqrt\kappa},
 \qquad
 \gamma=4\sqrt\kappa,
 \qquad
 Q=Q_{1/(4\sqrt\kappa),\,4\sqrt\kappa}^{U},
\end{equation*}
there is a universal
constant $C_1<\infty$ such that, for every $\kappa>1$, $d\ge1$,
$U\in\mathcal U_\kappa^d$, every initial state $z$, and every
$\varepsilon\in(0,1)$,
\begin{equation*}
 t_{\mathrm{mix}}(z,\varepsilon;Q,\pi)
 \le C_1\kappa\log\!\left(\frac{C_1\kappa(1+W_2(\delta_z,\pi))}{\varepsilon}\right),
\end{equation*}
where $\pi$ is the unique invariant law of $Q$.
\item[\rm(ii)] Let $\mathfrak t$
be any numerically
stable fixed-parameter OBABO tuning rule, let $C,c>0$ and $a,b\ge0$
be constants, let $\tau:(1,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ satisfy
$\tau(\kappa)=o(\kappa)$ as $\kappa\to\infty$, and let
$\kappa_0>1$. Then there exist $\kappa\ge\kappa_0$ and
$U\in\mathcal U_\kappa^2$ such that $Q_{h_\kappa,\gamma_\kappa}^U$ has a
unique invariant law $\pi$, and there are $z\in\mathbb R^4$ and
$n\in\mathbb N$ for which
\begin{equation}
 \norm{\delta_z(Q_{h_\kappa,\gamma_\kappa}^U)^n-\pi}_{\mathrm{TV}}
 >C\kappa^a\bigl(1+W_2(\delta_z,\pi)\bigr)^b
   \exp\!\left(-\frac{cn}{\tau(\kappa)}\right).
\end{equation}
In particular, no such bound holds with $\tau(\kappa)=\kappa^\alpha$
for any $\alpha<1$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Sharpness of the diffusive scale

body:
[Thm 4 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] KCLGs in one dimension divide in three universality
classes:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $c(-1,0,\bone_{(-\infty,-1]})\neq0$ and $c(-1,0,\bone_{[0,\infty]})\neq0$,
then $q_{c}=0$. In this case the model is \emph{noncooperative} (see
\cite{Shapira2024Noncooperative} and Section \ref{subsec:noncooperative}
below).
\item If $c(-1,0,\bone_{(-\infty,-1]})=0$ and $c(-1,0,\bone_{[0,\infty)})=0$,
then $q_{c}=1$. We say in this case that the model is \emph{blocked}.
\item If $c(-1,0,\bone_{(-\infty,-1]})\neq0$ and $c(-1,0,\bone_{[0,\infty)})=0$
or vice versa, then $q_{c}\in(0,1)$. We call such models \emph{one-sided}.
\end{enumerate}
By $\bone_{(-\infty,-1]}$ (respectively $\bone_{[0,\infty)}$) we
mean the configuration filled in $(-\infty,-1]$ (respectively $[0,\infty)$)
and empty elsewhere. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
