body:
[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2608.18557, 'Randomly Permuted Orthogonal Products and Fast Dimension Reduction'] There exist couplings of an ORA walk \(Q_T^{\mathrm O}\) and an
	S-ORA walk \(Q_T^{\mathrm S}\), both of length \(T\), such that,
	possibly under different couplings,
	\[
	Q_T^{\mathrm S}
	=
	G_T^{\mathrm L}Q_T^{\mathrm O},
	\qquad 
	Q_T^{\mathrm S}
	=
	Q_T^{\mathrm O}G_T^{\mathrm R},
	\]
	where \(G_T^{\mathrm L}\), \(G_T^{\mathrm R} \in \mathcal H_d\) are signed
	permutation matrices. Consequently, for every $I\subseteq [d]$ and every $X\subseteq \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, we have
	\[
	\norm{Q_T^{\mathrm S}}_\infty
	\stackrel{\mathrm d}=
	\norm{Q_T^{\mathrm O}}_\infty,
	\qquad
	\kappa_I(Q_T^{\mathrm S})
	\stackrel{\mathrm d}=
	\kappa_I(Q_T^{\mathrm O}),
	\qquad
	\Theta_{Q_T^{\mathrm S}}(X)
	\stackrel{\mathrm d}=
	\Theta_{Q_T^{\mathrm O}}(X).
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Thm eq:RootDecomp of arXiv:2506.18207, 'Cartan's Path Development, the Logarithmic Signature and a Conjecture of Lyons-Sidorova'] Let $\Delta$ be the set of
all nonzero roots with respect to a given Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak{h}.$
Then $\mathfrak{g}$ can be written as the direct sum 
\begin{equation}
\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{h}+\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta}\mathfrak{g}^{\alpha}.
\end{equation}
In this decomposition, one has $\dim\mathfrak{g}^{\alpha}=1$ for
each $\alpha\in\Delta$. Moreover, if $\alpha,\beta,\alpha+\beta\in\Delta$
then $[\mathfrak{g}^{\alpha},\mathfrak{g}^{\beta}]=\mathfrak{g}^{\alpha+\beta}.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Root Space Decomposition

Let a<b be finite, f in C-infinity([a,b]), t_1,...,t_m distinct nodes in [a,b], m>=1, and k_1,...,k_m positive integers. Put D=sum_i k_i and g(t)=product_i(t-t_i)^(k_i). There is a unique polynomial p of degree<D with p^(j)(t_i)=f^(j)(t_i) for 0<=j<k_i. For t in [a,b] outside the nodes, there exists xi strictly between min(t,t_1,...,t_m) and max(t,t_1,...,t_m) such that f(t)-p(t)=f^(D)(xi)g(t)/D!. At a node the error is zero; no strict-interior witness is asserted for a collapsed interval. In particular, if every k_i is even and f^(D)>=0 on [a,b], then p(t)<=f(t) throughout [a,b]. Derivatives at endpoints are understood one-sided.

Let X, Y, Z be Banach spaces, T in B(X,Y) and S in B(Y,Z) both Fredholm. Then S T in B(X,Z) is Fredholm and ind(S T) = ind S + ind T. In particular, composing with an invertible operator does not change the index, and if S T is a compact perturbation of the identity then ind S = -ind T.

[Theorem theo.generalcluster of arXiv:2411.19145, 'On the intersection of critical percolation clusters and other tree-like random graphs'] Assume that $\mathcal G$ satisfies the BK inequality and (equation Halpha of the paper), for some $\alpha\in (d/2,d)$. Let $(\mathcal C_0^i)_{i\ge 1}$ be independent copies of the connected component of $0$ in $\mathcal G$. 
\begin{itemize}
\item[$(i)$] If $\alpha \in (\frac{(k+1)d}{2k},\frac{kd}{2(k-1)})$, for some $k\ge 2$, then there exists $\kappa>0$, such that  
$$\mathbb E\left[\exp\left(\kappa \cdot |\mathcal C_0^1 \cap \dots\cap \mathcal C_0^k|^{\frac{2\alpha}{d}-1}\right)\right]<\infty.  $$
\item[$(ii)$] If $\alpha = \tfrac{kd}{2(k-1)}$, for some $k\ge 3$, then there exists $\kappa>0$, such that for any $t>e$, 
$$\mathbb P(|\mathcal C_0^1 \cap \dots\cap \mathcal C_0^k|>t)\le \exp\Big(-\kappa (\frac t{\log t})^{\frac {2\alpha}d-1}\Big).$$
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let Gamma be a C^2 embedded (D-M)-dimensional manifold of local minima of a C^3 function L on R^D, with rank(Hess L(x))=M for every x in Gamma. Let U be an open neighborhood of Gamma such that gradient flow from each point in U exists for all t>=0 and converges to an endpoint Phi(x) in Gamma. Assume Phi:U->Gamma is C^2. Then for x in Gamma, D Phi(x) is the Euclidean orthogonal projection onto T_x Gamma. In particular, ker(Hess L(x))=T_x Gamma, range(Hess L(x)) is its normal space, D Phi(x) is identity on tangent vectors, and it vanishes on normal vectors. This derivative assertion is at x in Gamma; it does not say Phi agrees with the nearest-point projection away from Gamma. Source: Li, Wang and Arora, Lemma 4.3, PDF p7, proof PDF pp29--30.
Gamma is a C^2 embedded manifold of local minima of L in Euclidean R^D
L is C^3 and Hess L has constant rank equal to codimension M on Gamma
U is an open neighborhood of Gamma with globally existing convergent gradient flow
The endpoint map Phi:U->Gamma is C^2

body: A space is a Baire space if every countable intersection of dense open sets is dense. Baire category theorem: every complete (pseudo)metric space - hence every Banach space - is a Baire space, and so is every locally compact Hausdorff space. It underlies the uniform boundedness principle, the open mapping theorem, and the closed graph theorem.
title: Baire category theorem

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Brown-measure universality beyond complex entry densities structural calculation Result: Every one-matrix holomorphic polynomial is already reducible to the circular law. If X_N has a circular-law limit and P is a fixed complex polynomial, spectral mapping gives mu_(P(X_N))=P_pushforward(mu_(X_N)) exactly, including algebraic multiplicities. The continuous mapping theorem therefore yields the pushforward of the circular law. The Brown measure of P(c) is the same pushforward, by factorizing P(z)-lambda and using multiplicativity of the Fuglede-Kadison determinant. Check: For each test function h bounded and continuous, h composed with P is bounded and continuous, so weak convergence passes through P. At the logarithmic-potential level, P(c)-lambda factors into commuting(c-root_j) terms, and determinant multiplicativity gives the same transformed Brown measure. Existing real-Gaussian and Bernoulli circular laws supply the initial one-matrix convergence. Obstruction: For several noncommuting input matrices there is no joint eigenvalue spectral mapping. Arithmetic and structural dependence in least-singular-value estimates remain unresolved here.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Global Kuramoto synchronization of random cubic graphs special-case or structural calculation Result: On the cubic prism C_m times K_2, m>=5, put theta_(j,a)=2 pi j/m for both layers. The sine forces along the two cycle neighbors cancel and rung forces vanish. The Hessian is a weighted Laplacian with cycle weights cos(2 pi/m)>0 and rung weights1, so it is positive definite modulo the global rotation. This is a nonconsensus strict local minimum modulo rotation. Check: Both the vanishing gradient and Hessian signs were checked; the graph is connected and cubic. This is an exact deterministic obstruction to a connectivity-only proof. Obstruction: Must show that uniformly random cubic graphs avoid all such stable phase arrangements with probability tending to one; the prism family itself has vanishing probability.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0067-global-kuramoto-synchronization-of-random-cubic-graphs

Convention $\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi i x\xi}dx$. Let $a,b>0$ and let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be measurable with $|f(x)|\le Ce^{-\pi a x^2}$ for a.e. $x$ and $|\hat f(\xi)|\le Ce^{-\pi b\xi^2}$ for a.e. $\xi$ (the first bound makes $f\in L^1$, so $\hat f$ is defined pointwise). Then: (i) if $ab>1$, $f=0$ a.e.; (ii) if $ab=1$, $f(x)=ce^{-\pi ax^2}$ for some constant $c$; (iii) if $ab<1$, there are infinitely many linearly independent such $f$ (for instance $p(x)e^{-\pi a'x^2}$ for any polynomial $p$ and any $a'$ with $a<a'<1/b$). So a function and its Fourier transform cannot both decay strictly faster than the self-dual Gaussian $e^{-\pi x^2}$.

[Lemma 18 (Tail flow from general initial data) of arXiv:2608.10992, '2608.10992'] Let $\mu$ be a probability law on $\N$. There exists a unique family
$q^\mu=(q_k^\mu)_{k\geq1}$ such that $q_1^\mu\equiv1$,
$q_k^\mu\in C^1([0,\infty))$ for $k\geq2$,
$q_k^\mu(0)=\mu([k,\infty))$, and
\begin{equation}

        (q_k^\mu)'
        =
        \sum_{u=1}^{k-1}q_u^\mu
        (q_{k-u}^\mu-q_k^\mu)
        +q_k^\mu(1-q_k^\mu),
        \qquad k\geq2.
\end{equation}
For every $t\geq0$,
\[
        1=q_1^\mu(t)\geq q_2^\mu(t)\geq\cdots\geq0,
\]
and each $q_k^\mu$ is non-decreasing in $t$. Consequently,
$q^\mu(t)$ is the tail of a unique probability law $\mu_t$ on
$\N\cup\{\infty\}$, with
\[
        \mu_t(\{\infty\})
        =
        q_\infty^\mu(t)
        :=
        \lim_{k\to\infty}q_k^\mu(t),
\]
and $(\mu_t)_{t\geq0}$ is non-decreasing in stochastic order.

[Lemma lem:riesz of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] The following statements hold not only for the right regular action on
$\mathcal H$ but for every finite-dimensional unitary
$\mathrm{SO}(n)$-module: in that formulation $P_i$ is the orthogonal
average of the circle $\pi(R_i(\theta))$, and the definitions above use
$N^{-1/2}\pi(R_i(\theta))$ in place of $\mathscr T$.
On the orthogonal complement of the $\mathcal K$-invariant functions,
with $(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger$ denoting the Moore--Penrose inverse,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|\mathscr D(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr D^*\|&\le1,\\
 \|\mathscr G(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr G^*\|&\le2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.3}
\]
On functions of circle Fourier degree at most $d$,
\[
 \|\mathscr L(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr L^*\|\le d^2.
\tag{3.2.4}
\]
The mixed blocks satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|\mathscr D(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr G^*\|&\le\sqrt2,
 &\|\mathscr G(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr D^*\|&\le\sqrt2,\\
 \|\mathscr L(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr D^*\|&\le d,
 &\|\mathscr D(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr L^*\|&\le d,\\
 \|\mathscr L(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr G^*\|&\le\sqrt2\,d,
 &\|\mathscr G(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger\mathscr L^*\|&\le\sqrt2\,d.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.2.4a}
\]
All these bounds remain true after tensoring by $I_V$.  They also hold,
with the same constants, when $(I-\mathcal K)^\dagger$ is replaced
everywhere by a finite Green kernel
$R_s=\sum_{\ell=0}^s\mathcal K^\ell$ acting between centered channels.

body: Record of an outside reading, 14 October 2026, of Y. Shmalo, The relaxation time does not control the normal approximation of stationary additive functionals (repository yspennstate/relaxation-time-normal-approximation, commit 40395f256c67), which answers Aldous-Fill Open Problem 4.30 negatively. The reader (a Claude model, fresh clone, no access to the author's internal reviews) found it correct: the construction answers the question as printed (Aldous-Fill p. 137; 'Open Problem 30' of the 1994 chapter, p. 26), and because it evaluates the distribution function at x = 0 the answer holds under any normalization; the parameter the question omits is sigma^2/tau_2, with sigma^2 of order 2b^2/s^2. All five findings are presentational: display (1.2) is a weakening of Lezaud's Theorem 3.1, and Remark 2 lacks one limsup line. An independent sampler gives P(S_8 <= 0) = 0.8838 +- 0.0051 at b = 2 against the repository's 0.8844, and the bound P(S_s <= 0) >= 1 - 4/s held on all 25 (b, s) pairs tried. A second independent reading (a Codex model) was still in progress on 14 October. Not refereed.
title: Outside reading of the answer to Aldous-Fill Open Problem 4.30, 14 October 2026: found correct, a second reading in progress

[Lemma Approximate capacity additivity of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] Let
\(A_{i},A_{j} \subset M\) be targets, each comparable to an
intrinsic \(\varepsilon\)-ball, whose intrinsic distance is at
least a separation parameter \(\varrho > 0\) with
\(\varepsilon < \varepsilon_{0}\varrho\). Then there exists
\(\theta = \theta(\varepsilon/\varrho) \in \lbrack 0,1)\), with
\(\theta(t) \rightarrow 0\) as \(t \rightarrow 0\), such
that

\[(1 - \theta)\left( \operatorname{Cap}_{N}\left( A_{i} \right) + \operatorname{Cap}_{N}\left( A_{j} \right) \right) \leq \operatorname{Cap}_{N}\left( A_{i} \cup A_{j} \right) \leq \operatorname{Cap}_{N}\left( A_{i} \right) + \operatorname{Cap}_{N}\left( A_{j} \right).\]

Consequently, by the comparison of Proposition 5.1, the killed
eigenvalues satisfy, for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\),

\[\lambda_{A_{i} \cup A_{j}} \geq c_{ce}\, C_{ce}^{- 1}(1 - \theta)\left( \lambda_{A_{i}} + \lambda_{A_{j}} \right).\]

[Corollary cor:conjugacy-poc-transfer of arXiv:2607.00149, '\bf Uniform-in-time Propagation-of-Chaos for\\ Stein Variational Gradient Descent'] Let $(\widetilde\pi,\widetilde K)$ be a finite-rank base pair with Stein
feature vector $\widetilde F$, and let $(\pi_H,K_H)$ be any conjugate pair
constructed from a diffeomorphism $H$ as in (equation eq:potential-transform of the paper)
and (equation eq:kernel-transform of the paper).  Denote its Stein feature vector by $F_H$.

Fix an initial law $\widetilde\mu_0$ for the base system, and define the conjugate initial law \( \mu_0^H := H_{\#}\widetilde\mu_0 . \) Let $(\widetilde\mu_t)_{t\ge0}$ be the base mean-field solution started from $\widetilde\mu_0$, and let $(\mu_t^H)_{t\ge0}$ be the transformed mean-field solution started from $\mu_0^H$. Let \( \widetilde X_1(0),\ldots,\widetilde X_N(0) \quad\text{be i.i.d. with law }\widetilde\mu_0, \) and define the transformed initial particles by \( X_i^H(0):=H(\widetilde X_i(0)), \, i=1,\ldots,N. \) Let $\widetilde\mu_t^N$ and $\mu_t^{H,N}$ denote the corresponding empirical particle solutions.

Then, for every $t\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
        d_{F_H}(\mu_t^{H,N},\mu_t^H)
        =
        d_{\widetilde F}(\widetilde\mu_t^N,\widetilde\mu_t).
\end{equation}
Consequently, any propagation-of-chaos estimate for the base pair in the
restricted feature metric transfers to every conjugate pair with the same rate
and the same constant.  In particular, if for some rate $\varepsilon_N\to0$,
\[   
        \mathbb E\left[\sup_{t\ge0}\, d_{\widetilde F}^2(\widetilde\mu_t^N,\widetilde\mu_t)\right]
        \le C\varepsilon_N,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
        \mathbb E\left[\sup_{t\ge0}\, d_{F_H}^2(\mu_t^{H,N},\mu_t^H)\right]
        \le C\varepsilon_N .
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Transfer of feature-level POC rates within a conjugacy class

[Lemma lem:sepstatdetconP of arXiv:2606.02472, 'Correlated uniform attachment trees'] Under the setup of Lemma~(lem:sepstatdetcon of the paper), assume that (item:kcentralstat of the paper) and~(item:kcentdegsmall of the paper) hold, and, in addition, that the following holds. 
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*'), start=3]
         \item After time step $m$, the weighted sum of squares of the differences in the number of nodes connecting to $A_{K_j}^{i}(m)$ in each of the two trees satisfies the bound
        \[
        \frac{1}{\ell + 1} \sum_{j=0}^{\ell} \frac{1}{K_j} \bbbclr{  \sum_{k=m+1}^{n} \mathbbm{1}_{ \left\{ X_k^{1} \in A_{K_j}^{1}(m) \right\} }  - \sum_{k=m+1}^{n} \mathbbm{1}_{ \left\{ X_k^{2} \in A_{K_j}^{2}(m) \right\} } }^2 < C\log(n),
       \]
       for some fixed  $C>0$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then
    \ba{
        \frac{1}{(\ell + 1)\log(n)} \sum_{j=0}^{\ell} \frac{1}{K_j} &\bbbclr{ \sum_{x \in A_{K_j}^{1}(n)} \deg_{T_n^{1}}(x) -  \sum_{x \in A_{K_j}^{2}(n)} \deg_{T_n^{2}}(x)  }^2 \\
         &< C  + \frac{1}{(\ell + 1)\log(n)} \sum_{j=0}^{\ell} \frac{2(m+1) \log(n)^{2/3} + (m+1)^2}{K_j}. 
    } (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let H = (L, R, E) be a finite bipartite graph and take the network with a source s, a sink t, arcs s->u of capacity 1 for u in L, arcs u->v for each edge uv, and arcs v->t of capacity 1 for v in R, every middle arc u->v of capacity M = |L| + 1. For a minimum s-t cut with source side S, put X = S n L and Y = S n R; then Y = N(X) and the cut has capacity |L| - |X| + |N(X)|. Conversely, for every X in L of maximal deficiency |X| - |N(X)|, the set {s} u X u N(X) is a minimum cut. So the minimum cut value is |L| - max over X in L of (|X| - |N(X)|). The strict inequality M > |L| is needed: with one edge and M = |L| = 1, the cut {s, u} is minimum and crosses the middle edge.

Author-derived obstruction pending w539: for finite N>=2 and s>0, a Riesz pair energy plus a C^2 external/background term near an interior point has a transverse second derivative -s epsilon^(-s-2)+O(1) when one pair approaches distance epsilon and other particles stay a positive distance away. It is negative for small epsilon, so no positive pointwise global Hessian lower bound holds on the full finite-particle configuration space. This does not analyze a renormalized infinite-volume Hessian or the Hessian restricted near a fixed crystal. A controlled-region/complement argument or a nonconvex inequality is required instead.
Finite N>=2
s>0
Interior near-collision pair
Other particles a fixed positive distance away
External/background potential C^2 with bounded Hessian nearby
title: DRAFT: finite Riesz near-collision curvature blocks global convexity

Put probability n^(-1/4) at K_n=1 and the remaining probability at ceil(n^(1/3)). Then convergence in probability holds but E[1/K_n]>=n^(-1/4). This is an audit counterexample to a typical-scale inference, not an FPP law and not a counterexample to the KPZ conjecture.

[Lemma 25 of arXiv:2608.08242, 'Bang--bang representation of $3\times 3$ embeddable stochastic matrices'] For $g\in(g_{\min},0)$, the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]	
\item
The admissible endpoint for $q_g$ is
	\[
	\bar c=\frac{r+1}{r+2x}.
	\]

\item
The coefficients of $q_g$ satisfy 
	\[
	\alpha(g)=(r+2x)m(g)T_{33}(U_g),
	\qquad
	\beta(g)=-2m(g)B(g),
	\qquad
	\gamma(g)=V_{32}(U_g),
	\]
	where
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		B(g)={}&-(r^2+rx-r-2x)\\
		&+g\bigl(yr^2+yrx-2yr-3yx-y-r^2-rx+x\bigr).
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	
\item	
	The vertex-location expression satisfies
	\[
	2\alpha(g)\bar c+\beta(g)
	=2m(g)\bigl(T_{31}(U_g)+1\bigr).
	\]
	
	
\item	
The reduced discriminant factor from
	Lemma~\ref{lem:Frydman-discriminant-factorization} is
	\[
	\widetilde H_{23}(U_g)=4\Theta(g),
	\]
	where
	\[
	\Theta(g)=h_2g^2+h_1g+x^2(r-2).
	\]
	Here
	\[
	h_2=-(r+2x)T_{21}(U)>0,
	\]
	and the explicit formula for $h_1$, together with the remaining
	polynomial identities used below, is recorded in
	Appendix~\ref{app:X23-Frydman-formulas}.
\end{enumerate}

Let S be a separable metric space, and let \mu_n, \mu be Borel probability measures on S such that \mu_n \Rightarrow \mu weakly. Then there exists a single probability space (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P}) and S-valued random variables X_n, X defined on \Omega such that the law of X_n is \mu_n for all n, the law of X is \mu, and X_n(\omega) \to X(\omega) as n \to \infty for \mathbb{P}-almost every \omega \in \Omega.

body:
[Defi 13 of arXiv:2608.28148, 'Flows and homotopies of Banach Lie algebroids'] An \emph{almost Lie bracket} on an anchored bundle $\left(A,\pi, M,\rho\right)$ is a sheaf of antisymmetric bilinear maps
\[
\LB_{A_U} \colon \Gamma\left( A_{U}\right)  \times\Gamma\left(  A_{U}\right)
\to\Gamma\left(  A_U\right), U\subseteq M \text{open}
\]
which satisfies the following properties
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\textbf{AL \arabic*})]
\item  the Leibniz identity:
\[
\forall\left(   \mathfrak{u}_{1}, \mathfrak{u}_{2}\right)  \in \Gamma \left(A_{U} \right)  ^{2}, \forall f \in C^{\infty}(U)
,\ \LB[\mathfrak{u}_{1},f \mathfrak{u}_{2}]_{A_{U}}=f.\LB[\mathfrak{u}_{1}, \mathfrak{u}_{2}]_{A_{U}}+df(\rho( \mathfrak{u}_{1})). \mathfrak{u}_{2}.
\]
\item For any  open set $U\subseteq M$ and any $(\mathfrak{u}_1,\mathfrak{u}_2) \in \Gamma(A_{U})^2$, the maps
\[
\mathfrak{u}_1,\mapsto \LB[\mathfrak{u}_1,\mathfrak{u}_2]_{A_{U}} \textrm{ and } \mathfrak{u}_2,\mapsto \LB[\mathfrak{u}_1,\mathfrak{u}_2]_{A_{U}}
\]
only depend on the $1$-jets of $\mathfrak{u}_1$ and $\mathfrak{u}_2$, respectively.
\end{enumerate}
By abuse of notation, such a sheaf of almost Lie brackets will be denoted $\LB_A$. The quintuple $(A,\pi, M,\rho,\LB_A)$ is called an \emph{almost algebroid}.
title: Definition 13 of arXiv:2608.28148

body:
At the regular 24-cell (vertices the 24 permutations of (+-1,+-1,0,0); facets a.x = 1 with a = +-e_i or a = (+-1/2,+-1/2,+-1/2,+-1/2)), the 144 vertex-facet incidence equations a_j.v_i = 1 in the 192 coordinates of the 24 vertices and 24 facet normals have rank 140: four of them are dependent at this point. The Zariski tangent space of the realization space therefore has dimension 52, against the expected dimension 48 (28 against 24 after quotienting by the 24-dimensional projective group), so a first-order count cannot certify the local dimension. This is why Brysiewicz and Sinn (arXiv:2609.02818) use a second-order (quadratic obstruction) test; the local dimension they certify is the expected one, 48, so the regular 24-cell is not locally projectively rigid.

Assumes: realization space in vertex and facet-normal coordinates, facets normalised as a.x = 1 (the origin is interior)

[Def frame bundle of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Let $\mathcal{Y} \to \mathcal{Z}$ be a degree $d$ finite \'etale morphism of smooth separated Deligne--Mumford stacks. 
Then, the {\em frame bundle} $\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{\mathcal{Z}}(\mathcal{Z}^{\sqcup \, d}, \mathcal{Y}) \to \mathcal{Z}$ defined as follows: suppose $T \to \mathcal{Z}$ is an \'etale morphism where $T$ is a complex scheme, then
\[
\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_{\mathcal{Z}}(\mathcal{Z}^{\sqcup \, d}, \mathcal{Y})(T) := \underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_T(T^{\sqcup \, d}, \mathcal{Y} \times_{\mathcal{Z}} T)
\]
where $\underline{\mathrm{Isom}}_T(T^{\sqcup \, d}, \mathcal{Y} \times_{\mathcal{Z}} T)$ is the usual Isom scheme (see [SGA2]).
The frame bundle naturally defines a principal $S_d$-bundle induced by the canonical left action of $S_d$ on $\mathcal{Z}^{\sqcup \, d}.$

[Proposition nest of arXiv:2608.07236, 'Negative association of Busemann functions \\in exponential last-passage percolation'] Fix $k<m<n$.
For any vertices $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}$ above or along level $n$, we have 
\begin{align} 
G^{\textup{S}}_{m, \mathbf{x}}(h) - G^{\textup{S}}_{m, \mathbf{y}}(h) = G^{\textup{S}}_{n, \mathbf{x}}(\sigma^{n-1}\cdots\sigma^m h) - G^{\textup{S}}_{n, \mathbf{y}}(\sigma^{n-1}\cdots\sigma^m h).
\end{align}
Similarly, for any vertices $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}$ below or along level $k$, we have 
$$G^{\textup{N}}_{\mathbf{a}, m}(h) - G^{\textup{N}}_{\mathbf{b}, m}(h) = G^{\textup{N}}_{\mathbf{a}, k}(\sigma_{k}\cdots\sigma_{m-1} h) - G^{\textup{N}}_{\mathbf{b}, k}(\sigma_{k}\cdots\sigma_{m-1} h).$$
title: Nested LPP property

[Proposition 22 of arXiv:2507.06186, '2507.06186'] For every $\eps,\ka>0$,
the operator $H_{\ka,\eps}$ is self-adjoint on $L^2(D)$.
Its spectrum $\la_1(H_{\ka,\eps})\leq\la_2(H_{\ka,\eps})\leq\cdots$ is purely discrete, bounded below, and has no accumulation point.
Moreover, the corresponding eigenfunctions $\psi_1(H_{\ka,\eps}),\psi_2(H_{\ka,\eps}),\ldots$
form an orthonormal basis of $L^2(D)$. Finally, for any $f\in L^2(D)$,
\begin{align}

\mr e^{-t H_{\ka,\eps}}f=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\mr e^{-t\la_n(H_{\ka,\eps})}\big\langle\psi_n(H_{\ka,\eps}),f\big\rangle\psi_n(H_{\ka,\eps}).
\end{align}

m &\longmapsto G_mf

body:
Let A be the infinitesimal generator of a strongly continuous (C_0) semigroup on a Banach space. Then the semigroup is UNIQUELY determined by A: if (S(t)) and (T(t)) are C_0-semigroups with the same generator then S(t) = T(t) for every t >= 0. Equivalently, the Laplace transform of the semigroup is the resolvent of A, and the resolvent determines the semigroup. The Hille-Yosida theorem says which operators are generators: A is the generator of a contraction semigroup exactly when A is densely defined and closed and every lambda > 0 lies in the resolvent set with ||(lambda I - A)^{-1}|| <= 1/lambda.
Both semigroups strongly continuous with the SAME generator including the same domain - two operators that agree on a common core but have different domains can generate different semigroups, which is precisely the non-uniqueness phenomenon for symmetric operators with several self-adjoint extensions.

body:
Load-bearing hypothesis in the stability theorem: the approximating functions must be VISCOSITY sub/supersolutions and the convergence must be LOCALLY UNIFORM. Neither can be dropped. (1) Almost-everywhere solutions are not closed under uniform convergence: let u_k(x) := dist(x, (1/k)Z) on R. Then |u_k'| = 1 at every point of differentiability, 0 ≤ u_k ≤ 1/(2k), so u_k → 0 uniformly, yet the limit u ≡ 0 satisfies |u'| = 0 and solves the eikonal equation nowhere. The u_k are not viscosity solutions of |u'| - 1 = 0 (at each of their convex kinks, on (1/k)Z, the supersolution test with the touching slope p = 0 fails), which is exactly why the stability theorem does not apply. (2) The convergence hypothesis cannot be weakened to pointwise or weak-* convergence. What goes wrong in the a.e. setting is already visible in (1): Du_k = ±1 a.e. while Du_k ⇀ 0 weakly-*, and the nonlinear expression H(Du_k) does not pass to weak limits. For genuine viscosity sub/supersolutions the proof of the stability theorem uses LOCALLY UNIFORM convergence to move maximum points of u_k - φ to a maximum point of u - φ; for a family that is merely locally uniformly bounded the correct substitutes are the half-relaxed limits limsup* u_k and liminf* u_k (Barles-Perthame), which are respectively a subsolution and a supersolution but in general differ from a pointwise limit. (If the u_k are locally equi-Lipschitz, pointwise convergence already forces locally uniform convergence, so the gap between the two modes of convergence bites only in the absence of equicontinuity.) Auditor's check: any passage to the limit in a nonlinear first-order PDE that is justified only by 'u_k → u and each u_k solves the equation a.e.' is invalid.
Counterexample: sawtooth functions u_k = dist(·, (1/k)Z) for the eikonal equation |u'| = 1 on R
Viscosity stability requires locally uniform convergence of the solutions (convergence of the equations must also be locally uniform)
Half-relaxed limit techniques replace uniform convergence only when combined with semicontinuous envelopes, not with a.e. solutions
title: Pitfall: Stability under Uniform Limits Needs Viscosity Solutions, Not a.e. Solutions

\vskip 3pt

Let $x\in\mbb R^2$ and $t>0$ be fixed,
and suppose that $Z$ is either $B^x$ or $B^{x,x}_t$.
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item Let $0\leq a<b\leq c<d\leq t$.
There exists a random variable $\be_{[a,b]\times[c,d]}(Z)$ such that
\[\be_{[a,b]\times[c,d]}(Z)=\lim_{\eps\to0}\be^\eps_{[a,b]\times[c,d]}(Z)
\qquad\text{in probability.}\]
\item If $0\leq a<b\leq t$, then
there exists a random variable $\ga_{[a,b]^2_\leq}(Z)$ such that
\[\ga_{[a,b]^2_\leq}(Z)=\lim_{\eps\to0}\Big(\be^\eps_{[a,b]^2_\leq}(Z)-\mbf E\Big[\be^\eps_{[a,b]^2_\leq}(Z)\Big]\Big)
\qquad\text{in probability.}\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let (S, A) be a measurable space and mu a sigma-finite measure on it, the intensity measure. A Poisson point process with intensity mu is a random counting measure N on S (N(A) is a random element of {0, 1, 2, ...} union {infinity} for each A in A, and N is a measure for each outcome) such that (i) for every A with mu(A) < infinity, N(A) has the Poisson distribution with mean mu(A), and (ii) for pairwise disjoint A_1, ..., A_k the counts N(A_1), ..., N(A_k) are independent. Such a process exists for every sigma-finite mu (construct it on each piece of finite measure by throwing a Poisson(mu(A)) number of independent points with law mu restricted to A and normalised, then superpose the pieces). When mu has no atoms the points are almost surely distinct; when mu is a multiple of Lebesgue measure on R^d the process is homogeneous with rate equal to that multiple. Basic calculus: the mapping theorem (the image of a Poisson process under a measurable map is Poisson with the image intensity), superposition (independent Poisson processes add to a Poisson process with the summed intensity), thinning (keeping each point independently with probability p(x) gives a Poisson process with intensity p mu), and Campbell's formula E sum_{x in N} f(x) = integral f d mu.

body: [Theorem of arXiv:2606.00325, 'Ergodicity for a class of stochastic Hasegawa-Mima equations with dissipation'] Let $G : \mathbb{X} \rightarrow R$ be collection of functions which determines measures. Assume that there exists a measurable $\mathbb{X}_0 \subset \mathbb{X}$ such that for any $(u_0,v_0) \in \mathbb{X}_0 \times  \mathbb{X}_0 $ and any $\phi \in G$ there exists a $\Gamma= \Gamma(u_0, v_0, \phi) \in \tilde C(\delta_{u_0}P^\mathbb{N}, \delta_{v_0}P^\mathbb{N})$ such that $\Gamma( D_\phi)>0$. Then there exist at most one ergodic invariant measure $\mu$ for $P$ with $\mu(\mathbb{X}_0) > 0$. In particular if $\mathbb{X}_0 = \mathbb{X}$, then there exists at most one, and hence ergodic, invariant measure. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Random variables X_n converge in distribution to X if and only if their characteristic functions converge pointwise, phi_{X_n}(t) -> phi_X(t) for every t. More usefully: if phi_{X_n}(t) -> psi(t) pointwise and psi is continuous at t = 0, then psi is the characteristic function of some random variable X and X_n -> X in distribution. This is the engine that turns the characteristic-function computation in the Central Limit Theorem into convergence in distribution.

Here the random variables are real-valued and phi_X(t)=E[exp(i t X)]. In the forward direction X_n converging in distribution to X implies the stronger conclusion that, for every T<infinity, sup_{|t|<=T}|phi_{X_n}(t)-phi_X(t)| tends to zero. Equivalently, for probability measures mu_n on R, weak convergence to mu gives convergence of their characteristic functions uniformly on every compact subset of R; the pointwise-convergence converse still requires continuity of the limit at 0.
for the converse, the limit function is continuous at 0

Let H and B be jointly translation-invariant disjoint binary fields on Z^d, marking holes and active sites. Use graph distance, put h=E H(0)>0, S=sum_{0<|x|<=2R}E[H(0)H(x)], T=sum_{|x|<=2R}E[H(0)B(x)], and let B_R be the graph ball of integer radius R>=1. The probability that the origin is strictly nearer a hole than an active site is at least |B_R|(h-T)_+^2/(h+S). Fix d≥1. Let H(x),B(x) be jointly translation-invariant binary fields on Z^d indicating holes and active sites, with H(x)B(x)=0 and h=EH(0)>0. Distances are graph distances. For an integer R≥1, put V_R=|B_R(0)| and

S_{2R}=sum_{0<|z|_1≤2R}E[H(0)H(z)],
T_{2R}=sum_{|z|_1≤2R}E[H(0)B(z)].

The z=0 term in T is zero by disjointness. If F is the event that the origin is strictly closer to some hole than to every active site, then

P(F)≥V_R (h−T_{2R})_+²/(h+S_{2R}).

Thus a time-indexed d4 configuration with h_t→0 has positive closer-hole liminf if, for some fixed b>0,C<∞,θ<1 and R_t=floor(bh_t^−1/4),

S_{2R_t}≤C h_t and T_{2R_t}≤θ h_t

eventually. The resulting lower limit is at least (2^4/4!)b^4(1−θ)²/(1+C). Unlike C2, this criterion allows an arbitrarily large fixed finite conditional expected number of neighboring holes; it requires a separate hole–active bound instead.

## Proof

Define G(x)=H(x)1_{there is no active site within distance 2R of x}. Its intensity g satisfies g≥h−T_{2R}, by applying the union bound to H(0) together with the active-site events. Since G≥0, g≥(h−T_{2R})_+.

If G(x)=1 and w is within distance R of x, then any active site y satisfies |y−x|_1>2R. Consequently

|w−y|_1≥|y−x|_1−|w−x|_1>2R−R≥|w−x|_1.

Thus every site within radius R of a G-center is strictly nearer a hole than every active site. If the active set is empty the same conclusion holds, with its nearest distance interpreted as infinity.

EM²≤sum_{x∈B_R}EH(x)+sum_{x,y∈B_R,x≠y}E[H(x)H(y)]

=V_R(h+S_{2R}).

The second inequality follows by fixing x and enlarging the possible differences y−x to B_{2R}\{0}; all terms are nonnegative. Cauchy–Schwarz gives (EM)²≤P(M>0)EM². Hence

P(F)≥P(M>0)≥V_R g²/(h+S_{2R})≥V_R(h−T_{2R})_+²/(h+S_{2R}).

The denominator is positive since h>0. If EM=0 the asserted bound is zero, so no division by a vanishing EM occurs. All sums are finite and require no independence.

Let X be a real random variable with E[X^2] < infinity, G a sub-sigma-field, and Var(X | G) = E[(X - E[X | G])^2 | G]. Then Var(X) = E[Var(X | G)] + Var(E[X | G]), both terms on the right are finite and nonnegative, and so Var(E[X | G]) <= Var(X), with equality if and only if X = E[X | G] almost surely, that is, X is almost surely equal to a G-measurable variable.

[Thm Existence-r of arXiv:2506.01746, '\bf Optimal Bregman quantization: existence and uniqueness of optimal quantizers revisited'] Let $r\!\in [2, +\infty)$. Assume that  the distribution $P$ of $X$ satisfies the  moment assumption~(equation eq:Integrabilite of the paper), that  

$F$ is $C^2$ on $U$ with $\nabla^2F(x)$ (symmetric) positive definite for  every $x\!\in U$.
Assume that at every $\bar x \!\in\hat\partial U =  \partial   U$, 

\noindent either
\begin{equation} 
\nabla^2F \mbox{ can  be continuously extended at } \bar x \mbox{ and } \nabla^2F(\bar x) \mbox{ is (symmetric) positive definite}
\end{equation}
or \\
\indent the l.s.c. extensions $\phi_{_F}(\xi, \cdot)$  on $ \bar U^{\widehat{\mathbb{R}^d}}$ satisfy at $\bar x$ 
\begin{equation}

 \forall\, \xi \!\in U, \qquad \phi_{_F}(\xi, \bar x) =\displaystyle  \sup_{x\in U}\phi_{_F}(\xi,x).
\end{equation}
Finally,  if $U$ is unbounded, assume that $\bar x = \infty$ satisfies the above condition~(equation eq:Cond-rb2 of the paper).

\medskip
\noindent $(a)$ Then for every $n\ge1$ there exists an $n$-tuple $x^{(r,n)}= \big(x^{(r,n)}_1, \ldots, x^{(r,n)}_n\big) \!\in U^n$ which minimizes $G_{r,n}$ over $U^n$. Moreover, if  the support (in $U$) of the distribution $P$ has at least $n$ points then $x^{(r,n)}$ has pairwise distinct components and $P\big(\mathring C_i(x^{(r,n)})\big)>0$ for every $i\!\in \{1,\ldots,n\}$.

\smallskip
\noindent $(b)$ The distribution  $P$ assigns no mass to the   boundary of  any $\phi_{_F}$-Bregman--Voronoi partitions of $x^{(n)}$ i.e.
\[
P\left (\bigcup_{i=1}^n\partial C_i\big( x^{(r,n)})\right) = 0
\]
and $x^{(r,n)}$ satisfies the $(r,\phi_{_F})$-stationary (or $(r,\phi_{_F})$-master) equation
\begin{equation}
 x^{(r,n)}_i = \frac{ \int_{C_i(x^{(r,n)})}\xi \phi_{_F}( \xi,x^{(r,n)}_i )^{\frac r2-1}P(\mathrm{d}\xi)}{\int_{C_i(x^{(r,n)})}\phi_{_F}( \xi,x^{(r,n)}_i )^{\frac r2-1}P(\mathrm{d}\xi) } , \quad  i=1,\ldots,n.
\end{equation}
 
\noindent $(c)$ The sequence $\displaystyle G_{r,n}\big( x^{(r,n)}\big) = \min_{U^n} G_{r,n}$ decreases as long as it is not $0$ and converges to $0$ as $n$ goes to infinity. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:positive-finite-energy-potential of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] For every finite positive Radon measure $\mu$ with $I_D(\mu)<\infty$, there is
a unique potential $U_D\mu\inH$ characterized by
\[
 \mathcal E(U_D\mu,v)=\int_D\widetilde v\,d\mu,
 \qquad v\inH.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \mathcal E(U_D\mu,U_D\mu)=I_D(\mu),
\]
and its quasi-continuous representative is given by
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde{U_D\mu}(z)
 =\int_DG_D(z,w)\,\mu(dw)

[Theorem bhp of arXiv:2411.14921, 'A boundary Harnack principle and its application to analyticity of 3D Brownian intersectio'] Let $U$ be a domain in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $K$ a compact set such that $K\subseteq U$. For $\mathbb{P}_{\vec x}$-almost every $\mathcal{W}$, there exists $C(U,K,\mathcal{W})\in (0,\infty)$ such that for all closed subset $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{W}$, if $u$ and $v$ are bounded positive harmonic functions in $U\setminus \mathcal{A}$ that vanish continuously on regular points of $\mathcal{A}\cap U$, then
    \begin{equation}
        u(x_1)\,v(x_2)\leq C\,u(x_2)\,v(x_1) \quad \text{for all $x_1,x_2\in K\setminus \mathcal{A}$}.
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Both hypotheses are used, and each failure has a clean counterexample on the unit disk D. (1) The set E where pointwise convergence is assumed must have an accumulation point in the open set U, not merely on its boundary. Take a_k = 1 - 1/k^2, so that the sum of (1 - a_k) converges, and let B be the Blaschke product with simple zeros exactly at the a_k; B is holomorphic on D with |B| < 1 and B is not identically zero (B(0) = product of the a_k, nonzero). The sequence f_n = (-1)^n B is uniformly bounded by 1 and converges (to 0) at every point of E = {a_k}, a set whose only accumulation point is the boundary point 1, yet f_n diverges at every point where B ≠ 0, for instance at 0. (2) Local uniform boundedness cannot be dropped: on U = D(0,2) the functions f_n(z) = z^n converge pointwise on E = D (a set with plenty of interior accumulation points) but diverge for |z| > 1; the family is not bounded on compact subsets of U. (3) Connectedness of U matters in the same way as for the identity theorem: if U has several components, the hypothesis must be met on each component separately, since the identity theorem step is applied there. When auditing an argument that upgrades pointwise convergence of holomorphic functions to locally uniform convergence, check exactly these three things, and check that the pointwise limits are finite complex numbers rather than ∞.
title: Pitfall: Vitali–Porter needs the convergence set to accumulate inside the domain, and local boundedness

Let (M,g) be a complete, simply connected Riemannian manifold with nonpositive sectional curvature at every point (K <= 0 for every tangent 2-plane at every point). Then for any point p in M, the exponential map exp_p: T_pM -> M is a diffeomorphism. In particular M is diffeomorphic to R^n, n = dim M, and any two points of M are joined by a unique geodesic.
M is complete

[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2609.02779, '2609.02779'] There exist $\rho_0,\mu,C,\lambda_0,e_0>0$ such that the following holds for
$0<\rho\le\rho_0$ and every real interval $[a,b]$.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item If $0<\lambda\le\lambda_0$ and
$Z_\lambda:[a,b]\to T^*M$ is the lift of a $u_\lambda$-calibrated curve with
\[
 d_{T^*M}(Z_\lambda(s),\Gamma)<2\rho
 \qquad\text{for every }a\le s\le b,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 d_{T^*M}(Z_\lambda(s),\Gamma)
 \le C\rho\bigl(e^{-\mu(s-a)}+e^{-\mu(b-s)}\bigr)+C\lambda
 \qquad\text{for every }a\le s\le b.
\end{equation}

\item If $Z^0:[a,b]\to T^*M$ is a conservative orbit satisfying
\[
 \dot Z^0=X_H(Z^0),
 \qquad
 H(Z^0(s))\equiv c+e,
 \qquad |e|\le e_0,
\]
and
\[
 d_{T^*M}(Z^0(s),\Gamma)<2\rho
 \qquad\text{for every }a\le s\le b,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 d_{T^*M}(Z^0(s),\Gamma)
 \le C\rho\bigl(e^{-\mu(s-a)}+e^{-\mu(b-s)}\bigr)+C|e|
 \quad\text{for every }a\le s\le b.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

Owner draft: independently checked proof (C015 v1). Suppose a d-dimensional body is decomposed up to null sets into finitely many nondegenerate d-simplices with disjoint interiors and volume fractions q_j/D, where q_j are positive integers and D=sum q_j. Then its uniform law is n-CM at n=kD whenever every k*q_j>=d+1. Take a complete mix of k*q_j uniform points in each simplex, concatenate the groups, and randomly permute all output positions. Deterministic volume-matched counts give the full uniform marginal and total n times the whole-body centroid despite differing piece centers. Rational-coordinate convex polytopes have such a rational-volume triangulation, so admit arbitrarily large commensurate-order mixes. This does not prove critical order for a multi-piece decomposition or all nonmultiple orders, and variable-order approximation cannot be passed to a fixed-order mix. Novelty UNKNOWN.

Positive rational piece-volume fractions
n=kD with every group size k*q_j>=d+1

For f, g in L^1(R^n) the convolution (f * g)(x) = integral over R^n of f(x - y) g(y) dy is defined for almost every x, belongs to L^1(R^n) with ||f * g||_1 <= ||f||_1 ||g||_1, and its Fourier transform is the product of the transforms: (f * g)^(xi) = f^(xi) g^(xi) for every xi, with f^(xi) = integral f(x) exp(-2 pi i x . xi) dx (with another normalisation of the transform a constant factor appears). Dually, for f, g in L^2(R^n) (or in L^1 with transforms in L^1) the transform of the pointwise product is the convolution of the transforms: (f g)^ = f^ * g^. The same identity holds for the Fourier series of 2 pi-periodic functions (the convolution on the circle, coefficients multiply), for the discrete Fourier transform of finite sequences with cyclic convolution (the basis of fast convolution by FFT, O(N log N) instead of O(N^2)), and for the Laplace transform with the convolution on [0, infinity). Consequences: L^1(R^n) with convolution is a commutative Banach algebra without unit whose Gelfand transform is the Fourier transform; convolution with an approximate identity converges to the function (the transforms tend to 1 pointwise); a convolution operator f -> k * f is diagonalised by the Fourier transform, with symbol k^, which is how constant-coefficient linear PDE and filters are analysed.
f, g in L^1(R^n) for the basic identity; the dual identity needs f, g in L^2 (or transforms in L^1)
normalisation exp(-2 pi i x . xi); with exp(-i x . xi) the identity acquires the factor (2 pi)^{n/2} or (2 pi)^n depending on the convention

[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2606.14812, 'Joint convergence in Wiener chaos via transport hierarchy and Malliavin covariances'] Let $(X_N = I_p(f_N), N\geq 1)$ with $p\geq 2$ satisfying \eqref{c1}. 
	Let us consider a sequence $(\mathbb{Y}_N=(Y_{1,N},\ldots,Y_{d,N}), N\geq 1)$ 
	of $d$-dimensional random vectors, with components in the $p$th Wiener 
	chaos, which converges in distribution to $\mathbb{Y}=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_d)$. 
	Assume
	\begin{equation}
		\mathbf{E}\!\left[X_N Y_{j,N}\right] \to_{N\to\infty} \rho_j, 
		\quad\text{for every } j=1,\ldots,d.
	\end{equation}
	Let $\rho=(\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_d)\in\mathbb{R}^d$. Then
	\begin{equation}
		(X_N,\mathbb{Y}_N) \xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{(d)} (Z,\mathbb{Y}),
	\end{equation}
	where $Z\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ and the characteristic function of 
	$(Z,\mathbb{Y})$ is given by, for every $u\in\mathbb{R}$, 
	$v\in\mathbb{R}^d$,
	\begin{equation}
		\varphi_{(Z,\mathbb{Y})}(u,v) 
		= \mathbf{E}\!\left[e^{i\langle v,\mathbb{Y}\rangle}\right]
		e^{-\frac{\sigma^2 u^2}{2} - u\langle\rho,v\rangle}.
	\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 7 of arXiv:2606.14812

body: Let W_t be a standard Brownian motion and let X_t solve the Ito stochastic differential equation dX_t = mu_t dt + sigma_t dW_t for adapted, sufficiently integrable processes mu_t, sigma_t. If f(t,x) is continuously differentiable once in t and twice in x, then Y_t = f(t,X_t) satisfies dY_t = [f_t + mu_t f_x + (1/2) sigma_t^2 f_xx] dt + sigma_t f_x dW_t, all partial derivatives evaluated at (t,X_t). Equivalently df = f_t dt + f_x dX_t + (1/2) f_xx d[X]_t, using the Ito rule (dW_t)^2 = dt. The stochastic-calculus chain rule; due to Kiyoshi Ito.
title: Ito's lemma

	\(D_\xi  \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) be a Rademacher diagonal, let \(\pi\) be an
	independent uniform permutation on \(S_d\), and let \(0<\eta<1/2\). Set
	\[
	U=AD_\xi P_\pi B, \qquad
	\ell=\log\left(\frac{8d}{\eta}\right),
	\qquad
	L_m=\log\left(\frac{8dm}{\eta}\right).
	\]
	Suppose that $m\ge600\ell$ and
	\[
	36\kappa_I(A)\norm B_\infty^2\,mL_m\le1.
	\]
	Then, with probability at least \(1-\eta\),
	\[
	\kappa_I(U)\le2.

body: [Cor fineET of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a cooriented $C^0$-foliation on $M$ transverse to $\partial M$ without compact planar leaves nor $\mathbb{T}^2$-type planar minimal sets. [campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is the supporting identity used in the campaign partial answer to Problem 3.11 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution, the distribution of a sum of freely independent self-adjoint variables with the indicated laws, and * for classical convolution of independent real variables. For t>0 let C_t have density t/[pi(t^2+x^2)] on the real line. For every probability measure mu on R, mu boxplus C_t = mu * C_t. In transform notation, G_mu(z)=integral_R (z-x)^(-1) mu(dx) for Im(z)>0, and G_{mu boxplus C_t}(z)=G_mu(z+i t), where i^2=-1. The record explicitly treats the identity as classical rather than claiming novelty for it. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
t>0 and mu is any probability measure on R.

The whole point is an identity that is special to the Cauchy family. Its Cauchy transform is
$G_{C_t}(z) = 1/(z+it)$ on the upper half plane, so $K_{C_t}(w) = 1/w - it$ and the $R$-transform is the
constant $R_{C_t}(w) = -it$. Free convolution adds $R$-transforms, so for any $\mu$,
$$K_{\mu\boxplus C_t}(w) = K_\mu(w) - it \quad\Longrightarrow\quad G_{\mu\boxplus C_t}(z) = G_\mu(z+it).$$
On the other side, the density of $\mu * C_t$ at $x$ is the Poisson integral
$\tfrac1\pi\int t\,d\mu(y)/((x-y)^2+t^2) = -\tfrac1\pi\operatorname{Im}G_\mu(x+it)$, so
$G_{\mu*C_t}(z) = G_\mu(z+it)$ as well. Hence
$$\mu \boxplus C_t \ = \ \mu * C_t \qquad\text{for every } \mu \text{ and every } t>0,$$
the free and classical convolutions with a Cauchy law coinciding.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:41d53089fc9154dfc68427cb689fc659cab94c6fae196dceb869ccf188d76c60","revision_digest":"sha256:692d5257f04848621ef0a15c85ace5ae808ba7700ca47e9f5495cb8d32102dac","source_id":"doi:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15","source_revision":"problem source: ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374; own campaign record: 2026-09-14","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma eq:shifted-r-derivative of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[lemma]{lem:conditional-aggregate-remainder}
Assume (equation eq:array-assumptions of the paper), and write \(r=m+1\).  Fix
\(O\in\mathcal O_{N,L}\), \(t\in[0,1]\), \(I\in[N]^p\), and
\(z_{-I}\in\mathbb R^{[N]^p\setminus\{I\}}\).  Define
\[
 \phi_I(s)=F_O(z_{-I},s),\qquad
 a_I^0=\abs{\partial_I\Psi_O(z_{-I},0)},\qquad
 B_I=\int\phi_I(s)\mu_{I,t}(\,\mathrm d s),
\]
and
\[
 \Delta_I(z_{-I})
 =\int\phi_I(s)\gamma(\,\mathrm d s)
  -\int\phi_I(s)\mu_I(\,\mathrm d s).
\]
Then, for all sufficiently large \(N\), the following estimates hold
uniformly in \(O,t,I,z_{-I}\):
\begin{align}
 \abs{\phi_I^{(r)}(s)}
 &\le C\phi_I(s)
 \left\{(a_I^0+\mathfrak d_I\left\lverts\right\rvert)^r
       +\mathfrak d_Iq_N^{r-2}\right\},
 \\
 c\phi_I(0)\le B_I&\le C\phi_I(0),\qquad
 \int\left\lverts\right\rvert^k\phi_I(s)\mu_{I,t}(\,\mathrm d s)
 \le C_kB_I,\quad 1\le k\le2r,
 \\
 \abs{\Delta_I(z_{-I})}
 &\le CB_I
 \left\{(a_I^0)^r+\mathfrak d_Iq_N^{r-2}\right\}.
 
\end{align}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{I\in[N]^p}
 \int\abs{\Delta_I(z_{-I})}\lambda_{t,-I}(\,\mathrm d z_{-I})
 \le CNq_N^{r-2}A_O(t).
\end{equation}

Method: Explicit calculation or obstruction with source-specific scope Result: The circle contour calculation shows why simply integrating the constant mode over a real period imposes neutrality. For an integer screening expansion, the integral of exp(i*k*beta*c) over a full period vanishes unless k=0. A noncompact complex Hankel-type contour can avoid that selection rule, but requires a large-argument estimate for the complex GMC Laplace transform along its two infinite legs. Finite exponential moments only ensure finiteness for each fixed argument, not decay along those legs. Check: For a deterministic complex random variable M=-1, every exponential moment is finite but E exp(-z*M)=exp(z) grows on the positive real ray. Thus existence of all moments cannot provide the needed contour decay. This diagnostic does not assert that the actual imaginary GMC has this behavior. Obstruction: The missing sphere Laplace estimate and identification with the imaginary DOZZ expression remain unresolved in the read source. Current status requires later papers beyond the read2025 proposal and April2026 charge-neutral result; it is not certified open solely from the survey.

Method: Union small-ball lower bound and one-normal upper bound Result: For a standard M-by-M real Gaussian matrix A, sigma_min(A)<=t implies that some column has distance at most sqrt(M)t from the span of the other columns: project a minimizing unit vector equation using a coordinate of magnitude at least 1/sqrt(M). The M remaining row projections are independent N(0,1), and omega is at most their minimum absolute value, giving omega<=C log(M)/M with probability tending to one for sufficiently large C. [Dfn smooth of arXiv:2608.25471, 'Exact Hausdorff measures and fine geometry of collisions of independent Markov processes'] [{Smooth measures}] 
  A Borel measure $\nu$ on $M$ is said to be a \textit{smooth measure} if it satisfies the following conditions:
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (\roman*)]
    \item 
      $\nu$ charges no semipolar sets, i.e., 
      $\nu(E) = 0$ for any semipolar $E \in \mathcal{B}(M)$;
    \item 
      there exists an increasing sequence $(E_{n})_{n \geq 1}$ of Borel subsets 
      such that $M = \bigcup_{n \geq 1} E_n$, $\nu(E_{n}) < \infty$ for each $n$, 
      $\int_{E_n} r_1(x,y)\, \nu(dy)$ is bounded in $x$ for each $n$,
      and $P_x( \lim_{n \to \infty} \tau_{E_n} \geq \zeta) = 1$ for all $x \in M$,
      where $\tau_{E_n} \coloneqq \inf\{t > 0 \mid X_t \notin E_n\}$.
  \end{enumerate}
title: Dfn smooth of arXiv:2608.25471

For odd m>=5, the degree-four arc-transitive graph C_m[empty K_2] has n=2m vertices, relaxation time 1/(1-cos(2*pi/m)), maximal commute time 2*floor(m^2/4)+2*m and stationary-average hitting time (m^2-1)/6+m. These violate proposed O(n) relaxation and O(n log n) commute bounds; the commute/ twice-average-hitting ratio tends to3/2. The source has a variable-assignment typo in its arc-transitivity definition; the proof uses the standard intended definition. Thirteen exact rational finite controls agree, but do not supply independent review.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:9ea5b85517036020530e7b15f2ed4969895ef72e4547a77140109f9419efb64b","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/9e/9ea5b85517036020530e7b15f2ed4969895ef72e4547a77140109f9419efb64b.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:782e3ef5bbb0faf01a685eb529732c0d77bfa3843ab0c5c3cb1c854a588ec117","bundle_entry_key":"wreath-graph-counter","bundle_id":"population.probability-candidate-obstructions-and-spatial-lemmas-005","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability theory","draft":"codex-probability-1000-20h-20260906/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.markov:candidate-arc-transitive-wreath-graph-hitting-relaxation-obstruction","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# P0208: the wreath graph and Aldous–Fill Problem 7.27

Status: complete counterexample candidate, checked by the author through hitting-time and spectral calculations. No independent review or novelty certificate. The graph itself is an established construction, not an invention here. This is a response to a historically sourced question; present-day open status remains unverified.

Primary question: Aldous and Fill, *Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs*, 2002 unfinished monograph, 2014 recompilation, Open Problem 7.27, PDF p.259, https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.pdf . Section 7.2 is internally dated January 31, 1994. It asks, for arc-transitive graphs other than cycles on n vertices, whether maximal mean commute time is O(n log n), relaxation time is O(n), and the ratio of maximal commute time to twice stationary-average hitting time tends to one. The three assertions are counted as one related question.

## Source scope and a printed definition error

Page 254 prints an inconsistent variable assignment in the definition of arc-transitivity: the images of two possible identical starting vertices would be allowed to be distinct. Read literally, that formula excludes any graph with a vertex having two neighbors. The surrounding discussion, examples of tori and Cayley graphs, and Lemma 7.19 unmistakably use the usual definition: the automorphism group is transitive on ordered adjacent pairs. Our result concerns that intended standard definition, and does not silently claim to satisfy the misprinted formula.

Conder's 2013 Rogla summer-school notes, p.8, independently describe the same established wreath/necklace graph and its arc-transitivity: https://www.famnit.upr.si/sl/resources/files/konference/rogla2013/conderlecturenotes.pdf . This is evidence that the construction is prior art. It does not establish when the probability question was answered.

## Construction and symmetry

Let m be an odd integer at least five, and put

\[
 V_m=(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)\times\{0,1\},\qquad
 (i,b)\sim(i+1,c),\ (i,b)\sim(i-1,c)\quad(c=0,1).
\]

This is the lexicographic product of a cycle with an edgeless two-vertex graph. It is connected, simple, 4-regular, and has n=2m vertices, so it is not an n-cycle. Dihedral symmetries act on the first coordinate. Independently swapping the two vertices in any fiber preserves every edge. Given two directed edges, a dihedral symmetry sends their ordered base edges to each other, after which independent swaps in the two distinct endpoint fibers match both second coordinates. Thus the graph is arc-transitive.

Use discrete-time simple random walk, or its rate-one continuization. The book states on p.115 that the parameters at issue are unchanged by this continuization. The first-coordinate projection is simple random walk on the m-cycle, and the second coordinate is replaced at each step by a fresh fair bit independent of the base step.

## Exact hitting times

Write h(v,w) for the mean first hitting time, with h(w,w)=0. From a base position at cyclic distance j in {1,...,m-1}, the mean first arrival at base fiber zero is

\[
 H_j=j(m-j).
\]

Indeed H_0=H_m=0 and H_j=1+(H_{j-1}+H_{j+1})/2. At the first fiber arrival, the fair bit hits a specified vertex with probability one half.

Let h be the mean hitting time from its twin to the specified vertex. Starting in that fiber, the first positive return of the base walk has mean m. The arrival bit succeeds with probability one half; on failure the same twin state recurs. Hence h=m+h/2, giving h=2m. Therefore

\[
 h((j,b),(0,0))=j(m-j)+m\quad(j\ne0),\qquad
 h((0,1),(0,0))=2m.
\]

The formula is symmetric in source and target and gives 2m-1=n-1 for neighboring vertices, exactly as Lemma 7.19 requires. Its maximum is floor(m²/4)+m for m at least five. Thus

\[
 \tau^*=2\lfloor m^2/4\rfloor+2m.
\]

The stationary law is uniform. Summing the same hitting-time formula gives

\[
 \tau_0=\frac1{2m}\left[2m+2\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}
          \{j(m-j)+m\}\right]
       =\frac{m^2-1}{6}+m.
\]

On a vertex-transitive graph the stationary mean to a fixed target equals the source's stationary-average target parameter, so either equivalent convention yields this value.

## Independent spectral route

For functions constant on each two-vertex fiber, the transition operator is the cycle operator, with eigenvalues cos(2πk/m), k=0,...,m-1. For functions antisymmetric within every fiber it is zero. These orthogonal invariant subspaces both have dimension m and exhaust the state space. Consequently

\[
 \tau_2=\frac1{1-\cos(2\pi/m)}\sim\frac{m^2}{2\pi^2}.
\]

The fundamental-matrix trace is

\[
 \sum_{k=1}^{m-1}\frac1{1-\cos(2\pi k/m)}+m
 =\frac{m^2-1}{6}+m,
\]

which agrees with the direct hitting-time sum. The trigonometric sum can also be recovered from the already derived cycle hitting-time formula by stationary averaging; it is not needed as an unproved numerical identity for the counterexample.

## Consequences and limitations

Since n=2m, both τ* and τ2 are of order n². They violate the proposed n log n and n upper bounds. Moreover

\[
 \frac{\tau^*}{2\tau_0}
 =\frac{\lfloor m^2/4\rfloor+m}{(m^2-1)/6+m}
 \longrightarrow\frac32,
\]

which violates the third assertion. These are exact formulas, not simulation estimates.

The strongest reasons for caution are the old unfinished source, its definition typo, and the fact that wreath graphs have long been standard. Focused searches on September 6, 2026 located the original question and primary graph-theory descriptions but no verified later disposition of Problem 7.27. Absence from that search is not evidence of novelty. A future reviewer should check the intended arc-transitivity convention, rate-one normalization, and prior probability literature before any promotion.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:556c6b1fcc6b4db785822e5b4cae963c5ea31477c78e3e04ba1fa72416f504a4","revision_digest":"sha256:6953ca17d9e261b9f17c422ee3d80a50d1c860e65bbcef06c9e4366bd4afe678","source_id":"owner-original-probability-research-20260906:wreath-graph-counter","source_revision":"author-checked-20260906-v1","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma lem:weighted-exp-conc of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Let $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N$ be independent real-valued random variables, and let $F=F(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N)$ be real-valued and measurable. Let $\xi_i'$ be an independent copy of $\xi_i$, independent of all coordinates, and let $\xi^{(i)}$ be obtained from $\xi=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N)$ by replacing only $\xi_i$ with $\xi_i'$. Assume that, for deterministic numbers $\ell_i\geq0$, not all zero, for every $1\leq i\leq N$,
		\[
			|F(\xi)-F(\xi^{(i)})|\leq \ell_i|\xi_i-\xi_i'|\, .
		\]
		Write
		\[
			\|\ell\|_{\ell^2}\coloneqq\left(\sum_{i=1}^N\ell_i^2\right)^{1/2}\, ,
			\qquad
			\|\ell\|_{\ell^\infty}\coloneqq\max_{1\leq i\leq N}\ell_i\, .
		\]
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
			\item If $p\geq2$ and $\mathbb{E}|\xi_i|^p<\infty$ for every $i$, then there is
			$C=C(p)$ such that
			\[
				\bigl(\mathbb{E}|F-\mathbb{E} F|^p\bigr)^{1/p}
				\leq
				C
				\left[
				\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \ell_i^2\bigl(\mathbb{E}|\xi_i-\xi_i'|^p\bigr)^{2/p}\right)^{1/2}
				+
				\left(\sum_{i=1}^N \ell_i^p \mathbb{E}|\xi_i-\xi_i'|^p\right)^{1/p}
				\right]\, .
			\]

			\item If the $\xi_i$ are i.i.d.\ and
			$\mathbb{E} e^{\theta_0|\xi_1|}\leq K_0$, then there are $c>0$ and $C<\infty$, depending
			only on $\theta_0$ and $K_0$, such that, for all $r\geq0$,
			\[
				\mathbb{P}(|F-\mathbb{E} F|\geq r)
				\leq
				C\exp\left\{
				-c\min\left(
				\frac{r^2}{\|\ell\|_{\ell^2}^2}\, , 
					\frac{r}{\|\ell\|_{\ell^\infty}}
				\right)
				\right\}\, .
			\]

				\item If the $\xi_i$ are i.i.d.\ with $\mathbb{E}\xi_1=0$ and
				$\mathbb{E} e^{\theta_0|\xi_1|}\leq K_0$, then there are $c>0$ and
				$C<\infty$, depending only on $\theta_0$ and $K_0$, such that,
				for every $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ with
				$|\lambda|\,\|\ell\|_{\ell^\infty}\leq c$,
				\[
					\log\mathbb{E}\exp\Bigl\{\lambda\sum_{i=1}^N\ell_i\xi_i\Bigr\}
					\leq
					C\lambda^2\|\ell\|_{\ell^2}^2\, .
				\]

			\item Under the assumptions of part~\textup{(b)}, if
				$|\lambda|\|\ell\|_{\ell^\infty}<\theta_0$, then
				\[
					\mathbb{E} e^{\lambda(F-\mathbb{E} F)}
					\leq
					\exp\{C\lambda^2\|\ell\|_{\ell^2}^2\}\, ,
				\]
				where $C$ depends only on $\theta_0$, $K_0$, and
				$\theta_0-|\lambda|\|\ell\|_{\ell^\infty}$.
		\end{enumerate}

[Lemma 16 of arXiv:2609.00690, 'Boundary behavior and optimal pointwise H\"older exponent of the total local time of $(1+\'] Let $\{K_t : t \in [0,T]\}$ be a c\`adl\`ag stochastic process. Suppose there are constants $a > 1$, $b > 0$, and $C > 0$ such that for all $s,t \in [0,T]$,
	\[
	\mathbb{E}|K_t - K_s|^a \le C |t-s|^{1+b}.
	\]
	Fix $\gamma \in (0, b/a)$. Define
	\[
	\bar\rho_\gamma := \sup\{ r\in[0,T] : \forall s,t \in [0,T],\ |t-s| \leq r \Rightarrow |K_t - K_s| \leq |t-s|^\gamma \},
	\qquad \rho_\gamma:=\frac12\bar\rho_\gamma.
	\]
	Then 
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[{\rm(1)}] $|K_t - K_s| \leq |t-s|^\gamma$ whenever $|t-s| \leq\rho_\gamma$,\ $s,t \in [0,T]$;
		\item[{\rm(2)}] $\mathbb P(\rho_\gamma > 0) = 1$;
		\item[{\rm(3)}] for all $0 < h < h_{\gamma}/2$,
		\[
		\mathbb P(\rho_\gamma < h) \le C' h^{b - a\gamma_0},
		\]
		where $\gamma_0 =(\gamma+b/a)/2$, $h_\gamma= [2^{-\gamma_0}(1 - 2^{-\gamma_0})/3]^{1/(\gamma_0 - \gamma)}$ and 
		\[
		C' := \frac{CT(T\vee 1/T)2^{2b - 2a\gamma_0+1}}{1 - 2^{-(b - a\gamma_0)}}.
		\]
	\end{itemize}
title: Lemma 16 of arXiv:2609.00690

[Proposition 52 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(\xi\) be a fixed limiting point based at
\(q=q_\pi(\xi)\in Y^{\rm prod}\).  After forgetting the distinguished
conjugate heat measures, the underlying K\"ahler metric flow of every
tangent space at \(\xi\) is the shrinking cylinder
\[
 \left(\C^m\times\PP^1,
 g_{\rm E}+(-s)g_{S^2}\right)_{s<0},
 \qquad \Rc(g_{S^2})=\tfrac12g_{S^2}.
\]
More precisely, let \(\tau_i\searrow0\) realize such a tangent space and
let \(p_i\) be \(H_{2m+2}\)-centres of
\(\mu_{i,-1}=\mu_{1-\tau_i}\) with respect to
\(g_i(-1)=\tau_i^{-1}g(1-\tau_i)\) at backward scale one.
After passing to a further subsequence that still realizes the same
tangent space, there is \(D<\infty\) such that, for all sufficiently
large \(i\),
\[
 F_q\subset
 B_{\tau_i^{-1}g(1-\tau_i)}(p_i,D),
\]
and, for every finite \(A\ge0\), there is \(C_A<\infty\) such that
\[
 \sup_{B_{\tau_i^{-1}g(1-\tau_i)}(p_i,D+A)}
 |\Rm_{\tau_i^{-1}g(1-\tau_i)}|_{\tau_i^{-1}g(1-\tau_i)}
 \le C_A.
\]

[Lemma lem:interp of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] For $t_i\ne t_j$ let
$B_{ij}=\Bigl(\frac{t_iz_j-t_jz_i}{t_i-t_j},\ \frac{z_i-z_j}{t_i-t_j}\Bigr)
\in\mathbb{C}^2$ (the coefficients of the affine function of $t$ through the two
points) and $d_{ij}=|t_i-t_j|^2$. Then for every admissible $q$,
\[
  D(q):=1-|\mu|^2=\sum_{i<j}q_iq_jd_{ij},
  \qquad
  (a,b)=\sum_{\substack{i<j\\ t_i\ne t_j}}
  \frac{q_iq_jd_{ij}}{D(q)}\;B_{ij} .
\]
In particular $(a,b)$ is a convex combination of the pairwise interpolation
coefficients; the conditioning factor $(1-|\mu|^2)^{-1}$ is absorbed
entirely.

body: Rejected inference: a uniform first energy moment of a scalar Poisson transform, or a bounded density of the disorder-averaged spectral measure, implies almost-sure absolute continuity of the sample measures. This implication is false: delta_0 and the random scalar operator with uniform eigenvalue give exact counterexamples. A higher moment or another argument excluding sample singular mass is required.

body:
[Theorem 64 (Rank-uniform Newton element) of arXiv:2608.29585, '2608.29585'] For every zero-framed knot $K$, the series
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr H_K(X,A,q)=
 \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
 B_k(X;A,q)\mathsf H_k(K;A,q)
\end{equation}
converges in $\widehat{\mathscr C}_{A,q}$ and has the following
properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.8em]
\item For every $r\ge0$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathscr H_K(X_r(A,q),A,q)=\HH_r(K;A,q).
\end{equation}
\item For every $n\ge2$, the specialization $A=q^n$ gives the
fixed-rank Newton series with coefficients $H_k^{(n)}$.  After the
substitution $X=q^nx^2+q^{-n}x^{-2}$, it is the colored lift
$\mathscr J_K^{(n)}(x,q)$ of
\eqref{eq:colored-lift}.
\item For every $n\ge2$, $r\ge0$, and complex root of unity $\zeta$,
there is a canonical finite evaluation
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{ev}_{n,r,\zeta}(\mathscr H_K)
 =J_r^{SU(n)}(K;\zeta),
\end{equation}
where the right side means evaluation of the generic Laurent polynomial,
and $\operatorname{ev}_{n,r,\zeta}$ means first specializing $A=q^n$,
then $X=X_r(q^n,q)$, and finally $q=\zeta$.
\item The Newton coefficients in
\eqref{eq:two-variable-unified-element} are unique, and the full
family of color evaluations determines the element.
\end{enumerate}

Lemma~(lem:lower of the paper), the ordered elements
$a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_m$ of a positive reduced $D(\varepsilon N)$-tuple satisfy
\begin{equation}
 a_{i+\ell}>N^\gamma a_i
 \qquad(1\le i\le m-\ell),
\end{equation}
where $\ell<2^{35}$ and $\gamma>2^{-26}$.

body: In algebraic geometry, Bézout's theorem is a statement concerning the number of common zeros of n polynomials in n indeterminates. In its original form the theorem states that in general the number of common zeros equals the product of the degrees of the polynomials. It is named after Étienne Bézout.
title: Bézout's theorem

Let d>=2 and let an equal-weight identity-covariance three-Gaussian teacher have planar means (a,0),(-a/2,3sqrt(3)a/2),(-a/2,-3sqrt(3)a/2), a>0. For an equal-weight identity-covariance mixture-score student with planar means (s,0),(t,v),(t,-v), three reduced population DDPM excess-risk stationary equations imply full unrestricted criticality. For risk F=E||score_student-score_teacher||^2, define planar responsibilities w, posterior mean r, discrepancy h=r-r_teacher and J=[w_j(u_j-r)] over the two-dimensional teacher mixture. The full mean Hessian splits into a planar six-by-six block and d-2 identical perpendicular blocks K=2E[ww^T+J^T J-w h^T J-J^T h w^T]. Reflection decomposes the planar block into even/odd three-by-three blocks and K into a two-by-two block and a scalar. Thus for d>=3 positivity of blocks of sizes 3,3,2,1 is equivalent to positive definiteness of the full Hessian; for d=2 only the planar blocks occur. This is an exact finite-noise certificate reduction for arbitrary finite a,s,t,v, not a root enclosure, stability verdict, bifurcation location, new general symmetry theorem or resolution of Target 2.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:db304008efaf035d6a786c20db55eb6f0952fedbef4efe02440c187e6c5c25fb","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/db/db304008efaf035d6a786c20db55eb6f0952fedbef4efe02440c187e6c5c25fb.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:8b9df28b747be86db730665948e8487b9e0d4f11ab0f35d26292ab0cc7ae726f","bundle_entry_key":"t309-c21","bundle_id":"population.t309-finite-noise-stability-reduction-draft","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian mixture learning and diffusion objectives","draft":"w721/bundle_014.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.learning:gaussian-mixture-ddpm-finite-noise-reflection-perpendicular-hessian","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; T309-w721-C21 v1; proof (unaudited); Target 2 route 12 auxiliary certificate reduction.

# Exact finite-noise stability blocks for reflection-symmetric planar DDPM students

This supplies an exact reduction for the finite-noise stability step left by C20. It does not certify stability at any new amplitude or locate a bifurcation. No novelty finding or general-target move is asserted. The proof uses differentiated finite-mixture formulas and Gaussian integration, not a high-noise asymptotic expansion.

## 1. Setup and statement

Let d>=2 and fix a plane identified with R^2. The teacher is the equal-weight spherical mixture whose planar means are

    (a,0), (-a/2,3 sqrt(3)a/2), (-a/2,-3 sqrt(3)a/2), a>0,

and whose component covariance is I_d. Embed the student means in that plane, with

    u_0=(s,0), u_+=(t,v), u_-=(t,-v).

The student also has equal weights and covariance I_d. For general planar student means u_j, define

    w_j(y)=exp(y.u_j-||u_j||^2/2)/sum_l exp(y.u_l-||u_l||^2/2),
    r(y)=sum_j w_j u_j, h(y)=r(y)-r_*(y),
    J(y)=[w_0(u_0-r), w_+(u_+-r), w_-(u_--r)].       (1)

Here r_* is the teacher posterior mean and expectation E_y below is under its two-dimensional noisy mixture q_2. The population excess DDPM risk is F=E||score_student-score_teacher||^2, with no factor 1/2. At planar means it equals E_y||h(y)||^2 exactly.

The three equations partial_s F=partial_t F=partial_v F=0 imply full unrestricted mean criticality, including every ambient direction. At such a point the full mean Hessian is the direct sum of a six-dimensional planar block and d-2 identical perpendicular blocks

    K=2 E_y[ww^T+J^T J-w h^T J-J^T h w^T].          (2)

The planar block further splits into two explicit three-dimensional reflection blocks. The perpendicular block splits into a two-dimensional label-symmetric block and a one-dimensional label-antisymmetric block. Thus, for d>=3, positive definiteness of four matrices of sizes 3,3,2,1 is sufficient and necessary for positive definiteness of the full Hessian. For d=2 only the two planar blocks occur. This certifies a nondegenerate strict local minimum when the reduced gradient is zero; it does not characterize degenerate minima.

All expressions are exact two-dimensional expectations for arbitrary finite a,s,t,v. No noncollinearity is needed for the identities. Noncollinearity can be imposed separately when continuing the C06 branch.

## 2. Exact planar derivatives

For any planar direction p=(p_0,p_+,p_-), set

    L_j=(y-u_j).p_j, Lbar=sum_j w_j L_j,
    A_p=sum_j w_j p_j+sum_j w_j(u_j-r)L_j,
    B_p=2 Cov_w(p,L)+Cov_w(u,(L-Lbar)^2-||p||^2).

Cov_w(f,g)=sum_j w_j(f_j-E_w f)(g_j-E_w g), interpreted as a vector when f is vector valued. Direct differentiation of the softmax weights, including the second derivative -||p_j||^2 of each logit, gives

    D_p r=A_p, D_p^2 r=B_p,
    D_p^2 F=2 E_y[||A_p||^2+h.B_p].                 (3)

Polarization supplies the six-by-six planar Hessian. Equivalently the planar gradient for component j is

    grad_{u_j} F=2 E_y w_j[h+(y-u_j)((u_j-r).h)].    (4)

This form computes all reduced derivatives without differentiating a high-dimensional integral. At any fixed finite means, the score difference is bounded by the student and teacher mean norms. Parameter derivatives introduce polynomial factors in y with bounded softmax weights. Local Gaussian-mixture domination therefore justifies differentiation and polarization under the expectation to the finite orders used here.

## 3. The perpendicular Hessian and the essential logit bias

Perturb one perpendicular coordinate by mean components tau z_j, with z=(z_0,z_+,z_-). Let X denote the standard normal observation in that coordinate; it is independent of y under the teacher. At tau=0 define

    mu=w^T z, B=Jz, V=E_w z^2-mu^2.

The logit increments are tau X z_j-tau^2 z_j^2/2. Hence

    w'_j=w_j X(z_j-mu),
    w''_j=w_j[X^2((z_j-mu)^2-V)-(z_j^2-E_w z^2)]. (5)

The planar posterior derivative is X B and the perpendicular posterior derivative is mu. Averaging the planar second derivative over X, using E X^2=1, gives

    E_X r_planar''=-2 mu B.                       (6)

Indeed the average coefficient in (5) is -2 mu w_j(z_j-mu). The teacher has zero perpendicular posterior mean, so no perpendicular second derivative contributes to its inner product with the base score difference. Differentiating the squared error therefore yields

    D_z^2 F=2 E_y[mu^2+||B||^2-2 mu h.B]=z^T K z,

which proves (2).

The negative quadratic norm term in each logit is essential. Dropping it leaves a spurious Cov_w(u,z^2) contribution in (6), and generally changes the Hessian. As a simple consistency check, z=(1,1,1) gives mu=1 and B=0, so z^T K z=2: translating every mean equally in a normal direction changes the risk by exactly tau^2.

For multiple perpendicular coordinates, each first planar derivative contains its own independent standard Gaussian X_i. Cross products average to zero for distinct i, and the mean-norm logit has no mixed second derivative between distinct orthogonal axes. The normal posterior derivatives also occupy orthogonal coordinates. Consequently the perpendicular Hessian is I_{d-2} tensor K. Mixed planar/perpendicular Hessian blocks vanish by oddness in X_i. All perpendicular first derivatives vanish for the same reason.

## 4. Reflection blocks and full criticality

Order planar coordinates as (x_0,y_0,x_+,y_+,x_-,y_-). Reflection of the physical second coordinate together with exchanging labels + and - acts by

    T(x_0,y_0,x_+,y_+,x_-,y_-)
      =(x_0,-y_0,x_-,-y_-,x_+,-y_+).

The teacher and risk are invariant under this orthogonal involution. The proposed student lies in its fixed space. Thus its gradient has no T-odd component. The map (s,t,v) spans the fixed space with full rank, so the three reduced stationary equations force its entire planar gradient to vanish. Section 3 supplies the remaining ambient criticality.

Let e_i be the six standard basis vectors. Orthogonal bases for the T-even and T-odd spaces are

    Q_even=[e_1,(e_3+e_5)/sqrt(2),(e_4-e_6)/sqrt(2)],
    Q_odd =[e_2,(e_3-e_5)/sqrt(2),(e_4+e_6)/sqrt(2)].

At a reflection-fixed point, the planar Hessian H commutes with T, by differentiating the invariance twice. Therefore Q_even^T H Q_odd=0. Its two blocks are H_even=Q_even^T H Q_even and H_odd=Q_odd^T H Q_odd, both of size three. This splitting holds even before imposing stationarity.

On each perpendicular coordinate the same physical reflection leaves the perpendicular axis unchanged and swaps student labels +,-. Consequently K commutes with S(z_0,z_+,z_-)=(z_0,z_-,z_+). With three-dimensional standard basis f_j, set

    P_even=[f_1,(f_2+f_3)/sqrt(2)],
    P_odd=(f_2-f_3)/sqrt(2).

Then K_even=P_even^T K P_even has size two, K_odd=P_odd^T K P_odd is scalar, and the off-block term vanishes. Together with Section 3 this proves the stated fixed-size Hessian test in every ambient dimension.

For underlying locations nu with noisy means M=a nu, gradients and Hessians at fixed a acquire factors a and a^2 respectively. Therefore stationary points and Hessian signs are unchanged by that fixed-a parameter conversion. A changing-noise algorithm still needs C20's explicit learning-rate conversion.

## Scope and next unpaid certificate

This is an exact certificate reduction, not a finite-noise stability verdict. To establish continuation beyond the small-amplitude regime one must connect enclosed zeros of the three reduced equations to the C06 bad branch, for example by overlapping uniqueness boxes, and prove positivity of all applicable blocks over the relevant parameter/noise boxes. A positive excess-risk bound must separately certify nonglobality; enclosing some stationary point could instead locate the teacher's global minimum. Alternatively one may exhibit and certify a loss of positivity on the continued branch. Any computer-assisted implementation must use outward-rounded integration or exact bounds, with Gaussian tails controlled. Floating-point roots or sampled Hessian eigenvalues would be numerical evidence only.

The finite rational script checks (5)--(6), the common-normal-translation value, a wrong-logit-bias control and the reflection eigenspaces. It does not independently certify analytic differentiation, root existence or block positivity. [Definition 12 of arXiv:2608.25785, 'Proper Actions on Homogeneous Spaces of the Upper Triangular Matrix Group via Coarse Geome'] Let $S$ be a set.
    A family $\mathcal{B}\subset \mathcal{P}(S)$ of subsets of $S$ is called a \emph{bornology} on $S$ if it satisfies the following three conditions. 
    \begin{enumerate} 
        \item $\mathcal{B}$ is a cover of $S$ (i.e.~ $\bigcup_{B\in \mathcal{B}}B=S$).
        \item $B_1 ,B_2\in \mathcal{B}$ implies $B_1\cup B_2\in \mathcal{B}$. 
        \item $B\in \mathcal{B}$ and $B'\subset B$ imply $B'\in \mathcal{B}$. 
    \end{enumerate}
    The pair $(S,\mathcal{B})$ is called a \emph{bornological space}.

[Lemm 10 of arXiv:2608.30357, 'Mean convergence for Banach space-valued random elements indexed in measure spaces'] Let $X, Y$ be $\cX$-valued random elements.
\begin{enumerate}[\rm (i)]
\item If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then they are diagonally negatively dependent.

\item $X, Y$ are diagonally negatively dependent if and only if $Y, X$ are. Moreover, \eqref{def:PDND} holds for a set $A \in \cB(\cX)$ if and only if it holds for $A^c$.

\item Let $(\cY, \|\cdot\|_\cY)$ be a separable Banach space and let $f \colon \cX \to \cY$ be $\cB(\cX)/\cB(\cY)$-measurable. If $X, Y$ are diagonally negatively dependent, then so are $f(X), f(Y)$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Lemm 10 of arXiv:2608.30357

Then $T_c = \var_{\alpha_V}(x)$ and

 \inf_{\varphi}\partial^2_\varphi V_T(\varphi) = 
\frac{T - T_c}{T^2}.

Let U ⊂ C be open and let f_n be holomorphic on U with f_n → f uniformly on every compact subset of U. Then f is holomorphic on U, and for every k ≥ 1 the derivatives f_n^(k) converge to f^(k) uniformly on every compact subset of U. Quantitatively, if the closed disk of radius 2r about a lies in U and g is holomorphic on U, then sup over |z - a| ≤ r of |g^(k)(z)| ≤ k! r^{-k} sup over |z - a| ≤ 2r of |g(z)|. The same holds for series: a series of holomorphic functions converging locally uniformly may be differentiated term by term any number of times. The convergence of derivatives is locally uniform, not uniform on all of U.

[Lemma lem:1* of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] Fix $q\in (0,1/5)$ and $\Phi\in (0,1/10)$. 
   Then for all $b \in (0,1)$ sufficiently small (depending only on $q,\Phi$), the following is true. For all $z\in \mathbb{C},r>0$, there exist deterministic (depending only on $z,r,q,\Phi,b$) points $u_+,u_-,v_+,v_-$ satisfying $u_+,u_-\in B_{\Phi r}(z-r)$ and $v_+,v_-\in B_{\Phi  r}(z+r)$ such that the balls of Euclidean radius $2br$ around $u_+,u_-,v_+,v_-,u,v$ are all pairwise disjoint and the intersection of the following events, which we call $G_r(z)$, occurs with probability at least $q$.
   \begin{enumerate}
   \item  $\mathscr{X}_{u_-,v_-}^{u_+,v_+}$
   \item  $\Gamma_{u_+,u}\cup \Gamma_{u_-,u}\subseteq B_{\Phi r}(z-r)$ and $\Gamma_{v,v_+}\cup \Gamma_{v,v_-}\subseteq B_{\Phi r}(z+r)$.
   \item  $\mathrm{dist}(\Gamma_{u,v_+}\cup \Gamma_{u,v_-}, \{u_+,u_-\})\geq 2br$ and $\mathrm{dist}(\Gamma_{u_+,v}\cup \Gamma_{u_-,v}, \{v_+,v_-\})\geq 2br$

   \item $\mathrm{dist}(\Gamma_{u_-,u}\cup \Gamma_{u_+,u}, \Gamma_{v,v_-}\cup \Gamma_{v,v_+})\geq 2br$
   \end{enumerate}
   Further, the points $u_+,u_-,v_+,v_-$ can be chosen such that the family of events $\{G_r(z)\}_{z\in \mathbb{C}, r>0}$ is translation and scale invariant.

Let (S,g) be a compact, oriented, boundaryless smooth Riemannian 2-manifold (surface) with Gaussian curvature K. Then the integral of K over S with respect to the Riemannian area element dA equals 2*pi times the Euler characteristic of S: integral_S K dA = 2 pi chi(S). More generally, if S has piecewise smooth boundary, integral_S K dA + integral_{boundary S} k_g ds + sum of exterior angles at corners = 2 pi chi(S), where k_g is the geodesic curvature of the boundary.
