{"artifact_digest":"sha256:c7de1d1270fea600cf249739b297f9b29e8cca36a1ecb90de84a7fe77545d9f6","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/c7/c7de1d1270fea600cf249739b297f9b29e8cca36a1ecb90de84a7fe77545d9f6.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:a4580348d9302652f45d19888b6a16b5c5ba99c2420313b3517382602955fd39","bundle_entry_key":"tanh_relative_gap_noise","bundle_id":"population.w712-t250-c009-relative-gap-noise","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Quantitative Gaussian-process limits and empirical correlation matrices","draft":"w712/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.neural_networks:tanh-gram-gap-relative-conditional-bias-variance","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# C009 v1: relative conditional noise of a two-input tanh Gram gap

Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: moved, a conditional-noise component of the reviewer's named first rung. Target: T250(a). Novelty unverified. This is not a proof of the multi-layer relative gap recursion.

## Statement

Let 0<q<=1, -1<=c<=1, and n>=64. Independently across i, let (X_i,Y_i) be standard bivariate Gaussians with correlation c. Set F(q)=E tanh(sqrt(q)Z)^2 and

    U_i=tanh(sqrt(q)X_i)/sqrt(F(q)),
    V_i=tanh(sqrt(q)Y_i)/sqrt(F(q)),
    h=E[U_i V_i], delta=1-h,
    A=mean U_i^2, D=mean V_i^2, T=mean U_i V_i,
    Dhat=1-T/sqrt(AD).

This is the uncentered empirical Gram correlation: sample means are not subtracted. The denominators are positive almost surely. There is an explicit universal rational K, defined below, such that, if c<1,

    |E Dhat-delta| <= K delta/n,
    E(Dhat/delta-1)^2 <= K/n,
    Var(Dhat) <= K delta^2/n.                         (1)

At c=1 both gaps are zero almost surely. At c=-1 both gaps equal two. The same assertions hold conditionally on any past for which the current two Gaussian marginal variances are equal to q and the fresh paired rows are independent. No independence of A and D is required.

Define M=15!!=2027025 and

    a=64(4M+1), b=64(16M+1), d=2048M,
    J=64^20 sum_{j=0}^{20} binom(20,j) product_{r=1}^j (64-2r)^(-1),
    K=(1+a+b+d+J)^12.

An empty product is one. These constants are deliberately large, but finite, rational, and independent of q,c,n. The hardest step is controlling inverse empirical norms without losing a factor of the population gap near c=1.

## 1. Gaussian increment moments relative to the population gap

The elementary tanh inequalities from C002 v2 give

    q/(1+3q)<=F(q)<=q,
    x^2/(1+x^2)<=tanh(x)^2<=x^2.

Put u(z)=tanh(sqrt(q)z)/sqrt(F(q)). Then E u(Z)^2=1, u is odd, |u(z)|<=2|z|, and its Lipschitz constant is at most two. If alpha=E[Zu(Z)], weighted Jensen for z^2 dgamma gives

    alpha >= E[Z^2/sqrt(1+qZ^2)] >= (1+3q)^(-1/2)>=1/2.

Write u(z)=alpha z+r(z), where E[Zr(Z)]=0. Gaussian conditioning gives E[Xr(Y)]=c E[Yr(Y)]=0, and likewise for the other cross terms. Consequently

    2delta=E(u(X)-u(Y))^2
       =2alpha^2(1-c)+E(r(X)-r(Y))^2 >= (1-c)/2.

Thus delta>0 when c<1 and 1-c<=4delta. Set W_i=(U_i-V_i)^2/2. For every positive integer p,

    E W_i=delta,
    ||W_i||_p <=16 delta G_(2p)^2,
    ||U_i^2-1||_p, ||V_i^2-1||_p <=4G_(2p)^2+1,
    ||U_i^2-V_i^2||_p <=16sqrt(2)G_(2p)^2 sqrt(delta),       (2)

where G_k=(E|Z|^k)^(1/k). Indeed |U-V|<=2|X-Y| and X-Y has variance 2(1-c), so ||U-V||_(2p)<=4sqrt(2delta)G_(2p). For the last line use Holder on (U-V)(U+V), with ||U+V||_(2p)<=4G_(2p). The centered variable U_i^2-V_i^2 has mean zero because the CURRENT variances are equal.

## 2. Sample mean moments, with an elementary finite count

For an even integer p and independent centered identically distributed B_i,

    ||mean B_i||_p <=p^2 ||B_1||_p/sqrt(n).                (3)

To verify this, expand the p-th power. A term with an index occurring once has zero expectation. Every remaining ordered p-tuple uses at most p/2 distinct indices. Their number is at most sum_{r=1}^{p/2} n^r r^p <=p^(p+1)n^(p/2). Holder bounds each term's absolute expectation by E|B_1|^p. Taking p-th roots gives p^(1+1/p)<=p^2. This counts an overestimate of all tuples, so needs no sign assumption.

Let w=mean W_i, x=A-1, y=D-1, and s=A-D. For p=2,4,8, (2)-(3) imply

    ||x||_p,||y||_p <=a/sqrt(n),
    ||w-delta||_p <=b delta/sqrt(n),
    ||w||_p <=(1+b)delta,
    ||s||_p <=d sqrt(delta/n).                           (4)

Here G_(2p)^2<=M for these three p, p^2<=64, and 16sqrt(2)<=32. These loose inequalities explain each integer constant in the statement.

## 3. Uniform inverse empirical norms

Pointwise,

    u(z)^2 >= z^2/(1+z^2).

For a subset I of exactly 64 samples, let A_I=mean_{i in I} U_i^2 and S_I=sum_{i in I}X_i^2. Then

    A_I >= S_I/[64(1+S_I)].

S_I has chi-square distribution with 64 degrees of freedom. Direct integration of its density s^31 exp(-s/2)/(2^32 Gamma(32)) gives, for j=0,...,20,

    E S_I^(-j)=product_{r=1}^j (64-2r)^(-1).

All integrals converge because j<=20<32. Hence E A_I^(-20)<=J. For n>=64, the average of A_I over all size-64 subsets is exactly A: each index occurs in binom(n-1,63) subsets and binom(n-1,63)/(64 binom(n,64))=1/n. Jensen for the convex function t^(-20) gives E A^(-20)<=J, and the same proof gives E D^(-20)<=J. Thus, by Lyapunov and J>=1,

    ||A^(-r)||_p,||D^(-r)||_p <=J^r whenever rp<=20.       (5)

Subset averaging is an analytic argument, not a request to enumerate subsets. No dependence assumption between the two sample norms is used.

## 4. Keep the normalization bias at order delta/n

Let k=(AD)^(-1/2) and

    t=(sqrt(A)-sqrt(D))^2/(2sqrt(AD)).

The exact Gram identity, including its factor two, is

    w=(A+D-2T)/2,
    Dhat=w k-t,
    0<=t <=(A-D)^2/(8AD).                              (6)

The last inequality uses (sqrt(A)+sqrt(D))^2>=4sqrt(AD). Holder with (4)-(5) yields

    ||t||_2 <= d^2 J^2 delta/n.                         (7)

For example, ||(A-D)^2||_4=||s||_8^2 and ||(AD)^(-1)||_4<=J^2; dropping the factor 1/8 only weakens the bound.

The identity |A^(-1/2)-1|=|x|/[sqrt(A)(1+sqrt(A))] gives

    ||k-1||_4 <=2aJ/sqrt(n).                            (8)

Indeed k-1=(A^(-1/2)-1)D^(-1/2)+(D^(-1/2)-1), followed by Holder with exponents eight and (5).

We also need the linear Taylor term, rather than just (8). For g(z)=z^(-1/2), Taylor with its integral remainder gives

    g(A)=1-x/2+r_A,
    |r_A| <=(3/8)x^2(1+A^(-5/2)).

The same holds for D,y,r_D. Set R=k-1+(x+y)/2. Algebra gives

    R=r_A g(D)+r_D-(x/2)(g(D)-1).

Holder and (4)-(5) now give

    ||R||_2 <=(a^2/n)[(3/8)(1+J^(5/2))(1+sqrt(J))+sqrt(J)/2]
             <=2a^2 J^4/n.                            (9)

The strongest inverse moment here is E A^(-20): to bound the first term, use ||x^2||_4 and ||(1+A^(-5/2))D^(-1/2)||_4, then split the latter by Holder into L8 factors. Thus no inverse moment above the proved range is used.

Since E x=E y=0 and E w=delta,

    E[w(k-1)]=-(1/2)E[(w-delta)(x+y)]+E[wR].

Equations (4),(7),(9) imply

    |E Dhat-delta| <=[ba+2(1+b)a^2J^4+d^2J^2]delta/n.   (10)

Using only Cauchy-Schwarz on E[w(k-1)] would lose a square root of n. The centered linear term above is what avoids that loss.

## 5. Relative second moment and explicit constant

From (4),(6)-(8) and n>=1,

    ||Dhat-delta||_2
      <=||w-delta||_2+||w||_4||k-1||_4+||t||_2
      <=[b+2(1+b)aJ+d^2J^2]delta/sqrt(n).               (11)

Write H=1+a+b+d+J>=2. The bracket in (10) is at most 4H^7<=H^12. The bracket in (11) is at most 4H^4, whose square is at most 16H^8<=H^12. This proves (1) with K=H^12. Variance is no larger than the mean squared deviation from the fixed value delta. At c=1, U_i=V_i; at c=-1, U_i=-V_i, proving the endpoint statements directly. All constants and estimates are uniform in q,c and therefore can be applied to a past-measurable q,c by conditioning.

## 6. What this does and does not close

At an equal-current-variance state, write delta=1-H(q,q,c). The next empirical gap has relative conditional bias at most K/n and relative conditional variance at most K/n. This proves the conditional-innovation part of the reviewer's proposed rung, uniformly even as c increases to one.

It does NOT prove a C003-type relative recursion for the original multi-layer D_l. Equal initial variances are not preserved by empirical sampling. If q_0=r_0>0 and |c_0|<1, then Q_1!=R_1 almost surely: condition on all X_i and on Y_1,...,Y_(n-1). The remaining Y_n has a nondegenerate Gaussian conditional law; tanh(sqrt(q_0)Y_n)^2 has no atoms, so its sum with the fixed other terms cannot equal the specified X-sum with positive probability. Thus applying this equal-current-variance lemma at every layer would be invalid. A coupled radial-contrast estimate, or a general unequal-current-variance extension, remains necessary. This is the FIRST missing premise in that proposed iteration.

The lower width restriction is substantive for this normalization route. For n=1, the empirical uncentered correlation is sign(XY), so E Dhat=2 arccos(c)/pi: write Y=cX+sqrt(1-c^2)Z with independent standard Gaussians X,Z. Their planar angle is uniform, and the discordant-sign sectors have total angle 2 arccos(c). The Lipschitz bound and section 1 give (1-c)/4<=delta<=4(1-c). Consequently a uniform relative bias O(1/n) all the way to c=1 fails at n=1. This observation does not refute the n>=64 claim or the eventual large-width target.

body:
Let P be a product measure on {0,1}^n and let A and B be increasing events. Write A box B for the disjoint occurrence of A and B: the set of configurations omega for which there are disjoint index sets I and J such that every configuration agreeing with omega on I lies in A and every configuration agreeing with omega on J lies in B. Then P(A box B) <= P(A) P(B) (van den Berg and Kesten 1985). This runs in the opposite direction to the Harris-FKG inequality for the plain intersection, P(A and B) >= P(A) P(B); the two are not in conflict because A box B is a subset of A and B. In percolation the standard use is P(two disjoint open paths) <= P(open path)^2.
P is a product measure (independent coordinates)
A and B are increasing events (van den Berg-Kesten); Reimer's inequality removes this hypothesis
A box B is the disjoint-occurrence event, witnessed by disjoint coordinate sets, not the intersection

[Defn 2 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] Fix a KCLG (i.e., a constraint function $c$).
Two configurations $\eta,\eta'\in\Omega$ are \emph{connected}, denoted
$\eta\connected{}c\eta'$, if there is a sequence of configurations
$\eta_{0},\eta_{1},\dots,\eta_{n}$ starting with $\eta_{0}=\eta$
and ending at $\eta_{n}=\eta'$, such that $\eta_{i+1}=\eta_{i}^{x,y}$
for $x,y$ such that $c(x,y,\eta_{i})\neq0$. We denote $\eta\connected Lc\eta'$
for configurations connected in the interval $[1,L]$.

body:
[Lemma lem:haar-residual of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $V$ be any finite-dimensional orthogonal $\mathrm{SO}(n)$-module,
let $\mathcal K_V=N^{-1}\sum_iP_{i,V}$, and let $\Pi_V$ be the
orthogonal projection onto $V^{\mathrm{SO}(n)}$.  With
$Q_V=I-\Pi_V$, for every $\ell\ge0$,
\[
 \boxed{\mathcal K_V^\ell=\Pi_V+Q_V\mathcal K_V^\ell Q_V.}
\tag{3.2.10s}
\]
Consequently every empty chronological gap in a fixed reflected ribbon
child is exactly either a Haar separator or a residual gap.  Expanding
all gaps produces at most $2^h$ children when $h$ physical times are
used.  End components obey the same convention after inserting a common
auxiliary Haar conjugation in the conjugation-invariant squared-shell
scalar.

[Proposition 4 (A bounded Brownian perturbation in a mixed equation) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\wt\eta\in(1/\alpha,1)$, let $0<\lambda<1$, let $\kappa\ne0$, and let $r\in L^2(0,T)$ be deterministic. Consider
\[
  b(t,x)=\wt b(t,x)\equiv0,
  \qquad
  a(t,x)\equiv\kappa,
  \qquad
  \wt a(t,x)=\kappa+r(t),
\]
and
\[
  \sigma(t,x)=\wt\sigma(t,x)=1+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr).
\]
Then the baseline equation contains both the Brownian and stable terms, the perturbed equation is driven by the same two noises, and the stable coefficient is bounded, bounded away from zero, and non-Lipschitz at the origin. For any coupled solution pair satisfying Assumption~\ref{ass:solutions}, the coefficient distances are
\[
  B=0,
  \qquad
  A^2=\int_0^T |r(t)|^2\dd t,
  \qquad
  S=0.
\]
Consequently, if $x_0=\wt x_0$ and $A=\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}<1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:noncritical} gives
\[
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}
  \le C\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}}.
\]
Thus, in this mixed Brownian--stable equation, the estimate reduces to the Brownian diffusion error, while the stable coefficient is H\"older and fails to be Lipschitz.

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2609.02755, 'The Sharp Rate of Probabilistically Strong Convergence to the KPZ Equation'] Let $(\gamma, \eta) = (2 + 2 \kappa, \vartheta)$ and $(\tilde{\gamma}, \tilde{\eta}) = (3/2 + 2 \kappa, - \kappa)$ where $\vartheta \in (0, 1/2 - \kappa)$. Suppose that $(\Hb, \Hp, \mathcal{W}) \in \mcD^{\gamma, \eta} \times \mcD^{\gamma, \eta} \times \mcD^{\tilde{\gamma}, \tilde{\eta}}$ is a solution of the fixed-point problem
	\begin{equs}[eq:system-in-lemma]
		\Hb &= \mathcal{P}_\gamma \mathbf{1}_+ [(\partial_x \Hb)^2 + \<b0>] + \mathcal{G} \psi
		\\
		\Hp &= \mathcal{P}_\gamma \mathbf{1}_+ [(\partial_x \Hp)^2 + \<p0>] + \mathcal{G} \psi
		\\
		\mathcal{W} &= \mathcal{P}_{\tilde{\gamma}} \mathbf{1}_+ [\partial_x \mathcal{W} (\partial_x \Hb + \partial_x \Hp) + \<0t>]
	\end{equs}
	with respect to the BPHZ model $Z^{\eps,\delta}$ and that $\mathcal{G}\psi$ is the usual lift of the caloric extension of the initial data $\psi \in C^\vartheta(\mathbb{T})$ to a modelled distribution.
	
	Then $(\mathcal{R}\Hb, \mathcal{R} \Hp, \mathcal{R} \mathcal{W})$ solves the system \eqref{eq:main_sys}.

[Prop fourier-obstruction of arXiv:2606.08325, 'Digit Mixing under Polynomial Maps'] Let \(Q\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be an integer-valued polynomial of  degree $d$, say
			\[ Q(x)=a_dx^d+a_{d-1}x^{d-1}+\cdots+a_0, \qquad a_d\ne0.
			\]
			Then
			\begin{equation}
			\lim_{N\to\infty}
			\mathbb E\, e(2^NQ(X))=L_Q,
			\end{equation}
			where
			\[
			L_Q
			=
			\prod_{\ell=1}^{\infty}
			\exp\left(
			\lambda\bigl(e(a_dd!2^{-\ell})-1\bigr)
			\right).
			\]
			In particular, $0<|L_Q|<1$.
title: Prop fourier-obstruction of arXiv:2606.08325

For mixed-Poisson X with mixing Lambda>=0 finite a.s., its probability generating function G(s)=E exp((s-1)Lambda) is log-convex on [0,1]. Strict log-convexity holds iff mixing is nondegenerate. Cauchy-Schwarz equality holds iff Lambda is constant; then log G is affine.
Lambda finite and nonnegative almost surely

[Theorem thm:main-nontriviality of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Let $d\geq2$, let $(\mu_\rho)_{\rho\in(0,1]}$ be a family of laws with mean $\mathbb{E}_{\mu_\rho}\sigma(0)=\rho$, and let the masses be i.i.d.\ with law $\mu_\rho$. Suppose there are $\rho_0\in(0,1)$, $\nu_0>0$, $\theta_0>0$, and $K_0<\infty$ such that
\begin{equation}
    \inf_{\rho_0\leq\rho<1}\Var_{\mu_\rho}(\sigma(0))\geq\nu_0^2
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \sup_{\rho_0\leq\rho<1}\mathbb{E}_{\mu_\rho}e^{\theta_0|\sigma(0)-\rho|}\leq K_0\, .
\end{equation}
Then there is $\rho_+=\rho_+(d,(\mu_\rho))\in[\rho_0,1)$ such that $\mathcal T^{(\rho)}$ contains an infinite nearest-neighbor component almost surely for every $\rho\in(\rho_+,1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

On a honeycomb mesh of side length delta, choose a complete interior hexagonal face with counterclockwise vertices v_0,...,v_5. The complex midpoint field H((v_j+v_{j+1})/2)=delta/(v_{j+1}-v_j), with indices modulo 6 and H=0 elsewhere, satisfies every vertex relation sum_p(p-v)H(p)=0, has six support points of modulus 1, and vanishes at every boundary midpoint. Adding H to a solution preserves every boundary value. This is an author-proved auxiliary result, pending full independent review.

[Theorem thm:ci of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Under assumption~(ass:dynamics of the paper), let $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu \in
L^2(\mu)$, and let $\tilde\sigma_A^2$ and $c_A$ be sub-gamma parameters for which
Eq.~(equation eq:uq_general of the paper) holds with $\overline{A}_t \in
\{\overline{\rho}_t(V), \overline{J}_t(U)\}$. 
Fix a confidence level $1-\alpha$, with $\alpha\in (0,1)$, and define
\begin{align}
  r_A(\alpha,t)
  =
  \sqrt{\frac{2\tilde\sigma_A^2}{t}\log\left(\frac{2N_\nu}{\alpha}\right)}
  +
  \frac{c_A}{t}\log\left(\frac{2N_\nu}{\alpha}\right),
  \quad
  N_\nu \equiv \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)},
  
\end{align}
where $N_\nu$ is a prefactor encoding the initial condition with $N_\mu=1$.
Then for every $t > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(-r_A(\alpha,t) \leq \overline{A}_t - \E^\mu[\overline{A}_t] \leq r_A(\alpha,t)\right)
  \geq 1-\alpha ,
  
\end{align}
that is, with probability of at least $1-\alpha$, under $\mathbb{P}^\nu$, the stationary mean lies in the confidence interval
\begin{align}
  \E^\mu[\overline{A}_t]
  \in
  \left[\overline{A}_t - r_A(\alpha,t),
  \overline{A}_t + r_A(\alpha,t)\right].
  
\end{align}
Moreover, the corresponding one-sided guarantees hold with a smaller radius $r_A^{(1)}(\alpha,t)$, 
obtained from Eq.~(equation eq:ci_radius of the paper) by replacing $2N_\nu$ with $N_\nu$, i.e., 
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{A}_t - \E^\mu[\overline{A}_t]
  \leq r_A^{(1)}(\alpha,t)\right)
  \geq 1-\alpha,
  \qquad
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\E^\mu[\overline{A}_t] -  \overline{A}_t
  \leq r_A^{(1)}(\alpha,t)\right)
  \geq 1-\alpha.
  
\end{align}

Observe independent x_i~N(0,I_p), e_i~N(0,sigma^2 I_m), z_i=Delta x_i+e_i, with sigma>=0. Let X=[x_i], Z=[z_i], C=XX^T/n, D=ZX^T/n, W=D C^(-1). Independently initialize B0=0, A0 p-by-p with iid N(0,s^2) entries, any s>0. Almost surely C is positive definite and A0 is invertible.

For such a realization define

 lambda=lambda_min(C), c=||C||op, h0=lambda_min(A0 A0^T)>0,
 q0=||W C^(1/2)||F^2/2,
 J=||A0 A0^T||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(p)(J+2R).

Choose a measurable constant step, for example the minimum of the three displayed bounds,

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/(6Kc+||D||op),h0/[4(1+q0)]}.

Run simultaneous GD on the empirical factor loss ||BA X-Z||F^2/(2n). Then almost surely

 ||B_t A_t-W||F^2 <= (2q0/lambda) exp(-eta h0 lambda t/2),

so B_t A_t converges to W, the ordinary least-squares product. Because r=p, the rank-r reduced-rank-regression product equals W. Moreover,

 lim_(t->infinity) E ||B_t A_t-Delta||F^2
 =E||W-Delta||F^2
 =sigma^2 m p/(n-p-1).

Thus the limiting expected population excess risk equals that of rank-r reduced-rank regression, factor exactly one, for this full-input-rank family and this initialization-dependent step. The sample condition n>p+3 is more than the n>p+1 needed for the known OLS formula; the extra two samples support an elementary second-moment domination proof below. No uniform deterministic iteration count in expectation, efficiency or proper-bottleneck guarantee is claimed. This family satisfies the named target's sample-size condition whenever n is chosen large enough to satisfy that condition as well.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:66306f87358b8c94bfcb47780dffea9ca3362f4d33a2f0091be9cf10f969ac1c","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/66/66306f87358b8c94bfcb47780dffea9ca3362f4d33a2f0091be9cf10f969ac1c.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:6ab216f2bd8c79eac2b1976bf71f57838efe6ef2416fb288fbea2f08f8d174d5","bundle_entry_key":"full-input-risk","bundle_id":"population.t419-full-input-empirical-gd-risk-domination-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"LoRA finite-sample optimization and expected regression risk","draft":"w705/bundle_008.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.lowrank:lora-full-input-empirical-gd-expected-risk-gaussian-domination","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T419-C018 v1: full-input-rank empirical GD reaches OLS with convergent expected risk

Kind: narrowed. Target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claimed.
This is the full-input-rank family r=p=d_in, with output dimension m>=p. It includes arbitrary Gaussian initialization scales but uses an initialization-dependent constant step. It does not address the proper rank bottleneck r<p. The deterministic part builds on C014 and the published Du-Hu-Lee imbalance method; the OLS risk is known, not a new statistical formula.

## Statement

Let Delta be any fixed real m-by-p matrix, m>=p>=1, of exact rank p. Let n>p+3. Observe independent x_i~N(0,I_p), e_i~N(0,sigma^2 I_m), z_i=Delta x_i+e_i, with sigma>=0. Let X=[x_i], Z=[z_i], C=XX^T/n, D=ZX^T/n, W=D C^(-1). Independently initialize B0=0, A0 p-by-p with iid N(0,s^2) entries, any s>0. Almost surely C is positive definite and A0 is invertible.

For such a realization define

 lambda=lambda_min(C), c=||C||op, h0=lambda_min(A0 A0^T)>0,
 q0=||W C^(1/2)||F^2/2,
 J=||A0 A0^T||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(p)(J+2R).

Choose a measurable constant step, for example the minimum of the three displayed bounds,

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/(6Kc+||D||op),h0/[4(1+q0)]}.

Run simultaneous GD on the empirical factor loss ||BA X-Z||F^2/(2n). Then almost surely

 ||B_t A_t-W||F^2 <= (2q0/lambda) exp(-eta h0 lambda t/2),

so B_t A_t converges to W, the ordinary least-squares product. Because r=p, the rank-r reduced-rank-regression product equals W. Moreover,

 lim_(t->infinity) E ||B_t A_t-Delta||F^2
 =E||W-Delta||F^2
 =sigma^2 m p/(n-p-1).

Thus the limiting expected population excess risk equals that of rank-r reduced-rank regression, factor exactly one, for this full-input-rank family and this initialization-dependent step. The sample condition n>p+3 is more than the n>p+1 needed for the known OLS formula; the extra two samples support an elementary second-moment domination proof below. No uniform deterministic iteration count in expectation, efficiency or proper-bottleneck guarantee is claimed. This family satisfies the named target's sample-size condition whenever n is chosen large enough to satisfy that condition as well.

## Deterministic convergence, retaining the covariance metric

Subtract the constant empirical residual at W. The resulting loss is

 q(B,A)=||(BA-W) C^(1/2)||F^2/2,

with product gradient G=BA C-D. Let E=BA-W and F_t=A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t. C014 proves, for the first two step bounds above,

 q_(t+1)<=q_t-(eta/2)||grad q_t||F^2,
 ||F_t-F_0||F<=2eta q0,
 ||B_t A_t||F<=R.

Its proof establishes these inequalities without assuming factor boundedness in advance, and works with this anisotropic covariance, not a substituted isotropic GD. The third step bound makes

 2eta q0<=h0 q0/[2(1+q0)]<h0/2.

Hence F_t>=h0 I/2 and A_t A_t^T>=h0 I/2 for all t. The square input factor is essential. Since grad_B q=E C A_t^T,

 ||grad q||F^2 >=(h0/2)||E C||F^2
               >=h0 lambda q.

Combine this with descent to get q_(t+1)<=(1-eta h0 lambda/2)q_t. The multiplier is nonnegative: K bounds the initial factor-pair squared norm, so K>=h0, and eta<=1/(6Kc+||D||op) implies eta h0 lambda<=1/6. Iterate and use q>=lambda||E||F^2/2. If q0=0, the gradients vanish and the same conclusion is immediate.

No high-probability complement is discarded here. C and A0 meet these deterministic assumptions almost surely; the step is selected from their realized values. Defining an arbitrary measurable positive step on the null singular event has no effect on any expectation claim.

## An integrable product bound independent of the initializer

The fact that eta is allowed to depend on A0 does not itself establish expectation convergence. For every t on the almost-sure event,

 ||B_t A_t-Delta||F^2<=2R^2+2||Delta||F^2.

Here R depends only on the training data, because B0=0 makes q0 independent of A0. We now prove its expectation is finite.

Conditional on X, write W=Delta+N C^(-1/2), where N has iid N(0,sigma^2/n) entries and its conditional law is independent of X. Thus

 E[||W||F^2 | X]=||Delta||F^2+(m sigma^2/n)tr(C^(-1)),
 E[2q0 | X]=||Delta C^(1/2)||F^2+mp sigma^2/n.

Since R^2<=2||W||F^2+4q0/lambda, its conditional expectation is at most

 2||Delta||F^2+(2m sigma^2/n)tr(C^(-1))
 +2||Delta||F^2 ||C||op||C^(-1)||op
 +(2mp sigma^2/n)||C^(-1)||op.

It remains to check the covariance moments used in this expression. A fully elementary bound suffices; no asymptotic random-matrix approximation is needed.

## Exact finite inverse-covariance moment check

Let G=X^T be the n-by-p standard Gaussian design. For each column j let d_j be its distance from the span of the other p-1 columns. Almost surely these spans have dimension p-1. The j-th row of the left pseudoinverse G^+ has squared norm d_j^(-2): it is the normalized residual vector of column j after orthogonal projection onto the other columns. Consequently

 sigma_min(G)^(-2)<=||G^+||F^2=sum_j d_j^(-2),
 sigma_min(G)^(-4)<=p sum_j d_j^(-4).

Conditional on the other columns, d_j^2 is chi-squared with k=n-p+1 degrees of freedom, by Gaussian orthogonal projection. Its density is t^(k/2-1)e^(-t/2)/(2^(k/2) Gamma(k/2)). Direct integration gives, for k>4,

 E[d_j^(-4)]=1/[(k-2)(k-4)].

No independence between different d_j is assumed. Therefore

 E||C^(-1)||op^2
 <= n^2 p^2/[(n-p-1)(n-p-3)]<infinity.

Also ||C||op<=tr C and the sum of np independent squared standard Gaussians gives

 E||C||op^2<=E[(tr C)^2]=p^2+2p/n.

Cauchy-Schwarz now proves E[||C||op||C^(-1)||op]<infinity. The first inverse moments are finite by the second-moment bound, and tr(C^(-1))<=p||C^(-1)||op. This proves that the data-only dominating variable 2R^2+2||Delta||F^2 is integrable, including in the zero-noise case.

## Passing to expected risk and identifying the known comparator

Pointwise product convergence and the integrable bound allow the dominated convergence theorem on the joint probability space of training data and initialization. Hence the limiting expectation equals E||W-Delta||F^2. For standard Gaussian designs the known inverse-Wishart mean is E[(XX^T)^(-1)]=I_p/(n-p-1), n>p+1; conditioning on X gives

 E||W-Delta||F^2=m sigma^2 E tr((XX^T)^(-1))
                          =sigma^2 m p/(n-p-1).

This is the standard overdetermined OLS risk, also given by Zindari-Mulayoff-Stich, arXiv:2605.19018, Theorem 1 and Proposition 3 (printed p.4; inverse-Wishart computation in Appendix IV.1). The mean formula is used only to identify the finite risk explicitly; the elementary moment argument above already proves the expectation passage.

The rank-p constraint imposes no restriction on an m-by-p regression product, so reduced-rank regression with r=p is exactly OLS. This explains the factor-one comparison and the essential limitation: there is no proper input-side rank bottleneck. C013 does not contradict this theorem because its positive step must be chosen independently of the Gaussian initializer; the present safe step uses its smallest singular value and norm. All claims remain unaudited, and novelty is not asserted.

Let C be any real positive definite p-by-p matrix, D any real m-by-p matrix, and r>=1. Put lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op, ell=||D||op, W=D C^(-1), and

 q(B,A)=(1/2)||(BA-W) C^(1/2)||F^2,

with B m-by-r and A r-by-p. This is the empirical regression objective up to a constant when C=XX^T/n and D=ZX^T/n. Initialize at any finite deterministic factors B0,A0, and define

 q0=q(B0,A0), J=||A0 A0^T-B0^T B0||F+1,
 R=||W||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=sqrt(r)(J+2R), L=6Kc+ell.

For any fixed

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/L},

simultaneous ordinary factor GD satisfies, for every integer t>=0,

 q_t<=q0,
 ||B_t||F^2+||A_t||F^2<=K,
 ||(A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t)-(A0 A0^T-B0^T B0)||F<=2eta q0<1,
 sum_(t>=0) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/eta.

In particular the gradient tends to zero, every accumulation point is critical, and for every integer T>=1,

 min_(0<=t<T) ||grad q(B_t,A_t)||F^2<=2q0/(eta T).

All constants are finite and computable from C,D and the initialization. There is no Gaussian assumption and no low-rank assumption on W. No iterate-convergence, saddle-avoidance or statistical-risk assertion is included.

## Exact identities and product/factor bounds

Let G=BA C-D. The two factor gradients are G_B=G A^T and G_A=B^T G. With E_t=A_t A_t^T-B_t^T B_t the first-order cross terms cancel exactly, giving

 E_(t+1)-E_t=eta^2(G_A G_A^T-G_B^T G_B),
 ||E_(t+1)-E_t||F<=eta^2(||G_A||F^2+||G_B||F^2).

This cancellation only uses dependence on BA and does not require isotropic C. Also

 (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2
 <=r [||AA^T-B^TB||F^2+4||BA||F^2].

To verify it, write P=B^TB,Q=AA^T. Scalar trace Cauchy-Schwarz gives (tr(P+Q))^2<=r tr((P+Q)^2), and cyclicity of trace gives tr((P+Q)^2)=||P-Q||F^2+4 tr(PQ), tr(PQ)=||BA||F^2. No commutation is assumed.

When q<=q0, positivity of C gives ||BA-W||F<=sqrt(2q0/lambda), hence ||BA||F<=R. If additionally ||E-E0||F<=1, then ||E||F<=J, so the preceding trace bound implies

 ||B||F^2+||A||F^2<=sqrt(r) sqrt(J^2+4R^2)<=K.

The initialization meets these conditions and therefore has pair norm at most sqrt(K).

## Descent established before closing the boundedness induction

Suppose at the current iterate the pair norm is at most sqrt(K), and preceding steps have valid descent inequalities. Then

 ||grad q||F<=||BA C-D||op sqrt(||B||F^2+||A||F^2)
             <=(Kc/2+ell)sqrt(K).

Because eta<=1/(6Kc+ell), the proposed next point has pair norm at most 2sqrt(K). The connecting segment also lies in that ball. On that ball the Hessian quadratic form in a perturbation (dB,dA) is

 ||(dB A+B dA) C^(1/2)||F^2+2<BA C-D,dB dA>.

Its absolute value is at most

 [c(||A||op^2+||B||op^2)+||BA C-D||op]
 times (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2)
 <=[4Kc+(2Kc+ell)] (||dB||F^2+||dA||F^2).

Here the first summand uses Cauchy-Schwarz on dB A+B dA; the cross term uses |<G,dB dA>|<=||G||op||dB||F||dA||F. Thus the Hessian operator norm on the segment is at most L. Taylor's theorem along that segment proves

 q_next<=q-eta||grad q||F^2+(L eta^2/2)||grad q||F^2
        <=q-(eta/2)||grad q||F^2.

In particular q_next<=q0. Telescoping the descent inequalities, including the proposed step, and using q>=0 yields

 sum_(j=0)^t eta^2||grad q_j||F^2<=2eta q0
 <=2q0/(1+2q0)<1.

Summing the imbalance increments now proves ||E_next-E0||F<=2eta q0<1. The product/factor bound therefore puts the endpoint back in the smaller ball of pair radius sqrt(K). This closes the induction without assuming a bound before proving descent on the required larger segment. The q0=0 case is included: both gradients vanish, the sequence is constant, and all inequalities still hold.

## Consequences and exact remaining gap

Telescoping for every finite horizon gives the infinite summability bound. A nonnegative summable sequence tends to zero, so the gradients vanish. Bounded finite-dimensional factor pairs have convergent subsequences; gradient continuity makes every subsequential limit critical. The running-minimum bound follows by averaging the finite sum. These statements do not require that the entire sequence converges to one point.

For B0=0 and a Gaussian A0, this provides an allowed positive step after observing the initialization, conditional on every full-row-rank design. It does not supply a single positive step independent of the unbounded Gaussian initializer. C013 shows that unconditional expected-limit risk with such an initialization-independent fixed step can diverge even at rank one.

Combining this bound with the already verified empirical strict-saddle landscape C010 is insufficient to conclude global optimization. One must additionally show that the specified zero/Gaussian initialization does not approach a nonglobal critical point, with all hypotheses of a saddle-avoidance theorem checked for its lower-dimensional initial support and step rule. Vanishing gradients do not establish that. Even convergence almost surely would not by itself justify passing to expected population risk; a failure-tail/integrability or finite-stopping argument is separately required. The usual full-ambient absolutely-continuous random-initialization theorem cannot simply be cited for the plane B0=0.

Independent reviewer audit and any novelty assessment remain pending. Define D_p(mu,nu)=[(2^p-1)/2]sum_{ell>=1}2^(-p ell)sum_{F in P_ell}|mu(F)-nu(F)|. This is Notation4(a)p5 ofFournier-Guillin1312.2128v1. Its normalization makes D_p<=1: each cell-discrepancy sum is at most2 and sum_{ell>=1}2^(-p ell)=1/(2^p-1). Moreover D_p=0 precisely when mu=nu, because the positive weights force equality of all dyadic cell masses, and these partitions generate the Borel sigma field of Q.

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT, claim T323-OFFAXIS-001 v2, status proof (unaudited). For three tokens x_i in S^2 under self-inclusive normalized attention dot x_i=(I-x_i x_i^T) sum_j exp(beta x_i^T A x_j)V x_j / sum_j exp(beta x_i^T A x_j), take A=V=diag(1,1/2,-2), beta=2. There is a locally asymptotically stable equilibrium x1=(-q,0,-sqrt(1-q^2)), x2=(-1,0,0), x3=(-q,0,sqrt(1-q^2)), where q is the unique root in (19/1000,191/10000) of exp(2q)+3q exp(-4+6q^2)-q exp(4-2q^2)=0. Its three directions are distinct and noncollinear, and its basin is open with positive product volume. The hyperbolic sink persists in some open neighborhood of (A,V,beta)=(V0,V0,2), with V real symmetric of signature (2,1); A may be unaligned and is realizable as Q^T K. Thus an almost-everywhere two-antipodal-cluster conclusion is false on an open family. This does not classify all initial states. Full tangent-Hessian negativity is certified by exact outward-rounded dyadic intervals; the proof and implementation still require independent audit. Clustering attractors were reported numerically by Altafini 2025; no claim that the phenomenon itself is new.
n=3 on (S^2)^3; full attention includes self-indices
Base parameters A=V=diag(1,1/2,-2), beta=2
For continuation: parameters sufficiently close to the base point; V symmetric
Certificate depends on verified scalar reduction and full tangent-Hessian formula; independent audit pending
metadata_json:
{"artifact_digest":"sha256:31393958d812b62d481d9e2f1cf6fce9ce058d23d13a5315abc5d60b709c81ee","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/31/31393958d812b62d481d9e2f1cf6fce9ce058d23d13a5315abc5d60b709c81ee.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:bdb526644ece0ec96f727c75c4f88aa86664b2a7c86d01d5ccfa8a1aaf9f0998","bundle_entry_key":"three-direction-sink","bundle_id":"population.t323-certified-three-direction-sink-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"spherical self-attention dynamics","draft":"w696/bundle_003.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:analysis.dynamical_systems:t323-certified-three-direction-attention-sink-open-parameter-family","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T323-OFFAXIS-001 v2: a three-direction attracting equilibrium

Status: proof (unaudited), computer-assisted. Kind: moved; target 2.
The hardest finite step is negativity of the full six-dimensional tangent
Hessian, including directions out of the symmetry plane. It is checked
with outward-rounded exact dyadic intervals, not floating-point spectra.
Independent audit and literature priority checking remain separate.

## Statement

For three self-inclusive tokens on S^2, let

    V0 = diag(1, 1/2, -2), beta0=2, Q^T K=V0.

The normalized attention flow has a locally asymptotically stable
equilibrium with three distinct, noncollinear token directions

    x1=(-q,0,-s), x2=(-1,0,0), x3=(-q,0,s),
    19/1000 < q < 191/10000, s=sqrt(1-q^2).

It has an open basin of positive product volume. Consequently the claim
that almost every start has an antipodal two-cluster limit is false for
this signature-(2,1) model. The result is robust: such a three-direction
hyperbolic sink persists for all (A,V,beta) in some open neighborhood of
(V0,V0,2), where A=Q^T K is the score matrix and V is restricted to real
symmetric matrices. Thus the counterexample holds on an open parameter
family, including unaligned A. No explicit neighborhood radius or
classification of every other basin is asserted.

## Scalar reduction and exact existence

Write

    S=exp(-4+6q^2), O=exp(4-2q^2), M=exp(2q), L=exp(2).

These are the pair self-score, the opposite-pair score, the score
between a pair token and the middle token, and the middle self-score.
The symmetric unnormalized attention matrix is

    W = [[S,M,O],[M,L,M],[O,M,S]].

Let h_i=sum_j W_ij V0 x_j and alpha_i=x_i dot h_i. The middle
token is stationary by reflection symmetry. Both pair tokens are
stationary if and only if

    f(q)=M+3qS-qO=0.                                      (1)

Indeed h_1=(-q(S+O)-M,0,-2s(O-S)) and h_3 is its z-reflection.
Equation (1) gives h_i=2(O-S)x_i for i=1,3. Also
h_2=(L+2qM)x_2. Normalizing by the positive row sums does not change
stationarity. These identities give exactly

    alpha_1=alpha_3=2(O-S), alpha_2=L+2qM.                 (2)

The certificate proves f(19/1000)>0, f(191/10000)<0, and

    f'(q)=2M+3S+36q^2 S+(4q^2-1)O < 0

throughout the closed interval. Continuity and the intermediate value
theorem give a unique root in its interior. Its s is strictly positive;
q is neither zero nor one. The three stated unit vectors are distinct
and not collinear, and the two pair directions are not antipodal.

## Full tangent Hessian and attraction

Use the aligned interaction energy

    E(X)=(1/(2 beta)) sum_ij exp(beta x_i^T V x_j).

Its product-metric gradient has components P_i h_i; normalized attention
is the same gradient ascent under the positive metric
g_X(U,U)=sum_i Z_i |u_i|^2, Z_i=sum_j W_ij. This identity is the
known aligned variational structure from Geshkovski, Letrouit,
Polyanskiy and Rigollet, arXiv:2312.10794 Section 3.4.

At a critical point, geodesic differentiation for tangent U gives

    Hess E[U,U] = sum_ij W_ij u_i^T V u_j
                 -sum_i alpha_i |u_i|^2
                 +(beta/2)sum_ij W_ij
                  (u_i^T V x_j + x_i^T V u_j)^2.         (3)

Both ordered pairs and self-indices are included. The last term follows
by differentiating each exponential twice; the first two follow from
the mixed score derivative and the spherical geodesic acceleration
x_i''=-|u_i|^2 x_i. The factor 1/(2 beta) cancels the two symmetric
mixed-score contributions to give the first term in (3).

Use the following orthonormal tangent basis, each vector supported on
only the indicated token, in this order:

    (s,0,-q) at token 1; (0,0,1) at token 2;
    (s,0,q) at token 3; e2 at token 1; e2 at token 2; e2 at token 3.

The program evaluates the symmetric bilinear matrix of (3), using (2)
only at the unique root. Interval evaluation encloses that matrix for
the root without substituting an approximate root. It then computes
an interval LDL^T factorization of minus the Hessian. Every diagonal
pivot interval is strictly positive; the six lower endpoints exceed,
respectively, the integers

    106, 5, 78, 109, 3, 102.

The exact endpoints and all 36 entry intervals are in
logs/offaxis_certificate.json. The script additionally verifies a simpler
certificate: for D=diag(1,2,1,1,1,1), B=D(-H)D has positive diagonal
and strictly positive lower bounds for every diagonal-dominance margin
B_ii-sum_{j!=i}|B_ij|. Indeed, using 2|z_i z_j|<=z_i^2+z_j^2 gives
z^T B z >= sum_i (B_ii-sum_{j!=i}|B_ij|)z_i^2>0 for z!=0.
Thus negative definiteness can also be checked without the LDL routine.
Interval LDL^T encloses the exact
algebraic factorization entry by entry; each division is by an interval
bounded away from zero. Positive exact pivots imply that minus the
Hessian is positive definite. Thus the Hessian is negative definite
in all six tangent directions, not merely in the scalar ansatz.

At a critical point the normalized-flow linearization is G^{-1}H,
where G is the positive metric matrix and H the energy Hessian.
It is similar to the symmetric negative-definite matrix
G^{-1/2}H G^{-1/2}. All eigenvalues are strictly negative. The smooth
ODE linearization theorem gives a hyperbolic attracting equilibrium
and an open basin. Every nonempty open subset of (S^2)^3 has positive
product Riemannian volume.

## Persistence: an open family, including non-gradient models

In a fixed product of local sphere charts near the equilibrium, the
row-normalized vector field depends analytically on the entries of
A=Q^T K, on symmetric V, and on beta>0. Its state Jacobian at the
certified point is invertible. The implicit function theorem continues
the equilibrium to a neighborhood of (V0,V0,2). Eigenvalues of the
state Jacobian depend continuously as an unordered set, so their real
parts remain negative after shrinking the neighborhood. Distinctness
and noncollinearity of the three token directions are open conditions,
as is signature (2,1) of V. Shrink the neighborhood again to preserve
all three properties. This gives a positive-volume basin for each
parameter in an open family, without invoking a Lyapunov function
for the perturbed, possibly unaligned system. Any real A is realizable
as Q^T K by taking Q=I and K=A.

## Reproducible arithmetic and truncation bounds

Run from the worker folder:

    python -X utf8 T323/scripts/certify_offaxis.py

The script uses only Python's standard library, with integer and
Fraction arithmetic. Each interval endpoint is an integer multiple of
2^-96. Addition is exact on that grid; multiplication and division use
integer floor and ceiling on all relevant endpoint combinations.
Squaring handles zero-crossing intervals. Square root uses integer
isqrt at the scaled endpoints with an explicit ceiling correction.

To enclose exp(x), the script first evaluates each rational endpoint
after exact repeated halving until |t|<=1/4. It uses the Taylor
polynomial of degree N=24 and the rigorous error

    R <= |t|^(N+1) / ((N+1)! (1-|t|)).

This is the Lagrange remainder with exp(|t|)<=1/(1-|t|), the latter
following termwise from the exponential and geometric series. All
polynomial and remainder calculations use exact Fractions. The two
rational bounds are rounded outward to the dyadic grid, then squared
with outward rounding once per halving. Monotonicity of exp combines
the two endpoint enclosures. No floating-point comparison enters a
certificate assertion. The script also performs 55 arithmetic checks
against exact rational operations and elementary exact containments.
Its SHA256 is included in the certificate log. The LDL routine also
accepts a known positive-definite 2 by 2 matrix and rejects an indefinite
one as explicit controls, included in the 55 checks.

## Scope and provenance

The earlier floating-point trajectory locates the candidate only;
it is not used as a proof of a bound. The exact certificate and analytic
reduction establish the claimed equilibrium independently of that run.
Kuehn-Yoon arXiv:2604.26085 Theorem 5.2 concerns pure-mode equilibria
x_i=s_i e_p and does not directly describe this three-direction state.
The identity synchronization theorems do not apply to this indefinite
V. The known gradient metric and elementary persistence theorems are
not claimed as new. Altafini, arXiv:2511.11553, Section 5 Remark 6,
PDF p22, reports clustering attractors in simulations and explicitly
leaves their analytical stability unverified. This result is an exact
stability certificate for a specific open parameter family; multistability
and clustering attractors were already observed in that paper.
Altafini's newer arXiv:2610.13518 Theorem 2, PDF p8, treats a discrete-time
model and gives stability criteria for consensus and bipartite equilibria.
Its Proposition 1 characterizes existence of the clustering class
implicitly; it does not supply this continuous-time three-direction
certificate. Priority remains bounded by the recorded searches and
subject to specialist review. No assertion of an almost-everywhere
classification of all initial configurations is made.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:63d418c01a16816e641210447ff5648026d7371deb90ea60869cee1c14527401","revision_digest":"sha256:6e62f610bdea54cccad7eca1890ecf26cc98ef0664d9acca4a7d07411a41bcdd","source_id":"owner:w696:T323-OFFAXIS-001-v2","source_revision":"v2; proof (unaudited); scripts/certify_offaxis.py and logs/offaxis_certificate.json","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Theorem 3 (Lower-tail bound for weighted Bernoulli sums) of arXiv:2608.18392, 'On Samuels' Conjecture'] Let $T := \sum_{i=1}^nw_iB_i$, where $B_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i)$ independently, $0\leq p_i \leq1$ and $0\leq w_i\leq1$. Let $0<a_1\leq\cdots\leq a_n$ satisfy $w_ip_i\leq a_i$. Assume
\begin{equation}
d := 1-\mathbb{E}T = 1-\sum_{i=1}^nw_ip_i >0.
\end{equation}
For $1\leq i\leq n$, write $C_i := \sum_{j=i}^na_j$.
Then
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}(T<1)
\geq
\min_{1\leq i\leq n} \prod_{j=i}^n \left( 1-\frac{a_j}{d+C_i} \right).

\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lower-tail bound for weighted Bernoulli sums

[Defn d:ssm-pp of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] The Gibbs spin model~(equation eqn:gibbs of the paper) satisfies {\em averaged weak spatial mixing} on the graph $\Psi = \Psi(\cdot)$ with respect to the input process $\mathcal{P}$ if
the following conditions hold: 
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]

\item  for any finite subset ${\cal X } \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, there exists a spatial mixing function 
$\mathcal{A}_{\Psi({\cal X })}: 2^{\cal X } \times 2^{\cal X } \to [0, \infty)$ 
such that   
\begin{equation} 
d_{\textnormal{TV}} \big( \mathcal{L}(V_{{\cal X }''} \mid V_{\partial {\cal X }'} = \v_{\partial {\cal X }'}),  
\mathcal{L}(V_{{\cal X }''} \mid V_{\partial {\cal X }'} = {z}_{\partial {\cal X }'}) \big)  
\leq \mathcal{A}_{\Psi({\cal X })}({\cal X }'', \partial {\cal X }'),
\end{equation}  
for all subsets ${\cal X }'' \subset {\cal X }' \subset {\cal X }$ and boundary conditions $\v_{\partial {\cal X }'}, {z}_{\partial {\cal X }'}\in \mathbb{K}^{\partial {\cal X }'}$, and 
\vskip.2cm
\item   
for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$ the functions 

\begin{equation} 
\mathfrak{a}_p(k):=\sup_{B \in {\cal B}_b} \sup_{x_1,\ldots, x_p\in B}  
\mathbb {E} _{\bk x1p} \big[\mathcal{A}_{\Psi(\mathcal{P} \cap B)} (\bk x1p, \partial \mathfrak{B}_k(\bk x1p))\big],  \ \  k \in \mathbb{N},
\end{equation}  

are fast decreasing as \( k \to \infty \).  
Here, \(\mathfrak{B}_k(\bk x1p) = \bigcup_{i=1}^p \mathfrak{B}_k(x_i)\) and the boundary $\partial$ of \(\mathfrak{B}_k(\bk x1p)\) is again with respect to~\(\Psi(\mathcal{P} \cap B)\);
${\cal B}_b$ are the bounded Borel subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$. 
We  assume that the mapping $((\mathbb{R}^d)^p,\hat\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d}})\owns(\bk x1p,\tilde\mu)=(\bk x1p,\Psi(\mu)) \mapsto \mathcal{A}_{\Psi}(\bk x1p,\partial^\Psi\mathfrak{B}_k(\bk x1p))\in\mathbb{R}$ is measurable for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$. Without loss of generality, we assume that $\mathfrak{a}_p$ are increasing in $p$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Averaged weak spatial mixing of the Gibbs spin model on a random spatial  graph

body:
[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2512.05340, 'The rate of convergence of the critical mean-field $O(N)$ magnetization via multivariate n'] Suppose $V$ satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption: assumptions on V}, and let $\mu$ have Lebesgue density proportional to
  $e^{-V}$.
  Let $W,W'$ be identically distributed $\RR^d$-valued random variables, defined on the same probability space, such that if $\delta:=W'-W$ then
  $W$ and $\delta\delta^\transpose$ are both integrable. 
  Let $\sF\supseteq\sigma(W)$ be a $\sigma$-algebra, let $\lambda>0$, and define $R_1$ and $R_2$ so that
    \begin{equation}
      \mathbb{E}[\delta|\mathcal{F}] = \lambda(-\grad V(W) + R_{1}),
      
    \end{equation}
    and
    \begin{equation}

Let a_j be independent N(0,I_n), fix a deterministic unit signal x_*, put y_j=(a_j^T x_*)^2 and f(x)=(1/(4m)) sum_j ((a_j^T x)^2-y_j)^2. Fix a sufficiently small absolute constant C1>0 and sufficiently large absolute constants C2,c0. If m>=c0 n log n, then on a simultaneous event of probability at least 1-O(m n^(-10)), every point x with ||x-x_*||<=2C1 and max_j |a_j^T(x-x_*)|<=C2 sqrt(log n) satisfies ||x-eta grad f(x)-x_*||<=(1-eta/2)||x-x_*|| whenever 0<eta<=1/[5C2(10+C2)log n]. The event is uniform in x, so the point may depend on the samples. This is an absolute projection bound for unit signal, not the relative-error bound C2 sqrt(log n)||x-x_*||. The cited statement does not replace n log n samples by alpha n or by itself preserve the region along a trajectory.

[Lemma lem:sobolev-tightness of arXiv:2609.02829, 'Quantitative explosion and percolation of the divisible sandpile'] Let $0<\beta<d$ and $K<\infty$. For each $R\geq1$, let
		$(F_R(x))_{x\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ be a mean-zero random field satisfying
		\[
			\bigl|\Cov\bigl(F_R(x),F_R(y)\bigr)\bigr|
			\leq K(1+|x-y|)^{-\beta}
		\]
		for every $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^d$. Then, for every $s>\beta/2$, the fields
		$\bigl(R^{\beta/2}F_R^{(R)}\bigr)_{R\geq1}$ are tight in
		$H^{-s}_{\rm loc}(\mathbb{R}^d)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Tightness from covariance decay

body:
[Ppn 138 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] If $\psi:\bbR^{d_1}\to\bbR^{d_2}$ is Lipschitz, then $\psi$ preserves $\bbW_2$ convergence.
If $d_1=2,d_2=1$ and $\psi(X,Y)=XY$, then $\psi$ preserves $\bbW_2$ convergence for sequences on which $X$ is uniformly bounded.

\begin{proof}
The first statement follows because $L$-Lipschitz maps increase $\bbW_2$ distances by at most a factor of $L$.
For the second statement, suppose 
$X_N\to X$ and $Y_N\to Y$ in $L^2$, with $|X_N|\leq C$ almost surely for all $N$. 
We will argue that this implies $X_NY_N\to XY$ in $L^2$, and the assertion then follows. First,
the uniform bound on $X_N$ gives
  \[
  \E\Big[(X_NY_N-X_NY)^2\Big]
  \le C^2 \E\Big[(Y_N-Y)^2\Big]
  = o_N(1)\,,
  \]
so $X_NY_N$ and $X_NY$ are close in $L^2$. For $T$ growing sufficiently slowly with $N$, we then bound
  \[
  \E\Big[ (X_NY-XY)^2\Big]
  \le T^2\E\Big[ (X_N-X)^2\Big]
  + 4C^2\E\Big[Y^2; |Y| \ge T\Big]
  \le T^2 o_N(1) + o_T(1)\,,
  \]
where the last term is because $Y^2\in L^1$. Therefore $X_NY$ converges to $XY$ in $L^2$, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Ppn 138 of arXiv:2608.29416

body: [Theorem 9.1 of arXiv:2503.23159, 'Hall's marriage theorem'] A sufficient condition for a family A of hypergraphs to have an SDR is that, for every subfamily B of A, there is a matching M in S B which cannot be pinned by fewer than |B| disjoint edges from S B. If each edge in each hypergraph is a singleton, the hypothesis reduces to that of Hall’s theorem (each hypergraph can be represented as a set, the union of its singleton edges), and the conclusion is the same as Hall’s.
title: Theorem 9.1 of arXiv:2503.23159: Hall's marriage theorem

Given that the long-only gain is the estimation variance the constraint removes at the rows the stack is scored on, the amount of constraint was chosen with the evaluation inputs: a blend w(t) between the simplex and least-squares stacks with t minimising the cross-validated calibration error plus the excess bootstrap variance of the blend at the evaluation rows over the calibration rows, and a per-row version t_i = 1/(1 + kappa v_i/median v) that leans to the simplex where least squares is uncertain. P24 (a) HELD: on EMIT the per-cell blend reads +0.08 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 39 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 t* is at or above 0.5 on 30 of 30 cells and the blend reads +0.66 vs least squares; (c) REFUTED: the per-row blend vs the per-cell blend is +0.70 on Y2 and -0.14 on EMIT overall; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Fresh-split replication (P25, split C, SPLIT_SEED 11, the criterion uses no evaluation targets): P25 (a) HELD: on split C the EMIT blend reads +0.63 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 35 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend reads +0.84 vs the simplex (wins 30 of 30) and +0.65 vs least squares; (c) HELD: t* averages 0.34 on EMIT and 0.67 on OCO-2; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered.
the members' predictions on the rows to be scored are available (transductive setting); their targets are not

body: Load-bearing hypothesis: H^s(R^n) embeds into L^∞(R^n) ∩ C^0 only for s > n/2, strictly; the borderline s = n/2 is excluded. Concrete counterexample, n = 2 (s = 1): u(x) = log log(1/|x|) for 0 < |x| < e^{−1}, extended by 0. Then ∫|∇u|² = 2π ∫_0^{e^{−1}} dr / ( r log²(1/r) ) = 2π < ∞ and ∫ u² < ∞, so u ∈ H¹(R²), yet u is unbounded at the origin. General n: choose f with f̂(ξ) = (1+|ξ|)^{−n} (log(2+|ξ|))^{−1} ≥ 0; then ∫ (1+|ξ|²)^{n/2}|f̂|² dξ < ∞ (radially, ∫ dρ/(ρ log²ρ) converges) so f ∈ H^{n/2}(R^n), while ∫ f̂ dξ = ∞ (∫ dρ/(ρ log ρ) diverges); since f̂ ≥ 0, an L^∞ bound on f would force ∫ f̂ < ∞ (test against a Gaussian approximate identity with positive Fourier transform and use monotone convergence), so f ∉ L^∞. Consequences: an energy-critical argument may not conclude a pointwise bound from the energy norm; ‖u‖_{L^q_t L^∞_x} estimates at the critical regularity generally require Besov spaces, since Ḃ^{n/2}_{2,1} embeds into L^∞ while H^{n/2} does not. This is the same phenomenon that makes the Lebesgue-space wave Strichartz estimates carry the restriction r < ∞ (the Littlewood–Paley summation of the dyadic blocks needs r < ∞, and at r = ∞ one lands in Besov spaces). The failure of the endpoints (q,r) = (2,∞) — Schrödinger in n = 2, wave in n = 3 — is a separate matter, proved by explicit counterexamples of Montgomery-Smith and of Klainerman–Machedon, not a corollary of this embedding failure.
title: Pitfall: H^{n/2} Does Not Embed in L^∞ (the Critical Sobolev Endpoint Fails)

[Theorem 8 (Random regular graphs: pointwise version) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Fix \(d\ge 3\), \(u\in[0,1]\), and \(\theta\in\mathbb N\) with \(\theta>1\). Let \(G_n\) be the random \(d\)-regular graph on \(n\) vertices, with law \(p_{d,n}\). Assume
\[
d>2c_{\theta,u}
=
2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr).
\]
Then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
\[
t\ge T_{\theta,u}(d)+\delta,
\]
one has
\[
p_{d,n}\!\left(
\Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
\right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Random regular graphs: pointwise version

[Defn 5 of arXiv:2606.04636, 'A Thomson-type variational principle for diffusion coefficients'] $V_{0}$ is the space of admissible flows with vanishing
divergence, that we write formally as
\begin{equation}
V_{0}=\left\{ \phi\in\cH_{2}:\left\langle \div\phi,\div\phi\right\rangle =0\right\} .
\end{equation}
For $\phi\in\cH_{2}$, $\left\langle \div\phi,\div\phi\right\rangle =0$
should be understood by the completion under $\left\langle \cdot,\cdot\right\rangle $.
That is, there exists a sequence $(\phi_{n})_{n\in\N}$ of flows with
well defined divergence that converge in $\cH_{2}$ to $\phi$, such
that $\left\langle \div\phi_{n},\div\phi_{n}\right\rangle \xrightarrow{n\to\infty}0$.
title: Definition 5 of arXiv:2606.04636

Fresh-split replication (P25, split C, SPLIT_SEED 11, the criterion uses no evaluation targets): P25 (a) HELD: on split C the EMIT blend reads +0.63 vs the simplex and beats least squares on 35 of 40 cells; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend reads +0.84 vs the simplex (wins 30 of 30) and +0.65 vs least squares; (c) HELD: t* averages 0.34 on EMIT and 0.67 on OCO-2; falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT, or than least squares by more than 0.3 on OCO-2) not triggered. Bootstrap-size stability (P28, B = 16 against B = 8 on split B): P28 (a) HELD: t*(16) equals t*(8) on 86 pct of the 70 cells and is within 0.2 on 100 pct; (b) HELD: the blend's mean gain against the simplex moves from +0.08 to +0.06 on EMIT and from +0.83 to +0.83 on OCO-2, and the both-endpoints win count on OCO-2 is 30 of 30 at B = 16; falsifier (agreement below 50 pct or a gain moving by more than 0.5) not triggered. Break test: a fixed midpoint t = 0.5 matches the criterion on OCO-2 (+0.96 / +1.01 against +0.83 / +0.84 on the two splits) but loses 1.6 and 4.4 pct on EMIT where the criterion stays at +0.08 and +0.63 - the criterion's value is knowing, without labels, when not to leave the simplex; the EMIT shortfall against the hindsight-best t is the bias-shift term of the risk identity. Scarce calibration (P30, 240 of the calibration rows per cell, split B): P30 (a) HELD: at n = 240 the simplex beats least squares by +14.10 on EMIT (full calibration +8.83); (b) REFUTED: t* averages 0.22 on EMIT and the blend reads -2.61 vs the simplex; (c) HELD: on OCO-2 the blend beats both endpoints on 30 of 30 cells and the simplex reads +2.27 vs least squares (full calibration -0.18); falsifier (blend worse than the simplex by more than 1 on EMIT) TRIGGERED. The observable part of the bias shift (P31): adding t^2 (D_ev - D_cal), the shift in the two bases' mean squared disagreement between the evaluation and calibration rows, to the criterion - P31 (a) REFUTED: the R'-blend reads -0.71 vs the simplex on EMIT split B (R-blend +0.08) and +0.71 on split C (R-blend +0.63); (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the R'-blend is -0.11 vs the R-blend on split B and -0.12 on split C; (c) REFUTED: mean t** 0.39 against t* 0.33 on EMIT, share of the hindsight optimum 0.07 -> -0.62; falsifier (R'-blend worse than the R-blend by more than 0.3 on any corpus or split) TRIGGERED. Per-output mixing weights (P34, the criterion decoupled across outputs): P34 (a) REFUTED: the per-output blend reads -0.41 vs the per-cell blend on EMIT split B and -0.53 on split C; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 -0.02 and -0.08 on split C; (c) REFUTED: on Y2 the share of outputs at t_d = 0 is 0.20 and at t_d >= 0.5 is 0.34; falsifier (per-output worse than per-cell by more than 0.3 anywhere) TRIGGERED.

[Lemma 66 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] Assume the same notation as in Definition \ref{Def.LETop}. Then, $L^N_1, L^N_2$ are a.s. increasing paths on $\llbracket 0, M \rrbracket$. Fix $b \in \llbracket 1, M \rrbracket$, $A, B \in \mathbb{Z}$, and an increasing path $g$ on $\llbracket 0, b \rrbracket$, such that $\mathbb{P}_N(E(A,B,g)) > 0$, where
$$E(A,B,g) = \{ L_1^N(0) = A, \hspace{2mm} L_1^N(b) = B, \hspace{2mm} L^N_2 = g \}.$$
Then, for any $E \subseteq \Omega(0,b,A,B)$, we have 
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}_N(L^N_1 \in E \vert E(A,B,g)) = \frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{Geom}}^{0,b, A, B}(\{Q \in E\} \cap \{Q \succeq g\} )}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{Geom}}^{0,b, A, B}(Q \succeq g)},
\end{equation}
where $Q$ has law $\mathbb{P}_{\mathrm{Geom}}^{0,b, A, B}$.

Conditional reduction, independent review pending: let W be a continuous adapted real chordal Loewner driver, W_0=0, with dg_t(z)=2/(g_t(z)-W_t)dt in one usual filtration. For three real marks 0<a<b<c put X=g_t(a)-W_t and Y_i=g_t(b_i)-W_t, b_1=b,b_2=c. On each stopped compact localization with 0<X<Y_1<Y_2 and positive separations, assume BOTH C(X/Y_i) are local martingales, where C(u)=B(1/3,1/3)^(-1) integral_0^u [v(1-v)]^(-2/3)dv. Smooth inversion of the first makes W a semimartingale; the two Ito signed-measure equations force zero finite variation part and local martingale bracket 6dt. If the assumption holds for a countable mark/localization family covering every finite time, W/sqrt(6) is Brownian motion. The square-lattice martingale approximation needed to apply this reduction is unproved in this draft.

[Definition 5 (Bessel Space) of arXiv:2608.07365, 'A pathwise Ito formula \\for weakly differentiable functions'] For $p\in [1, \infty]$ and $\alpha> 0$ the Bessel space $\mathcal{L}^p_{\alpha}(\Rr^d)$ is defined by
\[
\mathcal{L}^p_{\alpha}(\Rr^d):=\{\, g_{\alpha}\star f\colon\, f\in L^p(\Rr^d) \,\},
\]
where $g_0:= \delta_0$, so that $g_{0}\star f =f$.  The space $\mathcal{L}^p_{\alpha}(\Rr^d)$ is endowed with the norm
\[
\|F\|_{\mathcal{L}^p_{\alpha}(\Rr^d)} :=\|f\|_{L^p(\Rr^d)}
\]
where $f\in L^p(\Rr^d)$ such that $F=g_{\alpha}\star f$.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Design the algorithm and check whether the exploration frontier remains Markov. Result: For bond percolation the peeling frontier is a two-colour boundary (free/blocked edges) and the algorithm peels the edge at the colour change, keeping the unexplored region a Boltzmann map with a boundary of the same type. For site percolation the colour lives on vertices and after peeling a face the newly exposed boundary vertices are uncoloured; the natural algorithm peels the edge whose left endpoint is black and right endpoint is uncoloured, colouring the new vertices as they appear. The unexplored region is then a Boltzmann map with a boundary condition that is a word in {black, white, uncoloured}, and the difficulty is that the length of the black segment is no longer a Markov chain by itself: the future depends on the positions of uncoloured vertices along the boundary. The frontier becomes Markov if one records the boundary word, which is an infinite-dimensional state. On triangulations the problem was solved (Angel-Curien) because degree-3 faces expose at most one new vertex per step, keeping the state finite; for general Boltzmann maps with large faces a peeled face exposes many uncoloured vertices at once. So a Markov site-percolation peeling exists exactly when faces expose boundedly many vertices, i.e. for bounded face degrees, and the general Boltzmann case requires a state space of boundary words; whether the threshold can still be computed from a word-valued Markov chain is the open part. Obstruction: Unbounded face degrees expose many uncoloured boundary vertices at once; the frontier state is a word, not an integer.

	\]

[Theorem 1 (Fraenkel's conjecture) of arXiv:2609.01570, 'A Proof of Fraenkel's Conjecture'] Let \(m\ge3\).  Suppose that the sets
\(S(\alpha_i,\beta_i)\), \(1\le i\le m\), partition \(\Z\), and that
the moduli \(\alpha_i>1\) are pairwise distinct.  Then
\[
 \{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m\}
 =\left\{\frac{2^m-1}{2^j}:0\le j<m\right\}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Fraenkel's conjecture

[Proposition 10 of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be a compact and metrizable topological abelian group, equipped with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Assume $X,Y,Z$ are $G$-valued random variables with finite entropies. Then

    $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Question of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $G = (V,E)$ be a finite connected graph. For any $t \in (0,1)$, let $\mathcal{U}$ denote the convex set of measures $\nu$ on $\{0,1\}^E$ such that the uniform even graph of $\nu$ has the law of $\ell_{G,t}$. How many extreme points does $\mathcal{U}$ have? (Stated as a question by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Unnumbered question of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'

body: [Definition 2 of arXiv:2603.24616, 'Pinning in non-critical half-space geometric last passage percolation'] For a finite set $\mathsf{S} = \{s_1, \dots, s_m\} \subset \mathbb{R}$, we let $\mu_{\mathsf{S}}$ denote the counting measure on $\mathbb{R}$, defined by $\mu_{\mathsf{S}}(A) = |A \cap \mathsf{S}|$. We also let $\mathrm{Leb}$ be the usual Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mu_{\mathsf{S}} \times \mathrm{Leb}$ the product measure on $\mathbb{R}^2$.
title: Definition 2 of arXiv:2603.24616

body:
Given a block size b_n in {1, ..., n - 1} with b_n -> infinity and b_n = o(n), the sample {1, ..., n} is partitioned into N_n = [n/b_n] non-overlapping contiguous blocks B_l = {(l - 1)*b_n + 1, ..., l*b_n} for l = 1, ..., N_n. The block sum for the i-th coordinate is S_{n,l}(i) = sum_{t in B_l} x_{i,t}.
b_n -> infinity and b_n = o(n)
N_n * b_n = n
title: Telescoping Sub-Sample Blocking Partition

Let N>=0 be an integer, and let nu be a real signed Borel measure on R for which every polynomial is absolutely integrable with respect to the total variation measure |nu|. The measure nu is positive definite up to degree N if integral f(t)^2 dnu(t)>0 for every nonzero real polynomial f of degree<=N. Equivalently integral f(t)^2 dnu(t)>=0 for all such polynomials, with equality only for the zero polynomial. This is Cohn-Kumar Definition3.4. It is positivity of a finite-degree quadratic form, not a claim that nu is a nonnegative measure or that squared norms in higher degrees are positive.
N nonnegative integer
real signed Borel measure; all polynomial absolute moments finite
strict positivity is required for every nonzero polynomial within the stated degree range

body: A set A of positive integers is sum-distinct if its 2^|A| subset sums are pairwise different. Exhaustive enumeration shows there are exactly two sum-distinct 5-element subsets of {1,...,13}, namely {3,6,11,12,13} and {6,9,11,12,13}, and none of the C(12,5) = 792 five-element subsets of {1,...,12} is sum-distinct, so the least such N is exactly 13. The 32 subset sums of {3,6,11,12,13} are 0, 3, 6, 9, 11 to 34, 36, 39, 42, 45. In Lean 4 (the formal-conjectures statement Erdos1.erdos_1.variants.least_N_5) the kernel decides the witness half, and the 792-set lower bound compiles in 425 s once maxRecDepth is raised. The corresponding statement for n = 9 (least N = 161) does not reduce to a finite witness check of the same size.

[Lemma 20 of arXiv:2606.01742, 'Large deviation principles for SPDEs with locally Lipschitz coefficients'] (\cite[Lemma A.1]{BMS} and \cite[Lemma A.4]{LWYZ17})
Let $K$ be a compact set in $\mathbb R$ and let $\{V^\varepsilon(t,x):(t,x)\in[0,T]\times K\}$ be a family of real-valued functions. Assume that
\begin{itemize}
  \item[(A1).] for any $(t,x)\in[0,T]\times K$,
     $$\lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}|V^{\varepsilon}(t,x)|=0;$$
  \item[(A2).] there exist $\beta_1,\beta_2>0$ satisfied that for any $(t,x),(t',x')\in[0,T]\times K$,
$$
|V^\varepsilon(t,x)-V^\varepsilon(t',x')|\le C_{6,4}(|t-t'|^{\beta_1}+|x-x'|^{\beta_2}),
$$
where $C_{6,4}$ is a constant independent of $\varepsilon$.
\end{itemize}
Then for any $\theta\in(0,1)$, we have
$$\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\|V^\varepsilon\|_{\theta\beta_1,\theta\beta_2}=0. $$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 20 of arXiv:2606.01742

body: Mordell-Weil theorem: Let A be an abelian variety over a number field K. Then A(K), the group of K-rational points of A, is a finitely generated abelian group, called the Mordell-Weil group; equivalently A(K) is isomorphic to Z^r x T, where r >= 0 is the rank and T is the finite torsion subgroup. The special case in which A = E is an elliptic curve and K = Q is Mordell's theorem, which answers a question apparently posed by Henri Poincare around 1901 and was proved by Louis Mordell in 1922; the general case is due to Andre Weil (1928). It is a foundational theorem of Diophantine geometry and of the arithmetic of abelian varieties.
title: Mordell–Weil theorem

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). A Nash inequality on a graph with Dirichlet form E and reference measure mu has the form ||f||_2^{2+4/d} <= C E(f,f) ||f||_1^{4/d} for all f in the domain of the form, where d is an effective dimension parameter. Such an inequality is classically equivalent, by results of Nash and later Carlen-Kusuoka-Stroock, to an on-diagonal heat-kernel upper bound p_t(x,x) <= C' t^{-d/2} for the associated Markov semigroup, and combining it with matching volume-growth and effective-resistance-growth estimates, within the general framework relating resistance growth to heat-kernel decay used for fractal-like and random graphs, yields two-sided sub-Gaussian or Gaussian heat-kernel bounds. On graphs where effective resistance to the complement of a ball of radius n grows like n^zeta and volume grows like n^alpha, this gives sub-Gaussian heat-kernel estimates with off-diagonal decay governed by the exponent alpha+zeta, a technique central to analysis on fractals and on random graphs such as critical percolation clusters or random walk among random conductances. The technique does not give the resistance or volume exponents themselves, which are separate geometric inputs, and a full two-sided heat-kernel estimate typically requires both the Nash-type inequality, giving the upper bound, and a separate lower-bound argument, often via a chaining construction or an elliptic Harnack inequality. Typical failure: Assuming ordinary Euclidean Gaussian heat-kernel scaling, of the t^{-d/2} exp(-|x-y|^2/4t) form, transfers automatically to a random or fractal-like graph without re-deriving the resistance exponent zeta; on structures such as the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or random conductance models with heavy-tailed conductances, the correct scaling is sub-Gaussian with zeta != 1, and using the Euclidean exponent silently mis-states both the walk dimension and the tail behavior of the heat kernel. Canonical reference: Nash, 1958, American Journal of Mathematics; Carlen, Kusuoka and Stroock, 1987, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare; Barlow, 2004, Annals of Probability; Kumagai, Random Walks on Disordered Media and their Scaling Limits, 2014, Springer.

a valid Nash-type functional inequality with a specified effective dimension d
for two-sided estimates: matching volume-growth and effective-resistance-growth bounds on balls

title: Technique: Nash Inequality and Heat-Kernel Bounds via Resistance

[Definition stoch_domination of arXiv:2504.00512, 'Localization-delocalization transition for a random block matrix model at the edge'] {\rm{(i)}} Let
	\[\xi=\left(\xi^{(N)}(u):N\in\mathbb N, u\in U^{(N)}\right),\hskip 10pt \zeta=\left(\zeta^{(N)}(u):N\in\mathbb N, u\in U^{(N)}\right),\]
	be two families of non-negative random variables, where $U^{(N)}$ is a possibly $N$-dependent parameter set. We say $\xi$ is stochastically dominated by $\zeta$, uniformly in $u$, if for any fixed (small) $\tau>0$ and (large) $D>0$, 
	\[\mathbb P\bigg(\bigcup_{u\in U^{(N)}}\left\{\xi^{(N)}(u)>N^\tau\zeta^{(N)}(u)\right\}\bigg)\le N^{-D}\]
	for large enough $N\ge N_0(\tau, D)$, and we will use the notation $\xi\prec\zeta$. 
	
	If for some complex family $\xi$ we have $|\xi|\prec\zeta$, then we will also write $\xi \prec \zeta$ or $\xi=\mathrm{O}_\prec(\zeta)$. 
	
	\vspace{5pt}
	\noindent {\rm{(ii)}} As a convention, for two deterministic quantities $\xi$ and $\zeta$, we will write $\xi\prec\zeta$ if and only if $|\xi|\le N^\tau |\zeta|$ for any constant $\tau>0$. 

 \vspace{5pt}
	\noindent {\rm{(iii)}} Let $A$ be a family of random matrices and $\zeta$ be a family of non-negative random variables. Then, we use $A=\mathrm{O}_\prec(\zeta)$ to mean that $\|A\|\prec \zeta$, where $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the operator norm. 
	
	\vspace{5pt}
	\noindent {\rm{(iv)}} We say an event $\Xi$ holds with high probability (w.h.p.) if for any constant $D>0$, $\mathbb P(\Xi)\ge 1- N^{-D}$ for large enough $N$. More generally, we say an event $\Omega$ holds $w.h.p.$ in $\Xi$ if for any constant $D>0$,
	$\mathbb{P}( \Xi\setminus \Omega)\le N^{-D}$ for large enough $N$.
title: Stochastic domination and high probability event

body: In mathematics, the term homology, originally introduced in algebraic topology, has three primary, closely related usages. First, there is the homology of a chain complex, a sequence of abelian groups, called homology groups, which are regarded as fundamental invariants of the chain complex. Secondly, when one can associate a chain complex to a different mathematical object, one can also associate its homology to that object. Distinct procedures of associating chain complexes to a given object are grouped into homology theories. Finally, homology is important in the study of topological spaces. Under nice conditions in which distinct homology theories for a single topological space produce the same homology groups, one can define a single homology of a topological space. This last notion of homology is closely related to topological ideas frequently discussed in popular mathematics such as the holes of a surface or the cycles of a graph. There is also a related notion of the cohomology of a cochain complex, giving rise to various cohomology theories, in addition to the notion of the cohomology of a topological space.
title: Homology (mathematics)

[Definition def:circuit-primitives of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] For an ordered finite set $S$ of oriented carrier labels, write
$\mathscr H_S=\bigotimes_{u\in S}H_u$, with every factor equipped with
the Euclidean Hilbert norm.  A \emph{normalized Brauer primitive} is a
signed carrier permutation, a wedge reversal, full transpose, a share
turn, a through string, the orthogonal antisymmetrizer, or a cup/cap
normalized so that its operator norm is one.  A share turn is the fixed
signed boundary permutation, possibly followed by full transpose,
induced when a principal pivot reverses one of the two ordered boundary
intervals.  The two coefficient primitives are
\[
 \widehat C_{uv}=\iota_{uv}C\pi_{uv}:H_u\otimes H_v\to H_u\otimes H_v,
\]
where $\pi_{uv}$ is the normalized orthogonal projection and
identification onto $\Lambda^2H$, and $\iota_{uv}=\pi_{uv}^*$; hence
$\widehat C_{uv}$ is zero on $\operatorname{Sym}^2H$ and has norm $K$.
The other coefficient primitive is the restriction/re-expression of
(eq:2.1.3 of the paper) as the Bianchi transfer
\[
 (\Phi_CY)_{ik}=\sum_{m,n}C_{in,mk}Y_{mn},
 \qquad Y\in\Lambda^2H.
\]
The first Bianchi identity identifies the latter with the physical action
of $C$.  A \emph{safe gate} is a typed composite of these primitives,
including the $AA$ words and correctly oriented $AB$ words used below.
Its degree is the number of coefficient primitives.  Thus a degree-$d$
safe gate $G:\mathscr H_S\to\mathscr H_T$ satisfies
$\|G\|_{\rm op}\le K^d$; untouched factors are ancillary identities.

A coefficient box has four darts
$L_{i,0},L_{i,1},R_{i,0},R_{i,1}$.  For a column pairing $q$, a
\emph{packet} is a connected component of the box-incidence graph whose
edges are the $q$-pairs joining different boxes.  A $q$-pair joining the
two darts of one wedge is forbidden and gives zero.  An allowed
\emph{smoothing} chooses at each box either
\[
 h_i^{\parallel}=\{L_{i,0}R_{i,0},L_{i,1}R_{i,1}\},\qquad
 h_i^{\times}=\{L_{i,0}R_{i,1},L_{i,1}R_{i,0}\}.
\]
The alternating circuits of $q\vee h$ are the \emph{smoothing
carriers}; adjoining one carrier means adjoining one identity factor
$I_H$.  The smoothing support $\operatorname{supp}_h(i)$ of a box is the
one- or two-element set of $q\vee h$ carriers containing its two
$h$-passages.  A \emph{ported pair comb} on two chosen carriers consists of all
boxes whose smoothing support is that pair, together with every singleton-support box
assigned to it exactly once; removing all other support groups leaves
their boundary darts as linearly ordered typed ports.  These definitions
fix the domains and codomains of every safe word, fold, comb, and
attachment below.

An \emph{ambient rooted ribbon record} $\Gamma$ consists of a common
finite dart set, its coefficient boxes and local wedge signs, a row
pairing $p$, a column pairing $q$, a rooted trace pairing $r$, and the
declared boundary/root data.  Thus $p\vee r$ is the disjoint union of the
original trace circuits in that record; its components, not temporary
proof cuts, receive the normalization bases below.  The more detailed
Weingarten data carried by $\Gamma$ are specified in
(def:ribbon-record of the paper).
title: Typed circuit primitives

DRAFT; independent referee pending. For a unit-rate Poisson process N, M^n_t=1-t+nN_{t/n}, 0<=t<=1, is a nonnegative true martingale in its own natural filtration. Its paths eventually equal 1-t on the entire interval almost surely, because the first Poisson jump time is positive. Thus it converges uniformly almost surely to a continuous deterministic non-martingale. Uniform integrability is absent: E[M^n_t]=1 but E[1-t]=1-t. Joint path convergence alone cannot pass a renormalized observable's conditional martingale identity to the limit.

[Definition 2 (Admissible deterministic diagonal resolution) of arXiv:2606.16662, '2606.16662'] A deterministic diagonal resolution for a finite family \(\cM\) assigns to
each label \(\tau\in\cM\) deterministic diagonal Volterra operators
\(\Ret^\tau_\Lambda\) and \(\Ctr^\tau_\Lambda\) such that
\begin{equation}
        D^\tau_\Lambda=\Ret^\tau_\Lambda+\Ctr^\tau_\Lambda .
\end{equation}
The first term is retained and the second is subtracted from the raw mixed
block.  The resolution is dyadically admissible if, for each label with
\(\Ret^\tau_\Lambda\ne0\), there exists \(\delta_\tau>0\) such that
\begin{equation}
        \|\Ret^\tau_{\Lambda,N,Q}P_Qw\|_{C_TL^2}
        \le C_{\mathfrak P}N^{-\delta_\tau}
        \bigl(\|P_Qw\|_{L_T^\infty L^2}
        +\|P_Q\partial_tw\|_{L_T^\infty L^2}\bigr)
\end{equation}
for \(0<T\le T_0\) and \(Q\le c_{\rm ap}N\), uniformly in \(\Lambda\).
For every fixed \((N,Q)\), the corresponding two-time scalar kernels are
also required to converge in
\(C_{t,s}\cL(\ell_q^2,\ell_q^2)\).

The retained term may be any prescribed finite linear combination of scalar
diagonal branches, provided the combined kernel satisfies
\eqref{eq:retained-block-bound} and fixed-block convergence.  The raw
resolution is \(\Ret^\tau_\Lambda=D^\tau_\Lambda\), while the fully
Wick-subtracted resolution is \(\Ret^\tau_\Lambda=0\).
title: Admissible deterministic diagonal resolution

Let S={4^k:k>=1}, sigma_n=min(sqrt(n)/4,1+dist(n,S)/4) for n>=0, and let epsilon be one fair random sign. On the ray with edges j-1 to j assign tau_j=1+(sigma_j-sigma_(j-1)) epsilon. These weights lie in [3/4,5/4], and their unique minimizing path to n has T_n=n+sigma_n epsilon. Its mean is n, variance is sigma_n^2, and E exp(alpha |T_n-E T_n|/sqrt(Var T_n))=exp(alpha) for every alpha>0. Define a as the upper uniform concentration threshold: inf q for which some alpha>0 makes sup_(n>=1) E exp(alpha |T_n-E T_n|/n^q) finite. Define b as the lower uniform variance threshold: sup q for which some N has inf_(n>N) Var T_n/n^(2q)>0. Then a=1/2 and b=0. The weights share epsilon and are nonstationary; this is not an iid undirected Z^2 law.
