[Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.23989, 'Collision Properties in Discrete and Continuous Time on Bounded-Degree Graphs'] Let~$P$ be an irreducible Markov kernel with~$n$-step transition probabilities~$p_n$, and suppose that, for some~$\alpha > 0$,
$$ \inf_{x \in \mathsf S} P^2(x,x) \ge \alpha.$$
Then, there exists~$a = a(\alpha) > 0$ such that
$$ \sum_{ \substack{\ell \ge 0: \\|\ell - m| \leq \sqrt{m}  } } \Psi(2m+\epsilon,2\ell + \epsilon) \cdot p_{2\ell + \epsilon}(x,y) \ge a \cdot p_{2m+\epsilon}(x,y) $$
for every~$x,y \in \mathsf S, m \ge 1$ and~$\epsilon \in \{0,1\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma 6 of arXiv:2608.23989

[Thm fineET of arXiv:2608.30031, 'Ziggurats, taut foliations, and contact structures'] Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a cooriented $C^0$-foliation on $M$ transverse to $\partial M$ with finitely many compact planar leaves. Let $L_1, \dots, L_m$ denote its unstable compact planar leaves, and let $\Lambda_1, \dots, \Lambda_k$ denote its unstable $\mathbb{T}^2$-type planar minimal sets. For each of those, choose a boundary point $p_i \in \partial L_i \subset \partial M$ and $q_j \in \partial \Lambda_j \subset \partial M$.
    
    Then $\mathcal{F}$ can be $C^0$-approximated by positive (resp.~negative) contact structures which dominate some foliation $\mathcal{G}$ on $\partial M$, obtained from $\partial \mathcal{F}$ by the following operations only:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Isotopies,
        \item Blowdowns and blowups of type $\natural/\sharp$ (resp.~$\natural/ \flat$) away from the boundaries of the aforementioned minimal sets,
        \item $\flat$ (resp.~$\sharp$) modifications near $p_1, \dots, p_m, q_1, \dots, q_k$.
    \end{itemize}
    Moreover, all of these operations can be made arbitrarily small, so that $\mathcal{G}$ is tangentially $C^0$-close to $\partial \mathcal{F}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Finest version of Eliashberg--Thurston

[Theorem thm:U_process- of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item Suppose $z=0$. For $r>0$, 
$\frac{r}{U(-r)+r}$ has distribution $\mathcal{B}(\frac{2-\delta+\widehat \delta}{2},\frac{\delta'}{2})$. 
\item The family $(Q^z,z\ge 0)$ defines a time-homogeneous Feller process. For each $z\ge 0$, the process $\left(U(-r)+r\right)_{r\ge 0}$ is a time-homogeneous $(\mathscr{W}^-_r)_{r\ge 0}$-adapted Feller process starting from $z$. 
\item Suppose $z>0$ and write $\mathrm{x}:=\inf\{r\ge 0\,:\, U(-r)>z\}$, $\mathfrak{U}:=U(-\mathrm{x})$. 
We have $\frac{z}{z+\mathrm{x}}\sim\mathcal{B}(\frac{\delta'}{2},1)$ and conditionally on  $\{{\mathrm{x}}=x\}$, $\frac{z+x}{\mathfrak{U}+x}\sim \mathcal{B}(\frac{2-\delta+\widehat{\delta}}{2},1)$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Theorem thm:U_process- of arXiv:2411.04773

[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2608.30875, 'A Decomposition Theorem for Topological Semi-small Maps'] Let $R$ be a closed topologically stratified space with the intrinsic stratification $R=\bigsqcup_{\alpha} S_{\alpha}$. Consider a finite decomposition $R=\bigsqcup_{\beta} T_{\beta}$ such that each $T_{\beta}$ is a topologically stratified space with a stratification $T_{\beta}=\sqcup_{\gamma} V^{\beta}_{\gamma}$. Assume the following:
    	\begin{enumerate}
		\item The inclusion $\overline{V^{\beta}_{\gamma}} \hookrightarrow R$ is locally flat, for all $\beta$ and $\gamma$.
		\item For each point $r \in R$ there is an open neighborhood that intersects finitely many connected components of finitely many $V^{\beta}_{\gamma}$. 
		\item The collection $\{ V_{\gamma}^{\beta}\}$ satisfies the frontier condition, i.e., $V^{\beta}_{\gamma} \cap \overline{V^{\beta^{\prime}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}} \neq \emptyset$ implies $V^{\beta}_{\gamma} \subseteq \overline{V^{\beta^{\prime}}_{\gamma^{\prime}}}$ for all $\gamma, \gamma^{\prime}, \beta,$ and $\beta^{\prime}$. 
	   \end{enumerate}
	   Then the decomposition $R=\bigsqcup_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma} (V_{\gamma}^{\beta} \cap S_{\alpha})$ is a topological stratification.
title: Lemma 14 of arXiv:2608.30875

Let d and K be positive integers, let mu_1,...,mu_K be arbitrary vectors in R^d, and let X_0 have the equally weighted mixture law K^(-1) sum_i N(mu_i,I_d). For t>0 let X_t=e^(-t)X_0+sqrt(1-e^(-2t))Z with Z~N(0,I_d) independent of X_0; denote its positive density by q_t and put mu_i,t=e^(-t)mu_i. Then q_t is exactly the equally weighted mixture K^(-1) sum_i N(mu_i,t,I_d). Each component retains covariance I_d, although its mean decays exponentially. The hypothesis is common known covariance I_d and equal mixture weights; this card does not state a learning guarantee.

\[
C_{I,n}

L_n\,\frac{2T_{\ell+1,n}}{M_I}, & M_I>0,\\[8pt]
+\infty, & M_I=0.
\end{cases}
\]
For a child \(J\subset I\), set \(
U_{J,n}^{\mathrm{cap}}=U_J\wedge C_{I,n}\), and define
\[
\overline U_{I,n}
=
\mathbb{E}[U_{J,n}^{\mathrm{cap}}\mid\mathcal F_\ell].
\]
This quantity is independent of the choice of the child \(J\subset I\), since the fresh child weights are independent copies of \(U\).

body: In the mathematical field of real analysis, the monotone convergence theorem is any of a number of related theorems proving the good convergence behaviour of monotonic sequences, i.e. sequences that are non-increasing, or non-decreasing. In its simplest form, it says that a non-decreasing bounded-above sequence of real numbers converges to its smallest upper bound, its supremum. Likewise, a non-increasing bounded-below sequence converges to its largest lower bound, its infimum. In particular, infinite sums of non-negative numbers converge to the supremum of the partial sums if and only if the partial sums are bounded.
title: Monotone convergence theorem

body:
[Lemma 3.4 of arXiv:2110.05374, 'When Janson meets McDiarmid: Bounded difference inequalities under graph-dependence'] (A step in the proof of Theorem 2.1; setting as in Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3.) Let f : Ω → R be c-Lipschitz and X be G-dependent for a Rooted and Ordered dependency tree G on [n] with parent map i ↦ p_i. Then for every i ∈ [n−1], x ∈ Ω and x'_i ∈ Ω_i, E[f(X) | X_{[i]} = x_{[i]}] − E[f(X) | X_{[i]} = x^{(i)}_{[i]}] ≤ c_i + c_{p_i}. By Lemma 3.3 the difference equals E[f(Y^{(i)}) − f(Z^{(i)})], and Y^{(i)}, Z^{(i)} differ at most in coordinates i and p_i. With McDiarmid's martingale lemma (Lemma 3.1) this gives Theorem 2.1's denominator c_n² + Σ_{i≠n} (c_i + c_{p_i})² = c_min² + Σ_{{i,j}∈E(G)} (c_i + c_j)².
c-Lipschitz (Definition 1.1 of the paper): Ω = Ω_1 × ... × Ω_n is a product of Polish spaces, c = (c_1, ..., c_n) ∈ R_+^n, and f : Ω → R is c-Lipschitz when |f(x) − f(x')| ≤ Σ_{i=1}^n c_i 1{x_i ≠ x'_i} for all x, x' ∈ Ω (Lipschitz for the c-weighted Hamming distance).
G-dependent (Definition 1.3 of the paper): X = (X_i)_{i∈V(G)} is G-dependent when for all disjoint S, T ⊂ V(G) with no edge of G between S and T, the families (X_i)_{i∈S} and (X_j)_{j∈T} are independent; this is stronger than pairwise independence of non-adjacent coordinates.
Proof setting (Section 3 of the paper): G is a dependency tree on [n] that is Rooted (rooted at vertex n, with c_n = c_min) and Ordered (j is a descendant of i only if j < i), which a topological sort always provides; p_i is the parent of a non-root vertex i, S_i := [i+1, n] \ {p_i}, and for x ∈ Ω and x'_i ∈ Ω_i, x^{(i)} := (x_1, ..., x_{i−1}, x'_i, x_{i+1}, ..., x_n). The paper writes conditional probabilities of point events; for non-discrete Ω_i read them as conditional distributions.

body:
[Theorem optimaliq>1 of arXiv:2605.10452, 'A secretary for Messrs. Luce and Mallows'] Consider the secretary problem
with either  the  Mallows distribution
or the $P_n^{\mathcal{L}_\text{inv};\{q_n^i\}_{i=1}^n}$-type Luce distribution with  $q=q_n\in(0,\infty)-\{1\}$
in the case that the smallest number is  of highest rank.

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1-\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=0$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1-\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*\sim\frac1c\left(1-\log(e-1)\right)n^\alpha\approx0.459\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent iii.
Let $q\in(0,1)$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M^*)$, where
$$
M^*=\begin{cases}&\max\left\{M\ge1: \sum_{j=M}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac 1{1-q}\right\}, \ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac1{1-q};\\
&0,\ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}<\frac1{1-q}.\end{cases}
$$
(If  $\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}=\frac 1{1-q}$, then $M^*-1$ is also optimal.)

\noindent The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\begin{cases}&(1-q)(1-q^{M^*})\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge(1-q^{-M^*}),\ \text{if}\ M^*\ge1;\\
&1-q>\frac1e,\ \text{if}\ M^*=0.\end{cases}
$$
This limiting probability is always greater or equal to $\frac1e$ and is
strictly greater than $\frac1e$ for all but at most a countable number of $q$ with no accumulation points in $(0,\infty)$.

\noindent iv. Let $q_n=1+\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=1$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent v.
Let $q_n=1+\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
n-M_n^*\sim\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent vi. Let $q>1$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*=n-L, \ \text{where}\ L \ \text{satisfies}\ \frac1{q-1}\le L<\frac q{q-1}.
$$
The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\frac{q-1}{q^L}L>\frac1e.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem optimaliq>1 of arXiv:2605.10452

Status: proof (unaudited), T411-w740-C008 v1, Target 2. This fills an implementation step in C007; no novelty claim about scalar Gaussian approximation is made. All complexity claims below are for fixed positive integers K and q. The calculations are analytic; numerical checks are supplementary.

## Statement and computational assumptions

Let D>=2 be an integer, K,q>=1 fixed integers, b in {0,1/2}, D^(-K)<=epsilon<=1, and D^(-K)<=u<=D^K. Let X have mass proportional to exp(-t^2/2) on t=epsilon(j+b), j in Z, and let Y=X+uG for an independent standard Gaussian G. Write s(x)=(log p_Y)'(x).

The scalar parameters are given by algorithms producing certified rational enclosures of width 2^(-l) in time polynomial in D and l. This includes rational parameters and the elementary computable parameters in the GPX source. Evaluations of x use the same convention; network construction only needs rational x. No exact comparison of arbitrary real parameters is assumed.

There is a uniform algorithm, polynomial in D for fixed K,q, which constructs a constant-depth ReLU network f with polynomially many parameters of polynomial magnitude such that

    E[(f(Y)-s(Y))^2] <= D^(-2q).

It uses only scalar exponential/arithmetic computations. A further explicit output-clipping layer gives a network g such that

    E[(g(Y)-s(Y))^2] <= 3 D^(-2q),
    |g(x)| <= 4(q+K+10) log(D)/u  for every x.

On the window |x|<=T=D^(2K+q+10), the un-clipped construction approximates s uniformly to error D^(-q)/4. The generated network has rational coefficients of polynomial bit length. The construction does not enumerate or invert a one-way function. The constants have been deliberately overestimated; the exponents are not proposed as optimal.

## 1. Conditional Gaussian lattice and its score

Completing the square in exp(-t^2/2-(x-t)^2/(2u^2)) gives a conditional lattice Gaussian with

    m=x/(1+u^2),  v^2=u^2/(1+u^2).

Let E_x denote expectation under weights proportional to exp(-(t-m)^2/(2v^2)). Differentiation of the convergent Gaussian sums gives

    s(x)=-x/(1+u^2) + E_x[t-m]/u^2,
    s'(x)=-1/u^2 + Var_x(t)/u^4.

Termwise differentiation is justified on every compact parameter/window set by Gaussian tails. These identities do not use a prior density on R.

Choose, for analysis only, an index j0 whose t0 is nearest to m. Put delta=t0-m, so |delta|<=epsilon/2, and divide every conditional weight by that of t0. Thus w0=1, and for the index offset n,

    w_n=exp(-((delta+n epsilon)^2-delta^2)/(2v^2)).

All w_n<=1. For |n|>=2,

    w_n <= exp(-epsilon^2 n^2/(4v^2)).                 (1)

Indeed the difference of squares is at least epsilon^2 |n|(|n|-1), and |n|(|n|-1)>=n^2/2. This relative normalization is essential: the unnormalized conditional mass of the nearest point can itself be exp(-poly(D)), and need not be bounded below by an inverse polynomial.

## 2. A uniform derivative bound

Because the relative partition sum is at least one, and v<=1,

    E_x[(t-m)^2]
      <=5+(9/2) epsilon^2 sum_{n>=2} n^2 exp(-epsilon^2 n^2/4)
      <=80/epsilon.                                  (2)

Here the nearest point and its two neighbors contribute at most 1/4+2(3/2)^2<5. To check the remaining constant, set alpha=epsilon/2<=1/2 and compare each summand with the integral on [n-1,n]:

    sum_{n>=1} n^2 exp(-alpha^2 n^2)
      <= integral_0^infinity (t+1)^2 exp(-alpha^2 t^2) dt
      =sqrt(pi)/(4alpha^3)+1/alpha^2+sqrt(pi)/(2alpha)
      <=2/alpha^3=16/epsilon^3.

The last inequality follows from sqrt(pi)<2 and alpha<=1/2. Substitution gives 5+72/epsilon<=80/epsilon.

The same bound applies to the conditional second moment truncated around the nearest point, since its relative partition sum remains at least one and its numerator is smaller. Therefore

    |s'(x)| <=u^(-2)+80/(epsilon u^4) <=L:=81 D^(5K)   (3)

for every real x. Also, for |x|<=T,

    |s(x)| <=T+sqrt(80/epsilon)/u^2 <=T+9D^(3K).       (4)

## 3. Certified finite evaluation of the score

Set eta=D^(-q), N=T=D^(2K+q+10), and M=2K+2q+20>=24. With the nearest-point normalization, delete the terms |n|>N. For each j=0,1,2, the deleted sum of |t-m|^j w_n is at most

    E0=1000 D^(3K) exp(-N^2/(8D^(2K)))
       <=D^(-(q+10K+20)).                            (5)

For the first inequality, use (1), epsilon<=1 and |t-m|<=|n|+1. Split exp(-n^2/(4D^(2K))) into two equal exponential factors and bound one by exp(-N^2/(8D^(2K))). The full sum of (|n|+1)^2 times the other factor is at most 1000D^(3K). This follows from the preceding integral comparison, now with alpha=1/(sqrt(8)D^K), applied to (t+2)^2; using sqrt(pi)<2 and sqrt(8)<3 gives a constant less than 200, so 1000 is sufficient.

For completeness, the elementary inequality used to absorb this exponential, and later tails, is

    D^M/32 >=(50M+100) log D  (D>=2, M>=24).         (6)

The function D^M/log D is increasing for D>=2. At D=2 it suffices that 2^M>=32(50M+100), true at M=24 and preserved by doubling. Since log 2<1, this proves (6). Also 1000<=D^10. These inequalities imply the second part of (5), because N^2/D^(2K)=D^M.

Let R and R_N be the full and truncated conditional means of t-m. The full and truncated partition sums are at least one. By (2), |R_N|<=9D^K. Equation (5) therefore gives

    |R-R_N| <=(1+9D^K)E0,
    |s-s_N| <=10D^(3K) E0 <=eta/16.                (7)

We next explain why this exact truncation can be evaluated with polynomial work, including near a lattice tie. Compute m/epsilon-b to absolute error at most 1/4 and take the floor of that rational approximation, an integer a. The exact nearest index lies within distance two of a. Use all indices in [a-N-3,a+N+3]. This set contains every term with |n|<=N, so its omitted tails satisfy (5)-(7), with the same constants. The nearest point is used in the estimates, but its exact identity is never needed by the algorithm.

Compute the energies (epsilon(j+b)-m)^2/(2v^2) on this finite set. Subtract the smallest of their rational approximations before taking negative exponentials. If each energy approximation has error at most kappa, every relative computed weight is at most exp(2kappa), and a maximum weight is at least exp(-2kappa). Thus the numerical denominator is bounded below by 1/2 once kappa is sufficiently small. There is no division by an exponentially small number. The common offset cancels from the normalized means regardless of which energy minimizes the rounded list.

Here are explicit precision budgets. Take

    kappa=eta/(2^20 D^(4K) (N+10)^3).

Obtain the individual weights and residual-weight products with absolute errors at most kappa, with a further constant-factor guard in their energy enclosures. There are at most 3(N+10) terms. For exact finite sums A,B with A>=1 in nearest-point units and |B/A|<=9D^K, errors at most 3(N+10)kappa in each sum change B/A by at most

    60 D^K (N+10) kappa.

If the implemented energy offset differs from the exact nearest energy, its common factor lies between exp(-2kappa) and exp(2kappa); allowing an additional factor four in the preceding estimate covers that normalization. After multiplication by u^(-2), this is less than eta/128 with the chosen budget. Perform the remaining scalar divisions and additions to error at most eta/128. Together with (7), the evaluation error is less than eta/8.

To see that those enclosures have polynomial cost, every index has magnitude at most O(T/epsilon+N), every residual has magnitude at most O(N), and v^(-2)<=2D^(2K). The energies, their derivatives with respect to the finitely many scalar inputs, and the reciprocal of every positive parameter denominator are bounded by fixed powers of D. Their certified evaluation to kappa accuracy needs O(poly(K,q) log D) input bits. Exponentials after the common shift have arguments bounded above by 2kappa; values below the requested precision may be replaced by a certified interval containing zero. Standard elementary-series or interval evaluation therefore has polynomial cost. There are polynomially many terms. This proves a uniform algorithm, rather than an existence assertion about network weights.

## 4. A rational ReLU network

Take n=16TL/eta, an integer under the present parameter choices, and use the n equal intervals covering [-T,T]. Their common length is Delta=eta/(8L). Compute each endpoint score to error at most eta/8 using Section 3 and retain a certified rational approximation. Interpolate the values linearly and extend constantly outside [-T,T]. Equations (3)-(4) show

    sup_{|x|<=T}|f(x)-s(x)|<=eta/4,
    |f(x)|<=H:=12 D^(3K+q+10) for every x.

Each segment slope has magnitude at most 3L, since the endpoint evaluation errors differ by at most eta/4. A continuous piecewise-linear function with knots t_i and slopes a_i, including slope zero outside the window, is represented by a constant plus sum_i (a_i-a_(i-1)) ReLU(x-t_i). Thus a two-layer network suffices, with polynomially many rational coefficients, each of polynomial magnitude and polynomial bit length. This also gives an explicit network-generation algorithm.

## 5. The tails do not hide an L2 error

The lattice normalizer is at least exp(-1/2)/epsilon: there are at least 1/epsilon lattice points in [-1,1]. For z>=2, comparing each positive lattice summand with its preceding interval of length epsilon, and doing the same on the negative side, gives

    Pr(|X|>z)<=4 exp(-z^2/8).

Indeed the two tails are at most 2 epsilon^(-1) integral_(z-epsilon)^infinity exp(-t^2/2)dt before division by the normalizer, and z-epsilon>=z/2 and >=1. Consequently

    pi_T:=Pr(|Y|>T)
      <=4 exp(-T^2/32)+2 exp(-T^2/(8u^2))
      <=6 exp(-D^M/32)
      <=D^(-(100K+100q+1000)),                       (8)

where (6) proves the last deliberately loose bound.

The Gaussian denoising identity s(Y)=-E[G|Y]/u and Jensen give E[s(Y)^4]<=3/u^4. Cauchy-Schwarz therefore bounds the error outside the window by

    E[(f(Y)-s(Y))^2 1_{|Y|>T}]
      <=2H^2 pi_T+2sqrt(3)u^(-2)sqrt(pi_T)
      <=eta^2/2.                                    (9)

For a direct check of the last inequality, its two terms are bounded by 288D^(-94K-98q-980) and 4D^(-48K-50q-500), respectively; each is at most eta^2/4 for D>=2,K,q>=1. Inside the window the squared error is at most eta^2/16. This proves the stated global L2 bound, with slack.

## 6. Bounded output and use in C007

Set B0=2(q+K+10)log(D)/u and choose a certified rational B in [B0,2B0]. Clip the network output to [-B,B], using two additional ReLU operations. Conditional Jensen applied to exp(lambda G) shows that u s(Y) is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy one. Integrating its tail gives

    E[(s(Y)-clip_B(s(Y)))^2]
      <=4u^(-2) exp(-(uB)^2/2)
      <=4D^(-2q-10).

The second inequality uses log D>=log 2>1/2 and (q+K+10)^2>2q+2K+10. Projection onto the interval is nonexpansive, so the squared error of the clipped network is at most twice the error of f plus twice this clipping error, below 3eta^2. Its magnitude is at most 2B0, as stated.

For q>K+1 this has the O(u^(-1)log(1/(u D^(-q)))) output bound used for the one-dimensional primitives in GPX Lemmas C.11/C.15. Arbitrarily fixed inverse-polynomial error budgets are obtained by increasing q, keeping polynomial complexity. Ordinary one- or two-component Gaussian primitives are even simpler finite sums and satisfy the same evaluation/interpolation argument. The source's network composition then uses these scalar primitives, its explicit decoder and forward-circuit evaluation, and switches. Composing constant-depth polynomial-size, polynomially bounded networks preserves those properties, and rounding scalar coefficients more finely by a fixed inverse-polynomial factor absorbs the polynomial sensitivity of that composition. The proof does not introduce any conditional circuit inversion.

This resolves the specific effective-scalar-network step needed by C007. It is not a new posterior hardness assumption, an exact-score oracle, or a result on Target 1. [Corollary 17 (Unique Pinkall-modulus limit) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:anchored-profile}, orient the
profiles consistently with the reduced flow.  Let
\(\mathcal A_t\in\R/4\pi\mathbb Z\) be the oriented area class
enclosed by \(\gamma_t\), and let \(\mathcal A_T\) be the corresponding area class for
\(\gamma_T\).  Then
\begin{equation}
 
 \mathcal A_t\longrightarrow\mathcal A_T
 \qquad\text{in }\R/4\pi\mathbb Z .
\end{equation}
For \(t\) sufficiently close to \(T\), choose compatible real
representatives such that \(\mathcal A_t\to\mathcal A_T\).  Pinkall's
lattice is
\begin{equation}
 
 \Gamma_t=
 \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Z}
 \left\{(2\pi,0),
 \left(\frac{\mathcal A_t}{2},\frac{L(\gamma_t)}2\right)\right\},
\end{equation}
and the corresponding modulus is
\begin{equation}
 
 \tau_t=\frac{\mathcal A_t+iL(\gamma_t)}{4\pi}\in\mathbb H .
\end{equation}
It satisfies
\[
 \tau_t\longrightarrow
 \tau_T:=\frac{\mathcal A_T+iL_T}{4\pi}.
\]
Its imaginary part satisfies the quantitative bounds
\begin{equation}
 
 \frac14\leq\operatorname{Im}\tau_T\leq\frac2\pi.
\end{equation}
Consequently the conformal classes
\[
 [\tau_t]\longrightarrow[\tau_T]
 \qquad\text{in }\mathcal M_1=\mathbb H/\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)
\]
have a unique finite-time limit, independent of the approaching time
sequence.  With the orientation induced by the fixed oriented profile
and the positively oriented Hopf fibres, the class \([\tau_T]\) is the
intrinsic oriented conformal class of the limiting \(C^1\) Hopf torus.
In particular, no conformal
degeneration occurs at the finite endpoint.

Fix a finite irreducible row-stochastic Q with stationary probability pi, p in [0,1]^d, c>0, f=cr^2 and 0<r with r+f<=1. For Z in the state space [0,1]^d, let X_i be conditionally independent Bernoulli((QZ)_i), and update Z prime=(1-r-f)Z+rX+fp. The stationary law is unique, has mean f*((r+f)I-rQ)^(-1)p, and Cov(Z) tends as r->0 to K*pbar*(1-pbar)/(2c+K) times the all-ones matrix, where pbar=pi.p and K=sum pi_i^2. For Q=(1), its exact variance is p(1-p)/(1+2c-c^2*r^2). This is a stationary moment result, not a functional diffusion convergence theorem.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Assume a fixed finite irreducible row-stochastic Q, its stationary probability row vector pi, p in [0,1]^d, c>0, r>0, f=c*r^2 and r+f<=1. Update

    Z'=(1-r-f)Z+r X+f p,

with conditionally independent X_i given Z, and P(X_i=1|Z)=(QZ)_i. There is a unique stationary law on [0,1]^d. Its mean is z*=f*((r+f)I-rQ)^(-1)p. Write pbar=pi.p and K=sum pi_i^2. As r decreases to zero, its stationary covariance satisfies

    Cov(Z) -> [K*pbar*(1-pbar)/(2c+K)]*1*1^T.

Proof of existence/uniqueness: the transition is Feller on a compact cube. Couple two states using the same independent uniforms for their Bernoulli coordinates. Because 1-r-f>=0, the weighted L1 distance has expected next value at most (1-f) times its present value; use pi Q=pi. Thus stationary laws are unique and the transition contracts in this Wasserstein distance. Taking expectations yields the displayed mean; the matrix is invertible because its eigenvalues have positive real part.

For synchronization, let D=diag(pi), S=pi.Z, and E_Q(z)=z^T D(I-Q)z=(1/2)sum pi_i Q_ij(z_i-z_j)^2. At stationarity, with Delta=r(X-Z)+f(p-Z),

    2r E[E_Q(Z)] = 2f E[<Z,p-Z>_D] + E[||Delta||_D^2]
                   <= 2f+(r+f)^2 = O(r^2).

Irreducibility makes E_Q(z)>=gamma*||z-1*(pi.z)||_D^2 for some fixed gamma>0: the finite symmetric quadratic form has kernel precisely the constants. Hence E||Z-1*S||_D^2=O(r). Also E[S]=pbar exactly, so z*_i tends to pbar.

The martingale innovation for S has conditional variance r^2 sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i); conditional independence is used exactly here. Total variance at stationarity gives

    (2f-f^2) Var(S)=r^2 sum pi_i^2 E[(QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i)].

Synchronization shows (QZ)_i-S tends to zero in L2. The variables are bounded, so for any subsequential limit V of Var(S), division by r^2 gives 2c V=K*(pbar*(1-pbar)-V). Its solution is unique. Every subsequence has that limit, and synchronization gives the full covariance limit.

For the scalar case Q=(1), stationarity gives the exact variance

    Var(Z)=r^2*p*(1-p)/(2f-f^2+r^2)
          =p*(1-p)/(1+2c-c^2*r^2).

For h in C^3([0,1]), the one-step scalar generator divided by r^2 converges uniformly to

    Lh(z)=c(p-z)h'(z)+(1/2)z(1-z)h''(z).

Indeed E[Delta]=c*r^2(p-z), E[Delta^2]=r^2*z(1-z)+c^2*r^4(p-z)^2, and |Delta|<=r+cr^2. Taylor's remainder, divided by r^2, is bounded by ||h'''||_infinity*r*(1+cr)^3/6, with the additional second-order drift term O(r^2). This identifies the candidate Wright-Fisher generator; path tightness and martingale-problem uniqueness are further steps.

Theorem (full stationary law). Under the same fixed-network assumptions and 0<pbar<1, the joint stationary law of Z converges weakly to Y*1, where

    Y ~ Beta(2c*pbar/K, 2c*(1-pbar)/K).

Proof: write S'=S+f*(pbar-S)+r*eta, where eta=pi.(X-QZ), E[eta|Z]=0, |eta|<=1 and E[eta^2|Z]=sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i). For every polynomial h, the stationary Taylor identity divided by r^2 gives

    0=c E[(pbar-S)h'(S)]
      +(1/2)E[sum pi_i^2 (QZ)_i(1-(QZ)_i)*h''(S)] + O(r).

The drift-square contribution is O(r^2), and the third-order remainder is uniformly O(r). The proved L2 synchronization implies that the sum inside the second term differs from K*S*(1-S) by a quantity tending to zero in L1. Every subsequence has a further weakly convergent subsequence of S because [0,1] is compact. If its limiting moments are mu_k, use h(s)=s^k, k>=1, to obtain

    [2c+K*(k-1)]*mu_k = [2c*pbar+K*(k-1)]*mu_(k-1), mu_0=1.

These are exactly the moments of the displayed beta law: iterating gives the product of (2c*pbar/K+j)/(2c/K+j) for j=0,...,k-1, which also follows by integrating the beta density. A probability law on [0,1] is determined by its moments, since polynomials approximate continuous functions uniformly. Hence all subsequential limits agree and S converges weakly. Synchronization gives Z-S*1 tending to zero in probability, so the joint law converges to Y*1. If pbar=0 or 1, positivity of pi forces every p_i to be that endpoint and the unique stationary law is the corresponding point mass.

This proof uses all polynomial moments, not an inference from the first two moments. It proves convergence of stationary laws, not a limit for trajectories begun away from synchronization. Without conditional independence, the innovation variance changes. For example, Q=J_d/d, constant p, and one shared Bernoulli coin across all coordinates preserve a synchronized state and give the scalar beta parameters 2cp and 2c(1-p), rather than 2cdp and 2cd(1-p).

For reproducible finite checks, the exact covariance identity is

    V=B V B^T+r^2*diag(s*(1-s)-diag(Q V Q^T)),
    B=(1-r-f)I+rQ, s=Q z*.

Checks: the scalar exact formula; first four scalar stationary moments; exact polynomial generators; finite-network covariance systems; first four moments of the exact consensus Markov chain for Q=J_d/d at d=2,3,5; a common-coin control that changes the beta variance. The conditional-independence hypothesis is essential for K, the covariance formula and the stationary beta law.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:97f3a85196e873990e9567366e0506ef248b0ce7c5366d200c12cde129cf9cd6","revision_digest":"sha256:71f11592c93dc1af9dff028a3e3fbbd66f755b9640b9f7629f748526e31a9a8f","source_id":"owner:campaign:w336:P0087:forced-network-urn-stationary-covariance-quadratic-forcing","source_revision":"author-proof-2026-10-10; independent audit w346 pending","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

Let n,s>=1 be integers. Let q be a probability density on [0,1] that is strictly positive and constant on each of the n intervals [i/n,(i+1)/n]. Let p be the product of Uniform[0,1] in the first coordinate and q in the second. There exists a feedforward ReLU network Phi:R->R^2 with affine final layer, depth s+3 and connectivity at most 6n+24s+2, such that W_1(Phi#Uniform[0,1],p)<=2 sqrt(2)/2^s. Here W_1 uses Euclidean distance, depth counts affine maps, and connectivity counts all nonzero weight and bias entries. Coefficients are unrestricted real numbers. Source: arXiv:2006.16664v2, Theorem 4.3, PDF pp5--6.

[Theorem Fourier_laplace of arXiv:2606.29622, 'Affine Structure of the Brownian Signature'] Let $\bm{\sigma}\in T(\mathbb{C}^2)$ such that $\deg(\bm{\sigma}) = N$ for some odd $N$ such that 
    
    $\lambda := \bm{\sigma}^{{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{1}}}^{\otimes N}} \neq 0$, and let $M$ be the martingale defined by (equation eq:sig_mart of the paper). Suppose that $v = (v_1, v_2) \in \mathbb{C}^2$ is such that 
    $$
    v_1 \in \{z\in \mathbb{C} \colon \, \mathfrak{Re}(\lambda z) < 0\} \cup \{0\}, \quad  \, \mathfrak{Re}\left(\lambda^2 v_2\right) < 0,    
    $$
    and $\mathbb{E}[\exp(v_1 M_T + v_2 \langle M \rangle_T) | \mathcal{F}_t] \neq 0\,$ a.s. for all $t \in [0, T]$.
    Then,
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(v_1 M_T + v_2 \langle M\rangle_T\right)\, |\, \mathcal{F}_t\right] = \exp(\bracket{\bm{\psi}_t^{\sigW}}{{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{\varnothing}}}})\,, \quad t \in [0\,,T]\,,
    \end{equation}
    where $\bm{\psi}^{\sigW[t]}$ is a solution to the Riccati equation (equation eq:Riccati_recentered of the paper) with $\sigX[] = \sigW[t]\,$,
    
    
    
    
    
    
    and $\bm{p}$ is given by
    \begin{equation}
        \bm{p} = v_1\left(\bm{\sigma}{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{1}}} - \dfrac12\bm{\sigma}|_{{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{1}}}}{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{0}}}\right) + v_2 \bm{\sigma}^{\mathrel{\sqcup \mkern -3mu \sqcup} 2}{\color{NavyBlue}{\mathbf{0}}}.
    \end{equation}
title: Theorem Fourier_laplace of arXiv:2606.29622

$ 0 \le s \le u \le t $ and $ i,j \in \left\{ 1,\dots,N \right\} $. Then
$ D_s^j X_u^{i,N} $ satisfies, on $ [s,t] $,
\begin{align}

D_s^j X_u^{i,N}
&=
\sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\Biggl(
\partial_x b\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right) D_s^j X_r^{i,N}
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu b\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right)\left( X_r^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^j X_r^{\ell,N}
\Biggr) dr
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\Biggl(
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right) D_s^j X_r^{i,N}
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right)\left( X_r^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^j X_r^{\ell,N}
\Biggr) dB_r^i.
\end{align}
Equivalently, for every $ \alpha \in \left\{ 1,\dots,m \right\} $, the column

\sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)e_\alpha \mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}}
\nonumber\\

+
\int_s^u
\Biggl(
\partial_x b\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right) D_s^{j,\alpha} X_r^{i,N}
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu b\left( X_r^{i,N},\mu_r^N \right)\left( X_r^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_r^{\ell,N}
\Biggr) dr

+
\int_s^u
\Biggl(

For $s <  t \in [\theta, 1 - \theta]$, we can find a coupling of $\{\mathcal{H}_i\}_{i=1}^k, \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{Q}, \{\mathcal{D}_i\}_{i=1}^k$ such that each of the tuples $(\{\mathcal{H}_i\}_{i=1}^k, \{\mathcal{M}_i^s\}_{i=1}^k, \{\mathcal{D}_i\}_{i=1}^k)$ and  $(\{\mathcal{H}_i\}_{i=1}^k, \{\mathcal{M}_i^t\}_{i=1}^k, \{\mathcal{D}_i\}_{i=1}^k)$ has the same law as in (equation eq:cMdef of the paper), and 
			$$
			\mathbb{P}\left[\big\{\{\mathcal{M}_i^s\}_{i=1}^k \neq \{\mathcal{M}_i^t\}_{i=1}^k \big\}\cap \mathcal{E}[W] \right] \le C (t-s)^{2/3+\delta},
			$$
			where the constant $C$ can also depend on $\theta$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Corollary cor:canonical-borel-compression-traces of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] For every $0<a<b$, bounded real Borel function $v$, and $k\ge1$, the map
\begin{equation}
 x\longmapsto
 \Tr\!\left[(\Pi_{a,b}^x\operatorname{Mult}_v\Pi_{a,b}^x)^k\right]
 \in\mathbb R
\end{equation}
is measurable.  In particular, for rational $0<a<b$ and $v=q\in\mathcal Q_D$,
these are the power traces appearing in
(equation eq:minimal-borel-interface of the paper).

[Lem 19 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] The set $[-r,r]$ is a \emph{mobile cluster},
i.e.,
\begin{enumerate}
\item Let $\eta$ such that $\eta(x)=0$ for all $x\in x_{0}+[-r,r]$. Then
there exist $\eta'\connected{}{}\eta$ such that $\eta'(x)=0$ for
all $x\in x_{0}+1+[-r,r]$.
\item Let $\eta$ such that $\eta(x)=0$ for all $x\in x_{0}+[-r,r]$. Then
there exist $\eta'\connected{}{}\eta$ such that $\eta'(x)=0$ for
all $x\in x_{0}-1+[-r,r]$.
\end{enumerate}

body: Let Omega be a bounded domain in R^n with Lipschitz boundary, let 1 <= p < n, and let p* = np/(n-p) be the Sobolev conjugate exponent. Then the Sobolev embedding W^{1,p}(Omega) -> L^{p*}(Omega) is continuous, and the embedding W^{1,p}(Omega) -> L^q(Omega) is compact for every q with 1 <= q < p*: any sequence bounded in the W^{1,p} norm has a subsequence converging strongly in L^q(Omega). If p = n, the embedding into L^q(Omega) is compact for every finite q; if p > n, W^{1,p}(Omega) embeds compactly into C(closure of Omega). Named for Franz Rellich and Vladimir Kondrachov.
title: Rellich-Kondrachov theorem

body:
[Conjecture conj:quenched full of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] For $f\in D$, let $\theta$ be the optimizer in~(equation eq:quenched conj of the paper) and $\zeta$ the minimizer
		in~(equation def:tildeLambda of the paper) for this~$\theta$.
		Then:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\emph{(\roman*)}]
			\item \emph{(Ultrametric structure.)} The TAP critical points at free-energy level $f$ are organized in an ultrametric tree: the overlap between any two TAP states at level $f$ taken uniformly takes values in the support of $\zeta$.
			\item \emph{(Separation of free-energy levels.)} Whenever $f\neq f_\mathrm{eq}:=\inf_\zeta \mathcal{P}\mathrm{arisi}(\zeta)$, the ancestor states in this ultrametric tree have TAP free energy $\mathcal{P}\mathrm{arisi}(\zeta)\neq f$, i.e., the ancestors live at a different free-energy level than their descendants.
			\item \emph{(Subexponential number of ancestors.)} The quenched complexity of the ancestor states is $0$: they exist, but their number grows at most subexponentially in $N$.
		\end{enumerate} (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)
title: Ultrametric organization of TAP states

    the following map is a continuous group homomorphism:
    \begin{align*}
        \Phi_{ij}: \rmB(n) &\to \rmB(j-i+1), \\
        \begin{pmatrix}
            x_{11} & x_{12} &\cdots & x_{1n}\\
            0 & \ddots &\ddots & \vdots\\
            \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & x_{n-1 n }\\
            0 & \cdots & 0 &x_{nn}
        \end{pmatrix} &\mapsto 
        \begin{pmatrix}
            x_{ii} & x_{ii+1} &\cdots & x_{ij}\\
            0 & \ddots &\ddots & \vdots\\
            \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & x_{j-1 j }\\
            0 & \cdots & 0 &x_{jj}
        \end{pmatrix}.
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

 such that if $u$ is a solution to \eqref{eq1}-\eqref{bin1} from the restricted 
 Leray-Hopf class, satisfying 
\begin{equation*}

 $$
 |u_t-v_t|_{\cH}\leq |u_0-v_0|_{\cH}e^{-\gamma t}\quad\text{for $t\in[0,T]$}
 $$

 class with initial condition $v_t|_{t=0}=v_0\in\cH$, where 
 $\gamma:=\frc^{-2}(\nu-N\tilde u)>0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

$q>1$, and $\pi=(\pi_n)_{n\geq1}$ a sequence of partitions of
$[0,T]$ such that
$$
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|\pi_n|<\infty.
$$
Then
$$
\|\rho_{n,B}\|_{L^q([0,T])}^q
\longrightarrow
c_{q,d}T
\qquad \mathbb{P}_x\text{-almost surely},
$$
where
$$
c_{q,d}:=\mathbb{E}|Z|^{2q},
\qquad Z\sim N(0,I_d).
$$
In particular,
$$
\sup_{n\geq1}\|\rho_{n,B}\|_{L^q([0,T])}<\infty
\qquad \mathbb{P}_x\text{-almost surely}.
$$

body: In a multi-output stacking problem scored by the mean per-sample relative error $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \|\hat y_i - y_i\|/\|y_i\|$, the per-output least-squares stack minimises the unweighted squared error, which is dominated by the cases with the largest $\|y_i\|$, while the score is dominated by the cases with the smallest. Interpolating the per-output weights toward one pooled simplex weight vector fitted on the relative error therefore improves the score even IN-SAMPLE on the very calibration rows on which least squares is optimal in squared error - the signature that distinguishes an objective mismatch from a generalisation (variance) effect, which can only appear out of sample. Measured on the EMIT lookup-table pool (seed 101, component Y2, 23 members, 932 calibration rows, 285 outputs): in-sample relative error 0.1105 for least squares against 0.1026 at interpolation weight 0.4 (-7.2 percent), the in-sample optimum at the same weight as the out-of-sample optimum (0.1292 to 0.1186), while the in-sample squared error is minimal at least squares (8.8e-5 against 1.2e-4); the out-of-sample gain is +15.9 percent in the smallest-norm quartile of targets and -9.6 percent in the largest, and 45 percent of the least-squares score comes from its worst decile of cases. Consequently no model of the sampling noise of the weight rows reproduces the cross-validated interpolation weight: the known-noise James-Stein amount is 0.00 and the heteroscedasticity-robust amount 0.03-0.05 where cross-validation chooses 0.10-0.40. Shrinking toward the pooled UNCONSTRAINED least-squares weights (entries up to 90 in magnitude) or toward the mean of the rows is much worse; the simplex constraint together with the relative objective carries the effect. The practical rule: when a stack is scored in a metric that weights cases differently from the fitting loss, the first question is the objective, not the estimator's variance.

gradient $h$ with minimal cone representation
$h+\alpha a_i+\beta c_j=0$, $\alpha,\beta>0$, where $a_i\in A$ and
$c_j\in C$. The \emph{rectangle branch} is the case where two cross types

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited), T381-C004/C005/C006 v1. A fixed next-token model M can output |p| fair bits then terminate on prompt p. For a stateless robust watermark satisfying standard soundness and repeated-query undetectability uniformly over polynomial-length prompts, use p_lambda=1^n to instantiate the zero-bit PRC reduction at any polynomial length n with b_lambda(n+1)<=n. If b_lambda(L)<=A(lambda)L^alpha above a polynomial onset L0, where A,L0>=1 are efficient integer-valued polynomially bounded functions and fixed 0<=alpha<1, take n=max(L0,(2A)^d) for a fixed integer d with d(1-alpha)>=1. Then b_lambda(n+1)<=n. In particular O(lambda sqrt L) thresholds admit n=lambda^3 eventually, without knowing the implicit constant. The channel robustness is assumed, not obtained from entropy. If instead b_lambda(n+1)>n, uniform sampling with an always-rejecting detector has vacuous entropy-qualified completeness and fails the direct PRC reduction.

Let U and V be non-degenerate cumulative distribution functions on \mathbb{R}. Let (F_n)_{n=1}^\infty be a sequence of distribution functions, and let a_n > 0, b_n \in \mathbb{R}, c_n > 0, d_n \in \mathbb{R} be constants such that F_n(a_n x + b_n) \Rightarrow U(x) and F_n(c_n x + d_n) \Rightarrow V(x) weakly as n \to \infty. Then there exist constants a > 0 and b \in \mathbb{R} such that \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{c_n}{a_n} = a, \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{d_n - b_n}{a_n} = b, and V(x) = U(a x + b).
U, V are non-degenerate CDFs

Let 𝔄 be a unital Banach algebra (for instance the algebra B(E) of bounded linear operators on a Banach space E, or the n×n complex matrices), and for A ∈ 𝔄 define exp(A) = e^A := Σ_{k=0}^∞ A^k / k!, a series that converges absolutely in norm for every A (‖A^k/k!‖ ≤ ‖A‖^k/k!), so that ‖e^A‖ ≤ e^{‖A‖}. If A, B ∈ 𝔄 COMMUTE, AB = BA, then e^{A+B} = e^A e^B = e^B e^A. Consequences: for every A and all scalars s, t, e^{(s+t)A} = e^{sA} e^{tA} (the one-parameter group law), e^A is invertible with (e^A)⁻¹ = e^{−A}, e^0 = 1, and t ↦ e^{tA} is norm-differentiable with derivative A e^{tA} = e^{tA} A. If P is invertible, e^{PAP⁻¹} = P e^A P⁻¹. Sharp edges. (1) Commutativity cannot be dropped: for the 2×2 matrices A = [[0,1],[0,0]] and B = [[0,0],[1,0]] one has e^A = I + A, e^B = I + B, so e^A e^B = [[2,1],[1,1]], whereas A + B = [[0,1],[1,0]] gives e^{A+B} = [[cosh 1, sinh 1],[sinh 1, cosh 1]] ≠ e^A e^B (and e^B e^A = [[1,1],[1,2]] ≠ e^A e^B, so the two products differ as well). For non-commuting A, B the product e^A e^B is instead described by the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff series e^{A+B+[A,B]/2+…} when it converges, and by the Lie–Trotter formula e^{A+B} = lim_{n→∞} (e^{A/n} e^{B/n})ⁿ. (2) The converse is false in general: e^A e^B = e^{A+B} does not imply AB = BA (there are non-commuting complex matrices with e^A = e^B = e^{A+B} = I); it does hold for Hermitian (self-adjoint) matrices A, B, because then e^{A+B} Hermitian forces e^A e^B = (e^A e^B)* = e^B e^A, so the positive definite matrices e^A and e^B commute, and hence so do their unique Hermitian logarithms A and B. (3) For UNBOUNDED operators (generators of semigroups) the series definition is unavailable and 'commuting' must be formulated with care (e.g. commuting resolvents / commuting semigroups); this statement is only about bounded operators and Banach algebras.
𝔄 is a unital Banach algebra (e.g. bounded operators on a Banach space, or square matrices)
A and B are elements of 𝔄 (bounded operators)
AB = BA

Let α be irrational with regular continued fraction [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...], convergents p_n/q_n (p_{-1} = 1, q_{-1} = 0, p_0 = a_0, q_0 = 1, p_{n+1} = a_{n+1}p_n + p_{n-1}, q_{n+1} = a_{n+1}q_n + q_{n-1}) and complete quotients α_{n+1} = [a_{n+1}; a_{n+2}, ...], so a_{n+1} < α_{n+1} < a_{n+1} + 1. Write ||t|| = dist(t, Z) and δ_n = |q_n α − p_n| (so δ_{-1} = 1).

(1) Exact size and alternating sign. For all n ≥ 0, q_n α − p_n = (−1)^n / (q_n α_{n+1} + q_{n-1}). Hence 1/(q_n + q_{n+1}) < δ_n < 1/q_{n+1}, the errors alternate in sign, δ_n is strictly decreasing, and δ_n = ||q_n α|| for every n ≥ 1 (because q_{n+1} ≥ 2 gives δ_n < 1/2); for n = 0 this holds when a_1 ≥ 2.

(2) The distances obey the same recursion as the denominators: δ_{n-1} = a_{n+1} δ_n + δ_{n+1} for all n ≥ 0. Equivalently δ_n = 1/(α_1 α_2 ··· α_{n+1}).

(3) Closest returns (Lagrange's theorem on best approximations of the second kind). For every n ≥ 0 and every integer q with 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1}: ||q α|| ≥ δ_n, with equality if and only if q = q_n. In dynamical words: for the rotation t ↦ t + α (mod 1), among all times 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1} the orbit of any point comes closest to its starting point exactly at time q_n; the record-breaking (closest-return) times of the orbit are precisely the denominators q_0 (when a_1 ≥ 2), q_1, q_2, ..., and successive closest returns land on alternate sides of the starting point, at distances δ_n.

(4) Growth. q_{n+1} ≥ q_n + q_{n-1}, hence q_n ≥ F_{n+1} (Fibonacci) and q_n ≥ 2^{(n−1)/2} for n ≥ 1; the golden ratio (all a_k = 1) is the slowest case.

Where it fails. For rational α the expansion terminates, the last δ is 0 and the recursion (2) stops. Statement (3) is about ||qα|| = min_p |qα − p| (best approximations of the SECOND kind). For the FIRST-kind problem of minimising |α − p/q| over q ≤ Q, intermediate fractions (p_{n-1} + k p_n)/(q_{n-1} + k q_n) with k > a_{n+1}/2 can also be best approximations, so the two notions must not be conflated. When a_1 = 1 one has q_0 = q_1 = 1, the n = 0 case of (3) is vacuous, and ||α|| equals δ_1, not δ_0.
α irrational (for the rational case the expansion terminates)
regular (simple) continued fraction with integer partial quotients a_k ≥ 1 for k ≥ 1
||t|| denotes the distance from t to the nearest integer

[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2606.11068, '2606.11068'] Let \(S=(S_m)_{m\ge0}\) be a nearest-neighbour motion on \(\mathbb Z\), started
from \(S_0=0\), and let \(\Xi\) be an independent lifetime with tail \(G\).
Define
\[
  D^*:=\max_{0\le k\le \Xi}|S_k|.
\]
Let
\[
  \tau_n:=\inf\{m\ge1: |S_m|=n\},
  \qquad n\ge1,
\]
with the convention \(\inf\varnothing=\infty\). Then
\[
  \Pbb(D^*\ge n)=\E[G(\tau_n)].
\]
If
\[
  D^\to:=\max_{0\le k\le\Xi}S_k,
  \qquad
  \tau_n^+:=\inf\{m\ge1:S_m=n\},
\]
then
\[
  \Pbb(D^\to\ge n)=\E[G(\tau_n^+)].
\]
Analogously, if
\[
  D^\leftarrow:=\max_{0\le k\le\Xi}(-S_k),
  \qquad
  \tau_n^-:=\inf\{m\ge1:S_m=-n\},
\]
then
\[
  \Pbb(D^\leftarrow\ge n)=\E[G(\tau_n^-)].
\]
In the last two identities, we again use the convention \(G(\infty)=0\).

body:
Let X be a compact topological space and T: X → X a map. Then every nonempty closed set A ⊂ X with T(A) ⊆ A contains a minimal set: a nonempty closed set M ⊆ A with T(M) ⊆ M that has no proper nonempty closed T-invariant subset. In particular (A = X) every compact dynamical system has at least one minimal set. If moreover X is Hausdorff and T is continuous, then M = cl{Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} for every x ∈ M, T(M) = M, and (X metrizable) M carries a T-invariant Borel probability measure by the Krylov–Bogolyubov theorem, so every compact metrizable system has an invariant probability measure supported on a minimal set. The same statement and proof hold for a commuting family (or any semigroup) of maps X → X, with 'invariant' meaning invariant under every map of the family, and for flows. Sharp edges. (1) Compactness cannot be dropped: for the translation T(x) = x + 1 on ℝ, any nonempty closed invariant set A contains, for some a ∈ A, the closed invariant set {a + n : n ≥ 0}, which has the proper closed invariant subset {a + n : n ≥ 1}; so ℝ has NO minimal set, although it has plenty of nonempty closed invariant sets. (2) Existence uses only compactness and Zorn's lemma (the intersection of a chain of nonempty closed sets in a compact space is nonempty by the finite intersection property); continuity of T is needed only for the orbit-closure description and for T(M) = M. (3) Minimal sets need not be unique: the identity map has every single point as a minimal set; a system with a fixed point and a dense orbit (e.g. the doubling map) has minimal sets that are not the whole space. (4) 'Minimal' is with respect to inclusion among closed invariant sets; a nonempty invariant set that is not closed (a single dense orbit) is not a minimal set.
X is a compact topological space
T: X → X is a map (continuity needed only for the orbit-closure supplement and T(M) = M)
A ⊂ X is nonempty, closed, and T(A) ⊆ A
Zorn's lemma (axiom of choice) is available

CURRENT AUDIT STATUS: independently checked proof, T336-w727-C005 v2; claude-5693aca3 PASS in AUDITS_FROM_REVIEWER.tsv. Exact proof SHA256 22df67c6b2aaec99499aac6bf3440e8d5d6305204deedcc98fe9b4a621583b40. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed. The following original submission text retains historical pre-audit status notices.

Every continuous real symmetric PSD kernel of rank <=p and diagonal <=R^2 on a nonempty compact X subset R^d admits an explicit raw-input normalized-ReLU-attention transformer for uniform noisy predictive forward KL <=eps, with positive noise s, labels bounded by B, and contexts <=n. The complete width/depth/MLP/head bound is given in C005 Section 1 in terms of the canonical kernel modulus Omega(r), a finite h-net cardinality J, and the solver constants. A fixed finite Gram factorization supplies all encoder feature values; no feature computation is hidden outside the count. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C005 v2. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Target 1 for continuous finite-rank kernels on compact raw domains

Claim T336-w727-C005 v2. Status: proof (unaudited), dependent on C002 v1 and the deterministic perturbation/encoder constructions in C004 v1. The entire result is not Lean-checked. No independent review or novelty certification is claimed.

The hardest step is removing the supplied-feature oracle without adding a hidden feature-computation cost. A finite Gram factorization fixes the encoder weights; a kernel modulus controls its error. The size explicitly includes the resulting encoder.

## 1. Statement and all parameters

Let X be a nonempty compact subset of R^d, d>=1. Let k:X times X -> R be a continuous real symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel of rank at most p, p>=1, with k(x,x)<=R^2 for R>=0. The prior is the zero-mean GP with kernel k. Observation noise is independent N(0,s), s>0. Labels are bounded by B>=0, contexts have length <=n with n>=0 an integer, and eps>0. The prediction concerns a new noisy observation.

Define the canonical kernel modulus in the ambient L1 metric by

    Omega(r)=sup_{x,y in X, ||x-y||_1<=r}
                sqrt(k(x,x)+k(y,y)-2k(x,y)).

The expression is nonnegative by positive semidefiniteness. Omega(r) tends to zero as r decreases to zero, as proved below.

Retain the following explicit constants from C004's deterministic perturbation bound:

    S=R+1, C_A=n(2R+1),
    C_m=nB[(R+S)/s+S C_A R/s^2],
    C_v=R+S+S^2 C_A/s>0,
    eta=min(1,sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_m)),s sqrt(eps)/(2C_v),s/(4C_v)),
    eps0=min(eps/4,1/16), e=eta/sqrt(p)>0.

Choose any **fixed admissible** r>0 with Omega(r)<=e/2. An explicit upper modulus for k can be used to choose r; continuity guarantees existence, not an algorithm for computing a modulus of an arbitrary black-box kernel. Put

    A_cone=(2R+e)/r>0, h=e/(2A_cone)>0.

Choose a finite h-net G contained in X, of cardinality J>=1. The size bound is explicit in J (or in a known upper bound for the covering number). For X=[0,1]^d one may take the regular grid with

    m=max(1,ceil(d A_cone/e)), J=(m+1)^d.

For the attention solver define

    kappa=1+max(1,n)S^2/s, M=nS^2B/s,
    delta0=min(1/2,s/(2S^2),sqrt(s eps0)/(1+M),s sqrt(eps0)/S^2),
    T=ceil(sqrt(kappa) log(2/delta0)/2).

There is a transformer, using normalized residual ReLU attention and tokenwise residual ReLU MLPs, with

    D=7p+6+d+Jd+pJ,
    H=2Jd+pJ+4p+1,
    L_total=T+5+ceil(log_2 J),
    at most five attention heads per layer,
    at most L_total(15D^2+2DH)+2D dense scalar parameters,

whose positive-variance Gaussian output has forward KL<=eps from the exact noisy GP predictive, uniformly over all admissible raw-input contexts and queries. Its input contains only raw coordinates, labels, fixed context/query flags, and constants. The encoder is counted. These are arbitrary-real-weight size bounds; no finite-bit, kernel-evaluation, offline factorization-time, SGD, or ERM-generalization bound is asserted.

## 2. Canonical finite-dimensional features and the kernel modulus

Form the vector space of finite formal combinations of symbols delta_x with bilinear form

    <sum_i a_i delta_{x_i},sum_j b_j delta_{y_j}>
       =sum_{i,j}a_i b_j k(x_i,y_j).

Positive semidefiniteness makes this a nonnegative quadratic form. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality follows by applying nonnegativity to u+t v for all real t; in particular a zero-norm vector is orthogonal to every vector. Quotient by the zero-norm subspace. For any finite list of symbols, the dimension of their quotient span is the rank of their Gram matrix. Every finite list of quotient vectors is contained in the span of finitely many symbols. Thus the dimension of the resulting inner-product space is the supremum of these Gram ranks, which is the kernel rank and is at most p. It is finite dimensional, so no completion issue remains.

Choose an orthonormal basis and pad with zeros in R^p. The coordinates z(x) of delta_x then satisfy

    k(x,y)=z(x)^T z(y), ||z(x)||<=R,
    ||z(x)-z(y)||^2=k(x,x)+k(y,y)-2k(x,y).

Thus z is continuous and ||z(x)-z(y)||<=Omega(r) whenever ||x-y||_1<=r. To justify Omega(r)->0 directly, suppose the contrary. There are sequences r_j->0 and x_j,y_j in X at distance <=r_j with feature distance bounded away from zero. Compactness supplies a subsequence x_j->x; then y_j->x as well. Continuity of k makes the squared feature distance tend to k(x,x)+k(x,x)-2k(x,x)=0, a contradiction. The supremum is finite because the kernel is continuous on the compact product. In particular every fixed positive e admits the required r.

The factorization at the finite net does not require evaluating any feature map on runtime inputs. Form the fixed J-by-J Gram matrix K_G=(k(a,b))_{a,b in G}. It is PSD of rank <=p, so a finite spectral factorization gives vectors v_a in R^p with v_a^T v_b=k(a,b). There is an isometry between the spans of z(a) and v_a: the map sum c_a z(a) -> sum c_a v_a is well defined and norm preserving because both squared norms equal c^T K_G c. Extend orthonormal bases of the two spans to R^p. The isometry extends to an orthogonal map on R^p. Applying it to all z(x) gives a representation, still called z, with z(a)=v_a for every a in G and with the same norm and modulus bounds.

Consequently **all feature values used as weights below can be obtained from the finite prior Gram matrix on G**. Computing this fixed factorization is preprocessing of the fixed prior, not an input-dependent inverse hidden in the predictive head. Its real entries are included in the encoder's parameter count.

## 3. Cone envelope for a general continuous feature map

Define, using the finite Gram feature values,

    ztilde_j(x)=min_{a in G}[v_{a,j}+A_cone ||x-a||_1].

This formula is valid even though z_j need not be Lipschitz. We claim |ztilde_j(x)-z_j(x)|<=e for every j,x.

For a with ||x-a||_1<=r, the modulus gives v_{a,j}>=z_j(x)-Omega(r)>=z_j(x)-e/2. Adding a nonnegative cone term preserves this lower bound. For a with ||x-a||_1>r, the coordinate bound |z_j|<=R gives

    v_{a,j}+A_cone ||x-a||_1
      >z_j(x)-2R+A_cone r=z_j(x)+e.

So every candidate is >=z_j(x)-e/2, and the finite minimum is too.

For the upper bound choose a net point with ||x-a||_1<=h. Since h=e r/(2(2R+e))<=r/2, the modulus bound applies. Therefore

    ztilde_j(x)<=z_j(x)+Omega(r)+A_cone h
                  <=z_j(x)+e/2+e/2=z_j(x)+e.

It follows that sup_x ||ztilde(x)-z(x)||<=sqrt(p)e=eta and ||ztilde(x)||<=R+eta<=S. All denominators above are positive, including R=0. For a cube grid, coordinate rounding gives L1 distance <=d/(2m)<=e/(2A_cone)=h, which verifies the displayed grid size.

## 4. Exact network realization and original-posterior KL

Use C004 Section 4's explicit register construction, with the J centers now the net points a and with the slope K in the cone layer replaced by A_cone. Layer 1 computes all Jd absolute differences with 2Jd ReLUs. Layer 2 forms the pJ affine cone values using these nonnegative absolute registers and the constant register. A balanced residual-min tournament takes ceil(log_2 J) layers, including zero layers when J=1. The last gating layer, using the binary context/query flags and |ztilde_j|<=S, writes the context/query feature registers exactly. For padding choose a fixed anchor point in X as its raw coordinates, rather than assuming the ambient origin belongs to X. Its flags are zero, so the computed features are gated to zero.

This uses E=3+ceil(log_2 J) encoder layers and precisely the width and hidden-width bounds in Section 1. This invokes the exact algebraic encoder construction, **not the Lipschitz-error assertion** of C004 Section 3. Section 3 above supplies the replacement uniform approximation guarantee.

C004 Section 2's perturbation proof uses only ||ztilde-z||<=eta<=1, not feature Lipschitzness. It therefore gives original-versus-encoded predictive errors

    |mu-mutilde|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,
    |v-vtilde|<=min(s/4,s sqrt(eps)/2).

Apply C002 v1 to the encoded features with bound S and accuracy eps0. The one-head query broadcast, T five-head Chebyshev layers, and four-head readout produce muhat,vhat with vhat>=s and errors

    |mutilde-muhat|<=sqrt(s eps)/2,

## 1. Statement and all parameters

Let X be a nonempty compact subset of R^d, d>=1. Let k:X times X -> R be a continuous real symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel of rank at most p, p>=1, with k(x,x)<=R^2 for R>=0. The prediction concerns a new noisy observation.

Define the canonical kernel modulus in the ambient L1 metric by

    Omega(r)=sup_{x,y in X, ||x-y||_1<=r}
                sqrt(k(x,x)+k(y,y)-2k(x,y)).

The expression is nonnegative by positive semidefiniteness. Omega(r) tends to zero as r decreases to zero, as proved below.

Retain the following explicit constants from C004's deterministic perturbation bound:

    S=R+1, C_A=n(2R+1),
    C_m=nB[(R+S)/s+S C_A R/s^2],
    C_v=R+S+S^2 C_A/s>0,
    eta=min(1,sqrt(s eps)/(2(1+C_m)),s sqrt(eps)/(2C_v),s/(4C_v)),

Form the vector space of finite formal combinations of symbols delta_x with bilinear form

Positive semidefiniteness makes this a nonnegative quadratic form. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality follows by applying nonnegativity to u+t v for all real t; in particular a zero-norm vector is orthogonal to every vector. Quotient by the zero-norm subspace. For any finite list of symbols, the dimension of their quotient span is the rank of their Gram matrix. Every finite list of quotient vectors is contained in the span of finitely many symbols. Thus the dimension of the resulting inner-product space is the supremum of these Gram ranks, which is the kernel rank and is at most p. It is finite dimensional, so no completion issue remains.

Choose an orthonormal basis and pad with zeros in R^p. The coordinates z(x) of delta_x then satisfy

    k(x,y)=z(x)^T z(y), ||z(x)||<=R,

[Lemma lem:whiten of arXiv:2608.28007, 'Exact Risk Ratios for Weighted Data Selection in Linear Regression'] Let $H=\frac1N\sum_i x_ix_i^{\top}\succ0$ and $L_D^{\star}>0$. Let $w^{\star}$ be the
unique full-data optimum and $r_i=y_i-\ip{w^{\star}}{x_i}$. Set
\[
\xi_i=H^{-1/2}x_i,\qquad
\eta_i=\frac{r_i}{\sqrt{L_D^{\star}}},\qquad
q=\frac{H^{1/2}(w-w^{\star})}{\sqrt{L_D^{\star}}}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
\frac1N\sum_i\xi_i\xi_i^{\top}=I_d,\qquad
\frac1N\sum_i\eta_i\xi_i=0,\qquad
\frac1N\sum_i\eta_i^2=1,
\end{equation}
and for every $w$,
\begin{equation}
\frac{L_D(w)}{L_D^{\star}}=1+\lVert q\rVert^2 .
\end{equation}

body: Let a finite group G act on a finite set X. Burnside's lemma states that the number of orbits of this action equals the average number of points fixed by the elements of G: number of orbits = (1/|G|) times the sum over g in G of |Fix(g)|, where Fix(g) is the set of points of X fixed by g and |G| is the group order. This lets one count objects up to symmetry, such as distinct colorings of a necklace under rotation. The result was known earlier to Cauchy and Frobenius; it is often called the Cauchy-Frobenius lemma, with Burnside merely popularizing it in his 1897 textbook.
title: Burnside's lemma

body:
Julia operator and defect intertwining identity (P. L. Robinson, arXiv:1803.09329, Theorem0 p.1 and Theorem1 p.2). Let H,K be complex Hilbert spaces and F:K->H a bounded contraction, ||F||<=1. Define D_H=(I_H-FF*)^(1/2) and D_K=(I_K-F*F)^(1/2), the positive square roots. The Julia operator J=[[D_H,F],[-F*,D_K]] on H direct-sum K is unitary. The positive defect square roots satisfy D_H F=F D_K. Switching J's two column blocks gives the unitary map Q=[[F,D_H],[D_K,-F*]] from K direct-sum H to H direct-sum K. In finite-dimensional real spaces this is an orthogonal dilation whose top-left rectangular compression is F; real contractions and singular values equal to1 are allowed. In the special case H=K, Q is the usual Halmos dilation (Theorem2 p.2). These are classical dilation facts, not GD convergence theorems.
H,K complex Hilbert spaces and F a bounded contraction; real finite-dimensional specialization included
Defect square roots are the unique positive square roots; no invertibility of a defect operator is assumed

[Lemma L:boundoffm of arXiv:2606.03079, 'Mean Field Limits for Stochastic, Underdamped Reactive Langevin Dynamics Models'] For the $\ell-$th reaction, $1 \leq \ell \leq L,$ let $\eta$ be sufficiently small, $\varepsilon >0,$ and $R \in \mathbb{R}$ large enough as in Assumption (A:AssumptionRho of the paper). Consider a fixed constant $D> \left\{\frac{2m_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}, \frac{2m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}\right\}$ entering only in the case of a second order reaction $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ of the form $S_i + S_k \rightarrow S_j + S_r$. Also, let $\sigma^{*}\in [1,2)$ be  another fixed constant depending only on the stoichiometric coefficients $\alpha_{i}$ and particle masses $m_1,m_2,m_3$ for a second order reaction $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ of the form $S_i + S_k \rightarrow S_j$ (to be explicitly determined in the proof). The following estimates hold for $m$ large enough,
\begin{align*}
&\mathbb{E}\biggl[\displaystyle\sup_{t\in [0,T]}\int_0^t \int_{\tilde{\mathbb{X}}^{(\ell)} \otimes \tilde{\mathbb{V}}^{(\ell)}}\frac{1}{\bm{\alpha}^{(\ell)}!}K_\ell(\bm{x},\bm{v})\biggl(\int_{\mathbb{Y}^{(\ell)} \otimes \mathbb{V}'^{(\ell)}}\left(\sum_{r=1}^{\beta_{\ell j}}f_m\left(y_r^{(j)},{v'}_{r}^{(j)}\right)\right)\\
&\phantom{=}\times m_{\ell}^{\eta}\left(\bm{y},\bm{v'}|\bm{x},\bm{v}\right)d\bm{y}d\bm{v'}\biggr)\lambda^{(\ell)}[\mu_{s-}^{\zeta}](d\bm{x}, d\bm{v}) ds\biggr]\\
\leq&2 C(K)(C_{\circ} \vee 1) \displaystyle \sup_{1\leq i\leq J} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\int_0^t \left\langle f_{m-1-(D+2)R}(x,v), \mu_{s-}^{\zeta,i}(dx,dv)\right\rangle ds \right]\\
&\phantom{=}+2C(K)C_{\circ}\displaystyle \sup_{1\leq i\leq J} \mathbb{E}\left[\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\int_0^t  \left\langle f_{\floor{\frac{m-1}{1+\sigma^{*}}}}(x,v), \mu_{s-}^{\zeta,i}(dx,dv)ds \right \rangle ds\right]\\
&\phantom{=}+ 2 C(K) C_{\circ}^2\left\|f_{m}\right\|_{C_{b}^{2}\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times \mathbb{R}^{d}\right)} T \left(\varepsilon + C\eta \right).
\end{align*}

DRAFT narrow sublemma independently checked by w389; validating-coordinator review remains required. Take edgewise independent triples X_e~G,U_e uniform[0,1],Z_e~G conditioned on[b,infinity), independent across edges. Let a<b, p_a=G([0,a])>0,p_b=G([b,infinity))>0 and deterministic0<=delta_e<p_a on a finite deterministic set F. Put xi_e=1{X_e<=a,U_e<=delta_e/p_a}, Y_e=Z_e if xi_e=1 and X_e otherwise; outside F keep Y_e=X_e. Given the ENTIRE individual output Y, including exterior, the xi_e are independent Bernoulli with theta_e=1_[b,infinity)(Y_e)delta_e/(p_b+delta_e). Divide the joint raised-output density by the output density and factor independent coordinate kernels. A finite simple path prefix selected from Y alone is fixed by this conditioning and inherits that kernel. No other site's output or later marking success is conditioned on. This checks the September2026 manuscript's Lemma7.2 only, not its main theorem.

[Dfn 207 (coarsened buckets) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall from Definition~\ref{d:buckets}
the progressive partition
$\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$. 
For each time $q_d$, and for each of the spatial blocks $J_{\vl}$ defined by \eqref{e:J.blocks}, we now define a single bucket
	\beq
	B^{\frozen,\coarse}
	\equiv B^{\frozen,\coarse}(q_d,J_{\vl})
	\equiv \bigg\{
	a\in [M^+]
	: \vX^\frozen(q_d,a) \in J_{\vl}
	\bigg\}\,.\eeq
Each such $B^{\frozen,\coarse}$ is a union of buckets $B^\frozen\in\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$.
For any $B^\frozen\in\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$ not covered by one of the above (i.e., singleton buckets corresponding to particles that have left $[-\trK,\trK)^3$), we define simply
$B^{\frozen,\coarse} = B^\frozen$.
We define $\mathcal{C}^\frozen(q_d)$
to be the coarsening of $\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$ given by all these buckets $B^{\frozen,\coarse}$. We analogously define
the coarsening $\mathcal{C}^{\frozen,\Ising}(q_d)$ of $\mathcal{B}^{\frozen,\Ising}(q_d)$.
title: coarsened buckets

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Second-order expansion of E[|level set|] by the local CLT for the DGFF at a point, then a variance computation from the two-point Gaussian density. Result: The first-order correction to the mean is computable: with h_x ~ N(0, g log N + O(1)) the mean of the level-set size is N^{2(1-lambda^2)} times (c + O((log N)^{-1/2})) where the (log N)^{-1/2} term comes from the Gaussian tail with the boundary correction G_N(x,x) - g log N. The variance is dominated by pairs at distance N^{1-lambda^2 t} for t in (0,1) and its exponent is 2(1-lambda^2) + something strictly positive, so the normalised fluctuation is not of CLT type but is driven by the field at mesoscopic scales; the natural conjecture is that the fluctuation is Z^D_lambda-mixed Gaussian with variance proportional to the integral of e^{2 alpha lambda h} over a scale window, but I could not close the identification of the mixing measure. Obstruction: No local limit theorem for pairs at every mesoscopic distance uniformly; the fluctuation law is a functional of the whole scale ladder, not of one scale.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0002-fluctuations-and-large-deviations-of-intermediate-level-sets-of-the-2d
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

For a doubly indexed family (a_{ij}) of NONNEGATIVE reals, sum_i sum_j a_{ij} = sum_j sum_i a_{ij} = sup over finite rectangles of the partial sums, all three being equal in [0, infinity] with no further hypothesis; this is Tonelli's theorem for two copies of counting measure, which is sigma-finite. For SIGNED a_{ij} the interchange is valid as soon as sum_i sum_j |a_{ij}| < infinity (absolute summability), and can fail otherwise even when both iterated sums exist and are finite. Concrete failure: index i, j >= 1 and set a_{ii} = 1, a_{i,i+1} = -1, and a_{ij} = 0 otherwise. Every row sums to 1 - 1 = 0, so sum_i sum_j a_{ij} = 0. The column j = 1 has only the entry a_{11} = 1 and sums to 1, while every column j >= 2 has entries a_{jj} = 1 and a_{j-1,j} = -1 and sums to 0; hence sum_j sum_i a_{ij} = 1. Both iterated sums exist, both are finite, and they differ. [standard; the counterexample is classical]
for the unconditional statement: a_{ij} >= 0
for the signed statement: sum_{i,j} |a_{ij}| < infinity

[Thm lwc-meso of arXiv:2510.18856, 'Evolution of recursive trees with limited memory'] Consider the sequence of random trees $\left\{\mathcal{T}_n:n\geqslant 2\right\}$ in the mesoscopic regime with parameter $\beta \in (0,1)$. Then $\left\{\mathcal{T}_n:n\geqslant 2\right\}$ converges in probability in the extended fringe sense (Def.~(def:local-weak of the paper)~(equation it:fringe-b of the paper)) to the unique infinite {\tt sin}-tree with fringe distribution $\boldsymbol{\varpi}_{{\sf Poisson} , 1}$. This implies in particular, the degree distribution satisfies the asymptotics for $k\geqslant 1$,
     \[
\frac{N_k(n)}{n} \stackrel{P}{\longrightarrow} \frac{e^{-1}}{(k-1)!} \text{ as } n\to\infty,
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let P be a monotone increasing graph property. A function p*(n) is called a threshold function for P in the Erdos-Renyi random graph G(n, p) if for any p = p(n), P(G(n, p) has P) -> 0 when p(n) / p*(n) -> 0, and P(G(n, p) has P) -> 1 when p(n) / p*(n) -> \infty as n -> \infty.
P is monotone increasing

body: In mathematics, low-rank approximation refers to the process of approximating a given matrix by a matrix of lower rank. More precisely, it is a minimization problem, in which the cost function measures the fit between a given matrix and an approximating matrix, subject to a constraint that the approximating matrix has reduced rank. The problem is used for mathematical modeling and data compression. The rank constraint is related to a constraint on the complexity of a model that fits the data. In applications, often there are other constraints on the approximating matrix apart from the rank constraint, e.g., non-negativity and Hankel structure.
title: Low-rank approximation

[Lemma 3 (Galligo--Najnudel--Vu) of arXiv:2607.16954, 'Repeated differentiation of deterministic polynomials with asymptotically radial root dist'] Suppose $k$ is a non-negative integer and $m$ is a positive integer and suppose $P$ is a polynomial of the form
\[
P(z)=z^k p(z^m),
\]
where $p$ is a nonconstant polynomial with real, positive roots. Then $P'(z)$ has the form
\[
P'(z)=mz^{m-1}p'(z^m),\quad (k=0)
\]
and
\[
z^{k-1}\tilde p(z^m),\quad (k>0),
\]
where $\deg(\tilde p)=\deg(p)$ and where $\tilde p$ has all real, positive roots. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Galligo--Najnudel--Vu

[Thm 4 of arXiv:2607.21759, 'Marchenko--Pastur law for tensor powers of exchangeable unconditional vectors'] Let $d$ be fixed, and let $\mathbf X = (X_1,\dotsc,X_n)$ be the exchangeable unconditional base vector. If 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\E X_1^2 \to 1$, 
        \item  $\E(X_1^2X_2^2) - \E(X_1^2)\E(X_2^2) \to 0$, and
        \item  there exists some $\epsilon > 0$ such that $\sup_n \E(\abs{X_1}^{4d + \epsilon}) < \infty$,
    \end{enumerate} then the three conditions in \cref{thm:main} are satisfied, and we have with probability $1$ that \[\ESD(K_{\PrincipalT}) \wkconv \mu_{\MP(c)}.\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

DRAFT proof-method concept; this special-case argument was independently checked by w355 and assigned referee w356. No novelty or full KLS claim. Let d>=2, K=(d+1)(d+2), X be uniform on Delta_d={x_i>=0,sum_i x_i<=1}, m=(1,...,1)/(d+1), Sigma=(I-J/(d+1))/K with J the all-ones matrix, A=Sigma^(-1/2), Y=A(X-m), a=sqrt(2K), and v=Ae_1/a. Put Z=Proj_(v-perp)Y, T=<v,Y> and S=sum_(j=2)^d X_j. Given 0<epsilon<1, choose a nonzero smooth eta supported in (epsilon/4,epsilon/2) and put f(Y)=eta(S) sin(pi T/(a(1-S))). Each such f has finite full energy, E[f|Z]=0, E Var(f|Z)=E eta(S)^2/2 and E|partial_v f|^2=(pi^2/(2a^2)) E[eta(S)^2/(1-S)^2]. Its directional quotient is at least (2K/pi^2)(1-epsilon)^2, and the support has positive probability. Letting epsilon go to zero proves that the optimal directional conditional coefficient is 2K/pi^2. This card records the localized admissible witness method, rather than duplicating the common simplex-constants card. It does not bound the full-gradient KLS constant.

eta is nonzero smooth with the indicated support
Each fixed-epsilon full gradient energy is finite

[Lemma 22 (Top-degree connecting homomorphism) of arXiv:2608.30875, 'A Decomposition Theorem for Topological Semi-small Maps'] Let $\pi : E \longrightarrow B$ be an oriented spherical bundle with fibre $S^k$, $k \ge 0$.
       	Suppose that $B$ has finite cohomological dimension, i.e., there exists an integer $N$ such that $H^{i}(B) = 0$ for all $i > N$, and $H^{N}(B) \neq 0$. Then the connecting homomorphism of the associated Gysin sequence $\delta \colon H^{N+k}(E) \longrightarrow H^{N}(B)$
       	is surjective. In particular, it is non‑zero.

[Proposition prop:11 of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] Fix $\gamma\in (0,2)$ and consider a whole plane GFF $h$ and the associated LQG metric $D_h$. 
  Then, almost surely, simultaneously for all $D_h$-geodesics $P: [0,T] \to \mathbb{C}$ and $0<s<t<T$, $P|_{[s,t]}$ is the unique $D_h$-geodesic between $P(s)$ and $P(t)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

OWNER OWN WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited), no novelty established. For a centered equilateral equal-weight three-Gaussian teacher with covariance I_d, exact population DDPM GD on centered mean parameters, physical step 1 and centered Gaussian factor initialization, converges to the teacher up to permutation with probability at least 7/20. At the inverse-polynomial noisy radius chosen in C07, normalized mean accuracy epsilon costs O(a^(-2) log d+a^(-4) log(C/epsilon)) iterations, hence polynomial d and 1/epsilon. Here M=a sqrt(3/2) Z V^T, V=sqrt(2/3)U^T for unit equilateral vertices U, and Z_0 has iid N(0,1/d) entries. Mean error is ||M-M_teacher,permuted||_F<=a epsilon. This enforces zero centroid, known weights, covariance and radius; no empirical or arbitrary-triangle theorem is claimed.
d>=2
centered equilateral teacher and equal weights 1/3
known identity component covariance
known teacher radius for choosing smoothing time
centered-parameter exact population GD with physical step 1
Gaussian factor initialization at noisy scale, independent entries N(0,1/d)
a and fixed small rho chosen as in C07, with a^2 proportional to rho*(rho/(8000 sqrt(d)))^760
real arithmetic only
