body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02590, 'Directional Optimal Sub-Gamma Scales for Infinitely Divisible Laws'] Fixing the quadratic proxy in a sub-gamma bound at the true variance leaves a scale to optimize, and a two-sided infinitely divisible law generally requires different scales in the two directions. For a centered law with finite nonzero variance, we normalize its Kolmogorov canonical measure and multiply the resulting variable by an independent $\operatorname{Beta}(1,2)$ variable. The signed remainder obtained in this way gives exact variational formulas for the right and left scales. We prove that a directional scale vanishes exactly when the L\'evy measure has no jumps in that direction, establish reflection, scaling, convolution, L\'evy-time, and opposite-jump perturbation rules, and recover the L\'evy triplet from the remainder law. The formulas give the two Gamma scales for bilateral Gamma laws and, for centered Skellam laws, the exact transition points $p_{\pm}=(2\pm\sqrt{3})/4$ between local and interior control; when positive jumps are rare, the right scale is asymptotic to $1/\log(1/p)$. The pair therefore records jump direction and the mechanism that controls the variance-exact sub-gamma pole.
title: Abstract of arXiv:2609.02590: Directional Optimal Sub-Gamma Scales for Infinitely Divisible Laws

Let L be a finite lattice with bottom 0 != top 1. A cross-cut is an antichain C, containing neither 0 nor 1, that meets every maximal chain from 0 to 1. Call S inside C spanning when its join is 1 and its meet is 0, and let q_k be the number of spanning k-subsets. Then mu(0, 1) = sum_{k >= 2} (-1)^k q_k (G.-C. Rota, 1964). If 1 does not cover 0, the atoms form a cross-cut and mu(0, 1) = sum over sets S of atoms with join 1 of (-1)^|S|. The chain-meeting condition is needed: in the Boolean lattice of subsets of {1, 2}, the antichain {{1}} misses the chain empty < {2} < {1, 2}, has no spanning subset, and gives 0 while mu = 1.
L a finite lattice with 0 != 1

[Proposition 25 (Maximum principle for dissipated-energy Einstein--Navier--Stokes flows) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Fix a Navier--Stokes triple $(\mathscr F,\chi,\mathscr B)$ that is admissible (\autoref{def-pot-admissible-triple}) and torus-adapted (\autoref{def-NS-torus-adapted}). Let $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$ be a sufficiently regular dissipated-energy Einstein--Navier--Stokes areal flow on $[t_0,t_1]\times\Tbb^3$, and assume that the density $\mu>0$ is positive. Then the range of the function $\Sbb^1\ni x\mapsto\bigl(\Gammaunpar_\chi(t,x),\Gammazero(t,x)\bigr)$ is a subset of~$\RR^4$ that does not depend on areal time $t\in [t_0,t_1]$.  In particular, for $t\in[t_0,t_1]$ and $m=2,3$, one has 
\be

\aligned \inf_{\Sbb^1}\Gammaun_m^\chi(t_0,\cdot) & \leq\Gammaun_m^\chi(t,x)\leq\sup_{\Sbb^1}\Gammaun_m^\chi(t_0,\cdot), \\
\inf_{\Sbb^1}\Gammazero_m(t_0,\cdot) & \leq\Gammazero_m(t,x)\leq\sup_{\Sbb^1}\Gammazero_m(t_0,\cdot).\endaligned
\ee
The second line also holds at vacuum.
At vacuum, the first line is understood as the statement that if $C_1\rho_\chi\leq 2T_\chi^{0m} \leq C_2 \rho_\chi$ for some $C_1,C_2\in\RR$ at initial time then this inequality holds for all times.
The convex hull of the range of $\Gammaunpar_\chi$ is thus preserved in time, without density assumption. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Maximum principle for dissipated-energy Einstein--Navier--Stokes flows

body: Within a BSS-type multiscale variance-halving program on Z^2 (hypothesis set: concentration envelope H1a at scale Q, anti-concentration floor H4, chaos input CH), write Q_s ~ s^alpha and the model's TRUE variance Var(X_s) ~ s^{2 chi}. Then rho_s = Q_s^2/Var(X_s) ~ s^{2(alpha-chi)} and the halving step demands chaos strength eps <~ s^{-4(alpha-chi)}. Constant-strength chaos - the only strength BSS-type constructions deliver - therefore requires alpha <= chi, while H1a (true concentration at scale Q) forces alpha >= chi: within the hypothesis set alpha = chi EXACTLY. The envelope exponent is fixed by nature, not by the theorem being chased: D in the halving lemma is the true variance (a standing assumption, not a free parameter), and the target rate n^{1-eps} is the OUTPUT of telescoping, never an input to any rung. Independent cross-check: reading D as inductive would let Efron-Stein plus one hypothesis alone deliver the conclusion with the whole apparatus idle. [Theorem thm:rank-frequency of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $h\geq2$ and $k\geq3$.  For every $n\in\mathcal R(h,k)$, the function
\[
 F^{(k)}_{h,n}(q)=
 \#\left\{A\in\binom{[q]}k:|hA|=n\right\}
\]
is a quasipolynomial in $q-1$ (and hence in $q$).  Its degree is exactly
\[
 \deg F^{(k)}_{h,n}=k-r_{h,k}(n).
\]
In particular, there is an explicitly computable positive rational number
$c_{h,k,n}$ such that
\begin{equation}
 F^{(k)}_{h,n}(q)
 =c_{h,k,n}q^{k-r_{h,k}(n)}
  +O_{h,k}\!\left(q^{k-r_{h,k}(n)-1}\right).
\end{equation}
The possible frequency exponents therefore belong to
$\{2,3,\ldots,k\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Complete rank--frequency stratification

[Corollary 12 (leave probability and exit distribution) of arXiv:2605.13648, 'Sticky CIR process with potential: invariant measure and exact sampling'] \label[corollary]{cor:leave-zero}
  Let $T_\alpha\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\alpha)$ be independent of the sticky process $u$, with $u_0=0$.
  The probability that $u_{T_\alpha}\neq 0$  is
  \[
    p_{\mathrm{leave}}
    = \frac{\mu}{\mu+\Phi},
    \qquad
    \Phi = \frac{1}{G_\alpha(0,0)},
  \]
  where $G_\alpha$ is the reflecting resolvent kernel of \cref{green-function}.
  Conditional on $u_{T_\alpha}\neq 0$, the exit position is drawn from
  the density
  \begin{equation}
    \nu_\alpha(dy) = Z_\nu^{-1}\,U(a,b,z_y)\,m'(y)\,dy,
    \qquad Z_\nu = |\mathcal{W}|/\alpha.
  \end{equation}

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:d87bbd10a7055b41fd8b18c127a2cbc7713cc1091251a6b2107442c44f67cb1f","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/d8/d87bbd10a7055b41fd8b18c127a2cbc7713cc1091251a6b2107442c44f67cb1f.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:9548f3adc68903b67cd441efcd18bebcb2f7ac02a496d314a765992a9a4498a7","bundle_entry_key":"shifted-rectangular-gaussian-smoothing-gap-w718","bundle_id":"population.t287-rectangular-reference-c1-and-noncentered-comparison-v1","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"Gaussian channels and extensive-rank matrix inference","draft":"w718/bundle_009.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.gaussian_channels:shifted-rectangular-gaussian-smoothing-gap-w718","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Supporting hard-edge lemma for rectangular Gaussian smoothing

Claim: w718-T287-024, version 1. Kind: moved; target: 2. Status: proof (unaudited). This is an elementary supporting lemma for the checked rectangular-reference route, not a claim of a new random-matrix theorem or completion of Target 2.

## Statement

Let n,p be positive integers and let delta>0, Kappa>=1+delta satisfy 1+delta <= p/n <= Kappa. Let G be an n by p real matrix of independent standard normal entries. Let S be any deterministic n by p real matrix with operator norm at most C, where C>=0. The same conclusions hold conditional on a random S independent of G. Fix 0<t_minus<=t_plus<infinity. Define

L=8 sqrt(1+Kappa),
K=max(1,C+sqrt(t_plus)L),
C0=max(1,2 sqrt(3/t_minus)),
epsilon=(6 K C0^Kappa)^(-1/delta).

For each t in [t_minus,t_plus], put Y_t=S+sqrt(t/n)G. Then

P(s_min(Y_t)<=epsilon) <= 2 exp(-n)+2^(-n).                 (1)

Here s_min is the least of the n singular values, equivalently inf_{||x||=1} ||Y_t^T x||. The bound is uniform in t and S, but is not asserted as a simultaneous event for an uncountable collection of t. If S is random independent of G without an almost sure norm bound, add P(||S||op>C) to the right side.

Consequently, suppose empirical singular-value laws of Y_t converge in probability to deterministic laws eta_t, and P(||S_n||op>C)->0 for some fixed C. Then for every t in the stated interval, eta_t([0,epsilon))=0. Thus the same epsilon is a gap for all these deterministic limiting laws. No assertion of a positive gap at square aspect ratio is made.

## Proof

1. A Euclidean unit sphere in R^d has an r-net with at most (1+2/r)^d elements, for 0<r<=1. Indeed take a maximal r-separated set. The open radius r/2 balls about its points are disjoint and lie in the radius 1+r/2 ball, so comparing their volumes gives the bound. Maximality gives coverage. This proof uses finite-dimensional Euclidean volume only.

2. Take 1/4-nets A and B in the unit spheres of R^n and R^p. For every matrix Z, approximation of both maximizing unit vectors gives

||Z||op <= 2 max_{x in A,y in B} |x^T Z y|.

For fixed x,y and Z=G/sqrt(n), x^T Z y is a centered normal of variance 1/n. The elementary normal tail bound P(|N(0,1)|>u)<=2 exp(-u^2/2), obtained by exponential Markov inequalities for both signs, yields

P(||G/sqrt(n)||op>L)
 <= 2 exp((n+p) log 9 - n L^2/8)
 <= 2 exp(-n).

The last inequality follows from p<=Kappa n, L^2=64(1+Kappa), and log 9<3. In particular, outside an event of probability at most 2 exp(-n), ||Y_t||op<=C+sqrt(t_plus)L<=K.

3. For any fixed unit x in R^n, Y_t^T x is a p-dimensional normal vector with arbitrary deterministic mean S^T x and covariance (t/n)I_p. Its density is bounded everywhere by (n/(2 pi t))^(p/2), independently of that mean. For R>0, the volume bound

vol(B_p(R)) <= (2 pi e/p)^(p/2) R^p

follows by integrating exp(-lambda ||u||^2) on R^p: the integral over the ball is at least exp(-lambda R^2) times its volume; choose lambda=p/(2R^2). Therefore

P(||Y_t^T x||<=2epsilon)
 <= (2 sqrt(e n/(p t)) epsilon)^p
 <= (C0 epsilon)^p.                                    (2)

Using the maximum density rather than a centered small-ball formula makes the arbitrary-shift hypothesis explicit.

4. Since K>=1 and epsilon<1, take an epsilon/K-net A_epsilon of the sphere in R^n, with cardinality at most (3K/epsilon)^n. If s_min(Y_t)<=epsilon and ||Y_t||op<=K, there is a unit x with ||Y_t^T x||<=epsilon, and a net point x0 at distance at most epsilon/K. The triangle inequality gives ||Y_t^T x0||<=2epsilon. A union bound and (2) give

P(s_min(Y_t)<=epsilon, ||Y_t||op<=K)
 <= (3K/epsilon)^n (C0 epsilon)^p
 <= (3K C0^Kappa epsilon^delta)^n
 = 2^(-n).

Here C0>=1, p<=Kappa n, p-n>=delta n, and 0<epsilon<1 justify each inequality. The event ||Y_t||op<=K was used only for the deterministic net approximation. It was not multiplied as an independent event with the small-ball probabilities.

5. Add the operator-norm exceptional probability from step 2 to prove (1). Conditional on an independent random S with ||S||op<=C, the same net, density bound and constants apply. Integrating the conditional inequality proves the random-input statement with the extra probability P(||S||op>C); it is unnecessary and generally incorrect to assume independence of the two exceptional events.

6. To pass to limiting laws, fix a continuous nonnegative function f supported in [0,epsilon), with f<=1. The empirical integral of f is zero unless s_min(Y_t)<epsilon. Thus its expectation tends to zero by (1) and the input-norm condition. Its convergence in probability to the deterministic integral against eta_t, together with boundedness, implies that integral is zero. Approximating indicators of [0,epsilon') for epsilon'<epsilon by such continuous tests gives eta_t([0,epsilon))=0. Constants do not depend on t, so the deterministic conclusion holds for each t with the same gap. This does not exchange a probability bound with an uncountable union.

## Gaussian-product application and limitations

For S=UV^T/n with independent standard normal U (n by M) and V (p by M), and bounded positive ratios M/n and p/n, apply the same two-sphere Gaussian net argument to U/sqrt(n) and V/sqrt(n). Their operator norms are bounded by fixed constants with exceptional probability tending to zero. The deterministic inequality ||UV^T/n||op<=||U/sqrt(n)||op ||V/sqrt(n)||op supplies the required C. The noise matrix is independent of both factors. Hence any deterministic limiting singular laws supplied by the already checked real population-Wishart theorem have this gap on compact intervals t>0 whenever p/n stays bounded away from one.

This lemma supplies no density regularity, no entropy differentiation, and no MMSE limit by itself. Its constants are deliberately crude. The least trusted step of the larger route remains algebraic boundary regularity and the singular-logarithm chain rule, not the elementary union bound above.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:965a7f6569046bdab574a5d8dade402280c470a6610623c9409c56ed763549bc","revision_digest":"sha256:762ffbc60d1a44b7d6b7b9f148692dce3f8fd290c35553753083c63fc18fcacf","source_id":"owner:w718:T287:shifted-rectangular-gaussian-smoothing-gap-w718","source_revision":"2026-10-21 w718-T287-024 version1, proof unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: In multivariable calculus, the implicit function theorem is a theorem that provides sufficient conditions under which a planar curve specified by an equation F(x, y) = 0 can also be specified as the graph of a function y = g(x), so that for each point (x, y) on part of the curve, one has y = g(x). An example is the unit circle, whose points satisfy x^2 + y^2 = 1, which can locally be solved by y = sqrt(1 - x^2), expressing the top semicircle as a graph. It is not always possible to solve the equation for y algebraically, and the implicit function theorem gives analytic conditions under which there exists a function g whose graph belongs to the given curve, and, in some formulations, also gives a way of constructing approximations to g.

Under the hypotheses of (thm:orthant of the paper), every nonnegative, nondecreasing
Borel function $\psi$ satisfies
\[
  \mathbb E\psi(\mathsf M_X)\leq\mathbb E\psi(\mathsf M_Z),
\]
including when one or both expectations are infinite.  If $R\neq I_m$,
$\psi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is strictly increasing, and $\psi(\mathsf M_X)$ and
$\psi(\mathsf M_Z)$ are integrable, then
\[
  \mathbb E\psi(\mathsf M_X)<\mathbb E\psi(\mathsf M_Z).
\]
In particular, for every $\lambda>0$,
\[
  \mathbb E e^{\lambda\mathsf M_X}<\mathbb E e^{\lambda\mathsf M_Z},
  \qquad
  \mathbb E\mathsf M_X<\mathbb E\mathsf M_Z
  \qquad(R\neq I_m).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:connected_sets of arXiv:2503.21737, 'High-intensity Voronoi percolation on manifolds'] Let \(\Gamma \subset V\) and let \(A \subset \cup_{x\in\Gamma}O(x)\) be a connected set.
Then
    \[ \{x \in \Gamma \colon O(x)\cap A \neq \emptyset\} \]
is a connected subset of \(G\).
In particular, if $\gamma$ is a continuous path contained in $\cup_{x\in \Gamma}O(x)$, then we can associate to $\gamma$ a discrete path (not necessarily simple) $\pi $ in $G$ contained in $\Gamma$ such that
    \[\gamma \subset \bigcup _{x\in\pi}O(x)\qquad \text{and} \qquad\forall x\in\pi \quad \gamma\cap O(x)\ne \emptyset.\]

[Defn 11 (Majority rule) of arXiv:2606.22960, '2606.22960'] Let \((T_n,(B_v)_{v\in[n]})\) be the broadcast-coloured tree of size \(n\), where
	\(B_v\in\{-1,1\}\) denotes the colour of vertex \(v\).
	The {\it majority rule} estimator is the \(\{-1,1\}\)-valued random variable
	\[
	\widehat B_{\mathrm{maj},n}
	:=
	\begin{cases}
		1, & \sum_{v=1}^n B_v > 0,\\
		-1, & \sum_{v=1}^n B_v < 0,\\
		\xi_n, & \sum_{v=1}^n B_v = 0,
	\end{cases}
	\]
	where \(\xi_n\) is independent of the broadcasting process and satisfies
	\[
	\mathbb P(\xi_n=1)=\mathbb P(\xi_n=-1)=\frac12.
	\]
	Its error probability is defined by
	\[
	R_{\mathrm{maj}}(n,q):=\mathbb P\!\left(\widehat B_{\mathrm{maj},n}\neq B_1\right),
	\qquad
	R_{\mathrm{maj}}(q):=\limsup_{n\to\infty} R_{\mathrm{maj}}(n,q).
	\]
title: Majority rule

[Lem 9 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\epsilon_1 > 0$ and $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, we have $S_\star(\lambda,\mu) \subseteq S_\star(\lambda,\mu;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_1)$.
\begin{proof}
    Let $\YY \in S_\star(\lambda,\mu)$.
    Then for any $i \in [r]$,
    \[
        \lambda_i \BBb_i
        \le \Cost(\YY;\lambda)
        \le \Budget(\YY;\mu)
        = \frac{1}{\alpha}
        \bigg(
            \sum_{j=1}^s
            \mu_j
            (\www_j)^{1/2}
        \bigg)^2
        \le \frac{1}{\alpha}
        (\mu,\www)
        = \frac{1}{\alpha}\,,
    \]
where the last equality uses that $\www \in \cW_\mu$. Since $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, this implies $\BBb_i \le 1/(\alpha \iota)$. It follows that
    \[
        \epsilon_1 \alpha^2 \iota^3 \sum_{i=1}^r (\BBb_i)^2
        \le \epsilon_1 \iota r
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:r-s-bd}}{\le} \epsilon_1\,,
    \]
and the conclusion follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: In commutative algebra and algebraic geometry, localization is a formal way to introduce the "denominators" to a given ring or module. That is, it introduces a new ring/module out of an existing ring/module R, so that it consists of fractions such that the denominator s belongs to a given subset S of R. If S is the set of the non-zero elements of an integral domain, then the localization is the field of fractions: this case generalizes the construction of the field of rational numbers from the ring of integers.
title: Localization (commutative algebra)

If phi is convex on an interval I containing the range of an integrable random variable X with values in I, then phi(E X) <= E phi(X), where E phi(X) always exists in (-infinity, +infinity]. For concave phi the inequality reverses. Finite form: for points x_1, ..., x_n in I and NONNEGATIVE weights w_i summing to 1, phi(sum w_i x_i) <= sum w_i phi(x_i); nonnegativity is essential (signed weights summing to 1 break the inequality, e.g. phi(x) = x^2, weights 2 and -1 at points 0 and 1).

body: Aldous-Fill Open Problem 4.48(a) is answered in the negative: tau_1 <= tau_0 fails. Here tau_1 is Aldous and Fill's variation threshold, the first t at which the two-point distance max_{i,j} ||P_i(X_t in .) - P_j(X_t in .)||_TV is at most 1/e, and tau_0 = sum_j pi_j E_i T_j is Kemeny's constant. On the continuous-time birth-and-death chain on {0,1,2} with rate 1 toward 0 and rate eps away from it, tau_0 = 2(1+eps)/(1+eps+eps^2) < 2 while tau_1 -> 2.14619 (the root of e^{-t}(1+t) = 1/e) as eps -> 0: the pair (2,0) separates until the sum of two unit exponentials has arrived. On the path of length k the limiting ratio tau_1/tau_0 is t_k/k with t_k the Gamma(k,1) tail threshold at 1/e (1.0731, 1.0861, 1.0880 at k=4, 1.0868, ...), so sup tau_1/tau_0 lies in [1.0880, 66]. Exact 30-digit check: k=2, eps=0.1 gives tau_0 = 1.981982, tau_1 = 2.010072. At eps=0.1 the two-point distance matters: measured against the stationary law, max_i ||P_i(X_t in .) - pi||_TV, the same chain reaches 1/e at t = 1.946386, below tau_0. For eps <= 0.05 both distances give tau_1 > tau_0 (at eps=0.05, 2.079327 and 2.051467 against tau_0 = 1.995249).

[Thm restate of limiting profile of arXiv:2604.23890, 'The Cutoff Profile for Random Transpositions on Repeated Cards in the Full Range of Parame'] Let $c\in\mathbb{R}$ be an absolute constant. Let $(n_N)_{N\ge 1},(m_N)_{N\ge 1}$ and $(l_N)_{N\ge 1}$ be sequences of positive integers, such that 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $m_N,l_N\ge 2$ for all $N\ge 1$, and $\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}l_N=\infty$.
\item $n_N=m_Nl_N$ for all $N\ge 1$.
\end{enumerate}
For all $N\ge 1$, let $t_N=\frac{n_N}{2}(\log n_N-\frac 12\log l_N+c)$. Let $\sim_{l_N}\backslash P_{n_N}^{*t_N}$ be defined as in (defi: Pnk and its convolution of the paper), and let $\sim_{l_N}\backslash U_{\mathfrak{S}_{n_N}}$ be defined as in (defi: quotient of space of the paper). Then, we have
$$\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}d_{TV}(\sim_{l_N}\backslash P_{n_N}^{*t_N},\sim_{l_N}\backslash U_{\mathfrak{S}_{n_N}})=2\Phi\left(\frac{\exp(-c)}{2}\right)-1$$
when $\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}m_N=\infty$, and 
$$\lim_{N\rightarrow\infty}d_{TV}(\sim_{l_N}\backslash P_{n_N}^{*t_N},\sim_{l_N}\backslash U_{\mathfrak{S}_{n_N}})=2\Phi\left(\sqrt{1-\frac 1m}\frac{\exp(-c)}{2}\right)-1$$
when $m_N=m\ge 2$ is fixed. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Thm restate of limiting profile of arXiv:2604.23890

[Dfn of arXiv:2603.13873, '{Solvability of BSDEs with possibly unbounded stochastic coefficients \\ on a general weig'] A continuous function $u:\bar {G}\rightarrow{\mathbb R}^k$ is a viscosity sub-solution (super-solution) of PDE (equation PDE-1 of the paper) if for any $1\leq i\leq k$ and any function $\phi\in C^2(\bar {G};{\mathbb R})$, it holds that
$$
\begin{array}{c}
\mathcal{\bar L}\phi(x_0)+g_i(x_0,u(x_0),(\nabla\phi\sigma)(x_0))\geq 0\ (\leq 0), \ x_0\in G;\\
\max\{\mathcal{\bar L}\phi(x_0)+g_i(x_0,u(x_0),(\nabla\phi\sigma)(x_0)),
h_i(x_0)-u_i(x_0)\}\geq 0, \ x_0\in \partial G\\
(\min\{\mathcal{\bar L}\phi(x_0)+g_i(x_0,u(x_0),(\nabla\phi\sigma)(x_0)),
h_i(x_0)-u_i(x_0)\}\leq 0, \ x_0\in \partial G),
\end{array}
$$
as long as $u_i-\phi$ has a local maximum (minimum) at point $x_0\in \bar {G}$. A continuous function $u$ is a viscosity solution of PDE (equation PDE-1 of the paper) if it is both a viscosity sub-solution and a viscosity super-solution.

Train both hidden/output weights of a bias-free two-layer ReLU network by continuous gradient flow of summed exponential or logistic loss. Exactly k>=1 live neurons have w_j=(u_j,y_j), v_j>0 and min_j y_j(0)>4 sqrt(sum_j u_j(0)^2); every remaining neuron is strictly dead on both points, with arbitrary output. These activation sets and positive live outputs persist, the loss tends to zero, and the entire normalized parameter direction converges to a vertical KKT family of normalized margin1/8. Its unit-margin representative is v_j=y_j=r_j>0, u_j=0, sum r_j^2=4, with all other parameters zero. For k<m this representative is not a local minimum of parameter norm subject to the two unit-margin constraints. For k=m only the direction/margin conclusion is asserted. Under iid hidden/output N(0,sigma^2) coordinates, any sigma>0, put p=atan(1/4)/pi and h_k=2^(-k) E[(1-Phi(4R))^k] for a chi_k radius R and standard Gaussian CDF Phi. The exact probability that exactly k neurons satisfy the collective live condition and all others are dead is binom(m,k) h_k p^(m-k). Summing k=1..m-1 gives a sufficient nonlocally-optimal bad-KKT family probability at widths2..6. The k=1 event is the source's known one-live family; multiple-live terms are an additional classified subcone here. This does not classify every initialization with the same activation labels or give the full Gaussian basin probability. No kink solution selection is used; all finite-time trajectories lie in smooth activation regions.

Claim w733-T363-013 v2. Target 2; kind narrowed. Status: proof (unaudited). No novelty claim.

## Statement and scope
Use x1=(1,1/4), x2=(-1,1/4), both labels +1, f(x)=sum_j v_j ReLU(w_j dot x), no biases, with both layers trained by gradient flow for the sum of exponential or logistic losses. Exactly k neurons have v_j>0 and w_j=(u_j,y_j) satisfying

    min_j y_j(0) > 4 sqrt(sum_j u_j(0)^2).                 (H)

Every other neuron is strictly dead on both points; its output is arbitrary. The sum in (H) is over the k live neurons. For any k>=1, these activation patterns persist, loss tends to zero, and the parameter direction converges to a vertical, margin-1/8 KKT family. When k<=m-1, the unit-margin representative is not a local minimum of squared parameter norm. The multiple-live case k>=2 extends the source's one-live-neuron sufficient event; it does NOT classify every initialization with the same activation pattern. It does not assert a full Gaussian basin probability.

## 1. Barrier and existence
While the activation sets persist let a_i=-ell'(f_i)>0, A=a1+a2, d tau/dt=A, and g=(a1-a2)/A. Set b_x=sum v_j u_j, b_y=sum v_j y_j. Then f1=b_y/4+b_x and f2=b_y/4-b_x. The derivative magnitude a(f) is strictly decreasing for both losses, so b_x*g<=0 and |g|<=1. In the tau clock:

    u_j'=v_j*g,  y_j'=v_j/4,  v_j'=u_j*g+y_j/4.

For U=sum u_j^2, U'=2 b_x*g<=0. Write M=sqrt(U(0)). As long as the sector and positive outputs persist, y_j increases, and v_j'>=y_j/4-|u_j|>=y_j(0)/4-M>0. Thus v_j stays positive, y_j>=y_j(0)>4M>=4|u_j|. A first-exit argument closes the strict invariant region: no finite-time exit is possible. Dead neurons remain constant since their ReLU values and derivatives vanish at the two data points.

The physical-time vector field grows at most linearly in parameters: all live contributions are positive, hence f_i>0 and a_i<=1. Consequently the solution exists for all physical times. The tau clock is unbounded: if tau had a finite limit, the displayed linear-coefficient system (|g|<=1) would keep parameters bounded, hence f_i bounded and A bounded away from zero, contradicting bounded tau as t tends to infinity. All these arguments take place strictly inside smooth activation regions and invoke no convention at a ReLU kink.

## 2. Direction and margin
Let s_j=v_j+y_j and d_j=v_j-y_j. Their equations are

    s_j'=s_j/4+u_j*g,  d_j'=-d_j/4+u_j*g.

Since |u_j*g|<=M, e^(-tau/4)s_j has an integrable derivative and converges to c_j. Moreover c_j>=s_j(0)-4M>0. The variation-of-constants formula gives |d_j(tau)|<=|d_j(0)|+4M, while |u_j|<=M. Thus

    e^(-tau/4) v_j -> c_j/2,  e^(-tau/4) y_j -> c_j/2,
    e^(-tau/4) u_j -> 0.

All dead parameters become zero after normalization. With N the total squared parameter norm and C=sum c_j^2>0, N/e^(tau/2)->C/2, b_y/e^(tau/2)->C/4, and b_x/e^(tau/2)->0. Therefore f_i/N->1/8 and f_i->infinity. In particular the entire parameter direction converges, not merely its margin. Its unit-margin representative has live v_j=y_j=r_j>0, u_j=0, sum r_j^2=4; dead neurons are zero. Both margins equal 1 and N=8.

## 3. KKT and strict local suboptimality
For minimizing N/2 under f_i>=1, multipliers lambda1=lambda2=2 certify KKT stationarity: at each live neuron the vertical and output derivatives of 2f1+2f2 are r_j and r_j, respectively, and the horizontal derivatives cancel. At a zero neuron the output-hidden product ReLU has derivative zero at the origin, so its first-order stationarity equation holds as well. Constraints are active and multipliers positive.

For k<=m-1 select a zero neuron and one live coefficient r>0. Put a=||x1||=sqrt(17)/4. For delta>0 small, change the selected live parameters to

    v=r, u=-delta/(2r), y=r-2delta/r.

It remains active on both points if delta<r^2/4. Its prediction changes are (-delta,0). At the zero neuron introduce w=t*x1/a and v=t, where t=sqrt(delta/a)>0. Since x1 dot x2=-15/16<0, this adds (delta,0). Both constraints therefore remain exactly equal to one. The total squared norm change is

    Delta N = (-4+2/a)*delta + (17/4)*delta^2/r^2.

Here 2/a<4 because sqrt(17)>2. For sufficiently small delta the change is strictly negative; all perturbations tend to zero with delta. This proves failure of local optimality. For k=m there is no spare zero neuron and this local argument is NOT claimed, though the margin/direction conclusions still hold.

For comparison a feasible network at this width can use x1-only and x2-only directions: two neurons w_i=s*x_i/a, v_i=s with s=1/sqrt(a). Each point has margin one and squared norm 4/a=16/sqrt(17)<8. Its normalized margin is sqrt(17)/16>1/8. This is only a witness of suboptimality; no global optimality proof is needed here.

## 4. Exact Gaussian event probability
Let all hidden and output coordinates be independent N(0,sigma^2), sigma>0. Write p=atan(1/4)/pi, the hidden dead-sector probability. For a specified set of k live neurons, the probability of (H) and all positive outputs is

    h_k = 2^(-k) E[ (1-Phi(4 R))^k ],  R~chi_k,
        = 2^(-k)/(2^(k/2-1) Gamma(k/2))
          integral_0^infinity r^(k-1) exp(-r^2/2) [1-Phi(4r)]^k dr.

Indeed, after dividing by sigma the k horizontal coordinates are independent standard Gaussians; conditionally on their radius R each vertical coordinate must exceed 4R, independently; output signs contribute 2^(-k). For k>=1 this integral is strictly positive. The exact probability of exactly k barrier-live neurons and all others dead, with arbitrary placements, is

    P_{m,k} = binom(m,k) h_k p^(m-k).

These placement events, and the events for different k, are disjoint since live and dead sectors are disjoint. For widths2..6 the sufficient non-local-minimum bad-family probability is sum_{k=1}^{m-1} P_{m,k}. The k=1 term is the already known source family, since h_1=p/2. The additional terms k=2..m-1 (ten width/k pairs for m=3..6) are the new part of this slice. For widths2..6 the coefficient rows multiplying h_k p^(m-k) are respectively [2], [3,3], [4,6,4], [5,10,10,5], [6,15,20,15,6]. These are exact event masses, not certified numerical approximations to h_k and not total bad-basin probabilities. The cone condition is scale-invariant, so these formulas apply in particular to sigma=1e-6.

[Corollary cor:bipartite of arXiv:2507.16188, 'The noisy voter model with general initial conditions'] Fix $\theta\in(0,1]$. Let $G^{(n)}$ be a sequence of bipartite graphs on $n$ vertices satisfying (eq:expansion of the paper) for the same $\upalpha,\mathfrak{c}_0$. Let $\mathsf{x}_\mathrm{alt} = \mathsf{x}_{\mathrm{alt}}^{(n)}$ denote the alternating condition on $G^{(n)}$ as in (eq:alternatingbipartite of the paper). Then, for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$, the binary noisy voter model on $G^{(n)}$ with noise $\theta$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
t_\textsc{mix}^{\mathsf{x}_{\mathrm{alt}}}(\varepsilon) = \frac{1+o(1)}{\min\{4-2\theta,4\theta\}}\log n\,,
\end{equation}
where the $o(1)$-term is $ O\big(\log^{-\upalpha/2} n\big)
$ with a constant depending on $\varepsilon,\theta,\upalpha,\mathfrak{c}_0$ (but not on $G^{(n)}$).
Furthermore, if $\mathsf{x}_0=\mathsf{x}_0^{(n)}$ is any arbitrary sequence of initial conditions, we have
\[
\liminf_{n \to \infty}\frac{t_\textsc{mix}^{\mathsf{x}_0}(\varepsilon)}{t_\textsc{mix}^{\mathsf{x}_{\mathrm{alt}}}(\varepsilon)} \geq 1\,,
\]
thus $\mathsf{x}_{\mathrm{alt}}$ is the asymptotically fastest initial condition on $G^{(n)}$. In particular, for Glauber dynamics for the Ising model on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ (the case $G^{(n)}=\mathbb{Z}_n$) at any inverse temperature $\beta>0$, the alternating initial condition $\mathsf{x}_{\mathrm{alt}}$ is the asymptotically fastest initial condition. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Corollary cor:bipartite of arXiv:2507.16188

body: Let (Omega, F, mu, T) be an ergodic measure-preserving system and A: Omega -> GL(d,R) measurable with log^+||A|| and log^+||A^{-1}|| integrable, generating the cocycle A_n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x) ... A(Tx) A(x). The Oseledets multiplicative ergodic theorem states there exist real numbers lambda_1 > ... > lambda_r and, for almost every x, a filtration R^d = V_1(x) > ... > V_r(x) > V_{r+1}(x) = {0} with A(x) V_i(x) = V_i(Tx), such that for v in V_i(x) minus V_{i+1}(x), (1/n) log ||A_n(x) v|| -> lambda_i as n -> infinity. The lambda_i are the Lyapunov exponents. Due to Valery Oseledets.
title: Oseledets theorem

[Definition 3 of arXiv:2604.24664, 'Absolute continuity of Rosenblatt measures'] Let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ and $f: [0, T] \to \Rbb$. The \emph{left} and \emph{right Riemann--Liouville fractional derivatives of $f$ of order $\alpha$} are defined by
	\begin{align*}
		(I^{-\alpha}_{0+} f)(x) &= \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \frac{\d{}}{\d{x}} \int_0^x (x-y)^{-\alpha} f(y) \d{y},
		\\
		(I^{-\alpha}_{T-} f)(x') &= \frac{1}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)} \frac{\d{}}{\d{x'}} \int_{x'}^{T} (y-x')^{-\alpha} f(y) \d{y},
	\end{align*}
	for almost all $x,x' \in [0, T]$.

[Proposition prop:chi2 of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] Under the pseudo-wave map the semigroup acts by
$\psi_{\pi_t}=D^{-1}T_tD\,\psi_{\pi_0}=e^{\Lambda t(A-\mathrm{I})}\psi_{\pi_0}$ with
$A=A^{T}$, so $T_t$ is self-adjoint in $L^{2}(1/\nu)$. The stationary law maps to
the unit vector $\psi_\nu=\sqrt\nu$, and the $\chi^{2}$ divergence is the
corresponding squared distance to it,

\begin{equation}
\chi^{2}(p\,\|\,\nu)=\sum_i\frac{(p_i-\nu_i)^{2}}{\nu_i}=\|\psi_p-\psi_\nu\|^{2}.

\end{equation}

Consequently, with $\gamma$ the spectral gap of the chain,
$\chi^{2}(\pi_t\,\|\,\nu)\le e^{-2\gamma t}\,\chi^{2}(\pi_0\,\|\,\nu)$.

[Theorem Informal; bounded-disorder coexistence of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:intro-coexistence}
For every \(p\ge3\), there is a symmetric, compactly supported law
\(\mu\) with a \(C^\infty\) density, matching the standard Gaussian moments through
order \(2p\), for which the following hold simultaneously.  Every fixed
admissible incoherent-frame regularization has expectation asymptotic to
its Gaussian counterpart, whereas for some compact interval
\(B\subset(0,\infty)\),
\[
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B)
 >
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_N^G(B).
\]
The count on the left is unregularized and unrestricted in space.  The
same dichotomy holds in the standard symmetric-coordinate model. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Publication record. Y. Shmalo, A necessary and sufficient condition for convergence of the quantile process in L^p(0,1) (October 2026), proves that for 1 <= p < infinity the empirical quantile process sqrt(n)(Q_n - Q) converges in distribution in L^p(0,1) if and only if the quantile function Q is locally absolutely continuous on (0,1) and the integral of q(t)^p [t(1-t)]^{p/2} dt over (0,1) is finite, where q = Q'. The limit is -qB, with B a Brownian bridge. No density is assumed and atoms are allowed. The case p = 1 is due to Beare and Kaji (arXiv:2502.01254); for p > 1 this answers Problem 2 in Section 7 of the survey of del Barrio, Gonzalez-Sanz, Loubes and Rodriguez-Vitores (arXiv:2505.19104). Paper: https://github.com/yspennstate/quantile-process-lp (commit 4f78b53fc32e). Not refereed.

Let psi_X be the cumulant generating function of a random variable X. The Cramer transform, in the one-sided convention used for upper-tail (Chernoff) bounds, is psi_X^*(t) = sup_{lambda >= 0} (lambda * t - psi_X(lambda)). For t >= E X it equals the Fenchel-Legendre dual (convex conjugate) sup over all real lambda of (lambda * t - psi_X(lambda)), which is Cramer's rate function; for t < E X the one-sided transform is 0, while the conjugate is in general positive (for a standard normal X the conjugate is t^2/2 for every t).

[Theorem thm:vrjp-on-G-r-pos-rec of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] Let $G=(\Lambda,E)$ be a connected undirected graph without self-loops
  and take $l,r\in{\mathbb N}_0$ with $l\le r$.
  Let $(X,T)$ be vrjp in exchangeable time scale on the subdivided graph $G_r$ with
  starting point $\rho\in\Lambda$ and random weights $W_e>0$, $e\in E_r$, with
  respect to some probability measure with corresponding expectation ${\mathbb E}$. Its restriction
  $(X^{\Lambda_l\neq},T^{\Lambda_l\neq})$ to $\Lambda_l$
  with self-loops removed is again a mixture of vrjps on $G_l$ with random
  weights denoted by $W^{(l)}=(W_e^{(l)})_{e\in E_l}$. If the family $W=(W_e)_{e\in E_r}$ is
  independent or i.i.d., then so is the family $W^{(l)}$. Given $W$, the conditional
  law of $W^{(l)}$ can be described in terms of the restriction
  $\beta_{\Lambda_r\setminus\Lambda_l}$ of a $\nu_{\Lambda_r}^W$-distributed
  random field $\beta$. 
  For any finite subgraph $\tilde G$ of $G$ and the corresponding subdivision
  $\tilde G_l=(\tilde\Lambda_l,\tilde E_l)$, the restriction of $W^{(l)}$ to
  $\tilde E_l$ equals $W^{\tilde\Lambda_l}$ given in (equation def:W-J of the paper) with $J=\tilde\Lambda_l$
  and $I=\tilde\Lambda_r\setminus\tilde\Lambda_l$, and
  fulfills the recursion equations described in 
  Lemma (le:aux-W-l-1 of the paper), below. In particular, one has 
  \begin{align}
    
    &P_\rho^{W,\Lambda_r}((X^{\Lambda_l\neq},T^{\Lambda_l\neq})\in\cdot)=\int_{{\mathbb R}^{\Lambda_r}}
      P_\rho^{W^{(l)\neq}(\beta),\Lambda_l}((X,T)\in\cdot)\,
      \nu_{\Lambda_r}^W(d\beta).
  \end{align}
  Assume that the vertex degree of $G$ is bounded by $d$. Moreover, assume
  that the weights $W_e$, $e\in E_r$, are i.i.d.\ and satisfy
  ${\mathbb E}[W_e^\alpha]\le{c_1} 2^{\alpha(r-l)}$ for some $\alpha\in (0,\tfrac14]$
  with the 
  constant ${c_1}(d,\alpha)$ from Fact (fact:sabot-tarres-recurrence of the paper). 
  Then, the process $X^{\Lambda_l\neq}$ is a mixture of positive recurrent
  reversible Markov chains. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Vrjp on subdivided graphs

body:
Let U ⊂ C be open and F a family of holomorphic functions on U. F is normal (in the finite sense) if every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on every compact subset of U; the limit is then automatically holomorphic, and it need not belong to F. F is normal in the extended sense if every sequence in F has a subsequence which, on each connected component of U, either converges uniformly on compact subsets to a holomorphic function or tends to ∞ uniformly on compact subsets (equivalently, the reciprocals tend to 0 uniformly on compact subsets). For families of meromorphic functions, normality means that every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets with respect to the chordal metric of the Riemann sphere; restricted to holomorphic families this coincides with the extended sense, because a spherical limit of zero-free reciprocals is, by Hurwitz's theorem, either holomorphic or identically ∞ on each component. Normality is a local property: F is normal on U if and only if every point of U has a neighborhood on which F is normal. Normality asserts the existence of convergent subsequences only; it does not assert convergence of the family itself, and the limit function may leave the family (for instance the limit of injective functions may be constant).

[Lemma key_lemma_delocalized_eigenvector of arXiv:2504.00512, 'Localization-delocalization transition for a random block matrix model at the edge'] Take $z=E+\mathrm{i} \eta\in \mathbf D\left({\tau}\right)$ with $E=\gamma_k\in \qa{E^{-},E^+}$ and $\eta\sim N^{-2/3+\varepsilon_L}k^{-1/3}$ for a small constant $\varepsilon_L>0$ (recall that we assume $k\in[\![{1,DN/2}]\!]$). Under the assumptions of (mix of the paper), there exists a constant $c_L>0$ (depending on $\varepsilon_L,\delta_A,\varepsilon_A$) such that 
\begin{equation}
\max_{z_1,z_2\in\{z,\overline z\}}\max_{a,b\in [\![{D}]\!]}\left|\left(\mathbb{E} L_{(1,2)}- K_{(1,2)}\right)_{ab}\right|
=\mathrm{O}\pa{N^{-1-c_L}\eta^{-2}} .
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma lem:wasser_converg of arXiv:2510.06891, 'Multivariate CLT for L\'evy processes: convergence rates without moment assumptions'] Let $\bm{X}$ be a L\'evy process and $\bm{Z}$ be a standard normal random vector with $\mathds{E}[|\bm{X}_1|^2]<\infty$. 
Then, for any $q \in [1,2]$, the limit $\lim_{t \to \infty}\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X}_t/\sqrt{t},\bm{Z})=0$ is equivalent to $\bm{X}_t/\sqrt{t} \xrightarrow{d} \bm{Z}$ as $t \to \infty$.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:3c210df31af9f94090845cbe395dccd17b2f6be4a74dcc2ebcd3cbe9245cf681","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/3c/3c210df31af9f94090845cbe395dccd17b2f6be4a74dcc2ebcd3cbe9245cf681.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:13d25ce3b13643b349718be969bf43c6ea3afcacc0535b4dfd300b20ecd25005","bundle_entry_key":"unbounded-supercritical-common-hessian","bundle_id":"population.t362-unbounded-supercritical-007","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"optimization; random reshuffling; unbounded condition number; optimal constant step","draft":"w732/bundle_007.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.randomreshuffling:common-hessian-random-reshuffling-supercritical-optimizer-without-curvature-growth-cap","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Target 1: supercritical ratios without an upper growth restriction

Status: proof draft (unaudited). No priority or general-T362 claim.

## Statement

Take the normalized common-Hessian model of C001, fixed n>=2, deterministic fixed x0!=0,y0 and fixed zero-sum linear terms with mean squares s1>=0,s2>0. Epoch permutations are fresh, independent and uniform, shared across coordinates. Let T=nK and suppose

    liminf_{T->infinity} kappa_T*log(T)/T > 4.            (H)

No finite limiting ratio, monotonicity, or upper growth bound on kappa is required. With A=x0^2/2 and P_T the exact expected final-epoch error,

    min_{eta>=0} P_T(eta) ~ A*exp(-4T/kappa_T).           (1)

Every sequence of global minimizing constant steps satisfies

    T*(eta_T-2/kappa_T) ->0.                             (2)

Equation (2) is additive on the 1/T scale. When T/kappa_T->0 it does NOT assert kappa_T*eta_T->2. The theorem is not uniform as the lower ratio gap in (H) tends to zero.

This extends C005's finite limiting ratio c>4 to unbounded and oscillating sequences. It does not re-prove the exact recursion. The split below also handles superexponential kappa, where a stability-edge candidate need not suppress the stiff deterministic initialization.

## Exact inputs

Use C001's diagonal recursion and C005's all-step lower bound, valid for q=kappa*eta>=0:

    P_T(eta) >= [s2*q^4/(2(n-1)*kappa)]
                    *sum_{j=0}^{K-1}(1-q)^(2nj).         (3)

In particular P_T(eta)>=s2*kappa^3*eta^4/[2(n-1)]. The objective is a continuous coercive polynomial, so global minimizers exist. All coordinates contribute nonnegative errors; coordinate-noise independence is unnecessary.

For 0<q<2, the stiff variance equals (s2/kappa)*J_n(q)*(1-(1-q)^(2T)), where J_n is the fixed-n stationary function from C004. Its endpoint behavior is J_n(2-delta)=O(delta^-1). The flat stationary variance at eta->0 is O(eta^3), as in C001. Constants depend only on the fixed instance.

## A bound valid for all kappa

1. The stable candidate eta=1/kappa has q=1. Its stiff deterministic term is zero after any epoch, even when kappa is very large and y0!=0. Its stiff variance is exactly s2/(2kappa): W_n(1)=n-1 and the geometric variance multiplier equals one. The flat transient is at most A eventually, and the flat variance is O(kappa^-3). Since (H) implies kappa->infinity,

    min P_T <= A+O(kappa^-1)+O(kappa^-3) = A+o(1).        (4)

Combined with the quartic bound from (3), every minimizer obeys

    eta_T <= C*kappa^(-3/4)                              (5)

for a fixed C and all sufficiently large T.

Choose a fixed d>4 such that kappa>=d*T/log T eventually; this is possible even if the liminf in (H) is infinite. Write ell=log T and B_T=A*exp(-4T/kappa). Then

    B_T >= A*T^(-4/d).                                  (6)

## Very large curvature: kappa>T^2

2. In this range (5) gives T*eta_T<=C*T^(-1/2)->0, and T/kappa<=1/T->0. Therefore the flat transient A*(1-eta_T)^(2T)->A, which is a lower bound on P_T. Bound (4) gives the matching upper bound. Since B_T->A, (1) holds in this range. Also both T*eta_T and 2T/kappa tend to zero, proving (2). These arguments require no upper bound on log kappa and no candidate near q=2.

## Remaining curvature: d*T/ell<=kappa<=T^2

3. Put delta=ell^-2, q_c=2-delta and eta_c=q_c/kappa. The stationary endpoint estimate gives stiff variance O(ell^2/kappa)=O(ell^3/T). By (6), this is o(B_T), because 4/d<1. The stiff deterministic term is at most

    (T^2*y0^2/2)*exp(-2T/ell^2)=o(B_T).

The flat variance O(kappa^-3)=O(ell^3/T^3) is also o(B_T). The flat transient divided by B_T equals

    exp(2delta*T/kappa + O(T/kappa^2)) ->1,

uniformly in this range, since delta*T/kappa<=1/(d*ell) and T/kappa^2<=ell^2/(d^2*T). Consequently

    min P_T <= B_T*(1+o(1)).                            (7)

4. Let q_T=kappa*eta_T for any minimizer in this remaining range. Eventually q_T<3: otherwise the last geometric summand in (3) yields a lower bound const*2^(2(T-n))/kappa, at least const*2^(2(T-n))/T^2, contradicting (4).

If 2<q_T<3, put epsilon=q_T-2. Since log(1+epsilon)>=epsilon/2 on [0,1], the same last summand and (4) give

    epsilon*(T-n) <= log kappa + O(1).

Thus for all minimizers, including those with q_T<=2,

    q_T <= 2+O(log kappa/T).                            (8)

All constants may be chosen independently of kappa in the present range: log kappa<=2ell and the bound (4) is a fixed constant.

5. Because q_T<3, eta_T=O(1/kappa)->0 and T*eta_T^2=O(ell^2/T)->0. The flat transient therefore gives

    P_T(eta_T)/B_T
       >= exp(2*(2-q_T)*T/kappa + O(T/kappa^2))
       >= exp(-O(log kappa/kappa)-O(T/kappa^2)) ->1

as a lower bound. Here log kappa/kappa->0 uniformly for kappa>=dT/ell. Together with (7), this proves (1) in the remaining range.

Using the relative upper bound (7) in the first line above shows limsup (2-q_T)*T/kappa<=0. Bound (8) gives the matching liminf>=0, since its possible negative part is O(log kappa/kappa)->0. Hence (2-q_T)*T/kappa->0, precisely (2).

6. The ranges kappa>T^2 and kappa<=T^2 exhaust all sufficiently large T. The estimates in each range tend to their stated limits with the same fixed d; an oscillating sequence can be restricted to either range without changing those conclusions. This proves (1)-(2) for every sequence satisfying (H).

## Audit focus and unpaid scope

The new step beyond C005 is the huge-curvature branch (2), using q=1 to erase stiff initialization and the quartic variance bound to control every minimizer. Independent audit should check that the quartic bound remains valid at unrestricted steps, that the two ranges exhaust arbitrary oscillations, and that the additive step conclusion is not misread as kappa*eta->2.

Fixed n is used in the stationary estimates, s2>0 in (3)-(5), and x0!=0 to make B_T a positive comparison scale. n-1>0; stationary denominators are invoked only for the explicit 0<q_c<2 candidate. The proof does not cover a vanishing gap above 4, the ratio-only transition (handled separately in C007), x0=0, s2=0, growing n, or general finite-sum Hessians. No formal certificate, independent audit or priority claim is asserted. [Theorem thm:intro-scaling-limit-examples of arXiv:2512.20338, 'Up-down chains and scaling limits: \\ application to permuton- and graphon-valued diffusio'] Let
	$  \mathbb S  $ be the set of permutations (resp.~graphs),
	$  \mathbb S  _n$ be the subset of objects of size $n$,
	and $  E  $ be the space of permutons (resp.~graphons).
	Let $  X _n $ denote the up-down chain defined above on $   \mathbb S  _n $ and $  \iota  $ denote the map from $   \mathbb S   $ to $  E  $.
	Suppose that the initial distributions of these chains converge to $ \mu $, a distribution on $  E  $.

  Then there exists a Feller diffusion $F$ in $  E  $ with initial distribution $ \mu $ such that
  	$$
		\big(
			 \iota (  X _n (  \lfloor  n^2 t  \rfloor  ) )
		\big)_{ t \ge 0 }
			\Longrightarrow
        		\big(
        				 F ( t )
        		\big)_{ t \ge 0 }
	$$
    in distribution in the Skorokhod space $D([0,\infty),E)$.
    Moreover, this process is ergodic and its unique stationary distribution
     is the law of the recursive separable permuton (resp.~recursive cographon)
    of parameter $p$ introduced in [vfkrPermuton]. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm:intro-scaling-limit-examples of arXiv:2512.20338

[Proposition prop:Lq-J-thin of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Consider the coupling $(\bm{D}^{\bm{X},\kappa},\bm{D}^{\bm{Y},\kappa},\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa},\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa})$ defined in~(equation eq:comp_Poisson_measures of the paper) and~(equation eq:thining_coupling_defn of the paper). Then
\begin{equation}

\mathds{E}\bigg[\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\big|\bm{J}^{\bm{X},\kappa}_t-\bm{J}^{\bm{Y},\kappa}_t\big|^q\bigg]
\leqslant \int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})
    |\bm{w}|^q|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|\mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}),
\,\text{for any }q\in(0,1].
\end{equation}
In particular, the following inequality holds for any $q\in(0,1]$:
\begin{equation}

\begin{split}
\mathcal{W}_q(\bm{X},\bm{Y})
&\leqslant 
|\bm{\gamma}_{\bm{X},\kappa}-\bm{\gamma}_{\bm{Y},\kappa}|^q
+\bigg(4\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\1_{B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})
    |\bm{w}|^2|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|\mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w})\bigg)^{q/2}\\
&\qquad + 2^qd^{q/2}|\bm{\Sigma_X}-\bm{\Sigma_Y}|^q
+\int_{\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}}\1_{\mathbb{R}^d \setminus B_{\bm{0}}(\kappa)}(\bm{w})
    |\bm{w}|^q|f_{\bm{X}}(\bm{w})-f_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{w})|\mu(\mathrm{d}\bm{w}).
    \end{split}
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Locate the rate bottleneck in the Hermitisation argument. Result: The Hermitisation proof controls the log-potential U_n(z) = (1/n) log|det(n^{-1/2}M_n - z)| through the singular-value distribution of the shifted matrix; the error has three parts: (a) the rate in the Marchenko-Pastur-type convergence of the singular-value distribution, of order n^{-1/2}-ish under four moments and degrading to n^{-c(eps)} under 2+eps moments through the truncation at level n^{1/(2+eps)}; (b) the smallest singular value lower bound, which contributes only a log-factor to the log-potential error; (c) the conversion from log-potential convergence to weak convergence of the ESD, which costs a power through the smoothing of the Laplacian. The truncation in (a) is the eps-dependent bottleneck: entries are truncated at n^{1/(2+eps)}, the truncated variance differs from 1 by O(n^{-eps/(2+eps)}), and this variance error propagates to the singular-value distribution as a shift of the same order, giving delta of order eps/(2+eps) times the conversion loss in (c). So one expects delta(eps) = c eps/(2+eps) for small eps with c < 1 from step (c), and a plateau at the four-moment rate for eps >= 2. This is a heuristic scaling, not a theorem; the exact constant c requires the sharpest version of (c), which is the Kolmogorov-distance version of the log-potential-to-measure conversion. Key identity: Truncation at n^{1/(2+eps)} induces a variance error n^{-eps/(2+eps)}, which caps delta(eps) at a constant times eps/(2+eps) for small eps. Obstruction: Sharp conversion constant from log-potential to Kolmogorov distance.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Attempt the non-amenable direction through the spectral radius criterion of Benjamini-Schramm and Hutchcroft's p_c <= 1/spectral radius... type bounds. Result: Known route: if p_c < 1/rho where rho is the spectral radius of simple random walk, then at p slightly above p_c the expected number of open paths of length n to distance n grows slower than the number of returns... this gives p_c < p_u for graphs where p_c(G) < 1/(rho ... ) and is the content of the Benjamini-Schramm 1996 criterion p_c < 1/(1 + spectral gap)?; the general conjecture needs p_c < p_u even when p_c is close to 1/rho... For groups with p_c(G) < 1/rho(G) the conjecture holds; the remaining case is groups with a Cayley graph where p_c >= 1/rho, and the Pak-Smirnova trick replaces the generating set to make p_c small relative to rho. So the conjecture in its generating-set-free form (some Cayley graph) is settled by Pak-Smirnova, while the conjecture for EVERY Cayley graph reduces to showing p_c(G) < 1/rho(G)^{?}... I checked the inequality p_c <= 1/(1 + h) where h is the Cheeger constant... Benjamini-Schramm prove p_c <= 1/(1+h) and p_u >= 1/(1+h)?? no. The honest reduction: for every Cayley graph, p_c < p_u would follow from p_c < 1/rho (Benjamini-Schramm criterion) and the open question is whether every non-amenable Cayley graph satisfies p_c < 1/rho, which fails? For the free group with the standard generators p_c = 1/(2d-1) and 1/rho = (2d-1)/(2 sqrt(2d-1)) > p_c, consistent. No counterexample and no proof. Obstruction: Need p_c(G) < 1/rho(G) or another uniform criterion for every Cayley graph of every non-amenable group.

[Lemma lem:as-upgrade of arXiv:2608.18293, 'Critical tensor covariance at the Marchenko--Pastur threshold'] Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}$ and
\[
 T_n=\frac1{m_n}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{m_n}
 y_{n,\alpha}y_{n,\alpha}^*
\]
be $p_n\times p_n$, where $y_{n,\alpha}\in\mathbb F^{p_n}$, the samples
within each row of the triangular array are independent, and $*$ denotes
transpose or conjugate transpose according to the field. Suppose
$p_n/m_n\to c\in(0,\infty)$ and
\[
 \sum_{n=1}^\infty e^{-a p_n}<\infty
 \qquad\text{for every }a>0.
\]
If $\operatorname{ESD}(T_n)$ converges weakly in probability to a deterministic probability
measure $\mu$, then the convergence holds almost surely. No independence
between different rows of the triangular array is required.

Let Omega in R^n be open and A measurable with lambda|xi|^2 <= A(x)xi.xi and |A(x)xi.eta| <= Lambda|xi||eta| for a.e. x (0 < lambda <= Lambda). Let u in H^1_loc(Omega) be a weak solution of div(A grad u) = 0 in Omega. Then for every ball B_R(x0) contained in Omega, every 0 < r < R and every real constant k, integral over B_r(x0) of |grad u|^2 <= (16 Lambda^2 / (lambda^2 (R - r)^2)) times integral over B_R(x0) of |u - k|^2. The same inequality holds with u replaced by (u - k)^+ on both sides when u is only a weak subsolution (div(A grad u) >= 0), and with (u - k)^- when u is a supersolution. This is a reverse Poincare inequality: it bounds the energy of a solution by its oscillation in L^2, and it is the engine of both De Giorgi's and Moser's iterations.
Omega open in R^n
A measurable and uniformly elliptic with constants 0 < lambda <= Lambda (symmetry not needed)
u in H^1_loc(Omega) a weak solution (or subsolution/supersolution) of div(A grad u) = 0
B_R(x0) contained in Omega, 0 < r < R, k real

body: In mathematics, a real function of real numbers is said to be uniformly continuous if there is a positive real number such that function values over any function domain interval of the size are as close to each other as we want. [Prop lem:transfer of arXiv:2602.21277, 'A Limit in Law for the Cover Time and Last Visited Vertex of Wired Planar Domains'] Given $\eta \in (0,\tfrac{1}{2}-\gamma)$, there exists $c=c(\eta) > 0$ such that, if $k$ is large enough, for any $2 \leq T \leq {\rm e}^{ck^\gamma}$, $n \geq k$ and $x,\widetilde{x} \in {\rm D}_n$ with $x \in {\rm B}^-[\widetilde{x};T-1]$ and $\overline{{\rm B}^+[\widetilde{x};T]} \subseteq {\rm D}_n$, one has  
	\begin{equation}
		\frac{\mathbb{P} \Big( \big\{ Z_t[x;1] = (u,\overline{y})\big\} \setminus \mathrm{NR}^{\eta,[2,T-1]}_{n,t}(x) \,\Big|\,Z_t[\widetilde{x};T] = (v,\overline{z}) \Big)}{\mathbb{P} \Big( \big\{ \sqrt{\widehat{T}_{(v)}(1)} = u\big\} \setminus \mathcal{T}^{\eta,[2,T-1]}_{(v)}\Big)}=h_{k}(\overline{y})(1+O({\rm e}^{-ck^\gamma}))
	\end{equation} uniformly over all $t > 0$, $(u,\overline{y}) \in \mathcal Z_k[1]$ with $0 \leq \widetilde{u}_k \leq {\rm e}^{ck^\gamma}$ and $(v,\overline{z}) \in \mathcal Z_k[T]$ with $1 \leq \widetilde{v}_k \leq {\rm e}^{ck^\gamma}$, where $h_k$ is as in~(equation eq:defhk1 of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop lem:transfer of arXiv:2602.21277

[Corollary Persistence approximation of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] There exist
constants \(C > 0\) and \(\varepsilon_{0} > 0\) such that
for every \(0 < \varepsilon < \varepsilon_{0}\),
\(\delta \in (0,1)\), \(z \in M\), and every
\(T \geq C\left( s_{0} + \kappa_{d}(\varepsilon)^{- 1}\left( \log N_{\varepsilon}(M) + \log\frac{1}{\delta} \right) \right)\),
with probability at least \(1 - \delta\),

\[d_{B}\left( {Dgm}_{q}\left( \Gamma_{T} \right),{Dgm}_{q}(M) \right) \leq C\varepsilon\quad\quad\text{for every degree }q.\]

[Lem Gershgorin of arXiv:2506.01746, '\bf Optimal Bregman quantization: existence and uniqueness of optimal quantizers revisited'] Let $A= [a_{ij}]_{1\le i,j\le n}$  be an $d\times d$ symmetric tridiagonal matrix and let $L_i =  \sum_{1\le j\le d}a_{ij}$, $i=1,\ldots,d$. Assume that  
\[
\forall\, i \!\in \{1,\ldots, d\}, \quad a_{ii}\ge 0, \quad a_{ii\pm1}< 0, \quad    L_i \ge 0
\]
(with the convention $a_{10}= a_{d d+1}=-1$) and 
$$
L_1\quad \mbox{ or }\quad L_n>0.
$$ 
Then all the  eigenvalues of $A$ are (strictly) positive. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
In the normalized second Ray-Knight identity on a finite symmetric network pinned at a base vertex, the field identity in law is {L_(tau(t))^x + phi_x^2/2}_x =_d {(phi_x+sqrt(2t))^2/2}_x, with the left Gaussian field independent of the walk. It does not assert L_(tau(t))^x =_d (phi_x+sqrt(2t))^2/2. When Var(phi_x)=g>0 and t>0, the local-time marginal has mean t and an atom exp(-t/g) at zero, whereas the shifted Gaussian square has mean t+g/2 and no atom at zero. The omitted term in the earlier C0011 attempt invalidates that transfer step. This correction does not decide present openness of the full planar level-set problem.

g=Var(phi_x)>0
t>0
Gaussian field on the left independent of the walk

body:
OWNER OWN WORK, proof (unaudited), novelty unestablished.

U in R^(N by M), V in R^(P by M), N,P>=2,M>=1, have independent
iid real entries within each array; the arrays are independent.
Their fixed scalar laws u,v are centered with variance one and
finite fourth moments u4,v4. Assume measurable scalar functions
tau_U,eta_U,tau_V,eta_V,zeta_V satisfy, for bounded C1 functions h
with bounded derivative, including their bounded smooth compositions
in the proof,

 E[u h(u)]=E[tau_U(u) h'(u)],
 E[(u^2-1)h(u)]=E[eta_U(u) h'(u)],
 E[v h(v)]=E[tau_V(v) h'(v)],
 E[(v^2-1)h(v)]=E[eta_V(v) h'(v)],
 E[(tau_V(v)-1)h(v)]=E[zeta_V(v) h'(v)].             (1)

Assume |tau_U|<=T_U, |tau_V|<=T_V almost surely and
E eta_U^2,E eta_V^2,E zeta_V^2 finite. No differentiability of
these five functions and no posterior independence is assumed.
Bounded truncation of h(x)=x gives E tau_U=E tau_V=1.
Define the finite scalar constants

 t_U=E tau_U^2, t_V=E tau_V^2,
 e_U=E eta_U^2, e_V=E eta_V^2, z_V=E zeta_V^2,
 a_U=E[tau_U u^2], a_V=E[tau_V v^2],
 b_U=E[tau_U u], b_V=E[tau_V v],
 h_U=E eta_U, h_V=E eta_V,
 L_N=N-2+2*a_U^2+2*b_U^4.

Let independent Z have iid standard Gaussian entries, X=UV^T/sqrt(N),
Y=sqrt(s)X+Z, d=NP, alpha=P/N, beta=M/N, v_s=1+beta*s.
Set g=beta/v_s, m_N=E||X-E[X|Y]||^2/d and
B_N=log(v_s)/2-I(X;Y)/d, with natural logs.

## Explicit constants and result

Put A=beta^2*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^2 and

 E3=6*(N-1)*(P-1)*M*(t_U^2*t_V-1)/N^4,
 Ec=6*(N-1)/N^4 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*(v4+2*(P-1))+M*(M-1)*a_V^2],
 Eeta=2/N^3 * [M*P*e_U*T_V^2+M*(M-1)*h_U^2*b_V^2],
 Ezeta=2*N*M*z_V/N^3,
 E4=24*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^5 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^2*e_V*N+2*M*(M-1)*b_U^2*h_V^2],
 W=120*(N-1)*(P-1)*(P-2)/N^6 *
       [M*T_U^4*T_V^6*N*(N-1+u4)+M*(M-1)*L_N],
 F2=2*(Eeta+Ezeta), F3=2*(E3+Ec), F4=E4.            (2)

All constants are nonnegative. For all s>0,delta>0,

 g-m_N <= (1+delta)*s^3/v_s^2*(sqrt(A)+s*sqrt(W))^2
       +3*(1+1/delta)/v_s^2*(s^2*F2+s^3*F3+s^4*F4). (3)

For the exact R_N in038(10), define

 a=(N+u4-3)/N, b=(P+v4-3)/N,
 Q(s)=v_s^3+beta*(a+b)*v_s*s^2+beta*a*b*s^3,
 D(s)=v_s^2*Q(s), delta_N=1/floor(sqrt(N)),
 eps_N=delta_N*A+3*(1+1/delta_N)*(F2+F3+F4),
 K_N=A*(Q(1)-1)+(1+delta_N)*(A+2*W).

For 0<=s<=1 the requested estimate and its integral are

 0<=R_N(s)<=eps_N*s^2+K_N*s^4,                      (4)
 half integral_0^s R_N(t)dt<=eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10. (5)

In particular the full finite-N two-sided information bound is

 -A*(D(1)-1)*s^5/10
 <= B_N(s)-A*s^4/8
 <= eps_N*s^3/6+K_N*s^5/10.                         (6)

For fixed priors with positive aspect ratios bounded above,
F2,F3,F4=O(1/N), W,A,Q(1) are uniformly bounded,
eps_N=O(N^(-1/2)), and K_N is uniformly bounded.
If alpha_N->alpha>0,beta_N->beta>0, every limiting information
envelope therefore satisfies

 B(s)=alpha*beta^2*s^4/8+O(s^5), 0<=s<=1,            (7)

with the explicit remainder constants in (6). Existence or uniqueness
of the information limit is not required. The finite-N error in (6)
is additive O(N^(-1/2)*s^3), not a pure uniform Taylor remainder
after dividing by s^4 arbitrarily close to zero.

Equivalently the normalized mutual information has the explicit
finite-N polynomial

 P4_N(s)=beta*s/2-beta^2*s^2/4+beta^3*s^3/6
                              -(beta^4+A)*s^4/8,

and

 -eps_N*s^3/6-K_N*s^5/10
 <= I(X;Y)/d-P4_N(s)
 <= [beta^5+A*(D(1)-1)]*s^5/10.                     (6a)

The elementary identity log(1+x)=x-x^2/2+x^3/3-x^4/4
+integral_0^x t^4/(1+t)dt, valid for all x>=0, pays the log remainder.
Thus the limiting quartic term in I/(NP) is
-(beta^4+alpha*beta^2)*s^4/8, and no prior fourth cumulant enters
at that order within this class. The channel parameter is s=1/Delta;
I(UV^T;Y)=I(X;Y) because deterministic nonzero rescaling of the
input is invertible.

## Non-Gaussian example and whole-family scope

Both priors may independently be uniform on [-sqrt(3),sqrt(3)].
For either law take tau(x)=(3-x^2)/2, eta(x)=x-x^3/3;
for the V law take zeta(x)=-eta(x)/2. Their endpoint values vanish,
and their negative derivatives are x, x^2-1, and tau(x)-1,
respectively. Ordinary one-dimensional integration by parts proves
(1), without a Gaussian prior or a boundary contribution.
Exact constants are T=3/2, fourth moment9/5, t=6/5,
e=8/35, z=2/35, a=3/5, b=h=0.
Gaussian priors also satisfy (1) with tau=1,eta=x,zeta=0.
The result applies to every fixed law satisfying the stated kernel
conditions, not just these examples. Discrete Rademacher priors do
not satisfy (1) for arbitrary smooth tests and are not covered.
Specifically choose a compact smooth cutoff of (3*x-x^3)/2 which
equals that polynomial near {-1,1}. At a Rademacher input, h(u)=u
and h'(u)=0, so E[u*h(u)]=1 while E[tau(u)*h'(u)]=0 for every
finite function tau on its support. This is an obstruction to
applying the present derivative-transfer route to that law, not a
counterexample to quartic universality for discrete priors.

More concretely, each of U and V may have any standardized beta
law, with its own arbitrary fixed positive shape parameters p,q.
Let k=p+q, C=1/k, B=(q-p)*sqrt(k+1)/(k*sqrt(p*q)), and
x=(t-p/k)/sqrt(p*q/[k^2*(k+1)]) for t~Beta(p,q). Then

 tau(x)=1+C+B*x-C*x^2,
 eta(x)=tau(x)*(x+B)/(1+C),
 zeta(x)=B*tau(x)-C*eta(x).

The beta density times tau vanishes at both endpoints, including
when the density itself is unbounded there, because p,q>0.
Direct integration of its derivative proves E[x h]=E[tau h'].
Writing Q=x^2-1, the identity tau-1=B*x-C*Q and applying this
first identity to x*h(x) give
(1+C)E[Q*h]=E[tau*(x+B)*h']; this proves the eta identity.
The zeta identity follows by the same linear relation tau-1.
All kernels are bounded on the compact standardized support, so
every hypothesis of (1) is paid. This covers two asymmetric beta
priors as well as the symmetric subfamily. For an asymmetric exact
check, Beta(2,3) standardized as x=5*t-2 has
tau=(6+x-x^2)/5, eta=tau*(1+5*x)/6, zeta=tau*(1-x)/6.
Independent arrays and standard Gaussian channel noise; N,P>=2,M>=1; X=UV^T/sqrt(N)
Fixed centered unit-variance factor laws with finite fourth moments; bounded tau_U,tau_V
E[u h]=E[tau_U h'], E[(u^2-1)h]=E[eta_U h']; corresponding V identities and E[(tau_V-1)h]=E[zeta_V h'] for bounded C1 h with bounded derivative
Square-integrable eta_U,eta_V,zeta_V; precise constants and all rate bounds are in proof Eqs2,13
Positive finite convergent aspects only for limiting coefficient; no information-limit existence assumed

The beta density times tau vanishes at both endpoints, including
when the density itself is unbounded there, because p,q>0.
Direct integration of its derivative proves E[x h]=E[tau h'].
Writing Q=x^2-1, the identity tau-1=B*x-C*Q and applying this
first identity to x*h(x) give
(1+C)E[Q*h]=E[tau*(x+B)*h']; this proves the eta identity.
The zeta identity follows by the same linear relation tau-1.
All kernels are bounded on the compact standardized support, so
every hypothesis of (1) is paid. This covers two asymmetric beta
priors as well as the symmetric subfamily. For an asymmetric exact
check, Beta(2,3) standardized as x=5*t-2 has
tau=(6+x-x^2)/5, eta=tau*(1+5*x)/6, zeta=tau*(1-x)/6.

## Derivation of the relative-score decomposition

All identities here are under the original independent U,V,Z.
For compact smooth scalar f(Y), apply scalar Stein in V and Gaussian
IBP in Z to obtain, writing tau^U_ia=tau_U(U_ia) and similarly,

 E[Y_ij*f]/v_s-E[partial_ij f]
 =s/(v_s*N) sum_(a,k)
       E[(U_ia*U_ka*tau^V_ja-delta_ik)*partial_kj f]. (8)

For k=i split U_ia^2*tau^V_ja-1 into
(U_ia^2-1)*tau^V_ja+(tau^V_ja-1).
Use eta_U on the first part, zeta_V on the second. Each derivative
of Y with respect to a factor supplies sqrt(s/N) times the other
factor. This gives degree-two noise terms Ceta,Czeta below.

For k!=i use tau_U twice in its two independent coordinates. The
result is

 s^2/(v_s*N^2) sum_(a,k!=i,l,m)
 E[tau^U_ia*tau^U_ka*tau^V_ja*V_la*V_ma
                              *partial_il partial_km partial_kj f]. (9)

Partition its column indices into three disjoint cases:

 (i) l=m!=j: write V_la^2=1+(V_la^2-1). The1 part supplies
the leading cubic and its centered coefficient error. Apply eta_V
once to the centered part, obtaining the degree-four term C4.

 (ii) l!=m with l,m!=j: apply tau_V in the two distinct coordinates
V_la,V_ma. These derivatives never hit tau^V_ja, since j,l,m
are distinct. This gives the degree-five term W5.

 (iii) l=j or m=j: leave the expression unchanged, giving Cc.
These column coincidences have a vanishing tensor norm, bounded
explicitly below. No derivative of a Stein kernel is taken.

Define Wick products in standard noise Z by the generating function
exp(<t,Z>-||t||^2/2), allowing repeated indices. Noise IBP replaces
derivatives in (8)-(9) by the corresponding Wick products. Define

 A0_ij=(beta/N) sum_(k!=i,l!=j) :Z_il Z_kl Z_kj:,
 Ce_ij=N^(-2) sum_(k!=i,l!=j)
   [sum_a tau^U_ia*tau^U_ka*tau^V_ja-M] :Z_il Z_kl Z_kj:,
 Cc_ij=N^(-2) sum_(k!=i,l,m: l=j or m=j)
   [sum_a tau^U_ia*tau^U_ka*tau^V_ja*V_la*V_ma]
                                             :Z_il Z_km Z_kj:,
 Ceta_ij=N^(-3/2) sum_l
   [sum_a eta^U_ia*tau^V_ja*V_la] :Z_il Z_ij:,
 Czeta_ij=N^(-3/2) sum_r
   [sum_a zeta^V_ja*U_ra] :Z_rj Z_ij:,
 C4_ij=N^(-5/2) sum_(k!=i,l!=j,r)
   [sum_a tau^U_ia*tau^U_ka*tau^V_ja*eta^V_la*U_ra]
                                          :Z_il Z_kl Z_kj Z_rl:,
 W5_ij=N^(-3) sum_(k!=i,l!=m,l,m!=j,r,t)
   [sum_a tau^U_ia*tau^U_ka*tau^V_ja*tau^V_la*tau^V_ma*U_ra*U_ta]
                                      :Z_il Z_km Z_kj Z_rl Z_tm:.

The exact relative-score identity is

 r(Y)=grad log p_Y(Y)+Y/v_s
 =E[(s^2*A0+s^2*(Ce+Cc)+s^(3/2)*(Ceta+Czeta)
                                +s^(5/2)*C4+s^3*W5)/v_s | Y]. (10)

## Justification and Wick norm bounds

Gaussian convolution gives a smooth positive output density and a
square-integrable score by the conditional-noise formula. Every
coefficient in (10) is independent of Z. The estimates below prove
all fields in (10) are square integrable. Scalar Stein identities
are applied only to bounded smooth compositions with bounded scalar
derivatives for each fixed other coordinate; their polynomial random
prefactors are integrable by the stated moment hypotheses. Truncation
of those prefactors, followed by dominated convergence, justifies
successive integrations. The noise IBPs use bounded derivatives
and polynomial noise moments. No density-ratio Taylor series or
conditional independence assumption enters the proof. Equality
against every compact smooth f identifies the L2 score in (10).

For a degree-h ordered coefficient tensor independent of Z, the
Wick norm is h! times the squared Hilbert-Schmidt norm of its
symmetrization, at most h! times its ordered squared norm.
For each field above, its summation indices map injectively to its
ordered noise positions. The explicit restrictions on k,l,m are
retained in counting these ordered coefficients.

The three noise positions in A0 are distinct. Between two such
triples with fixed output i,j, only the identity Wick matching
survives: every other matching would force k=i or l=j. Hence

 E A0_ij^2=beta^2*(N-1)*(P-1)/N^2=A.                (11)

Hidden-index sums are sums of M independent copies. Their second
moments equal M times the single-copy second moment plus
M*(M-1) times its squared mean. Applying this observation and the
ordered Wick inequality gives, for every i,j,

 E Ce_ij^2<=E3, E Cc_ij^2<=Ec,
 E Ceta_ij^2<=Eeta, E Czeta_ij^2<=Ezeta,
 E C4_ij^2<=E4, E W5_ij^2<=W.                       (12)

Here are all moment and index counts paying (12):

Ce: (N-1)*(P-1) ordered triples. The coefficient's single-copy
mean is1, second moment t_U^2*t_V, so its variance is
M*(t_U^2*t_V-1). The Wick factor is3!=6.

Cc: for fixed k!=i the colliding column set has 2*(P-1) off-diagonal
pairs and one (j,j) pair. Summing the single-copy squared coefficients
is at most T_U^4*T_V^2*[2*(P-1)+v4]. Its mean is zero except at
(j,j), where it is a_V. Multiply by N-1, N^(-4), and3!.

Ceta: the single-copy second moment is at most e_U*T_V^2 for
each of P choices of l. Its mean is zero unless l=j, where it is
h_U*b_V. Multiply the hidden-index second-moment expression by
N^(-3) and2!.

Czeta: independence and E U_ra=0 give zero coefficient mean and
single-copy second moment z_V for each of N choices of r.
Multiply by M, N^(-3) and2!.

C4: there are (N-1)*(P-1) choices of k,l. The sum over r of
single-copy second moments is at most T_U^4*T_V^2*e_V*N.
Its mean is zero except r=i or r=k, where it equals b_U*h_V.
The summed squared means therefore equal2*b_U^2*h_V^2.
Multiply by N^(-5) and4!=24.

W5: there are (N-1)*(P-1)*(P-2) choices of k,l,m.
The summed single-copy second moments over r,t are at most
T_U^4*T_V^6*E(sum_r U_ra^2)^2
=T_U^4*T_V^6*N*(N-1+u4).
The V kernel product has expectation1 because j,l,m are distinct.
The summed squared means over r,t consequently equal L_N:
N-2 diagonal pairs outside {i,k} contribute1 each;
(i,i),(k,k) contribute a_U^2 each;
(i,k),(k,i) contribute b_U^4 each;
every other pair contains a centered independent unweighted U.
Multiply by N^(-6) and5!=120. At P=2 this field is empty.

All counts are per output entry; summing over i,j then dividing by
NP introduces no extra factor. The moment bounds use finite fourth
moments for U,V, bounded tau kernels, and square-integrable eta,zeta,
not uncontrolled sixth moments of either prior.

## Conclude the residual and information bounds

Conditional expectation contracts L2. Group Ceta+Czeta, Ce+Cc
using ||x+y||^2<=2||x||^2+2||y||^2, and use (10)-(12) to obtain

 sqrt(E||r||^2/d)
 <=[s^2*sqrt(A)+s^3*sqrt(W)
                   +s^(3/2)*sqrt(F2)+s^2*sqrt(F3)+s^(5/2)*sqrt(F4)]/v_s.

Split the first two and last three summands. Apply
(x+y)^2<=(1+delta)x^2+(1+1/delta)y^2, and bound the square of
the three-term error by three times the sum of its squared terms.
The Gaussian-channel identity E||r||^2/d=s*(g-m_N) proves (3).

038 defines R_N=(g-m_N)-A*s^3/[v_s^2*Q(s)] exactly. Q has
nonnegative coefficients and Q(0)=1, hence for 0<=s<=1,
1-1/Q(s)<=Q(s)-1<=s*(Q(1)-1).
Subtracting038 from (3), bounding v_s^(-2)<=1 and s^3,s^4<=s^2
in the vanishing error terms, gives

 R_N<=eps_N*s^2+
  [A*(Q(1)-1)+(1+delta_N)*(2*sqrt(A*W)+W)]*s^4.

Finally 2*sqrt(A*W)<=A+W proves (4). Integrating gives (5).
038's explicit lower bound, and D>=1 in its exact integral, give
(6), with denominators6 and10 from integrating s^2 and s^4.

Every rate claimed after (6) follows directly from (2): fixed scalar
constants and bounded P/N,M/N imply E3,Ec,Eeta,Ezeta,E4=O(1/N),
W=O(1), A=O(1), Q(1)=O(1); floor(sqrt(N)) lies between
sqrt(N)/2 and sqrt(N), so eps_N=O(N^(-1/2)). No SNR derivative
is interchanged with the dimension limit to obtain (7).

For completely dimension-independent constants, if alpha<=alpha_*
and beta<=beta_*, let A_*=alpha_* beta_*^2 and put

 C3_*=6 alpha_* beta_* (t_U^2*t_V-1),
 Cc_*=6[beta_* T_U^4 T_V^2(v4/2+2 alpha_*)+beta_*^2 a_V^2],
 Ceta_*=2[alpha_* beta_* e_U T_V^2+beta_*^2 h_U^2 b_V^2],
 Czeta_*=2 beta_* z_V,
 C4_*=24 alpha_*[beta_* T_U^4 T_V^2 e_V
                                  +2 beta_*^2 b_U^2 h_V^2],
 C_*=2(Ceta_*+Czeta_*)+2(C3_*+Cc_*)+C4_*,
 W_*=120 alpha_*^2[beta_* T_U^4 T_V^6(1+u4)/2
                                  +beta_*^2(1+a_U^2+b_U^4)],
 a_*=1+max(u4-3,0)/2,
 b_*=alpha_*+max(v4-3,0)/2,
 Q_*=(1+beta_*)^3+beta_*(a_*+b_*)(1+beta_*)+beta_* a_* b_*.

Then E3<=C3_*/N, Ec<=Cc_*/N, Eeta<=Ceta_*/N,
Ezeta<=Czeta_*/N, E4<=C4_*/N and W<=W_*.
For W, use N(N-1+u4)<=N^2(1+u4)/2 and
L_N<=N(1+a_U^2+b_U^4), valid because N>=2,u4>=1.
Also Q(1)<=Q_*, and

 eps_N<=(2 A_*+6 C_*)/sqrt(N),
 K_N<=A_*(Q_*-1)+2(A_*+2 W_*).                      (13)

The lower fifth-order constant in (6) is at most
A_*[(1+beta_*)^2 Q_*-1]/10. Thus every constant in the
limiting O(s^5) assertion has an explicit dimension-independent value.

Exact validation is in scripts/check_two_stein_score.py and
logs/two_stein_score_checks.json: polynomial Gaussian-noise integration
and rational uniform/Beta(2,3) moments test the unsimplified weak
score identity. Separate exact Wick norm computations test the
coefficient bounds. These finite checks exercise diagonal, collision,
fourth-order and fifth-order fields, including asymmetric kernels;
they do not independently audit the analytic theorem for all dimensions.

The first step still unpaid for full Target1 is replacing the scalar
Stein transfer hypotheses (1) by arbitrary finite-moment iid laws,
including discrete priors, with a similarly uniform remainder.
This theorem also does not locate the first prior-dependent term
beyond the now-universal quartic coefficient in its stated class.

For the conditioned covariance mixture in the previous NEXT,
specialize V to Gaussian and impose the sub-Gaussian U hypothesis
of034. The same two-sided inequality (6) holds for its conditioned
normalized KL K_E,N after subtracting H_N(s) from the lower bound
and adding H_N(s) to the upper bound, using the exact transfer
|K_E,N-B_N|<=H_N from038(9). Standardized beta U is bounded, hence
has a finite Hoeffding sub-Gaussian proxy. This pays the requested
conditioned-mixture sharp coefficient on that family; the previously

body: In mathematics, a real-valued function is called convex if the line segment between any two distinct points on the graph of the function lies above or on the graph of the function between the two points. Equivalently, a function is convex if its epigraph (the set of points on or above the graph of the function) is a convex set. In simple terms, a convex function graph is shaped like a cup $\cup$ (or a straight line like a linear function), while a concave function's graph is shaped like a cap $\cap$.

body: [Abstract of arXiv:2609.02362, '\textbf{Farthest-cell triplet entropy: high-dimensional shell limits and hyperbolic...'] We introduce farthest-cell triplet entropy, the conditional Shannon entropy of the farthest-prototype label given three random prototypes. For independent queries and prototypes, its estimator records only the farthest label, not coordinates or numerical distances. The statistic is bounded by $\log 3$, is invariant under common strictly increasing transformations of the dissimilarities, and has an exact mutual-information interpretation. In high-dimensional isotropic radial models $X_d=R_dU_d$, the Euclidean ordering reduces to scores $\lambda_d\xi_{i,d}-Z_i$, where $\lambda_d=\sqrt d\,\operatorname{sd}(R_d)/\E R_d$ and the $Z_i$ are independent standard Gaussian variables. This gives angular-dominated, intermediate, and radial-dominated entropy limits $\log 3$, $\Hinf(\lambda;F)$, and $0$. In hyperbolic space of curvature $-\kappa_d^2$, the same master curve appears at $\lambda_{d,\mathbb H}=\sqrt d\,\tau_d A(s_d)$, where $\tau_d=\operatorname{sd}(R_d)/\E R_d$, $s_d=\kappa_d\E R_d$, and $A(s)=s\coth s$. With a calibrated radial law and $\tau_d$, and a monotone operating interval, entropy inversion identifies the scale-invariant target $s_d^2$; absolute curvature requires an external length unit. CPU simulations give Euclidean and hyperbolic master-curve RMSEs of $0.0164$ and $0.0209$. Inversion from observed synthetic latent coordinates has a median relative error in $\kappa$ of $6.6\%$, while angular anisotropy increases this error to $68.9\%$. Thus the entropy statistic is comparison-based, whereas curvature recovery remains model-calibrated, is not graph-only, and is not robust to anisotropy.

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2607.08242, 'Convergence of random sums in non-commutative probability'] Let $\{N_n\}$ be non-negative integer-valued rvs

independent of iid rvs $\{Y_n\}$ with $0<\mathbb{E}[Y_n^2]<\infty$. Let $Z$ be a standard Gaussian rv. \vskip5pt

\noindent (i) Suppose $\mathbb{E}[Y_1]\neq0$, and 

as $n\rightarrow\infty$, $\sigma_n^2\rightarrow\infty$, then for $t_1,t_2\in\mathbb{R}$, we have 
\begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{E}\exp\Big[\iota t_1(\frac{S_{N_n}-\mathbb{E}[N_nY_1]}{\sigma_n})
    
    +\iota \delta_nt_2\tilde{N}_n\Big]=\mathbb{E}\exp[\iota\delta_n(t_1+t_2)\tilde{N}_n]\mathbb{E}\exp[\iota t_1\sqrt{1-\delta_n^2}Z]+o(1).
\end{equation*}
\noindent (ii) Suppose $\mathbb{E}[Y_1]=0$. 
If as $n\rightarrow\infty$, $\mathbb{E}[N_n]\rightarrow\infty$, and the probability measures of $\frac{N_n}{\mathbb{E}[N_n]}$ weakly converge to a probability measure $\mu$, then
\begin{equation*}
    \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\exp\Big[\iota t_1\frac{S_{N_n}}{\sigma_n}
    +\iota t_2\frac{N_n}{\mathbb{E}[N_n]}\Big]=\int_{0}^{\infty}\exp(-\frac{t_1^2}{2}x+\iota t_2x)\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x),\ t_1,t_2\in\mathbb{R}.
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem thm:Errw-on-subdivided-graphs of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] Let $G=(\Lambda,E)$ be a connected undirected graph without
  self-loops and with vertex degree
  bounded by $d$. For all $r\in{\mathbb N}_0$ consider the subdivided graph $G_r$. 
  Let $X$ be errw on $\Lambda_r$  with starting point $\rho\in\Lambda$
  and with constant initial weights $a>0$. 
  Assume that $\alpha\in\left(0,\tfrac14\right]$, $r\in{\mathbb N}_0$, and 
  $l\in\{0,\ldots,r\}$ satisfy
  $\Gamma(a+\alpha)/\Gamma(a)\le{c_1}(d,\alpha)2^{\alpha(r-l)}$
  with ${c_1}$ as in Fact (fact:sabot-tarres-recurrence of the paper). Then, 
  the restriction $X^{\Lambda_l\neq}$ of errw to $\Lambda_l$ with self-loops
  removed is a mixture of
  positive recurrent Markov chains. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Errw on subdivided graphs
