ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Analyse M(1,1) on Z^2 through the range of the first-coordinate walk. Result: In M(1,1) the first coordinate moves only at first visits and the second at later visits; the set of visited vertices is the range, and the first-coordinate process is a simple random walk on Z run at the rate of new visits. Recurrence of M(1,1) would follow if the walk returns to the origin infinitely often; since the second coordinate performs a simple random walk on the column above the current first coordinate whenever the vertex was visited before, the walk behaves in each column like a 1D random walk (recurrent) until it hits an unvisited vertex, at which time the first coordinate steps. The number of new visits up to time n is the range R_n; the first coordinate after n steps is a simple random walk at time R_n, so |X^1_n| is of order sqrt(R_n), and R_n <= n, so |X^1_n| is typically at most of order sqrt n - not deterministically: n first-visit moves to the right, which have probability 2^-n, give X^1_n = n; a return to the origin requires both coordinates to vanish. A heuristic: if R_n ≍ n/log n as for planar simple random walk then the first coordinate is diffusive at the slower clock, and the walk is 'more recurrent' than planar simple random walk, supporting the conjecture; but the range of M(1,1) is not that of simple random walk because the exploration is column-wise. A rigorous partial fact: M(1,1) is recurrent if and only if the first coordinate returns to 0 infinitely often at times when the second coordinate is 0; since within a column the second coordinate is a recurrent 1D walk that keeps returning to 0 until it finds a new vertex, and new vertices in a column are found at the ends of the visited interval, the question is whether the first-coordinate walk (which is a simple random walk in the clock of new visits) visits 0 infinitely often, which it does a.s. (1D recurrence), and whether at those visits the second coordinate is 0 - not automatic. So recurrence of M(1,1) reduces to: at the (infinitely many) times the first coordinate is 0, the second coordinate, which then performs a 1D walk in the column of 0 with the visited interval of that column, returns to height 0 before finding a new vertex - which has probability bounded below by a constant each time if the visited interval around height 0 in column 0 has length bounded... the visited interval in column 0 grows, and the probability of returning to 0 from the boundary of an interval of length L before exiting is of order 1/L... summing over the visits to column 0 gives a divergent series only if the interval lengths grow slowly enough. This is the crux and I did not settle it; the reduction is recorded. Key identity: M(1,1) recurrent iff, at the infinitely many returns of the first coordinate to 0, the second coordinate returns to 0 in column 0 before finding a new vertex; the return probability is of order 1/(visited interval length). Obstruction: Growth rate of the visited interval in column 0 not controlled.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0132-transience-and-recurrence-of-the-m-d1-d2-balanced-excited-random-walks

[Proposition prop:pop-hk-summatory of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] For integers $m\geq0$ and $k\geq3$, write
\[
 K_{m,k}=\sum_{r=2}^{m}\kappa_{k,r},
\]
with the empty sum equal to zero when $m=0$ or $1$.
Let
\[
 I_k=\int_{\substack{c\in\mathbb R^{k-1}\ {\rm mixed}\\
                      \delta_k(c)\leq1}}w_k(c)\,dc.
\]
Then $0<I_k<\infty$ and, for fixed $k\geq3$,
\begin{equation}
 K_{h,k}=\sum_{r=2}^h\kappa_{k,r}
 \sim\frac{I_k}{2\zeta(k-1)}h^{k-2}.
\end{equation}
Here the asymptotic is as $h\to\infty$.  For $k=4$, these constants agree
with the preceding ones: $\kappa_{4,r}=\kappa_r$ and $I_4=I$.
In particular, $K_{h,k}\asymp_k h^{k-2}$.

[Lemma 7 (Signed threshold coordinate) of arXiv:2609.02788, '\textbf{Quantized Einstein Metrics on \(S^7\) with \(SU(3)\)-Symmetry}'] After orienting $a$, the function $a(c)$ changes sign at $c_*$.  More
precisely, for some finite odd integer $m\ge1$,
\begin{equation}
 a(c)=\kappa(c-c_*)^m+O((c-c_*)^{m+1}),
 \qquad \kappa\ne0.
\end{equation}
Consequently $a$ is a strictly monotone local coordinate and its inverse is
continuous, though it need not be differentiable when $m>1$.

body: Little Picard theorem: if f : C -> C is entire and non-constant, then the image of f is either all of C or C minus a single point, i.e. f omits at most one complex value. If moreover f is transcendental (not a polynomial), then f takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often. Great Picard theorem: if f is holomorphic on a punctured neighborhood of z_0 and z_0 is an essential singularity, then on every such punctured neighborhood f takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely many times. The little theorem's transcendental case follows from the great one applied to g(z) = f(1/z) at its essential singularity 0.
title: Picard theorem

body: A metric space is a set X with a function d : X x X -> R such that d(x,y) >= 0 with equality iff x = y (identity of indiscernibles), d(x,y) = d(y,x) (symmetry), and d(x,z) <= d(x,y) + d(y,z) (triangle inequality). Completeness means every Cauchy sequence converges in X.

[Lemma lem:star of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] Fix an atom $i$ and set $P_{ij}=\frac12p_jd_{ij}$ for $j\ne i$. Then
$\sum_jP_{ij}=1$, the valid star coefficients $B_{ij}$ lie on a real
two-dimensional affine plane through
$m_i$ with $\lVert m_i\rVert^2=\frac12|z_i|^2$, and
$\sum_jP_{ij}B_{ij}=m_i$; their variance is
$V_i=E+\frac{|z_i|^2}2-L_i$ where
$L_i=\sum_{j:t_j=t_i}p_j|z_j-z_i|^2\ge0$. Consequently there exist two star
neighbours whose segment contains a point $\delta$ with
\[
  \Wnorm\delta^2\ \le\ \frac E4+\frac{5|z_i|^2}8-\frac{L_i}4 ,
\]
and $\delta$ is a closure point of three-point selections
(Lemma~(lem:closure of the paper)). Choosing $i$ with $|z_i|^2\le E$:
\begin{equation}
  \inf_{\substack{|\operatorname{supp} q|\le3\\ |\mu|<1}}C(q)\ \le\ \frac{7E}8,
  \qquad\text{so}\qquad \Gamma_3\le\frac78 .
\end{equation}

[Lemma 30 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Write \(D(\cE)^*\) for the continuous anti-dual of the form domain.
With the preceding first-slot-linear convention, the standard Gelfand
triple is
\[
                 D(\cE)\subset L^2(\mathfrak m)\subset D(\cE)^*.
\]
Let $u:Z\to\C$ be holomorphic and globally Lipschitz.  For $s\le0$ set
\begin{equation}
                           U(s,x)=u(\Psi_{-s}x).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
                         \|U(s)\|_{L^2(\mathfrak m)}\le Ce^{-s/2},
                         \qquad s\le0,
\end{equation}
and on every finite interval $[s_0,s_1]\subset(-\infty,0]$,
\begin{equation}
 U\in L^2([s_0,s_1];D(\cE)),\qquad
 \partial_sU+A_{\rm form}U=0\quad\text{in }D(\cE)^*,
\end{equation}
where $\langle A_{\rm form}v,\phi\rangle=\cE(v,\phi)$ is the form
operator.  On $\Dom A$, $A_{\rm form}$ agrees with the self-adjoint
operator $A$.
Moreover $s\mapsto U(s)$ is continuous into $L^2(\mathfrak m)$ and
\begin{equation}
                              U(0)=e^{sA}U(s),
                              \qquad s<0.
\end{equation}

Source-scope reference, reviewer claude-738954b6 PASS on C05 v1 recorded: Kwon, Xu, Yaras, Song, Balzano and Qu, The Effect of Training Task Diversity on In-Context Learning through the Lens of Low-Dimensional Subspaces, arXiv:2606.06814v1 (5 June 2026). Definition 1 (printed p.6) models training tasks by a centered Gaussian mixture on low-dimensional subspaces; its task-diversity notion concerns function classes and subspace overlap rather than merely counting a finite fixed task pool. For the paper's reduced linear-attention model, infinite training context and isotropic initialization, Proposition 1 (p.8), equation (9) and Lemma 1 (p.9) give a spectral reduction of separately trained query/key matrices and scalar value parameter. In particular the active squared spectral weights balance the scalar squared under the stated balanced initialization. This is prior architecture for finite-pool selector analysis. This scope card does not assert its assumptions cover unconstrained off-diagonal blocks or an empirically noncentered finite task distribution. Theorems 1-3 (pp.15-17) concern optimal-model subspace generalization under the source's covariance-regularization then training-context then test-context limits; they are not a raw-coordinate fixed-M gradient-flow selector.

[Lemma lem:finite-chaos-brownian-probe of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Fix $\alpha\geq0$.  For every $\delta_{\rm pr}>0$ there exist $n\geq2$,
$\varphi_{\rm pr}\in C_c^\infty((0,1))$, and a smooth field $q$ on
$[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d$ with
\begin{equation*}
 h_n(\xi):=\frac{\operatorname{He}_n(\xi_1)}{\sqrt{n!}},
 \qquad
 \Theta_n(s):=s^{n/2}\int_s^1
 \tau^{-n/2}\varphi_{\rm pr}(\tau)\,\mathrm d\tau,
 \qquad
 q(s,y):=\Theta_n(s)h_n(y/\sqrt s),\qquad 0<s\leq1,
\end{equation*}
where $\operatorname{He}_n$ is the probabilists' Hermite polynomial.  The
associated source is
\begin{equation*}
 F_0^{\rm tan}:=-\left(\partial_s+\frac12\Delta_y\right)q
 =\varphi_{\rm pr}(s)h_n(y/\sqrt s)\not\equiv0
\end{equation*}
The corresponding Hessian estimate is
\begin{equation}
 \left\lVert D_y^2q\right\rVert_{L^2(s^\alpha\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d\gamma_s)}
 \geq(C_\alpha^{\mathrm{Br}}-\delta_{\rm pr})
 \norm{F_0^{\rm tan}}_{L^2(s^\alpha\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d\gamma_s)}.
 
\end{equation}
The field vanishes on a terminal strip, and all its derivatives are
uniformly of polynomial growth in the spatial variable.

[Thm 11 (CLT for the normalized traces) of arXiv:2604.26499, 'Spectrum of Random Matrices with Exploding Moments'] Let $C_N$ be the random circulant matrix satisfying
Condition \ref{condition:Circulant Ensemble with Exploding Moments}
with $\alpha=1$. Then for $k\ge1$,
$$
Z_N(k)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\Tr(C_N^k)-\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\Tr(C_N^k)\right]
$$
converges in distribution to a centered Gaussian random variable $z(k)$. Moreover, the Covariance kernel is given as follows. 
\begin{align}
\mathrm{Cov}(z(k), z(l))
=
\begin{cases}
k!  , & \text{if } k=l, \\
0, & \text{if } k \neq l. 
\end{cases} +o(1),
\end{align}

body:
Let H be a separable complex Hilbert space and T a trace-class operator on H. List the nonzero eigenvalues lambda_1, lambda_2, ... of T according to their algebraic multiplicities (each finite, by the Riesz-Schauder theorem; the list may be finite or empty). Then sum_n |lambda_n| <= ||T||_1 < infinity and tr T = sum_n lambda_n. Self-adjointness is not assumed; the theorem is exactly what makes the trace computable from the spectrum of a non-normal operator.
H is a separable complex Hilbert space
T is trace class on H
eigenvalues are counted with algebraic (not geometric) multiplicity
no self-adjointness or normality is assumed

By Weyl's majorant theorem, sum_n |lambda_n| <= sum_n s_n(T) = ||T||_1, so the eigenvalue series converges absolutely. Step 2. Let M be the closed linear span of all generalized eigenvectors of T belonging to nonzero eigenvalues; M is T-invariant. Order a basis of generalized eigenvectors along Jordan chains so that the span of each initial segment is T-invariant, and apply Gram-Schmidt: the resulting orthonormal basis (u_n) of M puts T|_M in upper triangular form with diagonal entries <T u_n, u_n> = lambda_n. Complete by an orthonormal basis (v_m) of the orthogonal complement of M. Computing the (basis-independent) trace in the basis (u_n) together with (v_m) gives tr T = sum_n lambda_n + tr Q, where Q is the compression of T to the orthogonal complement of M, a trace-class operator that is quasinilpotent, since a nonzero eigenvalue of Q would produce a generalized eigenvector of T not accounted for in M. Step 3. A quasinilpotent trace-class Q has tr Q = 0. Its Fredholm determinant d(z) = det(I + zQ) is entire, has no zeros (the zeros of the determinant occur at -1/mu for the nonzero eigenvalues mu of Q, and there are none), satisfies the bound |d(z)| <= product over n of (1 + |z| s_n(Q)), whose logarithm is o(|z|) as |z| -> infinity because sum_n s_n(Q) < infinity, and has d'(0) = tr Q. Writing d = exp(g) with g entire and Re g(z) = o(|z|), the Borel-Caratheodory estimate forces g to be affine, hence g(z) = z tr Q; then Re(z tr Q) = o(|z|) in every direction forces tr Q = 0.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:2225456d23e042d16fa41a4883a1acf0ad8f28160beb6e99ce53d176a31bf47b","revision_digest":"sha256:7c9ac220f720c0750aa262568574b7bc9a239b32d467821b92feb72018290632","source_id":"wikipedia:Trace class","source_revision":"as-known-2026-09-12","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Theorem 38 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Suppose that Assumptions~\ref{Assumptions_Theta}, \ref{Assumptions_basic}, \ref{Assumptions_offcrit}, \ref{Assumptions_analyticity} hold and that the equilibrium measure has no saturations. Let $k_1,\ldots,k_L \in [H]$ be a $\N$-independent tuple and call $h_l = h^{k_l}$. Let $\boldsymbol{f}(z) = (f_l(z))_{l = 1}^{L}$ be functions such that $f_l(z)$ is holomorphic for $z$ in some $\N$-independent compact neighborhood of $[\alpha_{k_l} - \eps,\beta_{k_l} + \eps]$ where it is bounded independently of $\N$, for any $l \in [L]$. Let $\textnormal{\textsf{\textbf{Gau\ss{}}}}[\boldsymbol{f}]$ be a $L$-dimensional random Gaussian vector with covariance
\[
\textnormal{\textsf{Cov}}_{l_1,l_2}[\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{f}] = \oint_{\gamma_{l_1}} \oint_{\gamma_{l_1}} \frac{\dd z_1\dd z_2}{(2\ii\pi)^2} \mathcal{F}_{l_1,l_2}(z_1,z_2) f_{l_1}(z_1) f_{l_2}(z_2)
\]
in terms of the fundamental solution \eqref{FFFFFFFFFFF} associated to the bands of $\mu$ and the matrix $(\theta_{h_{l_1},h_{l_2}})_{l_1,l_2 = 1}^{L}$. Then, as  $\N \rightarrow \infty$ we have
\[
\bigg( \textnormal{\textsf{Lin}}_{k_l}[f_l] - \N \int_{\alpha_{k_l}}^{\beta_{k_l}} f_l(x)\mu_{h_l}(x)\dd x \bigg)_{l = 1}^{L} \,\, \mathop{\sim}^{\textnormal{d}}\,\,\textnormal{\textbf{\textsf{Gau\ss{}}}}[\boldsymbol{f}] + \bigg( \sum_{m = 1}^{L} \big(\textnormal{\textsf{Gau\ss{}}}_{\amsmathbb{Z},m} - \N \hat{n}^{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_m\big) \cdot  \omega_{k_l,m}[f_l]\bigg)_{l = 1}^{L}.
\]
where the discrete Gaussian $\textnormal{\textsf{\textbf{Gau\ss{}}}}_{\amsmathbb{Z}} = \textnormal{\textsf{\textbf{Gau\ss{}}}}_{\amsmathbb{Z}}[\Qu,\L,\boldsymbol{u}]$ is the same as in Theorem~\ref{Theorem_CLT_for_filling_fractionsi}. [Corollary of arXiv:2608.13452, 'Wasserstein stability of the zero cell of a Poisson hyperplane tessellation under directio'] Let $\hat{f}^{(1)}_{\gamma, n}$ and $\hat{f}^{(2)}_{\gamma, n}$ be the estimators of a density $f$ as defined in Proposition (prop:density-robust of the paper).
    Assume that the hypotheses of Proposition (prop:density-robust of the paper) are satisfied.
    Further assume that $f$ is globally $L$-Lipschitz and $\operatorname{supp}(f) \subseteq [0,1]^d$, and that \(\phi_2\) satisfies (equation eq:phi_2_close_condition of the paper).
    Then there exist random probability densities
    $\hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(1)}$ and
    $\hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(2)}$, defined on a common probability space,
    such that, for every fixed $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$,
    \[
    \hat{g}_{\gamma,n}^{(i)}(x)
    \overset{(d)}{=}
    \hat{f}_{\gamma,n}^{(i)}(x),
    \qquad i=1,2,
    \]
    and such that for constants $C(\phi_1, d)$ and \(\tilde{C}(\phi_1,d)\) depending only on $\phi_1$ and $d$ we have
    \begin{align*}
    &\mathbb{E} \left[\int_{[0,1]^d} \left|\hat{g}^{(1)}_{\gamma, n}(x) - \hat{g}^{(2)}_{\gamma, n}(x)\right| \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x \right] \\
    & \leq \min\left\{\frac{\gamma^{d/2} \|f\|_{\infty}^{1/2} \left(\mathrm{vol}(\Pi_1)^{1/2} + \mathrm{vol}(\Pi_2)^{1/2}\right)}{n^{1/2}} + \frac{L \tilde{C}(\phi_1, d)}{\gamma}W_{\mathrm{geo}}(\phi_1,\phi_2)^{\frac{1}{d}}, C(\phi_1, d)W_{\mathrm{geo}}(\phi_1,\phi_2)^{\frac{1}{d}}\right\}.
    \end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma le:bounds-W-l-one-step of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] \mbox{}\\
  Consider the setup of Theorem (thm:from-r-to-l of the paper). 
  For $l\in\{1,\ldots,r\}$, $\bar e\in E_{l-1}$, and $e'\in E_l$, 
  we have
  \begin{align}
    
    &{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]\le 2^{-\alpha}{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{e'})^\alpha]
      \quad\text{for }\alpha\in[0,1],\\
    
&{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]\le C_\alpha {\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{e'})^\alpha]^2
      \quad\text{for }\alpha\in[0,\tfrac12),\\
    
    &{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e}]\le\min\{{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]-\log 2,2{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]+{c_2}\}
  \end{align}
  with the constants $C_\alpha$ and ${c_2}$ from Theorem (thm:from-r-to-l of the paper).
  For $\alpha\in[0,\frac12)$,
  the bound  in (equation eq:bound-exp-w-l-alpha of the paper) is stronger than
  the bound in (equation eq:bound2-exp-w-l-alpha of the paper) if and only if
  ${\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{e'})^\alpha]>2^{-\alpha}C_\alpha^{-1}$.
  Similarly, the minimum in bound (equation eq:bound2-exp-w-l-log of the paper) equals
  ${\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]-\log 2$ if and only if
  ${\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]\ge -\log 2-{c_2}$.
  Note that the expectations do not depend on the choice of $\bar e$ and
  $e'$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Let F be C, R or Q, r >= 3 an integer and 0 < eps <= 1, and let xi be uniform on {-1,1}^n. (Thm 1.1) There is C = C(r, eps) such that: if f in F[x_1,...,x_n] is a quadratic polynomial all of whose coefficients have absolute value <= 1 and sup_x P(f(xi) = x) >= C (log n)^{r/2} / n^{1 - 2/(r+2)}, then there is a quadratic form h of rank < r such that the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients of f - h is at most eps n^2. (Thm 1.2) If instead the degree-2 coefficients of f lie in a fixed finite set S (C = C(r, eps, S)), the same hypothesis gives h of rank < r differing from f in at most eps n^2 coefficients. With r = 3: point probabilities much larger than n^{-3/5} force f to be close to a form of rank <= 2, which over C splits into two linear factors.

Assumes: Rademacher variables; coefficients bounded by 1 (Thm 1.1) or taken from a finite set (Thm 1.2)

Author-derived counterexample, independent review pending: let f be majority of three independent bits, mu=Bernoulli(epsilon)^3, nu=Bernoulli(1-epsilon)^3 with 0<epsilon<1/2. Each endpoint exterior makes a cell section nonconstant with probability 2 epsilon(1-epsilon), and each cell TV is 1-2 epsilon. Substituting endpoint sensitivities into a telescoping bound would give 6 epsilon(1-epsilon)(1-2 epsilon), tending to zero, whereas E_nu f-E_mu f=1-6 epsilon^2+4 epsilon^3 tends to one. For replacement order 1,2,3, the actual hybrid sensitivities are 2 epsilon(1-epsilon), (1-epsilon)^2+epsilon^2, 2 epsilon(1-epsilon); their TV-weighted sum equals the true difference. At epsilon=1/100 the false bound is 14553/250000 and the difference is 249851/250000. The valid inequality with actual hybrid laws is not refuted.

[Ppn 90 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recalling \eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym} and Definitions \ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}--\ref{d:measure.classes.sym}, we have
	\[\sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha) \subseteq \sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0)\,.\]

\begin{proof}
Consider any $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)$, as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym}. 
    By Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.Lip.to.Lip.sym}, we can find $\tilde\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$ with $\sym(\tilde\mu) = \mu$.
It was shown in the \hyperlink{p:thm.control.problems.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:control.problems.main}} that $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha) = \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0)$, so $\tilde\mu \in \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0)$.
Therefore, for any $\epsilon>0$ we can find $L>0$ and controls 
    \beq
        
        (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
    \eeq
such that (recalling that $\sym$ is a contraction) we have
    \[
        \bbW_2\Big(\mu, \mu^{\sym}(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)\Big)
        \le\bbW_2\Big(\tilde \mu, \mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)\Big)
         \le \epsilon\,.
    \]
We see from Definitions~\ref{d:SDE.classification} and \ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}
that the sets of controls $\Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ and $\Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ are in fact identical, so the controls \eqref{e:Lip.general.in.IAMP.sym.controls} belong to $\Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$, and 
    \[
        \mu \in \cB_\epsilon\Big(\cM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)\Big)\,.
    \]
    Since for all $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $L > 0$ so that this holds, we conclude $\mu \in \sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0)$.
    As this holds for all $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)$, the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Dfn 1. dfn: BTM of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [The Bouchaud trap model] 
  Fix an electrical network $G$.
  Let $\{\xi_{x}^{G}\}_{x \in V_{G}}$ be i.i.d.\ random variables with $\xi_{x}^{G} \stackrel{\mathrm{d}}{=} \xi$.
  Set $\nu_{G} \coloneqq \sum_{x \in V_{G}} \xi_{x}^{G} \delta_{x}$,
  which is a random measure on $V_{G}$.
  Conditional on $\nu_{G}$,
  the (symmetric) Bouchaud trap model (BTM) is defined as the continuous-time Markov chain $X_{G}^{\nu_{G}}$. 
  The random measure $\nu_{G}$ is called a \textit{trap}.

		$A\geq1$, all $R\geq1$, all $t\leq TR^2$, and all $x\in\mathbb{Z}^d$,
		\[
			0\leq
			\mathbb{E} u_t(0)-\mathbb{E} u_t^{Q(x,AR)}(x)

		\]

body: Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold with curvature tensor R. The Ricci curvature is the symmetric bilinear form Ric obtained by tracing the curvature tensor over one pair of indices: Ric(Y,Z) = trace of the linear map X |-> R(X,Y)Z. For a unit tangent vector v in T_pM, extend v to an orthonormal basis v, e_1,...,e_{n-1} of T_pM; then Ric(v,v) = sum_{i=1}^{n-1} K(sigma_i), where sigma_i is the 2-plane spanned by v and e_i, i.e. Ric(v,v) is (n-1) times the average sectional curvature of the 2-planes containing v. For general (nonzero, not necessarily unit) v, Ric(v,v) = |v|^2 Ric(v/|v|, v/|v|) by homogeneity. A further trace of Ric against the metric gives the scalar curvature.
title: Ricci Curvature

Let H and K be Hilbert spaces and T: H -> K compact. Let s_1 >= s_2 >= ... > 0 be the nonzero singular values of T, repeated according to multiplicity (a finite list or a sequence tending to 0). Then there are orthonormal systems (e_n) in H and (f_n) in K, indexed by the same set, such that T x = sum_n s_n <x, e_n> f_n for every x in H, the series converging in K; moreover the series converges in operator norm, with ||T - sum_{n <= N} s_n <., e_n> f_n|| = s_{N+1}. Here (e_n) is an orthonormal basis of (ker T)^perp, (f_n) is an orthonormal basis of the closure of ran T, T e_n = s_n f_n, T* f_n = s_n e_n, and |T| x = sum_n s_n <x, e_n> e_n. T is Hilbert-Schmidt iff sum_n s_n^2 < infinity and trace class iff sum_n s_n < infinity.
H and K are Hilbert spaces
T: H -> K is compact
singular values are listed in nonincreasing order with multiplicity

[Prop 2. prop: atom convergence from simple measure convergence of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] Let $\nu, \nu_{1}, \nu_{2}, \cdots$ be simple measures on $S$.
  For each compact subset $K$ of $S$,
  consider the following condition.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (VC), leftmargin = *]
    \item 
      Write $\{x_{i}\}_{i \in I_{K}} = \At(\nu) \cap K$ for the atoms lying in $K$.
      (NB. $I_{K}$ is a finite set.)
      Then, for all sufficiently large $n$,
      we can write $\At(\nu_{n}) \cap K = \{x_{i}^{(n)} \mid i \in I_{K}\}$ 
      in such a way that $x_{i}^{(n)} \to x_{i}$ for each $i \in I_{K}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then, the statements below are equivalent with each other.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (\roman*)]
    \item 
      The measures $\nu_{n}$ converge to $\nu$ vaguely.
    \item 
      Any compact subset $K$ of $S$ with $\nu(\partial K) = 0$ 
      satisfies (2. prop: characterization of vague convergence of simple measures of the paper).
    \item 
      There exists an increasing sequence $(D_{k})_{k \geq 1}$ of relatively compact open subsets of $S$ 
      such that $\bigcup_{k \geq 1} D_{k} = S$, $\mu(\partial D_{K}) = 0$ for each $k$, 
      and each $\closure(D_{k})$ satisfies (2. prop: characterization of vague convergence of simple measures of the paper).
  \end{enumerate}

[Definition eq:AMF2 of arXiv:2606.13264, 'Interference Queueing Networks: A Replica Mean-Field Approach in the Symmetric Setting'] Let \(p^\star\in[0,1]\) be a solution of the MF2 self-consistency equation: $p^\star=\mathbb P(q^{p^\star}>0)$, and let
\(\nu_{p^\star}\) denote the law of the corresponding Bernoulli random environment.
For \(i\in\{1,\dots,N\}\), define
\[
\overline\mu_i(p^\star)
:=
\mathbb E_{\nu_{p^\star}}\left[
B\log_2\left(
1+
\frac{1}{1+\sum_{m\neq i} T_{i,m} l(d(i,m))}
\right)
\right],
\]
where the random variables \((T_{i,m})_{m\neq i}\) are independent Bernoulli
random variables with parameter \(p^\star\).

The average second mean-field approximation
\[
Q^{\mathrm{AMF2}}=(q_i^{\mathrm{AMF2}})_{i=1}^N
\]
is defined, for each \(i\in\{1,\dots,N\}\), by
\begin{align}
q_i^{\mathrm{AMF2}}(t)
&=
q_i^{\mathrm{AMF2}}(0)
+
A_i[0,t]
-
\int_{\mathbb R_+}\int_0^t
\mathbf 1_{\{q_i^{\mathrm{AMF2}}(z^-)>0\}}
\mathbf 1_{\{u\leq \overline\mu_i(p^\star)\}}
\,D_i(\mathrm du,\mathrm dz).

\end{align}

Method: Polynomial small bias sufficient to fool DNF events exact calculation or structural obstruction Result: For a single conjunction C of k literals, its Fourier coefficients have magnitude2^-k on subsets of those k coordinates. An epsilon-biased distribution therefore changes E C by at most epsilon*(1-2^-k). Inclusion-exclusion for a union of s clauses gives the valid but crude error at most(2^s-1)*epsilon, since each nonempty intersection of consistent clauses is another conjunction. Check: The constant coefficient contributes no expectation difference, while all other coefficients are paired with parity biases of magnitude at most epsilon. Expanding the union into its2^s-1 nonempty clause intersections proves the stated global bound without assuming independence of clauses. Obstruction: To obtain polynomial rather than exponential bias requirements, one needs a substantially more economical approximation or cancellation argument. Small errors for individual clause probabilities do not by themselves control their union.

For piecewise-linear functions realized by two-layer networks in dimension at least 3, kinks supported on distinct hyperplanes cannot cancel each other locally: the realized coefficient of each kink is bounded by twice the Lipschitz constant of the function. Consequently the function class has small metric entropy regardless of how large the parameters are. The principle genuinely fails in dimension 2, where an even cycle of kink circles with alternating coefficients cancels, and it fails for smooth activations, whose discrete-derivative families need unbounded parameters.

body:
Let H be a Hilbert space. A bounded operator T on H is trace class (nuclear) if it is compact and ||T||_1 := sum_n s_n(T) < infinity. Equivalently: sum_i <|T| e_i, e_i> < infinity for some (hence every) orthonormal basis (e_i), where |T| = (T*T)^{1/2}, and this sum then equals ||T||_1; equivalently, T = AB with A and B Hilbert-Schmidt operators. The trace of a trace-class T is tr T = sum_i <T e_i, e_i>; this series converges absolutely for every orthonormal basis and its sum does not depend on the basis. The trace-class operators S_1(H) form a two-sided ideal of B(H) and a Banach space under ||.||_1, with ||T|| <= ||T||_2 <= ||T||_1; finite-rank operators are ||.||_1-dense in S_1(H); under the pairing (T, B) -> tr(TB), S_1(H) is isometrically the dual of the compact operators K(H) and the predual of B(H). For a positive operator T >= 0 the sum sum_i <T e_i, e_i> in [0, infinity] is basis-independent and is finite exactly when T is trace class; for operators that are not positive, convergence (even absolute convergence) of sum_i <T e_i, e_i> in one basis does not imply trace class.
H is a Hilbert space
T is a bounded linear operator on H
title: Trace Class Operator

body: Aldous-Fill Open Problem 4.49(ii) fails for every constant. For the cone G = K_1 v H over a connected d-regular graph H on n >= d+2 vertices with second adjacency eigenvalue mu_2: the diameter is Delta = 2; the simple-random-walk spectrum is {1, -1/(d+1)} on functions constant on H plus mu_i/(d+1) otherwise, so tau_2 = (d+1)/(d+1-mu_2); routing every unit flow through the hub gives psi = 2(d+1)(1 - pi_v), where pi_v = (d+1)/(n(d+2)) is the stationary mass of a base vertex, and the LP dual (edge lengths) gives inf psi >= 2(d+1) (r/(r+d)) (1 - (1+B_r)/n) for every r >= 1, where 1 + B_r bounds a ball of radius r-1 in H (B_r = d((d-1)^(r-1) - 1)/(d-2) for d >= 3). So inf psi < 2(d+1) on every finite cone, and inf psi -> 2(d+1) only as n -> infinity. Along Ramanujan families inf psi / (tau_2 Delta) -> d+1-mu_2 >= (sqrt(d-1)-1)^2 + 1, which is unbounded in d; on every finite cone the ratio stays below d+1-mu_2. Here psi is the book's plain congestion (Lemma 4.21), with no path-length weighting. The surviving positive bound is inf psi <= 65 tau_2 Delta log D with D the maximum degree, chained from the book's Lemmas 4.21, 4.13, 4.12 and 4.23.

Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: At step k the free chain has exactly k sleeping particles on N=L^d sites. Thus Var(S_B)=Var(S_Bc) and Var(S_B)<=min(|B|,N-|B|)^2/4. Taking the proper box B=[0,L-2] times the full other d-1 coordinate intervals leaves only L^(d-1) sites outside B. In d=1, B has L-1 sites and Var(S_B)<=1/4, contradicting a size-uniform lower bound c*(L-1) at any fixed positive subcritical density. The contradiction does not depend on a simulation or the full-torus endpoint. Check: On a cycle, S_B=k-I_x for the omitted site x. Therefore Var(S_B)=Var(I_x)<=1/4 exactly. Translation invariance from uniform driving even gives Var(I_x)=(k/L)*(1-k/L). Obstruction: This is a scope counterexample to the unrestricted window quantifier. It does not settle variance growth for windows small compared with the torus, nor the critical exponent.

[Proposition 17 of arXiv:2609.03386, 'Twisted Gradient Flow Approach to Vegetation-Rainfall-Bushfire Interactions Model'] Let any finite time $T>0$ be prescribed and fixed.
There exists a finite time $T_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}} \in (0,T]$, which is independent of the approximate parameters $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $\nu \in (0,1)$, 
such that the approximate initial-boundary value problem $\text{(AP)}{}_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\varepsilon,\!\nu$}}}$ admits a strong solution 
$(u,v,w,z):=(u_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\varepsilon,\!\nu$}}},v_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\varepsilon,\!\nu$}}},w_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\varepsilon,\!\nu$}}},
z_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\varepsilon,\!\nu$}}})$ on $[0,T_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}}]$ satisfying the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}\leftskip10pt
\item[(1)] $(u,v,z,w) \in (W^{1,2}(0,T_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}}\,;L^2(\Omega)) \cap 
L^\infty (0,T_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}}\,;H^1(\Omega)) \cap L^2(0,T_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}}\,;H^2(\Omega)))^4$.\\[-0.3cm]
\item[(2)] The system \{(\ref{Equation-2-7})--(\ref{Equation-2-10})\} with boundary conditions (\ref{Equation-2-11}) is satisfied in the following variational sense 
for a.e. $t \in (0,T_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}})$:

\begin{gather}

u'(t)-D_1 \Delta_N u(t)=\beta_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}}(u(t))\{c_1 v(t)-c_2 w(t)\} \quad \mbox{in} \quad L^2(\Omega),\\

M_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!z(t)$}}} v'(t)-\nu \Delta_N v(t)+v(t)=M_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!z(t)$}}}g_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}}(u,v,w\,;t) 
\quad \mbox{in} \quad L^2(\Omega),\\

w'(t)-D_2 \Delta_N w(t)+c_5 w(t)=c_6-c_7 v(t) \beta_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}} (w(t)) \quad \mbox{in} \quad L^2(\Omega),\\

z'(t)-\varepsilon \Delta_N z(t)=v'(t) \quad \mbox{in} \quad L^2(\Omega).
\end{gather}

where we define $g_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}}(u,v,w):[0,T] \rightarrow L^2(\Omega)$ by

\begin{equation*}
g_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}}(u,v,w\,;t):=v(t)\{c_3 \beta_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}} (w(t))-c_4 \beta_{\text{{\tiny $\delta$}}} (u(t))\},\quad \forall t \in [0,T].
\end{equation*}

\item[(3)] $(u(0),v(0),z(0),w(0))=(u_0,v_0,z_0,w_0) \quad \text{in} \quad (L^2(\Omega))^4$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem 3 of arXiv:2511.05218, 'On the Color Discrepancy of Spanning Trees in Random and Randomly Perturbed Graphs'] Let $p=\frac{\log n+\omega(1)}{n}$. body:
[Corollary cor:uniform of arXiv:2507.16188, 'The noisy voter model with general initial conditions'] Fix $\theta\in(0,1]$ and $q\geq2$. Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph on $n$ vertices satisfying (equation eq:expansion of the paper) for some $\mathfrak{c}_0>0$ and $0<\upalpha<1$, and $\mathcal{U}$ be the uniform distribution on $\{0,\ldots,q-1\}^V$. Then, for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$, the $q$-state noisy voter model on $G$ with noise $\theta$ started from~$\mathcal{U}$ has
\begin{equation}
t_\textsc{mix}^{\mathcal{U}}(\varepsilon) = 

\frac{1+o(1)}{4\theta}\log n\,,
\end{equation}
where the $o(1)$-term is $ O\big(\log^{-\upalpha/2} n\big)
$ with a constant 

depending on $\varepsilon,\theta,q,\mathfrak{c}_0,\upalpha$ (but not $G$), and
\begin{equation} t_\textsc{mix}(\varepsilon)=\frac{1+o(1)}{2\theta}\log n\,,\end{equation}
i.e., the asymptotic worst-case mixing time (attained by the monochromatic $\mathsf{x}_0=\bf{1}$) is twice slower.
Moreover, if $G^{(n)}$ is a sequence graphs satisfying (eq:expansion of the paper) for the same $\upalpha,\mathfrak{c}_0$, then for any $\mathsf{x}_0=\mathsf{x}_0^{(n)}$,
\[
\liminf_{n \to \infty}\frac{t_\textsc{mix}^{\mathsf{x}_0}(\varepsilon)}{t_\textsc{mix}^{\mathcal{U}}(\varepsilon)} \geq 1\,,
\]
i.e., asymptotically, no deterministic initial state $\mathsf{x}_0$ is faster than the uniform initial condition $\mathcal{U}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Definition 2 of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] For any $n \geq 0$ and $-t < -s < 0$, define the following coupling events.
\begin{multline*} \mathsf{C}(n,t,s) := \{ R^{\Lambda_{n}, -t, -s}(\alpha^+)_0 = R^{\Lambda_n, -t, -s}(\alpha^-)_0  \} \\ \text{ and }~\mathsf{C}(n,t,\geq s) := \bigcap_{-r \in [-s, 0]} \mathsf{C}(n,t,r), \end{multline*}
and 
\begin{multline*} \lfloor \mathsf{C}(n,t,s) \rfloor_k := \{ \lfloor R^{\Lambda_n(v), -t, -s}(\alpha^+)_0\rfloor_k = \lfloor R^{\Lambda_n(v), -t, -s}(\alpha^-)_0 \rfloor_k  \} \\ \text{ and }~\lfloor\mathsf{C}(n,t,\geq s)\rfloor_k := \bigcap_{-r \in [-s, 0]}  \lfloor\mathsf{C}(n,t,r)\rfloor_k . \end{multline*}

Finally, when $s = 0$, we remove it from the notation \emph{e.g.} we write:
\[  \mathsf{C}(n,t,0) := \mathsf{C}(n,t).  \]

Observe that those events are the ones appearing in Theorem~\ref{thm:cftp}, which explains their name of ``coupling events''.
We will also name their complementary events by replacing $\mathsf{C}$ by $\mathsf{NC}$ (``non-coupling'') for the four events just defined.

upper tail P(T - E T >= lambda sqrt(||x||_1/log||x||_1)) <= c_1 e^{-c_2 lambda}: requires E[e^{alpha tau_e}] < infinity for some alpha > 0
lower tail P(T - E T <= -lambda sqrt(||x||_1/log||x||_1)) <= c_1 e^{-c_2 lambda}: requires only E[tau_e^2 (log tau_e)_+] < infinity
||x||_1 > 1, lambda >= 0

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE POINT: the lower-tail condition is strictly weaker than the upper-tail condition. A statement that gives both tails under one hypothesis has merged two theorems.
WHAT IT FEEDS: this is the source of exponential decay at chi = 1/2 + delta for every delta > 0, which is what the survey's own sketch uses to reach the wandering bound xi_x <= 3/4 in a direction of curvature (an alternative route to Newman-Piza's original one, which went through Kesten's and Alexander's chi' <= 1/2).
HISTORY: the first such exponential inequality was not for general distributions, only for the nearly-Gamma class.
OPEN, per the survey: whether the sqrt(||x||/log||x||) scale on the right side is optimal.
SOURCE: Damron, M., Hanson, J. and Sosoe, P., 'Subdiffusive concentration in first-passage percolation', arXiv:1401.0917. Read in Auffinger-Damron-Hanson, '50 years of first passage percolation', arXiv:1511.03262v2 (AMS University Lecture Series 68, 2017), theorem 'thm: subdiffusive', tex lines 1512-1528.

[Theorem thm:mspacings of arXiv:2606.23547, 'The location of the largest exponential spacing and Euler’s generalized pentagonal numbers'] Let $m\geq 1$ be fixed. With probability one, there exists a unique random index
\[
R^{(m)} := \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{r\geq 1} Z_r^{(m)}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
R_n^{(m)} \stackrel{{\cal D}}{\longrightarrow} R^{(m)} \qquad\text{as } n\to\infty.
\]
The limiting distribution has full support on the positive integers. More
precisely, if
\[
q_r^{(m)} := \mathbb{P}\bigl(R^{(m)}=r\bigr), \qquad r\geq 1,
\]
then
\[
q_r^{(m)}>0 \quad\text{for every }r\geq 1, \qquad \sum_{r=1}^{\infty}q_r^{(m)}=1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Load-bearing hypothesis: local solvability of F(Du,u,x) = 0 with u = g on Γ requires D_pF(p0,z0,x0)·ν(x0) ≠ 0, i.e. the characteristic direction must be transversal to the data surface; and the initial triple must be admissible (the tangential derivatives of g must match p0). If the surface is characteristic, existence can fail outright and uniqueness can fail catastrophically. Counterexample: the equation u_x = 0 in R^2 (F(p,z,x) = p_1, so D_pF = (1,0)) with data on Γ = { y = 0 }, whose normal is ν = (0,1): D_pF·ν = 0, so Γ is characteristic — indeed the characteristics are the horizontal lines y = const, which lie IN Γ. Every C^1 solution satisfies u(x,y) = u(0,y), so u(·,0) must be constant: if g is not constant there is NO solution in any neighbourhood of a point of Γ; if g ≡ c there are infinitely many solutions u(x,y) = h(y) with h ∈ C^1 arbitrary and h(0) = c. The same pathology occurs for u_t + u_x = 0 with data prescribed on the characteristic line { x = t }. Auditor's check: before invoking local existence by characteristics, compute D_pF·ν at the point in question; for quasilinear equations a(x,u)·Du = b this is a(x0,g(x0))·ν(x0) ≠ 0, and for the Cauchy problem u_t + H(x,Du) = 0 on { t = 0 } it is automatic (the coefficient of u_t is 1).
Counterexample: F(p,z,x) = p_1 (equation u_x = 0), Γ = {y=0}
Noncharacteristic condition: D_pF(p0,z0,x0)·ν(x0) ≠ 0
Compatibility (admissibility): F(p0,z0,x0) = 0 and p0 agrees with the tangential gradient of g on Γ
Even when the conditions hold, the conclusion is only local in a neighbourhood of the point

body:
[Theorem 1 (Main theorem) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(M\) be a closed connected three-manifold which admits a locally
homogeneous metric modeled on one of \(\RR^3\), \(\Nil\), or \(\Sol\), and let
\(g(t)\), \(0\leq t<\infty\), be any immortal Ricci flow on \(M\).  In all
three cases, for every basepoint \(\widetilde m\in\widetilde M\) in the
universal cover, the lifted blowdown flows
\((\widetilde M,\widetilde m,s^{-1}\widetilde g(s\tau))\), \(\tau>0\),
converge as \(s\to\infty\) in the pointed Cheeger--Hamilton sense to a
homogeneous expanding Ricci soliton solution.  The compact
and lifted limits are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(M\) has type \(\RR^3\), then, for every \(m\geq0\), \(g(t)\)
converges exponentially fast in the \(C^m\)-norm of any fixed smooth
background metric, as \(t\to\infty\), to a flat metric on \(M\).
The Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a point.
The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the flat expanding soliton solution
\[
        (\RR^3,0,g_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\tau)),
        \qquad
        g_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\tau)=dx^2+dy^2+dz^2,
        \quad \tau>0.
\]
\item If \(M\) has type \(\Nil\), then the Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a point.  The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the Nil
expanding soliton solution
\[
        \left(\RR^3,0,
        \frac{1}{3\tau^{1/3}}
        \left(dx+\frac12 y\,dz-\frac12 z\,dy\right)^2
        +\tau^{1/3}(dy^2+dz^2)
        \right).
\]
\item If \(M\) has type \(\Sol\), then the Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a metric circle or a compact
interval of positive length.  The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the Sol expanding soliton solution
\[
        \left(\RR^3,0,e^{-2z}dx^2+e^{2z}dy^2+4\tau\,dz^2\right).
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Main theorem

body: A monad on a category C is a triple (T, eta, mu) consisting of an endofunctor T: C -> C together with two natural transformations, the unit eta: 1_C => T and the multiplication mu: T T => T (where T T denotes T composed with itself), satisfying two coherence laws. Associativity: mu o T(mu) = mu o mu_T, as natural transformations from T T T to T, meaning it does not matter whether the outer or inner pair of T's is combined by mu first. Unit laws: mu o T(eta) = mu o eta_T = 1_T, as natural transformations from T to T, so the unit acts as a two-sided identity for the multiplication.

body:
[Theorem eq:bounded-block-max of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:bounded-block-counterexample}
Fix \(p\ge3\) and an integer \(r\ge2\).  There is a symmetric,
compactly supported probability law \(\mu\) with a \(C^\infty\) density
such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
\item \(\mu\) matches the standard Gaussian moments through order \(r\)
(hence is centered and has variance one);
\item for i.i.d.\ ordered-tensor entries with common law \(\mu\), there
is a compact interval \(B\subset(0,\infty)\) for which
\begin{align}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^J(B)
 &>\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^G(B),\\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B)
 &>\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_N^G(B).
\end{align}
The reflected local-minimum inequality holds on \(-B\).
\end{enumerate}
In particular, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in[0,1/2)\),
\begin{equation}
 \max_{I\in[N]^p}|J_I|\le N^{1/2-\varepsilon}
 \qquad\text{almost surely for all sufficiently large \(N\)}.
\end{equation}
Thus an \(N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\) entrywise cutoff, or even an
 \(N\)-independent entry bound, does not restore universality of the
 unregularized annealed count.  The obstruction in this theorem is a
 coherent block involving on the order of \(N^{1/p}\) coordinates,
 rather than a single quadratic-scale entry. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Bounded-disorder mesoscopic-block counterexample

body:
Let f be n+1 times continuously differentiable on [a,b], and let x_0,...,x_n be n+1 distinct nodes in [a,b]. Let p be the unique polynomial of degree at most n with p(x_i) = f(x_i) for i=0,...,n (the Lagrange interpolating polynomial). Then for every x in [a,b], there exists a point xi, depending on x, in the smallest open interval containing x and all the nodes x_0,...,x_n, such that f(x) - p(x) = ( f^{(n+1)}(xi) / (n+1)! ) * prod_{i=0}^{n} (x - x_i).
f is n+1 times continuously differentiable on [a,b]
x_0,...,x_n are n+1 distinct interpolation nodes in [a,b]
p is the degree-at-most-n polynomial interpolating f at those nodes

Then g has at least n+2 distinct roots in [a,b]: the n+1 nodes (where f-p=0 and the product term vanishes) plus x. By repeated application of Rolle's theorem, g' has at least n+1 roots, g'' at least n roots, and so on, until g^{(n+1)} has at least one root xi in the interval spanned by x and the nodes. body: In mathematical field of combinatorial geometry, the Littlewood–Offord problem is the problem of determining the number of subsums of a set of vectors that fall in a given convex set. More formally, if V is a vector space of dimension d, the problem is to determine, given a finite subset of vectors S and a convex subset A, the number of subsets of S whose summation is in A.

degree $d$, then
\[
  \|LTR\|_{\mathfrak M_C(E)}
  \le K^d\|T\|_{\mathfrak M_C(E)}.

\]
If a new physical carrier is adjoined, then
\[
  \|T\otimes I_H\|_{\mathfrak M_C(E\otimes H)}

\]
Normalized Brauer cups, caps, permutations, and defect cuts do not
increase the module norm.

body: The expander mixing lemma intuitively states that the edges of certain $d$ -regular graphs are evenly distributed throughout the graph. In particular, the number of edges between two vertex subsets $S$ and $T$ is always close to the expected number of edges between them in a random $d$ -regular graph, namely ${\frac {d}{n}}|S||T|$.

body: [campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Hasebe and Ueda, Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018) 353-374, Problem 3.3 asks for the optimal universal C such that mu (free additive convolution) S(0,t) is unimodal for all t >= C D_mu^2 and all compactly supported mu; the paper proves C <= 4 and prints 2 <= C <= 4. Our result (id P0174, 2026-09-08): C = 1, and it is attained. The function F_R(u) = integral d mu(x) / ((x-u)^2 + R^2) has no local minimum of value <= 1/D^2. Reweighting by dQ proportional to ((x-u)^2 + y)^-2 d mu (with y = R^2), two moment inequalities for a centred variable on an interval of length D (a <= D^2/4 and b + 3 a^2 <= D^2 a) combine with the identity 1/F_R(u) = (b + 2 a y + y^2)/(a + y) and a Jensen-derived second-derivative condition (y <= 3a) to give 1/F_R(u) - D^2 <= [(y - 3a)(y + a) + (4a - D^2) y] / (a + y) <= 0. Equality is attained at the symmetric Bernoulli law with u = 0, y = 3 = 3a and 4a = 4 = D^2, where F_R(0) = 1/4 = 1/D^2 is a strict maximum and never a local minimum. Re-deriving the printed Bernoulli threshold in the authors' own frame gives t >= 4 at D_mu = 2, but since the condition reads t >= C D_mu^2 that only forces C >= 1, not the printed 2 - flagged as either the printed constant dividing by D_mu instead of D_mu^2, or a different reading. Verification as the source words it: each step re-derived (the first moment inequality from E[(X-l)(h-X)] >= 0 with centring, the second from (X-X')^4 <= D^2 (X-X')^2 for an independent copy where E(X-X')^4 = 2b + 6a^2 and E(X-X')^2 = 2a give the coefficient 3 exactly, the second-derivative formula F_R''(u)/(2Z) = 3 - 4 y E_Q[1/((X-u)^2+y)] from scratch, and the factorisation, which expands correctly term by term); and because the prior on a refereed paper slipping is that the reader misread it, the Bernoulli threshold was re-derived inside the authors' own frame with their own criterion. Prior art not cleared. mu compactly supported with support diameter D_mu S(0,t) the semicircular law of variance t y = R^2, a and b the second and fourth centred moments under the reweighted law

[Theo right of arXiv:2411.19543, 'Feller property and convergence for semigroups of time-changed processes'] The following assertions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\rm(1)] The process $\check{\mathbb{X}}$ is a standard process on $X$.
\item[\rm(2)] $F=X$.
\item[\rm(3)] $P_F u = u$ for all $u\in \mathscr{B}_b(X)$.
\item[\rm(4)] $P_F$ is injective on $\mathscr{B}_b(X)$.
\end{enumerate}

Method: Growth exponent for common subcladograms of random trees structural calculation Result: For the uniform model, sampling consistency gives an exact first-moment count: the expected number of agreeing k-subsets is binom(n,k)/(2k-3)!!. Thus P(C_n>=k) is at most this ratio. Stirling gives log of the ratio=k*[log n-2log k+2-log2]+o(k) when k is of order sqrt n. Consequently the elementary bound stops at order sqrt n, with threshold constant e/sqrt2. Check: The agreement probability is the collision probability of two uniform induced k-cladograms, exactly1/(2k-3)!!. Existence of a common larger subset implies existence of one of size k. The coalescent model has a nonuniform induced law, so its collision probability must instead be sum_T p_T^2; the uniform formula is not transferred to it. Obstruction: First moments overcount many strongly overlapping agreeing subsets. They cannot reach the stronger known exponent bound or prove convergence of log E C_n/log n. The source centroid recursion constructs particular matches and is not automatically optimal.

[Definition def:TASEPcp of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] For each $\alpha>0$ and $d\in \mathbb{N}$, we defined the \textbf{$d$-coupling} of half-space TASEPs with boundary parameter $\alpha$, as follows.

        Take the Poisson process $\Pi$, and view this as a collection of Poisson clocks on $\Lambda_d$. These clocks generate half-space TASEPs as follows.
        Let $\pi:\{(x,a)\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\times \mathbb{Z}, x+a\in 2\mathbb{Z}\} \to \Lambda_d$ be the projection map.
        Recall that we can define half-space TASEP as a Markov process $(h_t: t\ge 0)$ on the state space $\SRW_+$ (from (equation eq:defSRW+ of the paper)). 
        We flip $h_t(i) \mapsto h_t(i) + 2$ according to the Poisson clock at the vertex $\pi(i, h_t(i))$. In words, there is a flip $h_{t}(i)= h_{t-}(i)+2$ if and only if the Poisson clock at $\pi(i, h_t(i))$ rings at times $t$, and $h_t(j)=h_{t-}(i)+1$ for $j\in \{i-1, i+1\}\cap \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.

        By using the same set of Poisson clocks, we get a coupling of half-space TASEPs with boundary parameter $\alpha$, started from all initial configurations and all times.
title: Definition def:TASEPcp of arXiv:2604.10020

body: In real analysis, the Riemann integral is a rigorous definition of the integral of a function on an interval. It defines the integral by approximating the region under the graph of a function by finite sums of areas of vertical rectangles. For suitable functions, including every continuous function on a closed bounded interval, these Riemann sums approach a single limiting value as the partitions of the interval become finer. That limiting value defines the integral, and Riemann sums that are suitably close to the limit can be used as numerical approximations.
title: Riemann integral

N^{\mathrm{Wend}}_{n,d}&=N^{\mathrm{Wend}}_{n-1,d}+N^{\mathrm{Wend}}_{n-1,d-1}, \qquad n\geq d+1,\\
    N^{\mathrm{walk}}_{n,d}&=(2n-1)N^{\mathrm{walk}}_{n-1,d}+N^{\mathrm{walk}}_{n-1,d-1}, \qquad n\geq d+1,\\
    N^{\mathrm{br}}_{n,d}&=(n-1)N^{\mathrm{br}}_{n-1,d}+N^{\mathrm{br}}_{n-1,d-1}, \qquad n\geq d+2.

Let G have order n>=2 and identity e. For 0<alpha<=1 let P(x,x)=1-alpha and P(x,y)=alpha/(n-1) for y!=x. Start P at e and stop at independent T with P(T=k)=p(1-p)^k, k>=0, 0<p<1. Put b=1-alpha*n/(n-1) and a=p/(1-(1-p)*b). The Metropolis kernel M with proposal P and target Law(X_T) has spectral-gap relaxation time tau(M)=tau(P)*(1+(n-1)*a), where tau(P)=(n-1)/(alpha*n). It is strictly increasing in p. With alpha=p=1/2 both kernels are lazy and tau(M)/[n*tau(P)] tends to 2/3 as n tends to infinity. This family has proposal degree n-1 and does not settle a fixed-degree variant or a differently parametrised monotonicity question.

[Cor 247 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Assume that $L\ge1$ and that condition \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} holds. Let $\vX\equiv \vX^N$ be the process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp}
 and \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising}, and assume that condition~\eqref{e:w2.coupling.assumption} holds. Then the process $\vX^\trstar$ of Definition~\ref{d:trunc} satisfies
	\[
	\E'\Big[\|\vX(1)-\vX^\trstar(1)\|^2\Big]
	\le O(\epsilon) + o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
uniformly in $N$.

\begin{proof} 
For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$ we have $X^{\trstar,\sigma}(1,a)=X^\sigma(\tau(a),a)$, with $\tau$ the stopping time defined by \eqref{e:trstar.stopping.time}. It follows that, for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, we have
	\[
	\E'\Big[( X^\sigma(1)-X^{\trstar,\sigma}(1))^2\Big]
	\le O(1)
	\E'\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	X^\sigma(q_d)^2;\tau<1\bigg] 
	\le O(\epsilon) +o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
where the last bound is by Proposition~\ref{p:max.X.process.on.trstar.stopped.event}. Similarly,
	\[
	\E'\Big[( X^\Ising(1)-X^{\trstar,\Ising}(1))^2\Big]
	\le O(1)
	\E'\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	X^\Ising(q_d)^2;\tau^\Ising<1\bigg] 
	\le o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
again by Proposition~\ref{p:max.X.process.on.trstar.stopped.event}. The conclusion follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{L}_\text{inv};\{\theta^{(n)}_j\}_{j=1}^n}(\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.

in the case that the smallest number is  of highest rank.

M_n^*\sim e^{-\frac12}\thinspace n\approx0.6065\thinspace n,

Target 2, the mutual-information comparison only. Proof draft,
unaudited; novelty is unestablished. This does not prove a formula
for the limiting mutual information, nor an unconditional all-SNR
product-MMSE comparison.

Let N<=M<=P tend to infinity with M/N->beta and P/N->alpha,
where 1<=beta<=alpha<infinity. Let U in R^(N by M) and V in
R^(P by M) be independent arrays with centered iid entries of variance
one, using fixed entry laws with finite fourth moments q_U,q_V.
The laws of U and V may differ. Let B=U_G V_G^T/sqrt(N) use
independent standard Gaussian arrays of the same dimensions, and put
A=UV^T/sqrt(N). Independent standard Gaussian observation noise is G.

The claimed comparison is, for every fixed s>0,

 limsup [ I(A;sqrt(s)A+G)-I(B;sqrt(s)B+G) ]/(NP) <=0.       (1)

Thus whenever both normalized limiting mutual informations exist,
the Gaussian-factor value is at least the value for the iid priors
above. No existence assumption is needed for the limsup difference
statement (1). Transposition and deterministic rescaling give the
corresponding wedge P<=M<=N, with 0<alpha<=beta<=1.

## 1. Primary spectral theorem and exact normalization

N. Alexeev, F. Gotze, A. Tikhomirov, arXiv:1012.2586v2,
Theorem 1.1, PDF pp.1-2, proves convergence of the EXPECTED empirical
distribution of squared singular values of a product of independent
rectangular iid-entry matrices. The source starts with a nondecreasing
dimension chain p_0=n,p_1,...,p_m and assumes n/p_l->y_l in (0,1]
and a Lindeberg condition. We impose N<=M<=P exactly; no extension
to nonmonotone dimension chains is silently used.

Use m=2, p_0=N,p_1=M,p_2=P, X^(1)=U/sqrt(M),
X^(2)=V^T/sqrt(P). The two factors are independent; each has independent
centered entries with the required unit-variance raw variables.
The Lindeberg condition holds for each fixed finite-variance entry law
because the aspect ratios are bounded and
E[|U|^2 1_{|U|>tau sqrt(N)}] tends to zero (and similarly for V).
The limit law depends only on y_1=1/beta,y_2=1/alpha, hence is the
same for the Gaussian factors.

The normalized signal S=A/sqrt(N)=UV^T/N equals
sqrt(MP)/N times X^(1)X^(2). Its expected singular-value law therefore
has a deterministic universal weak limit mu after taking the positive
square root and this deterministic rescaling. The same holds for B.

## 2. Expected spectral convergence implies convergence in probability here

The theorem's expected-measure conclusion alone is insufficient for
the coupling lemma, so the concentration step is needed. View U and V
as N+P independent row blocks. Replacing one row of U changes S in
one row, hence by a rank-one matrix. Replacing one row of V changes
S in one column, again by rank one. In either case SS^T changes by
rank at most two: if D has rank one, (S+D)(S+D)^T-SS^T has column
space contained in the span of the column of D and S times its row.

The rank inequality for Hermitian empirical distribution functions
therefore bounds the change of F_N(x), the normalized empirical
distribution function of SS^T at any fixed x, by 2/N. Efron-Stein gives

    Var F_N(x) <= (N+P)(2/N)^2/2 = 2(N+P)/N^2 ->0.

Combining with the primary theorem at continuity points and using
monotonicity of distribution functions proves weak convergence in
probability of the empirical singular-value measures to mu.

## 3. Second moments, tail control, and W2

Put d=NP and b=M/N. Write

    T_N=||A||_F^2/(NP),   E T_N=b.

The fourth joint cumulant patterns in the dossier give the exact
variance identity

 d^2 Var T_N = d [2b^2+(M/N^2)(q_U q_V-3)]
       +d(P-1)(M/N^2)(q_U-1)
       +d(N-1)(M/N^2)(q_V-1).                           (2)

Terms on distinct rows and distinct columns vanish by independence
of the factor entries used. Under the aspect ratios above, (2) is
O(N^2), so Var T_N=O(N^-2). The empirical singular second moment of
S is

    (1/N)tr SS^T = (P/N) T_N -> alpha beta

in L^2. We must also verify that mu has exactly this moment.
Let C=max(1,|q_U-1|,|q_V-1|,|q_U q_V-3|).
For the trace of (SS^T)^2, the covariance pairings have total count
NP^2+N^2P+NP. Every fourth joint cumulant has absolute value at most
C M/N^2, and there are N^2P^2 summands. Hence

 E[(1/N)tr(SS^T)^2]
 <= b^2(NP^2+N^2P+NP)/N^3 + C M P^2/N^3 = O(1).       (3)

In particular the expected empirical singular second moments have
uniformly vanishing tails, since x^2 1_{x>L}<=x^4/L^2.
Expected weak convergence and (3) imply integral x^2 dmu=alpha beta.
Weak convergence in probability together with convergence of the
second moment now yields W2 convergence in probability to mu.

It remains to upgrade to expectation, as required by the coupling.
Pointwise Jensen gives

    E T_N^2 <= E A_11^4
      =3b^2+(M/N^2)(q_U q_V-3)=O(1).

Consequently the empirical second singular moment has a bounded
second moment. The inequality

    W2(mu_S,mu)^2 <= 2 integral x^2 dmu_S+2 integral x^2 dmu

implies uniform integrability of these squared W2 distances. Their
expectations therefore tend to zero. The Gaussian products satisfy
the same bounds. By the triangle inequality and (u+v)^2<=2u^2+2v^2,

    E W2(mu_{A/sqrt(N)},mu_{B/sqrt(N)})^2 ->0.           (4)

Independent draws of the singular-value vectors suffice in (4);
no unproved alignment or independence between individual singular
values is assumed. The optimal one-dimensional empirical W2 coupling
matches their singular values in the same order.

## 4. Orbit coupling completes the mutual-information inequality

Gaussian products B are bi-orthogonally invariant. Mix A over
independent Haar left and right orthogonal matrices to obtain tilde A.
Couple the ordered singular values as in (4) and use the same Haar
matrices for the two diagonal singular-value representatives. Then

    E||tilde A-B||_F^2/(NP)
      = (N/P) E W2(mu_{A/sqrt(N)},mu_{B/sqrt(N)})^2 ->0.

The finite-size inequalities in orbit_comparison.md give

    [I(A;sqrt(s)A+G)-I(B;sqrt(s)B+G)]/(NP)
       <= sqrt(s) [E||tilde A-B||_F^2/(NP)]^(1/2) ->0.

This proves (1).

For P<=M<=N apply the direct result to VU^T/sqrt(P) and use
A^T=sqrt(P/N) [VU^T/sqrt(P)]. Its channel parameter is s P/N,
which remains bounded and tends to a positive constant. The finite-size
bound just displayed is valid at these varying parameters as well,
so the rescaling does not require uniform convergence of a limiting MI.

## Remaining target

The source theorem is used only on monotone dimension chains.
Other aspect-ratio regions require a broader primary spectral theorem
or a justified reduction. Product-MMSE comparison follows from the
abstract lemma wherever the Gaussian limiting MI exists and is
differentiable; verifying all such hypotheses remains separate work.
The finite-size low-SNR reversal in finite_size_comparison.md is
consistent with (1), since its SNR interval shrinks with dimension.

Least-trusted steps to audit: the entropy/Wasserstein bound in the
abstract lemma; the upgrade from expected spectral convergence to
expected W2 convergence; and the normalization sqrt(MP)/N in the
application of Theorem 1.1. Let d>=1 and m>=1 be integers and D=[-1,1]^d. Suppose the real-valued function f admits the Fourier representation f(x)=integral_R^d exp(i x^T omega) F(f)(omega) domega and v_f,2=integral_R^d ||omega||_1^2 |F(f)(omega)| domega<infinity. Then there exists f_m(x)=b_0+a_0^T x+(v/m)sum_{k=1}^m b_k(a_k^T x-t_k)_+, where b_0=f(0), a_0=grad f(0), 0<=v<=2v_f,2, b_k in [-1,1], ||a_k||_1=1 and 0<=t_k<=1, such that sup_{x in D}|f(x)-f_m(x)|<=C v_f,2 sqrt(d+log m) m^(-1/2-1/d) for universal C. If instead the b_k are restricted to {-1,+1}, the paper supplies the weaker rate C v_f,2 sqrt(d+log m) m^(-1/2-1/(d+2)). The spectral moment uses the squared l1 norm, not the squared Euclidean norm. The affine part is explicit and is not bounded just by the displayed spectral moment. A standard one-hidden-layer ReLU realization can implement the linear term with two more neurons, since a_0^T x=(a_0^T x)_+-(-a_0^T x)_+.

Source-based draft, unaudited. Let Phi be a real m by n matrix of full rank min(m,n), sigma its smallest singular value, and c>0. A matrix W of the same size has deficiency margin c relative to Phi when ||W-Phi||_F<=sigma-c. Every matrix V of that size with ||V-Phi||_F<=||W-Phi||_F has smallest singular value at least c. This geometric lemma is not itself a convergence theorem and does not require whitened data or a neural-network initialization. Arora, Cohen, Golowich and Hu 1810.02281 use it in their separate whitened-data matrix-layer convergence theorem.

[Proposition 16 of arXiv:2608.07365, 'A pathwise Ito formula \\for weakly differentiable functions'] Let $\pi=(\pi_n)_{n\geq 1}$ satisfy Assumptions~1 and~2 and let
\[
F\in W^{2+,p}(\mathbb{R}^d)
   \cap W^{2,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)
   \cap W_{\mathrm{loc}}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^d),
\qquad 1<p<\infty.

Then, outside a polar set $E$ of starting points, the pathwise integral
constructed in Theorem~\ref{theorem:weakchangeofvar} agrees almost surely with the stochastic
It\^{o} integral, and
\[
\forall x\notin E,\quad 
\mathbb{P}_{x}\left( F(B(t))-F(B(0))
=
\int_0^t \nabla F(B(s))\,dB(s)
+
\frac{1}{2}[\nabla F(B),B]_{\pi}(t)\right)=1
\]
for every $t\in[0,T]$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Prop nonlinear-regression-regularity of arXiv:2608.30382, 'Convergence rates for the RMSprop optimizer with full control of the hyperparameters'] Let $\mathcal V\subseteq{\mathbb R}^d$ be nonempty and compact,
let $ r \in ( 0, \nicefrac{ 1 }{ 2 } ) $, $ \delta \in (0, \infty ) $,
and suppose that there exist nonempty compact sets
$ K_Z \subseteq \mathcal Z $ and $ K_Y\subseteq {\mathbb R}^m $ and a constant
$ B \in (0,\infty) $ with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]

\item
The random variables are compactly supported in the sense that
\begin{align}\begin{split} 
  {\mathbb P}\bigl( Z \in K_Z , \, Y \in K_Y \bigr) = 1 .
 \end{split}\end{align}

\item
For $ {\mathbb P}_Z $-almost every $ z \in K_Z $, the conditional law of $ Y $
given $ Z = z $ has a Lebesgue density~$ p_z $ satisfying
\bas{

  \| p_z \|_{ L^\infty } \le B .
}

\item
The map $ ( \theta, z ) \mapsto \Gamma^{ \theta }( z ) $ and, for every
$ i \in \{ 1, \dots, d \} $,
the map
$
  ( \theta, z ) \mapsto\frac{\partial\Gamma^\theta}{\partial\theta_i}( z )
$
are continuous on $ \mathcal V \times K_Z $.

\item
The coordinate derivatives satisfy the uniform moment lower bound
\bas{

D_r
=
\inf_{ \substack{ \theta \in \mathcal V } }
\inf_{
  1 \le i \le d
}
{\mathbb E}\biggl[
\Bigl|
\frac{\partial\Gamma^\theta}{\partial\theta_i}(Z)
\Bigr|^{r}
\biggr]
\ge \delta.
}
\end{enumerate}
Choose $R\in(0,\infty)$ such that $K_Y\subseteq B(0,R)$, let
$\omega_{m-1}$ denote the volume of the unit ball in ${\mathbb R}^{m-1}$, use the
convention $\omega_0=1$, and set
\bas{
\mu_r
&=\frac{\delta^{1/r}}{2B\omega_{m-1}R^{m-1}}
\left(\frac{1-2r}{1-r}\right)^{(1-r)/r},\\
C_X
&=\max_{\substack{\theta\in\mathcal V,\ z\in K_Z,\ y\in K_Y\\1\le i\le d}}
\left|
\left\langle
\frac{\partial\Gamma^\theta}{\partial\theta_i}(z),
\Gamma^\theta(z)-y
\right\rangle
\right|.
}
Then $\mu_r,C_X\in(0,\infty)$. The innovation $(X,U)$ defined in
(equation eq:nonlinear-regression-loss-innovation of the paper) is $(c_r,q_r)$-regular on
$\mathcal V$ with
\bas{
c_r
=\frac{(1-e^{-1})\mu_r^3}{8C_X},
\qquad
q_r=\frac{(1-e^{-1})\mu_r}{2C_X}.
}

Let d and K be positive integers, let mu_1,...,mu_K be arbitrary vectors in R^d, and let X_0 have the equally weighted mixture law K^(-1) sum_i N(mu_i,I_d). For t>0 let X_t=e^(-t)X_0+sqrt(1-e^(-2t))Z with Z~N(0,I_d) independent of X_0; denote its positive density by q_t and put mu_i,t=e^(-t)mu_i. Define w_i,t(x)=exp(-||x-mu_i,t||^2/2)/sum_j exp(-||x-mu_j,t||^2/2). Then grad_x log q_t(x)=sum_i w_i,t(x)mu_i,t-x for every x in R^d. For the additional symmetric two-component hypothesis K=2, mu_1=mu and mu_2=-mu, this is mu_t tanh(mu_t^T x)-x, with mu_t=e^(-t)mu. The tanh formula requires both opposite means and equal weights. This is a spatial-density score identity, not an identity for the DDPM parameter gradient or an exact equivalence of gradient descent with EM.

body:
[Proposition prop:imag-spectrum of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] Let $\lvert y_\pm\rangle:=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,\pm i)^{T}$ be the eigenvectors of $\sigma^y$,
with $\sigma^y\lvert y_\pm\rangle=\pm\lvert y_\pm\rangle$. Then the $2M$ orthonormal eigenpairs of
$H_{\mathrm{NUO}}$ are

\[
H_{\mathrm{NUO}}\,\bigl(\lvert y_\pm\rangle\otimes u_j\bigr)=\mp\,\alpha_j\,
\bigl(\lvert y_\pm\rangle\otimes u_j\bigr),\qquad j=1,\dots,M,
\]

so $\operatorname{spec}(H_{\mathrm{NUO}})=\{\pm\alpha_j\}$, symmetric about $0$. The Markov relaxation modes
and the quantum energy levels are the same list of numbers. The mode with semigroup
decay $e^{s(\alpha_j-1)}$ is the pair of energy levels $\pm\alpha_j$.

[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2506.11918, 'Central limit theorems for the Euler characteristic in the Random Connection Model for hig'] Let $W\in\Bf$ and $F=f(\Delta_W)$ with $\E{F}=0$, $\V{F}=1$ and $\E{F^4}<\infty$, where $f$ is a function defined for finite simplicial complexes with vertices in $\X$.
Moreover, assume that $\gamma_5,\gamma_6<\infty$.
Then it is true that
\begin{align*}
d_W(F,N) &\,\leq\, \gamma_1 + \gamma_2 + \gamma_3, \\
d_K(F,N) &\,\leq\, \gamma_1 + \gamma_2 + \gamma_3 + \gamma_4 + \gamma_5 + \gamma_6,
\end{align*}
where the quantities $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_6$ are defined by
\begin{align*}
\gamma_1 &\,:=\, 2 \Bigg[ \beta^3 \int_{W^3} \E{ \left( \Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_2,U_2)}^1F \right)^2 \left( \Lambda_{(x_2,U_2),(x_1,U_1)}^1F \right)^2}^\frac{1}{2} \\
& \qquad \enskip \times \, \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_3,U_3),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^2 \left(\Lambda_{(x_2,U_2),(x_3,U_3),(x_1,U_1)}^2 F\right)^2}^\frac{1}{2}  \; \lambda^3 \, (\d {(x_1,x_2,x_3)}) \Bigg]^\frac{1}{2} \hspace{-6pt}, \\
\gamma_2 &\,:= \left[ \beta^3 \hspace{-2pt} \int_{W^3} \hspace{-2pt} \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_3,U_3),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^2 \left(\Lambda_{(x_2,U_2),(x_3,U_3),(x_1,U_1)}^2 F\right)^2} \lambda^3 \, (\d {(x_1,x_2,x_3)}) \right]^\frac{1}{2}  \hspace{-6pt}, \\
\gamma_3 &\,:=\, \beta \int_W \E{ |\Lambda_{(x,U)}F|^3 } \; \lambda \, (\d x), \\
\gamma_4 &\,:=\, \frac{\beta}{2} \E{ F^4 }^\frac{1}{4} \int_W \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x,U)}F\right)^4 }^\frac{3}{4} \; \lambda \, (\d x), \\
\gamma_5 &\,:=\, \left[ \beta \int_W \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x,U)}F\right)^4 } \; \lambda \, (\d x) \right]^\frac{1}{2} \hspace{-6pt}, \\
\gamma_6 &\,:=\, \Bigg[ \beta^2 \int_{W^2} 6\; \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1)}F\right)^4 }^\frac{1}{2} \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^4 }^\frac{1}{2} \\
& \qquad \qquad \enskip + 3\; \E{ \left(\Lambda_{(x_1,U_1),(x_2,U_2)}^2 F\right)^4 } \; \lambda^2 \, (\d {(x_1,x_2)}) \Bigg]^\frac{1}{2}
\end{align*}
with independent marks $U,U_1,U_2,U_3\sim\Q$, which are also independent of $\Psi$.
Furthermore, we have $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_4<\infty$.

body: Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space and let f_1, f_2, f_3, ... be a sequence of Sigma-measurable functions from X to [0, infinity] (nonnegative extended-real-valued, with no domination or convergence assumed). Then the integral over X of liminf_n f_n dmu is less than or equal to liminf_n of the integral over X of f_n dmu, i.e. integral(liminf f_n) <= liminf integral(f_n). The inequality can be strict, for instance when mass escapes to infinity or travels along the domain, so equality needs an extra hypothesis such as domination.
title: Fatou's lemma

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the Erdos-Renyi random graph G(n,p) near the critical window p = 1/n + lambda n^{-4/3}, Aldous's exploration process encodes a depth-first search of the graph as a random-walk-like process Z_n(t) whose excursions above past running minima correspond exactly to the connected components, with excursion lengths equal to component sizes. After rescaling space by n^{-2/3} and time correspondingly, this process converges to a limiting process W(t) = B(t) + lambda t - t^2/2, a Brownian motion with parabolic drift, whose excursions above its running minimum encode the limiting rescaled sizes of the largest components in the critical window; the associated merging dynamics of component sizes as edges are added form the "standard multiplicative coalescent", a Markov process on sequences of masses matching the excursion structure. This gives the precise scaling limit, order n^{2/3} for the largest components with an explicit limiting joint law, for the Erdos-Renyi critical phase transition. It does not extend directly to other random graph models without re-deriving an analogous exploration or walk encoding, which may not exist in closed form, and the specific n^{2/3} spatial and n^{-1/3} time-window scaling is particular to models in the Erdos-Renyi (mean-field) universality class. Typical failure: Applying the Erdos-Renyi n^{2/3} critical scaling window and multiplicative-coalescent limit directly to a random graph model with heavy-tailed degrees, infinite third moment, or strong local clustering, where the correct scaling exponents and even the limiting process, as established for configuration models with power-law degree exponent tau in (3,4) by Bhamidi, van der Hofstad and van Leeuwaarden, differ substantially; universality of the Erdos-Renyi picture is a theorem for specific model classes, not a generic property of all critical random graphs. Canonical reference: Aldous, 1997, Annals of Probability; Aldous and Limic, 1998, Electronic Journal of Probability; Bhamidi, van der Hofstad and van Leeuwaarden, 2010, Annals of Probability.
Erdos-Renyi, or configuration-model-type with matching degree-tail conditions, random graph in the critical window p ~ 1/n + O(n^{-4/3})
a valid exploration (depth-first search) encoding of the graph as a walk whose excursions correspond to components
appropriate moment conditions, such as finite third moment of the degree for configuration models, for the walk-to-Brownian-motion scaling limit
the specific n^{2/3} spatial and n^{-1/3} time-window scaling matching the model's universality class

body: [Theorem 34 of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $[S,T]\subseteq\Rsf$ be an interval and let $n\in\Nsf$. Let $p\in [1,3)$, let $\omega$ be a control function on interval $[S,T]$, and let $X$ be an $n$-dimensional branched rough path on interval $[S,T]$ with regularity $p$ and control $\omega$. Let $M$ be a manifold, let $f: M\to R_n^2M$ be an admissible rough velocity field, and let $Y_0\in M$. Then there exists $\varepsilon\in (0,\infty)$ and an integral curve $Y:[S,(S+\varepsilon)\wedge T]\to M$ of $f$ driven by $X$ that satisfies $Y(S)=Y_0$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem 34 of arXiv:2609.01190

body: Let G be a connected linear algebraic group over a number field k. After enlarging a finite set S of places, G has a smooth model G/O_{k,S} with connected geometric fibres, and then H^1(O_v, G) = 1 for every finite place v not in S (Lang's theorem on the special fibre plus Hensel lifting). The local sets H^1(k_v, G) themselves need not vanish: for non-archimedean v, Kottwitz duality gives H^1(k_v, G) = Hom(Pic(G_{k_v}), Q/Z), a finite group (Proposition 2.12); accordingly the adelic set |BG(A_k^Sigma)| is the restricted product of the H^1(k_v, G), v not in Sigma, with respect to the trivial classes (Theorem 2.14).

body:
[Definition def:empirical_current of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] For a bounded, continuously differentiable vector field with bounded
derivatives, $U\in C^1_b(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)$, the \emph{current-type functional} (or empirical
current) is the Stratonovich integral
\begin{align}
  \overline{J}_t(U)
  \equiv \frac{1}{t}\int_0^t U(X_s)\circ\mathrm{d} X_s,
  
\end{align}
with $J_t(U)=t\overline{J}_t(U)$ the corresponding time-accumulated observable,
where $\circ$ denotes Stratonovich integration and $U(X_s)\circ\mathrm{d} X_s=\sum_i U_i(X_s)\circ\mathrm{d} X^i_s$.
title: Current functional

body:
[Lemma 17 (coefficient calculus) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $\Psi$ be real-analytic near the origin in a finite-dimensional matrix space. There is
$\delta_\Psi=\delta_\Psi(\Psi,n,s,v_{\rm A})>0$ such that, if
$\|M_1\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}+\|M_2\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}\le\delta_\Psi$, then
\begin{equation*}\tag{P}
\|\Psi(M_1)-\Psi(M_2)\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}
\ \le\ C_\Psi\|M_1-M_2\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}.
\end{equation*}
In particular
$\|\Psi(M_1)-\Psi(0)\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}\le C_\Psi\|M_1\|_{Y^{s-1,1}}$.

In addition, suppose that the pointwise ranges of $M_1,M_2$ lie in a fixed
compact convex set $\mathscr K$ on a neighbourhood of which $\Psi$ is defined and
$C^1$.  Then, for every $1\le p\le\infty$,
\[
\|\Psi(M_1)-\Psi(M_2)\|_{L^p}\le C_{\Psi,\mathscr K}\|M_1-M_2\|_{L^p},
\]
and, separately, for every $\partial\in\{\partial_t,\partial_a\}$, $1\le a\le n$,
for which the indicated weak derivative of $M_1$ belongs to $L^1_{\rm loc}$,
\[
\partial\Psi(M_1)=\Psi'(M_1)\partial M_1\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'.
\]
Consequently, the same difference estimates hold with $C_tL^p$ in place of
$L^p$. If $M\in C_tY^{s-1,1}$, then
$\Psi(M)-\Psi(0)\in C_tY^{s-1,1}$; more generally, differences
$\Psi(M_1)-\Psi(M_2)$ are continuous there by
\eqref{eq:coeff-lipschitz}. This formulation is necessary because
$Y^{s-1,1}$ is nonunital when $\Psi(0)\ne0$.

body:
[Theorem thm:transition of arXiv:2510.22778, 'Free denoising diffusion models'] Let $\rho=\tfrac12(\delta_{-a}+\delta_{a})$ and $\nu=\rho\boxplus\gamma_{v}$, $v>0$.
Then $\supp\nu$ is the union of two disjoint intervals if $v<a^{2}$ and a single
interval if $v\ge a^{2}$. The critical variance is
\begin{equation}
  v^{*}=a^{2}.
\end{equation}
In terms of the forward flow of Example~(ex:twoatom of the paper), with $a_{t}^{2}=\alpha_{t}a_{0}^{2}$
and $v_{t}=1-\alpha_{t}$, the spectrum is bimodal for
$\alpha_{t}>1/(1+a_{0}^{2})$ and unimodal thereafter.

        =

    \begin{equation}

        \begin{cases}
            \dfrac{\varsigma(\epsilon_3)\varsigma(\epsilon_4)\varsigma(\epsilon_5)}{\varsigma(\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2)}
            & n=2 \,, \\[0.95em]
            \varsigma(\epsilon_4)^2 \varsigma(\epsilon_5)^2

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); T379-C030 v1, route-failure, Target1. In the paired actual-iid truth experiment take d=1,N=3,K=3,r=2,ell=0 and zero source calibration budget. One pair has one arbitrary uniform 2-support A and one all-3 systematic S, with fair orientation; the third context is known S. Sources choose context uniformly then a truth uniformly. Condition on D_u: u>=1 copies of candidate0 in the left context followed by one copy of candidate0 in the right. A genuine certificate-consistency ERM over the VC1 orientation class, breaking ties toward the larger-count A side, has posterior orientation error e_u=2^(u-1)/(3^(u-1)+2^(u-1)), tending to zero. Certificate labels S arise only when more than r distinct truths occur; no partition tags are supplied. Under the uniform-support prior, every realized output must be exactly source-calibrated at equal-score bins in ALL four compatible worlds. Its optimal conditional posterior false mass is 7/72 for every u. The supplied-orientation oracle, retaining unknown A support, has optimal conditional mean 1/12 in either orientation. Thus the disclosure penalty is 1/72 for every u: no conditional-data upper bound by C e_u for finite C, or by a modulus tending to zero with e_u, is possible. A complete exact Fraction enumeration of all 21,147 partitions of nine atoms finds 89 robust-feasible partitions; their objectives are affine in orientation posterior pi. Endpoint minima at pi=0,1 are both 7/72 while KEEPING four-world feasibility, and a common explicit partition attains both, certifying every pi. Separate two-world oracle enumeration gives 1/12. This is a conditional-data obstruction, NOT an unconditional or fixed-world minimax lower bound; D_u becomes rare. It does not refute ERM bounds involving unresolved version-space probability. Independent mathematical/priority audits pending.
Specified finite paired source and uniform world prior
Data D_u has repeated identities but no >r distinct-truth certificate
Exact source calibration in every compatible world, not posterior-average calibration
