{"artifact_digest":"sha256:cbe9e4ed6fdc483573f34c7453ada190ee174833760b9c1ecbb8ea736f12aecc","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/cb/cbe9e4ed6fdc483573f34c7453ada190ee174833760b9c1ecbb8ea736f12aecc.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:08a01ae08f0e61ca76e7e86ee4635db12f2025829a430ca540f513027436bb66","bundle_entry_key":"multiple-top-parameter-escape","bundle_id":"population.t232-square-two-gaussian-second-step-chain-20261020","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"deep linear networks; asymmetric factorization; saddle-to-saddle dynamics","draft":"w704/bundle_004.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.deep_linear_networks:multiple-top-parameter-escape","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# T232 Target 1: dominant parameter escape with a multiple top eigenvalue

Status: proof draft (unaudited). This lemma replaces an unproved extension of the published local-minimum Gram theorem; it does not assume that extension.

## General local ODE lemma
Let F be C^2 near zero in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, F(0)=0, and J=DF(0) symmetric. Let lambda>0 be its largest eigenvalue, E its full eigenspace, and P the orthogonal projection onto E. The multiplicity of lambda is arbitrary. Fix a unit u in E. Let initial data d_epsilon satisfy
  P d_epsilon=p_epsilon u, p_epsilon>0, p_epsilon->0,
  ||d_epsilon||<=C p_epsilon.
Then the solutions shifted by tau_epsilon=log(1/p_epsilon)/lambda converge uniformly on every compact interval where the canonical solution exists to a unique path h solving
  h'=F(h),
  h(t)=exp(lambda t)u+integral_-infinity^t exp(J(t-v))N(h(v))dv,
  N(x)=F(x)-Jx.
In particular h(t)=exp(lambda t)u+O(exp(2lambda t)) backwards. The canonical path is defined on a negative half-line and extended by its ODE. Forward compact convergence is asserted only up to its maximal forward lifetime unless an independent global-existence argument is available.

## Proof
On a small ball, ||N(x)||<=K||x||^2 and ||N(x)-N(y)||<=K(||x||+||y||)||x-y||. In shifted time the initial time is -tau. The free evolution obeys
  ||exp(J(t+tau))d||<=C exp(lambda t), t>=-tau,
since J is symmetric and every eigenvalue is <=lambda. In a weighted supremum ||x(t)||exp(-lambda t), Duhamel bounds the quadratic term by
  (K/ lambda) A^2 exp(lambda T)
on [-tau,T] whenever the weighted norm is <=A. Choose a fixed negative T so a continuity bootstrap from C to 2C cannot cross 2C, and so the resulting ball stays in the local domain of F. Thus ||x_epsilon(t)||<=2C exp(lambda t) there, uniformly in epsilon.

The top part of the free evolution is exactly exp(lambda t)u. For an eigenspace with eigenvalue nu<lambda its free part has norm bounded by
  C p_epsilon^(1-nu/lambda) exp(nu t),
which tends to zero uniformly on each fixed shifted compact interval. No convergence of the bounded normalized lower initial components is needed. On each such interval, the solutions and their derivatives are uniformly bounded. Diagonal Arzela-Ascoli therefore yields a locally uniform subsequential limit on (-infinity,T].

The nonlinear integrand is bounded uniformly by
  exp(lambda(t-v)) K(2C)^2 exp(2lambda v)
    =K(2C)^2 exp(lambda t)exp(lambda v),
which is integrable at minus infinity. A fixed-tail split passes Duhamel to the displayed Volterra equation. Its operator is a contraction in the exp(lambda t) weighted ball on a sufficiently negative half-line: its Lipschitz constant is bounded by a fixed multiple of exp(lambda T)/lambda. Thus its solution is unique in the class O(exp(lambda t)); for two possible bounds choose a common larger bound and a more negative T. Existence follows from the subsequential limit. Uniqueness identifies every subsequential limit, proving whole-family convergence. Integrating the same quadratic bound gives the O(exp(2lambda t)) backward remainder. Finite-interval continuous dependence extends convergence along every compact part of the canonical solution. QED, subject to independent review.

## The two essential restrictions
The normalized FULL top projection must be fixed (or converge to u with an explicit equivalent argument). A rotating top vector need not converge when the top eigenspace has dimension above one. Also ||d||=O(p) cannot be omitted: for J=diag(2,1), initial data (p,sqrt(p)) have top projection p e1 but at the shift log(1/p)/2 their lower coordinate stays of order one and changes the limit. This is an exact linear boundary, not numerical evidence.

## Application to the actual rank-one saddle
Use the full parameter space of B,A and its Euclidean factor metric, centered at theta1=[zstar,0,...,0], where zstar is a nonzero balanced rank-one critical factor. The factor flow is negative gradient of the scalar loss, so its Jacobian is symmetric. Direct differentiation at zero dormant columns makes it block diagonal:
  Jfull=diag(Jact,Lstar,...,Lstar).
C009 proves largest eigenvalue(Jact)=r<s. Each frozen dormant block has eigenvalues s,0,0,-s. Thus the full largest eigenvalue is s, with multiplicity w-1, and its full eigenspace consists of v times arbitrary dormant hidden rows. A nonminimal active saddle does not change this strict spectral separation.

At the aligned arrival supplied by C009, the active endpoint error is O(p^2), the dormant norm is O(p), and the row v^T X has norm p. Make a hidden orthogonal rotation of the DORMANT columns only, fixed for the subsequent flow, taking that row to (p,0,...,0). This leaves theta1 unchanged. The full top parameter projection is now EXACTLY p times the fixed vector u having v in the first dormant column and zero elsewhere; total parameter error is O(p). The general lemma applies with lambda=s even though its top eigenvalue is multiple. This is a parameter theorem; it does not smuggle a simple-top assumption into a multiple-top Hessian.

## The canonical path has a nonzero width-two realization
The subspace with only the active and first dormant columns nonzero is invariant under the factor ODE. It is also preserved by J and the Volterra map because every zero factor column has identically zero derivative. Uniqueness therefore makes the canonical path have exactly this width-two realization. The backward expansion gives
  z(t)=zstar+O(exp(2st)),
  x(t)=exp(st)v+O(exp(2st)).
The input part of v is a nonzero residual singular vector perpendicular to astar, and its output part is perpendicular to bstar. The input and output square factors consequently have determinants with nonzero leading terms of order exp(st); both are invertible for all sufficiently negative finite t. This proves a nonzero rank-two canonical mode; rank is not inferred from limits of finite-rank matrices alone.

The factor balance matrix is conserved and tends to its value at theta1, which is zero, so the canonical width-two factors are exactly balanced. In the oriented endpoint frames, v=(delta lperp;rperp)/sqrt(2) up to simultaneous sign, with delta=sign det M by C003's determinant identity. The graph determinant of the canonical two-column plane is therefore delta at sufficiently negative times and remains so. Its loss is strictly below the first critical loss because the path is nonconstant gradient flow, and that critical loss is strictly below C(0) by the stationary energy identity in C010. C010 therefore gives global forward existence, factor convergence and endpoint product M for this canonical path.

## Clocks and original factor rotations
The parameter shift in this lemma is log(1/p)/s. At the actual C009 arrival, z-zstar=O(p^2) and v perpendicular to zstar, so
  a=v^T Z v=p^2+(v^T z)^2=p^2+O(p^4).
Therefore log(1/a)/(2s)-log(1/p)/s=O(p^2)->0. The parameter and Gram clocks agree asymptotically. Compose the original fixed seed rotation with the arrival's dormant rotation; their product is one rotation per alpha, fixed in time, so the asserted factor convergence has the required form.

## Scope
This establishes the central local escape link IF the upstream C006/C008/C009 hypotheses and proofs hold. Those analytic arguments and this lemma all await independent review. The multiple-top extension and canonical width-two realization are written explicitly; neither is certified by an algebra-only check or by the published simple-top theorem. A separate final composition must state data and initialization assumptions and prove the first canonical orbit has a nonzero critical endpoint. Owner draft: independently checked proof (C014 v1). Let d>=2, p=d-1, S a nondegenerate centered p-simplex, A invertible, c(y)=c_0+y*c_1, and r(y)=alpha+(beta-alpha)y with alpha,beta>=0 and alpha+beta>0. The uniform law on C={(y,z):0<=y<=1, z in c(y)+A(r(y)S)} is n-CM for every n>=d+1. This includes simplex prisms and truncated simplex pyramids/frustums and invertible affine images. The height density is proportional to r(y)^(d-1), so the same monotone-height mix and radius bound as for ellipsoidal frustums apply. Given the heights, d*max_i rho_i<=sum_i rho_i, and the measurable weighted-simplex theorem couples the section laws with zero sum. Affine section centers give the full centroid sum. General nonhomothetic/nonaffine sections remain outside the argument; novelty UNKNOWN.

Fixed invertible affine section shape
Affine center and affine nonnegative radius on [0,1], positive endpoint sum
n integer >=d+1

[Lemma lem:chirurgieloc of arXiv:2601.20502, 'Optimal matching under size priority'] Fix a rooted graph in $\Omega^{\mathrm{very\, good}}$ then fix a family of weights $w(e)_{e \in E(G_n)}$ and pick $e_1 \in B_H(G_n,o_n)$.
         Assume that $i(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_1})+i(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_1})=1$.
         Then there exists $e_2 \sim e_1$ such that $i(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_2})+i(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_2})=1$ and:
         \begin{itemize}
             \item If $e_1\in M_{\mathrm{opt}}$ then there exists $a>0$ such that setting $w'(e_2)=a$ and $w'=w$ elsewhere gives $\max(Z_-(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_2}),Z_+(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_2}))+\max(Z_-(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_2}),Z_+(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_2}))<w'(e_2)=a.$
             \item If $e_1 \notin M_{\mathrm{opt}}$, then there exists $b>0$ such that setting $w'(e_1)=b$ and $w'=w$ elsewhere gives $\max(Z_-(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_1}),Z_+(\overset{\rightarrow}{e_1}))+\max(Z_-(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_1}),Z_+(\overset{\leftarrow}{e_1}))<w'(e_1)=b$.
         \end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Author-checked lemma, not independently reviewed: suppose a Galton-Watson tree has an equivariant measurable finite-valued class c(T), its root class is a deterministic function of the root offspring number and child-class vector, and some child always has the root class. Choose uniformly among children of the root class. Then each conditional law GW(.|c=a) of positive mass is stationary for the selected-subtree kernel, and GW itself is stationary.
Finite nonzero offspring almost surely
A Borel subtree class as specified
At least one child has the parent class almost surely

Let (M,g) be a connected Riemannian manifold with induced distance function d. The following are equivalent: (1) (M,d) is a complete metric space; (2) M is geodesically complete, i.e. for every p in M the exponential map exp_p is defined on all of T_pM; (3) M is geodesically complete at some single point p, i.e. exp_p is defined on all of T_pM for at least one p; (4) every closed and bounded subset of M is compact. If any of these hold, then any two points of M can be joined by a minimizing geodesic, a geodesic segment whose length equals the distance between its endpoints.
M is a connected smooth Riemannian manifold

[Proposition p:mppmix_double of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Fix $p,q \in \mathbb{N}$ and $r \in (0, \infty)$. Assume that $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ satisfies condition~(ii:mppmix_double of the paper)  of Lemma~(p:mppmixcl_double of the paper). Let $\xi: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \to \mathbb{K}'$ be a marking function such that $\xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}) =  \xi^{(r)}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}) =\xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}\cap B_r(x))$ for all $(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mu}) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}}$. Consider the marked point process $\dbtilde\mathcal{P}=\sum_{x \in \mathcal{P}} \delta_{(x,V(x))}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d\times \mathbb{K}'$ where $V(x) := \xi(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})$.  

Then, for  all $f \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^p),$   $g \in \mathbb{B} ((\mathbb{K}')^q)$, for almost all $\bk x1{p+q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d(p+q)}$ such that $s:=d(\bk x1p,\bk x{p+1}{p+q}) >4r$, and with ${w}_0= 4(p+q)\theta_d r^d$
we have
\begin{align} \nonumber
& \Big| \mathbb {E} _{\bk x1{p+q}}[f(\bk V1{p})g(\bk V{p+1}{p+q})]\rho^{(p+q)}(\bk x1{p+q}) -
\mathbb {E} _{\bk x1p}[f(\bk V1p)] \rho^{(p)}(\bk x1{p}) \; \mathbb {E} _{\bk x{p+1}{p+q}}[g(\bk V{p+1}{p+q})]\rho^{(q)}(\bk
x{p+1}{p+q}) \Big|
\\
&\le 
\phi( \frac{s}{2})\sum_{l=1}^\infty \frac{w_0^l}{l!}  C_{l+p+q}
=:\phi( \frac{s}{2})\hat{C}_{p+q}<\infty.
\end{align}

Thus the marked point process
 $\dbtilde\mathcal{P}$ satisfies the inequality~(equation e.Bmppmixing of the paper)  in Definition~(B-omega-mixing of the paper)(Bmixing of the paper) 
for $s>4r$, with  $\omega_{p+q}(s):=\hat C_{p+q}\phi(s/2)$ where  $p,q,\phi$ are as above.

[Lemma le:replace of arXiv:2604.21142, 'Gaussian fluctuations for Internal DLA on cylinders'] Fix $y_0 > 0$ and $\n > 0$, and assume $a_N \gg \log N + \log_+ a_N$ as $N \to \infty$ and that Assumption~(a:spectral of the paper) holds for each $2 \leq k \leq K$. Let $T \coloneqq N \lfloor a_N y_0\rfloor$, $h \coloneqq T/N$, and let $(\Delta_N)_{N \geq 1}$ be positive reals satisfying $\Delta_N = O\!\left(\sqrt{a_N(\log N + \log_+ a_N)}\right)$ and
	\[ {\ensuremath{\mathbb P}} \big(R_{\lfloor h - \Delta_N\rfloor} \subseteq A(T) \subseteq R_{h + \Delta_N}\big) \geq 1 - N^{-\n} \qquad \text{for } N \text{ large enough}\,. \]
Let $\phi : V_N \times {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}}  \to {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}} $ be a test function of the form $\phi(x, y) = \sum_{k=2}^K \a_k(y)\, f_k^N(x)$, where each $\a_k : {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}}  \to {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}} $ is independent of $N$ and has bounded derivative in a neighbourhood of $y_0$; let $\varphi(x, y) \coloneqq \phi(x, y/a_N)$, and let $\psi$ be the discrete harmonic extension of $\varphi$ defined in~(equation eq:truepsi of the paper). Then
	\[ \frac{1}{\sqrt{Na_N}}\,\langle \! \langle D_T, \varphi - \psi\rangle \! \rangle \;\longrightarrow\; 0 \qquad \text{in probability as } N \to \infty\,. \]

[Lemma zygmund-marcinkiewicz of arXiv:2411.07737, 'On Asymptotic Behavior of Extinction Moment of Critical Bisexual Branching Process in Rand'] Let $\{ \xi_n \}_{n = 1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of i.i.d. r.v. with $\ER \abs*{\xi_n}^{\alpha} < \infty$, where $1 \leq \alpha \leq 2$, and $\ER \xi_n = 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
    Then, there is a constant $c_{\alpha} > 0$ such that
    \[
        \left( \ER \abs*{ \sum_{i = 1}^n \xi_i } \right)^{\alpha}
        \leq \ER \abs*{ \sum_{i = 1}^n \xi_i }^{\alpha}
        \leq c_{\alpha} \sum_{i = 1}^n \ER \abs*{\xi_i}^{\alpha}.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequality,~\cite{Marcinkiewicz1938}

body:
[Prop P:two-point-bd of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $n \in \mathbb{N}$, parameter $\alpha \ge 1/2 - n^{-1/6}$, and $x, y, z_0 \in \llbracket0, n/100 \rrbracket$, $a > 0$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
	
C_0 \max \left(\frac{z_0^2}{n}, \frac{z_0 |y-x|}{n}, z_0(1/2 - \alpha)\vee 0 \right) < a < C_* z_0,
\end{equation}
where $C_0>0$ is a universal constant, and $C_*>0$ is any large enough number.
Then for a constant $c>0$ depending only on $C_*$, we have
$$
\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{z \in\llbracket0,z_0 \rrbracket} \left|\bar X[x, 1; y + z, n]_\textsf{L} - \bar X[x, 1; y, n]_\textsf{L} \right| \ge a \right) \le 2\exp(- c a^2/z_0) + 2 \exp(-c \sqrt{n}).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop P:two-point-bd of arXiv:2604.10020

[Cor 15 of arXiv:2604.25725, 'What is The Probability That A Random Graph With A Given Degree Sequence is Connected?'] Fix $0<\eps<10^{-6}$ and let $\cD$ be such that $m$ is large enough and $n_1,n_2 \le 10^{-6} m$.
    Let $v\in[n]$ be fixed. Then the probability that there exists an $i$  with  $1\leq i \leq m$  such that  $2|E(H_{i-1})|+|X_{i-1}| \leq \eps m$, and such that neither
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
    \item $X_i \ge 0.9\sum_{j=1}^i d_j(v_j)-\frac{m}{\log m}$, nor
    \item  $D^*\ge \epsilon m$ and 
    $H_i$ contains a vertex of degree at least $\sqrt{m}(\log m)^{-2}$
\end{enumerate}
holds, is at most $e^{-m^{1/11}}$.
title: Cor 15 of arXiv:2604.25725

[Proposition 16 ($K_\infty$ is generically not Hilbert--Schmidt) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Let $k_\infty(\xi,\eta)$ be the limiting boundary kernel of the operator programme of Section 1.1, so that $k_\infty(\xi,\eta)\asymp
u_h(B_{\xi\wedge\eta})^{- eta}$ for some $ eta>0$ determined by the transmission/Martin exponents, where $\xi\wedge\eta$ is the confluence depth. Then
 egin{align*}
\|K_\infty\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2&=\iint_{\partial T	imes\partial T}|k_\infty(\xi,\eta)|^2\,d
u_h(\xi)\,d
u_h(\eta)\
&\asymp\sum_{n\ge0} r(T)^{2n eta}\cdot
u_h\otimes
u_h ig(\{|\xi\wedge\eta|=n\} ig)\asymp\sum_{n\ge0} r(T)^{n(2 eta-1)}
\end{align*}
whenever $2 eta\ge1$ and $g$ is supercritical ($ r(T)>1$). For the Martin-kernel construction one has $ eta\ge1$, since $K(x,\cdot)\asymp
u_h(B_{|x|})^{-1}$ on the cylinder of $x$ (the Martin kernel is the harmonic-measure density $d

body:
[Proposition 2.5 of arXiv:2512.19517v1, 'Spiking and Resetting' (Cédric Bernardin and Vsevolod Vladimirovich Tarsamaev); numbered Proposition 6 in the earlier card; corrected to the increment form]

## Proposition 2.5 (increment form)

Assume the standing hypotheses of Section 1: (f,h\in C^2([0,1])), (f(1)<0<f(0)), (h(1)=0), (h'(1)\ne0), and (h(x)>0) on ([0,1)). Let

\[
e_1^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t^\varepsilon>y_*^\varepsilon\},\qquad
e_2^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge e_1^\varepsilon:X_t^\varepsilon=0\},
\]

and define the post-(e_1^\varepsilon) holding time

\[
d_2^\varepsilon:=e_2^\varepsilon-e_1^\varepsilon.
\]

Then, for every (t\ge0),

\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathbb P(d_2^\varepsilon>t)=e^{f(1)t},
\]

so (d_2^\varepsilon\Rightarrow \operatorname{Exp}(-f(1))).

The proof in the paper restarts the deterministic flow at (e_1^\varepsilon) with local time (s=0); its displayed survival integral is therefore for (d_2^\varepsilon), not the absolute epoch (e_2^\varepsilon). The source says that after the stopping time “the process evolves deterministically until the next reset” (v1 HTML lines 252-257), which is precisely an increment statement.

## Later alternating holding-time sentence

For the recursively defined epochs (e_k^\varepsilon), the strong Markov property applies to the increments

\[
e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon-e_{2k}^\varepsilon,
\qquad
e_{2k+2}^\varepsilon-e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon,
\]

not to the increasing absolute epochs themselves. The alternating increments are the quantities that can be independent and have the two respective holding-time laws. Any downstream card should preserve this distinction.

## Why the absolute-time statement cannot hold as written

For every (\varepsilon), (e_2^\varepsilon\ge e_1^\varepsilon), hence

\[
\mathbb P(e_2^\varepsilon>t)\ge\mathbb P(e_1^\varepsilon>t).
\]

This stochastic order must persist at continuity points of any weak limits. Yet the paper permits (f(x)=1-3x) and (h(x)=1-x), for which (f(0)=1) and (f(1)=-2). Its two displayed absolute-time limits would require (e^{-2t}\ge e^{-t}) for (t>0), an immediate contradiction. No additional relation between (f(0)) and (f(1)) is present in the standing hypotheses.

body: A standard Brownian motion, or Wiener process, is a real-valued stochastic process (W_t)_{t >= 0} on a probability space such that (i) W_0 = 0 almost surely; (ii) for 0 <= s < t the increment W_t - W_s is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance t - s; (iii) increments over disjoint time intervals are independent; (iv) almost every sample path t |-> W_t is continuous. Existence is Wiener's theorem (constructed for instance by the Levy-Ciesielski series or as the Kolmogorov-extension limit with continuity from Kolmogorov's criterion, since E|W_t - W_s|^4 = 3 (t - s)^2). Consequences packaged with the definition: the covariance is E[W_s W_t] = min(s, t); paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable and have unbounded variation on every interval, with quadratic variation t; Brownian scaling c^{-1/2} W_{c t}, time inversion t W_{1/t}, and reflection are again Brownian motions; W is a continuous martingale and a Markov process with transition density the Gaussian kernel. Conditions (i)-(iii) characterise the finite-dimensional laws; (iv) selects the continuous version, which is the object meant in every theorem about paths.

Fix a finite class set Y, positive weights w_i summing to1, means mu_i in R^d, and a shared positive-definite covariance Sigma. Under the forward Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model dU_s=-U_s ds+sqrt(2)dW_s, put Sigma_s=exp(-2s)*Sigma+(1-exp(-2s))*I and p_s(x,i)=w_i*N(x;exp(-s)*mu_i,Sigma_s). Let p_s(x)=sum_i p_s(x,i) and q_s(i|x)=p_s(x,i)/p_s(x). Fix a class y, finite horizon T>0 and a constant guidance increment eta>=0. In increasing sampling time t, s=T-t, define guided DDIM by dX_t/dt=b_eta(X_t,t), b_eta(x,t)=x+grad_x log p_s(x,y)+eta*grad_x log q_s(y|x). Unguided DDIM is dZ_t/dt=b_0(Z_t,t). Let Phi_t be the guided flow and J_t(a)=D_a Phi_t(a), with J_0=I. Let M_t solve M_dot=(I-Sigma_(T-t)^(-1))*M, M_0=I; the unguided flow is affine Z_t=M_t Z_0+xi_t. For all a in R^d and 0<=t<=T, 0<det J_t(a)<=det M_t. For the fixed model and finite horizon, det J_t(a) is bounded above and bounded away from zero uniformly in a and t. This is the determinant comparison used in the paper's entropy proof; its constants are not dimension-free or uniform over eta.

body: Brouwer's fixed-point theorem is a fixed-point theorem in topology, named after L. E. J. (Bertus) Brouwer. It states that for any continuous function f mapping a nonempty compact convex set to itself, there is a point x_0 such that f(x_0) = x_0. The simplest forms of Brouwer's theorem are for continuous functions f from a closed interval I in the real numbers to itself or from a closed disk D to itself. A more general form than the latter is for continuous functions from a nonempty convex compact subset K of Euclidean space to itself.
title: Brouwer's fixed-point theorem is a fixed-point theorem in topology, named after L

[Prop eq:q(t|s) of arXiv:2604.20629, 'Rates of forgetting for the sequentially Markov coalescent'] The SMC jump chain $(X_{n})$ defined by ((eq:Xn+1 of the paper)) has
transition density
\begin{equation}
q_{\mathrm{SMC}}(t\mid s)=\frac{e^{-t}\left(e^{s\wedge t}-1\right)}{s},\quad s>0, t>0.
\end{equation}
It is irreducible and reversible with respect to 
\[
\mu(dt)=te^{-t} dt,
\]
and $\mu$ is the unique invariant probability measure.

The SMC' jump chain $(X'_{n})$ has transition density
$q_{\mathrm{SMC}'}(t\mid s)$ given above. 
It is irreducible and reversible with respect to 
\[
\mu'(dt)=\frac{3}{8} \bigl(2t+1-e^{-2t}\bigr)e^{-t} dt.
\]
and $\mu'$ is the unique invariant probability measure. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop eq:q(t|s) of arXiv:2604.20629

    \widehat{\mathfrak C}_{q,r,s}^{p}
    \mid Y_{1:N}
\right\}
\ge1-\alpha_T
\right]
\ge1-\alpha_D.

\end{equation}
Consequently, by independence of the calibration and deployment experiments,
with
\[
    \alpha
    =
    1-(1-\alpha_D)(1-\alpha_T),
\]
\begin{equation}
\inf_{\xi\in\mathfrak P^p_{q,r}(s)}
\mathbb P_\xi^{N,T}
\left\{
    \vartheta(\xi)
    \in
    \widehat{\mathfrak C}_{q,r,s}^{p}
\right\}
\ge1-\alpha.

\end{equation}

For $N$ above the fixed block threshold of the robust calibration-moment
construction, define
\begin{equation}
\rho_N(s)
=
C\left[
    (s\wedge\epsilon_N)
    +
    \left(s\wedge\frac{\epsilon_N}{s}\right)
    +
    \left(s\wedge\frac{\epsilon_N}{s^2}\right)
\right].

\end{equation}
Any two dictionaries retained by the same nonempty calibration region have
quotient-dictionary distance at most $\rho_N(s)$.  If
$\epsilon_N\le CN^{-1/2}$, then
\begin{equation}
    \rho_N(s)
    \le
    C\left(
        s\wedge\frac{1}{\sqrt N\,s^2}
    \right).
    
\end{equation}
Below the block threshold, retaining the full compact shell yields the same
order after adjustment of fixed constants.

For every realization,
\begin{align}
\operatorname{diam}_{\mathrm{pr}}
\left(
    \widehat{\mathfrak C}_{q,r,s}^{p}
\right)
\le{}&
C\rho_N(s)
\notag\\
&+
Cs\,
\mathbf 1
\left\{
    2\tau_{T,q}\ge m_S(\rho_N(s))
\right\}
\notag\\
&+
C\,
\mathbf 1
\left\{
    2\tau_{T,q}\ge m_G(\rho_N(s))
\right\}.

\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Coverage and resolution of the cross-dictionary correspondence

Let P_X be an input probability law and P_F a law on measurable functions F:X->{-1,1}, with measurable evaluation. Draw F and F_prime independently from P_F. Draw X_1,...,X_m iid from P_X, independently of both functions, where m>=1 is an integer; each sampled function is held fixed throughout the batch. Define CP_infinity = E_{F,F_prime}[(E_X F(X)*F_prime(X))^2]. Define CP_m=E[((1/m) sum_{i=1}^m F(X_i)*F_prime(X_i))^2]. Then CP_m=1/m+(1-1/m)*CP_infinity. Equivalently, for K(x,x_prime)=E_F[F(x)*F(x_prime)], CP_infinity=E_{X,X_prime}[K(X,X_prime)^2], with X,X_prime independent under P_X. Thus0<=CP_infinity<=1, CP_m>=1/m and CP_1=1. No balanced-label assumption is needed for these identities.
Binary-valued functions; measurable evaluation and the stated probability laws.
The input batch is iid and independent of two iid function draws.
The same function pair is reused throughout the batch; it is not redrawn per input.

\(
(Z_k)_{k\ge0}
\)
be a Galton--Watson process with 
\(
Z_0=1
\),
offspring distribution \(\xi\), and mean \(m=\mathbb{E}\xi>1\).
Assume that \(\xi\) is bounded. Then, for every 
\(
1<\beta<m
\),
\(
Z_k\ge \beta^k
\)
for all sufficiently large \(k\), almost surely on the survival event
\[
S=\{Z_k>0\text{ for all }k\ge0\}.
\]

[Definition def:vary of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] Let $\mathcal W$ be a white noise with respect to some filtration $\mathcal F$. Let $\overline{\delta}$ be a drift function with respect to $\mathcal F$. We call a collection of continuous processes $\mathcal S=(\mathcal S_{r,x}(a),\, x\ge r)_{r\in {\mathbb R},a\ge 0}$ a ${\rm BESQ}(\overline{\delta})$ flow driven by $\mathcal W$ if 
   
    (1) The restriction of $\mathcal S$ to each $A_i$ is a ${\rm BESQ}^{\delta_i}$ flow driven by $\mathcal W$.

    (2) The regularity conditions of Definition (def:BESQflow of the paper) hold.
 

If $E$ is a (possibly random) Borel set, we call $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow killed on $E$ the flow obtained from the $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow by absorbing the flow line $\mathcal S_{r,\cdot}(a)$ at $0$ at time $\inf\{x \in E\cap (r,\infty) \,:\, \mathcal S_{r,x}(a)=0\}$.

 If $E={\mathbb R}$, we will simply say that $\mathcal S$ is a killed  $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow. We call general  $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow a $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow or a  killed $\rm BESQ(\overline{\delta})$ flow.
title: Definition def:vary of arXiv:2411.04773

[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2609.03191, 'On lifting representations and actions on curves of the metacyclic groups $C_{p^s}\rtimes '] Let $V$ be a $k[H]$-module. Let $R$ be such that it contains $R_s$. Let $t\in\mathbb Z\setminus p\mathbb Z$. Let $o$ be the order of $[t]_{p^s}\in (\mathbb Z/p^s\mathbb Z)^{\times}$. Then the following properties hold.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} The following statements are equivalent.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (1.a)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is cyclic.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.b)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is indecomposable.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.c)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ is strongly indecomposable.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.d)} We have $\imath_V\in\{0,1\}$.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.e)} Each lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ is cyclic.

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (1.f)} Each lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ is cyclic and strongly indecomposable.

\medskip
{\bf (2)} The $k[H]$-module $V$ has a lift $\mathcal H$ to $R$ which is an end-hull of $V$ and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules. Moreover, if $\jmath_V=0$, then we can also assume that $r_{\mathcal H}=0$.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} Suppose that $V$ is cyclic. Let $\mathcal V_1$ and $\mathcal V_2$ be two lifts of $V$. Then the $R[H]$-modules $\mathcal V_1$ and $\mathcal V_2$ are isomorphic if and only if the $B[H]$-modules $\mathcal V_1\otimes_R B$ and $\mathcal V_2\otimes_R B$ are isomorphic.

\smallskip
{\bf (4)} The $k[H]$-modules $V$ and $V^{(t)}$ are isomorphic.

\smallskip
{\bf (5)} The following statements are equivalent.

\medskip\noindent
{\bf (5.a)} There exists a lift $\mathcal V$ of $V$ to $R$ which is $t$-invariant and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules (resp.\ which is $t$-invariant and a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules with $r_{\mathcal V^H}=0$).

\smallskip\noindent
{\bf (5.b)} For each $b\in\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket\setminus o\llbracket1,\lfloor\frac{p^s}{t}\rfloor\rrbracket$ such that $\mu_V(b)\neq 0$, $\mu_V(b)$ is a sum of cardinals of orbits of the action of $[t]_{p^s}$ on $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s)$ (resp.\ $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s^{\ast})$), equivalently of subsets $\Phi$ of $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s)$ (resp.\ $\mathcal P_b(\Xi_s^{\ast})$) with $[t]_{p^s}\cdot\Phi=\Phi$.

\medskip
{\bf (6)} Suppose that $p$ is odd, $[t]_{p^s}=[p^s-1]_{p^s}$ (equivalently, $o=2$) and $\dim_k(V)$ is even. Then $V$ has a lift to $R$ which is a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules and is $t$-invariant.

\medskip
{\bf (7)} Suppose that $p$ is odd, $[t]_{p^s}=[p^s-1]_{p^s}$, $\mu_V(d)$ is even for each odd $d\in\llbracket1,p^s\rrbracket$, and $\jmath_V=0$. Then $V$ has a lift $\mathcal V$ to $R$ which is a direct sum of cyclic $R[H]$-modules and is $t$-invariant with $r_{\mathcal V}=0$.

[Lemma 18 (Ricci quadratic estimate; cf.\ Lemma A.1 of \cite{Brendle2019}, Lemma 4.7 of \cite{Chen2024}) of arXiv:2608.26598, 'Pinching cones for positive isotropic curvature in dimensions seven and eight'] Let $0\le\zeta\le1$ and $0<\varrho\le1$, and let $H$ be a symmetric two-tensor whose largest
    eigenvalue is at most $\frac12\mathrm{tr}\,H$ and whose two smallest eigenvalues have sum at
    least $\frac{2(1-\zeta)}{n}\mathrm{tr}\,H$. Then, with
    $H^0=H-\frac1n\mathrm{tr}(H)\,\mathrm{id}$, every orthonormal pair $\{e_1,e_2\}$ satisfies
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{n-2}{n}\,\mathrm{tr}(H)\,\bigl(H_{11}+H_{22}\bigr)
        -\varrho\bigl((H^0)^2_{11}+(H^0)^2_{22}\bigr)
        \ge\frac{2}{n^2}\left((n-2)(1-\zeta)-2\zeta^2\varrho\,
        \frac{n^2-2n+2}{(n-2)^2}\right)\mathrm{tr}(H)^2.
    \end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

DRAFT, proof (unaudited), T318-C3 version 2 sections 1 and 4; no priority claim. Let p/d->psi>0, let f_j be independent uniform vectors on the sphere of radius sqrt(d), and let g~N(0,I_d) be independent. Fix a globally Lipschitz activation rho with E rho(G)=0 and v=E rho(G)^2>0 for G~N(0,1). Define W_jk=f_j^T f_k/d and C_jk=E_g rho(f_j^T g/sqrt(d))rho(f_k^T g/sqrt(d)). With b=(E G rho(G))^2 and tau=v-b, C=tau I+bW+E where E_jj=0, |E_jk|<=tau|W_jk|^2 and E||E||_F^2<=3 tau^2 p(p-1)/[d(d+2)]. The Schur product contraction gives ||C||<=v||W||. Hence C has limiting empirical law law(tau+b MP_psi), since its resolvent trace differs from that of tau I+bW by at most ||E||_F/(sqrt(p) s^2) at every s>0. Operator-norm equivalence is not asserted. For general sets contractibility of the intersections is not enough; the usual hypotheses are open sets, or closed convex sets.

The planar set C={(x,y): x>0 and |y-x^2|<1} is open, connected and unbounded, but contains no straight ray with nonzero direction. A ray with negative x direction exits x>0, a vertical ray exits the bounded vertical strip at its fixed x, and a ray with positive x direction has y-x^2 tending to minus infinity quadratically. This is a geometric counterexample to an unbounded-component implies straight-visibility inference; no permitted mirror configuration or reflected-ray trapping is asserted.

Thus all possible directions leave C in finite time.

This gives an explicit algebraic version of the previous spiral-corridor obstruction: unbounded connected vacancy alone does not supply a straight ray.         \item $\Lambda$ is a $\mathbb{T}^2$-type planar lamination.
    \end{enumerate}

Define the elementary factors E_0(w) = 1 - w and, for p ≥ 1, E_p(w) = (1 - w) exp(w + w^2/2 + ... + w^p/p). Let m ≥ 0 be an integer and let (a_n) be a finite or infinite sequence of nonzero complex numbers, repetitions allowed, with |a_n| → ∞ if the sequence is infinite. Choose nonnegative integers p_n such that the series Σ_n (r/|a_n|)^{p_n + 1} converges for every r > 0 (the choice p_n = n - 1 always works). Then the product P(z) = z^m Π_n E_{p_n}(z/a_n) converges absolutely and uniformly on compact subsets of C and defines an entire function whose zero set is exactly {0} (with multiplicity m, omitted if m = 0) together with the points a_n, each with multiplicity equal to the number of times it is listed. Conversely, every entire function f whose zeros are exactly these (with these multiplicities) has the form f(z) = exp(g(z)) P(z) for some entire function g. Consequently every entire function admits such a factorization, and every meromorphic function on C is a quotient of two entire functions.
the prescribed zeros form a sequence with no finite accumulation point (|a_n| → ∞ if infinite)

Let H be a complex Hilbert space. (a) If A is self-adjoint on H, then U(t) = e^{itA} (Borel functional calculus) defines a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: U(t + s) = U(t)U(s), U(0) = I, U(t)* = U(−t), and t ↦ U(t)x is continuous on ℝ for each x. Moreover D(A) = {x ∈ H : lim_{t→0} (U(t)x − x)/t exists} and for x ∈ D(A) that limit equals iAx; D(A) is invariant under each U(t). (b) Conversely, let (U(t))_{t ∈ ℝ} be a family of unitary operators with U(t + s) = U(t)U(s), U(0) = I, and t ↦ U(t)x continuous for each x ∈ H. Then there is a unique self-adjoint operator A with U(t) = e^{itA} for all t, namely Ax = lim_{t→0} (U(t)x − x)/(it) on the set where the limit exists. (c) Weak continuity suffices in (b): if t ↦ ⟨U(t)x, y⟩ is continuous for all x, y, the group is strongly continuous, since ‖U(t)x − x‖² = 2‖x‖² − 2Re⟨U(t)x, x⟩. If H is separable, weak measurability of t ↦ ⟨U(t)x, y⟩ already implies strong continuity (von Neumann). (d) A subspace D ⊂ D(A) that is dense in H and invariant under every U(t) is a core for A (Nelson's criterion via invariant domains).
H is a complex Hilbert space
in (a): A is self-adjoint, not merely symmetric
in (b): U(t) unitary for every real t, group law on all of ℝ, and strong (or weak) continuity

[Proposition prop:KW of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $\Lambda$ be a finite cubical subcomplex of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, $\mathbb{G}$ a finite abelian group, $1\leq k\leq d$, $(J_{\mathbf{c}})_{\mathbf{c}\in \Lambda^{*,k}}$ be positive coupling constants and $h:\mathbb{G}\to \mathbb{R}$ be even. Let $\Omega:=\mathrm{Im}(\partial_{d-k+1})$  and $\Sigma:=C^{k-1}$. Define $f:\Omega\to 2^{\Sigma}$ by $f(\eta) = \{\sigma \in \Sigma \mid d^k(\sigma) = \eta^* \} = (*\circ d^k)^{-1}(\eta)$ and
     $$
     \rho[\eta]\propto \prod_{\mathbf{c}\in {\Lambda_{d-k}}}\exp(J_{\mathbf{c}} h(\eta_{\mathfrak{c}})), \;\forall \eta\in \Omega, \qquad \gamma[\sigma]\propto 1,\;\forall\sigma\in\Sigma.
     $$
     Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
    \begin{enumerate}
		\item[(a)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$ is the spin model $\mu^{*}_{\Lambda^{k-1}}$. 
        For each $\eta \in\Omega$,  the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \eta]$ is the uniform measure on $f(\eta)$, that is the uniform assignment of a spin configuration consistent with the domain walls $\eta$.
		\item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$ is the domain wall measure $\mu_{\Lambda_{d-k}}$.  For each $\sigma \in\Sigma$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \sigma] = \delta_{(d^k(\sigma))^*}$, the Dirac measure on the dual of the co-boundary of $\sigma$ corresponding to taking the domain walls of the spin configuration. 
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Spin Models and Domain Walls

Let n>=1 and y_i in {-1,+1}, and let f(w;x_i) be continuously differentiable in w in R^D. Assume global constants rho>0 and beta>0 satisfy ||grad f(w;x_i)||_2<=rho and ||grad f(w;x_i)-grad f(v;x_i)||_2<=beta||w-v||_2 for every w,v and every training index i. Define L(w)=(1/n)sum_i log(1+exp(-y_i f(w;x_i))) and w_{k+1}=w_k-eta grad L(w_k), where eta>0 denotes the source paper's eta_tilde. At any iterate w with L(w)<=1/(eta rho^2), writing g=grad L(w) and w_plus=w-eta g, one has -eta(1+beta eta L(w))||g||_2^2<=L(w_plus)-L(w)<=-eta(1-(2rho^2+beta)eta L(w))||g||_2^2. In particular L(w)<=1/[eta(2rho^2+beta)] implies L(w_plus)<=L(w). The model need not be convex or twice differentiable. Near-homogeneity and linear separability are not hypotheses of this one-step result.
Finite nonempty binary-labeled training data and averaged logistic risk
Continuously differentiable predictor with globally rho-bounded gradients
Predictor gradients globally beta-Lipschitz, with rho,beta>0
Constant full-batch step eta>0 (source eta_tilde); arbitrary initialization
At the selected step L(w)<=1/(eta rho^2)

[Definition 7 of arXiv:2605.13727, 'Stochastic evolution equations\\ driven by arbitrary cylindrical Lévy processes'] A predictable process $\Psi \colon \Omega \times [0,T] \rightarrow L_2(U,H)$ is $L$-integrable if there exists a sequence $(\Psi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of processes in $\mathcal{S}_{\rm prd}^{\rm HS}$ such that
	\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
		\item[{\rm (1)}]  $(\Psi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges $P_T$-a.e. to $\Psi$;
		\item[{\rm (2)}] $\displaystyle \lim_{m,n \rightarrow \infty}d_T^{em}(I(\Psi_m),I(\Psi_n))=0.$
	\end{enumerate}
	In this case,  the stochastic integral process $(I(\Psi)(t):\, t\in [0,T])$ of $\Psi$ is defined as the limit 
	of $(I(\Psi_n))_{n\in\N}$ in $\dem_T$. The class of all $L$-integrable $L_2(U,H)$-valued predictable processes will be denoted by $\mathcal{I}_{{\rm prd},L}^{\rm HS}:=\mathcal{I}_{{\rm prd},L}^{\rm HS}(U,H)$.
title: Definition 7 of arXiv:2605.13727

body:
Let G be a finite connected undirected multigraph on n vertices, loops discarded, with Laplacian L = D - A where D is the diagonal degree matrix and A the adjacency matrix (A_{ij} the number of edges between i and j). Then the number of spanning trees of G equals every cofactor of L: deleting any row i and any column j and taking (-1)^{i+j} times the determinant gives the same value. Equivalently, if 0 = lambda_1 < lambda_2 <= ... <= lambda_n are the eigenvalues of L, the number of spanning trees is (lambda_2 lambda_3 ... lambda_n) / n.
G finite and undirected; for a disconnected graph every cofactor is 0
loops do not affect spanning trees and are removed

\[
  K_t(\rho):=\int_0^t |C(t,s,\rho)|^2\,ds ,
\]
where
\[
C(t,s,\rho)
=
-\pi\rho^{-2/3}
\Big[
 \Bi(-\rho^{2/3}t)\Ai(-\rho^{2/3}s)
 -
 \Ai(-\rho^{2/3}t)\Bi(-\rho^{2/3}s)
\Big].

Then
\[
  K_t(\rho)=\rho^{-2}+o(\rho^{-2})

\]
Equivalently,
\[

\]

body:
[Lem 39 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any constants $C,\delta > 0$, there exists a positive constant $c(C,\delta)$ such that the following holds: let $\bA$ be any $N\times N$ diagonal matrix with $\|\bA\|_{\op} \le C$, and suppose $\bg,\acute{\bg}$ are independent standard gaussian vectors in $\R^N$. Then,
    \[
        \frac{|(\bA \bg, \bg) - \Tr(\bA)|}{N}\,,
        \frac{|(\bA \bg, \acute{\bg})|}{N}
        \le \delta
    \]
    with probability at least $1-e^{- c(C,\delta) N}$.

\begin{proof}
We rewrite the random variables of interest as
    \begin{align*}
    (\bA \bg, \bg) - \Tr(\bA)
    &=
    \sum_{i=1}^N a_{i,i}
    \Big((g_i)^2-1\Big)\,,\\
    (\bA\bg,\bg')
    &=
    \sum_{i=1}^N a_{i,i}
        g_i\acute{g}_i\,.
    \end{align*}
The claim then follows by standard Chernoff bounds.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Theorem 30 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] For \(\mu_n, \mu \in \mathcal{D}\) and their corresponding PCAFs \(A^{\mu_n}, A^{\mu}\), if \(\mu_n\) converges to \(\mu\) in \(d_\mathcal{D}\), then \(A^{\mu_n}\) converges to \(A^{\mu}\) in \(L^1(\mathbb{P}_x)\) uniformly for \(x\) with the local uniform topology for \(t\), that is, for any \(T>0\),
\[\lim_{n\to \infty} \left\|\mathbb{E}_\cdot[\sup_{0\leq t\leq T} |A^{\mu_n}_t-A^{\mu}_t|]\right\|_{\infty,q} = 0.\]

	Let $T=D$ or $T=D^{\rm D}$. Let $0\le t_1<t_2<\infty$ and $\Omega$ be a connected opensubset of $\RR^d$. Assume that $f \in \mathcal{C}^{2,1}(\Omega\times (t_1,t_2))\cap \mathcal{C}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t_1,t_2])$ satisfies 
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $Tf(x,t)\geq 0$ for  $(x,t)\in \Omega\times(t_1,t_2]$,
		\item $f(x,t)\geq 0$ for $(x,t)\in\partial\Omega\times [t_1,t_2]\cup \Omega\times \{t_1\}$.
	\end{enumerate}

[Theorem 232 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider a solution $\boldsymbol{F}(z) = (F_h(z))_{h = 1}^H$ of the master Riemann--Hilbert problem with zero source, such that $\boldsymbol{F}(z) = O(z^d)$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$ for some $d \in \amsmathbb{Z}$. Then, for any non-zero $\boldsymbol{v} \in \amsmathbb{R}^H$, there exists a unique meromorphic function $F_{\boldsymbol{v}}$ on $\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}}$ such that, for any $\boldsymbol{w} \in \mathfrak{G}.\boldsymbol{v}$ and $p \in \Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{w}}$ we have
\[
F_{\boldsymbol{v}}(p) = \big \langle \boldsymbol{w} \cdot \boldsymbol{F}(z) \big \rangle = \sum_{h = 1}^H w_h F_h(z) \qquad \textnormal{with}\quad z = Z_{\boldsymbol{v}}(p).
\]
The function $F_{\boldsymbol{v}}$ can have poles only at ramification points with order at most equal to the tameness exponent of $\boldsymbol{F}$, and at $Z^{-1}_{\boldsymbol{v}}(\{\infty\})$ with order at most $d$. If the $\mathfrak{G}$-orbit of $\boldsymbol{v}$ is finite, then $\Sigma_{\boldsymbol{v}}$ is a compact Riemann surface, and
\[
\big\{\langle \boldsymbol{w} \cdot \boldsymbol{F}(z)\rangle \,\,\big|\,\,\boldsymbol{w} \in \mathfrak{G}.\boldsymbol{v}\big\}
\]
are the various branches of an algebraic function. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2609.03954, 'Galois representations ramified at one prime via relative deformation theory'] For every $m\in\Z$, the groups $H^i(G_{\{p\}},\Zp(m))$ are finitely generated $\Zp$-modules for $i=1,2$, and the canonical maps
\[
 H^i(G_{\{p\}},\Zp(m))\otimes_{\Zp}\Qp
 \longrightarrow
 H^i(G_{\{p\}},\Qp(m))
 \qquad \text{for}\quad i=1,2
\]
are isomorphisms.  In particular, the degree-two map
\[
 H^2(G_{\{p\}},\Zp(m))\otimes_{\Zp}\Qp
 \longrightarrow
 H^2(G_{\{p\}},\Qp(m))
\]
is an isomorphism.  Moreover
\[
 \dim_{\Qp}H^2(G_{\{p\}},\Qp(m))
 =
 \operatorname{corank}_{\Zp}
 H^2\!\left(G_{\{p\}},(\Qp/\Zp)(m)\right).
\]

Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^d)$ (equivalently, by the argument below, $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$). If both $\{x:f(x)\ne0\}$ and $\{\xi:\hat f(\xi)\ne0\}$ have finite Lebesgue measure, then $f=0$ almost everywhere. In particular $f$ and $\hat f$ cannot both have compact support unless $f=0$, and a nonzero bandlimited function cannot vanish outside a set of finite measure. Quantitative companion (Amrein-Berthier, Nazarov in $d=1$): for sets $S,\Sigma\subset\mathbb R^d$ of finite measure there is $C=C(S,\Sigma)>0$ with $\|f\|_2\le C(\|f\|_{L^2(S^c)}+\|\hat f\|_{L^2(\Sigma^c)})$ for all $f\in L^2$.

BOTH the support of f and the support of its transform have finite Lebesgue measure

body: For an n by n complex matrix A, the numerical range (field of values) of A is the set W(A) = {x* A x : x in C^n, x* x = 1}, a subset of the complex plane. W(A) contains every eigenvalue of A, and if A is normal (A A* = A* A), W(A) equals the convex hull of the eigenvalues of A. [standard, e.g. Horn and Johnson, Topics in Matrix Analysis]
title: Numerical Range (Field of Values) of a Matrix

[Def Exceptional Divisor of arXiv:2609.04023, 'Characterizing Contractions and Weighted Blowdowns'] Suppose $Y_\bullet \hookrightarrow X$ is a weighted embedding defined by $I_\bullet.$ 
   The inclusion $I_{\bullet +1} \subset I_\bullet$ induces an inclusion $\mathcal{O}_{\operatorname{Bl}_Y X}(1) \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}_{\operatorname{Bl}_Y X}$ of invertible sheaves.
   The {\em exceptional divisor} $\mathcal{E}$ is the Cartier divisor associated with this inclusion. 
   In particular, $\mathcal{O}_{\operatorname{Bl}_Y X}(-\mathcal{E}) \simeq \mathcal{O}_{\operatorname{Bl}_Y X}(1).$
title: Exceptional Divisor

body: Certificate (campaign status: proved): (S14 (10)-(20).) Put d = ceil(n/3), s = 3d-n in {0,1,2}; choose cyclically ordered U = {u_1,...,u_d} with exactly s gaps of length two and d-s of length three (lengths sum 2s+3(d-s) = n). Write a length-two gap as u_j,m_j,u_{j+1} and a length-three gap as u_j,m_j,w_j,u_{j+1}. Then B_n = {A} u {C_{u_j,m_j} : all j} u (length-three gaps) {C_{m_j,w_j}, B_{w_j}} u (length-two gaps) {B_{m_j}} has 1+d+2(d-s)+s = n+1 forms and is a coordinate basis: relative to A a length-two gap contributes B_{u_j}+B_{m_j}, B_{m_j}, a length-three gap B_{u_j}+B_{m_j}, B_{m_j}+B_{w_j}, B_{w_j}, on disjoint coordinate sets. Selectors: B_{u_j} -> -A (residual L_{u_j}); B_{m_j} -> C_{u_j,m_j} in a length-three gap (residual -L_{u_j}); with v_j = m_j or w_j, C_{v_j,u_{j+1}} -> B_{v_j} (residual L_{u_{j+1}}). Notes: All selector residuals lie in the d-dimensional R = span{L_u}, so d_cb(A_n) <= d, and with S10's lower bound this proves d_cb = d_geo = ceil(n/3).

body:
[Lemma lem:covering of arXiv:2412.04539, 'Counting minimal cutsets and $p_c<1$'] Let $n \geq 1$. Let $P=(p_{i,j})_{i,j \in [n]}$ be a symmetric matrix of non-negative entries such that\footnote{We can think of $P$ as the transition matrix of a Markov chain which is killed at $i$ with probability $1-\sum_{j} p(i,j)$.} $\sum_{j \in [n]} p(i,j) \leq 1$ for all $i \in [n]$. Let $\Gamma$ be the set of all sequences $\gamma=(\gamma_0,\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_k)$ in $[n]$ (for any $k \geq 1$) with $\gamma_0=1$ such that the unique element $i\in [k]$ satisfying both $\gamma_i=1$ and $\{\gamma_0,\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_i\} = [n]$ is $i=k$. For every such sequence $\gamma$, define
\[
          p(\gamma) := \prod_{i=1}^k p\left(\gamma_{i-1},\gamma_i\right).
\]
For each $\varepsilon > 0$, if every non-empty proper subset $I$ of $[n]$ satisfies
\begin{equation} 
          \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{j \in [n] \backslash I} p(i,j) \geq \varepsilon,
\end{equation}
then $\delta :=\frac{\varepsilon^2}{16e^2}$ satisfies
\[
          \sum_{\gamma \in \Gamma} p(\gamma) \geq \delta^n.
\]

For f in L^1_loc(R^d) define the centred maximal function Mf(x) = sup_{r > 0} (1/|B(x,r)|) integral_{B(x,r)} |f(y)| dy. Then M is of WEAK type (1,1): for every f in L^1(R^d) and every lambda > 0, |{x : Mf(x) > lambda}| <= 3^d ||f||_1 / lambda. For 1 < p <= infinity, M is bounded on L^p: ||Mf||_p <= C(d,p) ||f||_p, with C(d,p) blowing up like p/(p-1) as p decreases to 1. M is NOT bounded on L^1: if f is not almost everywhere zero then Mf(x) >= c_d ||f||_1 / |x|^d for |x| large, which is not integrable, so Mf is in L^1 only when f = 0 a.e. The uncentred maximal function (supremum over all balls containing x) is comparable to the centred one, with constants depending only on d. [standard; e.g. Stein and Shakarchi, Real Analysis, Theorem 1.1 and Chapter 3]
f in L^1(R^d) for the weak (1,1) bound; f in L^p for the strong bound

body:
Let X be a discrete random variable taking values in a finite set of size m, let Y be any random variable jointly distributed with X, and let X_hat = g(Y) be any estimator of X computed from Y alone, so that X -> Y -> X_hat forms a Markov chain. Let P_e = Pr(X_hat != X) be the error probability. Then H(X|Y) <= H_b(P_e) + P_e * log(m-1), where H_b(p) = -p*log p - (1-p)*log(1-p) is the binary entropy function. Consequently, if the conditional entropy H(X|Y) is bounded away from 0, the error probability P_e cannot be made arbitrarily small.

X_hat is a function of Y alone, so X -> Y -> X_hat is a Markov chain
P_e = Pr(X_hat != X)

Since E is a deterministic function of X and X_hat (itself determined by Y), H(E|X,Y) = 0. Conditioning cannot increase entropy, so H(E|Y) <= H(E) = H_b(P_e). For H(X|E,Y): when E=0, X = X_hat is already known, contributing 0; when E=1, X takes one of the remaining m-1 possible values, so H(X|E=1,Y) <= log(m-1); weighting by Pr(E=1)=P_e gives H(X|E,Y) <= P_e*log(m-1). OWNER OWN WORK, proof (unaudited); standard-form construction, novelty unestablished.
Let p be a Lebesgue density supported on a finite interval [a,b],
p(x)>=m>0 for almost every x in that interval. Assume E u=0,
E u^2=1. No continuity, differentiability, or upper bound on p is
assumed. Define, almost everywhere on its support,

 tau(x)=[integral_x^b y*p(y)dy]/p(x),
 eta(x)=[integral_x^b (y^2-1)*p(y)dy]/p(x),
 zeta(x)=[integral_x^b (tau(y)-1)*p(y)dy]/p(x).       (1)

Then, for every bounded C1 h with bounded derivative,

 E[u*h(u)]=E[tau(u)*h'(u)],
 E[(u^2-1)*h(u)]=E[eta(u)*h'(u)],

Write F_g(x)=integral_x^b g(y)*p(y)dy for centered integrable g.
It is absolutely continuous, F_g'=-g*p almost everywhere, and
F_g(a)=F_g(b)=0. Ordinary integration by parts for an absolutely

All integrals here are absolutely convergent: the interval is compact,
g is integrable, and h,h' are bounded. Dividing by p defines a
measurable kernel almost everywhere; since p>=m>0 it satisfies
|F_g/p|<=E|g|/m. The zero endpoint conditions are essential.

[Proposition 106 of arXiv:2609.03875, 'Measure theory without infinities'] Let $\mf A$ be an HTM, $\sm{\mf A}{k\in K}{f(k)}$, and $x = \sum_{k\in K}f(k)$.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item[(i)] Let $\sm{\mf A}{k\in K}{g(k)}$. Then $\sum_{k\in K}(f(k) + g(k)) = x + \sum_{k\in K}g(k)$.
  \item[(ii)] Let $\mf B$ be an HTM and $\varphi\colon\mf A\to\mf B$ be a continuous homomorphism. Then $\sum_{k\in K} \varphi(f(k)) = \varphi(x)$.   
  \item [(iii)] Suppose $\mf A$ is an HTG. Then $\sum_{k\in K}(-f(k)) = -x$.
  \item [(iv)] Suppose $\mf A$ is an HTG and $\sm{\mf A}{k\in K}{g(k)}$. Then $\sum_{k\in K}(f(k) - g(k)) = x - \sum_{k\in K}g(k)$.
  \end{enumerate}

  \tau\Big[\big(g(X_{t},t)-\sqrt{\alpha_{t}}X_{0}\big)^{2}\Big]

score-matching loss differ by a constant.

body:
Consider bond first-passage percolation on Z^2 with iid edge weights supported in [a,b], where 0<a<=b<infinity, and fixed distinct vertices u,v. Let X=T(u,v) and choose a measurable canonical topmost minimizing geodesic (atoms and ties are allowed). Partition the edges into deterministic blocks Lambda. For each block independently redraw its weights from the original law, independently of the environment, and write X^Lambda for the passage time with only that block replaced. Let U_Lambda be the event that the original chosen geodesic uses an edge in Lambda. Give the blocks iid Uniform[0,1] labels tau_Lambda independent of all original and redrawn weights. F_t reveals each labeled block and its original/redrawn weight pair when tau_Lambda<=t; equivalently, for the probabilities of U_Lambda one may reveal only original weights. Define A2=sum_Lambda E[1_U_Lambda (X^Lambda-X)^2], A2plus=sum_Lambda E[((X^Lambda-X)^+)^2], A4=sum_Lambda E[1_U_Lambda ((X^Lambda-X)^+)^4], and Pbar(kappa)=sum_Lambda E[P(U_Lambda|F_(1-kappa))^2]. For every 0<kappa<1, Var(X)<=kappa A2plus+sqrt(A4 Pbar(kappa))<=kappa A2+sqrt(A4 Pbar(kappa)). Positivity and boundedness localize all relevant paths to a deterministic finite edge set, so only finitely many blocks contribute. The proof needs independent blocks, off-geodesic monotonicity and conditional expectations; isotropy and FKG are not assumptions.
iid edge weights in [a,b] with 0<a<=b<infinity
Fixed distinct endpoints in Z^2 and measurable canonical topmost geodesic selection
Deterministic edge partition; independent same-law block redraws and independent uniform reveal labels

Let phi be real-valued and smooth on (a,b) with |phi^{(k)}| >= 1 there, where k >= 2, or k = 1 and phi' monotone. Then |int_a^b e^{i lambda phi(x)} dx| <= c_k lambda^{-1/k} for lambda > 0, with c_k depending only on k (for k = 1 the sharp constant is 2). Since the hypotheses hold on every subinterval, one integration by parts gives, for psi of bounded variation on [a,b]: |int_a^b e^{i lambda phi} psi dx| <= c_k lambda^{-1/k} (|psi(b)| + int_a^b |psi'(x)| dx), the integral read as the total variation. For an integrable psi of bounded variation on R and |phi''| >= 1 on R: |int e^{i lambda phi} psi| <= c_2 lambda^{-1/2} TV(psi).

body: Taylor's theorem: Let k >= 1 and let f be k times differentiable at the point a, and set P_k(x) = sum_{j=0}^{k} f^{(j)}(a) (x - a)^j / j!, the k-th order Taylor polynomial of f at a (the unique polynomial of degree at most k agreeing with f in value and in the first k derivatives at a). Peano form: f(x) - P_k(x) = o(|x - a|^k) as x -> a. Lagrange form: if in addition f is k+1 times differentiable on an open interval I containing a, then for each x in I there is a point xi strictly between a and x with f(x) - P_k(x) = f^{(k+1)}(xi) (x - a)^{k+1} / (k+1)!. The case k = 1 is the linear approximation and k = 2 the quadratic approximation; for a smooth f, P_k is the truncation at order k of the Taylor series of f at a.
title: Taylor's theorem

body: An explicit s-stage Runge-Kutta method for the initial value problem y' = f(t,y), y(t_0) = y_0, advances y_n to y_{n+1} = y_n + h * sum_{i=1}^{s} b_i * k_i, where k_i = f( t_n + c_i*h, y_n + h*sum_{j<i} a_{ij}*k_j ), and the coefficients a_{ij}, b_i, c_i (the Butcher tableau) typically satisfy c_i = sum_{j<i} a_{ij}. The method has order p if, for sufficiently smooth f, its Taylor expansion in h agrees with the Taylor expansion of the exact solution through the h^p term (equivalently, the local truncation error is O(h^{p+1})). Matching these Taylor expansions imposes polynomial equations on (a_{ij}, b_i, c_i) called order conditions: for example, order 1 requires sum_i b_i = 1, and order 2 additionally requires sum_i b_i*c_i = 1/2. In Butcher's rooted-tree theory there is one order condition per rooted tree up to order p, and the number of independent conditions grows faster than the number of stages s, which is why, for instance, no explicit Runge-Kutta method can reach an order equal to its stage count once the order exceeds 4.
title: Runge-Kutta Order Conditions

[Lemma lem:poisson-difference-cc of arXiv:2608.06159, 'Majority Dynamics on Resampled Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi Graphs:\\[0.5ex] Gaussian Winner '] Let \(P_X\sim\Pois(\lambda_X)\) and
\(P_Y\sim\Pois(\lambda_Y)\) be independent, and set
\[
S\coloneqq P_X-P_Y,
\qquad
\lambda\coloneqq\lambda_X+\lambda_Y,
\qquad
m\coloneqq\lambda_X-\lambda_Y.
\]
Suppose that for some fixed \(M>0\), \(|m|\le M\sqrt{\lambda}\) as \(\lambda\to\infty\). Then uniformly over integers \(k,\ell\),
\begin{subequations}
\begin{align}
\P(S\le\ell)
&=
\Phi\left(
\frac{\ell+1/2-m}{\sqrt{\lambda}}
\right)
+O_M(\lambda^{-1}),
\\
\P(S=k)
&=
\frac1{\sqrt{\lambda}}
\varphi\left(
\frac{k-m}{\sqrt{\lambda}}
\right)
+O_M(\lambda^{-3/2}).

\end{align}
\end{subequations}

[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked; reduction plus asserted conditional, not a solution] Svante Janson's Problem 18.39 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510, asks whether Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability is possible in the condensation regime 0 < nu < lambda. Janson conjectures that it is not possible for the full sequence and, more strongly, that there are always epsilon > 0 and a subsequence along which Y_(1) >= epsilon n w.h.p. (Example 18.36 gives Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability along a subsequence.) Setting: let w_k >= 0 with w_0 > 0, let Phi(z) = sum_k w_k z^k have radius rho in (0,infinity) with Phi(rho) < infinity, and put pi_k = w_k rho^k/Phi(rho), a law with generating-function radius one and finite mean nu > 0. Let m_n/n -> lambda > nu. (Y_1,...,Y_n) is n i.i.d. pi variables conditioned on sum m_n, Y_(1) = max_i Y_i, and M = (lambda-nu)n. Heuristic rate: carrying M in r = M/a boxes of size a has class weight binomial(n,r) pi_a^r up to the bulk's fluctuation, giving log P = M Lambda(a) + o(M) with Lambda(a) = [log pi_a + log(a/(lambda-nu)) + 1]/a. For pi_k ~ c k^(-beta) and for pi_a = exp(-a^gamma), 0<gamma<1, Lambda increases on large a, so the optimum is a = M (one box), matching the known condensation picture. Since limsup_a Lambda(a) = 0 and Lambda < 0 for large a, Lambda has infinitely many upper records a_1 < a_2 < ... (Lambda(a_j) > Lambda(a) for all a < a_j) exactly when Lambda(a) < 0 for every a; if Lambda(a) >= 0 for some a the maximum is attained and there are finitely many records (Lambda(1) = log pi_1 + log(1/(lambda-nu)) + 1 is positive once lambda - nu < e pi_1). The record asserts, as author-checked and with no proof given beyond reference to an analogous step for Problem 18.40 in a companion memo, the following Proposition: if for some epsilon > 0 and every C, along infinitely many records, Lambda(a_j) - max_{a <= epsilon a_j} Lambda(a) > C a_j^(-1/2), then along n_j = a_j/(lambda-nu), P(Y_(1) >= ((lambda-nu)/2) n_j) -> 1, so the conjecture holds. Caveat: the only derivation offered is the heuristic rate with an o(M) error, which is coarser than the order sqrt(a_j) resolution this hypothesis requires, so the record does not establish the Proposition. The record poses the open Question whether, for every law pi on Z_{>=0} with radius one and finite mean, [log pi_a + log a]/a has infinitely many records with gap exceeding a_j^(-1/2) below max_{a <= epsilon a_j} for some fixed epsilon > 0. This is not a proved equivalence with the conjecture. A negative answer would only give a candidate counterexample, still requiring proof that the allocation spreads. The Question's normalisation and fixed threshold also differ from the Proposition's hypothesis. The problem remains open. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
The allocations are defined along sizes with positive conditioning probability.
0 < nu < lambda and the boundary-tilted law pi has generating-function radius one.

[Lemma 1 of arXiv:2604.01257, '2604.01257'] Let conditions $[{f_{\nu}}]$, $[{{\mathcal{L}}_{\nu}}]$ and $[{{\omega}_{\nu}}]$ be satisfied. Then
\begin{equation}                              
    \frac{1}{\Lambda(R(t;s))}-\frac{1}{\Lambda(1-s)}=\nu{t}+
    \int_{\tau(0;s)}^{\tau(t)}{\frac{\varepsilon(x)}{{x^{1-\nu}}\mathcal{L}(x)}dx}+
    \mathcal{O}\left(1/t\right)
\end{equation}
    as $t\to\infty$, where $\tau(t)={{(\nu{t})}^{1/\nu}}\big/{\mathcal{N}(t)}$ and $\mathcal{N}(t)$ is defined
    in {(\ref{IIB3.2})}. By incorporating the supplementary constraint {(\ref{IIB3.3})}, we directly derive the
    following fundamental identity:
\begin{equation}                              
    \frac{1}{\Lambda(R(t;s))}-\frac{1}{\Lambda(1-s)}=\nu{t}-\frac{1}{\nu}\ln\left[\Lambda(1-s)\nu{t}\right]+\rho(t;s),
\end{equation}
    where $\rho(t;s)=o(\ln{t})$ as $t\to\infty$ uniformly in $s\in[0,1)$.

This is a restrictive parameter interval, not the full population target and not the finite-sample target. No literature novelty is asserted. Only a reviewer PASS can make it independently checked.
Versions 1 and 2 are preserved in their original proof files. Version 2 strengthens the initialization restriction by an additional factor of mu and replaces the previous local-phase sketch with a self-contained basin argument.

## Theorem

Let Delta be an m-by-n real matrix of exact rank r, with 1<=r<=min(m,n), ||Delta||op=1, and sigma_r(Delta)=mu in (0,1]. Put N=m+n. Fix 0<rho<1, c=10r/rho, and a=10^(-12). Let
  B0=0, A0 have independent N(0,s^2) entries, 0<s<1,
  L=log(e*c^2*r*N/(mu*s^2)).
Suppose
  s L <= a mu^2/(c^3 N r^(3/2)),
  0<eta <= a mu s^2/(c^2 r).
For simultaneous GD on f(B,A)=(1/2)||BA-Delta||F^2, with probability at least 1-rho, for every 0<eps<1 and every integer
  t >= ceil(10000/(eta mu) * [L+log(e*r/eps^2)]),
one has ||B_t A_t-Delta||F<=eps.

For an unnormalized target, set lambda=sigma_1(Delta), replace s by s/sqrt(lambda), eta by eta*lambda, eps by eps/lambda, and mu by sigma_r/lambda. At the maximal indicated step size, the iteration order is O(c^2 r kappa^2 lambda/s^2) times the displayed logarithms, hence O(r^3 kappa^2 lambda/(rho^2 s^2)) times logarithms. The universal constant in this O includes 1/a.
The admissible interval is nonempty for every fixed target and rho, because s log(1/s) tends to zero as s tends to zero.

## Spectral inequalities from the literature, verified in the appendix

We use two deterministic spectral inequalities from Ye and Du, Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Asymmetric Low-Rank Matrix Factorization, arXiv:2106.14289. They are Lemma 3.2 and Lemma 3.3 in the PDF, and theorems/lemma_dynamic_S.tex and theorems/lemma_dynamic_P.tex in its source archive. Set their sigma_1=1, sigma_d=mu, beta=1/2.

(A) If W and Lambda are positive definite symmetric, ||W||op<=2 and mu I<=Lambda<=I, then for eta<=1/16 and w=lambda_min(W),
 lambda_min((I+eta(Lambda-W)) W (I+eta(Lambda-W)))
 >= (1+eta(mu-w))^2 w-22eta^2.

(B) If P is symmetric, ||P||op<=2, mu I<=Lambda<=I, and p=lambda_min(P), then for H=I-eta(Lambda-P), eta<=1/16,
 lambda_min(H P H) >= 0 if p>=0,
 and >=(1-eta mu)^2 p-22eta^2 if p<0.

These are sourced matrix inequalities, fully re-derived in the appendix rather than inferred from finite examples. Our proof below derives the uniform c-dependence from exact GD identities rather than interpreting the source's hidden constants as uniform.

## Coordinates and initialization

Rotate into the fixed left and right singular coordinates of Delta. Write Lambda=diag(sigma_1,...,sigma_r). As in the source, let U be the rotated B and V the rotated A transpose. Since the complementary output block J starts at zero, its exact update J_next=J(I-eta V^T V) keeps J=0. Thus U=[R;0], V=[T;K], where R,T are r-by-r and K is (n-r)-by-r. The reduced target is [Lambda,0].
Define
 S=(R+T)/2, D=(R-T)/2,
 P=Lambda-SS^T+DD^T, Q=SD^T-DS^T,
 E=Lambda-RT^T=P+Q.
The full residual is [E,-RK^T].

C004 supplies, with probability >=1-rho,
 sigma_min(S0)>=ell:=s/(c sqrt(r)),
 ||S0||op<=cs sqrt(r), ||D0||F<=crs,
 ||K0||op<=cs sqrt(N), D0=-S0, P0=Lambda, Q0=0.
The theorem's scale condition implies SS^T<=2Lambda initially. No independence between S0 and D0 is used. Fix this deterministic event for the remainder.

We repeatedly use the following direct consequences of the smallness conditions: L>=1, c>=10, N>=2r, eta<=1/100, eta<=c^2 N r s^2, 2crs<=1/4, cs sqrt(N)<=1/4, ell^2<=mu/4, and eta<=sqrt(mu)/128. Each follows by substituting sL<=a mu^2/(c^3 N r^(3/2)), mu<=1 and a=10^-12.

## Exact update identities

With W=K^T K the GD recurrences are
 R_next=R+eta(E T-RW),
 T_next=T+eta E^T R,
 K_next=K(I-eta R^T R).
Consequently,
 S_next=S+eta P S-eta Q D-(eta/2)(S+D)W,
 D_next=D-eta P D+eta Q S-(eta/2)(S+D)W.

Let C=SD^T+DS^T, M=Lambda-P, H=I-eta M. Direct expansion gives
 P_next=H P H+F,
where
 F= -2eta(P DD^T+DD^T P)+eta(QC-CQ)
    +eta sym(RWT^T)
    -eta^2 sym((ET-RW)R^T E)
    -eta^2 M P M,
and sym(X)=(X+X^T)/2.
The full residual identity and this P identity are verified by exact free noncommutative polynomial expansion in scripts/free_algebra_P.py. This check does not assume commuting matrices. Reversing the commutator sign fails that check.

## Warm-up bootstrap

Set Tbar=ceil(1000 L/(eta mu)). Up to this horizon bootstrap
 ell^2 I<=SS^T<=2Lambda,
 ||D||F<=2crs,
 ||K||op<=cs sqrt(N).
All are initially satisfied, and the estimates below close them with strict margins.

Write d=||D||op and k=||K||op. The bootstrap implies ||S||op<=sqrt(2), d<=1/4, k<=1/4, ||R||op,||T||op<=2, ||P||op<=2 and ||E||op<=4.
Indeed, -I<=Lambda-SS^T<=I, and DD^T has norm <=d^2.
By triangle inequalities in the exact F identity,
 ||F||op <=24eta d^2+4eta k^2+128eta^2
          <=400eta c^2 N r s^2.                         (1)
For the quadratic terms one may use
 ||(ET-RW)R^T E||op<80 and ||MPM||op<=18;
the factor 128 is an upper bound for their sum.
The linear terms are bounded by ||Q||op,||C||op<=2sqrt(2)d and ||P||op<=2.
The last inequality in (1) uses eta<=c^2 N r s^2.

Using (B) and Weyl's inequality gives the scalar recursion
 lambda_min(P_next)>= (1-eta mu)^2 min{lambda_min(P),0}
                       -500eta c^2 N r s^2.
Since P0=Lambda is positive definite,
 lambda_min(P_t)>=-500c^2 N r s^2/mu.                  (2)
Here 1-(1-eta mu)^2>=eta mu; no product of probability estimates appears.
Now
 SS^T=Lambda-P+DD^T
 <=Lambda+(500c^2Nrs^2/mu+4c^2r^2s^2)I
 <=Lambda+502c^2Nrs^2/mu I<=2Lambda.                   (3)
The scale assumption ensures the final inequality.

To control D, take the Frobenius inner product of its update with D.
The identity <D,QS>=-||Q||F^2/2 and positivity of W let us discard nonpositive terms. By (2),
 ||D_next||F^2 <= (1+p)||D||F^2+q,
 p=1000eta c^2 N r s^2/mu,
 q=3eta c^3 N r^(3/2) s^3+324eta^2 c^2 r^2 s^2.        (4)
For the first additive term use
 ||D^T S||F ||W||F <=2sqrt(2)c^3 N r^(3/2)s^3.
For the squared-update term use ||D_next-D||F/eta<=18crs: the three pieces are bounded by 4crs, 8crs and 2sqrt(r)c^2s^2N<=2crs, respectively.
Thus 18 is conservative.
For T<=Tbar, direct substitution gives
 pT<=3*10^6 a^2<1/100,
 qT/(c^2 r^2 s^2)<=4000a+4*10^5 a^3<1/100.
Iterating (4) and using exp(x)<=1/(1-x) for 0<=x<1 yields
 ||D_T||F^2 <= exp(pT)(||D0||F^2+qT)
             <=(101/99)c^2r^2s^2<4c^2r^2s^2.
This closes the D bound.

For K, eta<=1/4 and ||R||op<=2 imply
 0<=I-eta R^T R<=I.
Its operator norm therefore never increases, closing the K bound.

It remains to close the lower bound on S and reach a large signal.
Its update is
 S_next=S+eta(Lambda-SS^T)S+eta Z,
 ||Z||op<=11c^2 N r s^2.
The bound follows from
 ||Z||op<=3sqrt(2)d^2+(sqrt(2)+d)k^2/2
and N>=2r.
Let b=sigma_min(S). If ell<=b<=sqrt(mu/2), (A) and the singular-value triangle inequality give
 b_next>=sqrt((1+eta(mu-b^2))^2b^2-22eta^2)
                   -11eta c^2 N r s^2.
The radicand is positive because 22eta^2<=b^2. Using
 sqrt(x^2-y)>=x-y/x for x>0, 0<=y<=x^2,
the total subtracted perturbation is at most
 (22a+11a)eta mu b<=eta mu b/4.
It follows that
 b_next >=(1+eta mu/4)b.                               (5)
No division by mu-b_next^2 is made.
While below sqrt(mu/2), squared signal grows at least as exp(eta mu t/4).
Hence the first crossing occurs by
 T1<=ceil(4/(eta mu) log(c^2 r mu/(2s^2)))
    <=5 L/(eta mu).

After crossing, sigma_min(S)>=sqrt(mu/4) is invariant.
For b in [sqrt(mu/4),sqrt(mu/2)], (5) applies.
For b>=sqrt(mu/2), the bounded exact update gives
 ||S_next-S||op<=16eta,
so b_next>=sqrt(mu/2)-16eta>=sqrt(mu/4).
The step restriction eta<=sqrt(mu)/128 suffices.
Thus the lower bootstrap bound is preserved both before and after the crossing.

The estimates (1)-(5) are a simultaneous induction, not an argument that assumes its own endpoint: at a hypothetical first exit before Tbar, the estimates using earlier bounds give (2), the D bound, (3), the K bound and the lower S bound at that very next step. Each has the stated margin. Hence no exit occurs.

## Entering a small Euclidean basin

After T1, (5) and the barrier give lambda_min(SS^T)>=mu/4. Since d^2<=mu/8,
 mu/8 I <=M=SS^T-DD^T<=2I.
Thus the congruence term in the P identity contracts in operator norm with factor
 theta^2=(1-eta mu/8)^2.
By (1), for j>=0 while T1+j<=Tbar,
 ||P_(T1+j)||op<=2 exp(-eta mu j/4)+3200c^2 N r s^2/mu.
Set tau=mu^(3/2)/(10^6 sqrt(r)).
The second term is <=tau/2 by the smallness condition.
After
 T2=ceil(4/(eta mu) log(4/tau)),
the first term is <=tau/2. Since log(4*10^6)<16 and L>=1,
 T1+T2<=100 L/(eta mu)<Tbar.
At T0=T1+T2 we therefore have ||P||op<=tau.
Moreover
 ||Q||F<=2||S||op||D||F<=6crs,
 ||RK^T||F<=2sqrt(r)cs sqrt(N).
Consequently the full residual e0 satisfies
 e0:=||[Lambda,0]-R V^T||F
 <=sqrt(r)tau+6crs+2sqrt(r)cs sqrt(N)
 <=(10^-6+8a)mu^(3/2)<=mu^(3/2)/10^5.                (6)
All inequalities remain valid for an empty K block.

At this endpoint ||R||op,||V||op<=2. Also
 ||RR^T-Lambda||op<=||E||op+2||R||op||D||op<=mu/2,
so sigma_min(R)>=sqrt(mu/2).
This estimate uses a perturbation of the symmetric RR^T, avoiding a sign ambiguity in the source's local-phase sketch.

## Self-contained local GD convergence

Use the reduced factors U=R, V=[T;K]. Consider the Euclidean ball in factor-pair Frobenius norm of radius sqrt(mu)/8 around their T0 values.
Throughout this ball, ||U||op,||V||op<=3 and sigma_min(U)>=sqrt(mu)/2.
The residual operator norm is <=10, and the Hessian of
 g(U,V)=(1/2)||UV^T-[Lambda,0]||F^2
has operator norm <=||U||op^2+||V||op^2+||residual||op<=28.
Thus 100 is a valid smoothness constant on the ball.
Furthermore
 ||grad g||F^2>=||residual^T U||F^2>=mu/4 *||residual||F^2,
and ||grad g||F<=6||residual||F.

Since eta<=1/100, the descent inequality within the ball gives
 e_next^2<=(1-eta mu/4)e^2.
A first-exit argument keeps the trajectory in that ball: before a possible exit, total factor displacement, including the proposed exit step, is bounded by
 sum eta*6 e0*(1-eta mu/4)^(j/2)
 <=48e0/mu<=48sqrt(mu)/10^5<sqrt(mu)/8.
The proposed exit endpoint is therefore inside the ball, a contradiction. All relevant line segments lie in its convex interior, justifying the smoothness bound used for descent.
It follows for every subsequent k>=0 that
 e_k<=e0 exp(-eta mu k/8).
Combining this with T0<=100 L/(eta mu) proves the displayed theorem with the conservative constant 10000.

## Verification and remaining practical limits

- Initialization probability is proved analytically in C004, with a union bound; no unjustified multiplication of conditional probabilities is used.
- The GD identities pass 57 exact rational checks and six universal free noncommutative polynomial identities; a wrong commutator sign is detected.
- The scalar margins for a=10^-12 are checked by exact rational arithmetic in the accompanying script. These checks do not replace the sourced spectral inequalities.
- The requested Mathlib cancellation check returned RUNTIME_UNVERIFIED. This proof is not Lean-checked.
- The proof assumes exact target rank, positive scale, population isotropic loss, and the stated small step. Orthogonal-only signal initialization, s=0 and arbitrary step size are excluded for substantive reasons.
- The argument does not prove a result for moderate/large s or any finite-sample comparison with reduced-rank regression.
- The primary matrix-inequality inputs and all constants need independent reviewer audit before this counts as independently checked progress.


## Appendix: complete verification of the two normalized spectral inequalities

This appendix removes the need to treat (A) and (B) as unverified black boxes. Their source is still credited to Ye-Du. It keeps the negative second-order term in the residual case explicitly.

Let X be real symmetric with ||X||op<=2 and let mu I<=Lambda<=I. For either sign define H_+=I+eta(Lambda-X), H_-=I-eta(Lambda-X). Direct expansion, requiring no commutation between Lambda and X, gives
 H_+ X H_+ = [X/2-2eta X^2+eta^2 X^3] + C_+ X C_+ - eta^2 R,
 H_- X H_- = [X/2+2eta X^2+eta^2 X^3] + C_- X C_- - eta^2 R,
where
 C_+=I/sqrt(2)+sqrt(2)eta Lambda,
 C_-=I/sqrt(2)-sqrt(2)eta Lambda,
 R=Lambda X Lambda+Lambda X^2+X^2 Lambda.
Here ||R||op<=2+4+4=10.
Both identities are independently verified as universal free noncommutative polynomial identities in scripts/check_spectral_splits.py.

For (A), X is positive definite. On [0,2], the scalar polynomial
 h_+(x)=x/2-2eta x^2+eta^2 x^3
is nondecreasing because h_+'(x)>=1/2-8eta>=0 for eta<=1/16. If w=lambda_min(X)>0, spectral calculus therefore gives
 lambda_min(h_+(X))=h_+(w).
Since C_+ is positive definite and lambda_min(C_+)>=1/sqrt(2)+sqrt(2)eta mu,
 lambda_min(C_+ X C_+)>=w(1/2+2eta mu+2eta^2 mu^2).
Adding these bounds and subtracting the remainder gives
 lambda_min(H_+ X H_+)
 >=(1+eta(mu-w))^2 w
     +eta^2(mu^2 w+2mu w^2)-10eta^2
 >=(1+eta(mu-w))^2 w-22eta^2.
This proves (A).

For (B), if p=lambda_min(X)>=0, congruence preserves positive semidefiniteness.
If p<0, the polynomial h_-(x)=x/2+2eta x^2+eta^2 x^3 is nondecreasing on [-2,2], since h_-'(x)>=1/2-8eta>=0. Thus lambda_min(h_-(X))=h_-(p).
The matrix C_- is positive definite for eta<=1/16 and
 ||C_-||op<=1/sqrt(2)-sqrt(2)eta mu.
From X>=pI and p<0,
 C_- X C_->=p C_-^2>=p||C_-||op^2 I.
Consequently,
 lambda_min(H_- X H_-)
 >=(1-eta mu)^2 p
    +2eta p^2+eta^2 p^3+eta^2 mu^2 p-10eta^2.
The first two correction terms combine as eta p^2(2+eta p)>=0, since p>=-2 and eta<=1/16. Also mu^2 p>=-2. The whole correction is therefore >=-12eta^2, which is stronger than the required -22eta^2. This proves (B), including every sign condition in the congruence comparison.

This appendix uses only the real symmetric spectral theorem, scalar polynomial monotonicity, norm submultiplicativity and the elementary Loewner-order congruence rule. Let B be a positive self-adjoint trace-class operator on a closed subspace V of L2(Omega,tau), extended by zero on V-perp, with finite positive trace T and spectral kernel k(theta,thetaprime)=sum_j mu_j phi_j(theta)phi_j(thetaprime), mu_j>=0. Use the canonical positive spectral representative, including its diagonal k(theta,theta)=sum_j mu_j phi_j(theta)^2, so E_tau k(theta,theta)=T. For every fixed real q>=1 assume ||k||_(L2q(tau times tau))<=C(q)||k||_(L2(tau times tau)) and ||k(theta,theta)||_(Lq(tau))<=C(q) E_tau k(theta,theta). Draw theta_1,...,theta_N independently from tau, N>=2, and define Delta_ij=k(theta_i,theta_j)1_(i!=j), where the indicator removes sample-index diagonal entries. For every positive integer p there is K(p), depending only on p and the stated moment constant C(p), such that E||Delta||_op<=K(p){N||B||_op+[||B||_op T N^(1+2/p)log N]^(1/2)}. Sample points are independent; matrix entries generally are not. No centering of the kernel or deletion of its population leading mode is assumed.

For finite irreducible reversible chains, any universal K satisfying t_stop(P_hat)<=K t_stop(P) for every stationary-flow lumping must obey K>=3/2. Here t_stop(P)=max_i inf_T E_i T for randomized stopping times with terminal law pi. A four-state family with symmetric weights W=[[0,0,1,0],[0,2s,1,2s],[1,1,0,s],[0,2s,s,4s^2]], P_ij=W_ij/sum_k W_ik, s>0, and blocks {0},{1},{2,3}, has t_stop(P)->2 and t_stop(P_hat)->3 as s->infinity. This proves a candidate lower bound only; existence or sharpness of a universal K is not settled here. Independent review is pending.

Earlier work read: the original store attempt requiring strong lumpability, and `Probability_P0242_Aldous_Fill_open_problem_4_45_lumping_2026-09-14.md`. The latter disproves K=1 and reports a finite witness with ratio 1.48220..., but explicitly has no asymptotic argument. The source is Aldous--Fill, Open Problem 4.45, PDF p.149 of the 2014 recompilation, and its stopping-time/halting-state identity.

For s>0 take the following symmetric weight matrix on states 0,1,2,3:

    W = [[0, 0, 1, 0],
         [0, 2s, 1, 2s],
         [1, 1, 0, s],
         [0, 2s, s, 4s^2]].

Let w_i be its row sums: (1,4s+1,s+2,4s^2+3s), with total 4(s+1)^2. The discrete chain P_ij=W_ij/w_i is irreducible and reversible with pi_i=w_i/(4(s+1)^2).     W_hat = [[0, 0, 1],
             [0, 2s, 2s+1],
             [1, 2s+1, 4s^2+2s]].

This is stationary-flow lumping, rather than strong lumpability: from state 2 the transition probability into {0} is 1/(s+2), whereas from state 3 it is zero.

For each target j let H_ij be the expected hitting time, the unique solution of H_jj=0 and -sum_k Q_ik H_kj=1 for i!=j. The standard optimal-stopping identity is

    t_stop(P) = max_(i,j) D_ij,

[Definition 21 (Wishart distribution) of arXiv:2609.02790, 'Full-Model Optimality for Tunable Linear Generative Priors in Compressed Sensing'] Let $X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ have i.i.d. rows $x_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\Sigma)$, where 
$\Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ is positive definite.  
The random matrix
\[
W = X^\top X = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i x_i^\top
\]
is said to follow a \emph{Wishart distribution} with $n$ degrees of freedom and scale matrix $\Sigma$, written
\[
W \sim \mathcal W_p(\Sigma,n).
\]

Fix d>=1, sigma>0, x in R^d, and a finite label set Y of size K>=2 containing distinct classes cA,cB. Let 0<pB<pA<1 satisfy pA+pB<=1 and (K-1)*pB>=1-pA. Set R=(sigma/2)*(Phi^(-1)(pA)-Phi^(-1)(pB)). For every delta in R^d with ||delta||_2>R, there exists a deterministic measurable base classifier f_star:Y-valued on R^d for which P(f_star(x+epsilon)=cA)=pA and max_(c!=cA)P(f_star(x+epsilon)=c)<=pB, with equality for cB, but its Gaussian-smoothed classifier does not predict cA at x+delta. Here epsilon~N(0,sigma^2 I_d). The finite-label feasibility condition makes explicit the capacity needed to distribute the residual probability among the paper's other classes. In particular, binary sharpness is covered when pA+pB=1. This is a limitation of certificates using only these probability bounds, not a claim that every base classifier changes label outside R.
Nondegenerate isotropic Gaussian noise and a finite label set of specified size K
0<pB<pA<1, pA+pB<=1
Finite-label capacity: (K-1)*pB>=1-pA
Strictly outside R; the classifier may depend on the chosen perturbation
Existential worst-case statement, not pointwise failure for all classifiers
