[campaign status: author_checked_limited_argument - a first-pass structural calculation; no independent review, prior art unverified, and the other questions in the source are untouched] For Metropolis chains targeting a geometric-time law on a Cayley group, the source asks whether the relaxation time decreases monotonically in the tilt p. CLAIM: NO, and the counterexample is the smallest possible one - the two-element group - with relaxation defined the standard way as 1/(1 - lambda_2). (i) NONLAZY BASE. The base walk flips the two states; the target is mu_p = (1/(2-p), (1-p)/(2-p)); the Metropolis matrix is [[p, 1-p],[1, 0]], whose second eigenvalue is p - 1, so tau(p) = 1/(2 - p), STRICTLY INCREASING in p. (ii) LAZY BASE, which removes the convention ambiguity because its spectrum is nonnegative. The base matrix has all entries 1/2, mu_p = ((1+p)/2, (1-p)/2), the Metropolis off-diagonal rates are (1-p)/(2(1+p)) and 1/2, and tau(p) = 1 + p, again increasing. (iii) If laziness is imposed AFTER forming the nonlazy Metropolis kernel, tau(p) = 2/(2 - p), still increasing. WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO: it refutes the literal monotonicity direction only. It does not answer the source's other universal-bound questions and does not resolve its undefined tau(infinity). CONVENTION CAVEAT recorded with the result: if 'relaxation' meant the inverse absolute spectral gap of a nonlazy chain, that convention differs - the lazy example exists precisely to remove the ambiguity.
the group is the two-element Cayley group; the claim is a counterexample, not a general theorem
relaxation time is 1/(1 - lambda_2), the standard spectral-gap convention
the target is the geometric-time law of the base walk at tilt p

body: Concept (campaign status: proved on the family): for the odd m-cycle sharing graph, tightness(C_m) = m*beta / (m*beta + |log2(1 - 3^{-m})|) -> 1 from below as m grows, never reaching 1 - the largest tightness of any family the campaign measured (C5 gives 0.9971). An odd cycle gets no rank drop from bipartiteness, so its entire RC budget is the negativity of its own correlation, which vanishes like 3^{-m}. Density and positive correlation make RC easier, not harder: the dense bipartite K(n,n) family sits at tightness -> beta = 0.415 with asymptotic margin exactly 1/beta = 2.409, while sparse odd cycles crowd 1.
title: Odd cycles are RC's extremal family

DRAFT source-backed correction, pending referee check. In an infinite connected d-regular Cayley graph let rho be the normalized simple-random-walk spectral radius, so the adjacency norm is d*rho. The classical sufficient condition for bond nonuniqueness is p_c*d*rho<1: choose a supercritical p with p*d*rho<1, bound the connection kernel by the all-walk Neumann series, and exclude uniqueness by FKG. The degree-free p_c<1/rho condition in C0047-A001 is automatic when 0<rho<1 and p_c<=1, and is not that sufficient theorem. The correct condition is not necessary: on T4, p_c=1/3, rho=sqrt(3)/2 and p_u=1, while p_c*d*rho>1. This correction does not solve C0047.

For a finite family of events I let G_I = alpha_I^T Sigma_I^+ alpha_I be its Gallot-Kounias value, computed from the family's own probabilities and pairwise intersections. If J is a subfamily of I then G_J <= G_I. If B is an event whose indicator lies in span{1_{A_1}, ..., 1_{A_m}} in L2(P), then B is contained in the union of the A_i almost surely, so adding B to the family changes neither the union nor the Gallot-Kounias value.

Let T be an integrable, translation-invariant undirected lattice FPP metric, h(x)=E T(0,x), and g a norm with g(x)=lim_m h(mx)/m on lattice x. Write b(x)=h(x)-g(x) and X(x,y)=T(x,y)-h(y-x). Then b(x)>=0. If z lies on any attained minimizing path from 0 to v, then g(z)+g(v-z)-g(v)=b(v)-b(z)-b(v-z)+X(0,v)-X(0,z)-X(z,v) <= b(v)+X(0,v)-X(0,z)-X(z,v). In particular, if the three centered errors have magnitude at most s, the detour is at most b(v)+3s. No upper bound on the two interior mean biases is required.

Translation invariance of the edge law
A limiting norm g with the stated expectation limit

body:
Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with n >= 3, and let A be a measurable matrix field on Omega with |A(x)| <= Lambda and A(x)xi.xi >= alpha|xi|^2 for all xi in R^n and a.e. x, with alpha > 0 (bounded measurable uniformly elliptic coefficients; no continuity is assumed). Let f be in L^p(Omega) with p > n/2, and let u in H^1_0(Omega) be the weak solution of -div(A grad u) = f, i.e. integral_Omega A grad u . grad v = integral_Omega f v for all v in H^1_0(Omega). Then u is in L^infinity(Omega) and ||u||_{L^infinity} <= C ||f||_{L^p}, where C depends only on n, p, alpha and |Omega| (not on Lambda and not on any regularity of A). For n = 2 the same conclusion holds for every p > 1. WHERE IT FAILS: the exponent threshold is sharp. At p = n/2 the conclusion is false: on the unit ball of R^n, n >= 3, the function u(x) = log log(1 + 1/|x|) lies in H^1, is unbounded near the origin, and its Laplacian lies in L^(n/2); the borderline case only yields exponential integrability (Brezis-Merle type), not boundedness. Boundedness of Omega is used through the measure |Omega| in the constant. The estimate is one-sided in nothing: it bounds |u| because the argument is applied to u and to -u alike. Ellipticity is essential; for a degenerate A the truncation argument loses the Sobolev inequality it needs.

body:
Let n ≥ 1, T > 0, and let u ∈ C²([0,T]×R^n) solve ∂_t²u − Δu = 0 (no support or decay assumption is needed). Fix x0 ∈ R^n and t0 ∈ (0,T]. Then the local energy e(t) = (1/2)∫_{B(x0, t0−t)} ( |∂_t u(t,x)|² + |∇u(t,x)|² ) dx is nonincreasing on [0,t0). Consequences: (i) if u(0,·) = ∂_t u(0,·) = 0 on the ball B(x0,t0), then u ≡ 0 on the cone {(t,x): 0 ≤ t < t0, |x − x0| < t0 − t}; (ii) (uniqueness / domain of dependence) two C² solutions with the same Cauchy data on B(x0,t0) coincide on that cone, so the Cauchy problem has at most one C² solution; (iii) if supp u0 ∪ supp u1 ⊂ B̄(0,R), then supp u(t,·) ⊂ B̄(0,R+t) for 0 ≤ t ≤ T. The same holds for □u = F: u on the cone depends only on the data on B(x0,t0) and on F restricted to the cone.

body:
[Corollary 8 (Large cycles) of arXiv:2606.18047, 'Analysis of the asymmetric shelf shuffle'] Fix $p\in(0,1)$ and $k\geq 1$. Let $m=m_n$ be any sequence of positive integers, fixed or growing with $n$.  If $\pi_n\sim \nu^{(p)}_{n,m_n}$ and $\sigma_n$ is uniform on $S_n$, then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sup_{0\leq t_1,\ldots,t_k\leq 1}
\Bigg|&
\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{L_1(\pi_n)}{n}\leq t_1,\ldots,\frac{L_k(\pi_n)}{n}\leq t_k\right)\\
&-
\mathbb{P}\left(\frac{L_1(\sigma_n)}{n}\leq t_1,\ldots,\frac{L_k(\sigma_n)}{n}\leq t_k\right)
\Bigg|\longrightarrow 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, the ordered large cycles have the same $\operatorname{Poisson--Dirichlet}(1)$ limit as those of a uniform random permutation.

[Lemma 17 (Local split--merge--rewire rule) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Let \(\omega\) be a configuration, let \(\cL(\omega)\) be the associated loop
configuration, let \(e=\{x,y\}\in E\), and let \(s\in S^1\setminus T(\omega)\) be a
regular time. Consider the effect of inserting at \((e,s)\) either a cross or a bar.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item If \(I_{\neq}(\omega;e,s)=1\), then inserting either a cross or a bar
    merges the two loops containing \((x,s)\) and \((y,s)\) into one.

    \item If \(I_+(\omega;e,s)=1\), then inserting a cross splits the loop into two,
    whereas inserting a bar rewires the loop without changing the number of loops.

    \item If \(I_-(\omega;e,s)=1\), then inserting a bar splits the loop into two,
    whereas inserting a cross rewires the loop without changing the number of loops.
\end{enumerate}

Let pi(dx)=Z^{-1}exp(-V(x))dx be a smooth positive probability density on R, with V in C2(R) and bounded V_second. Let k:R-by-R->R be continuous, symmetric, positive definite and integrally strictly positive definite: its double integral against any finite nonzero signed Borel measure is strictly positive whenever that integral is defined. Assume integral k(x,x) pi(dx)<infinity. Let H_k be its RKHS and assume the embedding H_k into H1(pi) is continuous and dense. Define T f(x)=integral k(x,y)f(y)pi(dy). For phi in H_k set Q(phi)=integral [V_second(x)phi(x)^2+phi_prime(x)^2]pi(dx). Assume in addition that k(x,y)=h(x-y), where h is continuous on R, C1 on R minus {0}, absolutely continuous, and h(x)->0 and h_prime(x)->0 as x tends to either infinity. Then there is no lambda>0 satisfying the equivalent one-dimensional Stein curvature inequalities of Lemma 41. Equivalently exponential convergence near equilibrium fails in the precise Definition 32 sense. The claim does not assert that every individual solution fails to converge exponentially.

[Theorem 41 of arXiv:2608.25785, 'Proper Actions on Homogeneous Spaces of the Upper Triangular Matrix Group via Coarse Geome'] Fix $n\in \Z_{\geq 2}$. Then the following three conditions hold:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The map $\alpha_0=\mu_{(1,n,1,1)}\circ \iota_{\rmN(n)}$ is coarse.
        \item The map $\alpha_i$ is controlled for all $i\in [n-1]$.
        \item Fix a subset $I\subset [n-1]\cup\{0\}$ with $0\in I$ and $\Lambda\subset \Lambda_1(n)$.
        Then the following map is coarse:
        \[
        (\alpha_I, \mu_{\Lambda}):\rmN(n)\to \R^{I\sqcup \Lambda}, \quad X\mapsto (\alpha_i(X))_{i\in I}\oplus (\mu_\Lambda(X)).
        \]
        Here, in case $\Lambda=\emptyset$, put
        $(\alpha_I, \mu_{\Lambda}):=\alpha_I$.
    \end{enumerate}

body: The classical Čech complex and Vietoris-Rips complex on Poisson point processes embed into the marked stationary RCM framework: for Vietoris-Rips at scale $r$, $\varphi_1(x, y) = \mathbf{1}\{\|x - y\| \le r\}$ and $\varphi_j \equiv 1$ for all $j \ge 2$ (clique complex); for Čech at radius $r$, the grains are closed balls $B(x, r/2)$ in the Boolean model representation. The CLTs for Betti numbers and Euler characteristics developed by Dominik Pabst encompass both models as deterministic specializations.
title: Embedding of Čech and Vietoris-Rips Complexes in RCM

body:
[Lem -1 of arXiv:2411.13403, 'Path weighting method for spot sensitivities and its variance reduction'] Let $X$, $\tilde{X}$ be two $n$-dimensional random
variables such that $\mathbb{E}(X)=\mathbb{E}(\tilde{X})=x_{0}$,
and $g(x)\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$. Let
\begin{equation}
\kappa(r)=\max_{|x|\le r}|\partial_{x}^{2}g(x)|,\;r>0.
\end{equation}
Then
\[
\big|\mathbb{E}[g(\tilde{X})]-\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\big|\le C\mathbb{E}\big[\big(\kappa(|x_{0}|)+\kappa(|X|)+\kappa(|\tilde{X}|)\big)(|\tilde{X}-X|^{2}+|X-x_{0}||\tilde{X}-X|)\big].
\]
title: Lem -1 of arXiv:2411.13403

body:
[Prop app-hilbert-flow of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] Let $\Gamma$ act on $\partial_\infty^{(2)}\Gamma\times\mathbb R$ by
\begin{equation}
  \eta\cdot(x,y,s)
  :=\bigl(\eta x,\eta y,s-c_H(\eta,y)\bigr).
\end{equation}
This action is properly discontinuous and cocompact, with the quotient 
\[
  X_H:=\Gamma\backslash
  \bigl(\partial_\infty^{(2)}\Gamma\times\mathbb R\bigr)
\]
admitting the translation flow
\[
  [x,y,s]\longmapsto[x,y,s-t]
\]
that satisfies:
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] The translation flow on $X_H$ 
is H\"older conjugate to a H\"older reparametrization of $\phi_t$ on
$T^1S$.  (In what follows, we use this conjugacy to regard it as a flow $\psi^H_t$ on $T^1S$.)

\item[(ii)] The topological entropy of $\psi^H_t$ is $h_H$.

\item[(iii)] The  closed
orbits of the flow correspond to  closed geodesics
on $S$, and the orbit corresponding to a geodesic $\gamma$ has period
$\ell^H_{\rho_0}(\gamma)$. 

\item[(iv)] $\psi^H_t$ has a unique invariant
probability measure of maximal entropy, denoted by $\widetilde m_H$.
\end{itemize}

[Theorem thm:CvChainPermuton of arXiv:2512.20338, 'Up-down chains and scaling limits: \\ application to permuton- and graphon-valued diffusio'] Let $\{ \sigma_{n,0} \}_{ n \ge 1 } $ be a sequence of (random) permutations converging to a (random) permuton $\mu_0$.
  For all $n$, let $ X _n$ be the up-down chain with transition kernel $  p^\uparrow _n  p^\downarrow _{ n + 1 } $ and initial distribution $\Law( \sigma_{n,0} )$. 
  Then there exists a Feller process $ F $ in $  \mathcal P   $ with initial distribution $\Law(\mu_0)$ and sample paths in $D([0,\infty),  \mathcal P  )$ satisfying the path convergence
	$$
		\big(
			 \iota (  X _n (  \lfloor  n^2 t  \rfloor  ) )
		\big)_{ t \ge 0 }
			\Longrightarrow
        		\big(
        				 F ( t )
        		\big)_{ t \ge 0 }
			.
	$$
	
	\noindent
	Here $  \iota  $ denotes the inclusion from the set of permutations to the space of permutons. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

Owner-own-work derived corollary; status proof (unaudited), independent review and priority assessment pending. Fix D>=k>=2, 0<a<=b, delta in (0,1) and an (a,b)-bi-Lipschitz map F:[0,1]^k to R^D. Let P_delta contain all measurable probability densities with 1-delta<=p<=1+delta and no common Lipschitz bound. Let C_N contain all continuous piecewise-affine curves from [0,1] to R^D with at most N pieces, including constant plateaux. Define E_N=sup_(p in P_delta) inf_(g in C_N) W1(g#Unif[0,1],F#(p dx)). There are positive constants c1,c2 depending only on k,D,a,b,delta such that c1*(N log(N+2)^2)^(-1/k)<=E_N<=c2*N^(-1/k) for N>=2. Consequently log(E_N)/log N tends to -1/k and no uniform exponent beta>1/k is possible on this density class, even for the flat inclusion. The upper uses cube quantization and positive-time plateau/connector curves, with the connector mass tending to zero inside an infimum. The lower applies audited density packing and unrestricted-real-weight VC covering, using a single N-hidden-unit shallow architecture with (D+2)N+D charged edge weights and biases containing every N-piece curve. The faster exponent 2/(2k-1) requires extra hypotheses such as common density regularity; this corollary does not contradict such a theorem. Densities in the supremum may depend on N. No lower rate for one fixed density or a singleton uniform-surface law is asserted. The logarithmic gap remains unresolved. Known ingredients: Yang-Li-Wang arXiv:2101.12353 Lemma 3.2 p.10 and audited w728 T2-001 v1, T2-005 v1/v2; no new-construction or novelty claim.
Exactly the fixed bi-Lipschitz cube map and varying bounded density class above; unrestricted real coefficients, scalar uniform source, at most N continuous affine pieces. Analytic proof unaudited.
title: Draft: shallow scalar-noise generators have minimax exponent 1/k over bounded cube densities

body: For a linear operator (or square matrix) A, a nonzero vector v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue lambda if A v = lambda v. The eigenvalues are exactly the scalars lambda for which A - lambda I is singular, i.e. the roots of the characteristic polynomial det(A - lambda I). The set of eigenvectors for a fixed lambda together with 0 is the eigenspace, a subspace; its dimension is the geometric multiplicity, at most the algebraic multiplicity (the root's multiplicity in the characteristic polynomial).
title: Eigenvalue and Eigenvector

[Dfn 53 (controlled processes and endpoint measures) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $q_0 \in [0,1)$ and $q_* \in [q_0,q_0+\epsilon]$, define the following mutually independent random variables.
    Let $B,W$ be Brownian motions on the time interval $t\in [q_*,1]$ with $B(q_*) = W(q_*) = 0$. Let $U,U' \sim \unif([0,1])$.
    For measures $\zeta, \zeta^\Ising \in \cP_2(\R)$, let $X(q_*) \sim \zeta$ and $Y(q_*) \sim \zeta^\Ising$.
    Define the filtrations $\cF_X$ and $\cF_Y$ by
    \beq
        \begin{aligned}
            \cF_X(t) &= \sigma\Big(
                (B(s): q_* \le s\le t),
                U,X(q_*)
            \Big)\,,\\
            \cF_Y(t) &= \sigma\Big(
                (W(s) : q_* \le s\le t),
                U',Y(q_*)
            \Big)\,. 
        \end{aligned}
    \eeq
Recall from \eqref{e:s.sqrt.fn} that $s(t) \equiv [(tp)'(t)]^{1/2}$.  Recall the notations of Definition~\ref{d:achievable-msrs-sym}.
    For $p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$
    (see Definition~\ref{d:incr.p}) and control processes $b,\sigma \in \ProgMsrbl(\cF_X)$, $w\in \ProgMsrbl(\cF_Y)$, define
    \begin{align}
        
        X(t)
        &= X(q_*) + \int_{q_*}^t p'(u)^{1/2}\,b_u\,du
        +\int_{q_*}^t s(u)\sigma_u \,dB(u)\,,
        \\
        
        Y(t)
        &=Y(q_*) + \int_{q_*}^t w_u \,dW(u)\,,
    \end{align}
    with initial conditions $X(q_*) \sim \zeta$ and  $Y(q_*) \sim \zeta^\Ising$ as described above. Define
\beq

Method: Metric scaling of critical random-walk vacant components structural reduction Result: A high degree need not imply large escape capacity. Attach K leaves to a vertex v that has just one additional edge leading into a fixed transient infinite tree. Every walk step from v into a leaf returns to v with probability1; only the remaining edge can contribute to escape. Thus d_v*P_v(no return after time0) is at most1, uniformly in K. Check: Condition on the first step from v. Each leaf contributes0 to the sum of neighbor escape probabilities, and the one transient branch contributes at most1. This is the usual unit-conductance singleton capacity calculation. Obstruction: The example is not a configuration-model limit theorem. It shows why deleting hubs based only on degree can fail: escape geometry, not stationary occupation alone, controls avoidance.

For every complex (or real) m x n matrix A there is a unique n x m matrix A^+ satisfying the four Penrose equations A A^+ A = A, A^+ A A^+ = A^+, (A A^+)^* = A A^+ and (A^+ A)^* = A^+ A. If A = U Sigma V^* is a singular value decomposition with Sigma carrying the nonzero singular values sigma_1, ..., sigma_r, then A^+ = V Sigma^+ U^* where Sigma^+ inverts each nonzero singular value in place and transposes the shape. A A^+ is the orthogonal projector onto the range of A and A^+ A the orthogonal projector onto the row space (the orthogonal complement of the kernel). For every b in C^m, x = A^+ b minimises |A x - b| over all x and has the smallest norm among the minimisers; if A has full column rank then A^+ = (A^* A)^{-1} A^*, and if A is square and invertible then A^+ = A^{-1}.
A any m x n complex or real matrix (no rank condition)
* denotes the conjugate transpose; the SVD exists for every matrix

body: Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold with curvature tensor R (sign convention R(X,Y)Z = nabla_X nabla_Y Z - nabla_Y nabla_X Z - nabla_{[X,Y]} Z), and let p in M. For a 2-dimensional subspace (2-plane) sigma of T_pM spanned by linearly independent vectors u, v, the sectional curvature is K(sigma) = g(R(u,v)v,u) / (g(u,u)g(v,v) - g(u,v)^2). This value does not depend on the choice of basis u, v of sigma, and it equals the Gaussian curvature at p of the 2-dimensional surface swept out by the geodesics through p tangent to sigma. Sectional curvature determines the full curvature tensor R.
title: Sectional Curvature

[Dfn 204 (spatial rerandomization for spherical perceptron) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] We use the buckets from Definition~\ref{d:buckets} to
 define a new process $\vY\equiv\vY^{\RomI:\RomIII}$, as follows. First let $a(q_0)$ be sampled uniformly at random from $[M]$. Then, conditional on $a(q_0), \ldots, a(q_d)$, we let $a(q_{d+1})$ be sampled from the measure $\bP$ conditional on the bucket at time $q_d$, that is,
    \[a(q_{d+1})
    \sim \bP
    \bigg( a = \cdot \,\bigg|\, 
    a\in B(q_d,a(q_d)) \bigg)\,.
    \]
We then let $\vY(q_d)$ be the average of $\vX^\trunc$ over all the particles in the bucket containing $a(q_d)$, 
    \beq
    \vY(q_d)
    =
    \sum_{a\in B(q_d,a(q_d))}
    \frac{\vX^\trunc(q_d,a)}{|B(q_d,a(q_d))|}
    \,.
    \eeq
Informally, $\vY$ is the process $\vX^\trunc$ with ``spatial rerandomization at scale $\eta$.'' It is easy to check (by induction) that each $a(q_d)$ is marginally uniform on $[M]$, which implies that $\vX^\trunc(q_d)$ and $\vY(q_d)$ are within $W_{\infty}$ distance $O(\eta/\delta)$ for each fixed $d$.  Likewise, we define $\vY^\frozen\equiv\vY^{\frozen,\RomI:\RomIII}$ to be the spatial rerandomization of $\vX^\frozen$ at scale $\eta$, with random indices $a^\frozen(q_d) \in[M^\frozen]$
and buckets $\mathcal{B}^\frozen(q_d)$.
title: spatial rerandomization for spherical perceptron

(2) For a random (d, k)-regular hypergraph, let w_i, w'_i be unit eigenvectors of B associated with two eigenvalues mu_i, mu'_i given by (6) with mu_i, mu'_i not in {1, -(k - 1)}. Then, for d > k >= 3, with high probability, for all i in [n], ||w_i||_inf, ||w'_i||_inf <= ((sqrt(k - 1) + o(1)) / (sqrt(d - 1) - sqrt(k - 1))) ||v_i||_inf.

Status: independently checked proof; reviewer PASS on the listed claim version. Target 1, kind moved. The drift and variance coefficients were already predicted in the dossier; the result here is a finite-moment regularization and bounded-test-function argument. No entrance theorem or full weak path limit is claimed.

## Statement

Fix 0<d<K<infinity. Uniformly for u in [d,K], put theta=1/(nu). Let a,g be independent standard Gaussian vectors in R^n, X=a_+, and Y=(cos(theta)a+sin(theta)g)_+. An explicit event G below has probability at least 1-C exp(-c n), uniformly in u. Define U'=1/(n angle(X,Y)) on G and U'=u off G. For every bounded C^3 function f on [0,infinity) with bounded derivatives through order three,

    n E[f(U')-f(u)] = (2u+1/(3 pi)) f'(u) + u^2 f''(u) + O_{d,K,f}(n^-1/2).

The same assertion for the exact angle transition, killed at extinction or angle zero and with any bounded value for f at the cemetery state, follows by changing the generator by at most 2n||f||_infinity C exp(-cn). This is local generator convergence, not a compact-containment or entrance assertion.

## 1. Good event and quantitative elementary bounds

Write A={i:a_i>0}, k=|A|, S=sum_A a_i^2, C0=sum_A a_i g_i, V=sum_A g_i^2 and R=V-C0^2/S when S>0. Conditional on k>=2, S has chi-square k law; R has chi-square k-1 law and is independent of S. Indeed conditional on a, projection of g_A perpendicular to a_A is independent standard Gaussian on a (k-1)-dimensional subspace. Its squared norm has a law depending only on k, not on a.

Let J=sum_i g_i^2 1{|a_i|<=2 theta |g_i|}. Choose a fixed sufficiently small eta>0 (for example eta=10^-8), and let G be the intersection of

    n/3 <= k <= 2n/3; n/8 <= S,R <= 2n;
    ||a||^2 <= 2n; ||g||^2 <= 2n; J <= eta n.

For all sufficiently large n (depending on d), P(G^c)<=C_d exp(-c n). The binomial and chi-square bounds follow by applying Markov's inequality to their explicit moment-generating functions. For J, with any fixed 0<lambda<1/4,

    E exp(lambda g_i^2 1{|a_i|<=2 theta |g_i|})
    <= 1 + C theta E[|g_i| (exp(lambda g_i^2)-1)] <= 1+C_lambda theta.

Consequently E exp(lambda J)<=exp(C_lambda n theta)<=exp(C_lambda/d). Markov gives P(J>eta n)<=exp(C_lambda/d-lambda eta n). This also proves E[J^p]<=C_{p,d} for every fixed p, by integrating the exponential tail. Constants need not be efficient.

On k in [n/3,2n/3], all fixed positive and inverse moments of S/n and R/n are uniformly bounded for sufficiently large n. Their centered fluctuations have L^p size O_p(n^-1/2). Thus deleting the exponential-probability failures of the other conditions changes fixed such moments, including logarithmic moments, by exponentially small terms (Cauchy–Schwarz with a moment of twice the order). Small k is excluded before making this argument; no logarithm or inverse of a zero chi-square is taken.

## 2. Flip moments

Set b=cos(theta)a+sin(theta)g, Z=(b-a)1_A, r=Y-X-Z. The vector r is supported on sign flips. For theta sufficiently small, any flip satisfies |a_i|<=2 theta |g_i|. On that set,

    |r_i|+|Z_i| <= C theta |g_i|,  |X_i r_i| <= C theta^2 g_i^2.

Hence H=2<Z,r>+||r||^2 and B=<X,r> obey

    ||H||_p + ||B||_p <= C_{p,d} theta^2,  p fixed.

For the expectation of H use the exact Gaussian polar integral. A flip from a>0 to b<0 contributes 2ab-b^2; the opposite flip contributes b^2. Swapping a,b converts the latter contribution to a^2 on the first flip sector. In polar coordinates a=r0 sin(e), b=r0 sin(e-theta), 0<e<theta, with E r0^2=2 and uniform polar angle,

    E H_i = (1/pi) integral_0^theta [sin^2(e)+2 sin(e)sin(e-theta)-sin^2(e-theta)] de
          = (theta cos(theta)-sin(theta))/pi
          = -theta^3/(3 pi) + O(theta^5).

The last error follows from |sin x-x|<=|x|^3/6 on this interval, whose integrand error is O(theta^4) and length theta. Therefore EH=-n theta^3/(3 pi)+O(n theta^5). This recovers the dossier's settled coefficient and does not claim it as new.

## 3. Angular decomposition on G

Let P project perpendicular to X. Then PZ=sin(theta)Pg_A, and

    ||P Y||^2 = sin^2(theta) R + Htilde,
    Htilde = H - 2[(cos(theta)-1)+sin(theta) C0/S] B - B^2/S.

On G, S and R are of order n and |C0|<=sqrt(SV)<=2n. The J bound with eta small makes |Htilde|/(sin^2(theta)R)<=1/2. Also

    <X,Y>/S = Q = cos(theta)+sin(theta) C0/S+B/S

is bounded above and below by constants tending to 1 uniformly as n increases. In particular the angle is well-defined, positive and small on G. Set xi=Htilde/(sin^2(theta)R). The preceding moment bounds and chi-square inverse moments give

    E[xi 1_G] = -2 theta/(3 pi)+O_{d,K}(n^-3/2),
    E[|xi|^p 1_G] = O_{p,d,K}(n^-p), p=2,3.

For clarity, the denominator replacement uses ||H/theta^2||_2=O_d(1) and

    ||1/R-2/n||_2 = O(n^-3/2)

on the central-k region, including binomial variation of k. Thus replacing R by n/2 in the expectation costs O(n^-3/2); replacing sin^2(theta) by theta^2 costs O(n^-3). The projection corrections cost O(n^-5/2)+O(n^-3): use ||C0/S||_p=O(n^-1/2), ||B||_p=O(theta^2), and 1/S=O(1/n). Exponentially small deletions are controlled as in section 1. No untruncated inverse of the exact output angle is used.

From tan(theta')=||P Y||/(sqrt(S) Q), the logarithmic angular increment on G is

    z=log(theta'/theta)
      = (1/2)log(R/S)+(1/2)log(1+xi)-log Q+E0,

where |E0|<=C theta^2 on G. This uses sin(theta)/theta=1+O(theta^2) and arctan(v)/v=1+O(v^2); R/S and Q are bounded on G. Furthermore

    |E[log Q 1_G]|=O(n^-2),  ||log Q 1_G||_p=O(n^-3/2)+O(n^-2).

To see the expectation bound, E[C0/S; central k]=0 by Gaussian symmetry before the other restrictions; removing G^c changes it exponentially little by Cauchy–Schwarz. The remaining terms are O(theta^2), O(theta^2/n), and O(theta^2 E(C0/S)^2). These estimates hold uniformly on the fixed compact [d,K].

## 4. Baseline chi-square ratio and the generator

Define z=0 off G. For central k, the independent chi-square logarithms give

    E[(1/2)log(R/S)|k] = (1/2)[psi((k-1)/2)-psi(k/2)] = -1/(2k)+O(k^-2),
    Var[(1/2)log(R/S)|k] = (1/4)[psi1((k-1)/2)+psi1(k/2)] = 1/k+O(k^-2).

Here the expansions follow from the usual positive-real large-argument gamma logarithmic derivatives; they can equivalently be obtained by Taylor expansion of log(chi-square/k) on its central event and exponential tail bounds. Since E[1/k; central k]=2/n+O(n^-2), the mean is -1/n+O(n^-2) and variance 2/n+O(n^-2). Fixed centered third absolute moments are O(n^-3/2), from chi-square centered sixth moments and the same truncation. Deleting G^c is exponentially negligible as above.

Combining sections 2–3, and using Cauchy–Schwarz for the baseline/flip covariance, yields

    Ez = -1/n-theta/(3 pi)+O(n^-3/2),
    Ez^2 = 2/n+O(n^-3/2), E|z|^3=O(n^-3/2).

Moreover |z| is bounded on G by an n-independent constant. Thus Taylor's remainder for exp(-z) is bounded by C|z|^3. Since U'=u exp(-z), uniformly for u in [d,K],

    n E(U'-u)=2u+1/(3 pi)+O(n^-1/2),
    n E(U'-u)^2=2u^2+O(n^-1/2),
    n E|U'-u|^3=O(n^-1/2).

Taylor's theorem for f proves the stated generator formula. Bounded f makes comparison with the killed exact kernel immediate from P(G^c)<=Ce^-cn, even though the latter has infinite raw inverse-angle moments.

## What this does not settle

The argument is uniform only on fixed compact intervals [d,K] with d>0. It supplies no passage from fixed theta_0 to u>0 at time o(1), no compact-containment theorem, and no convergence rate for the final two-input outputs. Those remain the hardest target-1 requirements. The constants in the exponential deletion bound are inefficient; no numerical performance of that bound is asserted.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:c6924ed4fbeaf5d90fdf5114b0b93de31bd962d24a9c78646726cf7f392aec86","revision_digest":"sha256:853e9e56a5ede8d6cbc9d892220bc47974eee7136bb5ff5a8cad3399df3a4696","source_id":"owner-own-work:T244-w691-C004:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v1-reviewer-pass","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: For alpha >= 1 let psi_alpha(x) = exp(x^alpha) - 1. The psi_alpha norm of a random variable X is ||X||_{psi_alpha} = inf{k in (0, infinity) : E[psi_alpha(|X|/k)] <= 1} = inf{k > 0 : E[exp((|X|/k)^alpha)] <= 2}. A random variable with finite psi_2 norm is sub-Gaussian and one with finite psi_1 norm is sub-exponential, and ||X||_{psi_p} < infinity if and only if P(|X| >= x) <= K exp(-K' x^p) for some constants K, K' > 0. (For 0 < alpha < 1 the same formula defines a quasi-norm, the 'sub-Weibull' case of later papers; the cited source covers alpha >= 1 only.)

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT C016 v1, proof (unaudited); no novelty or independent-review claim. Let f_theta(x)=m^(-1)sum_i a_i sigma(w_i dot x), d>=1, m>=28 and fixed finite total mean-field time T>=0. Assume sigma globally C2 with absolute values of sigma and its first two derivatives <=1, bounded data ||X||<=1, |Y|<=1, and population half-squared loss. Initialize two independent collections of iid pairs with common product law a~N(0,1), w~N(0,Gamma), Gamma PSD with trace <=1. Train BOTH layers simultaneously with mean-field SGD multiplier m, fresh samples or finite minibatch averages conditional on initialization and the JOINT past, and common deterministic nonnegative steps eta_n summing to <=T. Independent streams or common fresh samples are allowed; there is no teacher assumption. One joint initial permutation of (a,w) yields expected population loss-chord barrier <=2Lambda_T sqrt(3Astar_T)[2r_G(m)+2sqrt(2)G_T sqrt(sum eta_n^2)]^(beta_T/2)+49exp(2T)/sqrt(m), with explicit constants from proof statement and beta_T=exp(-kappa_T T)>0. Here r_G is the trace-bounded Gaussian covariance matching bound of C015 v1. If eta_max<=1/log(m+e), this gives O_T((log log m)^(beta_T/2)(log m)^(-beta_T/4)), uniformly over d,Gamma and bounded data laws. body:
Let $x_1, \dots, x_n \in \mathbb{R}^p$ be i.i.d. with mean zero, covariance $\Sigma$ and finite eighth moments, $S = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i x_i^T$, and let $\mu = \operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)/p$, with the scaled Frobenius norm $\|A\|^2 = \operatorname{tr}(A A^T)/p$. Define $\alpha^2 = \|\Sigma - \mu I\|^2$, $\beta^2 = E\|S - \Sigma\|^2$, $\delta^2 = E\|S - \mu I\|^2 = \alpha^2 + \beta^2$. THEOREM (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004). Among all estimators of the form $\rho_1 I + \rho_2 S$ with nonrandom $\rho_1, \rho_2$, the expected loss $E\|\hat\Sigma - \Sigma\|^2$ is minimized by $$\Sigma^* = \frac{\beta^2}{\delta^2}\, \mu I + \frac{\alpha^2}{\delta^2}\, S,$$ a convex combination of the sample covariance and the scaled identity, with expected loss $\alpha^2 \beta^2 / \delta^2$. The constants have consistent plug-in estimates under general asymptotics $p/n \to \gamma \in (0, \infty)$: $\hat\mu = \operatorname{tr}(S)/p$, $\hat\delta^2 = \|S - \hat\mu I\|^2$, $\hat{\bar b}^2 = \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_i \|x_i x_i^T - S\|^2$, $\hat\beta^2 = \min(\hat{\bar b}^2, \hat\delta^2)$, $\hat\alpha^2 = \hat\delta^2 - \hat\beta^2$, and the resulting estimator $\hat\Sigma^* = \frac{\hat\beta^2}{\hat\delta^2}\hat\mu I + \frac{\hat\alpha^2}{\hat\delta^2} S$ has the same asymptotic loss as $\Sigma^*$, is always well conditioned and invertible, and is uniformly no worse than $S$. The shrinkage target is the scaled identity, so the estimator pulls all eigenvalues of $S$ toward their mean $\hat\mu$; when one eigenvalue of $\Sigma$ dominates the trace (a strong spike), $\hat\mu$ is dominated by that spike and the target is far from the small eigenvalues.
i.i.d. rows with finite eighth moments (mean zero, or centered)
p/n -> gamma in (0, infinity)
loss is the scaled Frobenius norm tr(A A^T)/p

body: In probability theory, a martingale is a stochastic process in which the expected value of the next observation, given all prior observations, is equal to the most recent value. In other words, the conditional expectation of the next value, given the past, is equal to the present value. Martingales are used to model fair games, where future expected winnings are equal to the current amount regardless of past outcomes.
title: Martingale (probability theory)

r_\theta^{(L+1)/2}.

\longrightarrow

[Proposition prop:mu0 of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] A proof of Conjecture~(conj:CE of the paper) cannot restrict to selections with
$\mu=0$. Concretely, for the seventh-roots system
$t_j=\zeta^j,\ z_j=\zeta^{3j},\ p_j=\frac17$ ($\zeta=e^{2\pi i/7}$), every
$q$ with $\mu=0$ satisfies $C\ge\frac{7/k-1}2$ for support $k$ (a discrete
Parseval identity), i.e.\ $C\ge\frac38>\frac14$ at $k=4$ and
$C\ge\frac23>\frac58$ at $k=3$; yet unconstrained selections achieve
$C=\frac27$ at three points (the difference set $\{0,1,3\}$) and $C<\frac14$
at four consecutive points (an exact algebraic computation modulo
$x^3+x^2-2x-1$). Similarly, for the regular hexagon third-harmonic system
($t_j=e^{\pi ij/3}$, $z_j=(-1)^j$, $p_j=\frac16$) all $\mu=0$ selections of
support $\le3$ have $C=1$, while $\{0,1,2\}$ at weights $2{:}3{:}2$ attains
the exact three-point optimum $C=\frac12$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Let f : R^d -> C be Lebesgue measurable and finite almost everywhere, let E be a measurable set of FINITE measure, and let eps > 0. Then there is a compact (hence closed) set F contained in E with |E \ F| < eps such that the RESTRICTION of f to F is continuous. Moreover one may take g in C_c(R^d) with g = f on F and sup |g| <= sup |f|. The theorem does not assert that f is continuous AT the points of F as a function on R^d: the indicator of the rationals is nowhere continuous on R, yet it agrees with the zero function off a set of measure zero, and Lusin's F can be taken to be any closed set of irrationals of nearly full measure. Finiteness of |E| may be relaxed to sigma-finiteness by exhausting E, at the price of stating the conclusion with |E \ F| < eps for each piece. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 2.24]

Converse (Lusin's criterion): let E be a Lebesgue measurable subset of R^d of finite measure and let f:E->C be a function. If for every eps>0 there is a closed F contained in E with |E\F|<eps such that f restricted to F is continuous, then f is Lebesgue measurable on E. Thus measurability of an a.e.-finite function on such E is equivalent to continuity of its restriction on closed subsets missing arbitrarily small measure. Applied on every bounded measurable piece, this gives the local criterion on R^d.
f measurable and a.e. finite
|E| < infinity (or E sigma-finite, applied piecewise)
the measure is Borel regular, so that inner regularity by closed sets is available

A uniform limit of continuous functions on F is continuous on F. [Lemma 13 of arXiv:2607.16954, 'Repeated differentiation of deterministic polynomials with asymptotically radial root dist'] Consider positive integers $k,l\leq n$  such that when $n\to\infty$ we have $1-k/n\to \alpha$ and $l/n\to t$. In the case $\Delta<0$, we assume
\[
\alpha>\alpha_{\min}=t\vert\Delta\vert. 
\]
Then 
\begin{equation}
\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[\prod_{j=0}^{ml-1}\frac{\falling{mn-mk+j\Delta}{b}} {\falling{mn-mk+m+j\Delta}{b}}\right]^\frac{1}{m}=\begin{cases} e^{-\frac{ta}{\alpha}} & \text{if } \Delta=0, \\
\left(1+\frac{t\Delta}{\alpha}\right)^{-\frac{b}{\Delta}} & \text{if } \Delta\neq 0.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Here, it does not matter if $m$ is fixed or if it tends to $\infty$.
title: Lemma 13 of arXiv:2607.16954

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma 3 (Young integration) of arXiv:2607.04193, 'Onsager--Machlup Functionals for Generalized Newtonian Equations of Motion with Time-Varyi'] Let \(f\in C^\beta([0,T];\mathbb R)\) and
\(g\in C^\gamma([0,T];\mathbb R)\), where
\(\beta,\gamma\in(0,1)\) and \(\beta+\gamma>1\). Then the
Riemann--Stieltjes integral
\[
    \int_0^t f_s\,dg_s
\]
is well defined pathwise for all \(t\in[0,T]\). Moreover, there exists a
constant \(C_{\beta,\gamma,T}>0\) such that, for any
\(0\le s<t\le T\),
\begin{equation}
    \left|
        \int_s^t f_r\,dg_r
        -
        f_s(g_t-g_s)
    \right|
    \le
    C_{\beta,\gamma,T}
    [f]_{\beta}
    [g]_{\gamma}
    |t-s|^{\beta+\gamma}.
    
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition 9 (Consequences of delocalization and balance) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Under \eqref{eq:spike-package},
\begin{align}
 \max_i x_i^2&=o(N^{-1/2}),
 \\
 \sum_i x_i^4&=o(N^{-1/2}),
 \\
 \max_{i<j}|s_{ij}|&=o(1).
 
\end{align}
The linear profile satisfies
\begin{align}
 \max_{i,j}|p_{ij}^{(1)}|&=o(1),
 \\
 \frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}|p_{ij}^{(1)}|&=O(N^{-1/2}),
 \\
 \frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}(p_{ij}^{(1)})^2&=O(N^{-1}),
 \\
 N\left|\frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}p_{ij}^{(1)}\right|&=o(1),
 \\
 \max_i\frac1N\sum_j|p_{ij}^{(1)}|&=o(N^{-1/4}).
 
\end{align}
The quadratic profile satisfies
\begin{align}
 \max_{i,j}|p_{ij}^{(2)}|&=o(1),
 \\
 \frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}|p_{ij}^{(2)}|&=O(N^{-1}),
 \\
 \frac1{N^2}\sum_{i,j}(p_{ij}^{(2)})^2&=o(N^{-1}),
 \\
 \max_i\frac1N\sum_j|p_{ij}^{(2)}|&=o(N^{-1/2}).
 
\end{align}
No stronger polynomial rate follows from \eqref{eq:spike-package} alone.

Then the damped Sine--Gordon Markov cocycle \eqref{e.060402} has a unique stationary measure $\mu_\s^{\eps}$ that attracts transition probabilities exponentially under the Wasserstein metric $\mathbb{W}_{\|\cdot\|_X\wedge1}$.

body:
[Lem 143 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $0\leq \ell\leq \ubl$ we have:
  \begin{align}
  
  \bbE[
  U^\ell-U^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,\cF^U(\ell-1)]
  &=0,
  \\
  
  \bbE[
  Y^\ell-Y^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell-1)]
  =
   \bbE[
  Y^\ell-Y^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^U(\ell-1)]
  &=
  0,
  \\
  
  \bbE[
  V^\ell-V^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^V(\ell-1)]
  &=0,
  \\
  
  \bbE[
  M^\ell-M^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^M(\ell-1)]
  =
  \bbE[M^\ell-M^{\ell-1}
  \,|\,
  \cF^V(\ell-1)]
   &=
  0
  .
  \end{align}

\begin{proof}
We will show inductively that
\eqref{eq:u-increments-orthogonal}
implies
\eqref{eq:y-increments-orthogonal},
which implies
\eqref{eq:v-increments-orthogonal},
which implies 
\eqref{eq:m-increments-orthogonal},
which finally implies
\eqref{eq:u-increments-orthogonal}
with $\ell+1$ in place of $\ell$.
In the base case, \eqref{eq:u-increments-orthogonal} with $\ell=1$ is trivial, since $U^0=0$, $\mathcal{F}^U(0)$ is the $\sigma$-field generated by $Y[0]$, and $U^1$ is a centered gaussian random variable independent of $Y[0]$. We therefore proceed with the inductive argument:

\begin{itemize}
\item
\eqref{eq:u-increments-orthogonal} $\Rightarrow$ \eqref{eq:y-increments-orthogonal}: from the definition
\eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments},
  \[
  \E\Big(Y^\ell-Y^{\ell-1} 
  \,\Big|\,
  \cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell-1)\Big)
  = \frac{w^{\ell-1}
  (\prxY^{\ell-1})}{\gamma(\ell-1,\delta)}
  \E \Big(U^\ell-U^{\ell-1} 
  \,\Big|\,
  \cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell-1)\Big)\,.
  \]
We also claim
that $\cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell)$
is contained in 
$\cF^U(\ell)$ for all $\ell$: indeed, in the base case we have $\cF^{Y,\prxY}(0) =\cF^U(0)$, so if we suppose inductively that 
$\cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell)$ is contained in $\cF^U(\ell)$, then
\eqref{e:state.evol.x.y.increments}  implies 
\[\cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell+1)
\subseteq \sigma\Big(
\cF^{Y,\prxY}(\ell),
\cF^U(\ell+1)
\Big)
\subseteq \cF^U(\ell+1)
\,,\]

STATUS: proof (unaudited). For equal-variance q>0 critical tanh inputs, the exact infinitesimal angular multiplier satisfies H_q^2=q*h^T D P_x D h/||x||^2, with x=tanh(sqrt(q)g), D=diag(sech^2(sqrt(q)g)), independent standard Gaussian g,h. The norm multiplier is M_q=||x||^2/(nq); conditional tangent weights and denominator share g. At fixed n>=2, q->0 gives jointly (M_q,H_q)->(S/n,sqrt(R/S)) with independent S~chi-square_n,R~chi-square_(n-1). Assumptions: Zero biases, Gaussian weight variance exactly 1/n, no shaping normalizer; equal input diagonal variances; theta derivative at 0 taken first; n>=2. Scope: Exact one-step infinitesimal-angle identity only. Not a finite-angle tanh network limit; no drift or cumulant expansion asserted. Independent audit pending.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:61540c5a30665f23d715dfa877ed36851d4f5e6b8bcc57c61ae9d265cd7eb3e0","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/61/61540c5a30665f23d715dfa877ed36851d4f5e6b8bcc57c61ae9d265cd7eb3e0.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:77287f4d4792c9d694f179b6884ade1129b6f8376e899da074d1e85d979a5106","bundle_entry_key":"tanh-tangent-shared-quadratic-form","bundle_id":"population.t244-tanh-tangent-shared-wishart-noise-017","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"probability; random neural networks","draft":"w691/bundle_017.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.randomnetworks:t244-tanh-tangent-shared-quadratic-form","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Critical tanh: exact tangent kernel and its shared Wishart noise

20 October 2026. C050/C051; Target 3. Proof drafts, unaudited.
These are infinitesimal-angle one-step results, not a two-input tanh
diffusion theorem or an all-order cumulant expansion. No novelty asserted.

## C050: exact positive-variance kernel

Fix n>=2 and q>0. Let g,h be independent N(0,I_n) vectors. For two inputs
with equal preactivation variance q and angle theta, the next activated
vectors are exactly distributed as

    x = tanh(sqrt(q) g),
    y(theta) = tanh(sqrt(q)(cos(theta)g+sin(theta)h)).

The independent Gaussian weight rows give these conditional marginals
given the present Gram matrix. The tanh critical weight variance is 1/n;
thus the next diagonal variance is K'=||x||^2/n and the radial multiplier
is M_q=||x||^2/(nq). There is no width-dependent shaping normalizer.

Set D=diag(sech^2(sqrt(q)g_i)), P_x=I-xx^T/||x||^2. Then the right-hand
derivative H_q of the angle between x and y(theta) at theta=0 is

    H_q^2 = q h^T D P_x D h / ||x||^2.

Proof: y(0)=x and y'(0)=sqrt(q)Dh. The derivative of y/||y|| is
sqrt(q)P_x Dh/||x||, whose norm is the nonnegative angular speed.
Almost surely x is nonzero and this speed is positive for n>=2.

Conditionally on g, Q_q=h^T D P_x D h is a sum of n-1 independent
chi-square_1 variables with positive weights equal to the nonzero
eigenvalues lambda_j of D P_x D. These satisfy

    d_min^2 <= lambda_j <= 1,
    d_min = min_i sech^2(sqrt(q)g_i).

Indeed these nonzero eigenvalues equal those of P_x D^2 P_x restricted
to x-perp, whose Rayleigh quotients lie in that interval. Both M_q and
the conditional weights depend on the same g. In particular the exact
positive-q model must retain this conditioning; replacing Q_q by an
independent chi-square is a different kernel. Even the radial sum
||x||^2/q is bounded above by n/q, unlike a chi-square variable.

For fixed n, q decreases to zero gives jointly, almost surely under the
original (g,h) coupling,

    M_q -> S/n,      H_q -> sqrt(R/S),
    S=||g||^2 ~ chi-square_n,
    R=h^T P_g h ~ chi-square_(n-1),  R independent of g and hence of S.

The independence follows because the conditional law of R given g is
the same chi-square_(n-1) law for every nonzero g. The SAME S appears in
the radial multiplier and angular denominator. For n=1 the tangent
speed is zero, so logarithmic angular statements below exclude n=1.

## C051: uniform leading noise at the critical variance scale

For every fixed C<infinity, uniformly over 0<q<=C/n, define

    A_q=log M_q,       B_q=log H_q.

As n increases,

    n Cov((A_q,B_q)) -> [[2,-1],[-1,1]].

Here Cov is centered covariance. Equivalently, replacing B_q by the
logarithmic reciprocal-angle multiplier -B_q changes both off-diagonal
entries to +1. This only identifies one-step noise, not a drift limit.

### Coupling and quantitative error

Draw g and, independently, eta_1,...,eta_(n-1) iid standard normals.
Use a measurable ordering of the eigenvalues above and put

    Q_q^* = sum_j lambda_j(g) eta_j^2,
    R^* = sum_j eta_j^2,       S=||g||^2.

The pair (M_q, sqrt(q Q_q^*/||x||^2)) has EXACTLY the required joint
law (M_q,H_q), by the conditional quadratic-form law. Also S and R^*
are independent chi-squares with the stated degrees of freedom.
Thus this construction verifies both coupled marginals. No pointwise
comparison with the original h projection is being asserted.

For z>=0, sech^2(z) <= tanh(z)/z <= 1, with the continuous value at zero.
Consequently, with Z=max_i |g_i|,

    d_min^2 <= ||x||^2/(qS) <= 1,
    d_min^2 <= Q_q^*/R^* <= 1.

Since log(cosh z)<=z^2/2, this yields the deterministic coupling bounds

    |A_q-log(S/n)| <= 2q Z^2,
    |B_q-(1/2)log(R^*/S)| <= q Z^2.

A Gaussian union bound P(Z^2>r)<=min(1,2n exp(-r/2)), integrated as
E Z^4=integral_0^infinity 2r P(Z^2>r)dr, gives
||Z^2||_2 <= C_0 log(2n). Hence each logarithmic error has L2 norm at
most C_1 q log(2n), without deleting any event or inverse tail.

### Covariance calculation

Let A_0=log(S/n), B_0=(log R^*-log S)/2. Gamma integration gives

    Var A_0 = psi_1(n/2),
    Cov(A_0,B_0) = -(1/2)psi_1(n/2),
    Var B_0 = (psi_1((n-1)/2)+psi_1(n/2))/4.

The trigamma series psi_1(z)=sum_(k>=0)(z+k)^(-2) and integral comparison
give psi_1(z)=1/z+O(z^-2). These identities can alternatively be obtained
by differentiating E S^t=2^t Gamma(n/2+t)/Gamma(n/2) at t=0.
The displayed baseline covariance therefore has the claimed limit
after multiplying by n, and its centered L2 norms are O(n^-1/2).

For centered random variables, covariance perturbation by L2 errors e
has size at most C(n^-1/2 ||e||_2 + ||e||_2^2); centering an error costs
no more than its L2 norm. After multiplying by n, our bound is

    O(sqrt(n) q log(2n) + n q^2 log(2n)^2)
       = O_C(log(2n)/sqrt(n) + log(2n)^2/n),

uniformly over 0<q<=C/n. This tends to zero and proves C051.

## Scope left open

The limits are: first the angle derivative at zero for fixed n,q,
then n -> infinity with q<=C/n. C051 does not justify exchanging the
infinitesimal-angle limit with a finite-angle network evolution, does
not give the order-1/n drift, and does not establish that actual tanh
input correlations approach one. The scalar critical-tanh diffusion
and cumulant-rate work remain separate claims C026-C027 and C044-C047.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:22c6d532d863fd81ef53240a00570657817f6c17e8e5fb0515c76a33cfbda523","revision_digest":"sha256:85f5ca6e4c11faf59b3859d20fd8b9c840a142c102084630954bf5c6cc79c24a","source_id":"owner-own-work:T244-w691-C050:v1","source_revision":"2026-10-20T13:53:12.705197","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

body: Let X be a Banach space and (x_n) a sequence in X converging weakly to x. Then there exists a sequence (y_k) of finite convex combinations of the x_n, that is, each y_k = sum_i lambda_i^{(k)} x_i for finitely many indices i with lambda_i^{(k)} >= 0 and sum_i lambda_i^{(k)} = 1, such that y_k converges to x in norm. Equivalently, the norm-closed convex hull of {x_n : n >= 1} contains x and equals its weak closure. [standard, e.g. Brezis, Functional Analysis, Sobolev Spaces and PDEs]

Let H: R^n → R be convex and superlinear (H(p)/|p| → ∞), let L = H* be its Legendre transform, and let g: R^n → R be Lipschitz. Define u(x,t) := min_{y ∈ R^n} ( t L((x-y)/t) + g(y) ) for t > 0, u(x,0) := g(x). Then: (i) the minimum is attained, u(·,t) is Lipschitz with constant at most Lip(g) for every t > 0, and |u(x,t) - g(x)| ≤ C t with C = max( |L(0)| , max_{|p| ≤ Lip(g)} |H(p)| ); hence u is Lipschitz on R^n × [0,∞) and attains the initial data continuously. (ii) u is differentiable almost everywhere in R^n × (0,∞), and at every point of differentiability u_t(x,t) + H(Du(x,t)) = 0. (iii) u is a viscosity solution of u_t + H(Du) = 0 in R^n × (0,∞) with u(·,0) = g. (iv) If in addition g is bounded, then for every T > 0, u is the unique viscosity solution of this Cauchy problem in the class of bounded Lipschitz functions on R^n × [0,T].
H: R^n → R finite, convex, superlinear (continuity is automatic from finiteness and convexity)
L = H* so that L is finite, convex and superlinear and L* = H
g: R^n → R Lipschitz continuous
for (iv): g in addition bounded, and uniqueness asserted only among bounded Lipschitz viscosity solutions
(ii) asserts the equation only at points of differentiability; a.e. solutions are not unique, so (ii) alone does not characterize u

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For f: {-1,1}^n -> R with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_S hat{f}(S) chi_S and the noise operator T_rho, which independently resamples each coordinate to a fresh uniform sign with probability 1-rho (equivalently, flips each coordinate with probability (1-rho)/2, so that each coordinate keeps correlation rho with the input), the Bonami-Beckner inequality states ||T_rho f||_q <= ||f||_p whenever 1 <= p <= q and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1)). Equivalently, T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} hat{f}(S) chi_S, and the inequality forces the Fourier weight of f on high-degree levels to decay geometrically once rho<1, giving sum_S rho^{2|S|} hat{f}(S)^2 <= (E[|f|^p])^{2/p} for suitable p. This is the central tool converting L^2 Fourier information into higher-moment (typically L^4) control, and it underlies the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem on the existence of an influential coordinate, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm noise-sensitivity theorems, and Friedgut's junta theorem for low-influence functions. It does not directly give influence bounds without further combination with such machinery, and the sharp constant and range of rho given here hold for the uniform measure on {-1,1}^n; biased-p product measures or non-product (dependent) measures require different, generally weaker, p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractive inequalities. Typical failure: Applying the sharp uniform-measure {-1,1}^n hypercontractive constant to a biased-p product measure or to a dependent measure such as the random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure without switching to the correct p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractivity inequality, whose constants generally degrade as p approaches 0 or 1; this silently invalidates quantitative noise-sensitivity conclusions claimed for critical percolation at p != 1/2 or for genuinely non-product models. Canonical reference: Bonami, 1970, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Beckner, 1975, Annals of Mathematics; O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, 2014, Cambridge University Press.

The characteristic exponent \alpha \in (0, 2] of a stable distribution determines the decay rate of its tails. When \alpha = 2, the distribution is normal (Gaussian), all moments exist, and the tails decay exponentially. When 0 < \alpha < 2, the distribution has heavy tails: \mathbb{P}(|X| > x) \sim c x^{-\alpha} as x \to \infty, so \mathbb{E}[|X|^p] < \infty for all 0 < p < \alpha, but \mathbb{E}[|X|^p] = \infty for all p \ge \alpha.
\alpha \in (0, 2]

body: Concept (campaign status: open, evidence strong): CONJECTURE - for every linear NAE triangle system, SOME choice of one pair per triangle yields a pair-sum span that is an admissible residual space (valid_R). Since c = k*beta - ell is intrinsic, every choice-graph shares one Z, so the choice is free on the Ising side, and the lemma would give d_cb <= |V| - b and hence Conjecture RC for ALL linear systems via cut-inflation. Evidence: on the single system where the fixed shared-pair rule failed, 725 of 729 pair-choices are admissible (min dim 5); a 60-system chosen-pair sweep found zero systems with no admissible choice, tight on trees (slack exactly 0). Structure of the obstruction: a signed extra like e_0 - e_1 + e_2 is covered exactly when the choice-graph places its two same-signed coordinates in one component on the same bipartition side (their difference then dies in R) or in a non-bipartite component (whose generator vanishes) - so the general lemma is a simultaneous matching problem over the 3^k choices.

[Definition 5 of arXiv:2605.31300, 'Cone-Additive Functions for Random Walks on Free Products of Graphs'] Consider a function 
$$
f: \Pi\to\mathbb{R}, \pi \mapsto f(\pi).
$$
Then $f$ is called  \textit{cone-additive} w.r.t. $P$ if the following two properties hold:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item 
Additivity property: for all $n\in\N$,
$$
f\bigl([X_0,\ldots,X_n]\bigr)= \sum_{j=1}^{\mathbf{k}(n)} f(\pi_j) + f(\pi^\ast_{n}) \quad \textrm{ almost surely.}
$$
\item Shift invariance: for all $j\in\N$, 
\begin{equation}
f(\pi_j)=f\bigl(X_{\e_{j-1}}^{-1}\pi_j\bigr).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

Let p and q be probability mass functions on a nonempty finite set and p x q their independent coupling, whose disagreement probability is 1 - sum_x p(x) q(x). The following are equivalent: (i) p x q has the least disagreement d_TV(p, q) among couplings; (ii) it has the greatest, 1 - max_x (p(x) + q(x) - 1)_+; (iii) all couplings of p and q have the same disagreement probability; (iv) p and q have disjoint supports, or p or q is a point mass. Otherwise the independent coupling's disagreement lies strictly between the least and the greatest.

[Prop P:weighted-quadrangle of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Consider a weighted directed acyclic graph $G = (V, E, M)$, and let $H = (V, E, M')$ be another one with the same vertices and edges, but different weights satisfying $M' \le M$, with equality on a set $W \subset V$. Consider vertices $x_1 \prec y_1$ and $x_2 \prec y_2$ and suppose that we have the following {\bf path-crossing} property:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Let $\tau$ be any path from $x_1$ to $y_1$ and $\pi = (\pi_0, \dots, \pi_k)$ be any path from $x_2$ to $y_2$. Then if $\pi_i \notin W$ for some $i \in \llbracket1, k-1 \rrbracket$, there are indices $i^- < i < i^+$ such that the vertices $\pi(i^-), \pi(i^+)$ are on the path $\tau$.
\end{itemize}
Then
$$
H(x_1; y_1) + G(x_2 ; y_2)  \le G(x_1; y_1) + H(x_2 ; y_2).
$$

body: In spectral graph theory, the Alon–Boppana bound provides a lower bound on the second-largest eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix of a -regular graph, meaning a graph in which every vertex has degree . The reason for the interest in the second-largest eigenvalue is that the largest eigenvalue is guaranteed to be due to -regularity, with the all-ones vector being the associated eigenvector. The graphs that come close to meeting this bound are Ramanujan graphs, which are examples of the best possible expander graphs.

[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $m,n\in\Nsf$, $[S,T]\subseteq\Rsf$ be an interval, $p\in[1,3)$, and $\omega$ a control function on interval $[S,T]$. Let $X=(X^\tau)$ be an $n$-dimensional branched rough path on $[S,T]$ with regularity $p$ and control $\omega$. Let $M$ be an $m$-dimensional manifold and let $f: M\to R_n^2M$ be a rough velocity field. Let $Y:[S,T]\to M$ be a continuous function such that for every $r\in [S,T]$ there exists
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\itemsep0em
    \item an interval $[u,v] \subset [S,T]$ that contains $r$ in its relative interior and such that we either have $v = T$ or $\omega(r,v) > 0$,
    \item a chart $(U, x)$ whose domain contains the image of $[u,v]$ under $Y$, and
    \item a constant $C\in (0,\infty)$
\end{enumerate}
such that inequality~\eqref{eq:integral-curve}, where $(Y^i)$ is the representation of $Y$ in the chart $(U,x)$ and $(f^i_\tau)$ is the representation of $f$ in the induced chart $(\overline{U},\overline{x})$, holds for every $i\in \llbracket 1,m \rrbracket$ and $(s,t)\in\Delta [u,v]$. Then $Y$ is an integral curve of the rough velocity field $f$ driven by the rough path $X$.

body:
Let X be a real N-by-n design of rank q>=1 with q<n, Y an N-by-m response matrix, and hidden width h>=min(m,n). Consider continuous Euclidean gradient flow on L(U,V)=||Y-X U V^T||F^2/2, U n-by-h, V m-by-h. Choose an orthonormal basis Phi1 of the data row space, set U1=Phi1^T U, and let a=lambda_q(X^T X)>0 be the smallest positive design-covariance eigenvalue. The latent imbalance D=U1^T U1-V^T V is constant along the flow. Using decreasing eigenvalues with lambda_i=0 when i exceeds the matrix dimension, define delta_eff=max(lambda_q(D),0)+max(lambda_m(-D),0). If delta_eff>0 at initialization, the excess over the unrestricted linear-regression optimum obeys L(t)-L_star<=exp(-2a delta_eff t)(L(0)-L_star) for every t>=0. This is the sufficient-imbalance specialization of Min, Tarmoun, Vidal and Mallada, Convergence and Implicit Bias of Gradient Flow on Overparametrized Linear Networks, arXiv:2105.06351, Theorem 3 and Corollary 4 (printed pp.9-10), with the zero-padding convention on p.4 and delta_eff in equation (20), p.8. Positive definiteness of the h-by-h D alone is insufficient when q>h: its q-th eigenvalue is zero by convention, while all eigenvalues of -D are negative (or zero-padded). This is a continuous-time sufficient condition, not a discrete-GD or proper-bottleneck initialization theorem.
Real finite data with 1<=rank(X)=q<n; hidden width h>=min(m,n)
Euclidean continuous gradient flow; unrestricted linear-regression comparator
Effective imbalance delta_eff>0, with the precise zero-padded eigenvalue indices

[Lemma 20 (Weak-profile transfer by diagonal congruence) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let \(H\), \(S\), \(D\), and \(\widetilde H\) be as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:R3-stochastic-normalization}.  Suppose in addition that
\begin{equation}
 \norm{D-I}_\infty=o(N^{-1/2})
\end{equation}
and that the variables \(\sqrt N H_{ij}\) are uniformly bounded.  Let
\(m^S(z)=(m_i^S(z))\) solve
\begin{equation}
 -\frac1{m_i^S(z)}=z+\sum_jS_{ij}m_j^S(z),
 \qquad
 \overline m^S(z):=\frac1N\sum_i m_i^S(z),
\end{equation}
and let \(m(z)=m_{\rm sc}(z)\).  On every fixed analytic LSS contour
\(\Gamma\) at positive distance from \([-2,2]\), with the standard spectral
confinement cutoff,
\begin{equation}
 \sup_{z\in\Gamma}\E\left|
 \left[\Tr(H-zI)^{-1}-N\overline m^S(z)\right]
 -\left[\Tr(\widetilde H-zI)^{-1}-Nm(z)\right]
 \right|^2=o(1).
\end{equation}
Consequently, uniformly for \(z,w\in\Gamma\),
\begin{align}
 &\left[\E\Tr(H-zI)^{-1}-N\overline m^S(z)\right]
 -\left[\E\Tr(\widetilde H-zI)^{-1}-Nm(z)\right]=o(1),
 \\
 &\Cov\!\left(\Tr(H-zI)^{-1},\Tr(H-wI)^{-1}\right)
 \nonumber\\
 &\qquad-
 \Cov\!\left(\Tr(\widetilde H-zI)^{-1},
              \Tr(\widetilde H-wI)^{-1}\right)=o(1).
 
\end{align}
The same comparison holds for joint characteristic functions of finitely many
analytic LSS after subtracting the exact Dyson centering
\(-N(2\pi\ii)^{-1}\oint\varphi\overline m^S\) at the \(H\) endpoint and the
scalar semicircle centering at the \(\widetilde H\) endpoint.

[Theorem thm-ig1 of arXiv:2411.19810, 'Radial conformal welding in Liouville quantum gravity'] Fix $\kappa>0$, a vector $\underline{\rho}$ of weights and a vector $\underline{x}$ of force points. Let $(K_t)_{t\ge 0}$ be the hull at time $t$ of the SLE$_\kappa(\underline{\rho})$ process $\eta$ described by the Loewner flow (equation eqn-def-sle of the paper) with $(W_t, V_t^{i,q})$ solving (equation eqn-def-sle-rho of the paper). Let $\mathfrak{h}_t^0$ be the harmonic function on $\mathbb{H}$ with boundary values 
	 	$$
	 	-\lambda(1+\sum_{i=0}^j \rho^{i,L})\ \ \text{on} \ [V_t^{j+1, L}-W_t, V_t^{j,L}-W_t)\ \  \text{and}\ \ \lambda(1+\sum_{i=0}^j \rho^{i,R})\ \text{on}\ \ [V_t^{j, R}-W_t, V_t^{j+1,R}-W_t)
	 	$$
	 	where $\rho^{0,R} = \rho^{0,L}=0$, $x^{0,L} = 0^-, x^{0,R} = 0^+, x^{k+1, L} = -\infty, x^{\ell+1, R} = +\infty$, $V_t^{0,L} = g_t(0^-)$ and $V_t^{0,R} = g_t(0^+)$. Set $\mathfrak{h}_t(z) = \mathfrak{h}_t^0(g_t(z))-\chi\arg g_t'(z)$. Let $\mathcal{F}_t$ be the filtration generated by $(W, V^{i,q})$. Then there exists a coupling $(K,h)$ where $h = \tilde{h}+ \mathfrak{h}_0$ with $\tilde{h}$ being a zero boundary GFF on $\mathbb{H}$ such that the following is true. For any $\mathcal{F}_t$-stopping time $\tau$ before the continuation threshold, $K_\tau$ is a local set for $h$ and the conditional law of $h|_{\mathbb{H}\backslash K_\tau}$ given $\mathcal{F}_\tau$ is the same as the law of $\mathfrak{h}_\tau+\tilde{h}\circ g_\tau$. Moreover, the curve $\eta$ is measurable with respect to $h$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem thm-ig1 of arXiv:2411.19810

Result: For oriented percolation the lace expansion converges when the oriented triangle (bubble) diagram is small, controlled by the random-walk return probabilities of the d-dimensional walk, of order 1/d; the nearest-neighbour model in d = 5, 6, 7 has no small parameter, exactly as for unoriented percolation below d = 11. (i). If $L=2$ and $\mu(0)=\mu(1)=1/2$, then for $n\geq 1$, 
$$\mathbb{E} \chi_1^{(2)}(S_n)=2\mathbb{P}(S_n=0)-1=\mathrm{i}^n R_n(0).$$ 
(ii). If $L\geq 3$ and $\mu(-1)=\mu(1)=1/2$, then for any $j\in [L-1]$ and $n\geq 1$, $\mathbb{E} \chi_k^{(L)}(S_n)=R_n(\cos (2 k\pi/L) )$.

[campaign result 2026-09-14, Author-checked, no independent read.] This is an exactly solved adjacent case of Open Problem 14.12 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html). For n>=3 let C_n be the simple cycle on n vertices. Start a particle at every vertex. Each particle independently jumps at rate one to a uniformly chosen neighbor, and particles merge on meeting. Let T_coal be the first time only one particle remains. Then E[T_coal]=(n^2-1)/6. If P is the cycle's discrete-time simple-walk matrix, define its mean spectral hitting-time quantity K=sum_{j=2}^n 1/(1-lambda_j(P)); then K=(n^2-1)/6 also. Thus E[T_coal]=K exactly. Its relaxation time tau_2=1/(1-cos(2pi/n)) satisfies tau_2/K -> 3/pi^2, so this family has the equality conclusion even though the small-relaxation-time hypothesis in the source problem fails. In the extracted optional-stopping proof, EC in a stopping-time subscript denotes the random coalescence time; the final displayed EC denotes its expectation. This is an unrefereed campaign result.
Continuous-time rate-one simple walks; one initial particle per vertex.
n>=3 and coalescence occurs on occupying the same vertex.

[Theorem 10 (Simple bounded-degree configuration model: pointwise version) of arXiv:2604.20514, 'Macroscopic loops in the random loop model on sparse random graphs'] Let \(G_n\) be the simple graph obtained from the configuration model with degree sequence \((d_i^{(n)})_{i=1}^n\), that is, the pairing model conditioned on simplicity. Assume that
\[
1\le d_i^{(n)}\le \Delta
\qquad\text{for all }i,n,
\]
and
\[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^{(n)}\to \rho.
\]
Fix \(u\in[0,1]\) and \(\theta\in\mathbb N\) with \(\theta>1\). If
\[
\rho>2c_{\theta,u}
=
2\bigl(1+\theta\max\{u,1-u\}\bigr),
\]
then for every \(\delta>0\) there exist \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that for every
\[
t\ge T_{\theta,u}(\rho)+\delta,
\]
one has
\[
\Pbb\!\left(
\Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\ge c
\right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Simple bounded-degree configuration model: pointwise version

Write D=[[0,M Sigma],[Sigma M^T,0]], H(P)=[[0,P Sigma],[Sigma P^T,0]], and let v1,v2 be its positive unit eigenvectors. Fix one finite seed U0=(B0;A0^T) and one hidden orthogonal rotation R with v1^T U0 R=(c1,0,...,0), c1>0. Write U0 R=[z0,X0] and assume c2=v2^T X0 is nonzero. Start the factor flow at alpha U0 R. Put tau=log(1/alpha)/s1 and epsilon=alpha^(1-s2/s1), and write shifted U_alpha(t)=[z_alpha(t),X_alpha(t)] for physical time tau+t.

For the exact c1 canonical path zbar of C014, on every FIXED shifted compact I,
 sup_I ||z_alpha-zbar||<=C_I epsilon.
The constant depends on I, seed and data. This is an entire active-vector bound, including the extra output directions, not a substitution of frozen dormant transport for active variation.

Moreover C014, this estimate, the reduced square transport C003 and C016 imply the following proposed Gaussian-arrival conclusion. For almost every ONE fixed iid standard Gaussian seed, subsequently scaled by alpha, there are physical arrival times T_alpha and p_alpha>0 tending to zero with
 ||z_alpha(T_alpha)-zstar||=O(p_alpha^2),
 ||X_alpha(T_alpha)||_F=O(p_alpha),

 ||Z_alpha(T_alpha)-zstar zstar^T||_F<=K p_alpha^2,

Here zstar is the nonzero-product critical endpoint of the canonical first path, Z_alpha=U_alpha U_alpha^T, and vstar is the unit top frozen residual vector. In these arrival formulas z_alpha and X_alpha are evaluated in physical time, with the first fixed hidden rotation R. K is fixed for the chosen seed and data. Thus arrival is strongly relatively aligned without an initial alignment hypothesis. This statement alone does not construct the subsequent canonical escape or its forward endpoint.

T232-w704-C017 v1. Kind: moved; Target 1. Status: proof (unaudited). This closes a proposed rectangular entrance handoff, conditional on correctness of the cited rectangular drafts, not their independent audit. No complete second-step or novelty claim.

## Statement
Use C014's setting: finite m>=2,w>=2, real rank-two m-by-2 M, SPD 2-by-2 Sigma, distinct positive singular values s1>s2 of M Sigma. Write D=[[0,M Sigma],[Sigma M^T,0]], H(P)=[[0,P Sigma],[Sigma P^T,0]], and let v1,v2 be its positive unit eigenvectors. Fix one finite seed U0=(B0;A0^T) and one hidden orthogonal rotation R with v1^T U0 R=(c1,0,...,0), c1>0. Write U0 R=[z0,X0] and assume c2=v2^T X0 is nonzero. Start the factor flow at alpha U0 R. Put tau=log(1/alpha)/s1 and epsilon=alpha^(1-s2/s1), and write shifted U_alpha(t)=[z_alpha(t),X_alpha(t)] for physical time tau+t.

For the exact c1 canonical path zbar of C014, on every FIXED shifted compact I,
 sup_I ||z_alpha-zbar||<=C_I epsilon.
The constant depends on I, seed and data. This is an entire active-vector bound, including the extra output directions, not a substitution of frozen dormant transport for active variation.

Moreover C014, this estimate, the reduced square transport C003 and C016 imply the following proposed Gaussian-arrival conclusion. For almost every ONE fixed iid standard Gaussian seed, subsequently scaled by alpha, there are physical arrival times T_alpha and p_alpha>0 tending to zero with
 ||z_alpha(T_alpha)-zstar||=O(p_alpha^2),
 ||X_alpha(T_alpha)||_F=O(p_alpha),
 ||vstar^T X_alpha(T_alpha)||_F=p_alpha,
 ||Z_alpha(T_alpha)-zstar zstar^T||_F<=K p_alpha^2,
 vstar^T Z_alpha(T_alpha)vstar>=p_alpha^2.
Here zstar is the nonzero-product critical endpoint of the canonical first path, Z_alpha=U_alpha U_alpha^T, and vstar is the unit top frozen residual vector. In these arrival formulas z_alpha and X_alpha are evaluated in physical time, with the first fixed hidden rotation R. K is fixed for the chosen seed and data. Thus arrival is strongly relatively aligned without an initial alignment hypothesis. This statement alone does not construct the subsequent canonical escape or its forward endpoint.

## 1. Negative-half-line comparison
C014's proof gives, on [-tau,T] for a sufficiently negative FIXED T,
 ||U_alpha(t)||,||zbar(t)||<=C exp(s1 t),
 ||X_alpha(t)||_F<=C epsilon exp(s2 t),
 zbar(-tau)=alpha c1 v1+O(alpha^3).
These follow from the full operator bounds and weighted bootstrap, including all zero modes.

Let e=z_alpha-zbar. At -tau,
 e(-tau)=alpha(z0-c1 v1)+O(alpha^3).
The displayed first vector has zero v1 component EXACTLY. The spectrum of D outside v1 is bounded above by s2: it consists of s2, -s1, -s2, and m-2 zeros. Hence for t>=-tau its first free term is bounded by
 C alpha exp(s2(t+tau))=C epsilon exp(s2 t).
The O(alpha^3) remainder propagates to at most C alpha^2 exp(s1 t). After division by epsilon exp(s2 t), its size is at most
 C alpha^(1+s2/s1) exp((s1-s2)T).
This is bounded and tends to zero. In particular there is no uncontrolled O(alpha) remainder in the fastest free direction. The transverse zero-mode free terms, though larger than negative-mode terms in normalized dormant matching, are smaller than the positive s2 bound used here.

Put N1(z)=H(b a^T)z. On the segment between actual and reference active vectors, its cubic derivative is bounded by C exp(2s1 t). With X=(V;W), the exact equation is
 e'=De-[N1(z_alpha)-N1(zbar)]-H(VW^T)z_alpha.
The last term is bounded by C epsilon^2 exp((s1+2s2)t). No frozen-transport equation is used for e.

Using ||exp(D(t-u))||<=exp(s1(t-u)), define the finite weighted supremum A_t=sup_{-tau<=u<=t} ||e(u)||/(epsilon exp(s2 u)). The Lipschitz integral, after division by this weight, is at most
 [C exp(2s1 T)/(s1+s2)] A_t.
Indeed its remaining integral is exp((s1-s2)t) integral_{-tau}^t exp((s1+s2)u)du. The dormant-feedback integral is at most
 C epsilon exp((s1+s2)T)/(2s2),
since its remaining integral is integral_{-tau}^t exp(2s2 u)du. Both denominators are positive. Thus
 A_t<=C_free+[C exp(2s1 T)/(s1+s2)]A_t+C epsilon exp((s1+s2)T)/(2s2).
Shrink T until the bracket is below 1/2, and absorb it. For alpha small with -tau<=T and alpha<=1, the rightmost term is bounded uniformly. This proves a uniform bound on A_t through T. All constants are independent of alpha for the fixed data and seed.

## 2. Extension to fixed compacts only
C014 gives uniform bounded factors and X_alpha=O(epsilon) on each fixed interval [T,T1]. The active vector field is Lipschitz on the relevant fixed bounded set, and dormant feedback is O(epsilon^2). Finite-interval Gronwall propagates e(T)=O(epsilon) to e=O_I(epsilon). No interval with T1 depending on alpha is covered. This proves the quantitative active assertion.

## 3. The first endpoint and ideal transport reduce exactly to square dimension two
Let Q span col(M) orthonormally. C014 places both bbar and chi_b inside col(M), and the reduced equations are exactly those for the invertible square Mtilde=Q^T M and the same Sigma. Their positive origin singular values remain s1,s2. The first canonical path is balanced and nonconstant, bounded by its energy sublevel and balance identity. The analytic-gradient convergence argument in C012 Section 2 gives a stationary limit. A fixed finite-time loss is strictly below C(0), hence the limiting loss is also strictly below C(0). It cannot have zero product. In the reduced square representation, zero outer product forces one factor zero and balance forces the other zero. Thus zstar has NONZERO PRODUCT, the premise needed by C015 and C016. This transfers back isometrically to the rectangular output space.

The reduced canonical pair has the two positive origin boundary modes and their canonical Volterra prescriptions. Thus it is exactly the square pair of C006, with its J-null graph orientation. C003 applies to the nonzero first endpoint and implies chi/||chi|| tends, up to sign, to its positive frozen residual vector. This statement does not require exponential endpoint convergence. The full rectangular residual has columns in col(M), by C015, and rank one. Its unique positive vector vstar is the isometric lift of the reduced vector; all added output directions are dormant zero eigenvectors. Therefore the same normalized transport alignment holds in the full rectangular space. The nonzero solution chi of a continuous linear ODE never vanishes at a finite time; c2 is fixed and nonzero.

## 4. One fixed cone entrance, followed by the separate local argument
Choose a single sufficiently late shifted first-path time T0 so the reference remains inside C016's endpoint neighborhood and chi(T0)c2 lies strictly inside its prescribed cone. Such T0 exists by the transport limit just proved. It is chosen before alpha tends to zero. By C014,
 X_alpha(T0)/epsilon -> chi(T0)c2.
Consequently there are fixed positive c0,c1 and a fixed small-alpha cutoff such that the actual projected dormant row has norm between c0 epsilon and c1 epsilon and the actual block is inside the cone. The strict cone margin absorbs any eventually-small normalized error; no false O(epsilon) bound on that normalized error is imposed.

Sections 1-2 give ||z_alpha(T0)-zbar(T0)||<=C0 epsilon at the SAME fixed T0. These are all of C016's entrance hypotheses, with uniform constants for the fixed seed and data. Apply C016 with epsilon=alpha^(1-s2/s1), a monotone parametrization tending to zero. Its own local comparison inequalities and all-smaller-epsilon diagonal cutoffs give the physical arrival times and O(p_alpha^2) active endpoint error stated above. This uses C016 to control the growing local interval; it does not extrapolate Section 2 Gronwall beyond a fixed compact.

## 5. Gaussian event, status and remaining piece
For iid Gaussian U0 the two orthonormal eigenrows v1^T U0 and v2^T U0 are independent standard Gaussian rows in R^w. Almost surely c1>0 and the projection of the second onto the (w-1)-dimensional complement of the first is nonzero. This is an initialization statement, not later-flow independence. The seed is fixed while alpha varies.

C014-C017 are unaudited rectangular drafts. C003/C006/C008/C009/C010/C011/C012 have PASS only at their recorded square or general-ODE scopes; no PASS is inherited merely by analogy. The strongest remaining obligation for the full rectangular second-step theorem is the canonical escape and forward-endpoint composition: verify its full parameter Jacobian, fixed full-top projection, invariant output/hidden subspaces at the negative-infinite boundary, and apply C010 only after reducing the canonical path to square width two. That composition is not asserted here. Literature priority remains unresolved.

Sources: C014, rectangular_origin_matching.md; C015, rectangular_endpoint_spectrum.md; C016, rectangular_local_arrival.md; C008 v2, active_first_escape_error.md (square precedent); C003/C006/C012 v2 (reduced square ideal geometry, transport and analytic endpoint). [Corollary No finite-moment determination of annealed complexity of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[corollary]{cor:no-finite-moment}
For every fixed integer \(r\ge2\) and every \(p\ge3\), there exist two
symmetric, centered, unit-variance sub-Gaussian laws \(\mu_1,\mu_2\), both
with strictly positive \(C^\infty\) densities and with identical moments
through order \(r\), and a compact interval \(B\subset(0,\infty)\), such
that
\[
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E_{\mu_1}\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B)
 >
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathbb E_{\mu_2}\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B).
\]
Thus no prescribed finite collection of moments forces the Gaussian
energy-window rate for the spatially unrestricted, unregularized annealed
count: the non-Gaussian liminf may be strictly larger.  The statement
does not assert existence of the non-Gaussian limit. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

We assume $\omega_X \simeq \cO_X$.
Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $X$ is HT-split.
\item The homomorphism
\[
H^d(X,\cO_X) \xrightarrow{F^{\dR}_X} H^d(X,F_*\Omega_X^{\bullet})
\]
is injective.
\item The Hodge-to-de Rham spectral sequence is $E_1$-degenerate.
\end{enumerate}

    eta = min(p_c/2, (delta_star-delta)/(2M)) > 0.

Let d>=2, X standard Gaussian, u a unit teacher, fixed +1 outer weights, sphere directions, student f_rho(X)=E_rho sigma(w.X), and risk E[(f_rho(X)-sigma(u.X))^2] without 1/2. Let sigma be smooth with Gaussian-L2 expansion sum c_k He_k/sqrt(k!), c1=0, a_k=c_k^2, sum_{k>=2}a_k=1, A=a2>0 and sum k^4 a_k finite. The arbitrary constant coefficient cancels. Put tau=sum_{k>=3}k a_k; odd degrees are allowed. For 0<eps<=1 define delta=sqrt(eps)/8, S=log(32d/delta^3), T=S/(8A delta), H=min(delta^2/16,1/(256A^2T^2)), K=8(1+16AdT)^6 and lambda0=H/(8dTK). If tau<=eps/32 and tau^2<=H/(64KT^2), population sphere MFLD from the uniform law with lambda(t)=lambda0/(1+t/T) has R(rho_T)<=43eps/384<eps/4. Time and inverse positive temperature have explicit polynomial bounds in d,1/eps,1/A. The allowed tail threshold also has a polynomial reciprocal bound. The altered-kernel coupling uses h prime<=16A r_nu h+16A h^(3/2)+8tau sqrt(h)+2d lambda; only the quadratic reference residual enters the integrated clock. [Defn def:size-biased-tree of arXiv:2601.00119, 'The largest common subtree of two random trees'] Let $\tau_\infty$ be a random infinite plane tree and $U_\infty=(J_i)_{i\geq 1}$ be a sequence of random positive integers. Set $U_0=\varnothing$ and $U_n=(J_1,\ldots,J_n)$ for all $n\geq 1$. We say that $(\tau_\infty,U_\infty)$ is a \emph{size-biased Bienaymé tree with offspring distribution $\mu$} if it satisfies the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] For all $n\geq 0$, $U_n$ is almost surely an element of $\tau_\infty$.
    
    \item[(b)] The random pairs $(\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty),J_{n+1})$ for $n\geq 0$ are i.i.d.~and distributed as follows:
    \[\forall k,j\in\mathbb{N}^*,\quad \mathbf{P}(\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty)=k\, ;\, J_{n+1}=j)={\mathbf 1}_{\left\{j\leq k\right\}}\mu(k)/m_\mu.\]
    
    \item[(c)] Conditionally given $(\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty),J_{n+1})_{n\geq 0}$, the random plane trees $\theta_{U_n*(j)}\tau_\infty$ for $n\geq 0$ and $j\in \{1,\ldots,\mathrm{k}_{U_n}(\tau_\infty)\}\setminus\{J_{n+1}\}$ are independent Bienaymé trees with offspring distribution $\mu$.
\end{enumerate}
title: Defn def:size-biased-tree of arXiv:2601.00119

body: In statistics and control theory, Kalman filtering is an algorithm that uses a series of measurements observed over time, including statistical noise and other inaccuracies, to produce estimates of unknown variables that tend to be more accurate than those based on a single measurement, by estimating a joint probability distribution over the variables for each time-step. The filter is constructed as a mean squared error minimiser, but an alternative derivation of the filter is also provided showing how the filter relates to maximum likelihood statistics. The filter is named after Rudolf E. Kálmán.
title: Kalman filter
