Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables and f a square-integrable function of them, Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n). Let X_1', ..., X_n' be an independent copy of the X_i and Z_i' = f(X_1, ..., X_i', ..., X_n) the value with the i-th coordinate resampled. Then Var(Z) <= (1/2) sum_{i=1}^n E[(Z - Z_i')^2] = sum_{i=1}^n E[(Z - E_i Z)^2], where E_i denotes expectation over X_i alone (Efron and Stein 1981; Steele 1986 for the constant 1/2). Equivalently Var(Z) <= sum_i E[Var_i(Z)]. The inequality is tight for linear f. It needs independence of the coordinates (it is the sum over coordinates of one-coordinate variances, a tensorization statement) but no boundedness; the bounded-differences (McDiarmid) inequality is the exponential-tail counterpart under the extra assumption that changing one coordinate changes f by at most c_i, in which case Var(Z) <= (1/4) sum c_i^2.
X_1, ..., X_n independent (not necessarily identically distributed)
f(X) square-integrable
no boundedness or Lipschitz assumption; those are needed only for the exponential tail (McDiarmid), not for the variance bound
title: Efron-Stein inequality (variance of a function of independent variables)

The campaign's P0104 record groups Questions 13 and 15 of Auffinger--Damron--Hanson's 50 years of first passage percolation (arXiv:1511.03262v2, PDF page 37): strict exponent below 1/2 in dimensions at least two under suitable edge-law conditions; exponent 1/3 in the plane; and a positive exponent in a suitable dimension. The source leaves suitable hypotheses and the exact variance-scaling convention to be specified. A bounded Uniform[1,2] planar variance-exponent attempt covers a restricted slice. The April 2026 arXiv:2604.01214v1 polynomial improvement is for its specified isotropic Riemannian continuum model and supplies no proved iid square-lattice transfer. October 2026 current openness is UNKNOWN under this targeted check, and no P0104 solution is claimed. Verified source hashes establish provenance, not mathematical proof.

body: [Lemma of arXiv:2609.04045, 'Heat content and spectrum for subordinated sub-Laplacians'] Let $\Omega=\mathbb{B}_{\rho}(e,R)$ for some $R>0$. Then $p=(\xi_1,\xi_2)\in\partial\Omega$ is a characteristic point if and only if $\xi_1=0$ and $|\xi_2|=\kappa R^2$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Lemma Eigenfunction lower bound for a small target of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] There exist \(\rho_{0} > 0\), \(c_{\varphi} > 0\)
and \(\varepsilon_{1} > 0\), depending only on the data of
the fixed ambient domain \(M\), such that for every centre
\(x_{*} \in M\) and every
\(\varepsilon < \varepsilon_{1}\), the process killed on
\(A_{\varepsilon} = B_{M}\left( x_{*},\varepsilon \right)\)
satisfies, for all \(t \geq 0\) and all starting points
\(x\) with
\(d_{M}\left( x,A_{\varepsilon} \right) \geq \rho_{0}\),

\[P_{x}\left( \tau_{A_{\varepsilon}} > t \right) \geq c_{\varphi}\, e^{- \lambda_{A_{\varepsilon}}t}.\]

[Lemma conjugating piecewise linear lip maps of arXiv:2608.30346, '\textbf{Classification complexity of homeomorphism group actions}'] Let \(0 \leq a_1 < b_1 \leq 1\) and \(0 \leq a_2 < b_2 \leq 1\). Let 
    \[f_i(t) = 
    \begin{cases}
        2t-a_i, \quad &t \in [a_i,a_i + \frac{b_i-a_i}{3}] \\
        \frac{1}{2}t+\frac{1}{2}b_i, \quad &t \in [a_i + \frac{b_i-a_i}{3},b_i].        
    \end{cases}\]
    Then there is a homeomorphism \(\varphi: [a_1,b_1] \to [a_2,b_2]\) such that \(\Lip(\varphi) = \frac{b_2-a_2}{b_1-a_1}\), \(\Lip(\varphi^{-1}) = \frac{b_1-a_1}{b_2-a_2}\) and \(\varphi \circ f_1 = f_2 \circ \varphi.\)

[Lemma lem:pole-projected-positive-strip-closure of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Assume the coefficient and weight hypotheses
(equation eq:pole-coefficient-class of the paper) and (equation eq:pole-weight-threshold of the paper), with
$0\leq\alpha<1/2$.  Fix an integer $N_{\mathrm H}\geq1$,
$0<\theta<1$, $K\geq K_\theta^\star(a)$, $0<r\leq T$, and
$0<\varepsilon<1$.  Let
$\varphi=\Pi_{\mathrm{hi}}\varphi$ belong to
\begin{equation*}
 W^{1,2}\bigl([\varepsilon,1];L^2(\gamma_d)\bigr)
 \cap L^2\bigl([\varepsilon,1];\mathscr D_\gamma\bigr),
\end{equation*}
with $\varphi=0$ on a strip immediately below $s=1$.  Suppose that, for some
$C_{\mathrm{hi}}>0$, for almost every $s\in(\varepsilon,1)$ and every
$\vartheta\in\mathscr D_\gamma$ satisfying
$\vartheta=\Pi_{\mathrm{hi}}\vartheta$, the fixed-time estimate
\begin{equation}
 \norm{\nabla^{\mathsf A_r^{-1}}\vartheta}_{L^2(\gamma_d)}^2
 \leq\frac{C_{\mathrm{hi}}}{N_{\mathrm H}}
       \norm{\mathsf A_r^{1/2}\operatorname{Hess}_{\mathsf A_r^{-1}}\vartheta
                     \,\mathsf A_r^{1/2}}_{L^2(\gamma_d)}^2
 
\end{equation}
holds, and put
$\Theta_{\mathrm{hi}}
:=\theta+(1-2\alpha)C_{\mathrm{hi}}/N_{\mathrm H}$.  Then
\begin{equation*}
 (1-\Theta_{\mathrm{hi}})
 \left\lVert \mathcal J_r\varphi\right\rVert_{\mathscr Y_{\alpha,K,r};(\varepsilon,1)}^2
 \leq4\left\lVert \mathcal P_r\varphi\right\rVert_{\mathscr X_{\alpha,K,r};(\varepsilon,1)}^2.
\end{equation*}
The estimate is uniform in $\varepsilon$.

Every regular Dirichlet form (E, F) on L^2(E; m) admits a unique Beurling-Deny representation: for any u, v in F cap C_0(E), E(u,v) = E^{(c)}(u,v) + iint_{E x E \ diag} (u(x)-u(y))(v(x)-v(y)) J(dx, dy) + int_E u(x) v(x) k(dx), where E^{(c)} has the strong local property, J is a symmetric Radon jumping measure off the diagonal, and k is a Radon killing measure.
(E, F) is regular Dirichlet form on L^2(E; m)

[Theorem 10 of arXiv:2606.18047, 'Analysis of the asymmetric shelf shuffle'] Let $m, n\geq 1$ and $p\in (0, 1)$ be fixed. Let $G_{n, m}^{(p)}(t) := \mathbb{E}_{\nu_{n, m}^{(p)}}[t^{\des(\pi)+1}]$.

Then, 
\[
G_{n, m}^{(p)}(t) = \frac{1}{m^n}[u^n](1+u)^{m-1}\left(A_t(u)\frac{1-\omega_t(u)}{1+\omega_t(u)}\right)^{n+1}\,\, \sum_{k\geq 1}k^n\omega_t(u)^{k}\;.
\]
title: Theorem 10 of arXiv:2606.18047

[Lemma 57 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(d\ge3\), \(1\le k<d\), \(r_b>0\), and \(\Lambda\ge1\).  There
exist constants
\[
 a_0=a_0(d,k,r_b,\Lambda)>0,
 \qquad
 R_0=R_0(d,k,r_b,\Lambda)<\infty
\]
with the following property.  Let \((M^d,h)\) be a Riemannian manifold
and \(p\in M\).  Suppose that \(\exp_p\) is a diffeomorphism from
\(B_{T_pM}(0,2r_b)\) onto its image and that, in these exponential
coordinates,
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda^{-1}g_{\rm E}
 \le \exp_p^*h\le\Lambda g_{\rm E},
 \qquad
 \|\exp_p^*h\|_{C^2(B(0,2r_b))}\le\Lambda.
\end{equation}
Let
\[
 H:\exp_p\bigl(B_{T_pM}(0,2r_b)\bigr)\longrightarrow\R^k
\]
be smooth, with \(H(p)=0\), and suppose that
\begin{equation}
 |dH|_h+|\nabla dH|_h\le\Lambda
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 \Lambda^{-1}|a|^2
 \le
 \left|\sum_{\alpha=1}^k a_\alpha dH^\alpha\right|_h^2
 \le\Lambda |a|^2
 \qquad(a\in\R^k).
\end{equation}
Then the component of \(H^{-1}(0)\) through \(p\) contains an embedded
closed \((d-k)\)-disk \(\mathcal D_p\) such that
\begin{align}
 \mathcal D_p
 &\subset
 B_{H^{-1}(0),\,h|_{H^{-1}(0)}}(p,R_0),
 \\
 \Vol_{h|_{H^{-1}(0)}}(\mathcal D_p)
 &\ge a_0.
 
\end{align}
The ball in \eqref{ti:eq:level-disk-intrinsic-ball} is intrinsic to the
regular level.

[Definition of arXiv:2609.01557, '$L^\infty$ Variational Approximation of the Aubry Set'] Let $U\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be open. 
A function $u\in W_{\mathrm{loc}}^{1,\infty}(U)\cap C(U)$ is called an \emph{absolute minimizer} for $H$ in $U$ if, for every open set $V\Subset U$ and every
\[
v\in W^{1,\infty}(V)\cap C(\overline V)
\]
satisfying
\[
v=u \qquad \text{on } \partial V,
\]
we have
\[
\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in V} H(Du(x),x)
\le
\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{x\in V} H(Dv(x),x).
\]
title: Unnumbered definition of arXiv:2609.01557, '$L^\infty$ Variational Approximation of the Aubry Set'

no-section artifact. Thus a sequence of approximate sections whose
errors tend to zero cannot have uniformly bounded Lipschitz constants.

vertex, is at distance at least t from t v_i, since their angles
are obtuse. Thus s(t v_2) lies in T_2={||x-c2||_1<=1/2}, and

On T_2 we have x-y>=1/2, while on T_3 we have x-y<=-1/2.
Cauchy-Schwarz therefore gives distance(T_2,T_3)>=1/sqrt(2).
Equality is attained at (3/4,1/4) and (1/4,3/4).
Since ||t v_2-t v_3||=sqrt(3)t, we obtain
Lip(s)>=1/(sqrt(6)t). Let t decrease to e to obtain (1).

For clarity the divergence is unavoidable geometry, not an artifact

with E(s)=e and Lip(s)=1/(sqrt(6)e), as follows.

 s(t v_i)=p+(t/delta)(x_i(delta)-p),   0<=t<=delta,

The two definitions agree at delta and the three branches agree at 0.
The images stay in the convex square. On the inner part no other
positive support is encountered and direct substitution gives

body:
Compact operators are completely continuous: they send weakly convergent sequences to norm convergent ones. The converse needs the domain to be reflexive, because the proof runs 'bounded sequence -> weakly convergent subsequence -> norm convergent image', and the first arrow is exactly reflexivity (with the Eberlein-Smulian theorem). The counterexample is the identity of l^1: by Schur's property, every weakly convergent sequence in l^1 converges in norm, so the identity is completely continuous, yet it is not compact because l^1 is infinite-dimensional. A related trap in the other direction is the use of weak sequential compactness of the unit ball: in a nonreflexive space such as c_0 or L^1([0,1]) a bounded sequence need not have any weakly convergent subsequence, so arguments of the form 'the sequence is bounded, so pass to a weakly convergent subsequence, and then apply compactness of T' are invalid there. Also note that the older literature uses 'completely continuous' as a synonym for 'compact'; when reading a classical source, check which meaning is in force before transporting a statement.
the domain is reflexive for the converse direction
compactness always implies complete continuity, with no reflexivity needed
terminology must be checked in older sources, where 'completely continuous' can mean 'compact'
title: Pitfall: 'Maps Weakly Convergent to Norm Convergent' Implies Compact Only for Reflexive Domains

body: In mathematics, subadditivity is a property of a function that states, roughly, that evaluating the function for the sum of two elements of the domain always returns something less than or equal to the sum of the function's values at each element. There are numerous examples of subadditive functions in various areas of mathematics, particularly norms and square roots. Additive maps are special cases of subadditive functions.

[Proposition prop:averaging of arXiv:2608.30254, 'Exact Recovery Thresholds for Weighted Data Selection\\ in Vector-Valued Linear Regression'] A proof cannot either rely on selections that keep the original weights on a
subset. With $w_e=p_ip_jd_{ij}$, $y_e=w_eB_{ij}$,
$U=\sum_ew_e^2$, $Q=\sum_e\lVert y_e\rVert^2$, $R=4\sum_ip_i^2$,
$V=2\sum_ip_i^2|z_i|^2$, the exact averages over all $k$-subsets $S$ (with
$D_S=\sum_{e\subset S}w_e$, $G_S=\sum_{e\subset S}y_e$, and binomials
$A=\binom{N-2}{k-2}$, $B=\binom{N-3}{k-3}$, $H=\binom{N-4}{k-4}$) are
\[
  \sum_{|S|=k}\lVert G_S\rVert^2=(A-2B+H)Q+(B-H)V,\qquad
  \sum_{|S|=k}D_S^2=H+(A-2B+H)U+(B-H)R .
\]
For the fifth-roots system $t_j=\zeta_5^j$, $z_j=t_j^2$, $p_j=\frac15$ one
gets $U=\frac3{25},R=\frac45,Q=\frac15,V=\frac25$, so the best
original-weight three-point ratio guaranteed by these averages is
$\frac{Q+V}{U+R}=\frac{15}{23}>\frac58$: reweighting inside the selected
triangle (the freedom quantified by Lemma~(lem:closure of the paper)) is essential.

     hold for $X$ with operator $\mathcal{A}$. Then for any $t_0 > 0$, we have the following upper bound for Wasserstein-$p$ distance between $\mathcal{L}(X)$ and $\mathcal{L}(Z)$, 
    \begin{align}
        W_p(\mathcal{L}(X), \mathcal{L}(Z)) &\leq g_0(t_0,p) + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} g_k(t_0,p) \mathbb{E}[|a_{k}^{\mathcal{A}}(X) - a_{k}^{\mathcal{L}_{OU}}(X)|^p]^{1/p} \notag\\
        &= g_0(t_0,p) + g_1(t_0,p) \mathbb{E}[| a_{1}^{\mathcal{A}}(X) + X|^p]^{1/p} \notag\\

    where $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and the coefficients $g_k(t_0,p)$ for $k\ge 0$

body: In combinatorial mathematics and extremal set theory, the Sauer–Shelah lemma states that every family of sets with small VC dimension consists of a small number of sets. Here, the VC dimension is the largest size of a set with the property that all of its subsets can be formed by intersecting it with a member of the family. If the family has elements in its union, then the Sauer–Shelah lemma states that its number of sets is at most proportional to .

$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in [n]^d} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right).
$$
Let $a,b \in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$. Then for $2 \leq t \leq \infty,$
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf F}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf F}({\bf x})}_{2t}^{2t} ~\leq~ (2^d \sqrt{2}t)^{2t} \left( \sum_{1 \leq a+b
    \leq d}\norm{{\mathbb E} {\bf F}_{a,b}}_{2t}^{2t} \right).

 |H(E,z)-H(E_{\widehat\mu},0)|
 &\le \frac{C}{t}\bigl(\vartheta_b+|z|^2\bigr),
 \\
 |a(E,z)-a(E_{\widehat\mu},0)|
 &\le \frac{C}{t^2}\bigl(\vartheta_b+|z|^2\bigr).
 
\end{align}

body:
[Theorem 1 (Classification of entire logarithmic signatures) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, let $\gamma:[0,T]\to V$ be continuous and of bounded variation, and put
\[
\overline\gamma_t=\gamma_t-\gamma_0,
\qquad
 g=S(\gamma),\qquad l=\log g,\qquad v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0.
\]
Assume $R(l)=\infty$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item If $v=0$, then $g=1$; equivalently, $\gamma$ is tree-like.
\item If $v\neq0$, there is $t_*\in[0,T]$ such that, with
\[
\alpha=\overline\gamma|_{[0,t_*]},
\qquad a=S(\alpha),
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
S(\gamma)=a\e^v a^{-1}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Conversely, if $a$ is a bounded-variation signature, then $a\e^v a^{-1}$ has an entire logarithmic signature for every $v\in V$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Classification of entire logarithmic signatures

DRAFT, refuted inference: even uniform vanishing of fixed endpoint origin-hit probabilities does not imply vanishing of the adaptive union over all boundary endpoint pairs. If q_R is the largest pair probability on S_R, the bare union bound gives P(E_R)<=min(1,(32R^2-4R)q_R). It proves decay only with a stronger premise such as a subsequence on which (32R^2-4R)q_R tends to zero. This is a sufficient bound for that particular argument, not a necessary condition for absence. No independence or conditional multiplication is used. An environment-selected endpoint pair cannot be substituted into a deterministic-pair theorem without a selector or union argument.

[Lem ito of arXiv:2411.11759, 'Milstein-type schemes for McKean--Vlasov SDEs driven by Brownian motion and Poisson random'] For any real-valued $F\in \mathcal C^2(\mathbb R^d\times\mathscr{P}_2(\mathbb R^d))$
\begin{align*} 
	F(&x_t^{i,N},\,\mu_t^{x,N})=F(x_0^{i,N},\mu_0^{x,N})+\int_{0}^{t}\mathfrak{D}_x^bF(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N})ds
	-\int_{0}^{t}\int_Z \mathfrak D_{x}^{\gamma(z)} F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N}) \nu(dz)ds	\notag
	\\
	&
	+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^N\int_{0}^{t}\mathfrak{D}_\mu^b F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N},x_s^{k,N})ds
	-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\int_{0}^{t}\int_Z
	\mathfrak D_{\mu}^{\gamma(z)} F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N},x_s^{k,N})\nu(dz)ds
	\\
	&+\sum_{\ell=1}^m\int_{0}^{t}\mathfrak D_x^{\sigma^\ell}F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N})dw_s^{i\ell} \notag
	+\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\ell=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^N\int_{0}^{t}\mathfrak D_\mu^{\sigma^\ell}F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N},x_s^{k,N})dw_s^{k\ell} \notag
	\\
	&+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{t} \mathfrak D_{xx}^{\sigma}F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N})ds 
	+\frac{1}{N}\int_{0}^{t} \mathfrak D_{x\mu}^{\sigma} F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N})ds   \notag
	\\
	&+\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{k=1}^N\int_{0}^{t} \mathfrak D_{y\mu}^{\sigma}F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N},x_s^{k,N})ds
	+\frac{1}{2N^2}\sum_{k=1}^N\int_{0}^{t} \mathfrak D_{\mu\mu}^{\sigma}F(x_s^{i,N},\mu_s^{x,N},x_s^{k,N})ds \notag
	\\
	&+ \sum_{k=1}^{N}\int_{0}^{t}\int_Z\Big\{F\big(x_{s-}^{i,N}+1_{\{k=i\}}\gamma(x_s^{k,N},\mu_{s}^{x,N},z),\mu_{s-}^{x+\gamma(k,z),N}\big)
	-F(x_{s-}^{i,N},\mu_{s-}^{x,N})
	\Big\}n_p^k(ds,dz) 
\end{align*}
almost surely for  $t \in [0,T]$ and $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ where $\mu_{s-}^{x+\gamma(k,z),N}=\displaystyle \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\delta_{x_{s-}^{j,N}+1_{\{j=k\}}\gamma(x_s^{j,N}, \,\mu_{s}^{x,N}, \,z)}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
[Ppn 26 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall $F^{\riv}$ from \eqref{e:F.iv}, and
$F^{\rv}$ from \eqref{e:F.rv}. 
    For sufficiently large $N$, we have for all $t\in \R$
    \[
    \P(F^{\riv} \ge t)
    \le \P\bigg(
    F^{\rv}+ \frac{\epsilon'}{5}
    \ge t
    \bigg) + e^{-cN} \,.
    \]
That is, $F^{\rv}$
approximately stochastically dominates
$F^{\riv}$.

\begin{proof}
For each $j\in[r]$, let
    \[\bv_1(B_j)\equiv
    \frac{\bz(B_j)}{\|\bz(B_j)\|}\,,\]
and complete this to a (Haar random)
orthonormal basis
$(\bv_a(B_j) : 1\le a \le |B_j|)$
of $\R^{|B_j|}$. Let $\tau_j \equiv \|\bz^{B_j}\|^2 / |B_j|$. Then we can rewrite \eqref{e:F.v} and \eqref{e:bar.F.U} as
    \begin{align*}
    F_v(\bG,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j}{MN}
        \sum_{a=1}^{|B_j|}
        (
         \bv_a(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2
         \,,\\
    \bar{F}_U(\bG,\bz,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\tau_j \hU_j}{MN}
        ( \bv_1(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2\,.
    \end{align*}
If we split off the $a=1$ term of $F_v$ and combine it with $\bar{F}_U$, then we see that $F_v+\bar{F}_U$ is the same as the sum of the two terms
    \begin{align*}
    F_{v\setminus1}(\bG,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j}{MN}
        \sum_{a=2}^{|B_j|}
        (
         \bv_a(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2
         \,,\\
    \bar{F}_{U+}(\bG,\bz,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j+
            \tau_j \hU_j}{MN}
        ( \bv_1(B_j),\bG^{B_j} \by)^2\,.
    \end{align*}
Fix arbitrary representatives $a_j \in B_j$, and denote
    \begin{align*}
    \acute{F}_{v\setminus}
    (\bG,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j}{MN}
        \sum_{a\in B_j\setminus a_j}
        (\bg^a,\by)^2
    \le F_v(\bG,\by)\,, \\
    \acute{F}_{U+}
        (\tbmeta,\by)
    &= \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hv_j+
            \tau_j \hU_j}{MN}
    (\tbmeta^{r+j},\by)^2\,.
    \end{align*}
Recalling $F_w$ from \eqref{e:F.w} and
$\bar{F}_B$ from \eqref{e:bar.F.B}, define
    \begin{align*}
    \acute{F}_-(\bG,\tbmeta,\by)
    &\equiv F_w(\by)
    +\acute{F}_{v\setminus}
        (\bG,\by)
    +\bar{F}_B(\tbmeta,\by)
    +\acute{F}_{U+}
        (\tbmeta,\by)
    \\
    &\le F_w(\by)
    +\acute{F}_v(\bG,\by)
        +\bar{F}_B(\tbmeta,\by)
        +\acute{F}_{U+}
        (\tbmeta,\by)
    \equiv\ddot{F}(\bG,\tbmeta,\by)
    \end{align*}
By gaussian rotational invariance,
$\bar{F}$ has the same distribution (as processes indexed by $\by$) as $\acute{F}_-$, which in term is dominated by $\ddot{F}$. Finally, the difference between $\ddot{F}$ and $\acute{F}$
is bounded, for all $\|\by\|^2=N$, by
\[
        \bigg|\sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{(\tau_j-1) \hU_j}{MN}
        (\tbmeta^{r+j}, \by)^2\bigg|
        \le \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{|\tau_j-1| |\hU_j|}{M}
        \|\tbmeta^{r+j}\|^2\,.
    \]
It holds with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$ that
    \[|\tau_j-1| \le \frac{\alpha \iota \epsilon'}{20r},\quad
    \max_{j\in[r]}
    \frac{\|\tbmeta^{r+j}\|}{N^{1/2}}
     \le 2\,.
    \]
On this event, the above quantity is bounded by 
    \[
        r \cdot \frac{\alpha \iota \epsilon'}{20} \cdot \frac{\|\hU\|_\infty}{M} \cdot 4N 
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:fp-normalization-bd}}{\le} \frac{\epsilon'}{5}\,,
    \]
which concludes the proof.\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: Let (Omega, F, mu) be a finite measure space and (f_n) a sequence in L^1(mu) converging in measure to a measurable function f. If the family {f_n} is uniformly integrable, that is, sup_n integral over {|f_n| > K} of |f_n| d mu tends to 0 as K tends to infinity, then f is in L^1(mu), f_n converges to f in L^1(mu), and integral of f_n d mu converges to integral of f d mu. This generalizes the dominated convergence theorem, which is the special case where |f_n| <= g for a fixed integrable g. [standard, e.g. Folland, Real Analysis]
title: Vitali Convergence Theorem

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let mu_1, mu_2 be strictly positive probability measures on a common finite distributive lattice (e.g. {0,1}^E ordered coordinatewise). If the Holley condition holds, mu_1(x v y) mu_2(x ^ y) >= mu_1(x) mu_2(y) for all configurations x, y, then mu_1 stochastically dominates mu_2, meaning mu_1(A) >= mu_2(A) for every increasing (monotone) event A. This is a purely combinatorial, pointwise sufficient condition for stochastic domination between two measures that need not be product measures, and it strictly generalizes the FKG inequality, which is recovered as the special case mu_1 = mu_2. It is the standard tool for comparing Gibbs measures with different boundary conditions or parameters in the Ising model, the random-cluster model, and other lattice systems, and for monotone-coupling arguments more generally. The theorem does not establish the Holley condition itself, which can be as hard to verify as the comparison one is trying to prove; it gives only qualitative stochastic domination, with no quantitative bound on the total-variation distance between mu_1 and mu_2; and it requires strict positivity of both measures on the entire lattice. Typical failure: Assuming the Holley condition holds because mu_1 looks larger than mu_2 in some averaged or marginal sense; the condition is a pointwise, multiplicative statement that must hold for every pair of configurations including their join and meet, and it can fail even when mu_1 does stochastically dominate mu_2 for unrelated reasons, or when only checked on a generating set of configurations rather than genuinely all pairs. Canonical reference: Holley, 1974, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Georgii, Haggstrom and Maes, 2001, in Phase Transitions and Critical Phenomena, vol. 18, Academic Press.

[Prop smooth in sym of arXiv:2608.25471, 'Exact Hausdorff measures and fine geometry of collisions of independent Markov processes'] Assume that Assumption~(assum:main of the paper) holds.
  Moreover, assume that each $X^i$ is a Hunt process and $\mu$-symmetric, that is,
  for all non-negative Borel measurable functions $f$ and $g$ on $M$, 
  $\int_M E^i_x[f(X^i_t)] g(x)\, \mu(dx) = \int_M f(x) E^i_x[g(X^i_t)]\, \mu(dx)$
  for all $t \geq 0$,
  where $E^i_x$ denotes the expectation with respect to $P^i_x$.
  Then Assumption~(assum:smooth of the paper) is satisfied, 
  and thus the collision local time $(C_t)_{t \geq 0}$ is well defined.

[Theorem th:GFF of arXiv:2604.21142, 'Gaussian fluctuations for Internal DLA on cylinders'] Fix $y_0 \in (0, \infty)$. Let $\phi = \phi_N : V_N \times {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}}  \to {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}} $ be a test function of the form
	\[ \phi (x,y) = \sum_{k=2}^K \alpha_k(y) f_k^N(x) \]
for some finite integer $K \geq 2$ independent of $N$, where each coefficient $\alpha_k$ does not depend on $N$ and is differentiable on a neighbourhood of $y_0$ with bounded derivative there.
Let $\varphi = \varphi_N : V_N \times {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}}  \to {\ensuremath{\mathbb R}} $ be the extension
	\[ \varphi (x,y) \coloneqq \phi \Big( x , \frac{y}{a_N} \Big)\,, \qquad (x,y) \in V_N \times {\ensuremath{\mathbb Z}} \,, \]
with $a_N$ as in~(equation eq:aN of the paper). Assume that Assumption~(a:spectral of the paper) holds for each $2 \leq k \leq K$, and that
	\[ a_N \gg \log N + \log_+ a_N \qquad \text{as } N \to \infty\,. \]
Let
	\[ \sigma^2(\phi) \coloneqq \sum_{k=2}^K \alpha_k(y_0)^2 \, \frac{1 - e^{-2\g_k y_0}}{2\g_k} \,\geq\, 0\,. \]
Then, with $T = N \lfloor y_0 a_N \rfloor$,
	\begin{equation}
	 \frac{1}{\sqrt{Na_N}} \langle \! \langle D_T , \varphi \rangle \! \rangle \Rightarrow
	\mathcal{N} \big( 0\,,\, \sigma^2(\phi) \big)
	\end{equation}
as $N\to\infty$. 

Here $\Rightarrow$ denotes convergence in distribution, and $\mathcal{N} (0, \sigma^2)$ denotes a normal distribution with $0$ mean and variance $\sigma^2$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Theorem th:GFF of arXiv:2604.21142

body:
Let Omega in R^n be open, k >= 0 an integer and 0 < alpha <= 1. For a function v on a set S, [v]_{alpha;S} = sup over x, y in S with x != y of |v(x) - v(y)| / |x - y|^alpha. For bounded Omega, C^{k,alpha}(closure of Omega) is the space of u in C^k(Omega) such that every derivative D^beta u with |beta| <= k extends continuously to the closure and ||u||_{C^{k,alpha}} = sum_{|beta| <= k} sup_Omega |D^beta u| + sum_{|beta| = k} [D^beta u]_{alpha;Omega} is finite; it is a Banach space. The local space C^{k,alpha}(Omega) consists of u in C^k(Omega) with u in C^{k,alpha}(closure of U) for every open U with compact closure in Omega. C^{0,1} is the Lipschitz class; C^{1,1} (bounded second difference quotients, equivalently W^{2,infinity} locally) is strictly larger than C^2. A bounded open set Omega is a C^{k,alpha} domain if every boundary point has a neighborhood U such that, in suitable rotated coordinates, Omega intersected with U = {x in U : x_n > g(x_1, ..., x_{n-1})} for some g of class C^{k,alpha}. Schauder theory uses 0 < alpha < 1 strictly; it fails for alpha = 0 (mere continuity) and alpha = 1 (Lipschitz).
Omega open in R^n (bounded for the global space)
k >= 0 integer
0 < alpha <= 1

Let X, B, Y be Banach spaces with X embedded COMPACTLY in B and B embedded continuously in Y. Let 1 <= p < infinity and 1 <= q <= infinity, and set W = { u in L^p(0,T; X) : the distributional time derivative u' lies in L^q(0,T; Y) }. Then W is embedded COMPACTLY in L^p(0,T; B) (and, when p = infinity and q > 1, compactly in C([0,T]; B)). The typical PDE use is X = H_0^1, B = L^2, Y = H^{-1}: a sequence bounded in L^2(0,T;H_0^1) whose time derivatives are bounded in L^2(0,T;H^{-1}) has a subsequence converging strongly in L^2(0,T;L^2), which is what lets one pass to the limit in a nonlinear term.
COMPACTNESS of the embedding X into B is essential - continuity is not enough.
The time derivative must be controlled in the WEAKER space Y;
controlling it in B would be a much stronger and usually unavailable hypothesis.

Let d>=1, L>=m>0 and R>0. Let U:R^d->R be C1, have an everywhere-existing Hessian and globally L-Lipschitz gradient, with grad U(0)=0. Put Omega=R^d minus B(0,R). Assume V(x)=U(x)-(m/2)||x||_2^2 is convex on Omega in this precise sense: V(sum_j a_j x_j)<=sum_j a_j V(x_j) whenever a_j>=0, sum_j a_j=1, all x_j belong to Omega and their barycenter also belongs to Omega. Let mu have density proportional to exp(-U), and define rho_U by Ent_mu(g^2)<= (2/rho_U) integral ||grad g||_2^2 dmu for smooth compactly supported g, where Ent_mu(h)=integral h log(h/integral h dmu) dmu. Then rho_U >= (m/2) exp(-16 L R^2). In particular the deterioration is governed by L R^2; polynomial-dimensional consequences require that this quantity and the other algorithmic parameters be controlled.

[Theorem thm:locFriendClust of arXiv:2603.16824, 'Age-dependent random connection models with arc reciprocity: clustering and connectivity'] For all \(\beta>0,\gamma\in(0,1),\delta>1,\) and \(\Gamma\geq 0\), we have, in probability as \(t\to\infty\),
    \[
    	c^\textup{fc}_\textup{av}(\mathscr{D}_t) \longrightarrow \mathbb{E}_o c^\textup{fc}(\0,\mathscr{D}_o),
    \]
    where
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{aligned}
            \mathbb{E}_o c^\textup{fc}(\0, \mathscr{D}_o) & = 
            \int_0^1 \mathbb{P}(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(u)}\leftrightarrow\boldsymbol{X}^{(u)}) \mu^f_2(\,\mathrm{d} u),
        \end{aligned}
    \end{equation*}
    
    and \(\boldsymbol{X}^{(u)}\) and \(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(u)}\) are two independent random variables distributed according to the normalised measure \(\lambda_u^f/\lambda_u^f(\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,1))\) with
        \[
       \lambda_{u}^\textup{f}(\,\mathrm{d}(x,s)) =  \Big((\tfrac{s}{u})^\Gamma\rho\big(\beta^{-1} s^{\gamma}u^{1-\gamma}|x|^d\big)\1_{\{s<u\}}+(\tfrac{u}{s})^\Gamma\rho\big(\beta^{-1}s^{1-\gamma}u^\gamma |x|^d\big)\1_{\{s\geq u\}}\Big) \,\mathrm{d} s \, \,\mathrm{d} x,
    \]
    and \(\mu^f_2\) is the distribution on \((0,1)\) with density proportional to 
    \[
        1-e^{-\lambda_u^f(\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,1))}-\lambda_u^f(\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,1))e^{-\lambda_u^f(\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,1))}.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

In the household-contact epidemic model with X_L=0 almost surely, fixed population and initial infections, using the same global contact graph makes infection paths identical for every admissible household partition and local-to-global replacement probability. Let A be a real m x n matrix, the payoff matrix of a two-player zero-sum game in which the row player chooses a mixed strategy x in the simplex Delta_m = {x in R^m : x >= 0, sum_i x_i = 1}, the column player chooses y in Delta_n, and the row player's expected payoff is x^T A y (the column player's payoff being its negative). Then max_{x in Delta_m} min_{y in Delta_n} x^T A y = min_{y in Delta_n} max_{x in Delta_m} x^T A y. This common value v is called the value of the game, and any x*, y* attaining the respective maximum and minimum together form an optimal pair of strategies (a Nash equilibrium) for the game.

Independent review pending. Let T be the rooted tree in which each vertex at level n-1 has 8 children if n is a power of two and 2 children otherwise, for n>=1. T is infinite, connected, simple and locally finite, with maximum degree 9. For iid Bernoulli bond percolation, p_c(T)=1/2 and the root survives at criticality with probability at least 4/5. At p=1/2 the open generation mean is M_n=4^(1+floor(log_2 n)), and its normalized second moment is 1+(1/2)sum_{j<=n}1/M_j<=5/4. Two independent uniform-child rays on the host have E[2^K]=5/4, where K counts their common undirected edges. Below 1/2, M_n<=4n^2(2p)^n tends to zero. The degree-8 root is unique, so every automorphism fixes it and T has infinitely many vertex orbits. This example excludes replacing quasi-transitivity by bounded degree; it does not refute critical extinction on quasi-transitive graphs.

body:
[Corollary 21 (No transfer) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] A transform proven optimal for one regime carries no optimality guarantee for the other. In particular, for a generic spectrum the KLT (\Cref{thm:klt}), optimal for allocation-flexible
coding, leaves the energy profile bounded away from the within-group flatness that the
AbsMax step-size surrogate rewards (\Cref{thm:inversion},
\Cref{prop:schur}(ii)). Because that surrogate is not a functional of the global order at
all, the change relative to an arbitrary starting basis is not even signed: what fails to
transfer is the guarantee, the signed opposition of \Cref{thm:inversion} being a within-group
statement rather than a global one. The one exception is degenerate: if the spectrum is constant on every scale group in the eigenvalue-sorted order (plateaus of multiplicity $G$ aligned with the group boundaries, \Cref{rem:inv-scope}), the sorted KLT sits on the fixed-rate floor $E/G$ and both surrogates are minimized at once.

A real-valued stochastic process Z satisfies the downward crossing property if for any almost surely finite stopping time tau, P(forall h > 0, inf_{s in [0, h]} (Z(tau + s) - Z(tau)) < 0) = 1. This property ensures that upon hitting any boundary, the process immediately enters the lower half-plane with probability 1.
Z is a real-valued stochastic process
title: Downward Crossing Property of Driving Processes

body:
[Corollary cor:constant-overshoot-families of arXiv:2607.04620, 'The Exact Ville Identity\\ \large From the Absorbing Case to the General Law\\ with an App'] Consider the first passage of an additive mean-zero walk above an integer level.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \emph{Bounded integer up-steps (C1).} If the increments take integer values with maximal up-step $+1$, the walk lands exactly one unit above the level, so $\omega=1$. (For any such $X$, $\mathbb{E}[X\mid X>0]=1$.)
\item \emph{Geometric positive increments (C(2,$\cdot$)).} If the positive increment has the geometric law on $\{1,2,\ldots\}$ with success probability $q\in(0,1)$, namely $\mathbb{P}(X=k)=q(1-q)^{k-1}$, then by the memorylessness of the geometric the conditional overshoot is again geometric with the same law, and $\omega=1/q$. (Equivalently, the companion's parametrization gives $\mathbb{E}[X\mid X>k]=k+p/(1-p)$ in the decay-ratio convention; see (rem:geometric-param of the paper).)
\item \emph{Exponential right tail (C(3,$a$)).} If the positive increment has an exponential right tail, $\mathbb{P}(X>y)=c e^{-ay}$, then by the memorylessness of the exponential the overshoot is exponential with mean $\omega=1/a$, and $\mathbb{E}[X\mid X>y]=y+1/a$ (the constant $c$ is irrelevant).
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Constant-overshoot families

body: In probability theory, the central limit theorem states that, under certain circumstances, the probability distribution of the scaled mean of a random sample converges to a normal distribution as the sample size increases to infinity. Under stronger assumptions, the Berry–Esseen theorem, or Berry–Esseen inequality, gives a more quantitative result, because it also specifies the rate at which this convergence takes place by giving a bound on the maximal error of approximation between the normal distribution and the true distribution of the scaled sample mean. The approximation is measured by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance. In the case of independent samples, the convergence rate is n−1/2, where n is the sample size, and the constant is estimated in terms of the third absolute normalized moment. It is also possible to give non-uniform bounds which become more strict for more extreme events.
title: Berry–Esseen theorem

[Lemma lem:GKS of arXiv:2411.14111, 'Stochastic processes on preferential attachment models'] Consider two Ising measures $\mu$ and $\mu^\prime$ on graphs $G = (V, E)$ and $G^\prime= (V, E^\prime)$, with inverse temperatures $\beta$ and $\beta^\prime$, and external fields $\underline{B}$ and $\underline{B}^\prime$, respectively. If $E\subseteq E^\prime$, $\beta \leq \beta^\prime$, and $0 \leq B_i \leq B^\prime_i$ for all $i \in V$, then, for any $U \subset V$,
	\begin{equation}
		0\leq \left\langle{\prod\limits_{i\in U}\sigma_i}\right\rangle_{\mu}\leq \left\langle{\prod\limits_{i\in U}\sigma_i}\right\rangle_{\mu^\prime}.
	\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body:
Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT and OCO-2 stacking pools (70 cells, the pool protocol, full calibration, paired). After the optimism reading was refuted (P20), the gain was located row by row: the per-evaluation-row relative-score gain of the long-only stack over least squares against the bootstrap variance of the least-squares stack at that row. P22 (a) REFUTED at the pre-registered 0.2: the within-cell median Spearman between a row's gain and the least-squares variance load at that row is 0.13 over the 40 EMIT cells (positive in 36 of 40; 0.37 on Y2, 0.01 on Y1); (b) HELD on Y2, REFUTED as an every-group claim: the top-decile-load rows carry 47 pct of Y2's gain (a uniform spread gives 10) but only 11 pct on Y1 (20 on Y3, 32 on Y4); (c) HELD: across the 40 EMIT cells the gain rank-correlates 0.54 with the variance-load share of least squares' error, and 0.65 with the share the constraint removes (least squares minus nn1) - the between-cell statistic that optimism (P20) failed to be; (d) REFUTED as written: the OCO-2 top-decile share reaches 0.40 on sco2, but as the share of a gain of -0.55 pct it is the ratio of two near-zero numbers and does not test the clause; falsifier (within-cell correlation at or below zero) not triggered. Reading: where the gain is large (Y2, +18) it sits where least squares is uncertain - row-level rank correlation 0.37, 47 pct of the gain on the tenth of rows with the largest variance; where it is modest (+5 to +6) it is spread over the rows; between cells the variance-load share of least squares' error predicts the gain (0.54) and the variance the constraint removes predicts it better (0.65). The calibration and evaluation rows share the same target-norm distribution, so this is not a split shift; the gain leans toward the small-norm evaluation rows the reported metric weights most. Cell level: the variance the constraint removes (least squares' bootstrap variance share minus the long-only stack's) predicts the gain within every output group (Spearman 0.79, 0.87, 0.54, 0.43 on Y1-Y4; 0.69 across 40 cells with the group effect removed), while the L1 norm of the least-squares weights does not survive the group adjustment (0.02): the constraint pays what it saves in estimation variance at the rows it is scored on. Fresh-split replication (split C, SPLIT_SEED 11): P23 (a) REFUTED at the per-group 0.5, HELD in the aggregate: on split C the within-group Spearman between the gain and the variance removed is +0.59, +0.49, +0.64, +0.22 on Y1..Y4 and +0.74 across the 40 cells with the group effect removed (split B: +0.69); (b) REFUTED: the split-B variance-removed share predicts the split-C gain only on Y1 and Y2 (+0.72, +0.47; Y3 +0.09, Y4 -0.24; demeaned +0.17), and the split-B gain itself predicts the split-C gain only weakly (Y1 +0.82, Y4 +0.47, Y2 +0.15, Y3 -0.14); (c) HELD: the long-only stack beats least squares on 35 of 40 split-C cells (mean +9.59 against +8.83 on split B); falsifier (any group at or below 0.2, or the demeaned correlation at or below 0.3) not triggered. Fresh-split check of the calibration-side correlates (P32, the P20 driver on split C): P32 (a) HELD: on split C the between-cell Spearman of the gain with the least-squares L1 is +0.55 and with n_eff -0.44; (b) REFUTED: group-demeaned, L1 +0.29 and members kept +0.21; (c) HELD: the nn0 RMSE gain with the smallest relative eigenvalue +0.29 and with the condition number -0.31; falsifier (L1 above +0.3 after the group adjustment) not triggered. The gain off the tail (P36, the top tenth of evaluation rows by |gain| removed): P36 (a) HELD for the sign, REFUTED for the size: the trimmed gain is positive on 36 and 36 of 40 EMIT cells (splits B, C) but reads +7.67 and +8.30 against untrimmed +8.83 and +9.59 - the body keeps 87 pct of the gain, not less than half; (b) HELD: on OCO-2 the trimmed gain is +0.25 against -0.18 untrimmed; (c) REFUTED: the smallest trimmed gain is on Y4, not Y1; falsifier (negative trimmed gain on EMIT) not triggered. Removing the two-sided tail leaves 87 pct of the EMIT gain: the constraint pays broadly across the rows, and the non-transfer between splits comes from the tails' noise, not from where the gain sits.

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); T232-w704-C016 v1. No independent PASS or established novelty/priority. Let finite m>=2,w>=2, rank-two M in R^(m-by-2), and SPD 2-by-2 Sigma define the asymmetric factor gradient flow. Suppose a balanced rank-one reference zbar(t) converges to a stationary endpoint zstar=(bstar;astar) with NONZERO PRODUCT bstar astar^T. Put Gstar=(bstar astar^T-M)Sigma and let v be the unit top eigenvector of Lstar=[[0,-Gstar],[-Gstar^T,0]]. At one sufficiently late FIXED entrance time, write actual flows U_epsilon=[z_epsilon,X_epsilon]. Assume uniformly for all small positive epsilon that ||z_epsilon(0)-zbar(0)||<=C0 epsilon, c0 epsilon<=||v^T X_epsilon(0)||_F<=c1 epsilon with fixed 0<c0<=c1, and ||(I-vv^T)X_epsilon(0)||_F<=h||v^T X_epsilon(0)||_F for a sufficiently narrow fixed cone aperture h. The reference future tail must be inside the chosen fixed local endpoint neighborhood. Then convergence alone permits thresholds delta_epsilon tending to zero and first-hit times t_epsilon tending to infinity with p(t_epsilon)=||v^T X_epsilon(t_epsilon)||_F=delta_epsilon, ||z_epsilon(t_epsilon)-zstar||<=D delta_epsilon^2, and ||X_epsilon(t_epsilon)||_F<=sqrt(1+h^2)delta_epsilon, for fixed D. For Z_epsilon=U_epsilon U_epsilon^T and Z1=zstar zstar^T, a fixed K>0 gives ||Z_epsilon(t_epsilon)-Z1||_F<=K delta_epsilon^2 and v^T Z_epsilon(t_epsilon)v>=delta_epsilon^2, hence strong relative Gram alignment at least 1/K. C015 supplies the strict active/dormant gap and the nonpositive dormant complement. No exponential reference rate or actual-family balance is needed. This does not prove the Gaussian active O(epsilon) entrance premise: C014's qualitative convergence alone is insufficient. It does not prove the complete rectangular second-step composition.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:4a054a169c86083274f88d6e8fb68681913e099c83326d578db28eb6369c9656","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/4a/4a054a169c86083274f88d6e8fb68681913e099c83326d578db28eb6369c9656.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:d69cab3a62309597bdd696021668bf7b390642f1eda259975dfea1d109804dfb","bundle_entry_key":"rectangular-strong-gram-arrival","bundle_id":"population.t232-rectangular-origin-spectrum-arrival-20261021","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"deep linear networks; asymmetric factorization; saddle-to-saddle dynamics","draft":"w704/bundle_005.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:optimization.deep_linear_networks:rectangular-strong-gram-arrival","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Rectangular local arrival: strong Gram alignment from a fixed cone entrance

T232-w704-C016 v1. Kind: moved; Target 1, conditional local arrival on the whole m-by-2 range. Status: proof (unaudited). This is not a complete Gaussian second-step theorem. Dependencies C015 v1 and the proof below require independent audit; the square C009 PASS does not certify this extended statement.

## Theorem and load-bearing entrance hypotheses
Let m>=2 and w>=2 be finite, M in R^(m-by-2) have rank two, and Sigma be 2-by-2 symmetric positive definite. Let a balanced rank-one reference zbar(t)=(bbar;abar) solve the factor gradient flow and converge to a critical endpoint zstar=(bstar;astar) with NONZERO PRODUCT bstar astar^T. Set Gstar=(bstar astar^T-M)Sigma, Lstar=[[0,-Gstar],[-Gstar^T,0]], s=||Gstar||op, and let v be its unit top eigenvector.

Choose a sufficiently late reference time as the fixed local time zero. Consider any actual width-w flow family U_epsilon=[z_epsilon,X_epsilon], with positive epsilon tending to zero, satisfying at this ONE fixed entrance time, with constants independent of epsilon,
 ||z_epsilon(0)-zbar(0)||<=C0 epsilon,
 c0 epsilon<=||v^T X_epsilon(0)||_F<=c1 epsilon,  0<c0<=c1,
 ||(I-vv^T)X_epsilon(0)||_F<=h||v^T X_epsilon(0)||_F.
Here h>0 is a sufficiently narrow fixed aperture, and all entrance conditions hold for every sufficiently small epsilon. No independence of evolving factors, exponential reference convergence, or balance of the actual family is assumed.

Then there are first-threshold times t_epsilon tending to infinity and positive thresholds delta_epsilon tending to zero such that
 p(t_epsilon)=||v^T X_epsilon(t_epsilon)||_F=delta_epsilon,
 ||z_epsilon(t_epsilon)-zstar||<=D delta_epsilon^2,
 ||X_epsilon(t_epsilon)||_F<=sqrt(1+h^2)delta_epsilon.
With Z_epsilon=U_epsilon U_epsilon^T and Z1=zstar zstar^T, a fixed K>0 satisfies
 ||Z_epsilon(t_epsilon)-Z1||_F<=K delta_epsilon^2,
 v^T Z_epsilon(t_epsilon)v>=delta_epsilon^2.
Hence the liminf of their relative alignment ratio is at least 1/K>0. Constants may depend on fixed data, endpoint, reference and entrance constants; there is no uniform quantitative lower bound across data.

## 1. Rectangular spectral premises
C015 proves, under exactly the nonzero-product endpoint premise, rank(Gstar)=1, s>0, simple top s of Lstar, nonpositive complementary spectrum (one -s and m zeros), and v perpendicular to zstar. The full active derivative Jact=DF(zstar) is symmetric with top rate r satisfying 0<=r<s. Its added m-2 transverse active directions have eigenvalue -astar^T Sigma astar<0. Thus neither the dormant zero modes nor the additional active directions introduce a competing positive top rate.

Choose rplus in (r,s). Continuity makes the largest eigenvalue of DF at most rplus on a small convex active ball of radius R about zstar. Choose h>0 and then eta>0 small enough that
 eta(1+h)^2<h s,
 a=s-eta(1+h)>rplus,  b=s+eta(1+h).
These choices are possible since rplus<s. Fix active and dormant balls, of radii R and R_X, so the exact dormant generator differs from Lstar by at most eta throughout them. The generator difference is -H(P-Pstar), where P=z_b z_a^T+VW^T for X=(V;W). It is continuous and vanishes at (zstar,0). Shift the reference sufficiently late that its entire future tail lies in the active ball of radius R/4. The theorem assumes the uniform entrance hypotheses at that chosen time.

## 2. Dimension-independent cone and active comparison
Write Y=v^T X, Q_X=(I-vv^T)X, p=||Y||_F, q=||Q_X||_F. Up to first exit from the local balls, the exact equation X'=(Lstar+R(t))X has ||R(t)||op<=eta. For p>0,
 sp-eta(p+q)<=p'<=sp+eta(p+q).
The symmetric nonpositive complementary spectrum gives D^+q<=eta(p+q), including q=0 by the norm triangle inequality. At q=hp,
 D^+(q-hp)<=[eta(1+h)^2-hs]p<0.
Thus the cone q<=hp is invariant before exit. The initial p is positive, and p'>=ap preserves positivity. Inside the cone,
 ap<=p'<=bp,  ||X||_F^2<= (1+h^2)p^2.
This calculation uses only a nonpositive complement, not its dimension or absence of zeros.

The exact active equation is z'=F(z)-H(VW^T)z. On a fixed bounded active ball, ||H(VW^T)z||<=C||X||_F^2, for a fixed C. With E=||z-zbar||, symmetry of DF and integration along the segment between z,zbar give
 D^+E<=rplus E+C(1+h^2)p^2.
For u<=t, lower cone growth gives p(u)<=p(t)exp(-a(t-u)). Integration therefore yields
 E(t)<=C0 epsilon exp(rplus t)+C1 p(t)^2,
 C1=C(1+h^2)/(2a-rplus).
The denominator is strictly positive because a>rplus>=0. This uses the full active derivative; frozen dormant transport is not substituted for it.

## 3. A uniform cutoff for each fixed threshold
Set k=rplus/a<1 and C_H=max(1,C0 c0^(-k)). Choose delta0 in (0,1) so
 (1+C1)delta0^2<R/4,  sqrt(1+h^2)delta0<R_X/2.
For any fixed delta in (0,delta0], reference convergence supplies a finite t_delta>=0 such that ||zbar(t)-zstar||<=delta^2 for every t>=t_delta. Impose
 epsilon<=epsilon_ent,
 epsilon<=delta/(2c1),
 epsilon<=[delta^(2-k)/(2C_H)]^(1/(1-k)),
 epsilon<=delta exp(-b t_delta)/(2c1).
Here epsilon_ent is the fixed entrance cutoff. All four bounds are positive at fixed delta and hold for every smaller epsilon as well.

Before the first threshold p=delta or the first exit, lower growth gives the elapsed-time upper bound T_upper=log(delta/(c0 epsilon))/a: an interval without either event cannot extend past this value. Therefore its homogeneous active error is at most
 C0 epsilon exp(rplus T_upper)<=C_H delta^k epsilon^(1-k)<=delta^2/2.
Consequently E<=(C1+1/2)delta^2<R/4 and z remains within R/2 of zstar, while ||X||<R_X/2. There is a strict margin to both exit boundaries. Smooth local continuation in these bounded balls excludes exit first and, by the lower growth bound, ensures that the threshold is attained by T_upper.

Upper growth gives the stopping-time lower bound
 t_stop>=log(delta/(c1 epsilon))/b>=t_delta+log(2)/b.
Thus the reference endpoint error is at most delta^2 at this stop. Combining it with E yields
 ||z-zstar||<=D delta^2,  D=C1+3/2.
The Gram expansion gives
 ||zz^T+XX^T-zstar zstar^T||_F<=K delta^2,
 K=2||zstar||D+D^2 delta0^2+1+h^2.
Indeed the active difference is bounded by 2||zstar||||z-zstar||+||z-zstar||^2, and ||XX^T||_F<=||X||_F^2. Positivity gives v^T Z v=(v^T z)^2+||v^T X||^2>=delta^2. In particular K is fixed independently of delta and epsilon.

## 4. One diagonal selection; all smaller epsilon, not a subsequence only
Let delta_n=delta0 2^(-n), n>=1. Choose epsilon_n strictly below half of epsilon_(n-1) for n>1, delta_n^n/2, epsilon_ent/2, and half of each of the other three cutoffs in Section 3 evaluated at delta_n. Every epsilon_n is positive, epsilon_n strictly decreases to zero, and the delta_n stop is valid for EVERY epsilon<=epsilon_n.

For epsilon<=epsilon_1 set n(epsilon)=max{n>=1:epsilon<=epsilon_n}. This set is nonempty and finite because epsilon_n tends to zero. Its maximum tends to infinity as epsilon tends to zero. Choose the actual first delta_n(epsilon) stop and put delta_epsilon=delta_n(epsilon). All estimates above apply uniformly there, so delta_epsilon tends to zero and the claimed alignment follows. Moreover epsilon<delta_n^n implies
 t_stop>=[(n-1)log(1/delta_n)-log c1]/b,
which tends to infinity. This checks the index direction and the number n-1 explicitly.

The reference convergence modulus t_delta may be arbitrarily slow. It only shrinks positive epsilon cutoffs; no rate or interchange of growing-time limits is used. QED, subject to independent review.

## Remaining frontier obligations
This establishes conditional local arrival over the whole m-by-2 range if its proof and C015 are correct. It does NOT establish the entrance hypotheses for Gaussian initialization, a complete rectangular canonical escape or its forward endpoint. C014 supplies fixed-compact origin matching and ideal output confinement, not a growing-time comparison or an active O(epsilon) error estimate by itself. In particular normalized dormant convergence cannot be substituted for the active O(epsilon) entrance premise without a separate argument. That Gaussian handoff remains the hardest open link of the rectangular extension.

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Exact conditioning, spectral integral estimate, deterministic graph comparison or order-statistic asymptotics Result: Put delta=sqrt(6*k*log(n)) and assume k>2*delta. Threshold edge weights at t=(k-delta)/(n-1). Each threshold degree B_v is binomial with mean k-delta. Chernoff and a union bound give k-2*delta<=B_v<=k for all vertices with probability at least 1-2/n^2. On that event every threshold edge is preferred at both endpoints, so k-2*delta<=D_v<=k simultaneously. Thus k/log(n)->infinity suffices for relative concentration. The argument uses independence of the underlying edge weights, and never independence of vertex degrees. Check: Upper and lower Chernoff exponents are at least delta^2/(2*k)=3*log(n), followed by a union over n vertices. The deterministic threshold inclusion follows directly from having at most k incident edges below t at each endpoint. Obstruction: A sufficient-condition partial only. Sharp tails and the logarithmic boundary are not determined; below connectivity isolated vertices rule out concentration of every degree near k.

Let $(\Sigma, g_0, h_0)$ be an asymptotically flat Cauchy initial data set satisfying the vacuum Einstein constraint equations. If the mean curvature $H_0 = \operatorname{tr}_{g_0} h_0$ satisfies a suitable smallness condition in weighted Sobolev spaces, then there exists a local maximal foliation of the maximal Cauchy development of $(\Sigma, g_0, h_0)$ in a neighborhood of $\Sigma$.
(\Sigma, g_0, h_0) is asymptotically flat vacuum initial data
Mean curvature H_0 is small in weighted Sobolev norm
Linearized operator Delta - |h|^2 is invertible on weighted spaces

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Use the Apollonian structure of the limit to predict the local statistics in each patch. Result: The Pegden-Smart limit is a piecewise-quadratic function whose Hessian takes values in the set Gamma of integer superharmonic matrices; inside a patch where the Hessian is a fixed matrix A in Gamma, the sandpile is (Levine-Pegden-Smart) a periodic pattern determined by A, so the height-j fraction in a patch converges to the frequency of height j in that periodic pattern, which is a computable rational number. Hence the refinement holds in the interior of every patch; the question reduces to the boundary set between patches (the Apollonian gasket of patch boundaries), which has Lebesgue measure zero in the limit but whose discrete neighbourhood might carry a positive fraction of sites at scale n if the boundary layers have width of order n^{alpha}, alpha > 0... the patches are of all sizes (Apollonian), and the total area of patches of diameter < eps tends to zero as eps -> 0 (the gasket has Hausdorff dimension < 2), so for any delta the fraction of sites within the small patches is < delta for eps small, and within large patches the convergence holds; therefore the height-j fraction converges PROVIDED the discrete configuration inside a large patch is exactly the periodic pattern except in a boundary layer of o(n) width, which is the content of the Levine-Pegden-Smart 'Apollonian structure in the abelian sandpile' theorem (they prove the patterns appear; the width of the transition layers is what I could not confirm from memory). Conditional resolution recorded: the height-fraction convergence follows from the patch-pattern theorem plus an o(n) transition-layer bound plus the measure-zero gasket; the identity-element scaling limit remains open beyond the Caracciolo-Paoletti-Sportiello special case. Key identity: Inside a patch with Hessian A the height-j frequency is the frequency of j in the A-pattern; the gasket of boundaries has area zero, so convergence reduces to o(n) transition layers. Obstruction: Transition-layer width between patches not confirmed; identity element limit open.

body:
Let (X,d) be a compact metric space and T: X -> X continuous. For n >= 1 define the Bowen metric d_n(x,y) = max_{0 <= i <= n-1} d(T^i x, T^i y). A set E contained in X is (n, eps)-SEPARATED if d_n(x,y) > eps for all distinct x, y in E; let s_n(eps) be the largest cardinality of an (n, eps)-separated set. A set F is (n, eps)-SPANNING if for every x in X there is y in F with d_n(x,y) <= eps; let r_n(eps) be the smallest cardinality of an (n, eps)-spanning set. Both are finite by compactness. THEOREM (Bowen, Dinaburg): h_top(T) = lim_{eps -> 0+} limsup_{n -> infinity} (1/n) log s_n(eps) = lim_{eps -> 0+} limsup_{n -> infinity} (1/n) log r_n(eps), and this common value coincides with the Adler-Konheim-McAndrew topological entropy defined through open covers. The limits in eps exist in [0, +infinity] because s_n(eps) and r_n(eps) are nonincreasing in eps, so the inner quantities are nonincreasing in eps. The two counts are comparable at shifted scales: r_n(eps) <= s_n(eps) <= r_n(eps/2). SHARP EDGES. (a) The order of the limits is not negotiable: for a FIXED eps the quantity limsup_n (1/n) log s_n(eps) is in general strictly smaller than h_top(T) (it is the 'entropy at scale eps'), and it is only after eps -> 0 that one gets the entropy. The single exception worth remembering is an expansive homeomorphism, where any eps below the expansive constant already gives the answer. (b) Compactness is used to make the counts finite and to make the value a topological invariant. Bowen's extension to a uniformly continuous map of a possibly non-compact metric space, taking the supremum of the above over compact subsets, defines a quantity h_d(T) that depends on the METRIC and not only on the topology: uniformly equivalent metrics give the same value, but merely topologically equivalent ones need not, so on non-compact spaces 'the topological entropy' is not well defined without naming the metric. (c) Separated and spanning counts measure ORBIT distinguishability over a finite time window; they say nothing by themselves about invariant measures. The link to measures is the variational principle, h_top(T) = sup over T-invariant Borel probabilities mu of h_mu(T), which is a separate theorem and is not proved by the counting argument below. (d) The definition uses only forward iterates 0, ..., n-1, and for a homeomorphism this already gives the entropy of T; the two-sided window max over |i| <= n gives the same number, not twice it.
(X,d) is a compact metric space
T: X -> X is continuous
for the non-compact extension, T is uniformly continuous and the entropy is taken as a supremum over compact subsets, and then depends on the uniform equivalence class of d

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine whether the Gaussian free field characterisation can be made asymptotically exact. Result: DLP show t_cov ≍ |E| (E max GFF)^2; the later result of Ding (2012, 'Asymptotics of cover times via Gaussian free fields: bounded-degree graphs and general trees') gives asymptotic equality t_cov ~ |E| (E max eta)^2 for bounded-degree graphs when t_cov/t_hit -> infinity, and Zhai (2018) proved the asymptotic formula for general graphs under the same condition. Given the asymptotic formula, a (1+eps) approximation of t_cov reduces to a (1+eps) approximation of E max of a Gaussian vector with given covariance (the Green function), which is a deterministic computational problem: computing E max of a Gaussian vector to within 1+eps is not known to be in deterministic polynomial time in general (the majorizing-measure/generic-chaining bounds are only within constants; exact computation of Gaussian maxima expectations is #P-hard in some formulations). So the question reduces, for graphs with t_cov/t_hit -> infinity, to the deterministic approximability of E max of a Gaussian vector with a graph-Laplacian covariance; a positive answer would follow from a deterministic FPTAS for Gaussian expected maxima on such covariances, which is open; graphs with t_cov ≍ t_hit (e.g. cycles, where the cover time is dominated by hitting times) need a separate treatment and are the easier case since hitting times are computable exactly. Reduction recorded. Key identity: t_cov ~ |E| (E max GFF)^2 when t_cov/t_hit -> infinity (Ding; Zhai), so (1+eps)-approximation reduces to approximating a Gaussian expected maximum. Obstruction: No deterministic (1+eps) algorithm for Gaussian expected maxima with general covariance.

[Prop P:temporal-est of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $n < n+r \le 2n \in \mathbb{N}$, and parameter $\alpha \ge 1/2 - n^{-1/6}$. For any $x, y_2\in \llbracket0, n/1000 \rrbracket$, denote $y_1 = \lfloor x + n(y_2-x)/(n + r) \rfloor$, and 
$u_1 = [x, 0; y_1, n]_\textsf{L}$, $u_2 = [x, 0; y_2, n + r]_\textsf{L}$.
Take any $\epsilon > 0$ satisfying the constraints:
\begin{equation}
	
	C_0 \max \left(\frac{|x-y_2|^2}{n^2}, ((1/2 - \alpha)\vee 0)^2\right) < \epsilon < C_* r^{-1/3},
\end{equation}
where $C_0>0$ is a universal constant, and $C_*>0$ is any large enough number. 
Then for a constant $c>0$ depending only on $C_*$, we have
$$
\mathbb{P}\left( \left|\bar X(u_1) - \bar X(u_2)\right| \ge \epsilon r \right) \le 2\exp\left(-c \epsilon^{3/2} r \right).
$$
title: Prop P:temporal-est of arXiv:2604.10020

DRAFT proof (unaudited), T318-C8 v1. Let a test input x have an arbitrary finite-dimensional Gaussian law, let A be PSD, V=xprime A x, q=EV, and f=xprime delta with deterministic delta conditional on the training environment; f and V need not be independent. Put R=Ef^2 and v=Var(V)<infinity. Then abs(E[(1+f^2)/(1+V)]-(1+R)/(1+q))<=sqrt(3v)(1+R), and abs(E log(1+V)-log(1+q))<=sqrt(v). This follows from the noncentral scalar Gaussian bound Ef^4<=3R^2 and the 1-Lipschitz reciprocal/log functions on nonnegative arguments. The ratio error is relative to 1+R, so a uniform lower risk bound can survive even when R is unbounded as a regularization parameter approaches zero: first require 1/(1+q)-sqrt(3v)>0, then insert a common lower bound on R. For any PSD covariance C, teacher w and fitted vector w_hat in a subspace S, the bound (w_hat-w)prime C(w_hat-w)>=wprime C^(1/2) P C^(1/2)w holds with P the orthogonal projection onto (C^(1/2)S)^perp. A Euclidean nullspace projection does not supply the same bound. These two facts yield C8 realized-teacher non-tightness of global likelihood-temperature minimizers in C7 offset-linear random features; that application requires all C7 assumptions and is not a probability-one escape claim. No novelty or independent-audit claim.
Finite-dimensional Gaussian test input, PSD quadratic denominator, scalar linear Gaussian numerator as stated; conditional training quantities fixed.
For the lower-risk substitution the relative coefficient must be positive; no independence of numerator/denominator.

body: In mathematics, the multiplicative ergodic theorem, or Oseledets theorem provides the theoretical background for computation of Lyapunov exponents of a nonlinear dynamical system. It was proved by Valery Oseledets in 1965 and reported at the International Mathematical Congress in Moscow in 1966. A conceptually different proof of the multiplicative ergodic theorem was found by M. S. Raghunathan. The theorem has been extended to semisimple Lie groups by V. A. Kaimanovich and further generalized in the works of David Ruelle, Grigory Margulis, Anders Karlsson, and François Ledrappier.
title: Oseledets theorem

Let (X_n)_{n=1}^\infty be independent real random variables, and fix c > 0. Define the truncated variables Y_n = X_n \mathbf{1}_{\{|X_n| \le c\}}. Then the series \sum_{n=1}^\infty X_n converges almost surely if and only if all three of the following series converge: (1) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb{P}(|X_n| > c) < \infty; (2) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \mathbb{E}[Y_n] \text{ converges in } \mathbb{R}; (3) \sum_{n=1}^\infty \text{Var}(Y_n) < \infty.

[Corollary 3 (Maximal EPI on connected compact groups) of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be a compact and metrizable topological abelian group,
equipped with its Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For any pair
of independent random 
variables $X,Y$ on $G$,
$$h(X+Y)\geq \max\big\{h(X),h(Y)\big\}.$$
Moreover, suppose that $G$ is connected and 
$\max{\{h(X),h(Y)\}} = h(Y) >-\infty$. Then we have
equality if and only if either $Y$ is uniformly distributed
on $G$ or $h(X)=-\infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Maximal EPI on connected compact groups

Method: Relaxation of linear-polymer coagulation and fragmentation structural calculation Result: The cluster-count coordinate K has exact rates K->K+1 at beta*(n-K) and K->K-1 at K*(K-1)/n. Its deterministic equilibrium density mu solves mu^2=beta*(1-mu), and linearizing the density drift gives restoring rate beta+2*mu=sqrt(beta^2+4*beta). At beta=b/n this is order n^-1/2. The source edge coupling has discrepancy killing rate at least beta+(K-1)/n, so it also suggests this scale once K is near sqrt(b*n). Check: For n=3 the partition states3,21,111 have rates3->21=2beta,21->3=2/3,21->111=beta,111->21=2. Direct characteristic-polynomial calculation gives gap[3beta+8/3-sqrt(beta^2+16/9)]/2. Thus finite-n small-beta behavior cannot simply be substituted for the joint n,beta_n limit. Obstruction: The required upgrade is a uniform exponential bound on the coupling survival functional E exp[-integral(beta+(K_u-1)/n)du], including atypically small K. Replacing K by its stationary mean inside the exponential has the wrong Jensen direction and is not a proof of the desired upper bound.

body: In algebra and number theory, Wilson's theorem states that a natural number n > 1 is a prime number if and only if the product of all the positive integers less than n is one less than a multiple of n. That is (using the notations of modular arithmetic), the factorial $(n-1)!=1\times 2\times 3\times \cdots \times (n-1)$ satisfies $$(n-1)!\ \equiv \;-1{\pmod {n}}$$

[Proposition 13 of arXiv:2606.16164, 'A Low-Regularity Semigroup Sewing Lemma via Quotient Structures'] Let $h\in Z\hat C(\Delta_T^3;B_\alpha)$ and let $(r^\tau)_{\tau\in[0,T]}$ be a compatible frozen increment family over $h$. For $0\le s\le t\le T$, define $R_{ts}:=r^t_{ts}$. Then
\[
R\in C(\Delta_T^2;B_\alpha)\  \text{\,and\,} \ \hat\delta R = h.
\]
Moreover, if $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and for every $0<\varepsilon<\gamma$, $$ \sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r^\tau\|_{\gamma-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon;\tau}<\infty,$$ then
$R\in E^{\gamma}(\Delta_T^2; B_\alpha)$ and for every $0<\varepsilon<\gamma$,
\begin{equation}

\|R\|_{\gamma-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon}
\le
\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}
\|r^\tau\|_{\gamma-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon;\tau}.
\end{equation}
Similarly, if 
$$\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r^\tau\|_{1,\log;\tau,\alpha}+\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r^\tau\|_{1-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon;\tau}<\infty$$
for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, then $R\in E_{\log}^{1}(\Delta_T^2; B_\alpha)$ and
\[
\|R\|_{1,\log;\alpha}\le\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r^\tau\|_{1,\log;\tau,\alpha}, \quad \|R\|_{1-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon}\le\sup_{\tau\in[0,T]}\|r^\tau\|_{1-\varepsilon,\alpha+\varepsilon;\tau}.
\]
title: Proposition 13 of arXiv:2606.16164

body:
[Proposition 12 of arXiv:2609.01460, 'On cost-induced Santal\'o-type inequalities \\ in Polish measure spaces'] Let $d\in \N$ and $\alpha>0$. Let $\Omega:\R_+\to \R_+$ be a measurable function such that 
    \[
    0 < \int_{0}^{\infty}\Omega\left(t^\alpha\right)t^{d-1}\,dt < +\infty.
    \]
    Then, for every star body $L\subset \R^d$, it holds that
    \begin{equation}
    
    \vol[d](L) = \frac{1}{d} \frac{\int_{\R^d}\Omega\left(\|x\|_{L}^\alpha\right)\,dx}{\int_0^\infty \Omega\left(t^\alpha\right)t^{d-1}\,dt}.
    \end{equation}
title: Proposition 12 of arXiv:2609.01460

Let d>=1, L>=m>0 and R>0. Let U:R^d->R be C1, have an everywhere-existing Hessian and globally L-Lipschitz gradient, with grad U(0)=0. Put Omega=R^d minus B(0,R). Assume V(x)=U(x)-(m/2)||x||_2^2 is convex on Omega in this precise sense: V(sum_j a_j x_j)<=sum_j a_j V(x_j) whenever a_j>=0, sum_j a_j=1, all x_j belong to Omega and their barycenter also belongs to Omega. Put mu(dx) proportional to exp(-U(x))dx and kappa=L/m. For epsilon in (0,1), initialize X_0~N(0,I_d/L). Run the unadjusted Langevin algorithm X_{k+1}=X_k-h grad U(X_k)+sqrt(2h)G_k with independent G_k~N(0,I_d), choosing h=c exp(-16 L R^2) kappa^{-1} L^{-1} epsilon^2/d for a sufficiently small positive absolute constant c. Then the number of iterations needed for total-variation distance to mu at most epsilon is at most ceil(C exp(32 L R^2) kappa^2 (d/epsilon^2) log(d/epsilon^2)) for an absolute C. The bound is polynomial in d only when its displayed parameter dependence is also polynomial.

Tang, Chen and Liu, Beyond Quadratic Loss: The Stability Phase Diagram of Adam, arXiv2609.18314v1, Theorem3, treats L(x)=k|x|^n with k>0,n>2,1/2<beta1<1,0<beta2<1,v0>0,epsilon=0 and the imposed recurrence v_next=beta2*v. Conditional on attraction to either nonzero fixed point of the rescaled dynamics, the source concludes eventual absence of EoS-triggered spikes when beta1*beta2^(-n/(2*(n-2)))<1. Rescaling x_t=q^t*y_t with q=beta2^(1/(2*(n-2))) gives a second-order recurrence whose previous-position coefficient is beta1*beta2^(-n/(2*(n-2))). The imposed variance recurrence omits the ordinary squared-gradient addition. This theorem therefore does not cover n=2, positive epsilon, standard v0=0, or generic convergence to a quadratic unstable origin. Section3 Figure3(a) instead reports a numerical quadratic beta-boundary from finite trajectories, not a theorem about standard-initialization basin measure.

body: In probability theory, Markov's inequality gives an upper bound on the probability that a non-negative random variable is greater than or equal to some positive constant. Markov's inequality is tight in the sense that for each chosen positive constant, there exists a random variable such that the inequality is in fact an equality.
title: Markov's inequality

[Defn 9 (Likelihood ratio for i.i.d. prior) of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] For an $N \times N$ Wigner matrix $W = (W_{ij})$ and a prior $\caX$, we define the likelihood ratio $\ol \caL (\SNR)$ by
\beq 
	\ol \caL (\SNR) = \E_\caX \left[ \prod_{i<j} \frac{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_i x_j)}{p(\sqrt{N} W_{ij})} \prod_k \frac{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk} - \sqrt{\SNR N} x_k^2)}{p_d(\sqrt{N} W_{kk})} \right].
\eeq
title: Likelihood ratio for i.i.d. prior

Owner campaign draft, proof (unaudited); standard finite-population identities, independent audit and novelty assessment pending. Let P0=P on R^d have finite second moment, n>=1, h>=0, and r=0. Each generation draws n conditionally iid samples from Pt and forms their equal-weight Gaussian KDE with covariance h^2 I_d; bandwidth is constant within a trajectory. Let a=1-1/n, v0=tr Cov(P), mt=mean(Pt), and vt=E tr Cov(Pt), using the KDE's divisor-n covariance. For t>=1, vt=a^t v0+n d h^2(1-a^t), and E|mt-m0|^2=v0(1-a^t)+d h^2[t-n(1-a^t)]. Thus expected second moment about m0 is v0+t d h^2, although fixed-h within-generation variance approaches n d h^2. At h=0 the mean martingale converges in L2 to random M_infinity and E W2^2(Pt,delta_M_infinity)=2a^t v0. For n tending to infinity and t_n/n tending to infinity, centered expected variance tends to zero if and only if n h_n^2 tends to zero; h_n tending to zero alone is insufficient. If n h_n^2 tends to finite lambda, vt_n tends to d lambda. Covariance calculations do not determine the complete positive-bandwidth limit distribution or keep the random mean near m0 for all times. Proof: C003 v2, T356/proofs/review/c003_v2.md.

[Corollary Weak Simplex Conjecture of arXiv:2607.14087, 'Stochastic Domination of Gaussian Maxima: A Resolution of the Weak Simplex Conjecture'] \label[corollary]{cor:wsc}
Let $m=d+1$, let $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ be unit vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, and let the
message $I$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,m\}$.  Under the channel
\[
  Y=\lambda x_I+Z,
  \qquad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d),\quad \lambda>0,
\]
the average probability of correct maximum-likelihood decoding is no larger
than for a regular simplex.  For every fixed $\lambda>0$, equality holds if
and only if the $x_i$ form a regular simplex.  Thus the regular simplex is the
unique maximizer up to rotation and relabeling. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Weak Simplex Conjecture

Version 1, Target 1, kind bound; proofs (unaudited), 20 October 2026.

## C033: discrete-time semigroup subtraction

Let a=1/(3pi), b=1/(6pi^2), and A,B be the differential operators in C032.
One step of duration 1/n has P_n=I+A/n+B/n^2+O(n^(-5/2)) on positive
compacts. A diffusion step has exp(A/n)=I+A/n+A^2/(2n^2)+O(n^-3), for
sufficiently smooth local tests. Thus the local weak-error operator is

    C=B-A^2/2
     =(8u+a/5+b/u)D+(4u^2-3au/5)D^2.               (3)

This is an algebraic identity, not a global semigroup expansion at zero.
Direct differentiation gives

    A^2=(4u+2a)D+(14u^2+6au+a^2)D^2
                  +(8u^3+2au^2)D^3+u^4 D^4.

Subtracting half of this from C032's B proves (3); the third- and fourth-
derivative terms cancel exactly. Their inclusion before subtraction was
necessary. A global modified diffusion with this C is not asserted:
the drift b/u is singular and its second-order coefficient can be negative
near zero at finite n.

## C034: a rigorous logarithmic divergence of the limiting Duhamel functional

Use the reviewer-PASS C017 diffusion dU=(2U+a)ds+sqrt(2)U dW, U0=0,
and its semigroup P_s. Fix t>0 and f(u)=1-exp(-u). Define, for 0<epsilon<t,

    I_epsilon(t)=integral_epsilon^t E[(C P_(t-s)f)(U_s)] ds,
    D_t=(D P_t f)(0)=E[J_t exp(-U_t)],
    J_t=exp(t+sqrt(2)W_t).

Then 0<D_t<infinity, and there is a finite H_t such that

    I_epsilon(t)=(D_t/(2pi))log(1/epsilon)+H_t+O_t(sqrt(epsilon)). (4)

This statement concerns the specified cutoff integral for the limiting SDE.
It does not replace epsilon by 1/n inside a network weak-error theorem.

Proof of regularity. The solution from initial value u is U_v^u=U_v^0+uJ_v.
Consequently D^j P_v f(u)=E[J_v^j f^(j)(U_v^0+uJ_v)] for j>=1.
All these derivatives are bounded uniformly for 0<=v<=t, because Gaussian
exponentials J_v have every positive moment. Differentiation under expectation
is justified by these dominating moments. The time derivative of D P_v f
is bounded too: Af and (Af)' are bounded (polynomials times exp(-u)), and
the semigroup identity P_v f-f=integral_0^v P_r Af dr allows differentiation
in u. In particular, with h(s,u)=D P_(t-s) f(u),

    |h(s,u)-D_t|<=C_t(s+u), 0<=s<=t, u>=0.          (5)

The same bounded-derivative estimates apply to D^2 P_(t-s)f.

Proof of the entrance estimate. The explicit solution gives

    U_s=a integral_0^s exp((s-r)+sqrt(2)(W_s-W_r)) dr.

Let M_s=sup_(r<=s)|W_r| and H_s=s+2sqrt(2)M_s. Then
exp(-H_s)<=U_s/(as)<=exp(H_s). Brownian scaling and the Gaussian tail of
M_1 show, for each fixed t,

    E(1/U_s)<=C_t/s,
    E|1/U_s-1/(as)|<=C_t/sqrt(s), 0<s<=t.           (6)

For the second inequality use |1/(U_s/(as))-1|<=exp(H_s)-1 and
E(exp(H_s)-1)<=C_t sqrt(s). The moments of U_s of each fixed order are
O_t(s^j), by the same pathwise bound.

Equations (5)-(6) imply

    E[h(s,U_s)/U_s]=D_t/(as)+O_t(s^(-1/2))+O_t(1).

The nonsingular terms in C have bounded expectation near s=0, by the
derivative and U_s moment bounds. Therefore

    E[(C P_(t-s)f)(U_s)]= (b/a)D_t/s+O_t(s^(-1/2)). (7)

The difference between the integrand and (b/a)D_t/s is integrable at zero.
Integrating it proves (4), including its remainder. Finally b/a=1/(2pi).

## Consequence and the unpaid step

The natural candidate network leading correction for this bounded test is
(D_t/(2pi))log(n)/n, with a theta0-dependent constant/n at the next order.
This is a prediction, not proved network asymptotics. A proof still needs
uniform control while u approaches zero, a matching scale and remainder,
and the accumulated exact-to-regularized bounded-test comparison through
the entrance. A lower-cutoff contribution might alter or cancel a formal
coefficient unless controlled. C029's deterministic logarithmic offset is
compatible with this prediction but cannot supply that missing stochastic
matching theorem. [Lemma 4 (\citenum{mrAritheoremeticHyperbolic3Manifolds}, Lemma 5.3.10) of arXiv:2608.29855, 'Growth of Simple Closed Geodesics in closed Hyperbolic $3$-Manifolds'] Let $A\subset\hts$ be a geodesic whose stabilizer in the discrete torsion-free group $\Gamma$ contains a nontrivial loxodromic element. Then
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $\Stab_\Gamma(A)\cong\Z$, and every element of $\Stab_\Gamma(A)$ preserves the orientation of $A$ as a line.
\item If $g\in\Gamma^+$ is loxodromic, then $g$ is simple if and only if
$$
A_g\cap hA_g=\varnothing
$$
for every $h\in\Gamma\setminus\Stab_\Gamma(A_g)$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: \citenum{mrAritheoremeticHyperbolic3Manifolds}, Lemma 5.3.10

[Theorem 1 (Noiseless optimality of the full model) of arXiv:2609.02790, 'Full-Model Optimality for Tunable Linear Generative Priors in Compressed Sensing'] Fix an invertible matrix \(G_n\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) with singular value
decomposition
\[
    G_n=U\Sigma V^\top,
    \ \Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n),
    \
\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_n>0,
\]
where \(U,V\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) are orthogonal.
For each \(k\in[n]\), define the rank-\(k\) linear generative model
\[
    \mathcal G_k:=U_k\Sigma_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times k},
    \qquad
    \Sigma_k:=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_k),
\]
where \(U_k\) consists of the first \(k\) columns of \(U\).
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have i.i.d.\
\(\mathcal N(0,1)\) entries, where \(2\le m\le n\).
Let \(z^\star\sim\mathcal N(0,I_n)\) be independent of \(A\), and define
\[
    x^\star:=G_nz^\star,
    \qquad
    y:=Ax^\star .
\]
For each \(k\in[n]\), let \(\widehat x(k)\) be the reconstruction signal obtained
from the model \(\mathcal G_k\) according to the reconstruction rule
\eqref{eq0}, and let \(E(k)\) denote the expected reconstruction error
defined in \eqref{eq:recon err}.\footnote{The quantity \(E(k)\) is
interpreted as an extended-real-valued expectation. In particular,
\(E(m-1)=E(m)=+\infty\); see
Proposition~\ref{prop:boundary-divergence}.}
Then
\[
    E(n)\le E(k)
    \qquad\text{for every }k\in[n].
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Noiseless optimality of the full model

[Definition 38 of arXiv:2607.18104, '2607.18104'] Let $\UC$ denote the space of upper semi-continuous functions $f \colon \R \rightarrow \R \cup \{ -\infty\}$ such that for some $x\in \R$, $f(x)\neq -\infty$ and such that there exists some constants $m,C>0$ so that for all $x\in \R$
$f(x) \leq m |x| + C$. For any $\mathfrak{h}_0 \in \UC$ and $\mathcal{L}$ an independent (of $\mathfrak{h}_0$) full-space directed landscape, we define the \textbf{full-space KPZ fixed point} with initial data $\mathfrak{h}_0$ as the random function $(y,t) \mapsto \hfix(\mathfrak{h}_0;y,t)$, where
\begin{equation}
\hfix(\mathfrak{h}_0;y,t) := \sup_{x\in \R} \big(\mathfrak{h}_0(x) + \mathcal{L}(x,0;y,t)\big).
\end{equation} For multiple initial data this provides a coupling of full-space KPZ fixed points.
title: Definition 38 of arXiv:2607.18104

[Proposition Certificates: recovery and existence of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] (i) If \(\mathcal{A}\) is a degree-\(q\),
radius-\(r\) certificate, then
\(H_{T}\left( \mathcal{A} \right) \subseteq R_{q}(T,r)\); if
\(\mathcal{A}\) is full, then
\(H_{T}\left( \mathcal{A} \right) \subseteq R(T,r)\).

(ii) There exist constants \(C_{low},C_{up},\varepsilon_{0} > 0\)
such that for every \(0 < \varepsilon < \varepsilon_{0}\)
and every intrinsic \(\varepsilon\)-net
\(\{ x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}\}\) of \(M\) with
\(N = N_{\varepsilon}(M)\), the family

\[\mathcal{A}_{\varepsilon} = \{ B_{M}\left( x_{1},\varepsilon \right),\ldots,B_{M}\left( x_{N},\varepsilon \right)\}\]

is a full homological certificate at every radius \(r\)
with
\(C_{low}\,\varepsilon \leq r \leq C_{up}\, \operatorname{reach}(M)\). In
particular, full certificates of size \(N_{\varepsilon}(M)\)

body:
[Corollary 10 of arXiv:2605.13727, 'Stochastic evolution equations\\ driven by arbitrary cylindrical Lévy processes'] Let $(\Psi_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of $L$-integrable, predictable processes 
	converging to an $L_2(U,H)$-valued predictable process $\Psi$  $P_T$-a.e. If we have
    \[\esssup_{\omega\in\Omega}\sup_{s\in (0,T]}\sup_{n\in\N} \norm{\Psi_n(\omega,s)}<\infty,\]
    then $\Psi$ is $L$-integrable  and satisfies
	\[\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty} d_T^{em}(I(\Psi_n),I(\Psi))=0.\]

body: [Theorem 2.2 of arXiv:1908.07093, 'Uniform Reliability of Self-Join-Free Conjunctive Queries'] [DS07]. Let Q be a CQ without self-joins. If Q is hierarchical, then PQE(Q) is solvable in polynomial time. Otherwise, PQE(Q) is #P-hard. Recall that #P is the complexity class of problems that count witnesses of an NP-relation (e.g., satisfying assignments of a logical formula, vertex covers of a graph, etc.).
title: Theorem 2.2 of arXiv:1908.07093: Uniform Reliability of Self-Join-Free Conjunctive Queries
