{"artifact_digest":"sha256:d86de94316bdcb0f9c2774df16ccd6ecb01559c5bd9b186023902dc90f306cc4","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/d8/d86de94316bdcb0f9c2774df16ccd6ecb01559c5bd9b186023902dc90f306cc4.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:21d94ddd43c6a5932560be19f51c54887d3448247219d922219e6b170542073f","bundle_entry_key":"stein-companion-log-regularity","bundle_id":"population.w722-t311-logarithmic-regularity-002","claim_kind":"lemma","conditions":[],"domain":"analysis","draft":"w722/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:analysis.stein:w722-t311-stein-companion-logarithmic-hermite-regularity","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# Target 2: logarithmic regularity and companion semigroup decay

Status: proof (unaudited), conditional on the operator comparisons explicitly stated below. This is an application of classical resolvent and fractional-power order methods; novelty is not claimed. It concerns the symmetric companion, not a nonlinear SVGD law or a density-profile decay theorem.

## Statement

Let (psi_j)_(j>=0) be an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space. Fix q>=1 and 0<B<1. Put

    Q psi_j=(j+1)psi_j,
    R psi_j=d_j psi_j,       d_j=(j+1)(1-B)B^j.

Let S be a bounded positive self-adjoint operator satisfying, as bounded forms,

    q^(-1) R <= S <= q R.                                      (A)

Let H be positive self-adjoint and suppose, as closed quadratic forms,

    q^(-1) Q <= H <= q Q.                                      (B)

In the Gaussian/RBF application these are exactly the S, R, Q and H of proofs/spectral_order.md. Here H is the ordinary Gaussian number operator plus identity, transported to flat space, whereas Q is the squeezed oscillator plus identity.

Set kappa=e*q/(1-B), and define the positive self-adjoint operator L=log(kappa/S) by spectral calculus. Then, for 0<r<=1/2,

    Dom(L^r)=Dom(Q^r)=Dom(H^r),                                (C)

with equivalent norms. Moreover, there are positive constants a_r,b_r depending only on q,B,r such that for every t>=1,

    a_r [log(1+t)]^(-2r)
      <= sup_{u in Dom(H^r), ||H^r u||<=1} ||exp(-tS)u||^2
      <= b_r [log(1+t)]^(-2r).                                (D)

The supremum allows u to depend on t. The lower bound is not a decay assertion for one fixed initial law.

## 1. Logarithms of the compact sandwich

The scalar sequence d_j is positive and summable, with sum_j d_j=1/(1-B). Thus R is injective, trace class and bounded by I/(1-B). Assumption (A) makes S injective: <u,Su>=0 forces sum_j d_j |<u,psi_j>|^2=0, hence u=0. Also ||S||<=q/(1-B), so L>=I by the choice of kappa. Compactness is not needed for the logarithm argument, but follows from (A), for example by summing diagonal forms to bound the trace of S.

We first justify the logarithm comparison, including its domains. For bounded positive operators X,Y that are bounded below by a positive scalar, X<=Y implies (X+tI)^(-1)>=(Y+tI)^(-1). To see inverse order, conjugate X<=Y by Y^(-1/2), invert the resulting positive operator bounded by I, and conjugate back. Apply the same argument to X+tI and Y+tI.

The scalar identity

    log x = integral_0^infinity [1/(1+t)-1/(x+t)] dt

holds for x>0 by integration of the two fractions. On a compact positive spectral interval the truncated integrals converge in operator norm to log X. The inverse order above therefore proves log X<=log Y in the bounded, bounded-below case. Scalar multiplication commutes with spectral calculus: log(aX)=log(a)I+log X for a>0.

For epsilon>0, (A) implies

    q^(-1)(R+q epsilon I) <= S+epsilon I
                            <= q(R+epsilon I/q).

The bounded logarithm comparison consequently gives

    log(kappa/(R+epsilon I/q))-log q I
      <= log(kappa/(S+epsilon I))
      <= log(kappa/(R+q epsilon I))+log q I.                    (1)

Let epsilon decrease to zero. For each of the three spectral calculi, the scalar logarithms increase to log(kappa/x). For 0<epsilon<=1 these functions have a common finite lower bound; subtracting that bound makes the functions nonnegative. Monotone convergence of their spectral integrals applies to every vector and permits the value +infinity. Thus the central limit is finite exactly when the diagonal logarithm form is finite. In particular

    Dom(L^(1/2))=Dom(log(kappa/R)^(1/2)),
    log(kappa/R)-log q I <= L <= log(kappa/R)+log q I           (2)

as closed forms on that common domain. This limiting argument does not assume that the logarithms commute.

## 2. Comparison with the number operator and its fractional powers

Write b=-log B>0 and

    ell_j=log(kappa/d_j)
         =b*j-log(j+1)+log(kappa/(1-B)).

Since d_j<=sum_k d_k=1/(1-B), ell_j-log q>=1. Also both sequences

    (ell_j-log q)/(j+1),       (ell_j+log q)/(j+1)

converge to b. Therefore the constants

    c=inf_{j>=0} (ell_j-log q)/(j+1)>0,
    C=sup_{j>=0} (ell_j+log q)/(j+1)<infinity                 (3)

are well defined. Positivity of c follows by separating a tail where the ratio is at least b/2 from the remaining finite collection of positive terms. Equations (2)-(3) give

    c Q <= L <= C Q                                          (4)

as closed forms, with common form domain Dom(Q^(1/2)). By (B), also

    (c/q) H <= L <= Cq H.                                    (5)

For completeness, the fractional-power order step used next can be derived by resolvents. If positive self-adjoint E<=F in form order, the variational identity

    <u,(E+tI)^(-1)u>
      =sup_v [2 Re<u,v>-||E^(1/2)v||^2-t||v||^2],

where v runs through Dom(E^(1/2)), gives (E+tI)^(-1)>=(F+tI)^(-1). The inclusion of form domains in the definition of E<=F gives the correct direction of the two suprema. Hence

    E(E+tI)^(-1)<=F(F+tI)^(-1).

For 0<theta<1 the scalar formula

    x^theta=(sin(pi theta)/pi)
              integral_0^infinity t^(theta-1) x/(x+t) dt

follows by substituting t=xs in the convergent beta integral. Spectral calculus and Tonelli's theorem express the corresponding quadratic forms as integrals of the positive resolvents above. Therefore E^theta<=F^theta in form order, including the relevant domain inclusions. The endpoint theta=1 is the original form order.

Apply this fact to both sides of (5) with theta=2r in (0,1]. The result is

    (c/q)^(2r)||H^r u||^2 <= ||L^r u||^2
                              <= (Cq)^(2r)||H^r u||^2,        (6)

with equality of the domains of these norms. Applying the same argument to (4), or to (B), proves the remaining equality with Dom(Q^r) in (C). No assertion for r>1/2 follows from this power-order argument.

## 3. Upper semigroup bound

For t>=1 put T=log(kappa*t). Since kappa>=e, T>=1. A spectral value lambda of S corresponds to m=log(kappa/lambda)>=1, and

    exp(-2t lambda)=exp(-2 kappa*t*exp(-m)).

For m>=T/2, the product exp(-2 kappa*t*exp(-m))*m^(-2r) is at most (2/T)^(2r). For 1<=m<T/2 it is at most exp(-2 exp(T/2)). The elementary inequality exp(T/2)>=T for T>=1 and exp(2x)>=2x give

    exp(-2 exp(T/2)) <= 1/(2T) <= (1/2)T^(-2r),

where the last step uses 2r<=1 and T>=1. Thus

    sup_{m>=1} exp(-2 kappa*t*exp(-m))*m^(-2r)
      <= 2^(2r) [log(kappa*t)]^(-2r).

Spectral calculus and (6) now yield

    ||exp(-tS)u||^2
      <= (2Cq)^(2r)[log(kappa*t)]^(-2r)||H^r u||^2.

For t>=1, kappa*t>=1+t, so this proves the upper bound in (D) with b_r=(2Cq)^(2r).

## 4. Matching lower bound on the Sobolev ball

For t>=1 choose n=ceil((2/b)log(1+t)). Then B^n<=(1+t)^(-2), and

    t*q*d_n <= q(1-B)(n+1)/(1+t)
              <= q(1-B)(2/b+2)=K.                            (7)

Here ceil(x)<=x+1 and log(1+t)/(1+t)<=1 were used. Also

    n+1 <= M log(1+t),       M=2/b+2/log 2.                   (8)

From (B) and fractional-power order, ||H^r psi_n||<=q^r(n+1)^r. Hence

    u_t=q^(-r)(n+1)^(-r)psi_n

belongs to the H^r unit ball. The spectral measure of S at the unit vector psi_n is a probability measure. Convexity of x -> exp(-2tx), Jensen's inequality, and (A) give

    <psi_n,exp(-2tS)psi_n>
      >= exp(-2t<psi_n,S psi_n>) >= exp(-2tq d_n).

Combining with (7)-(8),

    ||exp(-tS)u_t||^2
      >= q^(-2r) M^(-2r) exp(-2K) [log(1+t)]^(-2r).

This proves (D), with the displayed positive constant as a_r.

## 5. Exact remaining transfer gap

In the Gaussian application H=DD* has ordinary normalized Hermite eigenfunctions and eigenvalues j+1. Thus the class in (D) is an ordinary Hermite Sobolev class for the companion initial variable u. If those coefficients are bounded by a constant times (j+1)^(-s), then u belongs to Dom(H^r) whenever r<s-1/2. This is just convergence of sum_j (j+1)^(2r-2s), not identification of Stein eigenvectors with Hermite functions.

The density generator is A=CC*, where C=D*T^(1/2), whereas S=C*C. Let V be the polar unitary from the companion Hilbert space to the mean-zero density space, so A=VSV*. Transporting (D) to a density perturbation f requires control of ||H^r V*f|| by the ordinary density norm ||H^r f||. The boundedness of H^r V*H^(-r) on the appropriate mean-zero space is NOT established by this proof. Equality of spectra and unitarity in L2 alone do not supply it.

This leaves a precise linear transfer question, and leaves all nonlinear regularity propagation questions open. No statement here identifies a fixed positive initial probability law achieving the Sobolev-ball lower bound.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:559b2d4a17cda971141e8b93f8b6fa97539dc237743f2691a7ac21016844fd7f","revision_digest":"sha256:8ba5546065d6a545db7e2706544d5288f35652cb1836c9935703dcfd3f7bd11b","source_id":"owner-own-work:w722:T311:w722-log-regularity-bridge-v2","source_revision":"w722-log-regularity-bridge-v2","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Corollary 4 of arXiv:2506.09592, 'Extremal process of the local time of simple\\random walk on a regular tree'] Given~$n\ge1$ and a sample~$\ell_{\tau_\varrho}$ on~$\T_n$ under~$P^\zero$, let~$Y_n$ denote the a.s.-unique maximizer of~$x\mapsto\ell_{\tau_\varrho}(x)$ on~$\BbbL_n$. Then~$\theta_n(Y_n)$ converges in law to a random variable~$U$ on~$[0,1]$ described as follows: Given a sample~$\{Z_{T_k}\}_{k\ge1}$ of the measures in Corollary~\ref{cor-1.3}, let~$K$ be the smallest~$k\ge1$ maximizing
\begin{equation}

k\mapsto \log Z_{T_k}\bigl([b^{-1},1]\bigr)-2k\log b+G_k
\end{equation}
where~$\log0:=-\infty$ and $\{G_k\}_{k\ge1}$ are i.i.d.\ standard Gumbel 
independent of $\{Z_{T_k}\colon k\ge1\}$.
Then $K<\infty$ a.s.\ and $U$ is uniform on~$[b^{-k-1},b^{-k})$ conditional on~$\{K=k\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

For independent Bernoulli trials with probabilities p_1,...,p_M followed by fair trials, let F_m count failures before the m-th success. For m>=M and m>=1, s=sum p_i, t=sum p_i(1-p_i), and delta=sum(2p_i-1), E F_m=m-delta and Var F_m=2(m-s)+4t. This is a quenched single-stack identity; it assumes no independence between stacks. It does not settle the stationary-ergodic excited-walk recurrence criterion.
All hypotheses and scope restrictions in the statement apply.

Status: proof written; w346 KEEP pending. The stationary-ergodic recurrence criterion remains unresolved by this round. The cached 2012 review poses Problem 3.11. The prior attempt alternates between a log-mean argument and an averaged-drift claim; neither is a proof of the general criterion.

Fix a cookie stack of length M, with independent Bernoulli success probabilities p_1,...,p_M in its first M trials and probability 1/2 thereafter. Let F_m count failures before the m-th success. For every integer m>=M with m>=1, set s=sum p_i, t=sum p_i(1-p_i), and delta=sum(2*p_i-1). Then

    E[F_m]=m-delta,
    Var(F_m)=2(m-s)+4t.

Proof: sample all M prefix trials and let S be their number of successes. When m>=M, the stopping time processes the whole prefix, except that it may finish precisely at its end when m=M=S; that exception has zero tail and satisfies the same representation. Conditional on S,

    F_m = M-S + NB(m-S,1/2),

where NB(k,1/2) counts failures before k fair-coin successes, with mean k and variance 2k (and NB(0)=0). Conditional expectation is m+M-2S, whose variance is 4t. The total-variance identity gives the formulas. They hold quenched, without any independence between stacks at different sites.

The associated map F_{k+1} has conditional expectation k+1-delta for k+1>=M. Its large-population linear coefficient is exactly 1 at every site. Therefore a nontrivial product of site-dependent offspring means is not supplied by this identity; a standard subcritical/supercritical BPRE log-mean test cannot be used to settle the cookie criterion merely by calling this a BPRE. Additive migration and low-population behavior still matter. This refutes that proposed mechanism, not the possible averaged-drift criterion or every BPRE method.

Boundary check: with M=2 and p_1=p_2=3/4, m=1 is outside the hypothesis. Its actual mean is (1/4)*(3/4*1+1/4*3)=3/8, whereas m-delta=0. The cutoff must stay on the card. No periodic-environment recurrence/transience claim is certified here.

Checks: enumerate prefix outcomes exactly using rational probabilities, check means and variances, and verify the m<M counterexample. These are checks of the local moment lemma, not of the full walk criterion.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:ef2146ca3f9350a01d1a1b2ce5a7c9fed3b949a2d235b788a148af63373ea6fe","revision_digest":"sha256:8baea3c12c7d597713ebf5afcbb72a53222fb3c52cb4181df4aa5fc8fad7c860","source_id":"owner:campaign:w336:C0129:finite-cookie-prefix-failure-mean-and-variance","source_revision":"author-proof-2026-10-10; independent audit w346 pending","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Prop lem:triangular of arXiv:2606.08325, 'Digit Mixing under Polynomial Maps'] Fix an integer \(q\ge1\) and a real number \(0<\rho<1/2\). There exist constants $c=c(q,\rho)>0$ and $C=C(q,\rho)<\infty$ with the following property.
			Let \(A(k_1,\ldots,k_q)\), \(1\le k_1,\ldots,k_q\le L\), be real coefficients satisfying
			\begin{align}
				&\left\|A(k,k,\ldots,k)\right\|\ge\rho \qquad(1\le k\le L) , \\
				\text{and} \quad &A(k_1,\ldots,k_q)=0
				\quad\text{if}\quad (k_1,\ldots,k_{q-1})\succ(k_q,\ldots,k_q).
				
			\end{align}
				Let \(U_{j,k}\) be as in Lemma~(lem:GCS of the paper). Then
			\begin{equation}
				\left|\mathbb E e\!\left(\sum_{k_1,\ldots,k_q=1}^{L} A(k_1,\ldots,k_q) \prod_{j=1}^{q}U_{j,k_j}\right)\right|
				\leq C e^{-cL}.
			\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Prop lem:triangular of arXiv:2606.08325

[Theorem Offset reconstruction of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] There exist
constants \(\varepsilon_{rec} > 0\), \(C_{low} > 0\),
\(C_{up} > 0\), depending only on the positive-reach
reconstruction constants of \(M\), such that the following holds.
Let \(S \subset M\) be compact with
\(d_{H}(S,M) \leq \varepsilon\) and
\(0 < \varepsilon < \varepsilon_{rec}\). Then, for every
reconstruction radius \(r\) with

\[C_{low}\,\varepsilon \leq r \leq C_{up}\, \operatorname{reach}(M),\]

the offset \(S^{r}\) is homotopy equivalent to
\(M\); in particular \(H_{q}\left( S^{r} \right) \cong H_{q}(M)\)

Let (X, d) be a complete metric space and let U_1, U_2, U_3, ... be countably many dense open subsets of X. Then their intersection is dense in X; in particular, if X is nonempty the intersection is nonempty. Equivalent formulation: a nonempty complete metric space is not the union of countably many nowhere dense sets (sets whose closures have empty interior); such spaces are Baire spaces.

TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). On a product probability space (Omega_1 x ... x Omega_n, mu), define the convex distance d_T(x,A) = sup_{alpha>=0, |alpha|=1} inf_{y in A} sum_i alpha_i 1_{x_i != y_i}, a weighted Hamming-type distance from x to a set A, maximized over convex combinations of nonnegative unit-norm weight vectors. Talagrand's inequality states integral exp(d_T(x,A)^2/4) dmu(x) <= 1/mu(A), which implies mu(A) mu({x : d_T(x,A) >= t}) <= exp(-t^2/4), a strong concentration of any set A around itself in convex distance. Applied to a function f that is certifiable, meaning any difference f(x) - f(y) can be witnessed by a bounded number of coordinates with bounded weight, this yields subgaussian concentration of f around its median without requiring f to be linear or even close to it, making the method far more flexible than Azuma-Hoeffding for combinatorial optimization functionals such as the longest increasing subsequence, bin-packing cost, or chromatic number. It does not directly give concentration around the mean, only the median, so a separate median-to-mean gap argument is needed, and it requires exhibiting an explicit certificate structure for f, which can be technically demanding to construct. Typical failure: Applying Talagrand concentration by treating f as ordinary Hamming-Lipschitz (uniform weight 1 per coordinate change) when the natural certificate for f actually requires nonuniform or superlinear weighting, since changing one coordinate can move f by an amount depending on many other coordinates; using the wrong or absent certificate yields either the wrong concentration scale or, more commonly, no valid proof at all, since the convex-distance formulation is easy to state and easy to misapply. Canonical reference: Talagrand, 1995, Publications Mathematiques de l'IHES; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM.

the function or event of interest admits a certifiable Lipschitz-type structure with bounded, possibly nonuniform, weights

    \leq 
    R_{G}(x,y) 
    \leq 
    R_{\tilde{G}}(\pi(x), \pi(y)) + \mu_{G}(a, b)^{-1}.
  \end{equation}

body:
[Lemma lem:distribution of cumulative arrivals of arXiv:2412.06452, 'Time-dependent queue length distribution in queues fed by $K$ customers in a finite interv'] For $(t,k) \in (0,T) \times \{0,1,\ldots,K\} \cup [T,\infty) \times \{K\}$,
$m \in \{1, 2, \ldots\}$, 
$t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_m \in [0, t]$, and 
$k_1, k_2, \ldots$, $k_m \in \{0, 1, \ldots, k\}$, 

\begin{align}
\lefteqn{
\Pr\bigl[A(t_1) = k_1, A(t_2) = k_2, \ldots, A(t_m) = k_m \mid A(t) = k\bigr]
}\qquad
\notag 
\\
&= 
\Pr\bigl[
\widehat{A}(t_1) = k_1, \widehat{A}(t_2) = k_2, \ldots, \widehat{A}(t_m) = k_m 
\mid \widehat{A}(t) = k
\bigr].

\end{align}

In particular, for $t \geq T$

\begin{align}
\lefteqn{
\Pr\bigl[A(t_1) = k_1, A(t_2) = k_2, \ldots, A(t_m) = k_m\bigr]
}\qquad
\nonumber
\\
&
=
\Pr\bigl[\widehat{A}(t_1) = k_1, 
\widehat{A}(t_2) = k_2, \ldots, \widehat{A}(t_m) = k_m 
\mid \widehat{A}(t) = K\bigr]
\nonumber
\\
&=
\Pr\bigl[\widehat{A}(t_1) = k_1, 
\widehat{A}(t_2) = k_2, \ldots, \widehat{A}(t_m) = k_m 
\mid \widehat{A}(T) = K\bigr].

\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Lemma lem:distribution of cumulative arrivals of arXiv:2412.06452

[Lemma 46 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] Let \(F\subset\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\) be nonempty and finite, let \(C_F\) be the
covariance matrix of \(B_F\), and put \(\mathsf P_F=C_F^{-1}\).  Then
\begin{equation}
  (\mathsf P_F)_{s,t}\leq0\quad(s\neq t),
  \qquad
  \mathsf P_F\mathbf1_F\geq0
  \quad\text{coordinatewise}.
  
\end{equation}
For every nonempty \(I\subseteq F\), the conditional precision
\((\mathsf P_F)_{II}\) and the marginal precision \(C_{II}^{-1}\) have the
same two properties.  If \(J:=F\setminus I\) is nonempty, the latter is the
Schur complement of \((\mathsf P_F)_{JJ}\) in \(\mathsf P_F\).

[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.29984, 'On Cauchy Problems for Parabolic Equations with Rough Coefficients'] For any $ 0<s<\frac{1}{2}$, there exists a universal constant $\delta_{0}$ only depends on $c_{0}$ and $s$, such that: under the assumptions (H1), (H2), $(H3)_{\delta_{0},s}$, for any continuous initial data $u_{0}(x)$ with $u_{0}(x)\in \dot{H}^{1}(\R)\cap \dot{H}^{1+s}(\R)$ and force term $f(t,x)\in L^{2}([0,T];H^{s}(\R))$, the non-divergence form equation \eqref{heateqnondiv} exists a unique strong solution $u(t,x)$, which satisfies
\begin{equation}
\sup_{0\leq t \leq T}\|\partial_{x}u(x,t)\|_{H^{s}_{x}}^{2}+\int_{0}^{T}\|\partial_{x}^{2}u\|_{H^{s}_{x}}^{2}dt\lesssim \|u_{0}(x)\|_{\dot{H}^{1}\cap \dot{H}^{1+s}(\R)}^{2}+\|f(t,x)\|_{L^{2}([0,T];H^{s}(\R))}^{2}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[Proposition prop:equiv of arXiv:2511.01851, 'Percolation on graphs of polynomial growth is local:\\analyticity, supercritical sharpness'] The following statements are equivalent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item every graph in $\mathfrak{A}$ satisfies $\theta(p_c)=0$,
        \item for every $\mathscr{G}\in \mathfrak{A}$, the map $p\longmapsto \theta_\mathscr{G}(p)$ is continuous from $[0,1]$ to $[0,1]$,

        \item the map $(\mathscr{G},p)\longmapsto \theta_\mathscr{G}(p)$ is continuous from $\mathfrak{A}\times [0,1]$ to $[0,1]$,
        \item the map $\mathscr{G}\longmapsto \theta_\mathscr{G}$ is continuous from $\mathfrak{A}$ to $\mathcal{L}^\infty([0,1],\mathbb{R})$,
        \item the map $\mathscr{G}\longmapsto \theta_\mathscr{G}$ is well defined and continuous from $\mathfrak{A}$ to $\mathcal{C}([0,1],\mathbb{R})$ endowed with the uniform topology.~\hfill\hyperlink{target:equiv}{\footnotesize\color{mycolor}$\downarrow$ context and proof}

[Prop linrel of arXiv:2412.09535, 'Local limit theorem for joint subgraph counts'] Let $\mu_H$ and $\nu_H$ denote any two of
\[X_H,\quad X_H^*,\quad (p(1-p))^{e(H)/2}\gamma_H,\quad\text{or } (p(1-p))^{e(H)/2}\gamma^*_H.\]
Then, for any $H$, one can write $\nu_H$ as a linear combination $\sum_{H'\preceq H} a_{H'} \mu_{H'}$, where $a_{H} \asymp_H 1$, $a_{H'} \lsim_H 1$ for all $H' \preceq H$, and $a_H =1$ if $H$ is connected. (Note that these bounds are independent of $p$.)

[Proposition prop:jensen of arXiv:2608.16915, 'Exact mean--covariance dynamics of the Weber field in the stochastic Lagrangian representa'] For every $N\in\mathbb N$ there is a two-valued random smooth volume-preserving
diffeomorphism $A$ of $\mathbb{T}^3$, isotopic to the identity, with
\[
  \norm{\mathbb{E}\nabla A}_{C^\alpha}=1,\qquad
  \mathbb{E}\left\lVert \nabla A\right\rVert_{C^\alpha}\ge c_\alpha N .
\]
Moreover, volume preservation places no lower bound on the smallest singular value of a
mean: the four rotations
$R_0=\mathrm{diag}(1,1,1)$, $R_1=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1)$, $R_2=\mathrm{diag}(-1,1,-1)$,
$R_3=\mathrm{diag}(-1,-1,1)$ all lie in $SO(3)$, yet $\tfrac14\sum_jR_j=0$.

body:
Let f be an orientation-preserving C^1 diffeomorphism of the circle with irrational rotation number alpha, and suppose log f' has BOUNDED VARIATION (in particular this holds if f is C^2). Then f is topologically conjugate to the rigid rotation R_alpha; in particular f is minimal and has no wandering intervals. The engine is Denjoy's inequality: for every n the distortion is controlled, exp(-V) <= (f^n)'(x) / (f^n)'(y) <= exp(V) where V is the total variation of log f', valid whenever the intermediate iterates of the interval between x and y are disjoint - which the combinatorics of closest returns to an irrational rotation number supplies. Regularity is sharp: Denjoy also constructed C^1 examples with irrational rotation number and a wandering interval, so the bounded-variation hypothesis cannot be dropped.
Orientation-preserving, irrational rotation number, and log f' of bounded variation (C^2 suffices, C^1 does not).
The conjugacy produced is a homeomorphism;
its smoothness requires Diophantine conditions on alpha and much more regularity (Herman-Yoccoz theory).

body:
Let (F_n) be a sequence of distribution functions on R, that is nondecreasing right-continuous functions with values in [0,1]. Then there exist a subsequence (F_{n_k}) and a nondecreasing right-continuous F : R -> [0,1] such that F_{n_k}(x) -> F(x) at every continuity point x of F. The limit F need NOT be a distribution function: mass can escape to plus or minus infinity, and with F_n the distribution function of the point mass at n one gets F identically 0. This is exactly the gap that tightness closes: when every F_n is a proper distribution function (F_n(x) -> 0 as x -> -infinity and F_n(x) -> 1 as x -> +infinity), the family is tight, meaning sup_n (1 - F_n(M) + F_n(-M)) -> 0 as M -> infinity, if and only if every such subsequential limit is a proper distribution function, which is Prokhorov's theorem on R (without properness the 'if' fails: a single improper F_1 makes the family non-tight while every subsequential limit can be proper). For the selection itself nothing is assumed about the F_n beyond monotonicity, right-continuity and the range [0,1] - no continuity, no tightness, no common support. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.2.6]
each F_n nondecreasing, right-continuous, with values in [0,1]
no tightness is assumed, and without it the limit can be defective

[Theorem thm:twistbc of arXiv:2604.15146, 'Renormalised two-point functions of CLE$_4$ gaskets'] The twist field two-point correlation 
$\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D,v}(z_{1}, z_{2})$ for constant boundary condition $v \in \mathbb{R}$ can be defined in the following equivalent ways.
\begin{enumerate}[i)]

\item
As $\max(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)\to 0$, we consider the limit of
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\pi/2}{(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{1/8}\sqrt{|\log \varepsilon_1|\,|\log \varepsilon_2|}} 
\exp\Bigg[
-\mu^{\rm loop}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}
\bigl(\indx_\gamma(z_1)+\indx_\gamma(z_2)\text{ odd}\bigr) \\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad
-v^2\mu^{\rm exc}_{D}
\Bigl(
\indx_\gamma(z_1)+\indx_\gamma(z_2)\text{ odd },\,
\gamma\subset D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)
\Bigr)
\Bigg].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
\item
Consider
$\mathcal{L}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}$
the Brownian loop soup in
$D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)$
with intensity
$\frac{1}{2}\mu^{\rm loop}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}$.
For $v\geq 0$, denote by
$\Xi^{v^2/2}_{D, D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}$
the Poisson point process of boundary excursions in
$D$ with intensity
\[
\dfrac{v^2}{2}\,
\1_{\{\gamma\subset D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)\}}
\mu^{\rm exc}_{D}(d\gamma).
\]
As $\max(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)\to 0$, we consider the limit of
\begin{equation}
\frac{\pi/2}{(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2)^{1/8}\sqrt{|\log \varepsilon_1|\,|\log \varepsilon_2|}}
\mathbb{P}\Big(
\text{No cluster of }
\mathcal{L}_{D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}
\cup
\Xi^{v^2/2}_{D, D_{\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2}(z_1,z_2)}
\text{ disconnects } z_1 \text{ from } z_2
\Big).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
\noindent Moreover, for all $v\in\mathbb{R}$, its value is equal to
\begin{equation}
\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D,v}(z_1,z_2)
=
\sigma_{\rm tw}^{D}(z_1,z_2)
\exp\bigl(-v^2 \mathcal{M}_D(z_1,z_2)\bigr),
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{M}_D(z_1,z_2) = \mu^{\rm exc}_{D}
\bigl(\indx_\gamma(z_1)+\indx_\gamma(z_2)\text{ odd}\bigr)$.
Further, $\exp(-\frac{\pi}{4}\mathcal{M}_D(z_1,z_2)) = \hat q$,

where $\hat q$ is the complementary nome to nome $q$ (i.e. $\log q \log \hat q = \pi^2$), that in turn is by Lemma (lem:parametr of the paper) uniquely defined via 
$$\exp\Big(\pi G_D(z_1,z_2)\Big) 
= \dfrac{\theta_3(q^{1/2})}{\theta_2(q^{1/2})}.$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)
title: Two-point correlation of twist field with boundary data

[Lemma 18 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Let $(\vertexset,w)$ be a weighted graph, and let $\graph = (\vertexset,\edgeset)$ be the subgraph induced by the edges with positive conductances. Let $x,y,z_1,\ldots,z_N \in \vertexset$ such that $\{z_1,\ldots,z_N\}$ separates $x$ from $y$ in $\graph$. Let $K_x$ be the subgraph induced by removing the vertices that are strictly separated from $x$ by $\{z_1,\ldots,z_N\}$. Let H and K be Hilbert spaces (not necessarily separable) and let T: H -> K be compact. Then there exist finite-rank bounded operators T_N with ||T - T_N|| -> 0. Explicitly, if T = sum_n s_n <., e_n> f_n is a Schmidt decomposition, the truncations T_N = sum_{n <= N} s_n <., e_n> f_n satisfy ||T - T_N|| = s_{N+1}(T) -> 0. Combining with the closedness of K(H,K) in operator norm: a bounded operator between Hilbert spaces is compact if and only if it is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank operators. (This equivalence uses the Hilbert structure; in a general Banach space it can fail, see the approximation-property pitfall.)

[Defn def:local-weak of arXiv:2510.18856, 'Evolution of recursive trees with limited memory'] Fix a probability measure $\varpi$ on $\mathbb{T}$.
	\begin{enumeratea}
 \item  Say that a sequence of trees $\left\{\mathcal{T}_n\right\}_{n\geqslant 1}$ converges in {\bf expectation}, in the fringe sense, to $\varpi$, if \[\E[\mathfrak{P}_n^{0}] \to \varpi, \quad \text{ as } n\to\infty. \]
 Denote this convergence by $\mathcal{T}_n\stackrel{\mbox{$\E$-\bf fr}}{\longrightarrow} \varpi$ as $n\to\infty$.
	    \item   Say that a sequence of trees $\left\{\mathcal{T}_n\right\}_{n\geqslant 1}$ converges in the probability sense, in the fringe sense, to $\varpi$, if \[\mathfrak{P}_n^{0} \stackrel{\mathrm{P}}{\longrightarrow} \varpi, \quad \text{ as } n\to\infty. \]
	Denote this convergence by $\mathcal{T}_n\stackrel{\mbox{$\operatorname{P}$-\bf fr}}{\longrightarrow} \varpi$ as $n\to\infty$.
	    \item  Say that a sequence of trees $\left\{\mathcal{T}_n\right\}_{n\geqslant 1}$ converges in probability, in the {\bf extended fringe sense}, to a limiting infinite random {\tt sin}-tree $\mathcal{T}_{\infty}$ if for all $k\geqslant 0$ one has
	  \[\mathfrak{P}_n^k \stackrel{\mathrm{P}}{\longrightarrow} \mathbb{P}\left(F_k(0,\mathcal{T}_{\infty}) \in \cdot \right), \qquad \text{ as } n\to\infty. \]
	Denote this convergence by $\mathcal{T}_n\stackrel{\mbox{$\operatorname{P}$-\bf efr}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{T}_{\infty}$ as $n\to\infty$.
	\end{enumeratea}

ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Source-specific calculation, conditional implication or exact obstruction Result: The grand partition function contains its exactly neutral canonical summand, giving one free-energy inequality immediately. Concentration of the particle number around neutrality does not give the opposite inequality. For example, a law supported equally at N-floor(sqrt(N)) and N+floor(sqrt(N)) has particle number divided by N tending to1 but assigns probability zero to exactly N. Check: The relative deviation is at most1/sqrt(N); nevertheless its central mass is identically zero. Thus a law-of-large-numbers neutrality argument supplies no logarithmic lower bound on the exact neutral sector. Obstruction: A proof needs uniform energy and entropy control when inserting or removing the subextensive excess charge, or a local partition-function comparison. Long-range background energy makes that repair nonlocal. No reverse free-energy inequality is proved here.

[Theorem 9 (Random environment: simple sufficient conditions) of arXiv:2605.04048, 'Catastrophe--dispersion models in random and varying environments across generations'] Consider the Poissonian growth with binomial survival of Example~\ref{ex:poisson-binomial}.  Let $(\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stationary ergodic random environment whose marginal distribution is that of the random vector $\mathcal E=(\theta,\lambda,p,d)$ with $\theta>\lambda$\ a.s.\ and $d\in\mathbb N$, $d\ge2$.  Assume
\[
\E[|\log p|]<\infty,\qquad
\E[|\log(1+\lambda/\theta)|]<\infty,
\]
and that $\E\bigl[\bigl|\log\bigl(\p(\xi_{1,0}>0\mid\mathcal E_0)\bigr)\bigr|\bigr]<+\infty$ (which is automatically satisfied for this model under the previous hypotheses).  Then, for every dispersion mechanism $\Delta^{(j)}$, $j=1,2,3,4$:
\begin{itemize}
  \item if
  $\displaystyle \E[\log p] < \E\!\left[\log\frac{\theta}{\theta+\lambda}\right]$,
  the process becomes extinct almost surely;
  \item if almost surely
  \[
  p > \frac1d \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{\lambda}{\theta} > \frac1{(d-1)p},
  \]
  the process survives with positive probability.
\end{itemize}

Let sum_n a_n be a series of REAL numbers that converges but not absolutely (a conditionally convergent series). Then for every alpha in the extended reals [-infinity, +infinity] there is a permutation sigma of the indices with sum_n a_{sigma(n)} = alpha, and there are permutations for which the partial sums have any prescribed pair liminf <= limsup in the extended reals. Consequently a real series is unconditionally convergent (every rearrangement converges to the same sum) if and only if it is absolutely convergent. In R^d with d >= 2 the analogous statement is FALSE and is replaced by the Levy-Steinitz theorem: the set of sums achievable by rearranging a convergent series in R^d is an AFFINE SUBSPACE of R^d, that is a translate of a linear subspace, so it can be a single point, a line, a plane, or all of R^d, but never for instance a disc or two isolated points. In infinite-dimensional Banach spaces unconditional and absolute convergence differ (Dvoretzky-Rogers), so the equivalence in the first sentence is a strictly finite-dimensional phenomenon. [Riemann (1854); Levy (1905) and Steinitz (1913); Dvoretzky and Rogers (1950)]
the series is real-valued and conditionally convergent
for the affine-subspace conclusion: finite-dimensional target R^d and a convergent (not necessarily conditionally convergent) series

[Proposition 16 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $b\in\{0,1\}$. Then there exists a mutually independent family of smooth, centered, autonomous, Gaussian fields $\{u^j\}_{j\geq 0}$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $U^{\alpha,b}$ is equal to $\sum_{j= 0}^\infty u^j$ in law,
    \item for each $j\geq 1$, $u^j$ has a finite spatial range of dependence $2^{-j}$,
    \item and there exists $C(d,\alpha)>0$ such that for all $j\geq 0$, $p\geq 1$, and $n\in\{0,1,2\}$,
    \[\|\nabla^n u^j\|_{L^p_\omega C^0_x}\leq  C (p^{1/2}+j^{1/2})2^{(n-\alpha)j}.\]
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, if $b=1$ and $d\geq 2$, then
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] $\nabla\cdot U^{\alpha,b}=0$,
    \item[(ii)] and almost surely, letting $Z_\eps$ be defined as in~\eqref{eq:zero sets}, for all $0 \leq \alpha'<\alpha$,
    \[\lim_{\eps\rightarrow 0} \eps^{-\alpha'd}|Z_\eps|=0.\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

body: [Theorem thm:semi of arXiv:2412.01381, 'Ergodicity and mixing for locally monotone stochastic evolution equations'] Assume that $\mathbf{f}$ and $g$ satisfy~(equation eq:g1 of the paper),~(equation eq:g2 of the paper),~(equation eq:g5 of the paper),~(equation eq:g3 of the paper)~and~(equation eq:g4 of the paper) and assume that $B\in L_2(U,W_0^{1,2}({\mathcal O}))$. Assume that Hypotheses~(hyp:quant of the paper)~and~(hyp:mixing of the paper) hold. Then the Markovian Feller semigroup $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$ of the stochastic semilinear equations of the form~(equation eq:semi of the paper) for $d=1,2$, with degenerate additive Wiener noise is exponentially mixing and exponentially ergodic and possesses a unique invariant measure $\mu_\ast$ with finite second $V$-moments. In particular, this holds for the stochastic Burgers equation in 1D for $f_1(x)=x$.

body: Lagrange's four-square theorem, also known as Bachet's conjecture, states that every nonnegative integer can be represented as a sum of four non-negative integer squares. That is, the squares form an additive basis of order four: $p=a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2},$ where the four numbers $a,b,c,d$ are integers. For illustration, 3, 31, and 310 can be represented as the sum of four squares as follows: ${\begin{aligned}3&=1^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2}+0^{2}\\[3pt]31&=5^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}+1^{2}\\[3pt]310&=17^{2}+4^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}\\[3pt]&=16^{2}+7^{2}+2^{2}+1^{2}\\[3pt]&=15^{2}+9^{2}+2^{2}+0^{2}\\[3pt]&=12^{2}+11^{2}+6^{2}+3^{2}.\end{aligned}}$

body:
[Lemma 14 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] Let \(Y\) have a centred, possibly singular, Gaussian law on
\(\mathbb R^d\), let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be Borel and convex with
\(\PP(Y\in C)>0\), and let
\(b=\EE(Y\mid Y\in C)\).  For every nonnegative convex Borel function
\(\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)\),
\begin{equation}
  \EE\left[\varphi(Y-b)\,\middle|\,Y\in C\right]
  \leq \EE\varphi(Y),
  
\end{equation}
whenever the right-hand side is finite.  In particular, for every linear
functional \(\ell\) and every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\),
\begin{equation}
  \EE\left[
    e^{\lambda\ell(Y-b)}\,\middle|\,Y\in C
  \right]
  \leq
  \exp\left(\frac{\lambda^2}{2}
  \operatorname{Var}(\ell(Y))\right).
  
\end{equation}

[Theorem 10 (Relative-entropy net to covering) of arXiv:2606.16005, '\bfseries An Algebraic Matrix Spencer Theorem'] Let $\Delta$ be a block-diagonal spectraplex, and for $S\subseteq[n]$ define
\[
  \mathcal A_S(X)=\bigl(\Tr(A_iX)\bigr)_{i\in S}\in\R^S.
\]
Suppose $T_0\subset\Delta$ has size $\exp(O(s))$, where $s=|S|$, and every
$X\in\Delta$ has some $Y\in T_0$ with $\KL{X}{Y}\le D$.  Then
\[
  N\!\left(\mathcal A_S(\Delta),
    C\sqrt{D/s}\,B_\infty^S\right)
  \le \exp(O(s)).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)

[campaign status: proved - the campaign's own proof, author-checked, unrefereed; the prior-art search was not completed] Let B_{m,n} be the balls-in-boxes model with a weight sequence (w_j), partition function Z(m,n), radius of convergence rho > 0 and w_0, w_1 > 0, and let Y(1) be the largest box occupancy. CLAIM (Janson, Conjecture 18.4): if m = o(n) then Y(1) = o_p(log n). Quantitatively, for m <= n/4, with gamma = min(1, w_1/w_0) and any r < rho such that gamma r n / (2m) > 1 (true for all large n when m = o(n) and r is fixed; otherwise the logarithm is not positive and the bound says nothing), Y(1) <= (1 + delta) log n / log(gamma r n / (2m)) with high probability, i.e. Y(1) = O_p(log n / log(n/m)). The case w_1 = 0 (span 1) follows by the same comparison, writing j as a fixed sum of parts from a finite allowed set F by Frobenius, with constant max F / log(gamma_F r^{max F} n / (2m)), again once that logarithm is positive; span d > 1 reduces to span 1 by dividing box counts by d. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: the finer multinomial asymptotics log n / log(n log n / m) of Gonnet and of Raab and Steger have no general-weight analogue here.

[Lemma lem:logarithm_of_unit_perturbation of arXiv:2607.04514, 'Boundary-layer asymptotics for Gaussian-smoothed singular measures'] Let \(s\geqslant0\) be an integer and let \(B\in\mathfrak B_s\) on \(\mathcal
  D_{A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma_0}\). There is \(\sigma'_0>0\) such that
  \begin{equation}
    \log\Bigl( 1+\sigma B(a,x,\sigma)\Bigr) = \sigma B(a,x,\sigma)
    + \sigma^2\mathscr R_{\log}(a,x,\sigma)
  \end{equation}
  for some \(\mathscr R_{\log}\in\mathfrak B_s\) on \(\mathcal D_{A,\mathcal{K}_{\mathcal{S}}, \sigma'_0}\).

body: [Theorem 1.3 of arXiv:2607.29403, 'Strong invariants and Tverberg numbers in convexity spaces'] Let $(X,\mathcal{C})$ be an $S_{3}$ -separable convexity space with Helly number $h$, and let $\mathcal{B}$ be its family of halfspaces. If $\textup{VC}(\mathcal{B})\leq d$, then $r_{t}=O\bigl(dh\log h\bigr)t.$ In particular, if the Radon number is $r$, then $r_{t}=O(r^{2}\log r)t.$

body: Let X be a square-integrable function of independent coordinates and X^L its value after an independent resampling of a block L, and suppose the pair (X, X^L) is exchangeable (automatic for independent block resampling). Then E[((X^L - X)^+)^2] = Var(X) - Cov(X, X^L). Proof in two lines from facts that hold separately: exchangeability gives E[(X - X^L)^2] = 2 Var(X) - 2 Cov(X, X^L), and the symmetry of X^L - X gives E[(X - X^L)^2] = 2 E[((X^L - X)^+)^2]; equate. Consequences: Cov(X, X^L) <= Var(X) always; summing over a partition of blocks turns Efron-Stein into the exact statement Sum_L E[((X^L - X)^+)^2] = Sum_L (Var(X) - Cov(X, X^L)), so bounding the positive-part functionals a resampling engine consumes is EXACTLY the problem of lower-bounding the block covariances. Numerically checked on a nonlinear functional (relative difference 0.008 at 200,000 samples).

body:
[Proposition 6 (A mixed example with all three coefficient distances) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\wt\eta\in(1/\alpha,1)$, let $0<\lambda<1$, let $\varpi>0$, and let $b_0,a_0\in\R$. Let $\beta\in L^1(0,T)$ and $r\in L^2(0,T)$ be deterministic. Consider
\[
  b(t,x)\equiv b_0,
  \qquad
  \wt b(t,x)=b_0+\beta(t),
\]
\[
  a(t,x)\equiv a_0,
  \qquad
  \wt a(t,x)=a_0+r(t),
\]
and
\[
  \sigma(t,x)=1+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr),
  \qquad
  \wt\sigma(t,x)=1+\varpi+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr).
\]
Then both stable coefficients are bounded, bounded away from zero, and H\"older while failing to be Lipschitz at the origin. For any coupled solution pair satisfying Assumption~\ref{ass:solutions}, the coefficient distances satisfy
\[
  B=\|\beta\|_{L^1(0,T)},
  \qquad
  A=\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)},
  \qquad
  S=\varpi T^{1/\alpha}.
\]
Consequently, if $x_0=\wt x_0$ and these three quantities are smaller than one, then Theorem~\ref{thm:noncritical} gives
\[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}
\le C\max\left\{
\|\beta\|_{L^1(0,T)}^{\frac{\alpha\wt\eta-1}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+1}},
\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}},
(\varpi T^{1/\alpha})^{\alpha-1/\wt\eta}
\right\}.
\]

$\phi_1,\dots,\phi_m$ be supported in $\overline B_{R_0}$ with

F^{(m)}_n(\vec y)\;\le\;\bigl(K_3/\mathfrak a\bigr)^{m}K_3^{m-1}\,M_0^m

\prod_{v}du_v ,\qquad u_0=0,\ u_i=y_i .

Moreover $\int_{(\R^d)^m}\sum_{T}D_T(\vec y)\prod_i

body: Carleson's theorem: the Fourier series of every L^2 function on the circle converges pointwise almost everywhere (extended by Hunt to L^p for p > 1). By contrast Kolmogorov constructed an L^1 function whose Fourier series diverges almost everywhere, so the integrability threshold is sharp in this sense. The proof is one of the deepest in classical analysis, via time-frequency decomposition of the Carleson operator.
title: Carleson's Theorem (pointwise convergence)

OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited), w730-T355-C003 version 2. Not independently checked. Let d,q>=1 be finite integers. Let u in R^d, v,z in R^q, and
A in C^4(R^d,R^{q x q}). Put H=A^T A and assume globally

    0<m I<=H(u)<=M I,
    (sum_{i=1}^d ||partial_i A(u)||^2)^(1/2)<=D,
    ||D^j H(u)[e_1,...,e_j]||<=B_j product_l |e_l|, j=1,...,4.

All vector norms are Euclidean; matrix norms are operator norms. The bounds
on the derivatives of H are multilinear operator bounds, not coordinatewise
bounds. No common eigenbasis or commutation assumption is made. Let sigma>=0,
0<eta<=min(1,1/M). Let z_k be iid, independent of the past, centrally
symmetric with E z_k z_k^T=I_q, and mu_6=E|z_k|^6<infinity;
mu_4=E|z_k|^4. Start at deterministic u_0 and v_0=0. The full-gradient
label-noise recursion for residual A(u)v is

    u' = u + h,
    h_i = -eta v^T (partial_i H)v/2
          -eta sigma z^T (partial_i A)v, i=1,...,d,
    v'=(I-eta H)v-eta sigma A^T z.

Define the global ODE

    U'=b(U), b=-(sigma^2/4) grad tr H, U(0)=u_0.

For bounded C^3 observables F with bounded derivatives put f(u)=F(u,0),
F_j=sup ||D^j f||, j=1,2,3, and F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||.
For T>=0 define the following finite nonnegative constants:

    c2=sigma^2 q M/m,
    c4=[sigma^2 M(2q+4)c2+sigma^4 M^2 mu_4]/m,
    c6=[sigma^2 M(3q+12)c4+15 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 c2
        +sigma^6 M^3 mu_6]/m,
    J2=B_1^2 c4/4+sigma^2 D^2 c2,
    Jcv=B_1^2 c6/4+B_1^2 sigma^2 M q c4/4
         +sigma^2 D^2 q c4+sigma^4 D^2 M mu_4 c2,
    beta_j=sigma^2 q B_{j+1}/4, j=0,1,2,3,
    G1=F_1 exp(beta_1 T),
    G2=exp(2 beta_1 T)(F_2+beta_2 T F_1),
    G3=exp(3 beta_1 T)[F_3+3 beta_2 T F_2
                    +(beta_3 T+3 beta_2^2 T^2/2)F_1],
    Gtu=beta_1 G1+beta_0 G2,
    Gtt=beta_0 beta_1 G1+beta_0^2 G2,
    S0=B_1/(2m), S1=(B_2+2B_1 S0)/(2m),
    S2=(B_3+2B_2 S0+4B_1 S1)/(2m),
    C0=G1 S0/2, C1=(G2 S0+G1 S1)/2,
    C2=(G3 S0+2G2 S1+G1 S2)/2, Ct=Gtu S0/2,
    Qg=G2 J2/2+Gtu sqrt(J2)+Gtt/2,
    Qc_d=C0 M^2 c2+C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 q M c2)/2
         +2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(d M) D c2+2 C2 Jcv+Ct c2,
    C_d(T)=(C0+F_vv/2)c2+T(Qg+Qc_d).

Then

    sup_{0<=k<=T/eta^2}
      |E F(u_k,v_k)-F(U(k eta^2),0)| <= C_d(T) eta.       (1)

The supremum is over integer k. Thus a=1, with an explicit constant for
all finite tangential and normal dimensions. The dependence on dimension
is displayed or contained in the stated derivative and noise norm bounds;
no dimension-free rate constant is asserted.

{"artifact_digest":"sha256:d51fce0785edbe4ed45244f911f14dbc2682d9d4c0e0a7edcb5ab3acfd93858f","artifact_path":"objects/sha256/d5/d51fce0785edbe4ed45244f911f14dbc2682d9d4c0e0a7edcb5ab3acfd93858f.md","bundle_digest":"sha256:247dae2f2ad9f7fa2f3b76e27faa583ce4fab2eeb096b870775440ac64ebccd3","bundle_entry_key":"t355-all-finite-dimensions","bundle_id":"population.t355-finite-dimensions-and-constant-hessian-second-moments-002","claim_kind":"theorem","conditions":[],"domain":"probability","draft":"w730/bundle_002.json","evidence_ids":[],"logical_id":"math:probability.stochastic_approximation:t355-multidimensional-matrix-lyapunov-label-noise-weak-order-one","overlay_schema_version":1,"proof_text":"# All finite tangential dimensions: extension of C002 v2

Claim w730-T355-C003, version 2. Kind: narrowed. Target: 1 (the dossier
repaired label-noise model). Status: proof (unaudited). Exact algebra checks pass; independent review is pending.
This extends the saved C002 v2 proof; it does not assume scalar projection
cancellation for multiple outputs. The known limiting vector field remains
Li-Wang-Arora's Corollary 5.2, arXiv:2110.06914v4, pp.8-9,33.

## Statement and explicit constants

Let d,q>=1 be finite integers. Let u in R^d, v,z in R^q, and
A in C^4(R^d,R^{q x q}). Put H=A^T A and assume globally

    0<m I<=H(u)<=M I,
    (sum_{i=1}^d ||partial_i A(u)||^2)^(1/2)<=D,
    ||D^j H(u)[e_1,...,e_j]||<=B_j product_l |e_l|, j=1,...,4.

All vector norms are Euclidean; matrix norms are operator norms. The bounds
on the derivatives of H are multilinear operator bounds, not coordinatewise
bounds. No common eigenbasis or commutation assumption is made. Let sigma>=0,
0<eta<=min(1,1/M). Let z_k be iid, independent of the past, centrally
symmetric with E z_k z_k^T=I_q, and mu_6=E|z_k|^6<infinity;
mu_4=E|z_k|^4. Start at deterministic u_0 and v_0=0. The full-gradient
label-noise recursion for residual A(u)v is

    u' = u + h,
    h_i = -eta v^T (partial_i H)v/2
          -eta sigma z^T (partial_i A)v, i=1,...,d,
    v'=(I-eta H)v-eta sigma A^T z.

Define the global ODE

    U'=b(U), b=-(sigma^2/4) grad tr H, U(0)=u_0.

For bounded C^3 observables F with bounded derivatives put f(u)=F(u,0),
F_j=sup ||D^j f||, j=1,2,3, and F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||.
For T>=0 define the following finite nonnegative constants:

    c2=sigma^2 q M/m,
    c4=[sigma^2 M(2q+4)c2+sigma^4 M^2 mu_4]/m,
    c6=[sigma^2 M(3q+12)c4+15 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 c2
        +sigma^6 M^3 mu_6]/m,
    J2=B_1^2 c4/4+sigma^2 D^2 c2,
    Jcv=B_1^2 c6/4+B_1^2 sigma^2 M q c4/4
         +sigma^2 D^2 q c4+sigma^4 D^2 M mu_4 c2,
    beta_j=sigma^2 q B_{j+1}/4, j=0,1,2,3,
    G1=F_1 exp(beta_1 T),
    G2=exp(2 beta_1 T)(F_2+beta_2 T F_1),
    G3=exp(3 beta_1 T)[F_3+3 beta_2 T F_2
                    +(beta_3 T+3 beta_2^2 T^2/2)F_1],
    Gtu=beta_1 G1+beta_0 G2,
    Gtt=beta_0 beta_1 G1+beta_0^2 G2,
    S0=B_1/(2m), S1=(B_2+2B_1 S0)/(2m),
    S2=(B_3+2B_2 S0+4B_1 S1)/(2m),
    C0=G1 S0/2, C1=(G2 S0+G1 S1)/2,
    C2=(G3 S0+2G2 S1+G1 S2)/2, Ct=Gtu S0/2,
    Qg=G2 J2/2+Gtu sqrt(J2)+Gtt/2,
    Qc_d=C0 M^2 c2+C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 q M c2)/2
         +2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(d M) D c2+2 C2 Jcv+Ct c2,
    C_d(T)=(C0+F_vv/2)c2+T(Qg+Qc_d).

Then

    sup_{0<=k<=T/eta^2}
      |E F(u_k,v_k)-F(U(k eta^2),0)| <= C_d(T) eta.       (1)

The supremum is over integer k. Thus a=1, with an explicit constant for
all finite tangential and normal dimensions. The dependence on dimension
is displayed or contained in the stated derivative and noise norm bounds;
no dimension-free rate constant is asserted.

## 1. Normal moments and increments

The second, fourth and sixth normal recurrences in C002 v2 section 2
condition on (u_k,v_k), so changing the dimension of u does not change
any of their terms. In detail with r=|v|, w=(I-eta H)v and
n=-eta sigma A^T z, symmetry gives

    E[|v'|^2|past]<=(1-eta m)r^2+eta^2 sigma^2 qM,
    E[|v'|^4|past]<=(1-eta m)r^4
       +eta^2 sigma^2 M(2q+4)r^2+eta^4 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4,
    E[|v'|^6|past]<=(1-eta m)r^6
       +eta^2 sigma^2 M(3q+12)r^4
       +15 eta^4 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 r^2+eta^6 sigma^6 M^3 mu_6.

These follow by expanding (|w|^2+2w.n+|n|^2)^j, j=1,2,3;
odd powers of n vanish. The contraction uses eta m in [0,1]. Starting
at r=0, induction gives E r^2<=c2 eta, E r^4<=c4 eta^2,
E r^6<=c6 eta^3. All expectations used below are consequently finite.

The deterministic part of h is bounded in Euclidean norm by
eta B_1 r^2/2, by testing its inner product with an arbitrary unit
vector e and using v^T DH[e]v. For its noise part,

    E|h_noise|^2=eta^2 sigma^2 sum_i |partial_i A v|^2
              <=eta^2 sigma^2 D^2 r^2,
    |h_noise|<=eta sigma D |z| r.

Consequently E|h|^2<=J2 eta^3 and E|h|<=sqrt(J2)eta, using eta<=1.
The same product estimate as in C002 v2, with |h| replacing |d|, gives

    E[|h|^2 |v'|^2]<=4 Jcv eta^3.                     (2)

Indeed |h|^2<=2 eta^2[B_1^2 r^4/4+sigma^2 D^2 |z|^2 r^2]
and |v'|^2<=2r^2+2eta^2 sigma^2 M |z|^2. Multiplying these inequalities
and conditioning on the past gives exactly the four terms in Jcv, since
E|z|^2=q. The powers of eta in those four terms are respectively
5,6,4,5, all bounded above by eta^3 for 0<eta<=1. No sum over d
is omitted: it is absorbed by the specified square-sum bound D.

## 2. Vector backward flow

For every j=0,1,2,3, ||D^j b||<=beta_j. To see this, for unit vectors
e_0,...,e_j, take the inner product of D^j b[e_1,...,e_j] with e_0:
its absolute value is sigma^2/4 times
|tr D^{j+1}H[e_0,...,e_j]|<=q sigma^2 B_{j+1}/4.
Thus b is bounded and globally Lipschitz. For a terminal integer K with
tau=K eta^2<=T, let g(t,u)=f(S_{tau-t}u), where S is its global flow.
The vector variational equations for J=DS, K2=D^2S, K3=D^3S are

    J'=Db J,
    K2'=Db K2+D^2b[J,J],
    K3'=Db K3+sum_of_three D^2b[J,K2]+D^3b[J,J,J].

The operator norm inequalities are precisely the scalar inequalities
used in C002 v2. Variation of constants gives
||J_s||<=exp(beta_1 s), ||K2_s||<=beta_2 s exp(2 beta_1 s),
||K3_s||<=(beta_3 s+3 beta_2^2 s^2/2)exp(3 beta_1 s).
This remains valid at beta_1=0, without division by beta_1.
The chain rule gives the displayed G1,G2,G3 for the first three spatial
derivatives of g. The backward equation is g_t+b.grad g=0;
its derivatives give ||D g_t||<=Gtu and |g_tt|<=Gtt.

## 3. Matrix-valued one-form corrector

For each u define a linear map S_u:R^d->Sym_q by

    H S_u[e]+S_u[e] H=DH(u)[e].

The inverse Lyapunov operator on symmetric matrices has norm <=1/(2m),
as shown by its exponentially convergent integral in C002 v2 section 3.
Thus ||S_u[e]||<=S0|e|. Differentiating in a direction a gives

    H (D_a S)[e]+(D_a S)[e] H
       =D^2H[a,e]-DH[a]S[e]-S[e]DH[a].

A second derivative gives the B_3 term, two B_2 S0 terms, and four
B_1 S1 terms. Therefore the first two u derivatives of this one-form
have multilinear norms <=S1,S2 respectively. Define

    C(t,u)=-S_u[grad g(t,u)]/2,
    G(t,u,v)=g(t,u)+v^T C(t,u)v.

The chain rule gives ||C||<=C0, ||DC||<=C1, ||D^2C||<=C2,
||C_t||<=Ct, with the constants stated above. In particular

    HC+CH=-DH[grad g]/2,
    sigma^2 tr(CH)=-(sigma^2/4) tr DH[grad g]=b.grad g. (3)

These are identities without a commutation hypothesis. The frozen
quadratic increment is exactly

    E[v'^T C v'-v^T C v|past]
       =-eta v^T(HC+CH)v+eta^2 v^T HCH v
        +eta^2 sigma^2 tr(CH).                       (4)

The first term cancels the deterministic normal-quadratic term in the
increment of g; (3) cancels its eta^2 g_t term.

## 4. Shared-noise tensor contraction

The coefficient expansion is C(t,u+h)=C+DC[h]+R,
||R||<=C2 |h|^2/2. Equation (2) bounds its expected contribution by
2 C2 Jcv eta^3. The time coefficient change costs Ct c2 eta^3.
The drift part of DC[h] costs at most
C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 qM c2)eta^3/2, as in C002 v2.

For the noise part write A_i=partial_i A, C_i=partial_i C,
a_i=A_i v, and w=(I-eta H)v. Conditional on the past, symmetry and
E zz^T=I imply the exact identity

    E[(z^T a_i)(w-eta sigma A^Tz)^T C_i(w-eta sigma A^Tz)]
       =-2 eta sigma w^T C_i A^T A_i v.

Summing over i and multiplying by -eta sigma gives

    E[v'^T DC[h_noise]v'|past]
       =2 eta^2 sigma^2 sum_i w^T C_i A^T A_i v.       (5)

The index sum cannot be discarded or replaced by its scalar version.
For every u, each ||C_i||<=C1, and sum_i ||A_i||^2<=D^2.
Cauchy-Schwarz in the i index yields

    sum_i ||C_i|| ||A_i||<=sqrt(d) C1 D.

Using |w|<=r, ||A||<=sqrt(M), and E r^2<=c2 eta, the absolute
expectation in (5) is <=2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(d M) D c2 eta^3.
This is the only new explicit dimension factor relative to C002 v2.

The g Taylor remainder is bounded by Qg eta^3, since its spatial
second derivative is bounded by G2, its mixed derivative by Gtu,
and its time second derivative by Gtt. The HCH term in (4) costs
C0 M^2 c2 eta^3. Combining all terms gives

    |E[G(t+eta^2,u',v')-G(t,u,v)]|<=(Qg+Qc_d)eta^3.   (6)

## 5. Endpoints and full observables

Telescope (6) for K steps. The initial quadratic correction is zero;
the final correction has expectation bounded by C0 c2 eta. Hence
|E f(u_K)-f(U(tau))|<=[C0 c2+T(Qg+Qc_d)]eta.
The law of (u_k,v_k) is invariant under (u,v)->(u,-v): applying
(v,z)->(-v,-z) leaves every component of u' fixed and reverses v'.
Induction starts from v_0=0 and uses the central symmetry of each fresh
z_k. The linear normal term in Taylor expansion of F(u,v) at v=0
therefore has mean zero. Its quadratic remainder is bounded in
expectation by F_vv c2 eta/2. This proves (1) for arbitrary K and
the same constants for all K eta^2<=T, including K=0.

## Boundary of this result

This treats arbitrary finite d,q in the repaired quadratic-normal model.
It does not prove the general curved-manifold problem, handle fixed
off-manifold starts in a uniform supremum including zero, or establish
priority over all later literature. Symmetry of labels is used explicitly;
no nonsymmetric-label result is claimed. All proof claims remain unaudited.
The next unpaid model extension is nonsymmetric finite-moment labels or
an explicitly corrected off-manifold initial layer.","release_manifest_digest":"sha256:187fcaa1123ef86d82609c8874d3b3e63fce8e93ce7a1a85148d5aa8311216e5","revision_digest":"sha256:8d156243bb4b38cd384035c284eb21cb9225cfd962d41818e04245168d977da0","source_id":"owner-own-work:w730:T355:w730-T355-C003:v2","source_revision":"2026-10-20-v2-unaudited","statement_fidelity_reviewed":false,"supersedes":[],"trust_class":"curated_secondary","truth_status":"unverified"}

[Lemma lem:uniform-moving-cubic of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $C\geq1$.  There is $C_1=C_1(C)$ such that, uniformly for $N\geq3$,
integers $L$ satisfying $|L|\leq CN^2$, and arbitrary sets
$E\subset[-CN,CN]\cap\mathbb Z$, one has
\begin{equation}
 \int_0^1\left|
  \sum_{x\in E}\exp\bigl(2\pi i\alpha(x^3+Lx)\bigr)
 \right|^8d\alpha
 \ll_C N|E|^4\Delta_3(C_1N^3).
\end{equation}
In particular, when $|E|\ll_C N$, the right side is
\begin{equation}
 N^5\exp\!\left(O_C\!\left(
  \frac{\log N}{\log\log N}\right)\right).
\end{equation}

[Proposition heat_longtime_1 of arXiv:2504.04792, 'Uniqueness and Longtime Behavior of the Completely Positively Correlated Symbiotic Branchi'] Let $f \in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ and let $u(t,\cdot)= S_tf(\cdot)$. Denote $M = \langle f, \bold{1} \rangle$. Then,
 \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
     \item For all $t \geq 0$: $\langle u(t,\cdot), \bold{1} \rangle = M.$
     \item $\lim_{t \to \infty} \langle |u(t, \cdot) - Mp_t(\cdot) | , \bold{1}\rangle = 0.$
